At most, they called it a five-nut fruit mooncake,” says Tse Jing-yuen, the second-generation operator of Tai Tung Bakery, one of the oldest bakeries in Hong Kong. According to Tse, there have been many variations of the five-kernel filling. The most common sweet version included candied winter melon, while the savoury version included preserved mustard greens. By the 1960s, palates had become increasingly discerning, and people wanted more novelty when it came to flavours. Gradually, fillings like five-kernel rose sweet mooncake, straw mushroom braised chicken mooncake, roast duck mooncake and even a luxury banquet mooncake appeared. “The five-kernel mooncake filling is quite interesting. The same flavour can be both sweet and savoury, which reflects different levels of quality,” Tse explains. “For example, the meatless five-nut fruit mooncake was the cheapest, the five-nut ham mooncake was slightly more expensive, and the luxury banquet mooncake was the most luxurious, because it contained dried oysters.” Traditional five-kernel mooncakes include ingredients such as walnuts, cashews, sesame and melon seeds. Modern five-kernel mooncakes have evolved: for example, Lung King Heen, a two-Michelin-starred Chinese restaurant in Hong Kong, has added pistachios for extra texture and a more satisfying bite. “For our mixed nuts mooncakes with candied citrus, we use a generous selection of nuts and seeds, including walnuts, cashews, melon seeds, sunflower seeds, pine nuts, sesame, pumpkin seeds, pistachios and whole almonds,” says Lo Kin-ming, dim sum head chef at Lung King Heen. “While we respect the traditional foundation of [five-kernel] mooncakes, we have added a few ingredients to enhance the overall flavour and texture. We also added candied citrus that brings a distinctive aroma and refreshing citrus note. It helps balance the richness of the nuts and gives the mooncake a more elegant and fragrant finish.” Protein-forward mooncakes A recent obsession with protein, driven by social media fitness trends, a cultural focus on longevity and the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, has made people worry about losing muscle. So might wuren mooncakes be a good protein-packed alternative for the Mid-Autumn Festival? “Because five-kernel mooncake is made with lots of nuts, the protein content is relatively higher than the lotus seed paste and salted egg yolk or custard versions,” registered dietitian Zoe Tsui says. “However, we still have to watch out for [portion control] when eating these nutty mooncakes as vegetable oil and sugar are added to make these treats. Indeed, nuts have good fat, but overeating food fats also affects body weight.” Lo echoes the sentiment. “Mixed nuts are generally believed to offer nutritional benefits and, compared with very rich or sweet fillings, this mooncake offers more texture, aroma and natural nuttiness,” he says. “At Lung King Heen, we also do not add any extra sugar; the sweetness comes naturally from the ingredients themselves, such as the dried fruit. Rather than calling it healthy, I would say it is a more balanced version.”

title: ‘Unshirkable responsibility’: tax chief apologises for e-filing failures
description: Benjamin Chan vows improvements after unclear wording in eTAX system results in more than 33,000 people leaving returns incomplete.
content: Hong Kong’s tax chief has apologised after the ombudsman found that unclear wording in the eTAX system led to more than 33,000 people leaving their returns incomplete, triggering penalty notices for almost 5,200 taxpayers and the prosecution of two. “Some taxpayers were unable to complete the submission of their tax returns; we apologise for the inconvenience caused to them,” Commissioner of Inland Revenue Benjamin Chan Sze-wai told a radio programme on Tuesday. “The system is under the Inland Revenue Department [IRD] and is not ideal; we have an unshirkable responsibility to address the problem … We will continue to improve the system and hope that such misunderstandings will not happen again.” The IRD said no taxpayers would be penalised over the incident, adding that penalty remissions would be granted, payments refunded and the two prosecutions withdrawn. In a report released on Monday, the Office of the Ombudsman said ambiguous instructions on the eTAX submission and signature interface led many users to believe that signing via the “iAM Smart” platform completed their filing, when in fact they had to return to eTAX until a confirmation page appeared. Between May 2 last year and January 31 this year, 489,425 taxpayers tried to submit electronic returns using a digital signature on the “iAM Smart” app for the 2024-25 tax year, the investigation found. Of these, 33,019 did not complete the submission process, 5,169 received penalty notices and two were prosecuted. About 14,000 successfully resubmitted on the same day as their initial attempt. Taxpayers must file returns within one month of issue so the department can prepare assessments and approve deductions. Late submission carries a maximum fine of HK$10,000 (US$1,275) and a further penalty of up to three times the undercharged tax. “The large number of taxpayers affected clearly indicated that the problem was not merely due to [operational] errors of individuals,” the office said. “The incident caused a great deal of inconvenience to those affected … The incident not only caused distress to those taxpayers, but also resulted in an extra workload for the [department] staff.” The report noted that the IRD had received similar complaints as early as 2022 and made system improvements, but the revised wording remained unclear. “When the problem emerged again in 2025, the IRD was not initially alarmed and only suggested that taxpayers resubmit their tax returns upon receiving inquiries,” the report stated. Asked why the department failed to resolve the issues when they were first raised in 2022, Chan explained that it had received only “single-digit” reports at the time. He noted that submission failures had multiple causes, including internet disconnections and computer freezes, and that the department’s priority was helping taxpayers complete their declarations. He said that among the 33,000 affected taxpayers, about 26,000 successfully submitted their returns before the deadline. Chan said enhancement measures were implemented before the 2025-26 individual tax return filing process began in May this year and these measures prevented further similar complaints. Those measures include a pop-up reminder to return to eTAX after iAM Smart signing, confirmation messages in users’ eTAX inboxes, enhanced on-screen and email prompts, and auto-saving of entered information to avoid re-entry. Chan added that the department was studying ways to simplify the steps required to submit tax returns via the eTAX system for a more seamless process. Dr Luk Che-chung, a former chief executive of the Hospital Authority’s Hong Kong East area, was among the affected taxpayers and urged the government to learn from the incident. Luk told a radio programme that he was fined HK$600 for failing to submit his tax return. “The department told me I had not submitted my tax return. I found it quite strange, as I remembered having already submitted it and could not think of any reason why I had not,” Luk said. “I am already in my sixties and I thought my memory must be really poor if I had failed to realise that I had not submitted the form.” Luk said he was relieved by the announcement of the probe. He urged the government to learn from the incident and improve its systems as soon as complaints arose.

title: Couple who survived Tai Po fire await trial for fraud, cannot leave Hong Kong
description: Wang Fuk Court residents allegedly obtained more than HK$330,000 in government-backed loans by overstating drop in revenue of their business.
content: A couple who survived the deadly Tai Po blaze last year have been barred from leaving Hong Kong pending trial for allegedly obtaining more than HK$330,000 (US$42,000) in government-guaranteed loans by overstating the decline in revenue of their decoration business. Former Wang Fuk Court residents Jason Kong Cheung-fat, 65, and Rosanna Cheung Yeuk-lan, 62, appeared in Sha Tin Court on Tuesday to face two counts of fraud and one of money laundering. The couple were not required to enter pleas after prosecutors applied a five-week adjournment to prepare the paperwork to transfer the case to the District Court for trial. According to a charge sheet available for press viewing, the defendants misrepresented to HSBC the decline in sales of Ace Interior Design & Engineering Company, of which they are directors, to support two applications under the 100 per cent Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme between February 8 and June 30, 2022. The scheme was a relief measure introduced in 2020 to provide fully government-guaranteed loans to companies struggling to stay afloat during the Covid-19 pandemic. Prosecutors also accused the couple of laundering the HK$331,300 they dishonestly obtained between April 4 and July 25 that year. Acting Principal Magistrate Cheang Kei-hong released each defendant on HK$10,000 bail, on condition that they remain in Hong Kong, reside at their current address in Hung Shui Kiu, report to police once a week and avoid contact with prosecution witnesses. The couple are expected to return to Sha Tin Court for a brief hearing on October 6. In April, Kong testified at an independent committee inquiry into the Wang Fuk Court fire in his capacity as a former management committee member of the owners’ corporation. He complained about suspected vote-rigging practices at general meetings and suggested the long-standing problem was linked to the appointment of a convicted contractor at the centre of the disaster that killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000. Kong and his wife were arrested on the morning of May 14, two weeks after the former resident representative petitioned the estate’s administrator to convene an extraordinary general meeting to address homeowners’ queries.

title: South Korea sets record US$600 billion budget, backed by chip windfall
description: The spending plan ‌represents a 12.8 per cent rise from 2026, marking the largest year-on-year increase in the country’s history.
content: South Korea on Tuesday unveiled its most aggressive financial spending plan on record, setting total government expenditure for 2027 at 821 trillion won (US$600 billion) to strengthen the country’s technological edge amid the global AI race. In its annual budget proposal, the budget ministry said the spending plan ‌represented a 12.8 per cent rise from 2026, marking the largest year-on-year increase in the country’s history. The proposal signals a shift in Asia’s fourth-largest economy under President Lee Jae Myung, who has championed an expansionary financial policy since taking office in June last year, pivoting away from three years of austerity under his predecessor. The historic spending increase is possible thanks to a windfall from the country’s semiconductor industry. Chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are generating unprecedented profits driven by global demand for high-bandwidth memory used in the AI boom. Total tax revenue is seen increasing 40.7 per cent next ⁠year to 584.4 trillion won, with corporate tax receipts alone projected to more than double to 216.7 trillion won. That revenue will help reduce South Korea’s ‌debt-to-GDP ratio by 3.3 percentage points to 48.3 per cent, down from 51.6 per cent estimated for this year. “The government plans to deploy fiscal resources pre-emptively and expansively, backed by the amplified national tax revenues projected for 2026 and 2027,” Budget Minister Park Hong-keun ‌told a news conference. “From 2028 onwards, a period when these fiscal investments are expected to yield tangible economic returns, we ⁠will gradually stabilise the spending growth rate, ⁠tapering it down in stages to around the 5 per cent level by 2030.” The government earmarked 2.6 trillion won for a special semiconductor budget, Park said at the cabinet meeting. It also proposed 3.4 trillion won in spending for a nuclear-powered submarine programme and other strategic weapons, presentation material during the meeting showed. The budget ‌proposal ‌will require parliamentary approval. Balancing needs Lee said on Tuesday the economy was at a point where an interest rate rise was unavoidable, risking ‌denting growth potential at a time the socially disadvantaged are feeling the impact of higher borrowing costs. “Against the backdrop of these sweeping changes, next year’s budget should serve as a solid foundation for Korea to emerge as a global leader in cutting-edge technologies,” Lee said. The country was at a critical juncture, facing a choice between prolonged low growth and a rebound in its potential growth rate, he said. “We need a productive strategy that uses expanded resources for future growth to enlarge the economic pie, strengthen industrial competitiveness and, in turn, create greater fiscal room.” Rather than channelling its projected 162.3 trillion ⁠won of excess tax revenue into short-term spending, the government plans to direct it into a strategic endowment called the Future Response Fund, designed for ⁠long-term investments. The fund will deploy 45.4 trillion won next year to expand initiatives in youth welfare, future growth engines and specialised education programmes. For 2027, a core pillar of spending will be to support next-generation semiconductor infrastructure. The government has allocated 21.3 trillion won for industrial water ‌systems, power grids and logistics networks ‌to strengthen national chip manufacturing and advance critical technology infrastructure nationwide. Part of the tax windfall will be allocated to reduce government bond issuance. Total government bond sales for next year will drop to 222.8 trillion won, down from 225.7 trillion won in this year’s budget. Net bond issuance, which reflects the creation of fresh sovereign debt, will decline even more sharply by 13.1 trillion won to 96.3 trillion won, down from 109.4 trillion won this year. The government also aims to complete the repayment of public funds injected during the 1997-98 financial crisis next year. “This officially concludes the country’s nearly 30-year journey to overcome the International Monetary Fund crisis while creating greater fiscal room for investment in future generations,” Park said. Additional reporting by The Korea Times

title: Pampered Asian Games cricket chiefs in moan over lack of 5-star accommodation for players
description: Japan will host both men’s and women’s T20 matches at newly built ground in Nisshin, but reports suggest not all facilities are up to scratch.
content: While players around the world are often happy if a ground has proper boundaries and there isn’t broken glass in the outfield, Asian Games cricket chiefs have been complaining about a lack of luxury accommodation for their pampered stars. A Sri Lankan official said the Asian Cricket Council had heard concerns over a lack of five-star hotels near the ground in Japan where games will be played, while India are reportedly threatening to send a second-string team. Both the men’s and women’s T20 cricket will be played at the host’s newly built cricket ground in Nisshin, with matches starting on September 17. But reports of tents serving as dressing rooms for players, distant washroom facilities and lack of top-class accommodation for cricketers have raised eyebrows. “There are some concerns with regard to the quality of accommodation being provided and also with regard to the logistics,” Prakash Schaffter, Sri Lanka Cricket secretary, told reporters in Colombo. He said the ACC executive committee had discussed the Asian Games with “some degree of detail” at its recently concluded meeting in Bangkok. Member states had agreed to send representatives to examine the grounds and other logistical arrangements, but hoped the tournament would still go ahead, he said. “There is a lack of available five-star rooms. Cricketers are generally provided with five-star accommodation,” he said, adding that the host city did not have luxury hotels to accommodate all athletes and spectators. However, he said the ground prepared for the T20 series was suitable for play. Media reports in India said the country’s all-powerful cricket board was unhappy with the Asian Games’ arrangements for the tournament and looking to send a second-string team. India have named a 15-member squad led by Shreyas Iyer and including teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi for the Games. The Bangladesh Cricket Board said the member boards of the ACC were looking at the concerns regarding player facilities. “The cricket part of the Asian Games will be looked after by the Asian Cricket Council,” Shahriar Nafees, the BCB cricket operations manager, said. “The individual boards have already discussed it at the ACC forum, and they will take a collective decision on the issue.”

title: Chinese script evolved like a living organism driven by natural selection: study
description: Research shows a small set of high-frequency building blocks shaped the writing system through a principle of economy.
content: Modern simplified Chinese characters form a tightly connected network from just 514 basic components that evolved through a process similar to natural selection, according to researchers who say their findings could change how Chinese writing is taught. “Chinese characters evolve like living organisms,” lecturer Xie Yonghui of Shanghai Normal University said on August 24. The research into the evolution of Chinese writing over thousands of years, led by Huang Wei, of Beijing Language and Culture University and Xie, was published in the peer-reviewed journal Digital Scholarship in the Humanities in January. Their study of “the structural formation system of modern simplified Chinese characters from a complex network perspective” reveals that a small number of core components – such as 日 (sun), 月 (moon) and 人 (human) – are repeatedly combined to create new characters. When existing elements were insufficient, entirely new components were invented. “From ancient times to the present, Chinese characters have evolved from complex to simplified forms, such as the shift from traditional to simplified characters, partly to make writing easier and partly through natural selection driven by usage frequency,” Xie said. The researchers said this evolutionary pressure produced a system in which a minority of high-frequency components dominated, while less-central elements remained on the margins. The pattern followed a principle of economy, mirroring the linguistic tendency towards greater output with less effort. China’s national “Specification of Common Modern Chinese Character Components and Component Names” includes 514 basic character components. The findings could have practical implications for Chinese-language education, both at home and abroad. Xie noted that a limited set of components might help learners acquire characters more quickly and reduce the memorisation burden but cautioned against teaching the system in isolation. “Chinese language formation is indeed systematic, but learners should not simply be taught the system itself,” Xie said. “Instead, they should be helped to develop an awareness that Chinese character forms have a structural system.” While the 514-component framework offers insight into how the writing system is organised, Xie said it was not a practical replacement for existing input methods. The Wubi, or five-stroke, input system, for example, already uses a smaller set of carefully selected radicals optimised for rapid typing. “Using more than 500 general-purpose components directly for an input method would create too much of a memory and input burden,” Xie said. Looking ahead, the researchers suggested that work could examine how this structural system could be applied to teaching, information processing and other fields.

title: Rate rise expectations mount in Hong Kong property market following Fed chief’s comments
description: But property consultancy Knight Frank says likelihood of near-term rise in prime rate by city’s note-issuing banks remains low.
content: With expectations of a quarter-percentage-point increase in the US Federal Reserve’s target interest rate increasing following comments by Fed chairman Kevin Warsh last week, the Hong Kong property market is bracing for its potential impact. Following Warsh’s comments at the Jackson Hole economic symposium on Friday, the CME FedWatch tool, which tracks Fed funds futures contracts, indicated that expectations of a rate rise in the United States this month had doubled, with markets pricing in a 60 per cent likelihood. However, global property consultancy Knight Frank said in a news release that the likelihood of note-issuing banks in Hong Kong raising the prime rate in the near term was low – projecting it would remain unchanged or rise by a maximum of one-eighth of a percentage point. In Hong Kong, the prime lending rate – the lowest rate of interest that banks charge commercial borrowers – remains a key reference rate for mortgage pricing and borrowing costs. Analysts said more homebuyers were now tending to opt for fixed-rate mortgages, with interest rates that remained unchanged even if the Hong Kong interbank offered rate (Hibor) or the prime rate rose. Under a currency peg known as the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong’s monetary policy has moved in lockstep with the Fed since 1983. However, commercial banks can decide when and by how much to adjust their prime and savings rates. “Market consensus suggests that local banks are only likely to follow with a prime rate hike after back-to-back Fed rate increases or a significant rise in funding costs,” said Esther Liu, director and head of Greater China research and consultancy at Knight Frank. “Because the prime rate directly governs the effective mortgage rate cap, which is currently at 3.25 per cent, actual mortgage financing costs are expected to remain broadly stable,” she added, even if some banks increased their fixed-rate mortgage plans by one-fifth of a percentage point to 2.93 per cent. Driven by marketing campaigns urging borrowers to catch the ‘last train’ for low interest rates, homeowners have accelerated the pace of mortgage refinancing Raymond Chong, StarPro Agency The results of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s residential mortgage survey, which were released on Monday, showed the proportion of newly approved fixed-rate mortgages rose to an eight-year high of 34.1 per cent in July – an increase of 9 percentage points from June. Eric Tso, chief vice-president at mReferral Mortgage Brokerage Services, said market expectations of an interest-rate increase in the US this month – coupled with concerns about Hong Kong banks following suit – had prompted more buyers to opt for fixed-rate mortgage plans. Raymond Chong, the CEO and founder of mortgage referral brokerage firm StarPro Agency, said: “Driven by marketing campaigns urging borrowers to catch the ‘last train’ for low interest rates, homeowners have accelerated the pace of mortgage refinancing.” He said the share of fixed-rate mortgages among new mortgages was likely to have peaked somewhere above 40 per cent last month. Of the three banks in Hong Kong offering fixed-rate mortgages, HSBC is the only one to have extended the application deadline until the end of the year. “HSBC has recently raised the fixed interest rate for new applications by 0.2 percentage points to 2.93 per cent, which means Hong Kong banks are considering the costs,” Tso said. He said the one-month Hibor rose to a nearly two-month high of 2.85 per cent on Monday, which meant banks were facing increased costs when sourcing capital for mortgage lending.

title: Letters | Today’s humanists don’t deserve the likes of a Fields Medal
description: Readers discuss recognition for humanities scholars, and the challenges of ethnic minority children in Chinese language acquisition.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I read with great interest the letter, “Why do the humanities not have awards like the Fields Medal or Nobel Prize?” (August 24). Your correspondent poses a question that I have wondered why so few people ask. As the bearer of a doctoral degree in English literature, I can confirm that major awards spur innovation and achievement, inspiring scholars to seek out the highest mountains of the mind. Why, then, is there no Fields Medal for historians, literary critics, philosophers and their ilk? After considering this question for the better part of a decade, I have arrived at a rather depressing answer: humanists simply don’t deserve one. Your correspondent notes that humanities “produce forms of knowledge whose impact is often difficult to quantify”. I wish this were true. The main difference between the sciences and the humanities does not have to do with quantifiability. It has to do with what passes for knowledge in the first place. During my more than 10 years in the academy, I found humanists operated under a categorically different model from, say, mathematicians and physicists. Whereas scientists generally try to uncover permanent laws that reveal the objective truths of the universe, humanists generally seek to produce popular paradigm shifts from the work of earlier generations. In literature, for example, a major revolution occurred when the New Criticism of the 1940s was supplanted by the New Historicism of the 1980s. Now, in 2026, the surviving New Historicists find themselves in the twilight of their careers, and they are largely dismissed, attacked or – worst of all – simply ignored by a younger generation of identity-focused scholars who could not build careers while also acknowledging the contributions of their blinkered elders. If young scientists stand on the shoulders of giants, then young humanists seem to succeed in another way: by slaughtering the giants. The differences in the incentive structures suggest a host of practical questions that would probably plague a Fields Medal for the humanities. Who would judge the award? What would be the criteria? And most critically, would the winners survive in the court of public opinion after winning? Even these basic questions have no easy answers, and this is a sad state of affairs. Perhaps one day humanists will be worthy of a Fields Medal. Not today. Andrew Williamson, founder, Williamson Education Parents can help children gain fluency in Chinese I refer to the letter, “Hong Kong’s ethnic minority students face a new challenge – Mandarin” (August 10). I strongly agree that Hong Kong’s Chinese-as-a-second-language curriculum should be improved to cater to the needs of our ethnic minorities in acquiring both Cantonese and Mandarin. I wish to point out that successful acquisition of Chinese does not hinge merely on formal education. Parents play a crucial role as well. Language classes can provide students with basic knowledge, but one can only become fluent in a language by constantly using it. In fact, even with an established English language curriculum, a lot of local students struggle with English precisely because they don’t use it in daily life. Parents from ethnic minority communities should encourage their children to use more Chinese at home or with friends. When dining out or visiting a store, parents should also encourage their children to interact more with locals in Chinese. Parents can themselves serve as a role model by learning and using Chinese in daily life. They need not be fluent in the language but at least they should show their children they are trying. This is not something difficult to imagine. My parents migrated to Hong Kong from rural villages on the Chinese mainland. Although they did not even finish their secondary school education, they tried hard to speak English with me at home during my childhood. It was through these conversations at home, on top of the formal education I received at school, that I eventually picked up the language. Given the additional challenge of Mandarin, which imposes more of a burden on children, the role of parents in education has become even more important. A. Chan, Guangzhou

title: Australia’s biggest property downturn since pandemic threatens economic growth
description: Home prices fell for a fifth month in August, threatening to erode household wealth and curb consumer spending.
content: Australian home prices fell for a fifth month in August in the biggest downturn since the pandemic, and there is further pain ahead as stubborn inflation puts upward pressure on interest rates. Figures from property consultant Cotality released on Tuesday showed national home prices fell 0.9 per cent in August from July, when they dropped 1.2 per cent. Sydney ‌and Melbourne again led the monthly decline with falls of 1.4 per cent and 1.1 per cent, leaving prices down about 7 per cent from their peaks. Falling house prices threaten to erode household wealth and curb consumer spending just as Australia’s economy faces the risk of a sharper slowdown. Data on Wednesday is expected to show annual economic growth eased to 1.8 per cent in the second quarter, from 2.5 per cent in the first quarter, a cooling engineered by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), which has warned interest rates can still go higher. “We are probably only about 35 per cent of the way through the slump both in terms ⁠of the percentage fall and months,” said Shane Oliver, chief economist at AMP, who is tipping a peak-to-trough home price fall of 10 per cent in this cycle ‌and a turnaround in the second half of next year. “The home price slump will weigh on economic growth, but is not significant enough yet to change the direction of the RBA rate moves from up to down given the inflation ‌problem,” he said. Separate data on Tuesday showed net exports added 0.1 percentage points to GDP growth in the second quarter, while government spending ⁠also contributed 0.1 percentage point, although that ⁠was more than offset by a 0.3 percentage point drag from business inventories, leaving quarterly growth stuck at a sluggish 0.3 per cent. A sustained slump in housing turnover would have wide implications for the economy ‌given the housing sector’s extensive links to industries ranging from real estate services to tradespeople and construction. Housing credit growth has already started to slow. Little relief in sight UBS analysts said it was increasingly likely ‌house ‌prices would drop towards 10 per cent in this cycle, which would be among the worst downturns in Australia, leaving the central bank facing a policy dilemma given falling ‌house prices and high inflation. “Overall, UBS still expect the RBA to raise the cash rate by another 25bps [basis points], by November,” they said in a note ⁠to clients. “The more likely timing remains in November, but the risk of an early hike at the next meeting in September is now material.” There is little relief ⁠in sight for the sector after the government’s tax changes announced in May cooled investor demand. The RBA has raised the cash rate three times this year to 4.35 per cent, and markets are fully pricing in another hike this year after a hot inflation print for July. Nearly ‌all capital cities recorded a fall for ‌August, with the heat finally coming out of boom markets like Brisbane and Perth, which fell 1 per cent and 0.8 per cent respectively after double-digit gains this year. Tim Lawless, Cotality’s research director, said the softer trend in values was underpinned by weaker transaction activity, adding that sales for the past three months were down 15.5 per cent from a year earlier. “Longer selling times, larger vendor discounting and persistently low auction clearance rates all point to a buyer’s market, yet buyers are lacking the confidence to transact at the moment.” The slump is hitting the nation’s biggest banks, with mortgage applications dropping as much as 20 per cent since the budget and one CEO saying “volatility and uncertainty” were more structurally present than for decades. Last week, one of Sydney’s biggest developers, Bathla Group, fell into insolvency owing A$3.3 billion (US$2.4 billion). The challenge is an extreme version of the one facing governments around the world after decades of leverage-fueled and state-sanctioned home price gains. Policymakers must figure out how to deflate frothy property markets and boost affordability, without derailing the economy at a time when inflationary pressures are driving up borrowing costs. The risk for Australia is any prolonged downturn could hit families in their pockets at an already tough time. A measure of consumer confidence fell to “deeply pessimistic” levels in June. About 60 per cent of household wealth is tied up with property, according to Commerzbank. “People don’t transact in a high-ticket item like property when they are not secure about their finances or the broader economy,” said Nicola Powell, chief residential economist for Domain, an online property portal. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: China tennis star Zheng Qinwen donates 1 million yuan to victims of Nepal disaster
description: Olympic gold medallist says money to be directed to ‘emergency relief, transitional resettlement and post-disaster reconstruction’.
content: China tennis star Zheng Qinwen has given 1 million yuan (US$150,000) to help the disaster relief efforts in Nepal and Tibet, a charity group has revealed. In a post on its official social media account, the China Charity Federation said Zheng had made the donation in response to the flash flood that has claimed the lives of at least 950 people, while more than 4,000 are still missing. The Olympic gold medallist, who is through to the second round of the US Open after beating Kristina Liutova on Monday in New York, reportedly told the China Charity Federation the funds were specifically for “emergency relief, transitional resettlement and post-disaster reconstruction”. “On August 26, a mudslide on the Nepal side caused heavy casualties and missing persons at Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Shigatse City, Tibet,” the federation wrote. “In response to the severe disaster, tennis player Zheng Qinwen generously donated 1 million yuan to the mudslide-affected area in Gyirong, Tibet, through the China Charity Federation. “Ms. Zheng Qinwen stated that she will continue to closely follow the progress of relief efforts in Gyirong and expressed her sincere wishes for the compatriots in the disaster-affected area to overcome the hardship soon and rebuild their homes.” The group subsequently announced that Chinese firms Anta Group, BYD, and Pinduoduo had each donated 10 million yuan for disaster relief. European football clubs such as Barcelona and Athletic Bilbao held a stadium-wide moment of silence before their La Liga matches to express solidarity with the victims in Nepal. This is not the first time Zheng has supported disaster relief efforts in her home country. In 2023, she donated 200,000 yuan (US$28,000) after an earthquake hit the rural Jishishan region.

title: South Korea’s top presidential aide resigns following cabinet reshuffle
description: Kim Yong-beom had drawn criticism over the rapid introduction of single-stock exchange-traded funds and ‘citizen dividend’ proposal.
content: South Korea’s chief presidential policy adviser has resigned, the presidential Blue House said on Tuesday, after President Lee Jae ‌Myung reshuffled his cabinet and senior aides amid a drop in his approval rating. Kim Yong-beom was a key adviser to Lee on economic policy, including on housing and ⁠stock market issues. Kim had offered to step down from the post on Monday, which oversees the administration’s economic and domestic policy agenda. During his term, Kim had drawn criticism over the rapid introduction of single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds tied to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The products, launched in May as part of an effort to draw retail money into domestic equities, later helped amplify extreme market swings and prompted regulators to tighten investor safeguards. His proposal for a potential “citizen dividend” funded by excess tax revenue from the AI boom also triggered public debate, and fuelled market speculation over how the government might use the windfall. Kim later said that the idea involved distributing excess tax receipts rather than tapping company profits. President Lee had accepted Kim’s ‌resignation on Tuesday, his office said. It did not immediately disclose the reason for his resignation or name a successor. The announcement follows a cabinet ‌reshuffle announced on Sunday, in which Lee’s office ⁠named ⁠six new ministers including replacements for the economy and ‌finance minister and the land minister, as well as new ‌presidential aides. ‌Lee also named a new trade minister ‌in late August. The reshuffle may be an attempt to put a brake on a slide in popularity, but analysts warn it gets increasingly difficult to change public opinions when existing policy is not seen to be addressing people’s main concerns. “Nobody thinks policy will change just because you replace the ministers,” said Shin Yul, a political-science professor at Seoul’s Myongji University. “Once people start thinking the government doesn’t know what it’s doing, it’s very difficult to change that perception.” Lee’s approval rating fell ⁠1.3 percentage points to 38.9 per cent, a Realmeter poll released ⁠on Monday showed, marking its first drop into the 30 per cent range since he ‌took office ‌in June last year. The pollster said concerns over housing prices and rental costs had weighed on public sentiment. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Thailand’s Pattaya pins hopes on arrival of 5,000 US sailors to boost tourism
description: Pattaya has faced a grim low tourist season, driven in part by the economic downturn triggered by the Iran war.
content: After more than 250 days at sea, much of it fighting the war on Iran – and amid reports of dire conditions on board – the USS Abraham Lincoln is finally set to dock near Pattaya this week, giving more than 5,000 American sailors and Marines shore leave as the Thai resort city hopes they will spend big during their last pit stop before home. The eastern Thai beach resort, known for its colourful nightlife, has faced a grim low tourist season, driven in part by the economic downturn triggered by the same war that has kept the carrier and its crew in combat. The Lincoln’s deployment, believed to be a record for a vessel of its size, was extended after it was unexpectedly redirected to the Middle East shortly before the US and Israel launched their February attack on Iran. It is set to dock on Wednesday in Thailand, allowing the crew up to four days of rest and recuperation before its onwards journey across the Pacific. Ahead of its arrival, a strict list of dos and don’ts has emerged for the crew. While Pattaya Mayor Poramet Ngampichet said the shore leave could see around 100 million baht (US$3 million) injected into the local economy over the four-day visit, he warned that the crew had been strictly warned to stay away from drugs and red-light areas. “We discussed with their [US] representative the restrictions on cannabis, as well as certain areas that are strictly off-limits after sunset,” he said in a social media post late on Monday. ‘’Some will be staying at hotels in Pattaya, while others will return to … the ship.” Thailand’s loosening of tight control laws around cannabis ostensibly for medicinal use has resulted in widespread recreational sale – including in stalls across Pattaya. The carrier, one of the world’s largest military boats, has also been at the centre of political controversy in the US. The row has pitted a defensive White House against reporters who have published complaints by crew members over apparent food and hygiene lapses after months at sea – as well as concerns over the mental health of some of the thousands on board. US President Donald Trump last Friday rejected reports of supply shortcomings on the carrier, saying the at-sea deployment was “not nearly long enough” and that the Lincoln “will return home soon”. But the controversy has raised questions in America regarding the treatment of its servicepeople and the scope of planning for a war on Iran, which was billed as an easy win but continues six months later. The Lincoln, a third of a kilometre long and built to carry dozens of fighter jets, will dock at Laem Chabang deep-sea port in Chonburi, eastern Thailand, on Wednesday, along with two support vessels. The port is a short drive to Pattaya, where businesses are in catching position for the unexpected but welcome spending of a crew trapped at sea – much of it spent in active combat – since last December, when it docked in Guam, a US territory in the Pacific. Hotels, restaurants and bars have had to contend with only a fraction of their usual low-season occupancy and sales rates, as the Iran crisis sent fuel costs soaring and complicated travel plans for many, including the crucial Middle East market seeking cooler climes during their sweltering summer months. “I’m glad that the sailors will be here to boost our local economy,” said Bhunanan Patanasin, president of the Pattaya Business and Tourism Association. “Our town has been very quiet with fewer visitors this year.” The presence of thousands of servicemen and women in Pattaya has stirred endless amusement across social media. The Thai meme factory has gone into overdrive, with influencers and celebrities joking about Pattaya bars stocking up for the fleet, women preparing to greet sailors at the beach and the inevitable cultural collision of thousands of service members docking in a city with a reputation for racy nightlife and visible sex work. Over the weekend, Thai police detained 25 sex workers operating on the beachfront, in what Thais say is a tokenistic clean-up ahead of Lincoln’s arrival. Prostitution remains illegal in Thailand, and advocacy groups say that instead of making jokes, the energy would be better spent campaigning for the legal and safety protections of people working in the sex industry as their only means to make money. “When people talk about Pattaya, they talk about money, jokes and nightlife – but why don’t we talk more about the workers?” Swing, a campaign group for sex workers, said on social media. “Enough with jokes that turn other people’s jobs into a punchline.” Thai authorities say police have also been briefed on how to sensitively manage any incidents that may occur as the Lincoln’s crew members hit bars and clubs for the first time in months.

title: Meta settlement not enough to protect teen mental health: whistle-blower
description: Deal does not meaningfully address the harms former safety engineer testified about; psychologists weigh in on time caps for Instagram and Facebook.
content:
Former Meta Platforms safety engineer Arturo Bejar, the whistle-blower whose testimony helped build a child-safety case against the tech giant, said its settlement with a coalition of US states has not meaningfully addressed the harms from social media that he described in court.
Bejar told a judge and eight jurors last week that the firm had knowingly under-reported the frequency with which teens were harmed on its platforms, pushed them towards content that made them feel bad about themselves and failed to correctly adjudicate reports of child predation.
On Wednesday, the states announced they and Meta had settled the case. California Attorney General Rob Bonta declared the settlement would “make social ‌media less dangerous for our kids”.
But Bejar said the proposed settlement does not meaningfully address the problems he was asked to testify about.
Meta, on its part, said it is “building on our long-standing efforts to empower parents and support teens”.
“We’re grateful for Mr Bejar’s advocacy and for his testimony in our case,” Bonta said in a statement. “We agree that there is more to be done by legislatures and industry, but believe that the settlement we announced yesterday institutes real and enforceable change, real transparency and real protections for children and teens across the country.”
The settlement involves Meta paying states up to US$18 billion (HK$141 billion) over the next decade. It also includes “remedies” ⁠such as limiting how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram.
In some instances, the remedies secured in the case are measures that Meta previously considered, leaked documents show, and rejected after determining they were relatively inconsequential on both user well-being and business grounds.
For example, Meta has agreed to hide likes and reaction counts on posts to prevent young users from comparing their posts’ performance with their peers’.
This effort to combat “negative social comparison” dates back to 2019, when Meta attempted to address its researchers’ concerns that social media might be harming ‌teenagers’ mental health.
The platform tested the effects of hiding like counts in an experiment called “Project Daisy”. It found that the change had at most a modest impact on users’ experience.
“We didn’t observe movements ⁠in overall well-being measures,” Facebook employees wrote in a 2020 ⁠slide presentation to Mark Zuckerberg. The effects on Meta’s business were similarly slight, with tests indicating that daily user count would likely fall by about 0.09 per cent if the change were adopted.
Meta ultimately allowed users to hide like counts as an opt-in feature.
Concerns about young people’s safety on Meta’s products have been raised for years, with some of the most concerning material emerging from internal Meta research leaked by employees or obtained via legal discovery.
Meta’s researchers had internally flagged algorithms’ tendency to recommend high doses of fitness and beauty content to teens with existing self-esteem issues.
They had also noted the intentional design of ‌features that ‌keep young users scrolling longer than they would independently choose.
Other concerns focused on shortfalls in Meta’s handling of user reports and moderation of inappropriate content. Bejar, for example, oversaw work at Meta that concluded users had ‌bad experiences on Meta’s platforms at rates greater than the company’s official prevalence estimates.
These allegations were central to the states’ case against Meta, but they are addressed only glancingly in the settlement. Instead, the remedies cited by the attorneys general ⁠focus on greater parental controls, time limits and boosting efforts to detect minors misrepresenting themselves as adults.
Meta’s ability to identify and remove underage users is itself far from guaranteed as users self-report their ages.
In Australia, where the government ⁠banned social media use by teenagers under age 16, regulators have found that eight in 10 young teens remain on social media, prompting authorities to consider additional enforcement.
Reaction from teen mental health experts to the settlement was mixed.
Dr Jane Conron, a clinical psychologist at the Feinberg School of Medicine at Northwestern University in Illinois, said the settlement only requires Meta to offer teens a non-algorithmically curated social media feed on an opt-in basis.
She predicted it would be a feature that would go largely unused.
However, ‌the settlement’s requirement that Meta cap the number of hours teens spend on Instagram and Facebook each day could be meaningful for some users, she said. Some of her young patients are so “emotionally overwhelmed by leaving the app” that they cry when their parents attempt to restrict how much time they spend on it, Conron said.
A built-in usage limit “will help”, she said, adding that she believes the settlement might also change the conversation around social media between teens and their parents.

title: China’s top brokerages step up global push as overseas profits surge
description: Citic, CICC and Guotai Haitong among those broadening cross-border deal-making and committing fresh capital to international arms as Beijing backs stronger investment banks.
content: China’s leading brokerages are accelerating their push overseas, pouring billions of yuan into their international arms as cross-border deals expand and profits from overseas operations grow, according to their latest interim reports. Citic Securities, one of China’s largest brokerages, saw revenue generated outside mainland China rise 45.5 per cent, year on year, to 15.86 billion yuan (US$2.4 billion) in the six months ended June, according to its interim report. The growth slightly outpaced the group’s 44.1 per cent increase in overall revenue. Its international arm, Citic Securities International (CSI), generated US$2.32 billion in operating revenue and US$829 million in net profit during the period, up 56 per cent and 114 per cent, respectively, from a year earlier. Total assets reached US$91.43 billion, 60 per cent higher than a year earlier. Citic also expanded cross-border deal-making, completing 44 overseas equity transactions worth US$4.22 billion, including two major Malaysian initial public offerings. The brokerage also handled 96 offshore bond transactions for Chinese issuers, as well as 28 global mergers and acquisitions that had a total value of US$22.88 billion and involved Chinese companies. Citic also completed deals across Southeast Asia and Europe, according to the report. China International Capital Corporation (CICC) reported a similar trend. Its overseas revenue in the first half of 2026 saw a year-on-year increase of 45 per cent to 9.19 billion yuan from 6.34 billion yuan a year earlier, faster than the investment bank’s 39.2 per cent overall revenue growth, according to its interim report. Overseas operations accounted for about 35 per cent of its revenue, up from 34 per cent a year earlier. Meanwhile, CICC sponsored 27 Hong Kong IPOs with an underwriting value of US$5.74 billion in the first half, compared with 13 deals worth US$2.87 billion a year earlier. The total assets of CICC International, its offshore arm, stood at HK$448.6 billion at the end of June, while net profit saw a year-on-year rise of 65 per cent to HK$4.35 billion. Guotai Haitong Securities, China’s largest brokerage by assets, also reported a sharp increase in offshore revenue. Revenue generated from Hong Kong and overseas markets reached 12.19 billion yuan in the first half, up 87.3 per cent from 6.51 billion yuan a year earlier, but the comparison was affected by the merger of Guotai Junan Securities and Haitong Securities. The overseas push by the leading brokers comes as Beijing seeks to build globally competitive investment banks and strengthen the securities industry’s cross-border capabilities. China Securities Regulatory Commission chairman Wu Qing said in December that China aimed to develop several leading brokerages with significant international influence during the 2026-2030 five-year planning period, while giving high-quality firms greater flexibility in their use of capital and leverage. The 36 overseas subsidiaries operated by 34 mainland Chinese brokerages had combined assets of HK$1.94 trillion at the end of 2025, up 31.95 per cent from a year earlier, according to the Securities Association of China. The international expansion has been accompanied by heavier capital commitments overseas by these leading brokerages. Citic raised 16 billion yuan through a private H-share placement completed in August, with the proceeds to be retained offshore for its international business. It has already injected the equivalent of 10 billion yuan into CSI. CSC Financial also injected HK$1.5 billion into China Securities International in February. Its offshore arm sponsored seven Hong Kong IPOs, raising HK$31.28 billion, during the first half of the year. It also had plans to further integrate its mainland and Hong Kong investment-banking operations while expanding into cross-border acquisitions and other products. The growing capital commitments to overseas businesses could also help improve brokerages’ returns on equity, according to analysts. Citi analysts led by Judy Zhang said in a report on Sunday that expanding overseas operations offered Chinese brokers “more tools to expand leverage”, alongside more accommodative onshore policies encouraging large securities firms to increase leverage.

title: 7 jewellery highlights for September from Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Boucheron and more
description: This month’s stand-out creations showcase elevated craftsmanship, wearable diamonds and bold new signatures.
content: From animal motifs to everyday diamonds – the world’s greatest maisons continue to delight with their enduring artistry. Here are our picks of the latest jewellery collections, some bringing fresh perspectives on iconic signatures and others showcasing groundbreaking design techniques. Boucheron Boucheron adds 12 new designs to its Serpent Bohème collection, the snake-inspired range that dates back to 1968. This latest iteration combines onyx and gold, representing shadow and light. Evoking a snake’s sinuous form, the creations include a stunning pendant necklace with a chain and a dainty bracelet partly set with diamonds. Buccellati The textured effect in Buccellati’s Macri creations is achieved through the maison’s signature “rigato” engraving technique. Delicate lines are hand-engraved onto the gold surface, giving the precious metal a fabric-like sheen. Embellished with brilliant-cut diamonds, the bracelets, rings and pendants in the range showcase the Italian jeweller’s savoir faire and its elegant Renaissance-tinged aesthetic. Cartier While the panther is Cartier’s undisputed icon, the jeweller has a long history with other animal creations, from zebras to crocodiles and even fantastical creatures like the chimera. Now the house is celebrating its menagerie of beautiful beasts with a series of pieces that showcase its ateliers’ ability to re-create in detail or subtly evoke animals ranging from tigers to rhinos. Graff Who says that diamonds are only for glamorous affairs? Graff’s Foufou collection offers rings perfectly suited to wearing every day. Adorned with yellow or white diamonds in cuts ranging from oval to heart and pear, the rings can be easily stacked for added oomph. Made of yellow or white gold, their delicate bands are set with pavé diamonds. Mellerio In 1951, French jeweller Mellerio filed a patent for a series of nail ornaments, which were never actually produced. Now, freshly inspired by that groundbreaking design, the house has finally realised the idea – fully 75 years later. Unveiled in Paris during the haute couture shows in July, these nail jewels can be worn separately or on each and every finger for maximum effect. They come in three combinations: white gold and white diamonds, white gold and black diamonds, and yellow gold and coloured gemstones. Palmiero Based in Valenza, a town in Northern Italy that has a very long tradition in jewellery manufacturing, Palmiero makes sculptural pieces where shapes, colours and volumes come together to create mini universes. This pendant necklace and matching ring – made of yellow gold and diamonds and available at Masterpiece by King Fook in Hong Kong – are part of the Rays of Sun collection, meant to evoke desert dunes illuminated by the sun. Van Cleef & Arpels Van Cleef & Arpels’ Alhambra collection needs no introduction. The four-leaf clover motif has become a signature of the maison and a symbol of good fortune. From mother of pearl to malachite and onyx, the famous motif appears in a wide variety of ornamental stones. A series of new creations in translucent pink enamel – developed after years of research in the brand’s workshops – adds a touch of whimsy to the colourful range. Additional contributions by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: Opinion | Going big and going green can work together for Hong Kong mega-events
description: By building green standards into event infrastructure, Hong Kong can stay competitive as an event host and irresistible to global organisers.
content: Hong Kong’s mega-event economy is thriving. In a blog post last month, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po noted that in the first half of 2026, the city hosted more than 130 mega-events, drawing 1.75 million visitors and injecting roughly HK$5.8 billion (US$739.9 million) into the local economy. These figures are the ongoing dividends of the government’s sustained policy and financial backing. This momentum is well-documented: in the last two years, the concerts of global A-listers such as Coldplay and Blackpink drew hundreds of thousands of fans and generated millions of dollars in ticket sales, while the 2025 Hong Kong Sevens delivered a HK$768 million boost. While sold-out stadiums and economic gains capture the headlines, a lesser-known aspect of these mega-events is their commitment to environmental sustainability. By introducing features such as a recycling leaderboard, Coldplay made going green fun, boosting LED wristband return rates to an impressive 94 per cent in Hong Kong and reducing their global tour emissions by 59 per cent compared to their previous tour. These efforts reflect a shift across the event sector. Blackpink’s management company, YG Entertainment, introduced event-level carbon tracking, ensuring their 2026 Hong Kong concert conducted rigorous carbon accounting. The 2024 Paris Olympics halved its carbon footprint compared to previous Games. As consumers and businesses increasingly value sustainability and extreme weather becomes more commonplace, greening Hong Kong’s mega-event economy should no longer be optional. A report by Our Hong Kong Foundation estimates that greening our mega-events could bring around HK$1 billion annually – all while reducing emissions. A 2023 Eventbrite survey found that 69 per cent of event organisers saw carbon mitigation as a key priority, so inaction could put us at risk of losing flagship events. Some might fear strict environmental rules will drive away events, but Singapore proves otherwise. After introducing its MICE Sustainability Roadmap in 2022, Singapore’s visitors for meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) still grew, showing environmental and economic gains can work in parallel. Moreover, a green transition could spawn a lucrative local market for specialised goods and services, driving job creation in fields such as carbon accounting and sustainable booth design. This is the right time to act. With the government expected to update its Climate Action Plan 2050 later this year, Hong Kong has an immediate policy window to future-proof its mega-event industry. First, the government should explicitly incorporate green mega-events into this coming update. Currently, green events are considered an event- or sector-specific agenda, which constrains cross-bureau cooperation and funding priorities. Making this a strategic priority will break down bureaucratic silos. This should be followed by a tailored decarbonisation road map for large-scale events. Drawing on guidelines already established in mainland provinces and cities, the road map should clearly define carbon accounting metrics, emission boundaries, and carbon offset mechanisms. Second, practical steps are needed to drive market demand. Flagship events such as Art Basel and the Hong Kong Sevens carry massive global visibility, making them perfect platforms to showcase sustainable best practices. The government could require a green event plan during funding applications, ensuring sustainability is embedded from pre-event planning to post-event teardown. This mirrors the approach by UK Sport, which has mandated similar requirements since 2023. To help the local industry adapt, a phased roll-out along with bonus funding of up to HK$1 million for voluntary submissions could be introduced. What about MICE events? While largely commercially funded, most take place in government-affiliated venues, specifically the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre and AsiaWorld-Expo. With contract renewals for both these venues approaching, the government has an opportunity to integrate green operating clauses into the tenders, greening the broader MICE industry by mandating venue-level environmental standards. Third, supply-side interventions should happen simultaneously. To help organisers confidently identify verified green suppliers, a centralised green supplier directory – managed by the government alongside accredited bodies like the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency – should be established. Following this, the “green premium” must be addressed. According to McKinsey, sustainable alternatives can carry a price premium of 16 to 40 per cent. The government could launch an e-green voucher scheme offering subsidies to organisers that procure goods and services from verified suppliers in the directory. Ultimately, environmental sustainability and economic vitality are two sides of the same coin. By embedding green standards into our event infrastructure, Hong Kong can ensure its position as an event host remains competitive and irresistible to global organisers. Katie Ho, a research manager at Our Hong Kong Foundation, also contributed to this article

title: HKIS settles bitter legal row with US church co-founder with substantial payment
description: Former chief justice Geoffrey Ma oversaw mediation between Hong Kong International School and Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod, source says.
content: An almost year-long legal dispute involving a prestigious Hong Kong international school and its US-based co-founder, a Lutheran church, has been resolved out of court, with the school making a substantial payment and ending its association with the religious body. A source familiar with the legal community told the South China Morning Post that former Hong Kong chief justice Geoffrey Ma Tao-li had overseen mediation between the two parties over two days in early August. Harold Kim, chairman of the board of managers of Hong Kong International School (HKIS), announced the move in a letter to parents on Tuesday, pledging that the settlement would not result in fee increases. “We are pleased to share that Hong Kong International School Association Limited (HKISAL) and the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod (LCMS) have reached a mediated settlement,” he wrote. “Under the terms of the settlement, LCMS will discontinue its legal proceedings against HKISAL, and both parties mutually agree to terminate the operating agreement, thereby concluding LCMS’ governance role with regard to HKIS. We are pleased to have reached this resolution.” Kim stressed that the settlement would not result in fee hikes. “HKIS remains in a strong financial position. The settlement will not affect our planned investments in the future of the school. Future tuition adjustments will continue to be reviewed through HKIS’ normal annual budget process,” he said. “The settlement will not affect tuition, nor will philanthropic donations be used to fund the settlement.” A financial statement previously seen by the SCMP showed that HKISAL had amassed financial reserves totalling HK$2.8 billion (US$357 million) as of July 31, 2024. Kim said that school operations would proceed as normal at its campuses in Repulse Bay and Tai Tam. “School leadership will continue unchanged under the governance of the board of managers, and the recent LCMS-initiated head of school search will be discontinued,” he said. Last year, LCMS said that the interim head of the school, Ron Roukema, was not a member of the church and called for him to be replaced. Kim said in the letter that Roukema continued to serve as the interim head. Both sides said details of the settlement were confidential. LCMS said in a statement that the settlement money would be used for religious, charitable and educational work. “As a church body, not one dollar goes to profit,” it said. “The agreement concludes proceedings in the High Court of Hong Kong, returns significant resources to LCMS and formally ends the relationship between LCMS and HKISAL.” The church stressed that its work in Hong Kong would continue after the agreement. “What has changed is that we have now secured our assets to fund that work on an even greater scale,” said Christian Preus, chairman of LCMS’ board of directors. A spokesman for the Education Bureau welcomed the resolution of the dispute, saying it had kept close contact with both parties. “The Education Bureau will continue to closely monitor the school’s operation and financial status, providing appropriate assistance to both parties in implementing the agreement,” he said. The agreement comes nearly a year after the church accused the school of serving only the rich and privileged and amassing excessive financial reserves. The church, which co-founded HKIS in 1966 with a group of American business professionals, earlier demanded that the school management pay it an indemnity of US$1.75 million. The school management, in turn, accused the church of exploring multiple options to develop part of the HKIS campus in Repulse Bay into a US$1 billion commercial project. The school’s primary and secondary sections follow the American curriculum. Primary school tuition fees for the 2026-27 academic year are HK$231,600, while those for secondary school range from HK$244,500 to HK$272,600. The dispute came to light when LCMS filed a lawsuit against the school’s management, alleging a breach of its 2013 operating agreement and demanding HKIS stop serving only the “rich and privileged few”. The church accused HKIS management of running the non-profit institution in a similar manner to a commercial business after accumulating HK$2.8 billion in financial reserves, even as it continued to raise tuition fees, collect cryptocurrency donations and sell HK$3 million priority debentures. In response, HKIS board chairman Kim rejected all the allegations as false, asserting that the school’s mission had always been to support the international expatriate business community by offering a top-tier education to attract global executives to Hong Kong. LCMS threatened to evict the school from its Repulse Bay campus, which the church owns, and to establish a cheaper alternative, named Hong Kong Pacific School, if HKIS failed to rectify the alleged breaches by 2027-28. But the school’s operator countered that the church’s sudden hostility in 2022 was financially motivated, pointing to LCMS’s prior property valuations and past sales of Hong Kong real estate to cover its global budget deficits. A source familiar with the matter said that HKIS would be able to “securely” operate its Repulse Bay campus under the agreement. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu and a group representing parents and staff earlier stepped in to emphasise that student learning must remain unaffected, even as the Education Bureau paused the church’s new school application pending litigation.

title: Nepal floods: meet the principal whose quick thinking saved 900 students
description: More than 4,400 remain missing in Nepal and China after the devastating flash floods, unleashed after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas.
content: Rajendra Dawadi was inside his classroom when a colleague rushed in with a warning: floodwaters were racing through Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, tearing apart homes, bridges and entire villages. Then a teacher received another warning by phone. Moments later, a parent arrived to take her child home. The danger had not yet been confirmed, but Dawadi, the principal, had little time to act. He rang the school bell and ordered his students and staff out of the building and towards higher ground. “I immediately decided to stop … school” and get the children out, he said. As he followed them to a nearby hill, the floodwaters rose behind him. From the safety of the hillside, he turned to watch the school where he had once been a student – and where he had spent years teaching – disappear beneath a torrent of water, mud, boulders and debris. Two staff members could not make it and remain missing. Dawadi’s decision to evacuate the school saved at least 900 students from last week’s devastating flash floods in Nepal, unleashed after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas. The disaster killed over 950 people in Nepal and Tibet, while more than 4,400 remain missing. As Nepal grapples with the catastrophic natural disaster, Dawadi’s story has emerged as a striking example of foresight and courage. The Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School had 1,643 students. At least 900 were on campus that morning, while some students were still making their way to school. Dawadi ordered those already there to leave and called bus drivers to tell them not to come. One bus, packed with students, had already reached the school when Dawadi told the driver to turn back, he said. The bus crossed a newly constructed bridge and, moments later, the old bridge beside it collapsed. For Dawadi, the scale of the destruction has become personal, as the school had been both his workplace and a large part of his life. “I have no words. I got education from that school. And I gave education at that school,” he said. The destruction of Dawadi’s school was not an isolated loss. Across northern Nepal, the floods have left thousands of children without classrooms, disrupted their education and raised fears that the disaster could cost them months of schooling. Aid group Save the Children said in a statement that at least 69 schools in northern Nepal were destroyed, putting the education of nearly 19,000 students at risk. Dawadi’s quick thinking and swift response during the disaster have been hailed as an act of heroism. When he returned to the site of the school days later, parents embraced him as they thanked him for saving their children. “Their parents hugged me, they cried with me,” he said. “They were emotional.” Student Suvina Tamang, 14, said the building was swept away shortly after the students had been evacuated. “I will thank him when I see him” for saving my life, she said. But Dawadi is reluctant to accept the role of hero. For him, rescuing his students was his responsibility. Now he says, students will need psychological counselling. Then, lessons must begin again, even if the school must temporarily relocate. His appeal to the Nepalese government is simple: rebuild the schools and get children back to classes.

title: US university to pay US$2.1 million settlement over claims it didn’t disclose China ties
description: Justice Department alleged Ohio State failed to reveal employees’ links to China in applications for federal grant funding.
content: A prominent American university has agreed to pay a US$2.1 million settlement to resolve allegations that it failed to disclose employees’ ties to China when applying for federal grant funding, the Department of Justice announced on Monday. Ohio State University’s (OSU) settlement relates to Nasa and National Science Foundation (NSF) grants that provided funding to the university from November 2012 to August 2023. Both Nasa and the NSF required the public university to disclose “foreign government support received by any principal investigator (PI) or co-PI on the grant application”, according to a Department of Justice press release. The NSF was established by Congress in 1950 and funds scientific research through grants, while Nasa oversees the US space programme, conducting research in areas including aeronautics and space exploration. The US$2.1 million settlement will specifically resolve allegations that, since 2014, annual faculty activity reports submitted to OSU identified affiliations with Chinese universities and state-run research organisations, but the university did not disclose this information to Nasa or the NSF. In addition, the university learned in 2019 that a principal investigator on Nasa grants was a participant in the Thousand Talents Programme, which the department said was established by the Chinese government “to recruit individuals with knowledge or access to foreign technology intellectual property”. OSU did not notify Nasa or the NSF until four years later in 2023, the release said, adding that the US had identified additional employees who worked on those grants who were affiliated with, collaborated with, or received funding from China. “The claims resolved by the settlement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability,” the Department of Justice stated. The Thousand Talents Programme is a state-backed recruitment initiative that began in 2008, aimed at attracting overseas Chinese academics through cash grants that fund research and living costs. American intelligence officials have accused the programme of “[facilitating] the legal and illicit transfer of US technology, intellectual property and know-how” to China. Beijing has consistently dismissed these allegations, framing it as a legitimate academic exchange. Also in Monday’s release, the Department of Justice noted that since 2011, US federal law has prohibited the use of grant funds for collaborations with China, Chinese universities, or any Chinese-owned companies. “American universities that benefit from the federal government’s support for scientific research and advancement must fully disclose all foreign funding in their grant applications,” said Brett Shumate, assistant attorney general at the Justice Department’s civil division. “We will continue to hold accountable any university that fails to comply with disclosure requirements designed to protect research security and federally funded scientific achievements.” The settlement comes amid a broader push from the Donald Trump administration, which has increasingly treated collaboration with China as a threat to the United States’ national security. In July, the NSF announced plans to prohibit NSF-funded projects from collaborating with Chinese entities on US restricted-party lists, including their employees. That policy, which the NSF intends to implement in federal financial year 2027, comes amid a broader congressional push by House Republicans to curb academic partnerships between China and the US.

title: The laptop, the social media user and the false alarm in Taiwan over a Beijing ‘spy’
description: Persistent fears of mainland infiltration risk raising unnecessary suspicion and eroding public trust, analysts say.
content: A false espionage alarm about a Taipei subway user has fuelled concerns that growing fears of Beijing are breeding unhealthy suspicion on the island and eroding public trust. The controversy erupted after a social media user posted a photograph of a man holding a laptop on a Taipei Main Station metro platform on Saturday. Seeing the words “2nd Theatre Photosynthesis System” appeared in simplified Chinese on the laptop’s screen, the social media user suspected that the man was a mainland Chinese spy on a mission. The social media user reported the man to several government agencies, including the police, immigration authorities, the Mainland Affairs Council and the Ministry of Justice’s Investigation Bureau. Ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) legislator Lin Chu-yin also raised the alarm, saying a similarly named “Photosynthesis public-opinion monitoring system” had been described as a mainland Chinese platform for monitoring online big data and gathering intelligence. She warned that if information about passenger flows, surrounding facilities and public movements at Taipei Main Station were collected and analysed by Beijing, it could potentially be used to plan wartime attacks or disrupt transport. “If this is true, this is definitely not simply someone using a computer, but a serious national security issue,” Lin said, calling for an immediate investigation. But claims unravelled just hours later. Taipei police tracked down the 48-year-old man, surnamed Kao, who told officers he had been waiting for a friend while listening to an online investment course. According to investigators, Kao’s account matched the course materials and the ominous-sounding “2nd Theatre Photosynthesis System” was simply a label used by the investment course. At the time of the incident, Kao had been listening to a course on compound interest. Police concluded that the incident was a misunderstanding. The episode has triggered a wider debate over whether concerns about mainland Chinese infiltration – intensified by years of cross-strait tensions and warnings about espionage, disinformation and “fifth column” activities – are creating excessive suspicion among parts of Taiwanese society. Beijing, which sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary, has repeatedly denied the espionage accusations. Mainland China’s counter-espionage agency has also warned of infiltration and influence efforts from Taipei. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Chang Yuan-hsiang, a political-science professor at Soochow University in Taipei, said collective “witch hunts” throughout history had typically been driven by fear, leading societies to manufacture enemies and hatred. He compared the atmosphere today with Taiwan’s White Terror era in the 1950s, when warnings by the then Kuomintang (KMT) authoritarian government that “communist spies are right beside you” were common. Chang said that since Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te had taken office, Lai’s “McCarthyist-style” anti-mainland China political messaging had helped to fuel excessive suspicion among some DPP supporters. He said some people genuinely believed that the opposition parties were “fellow travellers” of the mainland’s Communist Party and that large numbers of Beijing’s “fifth column” were hidden among opposition supporters. Chang said there was a danger of groups becoming driven by emotion and susceptible to extreme rhetoric and political cues rather than evidence. Confirmation bias then reinforced those beliefs, prompting people to “search for enemies among their fellow citizens” and spread their suspicions rapidly through social media, he said. The laptop controversy is just the latest false alarm. In June last year, DPP legislator Kuo Yu-ching posted online about a man in a park whom she said was acting suspiciously. The man was reportedly a former Taiwanese special forces soldier and conducting an ordinary live stream. Kuo deleted her post and apologised. Other cases cited by critics include a Hong Kong tourist who was confronted while photographing Taipei’s Ziqiang Tunnel and accused online of gathering intelligence. The tourist was later identified as a fan of Taiwanese rock band Mayday – the tunnel is mentioned in one of the group’s songs and is a popular destination among fans. In another incident, a man photographing streets while carrying equipment was flagged on social media as potentially suspicious amid warnings about mainland Chinese espionage. He turned out to be a land surveyor. Opposition politicians said repeated false alarms risk producing a “cry-wolf effect” in which the public eventually becomes desensitised to warnings about genuine espionage.
