On Monday, opposition New Party deputy secretary general Yu Chih-pin filed a complaint with Taipei prosecutors against Lin, accusing her of “potentially violating the Social Order Maintenance Act by spreading unverified claims capable of disturbing public peace”. DPP legislative caucus whip Chuang Jui-hsiung defended the need for public vigilance, saying there was “nothing wrong with alerting security agencies when people encounter something they believe could pose a national security concern”. But he acknowledged that once police established that Kao was simply taking an investment course, “his innocence should be made clear”. Chang warned that the broader danger was the erosion of social trust. He said trust was the “invisible glue” that held democratic societies together and once it disappeared, polarisation intensified, confidence in institutions declined and governing became more difficult. “Self-serving politicians, a lack of mutual trust among the public and the continuous fragmentation of society constitute Taiwan’s greatest crisis,” Chang said.

title: Chinese schools spark controversy over strict hair policy barring non-compliant male students
description: Schools are violating national education law by infringing upon students’ right to education over minor hairstyle issues, says lawyer.
content: Two schools in northwestern China have ignited controversy by enforcing a strict hairstyle policy on students, who may be stopped at the school gate or even turned away if they fail to comply with the requirements. August 23 marked the first day of the new school term at Yinchuan High School and Yinchuan No 24 Middle School in Yinchuan, the capital city of the Ningxia Hui autonomous region. Viral videos revealed that several teachers were stationed at the gates of these two schools, inspecting students’ hairstyles and prohibiting entry to those who did not adhere to the hair regulations, as reported by Jinyun News. Many students who were denied entry, along with their perplexed parents, were seen in the videos, with some parents making last-minute calls for hair styling services. Nearby the school gates, several barbers had set up makeshift stalls to accommodate the students in need of haircuts. Reports indicated that some students were queuing for their services. According to the grooming regulations set by the schools, male students are required to keep their hair above their eyebrows and ears, and it must not touch the collar in the back. Those who do not meet these standards must visit a barbershop for immediate adjustment before being allowed to enter the school. For female students, if their hair is short, it must not extend to their neck; if it is medium or long, it should be tied in a ponytail as per school rules. All students are prohibited from perming or dyeing their hair. Boys wishing to shave their heads completely must first obtain permission from the school. Some parents expressed to the media that they were unaware of these specific hairstyle requirements. An anonymous teacher from Yinchuan High School stated that they would permit students to enter after “their hair was corrected according to the school’s rules.” “Our intention is not to prevent students from entering the school. We simply wish to communicate with parents and collaborate to persuade students to adopt a standardised hairstyle,” the teacher was quoted as saying. An official from the Yinchuan Municipal Education Bureau mentioned that they are investigating the situation and have not yet determined an appropriate course of action. Meng Bo, a lawyer from Beijing Jingshi Law Firm, asserted that the schools have violated China’s Education Law by infringing upon students’ right to education, as they deny entry based on hairstyle issues. According to the country’s Ministry of Education, the Middle School Students’ Behaviour Regulation states that students should dress neatly and are not permitted to perm or dye their hair, wear make-up, or adorn themselves with jewellery. Male students are prohibited from having long hair, while female students are not allowed to wear high-heeled shoes, as per ministry guidelines. In addition to this general policy, many schools nationwide establish detailed requirements and enforce them stringently. In mid-August, a parent in Dongguan, southern Guangdong province, lodged a complaint with the local government, stating that a junior secondary school forced his son to cut his hair, threatening that he would not be allowed to register without compliance.

title: Survey finds that many Hong Kong pupils exceed daily limits on screen time
description: One in three kindergarteners spends at least an hour a day on social media, while 66.6 per cent of senior form students go beyond two hours.
content:
One in three Hong Kong kindergarten pupils spends at least an hour a day on social media, a survey has found. Also, more than 80 per cent of arguments between parents and kids are about screen time.
The Hong Kong Institute of Family Education’s survey found that 34.7 per cent of kindergarten kids spend at least one hour a day on social media. But the Department of Health says children ages two to five should have no more than one hour of screen time a day.
Sixty per cent of lower form secondary school students and 66.6 per cent of senior form students went beyond the global two-hour daily limit.
Tik Chi-yuen is the institute’s head. He said kids in kindergarten mostly used screens to watch videos and talk to family using their parents’ accounts.
He said the trend was “not that worrying” because it was not common among these parents to use screen time to keep children occupied.
Tik urged the government to tighten rules on children’s social media use. He suggested that those under 16 should not be allowed on these platforms.

title: US Treasury’s Bessent calls on Japan to boost yen through rate increases
description: A weak yen, which has pushed up import prices and broader inflation, has been blamed in part on the central bank’s slow pace of rate increases.
content: Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Monday she ‌met US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and agreed that orderly yen movement is critical for global market stability. The ⁠two countries also confirmed that ‌continued, cooperative measures would contribute to this common goal, ‌Katayama told reporters after attending the ⁠Group ⁠of 20 finance leaders’ gathering. She declined ‌to comment when asked if recent yen ‌moves ‌were orderly. Katayama and Bessent discussed ‌Japan’s financial policy, the earlier ⁠coordinated yen intervention and other topics, ⁠a senior Japanese official present at the ‌meeting told reporters. On Monday, Scott Bessent said he believed Japan’s government and central bank would take action leading ‌to a stronger yen, signalling a strong chance of a Bank of Japan (BOJ) interest rate increases in September. “I have information that the market doesn’t have, and it’s my belief that the Japanese government and the BOJ will do the things that will lead to a stronger yen,” Bessent told CNBC in an interview during a Group of 20 finance leaders’ gathering ⁠in Asheville, North Carolina. When asked whether that meant raising interest rates, Bessent said: “I think the market’s pricing that in now.” The yen gained against the dollar after ‌Bessent’s comments, which reinforced dominant market expectations the BOJ will raise rates at its next policy meeting in September. Bessent met Ueda on Sunday and Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama on Monday, a senior US Treasury Department official told Japanese ⁠public broadcaster NHK on Monday. In ⁠the meetings, Bessent called for the need for further rate increases and for Japan to clearly show markets how it would achieve fiscal sustainability, Erin Browne, undersecretary for international affairs at the ‌US Department of the Treasury, was quoted as saying in an interview with NHK. Sources have said the BOJ is set to raise rates ‌as soon ‌as its September 17-18 meeting and is considering hiking more aggressively than the current pace of roughly two times a year after that session. Bessent’s repeated ‌calls for BOJ rate increases have been among the factors that led markets to nearly fully price in the chance of a September increase. The ⁠Japanese central bank raised rates in June. An increase next month, rather than in October, could fuel market bets the BOJ would raise rates once every quarter, ⁠some analysts said. A weak yen has pushed up import prices and broader inflation, causing headaches for Japanese policymakers. It has been blamed in part on the slow pace of rate increases by the BOJ, which has kept Japan’s rate divergence with the US wide. Japan and ‌the US carried out a rare ‌joint yen-buying intervention on July 31, signalling their determination to prevent a sell-off in the yen and Japanese government bonds from spilling over into global markets. While that action failed to put a sustained floor under the yen, Bessent said he did not see recent yen moves as disorderly, suggesting Washington was in no mood to join Tokyo for another foray into the market to prop up the currency. Japan’s Finance Ministry announced on Friday that its intervention in the market over the preceding month hit a record 15.4 trillion yen (US$96.4 billion). The US has yet to disclose how much yen it bought, but the sum is expected to be far smaller. The Treasury secretary has repeatedly hinted over the past year that he would prefer that the BOJ raise interest rates to help the yen rather than see repeated intervention in the market. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Shein shares recover after 10% drop on Hong Kong debut
description: The fast-fashion retailer sold 280 million shares at HK$48.56 each, according to an exchange filing Monday.
content: Shein Global Holdings plunged as much as 10 per cent in its Hong Kong trading debut on Tuesday after raising HK$13.6 billion (US$1.7 billion), further shaking market confidence in the company’s valuation. The shares opened flat at the offer price of HK$48.56 before falling as much as 10 per cent to HK$43.72. They later pared most losses, trading at HK$48.50 by market close – a 0.1 per cent drop. Shein founder Sky Xu Yangtian attended the listing ceremony but remained low profile. He did not give any speeches or interviews. Instead, chief financial officer Leigh Gui spoke on behalf of the company. “This listing marks a new beginning for Shein,” Gui said. “Moving forward, we will continue to innovate while grounding our operations in compliance, transparency and ESG principles to bring fashion to consumers worldwide.” Shein’s Hong Kong public offering was oversubscribed 4.6 times, while the international offering was oversubscribed 1.6 times. On Monday evening its shares closed 13.1 per cent lower on the grey market at HK$42.2 after dropping as much as 28 per cent, according to Futu Holdings data. With a board lot size of 100 shares, each lot yielded a loss of HK$636, excluding transaction fees. Shein priced shares for its Hong Kong listing at just above the midpoint amount it had set. The fast-fashion retailer sold 280 million shares at HK$48.56 each, according to an exchange filing Monday, valuing the company at slightly over US$26 billion. That would be a significant markdown from its peak valuation of nearly US$100 billion in 2022, as well as its Series D+ funding valuation of around US$64 billion in 2023. To compensate investors who took part in the private funding rounds in 2022 and 2023, the prospectus reveals that Shein will pay around US$1.33 billion to holders of its pre-D, D and D+ preference shares. Shein successfully secured seven cornerstone investors, who together subscribed to about US$383 million worth of shares, accounting for around 22 per cent of the base offering size. Most of these cornerstone investors are existing backers. Based on Monday’s grey market close, they are already sitting on a paper loss of HK$410 million. The stock will start trading in Hong Kong on Tuesday, representing Shein’s third attempt to go public, after previous efforts in the United States and Britain stalled. The company, which relocated its headquarters to Singapore, eventually chose Hong Kong after facing setbacks in Western capital markets. Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing had launched weekly and monthly options for the stock, added it to a designated list for short selling and allowed derivative warrants to begin trading on the company’s first listing day. While Shein maintained annual revenue growth above 40 per cent from 2021 through 2023, the prospectus shows a compound annual net income growth rate of 14.2 per cent. In the first quarter of this year, Shein’s revenue growth nearly stalled, rising only 1.1 per cent year on year to US$9.05 billion, according to the prospectus. Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs are joint sponsors of Shein’s initial public offering, while Haitong International Securities, UBS, HSBC, Merrill Lynch (Asia-Pacific), Banco Santander and East West Bank are the joint bookrunners, according to its prospectus.

title: India line up Brazil, Uruguay friendlies, but domestic football chaos continues
description: Trio of international friendlies over next several weeks provides some light in a gloomy time for game in the country.
content: Against a backdrop of chaos in the domestic game, India’s national football team will at least have something to look forward to over the next couple of weeks – a trio of fixtures against World Cup winners and South American stars. While the Indian Super League stumbles towards what increasingly feels like another false start, football chiefs in the country have reportedly splashed out US$9.44 million (HK$74 million) to play Brazil, Uruguay and Panama in the coming international window. Initially pencilled in to be part of Fifa’s Asean Cup, which will see Hong Kong host the might of Brunei and Laos at Kai Tak Stadium this month, India withdrew so they could play Carlo Ancelotti’s side for the first time in their history. Other fixtures against Panama and Uruguay have now been added to what the All India Football Federation (AIFF) called “an unprecedented run of international football” for fans in the country, one they no doubt hope will mask the continued failings in the club game. After a disastrous 2025-26 season, which started five months late and involved just 13 games, this year’s ISL is scheduled to kick off on Friday, although even then, how many sides will take part, and in what format, remains to be seen. Earlier this month, Tata Steel pulled its funding of Jamshedpur FC, saying it wanted to concentrate on the game at a grass-roots level, a response that may have been linked to the AIFF’s decision that clubs should hold the commercial rights to the ISL. In a move this summer, the governing body said it was “retaining administrative control and oversight of key operational aspects”, in a move towards a more common model. “From our side, we are very committed to making this league one of the best in Asia,” Muthyalu Satyanarayan, the federation’s deputy secretary general, said. It is in that context, and in an attempt to better the ranking of a side that is nominally 138th in the world, but lost 1-0 to Hong Kong last year before winning a meaningless Asian Cup qualifier against the same opponents at home in March, that the games take place. Indian football legend Sunil Chhetri, who is still playing for Bengaluru at the age of 42 but has retired from the national team, said he would “feel a little jealous as a spectator”. “In my 24 to 26 years as a professional and nearly 20 years with the national team, I never got an opportunity like this,” said the ISL all-time top scorer, who also has the most caps, 157, and most international goals, 95, for his country. The hosts will kick things off against Panama in Bengaluru on September 26, with the five-time world champions the star attraction in Kolkata on October 3. Uruguay bring the curtain down on proceedings three days later in the same Salt Lake Stadium. While footing the substantial bill for hosting the matches, the AIFF will hope to break even, or make a small profit through the sale of tickets, hospitality packages, broadcast rights and other commercial activity. Work on improving the country’s ranking, and by association its standing within the game, began almost a decade ago. Ranked as low as No 173 in March 2015, India have been as high as 96 at times since, but dropped back over the past five years. Cricket is, and will always remain, the country’s passion, but the establishment of the AIFF-administered ISL in 2013 provided the foundation for the growth of football in India. French football stars Florent Malouda, David Trezeguet, Mikael Silvestre, Robert Pires and Nicolas Anelka, Italian duo Alessandro del Piero and Alessandro Nesta, former Liverpool left-back John Arne Riise, and even current Uruguay manager Diego Forlan all played in the early years of the top flight. The decision to host Brazil and Uruguay in Kolkata is also no coincidence, given it is home to a fierce rivalry between East Bengal and Mohun Bagan. A derby first played on August 8, 1921, it is considered by some to be the greatest rivalry in Asian football. Local media have said that while Kolkata residents might not have a clue what the Indian prime minister said on a given day, they “know the starting line-up of Brazil on the same day”. In an official announcement of the match earlier this year, the Brazil Football Confederation also hailed India as one of the world’s largest overseas fan bases for their national team. The CBF is expected to send a delegation of more than 90 people, and will arrive a week in advance to prepare, according to some Chinese media reports. India officials have also lined up matches against New Zealand, who also played in the World Cup this summer, in Auckland and Christchurch in November. Hong Kong, meanwhile, have yet to announce any plans beyond next month.

title: Bullying mayor ousted as Japan’s voters reject political abuse
description: The fall of Yokohama’s mayor suggests the end of an era for local Japanese leaders treating staff and public funds with contempt.
content: Yokohama’s mayor has become the latest local official in Japan to be forced from office by scandal, as analysts say voters are no longer willing to look the other way. Takeharu Yamanaka reportedly called his staff “human trash” and told a senior official to “commit seppuku” (ritual suicide) if the city failed to win a bid for an international conference. He stepped down on Friday after a prolonged investigation found he had repeatedly verbally abused city employees and humiliated subordinates. “Public attitudes have changed a lot in recent years,” said Hiromi Murakami, a political-science professor at Temple University’s Tokyo branch. This sort of behaviour has been going on for years in local governments Hiromi Murakami, political-science professor “This sort of behaviour has been going on for years in local governments, companies and organisations in Japan but there is far greater awareness about bullying now and people are less willing to tolerate it.” Yamanaka, a former university professor who was first elected mayor in 2021 and won re-election in August last year, became the subject of an external investigation after a senior city official accused him of harassment. The resulting report, released in late July, found that he had spent years terrorising his own staff – screaming at employees, hurling documents across desks and calling officials “useless”. It concluded that Yamanaka had committed “serious acts of power harassment that deeply damaged employees’ dignity and worsened the workplace environment”. By the time he faced reporters at city hall on Friday, there was little left to defend. “I did not sufficiently consider the weight of words spoken from the position of mayor or how my words and actions would be perceived,” he said, apologising and accepting what he called the city assembly’s “severe judgment” before confirming his resignation. Analysts say Yamanaka had no real alternative by that point. Once the report’s findings were public knowledge, the pressure became unsustainable. “We seem to be seeing more and more cases of people elected to high positions in local governments around the country who seem to believe that they hold huge amounts of power, that they are superior to everyone else and that they cannot be touched,” Murakami said. “But it is clear that has changed.” A familiar pattern Yamanaka is not the first Japanese politician to be brought low by scandal. In July last year, former Ito mayor Maki Takubo admitted she had not graduated from Toyo University as claimed on her campaign materials. She resigned within weeks and was later questioned by police after investigators found digital traces of the allegedly forged diploma on her computer. Ex-Ginan mayor Hideo Kojima resigned in March 2024 after 99 separate allegations of sexual harassment from female city hall employees, including accusations that he had groped a colleague. His resignation press conference was tearful yet not career-ending: he ran for a town council seat afterwards and won. In Maebashi, Akira Ogawa was forced out as mayor in November after it emerged she had met a male subordinate at a love hotel at least 10 times, meetings she insisted were purely professional. The municipal assembly was not persuaded, forcing her resignation, yet by January this year, Ogawa had staged a comeback, winning re-election as an independent on a platform built around “atonement”. And in Ichikawa, voters ousted Hirotami Murakoshi in March 2022 following revelations that he had spent 3.6 million yen (US$22,500) of public money on a private shower room and leased a Tesla as his official car. Untouchable no more For Toshimitsu Shigemura, a professor of politics at Tokyo’s Waseda University, the throughline connecting all these scandals in local Japanese politics is a culture of impunity that persisted for years. “This is the old culture that has long been part of Japanese politics at the local level,” he said. “These people have grown up seeing their elected representatives doing these sorts of things and nobody challenging them and the media effectively ignoring whatever they do, but suddenly that is changing.” Money is part of the story too. With households across Japan squeezed by a prolonged cost of living crisis, voters have far less patience for officials who splash public cash on themselves or their vanity projects. “Before, they had a lot of power and a lot of money so they felt untouchable,” Shigemura said. “But people and the media are now speaking out and they are being directly criticised.” Murakami agreed. “It is much harder to cover it up now,” she said, adding that the string of scandals could provide an opportunity to reset the terms of public office in Japan. “I hope that will have an impact,” she said, arguing that the added scrutiny should remind anyone seeking elected office that they ultimately answered to the people who put them there. Yokohama’s city council announced on Monday that voters would choose Yamanaka’s successor as mayor with a special by-election on October 18.

title: Elite Hong Kong schools urged to raise the bar, challenge high-ability students
description: External reviewers find top schools must design more demanding lessons for top performers and adjust difficulty for struggling students.
content: Some elite schools in Hong Kong have been criticised for failing to provide sufficient learning opportunities or challenging tasks to stretch top performers, with reviewers urging teachers to design questions and tasks with greater depth. The remarks appeared in the Education Bureau’s External School Review reports, which assessed 68 secondary and primary institutions. Some institutions were told to better cater for learners’ diversity, including by setting extended activities for pupils who finish tasks early. Reviewers, including bureau officers, urged teachers to set tiered tasks and higher-order questions for top performers, including through digital tools that allow self-paced advancement. They also called for adjusting lesson difficulty and adopting collaborative designs for struggling pupils. At least six elite schools were told to do more to maximise the potential of high achievers. Among them was Queen Elizabeth School in Mong Kok, a government secondary school known for its academic performance. It was told that its strategies for stretching the more able students remained limited and should be further strengthened. The school’s results in the university entrance exam, the Diploma of Secondary Education, typically exceed city averages. “Some lessons are teacher-led with low expectations. A few teachers provide excessive guidance, reducing opportunities for students to participate actively and think independently,” the report read. While questioning was frequently used to check students’ understanding, the queries were often straightforward and lacked depth, it added. “To cater for learner diversity more effectively, teachers should adjust lesson pace, assign differentiated tasks, and incorporate more higher-order thinking questions or extension activities to challenge the more able learners,” it said in the report. The report urged teachers to adopt a wider range of questions by using prompting queries at varying levels of difficulty to foster deeper thinking among students. In its response, the school’s management committee said it was formulating action plans. “To better cater to learner diversity, we will prioritise professional development focusing on stretching higher-ability learners. This includes implementing differentiated tasks and adopting a wider range of probing questions in daily classroom teaching,” the report read. Wa Ying College in Ho Man Tin, where students have also performed strongly in public examinations, received similar feedback. While students were observed to be attentive, eager to participate and capable of working independently, the school was told its classroom approaches for top performers still had room for refinement. The report advised staff to layer assignments by difficulty, set advanced supplementary challenges, and pose more analytical questions that would push high-ability pupils to investigate further. The school said it had been working to broaden self-evaluation data collection and initiate strategies to cater for learner differences. “Building on this foundation, we will explore strategies to conduct more in-depth analysis of the data and explore methods to further enhance the effectiveness of learning and teaching to unleash our students’ potential,” it said. Other institutions received similar guidance to set more demanding work for high-ability pupils. At St Joseph’s College in Central, where pupils were described as highly motivated and academically strong, reviewers said staff should broaden their pedagogical repertoire to address varying learning needs more effectively, particularly through more deliberate provision of challenging and extension tasks to stretch higher-ability learners. “In some lessons, task design offers limited opportunity to provoke deeper thinking, resulting in the more able students not always being sufficiently challenged and some becoming idle after completing the assigned work,” it said. Shun Tak Fraternal Association Leung Kau Kui College in Tuen Mun was told to craft more demanding and intellectually rigorous assignments, alongside specific constructive feedback, and to employ adaptive teaching methods that foster greater peer-to-peer exchange. At SKH Bishop Mok Sau Tseng Secondary School in Tai Po, reviewers found that “group learning tasks designed for more able students were relatively simple, mainly involving reciting facts and related information, while classroom questioning also lacked depth”. “Given the high calibre of students, the design of some group tasks is rather simple, focusing primarily on eliciting facts and information. Teachers should infuse challenging components in the task design in order to allow students to make use of their analytical minds and display creative ideas,” the report read. “Questions are frequently posed to check students’ understanding but often lack variety and depth. A wider range of questions should be adopted to foster higher-order thinking skills.” At Hennessy Road Government Primary School, reviewers noted that pupils who completed assignments early were not given further learning opportunities. It also suggested teachers deploy enrichment exercises and digital tools allowing children to advance according to their own readiness. At the same time, schools were told not to lose sight of weaker learners. SKH Lee Shiu Keung Primary School in Kwun Tong was advised to optimise questioning techniques and use “layered questions” to guide thinking and develop higher-order skills, while embedding more interaction in group activities to “strengthen care for different students’ learning needs”. At St Mary’s Canossian School in Tsim Sha Tsui, teachers were told they needed to “strengthen care for student diversity” by flexibly adjusting the difficulty of learning tasks according to student ability. The report also advised the school to increase collaborative elements in group work so that different learners could participate more fully.

title: Woman fatally shot by police after deadly stabbing attack in New York’s Times Square
description: One victim was killed and another was wounded; NYPD says suspect had a history of mental illness.
content: A woman randomly stabbed two people in New York City’s Times Square on Monday, killing one woman, and then was fatally shot by police, according to officials. The shooting happened just before 4.30pm next to a New York Police Department substation, just outside One Times Square, the building that hosts the city’s annual New Year’s Eve ball drop celebration. It is one of the most heavily touristed and policed spots in all of New York. The 49-year-old woman from Queens pulled out two knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man who had just come out of the subway station and was waiting to cross the street with his wife, striking him in the abdomen, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference. Seconds later, the woman stabbed a 32-year-old woman also in the abdomen, Tisch said. Both victims were taken to the hospital. The woman died and the man is in stable condition, according to police. Police didn’t say if the victims were tourists visiting the city or residents. Videos posted on social media show a group of at least 10 officers gathered around the woman, who was holding two large kitchen knives. Officers tried to convince the woman to drop the knives for several minutes before using a Taser, Tisch said. The woman told them: “I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you,” according to Tisch. The video shows the Taser not incapacitating her and the woman walking quickly towards the officers while waving the knives in front of her. Two officers then shot the woman, according to police. In the video posted by bystanders, the woman fell to the ground, where an officer handcuffed her. Officers rolled her onto her back and rendered first aid. “This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world,” Tisch said. The woman has a “documented mental health history with the NYPD”, which includes incidents in 2018 and 2019 but no arrest history with the department, Tisch said. She didn’t provide additional details. Police are investigating. Tisch said there was no evidence suggesting it was a terrorist attack. The names of the victims have not been released until next of kin are notified, according to police. “We know that those families’ lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both Mamdani and Tisch praised the officers, saying more people could have been hurt or killed if not for their actions. The NYPD temporarily closed part of 7th Avenue and warned the public to stay away from the area. Police tape cordoned off the area as a large group of law enforcement officers worked nearby. Violent crime has fallen sharply in New York City so far this year, with homicides down 24 per cent and on pace to potentially hit their lowest level in decades. But this is the second killing this year in Times Square. A man was fatally stabbed in the same area in May.

title: Editorial | Don’t let Iran sanctions derail US-China engagement
description: The US push to isolate Iran economically puts Beijing in the crosshairs. Ahead of Xi Jinping’s state visit, both sides must contain the fallout to protect vital broader ties.
content: The United States’ stalled war on Iran continues to loom large in its relations with China. In March, President Donald Trump delayed a state visit to Beijing until May to manage developments in the Iran conflict. Now, ahead of President Xi Jinping’s scheduled state visit to Washington on September 24, the Iran issue has again reared its head as the US tries to extract itself from a quagmire of its own making. Washington has widened US sanctions targeting dealings with Iran in what it described as an “economic D-Day” aimed at isolating the country from the global economy, following six months of conflict. This comes in the wake of failed peace talks and a US naval blockade, which was lifted after the parties reached a memorandum of understanding and reimposed after alleged Iranian attacks on commercial shipping. The two exchanged a round of military strikes over the weekend. Announcing the new measures, including sanctions on 60 entities around the world, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said any nation financially partnering Iran would be isolated, along with banks and businesses that refused to cut ties. Whether the measures are effective depends on the reaction from Iran’s trading partners. They include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil. The measures target mainland Chinese and Hong Kong-based procurement, financial and shipping intermediaries. But none of them are major banks or refineries. China has warned of reprisals against possible further US sanctions. “China will do everything necessary to firmly safeguard its rights and interests,” the foreign ministry said. Dialogue and negotiation were the only way forward, a spokesman added – rightly so, as economic warfare would only serve to fuel tensions and lead to spillover risks. The US needs to find a way out of its Iran dilemma, short of the military option – which would be a very expensive way to force Tehran back to the negotiating table. The other option is economic warfare. So far, economic sanctions have not been very effective. The US now hopes to isolate Iran by undermining China’s substantive relations with the Islamic Republic. In Trump’s trade war, China retaliated, stood firm and eventually prevailed. If a similar scenario unfolds over Iran, the world will watch how China responds. It remains to be seen how the escalating tensions will affect Xi’s planned visit to the US. But there are, thankfully, signs of another scenario – a tacit understanding between the two sides that gives room for differences, even sanctions and retaliation, within a policy of managed competition. At the same time as Bessent’s sanctions announcement, a US delegation visited Beijing for the third US-China Track 1.5 Dialogue, a mechanism established in 2023 to bridge official diplomacy and non-governmental exchanges between the two countries. This year’s visit was headed by John Thornton, co-chairman of the Asia Society think tank and former president of Goldman Sachs, who has served as a backchannel between the two governments. During the semi-official dialogue, Liu Haixing, head of the Communist Party’s International Department, called on both sides to “reject zero-sum games to achieve healthy stability with well-managed competition, and seek common ground while bridging differences to achieve normal stability with controllable disagreements”. Thornton and some of the other US delegates also met the fourth-ranked member of the Politburo Standing Committee, Wang Huning. The coming Xi-Trump summit is critical to bilateral relations. The Iran issue will be but one of many on the table. The two sides must not allow it to derail engagement. In that respect, we need go no further back than the Biden era to find a relevant case in point. Not long after former president Joe Biden and Xi had a good meeting in late 2022, tensions erupted in February 2023 over a high-altitude Chinese balloon that drifted into US airspace. In the absence of a strategy of managed rivalry, it eventually derailed diplomatic efforts to mend ties. There is a lesson there for both sides. The Iran issue is a potential trigger of destabilisation but the bilateral relationship is much bigger than that. Whatever eventuates with sanctions, it should not be allowed to affect the relationship or, particularly, Xi’s coming state visit.

title: How tourists are reacting to war, fuel prices and geopolitical strife in 2026
description: Regional conflicts and high fuel prices are affecting travel patterns as people prioritise flexibility and bypass trouble spots.
content: Geopolitical volatility and uncertainty have become an all-too-common part of life. The world is experiencing more active wars than at any point since World War II, according to the International Rescue Committee (IRC). Perhaps the most high-profile conflict this year has been the US-Israel attack on Iran, but it is hardly the only example of the violence and disruption affecting people and locations around the world. One in seven people globally is living with the threat of armed conflict, according to the IRC. That reality, in turn, is reshaping global travel patterns, altering airline economics and testing the resilience of tourism markets, according to a report from the consulting firm McKinsey & Company. People still want to see the world, even when geopolitical tensions are creating a fraught landscape. But consumers are taking a different approach to the travel process, including rethinking destination choices, how they get to where they are going and when they will visit. “The defining travel behaviour of 2026 has not been widespread cancellation, it’s been rapid substitution,” says Michael McCormick, founder and managing partner of Travel Again Advisory. “People still want to travel, but they are more willing than ever to change the destination, airline, routing or timing when geopolitical conditions become uncertain.” Travel demand remains firmly intact. Travel uncertainty is instead showing up via delayed bookings, altered travel patterns and changes in channel choices, according to McKinsey & Company. Travellers have grown far more risk-aware, but not necessarily more risk-averse, McCormick says. “They’re booking with greater attention to cancellation terms, travel insurance, nonstop flights, border requirements and the financial stability of the companies involved in their trips,” McCormick says. In addition, many travellers are waiting longer before committing to a trip as they watch global events carefully. Still other travellers are booking trips earlier, but are buying more flexibility to protect themselves from any unexpected disruptions that may arise. And those are not the only changes in consumer behaviour. “The most noticeable shift is that travellers are evaluating the entire journey, not merely the destination,” McCormick says. “They’re asking where the aircraft will fly, where they will connect, whether borders or visa requirements could change, and how easily they could return home if conditions deteriorate. “That represents a meaningful change from the traditional question of simply: ‘Is the hotel or destination safe?’” The biggest shifts in behaviour have been towards predictability, certainty and value, according to George Morgan-Grenville, founder and chief executive of Red Savannah, a luxury travel provider. “Travellers are seeking a stable experience, which has meant avoiding the Middle East either as a destination, or as a flight layover to Asia, for example,” he says. As once-popular Middle Eastern locations like Dubai and Abu Dhabi – which are historically popular winter and shoulder season destinations – experience a dramatic decline, countries like Spain, Greece, Portugal, Turkey, Italy and Morocco have emerged as the go-to alternatives for travellers seeking stable, sunny options free from conflict. Other “safe havens” have also emerged, Morgan-Grenville says, like Iceland, New Zealand and Japan, as well as Northern and Western European destinations such as Finland, Scotland and Ireland. The geopolitical instability that has dominated 2026 has indeed created a new normal. My overall view is that geopolitical instability is not eliminating travel demand. It is redistributing it Michael McCormick, founder and managing partner, Travel Again Advisory As the McKinsey & Company report explains, finding flights has become more difficult for consumers as airlines across the globe maintain reduced schedules in response to higher fuel costs. At the same time, making flight connections through Middle Eastern air hubs is not as easy or popular as it once was. Following the US-Israel attack on Iran, the total number of international passengers connecting via Middle Eastern hubs fell by 5.1 million (about a 53 per cent decrease) year over year as of March and April. Many travellers are opting to stay closer to home, according to a recent survey related to geopolitical events conducted by travel insurance marketplace Squaremouth. Just over 10 per cent of survey respondents said they actively chose travel destinations that were closer to home this year. And nearly one in four travellers scaled back a planned trip this year, while almost 9 per cent of survey respondents said they bought more travel insurance coverage than usual. Still, the consumer appetite for travel remains resilient. People are still willing to invest their hard-earned money even in an increasingly uncertain world. “My overall view is that geopolitical instability is not eliminating travel demand. It is redistributing it,” McCormick says. “In 2026, destinations that can communicate stability, accessibility and preparedness are gaining share from destinations that create even the perception of uncertainty. “The broader winner is not one particular country. It’s the destination that offers the traveller the fewest perceived points of failure.”

title: Foreign investors boost Chinese stock holdings as AI hardware, green energy lure inflows
description: Foreign exposures to yuan-traded stocks jump by a third, with QFII data showing holdings surging to more than US$40 billion.
content: Foreign investors boosted exposures to yuan-traded Chinese stocks by about a third in the second quarter, buying into companies tied to the artificial intelligence supply chain and China’s strategic green-energy industry. Global fund managers held a combined 10.1 billion shares in mainland-listed companies by the end of June, up from 7.5 billion in the first quarter, according to financial data provider Wind. The value of foreign holdings surged 87 per cent to 272.8 billion yuan (US$40.6 billion), taking into account the gains in stock prices, according to the Chinese firm’s data, based on interim reports from nearly 4,000 listed companies. The data only covered overseas investors taking part in the qualified foreign institutional investor (QFII) programme, which requires regulatory approval of licences and quotas. The scheme is separate from the cross-border Stock Connect, through which foreign traders can access China’s onshore stocks via the Hong Kong exchange without the need for government approvals. QFII holdings carry weight in the investment community, particularly China’s individual investors, who often view overseas traders as “smart money” and follow their disclosed positions. QFII exposure has become the only way for local investors to track foreign recalibration since the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses suspended disclosure of Stock Connect flows in 2024. Foreign buying in the second quarter focused on technology companies and those with solid earnings prospects across chipmaking, chemicals and hardware equipment, Wind’s data showed. Shengyi Technology, a maker of printed circuit boards used in AI infrastructure, Apple supplier Luxshare Precision Industry and Shandong Sinocera Functional Material, which makes multilayer ceramic capacitors for AI servers and data centres, were among those with the biggest foreign inflows during the period, each attracting more than 1 billion yuan. Shares of Shengyi surged 225 per cent in the second quarter, Luxshare rose 43 per cent and Shandong Sinocera soared 238 per cent. Gold producer Zijin Mining Group was also among foreign investors’ favourites. As a proxy for the yellow metal, the company returned to traders’ radar after concerns about US fiscal strain spurred hedging and diversification away from dollar assets. The stock fell 23 per cent in the April-to-June period before recouping all the loss this quarter. QFIIs ranked among the top 10 biggest shareholders in 1,102 mainland-listed companies in the second quarter, Wind data showed. The biggest were UBS Group, Goldman Sachs and BNP Paribas, with each of their holdings surpassing 20 billion yuan. Shengyi, Bank of Ningbo, Bank of Nanjing and Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited remained their biggest holdings. China had approved 999 overseas investors under the QFII scheme by late August. HSBC said in a report this week it saw opportunities in AI hardware, go-global strategy firms and new consumer companies on China’s onshore markets. The UK bank also said Chinese innovative technology companies could post an average of 90 per cent profit growth this year.

title: US Army Secretary Driscoll resigns after rifts in Pentagon leadership
description: Top civilian official’s departure marks the latest leadership upheaval following reported tensions with Pete Hegseth.
content: US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down after 18 months on the job, the White House said Monday, in the latest departure of a top military leader during the Trump administration. No reason was given for the departure of Driscoll, who is a friend of US Vice-President J.D. Vance, but tensions with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have been widely reported. It marks the latest in a series of shake-ups of the military leadership, with the US Army especially seeing major upheaval. “Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement. “The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added. The Pentagon abruptly announced in April that US Navy Secretary John Phelan was leaving the job, becoming the first head of a military service to depart during Trump’s second term. A US Army official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Driscoll spoke with President Donald Trump on the current state of the US Army and submitted his resignation. The official did not provide additional details. Driscoll’s departure follows the ouster of one of his allies from the US Army as well as the rollback of a drone programme he had championed. Hegseth had suddenly ousted the service’s top uniformed leader, General Randy George, in April, while the US Army’s commander in Europe and Africa, General Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down in June. General Christopher LaNeve, who has made a meteoric rise under Hegseth, took George’s place as the US Army’s acting chief of staff. Under LaNeve, the service is pulling the plug on a drone modernisation programme. A US Army unit based in Europe was building its own drones before LaNeve directed it to end its efforts and return to being a traditional infantry battalion, officials said in August. Driscoll was a George ally and lamented his departure, along with both Republican and Democratic lawmakers. The most senior Democrat on the Senate’s Armed Services Committee, Jack Reed, said in a statement that Driscoll “worked to transform the Army for the battlefield of the future, and he engaged with Congress candidly and consistently”. “Secretary Hegseth is cultivating a culture where dissent is punished and competence is secondary to personal allegiance,” said Reed, a former US Army officer, while noting that “hundreds of thousands of soldiers are deployed around the world, many in combat zones”. Driscoll is an Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to Vance, whom Driscoll met at Yale Law School. When nominating Driscoll in 2024, Trump called him “a disruptor and change agent”. As US Army secretary, Driscoll was tapped for the unusual role of key negotiator to try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. The US Senate confirmed him in February 2025, voting 66-28, following an Armed Services Committee hearing that was largely unconfrontational and focused on how the US Army could modernise its systems, improve recruiting and strengthen the military-industrial base. Driscoll noted that his father and grandfather served in the US Army, and he vowed to be a secretary focused on the needs of soldiers. According to the US Army, Driscoll served as an armour officer from August 2007 to March 2011, deploying to Iraq from October 2009 to July 2010. He also ran unsuccessfully in the Republican primary for a North Carolina congressional seat in 2020, getting about 8 per cent of the vote in a crowded field of candidates.

title: Trump praises China for remaining ‘relatively inactive’ during Strait of Hormuz crisis
description: US president also says he has ‘a lot of respect’ for Chinese leader Xi Jinping and believes feeling is mutual as planned summit in US nears.
content: US President Donald Trump praised China on Monday for remaining on the sidelines during the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to visit Washington. “Even with the Strait of Hormuz, he’s relatively inactive. He’s been relatively inactive by comparison to what he could have been,” Trump said while responding to a reporter’s question on Xi’s likely visit. “He’s coming in a couple of weeks. He looks forward to it. I look forward to having him. We have had a very good relationship.” Trump added that he had “a lot of respect” for the Chinese leader and believed the feeling was mutual. “I think he respects me, and I think he respects our country again. He didn’t respect our country two years ago. He laughed at our country.” Trump’s remarks came as US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent indicated that Chinese banks may not be targeted under the administration’s “Economic D-Day” secondary sanctions. “I would push back on that false narrative that somehow the media has jumped on this. Oh, you can’t do it without China. Well, you can,” Bessent said in an interview to CNBC on Monday. The comments appear to mark a climbdown by the Trump administration after it threatened to sanction Chinese banks and refiners over their commercial links with Iranian entities. The shift underscores the issue’s sensitivity and the risks of escalating economic pressure on Beijing just weeks before the Chinese leader visits Washington. Last week, Trump hinted that sanctions could be on the table for Chinese lenders. Asked why the US had not sanctioned Chinese banks for their dealings with Iranian entities, Trump said: “Who said I’m not? Well, I don’t have to announce everything, do I?” “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions,” Bessent also said last week when asked about the possibility of the US imposing secondary sanctions on Chinese banks. The Treasury Secretary announced new sanctions against 60 entities and individuals worldwide, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong, and demanded “immediate action” from nations maintaining economic and commercial ties with Iran. In response, the Chinese embassy in Washington said Beijing stood firmly against “illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law”. “We will firmly protect Chinese businesses’ legitimate and lawful rights and interests,” embassy spokesman Liu Chang said. China is the largest purchaser of Iranian oil, accounting for more than 80 per cent of the country’s total oil exports in 2025, according to data from analytics firm Kpler. A March report by the US-China Economic and Security Commission accused Beijing of helping Tehran circumvent global sanctions through trade and financial networks, technology transfers and trade in dual-use goods. China has rejected the accusations. The US measures are part of the administration’s broader campaign to increase economic pressure on Tehran after military strikes and diplomatic negotiations failed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or end the six-month conflict. US military strikes resumed on Sunday after US forces attacked two rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island. Tehran retaliated with strikes on American bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. Trump on Monday declined to say whether the latest attacks on Iran would continue, while asserting that the country’s economy and military had been largely degraded. “That doesn’t mean we won’t smack them. We’ll see what happens,” he said. However, Trump ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran when asked by a reporter, saying there was no reason for the United States to consider such an option. “They’re totally defeated militarily. So now I defeat them, and now I should use a nuclear weapon on top of them? What a stupid question!”

title: Trump wins Supreme Court ruling to continue White House ballroom construction
description: Divided 5-4 court lifts stay despite a warning from Chief Justice Roberts that Trump’s project is ‘likely unlawful’.
content: The US Supreme Court on Monday allowed President Donald Trump to continue construction of his White House ballroom, granting him a major victory as he works to leave a permanent mark on Washington. The conservative-dominated court ruled 5-4 to lift a lower order demanding most construction be halted, saying that the plaintiff in the case likely did not have legal standing to sue. Chief Justice John Roberts joined the court’s three liberals in dissenting, writing in an opinion that the major White House overhaul was “likely unlawful” due to the lack of congressional authorisation. The decision means construction can continue for now, while a lawsuit brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation remains unresolved in lower courts. The ballroom project is just one part of Trump’s second term push to reshape the US capital, which also includes renovation of Washington’s Reflecting Pool and erecting a huge triumphal arch. Trump celebrated Monday’s decision, saying it meant the project could go forward “without any further contingency, doubt, or threat”. However, the Supreme Court’s ruling was on procedural grounds and did not address the legality of the construction. National Trust President Brent Leggs said “we are deeply disappointed” by the decision, but “it is noteworthy that the majority did not weigh in on whether the ballroom project was in fact legal”. The National Trust’s case was brought on behalf of member Alison Hoagland, a Washington resident who claims that seeing the finished ballroom would result in damage to her “aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests”. The Supreme Court majority ruled those claims were likely insufficient to establish standing, citing previous rejections of similar arguments, but made clear they were not making a final ruling on the project’s legality. Roberts, writing for the dissenters, said that Hoagland clearly had standing under previous Supreme Court rulings. The project was “likely unlawful” because “Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’” for the administration to undertake it. Roberts last month allowed the project to proceed while the full court considered the matter. While the ballroom has drawn headlines, the project also includes a military bunker. A district court and, later, an appellate court, halted work on the above-ground ballroom while allowing construction on the military facility to continue. The president has trumpeted the ballroom as necessary for hosting galas and state dinners, while also stressing the national security need for the bunker. The project kicked off last year with the sudden demolition of the East Wing, which famously used to house the offices of the US first lady. The National Trust said last month that the administration was “working around the clock in an attempt to outrace judicial review”. Trump has repeatedly said that the ballroom would be privately financed, but US media outlets have reported that significant taxpayer funds are going to the project – which could cost as much as US$600 million.

title: In Focus | Will a new insurance scheme get China’s ageing population the long-term care it needs?
description: The central government has announced plans to provide nationwide coverage by 2028, but uneven regional development is a major hurdle.
content: Wu Boyao was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease 26 years ago. Now 86, he lives with his wife and one of their two daughters in a suburb straddling the border between the eastern Chinese cities of Shanghai and Suzhou. Originally from Shanghai, they moved to the area – which is administered by Suzhou – in search of a larger home. The trade-off was that Wu would no longer qualify for home care service sessions that were almost free. A decade ago, Shanghai was one of the first cities in China to roll out a pilot long-term care insurance (LTCI) scheme. Wu, who by then was largely dependent on others for daily functionality, had his application approved. The social security fund covered the lion’s share of the cost, leaving him with a token co-payment of just 6 yuan (88 US cents) a session. In exchange, he received daily one-hour visits from a carer who helped with bathing, foot and nail care, massages and other tasks. “It was a short service, but eased the burden for the family,” said his daughter Jenny Wu, who lives with him. But because local governments’ financing and payment arrangements are separate, that arrangement ceased after the family crossed the municipal border, even though Suzhou has also been piloting its own LTCI system in recent years. Wu is one of more than 40 million frail or cognitively impaired older adults in China, and among the first to use social insurance specifically designed for the needs of the country’s rapidly greying population. But coverage remains far from complete. The LTCI programme is a government-led system to cover the costs of daily living support and basic care for functionally disabled senior citizens. Funded jointly by individuals, employers and fiscal subsidies, similar models have been in place for decades in a handful of other countries, including Germany, Japan and South Korea. After 10 years of pilot programmes spanning more than 90 cities, the central government announced in March that it would expand the initiative nationwide, establishing a system covering all residents by 2028. While building a long-term care system could spur new industries, create jobs and boost consumption in a slowing Chinese economy, researchers say the country faces challenges that have yet to be fully confronted: a breakneck pace of ageing, stark regional economic disparities, and per capita GDP levels that remain a fraction of those in more developed economies. Ensuring the fund’s sustainability and providing sufficient professional carers will also be headaches, they added. “China is still in a phase of economic transition, with uneven development between regions and between urban and rural areas, and very uneven affordability,” said Wu Bei, a professor of public health and expert in gerontology at NYU Shanghai. “While Shanghai may have a fair number of nursing homes and care facilities, it may be quite difficult to find one in the central and western regions, or rural areas,” she said, adding that caring for rural “empty-nest” seniors – those whose adult children have left home – presented one of the biggest challenges. Last week, Chinese lawmakers incorporated language on LTCI into a Healthcare Security Law that will take effect from the beginning of next year, including a line saying the country will “establish and improve” a long-term care insurance system. According to guidelines issued by the central government in March, payments for the nationwide system will be split between workers and their employers. For those without jobs, the costs will be covered by the individual and government subsidies. Once a contributor is assessed and certified as being in a state of disability for more than six months, they will be able to apply for insurance benefits to receive care services either in a nursing home or at home. Only a small portion of contributors to the pilot schemes have benefited so far. They covered 308 million people around the country last year, but only 1.93 million received benefits, according to data released by the National Healthcare Security Administration in July. China had about 36 million senior citizens with disabilities and 17 million with dementia at the end of last year, according to a report issued recently by the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, the country’s top political advisory body. That number is expected to surge as population ageing deepens. By the end of last year, there were over 223 million people aged 65 or older in China, accounting for around 16 per cent of the population, according to data from the Ministry of Civil Affairs. It is on track to become a “super-aged” society by the early 2030s, when those 65 or older will account for 20 per cent of the population, according to a United Nations estimate. Globally, social insurance is not the mainstream model for providing long-term care for the elderly. They’re not used to buying insurance – if they don’t get a payout, they feel cheated He Wenjiong, Zhejiang University Systems in northern Europe primarily rely on public finance supported by high taxation, with local governments responsible for the delivery of services. In the United States, a combination of public aid and commercial insurance is used. He Wenjiong, a professor at Zhejiang University who specialises in social security, said it could solve some problems but could not be expected to solve them all, due to a lack of mature international experience and the absence of an “insurance gene” in Chinese cultural tradition. “Our society lacks a culture of mutual aid,” said He, who took part in preliminary research on China’s LTCI system. “Many people prefer to save money and get back their principal with interest. But they’re not used to buying insurance – if they don’t get a payout, they feel cheated.” At the current, early stage, contribution levels are relatively low. A worker earning 10,000 yuan (US$1,487) a month needs to pay 15 yuan a month, with their employer matching that amount, according to the central government’s guidelines. For rural residents and unemployed urban residents, if the local per capita disposable income from the previous year was 40,000 yuan – close to the national average last year – the annual contribution is set at 60 yuan, split equally between the individual and government subsidies. But He said even such seemingly low rates would be unaffordable for many rural residents, and called for full government coverage for those unable to pay. In countries such as Germany and Japan, LTCI premiums are dynamically adjusted rather than fixed to ensure the insurance fund’s sustainability. But sustaining these funds over the long term is no easy job. In June, Germany’s Health Ministry published a draft law designed to overhaul the country’s financially strained LTCI system, which is facing a multibillion-euro deficit, with proposed changes including raising the contribution assessment ceiling for higher earners and imposing stricter qualification criteria for lower care levels. “A few decades ago, we predicted that China would grow old before it grew rich,” said Wu of NYU Shanghai. “Today, we might say it’s at least growing old while growing rich.” While noting that the system used in the US had its own problems, she said its idea of a multi-tiered, income-based safety net was worth learning from. Her research shows that in the US, public funding – primarily Medicaid and Medicare – accounts for nearly 70 per cent of long-term care spending, with commercial insurance covering about 10 per cent and out-of-pocket expenses making up the remaining 20 per cent. Following a similar strategy, she said China should prioritise basic needs and direct more fiscal support to low-income families, while providing affluent households with diversified, personalised private insurance or high-end nursing homes. She said another step China could take would be offering more support to family carers. That could include the provision of adult day care centres, which would allow a family carer to work half a day instead of having to devote all their time to a disabled relative. Jenny Wu said that was critical. As her mother – her father’s primary carer – gets older and weaker, she has had to take on more duties. “I quit my job before retirement age and now take flexible work at home for lower pay to care for my family,” she said. Her experience since moving to the suburbs made her realise that at-home care services are, for now, still largely an urban privilege. Though they could not use the LTCI system in Suzhou, the local government offered a separate subsidy programme that was similar in principle and covered both in-home and nursing-home care. “But in reality, when I placed orders, no carer accepted them,” she said. “The suburbs are too far away – travelling an hour for a one-hour visit just isn’t worth it for them. “For users, one hour is also too short. You still have to have someone home to open the door – disabled people can’t – and there’s not even enough time for the family carer to make a round trip to the supermarket.” According to government data, China, with its tens of millions of disabled elderly people, had just 13,000 designated long-term care service institutions last year and 402,800 care workers. Zhejiang University’s He said the government’s push for LTCI was partly intended to boost employment. “There will be some kind of positive impact on the job market anyway – at least some people who could not afford a carer before can now hire one,” he said. “But the jobs created are unstable and low-quality.” Most people employed as carers nowadays were less educated and older than those in other fields, but some vocational schools had expanded elderly care programmes to bring in younger workers in recent years. “In the long run, things will improve,” He said. “But in the short term, it’s bleak – many graduates leave their positions within a short time of being hired. Retention is relatively low. The work is demanding, but benefits are not proportional.” That is an almost universal phenomenon. In more than one-third of Japanese households where care was provided at home, both the carer and the care recipient were aged 75 or older – a phenomenon known as “elderly-to-elderly caregiving” – the country’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare said last month, adding that was a record high. Despite all the challenges, Wu said ageing should not be seen only as a burden, arguing that for China it was also a strategic opportunity. “If done right, it could professionalise the care industry, create many jobs, and boost economic development,” she said.

title: Opinion | India needs to make up its mind about economic ties with China
description: New Delhi’s approach has gone from welcoming economic engagement with Beijing to containment to the latest calibrated reopening.
content: As India prepares for the Brics summit less than two weeks away, relations with China are warming up. On July 22, Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar met his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi during the East Asia Summit; five days later, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri visited China. Last week, Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval also visited Beijing, for border talks. But India remains deeply ambivalent when it comes to economic engagement with China: it seeks Chinese capital, technology and expertise while fearing the shocks they may bring. Justifying the latest economic engagement with China, Jaishankar said India’s long-term objective was to compete with China in manufacturing. After six years of sweeping curbs on Chinese investment, bilateral trade rose to US$151.1 billion in the financial year ended March 31. China remains India’s largest import source and has, after four years, displaced the United States as its top trading partner. India’s approach to engaging with China has evolved: from welcoming participation to containment after 2020 and, more recently, a calibrated reopening. During Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s first term and the early years of his second, India maintained a broadly open stance. Launched in 2014, the “Make in India” campaign sought to slash bureaucratic hurdles and attract foreign investment. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit that September, both sides signed a five-year economic cooperation plan. Modi’s 2015 China visit yielded a further US$22 billion in commercial deals. Economic engagement remained robust even after the 2017 Doklam stand-off. Both sides maintained senior economic dialogue, pursued the “China India Plus One” approach to projects in third countries and planned connectivity projects. Chinese investment in Indian start-ups grew twelvefold between 2016 and 2019, backing at least 18 of India’s 30 unicorns. In 2019, China proposed a manufacturing partnership. By early 2020, the stock of Chinese investment in India was estimated to exceed US$26 billion. But that was also the year the turning point came. In April, India introduced a requirement of prior government approval for foreign direct investment (FDI) from countries it shared a land border with, ostensibly to block “opportunistic takeovers”. After the deadly Galwan Valley border clash, restrictions against Chinese businesses expanded. India banned Chinese apps on national security grounds, tightened public procurement rules for bidders and required security clearance for directors from border countries. Visa delays, regulatory raids and other pressures suffocated Chinese business. In 2024, a limited reopening began. The government suggested that more stable border conditions could allow for an easing of investment scrutiny, while the Economic Survey 2023-24 argued that a full decoupling from Chinese supply chains was unrealistic. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman publicly endorsed improved economic ties. By March last year, a 250 billion rupee (US$2.6 billion) Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme to boost the manufacturing of electrical components was leading a surge of interest in Chinese partnerships. In March this year, FDI curbs were relaxed; in July, import duties of 7.5 and 5 per cent on selected electronics components were scrapped, potentially benefiting phonemakers such as China’s Xiaomi. The contradiction is that India needed to pursue capital inflows, technology and talent but was systematically constraining the Chinese sources best positioned to supply them. It reflected a paradox between the economic rationality of securing the inputs needed for a manufacturing ascent and the political logic of appeasing increasingly assertive nationalist sentiment. The 2020 FDI decision, while a turning point, was just a part of the larger picture. The PLI scheme offered manufacturing subsidies even as tariffs on inputs were raised under the “Atmanirbhar Bharat” (self-reliant India) policy. India proclaimed its ambition to join global value chains yet walked away from the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership at the eleventh hour. All the 2020 border crisis did was to accelerate the politicisation of the Sino-Indian economic ties. At the time, security agencies, economic hawks and protectionist business lobbies all converged to support the restrictions. Doval, the national security adviser, flagged concerns about Chinese tech dominance and the FDI curbs were backed by senior ministers including Home Minister Amit Shah, Finance Minister Sitharaman, External Affairs Minister Jaishankar and Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal. The Confederation of all India Traders launched a “China Quit India” campaign. A reassessment only came in 2024, prompted by slowing FDI, macroeconomic headwinds and a recognition that India could not capitalise on the “China India Plus One” approach while excluding Chinese supply chains and expertise. Years of frozen Chinese FDI in India had failed to reduce the country’s Chinese imports. Manufacturing output, especially in phones, expanded, but the result was often “Assemble in India” rather than a development of genuine depth in industrial capacity and the supply chain. Import dependence on Chinese components, machinery and intermediates grew instead, widening the bilateral trade deficit from US$44 billion in the 2020-2021 financial year to US$112.1 billion in the year ended March 31. “Modi-nomics” sought to replicate China’s manufacturing rise through industrial policies, infrastructure investment and selective policy incentives, but largely neglected the fact that the supplier ecosystems, skilled labour pools, logistics networks and scale economies took decades to build. India has thus neither reduced its reliance on Chinese supply chains nor achieved the autonomous industrial base it has long sought. The latest easing in key sectors only replaced blanket restrictions with controlled access, allowing Chinese capital and capabilities under defined strategic limits. Resources once framed as unacceptable risks have been recast as necessary inputs. Such a conflicted view of China, as simultaneously a life-threatening danger and an indispensable building block, is unlikely to bear fruit in the foreseeable future.

title: Can Chinese sleeper hit Dear You conquer the US box office next?
description: After grossing nearly US$300 million in mainland China, its North American release will test its popularity beyond Chinese-speaking diaspora.
content: China’s biggest box-office surprise this year – a Teochew-language family drama that became a hit in Southeast Asia – is finally coming to North American cinemas on September 4. Dear You, whose Chinese title translates as “Love Letters for Grandma”, has grossed nearly US$300 million in mainland China. Its North American release will test whether a Chinese film rooted in migration, family, and regional culture can find an audience beyond the Chinese-speaking diaspora. The seemingly non-political film also sparked debate over China’s cultural influence among overseas Chinese communities, raising questions about the role Chinese cinema can play in shaping perceptions of China overseas, and whether that cultural reach can translate into soft power. The film follows a debt-ridden grandson from the Teochew, or Chaoshan region of Guangdong Province, as he travels to Thailand to find the grandfather he believes abandoned his family, hoping the man behind years of qiaopi – letters sent by overseas Chinese migrants to their families, often accompanied by remittances – can help him repay his debts. He instead learns more about his family’s past and his grandparents’ relationship. Its distributors hope its near-universal themes will transcend language and cultural barriers even as others are sceptical. Bringing Dear You to the US Dear You is being released by Well Go USA, a Texas-based, family-owned distributor focused on bringing Asian cinema to North American audiences. The film will open in 86 screens across 23 US states and two locations in Canada, including major metropolitan areas, a modest roll-out for an indie film but with more showings expected. Doris Pfardrescher, president and CEO of the company, said the director “has crafted a deeply moving story about family, sacrifice, and the enduring power of human kindness that resonates across cultures”. Well Go USA released 17 Chinese films last year and is set to release 10 this year, positioning it as a major player in this niche market alongside China Lion Film Distribution, CMC Pictures, and Sony Pictures Classics. The distributor has also tailored its marketing for North American audiences with a trailer featuring highlights from film critics and media reviews, according to Will Zang, a Los Angeles-based publicist specialising in Asian cinema who is helping promote Dear You. “We expect [Dear You’s] North American release to connect with more audiences and help them appreciate the richness and emotional power of Chinese cinema and culture,” he said. Simon Abrams, a New York-based film critic, told South China Morning Post that Dear You is an old-fashioned melodrama with a “big three-hankie conclusion”. Still, he said, “it’s genuinely disarming and a real crowd-pleaser”. The release comes as Chinese films are increasingly seeking audiences outside China. In 2025, Chinese films generated US$140 million in overseas box office through October 20, according to a blog post by China’s National Film Administration, with films released in 46 countries and regions. Fifteen of China’s 20 highest-grossing domestic films had also received overseas releases. In North America, 54 new Chinese films were released in 2025, generating $US$38.44 million in box-office revenue – up 158 per cent from 2024, according to the state-affiliated Global Times. Ne Zha 2, helped by an English-dubbed version, became the fifth-highest-grossing Chinese film of all time in North America, surpassing Jackie Chan’s The Medallion. Will it win over American audiences? Chinese-language cinema was a strength of China’s soft power in the early 2000s, particularly through martial arts films, said Stanley Rosen, a professor at the University of Southern California who specialises in Chinese politics and soft power. Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, an Oscar-winning Chinese film released in 2000, grossed US$128 million in the US and held the record for the highest-grossing foreign-language film for two decades. But success in China does not necessarily translate into comparable success in North America. Today, Chinese films are reaching North America in greater numbers, although they remain far from mainstream. One recent example is Jia Ling’s YOLO, a 2024 Chinese New Year blockbuster about a woman who turns to boxing and rebuilds her life after a series of personal setbacks.
