The film grossed more than US$400 million in China, but earned only about US$2 million in the US and Canada after Sony Pictures acquired its international distribution rights and released it in more than 200 North American cinemas. China’s film industry still lags well behind Japan’s in the US market. Demon Slayer: Infinity Castle, a Japanese anime, alone made about US$135 million in the US market in 2025. Rosen expects Dear You’s audience to be primarily Chinese-speaking Americans, although he said it could perform better if strong reviews and positive word of mouth accompany its box-office success in China. “If it makes US$2 million, that would be very good,” he added. When cinema becomes soft power Despite its massive box-office success in the China market, Dear You has been embroiled in a wider debate over whether the film is strengthening a sense of shared Chinese identity among the diaspora. Beijing has strategic reasons to cultivate the diaspora beyond sentiment. Overseas Chinese communities are viewed as a channel for expanding geopolitical influence abroad – shaping opinion and cultivating sympathetic voices. In May, Singaporean journalist Sim Tze Wei argued that the film could be understood as a form of “non-coercive” United-Front work, a reference to Beijing’s external propaganda arm, suggesting its emotional appeal could strengthen a sense of Chinese identity among overseas Chinese. That drew a sharp rebuke from Chinese state media and Chinese online commentators, who accused the writer of politicising a film about ordinary family sacrifice. Wang Yan, an associate research fellow at Beijing Foreign Studies University, argued in a CGTN commentary titled “It’s cinema, not politics” that to call Dear You a “United Front work” is to impose a “contemporary political label onto a heritage that transcends borders and generations”. Rosen also expressed scepticism that uniting the Chinese diaspora was the filmmaker’s purpose. He noted that director Lan Hongchun has made films promoting Teochew culture before, suggesting that the film’s focus on shared Chinese identity does not necessarily mean it was designed as a united-front project. But he said the Chinese government may welcome the film as an opportunity to unite overseas Chinese, while noting it was unclear how China’s censorship system may have influenced the script. A 2025 report by scholars from Hong Kong and Germany found that Chinese-language film releases in North America have expanded steadily since 1992, shifting from festival-driven art-house pickups to genre films such as martial arts, horror, and triad films, and to day-and-date releases timed to the mainland market. The researchers argue that distributors’ acquisition, marketing and release strategies have played a critical role in determining which Chinese-language films reach North American audiences – a factor they say should be considered alongside questions of Chinese soft power. Rosen said China’s cultural influence extends beyond film, from Labubu dolls to Chinese coffee brands entering Western markets. But US-China rivalry remains a bigger factor in China’s global image, he added, citing Pew data showing perceptions of China improving as views of the US have declined. “What is moving the needle much more is Donald Trump,” Rosen said, referring to the US president. “That’s been much more helpful to Chinese soft power than [Dear You].”

title: US jury continues deliberations in Lindsay Clancy child killings case
description: Massachusetts jury weighs whether mother suffering from severe postpartum mental illness is criminally responsible for 2023 deaths.
content: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy trial on Monday spent a third day deliberating without reaching a verdict on whether the former labour and delivery nurse is criminally responsible for killing her three children in 2023 – a case that has drawn attention to maternal mental health after childbirth. The jurors began discussing the case on Thursday in Plymouth County Superior Court in Massachusetts after hearing testimony from more than 70 prosecution witnesses, including her former husband, and 10 defence witnesses over five weeks. The jury is scheduled to resume deliberations on Tuesday. While Clancy does not deny strangling her children, her lawyer said she did it because she had lost her grip on reality due to postnatal psychosis, a rare mental illness that can follow childbirth. In the months before the killings, Clancy sought treatment for her worsening mental health, including a stay in a psychiatric hospital. Prosecutors said Clancy knew what she was doing. They say she strangled the children because she was depressed and tired of living, and made a conscious choice to kill them before attempting suicide. The jury could find her guilty of murder or the lesser crime of manslaughter, or it could acquit her if it finds that she was not in control of herself due to psychiatric problems. Clancy’s sentence could be as severe as life in prison, or she could be released or remain confined in a mental health facility if acquitted. All three children – Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy, ages five, three and eight months – were strangled with exercise bands in the basement of the family’s home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts, before Clancy tried to kill herself while her husband was getting takeaway for dinner and going to a pharmacy on January 24, 2023. Clancy, 36, who grew up in Wallingford, Connecticut, has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility. She did not testify during the trial but jurors heard at length from medical professionals who treated her, as well as from friends and relatives she had told about her mental health problems. Jurors also heard from medical experts called by prosecutors and the defence who disagreed about her probable state of mind when she killed the children. The killings happened less than three weeks after Clancy was discharged from a psychiatric hospital. She cut herself before jumping from a second-floor window after strangling the children. She remains paralysed from the waist down. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Chile fines Chinese mafia inmate after cocaine found at maximum-security prison
description: Prosecutors link the inmate to a Chinese criminal network targeted in a major police operation last year and a second raid in June.
content: A Chilean court on Monday fined a Chinese man caught with cocaine inside a Santiago prison, where he is being held on charges of homicide, kidnapping and drug trafficking. It was the second such ruling in five involving a Chinese inmate in five months, with prosecutors linking the two men to the same criminal network. Officers had searched Haifeng Tang at Santiago Uno prison on August 12, a day before his move to La Laguna, the maximum-security jail at the centre of President Jose Antonio Kast’s tough prison policy. They found two sealed bags holding about a gram of powder, and a field test confirmed it was cocaine. The Seventh Guarantee Court of Santiago, which rules on pre-trial matters, set the fine at 71,649 pesos (US$75). Alternatively, the defendant can serve up to six months if he does not pay. Until last year, Chilean prosecutors had only identified one Chinese criminal network in the country; they are now running three separate investigations, from illegal casinos in the capital to a fraud operation in the far north. Tang also faces charges of weapons possession and criminal association, and prosecutors have identified the victim in the homicide count as another Chinese citizen. The discovery and subsequent penalty were a setback for Kast’s flagship security operation, since Tang had been cleared for transfer despite carrying cocaine. A judge in Iquique dealt a second blow later in August, ordering several Chinese defendants in a fraud case sent back from La Laguna to the prison where they had been held in the northern city, more than 1,700 km (1,056 miles) from the new complex. Kast launched Operation Cancerbero in August, fulfilling a campaign promise, modelled partly on the mass-incarceration approach of El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. The first phase moved 191 inmates, among them nine leaders of organised crime groups, to a maximum-security prison opened last year with capacity for 2,320 people and holding roughly 400 beforehand. Prison officers had found cocaine on another Chinese inmate at the same prison in March, and the same court imposed the identical penalty. Longliang Wang is charged with criminal association and kidnapping for ransom. The charges stem from a separate investigation that prosecutors have also tied to a group they call Hongmen. That case involved a Chilean businessman who exported fruit to China and was seized over a commercial debt he owed to Chinese counterparts, one of the few points where the networks touch the bilateral trade that sustains Chile’s economy. Wang had already been convicted in 2017 of trying to leave Chile on a false passport, and a court replaced his sentence with expulsion, an order that was never enforced. Tang is named among the leadership core of the network dismantled last year, alongside Huan Tao and Xingwang Cai. He became publicly known in July last year after firing a submachine gun near a residential building in Meiggs, the Santiago district with the largest Chinese commercial presence in the country, and police detained him that month along with 10 other Chinese nationals. The cases involve a community that remains small in a country of about 18 million people. Chilean migration authorities estimate that more than 10,000 Chinese nationals live there, while the last census counted between 13,500 and 17,000 Chinese-born residents. Their commercial weight is concentrated in Meiggs, a wholesale district behind Santiago’s main railway station that holds about 3,000 trading licences, of which Chinese merchants hold more than 440. Police seized about US$600,000 in cash in an operation known as Muralla Oriental, and found the group moved money through hawala, an informal transfer system that leaves no banking trail. The sum is believed to be linked to multiple illegal casinos through the country. A police officer on active duty was accused of taking payments of 500,000 pesos (US$500) to alert the group to inspections in Meiggs. The national police director, Eduardo Cerna, described the group as an “immense, dangerous and complicated criminal structure of Chinese origin”. Prosecutors turned their attention to the same network in June with Muralla Oriental II, raiding 27 illegal casinos in Santiago and the Valparaiso region, detaining 37 people and confiscating close to US$700,000. That stage targets the laundering structure behind the group and the finances of prominent businessmen in Chile’s Chinese community. Chilean prosecutors call the network Hongmen, a name that carries older and contested meanings since it refers to the Tiandihui (or Heaven and Earth Society), an 18th century Chinese fraternal organisation whose overseas branches operated as mutual aid societies, even as criminal groups claimed the title for themselves. Prosecutors said the operation last year revealed Hongmen in Chile for the first time, as a network separate from the Bang de Fujian, the Fujianese group detected in the country in 2020. The defendants returned to the north belong to a third network, a family organisation known as the Clan Chen, which prosecutors in Tarapaca say channelled more than US$180 million from international fraud through Chilean banks using shell companies around the Iquique free-trade zone. That investigation began after the Federal Bureau of Investigation alerted Chilean authorities. Several defendants are still awaiting trial, including Ping Lin, another man linked by prosecutors to Hongmen who was moved to La Laguna alongside Tang. He faces charges of human trafficking for sexual exploitation, drug trafficking and weapons possession, and prosecutors are seeking more than 55 years in prison.

title: US judge approves order to force-feed suspect who attacked National Guard troops
description: Accused gunman Rahmanullah Lakanwal has been hospitalised since July after refusing food.
content: A man refusing to eat food while jailed on charges he shot two National Guard troops near the White House, killing one of them, can be fed against his will under a judge’s emergency order. US District Judge Amit Mehta agreed on Saturday to order “non-consensual” nutrition and medical treatment for Rahmanullah Lakanwal, who was rushed to a hospital in July after he stopped eating. Mehta said Federal Bureau of Prisons medical staff can feed Lakanwal intravenously or through a medical tube to save his life. Redacted court filings have not specified a reason for Lakanwal’s refusal to eat but prosecutors noted that courts have held that prison officials can involuntarily feed “hunger-striking prisoners”. Justice Department lawyers asked Mehta to order the emergency life-saving measures for Lakanwal. “The defendant has medical capacity to make determinations regarding his health and he is refusing nutrition that is necessary to sustain his life,” they wrote. Lakanwal’s lawyers said he would oppose the government’s request. They noted that he has consumed some food, such as apple sauce, while hospitalised but also has been “adamant at times” that he did not want to eat. “At this juncture, the government does not indicate that Mr Lakanwal’s condition is so dire as to require this Court’s intervention and the provided medical records do not support that position,” they wrote in a redacted court filing. Defence lawyer Shelli Peterson declined to elaborate on Monday on Lakanwal’s medical condition and care. A spokesperson for US Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office also declined to comment. The Justice Department has not announced whether it will seek the death penalty in the case. “That is a very weighty decision,” Pirro said last year. The order authorising Lakanwal’s involuntary feeding expires on October 28 but can be renewed. Lakanwal, an Afghan national who lived in Bellingham, Washington, has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder and other charges in the November 2025 shooting that killed West Virginia National Guard Specialist Sarah Beckstrom and critically wounded Staff Sergeant Andrew Wolfe. Beckstrom, 20, and Wolfe, 24, were deployed to Washington as part of US President Donald Trump’s police surge in the nation’s capital, which began last summer. Lakanwal ambushed the Guard members outside a subway station three blocks from the White House, according to prosecutors. Another National Guard member heard gunshots and saw Beckstrom and Wolfe fall to the ground as Lakanwal fired a gun and screamed, “Allahu akbar!” according to a police report. Lakanwal was shot during the confrontation and made his initial court appearance from a hospital bed last year.

title: John Galliano cancels Met Gala exhibition after backlash over past racism, antisemitism
description: British designer apologises to Jewish and Asian communities for ‘words in the past’ as he pulls out of 2027 exhibition.
content: Top fashion designer John Galliano announced on Monday he is cancelling an exhibition of his work that was to kick off New York’s Met Gala next spring, following criticism from donors and political leaders over his past antisemitic remarks. “After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” Galliano, 65, wrote on Instagram. “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry,” he added. A French court convicted Galliano in 2011 of making racist and antisemitic comments, after he hurled Jewish and Asian slurs at a Paris bar. The Briton, famed for his flamboyant personality and daring designs, was also fired from his job as creative director of Dior after the incident surfaced. The Metropolitan Museum of Art had planned a nine-month exhibition of his work starting with the star-studded Met Gala next May but high-profile Jewish figures, including renowned art dealer Arne Glimcher and city council speaker Julie Menin, voiced opposition this month. “I do not want the debate surrounding me to place the Met in a difficult position or to distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute,” Galliano said on Monday, referencing the museum’s department dedicated to fashion. “I also recognise and respect that an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some,” he said. Galliano referenced the rehabilitation that followed his conviction, noting his “deepest gratitude to all those who have guided, supported and accompanied me throughout these fifteen years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction”. The Met confirmed that the “John Galliano: Horizons” show would not proceed as planned and that a new exhibition would be announced at a later date. Andrew Bolton, curator in charge of the Met’s Costume Institute, said he supported the decision. “I believe deeply in the responsibility of museums to examine difficult histories with rigour, candour, and care. I also recognise the pain and concern this exhibition has caused,” he said in a statement. Anna Wintour, the fashion icon and former Vogue editor who is a trustee of the Met, expressed her “full support” for Galliano and the museum. “John’s decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is,” she said. After Dior, Galliano took the reins as creative director at Maison Margiela. He stepped down in 2024 after 10 years at the French label that helped repair his scandal-tainted image. In March, he signed a two-year creative contract with Spanish retailer Zara. Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the charity Anti-Defamation League, said on social media that showcasing Galliano’s work was “the wrong move at the wrong moment”. “With antisemitism at crisis levels, the Met honouring John Galliano at this moment was misguided, and even Galliano ultimately recognised what the Met should have done from the start,” Greenblatt said.

title: Lithuania’s president says CIA chief’s Moscow trip ‘achieved its goals’
description: President Gitanas Nauseda says US briefed Baltic nation on John Ratcliffe’s unannounced visit that sparked global speculation.
content: Lithuania’s President Gitanas Nauseda said he has been briefed by the US on the content of CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s talks in Moscow, describing the visit as aimed at reducing regional tensions. “I can say at this stage that the meeting achieved its stated objectives, and it was aimed at reducing tensions in the region,” Nauseda said in Vilnius, according to Lithuanian media reports on Monday. “I very much hope that this message reached the Kremlin regime in good time.” He did not provide further details, citing the agreed approach with Washington. An unannounced visit by Ratcliffe to Moscow last week sparked global speculation about the purpose of the trip and the possible content of the talks. Little was officially confirmed after the meeting. US media reported, citing unnamed sources, that Ratcliffe had warned Russia during his Wednesday visit against attacking Nato allies. When asked about the reports, the Kremlin denied them and pointed the finger at the West. “We should not hide the fact that the meeting did not come about by chance and that the intention was to convey certain messages that had to be conveyed at this point in time,” Nauseda said. In general, however, too much attention is being paid to the meeting, he added. While the regional security situation remains tense, it has not deteriorated dramatically recently, he said. In the Baltic states and also in Poland, there are fears that Russia, due to its problems in the war in Ukraine, could increasingly provoke Nato member states. In Lithuania, the government has warned of possible sabotage attempts and hybrid attacks on critical infrastructure – and has therefore recently stepped up security measures at key transport and energy facilities.

title: US targets China’s global trade surplus at G20 meeting ahead of Xi-Trump summit
description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent raises concerns over China’s ‘excessive imbalances’ just weeks before crucial bilateral meeting.
content: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday targeted China’s global trade surplus, raising concerns over “excessive imbalances,” weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to arrive in Washington for a bilateral summit with US President Donald Trump. “We are confronting persistent global imbalances that undermine prosperity,” Bessent said in his opening address at the G20 Finance Ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. The United States holds the G20 presidency in 2026, leading a forum of the world’s major advanced and emerging economies. Without naming China, Bessent said that the grouping’s finance ministers and central bank governors “have broadly concurred that it is in the interests of both surplus and deficit countries to address excessive imbalances”. “We have seen how distorted policies that privileged countries’ own exports have harmed many of the economies represented here today,” he said, adding that a “durable global economy cannot rest on beggar-thy-neighbour acts that stifle fair market-based competition.” Washington has made trade imbalances a key theme of the G20 ministerial – part of decades-long complaints about Beijing’s high trade surpluses – as a surge in Chinese exports of major products such as automobiles, solar panels and batteries has raised concerns in many countries over Beijing’s alleged “overcapacity”. Governments have attributed the surplus production to weak pro-consumer policies and to state subsidies, a charge China denies. China’s global export volume surged to a record US$1.2 trillion in 2025, a 20 per cent increase over 2024. “The world cannot have a China with a US$1.2 trillion trade surplus,” Bessent said on Sunday in an interview with Reuters. “In China, the economy is quite weak, and they are trying to export their way out of it, and they need to rebalance their economy.” China on Monday pushed back on the trade allegations and Washington’s latest attempt to rally other G20 members over the issue. “China never deliberately pursues a trade surplus and opposes unilateral tariff measures in all forms,” foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a press briefing in Beijing. For its part, Washington has attempted to stem the flow of Chinese imports through a slew of measures, including tariffs, national security-based import bans, restrictions on Chinese companies and tighter scrutiny of Chinese goods entering the US. According to figures from the US Trade Representative, goods trade between China and the US totalled an estimated US$414 billion in 2025, down around 28 per cent from 2024. Economists say this might be deceptive, however, as more Chinese goods are routed through third countries. China denies industrial overcapacity due to state subsidies, weak domestic demand Last month, China rejected claims that its industrial overcapacity was driven by state subsidies and weak domestic demand, saying its manufacturing strength instead reflected technological innovation, market competition and structural reforms. “There is no necessary connection between industrial subsidies and overcapacity,” the commerce ministry said in a position paper. The document argued that governments routinely use subsidies to advance domestic development goals, citing Washington’s US$750 billion Inflation Reduction Act passed in 2022 to support domestic EV production. “It is imperative that all countries make the pie of global development bigger and introduce subsidies and other industrial policies in a rational and compliant manner, rather than use them as a tool to constrain the development of others,” it added. The US focus on trade imbalance at the G20 comes as Washington and Beijing race to finalise the economic deliverables for the expected Trump-Xi meeting in Washington next month. One major outcome is the likely launch of the bilateral Board of Trade, which will identify non-sensitive sectors and products the two sides can trade at reduced tariffs, capped at US$30 billion for each side. The South China Morning Post reported last week that the bilateral trade truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, is likely to be extended. The two sides at the time agreed to reduce some US tariffs on Chinese goods, suspend additional US restrictions on Chinese-affiliated companies, pause certain Chinese rare earth export controls for a year, and secure Chinese commitments on American soybeans and fentanyl precursors. On the sidelines of the G20 ministerial, Bessent held a meeting with the People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng on Sunday. “I had a very robust meeting with Governor Pan last night,” Bessent told CNBC on Monday, without providing details of the discussions. The Chinese G20 delegation also includes Chinese Vice Minister of Finance Liao Min. US ramps up efforts to economically isolate Iran The meeting comes as the US steps up efforts to build global support for its latest campaign to isolate Iran through tougher economic restrictions and secondary sanctions. Last week, Bessent announced the administration’s “Economic D-Day” sanctions targeting 60 individuals and entities, including Hong Kong companies and Chinese nationals, but stopped short of targeting Chinese banks doing business with Iranian firms. On Monday, he indicated that secondary sanctions against them may not be on the cards and questioned the assertion that economic pressure on Iran could not work without China’s help. “I would push back on that false narrative that somehow the media has jumped on this. Oh, you can’t do it without China. Well, you can,” Bessent said, claiming that only 30 million barrels of Iranian oil are left on the open waters because of a US-led blockade. “So even if they were to get remittances from China, that’s going to run out.” Bessent added that Washington and Beijing had “more in common” than they disagreed on Iran, noting that both countries agree that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon and that the Strait of Hormuz must remain open to free and fair ship transit. China last week condemned US actions and said Beijing’s cooperation with Tehran was conducted “within the framework of international law and should not be disrupted”. Economic wars and maximum pressure were “not the solutions”, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said. China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, purchasing more than 80 per cent of the country’s total oil exports in 2025, according to data from analytics firm Kpler.

title: Ex-gang leader found guilty in 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
description: Jury finds Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis guilty of orchestrating drive-by shooting, marking first conviction in decades-old case.
content: An ex-street gang leader accused of orchestrating the drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur three decades ago in Las Vegas was convicted of murder on Monday for his role in a long-unsolved crime that silenced one of rap music’s most influential voices. A jury in Clark County, Nevada, ‌deliberated for nearly three hours before finding Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, guilty of a single count of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, capping an 11-day trial in a downtown Las Vegas courtroom. Davis will face a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole at his sentencing on October 13. Davis told the judge “he plans to appeal this matter”. Several people in the gallery wiped away tears and hugged a prosecutor as the court adjourned. Binu Palal of the Clark County District Attorney’s Office told jurors that under the code of respect in street gangs, Davis could not ‌let the beating of his nephew slide. “So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr Shakur,” Palal said. Police say they long suspected Davis but did not have ‌enough evidence to charge him until he went public with his story in media appearances and a memoir, which, along with ⁠tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, ⁠make up most of the prosecution’s case. Davis’ lawyer Michael Sanft told jurors during his closing argument that his client’s story could not be corroborated by evidence and should not ‌be trusted. He also said the case was tainted by police corruption, mismanagement and missing files. “You’re reading a book that is fiction and not fact, but the state wants you to believe ‌that ‌this is somehow a confession,” Sanft said, referring to Davis’ 2019 memoir Compton Street Legend. Over the past two weeks, prosecutors played hours of recordings for jurors ‌in which Davis said he was enraged after Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis’ nephew. Davis and three other men, including his nephew, went looking ⁠for Shakur and his record executive Marion “Suge” Knight in a white Cadillac on the night of the beating, he told police during an unrelated investigation. ⁠Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat, and when they found Knight and Shakur’s car, one of the two men in the back opened fire. Prosecutors have not named the shooter, and the three other men in the car have since died. ‌Under Nevada law, Davis can be charged ‌with murder even if he did not pull the trigger. Davis was a leader of the South Side Compton Crips, a Los Angeles-area street gang that feuded with rival gang Mob Piru, which was associated with Shakur and his record label Death Row Records. Shakur’s 1996 killing became a seminal moment in rap history and heightened hip-hop culture’s violent image during “gangsta” rap’s heyday, an era defined by feuding between East and West Coast artists.

title: Trump to meet US oil executives as Iran war keeps fuel prices high
description: White House pushes for increased refining capacity after announcing huge US stake in Venezuela oil.
content: US President Donald Trump will meet oil refining executives on Tuesday as he tries to tame fuel prices sent spiralling by the Iran war ahead of midterm elections in November, the White House said. The talks at the White House also come days after Trump announced a deal for a huge US stake in the oil reserves of Venezuela, whose leader Nicolas Maduro was toppled by US forces in January. Republicans fear voters will punish them in November’s crucial US midterm elections after high fuel prices dramatically raised the cost of living for ordinary Americans. “The president will meet with industry leaders to collaborate on the best ways to increase refining capacity, further unleash American energy dominance across the entire supply chain, and bring down prices for the American people,” White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement on Monday. The talks were “especially timely as we increase Venezuelan crude flow to US refineries”, a White House official said separately. The White House did not release a list of companies attending Tuesday’s meeting but said it would include a “mix of small, medium, and large refiners and distributors”. Trump said on Friday that the deal – which he called the biggest in history – would provide “majority US control” of 65 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan petroleum reserves. Venezuela has the world’s largest proven reserves. Its government has operated under intense pressure and close scrutiny from the Trump administration since the US ousted and captured long-time ruler Maduro. Trump is hoping the Venezuelan oil can offset disruption of global oil supplies caused by the Iran war that he launched with Israel six months ago. The United States and Iran traded fire on Sunday for the first time in a month amid a stalemate in the war, with Iran keeping the strategic Strait of Hormuz closed and the US persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.

title: Lionel Messi retires from Argentina’s international team
description: Messi, who captained Argentina ⁠to the World Cup title in 2022 and ⁠the final in 2026, said the decision ‘hurt’ but ‘the time has come’.
content: Lionel Messi, who captained Argentina to World Cup victory in 2022 and the final in 2026, is retiring from international football, he ‌said on Monday. The record eight-times Ballon d’Or winner is his country’s record appearance-maker and scorer with 125 goals in 207 games, having transformed a complicated relationship with the national team into a story of redemption and triumph. “It was a decision that hurt – and still hurts deep down – but I understand that the time has come,” the 39-year-old Messi wrote on Instagram. “I swear to you that ⁠I always gave it my all – not just in these last few years when we won everything, ‌but before that too; I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to ‌be Argentine through football. “I leave with the peace ⁠of mind and pride ⁠of having given you – alongside my teammates – moments we once only dreamed of,” he added. Defeat in this year’s World Cup ‌final by Spain denied Messi a fairy-tale farewell but his place among the game’s greats had long since been secured. After years of ‌disappointment with ‌Argentina, including defeat in the 2014 World Cup final and successive Copa America finals, Messi ‌won his first major international trophy at the 2021 Copa America before leading his country to glory ⁠at the 2022 Qatar World Cup. The former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain forward who now plays for ⁠Inter Miami added another Copa America title in 2024 and arrived at his sixth World Cup hoping to complete an extraordinary final chapter. A 1-0 loss to Spain ensured that ‌did not happen but ‌Messi, who made his Argentina debut in 2005, walks away having emerged from the shadow of 1986 World Cup-winning captain Diego Maradona to forge a legacy of his own as another defining figure in his country’s football history.

title: Xi, Putin vow to deepen strategic ties after Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit meet
description: Xi said relevant departments from both sides are implementing initiatives he and Putin discussed during Putin’s state visit to China in May.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin both vowed to strengthen the role of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) during their meeting on Monday, as the two countries seek to deepen strategic coordination amid mounting tensions with Washington and its allies. The two leaders met on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Xi said the SCO has a mission to safeguard regional stability and promote regional development amid growing uncertainty and unpredictability in a fast-changing international situation, according to a readout from the Chinese side. “China is willing to work with all parties, including Russia, to discuss the future development of the organisation, help it achieve steady and long-term growth, and strengthen the force that leads the reform of global governance and advances an equal and orderly world multipolarity,” he said. Putin said Russia and China should enhance solidarity and cooperation within the organisation and play a guiding role, the readout said. The encounter, on the sidelines of the SCO’s 25th anniversary, was their second face-to-face meeting this year following Putin’s trip to China in May, just days after Donald Trump’s visit. Xi arrived in Bishkek on Sunday and held talks with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, according to state news agency Xinhua. Putin praises relations between Moscow and Beijing When talking on bilateral matters during Monday’s meeting, Putin praised how the relations between Moscow and Beijing have become a model for state-to-state relations, saying Russia is willing to strengthen cooperation with China in fields including trade, energy, industry, transport, science and technology, according to the Chinese readout. Xi said the relevant departments from both sides are actively implementing the initiatives he and Putin discussed during Putin’s state visit to China in May, and have already achieved substantial results. “We believe that under our strategic guidance and the joint efforts of both sides, the foundation of China-Russia relations will become more solid, the pace of development more steadfast, and the prospects even brighter,” said Xi. During Putin’s May visit, the two leaders extended the 2001 Treaty of Good-Neighbourliness and Friendly Cooperation, signed multiple cooperation documents and issued joint statements on comprehensive strategic co-ordination and a multipolar world. Trade between the two countries has rebounded this year following a dip in 2025. Figures for the first half of the year rose by around 25 per cent year on year, while the total for the first seven months of the year approached US$159 billion, according to official Chinese data. Energy is expected to feature prominently in the latest talks, including the stalled Power of Siberia 2 gas pipeline. Moscow has portrayed the project – which would carry as much as 50 billion cubic metres (1,765 billion cubic feet) of Russian gas annually to China through Mongolia – as central to its eastward economic pivot after losing many of its European markets. But the two sides have not reached agreement on pricing, financing, supply commitments and construction timelines. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in May that an “understanding” had been reached on the route and construction method, but no final commercial contract had been signed. Xi, Putin discuss international and regional issues Xi and Putin also discussed international and regional issues of common interest, according to the readout, without elaborating. Beijing has not condemned the invasion of Ukraine and called for negotiations to end the war while insisting it was not a party to the conflict. It has also rejected accusations from the West that it is supporting Russia’s defence-industrial base. Taking part in the talks on the Russian side were Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk, alongside officers from the Presidential Office. Notably, Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov and Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and the Rosatom State Corporation – the state nuclear energy and nuclear goods company – also attended the meeting, according to the Kremlin, which indicated potential cooperation areas. Xi and Putin have met in person more than 40 times since 2013, branding their relationship a “no limits” partnership in February 2022. While both have presented it as a strategic counterweight to Western pressure, they have stopped short of declaring it a formal alliance, and analysts have said the Ukraine war has left Russia increasingly reliant on China for trade, technology and diplomatic support. Both countries have also tried to promote the SCO as a platform for a more multipolar international system. China and Russia founded the 10-member security and economic forum in 2001, along with Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. India, Pakistan, Iran and Belarus have since become members. Chinese state media has framed the summit as an opportunity to expand the organisation’s role beyond traditional security cooperation into trade, connectivity, digital development and global governance. Former Kyrgyz prime minister Djoomart Otorbaev wrote in state-run China Daily on Monday that the group’s expanded membership had broadened its focus from security to economic development across Eurasia. However, it remains a loose grouping, with members divided over issues such as the wars in Iran and Ukraine, relations with Russia and the extent to which it should challenge Western influence. Member states such as India also have long-running territorial disputes with China and Pakistan.

title: France takes aim at ultra-fast fashion with fee per garment
description: New policy targets platforms like Shein and Temu, which have exploded in popularity in France.
content: France will from Tuesday impose a fee on ultra-fast fashion items that will eventually reach almost €20 (US$23.20) per garment, as the government targets major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein. The levy follows legislation passed by the French parliament in June to regulate “ultra-fast fashion” companies, known for selling large volumes of lower-quality clothing at rock-bottom prices. It is part of a push to rein in Asian e-commerce giants including Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which have exploded in popularity in France in recent years. “The harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion on our environment and our economy are well known and documented,” said Mathieu Lefevre, the minister for ecological transition on Friday as details of the measure were published. Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price. The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards. In 2026, companies will pay fines such as a 50 cent levy on underwear falling into the ultra-fast fashion category, rising to €2 for T-shirts, €9 for jeans and €12 for a jacket. The levy could reach up to €19.50 per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50 per cent of the product’s pre-tax price. A tool to collect data independently, rather than relying solely on companies’ own declarations, is under development, Lefevre’s office said. Shein – which on Monday was valued at US$26.3 billion in its long-awaited Hong Kong initial public offering – declined to comment when contacted by Agence France-Presse. Temu and AliExpress did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Alibaba Group owns AliExpress as well as the South China Morning Post. The measure has faced criticism over which retailers it will affect. In July, Lefevre’s office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European and French companies. French officials have made repeated statements that they view Shein, Temu and AliExpress as driving the surge in ultra-fast fashion. The European Commission had also raised questions over whether the legislation complied with EU law, but Lefevre’s office said those concerns had been “dispelled” and the measure was not expected to be blocked. China, meanwhile, warned in July of potential retaliation over the French law, slamming the regulation as “discriminatory” and in violation of trade principles. Imports of small parcels from China into the EU have already fallen by around 30 to 40 per cent since a separate €3 EU levy on such shipments came into force on July 1, according to the French government.

title: Central bar packed as Hongkongers aim to raise HK$50,000 for Nepal flood relief
description: Five Nepalese operators and bartenders launch signature cocktails at Orchard to raise funds for flood relief as community rallies.
content: Around a hundred patrons packed a bar in Central on Monday night to raise funds for victims of catastrophic flash floods and mudslides in Nepal, as members of Hong Kong’s Nepalese community rallied to support relief efforts for their homeland. The death toll in Nepal had risen to 919 as of 1pm on Monday, with 4,247 people still missing, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported. The disaster struck on Wednesday when a massive wall of mud and rock collapsed into a river along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet, unleashing devastating torrents downstream. At cocktail bar Orchard in Central, the fundraising event kicked off at 7pm on Monday in a collaboration between its Nepalese founder and fellow operators and workers from three other venues, who teamed up to craft signature drinks dedicated to their homeland. Hong Kong is home to a Nepalese community of roughly 30,000. Among the patrons was Shreya Rai, a 27-year-old Nepalese public relations professional who was born and raised in Hong Kong. Joining two friends at the bar, she described the fundraiser as a meaningful cause close to her heart. “There is no other reason to drink on a Monday,” Rai said. Though her relatives lived in a remote village in east Nepal, away from the affected area in the north, she remained worried. Their remote, mountainous village was prone to flooding, and rugged roads made evacuating with their belongings nearly impossible, Rai said, adding that she was in constant touch with them in a bid to ensure their safety. Bidhya Shrestha, a friend of Rai who works in the compliance industry, said she came to support families affected by the floods. The fundraising initiative also drew non-Nepalese residents. Delphine Kong, a 33-year-old Hongkonger who works in the food and beverage sector, said she felt duty-bound to support the fundraiser initiated by the community. “They were very fast to react,” Kong said. “It is a tragic event but the vibe here is still full of hope in raising funds for a meaningful initiative.” Dipesh Rai, a 27-year-old bartender at Orchard who grew up splitting his time between Nepal and Hong Kong, volunteered to work during his day off. “I had to come. The Nepalese community is small and it is great to gather for such a great cause,” Rai said. “The number of people affected has been increasing by the hour … it is really sad.” All proceeds from the night’s sales will be donated directly to the official government-run disaster relief fund in Nepal, according to Orchard founder Alex Pun. The 40-year-old restaurateur said the idea of the fundraiser took shape immediately after the flood, when he reached out to four fellow Nepalese operators and bartenders from three bars. With many Nepalese working in hospitality, Pun said he wanted to “mobilise people from the industry to help”. He said he was deeply touched after local friends texted him to ask after his family’s safety in Nepal, which spurred him to take action. Pun, who has been living in Hong Kong since 2003, said he aimed to raise HK$50,000 (US$6,400) from the night’s takings.

title: In flood-hit Philippines, ‘out of touch’ Marcos slammed for private birthday serenade
description: Observers say the public backlash was directed at Marcos’ ‘perceived insensitivity’ in light of the floods and related corruption scandal.
content: Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s birthday serenade for his wife might have been a private gesture, but as floodwaters overwhelmed much of Luzon – the country’s largest and most populous island and home to the capital Manila – a viral clip of him singing became a public-relations crisis. Observers told This Week in Asia that Marcos’ celebration of his wife, Marie Louise “Liza” Araneta-Marcos, on her 67th birthday struck the wrong chord with a public already angered by deadly floods, the government’s handling of disaster relief and long-running allegations of corruption in flood-control projects. By August 26, when Marcos quietly staged his wife’s party with a live band attended by family, close friends and political allies, Manila was almost at a standstill after days of heavy rain. Online responses sarcastically thanked the president and government for the scandal-hit flood-control projects under his watch. Two days later, a video of Marcos crooning “You” and “I Love Her” to his wife, taken by one of the party guests, Vigan City Mayor Bonito Singson, surfaced on social media. The clip soon went viral and several comments beneath one widely shared repost framed the video as proof of Marcos’ detachment. “No empathy,” one user wrote, while another called the president “out of touch” and a third said: “He really knows his priorities.” The national weather bureau Pagasa had earlier predicted strong monsoon rains for most of the week, enhanced by the near convergence of at least four cyclones, typhoons, tropical depressions and low-pressure areas. Rain had been falling almost nonstop since the middle of August, prompting Pagasa to issue multiple flood warnings, including the most severe Red alerts, late into the night. At least 33 people have died in various parts of the country because of the floods, according to the Office of Civil Defence, including a man who fell into an open street manhole concealed by raging waters in the central Luzon province of Pampanga. The backlash over the singing clip came despite Marcos staging photo events where he handed out ayuda (government flood aid) in the form of cash and goods and inspected flood-control pumping stations and dykes. A statement issued over the weekend by presidential communications undersecretary Claire Castro did little to stem the criticism. “The President is the President wherever he is,” Castro said in Filipino. “His devoting a few hours for his family does not mean his responsibility towards the nation stops and government operations stop. In the midst of severe rains, his monitoring and orders to agencies to ensure the safety and swift aid to our countrymen have continued.” For Dr Pamela Cajilig, a disaster anthropologist at the University of the Philippines, the criticisms against Marcos “show that citizens do not compartmentalise their expectations of a public servant of the highest order from that of a family man”. She said repeated disasters had taught Filipinos to expect that politicians and bureaucrats demonstrate kapwa (concern for others) that went beyond just handing out ayuda. “This means seeing oneself in their constituents – feeling the latter’s pain as they struggle – and sincerely demonstrating that,” Cajilig, who is also an architect and urban designer, told This Week in Asia. “This expectation of pakikipagkapwa [brotherly concern] is heightened by the deep distrust generated by the perceived lack of accountability and transparency in the flood-control programme.” Marcos’ staging of festivities amid a national tragedy, therefore, offended “a related collective value that is at stake: malasakit [compassion]”, Cajilig said. “Malasakit requires acting out of an ethics of care for your kapwa who is suffering, often at the cost of personal sacrifice.” Public anger over the floods was also sharpened by a wider loss of trust in Marcos’ handling of flood-control projects at the centre of corruption allegations. Recent surveys showed broad dissatisfaction regarding corruption, accountability and the president’s own role in the controversy. Momentum Research founding CEO Cleve Arguelles told This Week in Asia that Marcos’ singing video invited such scathing attacks because “political images are interpreted through the public mood in which they circulate”. “On its own, a president singing for his wife is ordinary and even potentially endearing. But President Marcos is currently operating in a very unfavourable political environment,” said Arguelles, who also teaches political science at the University of the Philippines. He pointed to Momentum’s latest survey in August, which found only 36.4 per cent satisfied with Marcos’ performance and 57.4 per cent dissatisfied, as well as its July poll showing “overwhelming dissatisfaction” with the administration’s handling of corruption in flood-control projects. “So the video encounters a public already predisposed to read presidential behaviour critically,” Arguelles said. The floods had acquired political meaning because they were now closely associated in the public imagination with “allegations of corruption, failed or nonexistent flood-control projects, and questions about government competence”, he added. “So the timing of the video’s circulation makes the contrast especially powerful: images of people struggling through floodwaters alongside images of the president singing at a private celebration.” While the events did not happen simultaneously, “social media collapses that chronology into a single political image”, Arguelles said. “The larger problem is therefore not really that Marcos sang for his wife. It is that, amid widespread frustration and suffering over floods and corruption, the video provided an unusually vivid image onto which that frustration could be projected.” Vic Rodriguez, a political ally of Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio, criticised the administration for “[worsening] the sufferings of the lives of ordinary people” by failing to ensure “full accountability” over flood-control funds. He said critics were justified in demanding “transparency on how the average annual budget of 227 billion pesos for flood control was utilised”, as well as accountability for those who had allegedly misused public funds. Rodriguez also noted that Marcos had spent 1.333 trillion pesos for flood-control projects from 2023 to 2025 but that “has not in any way mitigated any of the supposed flooding that it was meant to address […] making the misery on the lives of the hundreds of thousands [of] affected citizens unbearable”. For University of the Philippines political scientist Dr Jean Franco, “the optics of the president having a good time at a time when the country is reeling from floods is not good” given Marcos’ position. “He is accountable to the public in need of answers and assistance,” Franco said, noting that if the party could not be postponed, Marcos’ staff should have barred people from taking pictures and videos. Franco said the criticisms were directed at Marcos’ “perceived insensitivity” in light of the corruption scandal. “They were made not because they want to deprive the president from being a devoted husband but because the public is seeking accountability and empathy from the country’s highest official.”

title: India rejects ruling on water-sharing treaty with Pakistan by international court
description: The court says India must uphold the treaty and curb work on a hydroelectric plant in Kashmir pending a neutral expert’s assessment.
content: India must uphold a water-sharing treaty with ⁠Pakistan it suspended amid bilateral tensions and must limit work on a hydroelectric plant it is building in the Kashmir region, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague said on Monday. India in April last year suspended the treaty ‌that ensures water supply to 80 per cent of Pakistani farms, after India identified as Pakistani two of three assailants in an attack that killed 26 people at a tourist destination in Kashmir that month. Islamabad denied any role in the attack and took legal action after India last year also began work to boost reservoir holding capacity at two hydroelectric projects ⁠in the Kashmir region. This was seen as a first tangible step by India to operate outside agreements ‌covered by the Indus Waters Treaty between the two countries, which both have honoured since 1960 despite three wars and several other conflicts between them. The ‌Permanent Court of Arbitration said the Indus Water Treaty remained fully in force, ⁠as India had ⁠no justification for ending or suspending the agreement. “India must observe its obligations under the Treaty, including those relating to the ‌design and operation of its hydroelectric projects on the Western Rivers,” the intergovernmental court said. India, which is officially a member of ‌the court, ‌said it did not recognise the court and “categorically” rejected the verdict. “This so-called Court of Arbitration has ‌no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India’s sovereign decisions,” India’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in ⁠a statement. “Its pronouncements, now or in the future, will have no effect on India’s actions in ⁠connection with the projects being undertaken by India.” In a statement after the court’s ruling, Islamabad said: “Pakistan welcomes this finding by the Court that interim measures are warranted.” The court said a neutral expert, appointed by the World Bank, would judge by July 2027 whether the construction of hydroelectric plants ‌in the Himalayan region ‌was in line with the treaty. Agreeing with a demand by Pakistan, the court said India was not allowed to build the dam wall and power intake structure at the Ratle Hydro-Electric Plant above certain levels until 90 days after the neutral expert’s decision. Additional reporting by AFP

title: Sailor Halliday lays down Asian Games marker with historic top 10 at World Champs
description: Hong Kong’s Nick Halliday becomes first from city to finish in top 10 at the ILCA 7 Men’s World Championship.
content: Nicholas Halliday has racked up another “special achievement”, becoming the first Hong Kong sailor to finish in the top 10 at the ILCA 7 Men’s World Championship in Ireland. Halliday’s 10th place at the event in Dun Laoghaire marked a new high for the National Games gold medallist, and it was the first time an athlete from the city has performed that well in an Olympic class at the senior world championships. The success, according to Halliday, showed he was moving in the right direction with his training and was the result of “hard work and my passion for sailing”. “Top 10 at the World Championship of course has its own special meaning and significance as it’s the biggest and most difficult yearly ILCA event, and I am very happy to have achieved this milestone,” he added. With the Asian Games just around the corner, Halliday believes the results at the week-long event in Dublin Bay will have a positive effect on his competition in Japan. Of the 141 sailors from 45 countries and places who took part in the qualification races in Ireland, the 27-year-old ranked eighth, with reigning champion Ryan Lo of Singapore third. Ha Jee-min of Korea, who won silver three years ago in Hangzhou, and India’s Vishnu Saravanan who claimed bronze, were 32 and 37, respectively. “I am always taking things one at a time. The Asian Games is a very special event of great importance with different structure and demands than the worlds,” Halliday said. “To achieve a result like this at the worlds just before the Asian Games of course is a confidence booster, but it mostly confirms to me that I am in good condition heading into the Games.” Harris Tsolis, Halliday’s head coach at the Hong Kong Sports Institute, was adamant his charge was a medal contender in Japan. Speaking to the South China Morning Post, Tsolis said he considered the Hongkonger “the best ILCA 7 sailor in Asia”, but added that the talent in the region was very high. “Singapore and South Korea also have super strong and very experienced sailors, especially in the wind conditions expected in Gamagori,” Tsolis said. “India is also a very good one with a lot of good results; it’s a different ball game in the smaller Asian Games fleet.” Despite the display at the World Championship, Tsolis said there was a hint of regret, with Halliday knowing some mistakes over the last two days cost him an even better place. There were two “not so great starts” in both races on the final qualification day, and he was also over the line half a second early in the first final race, which required him to turn back and clear the start line again. Consistency is key at such big events, but it is not easy Harris Tsolis, Halliday’s head coach “ILCA 7 is the most competitive Olympic sailing class, so racing is extremely close at the World Championship,” Tsolis said. “Everyone is very skilled and high level, so just a very small mistake can send you to the back of the fleet with very few options and no easy passing lanes. “You do not have a lot of time and opportunities to recover. It’s not impossible, but it definitely hurts. Consistency is key at such big events, but it is not easy.” Tsolis said aside from the hard work Halliday put into his sport and the talent he had shown from a young age, the Hongkonger’s success over the past couple of years had served as a confidence boost. “Experience also plays a huge role in sailing, and that’s why you see most Olympic medallists are close to 25 to 30 years old,” the coach added. “It takes some time for everything to come together, and the thing that definitely made an impact for Nick was his wins in the Asian Championship that gave him the ticket to his first Olympics in Paris, and of course his amazing performance and win in the France Sailing Grand Slam in 2025. “Those moments boosted his confidence a lot, and he realised he is on the right track and the process is working. He now feels he belongs at the top and fights hard for it at every major event.”

title: Prediction markets have priced the Trump-Xi summit. Do the bets have any value?
description: Trump has announced a September 24 meeting, but Beijing has not. As prediction market bets multiply, they may begin to shape diplomacy.
content: US President Donald Trump has already announced the date: September 24. That is when, Trump says, Chinese President Xi Jinping will come to the White House for a visit following the “America first” leader’s own three-day trip to Beijing in May. But there is a diplomatic wrinkle. The Trump administration has publicly put the date on the calendar. Beijing has not formally announced Xi’s Washington visit. According to sources familiar with the plan, Xi is expected to arrive in Washington on September 23 and depart on September 25, mirroring Trump’s last three-day itinerary in China. The South China Morning Post first reported on August 1 that Xi is likely to remain in Washington rather than travel to another American city. Traders are already pricing the odds of the visit. As of August 27, Polymarket contracts on whether Trump would meet Xi in September and whether Xi would visit the US by September 30 were both priced at about 95 per cent. Polymarket put the probability of Xi visiting the US by the end of September at 94 per cent. At Kalshi, another prediction market, the chance of a visit before October stood at 88 per cent. The wager, however, is about to get more complicated. As the expected summit approaches, traders will move beyond the simple question of whether the Chinese president will get on the plane and begin pricing what will happen once he arrives. Will Trump and Xi announce a trade deal, cut tariffs, make progress on artificial intelligence, or discuss semiconductor controls? Will they say something about Taiwan, or at least strike a conciliatory tone? Sub-markets linked to Trump’s May visit to Beijing even included the prospect of the two leaders embracing, with “yes” odds that at one point ran into the teens before the market later resolved to “no”. The growing range of such wagers, observers note, may offer a new way to measure what the world expects next – while also creating the risk that those expectations begin to shape what happens next. Samuel Lazarus, a research associate at the Council on Foreign Relations, anticipates a “litany” of contracts to emerge around the expected Xi-Trump summit, covering everything from major policy decisions to the “buzzwords” the two leaders might use. “We should expect markets on potential tariff reductions, progress on the US-China Board of Trade, potential cooperation on AI safety, possible revisions to semiconductor export controls, new or updated purchase and sale agreements, the United States’ pending arms sales to Taiwan, and, of course, rumblings about a ‘fourth communique’,” Lazarus said. Some contracts will be tied to concrete policy outcomes. Others will be “mention markets”, where the wager comes down to whether Trump or Xi say a particular word or phrase. But Lazarus cautioned against mistaking every market movement for a meaningful shift in the relationship. “Markets and analysts are hardly pricing in a major shift in bilateral relations, such as major changes to baseline tariff levels or the status quo in the Taiwan Strait,” he said. Trump’s “spontaneity and bluster”, he added, made for “good fodder in mention markets, but his statements have generally proved to be noise, not signal, with respect to the trajectory of the relationship”. “Instead, the inertia of strategic competition has proved dominant, while prediction markets have proved useful in pricing tactical shifts,” he said. Hilton Root, a professor of public policy at the Schar School of Policy and Government of George Mason University, in Virginia, noted that during the May meeting markets covered attendance, particular words Trump might use, specific announcements and the possibility of a tariff agreement. “Kalshi has also offered contracts on a Xi visit to the United States, the tariff rate on China, and even the duration of a Trump-Xi handshake. I would expect many more contracts of this kind as another meeting approaches,” he said. However, Root added that the prediction markets’ “limitation is equally important to recognise”. “Prediction markets favour outcomes that are defined beforehand, publicly observable, and easy to settle,” he said. “They can price whether a tariff is reduced, an agreement is signed, or a particular phrase is used. They cannot readily price what may be the summit’s most valuable result,” he said, referring to the possibility of greater stability in the US-China relationship. That distinction could be particularly important for Beijing. Chinese officials have spent years learning how to operate around Trump’s unpredictability. Sourabh Gupta, a senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, said Beijing was unlikely to let individual presidential comments, or the prediction markets reacting to them, derail its broader objectives. “Beijing has learned to look beyond the president’s individual, erratic utterances,” Gupta said. It could still watch the overall direction of Trump’s comments “as a general pulse check of his inclinations”, he added, but individual statements would be unlikely to affect Beijing’s strategy. “While individual utterances may move prediction markets, [they are] unlikely to deflect Beijing from its summit goals and priorities,” Gupta said. Chinese officials “have learned to disregard that which is realistically beyond their control”. Instead, Beijing will focus on what actually happens. “Actions and adherence to commitments, and not sweet or sour words, are the bottom line by which they operate in their dealings with this administration,” Gupta said. But the markets carry risks of their own. The recent case of Gabriel Perez, a White House teleprompter operator placed on unpaid leave after using advance access to Trump’s remarks to bet on Kalshi, showed how quickly privileged information can acquire a dollar value. A US Army Special Forces soldier was also accused of using advance knowledge of the operation to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro to place winning bets on prediction markets. The stakes are potentially higher around a Xi-Trump summit. Knowing a president will utter “China” in a speech is one thing. Knowing in advance that the US is preparing to loosen semiconductor restrictions, change its position on Taiwan or announce a major tariff concession is something else entirely. Geopolitical prediction markets create “perverse incentives for government officials to trade on closely held, often classified, information”, according to Lazarus. At the same time, market transparency provided some protection, and most insiders were either prevented from trading or identified after the fact, he said. Still, regulators should narrow the scope of listed markets, particularly on offshore exchanges, to “minimise the risk of sensitive information leaking by way of insider trades”, Lazarus said. The damage caused by leaked government secrets, he warned, had the potential to be both permanent and highly costly. Prediction markets do not need privileged information to become influential. A relatively small amount of money can move a thin market, and the resulting price can take on a significance far beyond the original bet. Matthew Wein, a US national security policy expert, warned in a February commentary published by the Atlantic Council that a thinly traded market “could be meaningfully shifted by a single six-figure trade”. When it comes to a Trump-Xi summit, a sudden move in the odds on a tariff deal or Taiwan-related announcement could be interpreted as a signal that someone knows something, even when it may simply reflect one large bet. Treating such movements as transparent reflections of public belief, Wein cautioned, risked “granting disproportionate narrative power to actors with both the capital and the incentive to shape prices”. That possibility is especially interesting in the case of China, where summit diplomacy is typically tightly controlled and carefully choreographed. But Beijing may simply decide to ignore the noise. Gupta argued that prediction-market distortions could “throw a curveball or two and sour the atmosphere”. Still, he said, “Beijing is not the type of protagonist to be deflected by such forces”. These are “trivialities in the course of statecraft that just have to be stared down or, better yet, ignored”. Yun Sun, director of the China programme at Washington-based think tank the Stimson Centre, is similarly cautious about reading too much into the market. “As it stands now, the trip is expected to happen,” she said. But she sees a more fundamental question ahead: what can the summit actually deliver? “The market will react to any potential news,” Sun said. “But for this trip, it will be hard to expect major deliverables on specific industries or sectors. “The low-hanging fruits were picked during the May trip,” she said, adding that “implementation of existing agreements remains difficult, including follow-up to the Boeing deal”. “Rumours will always bubble,” Sun added. “But having a practical baseline expectation is more important at this stage.” Still, Lazarus contended that prediction markets remained “an indispensable tool for navigating an increasingly volatile international landscape and, of course, a uniquely improvisational president”. With appropriate guardrails, they could provide a “weighted average of popular expectations” at a time when geopolitical forecasting was becoming harder. “The stakes today are simply too high to outsource all geopolitical forecasting to the commentariat, the whims of the algorithm, or the promises of those who lead us.” And that may be the real test of the Xi-Trump summit: whether these markets can help reveal what the world expects next, without becoming part of what happens next.
