title: Spain PM blames Russia, Israel for Ceuta migrant crisis’ disinformation
description: Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also dismisses speculation on the involvement of Moroccan authorities in the crisis.
content: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Monday there were signs Russia and Israel had spread the disinformation over Spain’s migration policy that triggered last month’s rush of migrants into Ceuta, but no evidence of Moroccan involvement. Over 72,000 migrants irregularly crossed ‌from Morocco into the tiny Spanish territory between July 30 and 31 in an unprecedented surge at one of the European Union’s only two land borders with Africa, prompting alarm across the bloc. At least 100 people died in the attempt, according to Ceuta’s local authorities. Spanish opposition parties and some human rights groups have accused Rabat of deliberately allowing the mass crossing, an accusation Morocco has denied. “When people talk and speculate about the participation of Moroccan authorities, ⁠I deny this outright,” Sanchez told radio station SER. Videos on Instagram, TikTok and other social media spread misleading claims that migrants ‌reaching Ceuta by sea could remain in Spain, encouraging thousands to attempt the crossing, Spanish authorities have said. Sanchez said research by the EU’s diplomatic service EEAS had indicated that Russian and Israeli ‌networks had been behind the spread of disinformation in conjunction with far-right networks. He said it was clear that ⁠the two countries had ⁠used the crisis to criticise Madrid due to dissatisfaction with its position on the wars in Ukraine and Gaza, but gave no further details on the evidence ‌he had of their involvement. Later on Monday, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said in a post on social media that Sanchez was “lying shamelessly” when accusing Israel of ‌disseminating misleading ‌information about Ceuta, casting it as an attempt to distract from domestic policy failures. The Russian government rejected Spain’s allegations that Moscow was connected to the Ceuta migration crisis, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said ‌on Monday. The EEAS did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Roughly 5,000 migrants, some seeking asylum, have remained in Ceuta ⁠since the border rush, triggering near-daily protests from locals against the Spanish government’s handling of the crisis and sporadic attacks against ⁠a makeshift migrant camp at El Trampolin beach, according to police reports. Police arrested three Moroccan citizens on Sunday for throwing bottles filled with corrosive liquids against an army patrol in Ceuta, news agency EFE reported, citing ‌police sources. No one was injured ‌in the attack, the report added. Sanchez also announced on Monday that the cabinet would deploy an additional €168 million (US$195 million) in emergency funds to reactivate Ceuta’s economy, a figure equivalent to 8 per cent of the enclave’s gross domestic product, on top of €180 million pledged last week for medium-term recovery efforts.

title: US export controls on tungsten, battery ‘black mass’ seen pressuring Chinese recyclers
description: Washington’s new one-year measure reserves material for domestic buyers, but analysts point to limited processing capacity hindering efforts to build supply chains.
content: With Washington moving to ensure that tungsten scrap and lithium-ion battery “black mass” stay in the United States, analysts warn that the new restrictions will deprive Chinese refiners of a source of lower-cost feedstock and prompt Beijing to seek alternative supplies. China could also accelerate domestic recycling and use its own export controls on rare earths and magnets as leverage, they said. The administration of US President Donald Trump on Thursday barred exports of tungsten scrap and battery black mass – the shredded residue from used batteries that can be processed to recover valuable materials such as lithium, nickel and cobalt. Tungsten, known for its density, strength and exceptionally high melting point, is widely used in semiconductors, artificial intelligence chips, aerospace equipment and weapons. The year-long directive mandates that suppliers offer 100 per cent of their monthly output of tungsten scrap and black mass to US buyers and to keep the materials within the country. The order marks Washington’s latest attempt to shore up its strategic resource pipeline, coming after China imposed export controls on a range of tungsten products in February 2025 and required exporters to obtain government licences. Beijing subsequently moved to widen access to overseas recycling feedstock, formally allowing imports of compliant battery black mass in August 2025 and cutting the tariff to 3 per cent from 6.5 per cent at the start of 2026. China will be impacted in the short term, as this ban will reduce its refiners’ feedstock Liang Yan, Willamette University Chinese customs data showed that shipments of most controlled tungsten products to the US had fallen to zero in the first seven months of this year. However, the one-year timeline was unlikely to be long enough for the US to secure its supplies, as it lacked the capacity to process tungsten scrap and black mass, while building new refineries could take between two and five years, according to Liang Yan, a professor of economics at Willamette University in the United States. “What the one-year rule achieves is supply lock-up and government stockpile buying,” she said. “China will be impacted in the short term, as this ban will reduce its refiners’ feedstock.” Shipping electronic waste overseas is common in the US. The country generates about 6.9 million tonnes of electronic waste annually – second only to China – and exports roughly 1.5 million tonnes, according to electronics recycler EWaste Phoenix. US black-mass exports reached 100,667 tonnes in 2025, an increase of 48.7 per cent from a year earlier, according to S&P Global. Chinese customs data showed that the country imported 111,657 tonnes of industrial waste, including lithium-ion battery black mass, from the US in the first seven months of this year, accounting for nearly a tenth of China’s supplies. The restrictions could reshape global black-mass supply chains, reducing feedstock available to China’s battery recyclers while creating opportunities for domestic companies with advanced processing capabilities, S&P Global said in a report this month. [A]nything that the US faces Chinese export controls on could be included in the future: rare earths, antimony, gallium and germanium Xu Tianchen, Economist Intelligence Unit It said tighter export controls from the US could reduce overseas black-mass supplies available to Chinese refiners, though Chinese companies have stepped up overseas investment in recent years to secure raw materials and expand their global recycling networks. Xu Tianchen, a senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said the restriction, intended to bolster US domestic supplies, could eventually extend beyond tungsten and black mass to cover discarded rare earth magnets, other critical-mineral waste and any additional materials designated by the US government. “So, tungsten is the first tranche,” Xu explained. “But anything that the US faces Chinese export controls on could be included in the future: rare earths, antimony, gallium and germanium.” Liang also said the restrictions were likely to expand to other materials, including permanent magnets containing neodymium and dysprosium, aerospace-grade titanium and superalloy scrap. Beyond officially recorded trade, China has long had an active informal market for retired batteries and black mass, with unlicensed workshops competing against accredited recyclers for supplies, according to reports by the Financial Times and S&P Global.

title: Review | I Know Who You Are movie review: Hu Ge, Lei Jiayin lead absorbing Chinese spy drama
description: Feng Xiaogang’s drama set during the early years of the People’s Republic of China entertains but is let down by an unsatisfying ending.
content: 3/5 stars A righteous public security officer embarks on a 40-year game of cat and mouse with a suspected Kuomintang sleeper agent in I Know Who You Are, a sporadically entertaining historical drama by Feng Xiaogang. Lei Jiayin stars as Xiao Dali, a stubborn Chinese official convinced his next-door neighbour is a spy, while Hu Ge plays Feng Jingbo, who sees his secret mission repeatedly eclipsed by growing commitments to a community in rapid transition. Adapted from Zhang Ce’s novella No Regrets Tracking, the drama unfolds against a backdrop of seismic national upheaval, starting with the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949 and encompassing the Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution and sweeping economic reform. Throughout all this, Dali and Jingbo live side by side, their lives becoming increasingly and irreversibly intertwined. Both men live in the same Beijing hutong, where Dali is instantly suspicious of Jingbo, who has been hired as the new mathematics teacher at the local primary school. To observe his target, Dali moves into the same building as the teacher. While confused by some of Jingbo’s behaviour – not least his fixation on radio reports about Hong Kong vegetable prices – he struggles to find irrefutable evidence. The radio transmissions are, in fact, coded messages from Jingbo’s superiors, to which he responds using a hidden transmitter. Over time, the broadcasts become less frequent, but Dali’s suspicions never subside – not even when Jingbo asks him to play matchmaker for him and Liu Yemei (Zhang Yao), a proudly loyal member of the country’s growing political movement, whom he later marries. As the years pass, Jingbo becomes a respected and influential member of the community, and his secret political affiliations fade, while Dali’s behaviour leans ever further into self-destructive obsession. The two men’s families become close, especially after both men have children who form strong, lasting bonds, but when Jingbo eventually slips up, his nemesis is waiting to pounce. I Know Who You Are adopts a refreshingly level-headed and pragmatic approach to an issue that has divided families and communities for decades. Feng even has the temerity to suggest a man’s past might be forgiven, or at least forgotten, if he is willing to contribute to the greater good – an argument fuelled by a pair of contrasting yet equally compelling performances. Ultimately, however, the film insists justice must be served via a jarring, tacked-on denouement that attempts to have its cake and eat it too. It is a cynical and unsatisfying coda to a film that for much of its running time succeeds as an absorbing, if somewhat sanitised, exploration of a nation’s splintered and evolving ideological past. title: Beijing pushes back on Washington’s attempt to rally G20 over trade imbalance
description: After US Treasury Secretary Bessent called for coordinated response from G20 towards China, Beijing urged consultation instead.
content: China pushed back on Monday against Washington’s attempt to rally other Group of 20 members to pressure Beijing over its US$1.2 trillion trade surplus. “China never deliberately pursues a trade surplus and opposes unilateral tariff measures in all forms,” foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a press briefing in Beijing. Guo said China remained committed to “high-standard opening up” and would use its vast market to offer “new opportunities to all, including the United States”. His comment was a response to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s remarks that “the world cannot have a China with a US$1.2 trillion trade surplus” and that G20 members should reassess their trade terms with Beijing. “Both sides need to act on the important common understandings reached between the two presidents, resolve outstanding issues through consultation on the basis of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit, and strive to maintain the hard-won positive momentum in bilateral trade,” Guo said. Bessent made the remarks to Reuters on Sunday ahead of a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors, and called for a coordinated response on trade with China. The comments came as Beijing and Washington are preparing for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned visit to the US on September 24. Last month the US slapped tariffs of 10 to 12.5 per cent on goods from 60 economies following its forced labour investigation, with Chinese products facing the top rate of 12.5 per cent. Bloomberg reported last week that Washington was also considering an additional 7.5 per cent tariff on Chinese goods over allegations of excess manufacturing capacity. China’s goods trade surplus hit a record US$1.2 trillion last year, prompting concerns from Western politicians. The European Union has warned that it would be forced to take action if talks with Beijing fail to deliver “tangible results” on trade imbalances by October.

title: US visa delays leave Chinese students stranded with ‘frozen’ plans and ‘constant anxiety’
description: International students are being forced to defer enrolment at US universities as background checks and visa bottlenecks put them in limbo.
content: Late August marks the annual influx of international students to US campuses, but for many Chinese students, visa processing delays and diplomatic tensions have turned scheduled departures into open-ended delays. They say stringent visa scrutiny and expanding background checks have left them in limbo, delaying their timely arrival in the US and forcing them to defer enrolment. Under a provision of US immigration law known as “administrative processing” or visa checks, applicants may be asked to submit supplementary documents and undergo additional security reviews before their visas can be approved. Social media posts and interviews with affected students indicate these extended background checks are sweeping up a wider cross-section of applicants and fields of study. Ray Zhou, a Beijing resident admitted to a master’s degree programme in computer science, said the prolonged checks – now stretching beyond two months – had forced him to defer his enrolment until next year. Zhou, like the other students interviewed, asked not to give his full Chinese name or university because his visa was still being processed. “My mindset experienced a drastic shift,” he said. “At first, I felt relief from avoiding an immediate refusal and thought I would simply wait it out. But as the start of the semester got closer, the anxiety became overwhelming.” Hundreds of students across China have taken to social media to raise concerns about prolonged security checks that threaten to derail years of careful planning. The South China Morning Post has contacted the US embassy in China and the State Department for comment. Zhou manages a support group of more than 100 students caught in administrative processing, and he said the backgrounds of group members revealed the diversity of those affected. During US President Donald Trump’s first term, authorities started to impose stricter controls on international students in STEM fields – science, technology, engineering and mathematics – by intensifying security screenings to protect against the transfer of sensitive technology and research to foreign entities. Under Trump’s second administration, however, those measures appear to have expanded beyond hi-tech fields. “The definition of ‘sensitive’ has become so broad that even business, humanities programmes and course-based programmes with no research component are getting caught up,” Zhou said. Jack Jing, general manager of Beijing-based migration service provider WellTrend, said extended background checks had become standard procedure for US-bound students, though timelines varied by academic level and field of study. “Secondary school students typically face checks lasting three to five weeks, while postgraduate students in STEM fields can expect waits of two to six months,” he said. A PhD candidate in electrical and computer engineering, identified only by her surname Hu, attended her visa interview in July and has since chosen to defer her studies until next spring. “As my visa status is a complete black box, I cannot make any meaningful plans for my life,” the 26-year-old Changsha native said. “Pursuing a higher degree is one step in a much longer journey that I mapped out for myself. But having all your plans frozen is emotionally distressing.” The international student bottleneck comes amid a slew of tightening immigration policies in Washington, and more than a year after the Trump administration vowed to “aggressively” revoke the student visas of Chinese nationals. In September of last year, Trump raised the fee for new H-1B visa petitions from around US$1,000 to US$100,000. That move was blocked by a federal court earlier this summer, but the administration last week proposed a new regulation that would raise the fee for the skilled worker visas even higher, to over US$103,000. Earlier this month, the US temporarily suspended immigrant visa appointments at consulates around the world. Meanwhile, under a new rule effective from September 15, international students on F-1 visas will only be allowed to stay in the US for an initial period of up to four years. Previously, students were granted “duration of status”, which allowed them to stay without an expiration date as long as they maintained their student status. Students pursuing longer programmes must now formally apply to extend their permission to stay, creating extra paperwork and new uncertainty. Additionally, the post-graduation grace period for international students has been halved from 60 days to just 30. Those who have finished their studies must either leave the United States or change to another visa status within that narrow window. Desperate visa applicants are exhausting every possible avenue to expedite their cases. Standard embassy email inquiries go unanswered. Universities themselves have sent letters to authorities, with little effect. Zhou and Hu both said they had contacted US senators in their host universities’ electoral districts, but lawmakers could not compel federal agencies to accelerate background checks. In May 2026, a coalition of 32 university associations warned that continued processing delays could discourage international enrolment. Last week, 30 senators sent a letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanding answers about appointment unavailability and timely processing of student visas. The pervasive sense of powerlessness has made some students easy targets for online scammers claiming to have “internal connections at the embassy” who can fast-track approvals. Zhou said several students had been defrauded of substantial sums. “Students are already in such a desperate situation, waiting anxiously with no way out,” he said. “Taking advantage of the desperation is awful.” For those still waiting, the psychological toll mounts. Hu from Changsha said she had obtained a five-year US student visa in 2024 with no problems. “At that time, I did not take the offer to go because of family reasons. If I had known things would turn out like this, I would have planned far more carefully,” she said. The stakes are higher for another prospective student, identified only by his surname Qian, who has been admitted to an electrical engineering PhD programme. His university allows only one deferral with no option to postpone again, meaning any additional delay would result in his offer being revoked. He described living in “constant anxiety” that had taken a severe toll on his mental health. “I have been working towards this goal since my undergraduate years, and now at the final leg of the journey, the path is suddenly blocked,” he said. “Even if I defer, there is no guarantee I will ever get to go. I will be living with anxiety until I finally get an answer on my visa.” As the autumn semester begins, affected students are left to rethink their futures in an increasingly unpredictable geopolitical climate. For Zhou, the lessons for future students are stark: have a backup plan, apply for visa interviews as soon as possible, and never assume that academic merit alone will guarantee a smooth passage across the border. Additional reporting by Phoebe Zhang

title: Freed Hongkonger sent back to jail as storm delays deportation from Philippines
description: Lawyer says Tang Lung-wai’s return to maximum-security prison constitutes ‘illegal detention’ after severe weather halts deportation.
content: A Hong Kong man has been returned to a Philippine prison in what his legal team condemned as “illegal detention”, after severe weather halted his deportation following his release. Tang Lung-wai’s Philippine lawyer, Blessie Rose Carpena, told the South China Morning Post that prison authorities escorted Tang to the Bureau of Immigration last Friday. However, because government offices were suspended due to a passing typhoon, he was returned to the maximum-security New Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa. “[The Bureau of Immigration’s] delay of his release can constitute illegal detention,” Carpena said, describing Tang as “frustrated and devastated.” Tang was arrested in the Philippines in July 2000 for possessing methamphetamine, also known as ice, and sentenced to 40 years in prison in 2011. He has maintained his innocence and fought the conviction for more than two decades. In late July, a Manila court ruled that Tang’s sentence was fully served after factoring in good conduct time allowances, ordering his immediate release and deportation. Carpena said the prison was ready to release him, but the Bureau of Immigration could not accept him without approval from its commissioner. She added that deportation backlogs in the Philippines remained common, noting that another foreign client had waited six months for repatriation, while several others have faced delays exceeding a year. Former lawmaker Paul Tse Wai-chun, a lawyer assisting Tang for two decades, argued that the Hongkonger was now a free man and should be allowed to wait for deportation in a hotel rather than a prison. “It is outrageous. How can he be brought back after he is released from prison?” he said, echoing claims that holding Tang at the correctional facility amounted to unlawful detention because authorities no longer had grounds to imprison him. Tse said he had already sought help from Director of Immigration Benson Kwok Joon-fung, who pledged to follow up on the case with China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. However, former Secretary for Security Lai Tung-kwok said that since Tang has no rights of residence there, Philippine authorities had the power to confine him during a legal deportation process. He said he was confident Tang could return home in a reasonable time frame, subject to the Philippines’ administrative process. A spokesman for Hong Kong’s Immigration Department said the government placed great importance on the lawful rights of residents detained overseas. He said the department had immediately contacted Philippine authorities through the Chinese embassy in Manila to learn about Tang’s length of sentence served and his subsequent deportation arrangements. It had also forwarded relevant information to the embassy to facilitate identity verification and travel document issuance once deportation arrangements were finalised. Tang’s case previously drew high-level diplomatic attention. In 2018, then-city leader Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor wrote to Rodrigo Duterte, the country’s president at the time, to urge him to push immigration authorities to hasten their search for records believed to prove Tang’s innocence. Although the records indicated that Tang was not in the Philippines during the period local police said he was under surveillance, the Philippine Supreme Court dismissed his final appeal in 2020.

title: Former top European official adopts bullish tone on China-EU trade talks as deadline nears
description: The former president of the European Council says the two sides are approaching a common ground.
content: A former top European Union official has struck a bullish tone on the outlook for China-EU trade talks, saying he expects progress in the coming months. Charles Michel, president of the European Council from 2019 to 2024, told reporters in a media briefing in Shanghai on Monday that both sides were willing to pursue more common ground through talks. “On the EU side there is an expectation that by the end of October or November, or at least by the end of the year ... there will be some progress achieved in the fields of those four tracks,” he said, referring to a consultation mechanism between Beijing and Brussels established in June, where four topics – trade and investment, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization reform – had been discussed. At that time, Brussels set a three-month deadline for rebalancing trade ties, amid fears that cheap Chinese imports were helping to deindustrialise swathes of the European manufacturing economy. “China needs the access to the European Union’s markets, and China does not have the alternatives,” Michel said, who is now a professor at the China Europe International Business School. He added that EU market access was of important political and economic value, with Brussels using it as leverage during negotiations with Beijing. In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to announce new measures aimed at rebalancing ties with China, which national leaders will then debate at a summit in Brussels in October. Chinese exports of low-value goods to the bloc fell by 54 per cent in value terms and 40.8 per cent in volume terms in July, after a new tax of €3 (US$3.48) was levied on all packages worth less than €150 coming from outside the EU from July 1. But anti-subsidy tariffs on battery electric cars (EV), ranging from 17.8 per cent to 45.3 per cent, have yet to effectively curb surging sales of Chinese-made vehicles to the bloc. In July alone, China’s EV exports to France soared 365.5 per cent, while the figure was 530.9 per cent in the Netherlands. The Dutch figures are likely inflated, since Rotterdam is a main port of entry for goods bound for the rest of the bloc. Germany, Europe’s automotive hub, brought in 40.8 per cent more EVs from China in July than a year earlier. In January, the European Commission and Beijing reached a consensus to replace the tariffs with price undertaking agreements with individual Chinese carmakers through negotiations. “This minimum price [mechanism] is already an attempt to make progress in those negotiations,” said Michel. “On the other hand, from the European perspective, it’s not so easy because in terms of implementation of such an agreement, that would be quite complicated.”

title: Opinion | Move over Strait of Hormuz. Innovation chokepoints are the ones to watch
description: The strength of a chokepoint lies not only in the force of the initial blow but in the scale of the long-term damage it leaves behind.
content: In interstate rivalry, countries have many instruments at their disposal, from military conflict to coercive monetary and financial measures. What happens when rival powers have comparable strength, anticipate pressure through financial institutions and take pre-emptive steps to limit its effects, yet the confrontation continues? The struggle then shifts towards trade and sanctions, including attempts to block or control critical chokepoints in the global economy. The first type of chokepoint involves corridors for traditional resources. For example, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is like a shot from a weapon with enormous first-strike power but relatively little economic “memory” once the restriction is removed. Oil, liquefied natural gas and fertiliser flows are disrupted and prices jump, but the global trading system begins to adjust as alternative supply routes expand. Over time, such blockages encourage the development of new routes, reducing the importance of the original chokepoint. Blocking a resource corridor can inflict severe short-term damage, but its economic impact tends to diminish over the longer term. A second type of chokepoint concerns supplies of rare earth elements, which are critical to hi-tech industries. The problem is disruption to minerals whose alternative supplies are difficult to scale quickly. Here, what matters is not so much the force of the initial blow as the longer economic memory it leaves behind. A recent International Monetary Fund (IMF) paper is particularly revealing. It asks how severe the macroeconomic impact would be on economies dependent on Chinese rare earths if they suddenly lost a large share of their supplies? One result concerns an 80 per cent reduction in available rare earth supplies. In a short-run scenario with very limited substitution, the IMF estimates gross domestic product losses relative to the baseline of about 1.8 per cent in Japan, 1.5 per cent in the United States and 1.2 per cent in Germany. The key point is that alternative processing capacity cannot be created in a week, a month or even a year. China’s advantage therefore lies partly in its influence over complex supply chains whose disruption cannot be quickly repaired. A second IMF study from July reinforces this point. It suggests that the rare earth chokepoint has a longer economic memory because bypassing it requires not simply finding alternative routes but building new physical and technological production capacity. The fact that the IMF devoted two recent studies to rare earths underlines how important this vulnerability has become. An additional negative effect is that slowing the development of sophisticated industries, such as microelectronics and automobile manufacturing, can push a country out of markets that are difficult to re-enter later. This brings us to the most important type of chokepoint: advanced semiconductors, lithography and artificial intelligence – in other words, innovation chokepoints. Here, the initial impact of an economic weapon might be weak or even barely visible in the statistics, while its economic memory can be the longest. The reason is that lost time in a technological race, especially when technological progress is accelerating, can seriously constrain a country’s long-term development. Meanwhile, its competitor continues to accumulate technology, strengthen human capital with the necessary skills and, as a result, raise total factor productivity. Restrictions might eventually end and growth rates can recover, yet the affected economy can remain at a permanently lower level of development and productivity. According to IMF estimates, in the most severe scenarios, trade fragmentation could reduce the long-term level of global output by almost 7 per cent relative to a world without fragmentation. If technological lag is added, long-term output losses in some countries could reach as much as 12 per cent. Still, there is nothing new under the sun. We can find an ancient Hormuz analogue in the grain route to Athens through the Hellespont. During the Corinthian War, the Spartans assembled around 80 ships, moved into the Dardanelles and stopped grain vessels bound for Athens. This quickly pushed Athens towards peace in 386 BC. A medieval equivalent of rare earths was alum: small in volume but critically important for dyeing cloth and processing wool, and geographically concentrated. Research shows that Ottoman expansion in the eastern Mediterranean seriously disrupted the existing supply chain. Creating new production capacity was technologically difficult since alum ore had to be roasted, treated with water, boiled and crystallised. A medieval example of an innovation chokepoint is Byzantine silk. Silkworm eggs and knowledge of sericulture were brought into the empire, but one study shows that the idea of an immediate technological transfer is too simplistic. There is no firm evidence of well-established Byzantine sericulture before the 11th century, while dependence on imported raw silk persisted at least into the 10th century. What do history and today’s hybrid rivalry among major powers tell us? The strength of a chokepoint lies not only in the force of the initial blow but in the scale of the long-term damage it leaves behind. Lost shipments of oil can be replaced. Production chains have to be rebuilt. Lost time at the technological frontier can be almost impossible to recover.

title: Israel and Greece sign US$3.5 billion defence deal, largest ever between the 2
description: Buyers favouring Israel's battle-tested weapons have helped push its defence exports to record highs.
content: Israel signed a multibillion-dollar weapons deal with Greece, the largest between the two Mediterranean countries, as Israeli defence exports soar. Israel’s Defence Ministry said on Monday the nearly €3 billion (US$3.5 billion) defence export deal, coined Achilles Shield, was one of the country’s largest and included a multilayered air defence system for Greece using Israeli technology. “Israel and Greece share common strategic interests and face shared regional challenges. At a time when actors with hegemonic ambitions are seeking to expand their influence and undermine stability in the region,” said Defence Minister Israel Katz. The agreement comes as Israeli weapons exports have reached record highs with more than US$19 billion last year, a 30 per cent increase from 2024, according to official data, despite widespread criticism of Israel’s conduct in its wars in Gaza, with Hezbollah and with Iran. Experts say governments look to Israel because its weapons are battle-tested and they are able to see in real time that the munitions and systems work. Israel and Greece have deepened defence ties in the last decade. Monday’s signing, however, marks the most significant deal between the two as Greece focuses on modernising its armed forces to keep pace with its neighbour and fellow Nato member Turkey amid long-standing disputes over sea boundaries in the eastern Mediterranean. Previous deals have included a US$1.65 billion agreement with Israeli defence contractor Elbit to build a flight training school in southern Greece as well as the planned sale of Israeli rocket launchers, anti‑tank guided missiles and drones. Israel says Monday’s agreement was the first time it would provide a complete array of defence weapons against a range of threats from ballistic missiles to drones. It includes multiple Israeli systems such as David Sling and SPYDER as well as a new national command and control system. In addition to the agreement, a complementary deal valued at US$30 million (€26 million) was signed for the sale of Rafael’s Drone Dome systems, it said. “Modern conflicts have already altered the parameters of military defence and deterrence,” Greece’s Defence Minister Nikos Dendias said in a statement after the agreement was signed. “Technology, ballistic missiles, satellite communications, unmanned systems, cyber threats, hybrid forms of warfare and the interconnection of fields of operations have long rendered pre-existing defence doctrines completely unrealistic,” he said. More than half of the Israeli arms industry’s sales are for missiles, rockets and air-defence systems. For the first time, Israel has surpassed the United Kingdom in its share of global arms exports, making it the world’s seventh-biggest supplier, according to a March report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

title: Nearly all Wang Fuk Court owners accept buy-out, leaving 17 holdouts as offer ends
description: 17 of 1,984 Wang Fuk Court owners fail to accept offer as deadline ends, facing compulsory acquisition at lower compensation levels.
content: More than 99 per cent of homeowners at Hong Kong’s fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court have accepted a government buy-out of their flats, leaving just 17 households facing potential compulsory acquisition after the scheme closed on Monday. By the cut‑off time at 5pm on Monday, 1,967 or 99.1 per cent of the estate’s 1,984 flat owners had returned acceptance letters. The remaining 17 may face compulsory acquisition at lower compensation levels in the future. Among those who accepted, 1,559, or 78.6 per cent, have signed formal sale and purchase agreements with the government. “The government will continue to follow up on the procedures for acquiring the remaining titles at full speed to take forward the title acquisition exercise” it said on Monday. The HK$6.8 billion (US$867.24 million) scheme was announced in February after a fire tore through seven blocks of the Tai Po estate last November, killing 168 people and displacing about 5,000 residents in Hong Kong’s deadliest blaze in more than seven decades. In June, the government extended the buy-back offer to Wang Chi House, the only block spared by the fire, adding another HK$1 billion to the scheme’s cost. Officials have ruled out on‑site redevelopment. Under the scheme, the government is acquiring flats at HK$8,000 or HK$10,500 per square foot, depending on whether the owner has paid the land premium. Participating owners can use the cash compensation to purchase a flat on the private open market or join a special sales exercise to buy new subsidised housing under a flat-for-flat arrangement. Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said last Sunday that the buy-out offer was already 30 per cent above pre-fire valuations and would not be negotiated, as in a private sale. He acknowledged that some residents felt the sum was insufficient but warned that compulsory acquisition would yield substantially lower compensation. Vincent Ho Kui-yip, a former president of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors, earlier agreed that the acquisition price was a “generous offer”, noting that Wang Fuk Court was more than four decades old. He noted that the rate surpassed recent transaction prices for other Home Ownership Scheme flats in Tai Po. Pre-fire valuations by the institute put the market value of flats in the eight-block estate at about HK$6,000 to HK$8,000 per square foot. Lawmaker Bill Tang Ka‑piu previously suggested that the small group of owners were holding out for various reasons, including emotional attachments, misconceptions regarding compensation, unresolved inheritance procedures and family disagreements. The South China Morning Post earlier spoke to six residents determined not to sell, several of whom maintained that no financial package could compensate for the loss of their long-time homes and communal ties.

title: China to speed up bond issuance after national  meeting on stabilising investment: analysts
description: The fixed-income securities are to be used to fund national infrastructure and construction ventures to boost the economy.
content: After China’s top economic planner convened a rare national meeting to promote investments, analysts say that authorities are set to speed up bond issuance to fund government-led projects to keep growth on track for the rest of the year. The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) held a meeting on Friday with many of China’s key investment-related central government agencies, including the ministers of industry and information technology, housing and urban-rural development, and transport, alongside senior leadership from water resources and energy. Officials pledged to “maximise investment potential” in areas such as technological innovation, industrial upgrading and urban renewal, and accelerate the deployment of the policy-based financing tool and local government special bonds for major construction projects, according to a readout by state news agency Xinhua. “The current policy focus is clearly on boosting investment instead of consumption, more so than at any time since the global financial crisis,” said Song Yu, chief China economist at UBS Securities, in a report on Monday. The high-level turnout was “unusual” and showed the importance of the meeting, Song said, adding that the government now recognised the limits of consumer goods subsidies in boosting consumption to drive growth. Song noted that faster disbursement of fiscal funds could provide near-term support for infrastructure and related manufacturing activity, and that fixed-asset investment growth could show improvement in the rest of the year. Overall fixed-asset investment, covering major areas such as infrastructure, manufacturing and property construction, fell 6.7 per cent in the January-July period, underperforming market expectations and widening from the 5.7 per cent decline recorded in the first half of the year. This was despite 2026 being the first year of China’s new five-year plan cycle, which typically sees stronger investment as authorities begin work on planned projects laid out in the new development blueprint. Su Jian, an economics professor at Peking University, noted that the latest measures are largely in “non-traditional forms of investments” and aimed at stabilising China’s economy to meet its annual growth target, especially given slowing economic data in recent months. Authorities at Friday’s meeting said they would advance projects under the “six networks”, a national infrastructure programme to upgrade the country’s water, electricity, computing, telecommunications, logistics and underground pipe systems by 2030. This continues a shift away from projects in real estate, which were a primary driver of investment in China, now mired in a persistent downturn since 2021. The sector has continued to drag on economic performance, with growth becoming increasingly uneven as China seeks to expand its economy by between 4.5 and 5 per cent this year. Gross domestic product growth slowed to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, the softest quarterly expansion since late 2022, constrained by domestic consumption and investment but buoyed by strong exports. According to Goldman Sachs, bond issuance was already picking up. Around 61 per cent of this year’s 11.9 trillion yuan (US$1.77 trillion) total government bond quota had been issued as of the end of last week, the investment bank said, marking an increase from 56 per cent recorded the week before. The recent measures by the NDRC “suggest government-led investment may be accelerating to help meet this year’s growth target”, the bank’s analysts wrote in a Sunday note.

title: Why Japan’s hypersonic and underwater weapon plans might worry China
description: Beijing has hit out at Tokyo’s moves to arm submarine drones with long-range missiles and test hypersonic weapons in Australia.
content: In its latest swipe at Tokyo’s military build-up, China singled out Japan’s plans to arm its submarine drones with long-range missiles and test hypersonic weapons in Australia. Analysts say those moves could threaten People’s Liberation Army amphibious groups and surface combatants within the “first island chain” – potentially affecting the PLA Navy’s ability to operate in the event of a Taiwan conflict. The strategically important first island chain stretches from Japan to Taiwan, the Philippines and Borneo. China’s defence ministry spokesman Zhang Xiaogang highlighted the two initiatives on Thursday, saying Japan had “openly expanded its military arsenal”. Zhang said the “dangerous” moves had a “striking resemblance” to Japan’s pre-World War II militarisation, though he did not explain why these particular weapon programmes could pose challenges for the PLA. Japan has rapidly expanded its long-range strike capabilities since adopting a “counterstrike capability” in its 2022 security strategy. Under the policy, Tokyo says it could strike military targets in an adversary’s territory for self-defence following an armed attack, while pre-emptive strikes remain prohibited. Japan has already begun deploying domestically developed stand-off weapons, including the Type-25 hypervelocity gliding projectile (HVGP), which entered service in March. Japan does not currently have a system it designates as hypersonic in service, according to analysts. More advanced systems – including the Block 2 HVGP, which the defence ministry says will fly at hypersonic speed, and a scramjet-powered hypersonic cruise missile (HCM) – remain under development. Beyond land-based systems, Tokyo is also looking to take its long-range strike capabilities under water. Kyodo News on August 19 reported plans to develop an underwater-launched hypersonic missile, which analysts said would be an HCM fired from a crewed submarine. Separately, the news outlet reported that Tokyo planned to research technology that could enable unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) to launch long-range missiles. The research would build on Japan’s existing work on underwater drones. Defence analyst Yoshihiro Inaba, the Japan correspondent for Naval News, said the defence ministry’s technology agency was developing a modular UUV for surveillance, submarine tracking and mine-laying. While plans to arm the UUV remained at an early stage, he said they could eventually supplement Japan’s smaller submarine fleet. If equipped with such weapons, the UUVs could pose a “persistent threat” to PLA naval vessels operating around Japan’s southwestern Nansei Islands or supporting a potential attack on Taiwan, Inaba said. Timothy Heath, head of defence research firm Perceptum, said missile-armed UUVs could be difficult to detect because they might be quieter than submarines and launched from unexpected locations, giving Beijing little warning. He said their lower cost could also allow Japan to deploy them in greater numbers. If several launched missiles simultaneously, they could potentially overwhelm a target’s defences. Christopher Hughes, professor of international politics and Japanese studies at the University of Warwick, said China was “clearly irked” by Japan’s development of these capabilities and was “probably right to fear them”. Hughes noted that lessons from the Ukraine war were helping shape what Tokyo calls its “new ways of warfare”, influencing procurement and the coming review of Japan’s three strategic defence documents. He said Japanese defence planners had watched how Ukrainian drones and missiles severely constrained Russia’s Black Sea Fleet and were considering whether similar capabilities could constrain the PLA Navy. The two emerging technologies could pose different operational problems for the PLA. Hughes said the speed and manoeuvrability of Japan’s future HVGPs could make them difficult to intercept, while UUVs deployed in large numbers could also be difficult to counter. Japan’s more advanced hypersonic weapons could also significantly extend the country’s strike range, with Inaba saying Tokyo was pursuing more capable HVGP variants and the separate scramjet-powered HCM. Inaba said the planned Block 2A and Block 2B variants of the HVGP were expected to reach about 2,000km (1,240 miles) and 3,000km (1,860 miles), respectively, potentially putting some targets on the Chinese mainland within reach. But Masashi Murano, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, argued that the value of Japan’s future hypersonic weapons would lie primarily in anti-ship strikes rather than for land targets. Murano was more cautious about missile-armed UUVs. He said their size could severely limit the number of existing missiles they could carry, while reloading at sea would be difficult. “China’s ground targets are highly redundant and dispersed,” he said, noting that land attacks at the scale Japan could conduct would have limited impact unless integrated into a broader US campaign, while damaged infrastructure could be repaired. Targeting PLA naval forces would be the most efficient way to inflict losses on Beijing, according to Murano. China last week also took aim at Japan’s plan to test hypersonic weapons in Australia. On August 18, Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and his Australian counterpart Richard Marles agreed to advance arrangements for Tokyo to use Australian missile ranges over the next decade, including for its hypersonic programme. Koizumi called the move “groundbreaking”, while Marles said it built on discussions about Australia providing “strategic depth” to Japan. For Beijing, however, the cooperation could have implications beyond giving Japan more space to test its weapons. “Conducting tests in Australia would make Chinese intelligence collection considerably more difficult than if such activities were carried out in waters around Japan,” Inaba said. “Moreover, the arrangement clearly reflects the growing political and military alignment between Japan and Australia, which itself is likely to be viewed with concern in Beijing.”

title: China’s Z.ai revenue jumps 400% as total losses narrow on explosive cloud gains
description: First-half revenue from cloud-based deployment services soared over 2,700 per cent year on year.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence company Z.ai on Monday reported a 400 per cent increase in first-half revenue, driven by explosive growth in its open platform and application programming interface business, which helped narrow total losses despite higher research and development spending. Revenue for the six months ended June 30 rose to 953.89 million yuan (US$142 million). Full-year sales were expected to expand 514 per cent to 4.45 billion yuan, according to consensus estimates from analysts polled by Bloomberg. Beyond its first-half results, Z.ai said that its annual recurring revenue (ARR) – a key metric that projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period – had reached US$1.6 billion by the end of August. For comparison, Yan Junjie, CEO of rival firm MiniMax, said last week that his firm’s ARR had risen to US$800 million in August. Z.ai’s total loss for the six months ended June 30 narrowed 12.1 per cent to 2.07 billion yuan, while adjusted net loss increased 12.1 per cent to 1.96 billion yuan. Research and development expenses rose 33.6 per cent to 2.13 billion yuan as Z.ai – known domestically as Zhipu AI – continued to invest aggressively in computing power and base model performance. Shares of Hong Kong-listed Z.ai closed up 9.63 per cent at HK$1,195 on Monday ahead of the earnings release. The stock remains down about 60 per cent from its record high of HK$2,980 reached in June, when the company’s market capitalisation briefly approached HK$1 trillion (US$127.5 billion). Z.ai and Shanghai-based MiniMax, China’s first two publicly traded large language model developers, saw their valuations soar after blockbuster initial public offerings in January, though both now trade below their peaks. Top-line performance in the first half was primarily driven by cloud-based deployment services, where revenue jumped 2,736 per cent year on year to 825 million yuan from 29 million yuan. The segment accounted for 86.5 per cent of total revenue, up from 15.2 per cent a year earlier, reflecting Z.ai’s continuing shift away from customised, on-premise deployment towards cloud application programming interfaces and subscription-based agent products. Revenue from on-premise deployment fell 20.5 per cent to 128.7 million yuan. Gross profit increased 163.7 per cent to 252 million yuan, yielding a gross profit margin of 26.4 per cent compared with 50 per cent in the same period last year. Cloud inference generally carries lower margins than on-premises deployment because of its heavy computing overhead. The company has accelerated product releases this year to convert model capabilities into recurring revenue. It launched GLM-5-Turbo in March, introduced GLM-5.1 in April and released GLM-5.2 in June. Its latest flagship, GLM-5.3, launched in August and scored 60 on benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index – on par with Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, widely regarded as China’s benchmark open-weight model. Z.ai said GLM-5.3 improved coding and long-horizon agent capabilities entirely through post-training, without altering the underlying base model. The company last week also released GLM-5.3-Flash, a lower-cost multimodal model anonymously tested as Ox Alpha on OpenRouter and OpenCode. Z.ai said the test traffic was served on a large cluster of domestically developed AI chips. The launches come as Z.ai attempts to evolve from a model-as-a-service provider into an agent platform spanning its ZCode coding tool, AutoGLM and consumer-facing products. Registered users on Z.ai’s GLM model-as-a-service platform surpassed 7.4 million in August, up 144 per cent from the beginning of the year. Liu Debin, chairman of Z.ai, said the company had begun work on its next-generation model, which would feature a larger parameter size, longer context window and native multimodal capabilities. Z.ai was actively exploring overseas expansion through partnerships with global cloud service providers, one executive said. These agreements included local deployments of its open-source models and revenue-sharing arrangements. However, the transition remains constrained by computing supply and high inference costs. Z.ai previously acknowledged that shortages had affected service quality during peak periods, while arguing that customers continued to accept price increases because of model performance. Asked whether the company had sufficient computing power to sustain its model training and inference demands, an executive said Z.ai had been expanding compute capacity “at a very healthy pace” since earlier this year, adding that domestic chips would handle an increasing share of its inference workloads.

title: Land tender for flagship Northern Metropolis tech hub draws 6 bids
description: Operator Loop Hong Kong Park Company hails ‘enthusiastic response’ to tender that follows land sale for pilot project at Hung Shui Kiu.
content: Hong Kong’s flagship technology hub at the border received a better-than-expected six bids from conglomerates and hi-tech firms for its inaugural land tender by the deadline on Monday, with industry leaders describing the project as a springboard for mainland Chinese firms going global. The Loop Hong Kong Park Company, which operates the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park (HSITP), said it received strong interest in four land parcels with a combined gross floor area exceeding 76,000 square metres. The sites are earmarked for innovation and technology (I&T), and talent accommodation. The tender followed closely after a land sale for a Northern Metropolis pilot project at Hung Shui Kiu, which drew only two bidders in July. The Hung Shui Kiu site is the first large-scale land sale to combine property development with the creation of an I&T hub. The bidders for the tender, which opened in June, included high-end innovation and technology industries and large conglomerates, the operator said. “The enthusiastic response to this inaugural tender shows the industry’s full recognition of Hong Kong’s strengths in innovation and technology, as well as its confidence and high expectations for the park’s development,” it said. It added that the site sale used a weighted “two-envelope” scoring system, allocating 70 per cent to technical proposals and 30 per cent to financial offers. The operator said this framework encourages developers to submit forward-looking blueprints that bridge scientific research with commercial applications across the entire supply chain. Successful bidders will be responsible for the design, construction, financing and management of the relevant sites, including the accommodation facilities. Winning bids are expected to be announced in October. The Loop Hong Kong Park Company said it would evaluate submissions based on the criteria set out in the tender documents, with the contracts expected to be awarded before the end of the year. HSITP is located in the Hetao cooperation zone proposed by Beijing in 2017, comprising two parks on either side of the border between Hong Kong and the mainland. The project is part of the Northern Metropolis megaproject. Kathy Lee, head of research and retail at Colliers, said the response exceeded market expectations and highlighted keen corporate interest in the border innovation park. Backed by strong support from both local and mainland authorities, the park offered a unique competitive edge as a nexus where cross-border data flows, biological samples and international capital converge, she added. Lee said that this ecosystem enabled tech companies to scale up research and development while accelerating commercial expansion. Lawmaker Duncan Chiu noted that the park could serve as the first pilot project for cross-border innovation, achieving early breakthroughs in life sciences and the movement of research personnel. “Expectations for cross-border synergy remain high, and the project offers substantial advantages for tech firms,” he said. Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, said the project could serve as a launch pad for mainland tech firms to expand globally by adapting to Hong Kong’s institutional framework. According to the tender documents obtained by the South China Morning Post earlier, bidders must deposit a bank-backed, on-demand “construction bond” of HK$100 million as a financial guarantee upon signing the agreement as security for fulfilling contractual obligations. The four land parcels comprise two dedicated information technology sites and two sites for accommodation for workers, with a total gross floor area exceeding 76,000 square metres. Bidders also face an exceptionally tight deadline, as the document also stipulates that construction must be finished within 30 months of signing the sublease, with a “long stop date” final target set for April 1, 2030.

title: Historic Olympic Games qualification caps Thailand’s volleyball rise, China’s fall
description: Thailand beat China 3-2 to win Asian Women’s Volleyball Championship, earning a spot at a Games for the first time.
content: Thailand’s victory over China in the final of the Asian Women’s Volleyball Championship earned them their first-ever Olympics spot, underscoring both the former’s tactical ascension and deepening concerns over the latter’s future. The hosts led 2-1 in Tianjin, before Thailand rallied to win 3-2 and complete a clean sweep of Asian powerhouses, with victories over South Korea and Japan coming in the lead up to Sunday’s triumph. Qualification for the 2028 Games in Los Angeles comes 47 years after the start of the women’s programme, and after three previous near misses. At the heart of the rise, has been a highly coordinated tactical system, implemented by head coach Kiattipong Radchatagriengkai, who returned to lead the team in 2024. Despite an average height of 1.75 metres, compared to China’s 1.88 metres, Thailand compensated with tactical flexibility, recording a 65 per cent dig rate, eight service aces, and five attackers scoring in double digits. “We are very happy, it’s a miracle for us. This is our dream,” an emotional Kiattipong said afterwards. “For myself as a coach, I waited for 30 years and we qualified for the Olympics. And some of our players waited for this time for so long.” Kiattipong, who is married to former China team captain and Olympic gold medallist Feng Kun, also praised China, calling them “our teachers” who helped build Thai volleyball over decades. “In the next two years, China will 100 per cent qualify for the Olympic Games, I believe and I trust,” he added. “They still have more chances through the world rankings.” China will now need to rely on progressing through the World Championships or World Volleyball Nations League, and Hui Ruoqi, another former national team captain, noted the side’s struggles against a “more compact, flexible, Asian style”. “Our net dominance was not displayed,” Hui said, while noting that Thailand had some highly experienced veterans at key positions. Hui also highlighted critical difficulties at China’s setter position, citing both technical and physical challenges. She pointed out that although China had cruised through earlier rounds with 3-0 victories, several Chinese players suffered muscle cramps during the gruelling final, exposing the team’s struggle under sustained high intensity and long rallies. “This serves as a wake-up call for future matches – future training needs to be stepped up to a higher intensity,” Hui said, expressing hope that the national team would review the loss and grow faster in the future. Gong Xiangyu, the current China captain, pointed to psychological shortcomings during critical moments. “Today in this match, we indeed did not perform as well as the Thailand team in terms of handling pressure, and in terms of mindset when playing crucial points, we were not as firm and decisive as the Thailand team,” Gong said. “We need to focus more on on-court adaptability and demonstrate the desire to win through our play.” The defeat drew severe criticism from prominent Chinese sports commentator Yang Yi, who said it was the “weakest China women’s volleyball team in history” and called the loss to shorter opponents a “man-made disaster”. Yang said that while Chinese teams no longer feared defeat, the women’s volleyball side held a unique cultural status, making such a performance difficult to accept. “After losing the Asian Championship, this current state of the Chinese women’s volleyball team really must come to an end,” Yang added. “Change is imperative.”

title: PetroChina’s first-half profit jumps 22% as higher oil prices offset Iran war supply hit
description: As LNG and EV adoption bite into traditional fuel sales, higher global crude prices help the state-backed giant deliver strong earnings.
content: PetroChina, China’s largest oil and gas producer, has announced that it is gradually restoring operations at its Middle Eastern projects after the US-Israeli war in Iran severely disrupted global energy flows this year. On Monday, the company reported a 22 per cent jump in first-half net profit to 103.9 billion yuan (US$15.4 billion) for the six months ended June, as higher crude oil prices boosted earnings from its upstream operations while natural-gas operations offset weaker oil production and declining domestic demand for refined fuels. Overall revenue increased 5.3 per cent to 1.53 trillion yuan (US$227.55 billion), according to the company’s interim results. “We are steadily resuming production at our Middle East projects, with output in the region having recovered to nearly 90 per cent of pre-conflict levels,” said Ren Lixin, the company’s executive director and president, at a results briefing. The Beijing-based energy giant has benefited from a surge in oil prices amid geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. PetroChina reported that its average realised crude oil price rose 15.6 per cent year on year to US$76.53 per barrel, helping operating profit in its oil, gas and new-energy segment climb 15.3 per cent to 100.4 billion yuan. Higher prices have helped offset weaker oil production. Total crude output fell 2.8 per cent to 462.9 million barrels during the period, largely because overseas output declined 14.2 per cent amid lower production from Middle East projects, according to the interim report. Domestic crude production slipped 0.5 per cent, while domestic natural gas output rose 2.4 per cent. PetroChina’s downstream businesses also improved despite weakening demand for conventional fuels. Operating profit from refining, chemicals and new materials rose 31.4 per cent to 14.5 billion yuan, while the firm’s marketing segment operating profit climbed 50.3 per cent to 11.4 billion yuan, the earnings showed. However, the volume of crude processed fell 5.6 per cent, while refined-product output dropped 8.8 per cent, as higher oil prices and adoption of new-energy sources weighed on demand. PetroChina said domestic sales of petrol, kerosene and diesel also declined 7.3 per cent. “Although overall refined-fuel consumption may continue to decline in the second half, there are also some positive signs,” chief financial officer Wang Hua said. “The market generally expects the decline in petrol and diesel consumption to narrow from the first half.” Wang explained that the expansion of new-energy vehicles mainly drove the first-half weakness, along with liquefied natural gas and electric heavy trucks as well as elevated oil prices following the outbreak of the Iran war. Highlighting this transition, PetroChina’s vehicle LNG sales jumped 78.7 per cent, while charging volume increased 150 per cent, he added. The company also declared an interim dividend of 0.26 yuan per share, which would be paid on October 26. Its shares fell 0.2 per cent to close at HK$10.17 (US$1.29) in Hong Kong on Monday. PetroChina’s results mirror those of its rival, the China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC), which last week reported a 23.4 per cent increase in first-half net profit to a record 85.8 billion yuan, driven by higher oil prices and increased production. CNOOC’s revenue rose 16.9 per cent to 242.7 billion yuan, while net production increased 3.7 per cent to 398.7 million barrels of oil equivalent.

title: Hongkonger jailed 3½ years for molesting girlfriend’s daughter, filming assaults
description: Defendant, 47, jailed after police found nude photo of 11-year-old girl in his wallet during response to family quarrel.
content: A moving services manager has been sentenced to 3½ years in prison for molesting his girlfriend’s 11-year-old daughter at home and filming and photographing the assaults, with a Hong Kong judge imposing a heavier penalty to reflect the impact on the vulnerable child. Deputy District Judge Ivy Chui Yee-mei said on Monday that a deterrent sentence was necessary for the 47-year-old defendant, whose offence was “far worse” than most indecent assault cases because he possessed 233 videos and photos taken during the attacks between August 2023 and March 2024. Citing a psychologist’s report, Chui noted that the defendant was not a paedophile but had shown a sexual interest in his then-girlfriend’s daughter. The defendant told the psychologist he had been under the influence of alcohol and had mistaken the girl for his girlfriend. He pleaded guilty to 18 charges: seven counts of indecent assault and 11 counts of possession of child pornography. He admitted using his phone to take photos and a home security camera to record videos during the assaults. A nude picture of the girl was found in his wallet when he was arrested. The judge said that as the defendant was seen as a stepfather to the girl, the case involved a serious breach of trust. “Home is supposed to be where a child should feel safe and protected, but it turned out to be a place where [the victim] suffered from repeated assaults,” Chui said. The girl refused to assist the court by allowing a psychologist to assess her and prepare an impact report, and police had been unable to contact her mother. Chui pointed out that filming the assaults and storing the images on his digital devices had caused the victim “extra pain”. The defence submitted that the defendant did not coerce the girl into performing the indecent acts, but Chui said the acts were very serious. Evidence showed he molested the girl by touching her, forcibly kissing her and groping her chest. “A child would not have been able to understand what the defendant was doing, resist him, or handle their relationship,” she said. The court heard that the defendant was 35 years older than the victim at the time of the offences. The case came to light after officers arrived at the Yuen Long flat on April 5, 2024, to handle a report of a quarrel between the defendant and his girlfriend’s son. When they searched the defendant, they found a nude picture of a girl in his wallet; she was later confirmed to be the victim. The judge originally set the total sentence at 46 months but reduced it by four months after learning that the defendant is currently serving a term for another theft conviction.

title: Seoul Art Week 2026: Korean collectors on their passion, artists to watch, shows to catch
description: As Seoul Art Week kicks off, we talk to a variety of collectors on their journey and suggestions on who and what to see over the coming days.
content: South Korea is the epicentre of the Asian art calendar this week, with Frieze Seoul and the Korea International Art Fair converging alongside the opening of the Busan and Gwangju biennales. Yet behind the art-week frenzy – with some 300 galleries courting buyers at the two art fairs – questions remain about the depth and prospects of the Korean art market. The Korea Art Authentication and Appraisal Institute’s midyear report notes that local auction sales nearly doubled to 111 billion won (US$81 million) in the first half of 2026, but warns that the surge is top-heavy, driven by blue‑chip names such as Yoshitomo Nara, whose Nothing About It fetched a record 15 billion won in March. Are Korean collectors fixated on big, international names, or is a more diverse base emerging? As Seoul Art Week 2026 kicks off, we speak to several collectors – an educator, a designer, a collecting couple and an office worker with 200-plus works – on what fuels their passion, the artists they are watching and the shows they consider unmissable this season. The community educator Lee So-young is arguably one of the most recognisable figures in South Korea’s art community. She appears on some of the country’s most popular television programmes, reviews international exhibitions on her popular YouTube channel, writes books about art, and runs art education programmes for children and adults. “After I saw how many people viewed art as something difficult and unfamiliar despite the steady introduction of excellent exhibitions within the country, I started working to make art easier, more enjoyable and closer to people’s everyday lives,” she says. The enthusiasm that brought large amounts of money into South Korea’s art market during the pandemic has subsided somewhat, she says, but she believes the market is healthier as a result. “I see this as a period of transition towards a more stable market, as the people who remain are increasingly those who genuinely love art and want to continue engaging with it, rather than simply looking for short-term investment opportunities.” Korean collectors are also highly influenced by trends and what other collectors do, she says. “If I had to describe Korean collectors in one phrase, I would say they are highly sensitive to information and market signals,” she explains, adding that this is a result of the art market growing rapidly over a relatively short time. Another collector characteristic is an emphasis on stability. “They tend to buy work from blue-chip artists who are already established overseas,” she says. “Compared to other countries, Koreans don’t buy as much from younger, emerging artists.” Lee says the same tendency can be seen in corporate museums, which “generally build their collections around artists who occupy important positions in global art history”. But that is beginning to change as social media and the growing number of art fairs and exhibitions in Seoul, and beyond, influence a new generation of collectors, she says. “Collectors in their thirties and forties are discovering emerging Korean artists before they become established internationally, while interest in artists from China, Japan and Southeast Asia has grown considerably.” As examples of the shift, she points to recent exhibitions at the Leeum Museum of Art, run by the Samsung Foundation of Culture, featuring artists including Kang Seung Lee, Anicka Yi and Gala Poras-Kim. Her own collection of over 200 pieces is largely made up of Korean artists and she is a vocal supporter of young talent especially. She also focuses on female international artists and champions marginalised historic voices. Lee’s artist to watch: Sang Woo Kim – an artist as well as a British-Korean model – who uses his own face as both the subject and object of critique in his work. Must-see show in Seoul: “Muyeong Kim: Pig”, Art Sonje Centre The designer Teo Yang has been surrounded by art since childhood. His mother took him to auctions as a child, while works by artists such as Kim Whanki and Marc Chagall hung in his family home. Today, Yang encounters artists and their work up close as a designer. He has worked on spaces including Seoul’s Kukje Gallery and Thaddaeus Ropac Seoul, and now runs his own firm, Teo Yang Studio, focusing on spatial design and exhibition planning. His furniture and fragrance brand also reflects his philosophy of integrating Korean traditions and aesthetics into everyday life, which he showcases in his studio inside a traditional Korean hanok (house). For Yang, the size of the art market – and its current “cautious period” – is less important than the fact that “there are more opportunities to see and experience good art first-hand in Korea”. He also stresses the role collectors can play. “Collecting isn’t simply about buying and owning works that you like. Choosing to acquire an artist’s work and living with it can be an important form of support for that artist, beyond the financial significance,” he says. “Sometimes, buying a work by a relatively unknown artist and watching that artist grow over many years is one of the great pleasures of collecting.” Yang believes collectors need to support artists they like over the long term. “If we can build up enough of that experience over time, I hope Seoul can grow beyond being a city that hosts major international art events and become an art city with its own distinct tastes and sensibilities.” Yang’s artist to watch: Kishio Suga. Rather than trying to transform materials such as stone, wood and metal into something else, he reveals the inherent qualities of those materials and the ways in which they relate to one another. Exhibition to catch: “Si-gan: Time”, Horim Museum. The collecting couple For Kim Dong-un and Hwang Yoo-sun, collecting began with a birthday gift in 2022. Kim had taken a step back from his career in architecture and was discussing with his wife the possibility of finding something they could pursue and enjoy together. After he bought a print by a Korean artist for his wife’s birthday, they decided to embark on a crash course on art together. “We visited an extraordinary number of galleries – hundreds every year. Over the course of several years, I think we saw more than 1,000 galleries in total,” Kim says. “At this stage in our lives, we felt a certain sense of urgency – a desire to see and experience as much as we could.” Their overseas holidays have increasingly become art trips, while looking at and discussing artworks has become a nightly ritual. Kim says art has brought them closer. “Through art, we’ve learned more deeply about what the other person likes and dislikes, and we’ve come to understand each other better.” The couple have since become familiar figures in Seoul’s international gallery scene, developing a particularly close relationship with Thaddaeus Ropac Seoul, where they have found several works that have become meaningful within their collection. “When we first entered the art market, we received a great deal of advice about artists and works with strong potential. Over time, however, we realised that focusing too much on future value could distract us from what initially drew us to art.” It is a philosophy the couple hope to share with their two sons, who have also begun to build collections of their own. “I hope what we ultimately pass on to our children is not simply the collection itself, but a lasting relationship with art,” he says. Their artist to watch: Eom Yu-jeong. “A multitalented artist who has held our attention for quite some time with her exhibitions, movies and writings.” Exhibition to catch: “En attendant: Waiting” by Lee Bae at Museum San in Wonju The office worker collector When money poured into South Korea’s art market during the pandemic, many investors saw it as a new frontier for investment. The term “office worker collectors” became popular, helped by the bestselling Japanese book Let’s Buy Contemporary Art! by Daisuke Miyatsu, a salaryman who built a world-class contemporary art collection on an ordinary office worker’s income. Communities of office-worker collectors subsequently emerged on online forums and chat rooms in Korea, sharing investment strategies and market information. For Goo Chan-oo, however, making money was never the goal. The fashion industry employee began collecting almost by accident a decade ago, when he encountered a French street artist during a walk through his local park and bought one of his paintings for 10,000 won. “The sheer joy of that first purchase has surpassed any other collecting experience that I’ve had ever since,” he says. “Collecting art remains a pure hobby for me. It’s personal fulfilment, funded strictly by my salary.” Through his dedication to art collecting, Goo has established his own set of criteria for selecting pieces. “The most important thing is whether an artist expresses a distinct and unique mode of expression that makes their work instantly recognisable.” His hope for the Korean art scene is that such artists are appreciated and given a spotlight. Goo’s artist to watch: Kang Cheolgyu. “He exquisitely projects his inner emotions and autobiographical experiences onto a fictional canvas. I think of his work as ‘visualised philosophy’.” Exhibition to catch: “Do Ho Suh”, National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) in Seoul.

title: Hong Kong government loses appeal over Fanling golf course housing plan
description: Court of Appeal’s ruling is likely to result in fresh public consultations on developing 9.5 hectares of land at Fanling course.
content: The government’s push to boost short-term public housing supply has suffered a setback after it lost an appeal against a court decision overturning conditional approval for building 12,000 flats on part of Hong Kong’s oldest golf course. In a judgment delivered on Monday, the Court of Appeal found that the official endorsement of the project’s environmental impact assessment report was marred by an unfair public consultation process, the imposition of improper conditions and a failure to meet wildlife conservation objectives. The ruling is likely to result in fresh public consultations on developing 9.5 hectares (23.5 acres) of the 32 hectares that the government took back from the 172-hectare golf course in Fanling three years ago. The project was initially slated for completion in 2029. The government said it would review the judgment to decide whether to appeal further, adding that an announcement would be made “at the appropriate time”. The Hong Kong Golf Club welcomed the judgment, describing the course as a “precious living heritage” of the city that remained pivotal to the development of the sport. “The club will continue to communicate with the government, in the hope of preserving the old course and generating the greatest value for Hong Kong by fully utilising all resources and facilities at the club, which is in line with government policies of promoting golf and sports tourism,” a spokesman said. The club, which manages the course on the remaining 140 hectares, won a judicial review in late 2024 to quash the director of environmental protection’s approval of the study conducted by the Civil Engineering and Development Department.
