Mr Justice Russell Coleman, of the Court of First Instance, ruled that the government had failed to consult the public again when the civil engineering department provided additional information regarding the development’s ecological impact, which formed part of the report. The lower court also found it unfair and unreasonable for the director to disregard the club’s responses to the new information, and that the conditions he imposed for the report’s final approval were excessive and would effectively require an overhaul of project plans, as if the study had not actually been approved. Lawyers for the government urged the appellate court to dismiss the club’s challenge on the basis that it had become “academic” following legal amendments aimed at speeding up development of smaller plots. The Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance originally required a report for urban developments covering more than 20 hectares or involving a population exceeding 100,000. That definition was revised in June 2023 to cover projects of at least 50 hectares. Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung SC, on behalf of the director, argued the new regime allowed the government to press ahead with the project without going through an environmental impact assessment. But the court ruled that the amendments did not relieve the director of his duty to review environmental studies that commenced before the legal changes took place. The three presiding judges also dismissed the government’s argument that the report in the present case had become so obsolete or irrelevant it could serve no other meaningful purposes. “The [environmental impact assessment report] and the complaints raised against it in the judicial review are plainly matters which the government at least can and may well take into account in any further deliberation, even outside of the [Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance] regime, on the project and on the future use of the site,” the judges said. The three judges concurred with the lower court that the department’s additional analysis on various topics, including the development’s hydrological impact, was incorrectly excluded from the report for public inspection. They said the government’s failure to further consult the public on the matter rendered the overall process unfair. The panel also agreed with the Court of First Instance that the director had imposed “impermissible” conditions for approving the report, which involved making significant or even fundamental changes to the project’s layout, making his decision to approve the report lack finality and certainty. The Court of Appeal further held that the report failed to address the project’s impact on the site’s cultural heritage and ecology, such as trees classified as “old and valuable” by authorities. The Leisure and Cultural Services Department currently manages the 32 hectares of land returned to the government in September 2023. The government has continued to make the land available for the club’s use during international tournaments. LIV Golf Hong Kong, one of the international tournaments hosted by the club, faces an uncertain future after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund decided to pull its support. Considered a “mega-event” by authorities, the fourth edition of the tournament is scheduled to take place at the Fanling course in February next year. The league has long been expected to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States while it continues to secure funding for a downsized competition, referred to as LIV 2.0.

title: Xi Jinping’s Cairo trip marks ‘best ties in history’ as Egypt seeks to balance West
description: Chinese president’s visit comes amid expanding Suez investment and joint air force exercises.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping is returning to Egypt after a decade as Beijing deepens its economic, military and diplomatic ties with Cairo and seeks to work more closely with Egypt on crises across the Middle East and Africa. Xi will visit Egypt this week following his trip to Kyrgyzstan for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, which finishes on Tuesday. China’s foreign ministry last week described relations with Egypt as being “at their best in history” and said Xi’s visit would build on past cooperation while setting the direction for future ties. The visit coincides with the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations. It will be Xi’s first visit to Egypt since January 2016, when he addressed the Arab League in Cairo and witnessed the signing of agreements covering infrastructure, energy, finance and industrial development. By contrast, Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi has visited China eight times since taking office in 2014, most recently in May 2024. John Calabrese, a non-resident senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, said Xi’s visit offered political benefits to both sides. “The visit provides Beijing with an opportunity to showcase a durable, non-Western partnership with a major Arab, African and Global South state,” Calabrese said. For Egypt, it offered a way to show that it was “not a tool of the US or the West more broadly”. Calabrese expects the two governments to reaffirm their comprehensive strategic partnership and possibly announce agreements on trade, investment, belt and road cooperation and the use of the yuan in bilateral transactions. In 2023, Egypt became Africa’s first sovereign issuer of a panda bond, raising 3.5 billion yuan (US$520 million) on China’s domestic debt market. Beijing and Cairo renewed their bilateral currency-swap agreement in June, expanding it from 18 billion yuan to 30 billion yuan for another three years. China’s economic ties with Egypt have expanded rapidly, with bilateral trade reaching about US$20.8 billion in 2025, up from US$17.38 billion a year earlier, according to data from the Egyptian Commercial Service. Much of China’s industrial investment is concentrated near the Suez Canal, a maritime artery connecting Asia with Europe through the Red Sea and Mediterranean. By the end of 2025, the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone in Ain Sokhna was hosting nearly 200 companies, with reported investment of more than US$3.8 billion and about 10,000 jobs created. China Jushi, one of the zone’s largest manufacturers, has established a major fibreglass production base serving export markets in Europe, the Middle East and elsewhere. “The relationship is increasingly about industrial investment, not simply trade,” Calabrese said. Egypt was positioning itself as a manufacturing base for Chinese companies seeking access to European and African markets, Calabrese said. But foreign-currency shortages, debt pressures and bureaucracy remained obstacles, while Cairo’s reliance on Gulf and Western financing limited how far it could shift towards Beijing, he said. Amr Adly, an associate professor of political science at the American University in Cairo, said Chinese investment had risen rapidly over the past decade, although investors from Britain, the United States and Gulf states still held larger stocks of foreign direct investment. He said further growth could come from integrating Egyptian companies into Chinese-led supply chains serving European, African and Gulf markets. Military cooperation is also expanding. Egypt and China began their second Eagles of Civilisation joint air exercise on August 22, days before Xi’s visit. China deployed J-16 fighters more than 6,000km (3,730 miles) to Egypt, supported by mid-air refuelling from a YY-20A tanker, showcasing the growing ability of the Chinese air force to operate far from home. While Egypt has relied for decades on US military assistance, expanding exercises with China points to Cairo’s efforts to diversify its defence relationships. “Egypt is interested in balancing its relationship with the US by deepening cooperation with China,” Adly said. “On Gaza, there is broad alignment,” Calabrese said. “Both Beijing and Cairo support a ceasefire, Palestinian statehood and Egypt’s mediating and reconstruction role.” On Iran, he said: “I see only partial alignment.” “Both favour de-escalation and neither wants a wider conflict that disrupts Suez and Red Sea shipping.” But he added that Beijing’s deeper ties with Tehran and opposition to Washington’s pressure meant coordination with Cairo was likely to remain limited to calls for restraint. The Red Sea and Persian Gulf were important to Chinese interests, Adly said. Although China had acted as mediator in 2023 to restore diplomatic relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran, “the Chinese haven’t been as keen on intervening with the ongoing conflict”. Zhao Jun, director of the African Arab Countries Research Project and an associate professor at the Middle East Studies Institute of Shanghai International Studies University, said China needed Egypt as a regional “pivot” connecting the Arab world, Africa, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. Egypt, meanwhile, hoped to use Chinese investment, technology and market access to advance industrialisation and expand its diplomatic room for manoeuvre, he said. Zhao said the next phase of economic cooperation could focus on electric vehicles, solar power and energy storage, green hydrogen, desalination, artificial intelligence and port logistics. “Financing will also rely more heavily on [yuan] settlement, panda bonds, equity investment, industrial funds and public-private partnerships, reducing dependence on sovereign loans,” Zhao said. “Ultimately, the key measure of the visit’s success is not how many agreements are signed, but whether political trust can be translated into highly localised industrial projects that are bankable, operational and exportable.” Zhao said the “visit is expected to shape a division of labour in which Egypt leverages its advantages in on-the-ground mediation while China provides international political and development resources”.

title: Hong Kong emerges as Asia’s top hub for start-up potential, ranks fifth worldwide: study
description: City shows growing strength in nurturing scalable ventures and unicorns, CB Insights study says.
content: Hong Kong leads Asia in high-growth start-up potential and ranks fifth globally, showing the city’s growing strength in nurturing scalable ventures and unicorns, according to joint research published by technology market intelligence firm CB Insights and the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation. The white paper, released on Monday, said Asia operated on a distributed network where distinct markets specialised in different stages of the technology life cycle, unlike Silicon Valley’s single-hub model. Hong Kong served as the primary financial bridge connecting mainland Chinese and Asian tech innovations to global capital, international governance and cross-border buyers, the study added. As Asian companies target global markets from day one, Hong Kong functions as an essential gateway rather than an optional exit route CB Insights Foreign investors took part in 81 per cent of Hong Kong’s equity deals and channelled 84 per cent of their regional capital through the city, the report said. Furthermore, 55 per cent of unique equity investors in Hong Kong originated from outside Asia. “As Asian companies target global markets from day one, Hong Kong functions as an essential gateway rather than an optional exit route,” CB Insights said. Hong Kong companies showed the strongest growth momentum among Asian markets, according to CB Insights’ predictive measure of private company success across momentum, financing, market opportunity and leadership. “Looking ahead, our ... vision is built on four dimensions: broad and deep, far yet near,” said Cordelia Chung, the chair of Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP). “Broad means building a diverse talent ecosystem where human minds leverage technology, deep involves advancing tech-industry convergence, far entails expanding our global footprint and near focuses on drawing the future nearer with immediate action,” she added. Established in 2001 by the Hong Kong government, the HKSTP is a statutory body established to drive the city’s innovation and technology ecosystem. It has built a community of over 17,000 research professionals and 2,600 technology companies from 26 countries and regions across four strategic technology clusters. Mainland China led the region in frontier technology development, hardware manufacturing and large-scale deployment. It accounted for 52 per cent of all regional tech equity funding despite making up 38 per cent of total deals, with average deal sizes significantly larger than regional peers. India ranked second in deal volume through broad commercial partnerships, while Japan dominated regional liquidity, driving 50 per cent of all mergers and acquisitions. In physical artificial intelligence and advanced hardware, China operated virtually without regional competition. Neighbouring markets captured almost zero venture funding in foundational robotics models, humanoid robotics or autonomous vehicle AI stacks. The report showed that physical AI, robotics and AI infrastructure dominated funding across Asia. From January 2025 through June 2026, robotics and generative AI raised US$26.1 billion and US$20.7 billion across the region, respectively, outpacing agentic AI and fintech.

title: How a tree in Hanoi points to flowering of dissent among Vietnam’s Gen Z
description: To the outside world, Vietnam is a success story but the country’s youth believe that is not their reality.
content: A tree in Hanoi has become a symbol of how Vietnam’s Gen Z views its country – but it is not the enviable growth story sold by the government. Tree 55 on Nguyen Huy Tu Street – now dubbed the “Justice Tree” – was buried under bouquets earlier this month. It was an act of digital-age defiance over the death of a teenager in a road traffic accident in the area that went unpunished. Response to the accident, which triggered a belated explanation from the state, reveals unease with a system many young Vietnamese no longer believe can deliver on its socialist promises, analysts say. The Communist Party is seen to be cracking down on free expression since the rise of To Lam, a former police chief who is now both president and party general secretary – perhaps the most powerful Vietnamese leader in decades. The national narrative is one of a Southeast Asian nation on the rise, with region-topping economic growth and an international profile to match. But there is also simmering discontent from its 100 million population – especially from youth, connected to parts of the internet even one of the world’s tightest surveillance regimes is slow to reach. Tree No 55 is a case in point. Last May, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy and her father were hit by a BMW that swerved into their lane. The seriously wounded teenager died 10 days before her high school graduation exam. State-controlled media initially identified the driver as a 64-year-old man with the initials NSC. Rumours circulated that they stood for Nguyen Sy Cuong, a former Vietnam National Assembly deputy and husband of a high-ranking party official. The case went quiet for a year – until social media users revived it with memes about impunity and injustice. Virtual rebellion turned into real-life tributes as masked citizens laid flowers by the tree at the accident spot. Alarmed by the spontaneous public protest, Vietnamese authorities sent uniformed officers to cordon off the tree. Then, on August 17, they took the rare step of confirming the driver was Cuong – adding that his contrition was enough to avoid punishment. For many young Vietnamese the admission fell well short of accountability. “Justice is nonexistent. The rich and powerful can seal themselves off from the consequences of their actions,” claimed Nam*, 27, a Canada-based activist who uses Threads to organise political events. Social media – particularly Meta Platforms’ Threads – has helped the younger generation express their discontent. Threads “allows the youth to come together and occupy it easily, creating a culture sphere of their own”, said Susann Pham, a German-based researcher on Vietnam’s social movements, civil society and politics. “Threads also gives them some sort of anonymous identity compared to Facebook, where your network, your face, your family members might be easily seen.” The teenager’s death provided “an emotional identity – a hook – that the younger generation can jump on”, she added. “They can easily identify with the victim.” Gen Z rise From India’s ‘’cockroach’’ movement to revolutions in Nepal and Bangladesh, angry Gen Z protesters have proved to be powerful challengers to governments that had seemed firmly entrenched. While experts say opposition in Vietnam is a long way from turning into a similar threat – and a critical culture may stay in the digital world – the gripes of its youth are building. “Vietnam is also at an inflection point right now,” said Phil Robertson, the director of Asian Human Rights and Labour Advocates. “The economy is growing rapidly, but there is a widening gap between the rich and the poor, the connected and the disconnected, between party members and the ordinary people.” Even as the government aims for 10 per cent annual growth over coming years, anger is stirring in Gen Z over stagnant wages, rising property prices, pollution, corruption and environmental destruction. Gia*, a 26-year-old university graduate, earns 10 million dong (US$400) a month teaching English in a northern province. Even double that in Hanoi would not be enough to cover her cost of living, she said, locking her out from home ownership, a key metric of a middle class that is supposed to be surfing the country’s wave of growth. “There should be a range of affordable choices for people who want to settle,” she said. In Vietnam, average monthly wages are around 9 million dong. Yet Hanoi homes cost around 123 million dong per square metre – meaning that people, even university graduates, would have to work their whole life to afford a small flat. “One of the biggest issues facing us right now is the wages of everyday people. They are very low and creating a lot of pressure on the population,’’ said Nam, who is studying business in Canada. That struggle, juxtaposed against Vietnam’s surging economy, with its luxury malls and supercars, has raised awkward questions of the government’s core narrative. “I always thought we were living in a communist country, but now I see that it operates pretty much like a capitalist one, and a very ruthless one at that,’’ said Linh*, a 24-year-old now based in the UK. Vietnam in the past decade has deployed 10,000-strong military cyber-troops, known as Force 47, to fight off “wrongful information and anti-state propaganda”. Since To Lam became president in April, his government has stepped up its censorship and crackdown on dissent. Vietnamese journalist Le Anh Hung was arrested in March for “propagandising against the state”, while rapper MCK had to pull out over half the tracks on a new album after being approached by authorities “over sensitive content” and vulgar language. “Gen Z is critical of elites and children of elites … and in the short term: the censoring of the rapper – or the censoring of Gen Z culture – is felt like a personal insult to their identity,” Pham added. Mounting state repression is butting up against the aspirations of Vietnam’s politically aware youth, according to Robertson. “Authorities can repress it this time but it is going to keep coming up. You can’t have elite systems that operate in the dark with impunity,” he said. *Nicknames have been changed to protect identities

title: Meet Garth Brooks’ daughter Allie Colleen, whose Dolly Parton tribute has sparked backlash
description: The youngest child of the Grammy-winning country star shared a tribute to the ‘Jolene’ singer – but her message has rubbed many fans the wrong way.
content: Tributes continue to pour in following the death of beloved country legend Dolly Parton last week – though some have proven more controversial than others. Allie Colleen, country singer and daughter of Garth Brooks, has faced sharp criticism after her emotional tribute to the “Jolene” icon was deemed insensitive by fans. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Allie Colleen (@alliecolleenmusic) “My greatest fear in life is the day my dad loses his life, and I have to see the world mourn a man they never knew the way I knew him,” she wrote on Instagram, before extending her condolences to Parton’s family and friends. The post sparked a divided response online, with some users sympathising with her sentiment while others criticised the timing. “This is the weirdest condolence post I have ever seen,” one commenter wrote. “It’s giving how can I make something not about myself, about me. This is nepo baby at its worst.” “Allie, just a note. Next time, let someone read your work before you publish it. I know what you meant, however now was not the time to say it,” another added. Responding to a user questioning her message, Allie defended her post: “This is my account – I am saying I don’t know how to respond to these things in my industry because of my life experiences. I’m not telling anyone else how to grieve. I’m just acknowledging the family. You do you babe.” Here’s everything to know about Allie Colleen Brooks. What is Allie Colleen Brooks’ background? Born on July 28, 1996, Allie Colleen Brooks is the youngest of country star Garth Brooks’ three daughters with his ex-wife, Sandy Mahl – whom he married in 1986 and divorced in 2001. Her elder sisters are Taylor Mayne Pearl Brooks, 34, and August Anna Brooks, 32. During an appearance on the Children of Song podcast, Allie revealed that her parents “shut down everything” to raise her and her siblings. “I don’t know what it’s like to have celebrity parents. My dad was there every night,” she said, adding that Brooks and Mahl made them switch households every evening. Following his 2001 divorce from Mahl, the “Unanswered Prayers” singer married fellow country singer Trisha Yearwood in 2005. Yearwood embraced her role as a “bonus mum”, telling People in 2021: “They let me learn my way and allowed me to be that third parent in their lives.” She’s a musician just like her dad Allie Colleen took up songwriting at age eight after struggling with communication, she told Ohio public radio station WOUB. However, her father insisted she earn a college degree before pursuing music professionally, according to Fox News. She went on to study songwriting and music business at Belmont University, graduating in 2018. Today, the 30-year-old musician is signed to Evangeline Records. Having released her debut album Stones in 2021 and toured alongside Jelly Roll, she remains driven by a strong work ethic: “I want to work my tail off and be just like my dad,” she told Entertainment Focus. What are some of her other interests? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Allie Colleen (@alliecolleenmusic) Allie Colleen grew up around animals through her family’s involvement with Wild Heart Ranch, a wildlife rescue service based in Bushyhead, Oklahoma. An avid rider with two horses, Jack and Einstein, she serves as an ambassador for Horses for Mental Health. Beyond her music, the singer enjoys weightlifting and body art – even penning a track titled “Tattoo”.

title: 50 arrested in HK$500m building maintenance bid-rigging crackdown
description: Independent Commission Against Corruption, police and Competition Commission launch joint operation triggered by public complaints.
content: Hong Kong authorities have arrested 50 people, including some with alleged triad backgrounds, in a crackdown on bid-rigging activities involving 27 housing estates and buildings and about HK$500 million (US$64.1 million) in contracts. The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), police and antitrust regulator the Competition Commission on Monday revealed details of their joint operation, which was conducted last week. The ICAC said the suspects included the alleged mastermind and core members of a syndicate behind bid-rigging activities for the repair and maintenance of residential buildings. “The ICAC, police and the Competition Commission call on the public to actively participate in building management affairs and proactively report any illegal activities to law enforcement agencies,” the anti-corruption agency said. The three agencies searched 39 premises, including the homes of suspects, and seized documents and accounting records. Officers also raided premises allegedly controlled by triads for suspected illegal activities. The ICAC and police arrested 50 people, aged 24 to 77. Corruption complaints from the public triggered the operation. They concerned maintenance work, leading the ICAC to a contractor for major renovation works for three composite and private residential buildings in Eastern, Wan Chai and Yau Tsim Mong districts with contracts estimated to be worth HK$200 million, the ICAC said. As a result of the complaints and subsequent investigation, the ICAC intercepted the construction contracts that had not yet been awarded. The contractor, believed to be the syndicate head, was suspected of bribing project consultants and some members of owners’ corporations to secure the three major contracts. “The project contractor allegedly obtained help through bribery, including concealing the company’s conviction records in tender analysis reports to win the bids, and splitting the major renovation project into small-scale works to circumvent procedures requiring approval by the owners,” the ICAC said. “As registered inspectors are also suspected of failing to perform their duties, the ICAC has referred the matter to the Buildings Department for follow-up action.” During the operation, the ICAC arrested eight men and two women, aged 39 to 77, including the contractor, project consultants, registered inspectors and chairpersons and a member of the owners’ corporations. It also seized more than HK$1.2 million in cash from the premises of a project consultant, suspected to be part of the bribes involved. The Competition Commission’s action concerned building maintenance projects of 23 housing estates and buildings in eight districts across Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and the New Territories, involving HK$300 million worth of contracts. Some of the project tenders were overturned, while others had started or were already completed before the commission’s investigation. The commission also found the syndicate had disseminated pricing instructions to its members, commonly referred to as “homework”, in the tendering processes, so as to control their bidding prices. The syndicate was found to have collaborated with another bid-rigging syndicate through a middleman, with each arranging for their own contractors to take part in the tendering processes of some projects to enhance their chances of winning. During the operation last Wednesday, police also cracked down on three illegal gambling establishments suspected to be controlled by triad-related personnel and arrested 25 men and 12 women, aged between 24 and 62. Separately, police detained a construction company director, a structural engineer and the director of a contractor company. The three men, aged 40 to 69, were arrested on suspicion of submitting 13 forged works completion certificates to the Buildings Department in 2022, for minor works at 13 flats in a housing estate on Hong Kong Island. The registered inspector’s signatures were allegedly signed after the person had died.

title: Countries must consider reparations for slave trade, UN committee says
description: At least 12.5 million Africans were ‌taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries, according to the committee.
content: A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination it says persists today. Guidance published on Monday by the Committee on the Elimination of ‌Racial Discrimination stated that the obligations arise from a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place. The committee described the approach as a “paradigm shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations claims. “States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for people of African descent, covering all ⁠aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms. At least 12.5 million Africans were ‌taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination called the largest forced displacement in history. Calls for reparations – ‌ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and ⁠institutions should not be held ⁠responsible for historical crimes. The European Union and Britain abstained from a UN resolution on slavery in March. Some states have sought ‌to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade at the time – the ‌so-called intertemporality principle. But ‌the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under ‌the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects. “Irrespective of ⁠the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, States parties remain bound by their present obligations under the convention ⁠to address structural inequalities,” the UN document states. Financial compensation alone is not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions. Pela Boker-Wilson, a committee expert ‌from Liberia who helped draft the ‌document, said she expected states to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws. “We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she said. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

title: Singapore to invest US$173m over 3 years to boost fintech innovation
description: The money will help co-fund at least 1,000 internships under the Financial Sector Technology and Innovation Scheme to build young talent.
content: Singapore will commit S$220 million (US$173 million) over three years to boost its fintech sector, including co-funding at least 1,000 internships in a strong push to build talent for AI and other emerging technologies. The funds come under the latest iteration of the Financial Sector Technology and Innovation Scheme (FSTI), which aims to strengthen the country’s fintech space and accelerate innovation and technology adoption in the financial sector. The industry currently has more than 1,800 firms employing close to 10,000 professionals across technology, data, artificial intelligence (AI), compliance, cybersecurity and business roles, with investments in fintech reaching S$2.9 billion in 2025, according to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) on Monday. The latest edition of the scheme, known as FSTI 4.0, includes a manpower track that will support firms in building young talent by co-funding an internship stipend. This will be facilitated through a new internship portal managed by the Singapore FinTech Association to connect students with internships across business, technology and other roles. MAS said it aimed to support at least 1,000 fintech internship opportunities over the next three years. Speaking to the media on Monday, Deputy Prime Minister and MAS chairman Gan Kim Yong said it was important for Singapore to build a talent pipeline, which was particularly critical in the fintech industry given that it was a new and rapidly evolving sector. “With the emergence of AI and frontier technologies, as you can imagine, the talent that we need, the capability we need to build is going to be very critical for the growth of this sector. And that’s why we want to invest in building our people, in giving them the skills and knowledge so that they are able, well positioned to seize the opportunities when they emerge,” Gan said. While the MAS was unable to provide the breakdown of how much of the S$220 million would go towards co-funding internships, it will fund up to 80 per cent of each internship. Holly Fang, president of the Singapore FinTech Association, told This Week in Asia that the internship track was extremely important because the skills fintech companies required were changing very quickly, and the industry needed people who could work at the intersection of finance and technology, and increasingly also data and AI. “We hear a lot of anxiety among young people about what AI means for entry-level jobs. I think fintech presents the other side of that story. AI will automate certain tasks, but it is also creating new roles and changing existing ones,” Fang said. The best way for young people to develop these capabilities was through actual exposure to companies and real-world problems, and internships were an important entry point into the fintech talent pipeline, Fang added. She also noted a challenge many small and growing fintech firms faced: a lack of graduate recruitment infrastructure, campus presence, or employer brand of a large bank or technology company, which meant students might not know what opportunities existed in the sector. “So there is a matching problem on both sides. Government funding helps because taking on an intern is not costless for a smaller company, it’s not just the salary component, but also supervision and training,” Fang said. Singapore has poured hundreds of millions into various versions of the FSTI over the years. The scheme, introduced in 2015, acts as a catalyst for financial institutions, tech vendors and fintech start-ups to test, build, and scale innovative financial solutions. Besides the internship support, FSTI 4.0 also includes an AI Pathfinder track, which supports scaling and deploying market-ready AI solutions to create stronger collaborations between financial institutions and tech providers. There is also an infrastructure and platform track to fund sector-wide platforms that will boost operational efficiency, drive innovation and advance Singapore’s role in establishing global financial standards. The Centre of Excellence track will also continue to anchor the innovative functions of leading global financial institutions and fintech firms locally. The initiative brings together specialised talent and expertise, while supporting the growth of emerging technologies including AI, quantum computing and digital assets. According to the MAS, the cumulative impact of FSTI on the fintech ecosystem has resulted in more than 350 projects being supported, over 30 centres of excellence established and S$3.8 billion in funds raised by early-stage start-ups who were finalists in the annual Global FinTech Hackcelerator. Asked how FSTI 4.0 could help the city state better compete with other regional financial hubs like Hong Kong, Gan stressed that Singapore competed not just with Hong Kong and that the financial industry was not a zero-sum game. He said the scheme would also spur innovation in the local financial and fintech sectors. “Hopefully, with this, it will keep Singapore’s financial sector and fintech industries … very competitive, and as we do better, many of the innovations [and] solutions will also benefit the financial industries in this region,” Gan said. “Really, it’s not a zero-sum game. We compete, but I think the development of the industry will benefit all countries in the financial sector.”

title: China film studio lets tourists act in short dramas for US$30 to fight low attendance
description: A local mother commissioned 17 short dramas in six months, finding it both entertaining and therapeutic.
content: China’s Hengdian World Studios, the world’s largest film and TV studio, is now offering tourists the chance to shoot their own short dramas for about 200 yuan (US$30) per person, as a response to the recession caused by artificial intelligence. Previously, tourists flocked to Hengdian World Studios to admire the sets of their favourite dramas and explore the national 5A-rated attraction, which features over 100 sub-studios spread across 30 sq km and showcasing 5,000 years of history. Now, these studios are undergoing a significant transformation, shifting from a focus on fans to embracing aspiring actors. In August, the site launched a service that allows tourists to film their own short dramas. Participants pay a minimum of 218 yuan for an hour of acting experience, with a fee of 388 yuan if make-up and styling are included. Group packages are also available, priced at 3,800 yuan (US$570) and 12,000 yuan, aimed at families and companies seeking team-building activities. This initiative not only aligns with the growing trend of experience economies in Chinese tourist attractions – where non-player characters (NPCs) engage with visitors – but also serves as a strategy for the studio to sustain itself amid the rising influence of artificial intelligence in the TV production industry. According to China National Radio, last year Hengdian experienced a shift from traditional landscape dramas to vertical short dramas, employing over 4,000 crew members and showcasing a year-on-year growth of 237 per cent. However, this boom quickly turned out to be a bubble. In the first quarter of this year, it was reported that of the 128,000 newly released short dramas, 95 per cent were produced using AI. This situation poses a serious threat to those who depend on work from Hengdian, aptly nicknamed heng piao or “people who float in Hengdian,” who now face significant unemployment. One short drama director mentioned he had only filmed two dramas so far this year, an unprecedented decline compared to previous years. Thanks to the new tourist programme, a director by the surname Zhang reported he could now create 20 short dramas within a single day. Some directors, who once worked as extras in Hengdian, are adept at guiding newcomers in acting. They demonstrate a scene, allowing clients to repeat their actions, advise them on when to stop blinking or giggling, and occasionally share their own experiences to evoke emotional performances. One short drama sub-studio in Hengdian revealed that a young mother commissioned them to produce 17 short dramas featuring her within six months, likening the experience to psychological consultation. Director Wu Yizhuo told China Newsweek that the most popular plot among tourists involves a previously arrogant character who is astonished to discover the powerful identity of the protagonist. Wu characterised this preference as a pursuit of emotional value. “This is truly a tour in our daydreams,” commented a netizen. “I want to play that character who slaps people in their face all day long,” joked another. “Finally, I can be in show business,” declared a third.

title: Huawei, with an eye on self-reliance, ploughs 25% of revenue into R&D at expense of profits
description: Revenue in first half rose 9.55 per cent to 467.8 billion yuan, bolstered by a strong rebound in smartphones and demand for AI chips.
content: Huawei Technologies poured more than a quarter of its first-half revenue into research and development, prioritising long-term technological independence over short-term earnings as first-half profit plunged 36 per cent. R&D expenses jumped 25 per cent year on year to 121.4 billion yuan (US$18 billion) for the six months through June, accounting for over 25 per cent of total revenue, according to a filing on Monday with the Shanghai Clearing House, the primary central clearing counterparty in China’s interbank market. The surging technology spending, as well as rising component costs, pushed net profit for the Shenzhen-based giant down to 23.8 billion yuan from 37.2 billion yuan in the same period last year. This marks the second consecutive year of declining first-half profits for the company. Net operating cash flow also took a heavy hit, swinging to negative 39.9 billion yuan from a positive inflow of 31.2 billion yuan in the same period last year. Still, revenue for the period rose 9.55 per cent to 467.8 billion yuan from 427 billion yuan a year earlier, bolstered by a strong rebound in smartphone shipments and accelerating demand for its artificial intelligence processors. As a privately held entity, Huawei occasionally releases its operational figures via bond issuance disclosures on the clearing venue. The heavy spending underscores Huawei’s dual challenge: defending its domestic market leadership against skyrocketing memory chip costs while pouring billions into home-grown chip architectures amid US trade curbs. Huawei led the Chinese smartphone market with a 22.6 per cent share in the second quarter, driven by a 19.4 per cent jump in shipment volume, according to data from research firm IDC. Among the top 10 handset vendors in the world’s largest smartphone market, Huawei was the only one to post quarterly growth. Other Chinese brands including Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi and Honor suffered sharp declines in shipment volumes, IDC data showed. Huawei gained ground in the market partly by raising prices more cautiously compared to its competitors, but the company warned that soaring component costs would eventually force its hand. “With memory prices skyrocketing, smartphone prices may be forced to rise across the board, otherwise [manufacturers] would be selling at a loss,” Richard Yu Chengdong, chairman of Huawei’s Consumer Business Group, said at a launch event earlier this month. Beyond smartphones, Huawei continues to benefit from expanding adoption of its Ascend AI chips as a domestic alternative to China-restricted Nvidia products. A growing list of China’s AI firms, including DeepSeek, Z.ai and iFlyTek, are looking to deploy Huawei chips and accelerators for running and even training their AI models. Huawei and other domestic chip suppliers were expected to capture nearly 80 per cent of China’s AI server market this year, further squeezing global rivals such as Nvidia, according to TrendForce data in June. In May, the US-sanctioned company, which has been cut off from foreign supplies of advanced semiconductors, introduced a new scaling law and a chip architecture designed to deliver products equivalent to an advanced 1.4-nanometre processing node by 2031 without the need for high-end lithography tools. The tech industry is watching closely for the launch of its coming Kirin 2026 processor, built on Huawei’s LogicFolding architecture, as it is set to power the firm’s flagship Mate handsets launching this autumn.

title: As China-US space race heats up, Shanghai unveils space-computing hub
description: Songjiang is already a vital link in China’s satellite supply chain as home to SpaceSail, the low-Earth-orbit challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink.
content: As China ramps up its efforts to build an orbital data ecosystem and counter the US in the commercial space race, Shanghai – home to several major domestic players – has kicked off an inaugural space-computing forum alongside a new industry hub. The dedicated centre in the city’s southwestern Songjiang district, unveiled at the forum on Sunday, brought together aerospace developers, semiconductor makers, artificial intelligence specialists, cloud vendors, as well as researchers and investors to advance in-orbit data processing, local news outlet Shanghai Observer reported. Space computing enables satellites to analyse data in orbit, reducing the need to transmit raw files back to ground stations and speeding up real-time intelligence. More ambitious long-term plans envision orbital data centres powered by solar energy to ease pressure on land-based power grids. Songjiang, which has made commercial space a focal point of its development guidelines, is already a vital link in China’s satellite supply chain. The district is home to SpaceSail, the Shanghai government-backed firm building Qianfan – China’s main low-Earth-orbit challenger to US giant SpaceX’s Starlink. Having launched over 200 satellites to date, SpaceSail aims to deploy a 15,000-satellite mega-constellation by the end of 2030. By comparison, Starlink has placed over 11,000 satellites in orbit to date, serving customers across more than 150 countries and territories. Songjiang is also home to satellite manufacturers including Gesi Aerospace and Xuntian Qianhe, as well as the Shanghai Aerospace Precision Machinery Research Institute. Local officials valued Songjiang’s satellite-internet sector at 23 billion yuan (US$3.4 billion) in 2025, supported by more than 100 companies across the supply chain. The area also hosts Shanghai’s only designated 6G industry zone, where 81 companies generated about 24 billion yuan in revenue last year, according to Chinese media reports. Under a new action plan, Songjiang is targeting more than 5 billion yuan in sales from space-computing and related industries by 2030. The initiative aligns directly with Beijing’s broader strategy to establish China as a major space power, an ambition highlighted for the first time in the country’s latest five-year plan. The document listed satellite internet as key digital infrastructure to be built “ahead of demand”, calling for accelerated low-Earth-orbit constellation deployments and tighter integration of satellite, airborne and ground-based systems across communication, navigation, remote sensing and computing assets. Other priorities include expanding commercial space manufacturing and launch capacity, alongside lunar and deep-space exploration. China has logged important advances in reusable rocket technology this year, successfully recovering boosters via a sea-based net and land-based landing legs, milestones which are critical to driving down launch costs. Shanghai is not alone in chasing the sector. In neighbouring Zhejiang province, state-backed research institute Zhejiang Lab is spearheading the Three-Body Computing Constellation – a satellite cluster designed to process data in space.

title: Singapore may require social media firms to set daily time limits for teens
description: If a social media platform does not want to introduce stronger safeguards, Singapore may require it to raise the minimum age of access to 18.
content: Singapore plans to introduce legislation early next year requiring social media platforms to roll out stronger safeguards for teens, including possibly setting a daily time limit, Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo has said. If a platform could not or did not want to introduce these stronger safeguards, Singapore intended to raise the minimum age of access to that platform to 18, Teo told journalists in an interview on Friday. The government wanted to know what platforms could do to protect teen users from “stranger danger”, or direct messages from people unknown to them, she said. Algorithmic feeds, autoplay and infinite scroll are also a concern, with discussions touching on how to introduce a natural stop point for infinite scroll. “The idea has been put forward when we engaged with many different groups, that a time limit for the use of a particular platform … could be one way of dealing with infinite scroll,” said Teo. Singapore currently has a code of practice that covers six designated social media services: Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, HardwareZone and X. Teo noted that the measures Meta Platforms agreed to in its US settlement would apply to users up to age 18, in line with Singapore’s intended approach, though the details differed in places. “Some of the areas which Meta has agreed to implement are the same areas that we have been discussing with them about … But there are some differences in the details,” she said. For example, Meta agreed to let parents of teen users turn off autoplay, but continuous autoplay remains the default. Singapore wants autoplay off by default, with parents able to switch it on. Meta’s settlement also included a daily limit of two hours across Facebook and Instagram, tightening to one hour per platform in a second phase. Teo said there was no “magic number” but called the arrangement a useful reference point. “It doesn’t mean if you use a service for 59 minutes it’s very safe, and then if you use it for 61 minutes it’s very unsafe.” An expert panel convened by the Ministry of Health to study social media’s impact on youth mental health found that one in three users aged 15 to 17 already spent more than three hours a day on social media, Teo noted. The panel also found that one in six users aged 10 to 24 showed signs of problematic social media use. “What it does suggest is that three hours is a bit too long. It ought to be less than that,” she said. Whatever figure Singapore settled on would not satisfy everyone, she added. “The daily time limit really is a reminder that we should get on with other aspects of our life.” Beyond the newly operational Online Safety Commission, which began work in June, engagement on other aspects of online safety has been ongoing. Teo said platforms had known about the age assurance measures “for a long time”, and about the stronger safeguards for nine to 12 months. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced in his National Day Rally speech in August that Singapore would require platforms to introduce stronger safeguards for young users. While most platforms already set a minimum age of 13, enforcement was largely left to them, he noted, calling self-declaration “just not good enough” and pushing for more robust checks to properly enforce the minimum age. Singapore already required app stores to implement age assurance measures, Teo said. This is done through one of three broad methods – age estimation, which uses information a platform has about a user to estimate their age; age inference, which uses similar information to conclude an age range; and age verification, which checks a user’s age against official records. When age assurance was made mandatory for app stores, operators were asked to propose their own methods, which were approved if they appeared “reasonably robust”. The government intends to take a similar approach with social media platforms. “When it comes to being able to properly ascertain a user’s age, some steps are needed. If you don’t have a certain expectation of accuracy, then the methods of arriving at an estimation or an inference of the person’s age, these could lead to a lot of errors,” Teo said. This means a single attempt to confirm a user’s age might not be enough, she added. If a platform later gets signals suggesting a user is younger than it thought, it might need to reconfirm their age, meaning some inconvenience for users. “If we want the platforms to be able to properly assess the occasions where they have a child user, then the rest of us have to support that these methods are implemented, and so we have some mental preparation that it may cause the rest of us some inconvenience.” She also acknowledged concerns over whether platforms could safeguard the user data collected for age assurance, saying the government would require that data be collected “in a proportionate manner” – enough to implement good safeguards, but robust enough to ensure accuracy. Asked how teens had reacted, Teo said engagements suggested they accepted the need for stronger safeguards but would rather not be shut out of social media entirely. “Generally speaking, the feedback we have received is that teens understand why the safeguards are useful, and that they also support the idea of tiered access,” said Teo, adding that teens were also concerned about users even younger than themselves. This story was first published by CNA

title: Amid food security concerns, China passes first law on farmland protection and improvement
description: Law orders provincial-level governments to ensure that total amount of arable land does not decrease.
content: China has passed its first law on farmland protection and improvement amid intensified efforts to ensure its food security as climate change and geopolitical tensions increase global concerns over food supplies. The law, which will take effect from the beginning of next year, tightens control on the use of China’s arable land – a limited resource relative to the country’s huge population – and seeks to develop new farmland as Beijing places increasing importance on self-sufficiency amid uncertainties in global markets. The latest legislation on arable land resources, which President Xi Jinping has called the “lifeblood” of food production, came as a potential super El Nino event and regional military conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have put the world on alert for a potential new round of food crises. Passed by China’s top legislative body on Friday, the farmland protection law marks a major step in Beijing’s multi-year effort to prevent farmland being used for non-agricultural purposes, reclaim wasteland and improve saline-alkali land. “China’s fundamental condition of a large population and limited farmland remains unchanged,” said Zheng Linyi, a researcher with the China Academy for Rural Development at Zhejiang University. “The problems of converting arable land to non-agricultural uses and away from grain production are still prominent.” He said China urgently needed stricter legal safeguards to ensure national food security. The new law stipulates that provincial-level governments must ensure that the total amount of arable land within their administrative regions does not decrease, that its quality is improved and its ecological functions remain stable. It also incorporates previous central government requirements that any amount of arable land that is occupied for other uses must be fully replenished with an equivalent amount of land. Technologies such as satellite remote sensing, the internet, big data, cloud computing and artificial intelligence will be used to monitor the status of farmland, according to the law. In terms of developing new resources, the law encourages and supports the transformation and utilisation of saline-alkali land, and promotes innovation in the breeding and cultivation of salt-tolerant crops. It also recommends the development and use of non-traditional arable land for agricultural production, including deserts with accessible water resources. Both HSBC and JPMorgan have issued warnings about tighter global food supplies and price increases in recent weeks, citing disruptions from the Middle East conflict, the Russia-Ukraine war and extreme weather. A revised Agriculture Law, with amendments aiming to improve food security, boost farmers’ incomes and advance agricultural modernisation, was also approved by Chinese lawmakers on Friday. China has long made the stable stock of farmland a “red line” as it strives to keep its 1.4 billion people fed. Policy to this effect has paid off in recent years, with the total size of farmland increasing by about 1.5 per cent between 2020 and 2024, according to government data. China’s total grain output reached 714.88 million tonnes last year, with total production and yield per unit area both hitting historic highs.

title: Dual defence betrayal: China reveals rare case of executive spying for 2 countries
description: Highly regarded employee who handled international business for Chinese military trading firm arrested for leaking sensitive information.
content: An executive at a Chinese military trading company has been arrested for leaking sensitive defence information to intelligence agencies from two countries, Beijing’s top spy and anti-espionage agency revealed on Monday. The Ministry of State Security regularly publicises espionage cases to raise public awareness, but the vast majority of these disclosures focus on individuals targeted by a single foreign intelligence service. Public disclosures involving a Chinese national recruited simultaneously by multiple separate foreign intelligence agencies are extremely rare. The ministry outlined the case of the suspect, identified only by his surname Zhang, in an article published on an official social media account. The report did not name the two foreign countries involved, referring to them only as “Country A” and “Country B”. It also did not provide the name of the Chinese company or an exact timeline for the case. According to the ministry, Zhang was fluent in an unknown number of foreign languages after spending years studying abroad. He returned to China and was highly regarded by his employer, frequently handling international business for the arms-trading firm. The ministry said Zhang was first recruited by a foreign spy agency “several years ago” at a diplomatic reception, where a diplomat from Country A named “Lucas” approached him. Lucas had complimented Zhang on his language fluency and expertise, and the two exchanged contact information. Months later, Lucas asked Zhang to translate a few pages of technical documents for several hundred US dollars. Zhang accepted the offer, unaware that he was stepping into a trap, the ministry report said. As the translation requests became more frequent and lucrative, Lucas began seeking sensitive details regarding China’s military imports and the division of labour among Chinese arms-trading firms. Even after realising Lucas was likely an intelligence officer, Zhang continued cooperating owing to greed and a belief he would not be caught, according to the ministry. Over time, Zhang handed over verbal briefings and physical contracts, collecting tens of thousands of dollars in return. While enmeshed with Country A, Zhang was simultaneously targeted by intelligence operatives from Country B during an overseas business trip, the ministry said. Zhang got to know an embassy official from Country B named “Mike”, after Mike helped with his visa application, which the ministry described as “deliberately delayed”. Mike subsequently introduced Zhang to his assistant “Sarah”, who is of a similar age. The ministry said Sarah then approached Zhang and built a close personal relationship. She soon revealed her identity as a foreign intelligence agent and asked Zhang to provide sensitive information. Aside from promising lucrative financial rewards, Sarah told Zhang that Country B would extract him if he were exposed, persuading Zhang to furnish confidential documents on Chinese weaponry. The ministry said it uncovered Zhang’s connections with foreign intelligence agencies in the two countries after an investigation and arrested him. Zhang confessed to all charges, and his case is now being investigated further. “This day has finally come. It is too late to regret,” Zhang was quoted as saying to investigators during interrogation. The ministry said it had highlighted the case as a cautionary example of how foreign intelligence agencies used personal relationships and financial lures to recruit Chinese nationals across various sectors, from military researchers to corporate employees. It urged citizens to guard against step-by-step intelligence traps in which spies gradually escalated demands from harmless requests to core state secrets. It also reminded the public that those coerced or tricked into joining hostile organisations overseas could avoid prosecution if they promptly reported their actions to Chinese diplomatic missions or state security bodies, citing Article 55 of China’s anti-espionage law.

title: Hot property: Big banks, fashion stores seek ‘cheaper’, eye-catching Hong Kong retail
description: HSBC to open its first flagship operation at the Capitol Centre, where market sources say the rent is much lower than its previous tenancy.
content: From big banks to fashion brands, tenants are taking advantage of potential lower rents for retail space in Hong Kong’s prime areas as they utilise eye-catching locations to boost visibility towards customers, according to agents. HSBC is unveiling its first flagship branch at the Capitol Centre, which was previously occupied by fashion retailers such as Chanel, Victoria’s Secret and Forever 21, as the bank prepares to close two branches in one of the city’s top shopping areas, Causeway Bay. The bank’s new Causeway Bay flagship branch and Premier centre will open on October 20, as its existing Premier centre at the Causeway Bay Plaza 2 on Lockhart Road, and the nearby Park Lane branch on Gloucester Road will be closed at the end of business on October 17 “due to lease expiry”, a spokesman said. The spokesman, who declined to share more leasing details by citing a confidentiality agreement, added that renovation was in progress for the new location in Capitol Centre. The 161-year-old bank, which established its operation in Hong Kong in 1865, agreed to pay HK$4 million (US$510,200) a month for the space – significantly lower than the rates paid by previous tenants, according to market sources. The bank did not comment on the rent. The deal made HSBC the first non-fashion long-term tenant of the prime retail space in one of the busiest lanes in the shopping district since 2008, when Giordano leased the basement and five levels for HK$5.06 million a month. The Capitol Centre location, which spans more than 3,716 square metres (40,000 sq ft), would be larger than the combined size of the other two previous Causeway Bay locations that HSBC rented, according to a party familiar with the leasing details. The lender signed a five-year lease that began in May for the space, comprising ground plus four floors of the building, according to Land Registry records. The deal was registered in late November. The records did not show the size or rent for the leased space, but agents said the five floors would have a total area of 3,900 square metres. “Hong Kong’s retail leasing market continues to benefit from the recovery in tourism and improving business sentiment, but we are also seeing growing demand from the financial sector,” said Jackie Wong, director of occupier services at Colliers. “A number of private banks, wealth management firms and insurance companies are leveraging the current rental environment in taking up retail space in prime locations to strengthen client engagement and increase brand visibility,” she said. “These occupiers are using high-profile street-front premises as client-facing hubs, meeting spaces and experience centres.” Meanwhile, on nearby Paterson Street, fast fashion brand W. Management is set to take over a large chunk of the space vacated by Swedish competitor H&M in Fashion Walk. The group agreed to pay more than HK$2 million in monthly rents, according to a spokeswoman. The outlet will measure about 2,790 square metres, covering three floors. H&M had reportedly paid as much as HK$10 million a month for the entire 4,370 square metres spanning all four floors of the building. “The property is situated in the prime location of Causeway Bay, Hong Kong’s core retail district,” W. Management’s spokeswoman said, adding that with its transport accessibility, among others, the space is “an ideal location” for their “global flagship store in Hong Kong and aligns with the brand’s long‑term strategic development in the city”. Physical retail stores are facing challenges with the rise of online shopping. Hong Kong’s retail sales rose 7.1 per cent year-on-year in the second quarter, while online retail sales surged 25.3 per cent in the same period, according to Savills. While prime street shop rents have stabilised – with rents in the four core retail districts of Central, Causeway Bay, Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui unchanged on a quarterly basis – rents of major shopping centres fell 1.8 per cent in the same period, the property consultancy added.

title: Hong Kong retail sales rise 4.5% in July, marking 15th straight month of growth
description: Retail sales value for the month reaches HK$31 billion, with momentum remaining ‘resilient’.
content: Hong Kong’s retail sector recorded growth for a 15th consecutive month in July, with the government reporting a 4.5 per cent increase year on year, although the pace of expansion slowed amid adverse weather and continued outbound travel by residents. Retail sales value for the month reached HK$31 billion (US$4 billion), while sales in the first seven months of the year grew by 8.9 per cent compared with the same period in 2025, according to provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Monday. A government spokesman said retail sales growth momentum remained resilient in July, with growth broadly steady from the previous month. “Looking ahead, continued economic expansion, rising household incomes, and stable labour market conditions should bolster consumer sentiment,” he said. “A series of coming mega-events is also expected to sustain growth in visitor arrivals, providing further support to retail businesses.” Sales of jewellery, watches and clocks, and valuable gifts recorded the strongest increase in July, rising by 19.7 per cent year on year, followed by electrical goods and other consumer durables at 11.5 per cent. Other consumer goods not elsewhere classified also grew 10.5 per cent. Motor vehicles and parts recorded the steepest decline, falling by 18.2 per cent, closely followed by fuels at 18 per cent, while sales of Chinese drugs and herbs dropped by 13.7 per cent. The latest figures followed a 4.6 per cent increase in retail sales in June, when the value reached HK$31.5 billion. For the first half of the year, retail sales rose by 9.6 per cent in value and 7.2 per cent in volume compared with the same period in 2025. Annie Tse Yau On-yee, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Retail Management Association, said the latest figure was weak given the low comparison base, noting that July 2025 had been the second-worst month last year. “Under such a low base, a 4.5 per cent increase is not very satisfactory, although at least we are still seeing positive growth,” she said. Tse said the HK$31 billion sales value was also the lowest monthly figure so far this year, with poor weather a major drag. The city had 25 rainy days during the month, while the start of the summer holiday season also prompted more Hongkongers to travel overseas. Looking ahead, the association’s latest survey, covering about 3,100 shops and 75,000 employees, found that August sales also fell short of expectations. About 40 per cent of surveyed members said performance was worse than expected, while more than 30 per cent said it was in line with forecasts. Tse said foot traffic in traditional tourist districts such as Tsim Sha Tsui, Mong Kok and Causeway Bay remained healthy, but visitor spending power was still relatively weak. Hong Kong’s economy grew by 4.3 per cent year on year in the second quarter, bringing the increase for the first half of 2026 to 5.1 per cent. Private consumption expenditure rose by 2.8 per cent in real terms in the second quarter compared with a year earlier, slowing from a 4.9 per cent increase in the preceding three months. This month, the government raised its full-year economic growth forecast to between 3.5 and 4.5 per cent, from its previous range of 2.5 to 3.5 per cent. But it warned that geopolitical tensions, uncertainties over US trade and monetary policies, and fluctuations in global financial markets could cloud the outlook. Hong Kong welcomed 4.5 million visitors in July, a 3 per cent increase from a year earlier. Mainland arrivals also rose by 3 per cent to 3.61 million, while long-haul arrivals jumped by 17 per cent to about 307,000. The July figure brought total arrivals for the first seven months of the year to 31.22 million, an 11 per cent year-on-year increase. Mainland visitors accounted for 24.16 million arrivals, up 13 per cent, while non-mainland arrivals grew by 5 per cent to 7.05 million.

title: Hong Kong keeps T1 signal in force as storm edges closer to Guangdong coast
description: Hong Kong Observatory says unless Saudel intensifies significantly, chance of strong winds generally over Hong Kong is not high.
content: Hong Kong’s weather forecaster will keep the No 1 typhoon warning signal in force until Wednesday morning, with alerts likely extending further into the week. The Observatory said on Tuesday afternoon that the signal would remain in force for the rest of today and Wednesday morning, but the chance of issuing a No 3 strong wind signal was low. “There are rather large uncertainties in its subsequent movement and intensity. The tropical cyclone warning signal may remain in force until later this week,” the forecaster said. Tropical Depression Saudel is expected to skirt within about 200km (124 miles) southeast of Hong Kong later on Tuesday afternoon, edging closer to the coast of eastern Guangdong in the evening and Wednesday morning. “With Saudel edging closer to the coast of eastern Guangdong and intensifying gradually from Tuesday afternoon to Wednesday, local winds are expected to strengthen progressively,” the forecaster said. “Unless Saudel intensifies significantly and its associated strong winds are closer to the vicinity of the Pearl River Estuary, the chance of strong winds generally over Hong Kong is not high.” Heavier showers and squally thunderstorms are expected on Tuesday and residents are urged to check updates from the Observatory before heading out. The Observatory said maximum temperatures would hit 29 degrees Celsius (84 Fahrenheit) on Tuesday, and that Saudel was expected to weaken slightly in the latter part of this week.

title: The View | Hong Kong and Singapore property shrug off fund tax breaks
description: While the two cities compete on wealth management incentives to draw talent and capital, the spillover into office and residential real estate remains negligible.
content: The long-standing rivalry between Asia’s two leading financial centres is heating up. As Hong Kong and Singapore compete harder for investment talent, tax incentives for fund managers have emerged as the new battleground. A government bill working its way through Hong Kong’s Legislative Council would result in sweeping changes to tax rules on carried interest. The legislation, which is expected to be approved later this year, would offer preferential tax treatment to a wider range of alternative investment groups. The move by Hong Kong prompted a swift response from Singapore. On August 19, Singapore’s central bank announced a package of measures designed to enhance the appeal of the asset management industry, including a proposal that would exempt a share of profits made by fund managers when they deliver strong returns for investors in qualifying funds. Wall Street banks are already assessing the broader implications of the reforms. In a report on July 31, Citigroup said the changes to Hong Kong’s preferential tax regime were “a structural catalyst for capital and talent inflows into [Hong Kong]” that would support demand in the real estate market. If 3 per cent of fund managers from mainland China and Singapore relocated to Hong Kong, creating 1,500 new asset management positions, the grade A office market in Central, Admiralty and West Kowloon would benefit from 150,000 sq ft of additional take-up. In the housing market, demand for high-end homes would increase by 2 per cent if the relocations occurred within a year, Citigroup said. That said, tax competition is not a key determinant of the performance of Hong Kong’s real estate market. “The read-across to the property market is not that clear,” said Cathie Chung, senior director of research at JLL in Hong Kong. The rivalry between Hong Kong and Singapore has had little bearing on the fundamentals of both cities’ property sectors. The heavy influence of mainland China on Hong Kong’s economy, Singapore’s safe-haven status, the vastly different supply-demand dynamics in both markets, the importance of domestic demand in Singapore’s housing market and a much more decentralised office market in Hong Kong have proved far more consequential. Already in the first quarter of this year – before the launch of Hong Kong’s tax reform – Hong Kong was the second-most actively traded market for residential properties above US$10 million among 12 “super-prime” housing markets tracked by Knight Frank. Mainland buyers accounted for nearly half the value of new home sales in the two years following the removal of property cooling measures in February 2024, according to Midland Realty data. Tellingly, concerns about Beijing’s clampdown on outbound investment, which could constrain mainland buyers’ ability to fund property purchases in Hong Kong, contributed to the sudden fall in the city’s home prices in July. Conversely, there is little sign that competition with Hong Kong has had an effect on Singapore’s residential market. In the first half of this year, Singaporean citizens and permanent residents accounted for about 90 per cent of luxury home sales in the city’s core central region. When the stamp duty for foreigners buying any residential property was doubled to 60 per cent in 2023, the collapse in overseas purchases only accentuated the importance of domestic demand. In fact, speculative activity in Singapore’s public housing system – which houses 80 per cent of Singaporeans – has been a source of concern. The number of second-hand flats resold for at least S$1 million (US$786,000) rose to a record high last quarter despite a slowdown in the broader market. In the office sector, structural differences far outweigh the impact of competition for capital and talent. In Hong Kong, non-core districts account for more than a third of the city’s office stock. The combination of the steep fall in rents in core locations, a surge in supply in decentralised areas and strong demand for premium buildings in the central business district has led to an unbalanced recovery. In Singapore, by contrast, the office stock is concentrated in the city’s central business district. Tight supply has contributed to record low vacancy rates for grade A offices. Even grade B buildings are experiencing rental growth. “No greenfield office sites were sold since 2017 in an effort to redevelop the CBD,” said Tricia Song, head of research for Southeast Asia at CBRE. In the two cities’ commercial property investment markets, safety and liquidity are the key factors. Among the leading cities in the Asia-Pacific, Singapore was the second-most actively traded market after Tokyo in the first half of this year, according to MSCI data. Cross-border investors have accounted for the bulk of deals this year, with volumes on course to reach a record high for the year as a whole. Investors are drawn to Singapore’s “safe-haven status [and] robust supply of investment-grade assets,” CBRE said. While tax exemptions for fund managers are a big deal for the asset management industry, they are a sideshow to the forces driving property markets in Hong Kong and Singapore.

title: Review | CCOHK’s Space Fantasy is a visual spectacle great for the whole family
description: What the City Chamber Orchestra of Hong Kong’s original family musical lacked in narrative coherence, it compensated for in visual splendour.
content: The City Chamber Orchestra of Hong Kong (CCOHK) has never been one to stick to the classical canon. After Wild (2022) and Shark Symphony (2024), the orchestra continues its run of original family musicals with Space Fantasy, created by founder and artistic director Leanne Nicholls. The premiere took a bold, if slightly wobbly, leap into the cosmos. And while the narrative didn’t always land, the sheer visual spectacle was hard to resist. The story is simple enough: 10-year-old Astrid, practising a Bach partita for her school competition, encounters Fluto, an alien from Pluto who has come to Earth in search of music. Their meeting sparks a fantastical journey to outer space, where they crash a talent show called “Stars of the Cosmos”. The plot, as one might forgive for a children’s piece, is more of a clothesline for spectacle than a tightly woven narrative. Act II’s talent-show format felt like a convenient device to showcase the array of international guest artists, and the story occasionally defies logic – how, for instance, does an alien invasion lead to an intergalactic talent show with no clear stakes? But for a show aimed at three-year-olds and up, perhaps we’re not meant to overthink it. What Space Fantasy lacked in narrative coherence, it compensated for in visual splendour. After setting up the premise in Act I with a few sweet domestic scenes, Act II exploded into a full-scale revue. Each planet took a turn in the spotlight, with circus performers and musicians vying for the audience’s attention. The undisputed star of the night was Gabor Vosteen (a German performer also known as The Fluteman), who plays Fluto, a mute alien who communicates solely through his recorder. Vosteen’s Act II classical music medley was a breathtaking display of showmanship: he played five recorders simultaneously (including using his nostrils!), juggled, performed magic tricks, all while tooting Mozart and Rimsky-Korsakov flawlessly. He is a virtuoso and comedian rolled into one. The other planetary acts were equally dazzling. Kazuho Monster, a popping dancer from Japan, emerged as an unexpected highlight. His moonwalking and hypnotic body control – popping is a style that requires sudden tensing and releasing of muscles – drew cheers from the crowd. The four-arm juggler ON created uncanny illusions as Uranus, while Grace Hoop’s luminous hoop-spinning against a dark stage, representing the rings of Saturn, was mesmerising. The costumes (Twinny Cheng) and make-up and hair design (Margo Lau and Betty Wan) were central to the visual feast, dressing each planet in a distinct, detailed palette: Neptune in shimmering blues, Mercury with glowing orange goggles, and the Security Guard in an eccentric, yellow headpiece. And yet, for a production led by an orchestra, the music sometimes seemed to be accompanying rather than driving the action. The score, by Emmy-nominated screen composer Luna Pan, was pleasant and atmospheric, with humming synths and wacky electronic textures. But its film-music quality, while effective, was more reminiscent of a soundtrack than a theatrical score. Whether this was a deliberate choice by Nicholls or simply a reflection of Pan’s background, it left the orchestra in a supporting role rather than at the centre of the spectacle. Space Fantasy also struggled to balance its other ambitions. The theremin, an instrument played without physical contact, was one of the most eagerly anticipated elements of the show – its eerie sound inextricably linked to sci-fi and the unknown. But it was regrettably underused. Played by Miles Brown, a leading thereminist from Australia, the instrument appeared in only two of the 18 tracks. The first theremin solo in Act I’s “Astrid Dreams” wasn’t even obvious, as the instrument was not shown on stage. Its otherworldly tone, so perfect for the theme, was a missed opportunity for greater integration as an anchor. Meanwhile, young Adeline Wong, as Astrid, showed remarkable accomplishment playing the harp and singing, but as a 10-year-old, naturally lacked the expressive range to match Vosteen’s magnetic presence.
