Despite these quibbles, Space Fantasy created a palpable warmth in the auditorium. Children squealed in delight at Fluto’s antics, parents chuckled along and the musicians seemed to be having just as much fun as the audience. No doubt, as the new venue partner of Tsuen Wan Town Hall, CCOHK will go full speed ahead with its eclectic, risk-taking programming. Space Fantasy offers an imperfect but promising glimpse of the wonders to come. Space Fantasy, City Chamber Orchestra of Hong Kong, Tsuen Wan Town Hall Auditorium. Reviewed: August 29.

title: What do China’s new housing presale rules mean for real estate developers?
description: Beijing aims to restore buyer confidence, trading near-term financial pain for some developers for long-term market stability, analysts say.
content: With China rolling out a stronger-than-expected package of measures to transition the housing market away from a presales model, analysts said the shift is a double-edged sword for real estate developers: tighter regulations are poised to squeeze cash inflows, even as the reforms aim to stimulate sales and stabilise prices over time. Under new rules released by the People’s Bank of China, presales would remain in effect but down payments and mortgage funds would be disbursed to developers only when residential projects are fully completed. Previously, developers could already access these funds when buildings were topped out. “From structural topping out through practical completion, residential projects take six to 12 months, depending on building height,” said a private developer on condition of anonymity, citing the sensitivity of the matter. “This will substantially delay fund disbursements and weigh heavily on our cash flow.” Official data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed funds secured by property developers totalled 4.57 trillion yuan (US$679.98 billion) in the January-July period. Deposits and advance receipts and mortgage proceeds stood at 2.04 trillion yuan, accounting for 44.6 per cent of the total funding pool. The share surpassed the 36.1 per cent coming from self-raised funds. “The PBOC’s new rules serve as a major near-term negative catalyst for developers across the country,” said Fang Chengqi, chief analyst at Zhejiang province-based Caitong Securities, who estimated that developers’ average levered return on investment could drop by about 60 per cent. “Going forward, the market will increasingly be dominated by large-scale central and local government-owned developers with low leverage and solid financing access. Small regional players carrying very low leverage will also survive. Aggressive mid-tier private developers – such as Sichuan-based Bontop Group – are likely to fall by the wayside,” Fang noted. Reflecting immediate market anxiety, developer stocks came under heavy selling pressure in Hong Kong on Monday. Large-cap firms such as Beijing-based China Jinmao Holdings, Zhejiang-based Greentown China Holdings and Yuexiu Property headquartered in Guangzhou, tumbled more than 10 per cent in morning trading. A source from the mortgage business of a state-owned bank, who maintains close contact with financial regulators and spoke on condition of anonymity, said regulators and lenders had been discussing the new rules – announced by the PBOC on Friday – for some time. With slower capital turnover and shrinking cash on hand, new home supply is set to shrink over the long run Fang Chengqi, Caitong Securities “Regulators are well aware of the negative fallout for developers,” the source said. “By comparison, reassuring homebuyers that their homes will not become stalled projects and thus shoring‑up confidence in new‑home purchases carries greater priority.” The National Financial Regulatory Administration said in a statement on Friday that the reforms would help to “fundamentally protect homebuyers’ legitimate rights and interests”. Alongside the new financing framework for developers, regulators also extended the maximum mortgage term from 30 to 40 years, among other measures. The policies would better support new home sales, according to analysts. “With slower capital turnover and shrinking cash on hand, new home supply is set to shrink over the long run. Coupled with new mortgage rules that ease homebuyers’ financial burdens, new home prices will see steady gains, especially in first- and second-tier cities,” said Fang of Caitong Securities. However, Fang noted that the impact on pre-owned home prices was expected to be limited, with mid- to high-end resale properties that compete directly with new homes unlikely to see a price rebound. “The reform was inevitable,” said Cui Ji, deputy director at Shanghai-based property consultancy E-house China Research and Development Institute. “During the previous housing boom, relentless price appreciation incentivised homebuyers to prepay for off-plan units and wait for project completion as a bet on future value gains,” Cui explained. “Now that real estate has been stripped of its financial attributes, the housing market has returned to its fundamental consumption nature. A prepayment‑based transaction without any form of risk compensation is economically untenable, calling for corresponding regulatory adjustments,” Cui added. Song Yu, chief China economist at UBS Securities, said in a note on Monday that the new policies could lead to weaker new housing starts and lower supply, helping stabilise prices and reduce inventories. “While the move happened amid more signals of policy loosening, we see it more as an institutional restructuring than as policy loosening,” Song said.

title: South Korea’s Unification Church leader Han Hak-ja jailed 2 years for bribing officials
description: Han is accused of giving luxury items to former first lady Kim Keon-hee and providing illegal funds to a prominent lawmaker.
content: A South Korean court sentenced the leader of the secretive and powerful Unification Church on Monday to two years in prison on charges of bribing officials, including the then-president’s wife. Han Hak-ja, 83, was accused of providing luxury items, including a designer handbag, to former first lady Kim Keon-hee while her husband, Yoon Suk-yeol, was president, in an attempt to secure policy favours. She arrived for sentencing at court on Monday in a wheelchair, wearing pyjamas and a surgical mask, surrounded by aides. The Unification Church has a range of significant business interests, including media, education and food distribution, and has long drawn scrutiny over its political ties in South Korea. “We have confirmed that she has been sentenced to two years,” by the Seoul Central District Court, a spokesman for the Unification Church said, adding that the church would issue a statement. Other allegations against Han include providing illegal funds to prominent lawmaker Kweon Seon-dong, a former floor leader of the opposition People Power Party. Founded in 1954 by Han’s late husband, Moon Sun-myung, the Unification Church has long drawn controversy over teachings that regard Moon as the Second Coming of Jesus Christ. Han, revered by church members as the “True Mother”, took the helm of the church after Moon’s death in 2012. She was arrested in September 2025 in connection with a bribery case involving the former first lady. The Unification Church is best known for its mass wedding ceremonies, in which couples of different nationalities are matched, held at its headquarters in South Korea. Han’s arrest rocked the church, which claims to have 10 million followers worldwide. Since her arrest, Han has repeatedly been transferred between a detention centre and hospital for medical treatment. The church came under renewed scrutiny in Japan after the 2022 assassination of former prime minister Shinzo Abe, with the suspected gunman blaming the organisation for his family’s financial ruin.

title: Student admits forging reference letter for PhD place at Education University
description: Defendant says she has learned a hard lesson, but magistrate calls offence serious for depriving another applicant of a fair chance.
content: A student has admitted forging a reference letter to secure admission to a doctoral programme at a university in Hong Kong, after repeatedly failing to secure a place despite high hopes for her academic career. Fanling Court heard on Monday that 31-year-old Li Zuer from mainland China pleaded guilty to one count of obtaining services by deception. She commissioned a Shenzhen-based agent to rewrite a reference letter endorsing her academic performance and falsely claimed it had been submitted by Ho Wai-yip, a former teaching staff member at the Education University of Hong Kong (EdU), in March 2024. In court documents, Li previously stated she was enrolled in EdU’s doctor of education programme. Her lawyer told Magistrate Kenneth Chan Ping-chau that she had since lost her place as a result of the offence. The court heard Ho had originally written a reference for Li, his former student at EdU. In that letter, he praised her character but noted she “still had room to improve her English proficiency”. Senior Counsel Edwin Choy Wai-bond, representing Li, said his client had “high hopes” of building a career in academia. After multiple unsuccessful applications to doctoral programmes in Hong Kong, she turned to a Shenzhen agency to have the letter rewritten. The altered version claimed Li had demonstrated exceptional academic performance and remarkable dedication to her studies. “[Li] has always wanted to work in education. But she took a wrong turn and now she has to suffer the consequences,” Choy said. He told the magistrate that with a conviction record, Li was unlikely to be hired by any educational institution in Hong Kong or the mainland. Choy said the defendant was genuinely remorseful and ashamed of her wrongdoing. In a mitigation letter, Li wrote that she had learned a hard lesson. Magistrate Chan stressed the offence was serious. “The defendant must understand that her action had caused at least one other applicant for the doctoral programme – who might otherwise have been admitted – to be unfairly deprived of an opportunity,” Chan said. He ordered a probation officer’s report to assess whether Li would be fit to perform community service, but added that a custodial sentence remained an option. Sentencing was adjourned to September 14.

title: Man, 87, arrested after gravestone of film star Linda Lin Dai found vandalised
description: Marble altar at Lin’s Happy Valley grave found covered in cement, with police saying cemetery staff reported suspected vandalism.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested an 87-year-old man after the gravestone of late film star Linda Lin Dai was found damaged. Lin’s grave at St Michael’s Catholic Cemetery in Happy Valley was discovered with its marble altar covered in cement. In response to South China Morning Post queries, a police spokesman said officers had earlier received a report from a cemetery staff member that a grave was suspected to have been vandalised. Following an investigation, the 87-year-old was arrested on August 4 and charged with one count of criminal damage. He appeared in Eastern Court on August 17. The cemetery office confirmed it had referred the case to police and that the suspect had been charged, but declined to comment further. Linda Ching Yuet-chue – known professionally as Lin Dai – took her own life in her bedroom at the age of 29 in 1964, shocking fans and the film community. Dubbed the “Elizabeth Taylor of the East”, she won the best actress award at the Asia-Pacific Film Festival four times. In 2008, Lin’s son donated her personal belongings, film-related memorabilia and items reflecting her life as a movie star in the 1950s and 1960s to the government for exhibition as he prepared to renovate her former home.

title: Hong Kong students, at-risk residents can get flu jabs 1 week early this year
description: Centre for Health Protection says the government’s seasonal influenza vaccination programmes for 2026-27 will begin on September 17.
content: Hong Kong school students and other at-risk residents can receive influenza vaccines one week earlier this year, after the government diversified its procurement efforts and streamlined administrative measures. Authorities also said on Monday they aimed to boost the injection rate among people aged 65 or above and children aged six months to two years, adding that they would rely on reminders from doctors during medical encounters as a prioritised measure. Dr Edwin Tsui Lok-kin, controller of the Centre for Health Protection, said the government’s seasonal influenza vaccination programmes for 2026-27 would begin on September 17, one week earlier than those in the previous year. “Influenza is still active in August despite it having slightly subsided from the peak, and as students gather after school starts, transmission will be quicker,” Tsui said. “We expect there will be some transmissions and outbreaks in schools after the new academic year starts, and therefore, we advise [students] to receive jabs as early as available.” The programmes include the Vaccination Subsidy Scheme (VSS), which offers subsidised doses to vulnerable groups such as children, residents aged 50 or above, pregnant women and adults with chronic diseases. The other covered schemes are the outreach vaccination programmes for schools and residential care homes. Tsui said the programmes could start early as the government had stepped up the diversification of vaccine procurement efforts. Similar to last year, the government has bought injectable inactivated vaccines from French manufacturer Sanofi and Chinese pharmaceutical company Sinovac, nasal spray live attenuated vaccines from Swedish-British firm AstraZeneca and injectable recombinant jabs from Sanofi, totalling 1.3 million doses. This year, the number of Sanofi inactivated doses was reduced from 900,000 to 660,000, while the number from Sinovac was increased to 530,000, up from 300,000 in 2025. Meanwhile, the number of procured nasal spray and recombinant vaccines had increased to about 60,000 each, up from 50,000 each last year. Health authorities noted that while the Sanofi vaccines would only arrive in batches from mid-October, those from Sinovac had started arriving in late August. Tsui said the early arrival of some vaccines enabled authorities to start their inoculation drives earlier. All of this year’s procured vaccines are trivalent doses intended to protect against three flu strains. The World Health Organization earlier said the inclusion of the Yamagata variant of influenza B was no longer warranted. Tsui said the introduction of e-consent forms for parents through the government’s eHealth system had also allowed schools to make administrative preparations before the academic year started. Authorities also strengthened a pilot scheme that helped private doctors procure vaccines with government contracts by tripling the supply and expanding the eligibility for those taking part. Dr Christina Maw Kit-chee, assistant director of the Health Bureau’s Strategic Purchasing Office, said the government had procured 300,000 jabs under the scheme, up from 100,000 last year. The policy covers doctors who signed up for the VSS and at least one other government-subsidised primary healthcare programme. Last year’s programme was only open to those who joined both the VSS and the Chronic Disease Co-Care Pilot Scheme. Maw added that the government would review the pilot scheme and decide whether to normalise it after collecting information about demand levels from targeted groups as well as the ratio of government-procured vaccines to those doctors bought from private markets. According to government statistics, 2.03 million vaccines were administered under the government schemes in 2025-26, down from nearly 2.09 million a year earlier. Tsui noted that 27.4 per cent of children aged between six months and two years were covered by vaccines, higher than the moving average of the previous three years, 19.9 per cent, but the number would still need to rise as the proportion was relatively low. Government data also showed that only 49.4 per cent of residents aged 65 or above had received vaccines, 1.3 percentage points lower than the average of the previous three years. “From academic research, one of the most effective measures to promote such measures is [through] messages given by doctors during medical encounters in clinics,” Tsui said. He added that the government would work closely with all doctors to remind patients to get their flu jabs.

title: Malaysia’s air quality turns hazardous as Indonesian wildfires burn
description: Pollution index hits 476 near the border, forcing school closures and triggering emergency cloud-seeding plans in Sarawak.
content: Air pollution in Malaysia’s Bornean state of Sarawak has surged into hazardous territory, with the air pollutant index (API) topping 400 in the worst-hit district, as forest fires raging in Indonesia continue to send thick smoke drifting across the border. Serian in Sarawak, closest to the frontier with Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province, recorded the highest reading of 476 as of Monday morning. Kuching, Samarahan and Sri Aman all logged readings above 300 as of 10am, according to Malaysia’s Environment Department. The API scale classifies anything above 300 as hazardous; readings of 201-300 are “very unhealthy”, 101-200 “unhealthy”, 51-100 “moderate” and 0-50 “good”. Malaysia has activated its National Open Burning Action Plan and National Haze Action Plan in response, mobilising government agencies to tackle both the fires and the health risks posed by the smoke. Government protocols call for the suspension of outdoor activities at schools once API readings exceed 100, with schools, kindergartens and childcare centres to shut immediately once readings pass 200. If API levels stay above 150 for more than 24 hours, authorities have said they will launch cloud-seeding operations to induce rain and activate the Disaster Management Committee. Satellites map blazes Satellite analysis by the Asean Specialised Meteorological Centre in Singapore had detected 1,190 active hotspots in Kalimantan and 18 in Sumatra, the Environment Department said. A further 13 hotspots were recorded inside Malaysia itself: nine in Sarawak, two in Perak and two in Sabah. Azuri Azizah Saedon, a deputy director general for development at the department, said dry conditions were persisting across much of the region, with the exception of northern Sumatra and Peninsular Malaysia, both of which had received some rain. “Moderate to dense haze was observed over western Borneo, while moderate to dense smoke plumes were also detected in several other parts of Kalimantan as well as central and southern Sumatra,” she said in a statement on Sunday, adding that cloud cover was obscuring a fuller picture of the regional hotspots and haze. Satellite data from Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System on Sunday showed dense concentrations of heat signatures in West Kalimantan, close to the Sarawak border. Indonesia’s national disaster management agency said on Sunday that haze conditions in Kalimantan were severe, with visibility in three priority provinces falling below 1.5km (0.9 miles) – worse than the 2.4km to 5km (1.5 miles to 3.1 miles) recorded in affected areas of Sumatra. Air pollution in parts of Kalimantan reached extreme levels, with Indonesia’s equivalent air pollutant standard index (ISPU) hitting 877 in Katingan, Central Kalimantan; 720 in Southeast Pontianak, West Kalimantan; and 715 in Barito Selatan Sanggu, Central Kalimantan, as of 4.41pm on Sunday, said Berton Panjaitan, the agency’s acting head of data, information and disaster communication. “When air quality reaches unhealthy or hazardous levels, we always advise people to minimise outdoor activities and, if they must go outside, to wear a mask,” Berton said, according to national news agency Bernama. Indonesia has around 50,000 personnel on standby for firefighting and monitoring operations, backed by 53 aircraft, including 34 for water bombing and 13 for aerial patrols. Firefighting efforts are also being stepped up in West Papua, where 35 hotspots and active fires have been detected. El Nino effect? Smoke from the fires continues to drift towards the Strait of Malacca and the Natuna Sea, creating transboundary haze in Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei as prevailing winds carry pollutants across the region. Climate scientists have linked the fires to El Nino, the climate pattern associated with reduced rainfall across much of Southeast Asia. Fredolin Tanggang, professor emeritus of climatology and climate change at the National University of Malaysia, said the phenomenon should be understood as triggering a chain of interconnected, and partly foreseeable, risks that could be anticipated and, at least to some extent, prevented. El Nino caused soils and vegetation to become progressively drier, he told local news outlet Utusan Sarawak, adding: “Peatlands lose moisture and become increasingly susceptible to fire. When fires occur on a large scale, smoke can be transported by winds across national borders.” The Environment Department has said it will continue working with Malaysia’s ministries and disaster agencies to respond “swiftly and proactively” with measures set out in the National Haze Action Plan as the fire season continues.

title: Meet Elizaveta Neretin, who plays Ukrainian spy Oleksandra in Lioness
description: She has a deep personal connection to her role in Taylor Sheridan’s thriller, and the Juilliard-trained actress wants to be a Bond girl.
content: The third season of Oscar-nominated writer Taylor Sheridan’s Paramount+ series, Lioness, is more than halfway through, with each episode leaving viewers on the edge of their seats. Starring acclaimed actors Zoë Saldaña, Nicole Kidman and Morgan Freeman, the show is considered one of Sheridan’s best works to date. View this post on Instagram This season explores the Russia-Ukraine war, with Saldaña’s character, Joe McNamara, directly involved on the front lines. Interestingly, a new addition to the Lioness cast shares a personal connection to this season’s storyline: Russian-Ukrainian actress Elizaveta Neretin portrays Ukrainian double agent Oleksandra Balakin, who reluctantly works alongside Joe. So, who is the 33-year-old actor joining the star-studded line-up? Here is everything you need to know about Elizaveta Neretin. What is Elizaveta Neretin’s background? Elizaveta Neretin was born in Cherkasy, Ukraine, to a Russian father and Ukrainian mother. Raised across Moldova, Russia and Ukraine, she moved to Montreal, Canada with her father at 14, and speaks English, Russian, Ukrainian and French. Per Decider, Neretin studied biology at university for seven years after her father pushed her towards science: “My father was a mechanical engineer, and he was really like, ‘You’re going to be a doctor, because that’s the best job.’” But after a heartbreak, she reconsidered what she wanted from life and admitted her true dream was to become an actress. She enrolled in the Vancouver Acting School, completing its intensive and conservatory programmes over 15 months. How did Elizaveta Neretin break into acting? Following her training, Neretin began taking on screen roles, appearing in television series such as The 100, The Flash and Taylor Sheridan’s Mayor of Kingstown – featuring in the latter’s pilot episode. “After the first day of shooting, [Sheridan] sat down next to me and said, ‘Why did I kill you?’ So, I took that as a good sign,” she told CTV Your Morning. Speaking on the breakfast television programme, the actress recalled auditioning for The Juilliard School over Zoom during the Covid-19 pandemic. She secured a place and graduated from the prestigious institution with a Master of Fine Arts in 2025. “It’s very rigorous training … It’s four years. It’s 12 hours a day. It’s six days a week,” she said. “They really work you, and it develops your stamina.” Upon graduating, she reconnected with Sheridan, who offered her a role in Lioness – a part deeply tied to her personal heritage. “It was quite challenging. I am half Russian, half Ukrainian. Saying ‘don’t call me Russian’ in that one scene was very difficult for me, and yet, as an actor, that is the job,” Neretin told Decider. “You take on someone’s perspective, and you play their truth. You must lean into it.” She has big goals Neretin’s acting career may have only just taken off, but she has already set her sights on a wide variety of projects. “I would very much like to be a Bond girl,” Neretin told Click and Tell, an interview show co-hosted by Sangita Patel. “I think that would be really cool and kind of in line with the things I’ve been doing.” Her aspirations do not end with action. Thanks to her rigorous tenure at Juilliard – where her training included singing and acting in period corsetry – she is eager to tackle both musicals and costume dramas. “I would love to at some point do a musical,” she added. “Doing a film musical would be on another level, [a] dream come true.”

title: Indonesia-US joint military drills with allies kick off with 4,700 soldiers
description: The exercises, which have been held for nearly two decades, will include special forces infiltration training and cyberdefence drills.
content: Indonesia, the United States and more than a dozen allies launched annual joint military exercises on Monday to boost defence capabilities and “deter aggression” in the Asia-Pacific region. Jakarta maintains a neutral foreign policy, what it calls “free and active”, as it walks a diplomatic tightrope seeking good relations with both Washington and Beijing. The Southeast Asian giant held a joint navy drill with China this month that was blasted by Taiwan as a “provocation”. Indonesia, the US and certain allies have taken part in the annual drills, known as the Super Garuda Shield, for nearly two decades. This year’s edition will entail 4,700 soldiers from countries including Britain, France and Japan drills in several locations including Sumatra and Borneo islands until September 11. East Timor, Italy, Thailand and other nations have sent observers. Patrick Ellis, commander of the US Fourth Infantry Division, said the exercise was critical for “building the human architecture that keeps the Indo-Pacific safe”. “The security landscape of the Indo-Pacific is complex and readiness cannot be surged when a crisis begins,” he said at a military school in Bandung, east of Jakarta, where the drills officially kicked off. The exercises would include special forces infiltration training and cyber defence drills, Ellis added. Indonesia elevated its defence cooperation with the US to that of a major defence cooperation partnership in April. Ellis said Monday that was a testament to the role of the world’s third-largest democracy as a “vital anchor to regional stability”. China’s foreign and defence ministers travelled to Indonesia this month for talks with their counterparts, agreeing on greater political and military cooperation. Later this year, the two countries will hold their own joint military exercises under Heping Garuda – a recurring drill focused on humanitarian aid, disaster relief and military-to-military cooperation. Indonesia joined the Brics bloc of emerging economies last year that includes Russia and China. But President Prabowo Subianto has also signed a trade deal with US President Donald Trump and joined his so-called Board of Peace.

title: China’s 6 biggest state banks post rare shared growth as margins show tentative rebound
description: Half-year results rise across China’s largest state-owned lenders amid tentative signs of margin stabilisation.
content: China’s six largest state-owned banks recorded their first simultaneous rise in first-half revenue and net profit since 2022, according to interim results released last week, as margins that had been under pressure for two years showed tentative signs of stabilising. Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC), China Construction Bank (CCB), Agricultural Bank of China (ABC), Bank of China (BOC), Bank of Communications (Bocom) and Postal Savings Bank of China (PSBC) together generated more than 2 trillion yuan (US$297 billion) in operating income for the first half. Combined net profit attributable to shareholders amounted to about 712.6 billion yuan. Revenue grew between 4 and 11 per cent across the six lenders, while net profit rose 4 to 6 per cent – the first time since 2022 that all six registered positive growth on both counts at the same time. The improvement was underpinned by a tentative rebound in net interest margin (NIM) – the spread between what banks earn on loans and pay on deposits – after two years of steady compression that dragged the industry average down to a record low of nearly 1.4 per cent in the first quarter. A structural inflection point has yet to be confirmed and will depend on broader economic recovery and shifts in the interest rate environment Dong Ximiao, Merchants Union Consumer Finance CCB led the turn, posting a half-year NIM of 1.37 per cent – up 0.03 percentage points from full-year 2025 and 0.01 percentage points from the first quarter. ABC’s margin climbed 0.02 percentage points from the first quarter to 1.28 per cent, while ICBC and BOC each edged up 0.01 percentage points year on year, to 1.29 and 1.27 per cent, respectively. Bocom’s NIM rose 0.02 percentage points to 1.23 per cent. PSBC’s margin slipped 0.07 percentage points to 1.63 per cent but remained the highest among peers. Disciplined liability-cost management proved crucial. CCB reported a 0.34 percentage point drop in time deposit payout rates relative to early 2026, while domestic demand deposit balances expanded. ABC reported a 4.7 per cent drop in interest expenses as high-cost, fixed-term deposits matured and were repriced at lower prevailing rates, cutting overall deposit interest costs by 0.21 percentage points compared with late 2025. ICBC president Liu Jun said in a press release on Friday the bigger driver was “more appropriate liability costs and a more optimised liability structure … not just repricing”. Analysts urged caution over declaring a full-fledged turnaround. The recent margin rebound marked a low-level bottoming phase rather than a clear trend reversal, said Ming Ming, chief economist at Citic Securities. As relief from deposit repricing diminished, “the core conflict surrounding bank interest margins would gradually shift from elevated liability costs to pressure on asset yields”. Ming added that, going forward, bank operations would “pivot from passively offsetting margin compression to refined asset-liability management, raising the proportion of low-cost liabilities and optimising loan structures”. Dong Ximiao, chief economist at Merchants Union Consumer Finance, described the margin recovery as an “L-shaped bottoming”, noting that the boost from lower deposit costs would fade in the second half of the year while asset yields continued to fall. “A structural inflection point has yet to be confirmed and will depend on broader economic recovery and shifts in the interest rate environment,” Dong said in a recent domestic report. Asset quality across the state-owned lenders remained resilient, with PSBC recording the lowest non-performing loan ratio at 1 per cent, while peers hovered between 1.22 per cent and 1.3 per cent. Underpinned by steady balance sheets, the six lenders announced combined interim dividend plans exceeding 220 billion yuan, raising their cash payout ratio to around 31 per cent – up by about 1 percentage point from previous levels. Upbeat half-year results buoyed investor sentiment across mainland markets on Monday, with BOC leading gains as its Shanghai-listed shares closed more than 5 per cent higher.

title: Meet Kelly Vohnn, the Dolly Parton impersonator who CNN mistook for the country legend
description: The network later apologised to the ‘Jolene’ singer’s family; Vohnn, who is based in Las Vegas and a big fan of Parton, has thoughts on the matter herself.
content: Country music icon Dolly Parton passed away on August 25 at the age of 80 from cancer. Tributes poured in from around the world as fans mourned her passing, but one news network found itself making headlines for all the wrong reasons. During a Laura Coates Live report last Tuesday, CNN displayed a montage dedicated to the Queen of Country. But one of the images in the montage did not feature Dolly at all. Instead, it showed Las Vegas tribute artist Kelly Vohnn, 58, attending a screening of the film Song Sung Blue (2025) at the Palms Casino Resort, with the network seemingly mistaking the impersonator for Parton herself. CNN later apologised with a statement, “We regret the error and apologise to the Parton family.” What do we know about Kelly Vohnn – a performer who has portrayed Dolly Parton over the years, and whose resemblance to the “Jolene” singer fooled even CNN? What is Kelly Vohnn’s background? Kelly Vohnn was born on May 29, 1968, to parents Nick and Fran in Toronto, and grew up with two siblings, Sean and Tracy. She studied Voice at the Royal Conservatory of Music and majored in Voice at Humber College in Toronto. She has three children, Brittany, Amanda and Chris, whom she raised and home-schooled as a single mother after her husband walked out on the family, per The Mirror. She married her current husband James Kirner in 2022, and the couple is based in Las Vegas. She’s not just a tribute artist Vohnn’s musical career began at the Keith Burton Tribute Show, where she impersonated Parton, Patsy Cline, Madonna, Shania Twain and Reba McEntire. She eventually launched her own label, Payback Records, and released her debut record A New Beginning in 1999, which found some small success in Europe. To balance her responsibilities as a single mum and her music career, she went on the road as a singing impersonator, taking her children along. She worked as a supporting vocalist for Lou Gramm, Fee Waybill, and Mickey Thomas, led the one-woman shows Kelly Vohnn Divas and The Women In Me, and performed in Cowboy Cabaret. She also impersonates Barbra Streisand and Marilyn Monroe. How did Kelly Vohnn react to CNN’s mix-up? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kelly Vohnn Haggerty (@kellyvohnn) As startling as the mistake was for fans, it was also distressing to Vohnn. “I started getting all these texts in from friends saying that I was on CNN, and I couldn’t believe it,” she told the New York Post, adding, “I was already heartbroken at losing Dolly because of how much she has given to me as a woman and an artist. But then to see these images of me on screen was just weird.” She did not mince her words while calling out the network either. “Somebody at CNN really messed up and didn’t do their research,” she said, emphasising how she “felt so sorry and apologetic for Dolly”.

title: China’s AI chip drive: MetaX and Iluvatar swing to profit, as Biren narrows losses
description: MetaX posted a net profit of 612 million yuan for the first six months, reversing a loss of 186 million yuan a year earlier.
content: China’s home-grown artificial intelligence chipmakers are starting to cash in on Beijing’s self-reliance drive, but a fresh wave of first-half earnings reveals a stark divide between the industry’s rising profit stars and loss-making players. Shares of Chinese AI chipmakers traded mixed on Monday as investors digested the financial updates. MetaX Integrated Circuits saw its Shanghai-listed stock rise 2.4 per cent to 691.2 yuan on Monday after reporting a swing to profitability late on Sunday. Cross-town rival Biren Technology surged 18.8 per cent to HK$46.62 in Hong Kong, while Iluvatar Corex dropped 2.2 per cent to HK$388.2 in Hong Kong. The stock moves followed reports of a pivotal half-year for domestic graphics processing unit (GPU) designers, who are beginning to reap financial rewards from Beijing’s push for tech self-sufficiency and an aggressive national AI infrastructure buildout. MetaX, which made a high-profile debut on Shanghai’s Star Market in December, posted a net profit of 612 million yuan (US$90.9 million) for the first six months, reversing a loss of 186 million yuan a year earlier. First-half revenue jumped 44.7 per cent to 1.32 billion yuan, driven by widespread customer adoption and a sharp increase in GPU shipments, according to its stock exchange filing on Sunday evening. Founded in 2020 by a team of former executives from US chip firm Advanced Micro Devices, MetaX has emerged as one of China’s most closely watched GPU developers as domestic firms race to build alternatives to Nvidia’s AI chips. The company has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong listing, targeting a debut in the city by the end of this year, the South China Morning Post reported in July. Iluvatar Corex reported a similar turnaround on Friday. The company posted a net profit of 106 million yuan in the first half, compared with a 609 million yuan loss in the same period last year. Revenue surged over 191 per cent to 945.7 million yuan, with its core general-purpose GPU products generating 916.1 million yuan. In contrast, Biren Technology’s results showed a starkly different path. The company remained in the red with a net loss of 377 million yuan, though that marked a sharp narrowing from a 1.6 billion yuan loss a year earlier. Its first-half revenue stole the spotlight, skyrocketing nearly 1,998 per cent year on year to 1.24 billion yuan – surpassing its total revenue for all of last year. Exponential growth in AI token consumption has pushed the industry into a new stage of system-level competition, Biren said in a filing on Friday, adding that the trend continued to fuel strong demand for general-purpose GPU computing solutions. The divergence comes as makers of general-purpose GPUs, an architecture popularised by Nvidia, continue to expand market share despite rising competition from application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) championed by domestic rivals including Cambricon Technologies and Huawei Technologies’ Ascend unit. Both Biren and Iluvatar went public in Hong Kong earlier this year amid a wave of fundraising by Chinese AI chipmakers, fuelled by Beijing’s push for semiconductor self-reliance in the face of tightening US export controls.

title: Physical woes dog Novak Djokovic in shock US Open first-round loss, first in 20 years
description: Argentinian Mariano Navone wins in five sets at Flushing Meadows, as Novak Djokovic says he’s suffered ‘every match’ this year.
content: Novak Djokovic suffered his earliest grand slam exit in 20 years in New York on Sunday and said he doesn’t know the solution to the physical problems he’s battled in “pretty much every match” this year. Argentine Mariano Navone’s 7-6, 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 victory in the first round of the US Open ended Djokovic’s latest bid for a record 25th grand slam title. It also ended his run of 78 first-round victories in major tournaments, a streak stretching all the way back to a 2006 loss to Paul Goldstein at the Australian Open. Djokovic vomited on court and struggled with late-match cramps and back pain – an “awful feeling” that he’s becoming used to. “It’s something that I’ve been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year. Vomiting, throwing up … Then my whole body starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain.” Although he reached the final of the Australian Open this year and the semi-finals at Wimbledon, Djokovic said he’s not equipped right now to go deep in tournaments – and he’s not sure what the fix is. “I’m just trying to address really what’s going on and how far I can go this way,” he said. Despite his struggles, Djokovic appeared to have finally taken control when he broke Navone for a 2-1 lead in the fourth set with a vintage backhand winner down the line. But Navone won the next five games, raising his arms in celebration after fighting off two break points for a 5-2 lead and breaking Djokovic again to force the fifth set. Djokovic took a medical timeout before the final set, receiving a massage on his spine and another delivery of medication. Navone jumped to a 3-0 lead in the decisive set and despite the urging of fans there was no road back for the Serb as his opponent dropped just one point on his own serve as he sprinted to the finish line. “It’s unbelievable,” an ecstatic Navone said after triumphing in his first meeting with his long-time idol after four hours and 36 minutes. “It was a tough match, a battle. Playing against Novak the first time in the biggest stage we have in the world of tennis right now … Like, until 20 years he never lose in the first round, so I mean, it’s crazy.” Navone, ranked 48th, was most pleased with his mental game. “I was two sets to one down, and then break down also in the fourth, but in that moment I felt it,” he said. Djokovic broke Navone in the second game of the match as he rolled to a 3-1 first-set lead. But he was clearly struggling and with Navone gaining confidence Djokovic had to claw out of 0-40 hole to hold for 4-1, looking weary as Navone began to extend the rallies. Djokovic’s double fault on break point allowed Navone to cut the deficit to 4-3, and after a brief pause to close the roof when showers struck, Navone held at love to knot the set at 4-4. Neither blinked until the tiebreaker, but pills delivered by the trainer didn’t solve Djokovic’s sluggishness. He fell behind 4-2 in the tiebreaker and after a cleverly angled forehand winner to make it 5-5, Djokovic hit a forehand long and another weakly into the net to give the set to Navone. In a tense second set, Djokovic missed break chances in the third and fifth games before breaking Navone at love for a 6-5 lead and holding at love to level the match at one set apiece. The third set was more of the same, with Djokovic looking spent after every long rally. He let a precious break chance go begging in the fifth game of the third and after Navone held for 3-2 Djokovic all but collapsed into his courtside chair and buried his face in a towel. The Serb pressed on and was rewarded with a crucial break for a 5-4 lead. He held for a two sets to one lead but couldn’t make the advantage stand. After breaking Navone for a 2-1 lead in the fourth Djokovic lost the next eight games. When it was all over, Djokovic embraced Navone, then departed, blowing kisses to the crowd that had tried to will him to victory. “So grateful to experience this,” he said of the crowd support. “They were trying to lift me up in important moments … the love and appreciation they gave me in the end really touched my heart.”

title: China warns of ‘major risk’ of glacier collapse as landslide death toll nears 1,000
description: Rescue teams continues their efforts to reach the Gyirong Port border crossing as bad weather is forecast over the coming days.
content: China warned on Monday there was a “major risk” of further glacier collapses and landslides along the border with Nepal as the death toll from last week’s deadly mudslide rose to close to 1,000. The Ministry of Water Resources said there was an ongoing threat along the Cuojian River in Nepal, a waterway that flows into the Purepuqiang River in Tibet, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported. Downstream in Tibet there was also a risk that further landslides would cause a new barrier lake to form, the ministry added. The death toll in Nepal has risen to 903, with 4,247 people still missing, according to data released by the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Monday. Chinese authorities said on Sunday that the death toll on their side of the border had risen to 16, with 546 people still missing. The death toll after Wednesday’s massive surge of ice, floodwater and rocks is expected to rise in the coming days as search and rescue operations continue. Worsening weather and persistent and heavy rain could further complicate rescue operations and disrupt transport, with state media urging heightened vigilance against secondary hazards. On Monday, the China Meteorological Administration warned of more rain in Gyirong county, Tibet autonomous region, over the next three days, warning it could complicate rescue operations and transport, and urged rescuers to stay on high alert. The rain could make roads slippery along the Shigatse-Gyirong and Gyirong-Gyirong Port routes, said Zhang Taiyuan, a weather presenter with the administration, who urged rescue and relief vehicles to take extra care. More than 60 rescuers trekked for more than 10 hours through mountainous terrain to reach the core area on Sunday. They have searched an area of about 40,000 square metres (430,560 sq ft) twice, according to CCTV. High-water marks on the mountainside opposite Gyirong Port show that floodwaters had reached more than 60 metres (197 feet) – roughly the height of a 20-storey building – at their peak, rescuers estimated, according to CCTV. Yao Xueqin, deputy head of a fire and rescue unit deployed to the disaster area, said teams would continue searching. He said initial searches had focused on surface debris, and they would dig deeper in later operations. People on both sides of the border have posted on social media asking for tips on finding missing relatives and friends who were near the Gyirong Port border crossing when the disaster struck. Of those missing, 261 were foreign nationals, state news agency Xinhua reported, including 104 from Nepal, 49 from India, 33 from Latvia and 18 from the United States. The deadly disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse at Langtang Lirung on the Nepalese side of the border at an altitude of about 5,200 metres. Some buildings were buried, and power, communications and road access were cut off following the mudslide. Efforts to reopen the damaged section of a national highway leading to Gyirong Port have been stepped up. The road was cut off by the mudslides, severely hampering rescue operations. As of 4pm on Monday, crews had cleared and reopened hundreds of metres of road, leaving about 1.1km (0.7 miles) to go before reaching Gyirong Port. “The most challenging section of the road-reopening effort has entered its final push,” CCTV reported. An emergency communications base station near the Gyirong Port border gate was put into operation on Sunday, CCTV reported. Communications repair workers were able to speak with rescuers at the port through the station. The disaster has focused attention on the challenges of monitoring and providing early warnings for high-altitude glacial hazards in the remote Himalayan border region. The mudslide created by the glacier collapse travelled 22km along the valley and reached Gyirong Port border crossing in just seven minutes. Scientists told the Chinese media platform Shangguan News they could draw on years of satellite imagery to map glaciers and glacial lakes, but small or sudden changes could be hard to capture in real time. Ground monitoring could help fill the gap, but remote areas often lacked reliable communications, making real-time transmission and monitoring difficult, they added. China has also developed online monitoring and early-warning systems for some high-risk glacial lakes, but scientists have warned that the effectiveness of such systems depends on who receives and assesses the data. Much also depends on who decides whether to issue a warning and how quickly people at risk receive such information as some hazards can appear within minutes, leaving little time to get people to safety. The challenge became even greater across an international border, the report added. China had been sharing important information with Nepal, including disaster-area imagery, satellite and hydrological data, as well as early warnings on the upstream barrier lake, the foreign ministry said on Monday. The disaster struck on Wednesday as an annual disaster risk reduction conference organised by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development was being hosted in Chengdu, in the southwestern Chinese province of Sichuan. Local media reported that the topics discussed at the event included cross-border disaster information-sharing and setting up regular coordination mechanisms between China, Nepal and other Himalayan countries.

title: Chip expert Chen Ye joins China’s Zhejiang University – as it overtakes Harvard
description: Semiconductor expert appointed Qiushi Distinguished Professor at university named world’s top academic institution by the Nature Index.
content: Chen Ye, a semiconductor quality control expert with more than 16 years of industry experience in the United States, has been appointed as a Qiushi Distinguished Professor at Zhejiang University’s College of Integrated Circuits, the university has announced. The university, based in Hangzhou, overtook Harvard University to become the world’s top academic institution in the 2026 Nature Index, ending its 11-year grip on the title which it had held since 2015. Chen most recently served as chief scientist at Semitronix Corporation in Hangzhou, China, a role he took on in 2024, after returning from the US. Before that, he spent over 16 years at top American chip firms, including KLA and Anchor Semiconductor, where he specialised in developing defect-detection and yield-analysis systems for advanced chip manufacturing. According to Zhejiang University, the tools developed under Chen’s leadership have been deployed in large-scale mass production at leading international wafer foundries such as TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company), Samsung and Intel. Chen’s connection to Zhejiang University runs deep. He earned his bachelor’s degree in electronics and information engineering at the university in 2003, followed by a PhD. His semiconductor career in the US began in 2008 at Anchor Semiconductor, a pioneer in hotspot management and analysis software for both foundries and integrated device manufacturers to improve manufacturing efficiency and chip yield. He graduated with his doctorate that same year. At Anchor, Chen rose from senior software engineer to principal engineer and director of advanced R&D. After KLA, a global leader in semiconductor wafer fabrication equipment and process control, acquired Anchor in 2021, he continued as a research scientist. His work frequently took him to integrated circuit fabrication facilities in China, Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, where he developed software on-site using classified manufacturing data. On his LinkedIn profile, he noted: “18+ years of experience as a software developer and a technical lead. 38+ visits to IC fabs in China, Taiwan, South Korea and Japan to define projects and develop software on-site.” In 2024, Chen returned to China and joined Semitronix as chief scientist, where he built China’s first intelligent inspection platform for the entire manufacturing process, called ConVision, from the ground up. Earlier reports on Zhejiang University’s website in June had already identified Chen as a leading talent in national scientific and technological innovation and a newly appointed Qiushi Distinguished Professor. The appointment was officially announced earlier this month. The South China Morning Post has contacted Chen for comment.

title: Malaysian state’s cash handouts for teen weddings trigger backlash
description: Perak’s plan to offer money to newlyweds as young as 15 risks endorsing child marriage, rights groups warn.
content: A proposal in Malaysia’s Perak state to pay young people 500 ringgit (US$124) for marrying for the first time has triggered a backlash after officials confirmed the scheme could apply to children as young as 15. Critics say extending the state-funded benefit to minors risks legitimising child marriage, reigniting a fraught debate in Malaysia over laws that still allow some under-18s to wed. The one-off payment, under consideration for Perak’s 2027 budget, would be open to first-time couples aged 15 to 35 who were born in the northwestern state or have lived there for at least a decade. Khairudin Abu Hanipah, chairman of Perak state’s education and youth committee, said the proposal was unanimously approved at the fifth sitting of the Perak Youth Assembly – an advisory forum for young people – and was intended to ease the financial burden on young couples. We view this as a positive initiative Khairudin Abu Hanipah, Perak youth committee chairman “We view this as a positive initiative that demonstrates the state government’s care and concern by providing some assistance to newly married couples,” he told reporters after a state youth awards ceremony on Friday. He said the proposed age range for the handout followed the definition of youth under Malaysia’s Youth Societies and Youth Development Act 2007. The plan has yet to be approved by Perak’s state executive council and is expected to be finalised before the state’s next budget is put forward in November. Rights groups and politicians alike have condemned the proposal’s inclusion of 15, 16 and 17-year-olds. “Any form of marriage incentive should not include children or individuals below the age of 18”, said Malaysia’s national human rights commission Suhakam in a statement issued on Sunday through its Office of the Children’s Commissioner. Offering money to minors in such a way risked creating the perception that child marriage was “accepted, supported or encouraged”, it said. Malaysia’s Child Act defines anyone under 18 as a child. Under Perak’s Islamic Family Law Enactment 2004, Muslim men must typically be 18 and Muslim women 16 to marry, though a sharia judge may grant written permission for marriages below those thresholds. For non-Muslims, federal law generally sets the minimum age at 18, although girls aged 16 or 17 may marry with a special licence. The controversy has also revived scrutiny of Perak’s record on the issue. In March 2022, the state government proposed raising the minimum marriage age, pointing to poverty, patchy access to education and permissive statutes as among the forces pushing children into wedlock. In 2021 alone, Perak recorded 144 underage marriages, according to official figures from Malaysia’s Department of Statistics – 130 of which involved girls under the age of 18. Children aged 15 to 17 “should be in school, not thinking about marriage”, Amira Aisya Abdul Aziz, president of youth-focused political party Muda, said on Friday. “The Perak state government needs to review its proposed first marriage incentive for young people,” she said. “This incentive would only encourage marriages involving children.” The proposal has also drawn criticism on social media, much of it directed at the decision to set the eligibility threshold at 15. “A 15-year-old has no business thinking about marriage,” one user wrote. Another asked how the measure had cleared the youth assembly unopposed: “How many school kids are married there for this to be voted [on] unanimously?” Even those seemingly unbothered by the age question found the sums involved faintly absurd. As one commenter put it, 500 ringgit “wouldn’t even cover the food for the wedding”. This Week in Asia has contacted Khairudin’s office for comment.

title: Demand for dog DNA tests surges after Hong Kong clampdown over attacks
description: Animal welfare groups also warn that the government’s response to a string of dog attacks could lead to a wave of pet abandonments.
content: A government clampdown following a spate of dog attacks in Hong Kong has sparked a rush for canine DNA testing, while animal welfare groups warn the aggressive enforcement could trigger a wave of pet abandonments. Amid mounting public backlash over the sudden seizure and impounding of suspected fighting dogs, an advocacy group on Monday urged authorities to introduce a one-year grace period for owners to voluntarily declare pets with fighting-breed traits. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department stepped up inspections and seizures across the city following a string of dog attacks, including one in which the 33-year-old owner of a pet training facility was mauled by a mixed-breed dog registered as a mongrel. She was found dead nearby shortly after the attack. The incident exposed major loopholes in the city’s self-declaration microchip registration system, after the animal was found to carry genetic traits of the pit bull terrier – one of four fighting breeds strictly banned from import and unauthorised breeding in Hong Kong. As panic spread among dog owners, commercial testing centres saw a surge in clients seeking genetic proof to prevent their pets from being impounded. Clement Lai Yat-lung, founder of pet testing firm Hero DNA, said inquiries had surged more than fivefold over the past week, jumping from about 10 to between 50 and 60. He said that many dog owners, particularly those with mongrels, were anxious about government enforcement and hoped a DNA test result would prevent authorities from seizing their pets. “They see that their dogs are not purebred and worry that the animals may be seized. So they come to us for help,” Lai said. He said one client who adopted two mongrels was recently harassed on the street, and “an elderly woman even hit one of the dogs with an umbrella”. To handle the surge in demand, Lai said his firm expedited turnaround times from 30 days to 10, despite higher operational costs. Mark Mak Chi-ho, founder of the Non-Profit Making Veterinary Services Society, said that while the crackdown boosted demand for DNA tests, it could prompt anxious owners to abandon their pets out of fear of breaking the law. “What I am particularly concerned about is free-ranging dogs. These dogs may not be registered yet, so their owners might simply decide [to abandon] them,” he said. “Most of them are mongrels, which have mixed appearances from many different breeds. If the animal’s head is bigger, or it is stronger, people may call it a fighting or dangerous dog.” Mak called for greater clarity and consultation before amending the regulations, while reassuring dog owners that if their pets were registered and sterilised, they would not be breaking the law, regardless of their breed profile. Shelters have recorded an uptick in surrender inquiries. Kent Luk Ka-chit, founder of Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter, said daily calls about abandonment had risen to two or three a day, compared with one or two a week previously. He cited a case in which a dog owner brought his licensed pet to the department for vaccination and was told the animal was suspected of being a fighting dog. The pet was subsequently detained and the owner later abandoned the dog, he said. “If their dogs are classified as fighting dogs, owners face heavy responsibilities going forward,” Luk explained. “They must use a leash no longer than 1.5 metres, fit the dogs with red-and-yellow collars and keep them muzzled. Some even say they may need to buy insurance.” Luk criticised the government’s approach as divisive and counterproductive, calling for public education rather than heavy-handed seizures. “Authorities could introduce a grace period so that owners who are uncertain about their pets’ breeds can bring them in for inspection,” he added. Lau Chun-hoi, coordinator of the NGO Animal Welfare Advocacy Alliance, said during a radio programme that enforcement actions had increased the pressure on dog owners, prompting some to abandon their pets. He said his group had recorded a 50 per cent month-on-month increase in dog abandonment cases, adding that he had personally handled 16 cases. Lau said the sudden seizure of suspected fighting dogs left many pet owners in panic. He also expressed concerns that detaining the canines could alter their temperament and make them more aggressive. “Regulating fighting dogs is necessary, but the current pace is too fast and too sudden, leaving dog owners at a loss,” he said. “I do not believe that keeping the dog for another one or two weeks will pose any major threat to society.” He warned that sudden seizures could distress the animals and cause unnecessary heartbreak for both pets and their owners. He added that such enforcement sparked conflict and ran counter to the government’s aim of boosting the pet economy and building a pet-inclusive society. Lau called on authorities to establish a one-year buffer period for owners to declare any dogs they knew or suspected of exhibiting fighting-dog traits. “I do not think a comprehensive screening is necessary … because, after all, there are a large number of mongrels,” he said. “If every dog has to be re-examined, the burden on the government, the administrative workload, and the pressure on owners will be very heavy.” Speaking on the same show, lawmaker Chan Pok-chi proposed setting up a dedicated channel for residents to report irresponsible dog owners who violate the law. The legislator, who represents the agriculture and fisheries sector, also discussed the issue of unregistered fighting dogs and noted that some owners who adopted pets or received them from friends might not be fully aware of the animals’ crossbreed characteristics. But he also acknowledged ongoing dog smuggling and illegal breeding in the city as a potential contributing factor, noting that some shops instructed customers on how to evade regulations. A check by the South China Morning Post on WeChat found multiple mainland Chinese shops advertising same-day delivery of dogs to homes in Hong Kong, offering a wide range of breeds. Chan called for interdepartmental enforcement action to curb dog smuggling at its source. He also urged the government to improve the current registration system by introducing photo analysis and using genetic testing to provide additional information for breed verification, while outlining a clear appeals mechanism. Hong Kong law stipulates that all imported dogs and cats from the mainland must undergo a mandatory 30-day quarantine. The importing, breeding, selling and keeping of fighting dogs without a licence is prohibited. Anyone in possession of a fighting dog commits an offence if the owner fails to produce a veterinary certificate proving that the animal has been neutered. Those convicted face a maximum penalty of a HK$50,000 (US$6,380) fine and six months in jail. The law also requires that any dogs weighing no less than 20kg (44lbs) must be secured in public with a leash of up to two metres, with offenders facing a maximum penalty of three months in jail and a HK$25,000 fine. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu earlier promised to review laws governing dangerous dogs and the related penalties in response to the dog attacks.

title: Hong Kong’s Diocesan Boys’ School to pioneer 3 university pathways
description: The prestigious school aims to offer DSE, IB, and IAL starting in 2027, setting a new standard.
content:
Hong Kong’s prestigious Diocesan Boys’ School is planning to introduce the International Advanced Level curriculum starting in 2027. If the school receives approval from the Education Bureau, it will become the first institution in the city to offer three university pathways.
Headmaster Ronnie Cheng Kay-yen announced this development on Saturday during a Primary One admission talk at the school’s Mong Kok campus. This announcement follows the school’s approval from both Cambridge International Education and the Hong Kong Examinations and Assessment Authority.
“We are now waiting for the Education Bureau’s green light,” Cheng said.
“We are going full throttle to offer the Diploma of Secondary Education, the International Baccalaureate and the International Advanced Level,” he added.
“We have 1,400 secondary students and 900 primary students. Their learning speed, ability and direction are very different. We should strive to find ways so they can find a suitable learning model.”
Cheng said Form Three students in the 2026-27 school year, which starts next Tuesday, were expected to opt for the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE), International Baccalaureate (IB) or International Advanced Level (IAL) curricula.
DSE is the city’s main university entrance pathway, while the IB and IAL are internationally recognised curricula.
The South China Morning Post earlier reported that Hong Kong public universities admitted a record number of students applying outside the local DSE exam system, jumping by 63 per cent from 2,706 in 2019-20 to 4,401 in 2025-26.
Meanwhile, the intake of home-grown students taking the DSE exam dropped by 7 per cent, from 12,355 to 11,503 over the same period.
Samuel Chan Sze-ming, founder of education consultancy Britannia StudyLink, said parents weighing the three curricula must balance international competitiveness against their child’s individual suitability.
He noted that the DSE showed weakness in overseas university applications and was better suited for students who performed well in rote memorisation.
“The DSE is newer compared with the IB and A-levels, and it can be seen as more of a spoon-feeding curriculum in overseas university applications,” he said.
Chan described the IB as more comprehensive, blending science and humanities through a project-based approach. But he cautioned that its framework required strong time management and self-discipline.
“It suits well-rounded students, but not those who struggle to balance different areas,” he said.
The IAL was better suited for students who excelled in specific subjects while avoiding weaker areas, Chan said.
“It has become a popular choice for students seeking a different route into top local universities through the non-JUPAS pathway,” he said, referring to the centralised system for local students applying to full-time undergraduate programmes.
He added that the IAL’s modular structure allowed students to pick subjects that matched their strengths, offering greater flexibility.
“If more Hong Kong Direct Subsidy Scheme schools follow the lead of institutions like Diocesan Boys’ School and embrace IAL, I believe Hong Kong will become more internationally competitive,” he said.
Currently, non-local curricula are offered at 53 international schools, eight private independent schools and 21 semi-private local schools in Hong Kong.
Florence Yu, whose elder son is enrolled in Form Two at the Diocesan Boys’ School, said she was glad to see the school offering more options.
“It’s up to him to choose the curriculum, whether he wants to enrol in local [universities] through the DSE, or he wants to challenge himself and try the IB or even IAL. More options are always better,” the mother in her thirties said.
But Yu noted that competition for admission into the school’s IB programme was intense.
She added that teachers would observe students’ academic performance and personality, and advise them to pick a suitable curriculum, noting that the IB and IAL might better align with overseas universities.
Another parent, surnamed Tsang, whose son is nearly five years old, said having more curriculum choices increased the school’s appeal.
His wife, surnamed Chau, said it was too early to tell which curriculum would suit her son, as circumstances could differ in nine years, such as the popularity and international recognition of the curricula.
She added that her child’s interest in certain subjects, and his language as well as time management skills, would also affect his choice.
The Education Bureau said on Saturday evening that it had received the application from the school and was reviewing it.

title: AI‑fuelled boom lifts global billionaire count, Hong Kong retains top spot in Asia
description: Last year, Beijing had 61 billionaires, while Shenzhen and Dubai tied for eighth place with 43 billionaires each.
content: Hong Kong maintained its lead as the Asian city with the most billionaires last year, though mainland Chinese cities were quickly catching up thanks to wealth accumulation from the artificial intelligence boom, according to New York-based Altrata. Globally, Hong Kong ranked second in number of billionaires behind New York, while Beijing and Shenzhen secured spots among the top 15 cities, according to the data company. While Hong Kong’s aggregate billionaire net worth continued to climb, the city’s billionaire headcount slipped to 106, two fewer than a year earlier, compared to New York, which saw 164 billionaires, an increase of 12 in the same period. “This year’s Billionaire Census shows a billionaire class being reshaped by AI at a pace we haven’t seen before, but the story doesn’t end there,” said Altrata’s vice-president of sales Paul Sutton in a statement. “Wealth is concentrating faster at the very top.” San Francisco, London, Singapore, Los Angeles and Beijing took the third through seventh spots, respectively. Beijing had 61 billionaires, while Shenzhen and Dubai tied for eighth place with 43 billionaires each. The global billionaire population recorded its strongest expansion since 2020. The US and China remained the only countries with more than one city in the top 15 rankings, though Asian cities were becoming increasingly prominent, Altrata noted in its report released on Thursday. Amid complex geopolitics, volatile capital markets and rapid technological disruption, the AI investment boom was emerging as a major driving force behind that growth, the data company said. Globally, billionaires have an average age of 71, with 86.9 per cent being male. By sectors, banking and finance accounted for the largest share at 19.6 per cent, more than double the proportion held by second-ranked business and consumer services. Among personal interests, sports, philanthropy and aviation were the top passions among the world’s billionaires, according to the data. Hong Kong was one of two cities in the top 15 to see its billionaire count decline, along with London. Persistent weakness in its property sector and relatively limited exposure to AI‑fuelled wealth gains contributed to the drop, Altrata found. Meanwhile, Singapore and Hong Kong have become increasingly popular destinations for the super affluent from mainland China and India. Along with the United Kingdom, the two Asian cities stood out for their high share of billionaires born elsewhere.

title: 5 days in Seoul: the best things to do, from palaces and museums to the DMZ
description: South Korea’s capital is a sprawling mix of old and new. Here’s a 5-day itinerary to help first-time visitors see why the city is so special.
content: Seoul is one of the most populous cities in the world, home to some 10 million people in the centre plus 25 million in the wider metropolitan area. And yet Seoul is not a city that overwhelms visitors. If you are looking for a diverse travel destination in Asia, the South Korean capital is the perfect spot. The city is well-organised and easy to navigate, nestled among mountains and steeped in history – a history found not only in museums but out on the streets, on city walls and in palace courtyards. If you can, spend five days there. Even that is not enough to understand Seoul, but it gives you a chance to know why you would want to come back. Day one: the palaces of the Joseon kings Your first day in Seoul is all about the kings. Gyeongbokgung – built in 1395, destroyed during the Imjin war (1592–1598) and reconstructed over decades – opens up behind its entrance gate like a city in its own right. The palace has sprawling ceremonial courtyards, curved roofs in shades of blue and green, and guards in historical uniforms who carry out the changing of the guard several times a day. The ritual is choreographed down to the last detail. But it is more than just a spectacle; it serves as a reminder that this place was the centre of power on the Korean peninsula for five centuries. If you use Gyeongbokgung as a starting point, head to the neighbouring Changdeokgung in the afternoon, which many historians consider the more architecturally accomplished of the two palaces. A guided tour of the Biwon, or the Secret Garden, is a must. It contains ponds, pavilions and ancient trees set within grounds that were for centuries reserved for kings and their royal courts. The best way to spend the evening is a stroll through Bukchon, the neighbouring hanok – traditional Korean houses – district with its cobbled lanes winding between old-style wooden homes that are still inhabited. Bear in mind anyone wearing traditional hanbok attire is granted free entry to all of Seoul’s royal palaces. Rental outlets are located right outside the entrance gates. Day two: the old city wall The Hanyangdoseong – Seoul’s historic city wall – is one of the great surprises of the South Korean capital. Originally built in the 14th century to enclose what was then the capital of the Joseon Empire (1392-1897), it still winds its way for more than 18km (11 miles) through the city today. The section along the Bugaksan ridge is particularly impressive: between granite cliffs and secured areas, you suddenly get a sweeping view of the metropolis. Here, Seoul’s logical layout becomes clear. The city is framed by four mountains – Bugaksan, Inwangsan, Naksan and Namsan – that act as natural ramparts. The wall followed this topography, and the walking trail still follows it today. Over Naksan, the route leads down into the Ikseon-dong neighbourhood, one of the liveliest in the city centre, with small cafes and Korean bistros in restored hanok houses. Day three: exploring Gangnam across the Han River The Han River both divides Seoul geographically and splits it into two worlds. To the north of the river lies the historic, somewhat rugged city centre with its palaces and markets. As the city was barely able to expand northwards after the Korean war (1950-1953), development continued on the other side of the river. New neighbourhoods sprang up on the southern bank of the Han – the best known of which is Gangnam. The neighbourhood, which became world-famous thanks to a pop song, is less of a cliché than you might expect, though it is also exactly what it purports to be: a hub of wealth, lifestyle and ambition. Further west, Garosu-gil – a tree-lined avenue in the Apgujeong neighbourhood – winds its way past coffee bars, galleries and fashion boutiques. Gangnam is also a hub of Korean nightlife; head here after midnight to experience a different side of the city. And then there is the ultimate test of your head for heights, not far from Gangnam: the Lotte World Tower in Jamsil-dong. At 555 metres (1821 feet), the tower is South Korea’s tallest building and offers a breathtaking view over Seoul, including from a glass platform. Day four: taking in 5,000 years of history at museums The National Museum of Korea in Seoul’s Yongsan district is one of the largest in the world and, at the same time, one of the most underrated places in the city. The permanent exhibition takes visitors through 5,000 years of Korean cultural history: bronze swords from the pre-Christian Gojoseon era (2333BC-108BC), Buddhist sculptures of serene precision and celadon ceramics from the Goryeo period (918-1392) in their characteristic light green hue. Give yourself plenty of time here. The National Folk Museum reconstructs everyday life in bygone eras: tools, clothing, household goods and rituals. The fourth day finishes at the Leeum, a private museum of contemporary Korean art in the Itaewon neighbourhood. The museum’s three buildings were designed by Mario Botta, Jean Nouvel and Rem Koolhaas, respectively. Three architectural styles offer three perspectives on contemporary South Korea. It is also worth visiting the architecturally unique National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, which opened in 2013. Designed by Mihn Hyun-jun, it skilfully plays on the contrast between traditional court architecture and modern museum architecture. Day five: the border with North Korea The final day takes you out of the city, into a landscape where the history of the 20th century remains unresolved. The demilitarised zone (DMZ) begins around 50km north of Seoul. What sounds like a day trip is, in reality, one of the most unusual experiences a trip to South Korea has to offer. Your starting point is Imjingak Park, a sprawling site on the banks of the Imjin River, where guided tours set off. Amid the relics of war and memorials, there is also a statue of peace here. Two seated girls commemorate the “comfort women” from South Korea and North Korea who the Japanese military forced to work in military brothels during World War II. This is a quiet place before the larger excursion. The journey further north begins with a first reminder of where you are heading. The bus stops at a checkpoint, soldiers board and walk silently through the rows checking ID cards. It is calm and professional, and this is precisely what makes it so unsettling. At the Dora Observatory, the nearest civilian viewpoint to the border, you can look through binoculars at the North Korean city of Kaesong on the horizon. You can see houses, chimneys, and beyond them nothing but uncertainty. A 1953 armistice agreement ended Korean war combat, but the Korean peninsula is still officially at war, and visiting the DMZ reminds visitors of that. Seoul, one of the world’s most dynamic cities, is just an hour’s drive from this line. Bear in mind you can only visit the DMZ on an authorised guided tour. Book several weeks in advance. You need to bring a passport. Strict rules of conduct and a dress code apply.

title: Pakistani nurse to be honoured for saving newborn from deadly hospital fire
description: The baby whom Razia Noreen saved was the sole survivor of a fire that killed 14 other infants at a major government hospital in Islamabad.
content: A Pakistani nurse who rescued the sole surviving newborn from a hospital nursery fire that killed 14 other infants will receive one of the country’s most prestigious civil awards. Fire engulfed Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, a major government hospital in Islamabad, on Wednesday. A 51-second segment of CCTV footage, widely circulated online, captures Razia Noreen running into the burning nursery and emerging seconds later with the newborn in her arms. She tries to go back in, but cannot because of the flames and thick smoke. Noreen told private broadcaster Samaa TV on Sunday, while in tears, that she had merely done her duty. “I did not do it for a reward. I love children, and caring for them is my passion,” she said, adding that she wanted to save the others, but “the fire spread through the nursery within two minutes”. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Strategic Insight (@the_strategic_insight) Noreen said she was heartbroken she could not save the others as the flames spread too rapidly for her to re-enter the nursery after carrying the first baby to safety, and memories continued to haunt her. “I cannot sleep. Those babies do not let me sleep.” She will receive the Sitara-i-Khidmat, or Star of Service, which recognises people who have rendered distinguished public service or made exceptional contributions to the nation, and about US$36,000. The announcement drew widespread praise online. An inquiry requested by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Noreen entered the nursery and emerged eight seconds later carrying the baby. The nursery “deteriorated catastrophically within approximately two minutes”, according to the report. Fifteen newborns were being cared for in the third-floor nursery when the fire broke out. Sharif said Noreen displayed exceptional courage and devotion to duty by risking her life to save the newborn moments before the nursery burned down. I cannot sleep.
