Those babies do not let me sleep Razia Noreen, a nurse at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences Eight officials have since been suspended, and disciplinary proceedings initiated against them following the inquiry. Sharif also ordered criminal proceedings against those ultimately found responsible. Investigators are yet to determine what caused the fire. The deaths have prompted broader reviews of fire-safety measures at hospitals across Pakistan. The fire was among Pakistan’s deadliest recent tragedies involving children. In June, 14 schoolchildren were killed when the roof of a tutoring centre under construction collapsed in the eastern city of Lahore.

title: China-Nepal floods, Japan to deploy fighter jets to India: 5 weekend reads you missed
description: From foreigners missing in the China-Nepal disaster to Canada ending a migration path for Hongkongers, here are five stories you may have missed over the weekend.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage last weekend to help you stay informed about news across Asia and beyond. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. What Japan’s coming fighter jet deployment to India means for China Japan plans to deploy fighter jets in India for the first time next month, a decision experts say reflects Tokyo’s desire to strengthen security cooperation with “like-minded” countries in the Indo-Pacific region as it ramps up defence spending in response to China’s growing military power. 2. China-Nepal floods: 261 foreigners missing in Tibet, online rumours targeted China said on Sunday that 261 foreign citizens were missing after last week’s deadly floods along the border between its Tibet autonomous region and Nepal. 3. China needs 600% child subsidy rise to prevent deeper birth crisis: scholars Beijing should drastically raise its nationwide childcare subsidies to stave off a deepening birth crisis, according to Chinese scholars, who warned the country’s fertility rate could soon fall to the lowest in the world unless action was taken. 4. ‘Stuck’: Canada ends Hong Kong migration pathway, some turn to US and UK The closure of Canada’s “lifeboat” migration scheme for Hongkongers has left some applicants who are struggling to meet permanent residency requirements in limbo, prompting others to consider alternative destinations such as the US and Britain. 5. How the Philippines missed a US$3.8 billion Korean gambling racket Recent arrests expose a long-running crime network that flourished in the shadow of the nation’s Pogo scandal.

title: Asean urged to take on Big Tech after Meta’s record payout
description: Asean cannot pass EU-style laws, but a ‘coalition of the willing’ could force Big Tech to adopt safeguards against scams and child harm.
content: Calls are growing for Asean to collectively crack down on Big Tech platforms that spread scams and harmful content, spurred on by Meta Platforms’ landmark US$18 billion US settlement last week. Meta agreed on Wednesday to enact sweeping changes to Instagram and Facebook – including default time limits and content restrictions – as part of the settlement with several US states, which had alleged the platforms damaged children’s mental health. Within hours of the deal being announced, advocacy group Scam Watch Pilipinas was urging the Philippines, as this year’s chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, to put platform accountability squarely on the bloc’s agenda. “For too long, countries like the Philippines have been dealing with the world’s biggest technology companies individually,” said Jocel de Guzman, co-founder of the group, in a statement. Because an individual nation state’s enforcement reach was limited, cooperation on removing scam ads, fake accounts and harmful content often came down to “the willingness of the platform”, he added, further calling for an Asean Big Tech accountability framework to be introduced. Analysts who spoke to This Week in Asia said the US settlement strengthened the case for Southeast Asian governments to demand comparable safeguards, though they cautioned it was not a template the region could simply copy wholesale. Still, it “most certainly helped the Philippines get agreement from Meta on the safety protocols that were requested” last week, said Asha Hemrajani, a technology policy expert and senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, referring to commitments extracted from Meta and Roblox executives in Singapore. These included age verification, parental controls, faster takedowns and closer cooperation with law enforcement, according to Manila’s Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda. Those talks followed a school shooting in the southern port city of Zamboanga on August 18 that officials said was live-streamed. It was the second fatal school shooting in under two months. While Hemrajani said the effectiveness of Meta’s new safety protocols “remains to be seen”, she called the latest developments “a turning point” that were likely to spur other governments into demanding change. Elina Noor, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said the Meta settlement showed “there is more to be done in holding Big Tech accountable for a range of harms”, affecting children in particular. But she said the picture was complicated by the fact that many of the same companies being pressed to pay billions in damages were also providing technical expertise and underwriting capacity-building efforts to help the region fight scams. Yesterday’s rules Asean’s existing digital cooperation mechanisms were not built around platform accountability, focusing instead on phone calls and SMS. The bloc’s current guidelines “expressly exclude scams conducted through social media and OTT services such as WhatsApp”, said Alejandro Reyes, chief strategic officer of non-profit organisation AI Safety Asia, referring to services delivered directly to users over the internet. “Yet much of the problem has shifted onto precisely those platforms,” he told This Week in Asia. As an example, Reyes pointed to Singapore, where social media accounted for roughly 30 per cent of scam cases last year, with messaging apps responsible for another 23 per cent. Digital governance analyst Hafizh Nabiyyin said Asean leaned too heavily on scam prevention and non-binding guidance, such as public education campaigns or knowledge-sharing exercises, rather than holding platforms to account. This was a function of the bloc’s non-interference principle, consensus-based decision-making approach and tendency to take “a middle-ground position”, he said. Even if it expanded its guidelines to cover platform accountability more explicitly, “they would just be guidelines and not regulations or legislation”, Hemrajani said. Asean was not the European Union and it could not feasibly introduce comparable legally binding rules for Big Tech companies, she added. ‘Coalition of the willing’ If bloc-wide legislation is seemingly off the table, then what can Asean do? Existing regional frameworks set baseline measures, backed by information sharing and joint investigations, for individual members to adopt. Asean’s Guideline for Digital Platform Regulation, for instance, recommends that member states verify the identity of all online sellers on digital platforms. When Taiwan adopted a similar measure, it saw scam advertisements drop sharply as a result, said David Lam, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, digital economy and technology policy. “As effective as this measure is, however, Asean leaves it to member countries to individually enforce it,” Lam said. Enforcement, not ambition, is where the region keeps stumbling. Malaysia’s social media licensing requirements – later codified under its Online Safety Act – were largely ignored or rejected by social media companies when first introduced. Meta had also reportedly ignored Philippine requests to take down deepfake videos of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr used to promote an investment scam, Lam said. Collective bargaining power against Big Tech platforms could be consolidated via an Asean-wide framework, Noor argued, enabling the bloc to take on companies “whose market valuation and even annual revenue rival Southeast Asian economies”. But she said the obstacles to enforcement were numerous. Not only are these the same companies that underpin much of the region’s digital economic growth, member states also have differing exposure to online harm and uneven levels of digital maturity. On top of that is the ever-present risk of US trade retaliation against governments seen as targeting American tech firms unfairly. Yet at least a subset of Asean member states clearly wanted tougher Big Tech regulation, Lam said, driven by the twin pressures of scams and child safety. He pointed to Project Nexus – a regional instant-payments system built by a founding group of countries around binding operation standards, with the door left open for others to join later – as a template for how a “coalition of the willing” might operate on platform accountability too. Reyes said pushing platform accountability up the Asean agenda would fit “naturally with Manila’s stated priorities on digital transformation and protecting vulnerable groups”. But as chair, the Philippines is merely a convenor. “The chair cannot impose a regional regulatory regime,” he said. “There is no Asean equivalent of an EU legislature and regulator imposing and enforcing a single platform law across the region.” A more realistic ambition, Reyes said, would be establishing a “common regional floor” of shared minimum standards on scam advertising, account verification, fraud reporting, evidence preservation, child safety and cooperation with law enforcement. “If the Philippines wants to lead this at Asean, the question is not only what regional framework it can broker, but what enforceable obligations it is prepared to put in place at home,” he said.

title: Xi is in Bishkek for SCO summit. How does bloc fit China’s Eurasian strategy 25 years on?
description: Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s 25th anniversary summit expected to offer clues to China’s ambitions for a more multipolar Asia, analysts say.
content: As Washington’s strategic focus shifts and energy and grain supply disruptions continue to unsettle the Middle East, Beijing’s expanding presence across Central Asia is expected to be in focus as Kyrgyzstan hosts the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit this week. Chinese President Xi Jinping’s presence in Bishkek is expected to put the spotlight on whether the increasingly diverse grouping can move beyond diplomatic signalling, according to analysts. The SCO’s 25th anniversary summit was also expected to offer crucial clues to Beijing’s ambitions for a more multipolar Eurasia at a time of shifting regional power dynamics, they said. The meetings over Monday and Tuesday are themed as “25 years of the SCO: together for sustainable peace, development and prosperity”. They are expected to focus on regional security, connectivity, energy and digital cooperation, while also addressing wider challenges including Iran, Afghanistan and food security. China-Central Asia goods trade hit a record US$106 billion last year, according to Chinese government data, making Beijing the largest trading partner of the five countries combined for the first time. Li Lifan, an expert on Russia and Central Asia at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, said the SCO and Central Asia held special significance for Beijing. “As global competition intensifies between the US-led West and the emerging Global South amid a fractured international order, Beijing has placed greater weight on the SCO and Central Asia as a whole,” Li said, adding that “by deepening engagement and aligning more closely with Central Asian partners, China seeks to build common ground and present a more united front”. “Through the SCO, China can project power and influence aspects of the global order,” he said, noting that the group’s expansion showcased China’s diplomatic appeal and influence. In China’s diplomatic hierarchy, the United Nations ranks as the highest-level platform, while the SCO follows as the most important regional body. Founded in 2001 by China and Russia, the now 10-member Eurasian security and economic forum brings together four Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan – and also newer entrants Belarus, India, Pakistan and Iran. Turkmenistan is the only non-SCO member in Central Asia but often attends summits as a guest nation. Zhu Yongbiao, director of the Centre for Afghanistan Studies at Lanzhou University, said security remained Beijing’s top priority in Central Asia, not only along its western border but across the wider region, including the protection of key connectivity projects. “I believe China’s primary interest in Central Asia is security, that is, ensuring a peaceful and stable neighbourhood,” he said. Regional security is expected to feature prominently on the Bishkek agenda, according to Li, with Afghanistan, intelligence sharing and counterterrorism cooperation among the main concerns. The potential for instability spilling over from Afghanistan, combined with Kyrgyzstan’s own security priorities, gives those discussions added weight. While the China-Central Asia trade figure reflects the rapid expansion of commercial ties, Zhu cautioned against overstating the region’s economic weight. He said Central Asia’s limited population and economic scale, as well as “overstated claims” about its mineral and energy resources, meant the region accounted for a relatively small component of China’s overall foreign trade. Zhu emphasised that the region’s true strategic value stemmed from its geography – sitting next to China’s western border in Xinjiang, and serving as a critical bridge between China, Russia, the Middle East, South Asia and Europe. Infrastructure is a central focus of the SCO, highlighted by the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway. Now under construction after two decades of negotiation and recent clearance from Russia, the line would create a pivotal trade artery, connecting China with Central Asia and onwards to the Middle East and Europe while plugging into an overland trade link to Afghanistan. Li cautioned that security would remain a major challenge for the railway, as the route passes through difficult terrain and long tunnels vulnerable to terror attacks. “Protecting this ‘steel lifeline’ is critical, as it is seen as China’s gateway to Central Asia and the Persian Gulf,” he said. As a local saying goes: We wear Moscow’s armour, but our heart beats in Urumqi Li Lifan, Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences The railway is part of a wider effort to develop alternative routes, such as the “Middle Corridor” linking Central Asia and the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus, Turkey and Europe. Potential routes through Iran could provide additional access to the Persian Gulf and South Asia, but remain at the planning stage because of sanctions on Iran and regional instability. Zhu said these projects were driven by demand from Central Asian and other states, rather than by Chinese strategy alone. “Central Asian states, South Asia and Iran all seek stronger links, making connectivity inevitable,” he said. “China’s involvement adds momentum, enhances cooperation, improves quality, and accelerates the development of related routes.” Energy and food security are also emerging as important non-traditional security concerns for the SCO, Li added, citing fuel disruptions linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine and the impact of climate change on harvests. Iran’s protracted conflict with the United States will also be closely watched, given the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz for both energy and grain shipments. Meanwhile, China’s expanding economic and technological role has raised questions about its ties with Russia, which remains the region’s principal security partner. “Central Asian economies increasingly lean on China for trade, investment, infrastructure and technology, while Russia retains military bases, security arrangements and deep political and cultural ties,” Li said. “As a local saying goes: ‘We wear Moscow’s armour, but our heart beats in Urumqi [capital of Xinjiang].’” Yun Sun, director of the China programme and co-director of the East Asia programme at the Stimson Centre, noted that the SCO had also served as a mechanism for managing China-Russia relations, and that its limited practical achievements reflected the geopolitical and economic differences among its members. “Some people call it a ‘nothing burger’. But conflict prevention and management of potential animosity are also of significant value,” she said. China’s messaging through the SCO might also evolve now that strategic pressure from Washington had eased, Sun added, saying: “This year is the first time for a decade that China does not face a dire threat on the US front.” She noted that while Beijing previously leveraged the SCO partly to help counter US pressure, its fundamental goal – demanding global governance reform and a “more just and reasonable international order” – remained unchanged. Li, however, cautioned that the SCO’s role in the US-China rivalry should not be overstated. “Central Asian states tend to pursue their own interests and resist taking sides. China has framed cooperation as open and inclusive, generally refraining from pressuring Central Asian governments to ‘choose sides’,” Li said. “Their approach is best described as hedging.” Central Asian leaders deliberately exploited great-power rivalry to preserve strategic autonomy, resisting pressure to align fully with Russia or any other power, he added. Meanwhile, the US has been stepping up engagement with Central Asia, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio expected to visit all five former Soviet states soon after the SCO summit. Last November, Trump hosted the leaders of the five Central Asian nations in a “C5+1” summit at the White House to sign multibillion-dollar trade and critical mineral supply chain deals. In recent weeks, the US has pressed dozens of countries including Kazakhstan to “choose sides” in artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation. There is even talk of inviting Trump to the region, underscoring Washington’s growing interest. Uzbekistan has approached the US about joining Pax Silica, its flagship initiative on AI supply chains, a month after it signed up for China’s own global grouping, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Kazakhstan – the first Central Asian nation to sign up to Pax Silica – joined Waico in July. Artyom Lukin, a professor at Russia’s Far Eastern Federal University, had a more sceptical take on the SCO’s practical impact. “I think the SCO can’t be regarded as an efficient organisation delivering tangible results,” he said. “It’s definitely a talking shop in the first place and in the second place as well. I think almost everyone understands this reality.” However, that does not make the organisation irrelevant. As Lukin put it: “The SCO does have a certain value as a forum for multilateral dialogue of Eurasian powers as well as a venue for diplomatic signalling.”

title: Seoul district offers foreigners multilingual help to navigate South Korean rental market
description: The foreign population in Gangbuk has nearly doubled over the past decade to roughly 7,000 residents.
content: Navigating the intricacies of South Korea’s residential real estate market is notoriously complex even for long-time local residents. For the country’s steadily growing international population, however, steep language barriers, unfamiliar administrative procedures, and unique tenant laws make securing rental housing a particularly daunting endeavour – and one fraught with potential financial risk. To help bridge this informational divide and protect vulnerable foreign renters, Gangbuk, a northern administrative district in Seoul, is expanding a comprehensive municipal programme designed to safeguard foreign residents throughout the housing lease process. Under the enhanced initiative, foreign tenants visiting local neighbourhood centres to register their move-in address or file for an official “fixed date” status (hwakjeong ilja) will receive automated administrative guidance stamped directly onto their documentation in nine languages. The legal stamp – covering English, Chinese, Vietnamese, Mongolian, Tagalog, Uzbek, Japanese, Taiwanese and Thai – outlines essential protections under the Housing Lease Protection Act. In the South Korean rental market, obtaining an official fixed date is a critical statutory step that grants tenants legal priority to reclaim key security deposits should a landlord face foreclosure or property auction. Alongside the multilingual stamps, district offices are distributing QR code stickers linking directly to My Seoul, a dedicated mobile application operated by the Seoul Metropolitan Government. By scanning the code, foreign residents can easily install the application to access multi-language housing guidelines, municipal safety updates and multicultural social services. To eliminate misunderstandings during contractual negotiations, Gangbuk is also publishing standardised, multilingual housing lease agreement templates on its official district website. Prominent instructional banners featuring QR codes and lease resources have also been installed across all neighbourhood community centres to ensure drop-in visitors receive immediate guidance. The administrative changes reflect a rapidly shifting demographic reality. In Gangbuk, the registered foreign population has nearly doubled over the past decade to roughly 7,000 residents, driven largely by international university students, trainees and marriage migrants. Across South Korea, lease security has become a high-stakes civic issue following widespread domestic rental fraud scandals, making proactive administrative transparency vital for foreign residents who often lack localised legal support networks. Launched in January 2025, Gangbuk’s expanded housing initiative reflects broader municipal efforts across the capital to integrate foreign nationals into urban safety nets. “We have strengthened on-the-ground administrative support so that foreign residents do not face unfair disadvantages during the housing lease process due to language and information barriers,” said Gangbuk Mayor Jung Chang-soo. “We will continue expanding multilingual rental assistance and essential lifestyle support so that international residents can settle into our community with stability and peace of mind.” This article was first published by The Korea Times

title: Letters | A greener Bangkok must also be fairer
description: Readers discuss the revitalisation of Bangkok, and the legacy of ‘designated schools’ in Hong Kong.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The commentary, “Bangkok branches out: secret to Thai capital’s green revival” (August 8), resonated with me considerably. As a regular visitor to the city, I have witnessed many of the changes. Benjakitti Forest Park is undoubtedly one of the city’s great successes. The transformation of industrial land into wetlands and woodlands has given Bangkok a new breathing space. The upgraded walkways, pocket parks and greener streets have also made the city noticeably more pleasant to explore on foot. Bangkok has a strong culture of outdoor activities. The expansion of accessible green spaces seems to encourage even more people to reclaim public space for recreation. Every morning and evening, parks fill with runners, cyclists and aerobics groups. However, Bangkok remains one of Southeast Asia’s most unequal cities. The contrast between luxury towers and informal settlements is highly visible. This raises the question of whether the benefits of greening are reaching all residents equally. One concern is green gentrification. Major parks often increase nearby property values, attracting new investment while making neighbourhoods less affordable for lower-income residents. Benjakitti’s success may have environmental benefits, but it is reasonable to ask who gains from rising land values around Bangkok’s most desirable green spaces and whether that also limits access to some green spaces for vulnerable communities. The creation of public parks comes with social costs. The eviction of the Pom Mahakan community to create a park is a reminder that green space can be created at the expense of multi-generational communities. Similar debates have surrounded the development of Pathumwananurak Park, where informal settlements overshadowed by swanky malls had to be removed before the park could open. There are also questions about ecological benefits. Planting millions of trees sounds impressive, but the real success lies in quantifiable long-term survival rates, biodiversity outcomes and the protection of mature trees and habitats. Nonetheless, Bangkok should be celebrated for improving public spaces so visibly in such a short period. I hope the newly re-elected Governor Chadchart Sittipunt will now focus on solving the environmental challenges deeply embedded in the city: for example, unpleasant smog emitted in traffic gridlock, urban sprawl and flooding problems that affect poorer peripheral communities more than affluent residents and tourists. The true test of Bangkok’s green revival is whether the city can become not only greener but also fairer and healthier for everyone. Ian Tan Yuk Hong, Sai Ying Pun ‘Designated schools’ remain a problem Since my last submission on “designated schools” in Hong Kong, I have had the opportunity to take legislator Adrian Pedro Ho King-hong and his team to my secondary school, which is a former designated school. Years ago, the Hong Kong government began providing special funding to schools it saw as experienced in caring for non-Chinese-speaking children. These designated schools were expected to create programmes for teaching Chinese as a second language and other support measures. The schools attracted children from minority communities around Hong Kong but ended up inadvertently separating these children from their Chinese peers. I arranged a tour for Ho and his team to show them that while the government says it ended the designated school programme in 2013, these schools still take in a large number of ethnic minority children. This creates an environment that is not conducive to Cantonese learning because of, among other reasons, a lack of exposure to local Chinese students. My suggestion is that legislation putting a percentage cap on the number of ethnic minority students in such schools would get rid of these designated schools once and for all, and this idea will be taken up for debate at the Legislative Council. In fact, this idea is borrowed from Singapore. It does the same in its neighbourhoods so that ethnic enclaves do not form in one neighbourhood. Let’s see if Hong Kong’s Education Bureau can finally correct the mistake it made in 2006. The thing that has made this whole issue so difficult to tackle is that most people don’t even know about this issue or these schools. Ayudh Sharma, Sheung Wan

title: Will fixing Hong Kong’s childcare bottleneck help lift the city’s birth rate?
description: Parents and social welfare groups say demand for childcare services remains high even as births fall below 30,000 for 12-month period.
content: Shortly after Erica Lam found out she was pregnant with her second child, submitting a day care application for her unborn daughter became a top priority, as places at Hong Kong childcare centres were insufficient to meet demand. Even though Lam, a nurse in her early forties, tried to secure a place early, her daughter Ho-yan only managed to enrol in day care services operated by the Sheng Kung Hui church’s St Christopher’s Home, a social welfare group, when she turned eight months old. Meanwhile, her elder son, born in late 2020, had not been able to secure a place. The boy’s grandparents helped care for him during that period. To raise two children and give them a good quality of life, Lam and her husband could not give up their jobs. Sending Ho-yan to day care helped take pressure off their shoulders. “Childcare service is essential for working parents like us. The government encourages childbirth, and we have two children,” Lam said. “If our daughter could not get a place at the day care, we probably would not have been able to cope.” According to official figures, Hong Kong recorded 29,700 births between mid-2025 and mid-2026, down 15.6 per cent from the 35,200 recorded during the same period a year earlier. Falling below 30,000 births in the midyear population update was a first for the city since official records began in 1962. The previous midyear low was 32,600 births in 2023. To support working parents and encourage more couples to have children, SKH St Christopher’s Home has called on the government to provide better childcare support. Silvia Mak Yun-wan, the organisation’s chief executive, said the centre had the capacity to enrol 88 children aged under three, but the waiting list had accumulated to more than 70 applicants. Mak said nearly all service users were working parents, and some families came from different parts of the city to the centre in Kwun Tong. “This shows that the demand is very high. Our extended service has expanded from a quota of 17 to 30, and it is operating at full capacity every day,” Mak said. According to Social Welfare Department data, 553 childcare centres were available in the city. As of the first quarter of 2026, these centres served 43,000 children. The department said on Friday that it did not keep a record of the centres’ waiting times because applications were handled separately by different operators. Lam’s husband, Charles Lam, said they tried to find a “community nanny” through the government-backed Neighbourhood Support Child Care programme to look after their son when he was under two years old, but they never received a response. The parents said that while they were away from their children, they wanted them to have quality time with their carers, who could provide for their developmental needs and help train their social skills. “I am more at ease when I know that at least Ho-yan is learning when she is at the centre,” the mother said. Hong Ho-ching, the organisation’s service director, said that what working parents valued most was time spent with their children, despite only having a few hours a day after they got off work. He said parents could learn from carers at the day care centre what their children enjoyed doing, or what they should follow up on at home to build better bonds with them. To give more comprehensive support to families, Mak suggested the government consider placing a social worker at each day care centre. She said the stress working parents faced was often overlooked, but this group was still in need of support when overwhelmed by childcare. Lawmaker Nixie Lam Lam, who has been outspoken about family-friendly policies, agreed that social welfare should be made more accessible for working parents. She said that in the “best scenario”, a resident social worker would be stationed at every day care centre. “When we talk about a safety net for parents, we are talking about helping them to access the resources and information they need and making it more child-friendly and easy for them to raise their children,” Lam said. Welfare authorities said they had already assigned social workers to 741 pre-primary institutions, which included some of the childcare centres.

title: China, US bond markets diverge as Warsh strikes hawkish tone at Jackson Hole
description: Strong momentum is predicted to drive the yield on China’s 10-year government bonds to a low of 1.65 per cent, according to analysts.
content: The divergence of the bond markets in China and the US risks widening further, as economic data releases from the world’s second-largest economy remained underwhelming and Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh’s hawkish tone and concerns about fiscal sustainability add to the headwinds for Treasuries. The yield on China’s 10-year government bond traded at 1.692 per cent on Monday, approaching its lowest rate in a year after a set of economic figures from July trailed analysts’ estimates. Brokerages such as Great Wall Securities predicted that strong momentum would drive the yield to a low of 1.65 per cent. In the US, the 30-year yield was wavering near a two-decade high of 5.304 per cent, with investors continuing to demand the so-called term premium even after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he would double a buy-back programme to rein in the bond rout. Warsh’s surprisingly hawkish comment at the Jackson Hole symposium on Friday came as the latest frustration for Treasuries. The front-end yields rose immediately after Warsh focused his speech on restoring price stability, implying policy priority of inflation over employment. Warsh’s scrapping of forward policy guidance in a shift of approach to market communications may add more volatility to US Treasuries, said Li Xianglong, an analyst at Great Wall Securities, adding it would have a “limited impact on China’s bond market, which will trade on its own logic”. The disconnect between the world’s two largest debt markets will have implications on reshaping global capital flows across assets, with investors seeking diversification from US assets amid record fiscal debts and unbridled bond issuance by the White House under President Donald Trump. The world’s two largest economies also face a policy disparity, with China under pressure to cut interest rates to overcome deflation and the US to raise borrowing costs to curb oil shock-induced inflation. China’s bond market has been on a roll over the past month, with investors flooding in to shield themselves from the turmoil in technology stocks and an economic slowdown. Retail sales, industrial production and fixed-asset investment all fell short of analysts’ projections in July, with a downturn in property prices lingering and a resurgence in deflationary pressure. Calls for cutting borrowing costs to prevent growth from worsening were growing louder among investors. The 10-year yield dropped to 1.677 per cent on August 14, the lowest since July last year. An appreciation of the yuan and strength in the bond market have also attracted overseas investors. They bought 9.5 billion yuan (US$1.4 billion) of China’s government bonds for a third straight month of purchase in July, according to data from the central bank. China’s debt market had combined values of nearly 200 trillion yuan by the end of 2025, second only next to the US. Foreign investors accounted for a roughly 2 per cent holding estimated at 4.3 trillion yuan. Long-end US Treasury yields may stay at the elevated levels for a while, because of a confluence of factors including a strong American economy, AI funding needs and rising Japanese bond yields that may squeeze out demand for American debts, according to rates traders. “Taken together, persistent inflation, volatile energy prices, resilient US growth, AI-related investment, rising fiscal and corporate supply and changing Japanese demand for overseas bonds leave us cautious on global duration,” said Scott Solomon, a portfolio manager at T. Rowe Price. “In our view, these structural forces could keep longer-dated sovereign yields under upwards pressure.”

title: Nepal floods: could foreign rescue teams have been brought in earlier?
description: In the immediate aftermath of the floods, the government refused overseas help, only to reverse its decision days later.
content: The Nepalese government has appealed for rescue aid from other countries just two days after it reportedly refused help, as several hundred people are still believed to be trapped in hydropower tunnels and thousands remain missing following the catastrophic flash flooding at the border with China last week. Kathmandu’s apparent reversal reflects caution born from its chaotic experience with foreign teams after the 2015 earthquake, according to observers. Other factors include the government’s need to tightly control relief operations and failure to anticipate how quickly domestic capabilities can be overwhelmed in the aftermath. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the country had requested “specific specialised assistance” – including technology to locate people in affected areas and provide quick forensics and DNA analysis, as well as mortuaries to preserve dead bodies. He dismissed media reports rejecting international help and support as “false”. “The scale of devastation is extremely huge and support and assistance are required, not just in the phase of rescue and relief but more so in the phase of reconstruction and rehabilitation,” Khanal told a press conference on Saturday. “Given these very complex challenges of geography, we had to be very sensitive.” The ice-rock avalanche and ensuing floods on Wednesday along the Nepal-China border, which is flanked by towering mountains and deep gorges, have obliterated settlements in both countries, with the churning water swallowing villages hundreds of kilometres downstream. In Nepal, the death toll surpassed 900 with more than 4,200 people still missing, including 592 foreigners, as of Monday. Across the border, China has reported at least 16 deaths and 546 people as missing. Official figures show 933 people working at some 11 hydropower projects along the flooded areas in Nepal are also missing. Nepal’s military has already rescued 272 from two stations. Tunnel rescue teams from India and China, as well as South Korean experts, are scrambling to find more survivors, as authorities warn of fresh flooding. On Friday, personnel from the Nepal Mountaineering Association were also dispatched to help with rescue efforts. “The government should have sent local and foreign specialised teams without any delay,” said Rajendra Lama, the association’s general secretary. “We’re not opposing the government, but they should have taken a timely decision, which could have saved more lives.” Fading hopes In Kathmandu, hospital walls are plastered with photos of the missing, along with those of recovered bodies of adults and children. Relatives crowd the street to identify loved ones or find information. “We’re sending the photos to parents and family members, but the photos are so difficult to identify because of the condition they are in,” said Rabin Lama, whose niece, nephew and brother-in-law are among the missing, along with 25 others from his village in Rasuwa. “Some photos are naked and some only have body parts left – it would be heart-wrenching for family members to look at.” A humanitarian worker said she had been unable to locate one of her relatives, missing in Rasuwa’s Ghatte Khola, near the border, where rescuers were largely absent even by the fourth day of the disaster. With each passing day, family members are losing hope and believe more search and rescue teams from abroad could have supported local units. The humanitarian worker suggested that the initial decision to refuse international rescue assistance might have stemmed from the 2015 earthquake, which “became a bit of a circus” after foreign teams with no knowledge of the local topography or language attempted rescue operations. Even so, local authorities ought to have been ready to reinstate mobile connectivity and specialised equipment to track down missing persons by the second day, said the humanitarian worker, who has nearly 20 years of experience in disaster relief management and requested anonymity to speak freely. “A blanket ‘no’ sounds egotistical in a situation where we do not have the required capacity and manpower,” the worker said. “There have been a lot of good efforts, but there seems to be a lack of strategy, preparedness and crisis leadership.” The worker further suggested that authorities should invest in sufficient “simulations and scenario mapping, or retention of trained people for any disaster”. “We should be planning for recovery, rehabilitation and social protection for the survivors alongside rescue.” Safety shortcomings Nepal has suffered a devastating 7.8-magnitude earthquake and multiple deadly floods and landslides in recent years, yet experts say disaster readiness remains inadequate. Early warning systems provide only phone alerts, failing to identify safe shelters or coordinate relief efforts. “The one-door policy means everything goes through the government channel, which might be limiting relief to survivors in many places,” said Gangalal Tuladhar, a former education minister and disaster risk-reduction expert. “Disasters are inevitable in Nepal and yet we still lack preparedness. If we have better preparedness, we will have better relief and ultimately better recovery.” He said the government should have sought international help from the first day for complex tasks like tunnel rescue and mass-casualty management, while also consulting neighbouring countries to learn from their disaster response strategies. Khanal defended the government, however, saying official coordination with international partners had allowed some teams to arrive as early as the third day after the disaster. Locally, young people in Kathmandu are collecting food, clothes, bedding and medicine to help survivors. Public contributions to the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund have surpassed 6.5 billion rupees (US$42.3 million). However, there are growing calls for transparent spending reports to build trust in an administration that came to power just five months ago promising good governance. Suraj Raj Pandey, an entrepreneur crowdsourcing relief supplies in Kathmandu, said there were shortfalls but “right now is not the time to question the government”. “Right now, we’re all helping,” said Pandey, who has a close relationship with the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party. “There will come a time when we will get the picture of what happened.”

title: China’s factory activity improves in August, but stays in contraction
description: The PMI index was up last month to 49.8 from 49.2 in July, according to figures from the National Bureau of Statistics.
content: China’s factory activity improved in August but remained in contraction territory for a second straight month, as a pickup in orders could not fully offset the impact of overall weak domestic demand and disruptions from extreme weather. The manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) was 49.8 in August, up from 49.2 in July, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Monday. The reading was largely in line with the 49.85 projection from economists polled by the financial data provider Wind. The monthly index measures factory activity through surveys of supply chain managers across various sectors. A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while one below 50 signals contraction. The index ended a four-month expansionary streak in July. The new orders subindex, a gauge of manufacturing demand, rose to 50.6 in August from 48.5 in July, while a separate measure for new export orders came in at 50.1, up from 49.6 a month earlier. “The overall business climate in manufacturing improved visibly in August, with 16 out of 21 surveyed industries registering month-on-month gains,” said Huo Lihui, an NBS statistician, in a statement. Huo noted that “both production and demand expanded in tandem,” anchored by solid gains in hi-tech manufacturing and large firms. “The data came in a little stronger than market expectations,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, adding this could set the stage for a slight recovery in the industrial production growth data for August, scheduled for release in a few weeks. “The data suggested better activities in August, which will weaken the necessity of stimulus going forward,” said Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research. However, he pointed out that service and construction activities remained subdued due to adverse weather. “Looking ahead, we expect targeted policy supports [are] more likely,” Xing said. The figures come as weak domestic demand continues to weigh on the growth of the world’s second-largest economy, which slowed to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter of this year. In July, growth in both retail sales and industrial output slowed, while overall fixed-asset investment – which covers areas including manufacturing and property construction – weakened further. Extreme weather has added to the pressure on businesses. A series of typhoons, influenced in part by El Nino, hit parts of China this month, bringing heavy rain and flooding that disrupted commercial activities and stalled construction projects. Beijing has pledged to step up macroeconomic support and accelerate fiscal spending to counter sluggish growth. In August, authorities expanded eligible loans and raised maximum loan caps for smaller businesses under a national interest-subsidy scheme. Meanwhile, China’s non-manufacturing PMI – which tracks activity in the services and construction sectors – was 49 in August, unchanged from July. Elsewhere, China’s official composite PMI – which tracks economic activity in both manufacturing and non-manufacturing sectors – came in at 49.5 in August, compared with 49.3 in July.

title: Chief of Japan’s biggest lower house opposition party confirms alliance’s split
description: The Centrist Reform Alliance was formed in January to counter the ruling coalition, led by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
content: The chief of Japan’s largest opposition party in the powerful House of Representatives effectively confirmed on Monday that it would split, following the failure of merger talks with other forces. The break-up of the Centrist Reform Alliance (CRA) comes around seven months after it was established in January by lower house lawmakers from the left-leaning Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan (CDPJ) and Komeito, which was the ruling Liberal Democratic Party’s (LDP) coalition partner for 26 years. CRA leader Junya Ogawa said at a meeting of party leaders that he hoped to find “a new framework” to allow members to “restart” efforts to achieve a change of government. He added that he called for the CRA and Komeito to seek to form a parliamentary group in the lower house, and maintain existing cooperation among the three parties. Talks on incorporating upper house lawmakers from the two parties into the CRA effectively collapsed on Friday amid CDPJ resistance to the move, ending discussions on a full merger aimed at countering the ruling coalition led by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In the February general election, the alliance won 49 seats in the lower house, which is controlled by Takaichi’s LDP and its coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party. The scale of its defeat in the lower house election stalled moves to unify Komeito and CDPJ further. As talks on the merger continued, lawmakers of the two parties have continued to sit separately in the upper house where the ruling coalition does not hold a majority. The departure of all 28 former Komeito members from the CRA would reduce it to 21 seats, making it the third-largest opposition party in the lower house. The former Komeito lawmakers’ group would tie for the top spot in the chamber with the Democratic Party for the People, both on 28 seats. The focus will now shift to the opposition parties’ future cooperation ahead of unified local elections next year, with political analysts saying the fragmentation of the opposition camp will benefit the ruling parties. After months of talks, CDPJ leader Shunichi Mizuoka said in a meeting with his counterparts from the alliance and Komeito on Friday that his party would not join the alliance. His call to explore new forms of cooperation, such as forming a joint caucus in the upper house, was rejected by a senior Komeito executive.

title: Exclusive | Singapore firms keen to tap Northern Metropolis’ ‘massive potential’, envoy says
description: Consul general says businesses see potential in AI, biotech and other research opportunities in the 30,000-hectare development.
content: Singaporean businesses are keen to explore the “massive potential” emerging in Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis megaproject after the country’s prime minister visited the site earlier this year, its top envoy to the city has said. In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, Singapore’s consul general to Hong Kong, Eric Teo Boon Hee, said the country’s business chambers were considering fact-finding missions to explore opportunities in the 30,000-hectare development. During a visit in March, Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong toured the 87-hectare Hong Kong park of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone. The park forms part of the wider Northern Metropolis scheme, the centrepiece of Hong Kong’s long-term development strategy. The plan will transform land near the border with mainland China into what authorities hope will become a new engine of economic growth and a housing hub. “The prime minister’s visit to the Northern Metropolis generated much interest in Singapore among some of the companies, and now they are interested to come and take a look,” Teo said, adding that the consulate was encouraging firms to visit. “I know that the business chambers in Singapore are now planning to have study trips to come to the Northern Metropolis in the near future to explore these potential opportunities.” He also said universities in Hong Kong and Singapore were in “preliminary discussions” over potential areas of future collaboration in the megaproject’s planned university town. Asked whether any particular sector held the greatest potential for Singaporean firms, Teo said he would leave that decision to the companies themselves. “Whether it is in AI, biotech, or other [research and development] areas, I think the potential is all there,” he said. “I will leave it to the businesses to assess it for themselves.” The megaproject includes an innovation and technology zone, a commerce and industry zone, and a high-end professional services and logistics hub. The Hetao area, in particular, plays a crucial role in advancing Greater Bay Area cooperation under the nation’s five-year plan covering 2026 to 2030. In August, the wider project reached a milestone when a consortium of mainland state-owned and private companies – including e-commerce giant JD.com – and a major Hong Kong developer won the area’s first “large-scale land disposal” project for HK$1.03 billion (US$132 million). Total investment is projected at HK$16.8 billion. But development still faces hurdles, including enormous capital requirements, a lack of existing transport infrastructure and a tepid response from local property developers. Teo described the Northern Metropolis as Hong Kong’s leading medium- to long-term development project, which was why his team had encouraged Prime Minister Wong to visit the site during his trip. He added that the city’s south-north dual-engine strategy – pairing its traditional financial-services sector with the new innovation and technology hub in the Northern Metropolis – was “complementary” to Singapore. When Prime Minister Wong visited the Hetao park, he saw the “potential” of the project, particularly in cooperation between Shenzhen and Hong Kong, Teo said. Since the project was unveiled in 2021, Beijing has positioned it as a technology and innovation corridor that would link Hong Kong more closely with neighbouring Shenzhen under the national five-year plan. Teo said Shenzhen had strengths in advanced manufacturing, while Hong Kong had its own “unique advantages” as an open financial centre with a common-law legal system. “If Shenzhen and Hong Kong are able to work together with their respective strengths, then I think this project has really massive potential,” he said. Asked whether Singapore viewed the Northern Metropolis primarily through a lens of competition rather than opportunity, Teo said it was “not zero sum”. “I think the Northern Metropolis has opportunities for our Singapore companies, so they should come in and take a look at what areas they can get involved in,” he said.

title: Chinese team maps South China Sea floor with ‘twice the resolution’ of Western models
description: More than two decades of effort sees Chinese researchers develop maps of ocean terrain up to five times more accurate than global models.
content: China has mapped the seabed of its claimed waters including the South China Sea, with twice the resolution and up to five times the accuracy of methods used by other countries after more than two decades of effort, according to scientists involved in the project. The importance of such work was underscored in October 2021, when the US Navy’s Seawolf-class nuclear submarine USS Connecticut struck an uncharted seamount while submerged in the South China Sea. The collision grounded the vessel and injured 11 crew members. A subsequent investigation blamed poor voyage planning by the officers on watch, who failed to heed sonar warnings that did not match their charts. Had detailed topographic data for that area been available, the billion-dollar advanced submarine might well have avoided its mishap. Beneath the ocean surface lies a landscape as rugged as any mountain range on land. Knowing the outline of that terrain is vital not only for covert military operations and seabed mineral development, but also for research into ocean currents and earthquakes. Yet today, only 28.7 per cent of the world’s oceans have been surveyed in detail; the remaining 71 per cent remain dark on the map. In July, a team led by Professor Wu Ziyin with the Second Institute of Oceanography, under the Ministry of Natural Resources, received a second-class National Science and Technology Progress Award. Using data compiled over more than 20 years, the team has developed precise techniques to map undersea geographic features. They created China’s first systematic seabed atlas, naming 769 features in surrounding waters. More notably, their standard for unmanned seabed mapping was also adopted as the international standard in May. The team’s work marks a leap from a starting point of weak theory, missing methods and outdated technology to a position of partial global leadership, according to the ministry-backed China Natural Resources News. One of the keys was better data processing. Over decades, China had accumulated marine survey data from multiple eras, projects, instruments and reference systems – a jumble of information that spoke in different “dialects”. Wu’s team developed new techniques to combine and model this data, producing a high-resolution and highly accurate digital map of China’s surrounding seas. Compared with the best global models, their version doubled the resolution and improved accuracy by two to five times – so even previously hidden underwater hills now have exact locations. The team also rolled out new survey gear, including 6,000‑metre‑class (19,685 feet) autonomous underwater vehicles like the Qianlong‑4 and Orange Shark III, which are capable of low‑noise, low‑power propulsion and high‑precision navigation, and have now entered routine operation. For precise depth measurement, they built a home-grown multi-beam echo sounder that matched world‑class performance. “Our equipment breaks the monopoly of Western countries, with leading performance,” Wu said in the news report. “Previously, importing a multi-beam system cost millions of yuan; now our domestic product costs only a few hundred thousand.” The team followed standard naming rules but drew on Chinese mythology, historical figures and classical poetry to give hundreds of undersea features culturally distinctive names. They compiled a dictionary of 769 such names for China’s surrounding seas in 2021, and this year they plan to release an English edition of the atlas internationally – a step that highlighted their technical progress and strengthened China’s global voice in the field. According to the newspaper, the team’s survey results and equipment have already been widely applied in domestic sectors such as water conservancy, navigation channels, marine surveying and offshore wind power, supporting shallow‑water mapping, complex island‑reef surveys, marine ranching and automated measurement in extreme areas. At the same time, the home-grown technologies have been exported to Russia, Japan and Singapore. “We used to import most of our key marine survey gear from abroad,” Wu said in the report. “Now we have not only replaced those imports but are also exporting our own. That is a true qualitative leap.” Beyond research, Wu has trained 45 graduate students, most of whom have become core personnel in marine science. “At the start, we could only envy the advanced equipment of others,” he recalled in an interview with Science and Technology Daily. “Now some of our technologies are leading globally – this is the result of generations of effort.”

title: Opinion | Don’t leave Hong Kong parents to their own devices on child social media use
description: While regulation of young people’s use of social media is gaining momentum worldwide, Hong Kong lags behind.
content: Hong Kong, a city of overachievers, especially when it comes to the young, is also filled with children who take to social media early. Almost 35 per cent of kindergarten pupils log at least one hour of recreational screen time daily. By the junior forms, 60 per cent exceed the international two-hour daily limit. The time children spend on screens creates friction at home, accounting for 85.5 per cent of family disputes. Governments must look into whether they are adequately protecting children from screen time addiction – the bread and butter of social media platforms – or if parents are being left to their own devices. A little over a week after the Hong Kong Institute of Family Education released findings that reaffirmed what most of us already know, Meta announced that it has started sending alerts to parents if it is found that their children have been repeatedly searching for content about suicide and self-harm on Instagram. I have my doubts that this is because Meta cares about our children. Last December, Australia became the first country to ban social media for children under 16. Youth are more susceptible to the systemic features that make social media harmful, such as algorithms designed to feed viewers content likely to hook them and the lack of safeguards against inappropriate content. While a ban by one country will hardly rein in social media’s damaging effect on young people, it is a way to hold social media platforms accountable for their reckless pursuit of profit at the expense of our children’s mental health. Years of failed industry self-regulation – for example, piecemeal, ineffective age limit requirements that are too easy to bypass – have made it necessary for governments to step in to protect children. The Australian law has teeth because social media companies that fail to block children face fines of up to A$49.5 million (US$35.8 million). Efforts to hold social media platforms accountable gained momentum this year. The US, which is home to these tech giants, has seen lawsuits against them. In March, Meta and YouTube lost their first personal injury case, paying US$6 million in damages. This month, in a landmark settlement, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.1 billion in penalties to 47 states, the District of Columbia and US territories, and to make major changes to its products – introducing time limits and banning features that stoke mental health issues. The United Kingdom plans to ban social media for those under 16 by spring next year. New Zealand will be taking this on, too, with the government planning to introduce a bill in parliament seeking to ban social media for children under 16 and fining platforms up to 10 per cent of their global revenue for non-compliance. In Hong Kong, calls for similar action have been rising. Last month, legislative councillor Duncan Chiu asked Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong whether our government had considered enacting legislation to restrict children’s social media use. From Sun’s answer, it looks like our government is reluctant to do so. Sun said the government does not have “sufficient basis” to prohibit or restrict young people from using social media, and that while, at this stage, the government does not plan to pursue legislation to ban adolescents from usual social media, it is open to issuing guidelines. He also said the Education Bureau is fostering information literacy among students and “encourages parents, through various channels, to establish reasonable rules regarding social media and screen time based on their children’s ages and developmental needs”. So parents are left to the shoulder the bulk of the burden. While the government “attaches great importance to the impact of social media on physical and mental health of adolescents”, it appears to be equally concerned about the impact a ban would have on “the local innovation and technology ecosystem and related industries” and about “public expectations on freedom of speech and information”. Sun made sure to mention the benefits of social media – that it “ may provide more opportunities for learning and socialising for adolescents”. When asked about the city’s alarming student suicide rate in June, Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin mentioned the negative impact of social media as one of the causes. Yet the government seems content to leave it to parents to deal with the ill effects of social media on the next generation, which include ⁠exposing children to harmful content, addictive technology and pressure they are not equipped to ‌deal with, even when this adversely affects their family life and mental health.

title: Huawei and Apple bend to a tougher market with foldable phones as memory crunch bites
description: A new foldable iPhone and the Mate XT 2 are coming as analysts predict a double-digit plunge in smartphone shipments this year.
content: Highly anticipated foldable launches from Apple and Huawei Technologies next week are expected to offer a much-needed lifeline to a subdued global smartphone market, which is bracing for an estimated 17 per cent decline in 2026. Apple’s September 9 event has the industry watching closely, with expectations building for its first foldable iPhone to take centre stage alongside standard model refreshes and the keynote debut of new CEO John Ternus. The US tech giant’s biggest product showcase of the year will arrive just two days after Shenzhen-based Huawei unveils the Mate XT 2, an upgrade to its flagship trifold device. Analysts are counting on Apple’s foldable debut to lift a sluggish smartphone sector reeling from soaring component costs. “Apple’s entry into the foldable market has done more than reignite growth in a category that was losing momentum,” Nabila Popal, senior research director at research firm IDC, said on Wednesday. “It has fundamentally altered the market’s trajectory.” Popal projected that Apple would ship more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027, capturing about 40 per cent of the global foldable market. “Apple is positioned to challenge Huawei and Samsung for leadership in markets where they have long dominated – an extraordinary outcome for a product expected to be less than two years into its life cycle,” Popal said. The memory tsunami that we warned about is now hitting the market in full, and consumers are starting to pay the AI bill Francisco Jeronimo, IDC The foldable segment is set to grow 13 per cent this year and a further 18 per cent in 2027, making it the “only silver lining” in a troubled mobile market, according to IDC’s expectations. Global smartphone shipments are expected to fall 16.7 per cent this year, which would mark their steepest annual contraction on record, according to IDC’s latest report. The forecast is down from the research firm’s previous estimate of a 13.9 per cent decline, issued last quarter. A severe memory supply crunch, triggered by surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, is expected to hit hardware makers hardest in the second half of 2026, dragging semi-annual shipments down by more than 27 per cent, year on year. As shipment volumes slump, device prices are soaring, according to IDC, which said the average global selling price of a smartphone is forecast to jump about 27 per cent this year to US$581, with price increases expected to spill into 2027. “The memory tsunami that we warned about is now hitting the market in full, and consumers are starting to pay the AI bill,” said Francisco Jeronimo, vice-president for worldwide client devices at IDC. “The era of the cheap smartphone has ended. “From here, the winners will be the vendors with the scale and supply leverage to hold demand at prices consumers have never had to pay before.” The memory-chip crisis is sending shock waves across the broader consumer electronics supply chain, dragging down profitability for personal computers, tablets and digital cameras. Chinese action camera maker Insta360, a major competitor to US-based GoPro, on Thursday reported a 94 per cent drop in first-half net profit, citing rising memory-chip costs as the primary culprit. The Shenzhen-based firm noted that high memory prices had “posed significant challenges to the company’s product costs and put pressure on short-term profitability”. Insta360 recorded a 30.4 million yuan (US$4.5 million) profit for the first six months of 2026, down sharply from 519.8 million yuan in the same period last year, despite revenue climbing 50 per cent to reach 5.5 billion yuan.

title: China teen with zero programming skills earns US$2,600 in 3 days selling AI study app
description: This development experience made me realise that as long as you have a great idea, AI can bring it to life, Shuhan says.
content: A 13-year-old girl in China has earned 18,000 yuan (US$2,600) in just three days from an artificial intelligence (AI) product she developed to assist parents in supervising their children’s study habits. Zhu Shuhan, a Grade Two student at a junior secondary school in Shanghai, has no programming background. She began using AI only last year, as reported by the Shanghai Morning Post. At a national AI product marketing competition held in Hangzhou from August 21 to August 23, Shuhan secured the third prize of 5,000 yuan, competing against over 50 participants. The contest did not include technical judges; instead, winners were selected based on their AI-generated apps’ income during the three-day period. The app Shuhan created, called Zai Chang (translated as On Site in English), garnered 90 orders, resulting in total sales of 18,000 yuan, which helped her attain third place in the competition. Once a parent uploads a photo of themselves using the app, the system assumes the role of a virtual parent, supervising their child while they complete homework. Should the camera detect that the child is playing on a mobile device or leaving their seat, the virtual parent displayed on the screen will issue a voice reminder. Upon completion of the homework, the app generates a “concentration report.” Shuhan shared that her inspiration for this app came from her own experiences. “My parents were so busy that they did not have time to accompany me while I studied. I often found myself distracted and discreetly using my phone while doing homework,” she stated. “Many of my classmates face similar challenges with self-discipline. I wanted to create a digital parent clone.” Despite her limited knowledge of programming, Shuhan’s understanding of AI began just last year. To create the app, she simply “told” the large language model (LLM) her idea in her own words, after which AI assisted her in generating the code. From designing to implementing the core functionalities, the entire process took her only three to four days. She consulted AI programming tools regarding specific technical issues. Notably, she removed a feature labelled “mother getting angry” from the app’s initial design, which aimed to alert parents to frequent distractions. “I dislike whistle-blowers. I want my app to be gentle and allow room for improvement for children,” she explained. “From this app development experience, I realised that as long as you have a good idea, AI can bring it to life,” she emphasised. Her younger brother, a Primary One pupil, is one of her first users. “After being monitored by this app, my brother studies more diligently,” she remarked. She expressed her intention to market the app to a broader audience at a lower price. “If many people are willing to pay for this app, I will continue developing it,” she said. Online users have praised Shuhan, with one stating: “She is incredible with a creative idea and the ability to leverage AI.” “What business acumen she has! Her app precisely meets parents’ demands,” noted another commenter.

title: In Focus | Golden hour: why Hong Kong may finally succeed in becoming precious metal’s trading hub
description: De-dollarisation tailwinds, ecosystem buildout and mainland China’s support plus foreign backing give city’s ambitions credible momentum.
content: For decades, Hong Kong has been a hub for gold jewellery. Brands such as Chow Tai Fook and Chow Sang Sang have drawn buyers from the world over, aided by the city’s duty-free status and its proximity to one of the world’s largest gold-consuming markets. Two years ago, when officials set the goal of making Hong Kong a global gold trading hub comparable to New York and London, it was met with scepticism. Similar efforts in the past had ended in failure. The doubts, however, began to fade in early July, when the city announced the launch of a central clearing and settlement system, alongside a delivery connect with the Shanghai Gold Exchange. “Hong Kong’s unique value is to be the superconnector and super value-adder between mainland China’s gold market and international bullion markets,” said Stephen Law Cheuk-kin, president of the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants (HKICPA). “The mainland is one of the world’s most important gold-consuming, importing and producing markets, while Hong Kong provides international capital, global banks, insurers, commodity traders, sophisticated legal and professional services, and multi-currency funding and hedging capabilities.” Tensions send gold prices soaring Hong Kong’s gold ambition has resurfaced at a time when geopolitical tensions – from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 to the US-Israel war on Iran launched in February – have profoundly transformed views on gold, long used as currency and a hedge in uncertain times. Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management, wrote in a blog post on August 11 that the freezing of Russia’s US$300 billion reserves by the US and its allies in 2022 in response to the invasion of Ukraine was “not some obscure footnote in the history of sanctions”. He added: “A dollar asset held offshore may be liquid, deep and backed by the world’s largest economy, but under extreme circumstances it is still somebody else’s liability sitting within somebody else’s financial architecture. “Gold is nobody else’s liability.” Central banks, many of which hold US dollar assets such as Treasuries, have increasingly turned to gold. Net purchases reached 289 tonnes in the second quarter of 2026, the strongest second quarter on record, compared with 166.5 tonnes a year earlier. The global surge in gold demand had been accelerated by worries over expanding US sovereign debt, volatile US Treasuries yield, fluctuating Federal Reserve inflation policies and the economic landscape under the Trump administration, analysts said. It enhances regional liquidity and settlement efficiency, and provides Asian clients with a local time-zone solution Guy Wolf, Marex For Beijing, concerns about Washington’s weaponisation of the US dollar have persisted for years, and gold has become one way to diversify its foreign exchange reserves and support the yuan’s overseas use. The People’s Bank of China raised its gold reserves to 76.08 million ounces, valued at US$306.35 billion, at the end of July after adding 640,000 ounces – the largest monthly increase since late 2023 and the 21st consecutive monthly purchase. China also cut its US Treasury holdings to a near 18-year low in June to US$633.4 billion. After retreating from its January peak price of more than US$5,600 per ounce – an all-time record – gold has rebounded on market worries over rising US Treasury yields, with 30-year tranches now approaching a panic level of 5.2 per cent. The metal’s price rose to about US$4,607 per ounce on Friday, extending a rally after the US Treasury said on August 19 that it would at least double the size of its liquidity-support buy-back operations for long-dated bonds. Hong Kong builds a gold ecosystem Hong Kong’s gold ambitions have gained momentum as Asian powers emerge as pillars of demand. China and India are the world’s largest gold jewellery consumers, while central banks have added strong institutional support. The city’s role as an international financial centre – with global standards and financial infrastructure, free capital flows and legal protections – has buoyed the push. Guy Wolf, global head of market analytics at London-headquartered global commodities broker Marex, said Hong Kong’s new gold clearing system was complementary to London and New York, rather than a competitor. “It enhances regional liquidity and settlement efficiency, and provides Asian clients with a local time-zone solution, helping to generate additional global gold market flows rather than displacing existing activity,” he said. The new system, operated by the wholly government-owned Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing, has drawn 11 Chinese and international banks, with plans to expand participation. Law of the HKICPA said it could facilitate cross-border physical settlement and make Hong Kong a practical location for trading, storing, financing and delivering gold with clearer links to demand in mainland China. Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), in its fourth attempt since the 1980s to build a viable gold derivatives venue, relaunched its US dollar gold futures contract on July 6. To boost liquidity, HKEX paired the launch with a market-wide waiver of its US$1 per contract trading fee until June 30, 2027. The biggest support came from Beijing, which introduced the initial phase of delivery connect between the Hong Kong and Shanghai gold exchanges in July. Unlike paper gold trading in many Western markets, physical bar delivery is handled in Hong Kong through HKEX’s approved depository. On final settlement, ownership of the gold moves from the seller’s vault account to the buyer. The Shanghai Gold Exchange’s first offshore certified vault in Hong Kong, launched last year, supports yuan-denominated gold trading and works alongside Hong Kong’s central clearing system to link mainland China and international bullion markets. Making gold a core asset class aligns with China’s 15th five-year plan and “acts as a powerful catalyst for renminbi internationalisation” through expanded yuan-denominated gold trading, settlement and delivery, said Ming Lam, divisional councillor of the Greater China division at CPA Australia. The London Bullion Market Association’s suspension of qualified delivery status for some Chinese gold companies blacklisted by the US Department of Homeland Security could further lift Hong Kong’s role, market analysts said. On August 19, the China Gold Association said the measures “lack any factual basis, violate market-oriented principles and disrupt the stability of the global gold industry chain”. On the same day, HKEX reported record physical deliveries and a surge in its US dollar-denominated futures trading, with 145kg (320lbs) delivered – the highest single-day tally since the product’s launch. Greater availability of physical metal can support trading, financing, lending and delivery activity and, in turn, help develop liquidity across the wider market Bernard Sin, MKS PAMP Hong Kong Foreign institutions join in Hong Kong’s gold dream has won confidence from foreign banks and institutions. Eleven banks including ANZ, JPMorgan, Standard Chartered Hong Kong, HSBC and UBS have joined the new clearing and settlement system. “Attracting more internationally held gold to Hong Kong could help build the physical inventory and market depth required for a successful regional gold hub,” said Bernard Sin, regional director of Greater China at MKS PAMP Hong Kong. The Swiss company, one of the world’s largest refiners and traders of precious metals, set up its regional headquarters in Hong Kong last November. “Greater availability of physical metal can support trading, financing, lending and delivery activity and, in turn, help develop liquidity across the wider market,” Sin said. The city’s government agencies have begun lobbying regional central banks, financial institutions and others to make Hong Kong their reserve-storage destination. Economies involved in the Belt and Road Initiative “look to diversify reserve assets and mitigate geopolitical risks, and Hong Kong provides a trusted venue for [gold] trading, storage, clearing and delivery in the Asian time zone”, said a spokesman for the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) in a written reply. Where and how central banks store their reserves has become a pressing question amid global polarisation. In May, FSTB promoted Hong Kong’s gold-market opportunities at the Asian Development Bank’s annual conference in Uzbekistan, attended by heads of central banks of member countries. In July, the bureau signed a collaboration with Laos to create a framework to channel accredited Lao gold into Hong Kong. Benjamin Wong, head of transport, logistics and industrials at InvestHK, the Hong Kong government’s investment promotion arm, said the agency was working closely with the FSTB to identify potential companies from mainland China and overseas. This partnership was aimed at “promoting Hong Kong’s gold initiatives across the entire value chain from refining and transport to storage, trading and insurance”, Wong said, while expanding gold fund and financial product offerings. The latest push came in mid-July, when Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu met Malaysian officials in Kuala Lumpur to explore closer collaboration in financial and gold markets. The vault rush As Hong Kong positions itself as Asia’s answer to London in gold trading, leading global companies are quietly investing in warehouses and manufacturing sites across the city to capture the bullion boom. The Hong Kong Airport Authority has repeatedly expanded the capacity of the airport’s precious metals depository, most recently setting a target of more than 2,000 tonnes within three years, up from its initial capacity of 150 tonnes.
