Still, that remains a fraction of the 5,500 tonnes held in the Bank of England’s gold vault, the world’s second largest after the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. “A lot of the physical gold bought by central banks is a kind of static position. They buy it and hold it for quite some time,” said Vikas Gupta, head of trading, Asia currencies and emerging markets at JPMorgan Chase. “It is important to attract gold inventory that can provide a base for active trading and settlement.” Non-monetary gold imports to Hong Kong rose to 242kg in July, up from 112kg in January, according to data released by the Census and Statistics Department. China’s largest courier, SF Express, was setting up a gold vault in Tsing Yi this year, according to a government list provided to the South China Morning Post. The site is in western Hong Kong, an area home to container yards and logistics warehouses. Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the mainland’s largest state-owned lender by assets, was developing a precious-metals storage facility, according to the list. Shenzhen-based Chow Tai King was building a gold refinery in Hung Hom and could further expand its Hong Kong operations, while Point Gold was moving into the city after acquiring a site for a gold refinery at Tai Po InnoPark last year, which it aimed to bring into operation by the end of 2026. Standard Chartered Hong Kong said it planned to build its first gold storage facility in the city. Family offices’ interest in gold has been broadening, even through a volatile year William Chow, Raffles Family Office Investment on the rise The average daily trading volume of HKEX gold futures reached 9,974 contracts between July 6 and August 19, with total value hitting US$1.35 billion. More than 30 participants had engaged with the contract since its relaunch, according to HKEX data. Gold futures could help investors hedge against price risk and gain leveraged exposure without holding the physical metal, said Tom Chan Pak-lam, honorary president of the Institute of Securities Dealers. Hong Kong’s ambition to build a comprehensive gold ecosystem is underpinned by its cross-border wealth management business, ranked the world’s largest at US$2.95 trillion, according to InvestHK, with the financial sector driving demand for gold funds and gold-related products. The government is also planning new tax incentives for hedge funds and family offices trading gold as an asset class. “Family offices’ interest in gold has been broadening, even through a volatile year” as they seek to “hold something that sits outside any single financial system when geopolitics turns unpredictable”, said William Chow, deputy group CEO of Raffles Family Office. The allocations have become “steadier and more deliberate, rather than speculative buying”, he added. They need a “trusted gold clearing and settlement, secure storage, deep liquidity, and a reference price they can rely on during Asian trading hours”. JPMorgan Chase’s Gupta said linking demand and supply through Hong Kong was expected to result in “better price discovery”. HKICPA’s Law, who is also a member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, said Hong Kong should improve transparency, liquidity and interoperability of the pricing relationship between yuan-denominated gold prices and international US dollar benchmarks, providing a “more credible” offshore platform for economies seeking to diversify currency and commodity-risk management. Hong Kong’s role must cover the full value chain – physical trading, storage, refining, logistics, clearing, risk management and investment products – rather than simply establish another venue, Law said. Over time, the objective should not be to force a single “Hong Kong price” or immediately displace London or New York, he added.

title: How to manage mess, from a tidying expert
description: Orange Tam teaches us the basics, from pausing impulse buys to decluttering your spaces and staying organised.
content:
Perhaps you were finally able to clean your room over the summer, but as soon as the new school term starts, you know piles of papers will build on your desk all over again. Soon, your bedroom floor will look like a disastrous art project exploded on it.
Sound familiar? To help you put an end to this vicious cycle, Orange Tam, a tidying expert based in Hong Kong, gave us some tips on staying organised and boosting your productivity.
“What better way to begin the new school year than with a clutter-free bedroom?” Tam said.
As an active professional member of organising associations in the United States, Britain and Japan, Tam helps Hongkongers take control of the messy chaos in their life.
But her work is not only about tidying up spaces.
Tam is also the founder of Jupp Uk, a local decluttering service, and encourages her clients to rethink what they buy in the first place.
“Much of the work is not about dealing with someone’s belongings, but with the person and their relationship with material things – which many people equate with happiness,” Tam said. “Material things can enhance our lives and improve our overall well-being. But, if they’re bought without thinking, they can create distraction.”
Tam said in Hong Kong, it could be very easy to buy things you do not need.
“With malls everywhere, it’s … not surprising that many of us succumb to compulsive buying ,” she said. Tam said fast fashion completely changed the way we shop for clothes, leading to excessive buying.
Another item on the guilty list is books: “Some students see books as a status symbol . They simply collect books and don’t read them,” she said.
For students, Tam suggests decluttering at least once every school term. She explained, “A messy living space can be mentally draining as we are subconsciously reminded of the tasks that are left unfinished. This adds to the anxiety of starting school.”
Spend some time sorting through old papers and notes. One tip is to store them in different-coloured plastic files or magazine holders by subject, and to keep them somewhere you can see them so they do not get neglected.
But Tam advised against buying more storage than you need, as the empty containers might encourage you to fill them up with more stuff.
She added that decluttering could benefit more than just your physical space, but also your mental well-being.
“Being organised allows you to focus better at school, save time looking for misplaced items, and reduces stress, so you’ll end up feeling good about yourself,” she added.

title: 7 phrases to help you break the ice and navigate new social situations
description: These English idioms will help you talk about hitting it off with someone – or, on the flip side, giving them the cold shoulder.
content:
How do you talk to someone you’ve just met? Do you say hello, shake hands or crack a joke?
At the start of the school year, you meet new teachers and have chances to make friends. Thus, it’s the perfect time to dive into English phrases to describe hitting it off, embracing a new crowd and navigating the complexities of modern relationships.
Meaning: to quickly become good friends with someone
Example: I was nervous about the dinner, but we hit it off immediately.
Meaning: to get along with someone and become friends very quickly
Example: I introduced her to my roommates, and they got on like a house on fire .
Meaning: to decline an invitation now but say you would like to accept it later
Example: I’m swamped at work, so I’ll have to take a rain check on dinner.
Example: to have a long, relaxed conversation with someone
Example: Let’s grab a coffee this weekend and just chew the fat .
Meaning: to go out and have a fun-filled night with friends
Example: There are so many new places I want to visit; let’s paint the town red .
Meaning: to ignore someone on purpose or treat them in an unfriendly way
Example: After their heated argument yesterday, Sarah decided to give him the cold shoulder all through lunch.
Meaning: the most energetic and funny person in a social gathering
Example: Even though Julian is usually quiet at work, he becomes the life of the party as soon as the music starts.

title: Hong Kong author talks children’s creativity, silly-sounding science discoveries and more
description: Rozana Lee, author of ‘Crazy Ideas That Work’, explains why she wrote her children’s science book and what she wants young readers to learn from it.
content:
Did you know hair can be used to clean up oil? American hairdresser Phil McCrory came up with this idea after seeing how oil spills harm the ocean. McCrory did an experiment to see how well human hair absorbed oil and learned it could soak up oil spills.
This is one of many stories of innovation in Crazy Ideas That Work by Hong Kong-based writer Rozana Lee. The book, published last year, is a collection of extraordinary experiments.
“Sometimes you think people are just born with creativity. But creativity can actually be trained,” the 39-year-old writer said. “And that’s why I put out this book – to try to train children’s creativity.”
The book goes around the world to help children learn about different scientific successes, starting in Hong Kong and travelling to Sierra Leone, the United States and Peru. Its yellow cover opens to pages that mix photographs, digital drawings and hand-drawn illustrations. They invite readers to add their own creations.
“I like to ask [kids] a lot of questions. When you make something fun, they’re more likely to engage and remember,” Lee said.
The book has experiments for children to do at home to help them understand the science behind each story.
The Hong Kong story focuses on two innovators, Shervin Sharghy and Sophie Chapman. The pair are transforming the city’s plastic waste into sustainable concrete bricks, called EcoBricks. Using plastic to create bricks for building diverts thousands of kilograms of waste from landfills, lowering the carbon footprint of construction.
Lee hopes this story and others will teach students to test ideas and figure out the “ cause and effect ” relationship through hands-on activities .
Lee also wanted the book to encourage parents to connect with their kids. She even got her own kids involved in creating the book – readers can see their hands in its photos.
“I got them to be like little experiment assistants,” Lee said. “I thought it would be an experience of what it’s like to work and … understand what I do.”
Before becoming an author, Lee spent 10 years in the corporate world . However, she did not want to have one job for her whole life.
“Life is an adventure. You’re out here to explore and experiment,” she said. She said she could imagine herself being a creator.
Whenever she entered a bookstore or a library, Lee said she would feel overwhelmed by the choices. That is why she tried to create a book that would be different from what’s already on the market.
Lee said she hoped readers learn that you do not fail – you either win or you learn. “If you really believe in yourself and you put in the time and effort, you will get there,” she added.

title: Hong Kong can play unique role in fostering robotics industry: Paul Chan
description: Finance chief also welcomes launch of Galbot’s humanoid robot-operated outlets in Hung Hom, Kai Tak and Wan Chai – a first for the city.
content: Hong Kong can serve a unique role in the development of the robotics industry, the finance chief has said as he welcomed the coming opening of the city’s first convenience stores operated by humanoid robots. Following an opening ceremony on Monday, the first “Galbot stores” will launch in Hung Hom, Kai Tak and Wan Chai on Tuesday. They are Beijing-based Galbot’s first outlets outside mainland China, with plans for 10 more stores in the city later. The embodied-intelligence robotics company launched its first store on the mainland last August and has since expanded to about 200 outlets across 50 cities nationwide. “This is a genuinely important step for us in going overseas as Hong Kong is an important window and platform for [mainland] China facing the international market,” said Zhao Yuli, chief strategy officer of Galbot, noting that the business had operated a Hong Kong office since 2024. She said Galbot planned to open about 10 more stores in high-footfall districts of Hong Kong in coming years. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said at the opening ceremony that Hong Kong could play an “important and unique role” in three areas of the robotics industry: it could provide a viable application scenario; act as a sustainable research and development ecosystem, and ensure a robust supporting capital chain. “Hong Kong has a dense population, with highly efficient and diverse application scenarios and a high degree of internationalisation,” he said. “Galbot, as one of the fastest-moving players in the embodied intelligence race, has chosen to bring its most advanced technology to Hong Kong for validation and demonstration, which would be a key first step for its technology and products to ‘go global’ and expand into international markets.” Chan cited a Morgan Stanley report that projected the world would have nearly 1 billion humanoid robots by 2050, adding that China would be a key industry player and account for about 300 million of them. Clara Chan Ka-chai, CEO of the Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC), said the launch was a “phased and outstanding outcome” since the firm had invested in Galbot two years ago. She said the corporation had invested in more than 200 companies, with more than 70 per cent of the capital deployed going to early- and growth-stage companies, reflecting its firm commitment to backing start-ups at an early stage. Chan added that 11 companies in the HKIC’s investment portfolio had listed in Hong Kong, with more than 30 firms having applied for or preparing for listing this year. As of the end of 2025, the HKIC had recorded a 14 per cent net internal rate of return from its portfolio. According to Zhao, each Galbot store is run by wheeled humanoid robots powered by the company’s embodied foundation model, AstraBrain. The robots can take orders, deliver goods and prepare drinks using a linked coffee machine, though a human attendant is still needed for certain store operations, including some replenishment tasks, with full automation expected eventually. Zhao said Galbot’s robots won gold, silver and bronze medals in the retail category at the World Humanoid Robot Games. The competition required robots to restock shelves, manage inventory and autonomously identify misplaced items and correct their positioning. “Although Hong Kong has had many robotics and artificial intelligence exhibitions before, those were all demos running for a limited time,” she said. “What residents have rarely seen is a robot that can actually keep working, continuously.” Zhao said the robot at the Hong Kong outlet would be able to understand Cantonese, which would be one of the highlights of the launch. The stores would also sell cultural and creative products, in addition to drinks and food. Asked about the city’s high rents and labour costs, she said the company was willing to invest in the business and estimated that it would break even within 12 to 18 months. She described that time frame as “common” for bricks-and-mortar retail. Zhao cited examples in Beijing and Jiangxi, where the company sold cultural and creative merchandise linked to local landmarks, including Beijing-themed items near the Summer Palace and porcelain blind boxes in Jingdezhen. She said stores at cultural and tourism sites had increased foot traffic at some locations by 20 to 30 per cent over the past year. She added that the autonomous robots could also help extend operating hours where round-the-clock staffing was difficult. She cited Galbot’s smart-pharmacy deployments on the mainland, which operate 24 hours a day across multiple cities. Established in 2023, Galbot saw domestic orders across all its robot models exceed 1,200 last year, Zhao said. The company only began systematic international expansion in earnest this year. “We are actively exploring collaboration models with local partners, and expect to see more deployment across different international markets before long,” she said. She added that the company would also plan to introduce other robots to Hong Kong, including the Galbot ET1, its first learning-capable agentic bipedal humanoid robot.

title: Esther Chu’s top pick: Disney and Pixar’s ‘Inside Out’
description: The 12-year-old student from Lam Tin Methodist Primary School shares why they love this animated feature film about emotions and growing up.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your recommendations using this form .
I watched Inside Out, and I really liked it. It’s about a girl named Riley and the feelings inside her head – Joy, Sadness, Fear, Anger and Disgust.
At first, Joy tries to keep Sadness away. But later, Sadness helps Riley when she cries with her parents. That part touched me because it shows that it’s OK to be sad sometimes.
The film is soft and warm. It made me feel understood. I think everyone should watch it, especially on days when you feel a bit down. It will make you feel less alone.

title: Letters from readers about their favourite animals, interests and a day out in Hong Kong
description: Readers write about dogs and birds, cycling in Kowloon Bay and eating noodles and ice cream.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your letters using this form .
My favourite animals are dogs because they are adorable. I have always wanted a puppy, but my parents refuse to get one. They said they would rather buy me a digital pet.
During our end-of-term ceremony, I received two awards from my teacher. When I walked onto the stage, everyone clapped and cheered for me. I was over the moon!
My favourite subject is English because we learn new words and how to write stories.
I also enjoy swimming very much. I started learning when I was seven. I learned how to swim in Sichuan province.
My favourite animals are birds because they are cute and cuddly. I have seven birds. Five of them are yellow and grey, one is white and light blue, and the last one is red and green.
I have a big family. I have a sister, a mother and a father. My mother and father are always nice to me, apart from when I do something bad. Then, they might shout at me.
I am going to tell you about my day out with my family. We went cycling in Kowloon Bay, where I learned how to ride a two-wheel bike! It was not as hard as I thought it would be. While cycling, my dad fell, but luckily, he did not get hurt too badly.
After cycling, we went to Mong Kok for mixed cold noodles, egg waffles and ice cream. Then, we played squash until 8.30pm.
It was late, so we had instant noodles for dinner. It was the yummiest dinner ever! We all felt very tired and fell asleep quickly. I loved my family day!

title: Feature of the Week: Naisha Ranjan’s short story ‘Chasing the Moon’
description: The 10-year-old student from Kowloon Junior School writes about an aspiring female footballer who refuses to give up on her dream.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
Twelve-year-old Jennifer had one dream: to be a professional football player. But as the only girl footballer in her school, the boys often pushed and kicked her, making fun of her and telling her to play with babies.
Fortunately, Jennifer was not a good listener. She often told her mum: “I don’t really care what they say. They are just trying to discourage me, which is not going to work.”
“I did it! I did it!” Jennifer screamed after getting an offer from a major football academy.
When training began, she was glad to play with other girls, but their coach was not.
“Now I have another stupid girl to handle! I wish I coached the boys’ team,” the coach said.
Jennifer’s happiness faded as the weeks went by. When her mother asked about training, Jennifer could not hold back her tears. “I want to quit,” she sobbed as her mother tried to comfort her.
“You don’t have to keep playing,” her mum said. “But try one more week and then decide if you want to quit.”
During the next training, Jennifer saw an unfamiliar face setting up cones for drills.
“My name is Coach Craig. I am a retired footballer,” he said.
As he led the team through drills, Jennifer noticed how kind and supportive he was, and her heart felt at peace. This could be the coach to carry her to her dream.
It was Jennifer’s first match in the starting 11.
“I believe in you, Jennifer. Show the world what you can do,” Coach Craig told her with pride.
During the game, she made good tackles and passes. But in the last 10 minutes, she got the ball a few metres away from the halfway line. Everyone expected her to dribble or pass the ball.
Instead, she kicked the ball with all her might. Goal!
The fans screamed, and her teammates gave her high fives.
This was the same young woman who was a step away from giving up on her dream. And Jennifer was just getting started.

title: Advice: My mum is pregnant, and the extra chores are interfering with my studies
description: On this page, you’ll find advice from our team of psychologists to help you through all the ups and downs of life.
content:
A new baby changes a family, and it is normal for everyone to take on different tasks now. But your studies and your concerns are still important. Here are some ways to start this talk with your parents.
Look for a time when your parents are not rushing or stressed. You could say something like, “Mum and Dad, I would like to talk to you about balancing my chores and schoolwork. When is a good time for you?”
Let them know that you understand why you are needed more right now and that you want to help with the new baby.
Then, share examples of how the extra chores affect your studies. For instance, are you staying up late to finish homework? Or maybe you are missing assignment deadlines and having trouble focusing. These details will help your parents understand the full situation.
Make it clear that you want to support your family while also succeeding in school. You might phrase it like this: “I want to help prepare for the baby, but I’m also worried about my grades. Can we work together to find a balance?”
Remember your parents want that for you. They just may not realise how much the work is affecting you unless you tell them.
If the first chat does not go well, wait a little while and try talking to them again. Sometimes, parents need time to think and understand, especially because they may also be stressed about the pregnancy.
This question was answered by Ken Fung, a clinical psychologist and founder of Your Relationship Clinic.

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong, Singapore aren’t ‘enemies’, our competition is healthy, envoy says
description: Consul General Eric Teo calls for ‘win-win collaboration’ in wealth management despite competing tax packages to attract capital.
content: Singapore and Hong Kong do not view each other as enemies, but rather admire one another’s accomplishments, the country’s top envoy to the city has said, calling for greater cooperation between the two jurisdictions often cast as fierce rivals. Eric Teo Boon Hee, Singapore’s consul general in Hong Kong, said Asia was big enough to accommodate two financial centres and that both sides should work together to “expand the pie” as capital rushed into the region. Speaking exclusively to the South China Morning Post shortly after marking his first anniversary in the city, Teo pushed back against the prevailing narrative that Hong Kong and Singapore were locked in a zero-sum race for the crown of Asia’s top financial centre. “The way we see it, healthy and natural competition between the two cities is not necessarily a bad thing,” Teo said. “Actually, it is healthy and constructive competition to actually improve both sides, and allow us to do better for our people, for our businesses.” He said that in all his conversations with local officials and business leaders over the past year, he had “zero sense” that they viewed Singapore as an enemy. “There is competition, yes, but we don’t look at each other as enemies. We actually admire each other,” Teo said. “The world is changing in a very dynamic way. I think almost all of them are thinking about how we can … go back to forging win-win collaboration in areas that we are able to do so, including in the financial sector [and] in the wealth management sector.” The two jurisdictions are frequently seen as rivals due to their geographic similarities and shared status as Asian financial hubs. At the beginning of the decade, in particular, Hong Kong was seen to have lost out to Singapore as talent and companies uprooted themselves from the city in the wake of the national security law and pandemic restrictions. Despite Hong Kong positioning itself as a hub for mainland Chinese firms looking to go global, many of those companies have also opted to establish themselves in Singapore in part to gain a foothold in Southeast Asia and as an apparent hedge against geopolitical risk. But as of late, officials from both jurisdictions have been shifting their tone to focus more on areas of potential collaboration. On a visit to Hong Kong in March, Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong met Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu, with both leaders highlighting shared beliefs in areas such as free trade and multilateralism, and a mutual desire for enhanced cooperation. However, the adversarial narrative reignited recently as both jurisdictions were widely seen as introducing rival tax concession packages targeted at wealth funds. Teo said that such developments should not be framed as “zero-sum” and that the growing flow of capital entering the region provided the two jurisdictions with an opportunity to work together to “expand the pie”. Investors were seeking to hedge and avoid having all their resources concentrated in one particular location, he noted. “We strongly believe that in this part of the world, in Asia, we can accommodate both very good and open financial centres,” he said. He described the two financial centres as being in “different business nodes” – with Hong Kong positioned in northeastern Asia and Singapore in Southeast Asia. “I think both financial centres should find ways to work together in a complementary way to actually expand the pie,” he said. “If we are able to do that, then actually both benefit, rather than trying to undercut each other.” When asked where the two sides were most complementary and where cooperation might not be possible, he did not provide examples, instead saying he would “leave it to the experts in the financial sector” to work out. “We cannot work together in every area,” he said. “But I strongly believe that there are areas where, amid the competition, we can still work together.” Beyond the financial sector, Teo said there were opportunities for cooperation in areas where both jurisdictions were facing similar challenges, including low fertility rates, ageing populations, public housing and the rise of artificial intelligence. He noted that since January last year there had been 15 ministerial-level visits to Hong Kong from Singapore, while also highlighting the permanent secretaries exchange programme – the most recent of which occurred in July. He also highlighted the two cities’ robust trade, investment and people-to-people ties, with Hong Kong home to the largest overseas Singaporean community in a single city at about 28,000 people. In a personal anecdote, Teo shared that his maiden flight as a child was to Hong Kong in 1980, where he flew into the old Kai Tak Airport. Teo said it was clear to him that Hong Kong today was making a “very remarkable economic rebound”, and that the impression was shared by visiting Singaporean officials. “I think you can sense that the vibrancy, the dynamism, as well as the buzz is actually coming back,” he said.

title: For love of the game: why some athletes chase impossible Olympic dreams
description: Some of the city’s best will never reach an Olympics, let alone a podium, so why do they continue to train as hard as those who do.
content: When lacrosse returns to the Olympic Games in 2028 after more than a century away, it is unlikely that Hong Kong will be involved in any capacity other than watching. Just 12 teams – six in the men’s competition, six in the women’s – will take part in the shortened sixes format of the sport in Los Angeles, and Hong Kong’s sides, ranked 13th and 21st in the world, respectively, in the 10s version, are some way off breaking into the rarefied air occupied by those who will battle for gold. There is only a slightly better chance of reaching next year’s World Lacrosse Sixes Championships, and even then, that will need a top-five finish at October’s regional championships in Australia. In that context, the city’s players might be forgiven if they struggled to muster the motivation to carry on in the face of such overwhelming odds, and yet they do and with a hunger that would surprise many. “Watching the Olympics since I was little, and it always felt so far away, if not impossible,” Sally Tang Yi-ting, the women’s team captain, said. “It’s like a golden challenge or target for any athlete. “Yes, that’s a long road ahead for us, but no matter how far the target is, it’s something for us to work hard for, and it’s worth it to shed our sweat.” At 19, Baron Lee Chun-long still has a long playing career ahead of him, and even he acknowledged that the Games could be out of reach. “We all realised it’s going to be very difficult, but there’s still a chance,” he said. “If the sport is to remain in the Olympics, it gives the younger children playing the sport a hope to reach the world stage.” Hong Kong’s men and women, like many around the world, are chasing their Olympic dream while also juggling jobs, education and the normal concerns that come with not being full-time athletes. The question then, is why. What is the motivation to continue working, training and fighting to be better every day when the ultimate goal remains so far out of reach? Karen Lo, a former Hong Kong swimmer and now sport psychologist, said the dreams embodied “deeply held values like excellence, courage, identity, belonging, or contribution that give life meaning and direction”. “The psychological trap is not the unattainable goal, but becoming fused with a single outcome, for example, ‘I must win a medal’, rather than valuing the person and athlete one is becoming through the pursuit,” she added. “For more experienced athletes, research shows that the focus often shifts from ‘medalling’ to seeking a breakthrough or a feeling of mastery that affirms who they are and what they stand for.” Lo, who was a member of the city’s swimming set-up for seven years before she quit in 2006 at the age of 17, also pointed out the difference in drive between elite athletes and those who are never likely to see a podium. “The raw drive may feel similar, but the quality of motivation differs from athlete to athlete based on how well autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs are met,” she said. In the case of someone such as quadruple Olympic medallist Siobhan Haughey, a high autonomy, or her chosen goals, linked with clear progress, or competence, and the support of coaches, officials, and fans drives the motivation. “Athletes with limited medal chances may still be highly driven, but repeated barriers can thwart competence and autonomy, shifting motivation towards more controlled forms, such as proving themselves, and making the pursuit psychologically costlier, even if the underlying values remain the same,” Lo said. There is no guarantee that lacrosse, which was last played at the 1908 Games in London, will survive to be played at the Brisbane Olympics in 2032. History is littered with examples of sports that made brief appearances at a Games before disappearing from view, as those who play lacrosse are only too aware. Veteran Tang, who has been playing for 10 years, acknowledged she could well be chasing a target that might not materialise before she ends her playing career. “When I started playing lacrosse, there wasn’t even an Olympics to aim for,” she said. “I played because I love the sport, and enjoyed the process of learning new things to keep improving myself. The motivation is about improving every day – individually and collectively. “You can’t control how strong the other national teams are as an athlete; you can’t control if they are using players from the US, which is not what we are capable of doing. You only put unnecessary pressure on yourself by caring too much about things that you can’t control. “Also, as a more experienced player, I felt that I am working hard to fight for the next generation, and demonstrate to them what it takes to reach the higher goals.” Lee, who started playing lacrosse nine years ago at La Salle College and is now captain of the city’s under-20s team, said he felt as though he was at the start of a six-year journey, with Brisbane as the final destination. “I wonder what role I will play six years from now,” he said. “I will be 25, 26 if we have lacrosse in Brisbane; I might then have a more prominent role on the team. This is the reason why I am doing this. It’s also about the honour of representing my birthplace, and what I get at the end of my career. “I might be just a young man playing lacrosse now, but at the end of the day, it’s about what I get as an athlete. Maybe it’s for my own happiness, or maybe it’s for a sense of satisfaction. I don’t want to have any regrets, so I keep pursuing my dream as a lacrosse player.”

title: Small state, big agenda: Singapore prepares to steer Asean through crisis
description: The city state takes the helm on Asean’s 60th anniversary amid civil war, tariff threats and rising global tensions.
content: Every bloc needs a chair capable of getting things done – and Southeast Asia watchers say that description fits no country better than Singapore. The city state will get the chance to prove it in the bloc’s 60th anniversary year, after it takes the Asean helm from the Philippines on January 1. Speaking at Singapore’s National Day Rally on August 22, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the world was becoming more fractured and dangerous – one that the city state would have to “endure and survive for many years to come”. “Our response cannot be to retreat and turn inward,” Wong said, calling for the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations to deepen integration “to create a more effective single market”. A litany of headaches stand in the way of that ambition, from Myanmar’s civil war to an unresolved Thailand-Cambodia border row, simmering South China Sea tensions and keeping a distracted United States engaged with the region. But if any country can rise to the challenge, it is Singapore, according to Thitinan Pongsudhirak, a professor of political science and international relations at Chulalongkorn University in Bangkok. There was a joke among regional observers, he said, that Singapore should chair Asean every year, because “it is the most equipped despite its small size”. Technocratic leadership Singapore last chaired Asean in 2018, launching a smart cities network, spearheading efforts against transnational cybercrime and terrorism, and helping negotiators agree on a single, shared draft for a South China Sea code of conduct. Analysts expect a similar chairmanship style this time around: efficient, unglamorous and results-driven. “Compared with the Philippines, whose position as a South China Sea claimant gives it greater urgency on maritime security, Singapore is more likely to act as an honest broker and focus on institutional follow-through and economic integration,” said Joanne Lin, senior fellow and Asean Studies Centre coordinator at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. I would expect Singapore’s chairmanship to be more technocratic and implementation-oriented Syaza Shukri, political scientist A similar contrast can be drawn with Malaysia’s recent stewardship, according to Syaza Shukri, an associate professor of political science at the International Islamic University Malaysia. “I would expect Singapore’s chairmanship to be more technocratic and implementation-oriented than some previous chairmanships, such as Malaysia’s, focusing more on normative and diplomatic agenda,” she said. Singapore tended to emphasise deliverables, Syaza said, though its effectiveness would still depend on its ability to build consensus among member states. Its greatest impact, in her view, will come in economic integration, trade resilience, energy and connectivity. An economically fragmented bloc was more vulnerable to pressure from major powers, she said. “In that sense, Singapore’s economic agenda and its geopolitical agenda are really two sides of the same coin.” ‘Tangible effects’ Sharon Seah, principal fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, points to a scheme launched under Indonesia’s 2023 chairmanship as a concrete integration success: an interoperable QR code payment system linking the bloc’s national banks that is now working with WeChat, the Chinese super-app used by over a billion people for messaging, social media and mobile payments. “Singapore can try to take this idea further with key Asean trading partners and promote a systems interoperability that can help millions of Asean small and medium-sized enterprises,” she said. “This will be a very tangible effect of Asean payment systems integration.” Lin sees another opening on trade: Singapore could push for a less fragmented regional response to US tariff pressures by cutting non-tariff barriers, simplifying customs and rules of origin procedures, and coordinating responses to trade diversion and transshipment concerns. “I don’t think Singapore can solve Asean’s major crises, but it can try to sustain momentum, preserve common principles and leave Asean better coordinated and more resilient,” she said. Underpinning this is decades of institutional muscle memory. As a founding member, Singapore has the bureaucratic capacity and personnel to manage the bloc’s machinery, not just chair its meetings. “There is no doubt among the community of Asean observers that Singapore possesses strong agenda-setting powers and has able personalities who can steer the organisation at the various levels,” Seah said – borne out in this year’s State of Southeast Asia Survey, in which 31.3 per cent of respondents named Singapore the strongest leader on the bloc’s key challenges. Conflicts of interest For all the promise of economic statecraft, Singapore’s chairmanship will also be judged on harsher metrics – and few loom larger than Myanmar. For Thitinan, success hinges on how the city state handles Myanmar’s civil war and what he calls its “civilian-disguised government after a bogus poll”. Elections held between December and January were widely criticised as a junta-engineered sham to legitimise coup leader turned president, Min Aung Hlaing. “If Min Aung Hlaing is readmitted after gaining recognition from Laos, Thailand, and Cambodia … then leaders of major dialogue partners might not join Asean-related summits next year,” Thitinan said, adding: “Min Aung Hlaing is Singapore’s chief challenge.” Asean barred Myanmar’s generals from high-level meetings after the 2021 coup, but has since signalled willingness to welcome them back into the fold. Singapore’s chairmanship would also be measured against the ongoing Thailand-Cambodia border row and South China Sea tensions, Thitinan said – as well as its ability to draw “the US back into the Asean fray in order to balance out China”. On the South China Sea, Syaza said Singapore’s status as a non-claimant state cut both ways: no territorial stake made it a plausible broker of dialogue, but that same distance limited how far it could speak for claimant states like the Philippines and Vietnam. Should the long-stalled Asean-China code of conduct for the disputed waterway remain unresolved by the end of the Philippines’ term, “Singapore could inherit the task”, she said. No less consequential will be energy security. Asean’s heavy reliance on Middle Eastern oil and gas was laid bare this year by the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran, spotlighting the need to move away from fossil fuels. “Asean needs to fast track the green energy transition,” said Pou Sothirak, a former Cambodian ambassador and now a senior adviser at the Cambodian Centre for Regional Studies, calling for the “practical adoption of renewable energy, including stronger and smarter grid interconnectivity”. Like every Asean chair before it, Singapore will ultimately need to build consensus among member states with divergent interests to achieve its ambitions. “Singapore’s unique convening powers will be tested in the year ahead,” Seah said.

title: Hong Kong Science Park celebrates 25 years of innovation and growth
description: As Hong Kong’s premier science and technology ecosystem marks its silver jubilee, PostMag revisits the legacy of connection and invention that sustained 25 years of innovation, and meets the leaders driving the vision for the institution’s next chapter.
content: A particular kind of energy settles over Hong Kong Science Park on a weekday morning: researchers, deep in conversation, cross footbridges with laptop bags slung over shoulders; engineers transport prototypes between buildings, hunting for the next set of testing conditions; the air is rich with the buzz and hum of a community that has, over a quarter of a century, grown from reclaimed land at Pak Shek Kok into the largest start-up incubation platform in the city. Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) kick-starts its silver-jubilee celebrations this year, and that industrious atmosphere is precisely what its new chairman, Cordelia Chung, wants people to understand about what has been built here. Not a laboratory, not a gadget: an ecosystem driving growth – one she intends to carry into its next phase. Chung took up the chairmanship on July 1, arriving with a résumé that speaks of more than two decades inside one of the largest technology companies in the world. At IBM, she held senior leadership roles and steered the mainland China, Hong Kong and Asean markets, served as the vice-president and general counsel for Asia-Pacific, and was appointed to the IBM chairman and CEO’s Global Strategy Council as its first Asian female executive, contributing to worldwide direction setting across more than 140 countries. Her international background – having lived and worked in Tokyo, Singapore, Shanghai, Beijing and Hong Kong – brings a broader outlook. She is no stranger to HKSTP, either, as her tenure on the board of directors, from 2017 to 2023, will show. Among Chung’s long list of achievements, receiving the Medal of Honour from the Hong Kong government in 2024, for her role in propelling the city’s innovation and technology (I&T) development, is arguably one of the most meaningful. It is that blend of corporate governance and lived experience in a future-focused sector that shapes Chung’s vision for HKSTP, along with her sense of service to the community, instilled early on during her formative years at a convent school, which guides her intentionality to empower and enable talents. China’s 15th five-year plan outlined high hopes for the continued advancement of Hong Kong’s I&T industry as an international hub for science and technology, and for it to deliver results. But Chung does not reach for a single headline figure to convince the audience of her ambition, instead framing her philosophy around four qualities: breadth, depth, height and strength. “Hong Kong’s economy has relied heavily on finance and service industries, but facing global challenges, industrial transformation is now imperative. What we’re currently looking for is the breadth of I&T. We want to fully integrate I&T into traditional industries in order to expand Hong Kong’s industrial base,” she says, explaining that expanding talent development, nurturing that passion early and planting the seeds will provide a clear pathway for the next generation. Once breadth is established, depth comes into play. “Besides pursuing advanced technology, we also aim for a wide application of technology,” she says, pointing to the investment in AI computing capacity as the base for something broader than any one company’s product road map. “It offers hope for transformation to traditional industries that have reached a bottleneck.” She counts off some of Hong Kong’s foundational economic pillars: “Financial services, construction, real estate, education – all of them can be pushed forward with technology, and it can be applied to so many different disciplines.” Height, the third quality, is where Chung’s own international career shines through most clearly. Hong Kong’s unique East-meets-West positioning must be leveraged to “proactively attract businesses and talent from around the world. At the same time, we must lead the world by helping local and mainland Chinese I&T ventures expand to global markets”. Last but not least, strength describes the pace and density she wants HKSTP to sustain. “It’s easier to create synergy when talent, capital and different resources are highly concentrated,” Chung says. Bumping into experts from different fields while walking through the park’s corridors and campuses encourages exchange and intellectual confluence. Removing friction at each stage of a company’s growth and creating a support network to match innovators with investors allows the start-ups to have the “sprint energy” to break through and thrive. Chung’s vision is grand, and to understand her framing of the next chapter, it helps to trace how HKSTP arrived at this one. Its roots stretch back to the 1970s, when the first of three industrial estates – in Tai Po, Yuen Long and Tseung Kwan O – was established, starting a lineage that eventually produced the Hong Kong Industrial Technology Centre Corporation in 1993. It was not until 2001 that the government consolidated these assets under the HKSTP umbrella as the city’s flagship innovation and technology body, with the Hong Kong Science Park at Pak Shek Kok as its centrepiece. With a quarter of a century under its belt, that foundation has grown into a multi-location operation spanning around 240 hectares (593 acres) of dedicated infrastructure. With a network of more than 210 investors and over 500 public- and private-sector partners, HKSTP credits these relationships with keeping talent, technology and capital moving through its community. In the past eight years alone, HKSTP has demonstrated rapid acceleration, raising more than HK$170 billion (US$21.7 billion) in funding for its start-ups, with its Corporate Venture Fund leveraging private capital at a ratio of roughly one to 13. Under Chung’s predecessors, the number of companies based in the park rose from around 600 to more than 2,600, 14 unicorns were nurtured and 23 start-ups went public. HKSTP counts more than 26,000 professionals from 26 markets among its ranks, including success stories such as SenseTime and Lalamove, all built and scaled within its own ecosystem. From its origins as an industrial asset manager, the evolution of HKSTP into a global technology catalyst has been defined by game-changing milestones. Following Hong Kong Science Park’s opening in June 2002, early operations focused on building research and development (R&D) capacity across four pillars: electronics, biotechnology, precision engineering and IT. Back then, Hong Kong’s technology scene was primarily designed to serve as an innovation engine for the city and the Pan-Pearl River Delta, reimagined in 2019 as the Greater Bay Area. An iconic symbol of this ambition arrived in 2010. Following Charles Kao Kuen’s Nobel Prize win the previous year for groundbreaking achievements in fibre optics, HKSTP named its central landmark – the striking ovoid Charles K. Kao Auditorium, affectionately dubbed the “Golden Egg” – in honour of Hong Kong’s own laureate, inspiring generations of local talent. In 2019 came the announcement of InnoHK, a flagship government initiative enabling research collaborations in artificial intelligence, robotics and healthcare with top global universities, while 2021 saw the repositioning of the three traditional industrial estates in Tai Po, Yuen Long and Tseung Kwan O as modern InnoParks. It was a pivotal era that culminated in a historic visit by President Xi Jinping, in 2022, cementing the park’s role in the national innovation agenda. HKSTP’s momentum has only accelerated. It extended its physical footprint with a Shenzhen branch in Futian district the following year and, in 2025, the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou Innovation Cluster was ranked No 1 in the world. If Chung supplies the vision for the road ahead, HKSTP CEO Terry Wong Ping-sau is responsible for the daily mechanics of getting there. Wong has more than 30 years of international executive experience across advanced mobility, smart cities, infrastructure and energy, including in markets such as Australia and Saudi Arabia, but he describes his own first year in the role as a process of listening intently before acting. “I spend a large amount of time almost every day meeting stakeholders, including universities, the government, start-ups, corporations, partnerships and investors,” he says, adding that he celebrated his one-year anniversary at HKSTP in much the same way. In fact, that instinct for stakeholder management is not so different from the discipline required to deliver an infrastructure project, despite the subject matter. Big budget, small budget, international, or local matters not. “We have to have a strategy, be clear about what we want to achieve, and work together so that big teams share the same goal.” What has changed is the expanded terrain that HKSTP now covers, a point that dovetails with Chung’s own emphasis on breadth as a strategic priority. “We have a broad technical arena,” says Wong. “Market development, AI and robotics – it’s so broad, no one can say they’re an expert in all of this.” But there is a method to the madness of managing that range. HKSTP has organised its support around four pillars that play to Hong Kong’s natural advantages: life and health technology, AI and data science, green technology and advanced manufacturing. Support is calibrated to a company’s stage of growth, moving from early incubation, global connections and talent scouting through to business development, early capital and elite programmes, as well as venture-capital networks designed to help mature firms expand abroad. Wong describes this as a journey “from ideation to IPO”, spanning over 20 initiatives, including funding, proof-of-concept support, business matching and market access. Central to delivering that support is Inno.OS, the corporation’s own platform, blending hardware, software and services to help companies build value. Physical infrastructure is equally important. Beyond Hong Kong Science Park, the three InnoParks, dedicated to advanced manufacturing, offer plug-and-play production facilities that let companies move quickly from R&D into commercial output. A GreenTech Hub focuses on sustainability, and a new I&T facility, InnoPole, has been announced at the San Tin Technopole, in the Northern Metropolis area of the New Territories, where Chung has separately been appointed to the board of the dedicated company overseeing the site. Successful support systems must also consider the well-being of the innovators at the heart of progress. InnoCell, a 17-storey smart-living and co-creation space next to Hong Kong Science Park, was built to house the talent on which the ecosystem depends. It embodies what HKSTP describes internally as a “Work, Live, Play, Learn” philosophy: proximity between researchers, engineers and entrepreneurs, whether in a laboratory or a shared kitchen, produces the kind of chance encounter that formal programming cannot manufacture. InnoCell is a physical expression of the same principle Chung raises when she talks about strength: put enough talent and capital within walking distance of one another, and ideas begin to take shape. Nowhere is that philosophy more apparent than in life and health technology. More than 350 companies within the HKSTP ecosystem are involved in such fields as drug discovery and digital health. PanopticAI, a start-up founded by Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) alumni, has developed a camera-based monitoring solution capable of reading vital signs, including heart rate, blood pressure and respiration rate, from little more than a short video clip. PanopticAI won clearance from the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for contactless pulse and respiratory rate measurement on its mobile application, making it the first Hong Kong company to secure such approval for a piece of software as a medical device. Early adopters now include Gleneagles Hospital Hong Kong and healthcare firm Bupa. Another example is Koln 3D, a Hong Kong Science Park company that has become the first medical metal 3D-printing manufacturer in the city, producing patient-specific body implants used in reconstructive surgeries as far afield as Central Asia and Europe. Its AI-powered technology can accurately tailor-make bone replacements and 3D models. Starting out in 2013, Koln 3D has since expanded its production into the Greater Bay Area and Switzerland, and partnered with hospitals in Singapore, France and Kazakhstan – exactly the kind of internationalisation Chung and Wong say they want to accelerate across the Hong Kong Science Park portfolio. Meanwhile, Lalamove, an on-demand delivery platform that grew from a local start-up within Hong Kong Science Park into a unicorn that operates in 17 markets across Asia, the Americas and the Europe, Middle East and Africa region, tells the story of scale centred on international expansion. Founded in 2013, Lalamove, formerly known as “EasyVan”, joined HKSTP’s incubation programme early on to connect with technology partners and unlock investments that accelerated its development. Within 18 months, the company received two major capital injections and expanded to mainland China and other Asian markets. In April, it successfully tested its low-altitude-economy logistics solutions in complex urban environments, flying a cargo-carrying drone from Hong Kong Science Park, over Tolo Harbour, to the Mars Centre in the Tai Po InnoPark. Positioning Hong Kong as a connector is an instinct that runs through HKSTP, supported by its own cross-border work. HKSTP presents itself as a two-way avenue for Hong Kong and mainland Chinese innovators seeking to expand internationally, while also helping overseas companies enter the Greater Bay Area, mainland China and beyond. Its Shenzhen branch has attracted more than 90 innovation companies, helped raise over 800 million yuan (US$119 million) in funding and supported more than 170 companies moving northbound into the mainland and 80 moving southbound into Hong Kong. “Whatever we do, the market here is too small, anyway,” says Chung. “We need to have that broader, connective outlook.” HKSTP says its Global Connect programme has brought together more than 8,000 stakeholders, advisers and innovators, while its Global Mixer programme has taken more than 200 partner companies to over 20 exhibitions in more than 10 countries, from Las Vegas to Dubai to Singapore. “We can provide what we call a one-stop service,” says Chung. “If you have an idea, we can incubate you, we can give you money. When we think you’re doing a good job, we can help you accelerate. We can introduce investors, lawyers, bankers, tax consultants, accountants – the full suite of things that you need to really grow your business. If what you do is something that can be produced, you can actually land in one of our InnoParks and do the pilot production there and test it out. “It’s about building the bridge, making sure people are connected, making sure that the people who have the ideas meet the people who can make it happen.” She explains that the park’s bridging ability can “support the scale and eventual maturity of the entire I&T landscape in Hong Kong. We’re ready; the infrastructure is ready. We’re not going from zero to one, we’re [going] from one to 10 or one to N”. For companies coming from different starting points, Wong notes, the support required is rarely identical. “For companies from mainland China, their main objective is to expand overseas, and they already have good products that are selling in China.” What HKSTP offers is help understanding global regulatory standards and linking them with the right industry players. Newer, earlier-stage companies tend to need more fundamental support: introductions to researchers, help refining a prototype, or access to corporate partners willing to run pilot trials. “Instead of doing it on their own, the people in our park get access to different stakeholders,” Wong says. “We proactively curate the people they actually need.” Chung brings the governance experience and the outward-facing conviction to argue that Hong Kong’s next phase depends on breadth of talent, depth of adoption, height of ambition and strength of concentration. Wong brings the operational discipline to turn that framework into an organisation whose real product is connective tissue: the funding relationships, the mentorship networks and the physical proximity that let Hong Kong’s researchers and entrepreneurs turn ideas into products, and products into global businesses. For an organisation that has spent 25 years building that infrastructure, both physical and relational, Chung’s four-part vision reads less like a slogan and more like a checklist for the next page. Breadth, so that more of Hong Kong’s economy and more of its young people have a stake in the outcome. Depth, so that the technologies built here change how entire industries operate. Height, so that Hong Kong’s position between mainland China and the rest of the world becomes a genuine advantage. And strength, so that the density of talent and capital already gathered keeps generating the kind of collaboration no five-year plan can fully script in advance. Chung feels confident about the future because she has seen first-hand the path that lies ahead and where it can lead, during her years as a board member of HKSTP. “When I first joined, the start-up population here was around 600. Now, we have over 2,600. It has really grown. But is it enough? I don’t think it’s enough. So, that is one thing that I want to steer: for us to become much more energetic in this area,” she says. “In the last 10 years, 20 years, we have created a solid foundation. Now, we can take it to the next level.” Much can change in the next 25 years. In fact, the chairman is counting on it. Chung muses on the next chapter with good humour: “I have to think of my own age, if I still have the ability to …” She trails off, deep in thought, imagining the possibilities. “In 25 years’ time, I hope that the various science parks in the entire Greater Bay Area will be truly integrated. With laws and regulations completely streamlined, HKSTP will be the largest innovation cluster globally,” she smiles. “A day at Hong Kong Science Park will look like being in the leading science and technology hub in the entire world: a SuperPark.” HKSTP kicks off its 25th anniversary on August 31 with its “Together to Next” prelude celebration, honouring the visionaries, partners and innovators of the I&T community. title: What does a black hole sound like? A scientist’s answer was turned into music
description: Astrophysicist translates X-ray data from a black hole system into musical notes.
content:
Astrophysicist Becka Phillipson wondered what a black hole might sound like.
Phillipson works at Villanova University in the US state of Pennsylvania. She found an answer to her question by translating X-ray data from a black hole system into musical notes.
The first time she listened to the audio, the sounds reminded her of someone pressing every key on an organ at once.
After roughly 30 seconds of this “chaos”, she heard a “coherent, beautiful major chord” ring out.
Her research inspired a 13-minute musical piece. It was performed earlier this month at a concert called “This Silent Music”.
The concert was meant to be a place where people could sit and deal with their feelings, said Liz Lang, one of the creators.

title: Iran war forces Cambodian families to choose between school and survival
description: The conflict has increased the cost of petrol, making it more difficult for children to get to school.
content:
Sou Sreynich dreams of becoming a teacher. But she knows she’s far behind.
The 13-year-old first entered a classroom at 10, when most Cambodian children had been in school for years.
Fearing the boat to school could sink, Sou’s mother waited until she was old enough to swim. The decision is familiar to many living on Cambodia’s Tonle Sap, Southeast Asia’s largest freshwater lake.
Now, the price of petrol has spiked because of the US-Israeli war on Iran, making it more expensive for children and teachers to get to school. It is also more difficult for governments to fund education.
The war’s effects are forcing struggling families to decide whether to pay for food, fuel, rent and electricity or keep their child in school.
When money is tight, Sou skips a day or two of school to work with her parents. She dreads every absence.

title: China’s Dongba script: the only hieroglyphic system still used today
description: Form of writing, dating back more than 1,000 years, uses pictures and symbols instead of letters.
content:
Stepping into the Old Town of Lijiang, a city in China’s Yunnan province, feels like entering the set of a Chinese period drama.
The Old Town is a thriving shopping district. And if you pay attention to the signage, you will see drawings underneath almost all of them.
This is not graffiti – it is Dongba script. It is the only hieroglyphic script still in use today. It uses pictures and symbols instead of letters.
Dongba is the traditional religion, culture and priestly class of the Naxi ethnic group. Most live in Lijiang. Others are spread across parts of Yunnan, Sichuan and Tibet.
The Dongba script traces its roots back over 1,000 years, with scholars estimating its origins between the seventh and 10th centuries during the Tang and Song dynasties.
Created by Naxi shamans for sacred rituals, these pictographs survived for centuries in Yunnan’s isolated canyons, drawn on countless religious manuscripts over the generations.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong puts its dual policy blueprints to work for future growth
description: Launching both the five-year plan and the policy address in tandem ensures the city’s policy objectives fully align with the nation’s development priorities.
content: The concurrent release of Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the chief executive’s policy address this year is not a haphazard decision by John Lee Ka-chiu. Put together for coherence and synergy, the unprecedented joint unveiling next month of these two important instruments offers Hong Kong an opportunity to match long-term national alignment with near-term delivery – a strategic move that fosters change amid continuity as the administration finishes its term in 10 months. Crucially, it sharpens the focus on what it takes to rise to the challenge as we strive to meet national goals for the benefit of city and country. The coming policy speech will be Lee’s fifth and final one in his current term. What sets it further apart is the joint release of the city’s five-year plan, a much-anticipated blueprint to steer its development alongside the nation’s priorities up to 2030. The city leader will present both documents to the Legislative Council on September 16, before attending a question and answer session with lawmakers the following day. Lee and other ministers are expected to host briefings to explain the plans and policies in greater detail to the public, as well as diplomats and foreign investors. The linkage of the leader’s final policy address in the current term with the city’s first endeavour to align with state development goals is both symbolic and pragmatic. Traditionally, the policy speech takes stock of what the government has achieved while seeking to address the city’s short- and longer-term issues. Linking it now with the national plan signals that the city’s future transcends the tenures of individual public office holders. Whoever is at the helm is obliged to map out the measures needed to achieve outcomes in line with the directions set by the country. Speaking after a district visit on Wednesday, Lee said tabling the city’s five-year plan and then his policy address shortly afterwards would help people better grasp how they complement each other in defining the vision for Hong Kong’s future. “The five-year plan draws the eyes of a dragon, while the policy address draws the entire dragon,” he said. The policy address would formulate measures and set out indicators for implementing the five-year plan, based on the international environment, economic forecasts and the latest developments, he added. Lee dropped some hints when he visited low-income households as part of the public consultations for the policy address. He pledged to ease burdens on older people and their carers to support ageing in place. “Enabling elderly people to live healthily and with dignity in familiar communities is an important direction of our elderly care policy,” he wrote in a social media post following the visit. He pledged to promote the integration of medical care, rehabilitation, community support and technology applications. Understandably, the public will look up to Lee and his team for more tangible improvements in livelihood matters. The government should also elaborate on how its policies will lead the city to achieve the goals under the five-year plan to invigorate the economy and improve people’s standard of living. In just over a fortnight, Hong Kong people will find out what is in store for them in the coming year. At the same time, a new chapter for the city’s next crucial stage of development will unfold under a comprehensive blueprint running into the new decade. Lee’s final policy address offers a natural opportunity to take stock of what has been achieved since he took over the helm in 2022, distinguish initiatives that are working from those that need adjustment or reinforcement, and double down on successful policies into the next five-year cycle. It also allows the administration to launch measures that can take effect quickly while embedding them in a longer development strategy even beyond 2030. This is how change can be fostered amid continuity. Having a five-year plan by no means turns Hong Kong into a planned economy as some have questioned. A visionary blueprint enables advance planning so Hong Kong can better grasp the opportunities arising from national development under “one country, two systems”, and be better prepared amid fast-changing geopolitical uncertainties. The government should also review and update the plan’s goals whenever necessary.

title: A Hong Kong festival shows how the arts can help seniors live happier lives
description: The Hong Kong Creative Aging Arts Festival will feature more than 40 performances highlighting the healing power of the arts for the elderly.
content: More than 130 artists aged between 55 and 90 are set to take the stage for the coming second Hong Kong Creative Aging Arts Festival, a powerful celebration of how the arts can help seniors lead happier lives Running from September 9 to 20 at the Jockey Club Creative Arts Centre in Shek Kip Mei, Kowloon, the mainly Cantonese event will feature more than 40 performances, including an opening performance titled Measuring Love directed by the award-winning UK theatre director Alan Lyddiard. Other highlights include a drama production by Guangzhou’s Third Act Theatre, visual art exhibitions, and talks focusing on creativity and well-being during later life stages. The festival is organised by Arts’ Options, a non-profit charity established in 2011 to provide creative outlets and training for senior citizens in Hong Kong. “We want to create a ripple effect that continuously [influences] others,” says Rebecca Po Wan-ting, the charity’s executive director. “We want more members of the general public to understand the importance and the benefits of elderly arts.” The goal is not just fun, but also to give seniors the confidence to be cast in a professional environment, Po says. Since 2019, Arts’ Options has been running a “Train the Trainer” course for those who have completed drama training and want to teach others. The ethos behind Arts’ Options aligns with a growing global recognition of the physiological and social benefits of engaging in the arts. Daisy Fancourt thoroughly investigated these benefits in her recent bestseller, Art Cure: The Science of How the Arts Transform Our Health. The book has ignited fresh interest in how engaging in the arts – from listening to music and watching films to dancing and performing on stage – is good for you. For Lucy Siu May-yee, a former lecturer at the Education University of Hong Kong, these benefits have been life-changing. When she started taking acting classes at Arts’ Options five years ago, she finally began to look after herself. Until then, she had spent much of her time in retirement caring for her husband, who was nearing the end of his life. She loved him deeply, but the demanding role had taken a toll on her spirit, she says. Acting required the engagement of all her senses, and Siu soon discovered that it freed her mind and body, helping her regain a sense of purpose and agency. “I [found] that I live not for my beloved. I live for my own self,” she says. In the five years since her first class, Siu has gone on to write scripts and teach drama to other seniors. Her drama community was a major source of emotional support when her husband died last year, and she is looking forward to taking part in the coming festival, where she will be an exhibition guide. Another Arts’ Options participant, retired businessman and former television actor Bobby Chow Chun-ming, has seen similar benefits first-hand. Chow had a short television acting career from 1979 to 1982, before he transitioned into business. His business career kept him financially comfortable, but he missed the acting scene. Getting back into acting after his retirement has helped Chow exercise and improve his memory and mood, and has provided a respite from loneliness and the isolation that can come with retirement. “I was really lost,” Chow says. “And it really changed my life after I joined the acting group and I made new friends.” The therapeutic power of the arts is being recognised by institutions around the world. The National Gallery Singapore has just become the first museum in the world to be recognised as a Healing Arts Centre of Excellence. The gallery offers programmes such as “Art With You”, designed to provide relief to people with dementia and their carers, and “Slow Art”, an experience that focuses on mindfulness-based art. It also provides tactile resources for visually impaired visitors and a “Calm Room” to aid neurodivergent visitors who may feel overstimulated. Ong Zhen Min, director of learning and public engagement at the gallery, says museums across the globe are starting to incorporate wellness and inclusive offerings in their everyday visitor experiences. “It also reflects an evolving understanding of the role museums can play in people’s everyday lives – not only as places to encounter art, but as welcoming spaces where they can pause, connect and feel a sense of belonging,” she says. Cultural establishments are seen in Singapore as part of the country’s larger goals for community health. “Museums do not replace clinical or social care, but they can offer welcoming, non-clinical settings where people can slow down, express themselves and connect with others through art,” Min says. Siu says the lessons she has learned through teaching and acting have led to the one realisation that matters to everyone. As she was guiding elderly actors through a script about releasing negativity, saying goodbye and making peace with the end of life, her own fear of death started to subside. “I find that through drama or through creative arts, I [have] no more fear about nearing death, because I can find meaning in my life,” Siu says. “I will face death as just a bridge – as a bridge from this atmosphere to another universe.” The Second Hong Kong Creative Aging Arts Festival, Jockey Club Creative Arts Centre, 30 Pak Tin St, Shek Kip Mei, Kowloon, September 9-20.
