title: Hong Kong WhatsApp hijacking scams surge 170% to nearly 2,000 cases
description: Police say victims lost HK$146 million in first seven months of 2026, with some suffering individual losses exceeding HK$10 million.
content: WhatsApp account hijacking scams in Hong Kong surged by nearly 170 per cent to almost 2,000 cases in the first seven months of this year, with one victim losing as much as HK$12.2 million (US$1.55 million). Police said the 1,993 cases logged from January to July represented a 169.7 per cent increase from the 739 cases recorded over the same period last year. The figure also surpassed the 1,669 cases recorded in all of 2025. The cases over the first seven months resulted in losses of HK$146.3 million, down by 22.7 per cent from HK$189.2 million over the same period last year. Despite the lower total loss, police warned that the threat was far from subsiding, noting that some victims lost between HK$1 million and more than HK$10 million. “The rise in cases was related to the habits of our residents using these social media or instant messaging platforms,” said Superintendent Hui Yee-wai of the force’s cyber security and technology crime bureau. “On the other hand, we have also seen that artificial intelligence is a factor. Every scam involved fake websites, while AI has made generating these fake websites significantly easier.” WhatsApp account hijacking is a scam involving fraudsters impersonating friends and relatives or using fake WhatsApp websites to obtain telephone numbers and app registration codes. Once they gain access to an account, they message the victim’s contacts to solicit money or extract personal information. Chief Inspector Wong Cheung-hing said one case involved a 32-year-old man who fell victim to a WhatsApp hijacking scam in March. The victim, who was planning to buy a property, received fake WhatsApp messages from scammers who hijacked his account and impersonated his property agent and lawyer. They demanded the victim pay a large deposit on the property, resulting in a total loss of more than HK$1.1 million. In a separate case, a man lost more than HK$10 million after fraudsters hijacked his father’s WhatsApp account and impersonated his father using suspected AI-generated voice messages to scam the victim, demanding he make multiple transfers. Wong said another WhatsApp account hijacking scam case involved a financial manager at an investment company who lost HK$12.2 million. “Scammers would make seemingly plausible excuses such as a friend, supplier or business partner who was suddenly in urgent need of some funds, or needed to make a deposit,” he said. He appealed to the public to be vigilant, including avoiding relying solely on WhatsApp messages to determine someone’s identity. Residents should carefully verify the recipient’s account before transferring funds, regularly check linked devices on WhatsApp, and be mindful of personal information publicly available on social media, he said. Besides WhatsApp, police also recorded hijacking scams on other instant messaging platforms. The overall hijacking scams involving instant messaging accounts reached 2,020 cases from January to July this year, involving HK$150 million in losses. The number of cases was up 154.1 per cent from the 795 cases recorded over the same period last year. Among this year’s cases, 11 involved Telegram with losses of HK$3.7 million, and six involved Facebook with HK$18,000 in losses. Overall, the force recorded 16,437 cases of technology-related crimes between January and July this year, with a total loss of HK$3.08 billion. Police recorded 19,080 cases of technology-related crimes over the same period in 2025, with losses amounting to HK$3.64 billion. Philip Chua, Asia-Pacific director of public policy for products at Meta Platforms, which owns WhatsApp and Facebook, noted the challenges posed by transnational criminal syndicates. “Large transnational criminal syndicates are looking to profit in billions of dollars and they’re using all kinds of tactics, including interfering with broadcast powers, creating websites, trying to find ways to compromise people and to collect people’s personal information,” he said. He said Meta was committed to protecting its users in Hong Kong through measures, including displaying more information about unknown callers and preventing suspicious links from appearing in chats. “We are really seeing a very, very tough adversary. We want to make sure that the public is fully aware of what is happening, what they can do to protect themselves,” he said.

title: Citi’s China-US corridor thrives as mainland firms hedge risks amid trade turbulence
description: Chinese firms lean on global banks to manage trade friction and expand supply chains, keeping corporate activity resilient, Citi says.
content: Escalating US-China trade friction has failed to dampen corporate activity between the two economies, with Citi reporting steady revenue growth on its North America-China corridor as Chinese companies aggressively deploy risk-hedging strategies to protect their global market share. Instead of retreating from the US market, mainland Chinese firms had leaned heavily on global institutions to navigate financial friction and complex supply chains, Citi’s Greater China executives said at a media briefing in Hong Kong. “Our revenue has not decreased – there has been growth,” the bank’s China CEO Zhang Wenjie said, noting a 44 per cent year-on-year revenue surge across the bank’s China-US corridor in the first half of the year. Geopolitical headwinds boosted demand for cross-border financial services, he said. Because North America remained a vital market, Chinese enterprises increasingly turned to international banks to execute foreign exchange hedging, manage trade exposure and reconfigure capital flows, Zhang said. Chinese firms are exporting advanced technology, localised supply chains and high-value innovations that contribute to the development of host countries Zhang Wenjie, Citi The resilience comes as Chinese corporate expansion enters what Citi describes as a “Going Global 3.0” phase. Moving beyond low-cost manufactured exports and cross-border acquisitions, Chinese firms are now deploying entire hi-tech supply chain ecosystems abroad, with focus shifting towards green energy, electric vehicles, consumer electronics and artificial intelligence infrastructure. “We are seeing Chinese firms move away from competing strictly on cost,” Zhang said. “Today, they are exporting advanced technology, localised supply chains and high-value innovations that actively contribute to the economic development of host countries.” To manage global operations, mainland Chinese parent companies are adopting a “dual-hub strategy,” retaining domestic headquarters while establishing regional treasury centres in Hong Kong to orchestrate international capital. The shift has turned the Hong Kong-mainland China corridor into Citi’s largest and most active international banking route globally. Revenue from mainland clients’ cross-border business through Hong Kong ranked first among all of Citi’s corridors in the first half of 2026, rising 20 per cent year on year, according to Citi Hong Kong CEO Aveline San. “Mainland enterprises use Hong Kong to centralise treasury operations, manage multicurrency liquidity and raise international capital,” San noted. The corridor’s momentum was on full display on August 23, when Alibaba Group Holding priced a HK$80 billion (US$10.2 billion) share placement to fund its AI buildout – the largest primary follow-on share sale ever by a Hong Kong-listed company. Citigroup served as one of three co-bookrunners on the transaction. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. While traditional corridors remain robust, Chinese corporate footprint is also diversifying rapidly across emerging markets. Citi’s business tied to Central Asia had doubled over the past six months, driven by expanding trade and corporate activity between China and the region’s nations, according to bank executives. Strong activity was also surging across Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Latin America. Chinese companies were evolving from “Made in China” to “Created in China”, Zhang said. “Today, they are competing on innovation and technological leadership, enabling them to compete with global peers at a higher level.” To support this footprint, Citi is expanding its network of dedicated “China desks” – hubs staffed by senior Chinese-speaking bankers. The bank is adding locations in Brazil and Europe to complement existing centres in Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai, London, New York and South Africa. Financial technology is expanding in tandem. CitiToken Services – the bank’s blockchain-based platform enabling 24-7 real-time liquidity transfers across global time zones – had drawn strong demand since its 2025 launch, San said. Total capital raised year to date for mainland clients from global capital markets reached US$30 billion as of August, according to the bank.

title: Activities to keep your space tidy and build new organising routines
description: Add these small habits to your daily life to keep mess from becoming too much to handle.
content:
Organising can sound like a tiring chore. But all you need to do is add small, simple routines to your daily habits. You can turn a messy bedroom into a tidy one and feel much happier.
You don’t need to let a mess pile up. Instead, you can do small things every day to keep your space organised.
For example, you can make your bed every day and clean your desk before going to sleep. Spend just 10 minutes tidying your room every night.
Doing these quick, daily tasks stops the mess from becoming too much to handle.
When you add small, easy habits to your daily routine, you can also spend less energy making decisions. It also helps you save time.
1. Label the first jar “To Do” and the second jar “Done”.
2. Write down a list of the small, quick tasks you want to complete every night to keep your room neat. For example, fold clothes and clear the desk.
3. Write each task on its own popsicle stick using a permanent marker. Place all the sticks into the “To Do” jar.
4. Every night, 10 minutes before bedtime, pull one popsicle stick out of the “To Do” jar. Complete only that specific task. Once the task is complete, drop the stick into the “Done” jar.
5. Grab the next stick until the “To Do” jar is completely empty.
6. The next morning, put all the sticks from the “Done” jar back into the “To Do” jar so you’re ready for the evening.
labels (sticky notes can also be used as labels)
1. This storage system can be used to organise your past assignments, notes and exams for each subject. Add a label to each folder. Below it, add a sticky note.
2. On one label, write: “I’ll need it this month”. The next label should say: “I might need it later”. The third label should say: “I no longer need it (discard)”. You should recycle the work in this folder whenever you have the chance.
3. On the sticky notes, write: “This folder contains”. As you add things into the “this month” and “need it later” folders, write the title and date of your work on the sticky note.
4. Every month, look at the items in each folder and see if they need to be moved to a different one. This will also help you review previous assignments, notes and exams, keeping the information fresh in your mind.
5. If you remove assignments from the folders, update the sticky notes with what has been moved. Add more sticky notes as needed.

title: Sunburn can have long-term health risks for children, experts say
description: Sunburns in childhood can damage the DNA in skin cells and even double the risk of melanoma.
content:
We might not think twice about getting a sunburn. However, sun damage can lead to serious health risks later in life.
Research from 2024 shows that 59 per cent of children have been sunburned at least once. While the pain and redness fade, sunburn causes irreversible damage that can lead to skin cancer.
Experts warn that sunburn during childhood or adolescence can double the risk of developing melanoma. This is the most serious type of skin cancer.
According to the British Association of Dermatologists (BAD), a quarter of lifetime UV damage occurs before the age of 20. Sunburns can range from redness on the surface of the skin to more severe injuries (see graphic).
“Severe sunburn can cause blisters, heatstroke, and heat exhaustion,” Professor Tess McPherson said.
She is a consultant dermatologist at BAD. “Experiencing five or more bad sunburns before age 20 increases your melanoma risk by 80 per cent.”
Sophie Brooks is a health information manager at Cancer Research UK. She said that UV radiation damages the DNA in skin cells. “If enough DNA damage builds up over time, it can cause cells to grow out of control, leading to skin cancer,” Brooks said. She warned that a tan is not safe either. It is a sign the skin is trying to protect itself from damage.
Young people should take measures to protect themselves from sunburn. These include using a fragrance-free sunscreen with a minimum of SPF30 and UVA protection.
Reapply the sunscreen every two hours and immediately after swimming, sweating or towel-drying.
Remember that sunscreen does not offer 100 per cent protection. When outdoors, it is best to spend time in the shade and wear protective clothing.

title: Google Maps changes Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order
description: Canadian users continue to see the original name as the tech giant rolls out location-based labelling.
content: Google has updated its maps application to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for users in the United States, reflecting a recent order by US President Donald Trump that changed the name of the lake, the global technology giant said. The Google Maps update comes days after Trump’s order amid an escalating trade war with Canada that has led both countries to impose billions of dollars in added tariffs on each other’s goods. It echoes what Google did in 2025 when Trump issued an order to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. Google said in a blog post on Saturday that the decision was based on its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System, also known as GNIS. “People using Maps in the US will see ‘Lake America’, those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’, and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said in a brief statement. “These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now.” Trump’s decision on Thursday to rename the lake was met with mockery and indifference in both Canada and the United States. On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded to Trump’s order with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shore: “Lake Ontario. Now and forever”. The White House, the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ford’s office did not immediately comment on Sunday ⁠on Google’s decision. The internet company runs a leading search engine and major digital advertising network and is based in Mountain View, California. Its parent company is Alphabet.

title: Open Questions | Trita Parsi on why US air strikes strengthened Iran’s hand and failed to trigger a revolt
description: Iranian-born and Washington-based expert analyses Tehran’s leverage, China’s non-intervention strategy and shifting Persian Gulf alliances.
content: Trita Parsi is co-founder and executive vice-president of the Quincy Institute, a Washington-based think tank. He is an expert on US-Iranian relations, Iranian foreign policy and the geopolitics of the Middle East. He has written four books on US foreign policy in the Middle East, with a particular focus on Iran and Israel. Born in Iran, Parsi moved to Sweden with his family as a child and then to the United States as an adult. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. What is your take on US President Donald Trump’s so-called economic D-Day on Iran? Some mainland Chinese and Hong Kong companies are implicated in the new secondary sanctions. Can Trump achieve his goals with these measures or will they backfire? What results will these sanctions bring? Trump’s D-Day sanctions will either fail to squeeze Tehran very hard and not much happens, or they will be hard-hitting and then the question is whether Iran counter-escalates or surrenders. And the pattern so far is really clear: Iran fears capitulation much more than escalation. And given that [US Treasury Secretary Scott] Bessent has not listed any clear demands, Tehran will interpret the purpose of D-Day as a measure to force its surrender. So instead of this leading to an end to the conflict, it will just start another round of the escalatory cycle. What is your take on the latest developments regarding the US-Israel war on Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and the feasibility of the proposed Oman-Iran deal? We have seen contradictory signs from the Trump side, while Iran is raising even more demands. When will this escalation end? Unfortunately, I don’t see any end in sight right now. Despite the fact that [Iran and the US are] not necessarily far away from each other on some of the core issues on the strait, there still seem to be a couple of things in the talks that have dramatically reduced confidence and trust between the two sides, and that’s already in a scenario in which trust clearly has been in very limited supply. So, I do fear that in the near future we will not see any positive developments and, unfortunately, there is a risk of a further return to more conflict despite the fact that the conflict so far has been so tremendously non-constructive. It has not given the United States any additional benefit. We may still end up in another round of fighting. Given reports of a drain on US ammunition, are military conflicts still possible? They are still possible. It’s just that it will become riskier because what happens is that the US is running out of ammunition which it can fire from a long distance. In the next round of fighting, we may end up seeing that the US uses more aeroplanes that will have to fly into Iranian airspace and fly at lower altitudes, which will increase the risk for the US. And as a result we may see more aeroplanes getting shot down, and things of that nature. What is the prospect of the Strait of Hormuz reopening, and under what circumstances could it happen? Unfortunately, the prospect at this point seems very limited, but for it to open up it’s important to recognise that, even short of a deal, we may end up in a scenario in which some traffic will increase because both the Iranians and the Americans have a need for there to be traffic. Iran is also suffering from the fact that the strait is closed. So, this is not pain only on one side. So, the strait may still be blocked in name but some kind of traffic may still go through – even though the parties will not admit it? Yes, but it would be very limited. It would not be near normal levels. Five months into the war, what has changed in Iran politically and socially, and what has changed in its influence in the region? Iran’s influence in the region, arguably, has increased. At least its leverage has increased and, I think, a lot of countries are now of the view that this war has clearly not only failed but has also led to a scenario in which the Iranians have really survived an attack that almost no other country in the region would be able to survive. They have been attacked by two nuclear-weapon states and they have essentially come out on top. This is not something that any other country in the region could easily have done. And as a result, their deterrence [against] the other states has increased, and their leverage has increased internally. However, [while] the population is accepting that this is a war situation, they can only accept that for a period of time. They cannot accept a war situation for months, dragging into years. Now, of course, this was an aggression against Iran. They see this as a war of defence, which gives the government an amount of time in which the internal situation will be somewhat stable, despite shortages and economic problems. But if this goes on for more than a year and if there’s a perception – and I’m not saying that perception exists right now – that the Iranian government itself is an obstacle to a resolution, then you will start seeing a lot of anger and sentiments internally in the country welling up. It’s also important to recognise that the government has a lot of problems with the larger population. Those problems are now secondary because there’s a war. But once the war is over, these problems are going to come back. They haven’t gone away. They have not been resolved. And if this war goes on for too long and the population is suffering, that’s going to add to some of these challenges. But for now, it’s safe to say that the government’s internal position is stronger than it was six months ago. And in some ways, the war may have saved the Islamic Republic just as much as Saddam Hussein’s invasion of Iran in 1980 did. He thought he was going to overthrow the Iranian government, but he ended up saving the Iranian government. The revolution was still new. They had not consolidated their power, but because of the external threat, they did consolidate that power. They did manage to get control of the internal situation. Iran was facing some of the worst protests in decades. And then [this year] this attack comes and the country unites against an external threat. And in that way, the attack may have saved the Islamic Republic. Six months ago, huge protests took place and young people seemed to be very angry with the government. Are you saying the government’s control over the population has been strengthened because of the war? It has been strengthened because there’s a war and people are concerned about their security. When the US is bombing critical infrastructure, refineries and simultaneously saying that they’re trying to destroy the country and an entire civilisation, at this point it becomes clear this is not a war against a government. This is a war against the country as a whole, and that works in the favour of the government. Before the US and Israel started bombing Iran, Trump called for people to revolt against the government. And now it seems he is pushing the people closer to the administration because of the bombing? Absolutely. And it shows you the foolishness of this war and the massive miscalculation. What is your take on the Mecca defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan? Analysts say it is a sign these countries no longer view the US as a security guarantor for the Arab states. What will the Middle East look like if this perception persists? First of all, that is absolutely correct. This is a manifestation of the fact that a lot of countries in the region have lost faith in the American security umbrella, in its efficiency and reliability. They have seen that the security umbrella is ineffective against Iran and at the same time the American side is unwilling to really defend these countries from Israel. So, they have to look for alternatives and this is just going to be one of many things that I suspect will happen, and these are initial reactions. They may not end up becoming the end state. This pact also is explicitly said to be open. Additional countries can be added to it. It can go in that direction if the Iranians play their cards wrongly in this long-standing American effort to contain and isolate Iran, which has been the organising principle of American foreign policy in the region and was driven by American hegemonic desires. The US’ desire for hegemony in the region, which necessitated isolating Iran, may now be replaced by a regional desire for the same goal, meaning that the impetus will come from regional states that will seek to isolate and contain through a pact that isolates and encircles Iran because of a perception of threat. This would be a very bad development for the Iranians. It ultimately would be a very bad result for the region because the real conclusion that should be drawn is that you can’t contain or isolate Iran. That policy inevitably led to this war. And if you try that policy again, but without the US, the result will nevertheless likely be the same. It will just lead to another conflict. And we see that pattern in other bloc formations as well. Bloc formations are supposed to create stability, but oftentimes they make a long-term conflict more likely. What this can end up becoming, however, is the beginning step. It’s an embryonic agreement. Its end destination and objective is undecided and it may move towards becoming a larger regional security arrangement, not just a bloc between three countries, which ideally would be an inclusive security order [taking] inspiration from Asean. That would be much better for the region as a whole, and it would be based on creating economic integration and interdependence between the states in the region. That possibility is still there because this pact does not preclude it. But it can lead to a scenario in which this pact eventually becomes an obstacle to that vision. What is the likelihood of Iran becoming a regional power? If Iran somehow gets the US to lift some of the sanctions, will it become a regional power? Iran already is a regional power. The question is, is the region accepting Iran’s role as a regional power or is its role as a regional power contested? Iran needs to have a role that is commensurate with its geopolitical weight. And that is where diplomacy really comes in, and where the Iranians have to play their cards very cleverly and effectively and not rely entirely on hard power. Because if you rely too much on hard power, all you do is convince your neighbours that you are a threat and their reaction will be to try to balance you. How will China’s influence and role in the Middle East change as new dynamics and a new order are created in the region? And how will China’s relationship with the Gulf States and Iran change? Let’s first review what China has done in this war so far. China has really stayed out of this conflict, it has not taken sides. There is a revelation on the Iranian side that China was not hostile to Iran, of course, but China did not come to Iran’s aid in a very significant way. Yes, there may have been some intelligence sharing et cetera, and that may not have been unimportant, but that’s very different. There have been two main orientations in Iran: one that favoured orienting Iran towards the West; and the other one favoured leaning towards China and Russia. But both schools have been proven wrong. The first because a deal with the US was not possible, and the second because neither Russia nor China supported Iran meaningfully in the war. The conclusion is that Iran is alone. Iran has always been alone. It doesn’t mean that it doesn’t have friends, but it doesn’t have security pacts. Those strategic relations do not translate into security pacts. And as a result, it has to stand on its own [two feet]. And in some ways, that makes Iran’s outlook very similar to that of China. China is looking at itself similarly – it does not extend security pacts. The Iranians, as a result, are going to invest more, not to say that they’re going to walk away from China at all. On the contrary, they’re going to continue to invest in China relations, but with a clearer idea of what that relationship is. It is not a security relationship or a pact in which they can rely on Chinese support for their defence. Instead, it will be that Iran will have to invest in the region. It will invest in its forward defence, meaning its reliance on the Houthis, on Hezbollah and other groups, and then try to see how it simultaneously can improve relations with its regional neighbours. But the forward defence is a protection not against its neighbours. It’s a protection against the US and Israel. Hezbollah is Iran’s first line of defence against an Israeli attack. Israel only attacked when Hezbollah was weak. When Hezbollah has been strong, the Israelis have been more careful about attacking Iran. However, China has played its cards very well. It has stayed out of this conflict. It has not done anything to deliberately damage the US. It has not taken advantage of this to undermine the US. The US is doing enough to undermine itself – China doesn’t need to. At the same time, China has also realised that, yes, it always had a balance between its relationships with Iran and Saudi Arabia. But now China has realised that Iran is much stronger – not that Saudi Arabia isn’t but Saudi Arabia is dependent. Iran is independent. Iran alone defeated Israel and the US. Saudi Arabia, even with the help of the US, could not defeat the Houthis. And China’s perspective in the long term is to have very good relations with the countries that have the ability to provide stability in specific regions. And there, the outcome of this war has put Iran in a different light from Beijing’s perspective. How will Beijing’s relationship with the Gulf countries change, and how will these countries view Beijing? Because some may expect China to act to relieve or mediate the situation, but it has not. Beijing’s strategy so far has been very smart. It has not entered into any alliance with other states. It’s doing the opposite of the US. The US cannot help itself but get involved in everyone else’s conflict, whereas China very wisely stays out. But China is going to see an effort by the other GCC [Gulf Cooperation Council] states to become as close to China as possible economically to make sure that any future potential conflict between Iran and any GCC states would have a deep impact on China economically and, as a result, China would have a greater need for not necessarily getting involved militarily, but to get involved diplomatically. China has an ability that the US doesn’t have here. Everyone trades extensively with China. No one can afford to have a bad relationship with China because of economic reasons. And as a result, China can come in as a diplomatic force because everyone wants to make sure that they don’t move themselves too far away from China. The GCC will be hoping that China will get involved diplomatically and that it will feel a self-interest to get involved diplomatically because of economic reasons. Why did Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reject Trump’s Gaza proposal, and how will the US relationship with Israel change? Trump is under a lot of pressure internally, with Israel blamed for dragging the US into this war. There is a tremendous amount of frustration in the White House with Israel. Israel dragged the US into this war. We’re also seeing that Netanyahu is willing to say no to Trump. The Trump administration has not pushed back hard against Netanyahu on this issue, and there have even been statements saying that Netanyahu was faced with an election and, as a result, this is a sensitive period. If this was happening under the Biden administration, it would have gone out of its way to blame Hamas when Israel rejected a peace deal. We saw that repeatedly. Israel kept on rejecting peace deals, undermining peace deals, and the Biden administration protected Israel by blaming Hamas. The Trump administration did not do that this time. Everyone knows it’s Netanyahu who rejected this proposal. I find that interesting. Has Hamas been weakened so much that it’s hard to say it is Hamas any more? No, I don’t think so because it was the same situation before, and Hamas, even though it is weakened, still has some agency. So one could easily have done it back then as well. What we have seen is that Trump, even though he doesn’t put consistent pressure on the Israelis, is willing to go out and blame Israel and push back hard against Israel at times. It tends to be very temporary, but he has shown that willingness. Whereas the Biden administration had a policy in which they wanted to see no daylight between Israel and the US. And by that, allow the Israelis to completely set the agenda. Are you suggesting there is reduced US backing of Israel? We may end up seeing a significant distance between the two countries. The Israelis were very unhappy about the signing of the MOU [memorandum of understanding, by the US and Iran in June] and if the MOU had succeeded, and it still may, it would have led to a scenario in which there would have been a crisis in US-Israeli relations. How will Trump’s dealings with the Middle East, especially the war with Iran, affect the midterm elections? There’s going to be a general unhappiness because of inflation, gas prices, food prices, directly resulting from this. You’re already seeing that in some primaries, the US relationship with Israel has become a very hotly contested issue and the race is almost reduced to whether a candidate is in favour of the war, in favour of Israel, in favour of what Israel did in Gaza, or against it. This is very unusual. And it’s showing how things are changing in a very dramatic way in the US. But for these specific midterms, the Republicans are going to suffer defeats. Some members of Congress may come out and blame Trump and the war explicitly, either to save themselves or, if they lose, out of anger and frustration, because many of them are not just angry about the war. They are angry because they see that Trump does not care what happens to Republican members of Congress. He does not seem to be particularly concerned about this and as a result they’re facing an end to their careers politically because of what Trump has done and Trump does not do anything to support them. So, there’s a feeling of betrayal and abandonment. It’s very hidden right now but beneath the surface it festers. Will that increase the risk? Will that prompt Trump to take even more radical actions if there are failures in the midterms? There is a risk that after the midterms that Trump – because he has more difficulties in Congress – will become even more radical in his conduct. This is one of the potential miscalculations the Iranians are making in which they think the punishment of Trump in the midterms would be satisfactory to them, which perhaps on an emotional level it would be, but it can also lead to a scenario in which he increasingly does not care about certain constraints, and certain norms and guardrails. Look at how his behaviour changed after he lost the election in November 2020. Between November 2020 and January 2021, Trump considered some very radical options. One of them, which was actualised, was the protests on January 6, [an] attempt at a takeover, but he was also contemplating war with Iran during those two months as a way of staying in power. You may end up seeing a scenario in which the midterm elections and a loss will make him more radical.

title: Grand Canyon flash flooding leaves 1 dead, around 15 others missing
description: Search efforts continue as inner-canyon deluge destroys footbridges and cuts off park water supplies.
content: At least one person was killed and around 15 others are missing after a flash flood at the Grand Canyon, one of the most popular tourist sites in the United States, the National Park Service said in a statement on Sunday. The floods hit the Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area on Saturday, forcing dozens of people to evacuate and damaging the sole water pipeline serving the park. The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River in northern Arizona, the park service said. Video footage taken by hikers showed a torrent of muddy water rushing by trails and under footbridges as well as logs and other debris floating down swollen rivers, accompanied by a rumbling roar. The park service said it was working with Arizona authorities to evacuate people and account for missing individuals. As of Sunday morning, 62 people had been evacuated, with others scheduled for later, it said. It said around 15 people were thought to be missing, revising an earlier figure of more than 20. The flooding damaged the Transcanyon Waterline, a key water pipeline into Grand Canyon National Park, the park service said, announcing water restrictions in its most visited area and a ban on wood and charcoal fires. The 20km pipeline runs from the Roaring Springs source on the North Rim to the South Rim, providing drinking water and fire suppression, according to the park’s website. The flooding also resulted in “significant impacts to infrastructure,” destroying footbridges and blocking hikers from crossing Bright Angel Creek, the park service said. Overnight accommodations were to be closed from Monday, it added. “These measures are crucial for ensuring the safety and sustainability of water resources,” the park service said. The flash flood, which began about 2.30pm on Saturday, was caused by rain on the Kaibab Plateau, it said. More thunderstorms and heavy rainfall were possible through Monday, possibly leading to “additional flash flooding, debris flows, rockfall and changing trail and river conditions”, the park service warned. Flash floods are common in Northern Arizona because the arid, sparsely vegetated environments found in the area have little capacity to absorb rain, the park’s website says, urging visitors to be especially cautious from July to mid-September. The Grand Canyon is considered one of the greatest wonders of the natural world. Last year almost 5 million people visited the site.

title: Opinion | Reusable rocket milestone opens a door for Hong Kong’s space ambitions
description: Flurry of commercial activity offers opportunities for Hong Kong’s financial markets, research universities and the Northern Metropolis.
content: On the morning of August 19, LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 Y2 rocket lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Test Area. After deploying its second stage and payload into orbit, the rocket’s first stage touched down softly at a recovery site in Gansu province using deployable landing legs. It was China’s first successful land-based recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster that had just completed an orbital mission – a feat previously achieved only by SpaceX. Just over a month earlier, on July 10, state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corpartion recovered the first stage of a Long March-10B rocket using a sea-based net system. In less than six weeks, China displayed two distinct recovery methods – a rapid succession of milestones that underscores the country’s space ambitions. The benchmark for reusable rockets remains SpaceX’s Falcon 9, which pioneered vertical landing after launches of this kind and has conducted hundreds of recoveries. Through first-stage reuse, Falcon 9 has driven its launch price down to about US$2,700 per kg (US$1,225 per lb) – a reduction of 85 per cent from an average of US$18,500 in the pre-reusable era. In contrast, China’s commercial launch prices hover at between US$8,000 and US$14,000 per kg, depending on rocket type and mission profile. The Zhuque-3 is explicitly designed to close that gap. Standing 66 metres tall with a lift-off mass of roughly 570 tonnes, its first stage is powered by nine methane-liquid oxygen engines. Its stainless-steel structure – a deliberate departure from Falcon 9’s aluminium alloy – offers better heat resistance at a lower manufacturing cost. The booster is designed to be reused at least 20 times. But while the China-US technology gap in reusable launch vehicles has narrowed, it remains substantial. As a Zhuque-3 team engineer acknowledged anonymously in 2024: “China may have its own Falcon 9 rocket in five years and Starship in 20 years. We need to work hard to catch up.” The economic logic of reusability is straightforward. The first stage accounts for roughly 70 per cent of a rocket’s total cost. Reusing it just five times could cut per-launch costs by as much as 45 per cent; at 20 reuses, the marginal cost is dominated by the expendable second stage, fuel and refurbishment since the massive initial cost of the first stage is amortised across multiple flights. This compelling arithmetic has unleashed a wave of commercial activity. LandSpace is among at least 10 Chinese aerospace companies preparing for initial public offerings (IPOs) to fund their expansion, with many aiming for profitability by the end of the decade. The broader strategic context is China’s ambition to build low Earth orbit satellite constellations to rival SpaceX’s Starlink. Reusable rockets are the indispensable enabler; without them, deploying thousands of satellites remains economically unsustainable. Zhuque-3’s success presents three distinct, high-value opportunities for Hong Kong. Hong Kong’s financial markets can become the launch pad for China’s space unicorns. The Chapter 18C listing regime, which covers aerospace technology, has lowered market capitalisation thresholds – making it easier for deep-tech space ventures to go public in the city. With a wave of mainland rocket firms eyeing IPOs, Hong Kong can offer not just capital, but a full suite of insurance, legal and risk-management services tailored to a capital-intensive industry with long investment horizons. The sector is maturing, and Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem is ready to underwrite it. Hong Kong’s research universities have proven they can build hardware for the national space programme – and they should double down. From Hong Kong University of Science and Technology’s Multi-Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory, also known as the Tianyun camera, now operating aboard the Tiangong space station, to Polytechnic University’s next-generation space navigation cameras and City University’s lunar soil simulants, the city’s academic institutions are embedded in the space value chain. But the opportunity goes beyond government-funded projects: Hong Kong can become a regional hub for space science, translating its basic research into commercial applications and forging partnerships with mainland manufacturers. The Northern Metropolis could become a docking station for the commercial space industry. While the city is not built for heavy rocket manufacturing or launch pads, it is exceptionally well suited to high-value downstream services: satellite payload design, low-orbit data operations and command-and-control software development. One local start-up is developing a satellite constellation, and a 23-year-old PolyU undergraduate has raised nearly 100 million yuan (US$14.9 million) for his rocket venture. The government has reportedly held talks with mainland aerospace companies about setting up operations in the Northern Metropolis. Zhuque-3’s first stage landing in the Gobi Desert is not the finish line. The path from recoverable to reusable and profitable is long. But for Hong Kong, the door to the trillion-dollar global space economy is now open. The question is whether the city can move quickly enough to walk through it.

title: US strikes Iranian launchers in first action in a month, triggering retaliation
description: Tehran targets American bases in Jordan; UAE intercepts drone as regional tensions spike again.
content: US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in their first military action in a month on Sunday, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months. Vowing to retaliate for what it called a deadly attack, Iran later said it had launched missiles at US sites in Jordan. Forces with the Revolutionary Guard Corps were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for the US Central Command (CENTCOM). The US military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes. Semi-official news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait. The Guard in a statement carried by Iran’s state broadcaster noted “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots”. Later, Iranian state television showed what it said were ballistic missiles being fired by Iran at US bases in Jordan in response to the American strikes. Jordan’s armed forces said they intercepted eight missiles that penetrated the country’s airspace early Monday in the Middle East. The UAE Defence Ministry said its air force intercepted an Iranian drone over territorial waters and dismissed claims by Tehran that Dubai’s Al Minhad Air Base was targeted. US military officials disputed Iran’s claim that the latest American strikes were an act of aggression, calling them a “limited, precise action” against what they said were minelaying forces. A return to open conflict would be dangerous for the region, where Iran has targeted US military bases and infrastructure in Gulf countries since the war began on February 28. The last time the US military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, when it announced a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of Revolutionary Guard targets including coastal surveillance and defence sites. On August 1, US President Donald Trump said he would order the military to hold off on new strikes at the urging of Gulf allies Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. The attack comes just days after the Trump administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure – rather than military action – to try to end its war with Iran. The shifting strategy centres on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran. Sunday’s attack was a “fatal mistake by the Trump regime during the economic war” and the enemy would pay the consequences militarily and economically, a Guard spokesman, General Hossein Mohebi, said in a statement carried by Iranian media. The US turn to using sanctions came as the administration weighs diminished munitions stockpiles after months of war, sparking concerns that the prolonged conflict could undermine US military readiness in other parts of the globe. As the conflict grinds on, Trump’s talk of finding a quick end to the war also appears to be fading. He stressed last week that he was “not in a hurry” to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continued making the case that the Islamic Republic’s leadership was on the ropes. Appointments to Iran’s senior security leadership in the past month, however, have signalled Tehran’s defiance after weathering decades of sanctions as well as a lack of tolerance for dissent at home. Trump has consistently emphasised that the US and Israeli campaign has been devastating for Iran’s navy and air force. Iranian officials have said the country has suffered US$270 billion in direct and indirect damage. Israeli military strikes in the first weeks of the war wiped out much of the theocratic government’s leadership structure. But Iran has found leverage through its strikes against vessels on the Strait of Hormuz, where relatively few ships carrying oil and liquefied natural gas are risking passage. Iran still has enough drones and missiles to fire at vessels transiting the waterway through which 20 per cent of the world’s oil normally flows. Crude oil prices rose on Monday in response to the US attack. Brent crude futures were ‌up 3.26 per cent to US$90.97 a barrel at 1120 GMT (7.20pm Hong Kong time), while US West Texas Intermediate crude was up 3.49 per cent to US$86.31. Tehran continues to assert that even after it works out a management plan for the strait with Oman, its neighbour on the other side of the waterway, the US cannot use it until it fulfils its obligations under the memorandum of understanding the countries signed in mid-June. Trump has repeatedly declared that the “Strait of Hormuz is open”, saying 24 vessels passed through last week. But that was a fraction of the roughly 130 vessels that transited daily before the war began. Earlier on Sunday, a multinational coalition overseen by the US Navy said commercial traffic through the strait remained at “reduced levels”. And a monitoring agency run by the British military said an unknown projectile struck a tanker ship on Saturday north of Khasab, Oman, in the strait. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation said no casualties or environmental impact had been reported, and cited unspecified military authorities. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. The US military said that as of Sunday, it had redirected 83 commercial vessels and disabled three under its blockade of Iranian ports. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Colombia’s president warns armed groups after military kills key dissident leader
description: President Abelardo de la Espriella vows hardline crackdown will continue, warning criminals who do not surrender will ‘end up in a body bag’.
content: A prominent leader of the dissident factions of the defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia who operated in a volatile area in the country’s southwest region was killed on Sunday during a military operation, said President Abelardo de la Espriella. The president said the death of a man known as “Felipe” or “Arcadio” was a “crushing blow” to the dissident faction led by a man who goes by “Ivan Mordisco”. De la Espriella posted a video on social media presumably showing a person in a body bag near a weapon and ammunition seized by authorities during the operation. “We are closing the net on Mordisco and his networks,” warned the president, who announced that offensive operations against illegal armed groups would continue. “Any criminal who doesn’t surrender will end up in a body bag.” He said “Felipe” was responsible for multiple attacks on police stations in Valle del Cauca, using explosives dropped from drones. He commanded a unit within the Jaime Martinez faction, part of the dissident groups of the defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) that refused to join the government’s 2016 peace negotiations. The leader also took part in planting explosives-laden gas cylinders on roads in Valle del Cauca, attacking a military unit, torching cars, engaging in extortion and committing other criminal acts, de la Espriella said. This is not the first time de la Espriella has announced the killing of a leader of an illegal armed group since recently taking office. The president has vowed to take a hard line against such groups – marking a shift from the policy of his predecessor, Gustavo Petro – and has called on “Ivan Mordisco” and other leaders to surrender to authorities and face the consequences. On Friday, de la Espriella also announced the capture of Emilio Jose Cordero Sierra, known as “Fantasma”, who is accused of coordinating the exchange of cocaine for military hardware with Farc dissident groups. He is sought for extradition by the United States on charges related to terrorism, conspiracy to commit a crime and drug trafficking. In recent days, the president also gave the green light for the extradition to the United States of five suspects whose handover had been suspended as part of the peace process promoted by the previous administration – a process de la Espriella formally concluded through resolutions issued on Friday.

title: Trump calls for ‘punishment’ of NBC journalist over endorsement coverage
description: US president targets Kristen Welker after she noted ‘mixed results’ in primary races, prompting NBC to defend its anchor.
content: US President Donald Trump on Sunday threatened a prominent NBC broadcast journalist with possible punishment by US media regulators as the Republican expressed disappointment with coverage of his candidate endorsements ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump took to his Truth Social platform to attack Kristen Welker as the “unpopular ‘hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press” talk show. He objected to her having said the president had had “mixed results” on his endorsement of political candidates in party primaries, insisting the races had gone his way 98 per cent to 100 per cent of the time. Welker, speaking early Sunday to a local NBC affiliate, said Trump would “loom large over these midterms”. When it came to endorsements, she added, he “had some mixed results, but most recently, his pick of Senator Darline Graham … was successful in her primary battle”. Trump, in his comments, said “because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment”. The Federal Communications Commission assigns and oversees licences for radio and television broadcast frequencies. “Unfortunately, she is not the only one,” he added. “The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP.’” Welker is an award-winning journalist who earned bipartisan praise after moderating a 2020 presidential debate featuring Trump and Joe Biden, the Democrat who won that year’s election. An NBC News spokesperson, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, defended Welker on Sunday, telling Agence France-Presse that “Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her”. Trump’s endorsements overall have proved helpful for Republican candidates running for statewide office. But his approval ratings have slid, and at least 10 of Trump’s picks have been defeated this cycle, according to a tally compiled by Ballotpedia. They include four US House hopefuls and six candidates for governor, among them conspiracy theorist Mike Lindell in Minnesota. Billionaire Trump has used American media to his advantage over the years as a provocative real estate developer in New York. But as president he dramatically turned against the press and what he called “fake news”. Earlier in the week, he attacked New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman for reporting that he was skipping the annual September 11 commemoration in New York this year because he wouldn’t have a speaking role. He has sued several newspapers including the Wall Street Journal and New York Times, and ordered federal funding slashed for public media. His administration has ramped up restrictions and attempts to intimidate journalists, and the FCC – headed by a close Trump associate – has pressured broadcasters to toe the line. “I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” Trump said. The latest attack is part of the Trump administration’s months-long offensive against media outlets it deems overly critical. Such efforts are facing growing resistance from news organisations and major broadcast networks. Several of them have filed lawsuits against the FCC, arguing such pressure constitutes political retaliation that violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which protects freedom of speech. Relations between Trump and Welker have been under pressure for months. In June the president abruptly cut short an interview with her following a tense exchange, during which he grew irritated by Welker’s questioning, particularly on the war against Iran. Experts argue the FCC lacks the legal authority to punish broadcasters or reporters for their viewpoints. According to a 2025 paper by the Yale Journal on Regulation, the US Supreme Court has confirmed that US law “does not grant the FCC the power to ban controversial speech”. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Ukraine prepares for talks with Trump envoys as Kyiv reels from deadly strikes
description: Zelensky pursues diplomatic opening as Myla warehouse death toll reaches 38 and Russia threatens energy grid.
content: Ukraine is preparing for a new round of talks with representatives of US President Donald Trump, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday, expressing hope that diplomacy can prevent open conflict from remaining the only path forward. “There will be more details tomorrow. We will do everything we can so that war does not remain the only option for how events unfold further,” Zelensky said in a televised address. “It is important that America shares many of our views on the situation”. US-led diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, Europe’s deadliest since World War II, have been at a standstill for months. Russia has demanded sweeping territorial and political concessions from Ukraine, which Kyiv has ruled out as tantamount to capitulation. The United States has long been pressing Moscow and Kyiv to reach a peace agreement. However, trips to the warring nations by US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, which had been expected in August, did not take place. Zelensky’s diplomatic push comes as the death toll from a Russian strike on a warehouse west of Kyiv, the war’s deadliest attack this year, rose to 38 with four people still missing. The Friday night strike on the warehouse, which Ukrainian officials said was storing ammunition, sparked massive explosions and fires that swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings in the village of Myla. The attack came as Russia has sharply intensified its air campaign recently in the 4½-year-old war, with air raid sirens wailing repeatedly and explosions and the rumble of air defences resounding across Kyiv throughout the day. Emergency workers continued to extinguish fires and identify and neutralise explosives at the site, Zelensky said on social media. At least 52 people were injured, said Tymur Tkachenko, who heads the local regional military administration. On Saturday, Zelensky called the Myla attack “a terrible situation” and a consequence of “terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people”. He said an investigation was under way into why the ammunition came to be kept there. The escalation was a notable shift in tactics, putting more pressure on Ukraine’s already strained air defences while keeping civilians on alert for hours. Previously, daytime attacks on the capital had been relatively rare. The Defence Ministry in Moscow said Sunday it is preparing “massive strikes” on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. It described the planned strikes as retaliation for Kyiv’s drone campaign against Russian online retailers Wildberries and Ozon, as well as the country’s oil and gas sector. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said large-scale strikes against Ukraine’s energy sector would be “an appropriate response” to what he called Ukraine’s “path of escalation” and targeting of Russia’s civilian economy. Peskov told Russian state TV that Moscow has been launching “fairly systematic” strikes on what he called Kyiv’s military and war-related infrastructure. In the latest attack Sunday, an Ozon logistics facility was struck and set ablaze by a Ukrainian drone in the Belgorod border region of Russia, with the company saying it feared that there were multiple injuries. Ukraine said it was attacking Wildberries – the country’s largest online retailer, similar to Amazon – because it sells dual-use goods that have aided the military, although the company denies that. Ukrainian drones also have struck oil refineries and other energy infrastructure, prompting an unprecedented fuel crisis in one of the world’s biggest energy producers. During the war’s previous winters, Russia systematically battered Ukraine’s power grid, depriving thousands of heat and light. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that the coming winter may prove to be the most challenging since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022. Reuters, dpa, Agence France-Presse, Associated Press

title: Iceland votes to reject proposal to restart EU accession talks
description: Referendum fails as voters prioritise control over fishing grounds over pro-EU government’s push for geopolitical stability.
content: Iceland’s voters rejected restarting negotiations to join the European Union in a referendum that pitted concerns about geopolitical stability against keeping national control of Iceland’s prized fisheries, officials said on Sunday. Opponents defeated the measure by a margin of 52.8 per cent to 47.2 per cent, the National Electoral Commission said. The result puts the divisive issue to rest for now – more than a decade after a Eurosceptic government ended EU talks that had begun after the 2008 financial crisis. The vote Saturday was held in the shadow of repeated threats by US President Donald Trump to take control of nearby Greenland. Although Iceland is a Nato member, supporters said European solidarity would provide greater protection if Trump ever made similar threats towards the volcanic island. Iceland’s left-leaning coalition government, elected in 2024, moved up the EU referendum it had planned for next year after Trump mistakenly named Iceland four times while speaking about his designs on Greenland. The Trump administration respects “the sovereign decision” by Iceland, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement. “We look forward to strengthening our partnership with Iceland on all fronts including security, energy, innovation, and economic and cultural ties, to further advance our shared vision of peace and prosperity,” he said. Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir said she did not see the loss as a setback for her coalition government but as a win for democracy as more than 82 per cent of the eligible 270,000 voters cast ballots. She said she would respect the result but would not rule out a future attempt to reopen the issue. “Things happened in the past couple of years, though, that I could not have predicted,” she said. “But this government will not go forward with it. And something big has to change in the next 24 months for this to be at the top of the agenda.” Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, leader of the opposition Independence Party who opposed the measure, said the result is a blow to the government but not European relations. “The best way to heal the wounds is for the government to listen to the conclusion and put this path aside,” she told RUV, the national broadcaster. “Because we want to remain in close contact with the European Union, Europe and as many other countries as possible, the nation is sending a clear message that we intend to steer that course ourselves.” Voters faced a simple yes-or-no question: Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union? The capital of Reykjavik was the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people where a majority supported the referendum. The influential fishing industry led opposition to the referendum over fears the bloc’s common fisheries policy would open its waters to Spanish, Dutch and other trawlers. Descendants of Vikings, Icelanders, who won their independence from Denmark in 1944, have lived off the sea for centuries, and fishing is central to their national identity. Iceland has a proud history of refusing to be pushed around by bigger and richer European nations, winning the so-called Cod Wars with Britain in the 1970s over the right to control its waters. Opponents also rallied around the fact that Iceland already reaps benefits from being in the EU’s frictionless single market and the Schengen free-travel zone without the sovereignty compromises that come with full membership. They argued that Iceland’s voice would be muted in the large European Parliament and that it would be better off cutting its own trade deals, such as one with China. Backers said EU membership would lower inflation and interest rates, and the euro would bring more stability than Iceland’s volatile krona currency. They said it was also in the nation’s interest to get closer to its European neighbours to tackle issues that don’t respect borders, such as climate change. If the proposal had been approved, it would have been a preliminary step to revive the lengthy negotiating process with the EU’s executive branch, the European Commission, to discuss areas from the economy to human rights. Voters would have needed to approve any negotiated deal. The result is sure to disappoint many in the European Union. As a wealthy, stable and democratic country with vast fishing grounds, Iceland could have joined the bloc relatively quickly. Croatia was the last country to join, in 2013. Most of the other candidates waiting – including several countries in the Balkans, plus Moldova and conflict-torn Ukraine – must still undertake time-consuming reforms to bring their laws and standards into line with those of the EU. Getting Iceland into Europe’s rich club, perhaps along with Montenegro and possibly Moldova, over the next two years could have helped to lay to rest the damage to the EU caused by the departure of Britain in 2020, even though London now appears willing to mend ties.

title: At least 8 dead, 17 missing after ferry capsizes off Northern Cyprus
description: Captain and crew arrested after survivors report explosion on bow before vessel sank into deep waters.
content: A passenger ferry capsized and sank off Northern Cyprus Sunday, killing at least eight people and leaving more than a dozen missing, officials and media reports said, as police took the captain and seven crew members into custody. Several rescued passengers told local media a blast had gone off at the bow of the ferry before it rolled over, and said the boat had an insufficient supply of life-vests. The vessel capsized 6.5km (4 miles) off the coast of Cyprus, shortly after leaving a Northern Cyprus port bound for Turkey’s mainland. Images broadcast by Turkish television showed the upside-down ferry in the water, with people wearing life vests atop its orange hull. “Some people had to jump without lifebuoys or life jackets,” one young man, Efe Multici, told CNN Turk. “It was literally a fight for survival.” The ferry had been carrying a total of 267 people, according to authorities, of which 161 were rescued and taken to hospital and 76 have returned home. The official Cypriot news agency TAK, however, said 17 were missing. “Efforts to find the missing are continuing tirelessly,” Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said during a public ceremony. “We hope to receive positive news from these efforts.” The TRNC is dependent on Turkey, and Turkish Vice-President Cevdet Yilmaz said on X: “We are providing all necessary assistance to the search and rescue operations”. Unal Ustel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), said the ship’s captain and seven crew members had been arrested. The TRNC’s transport minister Erhan Arikli said the ferry had “completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres (1,686 feet)”. The vessel’s “black box” would help them understand what had caused the sinking, he added. But he also referred to allegations that an object might have hit the vessel. One rescued passenger who spoke of a blast on board told local TRNC television after he was taken back ashore: “The front part exploded, they tried to turn around. And the side windows blew out. The boat started taking on water”. The man, aged in his 50s and not named, said he spent an hour and a half in the water before being rescued. He said many people had been inside the ferry at the moment started taking on water. “Those who could, got out,” he said, adding that he saw the captain among the first to abandon ship “without organising anything”. Another witness, in his thirties, corroborated reports of an explosion. He said he had reported water leaks to the captain. “The seats started to float, the captain kept going, and the bow exploded,” he said. Many boats, including private ones, were involved in the rescue operation. Turkey’s interior ministry said on X that six Turkish navy ships had also been dispatched. “All necessary preparations are being made for a swift response from rescue and health services,” the TRNC’s health ministry said in a statement. Hospitals in the territory had been alerted, to provide any needed medical attention, it added. The ferry had departed from the Northern Cyprus port of Kyrenia – called Girne Kepuveia in Turkish – heading to the Turkish port of Tasucu. The TRNC, which is recognised only by Turkey, controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974. Ankara occupied that part of the island in response to an Athens-engineered Greek Cypriot coup seeking union with Greece. The territory is served with regular air and sea links to Turkey.

title: Theme park performer Bernice Yuen crowned Miss Hong Kong
description: The 26-year-old shines in final as fashion industry worker Ada Tang and ESG consultant Scarlett Li take second and third places.
content: Theme park performer Bernice Yuen Sze-hang outshone 11 other contenders to take the Miss Hong Kong 2026 title on Sunday night. The 26-year-old, one of the heavy favourites, dazzled both judges and the audience to claim the tiara in the beauty pageant final at TVB City in Tseung Kwan O. “We went through two or three hours [during the final], rushing through many things. Until the very end, when they announced the results, I hadn’t even realised it was time,” Yuen said. The Baptist University communication graduate has also worked as a theme park performer and actress in theatre and commercials, with additional experience as an event host and model. “When they called my name I was really shocked and happy,” she added, shortly after receiving the tiara from last year’s title-holder, Stacey Devina Chan. Her official aspiration is “to use her story to ignite the possibilities in everyone’s heart”. Ada Tang Hong-man, 24, a patternmaker’s assistant at a haute couture label, was first runner-up in the 54th edition of the broadcaster’s flagship pageant. She graduated two years ago from Kingston University in the United Kingdom, where she majored in fashion design, and was working in London before entering the contest. Scarlett Li Chak-yan, also 24, an ESG (environmental, social and governance) reporting consultant, took second runner-up. She holds a master’s degree from the Chinese University of Hong Kong. Li also won the Miss Photogenic title, impressing the judges with her elegance and stage presence. Meanwhile, 25-year-old piano teacher Chorie Li Tang Chengqing was awarded Miss Friendship. Earlier this year, Yuen was named second runner-up at the 2026 Miss Chinese World pageant held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. The 12 Miss Hong Kong finalists were selected following two rigorous interview rounds, which began with 84 candidates arriving at TVB City. The contestants were put through their paces in various segments, including a swimsuit showcase, talent performances, and a fast-paced question and answer session. With more than five decades of history, the Miss Hong Kong Pageant has launched the careers of some of Asia’s biggest stars, including Cannes Film Festival best actress Maggie Cheung Man-yuk and socialite Michele Reis.

title: New UK PM Burnham’s honeymoon ends as Trump, first budget loom large
description: Since succeeding Keir Starmer, Burnham has pleased voters with several low-cost sweeteners, including cutting electricity bills and bus fares.
content: Andy Burnham has enjoyed a honeymoon first month as UK prime minister, but the hard trade-offs involved in governing are about to get real as parliament returns from its summer break in the coming days. Since succeeding Keir Starmer on July 20, Burnham has pleased voters with several low-cost sweeteners, including cutting electricity bills and bus fares, while burnishing his casual man-of-the-people vibes. He has poured pints of beer with his finance minister, played guitar in Ukraine, and kept up a prolific output of slick social media videos during a self-styled “listening tour” of Britain. Projecting a sunnier outlook than the strait-laced Starmer, and benefiting from the woes besetting hard-right rival Nigel Farage, Burnham has sparked a poll bounce for his ruling Labour Party. A YouGov survey published on August 18 found that 46 per cent of Britons view him favourably, up 12 points from when he first arrived at Downing Street. With lawmakers on holiday, the new prime minister has largely been able to avoid thornier issues during his first weeks in office. “He’s benefited enormously from parliament not being there,” former senior civil servant Jill Rutter said, adding that it had allowed the 56-year-old Burnham to “control the narrative” so far. MPs return to Westminster on Tuesday, when Burnham is expected to deliver his first speech to Parliament as prime minister. His government will detail a watering down of contentious plans to release thousands of prisoners early to ease chronic overcrowding in jails. Burnham said on Sunday that hundreds of more serious offenders will remain behind bars, but conceded he was pushing the prison system to “the very limits of what’s possible without risking [it] collapsing within months”. Then on Wednesday, MPs and the public will learn whether Burnham is any good at facing down the weekly grilling by the leader of the opposition when he takes part in his first Prime Minister’s Questions session. Looming on the horizon is his government’s first budget on October 28, when Burnham must demonstrate that he can fund his pledges regarding cost-of-living support and ending rough sleeping, all while plugging a huge gap in defence spending. He must do so against a backdrop of strained public finances and with limited levers to pull due to his commitment not to raise income tax, employee payroll contributions, or a value-added tax on consumer goods. “That might be when reality starts to hit,” former minister Tony McNulty, who served alongside Burnham in Labour governments of the early 2000s, told reporters. McNulty, now a politics lecturer at Queen Mary University of London, insists Burnham is capable of taking tough decisions and “sticking” to them, despite opponents labelling him a “people pleaser”. Trump meeting? Plenty of sensitive issues lie ahead, including welfare reform, how to fund social care, and whether to proceed with the scrapping of jury trials for many offences. Whether to extract oil and gas at the controversial Jackdaw and Rosebank fields in the North Sea could be one of the most divisive questions. “You either alienate the unions by saying no and get noises off from [US President] Donald Trump in a very unhelpful way,” explained Rutter. Or, Burnham gives drilling a green light and “you alienate the Labour net zero [supporters] who say we’re going to lose more support to the Greens”. Burnham will host his first European leader since taking office when French President Emmanuel Macron visits London this week. It comes as he must decide how to proceed with a “reset” with the European bloc that was championed by Starmer ahead of a bilateral summit expected this year. Burnham has said Britain must be “bolder” in getting closer to the bloc, but has ruled out rejoining the single market, customs union, or allowing freedom of movement. “The EU isn’t handing out sweets just because we’ve got a sort of fun prime minister who likes [1980s English rock band] the Smiths,” added Rutter. A likely first meeting with Trump, possibly at the UN General Assembly next month, will be tricky for Burnham who once described the US president’s policies as “poisonous”. Labour lawmaker Jess Phillips said last week that Burnham must “show what his actual priorities are” but in doing so runs the risk of disappointing many MPs. MP Luke Akehurst said that Burnham’s positive start “gives him a significant bank of political capital” among Labour colleagues “who will need to trust his judgment in addressing the range of complex policy issues that the government faces.”

title: Fan Zhedong falls flat after cinemas sell out; China’s big 5 to skip Asian Championships
description: Fan Zhendong loses German Cup tie that sold out cinemas across mainland. Olympic trio opt to miss team tournament to manage busy schedules.
content: Olympic champions Wang Chuqin, Sun Yingsha, and Wang Manyu are among five big names to have made themselves unavailable for the Asian Team Championships in a bid to manage a demanding late-season schedule, China table tennis officials said. Along with the three Olympians, Chen Xintong and He Zhuojia opted out of the qualification process, while Zhou Qihao will not take part in the selection for men’s singles, men’s doubles, or mixed doubles. The China Table Tennis Association (CTTA) published its criteria for being picked for the tournament in Uzbekistan, which is scheduled to take place in Tashkent from October 19 to 25. Qin Zhijian, the China coach, said the decision to rest some of the players came because the national team faced “a heavy competition schedule”, with the Asian Games and the Mixed Team World Cup among the tournaments taking place between now and the end of the year. “After thorough communication with the players, considering subsequent major international tournament arrangements in 2026 and individual needs, the coaching staff agreed that five players, Wang Chuqin, Sun Yingsha, Wang Manyu, Chen Xintong and He Zhuojia, voluntarily gave up this selection qualification,” Qin added. The CTTA said places for Tashkent would be allocated based on ITTF world rankings as of August 17, internal trials and coaching recommendations, with long-term preparation aimed at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. One player still not part of the national team’s plans is superstar Fan Zhendong, and he had a night to forget playing for club side Borussia Düsseldorf in the German Cup. A clash against Ochsenhausen that had sold out cinemas across China ended badly for the former No 1, with a shock loss to Japan’s Shunsuke Togami on Friday, as his side was knocked out 3-1. The victory triggered an unprecedented surge in online traffic, causing the official Table Tennis Bundesliga website to crash. The match was live-streamed in commercial cinemas across mainland China, generating more than 1 million yuan (US$140,000) in pre-sales. On Sunday, veteran coach Wu Jingping, who trained world champions Ma Lin, Wang Hao, and Xu Xin, and began coaching Fan in 2013 when the star was 16, defended his former pupil, highlighting the distinct pressures facing top-ranked athletes. “When a Chinese athlete stands at the top of the world, all athletes take pride in defeating you,” Wu said. “They prepare meticulously for every match against you, try unexpected tactics to beat you, and play with a relaxed mindset, daring to fight aggressively. Meanwhile, you don’t have a specific opponent to study and can only solve problems on the spot.

title: PLA shift to systems warfare means Taiwan’s defences need to change: experts
description: Conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have shown the power of integration and the extension of targets to include critical civilian infrastructure.
content: The People’s Liberation Army is increasingly embracing broader “systems-oriented warfare” rather than relying on individual weapons platforms – a shift Taiwanese analysts say could pose new challenges to the island’s defences. Instead of focusing on individual weapons, the PLA has progressively emphasised integrating intelligence, AI, communications, weapons, logistics and infrastructure into an overall combat system, they warn. “The PLA is no longer concerned only with whose weapons are stronger, but with who can connect different weapons to generate greater overall combat power,” said Chen Chia-sheng, a researcher at a government-funded think tank in Taipei.
