In an article published last week by his organisation, the Institute for National Defence and Security Research, Chen wrote that for Taiwan, this meant the threat in a cross-strait conflict could extend well beyond attacks on its fighters, warships and missile batteries. Under what the PLA calls “systems destruction warfare”, Beijing could seek to disable critical nodes supporting Taiwanese forces, including satellites, radar, communications links, command centres, data networks and fuel and logistics facilities, he wrote. Once those links were severed, even sophisticated weapons could rapidly lose their effectiveness without being physically destroyed, he added. Chen’s assessment echoes observations by retired US Army foreign area officer Tye Graham, now a senior researcher at BluePath Labs, a Washington-based strategy and technology consulting company. In an opinion piece published on August 17 by the digital magazine Breaking Defence, Graham examined mainland Chinese military writings on the lessons to be learned from the US-Israel war on Iran. Graham said that PLA researchers saw the conflict as reinforcing a shift from “force-on-force confrontation” to “systems competition”, where advantage depended on fast, resilient and cost-effective networks rather than individual platforms. The approach emphasised distributed command, attacks on critical enabling nodes and dynamic “kill webs” capable of re-routing information and continuing to operate after parts of the network had been destroyed, he wrote. Analysts said the concept had serious implications for Taiwan’s extensive network of air defence systems, including the US-made Patriot, the locally developed Tien Kung and others. Beijing could exploit the cost imbalance between the PLA’s large numbers of inexpensive drones and rockets and Taiwan’s much more costly interceptors, they warned. “Even if Taiwan successfully intercepted the incoming threats, prolonged saturation attacks could exhaust its missile stocks and impose unsustainable costs,” said military expert Lu De-yun, a former defence ministry press secretary. To counter PLA threats, Taipei needed a “high-low mix” of sophisticated interceptors and cheaper countermeasures, including shorter-range missiles, electronic warfare, counter-drone systems, lasers and high-powered microwave weapons, he said. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies, a Taipei-based think tank, said the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran highlighted the importance of achieving the greatest battlefield effect with the least expensive combination of weapons. “The ‘high-low mix’, or using cheaper capabilities to overcome more expensive ones, is among the lessons learned over the past few years from the wars in Ukraine and Iran,” he said. But Wang added that this did not mean the performance or quality of sophisticated weapons was no longer important. “The key is finding the least expensive combination of capabilities that can deliver the greatest cost-effectiveness.” Command and control strategies present another challenge, according to analysts, who warned that the changing military environment required a different approach. Lu said that Taiwan’s large fixed radar installations and command facilities could become priority targets under the PLA’s “systems warfare” approach. He recommended that Taipei accelerate decentralising command, communications and distributed tactical networks. Wang agreed that changes to command structures were inevitable because the transmission of information had become critical to modern warfare. Whether Taiwan should adopt more distributed command or give frontline commanders greater decision-making authority still required careful consideration, but “there is no doubt that today’s battlefield environment is different from that of the past”, he said. Better integration between military services and platforms would also be critical, according to Chen, who stressed the need to strengthen the resilience of civilian infrastructure supporting military operations. Wang agreed that integrating cross-service data links and weapons systems would become increasingly important. “But the personnel operating those systems – and how the systems are employed – will be even more important,” he noted. Developing commanders capable of genuine joint operations remained difficult, Wang added, because “senior officers often retain a service-centric mindset”. The goal should be to cultivate commanders with a strong understanding of the battlefield who could effectively allocate resources across different services and platforms to generate greater overall combat power, he said. Wang observed that modern warfare was also developing towards two extremes – becoming either “super-fast” or “super-slow”, with the former relying on high-end weapons and concentrated precision strikes to achieve objectives within a short period. “Fighting a slow war becomes a contest of societal resilience and economic endurance,” Wang said, adding that prolonging a conflict could favour the defender because its costs were generally lower than those of the attacker. Systems warfare also expands the battlefield beyond conventional military facilities. Mainland Chinese researchers have identified airfields, ports, warehouses, pipelines, electricity infrastructure and data centres as militarily significant nodes whose destruction could degrade an opponent’s broader combat system. For Taiwan, this meant protecting civilian infrastructure had become inseparable from military defence, Lu said. “Power stations, telecommunications networks, hospitals, fuel supplies and transport systems would need sufficient redundancy and rapid repair capabilities to continue operating under attack,” he said.

title: Sony Music, Warner accuse Anthropic of ‘blatant theft’ in major new lawsuit
description: The case, brought by 35 music publishers, adds to the legal challenges facing Anthropic as the AI firm eyes a potential blockbuster IPO.
content: Some of the world’s biggest music publishers have launched a fresh lawsuit against Anthropic, accusing the artificial intelligence giant of conducting “one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history”. The case adds to the legal challenges facing Anthropic as the firm eyes a potential blockbuster initial public offering, as the AI industry confronts growing pushback over its use of human-made material to train its models. Sony Music Publishing, Warner Chappell Music and their affiliates – 35 publishers in total – filed complaints late on Friday with a court in California, accusing Anthropic and co-founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann of “illegally torrenting, scraping and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale”. The plaintiffs are seeking an injunction and statutory damages for the alleged violations, which they said had helped Anthropic “develop, operate and reap enormous profits from” its Claude series of AI models. “We disagree with the publishers’ claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court,” Anthropic said in a statement in response. The lawsuit comes as Anthropic reportedly pursues plans to go public in potentially one of the largest IPOs in history, with investors discussing a valuation of as much as US$2 trillion, according to the Financial Times. It is the latest in a series of music copyright lawsuits brought against the company. Concord, Universal Music Publishing and ABKCO Music & Records are pursuing separate cases over song lyrics, while BMG has filed its own claim covering works by artists including Bruno Mars, Ariana Grande and the Rolling Stones. “US courts have focused on whether training data was lawfully obtained, finding that acquiring copyrighted material through unauthorised means may itself constitute infringement,” said Yu Lin, a partner at Han Kun Law Offices focusing on intellectual property litigation. Many similar disputes have moved towards settlements and commercial partnerships, according to Yu. Anthropic also agreed last year to a US$1.5 billion settlement with authors and other book rights holders, who had accused the company of stealing their work. However, a judge on the case had earlier ruled that using books to train language models was permissible as long as the works were legally purchased. Documents unsealed in January revealed that Anthropic’s “Project Panama” had bought and destructively scanned millions of physical books from early 2024. In August, an investigation by news outlet 404 Media found that Amazon had engaged in a similar practice, buying up “massive quantities of books, scanning them for AI training data, and destroying them in the process”. Many other tech companies have faced lawsuits over their use of cultural works to train AI models. OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Google face related claims from authors, publishers and news organisations; Stability AI and Midjourney have been sued by artists; and music generators Suno and Udio have faced actions from record labels. Chinese developers are also under pressure. MiniMax faces litigation from Hollywood studios in the United States and from streaming platform iQiyi in Shanghai, while studios sent ByteDance a cease-and-desist letter over video-generation platform Seedance before agreeing to stronger safeguards. “China, by contrast, has focused more on AI-generated outputs,” Yu said. Courts had generally applied conventional copyright tests, asking whether outputs were substantially similar to existing works, but had yet to set a guiding precedent on the acquisition of training data, Yu added. In April, a Shanghai court found that a user had infringed copyright by publishing fine-tuned models that reproduced a character from a copyrighted anime cartoon, but cleared the platform after it promptly removed them.

title: Orangutan rescued from Borneo fire battles respiratory illness
description: Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain forest and land fires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra.
content: On Sunday morning, ⁠Jais, a farmer in ⁠Ketapang, West Kalimantan on Borneo island – the ⁠province hardest-hit by raging forest fires – was en route to his farm when he found an orangutan writhing on the ground in a weak state on a palm-oil plantation near the fire site. “It was very weak, then I gave it water,” ‌said Jais, who only goes by one name. Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze from forest and land fires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra islands after smoke triggered respiratory illnesses and forced thousands of schools to move classes online, including in neighbouring Malaysia. Wildfires burned at least 202,010 hectares of land from January to July, according to Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry, increasing from ⁠107,465 burned hectares from January to June. After finding the orangutan, Jais and other residents immediately called for ‌help. Some two hours later, a wildlife foundation – Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia – arrived with a veterinarian to provide the animal with treatment. It had fainted by then. The ‌orangutan was then named Sampurna, after the village where it was found. The foundation’s CEO Karmele ⁠Llano Sanchez said the ⁠orangutan fainted because it did not get enough oxygen. “The orangutan got hypoxia because of the very thick smoke in the area,” ‌Sanchez said. Komara, the veterinarian, said the orangutan did not have any severe burn-related injuries. But it had breathing problems and had ‌vomited. “We suspected ‌it was suffering from an acute respiratory infection,” he said, adding that the orangutan is ‌around 20 years old. At the palm-oil plantation, the orangutan lay on a net, appearing weak with its ⁠eyes closed. The veterinarian gave the orangutan oxygen through small tubes placed in its nose. Sampurna received fluids ⁠through an intravenous drip, with a makeshift infusion bag hanging from a palm-oil frond. The animal will be moved to a rehabilitation centre to get more treatment, she said. It ‌will be released back into ‌the wild once it recovers, said Komara, adding that they have rescued seven orangutans due to fires so far. Sanchez warned that the government must not only focus on containing fires, but prepare for the long-term effects on public health, forests and wildlife.

title: 13-year-old among 321 arrested as Hong Kong police seize drugs worth HK$130m
description: 19 boys and nine girls under the age of 18 among those taken into custody during seven-week citywide crackdown.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested 321 people, including a 13-year-old, and seized HK$130 million (US$16.5 million) worth of suspected illegal drugs during a seven-week citywide crackdown. Code-named “Tailbacker”, the operation ran from July 12 to August 29, and uncovered 234 drug-related cases, police said on Sunday. The 321 suspects, aged between 13 and 72, comprised 228 men, 65 women and 28 minors. They were arrested for suspected offences that included the manufacturing, possession, and trafficking of dangerous drugs, as well as operating a drug den and possessing Part 1 poisons. Some have already been formally charged. The underage suspects comprised 19 boys and nine girls, all under the age of 18. Over the course of the operation, officers seized 231kg (509 lbs) of suspected illegal drugs with a market value of HK$130 million, including 76kg of cocaine, 65kg of ketamine, 3.7 litres of liquid etomidate, and 6,400 etomidate vape pods, as well as some heroin, cannabis and methamphetamine. Police noted a significant increase in etomidate seizures compared with similar operations last year. “Investigations showed that drug syndicates lured teenagers with small monetary rewards to traffic and sell narcotics, attempting to shift legal liability onto the youth. In one case, a 14-year-old girl was arrested after being coaxed into trafficking 17 etomidate-infused vape pods,” police said in a statement. The force warned that manufacturing, trafficking and possessing dangerous drugs are all serious offences that could lead to life imprisonment and a HK$5 million fine upon conviction. Authorities vowed to crack down relentlessly on syndicates recruiting minors and stated they would apply to the courts for heavier penalties.

title: Opinion | Will US threats over Iran be the last straw for Beijing?
description: China’s measured stance since the Xi-Trump summit in May is reaching a tipping point as US pressure mounts.
content: Earlier this month, when US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened sanctions against any nation continuing to purchase Iranian crude oil, he did not name China. He did not need to. China, the Islamic Republic’s largest oil customer, is squarely in Washington’s crosshairs. The US has already unveiled new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels linked to Iranian trade, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong. Just three months after the May summit between President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump appeared to stabilise bilateral trade relations, the fragile calm is being tested again. So far, China has signalled it will not be coerced. The stand-off sets the stage for what could be the next major rupture in an already fraught relationship. Washington has not been idle since May. In June, the Pentagon added dozens of companies – including Alibaba, Baidu and BYD – to its list of “Chinese military companies”, a designation that can restrict these companies’ access to US capital and market. In July, it announced a 10-12.5 per cent tariff on goods from 60 economies, including China, following its Section 301 investigation into forced labour. This was followed by a ban on imports of Chinese robots and power inverters (July) and a 15 per cent tariff on polysilicon (August). The cumulative message is clear: Washington is tightening the screws on multiple fronts, and Iran is merely the latest lever. Beijing’s response to this onslaught has been deliberate and calibrated. Gone are the days of blanket tariff retaliation. Instead, China has preferred to hold its fire where the cost of escalation outweighs the benefits, striking back with precision when core interests are threatened. When the US imposed a forced-labour duty of 12.5 per cent, below the 20 per cent cap the US had reportedly agreed to, Beijing held off on retaliating. But when structural exclusions crossed the line – as when the US added 43 Chinese companies to an import blacklist over allegations of forced labour – China countered with targeted export controls and a national security trade investigation. Beijing now speaks Washington’s language fluently. On Iran, however, the calculation is starker. China has strongly opposed any dictate on which countries it may do business with. Should the US follow through with secondary sanctions, Beijing has signalled it will retaliate forcefully – and this is not a bluff. Beyond Iran, two other flashpoints will determine whether this managed friction stays in its lane or spirals into systemic rupture. The first is the looming US overcapacity investigation. The Commerce Department is expected to rule that Chinese state subsidies have created global gluts in industries such as solar, electric vehicles and steel. Yet any punitive duty exceeding 7.5 per cent – pushing total tariffs towards the 20 per cent ceiling – would almost certainly trigger retaliation, including stricter export controls over rare earths and critical minerals, where China’s supply chain dominance runs deepest. The second is the potential weaponisation of China’s Permanent Normal Trade Relations (PNTR) status. A bipartisan push in Congress to subject PNTR to annual review is more than rhetoric. A US International Trade Commission fact-finding report has turned political talking points into official data-backed analysis. While its just-published findings highlighting the high costs of revoking China’s PNTR status may make immediate, full revocation less tempting than some lawmakers hoped, it validated the push to do so as a serious policy option. Ending PNTR would push Chinese goods to Column 2 tariff rates, lifting average US duties to 35-45 per cent. The combination of high US tariffs and a likely forceful Chinese response would mark the most profound rupture in bilateral trade since China’s World Trade Organization accession in 2001. Importantly, Washington is moving from a tariff-centric conflict to a non-tariff war, deploying blacklisting, export controls and minimum import prices – a tool rarely used today. Moreover, its focus is now shifting from supply-side restrictions to constraining demand – particularly in green energy and hi-tech sectors. In coordination with the European Union and other allies, Washington is using tariffs, export controls and technical standards to restrict market access for Chinese products, effectively walling off demand. On its part, Beijing, now equipped with a full toolkit, would respond beyond tariffs. Parallel curbs on drones and components could extend to polysilicon and other sectors, inflicting more pain on American manufacturers than on Chinese suppliers, given China’s dominance in those supply chains. The probe into imported printers and photocopiers that use foreign-developed software – its first-ever foreign-trade national security investigation – signals that Beijing will not hesitate to use the same language of “national security” when warranted. The May summit was never designed to end the rivalry; it established mechanisms to prevent disagreement from spiralling out of control. Both sides recognise that complete decoupling is neither feasible nor desirable. Yet Washington’s core objective is not reciprocity but retardation – slowing China’s ascent through any means available. For Beijing, the response is equally clear: calibrated restraint where possible, sharp retaliation where necessary, and an unwavering commitment to safeguarding core interests. The era of strategic economic engagement is over. What replaces it is competitive coexistence: high tariffs maintained indefinitely, supply chains gradually reshaped, and technological boundaries slowly hardening. Further summits later this year may serve as pressure valves, temporarily suppressing friction. But they will not alter Washington’s fundamental calculus. Its deep-seated apprehension over China’s rise will drive it to tighten the screws – with Iran merely the latest turn.

title: Backlash grows after Hong Kong authorities seize  second ‘fighting dog’ in week
description: Owner says officers determined dog was a pit bull terrier after taking photos and videos and sending them to department vet.
content: Hong Kong authorities are facing a growing backlash after seizing a “fighting dog” from its owner following a neighbour’s complaint and detaining it for behavioural evaluation. It was the second dog with pit bull lineage that the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department had seized in a week. The department’s actions came amid heightened public concern over canine management, following a series of recent attacks, including one in which a woman was mauled and later found dead, and another that killed two small pet dogs. The department also stepped up inspections and enforcement action across the city, prosecuting three owners on Sunday for failing to keep large dogs on a leash. Many social media users said on Sunday that they had written to the department to complain about its seizure of unlicensed fighting dogs that did not have a history of attacks. Baku, an eight-year-old dog licensed as a mongrel under the government’s registration system, was taken from its home on Friday night after a complaint from a neighbour. His owner, Mr Lai, told the South China Morning Post that his whole family had been worried over the past few days that Baku might not pass the department’s assessments while nervous. He added that the officers did not explain the exact tests and assessments Baku needed to undergo. “It feels terrible and completely unfair. Baku did nothing wrong. He was taken away simply because someone said he looked like a fighting dog – that’s all the evidence they have,” Lai said. He said he had adopted Baku from a shelter, Home for Homeless Dog, four years ago. “The licence, which I obtained from the government in January, said he is a mongrel. The animal shelter also said so,” he added. “Baku has been a good dog. We trained the dog on our own, and the animal shelter also trained him before. Even when he saw the officers, he was just standing next to me and did nothing wrong.” Lai said he was allowed to see Baku for 15 minutes on Sunday. “Baku was nervous, terrified and curled up. He did not finish the food either,” Lai said. “I asked the staff if I could bring him home [on Monday]; they did not have an answer either.” Lai said department officers had contacted him before the Friday visit, saying that they would conduct an inspection and check the dog’s microchip. However, after sending photos and videos of Baku to their vet, they decided on the spot that he was a fighting dog and needed to be taken away. The officers told Lai that Baku would be “returned on Monday at the earliest”, but they did not leave a contact person. Lai had relied on a general line to contact the department over the weekend. In an open letter to the department on Sunday, the shelter urged the authorities to disclose the dog’s physical and mental condition, and release him as soon as possible. “This lack of professional judgment and transparency does nothing to protect public safety, but turns the department into a tool for people who hold grudges against pets,” it warned. “It ruins neighbourly relations, spreads unnecessary panic across the community, and could trigger a wave of pet abandonments.” It described Baku as “a gentle big boy” with a warm and friendly personality, and said he got along well with both cats and dogs. Baku has no record of attacking humans or animals. “However, your department’s officers completely negated the official licensing records issued in the past and detained the dog after receiving one unverified complaint. This not only undermined owners’ confidence in the system, but also shook public trust in the licensing regime,” it said. In response to SCMP queries, the department said it acted on a report of an allegedly unregistered fighting dog that was not restrained in public according to the law. Its staff contacted the owner and conducted an inspection with the owner’s consent to “safeguard public safety”. “There was evidence indicating that the dog is a pit bull terrier breed, which is classified as a fighting dog under existing law. The department then arranged to bring the dog back to the facility for further identification and observation,” it said. “The department noted that the dog has been neutered. However, the dog has been identified as a fighting dog, so our vet must still observe its behaviour and conduct a temperament test to determine whether it is still suitable to be returned to the owner.” It added that the owner would be required to undergo training to learn the relevant laws and how to manage and care for a fighting dog before it was returned. Breeds classified as “fighting dogs” are strictly regulated. The department earlier seized a 10-year-old dog in Stanley on Wednesday following a complaint. The dog was later confirmed to be a pit bull terrier and was returned to the owner after neutering. Under Hong Kong law, pit bull terriers, dogo Argentino, Japanese Tosa, fila Brasileiro and their crossbreeds are classified as fighting dogs. The law states that fighting canines must be neutered by a registered veterinary surgeon. Owners are also required to obtain a valid desexing certificate. Those dogs must be securely muzzled and held on a leash no longer than 1.5 metres at all times in public places, in addition to wearing special collars. Importing, breeding, selling and keeping fighting dogs without a licence is prohibited in Hong Kong. Anyone in possession of a fighting dog commits an offence if the owner fails to produce a veterinary certificate proving that the dog has been neutered. Upon conviction, offenders face a maximum penalty of a HK$500,000 fine and six months in jail. Any dogs weighing no less than 20kg must be secured in public with a leash of up to two metres, with offenders being subject to a maximum penalty of three months in jail and a HK$25,000 fine. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu earlier promised to review laws governing dangerous dogs and the related penalties in response to the dog attacks.

title: Arthritis drug restores 100% of hair on some patients with severe alopecia in global trial
description: Tests at hospitals in the US, Europe and China discover medication can help to reverse hair loss caused by the autoimmune disease.
content: For many, losing hair isn’t just a cosmetic worry – it is a deeply personal struggle that can chip away at confidence, social life and mental health. Now, a surprising candidate is offering new hope: a pill originally designed to treat arthritis. The condition is called alopecia areata. It is an autoimmune disease where the body’s own immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, causing unpredictable hair loss. Sometimes it is just a few patches but in severe cases, the entire scalp, eyebrows and even body hair can vanish. Until now, there has been no reliably effective treatment. Enter upadacitinib. This once-daily oral medication was previously approved to tame inflammation in various forms of arthritis. But scientists suspected it might also help with alopecia areata by calming the same kind of immune overreaction that destroys hair follicles. To test this, researchers at Harvard University ran two large, international clinical trials across hospitals in North America, Europe and China. They recruited people with severe alopecia areata. On average, the volunteers had lost about 84 per cent of their scalp hair. Some had not seen any regrowth for at least six months. Participants were randomly assigned to take either a 15mg dose, a 30mg dose, or a placebo pill every day. The results, published in JAMA Dermatology on August 12, were striking. Within just 24 weeks, roughly half of those taking upadacitinib – both doses combined – saw at least 80 per cent of their scalp hair grow back. Over 35 per cent of the 15mg group and 46 per cent of the 30mg group achieved “deep regrowth” – meaning more than 90 per cent coverage. Most remarkably, about one in five of them, or 20 per cent, reached a score of zero on the standard hair-loss scale. That’s a completely full head of hair – something almost never seen in the placebo group, where only about 1 per cent had any meaningful improvement. “These findings demonstrate both rapid onset and substantial depth of response with upadacitinib,” Arash Mostaghimi, a professor at Harvard and lead author of the study, told Medical News Today on August 24. “While this was not a direct head-to-head comparative trial, the data suggest that upadacitinib may be among the most effective systemic treatments evaluated for alopecia areata to date,” he added. Mostaghimi is an associate professor of dermatology at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, a teaching hospital of Harvard Medical School. Crucially, the safety profile in the trial matched what was already known from its use in arthritis – revealing no unexpected side effects. The drug works by blocking a specific cellular signal – the JAK/STAT pathway – that drives inflammation, essentially telling the immune system to stand down and let hair follicles recover. The research does not mean upadacitinib is a permanent cure and it is not yet approved specifically for alopecia areata, but the results represent a genuine ray of hope, according to the researchers. “In these two parallel Phase 3 replicate randomised clinical trials, upadacitinib showed a positive benefit-risk profile in adults and adolescents with severe [alopecia areata],” Mostaghimi wrote in the paper. “Upadacitinib may be a potentially effective treatment option for this patient population.”

title: Long queues mark final day as Hong Kong bookstore closes after raid
description: Have a Nice Stay’s closure follows mid-July operation by national security officers, who raided the shop over allegations of acts with seditious intent.
content: An independent Hong Kong bookstore has shut its doors six weeks after a national security police raid, drawing long queues of customers on its final day following four years in business. Readers wound down the dim staircase of a Prince Edward tenement building on Sunday afternoon, with some waiting up to 45 minutes to enter the third-floor bookstore, Have a Nice Stay. The closure followed a mid-July operation by national security officers, who raided the shop alongside nearby Greenfield Bookstore over allegations of acts with seditious intent. Five people were detained – three women aged 30 to 59 and two men aged 37 and 57 – including staff and co-founder Sum Wan-wah of Have a Nice Stay. They were later released on bail. After remaining closed for six weeks, the bookshop reopened from Wednesday until Sunday to clear its remaining stock and bid farewell to readers. Inside the cramped third-floor shop, customers browsed shelves of books on journalism, Hong Kong history and current affairs, while staff prepared to bring down the curtain on the four-year-old business at 9pm. Only cash was accepted. “Every time one of these bookstores closes, Hong Kong has one fewer space like this,” said a shopper leaving with several books, who declined to be named. “I came today because I wanted them to know that they are not closing because nobody wants what they offer. Just look at the queue.” Another customer, who also requested anonymity, said the turnout showed readers still valued independent bookstores, even as such establishments found it increasingly difficult to survive. Taking a more optimistic tone, another shopper, who had bought several titles including Below Victoria Peak: Hong Kong’s Cartographic Archives and Photographic Memories, said: “I’m sure as one closes, another like it can open in the future.” Booksellers declined interview requests. Have a Nice Stay was founded in 2022 by five former journalists after the media organisations they had worked for closed. Its founders sought to promote journalism and reportage while providing a gathering place for people who had chosen to remain in Hong Kong amid a mass exodus during the Covid pandemic. Announcing its closure in July, the bookstore said in social media posts that it had largely managed to break even during its four years of operation, but had suffered periods of financial deficit over the past six months. It cited Hong Kong’s economic conditions, uncertainty over its building, the personal and family circumstances of team members and “elusive red lines”. The shop said it lacked the capacity to read every book or determine which titles might be considered problematic, adding that it no longer had the “ability and courage” to fulfil its mission of spreading a broad range of knowledge. It also referred to persistent complaints from “enthusiastic complainants”, “unidentified individuals” and people hiding behind anonymous letters. The bookstore stressed that it had begun contemplating closure before the latest turmoil and that business difficulties, rather than “force majeure”, remained the bigger reason behind its decision.

title: 6 of the best new K-dramas to watch in September 2026, including The Scandal on Netflix
description: Must-sees in September include steamy period drama The Scandal, office comedy The Ordinary Jackpot and the return of Made in Korea.
content: The hot summer is finally winding down in South Korea, but the K-drama industry will still bring the heat in September with a number of major series, including a steamy literary adaptation and a splashy political thriller. Here is what to watch over the coming month. 1. Made in Korea season 2 Lead cast: Hyun Bin, Jung Woo-sung, Woo Do-hwan, Won Ji-an One of last year’s most high-profile dramas returns, with Hyun Bin and Jung Woo-sung reprising their roles in the big-budget period drama Made in Korea. Hyun plays ambitious political operator Baek Ki-tae, who consolidated his grip on power throughout season one and begins the second season as head of the Korean Central Intelligence Agency (KCIA) during a period of massive political turmoil in South Korea. Jung stars as Jang Geon-young, the dogged prosecutor determined to take him down. Joining them this season is Bloodhounds actor Woo Do-hwan in a new role. Woo Min-ho (Inside Men) is once again at the helm, while Park Eun-gyo (The Silent Sea) and Park Joon-suk (A Normal Family) return as co-writers. (Disney+, September 9) 2. The Ordinary Jackpot Lead cast: Lee Joon-hyuk, Seo Hyun-woo, Oh Dae-hwan Busy leading man Lee Joon-hyuk is back on screens in the workplace comedy The Ordinary Jackpot. He plays Eun-tae, a normal office worker burnt out from long hours and a dreary life that never seems to change. That is, until he buys a winning lottery ticket worth 1.3 billion won (US$950,000). It is a huge sum but not quite enough to buy a home in Seoul. Rather than quit his job, he decides to continue his current life, only with a new mindset backed by his financial windfall. Lee’s recent roles include The Art of Sarah, Mercy for None and Love Scout. He currently has several other projects in the works, including Vampire, a new horror-thriller from Exhuma director Jang Jae-hyun. (TVing, September 10/tvN, September 14) 3. A Love Other Than Yours Lead cast: Seo Kang-joon, Ahn Eun-jin, Lee Joo-ahn, Jo Aram Seo Kang-joon, fresh from Undercover High School, and Dynamite Kiss lead actress Ahn Eun-jin team up for the romantic melodrama A Love Other Than Yours, streaming globally on Prime Video. The actors play office worker Namgoong Ho and film director Lee Mi-do, a couple who, after being together for 10 years without tying the knot, are forced to navigate uncomfortable emotional changes in their relationship. Things come to a head when new people enter their lives – played by Lee Joo-ahn (Dream to You) and Jo Aram (The Auditors), formerly of the girl group Gugudan – forcing them to confront their feelings for each other. (KBS2/Amazon Prime Video, September 12) 4. The Scandal Lead cast: Son Ye-jin, Ji Chang-wook, Nana For this year’s Chuseok holiday, Netflix will launch the steamy period drama The Scandal, bringing together stars Son Ye-jin (No Other Choice), Ji Chang-wook (The Worst of Evil) and Nana (Mask Girl). The series is the second Korean adaptation of Pierre Choderlos de Laclos’ classic French novel Les Liaisons dangereuses, following 2003’s Untold Scandal starring Jeon Do-yeon, which was also set during the Joseon era (1392-1897). Son plays Lady Cho, a seemingly chaste noblewoman living in a time of strict Confucian order, while Ji co-stars as Cho Won, an aristocrat known as a playboy. The pair amuse themselves by secretly manipulating others romantically; their latest target is Hui-yeon (Nana), a beautiful widow. The series is directed by Jung Ji-woo, who is no stranger to erotically charged dramatic fare, having directed films such as Happy End and Eungyo. (Netflix, September 18) 5. Dive into You Lead cast: Bona, Park Seo-ham Bona (Twenty-Five Twenty-One), a member of the K-pop group WJSN, is heading to screens in September as Yun Ha-na, a beloved actress living a glamorous lifestyle at the peak of her career. All that changes one day when a mysterious incident causes her to switch souls with her twin brother, Yun Ha-ru (Jang Deok-su, Filing for Love), and travel back in time. Given this unexpected second chance, Ha-na is determined to save her first love, Jung Woo-jae (Park Seo-ham, The Murky Stream), a judo prodigy who became a bodyguard and died while trying to protect her. Meanwhile, Ha-ru is forced to reckon with his new circumstances when he wakes up in his sister’s body and navigates an unfamiliar relationship with Son Ye-rang (Moon Seung-you, Bon Appétit, Your Majesty), who is both his girlfriend and the CEO of Ha-na’s agency. (Disney+, September 26) 6. Mission Mompossible Lead cast: Jung Min-ah, Dong Ha Jung Min-ah (The Atypical Family) and Dong Ha (Queen of Mystery 2) lead the new KBS daily drama Mission Mompossible, in which two families, both led by matriarchs labelled “crazy” by others, become hopelessly entangled. One mother, known for going to extreme lengths for her children, is grappling with a terminal illness. The other is driven purely by her own desires and turns her back on her family, including her daughter. (KBS1, September 28)

title: Career finance official moves into pole position to become Shanghai’s next mayor
description: Zhu Zhongming, a former vice-minister for finance, has been appointed to a leading role in the city’s government.
content: Shanghai has named career finance official Zhu Zhongming as the municipal government’s new party chief, a role that puts him in line to become the city’s next mayor. His appointment as secretary of the Shanghai government’s Party Leadership Group was announced on Saturday in an official social media post that said he had chaired a meeting of the body. Zhu replaces the current mayor, Gong Zheng, in the post. However, the city’s most senior position is that of the secretary of the Shanghai Communist Party committee, which is currently held by Chen Jining. In China’s party-state system, municipal governments operate under the leadership of the party, which sets the broader political direction while the government handles day-to-day administration. Zhu’s appointment comes a year ahead of the next national party congress, which is expected to see a major leadership reshuffle. If Chen is promoted to a more senior role in Beijing, a move that would be in keeping with the precedent set over the past two decades, it would create vacancies at the top of Shanghai’s leadership. Zhu, 54, is a career finance official who spent much of his working life in his native province of Zhejiang, where he is believed to have crossed paths with Premier Li Qiang during the latter’s spell as governor. He started his career in the provincial finance department in 1993 after graduating from Wuhan University. In 2012, he was appointed deputy mayor of Wenzhou in Zhejiang and joined the city’s party standing committee later that year, serving in that post for about three years. He later served as deputy head of the Zhejiang provincial audit department for nearly two years before becoming its party secretary and director in April 2017. Zhu returned to the provincial finance department as its party secretary and director in 2020. In April 2020, he was transferred out of Zhejiang to become a vice-governor of Hunan province, with responsibility for education, civil affairs, healthcare and medical security. A year later, he moved to Beijing to serve as vice-minister of finance, remaining in the post until his transfer to Shanghai as deputy secretary to the city’s party committee in July 2024. At 52, he was one of the youngest provincial-level deputy party secretaries in China at the time. He was also appointed secretary of the city’s political and legal affairs commission the following month.

title: ‘A warning saved my life’: can Hongkongers trust smartwatches, or are they being misled?
description: Medical practitioners and fitness experts say wearable tech could support personalised, proactive healthcare as adoption hits 63 per cent among Hongkongers.
content: In the third instalment of a five-part Health Matters wellness series on Hong Kong’s growing wellness trends, Victor Ting examines how wearable devices are reshaping personal healthcare in the city, as experts caution that they should not replace professional medical advice. Alice Wong had little idea how seriously ill she might become until unusual patterns on her smartwatch prompted her to seek medical advice. A year ago, Wong, who was still in her twenties, had bought the device but paid little attention to it. That changed when she received an unusual notification warning her of an irregular heart rhythm. What followed was a health scare and a visit to a local doctor, who diagnosed her with atrial fibrillation, or AF – an irregular heart rhythm in which the atria, the heart’s upper chambers, beat chaotically. The condition can reduce the heart’s efficiency and significantly increase the risk of blood clots, stroke and heart failure. “I am a young and fit adult. I exercise regularly and have never previously had a serious medical episode. I don’t go for medical check-ups often, so I dread to think what could have happened if my device had not picked this up,” said Wong, who has since begun taking medication and expects to make a full recovery. While medical practitioners, fitness experts and technology developers told the South China Morning Post that wearable devices had significant potential to support personalised and proactive healthcare, some also warned against misusing the technology or treating wearables as substitutes for doctors. Commercial wearable technology differs from medical-grade wearables and diagnostic tools. It generally focuses on health and lifestyle tracking, monitoring metrics such as exercise, heart rate and sleep. The multibillion-dollar industry has grown rapidly in recent years, driven by advances in real-time data collection and artificial intelligence (AI). In Hong Kong, an estimated 63 per cent of the population owns a wearable device, with more than half of users wearing one every day, according to market research firm Rakuten Insight. Hong Kong users also topped a global ranking of average daily steps for the second consecutive year in 2025, recording an average of 10,663 steps a day, according to a Garmin Connect Data Report, which attributed the result partly to the city’s high-density urban environment and pedestrian-friendly public transport network. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong electronics manufacturer Dayton Industrial, which focused on sports watches, launched its first smartwatch line-up earlier this year called Link2Care. The company describes it as an AI-powered device that combines principles of traditional Chinese medicine with modern biosensors and Western medicine to produce wellness recommendations, rather than simply generate health data. The smartwatch tracks 38 physiological metrics, including sleep cycles and blood oxygen saturation, to provide reports on five organs: the heart, liver, spleen, lungs and kidneys. Its software was trained on more than 9 million historical health cases. It is activated when an organ’s score falls below 60 on a scale of 100. The system may then generate TCM-related suggestions, such as eating cooling foods to reduce “liver fire” or warming foods for spleen deficiency. It may also recommend acupressure at specific meridian points to help relieve stress, improve blood circulation or support what the company describes as organ vitality. Other recommendations include lifestyle adjustments, such as changing sleep schedules or avoiding particular environmental stressors. “By combining Eastern preventive healthcare, Western measurement science and large-scale AI analysis, we are giving users unprecedented visibility into their health and empowering timely, meaningful action,” Paul Yuen, a director of the company, said. Yuen said Western medicine, like a CT scan or periodic body checks, offered a “snapshot” that suffered from “data gaps” lacking baseline measurements of the body. In contrast, wearables were like a “movie”, offering continuous tracking down to every second. The company’s next-generation smartwatch, to be launched next week, would include continuous glucose monitoring to detect cardiovascular events, Yuen added. At a local trade fair in April, Triston Wong, a senior business development manager at Modern Dental Laboratory, also noticed growing interest in dental appliances that could be paired with wearable devices to give dentists a better understanding of patients’ clinical needs. In partnership with Belun Ring, a smart ring, the company tracks metrics such as blood oxygen saturation, pulse rate and sleep stages. The data is then provided to local dentists, who can use it to screen for potential obstructive sleep apnoea before designing an oral appliance to help keep the patient’s airway open during sleep. Wong said the wearable device played an “integral” role in the process by enabling home-based screening and a “seamless” experience in collaboration with healthcare professionals. Patients only need to wear the ring on their index finger while sleeping, rather than spend a night in a hospital sleep laboratory or undergo other conventional diagnostic procedures. The ring can also support post-treatment monitoring after the dental appliance has been fitted, with dentists continuing to receive data reports. “This is more reliable than patients’ subjective observations that they sleep better or feel less tired after using the appliance. It enables healthcare professionals to provide better care,” Wong said. But the fast-growing industry has also faced questions about the accuracy and reliability of wearable data, as well as doubts about how effectively the devices can detect diseases. Last year, the Consumer Council published test results showing that three of 44 locally available wearable models might count minor hand movements as steps, resulting in deviations of up to 59 to 74 per cent. Heart-rate measurement also varied considerably. Two models recorded deviations of more than 11 per cent during most activities and more than 21 per cent while cycling, prompting the watchdog to warn that the data were “suitable only for reference but not for medical use”. Dr Cheng Chi-man, president of the Hong Kong Medical Association and a family-medicine specialist, said more smartwatch users had visited his clinic for check-ups in recent years. He urged people to take a “balanced” approach to the technology. “We welcome technological advances that could lead to earlier diagnosis and treatment of otherwise unknown conditions, as well as promote healthy habits and lifestyles. But technology is a tool, not a replacement for professionally trained doctors,” Cheng said. Because smartwatch users come from all age groups and backgrounds, Cheng said he had diagnosed fit users with underlying thyroid problems that put them at risk of developing serious heart conditions. He had also seen frail elderly patients whose poor sleep scores suggested possible sleep apnoea. Rather than waiting to visit a clinic only after receiving an abnormal reading, Cheng advised users to take a proactive approach. This could include recording baseline measurements and discussing their use of smart devices with a family doctor, making it easier to identify meaningful changes over time. Cheng, who uses a smartwatch himself, also advised users to focus on long-term trends rather than place too much emphasis on daily fluctuations. “Single-day data points, such as heart-rate variability, can be affected by short-term factors including stress, weather and poor sleep, leading to a greater margin of error,” Cheng said. “Broader trends, such as weekly averages and patterns over several months, provide more useful behavioural insights.” Recent research has also supported a longer-term approach to interpreting biometric data from wearables. In a 2024 umbrella review of 249 studies involving watches, wristbands, armbands and other consumer wearables, researchers found that daily errors in estimated calorie expenditure ranged from minus 21.27 per cent to plus 14.76 per cent. Activity-intensity sensors also recorded a mean absolute error of between 29 and 80 per cent on individual days. But the researchers said these errors could cancel each other out or average out over longer periods, according to the study led by Cailbhe Doherty of University College Dublin. Wearables have also shown promise in detecting certain medical events and conditions, although their accuracy varies. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 studies led by Ben Singh of the University of South Australia found that wearable devices achieved varying levels of accuracy in detecting Covid-19, atrial fibrillation and falls. The pooled accuracy for Covid-19 detection was 87.5 per cent, while the pooled positive predictive value for AF detection was 87.4 per cent and sensitivity for fall detection was 81.9 per cent. Describing wearable health technology as an “emerging field with both significant promise and challenges”, the researchers highlighted the potential of continuous, real-time monitoring for conditions requiring regular surveillance. “They may empower patients to take a more proactive role in their healthcare by giving them immediate feedback and data about their condition. They may also contribute to improved surveillance and resource planning for healthcare systems, which could be particularly useful in times of epidemics or pandemics,” the researchers wrote. For fitness coach Kenny Cheung, however, wearables are not only tools for preventive or diagnostic healthcare. They can also serve as a “partner” in the fitness journeys of gym-goers in the city. Cheung said a bodybuilder seeking to burn fat could undertake endurance-based cardio at an intensity of 60 to 70 per cent of their maximum heart rate. This would encourage the body to use fat as a primary fuel source while improving cardiovascular fitness with relatively little joint or muscle fatigue. “Wearables can monitor this during workouts, giving trainers a picture of a client’s progress,” Cheung said. “But the data are not absolute. Weather conditions, such as heat, can affect how the body responds. It is therefore better to combine wearable data with perceived exertion – in other words, how hard the exercise feels. At that intensity, you should still feel comfortable and be able to speak in full sentences.” By contrast, someone seeking to improve peak cardiovascular performance would train in short, explosive bursts at 90 to 100 per cent of their maximum heart rate. At that intensity, the person would be breathless and able to manage only a few words at a time. For Wong, the story of wearable technology is far from over. “My life was saved after a warning from my watch prompted me to see a doctor,” she said. “I will definitely continue wearing it, and I believe it will empower me to make better choices about my health in the future.”

title: Hong Kong gives 45 Wang Fuk Court holdouts final call on buyout scheme
description: As of noon on Sunday, 1,939 of estate’s 1,984 flat owners have submitted acceptance letters, while 77.7 per cent have signed sale and purchase agreements.
content: Hong Kong authorities are making a final push to persuade 45 holdout homeowners at fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court to join a government buyout scheme before Monday afternoon’s deadline. As of noon on Sunday, 1,939 of the estate’s 1,984 flat owners – or 97.7 per cent – had submitted acceptance letters, while 77.7 per cent had signed formal sale and purchase agreements, according to the government. This leaves about 45 homeowners, or 2.3 per cent, who have yet to accept the government’s buy-back offer ahead of the August 31 deadline. The latest figure represents an increase of 25 completed acceptance forms compared with Friday’s official update. Under the acquisition scheme, the government will buy flats at HK$8,000 (US$1,020) or HK$10,500 per square foot, depending on whether the land premium has been paid. After selling their homes and receiving compensation, flat owners can either buy a property on the open market or join a special sales programme to acquire a new subsidised flat. Some homeowners who refused to sell told the South China Morning Post that the offer could not compensate for the loss of their properties and communal bonds. Others who lived in the less damaged Wang Kin House, one of the Tai Po estate’s eight residential blocks, had said they wanted to wait for a structural inspection report to see if repairs were possible. A spokesman for the Housing Bureau on Sunday urged the owners who were refusing to sell “not to miss the last opportunity” and to return the signed “Letter of Acceptance” to confirm their intention by 5pm on Monday. “With the reply deadline approaching, the engagement team coordinated by the Housing Bureau is stepping up efforts to contact owners yet to provide their response and offer the assistance required,” the spokesman added. Lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu called on the holdouts to sign the letters and “seize the last day”, adding that his appeal was based on “understanding and respect” for all residents who had different needs and feelings. “Signing the documents protects your own best interests and also helps the residents of the entire Wang Fuk community start a new life through everyone’s efforts,” he said. Tang added that while Wang Chi House was spared by the fire, earlier repair work had stripped away more than half of its external wall, leaving it structurally fragile, prone to leaks and spalling, and rendering it “uninhabitable”. Last November’s fire tore through seven blocks, killing 168 people and displacing some 5,000 residents in the city’s deadliest blaze in more than seven decades. The government announced in February that it would spend about HK$6.8 billion to acquire the flats in the affected blocks, using HK$4 billion in public money and HK$2.8 billion from a donation-backed support fund. In June, it extended the buy-back offer to the only unaffected block, Wang Chi House, adding another HK$1 billion to the scheme’s cost. It also ruled out on-site redevelopment.

title: Malaysia’s Anwar unveils cost of living measures as opposition rises
description: Anwar ⁠has faced declining support over a perceived failure to deliver on reforms as well as the mishandling of several high-profile corruption cases.
content: Malaysian Prime Minister ⁠Anwar Ibrahim on Sunday ⁠introduced measures to address rising living ⁠costs and support businesses, including restoring higher quotas for subsidised petrol and diesel purchases, as well as more funding for schools and small traders. The measures are expected to take effect on September 1, Anwar said in a televised address. “The economic ‌growth of the country must be returned to the people,” he said. Anwar has been under pressure to tackle higher living costs, even as Malaysia’s economy has outperformed most of its regional peers. The country’s gross domestic product grew 6 per cent in the second quarter this year, surpassing official projections. Anwar said the government would restore a quota for Malaysian citizens to buy ⁠the popular RON95 transport fuel to 300 litres per month, after reducing it to 200 litres ‌a month earlier this year amid a surge in global crude oil prices due to the US-Israeli war on Iran. The quota for diesel purchases for ‌certain categories of users would be similarly raised to 400 litres per month, he said. Anwar ⁠said a nwar said a governmen intelligence programme would be opened to Malaysians aged between 18 and 30 that would include free access to several ‌key applications including Google’s Gemini Enterprise and Wonderclip, and MuleRun by China’s Alibaba Cloud. He also unveiled increased funding for maintaining schools, improving ‌digital health ‌systems and micro-financing facilities for small businesses. He said the government would raise the revenue threshold ‌exempting companies from implementing e-invoicing to 3 million ringgit a year. Any funds seized or forfeited from ⁠anti-corruption legal proceedings would be channelled to government programmes, particularly in education and healthcare, he added. Anwar’s coalition ⁠has faced declining support over what critics have described as a failure to deliver on promised reforms and the mishandling of several high-profile corruption cases. The coalition has been ‌defeated in three successive regional ‌elections in recent months. The state elections are widely seen as an indicator of voter sentiment ahead of a general election that must be held by early 2028. Anwar has said he may call a snap election if divisions within his administration continue to widen.

title: Uzbekistan confirmed as second foreign operator of China’s J-10CE fighter
description: Uzbekistan’s defence ministry released official footage of the fighters on Sunday, which was also broadcast on state television.
content: Uzbekistan has confirmed that it has become the second foreign country to operate China’s J-10CE fighter, marking another breakthrough for Beijing’s advanced combat aircraft exports and a potentially significant inroad into a Central Asian defence market long dominated by Russian warplanes. Reports previously suggested that Uzbekistan had ordered 24 J-10CEs, although neither country confirmed the deal. However, at least six of the jets were shown in footage released by the Uzbek president’s office on Friday as part of the country’s independence day celebrations. The footage showed the Uzbek air force warplanes sitting on the runway, flying in formation and receiving a water-cannon salute, a ceremony that is traditionally used to mark significant arrivals. Uzbekistan’s defence ministry released an official video of the fighters later on Sunday, which was also broadcast by state television, describing them as “modern fighter aircraft guarding our air borders”. Chinese military aviation specialist Andreas Rupprecht said it was significant that Uzbekistan had become the second confirmed foreign operator of the J-10CE because the country had traditionally sourced its military equipment almost exclusively from Russia. “This demonstrates that China is gradually making inroads into markets with hi-tech systems,” he said, including sectors previously dominated by Russia. Rupprecht said Chinese systems were increasingly being seen as capable alternatives to Western and Russian equipment, while Russia was losing ground as an arms exporter because some products were either not competitive or could not be supplied in time. However, he cautioned that China would need to meet customers’ expectations for “after-sales support”, warranties, supplies and long-term product upgrades to establish itself as a successful arms supplier over the longer term. Beijing has been trying to promote international sales of the single-engine, multirole fighters and Bangladesh recently confirmed it was close to agreeing on a deal to buy the planes. Pakistan was the first foreign buyer of the plane, which played a prominent role in last year’s brief conflict with India. By May last year, it had received 20 of the fighters from China, according to the most recent Pentagon report on Chinese military power. The report said that Indonesia, Iran and Egypt had also expressed an interest in buying the planes. “Uzbekistan is, by any measure, a relatively small market, but the significance is in the fact that they are buying the jets at all,” said Brendan Mulvaney, director of the US Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute. “Not Russian ones, not French, or anyone else.” Mulvaney said the sales could be the start of Beijing’s efforts to “expand the customer base” to countries not typically served by the United States or other suppliers. Previous Chinese fighter exports have involved lower-cost jets such as the F-7 or the JF-17, which was jointly developed with Pakistan and sold to countries including Azerbaijan, Nigeria and Myanmar. But the J-10CE, the export version of the 4.5-generation warplane, marks China’s entry into the higher end of the international market for fighters. The PLA Air Force currently has more than 300 J-10Cs, according to the Royal United Services Institute, a UK-based think tank. The planes are equipped with electronically scanned array radars along with modern electronic warfare and data-link systems, and can be used for both air-to-air combat and strike missions. Its air-to-air arsenal includes the PL-10 short-range missile and the PL-15E, a radar-guided weapon designed to engage targets beyond its visual range. The fighters’ international profile rose sharply after Pakistan used them during its conflict with India in May last year, claiming they had shot down several Indian planes. The exact tally remains disputed, but US officials told Reuters that Pakistan had shot down at least two Indian military aircraft, including a French-made Rafale. Analysts warned that these engagements could not be used to draw direct comparisons between the warplanes involved, but the conflict still offered a rare opportunity to assess an advanced Chinese fighter and its weapons against Western-made aircraft. Bangladesh told Reuters that the conflict had played a role in the decision to buy the fighter, while Mulvaney said it was “a big part” of its appeal but “not the whole story”. “I’ve been saying since the Pakistan-India clash where Chinese equipment showed its worth that we are on the cusp of an expansion of higher-end military sales from China. I think this is the start of that trend,” he added. Uzbekistan’s decision to buy the planes indicates that China is gaining a foothold in a market traditionally dominated by Russian fighters. Mulvaney said price, availability, financing, weapons packages and the political conditions attached to sales would also have been factors in Tashkent’s decision to buy the planes. “As far as the jet itself goes, the J-10CE offers a better package than other competitors,” he said, pointing to its active electronically scanned array radar and the PL-15E missiles, which he said had a longer range than the weapons carried by many Rafales or Russian fighters. He added that the planes were cheaper than Western fighters such as the Typhoon or Rafale and could probably be delivered quickly while competitors were dealing with backlogs or – as in the case of Russia – the impact of sanctions. Buying the J-10CE could also be a way for countries to signal a shift away from US and European suppliers and represented “a bet on China over Russia for the future of aerospace”, he said.

title: Starry Lee seeks longer Legco session for joint policy address, 5-year plan debate
description: ‘For this first joint debate, I hope to secure a longer duration than before so that lawmakers will have more time for a comprehensive discussion,’ Legco president says.
content: Hong Kong lawmakers will hold a three-day joint debate in early October on the city’s annual policy address and first five-year plan, with Legislative Council president Starry Lee Wai-king seeking to extend the session so legislators have enough time to reflect residents’ views. The Legco earlier announced a combined debate from October 7 to 9, requested by the government, to cover both the motion of thanks on the policy address and a government motion on the five-year blueprint moved by the chief secretary. “For this first joint debate, I hope to secure a longer duration than before so that lawmakers will have more time for a comprehensive discussion,” Lee said on Sunday, adding that final arrangements would be confirmed with the chief executive. “The two [documents] are definitely interconnected, and delivering and debating them together will help highlight their connection.” Expecting key elements of the policy address to feature in the five-year plan, Lee said a joint debate was appropriate and pledged to ensure lawmakers were allotted sufficient time to discuss both documents. She also expected the five-year plan to outline middle- to long-term strategies for the city, particularly on technological advancement and economic growth, alongside targets for key livelihood issues such as housing, healthcare and labour. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced last week that he would unveil his annual policy address and the five-year plan at the legislature on September 16, to help residents better understand how the two are deeply connected. Although LegCo was originally scheduled to resume general meetings in October after the summer recess, it will convene a special session for Lee’s presentation. He will attend a question and answer session with lawmakers the following day. Hong Kong’s five-year plan aims to better align local development with efforts under the national blueprint for 2026–2030, while providing direction and strategic guidance for the future. It will outline the city’s vision for the Northern Metropolis megaproject, the advancement of innovation and technology, and the development of finance, shipping and trade.

title: Chinese viewers praise Korean dating show featuring serious illness survivors as lesson in love
description: Show producer reveals concept stems from curiosity about how awareness of mortality shapes young people’s perspectives on life and love.
content: Chinese audiences have been captivated by a new South Korean dating show that features young people battling serious illnesses, drawing inspiration from their courageous pursuit of love. The dating reality show, Love Against Time, released by the Seoul Broadcasting System (SBS) this summer, has gone viral on Chinese social media. While various dating reality shows have long served as a hallmark of South Korean entertainment, this new entry retains a unique appeal, bringing together eight individuals in their 20s and 30s who are confronting terminal diseases. Unlike other shows where participants engage in playful flirtation, the participants on Love Against Time immediately introduce their personal stories by reading heartfelt letters. One member, Kim Jong-eun, was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia just before he was set to take the test for his dream job as a firefighter, for which he had prepared for a year. After receiving a bone-marrow transplant, he faced serious complications, with the donated immune cells attacking his healthy tissues. As a result, his lungs, joints, and knuckles continue to function poorly. Another participant, Kim Seon-ho, ended his relationship with his girlfriend upon being diagnosed with rare lymphoma, fearing that he would be a burden. He had promised three fellow patients that they would share beers together once they recovered, but he became the only one to survive. Having endured the darkest moments of their lives, they have chosen to bravely pursue love once again. A female participant, Kim Na-young, lost her hearing in her left ear and gained 20kg within a month while treating her acoustic neuroma. She reflected on how this journey allowed her to contemplate life and death. “I have not been doing what I truly want in the past. I will cherish my precious time to love, work, have fun, and follow my heart,” she shared. The show’s producer, Lee Eun-sol, explained that the concept emerged from her curiosity about how awareness of mortality shapes young people’s perspectives on life and love, as reported by The Korea Herald. Her intention is for the show to centre on how young individuals “rebuild their lives and find love” after confronting illness, rather than focusing solely on their struggles. Participants are also encouraged to express their affection by dedicating a quota of 100 minutes to those they truly wish to spend time with. Many Chinese viewers have expressed their admiration for the show, commenting on how it inspires them to re-evaluate their own attitudes towards life and love. “I was profoundly moved by this show, witnessing these young individuals willing to open their hearts and courageously embrace new love after enduring significant pain and suffering,” one viewer remarked. Another noted that the show highlights the universal desire for love among those with serious illnesses: “Being diagnosed with cancer does not mean one does not deserve love. Love transcends physical ailments and is the connection of two souls.”

title: Cantopop diva Anita Mui’s mother dies at 102 after collapsing in flat
description: Tam Mei‑kam was being fed liquid oatmeal on Sunday morning when she suddenly collapsed in her Causeway Bay home.
content: The 102-year-old mother of the late Cantopop icon Anita Mui Yim-fong died on Sunday morning after collapsing at her home in Hong Kong. Tam Mei‑kam was being fed liquid oatmeal by her domestic helper at about 10.30am when she suddenly collapsed in her Causeway Bay flat. The helper, a 31-year-old Indonesian woman, immediately called police. Paramedics and officers arrived at her home in the Leigyinn Building at 62 Leighton Road to find Tam unconscious. She was rushed to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai, where doctors attempted resuscitation but she was pronounced dead at 11.27am. A police source confirmed that the woman was Mui’s mother. The source said Tam had a history of heart disease and hypertension, requiring regular medication and a liquid diet. Officers inspected her home and found no suspicious circumstances or injuries. The case is not considered suspicious and has been handed to the Wan Chai district miscellaneous inquiries subunit to follow up on. Mui died of cervical cancer and respiratory complications in December 2003 at age 40. Tam was well known for her relentless legal battles over her daughter’s estate. Despite Mui’s will establishing a trust to provide her mother with a monthly living allowance, Tam repeatedly challenged the arrangement in court, seeking lump‑sum payouts or full control of the inheritance. Her lawsuits stretched for more than a decade, ending in bankruptcy after she failed to pay legal fees. Courts consistently upheld Mui’s will, and with Tam’s death, the trust obligations cease. The remainder of the estate – estimated at more than HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) – will be donated to the Miu King Buddhist Association, as stipulated by Mui.

title: Lam’s brilliant birdie at last seals China Tour win, Japan Q-school beckons
description: Isaac Lam holds his nerve to claim inaugural Fanling Classic in front of home crowd at Hong Kong Golf Club.
content: A brilliant birdie on the last secured Isaac Lam a two-shot victory at the inaugural Fanling Classic on Sunday. Despite considerable pressure from China Tour points list leader Zizhao Jin, the 26-year-old Hongkonger held his nerve superbly to fire a final-round 65 over the Old Course at Hong Kong Golf Club to claim his second China Tour title by two shots on 17-under-par. Tied for the lead heading down the 72nd hole, Lam holed a 12-footer for birdie, while Jin could only bogey after coming up short with his approach. Jin finished second on 15 under, while Bowen Chai claimed third spot on 12 under. Hong Kong’s Jason Hak, who will represent the city at next month’s Asian Games, finished in a tie for fifth on seven under, alongside compatriot Jeffrey Shen who was awarded the top amateur prize. “I’m very happy to come out on top,” Lam, who heads to the Japan Tour Q-School next week, said. “I gave up my lead after nine holes but I was still cracking jokes with my caddie. It’s a great stepping stone to win again on the China Tour.” Lam is good friends with two-time Asian Tour champion Taichi Kho and said he was “100 per cent” motivated by his fellow countryman’s success. “There’s a quote my coach uses – ‘if he can do it, so can I’,” Lam said. “So I guess within our community I’d like to be pushed, and to push others. I think that’s what golf is about. It’s not just about your own successes but having successes around you. It really helps your career as well.”

title: CXMT joins growing list of Chinese tech firms suing US Pentagon over blacklists
description: Chipmaker CXMT has sued the US government to be removed from a Pentagon blacklist – joining a wave of legal challenges by Chinese tech firms.
content: Leading chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) has joined a growing list of Chinese technology companies suing the US government over their additions to Pentagon blacklists, as legal experts said US courts had shown a willingness to hold the Department of Defence to account. Recent rulings involving Chinese tech firms including lidar sensor maker Hesai Group, drone manufacturer DJI and biotech firm WuXi AppTec indicated that judges were prepared to scrutinise the US government’s evidence and grant interim relief, said Mark Shi, a compliance lawyer at Shanghai-based Co-Effort Law Firm. Other Chinese companies have cases pending – including the tech giant Alibaba Group Holding, which was granted a temporary reprieve over a lobbying restriction last month. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. The CXMT case would test whether a company’s broad ties to China’s industry ministry or state-asset regulator were enough to label it as a military-linked entity, and to what extent such US national-security determinations remained subject to evidence, reasoned explanation and due process, Shi added. CXMT, China’s largest maker of dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) chips, filed a lawsuit in a Washington federal court on Friday against the US Department of Defence, with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth named as a defendant. The company is seeking removal from the Pentagon’s Section 1260H list of Chinese companies with military ties. It was first added to the blacklist in January 2025, and kept on the list after a review in June. The designation bars the Pentagon from contracting directly with listed companies, with restrictions set to extend through defence contractors’ supply chains from June 2027. It can also discourage customers, banks and suppliers from doing business with them. CXMT said in its complaint that it was “not affiliated with the Chinese military” and produced DRAM chips for civilian and commercial uses. The Hefei-based company said it spent more than a year submitting information to the Pentagon in an effort to secure its removal. The department published a notice delisting CXMT in February, but withdrew it the same day, according to the firm. CXMT alleged that the Pentagon’s decision-making was arbitrary and violated its rights to due process. The question is not about ‘how’ but ‘when’ CXMT will be able to break into the ‘big three memory club’ Neil Shah, Counterpoint The lawsuit adds to a widening push by Chinese companies to challenge US blacklists in court. Companies were suing because the “designation now carries measurable costs, from lost government contracts and supply-chain restrictions to lobbying curbs and customers cutting ties”, Shi said. Some of these efforts have borne fruit. The Pentagon removed the Chinese semiconductor firm Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment from a blacklist in 2024, after it sued. Earlier this month, the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled that Hesai was entitled to see the unclassified evidence against it and respond, though it left the company’s designation as a military-linked entity in place. The court also revived part of DJI’s challenge because a lower court had not examined classified evidence. WuXi AppTec, meanwhile, secured a preliminary injunction blocking the Pentagon from enforcing its designation of the company as a military-linked firm while its case proceeds. The legal offensive comes as CXMT’s commercial position strengthens. This week, the firm reported its first-half revenue had surged by 874 per cent year on year to 150.3 billion yuan (US$22.4 billion). Its net profit reached 77.6 billion yuan, reversing a 2.3 billion yuan loss a year earlier. According to Counterpoint, CXMT was the world’s fastest-growing DRAM supplier in the second quarter of the year, with the firm holding a 7 per cent share of the global market. On Saturday, it announced it had begun mass production of its LPDDR6 memory, which is set to be used in Xiaomi’s 18 Fold smartphone handset from September. “The question is not about ‘how’ but ‘when’ CXMT will be able to break into the ‘big three memory club’,” said Neil Shah, a vice-president of research at Counterpoint.

title: Pakistan suspends 8 officials after maternity ward fire kills 14 infants
description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said those responsible do not deserve any concessions and that they will be brought to justice.
content: Pakistan’s prime minister said eight officials were suspended and called for criminal proceedings against them, after 14 infants were killed in a fire in a maternity ward in a hospital in the country’s capital. A preliminary report conducted by a four-person committee formed by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif found the deadly blaze had engulfed the unit “within approximately two minutes” just after 6.30am on Wednesday, with a nurse only able to save one of the 15 infants in hospital care. Among those suspended were hospital staff, including its executive director and the head of the neonatal department, as well as the director general of Islamabad’s emergency services. Sharif said late on Saturday “those responsible for criminal negligence do not deserve any concession” and that they will be “brought to justice.” He also approved taking action against the company responsible for the hospital’s security, without naming them. Emergency services were called within six minutes of the fire breaking out, with the first rescue services arriving at the scene 15 minutes later, the report said.
