Parents and other witnesses said the response had been slow and guards had reportedly prevented people from leaving the building. The hospital did not have detailed operating procedures or fire and emergency training, according to the preliminary report. Two nurses, a security guard and another officer were in the ward when the fire started, but there were no supervising staff, the report stated. Health Minister Mustafa Kamal said that a spark from an air conditioner is believed to have caused the fire. The report clarified an ignition source is yet to be determined as the investigation continues. Health Secretary Aslam Ghori, the country’s top civil servant for the department, was sacked on Wednesday following the devastating incident. Fires in large buildings are frequent in Pakistan, often due to poor safety laws and building codes as well as lax enforcement. In January, more than 65 people were killed in a shopping centre fire in the port city of Karachi. At least 11 people were killed in another shopping centre fire in Karachi in 2023. In 2012, at least 250 labourers died at a garment factory in Karachi.

title: ‘Stuck’: Canada closes Hong Kong migration scheme, some eye new paths
description: ‘Moving to the US is geographically convenient, but it is expensive,’ agent says, recommending UK BN(O) visa as Ottawa closes 2021 pathway.
content: The closure of Canada’s “lifeboat” migration scheme for Hongkongers has left some applicants who are struggling to meet permanent residency requirements in limbo, prompting others to consider alternative destinations such as the US and Britain. Hong Kong-based immigration agents made this observation after Ottawa announced on Friday that its dedicated pathways for Hongkongers would stop accepting new applications on Monday. Applications submitted before the deadline will continue to be processed. Launched in 2021 in response to Beijing’s imposition of the national security law in Hong Kong, the pathway allowed applicants to qualify for permanent residency either by completing a diploma or bachelor’s degree at designated Canadian institutions, or obtaining an open work permit and working full-time in the country for at least one year, or accumulating 1,560 work hours. Benny Cheung Ka-hei, director of immigration consulting firm Goldmax, said on Sunday that the scheme’s closure was widely expected amid Canada’s tightening immigration policy. He noted that some Hongkongers who moved to the country failed to meet the requirements, particularly struggling with the English proficiency test, and that the closure could shut down their route to permanent residence. “Some of our clients moved to Canada but are busy or need to take care of children and remain unable to pass the English test despite multiple attempts,” Cheung said. “Some of them are stuck at this stage.” He said some Hongkongers unable to qualify for permanent residency had begun seeking alternatives, prioritising the United Kingdom and the United States. “Moving to the US is geographically convenient for them, but it is expensive. Employment-based immigration costs a lot, while investment immigration requires at least US$800,000,” Cheung said. “The UK’s BN(O) visa does not cost much. So we do advise clients who have a BN(O) passport to consider moving to Britain.” Peggy Lau Pik-ki, head of business development at Uni Immigration Consultancy, noted that most Hongkongers intending to migrate to Canada had already submitted applications, meaning the closure would have only a minimal impact. “The deadline has been public for a relatively long time, and no extension is expected,” Lau said. “Those who failed the English-language test actually had ample time to retake it.” She added that the peak of the city’s emigration wave had passed, suggesting the scheme’s closure was unlikely to trigger a sudden surge in Hongkongers seeking other routes, such as the UK’s BN(O) visa pathway. Some internet users expressed concerns on social media before the Monday deadline. “I have been waiting for the permanent residence application for two years, but only received the acknowledgement of receipt,” a Threads user said five days ago. Another user said on August 16 that his reading score in CELPIP, an English exam for Canadian immigration, was one point short and asked internet users for suggestions. As of June, a total of 48,560 Hongkongers had applied for permanent residency under the scheme, with 13,485 approved and about 13,370 obtaining permanent residence status, according to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. Canada was among several Western countries to introduce emigration pathways for Hongkongers, with its scheme primarily targeting younger people, recent graduates and those who have already studied in the country.

title: How China’s liquor heartland traded old spirits for new energy
description: Home to one of the nation’s legendary baijiu makers, Yibin is racing to reinvent itself as a hi-tech manufacturing hub – though stark challenges remain.
content: Wuliangye, China’s second-largest liquor producer, is a household name. But Yibin, the lower-tier city in Sichuan province home to the famous baijiu maker, has long flown under the radar. So when I received an invitation earlier this month for a media trip to Yibin, the first question that sprang to mind was: where exactly is it? Tucked away behind the hills of western China, we had to fly to Chengdu, Sichuan’s capital, followed by a bus transfer. And when we finally arrived, local officials were keen to show us everything the city had to offer – except the liquor. “Wuliangye is old-fashioned,” local cadres said. What followed was a tour of a prefecture-level city trying hard to redefine itself: from a sleepy backwater into a manufacturing hub, with many of the costs typically associated with breakneck development. One of the first things that caught our eye was a 288-metre (about 944 feet), 57-storey skyscraper rising from a prime waterfront plot with sweeping vistas of the Yangtze River. The building, one of the tallest in Sichuan, is expected to house the province’s first five-star Westin hotel in 2027 after its developer signed a contract with America’s Marriott International. Before we had more time to gaze at Yibin’s expansive riverside skyline, we were whisked away to a suburban plant operated by state-owned transit giant China Railway Rolling Stock Corporation (CRRC). There, we were shown futuristic buses sold as “autonomous rapid transit (ART)” vehicles. If the idea sounds like a marketing gimmick, CRRC was eager to prove otherwise, as executives bragged about orders from South Korea and Malaysia. They let us board one of the 20-metre vehicles, where signs in Malay and English validated its destination. Set to be shipped to Kuching, Malaysia, the buses will serve main routes in a public transport network backed by the Sarawak state government. Other ART buses are expected to head to Daejeon in South Korea, while CRRC and Yibin’s city government hope the vehicles can enter Hong Kong after the company took part in a tender for a rapid transport system in Kai Tak. Yibin’s bet on advanced manufacturing, however, does not stop with transport. The city has also attracted Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL), the world’s largest battery maker, which is developing massive production bases there with a planned capacity of 270 gigawatt-hours. To further support the new energy sector, Yibin also hosts the World Power Battery Conference, an annual industry event backed by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. The arrival of companies like CRRC and CATL has helped lift Yibin’s economy. Since 2023, its gross domestic product has shot to third among Sichuan’s 21 prefecture-level cities. Only on the final day of the trip did we finally get the chance to taste Wuliangye. To our surprise, the version served was lighter and more refreshing than expected, with reduced alcohol content. “Baijiu sales across China are dropping and for time-honoured brands like Wuliangye, which traces its origins to the Song dynasty, it also has to adapt,” a local official said. Today, Wuliangye derives less than half of its revenue from liquor, and the company has substantial stakes in businesses such as Sichuan Airlines and Bank of Sichuan. Yet despite diversifying, Yibin’s wider transformation is far from straightforward. Like many lower-tier cities in central and western China eager to carve out new growth niches, it still faces long-standing constraints. The city is by no means rich, with many residents and sectors lagging as manufacturing rises. Average per capita annual disposable income was 36,690 yuan (US$5,459) in 2025, or 3,057 yuan a month, about 15 per cent lower than the national average. Retail sales fell 1.5 per cent year on year in 2025. Local government finances also show signs of strain. Fiscal income growth slowed sharply from 25.6 per cent in 2021 to 3 per cent in 2025, with the city recording a deficit of 50 billion yuan (US$7.44 billion) last year. Total government debt stood at 160 billion yuan. Like many other Chinese localities, Yibin is also ageing before it becomes rich. The number of newborns has fallen 37 per cent over the past decade, from 58,000 in 2015 to 36,000 in 2025, while a fifth of the population is now aged 60 or above. Meanwhile, the city faces environmental vulnerabilities. Eighteen years after the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake damaged 18,000 homes in Yibin – which sits on the edge of the Sichuan Basin, putting it at risk – large swathes of the old city have decades-old residential blocks, schools and hospital buildings with subpar resistance to seismic activity, locals said. For first-time visitors, anecdotal evidence also points to tepid sales despite the influx of investors and enterprises. The hotel where we stayed, managed by the UK’s IHG Hotels & Resorts, offered laundry services only every other day. Reception staff cited “inadequate guests”. International mass-market brands have also faced headwinds. Starbucks and McDonald’s have shut some stores in Yibin, in line with their strategy to concentrate sales in more affluent coastal areas. Young people continue to shun local jobs and flock to Chengdu and coastal cities. Still, local officials told us that economic development would, hopefully, address the city’s problems. “Yibin remains a small city and is never short of problems … which can only be solved through economic growth. At least our GDP is growing,” one local official said.

title: Opinion | Behind the Nepal-China border floods lie bad politics
description: While the solidarity on display in the wake of the disaster is commendable, the tragedy must not be viewed as an unpredictable, unpreventable act of nature.
content: As the waters of the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers recede, leaving behind mud, debris and damaged infrastructure, a familiar pattern is visible in Nepal. When disaster strikes, the country’s usual political divisions, cronyism and institutional mistrust give way, for a while, to real unity. Across party lines, political leaders worked around the clock alongside security forces. Digital channels opened for the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, a “one-door policy” was enforced to prevent duplication of relief efforts and telecoms operators made calls and internet free across affected areas. Diaspora communities and local volunteers stepped up alongside the state. But a familiar governance pattern is at risk of taking hold again: treating this disaster as an unpredictable, unpreventable act of nature. A natural event – glacier collapse, cloudburst, avalanche or wildfire – is a physical trigger. A disaster is something else. It is shaped by the human choices made around that trigger. What was first reported as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was, according to the US Geological Survey, a large mass of rock and ice breaking off a glaciated mountain in Langtang National Park, near the Tibet-Nepal border. The collapse released energy equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake, releasing a debris flow that travelled nearly 100km downstream. An unstable lake formed by remaining ice blockages still sits upstream. Emergency readiness now means moving from reactive rescue to continuous, real-time monitoring and staged evacuation planning downstream. Still, the scientific explanation is only part of the story. As Dr Nimesh Dhungana, a disaster scholar from the University of Manchester, has pointed out, every major disaster triggers a public search for a physical cause. But framing devastation purely as a natural event is a narrative that authorities can find convenient, since it shifts blame away from decisions they made and the accountability that might follow. The downstream destruction in this case was not simply an unavoidable tragedy. Much of it reflects choices already built into the country’s political economy. Building codes and environmental setbacks are routinely ignored or bypassed through cronyism, nepotism and manipulated environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards. Local leaders often build bridges, roads and structures to secure votes and reward allied contractors, not because an engineering assessment called for them. Hydropower projects are greenlit to quickly boost megawatt capacities and short-term profits, skipping rigorous, climate-resilient assessments. Down in the mid-hills and Terai plains, unchecked riverbed encroachment and unregulated sand mining choke natural water corridors. When a climate-induced deluge rushes downstream, these unengineered structures weaponise the river. During the height of a crisis, governments often operate under what is sometimes called a “state of exception”, a temporary loosening of normal procurement and oversight rules to prioritise speed. That trade-off can be reasonable during search-and-rescue operations. It should not extend into the longer phase of recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction. Reconstruction needs open, auditable data that shows why particular communities were left vulnerable in the first place, and that holds the officials who approved that development to account. This disaster also points to a regional blind spot. In the flood’s aftermath, some local reports accused China of delaying early warnings, allegations Beijing has denied. Regardless of the details, one thing is clear: managing the Himalayas primarily through narrow, militarised security lenses and border rivalries must end. We must shift urgently to ecological geopolitics. The region’s economic security depends on how well its governments manage shared terrain. Institutions like the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) must make a hard, diplomatic push to force regional governments into a binding, rules-based order for climate adaptation across the entire Hindu Kush Himalaya region. Nepal’s domestic governance failures sit alongside the gap between what wealthy, high-emitting countries have promised on climate finance and what they have delivered. Major historical carbon emitters, including the United States, have made commitments that have not translated into consistent climate loss and damage funding. China and India must also do more. Frontline countries like Nepal, which contribute very little to global emissions, are often left financing recovery through loans rather than grants, which adds debt to disaster. Nepal must move from emergency solidarity to systemic institutional accountability. First, institute mandatory risk audits with legal liability. Independent hydrological and social risk assessments should be required before any riverbank or hillside development is approved, with clear legal liability for officials and contractors when ignored codes or weakened standards contribute to failures. Second, open dashboard reconstruction. The emergency rules that apply during rescue operations should end once those operations conclude. Reconstruction spending should run through an open, trackable system so the public can follow funding from allocation to delivery. Third, pay attention to upstream risk management, such as real-time sensor networks and satellite monitoring for glacial blockages at high altitudes, paired with early warning systems and planned evacuation routes for downstream communities. Fourth, boost regional cooperation built on shared data. Increase support for institutions like ICIMOD to broker real-time data sharing on hydrology, permafrost and satellite monitoring between Nepal, China and India, separate from bilateral border disputes. Fifth, take a firmer position in climate diplomacy. Shift Nepal’s international posture from passive charity recipient to the leader of a mountain-state coalition. Explicitly demand grant-based loss and damage financing from major polluting nations and refuse debt-creating disaster loans. Nepal has shown that its people and its leaders can come together in a crisis. The harder task is carrying that same commitment into the ordinary, unglamorous work of governance and planning, before the next flood arrives.

title: Butter believe it – first Paris boutique devoted to France’s favourite fat opens
description: With flavours including garlic, shallot, fines herbes and raspberry, Le Butter Shop in Paris is a temple to all things butter.
content: Billed as Paris’ first boutique devoted entirely to butter, Le Butter Shop opened last month a short walk from the Eiffel Tower – with 30 varieties from small family producers in Brittany, the Loire Valley and northern France. France eats around 8kg (17.6 pounds) of butter per person a year, according to the country’s Ministry of Agriculture and Food. It is among the highest in the world. Yet the obesity rate is well below the average for wealthy nations – 14 per cent, compared to an average of 19 per cent. At the new boutique, customers taste by the spoonful before buying anything from a 10g pat to a kilogram block. Flavours include plain, shallot, pepper, seaweed, wild garlic, fine herbes and lemon with green pepper. At the sweet end: vanilla, raspberry, strawberry and chocolate. “Most people don’t expect to like a raspberry butter or to like chocolate butter,” says shop owner Erwan Leo, 34. “And when they try it, this is where they’re just like, ‘Oh wow, OK.’” Leo, who also runs a wine-tasting business, says butter should be used like wine to make a meal better – “the goal isn’t to get drunk”. Mehreen Himayat, 25, and Salman Bin Ehsan, 27, from Ireland – a country known for its rich golden butter – saw videos of the shop at home in Dublin before travelling to France. “We came here just to taste the butter,” Bin Ehsan says. Alexandra Incolano, a 36-year-old who lives near Paris, came to the shop with a specific mission. “I’m getting married on Saturday and I’m going to have a cheese centrepiece,” Incolano says. “I saw on Instagram that they had lots of great butters and I thought it could be a little something extra for my guests, a little surprise.” The reputation of French butter is also attracting visitors who work professionally with food. “I know that there’s some of the best butter in France, but I’ve never tried any,” says Aleksandr Balaban, a 31-year-old Estonian chef. “I work in Norway, they really like salted butter, and my friend asked me to bring him some French butter as well.” Leo says the secret to eating fatty butter is to be like Parisians: walk a lot and practise moderation. “We don’t go beyond four tartines a day,” he says, referring to a French open sandwich. Tasting butter works like tasting wine, he says: “You have to grab your spoon, you put it on your palate, on your tongue, it has to melt a little bit, and then the flavours are going to start coming one by one.” He adds: “The Italians choose olive oil, we choose butter. We learn how to master it.” Butter is the fat of France’s dairy-producing north and west, and of Brittany above all. Salt preserved it before refrigeration, and Brittany’s exemption from the gabelle, France’s old salt tax, kept Breton butter salted as much of the country’s butter went unsalted. The legacy lives on in crêpes, salted caramel and kouign-amann, whose Breton name means “butter cake”. Leo’s producers churn higher-fat milk from selected cows; an extra 2 or 3 percentage points, he says, “really makes a huge difference”. The tiny shop has drawn crowds through social media and now has a staff of four. “From day one, it’s been crazy,” Leo says. “Most people come in wanting to try one or two butters, they end up trying 25 butters because they’re just so curious.” Next up: a croissant-flavoured butter, and perhaps violet. “This is limitless,” Leo says.

title: 23,000 bronzes, 14 years, 60 volumes: how China is mapping lost heritage held abroad
description: Peking University study reveals seven times more relics held overseas than previously thought, creating crucial evidence trail.
content: In the quiet of a Peking University research room, shelves groan under the weight of 60 thick volumes. Stacked, they stand taller than an average human. Inside their pages lie the details of more than 23,000 ancient Chinese bronze vessels, weapons, chariot fittings and ritual objects that left China’s shores long ago and now sit in museums, private collections and auction houses across nearly 30 countries. Published in April by Shanghai Classics Publishing House, the Collection of Chinese Bronzes in Overseas Collections is the product of a painstaking 14-year investigation. It is also something more: an assembled toolkit for China’s intensifying campaign to reclaim cultural heritage lost to war, looting and smuggling, as well as an assertion of Beijing’s ambition to shape the global rules of repatriation. “To create archives for the cultural relics, to preserve evidence for history,” said lead editor and historian Zhu Fenghan, a Boya Chair Professor at Peking University, capturing the project’s dual purpose in an article in the People’s Daily last week. “We need to get a clear picture of our family assets and gain a more complete and comprehensive understanding of Chinese bronzes held overseas,” Zhu was quoted as saying. The effort began in 2012, when China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA) asked Peking University to map the true scale of the country’s dispersed bronzes, prompting a scholarly odyssey. Team members criss-crossed more than 10 countries to visit more than 260 institutions, scan rare catalogues, trawl auction records and photograph objects that had rarely, if ever, been systematically recorded by Chinese researchers. They returned with a massive trove of data, including about a terabyte of documents and 200 gigabytes of images. Earlier estimates had put the overseas number of bronzes at around 3,000 pieces. The new catalogue estimates more than seven times that figure. The team created an “identity document” for each piece or relic, Zhu told reporters at the work’s launch in Shanghai in April. Each entry functions like a personal file, containing high-resolution photos, measurements, inscriptions, where they were found, if known, transmission history and current locations. Nearly 300 types of bronzes appear, from celebrated ritual vessels to weapons, tools, lamps and northern-style pieces long sidelined in Western catalogues. Of the total, 3,462 carry inscriptions that reflect the politics, rituals and daily concerns of early Chinese states. Bronzes occupy a special place in China’s historical imagination. They were the physical embodiment of royal power and the ritual order that held society together. The earliest written use of the term Zhongguo (often translated as Middle Kingdom) on the Western Zhou He Zun artefact; the legendary Nine Tripods, or ding in Chinese; and enduring phrases such as “one word carries the weight of nine ding” all speak to their enduring symbolic force. From the late Qing dynasty to the mid-20th century, large numbers left China amid political chaos, wartime plunder and the activities of dealers who built efficient supply chains feeding Western museums and collectors. Only a minority of the objects now catalogued carry clear records of being exported legally or given as a diplomatic gift. China has reclaimed a measure of narrative control, regardless of where the objects currently sit Wang Wen, dean, Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University One emblematic case is the complete Western Zhou banjin altar set – a table and matching wine vessels – excavated in Baoji, Shaanxi, and once owned by the late-Qing official Duanfang. It was sold by his descendants and is now a star attraction at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. It is the most intact surviving set of its kind. Stories like this, repeated across the volumes, turn abstract loss into concrete, documented histories. China has stepped up the pace of recovery. During the 14th five-year plan period (2021–2025), some 35 batches totalling 537 lost relics and artworks were returned to China. Among them was the Western Zhou bronze ritual vessel Feng Xingshu Gui, Old Summer Palace columns and volumes of the Warring States-era Zidanku Silk Manuscripts, according to the NCHA. Early last year, US authorities handed back 41 items, including bronzes. Earlier, the swift recovery of a bronze group from a Tokyo auction in 2019 showed how legal, diplomatic and investigative tools could be combined to dramatic effect. Beijing has signed agreements with dozens of countries, co-authored the Qingdao Proposal on colonial-era cultural property, and taken a leadership role in Unesco heritage frameworks. Meanwhile, Washington’s withdrawal from the UN organisation will take effect at the end of this year. For legal scholars, the new catalogue directly addresses the biggest practical obstacle to further returns: the missing “chain of evidence”. “Recovering cultural relics lost overseas first requires a clear inventory of what was taken illegally,” said Huo Zhengxin, a professor at the China University of Political Science and Law. “This archive of bronzes is an important part of taking stock of our family assets. Bronzes hold exceptional value for an ancient civilisation, which is why documenting them matters so much.” He argues that the early return of illegally exported objects is a core element of cultural sovereignty. “Claims alone are not enough; evidence is required. This project clarifies the full chain of how these bronzes left China, and provides the foundation for future repatriation efforts.” Legal barriers remained, he said, but painstaking provenance work, thanks to the Chinese research teams and the cooperation with foreign institutions, was slowly closing the factual gaps. Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University, places the project in a broader cultural frame as modern losses have left Chinese scholarship with incomplete archives and broken research chains. By surveying more than 260 institutions and documenting 23,000 objects, the team had continued the unfinished work of earlier generations of scholars while rebuilding an evidentiary base for recovery claims, he said. The catalogue is an exercise in cultural confidence and sovereignty, according to Wang. He said Western scholars had for decades largely controlled the naming, dating and interpretation of overseas Chinese bronzes, and the Chinese team had revisited those judgments from the perspective of the civilisation that produced them, restoring ritual and historical meanings that had been obscured. According to Wang, the resulting archives prove that the Chinese cultural lineage was never severed by physical dispersal. For Chinese communities worldwide, the volumes turned scattered objects into a shared point of reference – a collective reminder that “lost cultural relics remain treasures of Chinese civilisation”, he said. “In practical terms, the right to archive, interpret and speak for one’s own heritage lies at the heart of cultural sovereignty. By producing an independent, systematic record, China has reclaimed a measure of narrative control, regardless of where the objects currently sit.” Wang said the detailed histories of how the artefacts were moved had also provided concrete evidence for future negotiations, strengthening Beijing’s hand in the evolving global conversation over looted and displaced heritage. The 60 volumes will not, by themselves, bring every bronze home. Full recovery of the estimated millions of Chinese relics that remain abroad remains a generational task. Yet, analysts say that by turning once-shadowy objects into documented cultural assets, the project supplies both scholarly scaffolding and diplomatic ammunition.

title: Not a token effort: beer meets artificial intelligence at bar in China’s capital
description: The AGI Bar in Beijing’s Zhongguancun tech hub offers free tokens to customers who order a drink.
content: Drinks, music, vibes … what else can a bar offer to attract customers? One in China’s capital, Beijing, is betting on unlimited access to artificial intelligence models. The AGI Bar in the Zhongguancun tech hub, known as China’s Silicon Valley, was packed with laptop-using customers on a recent night. One of the first things many did after ordering a drink was to connect to the in-house Wi-fi and configure an AI agent to access the free tokens the bar provides. Manager Yang Yuan said the bar, which opened in June last year, offered customers free tokens for any AI model as long as they ordered a drink and installed a plug-in on their laptop to access the bar’s AI agent. It offers more than a dozen drinks, with a glass of its bestselling AGI beer priced at just 9.9 yuan (US$1.47). The bar also runs DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally on two Nvidia DGX Spark computers, allowing customers to access the model without charge. When asked how many tokens the bar consumed each month, Yang declined to provide an exact figure, saying the costs were covered by the bar’s owner. Named after artificial general intelligence, a theoretical development that would see AI match or surpass human capabilities, the bar’s walls are covered with logos and merchandise from major Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba Group Holding and Tencent Holdings. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Close to the offices of several leading Chinese AI companies including Moonshot AI and DeepSeek, as well as the prestigious Tsinghua and Peking universities, the bar has become a meeting point for developers and AI enthusiasts, with events ranging from vibe-coding meet-ups to offline sessions hosted by AI professionals. The combination of drinks, coding tools and developer events has given the place a role that goes beyond that of a conventional bar. “Since we launched the free token offer, many AI enthusiasts and people working in the industry have come here specifically because of it,” Yang said. In a posting on the Dazhong Dianping restaurant review site in March, one customer described it as “a bar with futuristic vibes” that was a “prime example of the fusion of beverages and AI”.

title: China football bosses deny U23 coach Antonio Puche faces axe after Asian Games win or lose
description: Rumours swirl over Antonio Puche’s future, but officials hint that bigger things lie ahead for successful Spaniard.
content: China football officials have rushed to quash online rumours that men’s under-23 head coach Antonio Puche will be axed after the Asian Games no matter what his side does in Japan next month. Responding to rumours that the Spaniard would not have his contract renewed, officials from the Chinese Football Association (CFA) said that was “false information”, and hinted that he may be handed a bigger role. Speculation over Puche’s future came soon after former China men’s captain Li Weifeng used the sacking of Bora Milutinovic, who was fired immediately after leading the team to its only World Cup, as an example of the way unqualified officials were ruining football in the country. Puche is currently preparing a squad largely made up of U23 players, with some over-aged members allowed, for the Games in Nagoya. “The association fully affirmed the contributions of Antonio’s team in cultivating China’s national youth teams, steadily improving the team’s strength, and leading the U23 national men’s football team to win the runner-up title in the Asian Cup this year, achieving a historic breakthrough,” the CFA said in a statement. “Any online rumours about ‘not renewing the contract, changing coaches, and temporary personnel changes’ are all malicious speculations and do not reflect the actual situation.” The CFA statement added that it had a good relationship with Puche and his coaching staff, noted the remarkable work done by the 54-year-old, who coached the country’s U20 team from 2022 to 2023. “In accordance with the association’s requirements for building a ‘grand national team system’ … coaching teams that have met performance expectations, demonstrated effective management, and received positive assessments from experts and the public will have the opportunity to transition to coaching other national-level squads upon the conclusion of their current assignments,” the statement said. It finished by saying preparations for qualifying for the 2028 Olympics would begin immediately after the Asian Games. In January, Puche’s team famously beat Australia in the group phase and did not concede a goal en route to the AFC U23 Asian Cup final, but were thrashed 4-0 by Japan in Jeddah. Despite the loss, the results in Saudi Arabia marked a significant improvement for the U23 team, whose previous best result was finishing sixth in 2018. The team failed to reach the main draw in 2020 and 2022. In the Asian Games, the men’s football event runs from September 15 to October 3, with China in Group B alongside the United Arab Emirates, Iran and North Korea. The top two teams from the four groups advance to the knockout stages. Hong Kong have been placed in Group A, alongside the hosts, Thailand, and Kyrgyzstan. While the CFA has not set any performance targets for the regional Games, media reports suggested that Puche’s team aim to reach at least the quarter-finals, with the Spanish coach asking his team to “play their own style and showcase the level of the Asian Cup performance”.

title: Furore grows as Venezuela defends US oil deal with Trump
description: The agreement, which critics call an abdication of sovereignty, risks becoming a political liability for interim leader Rodriguez.
content: Venezuelan hardliners and opposition forces alike criticised acting president Delcy Rodriguez for agreeing to grant the US exclusive access to the country’s valuable oil resources. She may be betting that the deal with US President Donald Trump is her ticket to a tighter grip on power. One potential advantage for Rodriguez is if the deal to give the US majority control over 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan crude hems in the Trump administration’s incentive to press for swift election. “I think it can benefit Delcy to the extent that it reinforces Trump’s commitment to working with her and thus probably diminishes incentives to move quickly to a new vote,” said Risa Grais-Targow, Latin America director at Eurasia Group. That “is precisely why the opposition is so upset”, she said. Rodriguez defended the deal in televised comments on Saturday, saying it would bring prosperity and jobs to Venezuela. The agreement is expected to grant the nation around US$19 in profit per barrel of oil produced, she said. With decades of anti-US nationalism at her back, there is also the risk that the deal backfires into a political liability. Supporters of Chavismo, the political movement founded by the late president Hugo Chavez and built in part around state control of Venezuela’s oil, have their own reasons to be angry with Rodriguez. Both strands of criticism played out on social media immediately after the announcement in Washington late on Friday. Some commenters accused Rodriguez of giving away the country’s oil, while others questioned why neither Trump nor Rodriguez paired the economic agreement with commitments on election or a democratic transition. “But it’s also politically challenging for Delcy given sensitivities around resource nationalism and the perception that she’s betraying Chavismo’s principles, giving away valuable resources,” Grais-Targow said. The agreement was negotiated without the involvement of Venezuela’s opposition, according to people familiar with the matter. Maria Corina Machado, the most prominent opposition leader, was not involved in the discussions, they said. During Venezuela’s 2024 presidential campaign, it was Rodriguez – then allied with former president Nicolas Maduro – who accused Machado of taking orders from “masters” in the US and seeking the presidency so she could hand over Venezuela’s oil. Now Rodriguez is facing similar attacks. Hardline Chavistas reacted angrily to Friday’s announcement, according to text message discussions shared by participants, questioning its legality and describing it in social media posts as an abdication of sovereignty. Some said Venezuela had effectively been forced to give away oil under US threat. It is a sensitive moment for Rodriguez, whose popularity has slid in polls after what was perceived as a slow government response to two deadly earthquakes that killed more than 6,500 people in June. That could complicate her efforts to balance an increasingly close relationship with Washington against a political movement built for decades around resource nationalism and resistance to US influence. Until now, Trump’s enormous leverage over Rodriguez could be viewed as a tool to extract political concessions from her government. Negotiations have recently begun producing tangible results, including the National Assembly’s initial approval of a US-backed overhaul of the process for selecting Supreme Court justices. The oil agreement opens the door to a different scenario in which US companies, investors and eventually the government in Washington develop an economic interest in the stability provided by Rodriguez, political analyst Benigno Alarcon said. As US companies commit billions of dollars to Venezuela, Alarcon said, the US may gradually move from favouring “transition with stability” towards prioritising “stability that preserves the option of transition”. Some members of Machado’s party are already questioning whether any agreement signed by Rodriguez would survive a future political transition. “Anything Delcy Rodriguez has signed has no validity whatsoever,” said Jose Amalio Graterol, a member of Machado’s Vente party. “She may have signed it with Donald Trump, but it will never be valid because she lacks original legitimacy.” Francisco Monaldi, director of Latin American energy policy at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy in Houston, questioned the economic terms disclosed by Rodriguez and called the lack of transparency surrounding Venezuela’s oil policy “very alarming”. The US$209 billion in taxes she said the projects would generate amounts to roughly US$3.20 for each of the 65 billion barrels covered by the agreement, Monaldi said. If that figure represents nominal revenue collected over the life of the projects, its present value would be even smaller, he said. Rodriguez may face an even more uncomfortable challenge from Chavismo supporters. Former left-wing lawmaker Willian Rodriguez invoked Chavez, who died in 2013, in a sharp critique of the deal with Trump. “The oil is ours, and with it we recovered our homeland,” he quoted Chavez as saying. “This agreement does exactly the opposite: it gives away the homeland and renounces our national destiny,” Rodriguez said. “There’s no way to dress it up.”

title: Hong Kong police investigate viral video of dog trapped in running washing machine
description: Two Instagram stories circulating on Saturday show animal tumbling inside front-loading washing machine drum as it fills with water.
content: Hong Kong police are investigating social media videos that appear to show a dog trapped inside a running washing machine. Police confirmed on Sunday that they had received a report the previous night about a video circulating on a social media platform showing a suspect treating a dog inappropriately. Two Instagram stories that surfaced on Saturday night show a dog inside a front-loading washing machine, tumbling with the drum as the machine runs through its cycles and fills with water. One of the videos is captioned “OMG”, which is short for “Oh My God”. The original account and videos had been removed as of Sunday. Following an initial investigation, the case has been referred to the Mong Kok district animal crime team. No arrests have been made. Under Hong Kong’s Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance, anyone convicted of cruelty to an animal faces a maximum penalty of HK$200,000 (US$25,500) and three years in prison upon summary conviction.

title: Can Southeast Asian artists replicate K-pop’s global success with SEA-pop?
description: Even as more regional artists are performing overseas, they should not blindly copy the K-pop playbook, industry observers say.
content: At Tower Records in Tokyo’s Shibuya district earlier this month, fans flocked to a pop-up store set up for Filipino boy band SB19, buying exclusive merchandise including limited-edition CDs, T-shirts, stickers and phone straps. Due to overwhelming demand, the store ran for an additional five days. During the band’s tour in Japan, SB19 met fans in Yokohama and performed in Tokyo and Osaka during the Summer Sonic festival. Another Philippine act, the eight-member girl group BINI, made their debut at the music event. In July, SB19 performed at the Lollapalooza festival in Chicago for the first time, while in April, they played a sold-out home concert in the city of Paranaque, drawing almost 100,000 local and international fans, including from Hong Kong, Taiwan, Australia and Germany. BINI also made history in April during their inaugural performance at the Coachella festival in California. Their successes appear to reflect a wider trend in Southeast Asia’s entertainment scene, with more regional acts outperforming Western artists and K-pop bands on streaming charts. Data compiled by French music analytics platform Soundcharts found that the share of Indonesian artists on Spotify’s weekly top 10 soared from 39 per cent to 97 per cent in Indonesia between 2021 and the first half of 2026. The streaming data for the Philippines and Thailand were similar, rising from 31 per cent to 81 per cent and 71 per cent to 76 per cent, respectively, over the same period. An independent data analyst based in Japan, who goes by the moniker Tsurezure Lab and studies music streaming trends across global markets, tracked weekly aggregations of Spotify daily Top 50 charts in Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore from February 2023 to May 2026 and noticed strong intra-regional support in these countries based on linguistic and cultural similarities. The analyst, who asked to remain anonymous, cited the popularity of Indonesian pop on Malaysian charts and an increase in Mandopop streams in Singapore. As Southeast Asian music lovers continue to support local artists, industry players are betting that they can go further. This has raised a tantalising prospect: can artists from Southeast Asia replicate the success of their K-pop peers such as BTS and Blackpink and achieve global success? SEAPop rising Fans have coined a term to reflect the region’s growing music scene: SEA-pop, or Southeast Asian pop. “In recent years, SEA-pop has become increasingly vibrant, with local music dominating the charts like never before,” said Roslyn Pineda, Hong Kong-based president of Sony Music Publishing in Asia. “In the Philippines, where I entered the music industry in 2001, international music was once the trend. Today, original Pilipino music claims 81 per cent of Spotify’s weekly top 10, marking a significant shift in audience preferences,” she said. Thailand has also seen the market share of Thai pop, or T-pop, rise since 2023, according to Pineda. For Darynaufal Mulyaman, an assistant professor of international relations at Universitas Kristen Indonesia, whose research focuses on pop culture, soft power and Korean studies, SEA-pop mirrors the broader region. SEA-pop’s diversity reflected “Asean’s founding paradox playing out at the level of culture”, he said. Exemplifying the “unity in diversity” ethos of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the region’s historically, culturally, linguistically and religiously diverse countries had been “held together by consensus diplomacy rather than a shared identity”, Mulyaman said. “SEA-pop is reproducing that exact structure in music,” he said, with the genre united less by a common sound than a “shared posture towards the outside world, whether K-pop or Western pop”. Regional acts have infused local cultures, such as indigenous instruments, into their songs to reinforce their national identity, moving away from the K-pop model that initially inspired Southeast Asian music industry players who aimed to reproduce the success of the Hallyu phenomenon, or Korean wave. Nonetheless, K-pop’s practice of recruiting and training foreign talent had allowed performers, choreographers and producers from Southeast Asia to learn the ropes of the Korean entertainment industry and adapt lessons for their home countries, Mulyaman said. Going global However, exporting SEA-pop to the world would require more than strong streaming numbers. For now, the growth of the regional artists is driven largely by themselves, music labels and fans, rather than a comprehensive national-level approach that has turned K-pop into an entertainment powerhouse. As such, SEA-pop is “riding on a much thinner institutional floor than K-pop had, and thinner than what the EU’s cultural-integration machinery gives European pop”, according to Mulyaman. While South Korea had integrated pop culture into its export strategy, the region did not have a similar strategy or a government agency that could help accelerate SEA-pop’s global growth, Mulyaman said. “Asean’s cohesion is institutionally shallower than the EU’s by design,” he added, referring to the bloc’s traditional non-interference approach. Nonetheless, there is scope for Southeast Asia to unite and promote its soft power as it would entail less sensitivity than working together on security or economic issues, according to Mulyaman. Pineda identifies several regional artists that have what it takes to make it big on the global stage. “Acts like SB19 and BINI from the Philippines, Dolla from Malaysia, No Na from Indonesia, and 4EVE from Thailand are already making strides on international festival stages, producing bilingual tracks, dominating playlists, and showcasing high-fashion aesthetics,” Pineda said. According to Tsurezure Lab, the Philippines has the strongest potential to achieve international success due to the widespread use of English in its music and Filipino artists such as BINI and SB19 having a strong global following. The analyst said that Thailand ranked second, with the likes of singer Jeff Satur and Thai hip-hop artists having a growing global fanbase. However, the large populations in some Southeast Asian countries could ironically work against the goal of exporting SEA-pop to the rest of the world. Last year, fans in Indonesia and the Philippines generated 23.2 billion streams and 14.2 billion streams, respectively, on the Spotify Top 200. Both countries have a much larger population than South Korea, whose K-pop industry has to look outward to expand beyond its domestic market. “When home is that big and that loyal, the pressure to export is far weaker. Southeast Asia’s local music strength is, so far, largely inward-facing,” Tsurezure Lab said. For Southeast Asian artists to go global, they can look at following the K-pop template in which Korean acts initially targeted attracting more fans in Japan and China before they achieved wider success in the US and beyond, the analyst added. However, regional artists should establish their own identity instead of blindly copying their K-pop counterparts, according to industry observers. Mulyaman warned that if Southeast Asian artists were to become K-pop “derivative products”, they would “stop being SEA-pop”. Pineda said there was no need for Southeast Asian artists to “mimic K-pop” even as they learned from its success. “The expansion beyond their home bases is already under way. Achieving a global breakout hit and sustaining international fandom engagement is not far-fetched. It could be just around the corner.”

title: ‘Lone perpetrator’ Swiss man arrested after deadly shooting at rave
description: The rare shooting has left an Italian woman dead and five others injured in Aarau.
content: Zurich, Aug 31, 2026 (AFP) -A 43-year-old Swiss man was arrested on Monday on “strong suspicion” of being behind a rare deadly gun attack at a rave in Switzerland, police said. Gunfire erupted in the early hours of Sunday morning as an annual rave was winding down at the racecourse in Aarau, capital of Switzerland’s northern canton of Aargau. The attack triggered an international manhunt for the shooter, who left an Italian woman dead and wounded five others, some seriously. “A 43-year-old Swiss man was apprehended shortly before 1am on Monday (7am Hong Kong time),” Aargau police said in a statement. “The man was subsequently arrested on strong suspicion of having committed the crime. Investigations into the exact sequence of events, the background, and the possible motive are currently under way. “At this stage, it is believed a lone perpetrator was involved.” The shooting, which sent party-goers running for cover, is a rare event in the Alpine nation, despite widespread gun ownership. The last major shooting occurred in 2001, when 14 members of the parliament and local government of the canton of Zug, near Lucerne, were killed by a gunman who then took his own life. According to local media, shots were fired before 3am near the Aarauer Rave, an annual techno party attended by some 3,500 people at the Aarau racetrack from Saturday afternoon to Sunday morning. “A 22-year-old woman died of her injuries at the scene,” local police announced on social media. “Four men and one woman, aged between 24 and 27, were taken to hospital. They are suffering from injuries ranging from minor to serious.” Italy’s government said the killed woman was Italian, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni naming her as Maria Spinelli. Italy’s foreign ministry said two other Italians were lightly injured in the shooting. Officials from its embassy in Switzerland went to the scene “to closely follow the investigation”, the ministry added. All of the victims were Swiss residents, police said. Aargau cantonal police commander Michael Leupold said investigators had found evidence of two different calibres, from a pistol or submachine gun, and an assault rifle. He said the shots had been fired from two locations, at the rave itself and from next to a trailer park. Leupold said police were working on three hypotheses: “The first is a terrorist attack, the second a mass killing, and the third a simple criminal act, the motive for which remains unknown”. With the German border just a few dozen kilometres away, the investigation is being carried out in cooperation with Freiburg police, the DPA agency reported. Media reports said an army helicopter was deployed in the cantonal capital, Aargau, as well as numerous police officers, rescuers and medical teams. Witnesses told Blick newspaper that shots were fired at about 2.30am while the rave was still taking place. Initially, they were believed to be fireworks but one witness reported “shots fired in bursts”. Many people sheltered in a nearby gymnasium for safety. Swiss DJ Tekibo, who performed at the rave, wrote on social media that he was physically unharmed but deeply affected by the tragedy, in which he said he had lost a friend. “Techno and raves are supposed to be spaces of freedom and safety, never places where something like this happens,” he said, calling the events “absolutely heartbreaking”. A resident in Aarau posted a video on social media showing deserted streets and what sounded like several gunshots in the background. The Aargau cantonal police urged people to stay away from the area but asked for video recordings or photos from the rave. Army reservists in Switzerland are allowed to keep their weapons, but not ammunition, at home. As a result, weapons are widespread but with no federal register it is difficult to know exactly how many. According to the Geneva-based research centre Small Arms Survey, civilians had more than 2.3 million firearms in 2017 – nearly three for every 10 inhabitants. That made Switzerland the 16th country in the world in terms of weapons per capita.

title: Could joint oil and gas projects help ease Beijing and Manila’s South China Sea tensions?
description: China and the Philippines could build trust by cooperating in ‘low-sensitivity’ areas such as energy and the environment, analysts say.
content: China and the Philippines have been urged to resume joint South China Sea energy exploration as a way of easing tensions in the disputed waters. A joint report by Chinese and Philippine analysts also said the two countries should work together in other “low-sensitivity” areas such as marine environmental protection and combating crime at sea. The report, published on Monday by the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies think tank, said the relationship between the two countries was at a “rather sensitive and critical crossroads”. “Joint oil and gas exploration in the South China Sea by China and the Philippines could serve as a feasible early-harvest project,” the report said. “This would not only alleviate or even solve the Philippines’ energy needs and reduce the escalation of tensions between the two sides due to unilateral actions, thus contributing to regional security and stability, but also help resolve the lack of trust and confidence between the two sides due to the asymmetry in their military and economic strength.” The report also argued that Beijing and Manila should identify and pursue economic projects that served their shared interests and had low security implications as a way of building trust. Earlier this month, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr said there was a “distinct possibility” of undertaking joint oil and gas exploration with China, adding that he hoped to “reset” relations between the two countries. In March, Marcos declared a national energy emergency in the wake of the US-Israeli attack on Iran. Although Beijing and Manila signed a memorandum of understanding on oil and gas cooperation in 2018, little progress has been made since then. Their long-running territorial dispute in the South China Sea continues to overshadow the relationship, with regular clashes between their respective coastguards at disputed features such as Scarborough Shoal – called Huangyan Island by China – and the Second Thomas Shoal. The two countries have also clashed over the recent arrests of dozens of Chinese steel workers in the Philippines. The Philippine constitution says the state must retain full control over natural resources, but the report argued this did not eliminate the scope for joint oil and gas exploration in the disputed areas. “China and the Philippines can undertake the necessary and comprehensive institutional design for how future cooperation should be conducted and how fairness and justice can be promoted in the process of structuring such cooperation, so as to avoid differences and conflicts arising from the asymmetry in their respective strengths and their sovereignty disputes, which could trigger unnecessary confrontation,” it said. In 2005, the two countries signed an agreement with Vietnam to conduct seismic surveys in the South China Sea, but despite hopes that this might pave the way for further joint developments, the deal expired in 2008 and follow-up efforts did not get off the ground. According to the report, Anna Rosario Malindog-Uy, vice-president of the Manila-based Asian Century Philippines Strategic Studies Institute, said legal and political differences did not have to be “absolute obstacles” to economic cooperation, pointing to Beijing’s “pragmatic arrangements” with two rival South China Sea claimants, Malaysia and Vietnam. The report also said marine environmental protection was the area with “the greatest potential for cooperation”, arguing it was “characterised by low political sensitivity, a high degree of consensus and practical feasibility”. The authors – including Li Kaisheng, Zhou Shixin, Xue Chen and Zhang Qiyue, from the Shanghai think tank, as well as Lucio Blanco Pitlo, president of the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies – suggested that the two countries could resume joint scientific expeditions to monitor marine ecosystems, coral reefs and pollution.

title: Will Hong Kong see fewer creditor-led commercial property sales as assets stabilise?
description: City’s office and retail property segments have been mired in a multi-year slump that has triggered loan defaults.
content: Financial distress in Hong Kong’s commercial property market has moderated but not been completely eliminated, analysts say, with highly leveraged asset owners still expected to find refinancing their loans a challenge. The city’s office and retail property segments have been mired in a multi-year slump, with new supply outstripping demand in recent years as consumption slowed and interest rates surged, triggering loan defaults. “We do not expect defaults will increase noticeably from this time point, with transaction activity remaining relatively resilient, and much of the valuation correction has already been reflected in pricing,” said Thomas Chak, head of capital markets and investment services at Colliers Hong Kong. “Banks, however, continue to release distressed assets, and mortgagee sales remain an important source of transaction activity in order to recover cash and take advantage of the relatively more liquid market this year.” Savills said lower local interest rates had reduced debt-servicing pressure as the one-month Hong Kong interbank offered rate (Hibor) was about 2.6 per cent by the middle of this August, implying an effective funding cost of about 4.1 per cent to 5.1 per cent, compared with 7 to 8 per cent at end of 2023. In the first half of the year, Hong Kong saw HK$22.3 billion (US$2.84 billion) worth of non-residential property transactions above HK$50 million, up 120 per cent from the same period last year, with offices accounting for more than two-thirds or HK$15.1 billion, Savills added. Some of the office disposals involved receivers, banks, end users or strategic buyers, including the sale of 299 Queen’s Road Central. The 25-storey tower was taken over by Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (Macau), which appointed receiver Kroll to market the property for sale. Land Registry records show the building was sold in May for HK$611.4 million to New Success Holdings, whose directors are local investors. The deal represented a roughly 70 per cent discount to the HK$2.1 billion paid for the property in 2018. Another receiver-led sale was the One Bedford Place deal. The office building in Tai Kok Tsui was acquired by Singapore-based Wee Hur Holdings for HK$748.8 million for conversion into student accommodation. “The starting point remains challenging,” said Jack Tong, director of research and consultancy at Savills Hong Kong. “Around HK$200 billion of non-performing property loans are estimated to be in the system and around HK$20 billion of assets is in receivership, and distressed resales have generally cleared at discounts of 35 per cent to 56 per cent.” Those figures suggested that lower financing costs were providing breathing space for some borrowers, he added, but they did not resolve the refinancing problem for owners with high leverage, weak rental cash flow or substantial valuation shortfalls. The prevailing risk was “more asset-specific”, Tong said, because prime and well-positioned assets owned by financially stable groups should face a more manageable environment, while secondary offices, older retail properties and industrial assets with weaker leasing fundamentals remained exposed to refinancing pressure and possible creditor action. It would be premature to say that the concerns were overblown from a capital-markets perspective Jack Tong, Savills Hong Kong The improved outlook for the state of the city’s commercial property sector is underpinned by the easing in Hibor, which is used to price many mortgage loans, as well as Hong Kong’s improved economic prospects. In the first half of the year, prime office space recorded a positive net take-up of 600,000 sq ft, helping the overall office vacancy rate to edge down from 15.2 per cent in the first quarter to 14.8 per cent in the second quarter, Tong said. That had somewhat eased fears about the adverse impact of the Iran war and the risk of a potential interest rate increase in the coming months, he added. “Nevertheless, it would be premature to say that the concerns were overblown from a capital-markets perspective,” Tong said. “Office yields of roughly 3.5 per cent to 4.6 per cent remain low compared with Hong Kong borrowing costs of around 4.1 per cent to 5.1 per cent, leaving many locally financed office acquisitions negative-carry on a pure yield basis.” Tong said buying interest was largely concentrated among cash-rich purchasers, end users, buyers with alternative funding sources, and investors pursuing repositioning, conversion or longer-term capital-value opportunities – not buyers relying solely on current income yield. Oscar Chan, head of capital markets at JLL, said stability in commercial real estate would “vary by asset type” in the coming year. “Grade B en-bloc commercial buildings with potential for conversion into student accommodation could attract investors if priced appropriately,” Chan said. “Meanwhile, end users are actively seeking distressed office space, and retail properties with quality tenants offering yields above 6 per cent continue to draw long-term investors.” Savills’ Tong also predicted “divergence”, with “prime, supply-constrained and conversion-led assets” likely to outperform, while “secondary offices and properties exposed to substantial new supply will remain under pressure”. Colliers’ Chak said mortgagee sales and capital-loss disposals would remain part of the market landscape, particularly among secondary assets, noncore locations and owners facing refinancing pressures.

title: Even in the fertility heartland, China can’t stop its birth rate from falling
description: Economic pressure is outweighing traditional value of having large families in the Chaoshan area of eastern Guangdong.
content: Few places in China have held on to the ideal of big families as stubbornly as the people of the Teochew homeland, also known in Chinese as Chaoshan. The coastal region of eastern Guangdong – encompassing the cities of Chaozhou, Shantou and Jieyang and serving as the setting for the hit indie film Dear You – has long been known for its strong family ties and close-knit clans, with ancestral halls central to village life, and strong networks of siblings that serve as a safety net for family businesses, entrepreneurial endeavours and a far-flung overseas diaspora. That tradition has helped make Guangdong province China’s biggest source of newborns. The area recorded 1 million births last year, roughly one in eight of all births nationwide, with a birth rate of 7.82 per 1,000 people, well above the national rate of 5.63 per 1,000 people, according to official statistics. Yet even in this family-first heartland, the birth rate is falling fast. In Shantou, the local birth rate fell from 13.2 per 1,000 in 2021 to 7.89 in 2025, matching the provincial average. In nearby Jieyang, the rate declined from 16.2 in 2019 to 9.35 in 2025, a drop of about 40 per cent in six years. For Chaoshan’s younger generation, the region’s traditional preference for big families is increasingly running up against the realities of modern life. Both residents and demographers say that without stronger economic support and new measures to encourage births, those traditions may not be enough to keep the region’s fertility rate above the national trend for much longer. “If I could afford it, I would have three children,” said Sherry Chen, 32, a Chaozhou native. She says there are advantages to having more siblings, including better support for ageing parents and lifelong companionship. But among her peers back home, having only two children is increasingly common due to finances, she said. “Better-off Chaoshan residents in their 30s are still keen to have three or even four children. The old logic still works, if you have the money.” Under China’s one-child policy, which began in 1979 and ended in 2016, larger families were rare due to strict fines for additional births, though exceptions existed for parents without siblings who wished to have a second child, as well as for “daughter-only” couples in certain rural areas. The prevalence of multiple children in Chaoshan stemmed from a mix of exploiting policy loopholes and a willingness to pay penalties. Li Xian, a married mother of two from Shantou in her late 30s, sees this generational divide within her own family. Her father was one of eight siblings, but two children have become the norm for her generation. She said one of her younger brothers stayed in their hometown, where he married and had two children and has plans for a third, backed by housing provided by his parents and lower living costs in the area. Another brother moved to Guangzhou for work and chose to remain single due to the cost of living for urban families. “He thinks living on his own means far less money stress,” Li said. That trade-off is increasingly visible across China. China’s marriage registrations fell 7.5 per cent year on year to nearly 3.28 million in the first half of 2026, a drop of 264,000 from the previous year, according to data released by the Ministry of Civil Affairs earlier this month. Ren Zeping, a high-profile Chinese economist, recently highlighted that the unmarried rate for men aged 30 to 34 had reached nearly 28 per cent, driven by the rising cost of living and housing prices. Ren warned on his social media account on August 23 that China’s marriage market faced pressure from people marrying later, an increase in divorce and a growing pool of unmarried people, particularly men in their early 30s. For Li and Chen, the weakening of clan networks was continuing to reshape family planning decisions. Villages and clans once offered not just a social identity but practical financial backing, with youth returning to their hometowns for traditional customs that helped to reinforce clan-based business networks and systems built on shared capital, credit-sharing and mutual investment. “The village used to be a shared economic unit,” Li said. “Now people earn their livelihoods independently outside the village and even Chaoshan. Clan rituals are transitioning from a necessity to an optional tradition.” “For centuries, people here valued big families as a way to maintain our clan roots, overseas ties, family businesses, and local networks,” Li added. Yet, as she observed, even the thousand-year-old, deeply entrenched traditions are no match for the harsh financial realities facing the younger generation. “Now, city living and financial pressure are simply eroding those traditional values. Without strong policy support, urbanisation and financial stress will inevitably drag our birth rate down to match the rest of the country.”

title: Northern Metropolis ‘large-scale land disposal’ a win-win, Paul Chan says
description: Finance chief says megaproject’s success depends on attracting high-value industries and firms, with market forces steered into industrial development.
content: Fast-tracking the Northern Metropolis through a “large-scale land disposal” scheme underscores the government’s push to integrate technology, industry and talent while accelerating Hong Kong’s economic restructuring, the finance chief has said. In a blog post on Sunday, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said the megaproject’s success hinged on attracting “high-value-added, high-potential industries and high-quality companies to take root”, requiring market forces to be directed into industrial development. “We are building a diverse and powerful momentum for the ‘integrated development of technology, industry and talent’,” Chan said. “The government has set a clear vision, formulated long-term planning, and removed barriers, while the market has made investments, guided industries and conducted commercial operations. “This chain connecting land, capital, and industry will accelerate the reshaping of Hong Kong’s economic and industrial structure.” Chan’s remarks followed the recent award of the first pilot area under the “large-scale land disposal” scheme to a consortium of six companies, including mainland Chinese state-owned firms and a local developer. The 10.5-hectare (25.9 acres) development project in Hung Shui Kiu forms part of the 30,000-hectare Northern Metropolis near the city’s border with the mainland, which is set to be transformed into an economic powerhouse and housing hub. Chan said authorities had placed “greater emphasis on whether the bidders could introduce strategic industries, create jobs, and drive the development of industrial chains” during the tender evaluation. “We ensured that the successful bidder is not merely engaged in real estate development but is a long-term strategic partner with comprehensive strengths and a track record in development,” he said. Chan added that the “large-scale land disposal” project – which requires the winning bidder to develop commercially viable land alongside sites earmarked for public facilities – could leverage the private sector’s flexibility, market sensitivity, professional knowledge and experience while reducing the government’s cash outlay, describing it as a win-win approach. He noted that the government had been actively raising funds for the metropolis through the bond market, adding that surging demand for Hong Kong bonds amid geopolitical tensions provided ample room to finance the megaproject using market resources. Chan also emphasised that the ultimate success of the metropolis would rest on developing its innovation and technology sector, relying on the government’s investment arm, the Hong Kong Investment Corporation, and Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks to support and guide key industries and start-ups. Separately, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said that expanding storage capacity and developing gold refining industries were central to the city’s ambitions to become a trading hub for the precious metal. Hong Kong launched trial operations for its central gold clearing and settlement system in July, alongside the initial phase of Delivery Connect – a joint initiative with the Shanghai Gold Exchange to enable seamless cross-border physical gold settlement and delivery. “The clearing system is just one part of the value chain. The government has [expanded] gold vaults at the airport, while the market has responded with some financial institutions saying they want to build their own storage,” Hui told a radio programme. “Another important element is refining … Many overseas refiners are now actively looking to set up operations in Hong Kong, or some have already established a presence.” Addressing Hong Kong’s aim of tapping into the lucrative Islamic finance market, Hui said both sides had to deepen collaboration. He noted that Hong Kong’s gold market could better respond to demand from Islamic markets. He said the city could consider issuing yuan-denominated Islamic bonds to diversify its product suite.

title: Opinion | Singapore’s blueprint for economic success: plan, but be prepared to adapt
description: External shocks and changing domestic conditions often render plans unfeasible, so being agile is a better policy.
content: In the discussion on Hong Kong’s first ever five-year plan, much ink has been spilled on the merits of a planned economy. The most recent example of this was Anthony Rowley’s commentary that cited Singapore as an example of a highly successful planned economy. Unfortunately, he misrepresents what planning in Singapore is about. There are lessons that Hong Kong can draw from how the Singapore government navigated a changing environment – but not the ones Rowley highlights. It is quite understandable why an observer would view Singapore as a planned economy. After all, signs of order are all around. Nearly 80 per cent of Singaporeans live in public housing; the city is well-designed, green, and manicured. Clearly, this is a city that has been meticulously planned and engineered for decades. Above all, Singapore’s politics is carefully managed by a ruling party that has been in power since 1959, and political dissent is often constrained by a paternalistic state. But the idea of the Singapore economy as a top-down, dirigiste and planned one is a caricature at best. While various government agencies in Singapore engage in planning (loosely defined), the city state has never had five or 10-year plans, nor set production targets the way the Eastern bloc countries and China did. Policies, not plans Singapore’s first finance minister and deputy prime minister Goh Keng Swee was openly disdainful of socialist planning, saying that “planning as we know it has a limited value. Economic policy is more important”. In economic policy, perhaps the most important difference between the Singapore economy and Hong Kong’s is the role of the state in industrial development. Since the establishment of the Economic Development Board (EDB) in 1961, the Singapore state has promoted manufacturing as one of the key engines of the economy. Even today, manufacturing output comprises an astonishing 19 per cent of Singapore’s GDP, compared with less than 1 per cent in Hong Kong. The EDB – or any other economic agency – has never produced five-year plans, so that cannot be the reason for Singapore’s success in industrialisation and industrial upgrading. But thanks to industrial policy, Singapore is a key node in global value chains in various high value-added industries such as electronics, petrochemicals, precision engineering, and pharmaceuticals and biotech to name a few. The lesson from Singapore here is that five-year plans are much less important than specific policies that drive industrial diversification and upgrading. A plan is simply a declaration of intent; whether that intent becomes reality depends on the right policies being formulated and how they are implemented. It is also quite common for governments to come up with bold visions and ambitious intents; what is much rarer is the capacity to execute change effectively. With industrial policy, this means ensuring sound macroeconomic fundamentals and having the right microeconomic tools – such as tax incentives, foreign labour allowances, vocational training and worker upgrading programmes – to develop the desired industries. But none of this was static or unchanging: external shocks and changing domestic conditions often necessitated changes to Singapore’s economic policies in ways that no five-year plan can foresee. Quick to adapt A second common error is to mistake the precision of the plan for its validity or quality. Even in a free-market economy like Hong Kong’s, there is a fascination bordering on obsession with setting precise targets or key performance indicators (KPIs) for government. The logic is that since much of what government does not lend itself easily to market metrics, targets or KPIs impose the necessary discipline on government. This obsession is not always healthy. A target may be very precise, but it could also measure the wrong thing. This is not to diminish the value of planning, but to emphasise the importance of adapting quickly to changing conditions. Being large bureaucracies, governments are often creatures of habit; their behaviours do not change quickly or easily even when circumstances require them to do so. You just start it and hope for the best Goh Keng Swee, Singapore’s first finance minister When asked in 1992 if he had started out with a master plan in mind, Goh replied: “I had no initial vision. You just start it and hope for the best.” In many respects, Singapore’s economic success was the result of constant adaptation and improvisation. For example, Singapore’s original economic plan was import-substitution industrialisation. This was one of the motivations for Singapore to join the newly established Malaysian federation in 1963 – to create a common market. When Singapore separated from Malaysia in 1965, the plan was clearly no longer workable. Singapore adapted quickly and embraced export-oriented industrialisation, laying the foundations for the highly globalised economy it became a decade or so later. Another example of adaptation was the practice of adjusting Central Provident Fund (CPF) contribution rates as a macroeconomic stabilisation tool. Singapore has, on various occasions, adjusted employer contribution rates in response to changes in macroeconomic conditions – lowering them to maintain cost competitiveness when faced with negative demand shocks, and raising them to deal with wage and inflation pressures. Pay attention to process Finally, the real value of a plan lies in the process rather than the plan itself. A five-year plan is limited in at least two ways. First, the relatively short time horizon means that it is almost inevitable that the plan would be a collection of (achievable) goals that the various parts of the government have already set for themselves. It is unlikely to contain much that departs from existing priorities. Second, because the emphasis of a five-year plan is to come up with specific deliverables, it is unlikely to catalyse a creative (re-)imagination of the future. Five-year plans are usually linear extrapolations of present trends, with targets adjusted marginally upwards to reflect the government’s enthusiasm in new areas – such as artificial intelligence. Governments often overestimate their ability to change things in the short term but underestimate it over the long term. This bias informs Singapore’s approach to planning. Because much of what a government does on a routine basis is short term, the two main forms of planning that the Singapore government undertakes adopt a much longer time horizon. The emphasis is also on long-term strategy rather than near-term deliverables. In city planning, for instance, the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s concept plan is reviewed once every decade and covers a time horizon of 50 years. Meanwhile, its master plan guides the city’s physical development over the next 10 to 15 years. Since the turn of the century, the city state has also embraced scenario planning as a way of thinking (creatively) about the future. Unlike five-year plans, the main goal of scenario planning is not to come up with a single plan for government with specific goals, targets or KPIs. Neither is scenario planning meant to produce predictions or forecasts.
