Instead, it is to generate distinct, plausible stories about the future (even if they seem improbable), question long-held assumptions, and surface the challenges and opportunities in the various scenarios. Unlike five-year plans that are based on a particular view of the future, scenario planning is a much more divergent process that aims to anticipate various possible futures. More recently, the Singapore government has expanded its capabilities in what it calls “futures thinking”. It set up a Centre for Strategic Futures about a decade ago to “build a strategically agile public service ready to manage a complex and fast-changing environment”. The centre’s logo, with a black swan embedded, reflects its ambition to develop the government’s foresight and its ability to adapt. This idea of planning as thinking creatively about the future is about as far as one can get from the world of five-year plans.

title: How a Hong Kong psychiatrist with a taste for NSFW art built a gallery for the ‘unsuitable’
description: Dr Brian Ip set up Kabinett in Wong Chuk Hang to show inspiring works by female and LGBTQ artists – works he can’t hang in his office.
content: Dr Brian Ip Pak-in’s Kabinett art space taps into the look and feel of a Scandinavian cabin, complete with pine panels and floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking green hills. It acts as a fast-acting dose of Nordic tranquillity. But the practising psychiatrist did not design it with wellness retreats in mind, and neither is this an art therapy centre. Instead, Kabinett is where he can freely show pieces that he deems not safe for work, or, at least, not safe for his work. “I have to be very careful with what I show in the clinic and avoid anything that’s potentially triggering. The art on the clinic walls tends to be abstract,” he says of his practice in Melbourne Plaza, in Hong Kong’s Central neighbourhood, where his father, also a psychiatrist, has his office, too. “I love Miriam Cahn, but her portraits would be most unsuitable there.” He named Kabinett after the miniature solo or thematic exhibition sections at Art Basel fairs. The three-year-old Wong Chuk Hang space is partly a personal escape from the intense negativity that he, like other psychiatrists, absorbs daily. Ip, who believes collectors have the responsibility to share works rather than hide them away in storerooms, also intends Kabinett to be a semi-public platform for thematic exhibitions based on the psychologically complex creations he loves. His taste in art has been affected by the most significant loss of his life. In 2019, when he was 32, his mother died. Her death profoundly shaped his views on transience – reflected in the philosophy of Kabinett – and solidified his dedication to female artists with strong messages; they now make up more than half of his 200-piece collection. Shortly before his mother died, Ip bought his first painting by Cahn, a Swiss artist whose deeply unsettling, anti-war piece F*** abstraction! (2022) required the intervention of the French government regarding its display in Paris in 2023. The painting Ip acquired – zeige!, 2. + 29.12.13 + 19.04.18 – is a portrait of a female nude with a baby in her left arm and her right hand, looking bloody, tucked between her thighs. The artwork, which Ip has hung in his bedroom, symbolises strength emerging from darkness. “My mother loved the Miriam Cahn,” he says, adding that he sees zeige!, 2. + 29.12.13 + 19.04.18 as a painting about motherly love, an image of a woman protecting her newborn from the red, menacing surroundings. “Every time I look at the painting, I feel a sense of admiration for her and relief,” he says. “My mother’s passing taught me the biggest lesson in my life. She was my best friend, and we talked about everything. Despite her absence, her influence on me keeps evolving.” I personally feel these artists have inspired me tremendously through their innovative ideas and fearlessness Dr Brian Ip The instinct to collect, Ip says, was probably inherited from his father, who is a well-known antiquities collector. Since his mother’s death, Ip has also developed a deep connection with the work of Sonia Gomes, a Brazilian artist whose 2004 mixed-media sculpture Memory, housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, incorporates fabric donated by her friends who had lost their mothers. “This work allows me to see the shape and beauty of grief,” says Ip, who included Gomes’ Untitled (Tear series) (2024) in an earlier exhibition of female artists called “Pillars of Heaven”. The late Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama is another favourite, as is the Swiss painter Caroline Bachmann. Ip also has various works by Ren Hang, the openly gay mainland Chinese poet-photographer who committed suicide in 2017 aged 29 after a long struggle with depression. “I never did an estimate of how many works by LGBTQ artists I have in my collection,” Ip says, “but I personally feel these artists have inspired me tremendously through their innovative ideas and fearlessness.” Kabinett’s latest exhibition, “Una Corda”, runs until April 2027 and explores the intersection of landscapes and psychological states. Visitors are encouraged to sit on the gallery’s pine bench and feel the vibrations of Debussy’s Estampes while viewing Bachmann’s shifting, surrealist paintings of Lake Geneva, or Hong Kong artist Dony Cheng Hung’s mysterious monochrome forest, and works by Kong Lingnan, Patricia Leite and Joani Tremblay. In an idiosyncratic touch, Ip has left some works from “Pillars of Heaven” by the floor-to-ceiling windows, creating a dialogue of contrasts with the new show. These works include Hong Kong artist Leelee Chan’s Moth (Silver Cloud) (2023), which is made from salvaged industrial materials and natural magnesium and actively alters its appearance as it reacts to light and air. Nearby sits Liao Wen’s Stare (2022), an armless wooden female figure bending downward with a resin patch resembling a vagina at eye level for those sitting on the wooden benches. Its in-your-face placement may seem jarring against the spiritual vibe of “Una Corda”, but Ip views the sculpture as a compatible embodiment of quiet power and inner strength. Ultimately, Kabinett is an intimate salon where its owner’s personality looms large: a contemplative space indicative of a psychiatrist’s deep interest in human feelings and fragility. Kabinett does not have regular opening hours. Visits are by invitation.

title: Finland says it ‘makes no sense’ for Russia to risk attack on a Nato nation
description: President Stubb said he did not believe Moscow was ⁠in a position ⁠to go to war with the military alliance.
content: Finland’s President Alexander Stubb said he did not believe ⁠Russia would risk ⁠an attack against a Nato country, ⁠telling Germany’s Bild newspaper it would “make no sense” to test the resolve of the alliance. Western officials have warned of a growing risk of Russian hybrid operations, including cyberattacks, against European countries potentially leading to a direct ‌confrontation with the Nato alliance. German officials have said they assess Russia would be in a position to attack a Nato country by 2029. “If anyone has a crystal ball like that – that’s great. I simply see neither evidence nor facts to support it,” he told Bild in an interview published on Saturday, adding he did ⁠not believe that Russia “would ever want to attack Nato, the world’s most powerful military alliance”. Stubb, whose ‌country joined Nato in 2023, abandoning its previous policy of neutrality following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine a year earlier, said the alliance had ‌to be prepared for any scenario but he did not believe Moscow was ⁠in a position ⁠to go to war with Nato. He said Nato’s strength in conventional weapons, missiles and nuclear weapons was too ‌strong to attack, adding that he had intelligence information to back his assessment. “It makes no sense for any power in ‌the ‌world to test the resolve of this alliance,” Stubb said. He said Russia was trying ‌to spread alarm in Europe through its information war. But it was currently taking unsustainable losses ⁠in Ukraine, losing around 30,000-35,000 troops a month and recruiting only around 27,000. “So they have ⁠fewer and fewer soldiers in an increasingly complex situation,” he said. “I simply cannot see them suddenly being able to mobilise forces for two fronts.” Stubb said Ukraine ‌was in a stronger ‌position than at any time during the war and it was vital that Europe continued to support Kyiv. “We must understand – you in Germany and we in Finland – that Ukraine is the best security guarantee we have against Russia. If Ukraine loses, we lose,” he said.

title: China-Nepal floods: 261 foreigners listed missing in Tibet, cyber police target rumours
description: Nepalese and Indians account for more than half of nationals from 23 countries missing after devastating glacier collapse four days ago.
content: China said on Sunday that 261 foreign citizens were missing after last week’s deadly floods along the border between its Tibet autonomous region and Nepal. The missing foreigners were from 23 different countries and included 104 Nepalese citizens, authorities in Tibet’s Gyirong county told reporters. Also unaccounted for are 49 people from India; 33 Latvians; 18 from the United States; 15 from Britain; six each from Canada and Australia; four from South Africa; three each from Malaysia, Germany and Russia; two from Ireland, Estonia, France, the Netherlands and New Zealand; and one each from Kazakhstan, Finland, Lithuania, Portugal, Ukraine, Spain and Hungary. China has so far confirmed 16 deaths after Wednesday’s glacier collapse, while 546 people are missing. In Nepal, at least 788 have been confirmed dead, with more than 2,500 still unaccounted for. Sunday’s list of missing foreigners was China’s first release of country-by-country details. Beijing added that it had notified the diplomatic missions of the countries concerned. Gyirong officials also said no foreign survivors were stranded in the area. The worst-affected areas remain on high alert even four days on, with Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority warning on Sunday of a fresh surge in water levels on the Bhote Koshi River. The increase was linked to a new barrier lake that had formed on the Lhende River, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi. Search and rescue crews, relief workers and local residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan districts were advised to exercise the utmost caution following the alert. China’s Ministry of Natural Resources told state broadcaster CCTV on Sunday that it had launched a comprehensive assessment of geological risks in the affected areas. More than 60 potential geological hazards had been identified, it said, with eight preliminarily classified as high-risk sites. Meanwhile, more Chinese tunnel rescue specialists have arrived in the capital Kathmandu to help Nepal’s search and rescue efforts, along with emergency aid kits that include tents, blankets, sleeping bags, food and medical equipment. Beijing also promised to provide funding and further supplies following a phone call between the two countries’ foreign ministers on Saturday. The Chinese embassy in Nepal said on Sunday that it had been working with the local authorities to evacuate 94 of its citizens. Meanwhile in China, cyber police have taken action against at least 11 individuals over spreading false information about the disaster on social media. The people involved spread what authorities described as fabricated or exaggerated casualty figures, “causing public panic”, or had made unverified claims about the cause of the disaster. Authorities in Tibet, Hunan, Inner Mongolia, Jiangxi and Chongqing have imposed administrative penalties on most of them. In one case, a 43-year-old woman in Hunan province voluntarily deleted her “speculative and misleading” comments about the cause of the disaster after local authorities investigated the matter, according to the Ministry of Public Security’s Cyberspace Security Bureau. She was formally reprimanded and signed a pledge to comply with online conduct regulations, the bureau said. Wednesday morning’s deadly disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse at Langtang Lirung on the Nepalese side of the border. Debris from the collapse then dropped around 1,200 metres (4,000 feet), creating a high-speed wall of ice and mud that travelled across the valley within minutes, obliterating everything within its path, including the Gyirong Port border crossing. Chinese authorities said the speed of the debris flow – crossing the entire valley to Gyirong Port in the space of about six or seven minutes – meant that residents had no time to flee. On Sunday, authorities in Tibet said the main threat to the rescue efforts remained a barrier lake that had formed about 13km (8 miles) from the border on the Nepalese side – although the risk of a total collapse was low as it was gradually draining away. At its peak, it contained more than 2.5 million cubic metres (88 million cubic feet) of water – the equivalent of 1,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Debris from the disaster also created two other dams along the Tsogyal River in Nepal, which are now being monitored by satellites and drones. CCTV reported that these included reconnaissance and heavy-lifting drones from the Ministry of Emergency Management’s “swift emergency response mechanism”. The mechanism was set up in 2010 with the aim of using a public-private partnership model to organise drone units to support disaster relief operations. On Saturday evening, the unit detected a landslide around 3km downstream from a third barrier lake – which had formed on the Purepuqiang River in southwest Tibet near the Nepal border – forcing emergency response teams near Gyirong Port to halt operations while they moved to a “safe location”. Beijing has set up two 24-hour English-language hotlines to help families seeking information about the missing: 0086-891-6817-165 and 0086-183-08026-705. Additional reporting by Meredith Chen

title: Legal battle over Hong Kong tycoon Lim Por-yen’s HK$2.9b estate set to rumble on
description: Lim’s estate appeals ruling voiding his 2004 will, which found the late tycoon lacked testamentary capacity and allowed his third family to inherit.
content: A 15-year legal battle over late tycoon Lim Por-yen’s HK$2.9 billion (US$371.8 million) estate is set to continue, with rival parties preparing for further legal action after a Hong Kong court ruled that his third wife and children were entitled to inherit part of his estate. Lim’s estate lodged an appeal after losing the legal battle last year, while Pearl Ling Meng-chu, daughter of Lim’s third wife, told the South China Morning Post that she had not ruled out taking further action. “She is reviewing all options available to her and the estate and is not ruling anything out,” Ling’s spokesman said. Ling, also known as Pearl Lam, is the daughter of the late tycoon, founder of the conglomerate Lai Sun Group, and his third wife, Koo Siu-ying. Lim’s estate asked the court to validate a will purportedly signed by the tycoon in December 2004. Ling and Koo were named as defendants in a probate lawsuit that began in 2011, after each lodged a caveat asserting an interest in the tycoon’s estate. Lawyers for Lim’s estate had assessed the value to be about HK$2.9 billion. Lim, a former chairman of local broadcaster ATV, purportedly left most of his assets to the wives and children from his first two marriages, excluding members of his third family, before he died in February 2005 at the age of 93. In a judgment handed down in April last year, then High Court judge Wilson Chan Ka-shun ruled in favour of Ling and Koo. He dismissed the estate’s application to validate the December 2004 will, citing the “highly suspicious circumstances” surrounding its execution. Chan invalidated the 2004 will after finding that Lim, who had severe dementia, lacked the mental capacity required to revoke a will he made in 1973. Under the 1973 will, Lim directed that his assets be divided into 12 equal shares and distributed among family members in varying proportions. A judgment handed down in July in separate litigation related to the probate case showed that Lim’s lawyers had appealed Chan’s April 2025 decision. They argued that it involved judicial plagiarism, inadequacy of reasons and factual findings concerning “testamentary capacity, knowledge and approval” at trial. Chief Justice Andrew Cheung Kui-nung said on July 27 that he had asked Chan to retire early after reprimanding him for repeated judicial plagiarism in judgments. Cheung said the series of incidents had undermined public confidence. Chan retired on July 31. No hearing date has been set for the probate appeal. An SCMP search found that a directions hearing in the appeal has been scheduled for November this year. In a separate judgment on costs in the lengthy probate lawsuit, handed down on July 17 this year, Chan found Peter Lam Kin-ngok, Lim’s second son, liable for the costs of the lawsuit, alongside the other plaintiffs. Chan said there was “no dispute” that Lam had funded the trial. He also said it was indisputable that Lam, the incumbent Lai Sun group chairman who also chairs the Tourism Board, stood to benefit from the litigation. “Importantly, he stood to receive a greater proportion of the estate than under previous wills,” Chan wrote. Separately, the judgment in litigation related to the probate case revealed that Ling lodged a caveat in June last year against Lim’s late second wife, U Po-chu. U, Peter Lam’s mother, is the executor of the 1973 will and had obtained a grant of probate to administer Lim’s estate. The SCMP has contacted Lam for comment.

title: Letters | Focusing on ‘bad’ dogs will not do Hong Kong any good
description: Readers discuss the state of Hong Kong’s animal laws, and whether a ‘no-kill’ mandate for animals is the most humane approach.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The occurrence of two canine incidents in the past week or so has placed mongrels at the centre of debates. This is not the first time we have had this conversation. In autumn 1971, a 10-year-old left her home on the Tsz Wan Shan Resettlement Estate and was later found lifeless at the foot of a hill. Echoing popular opinion and turning a deaf ear to a father’s suspicions that his child may have been murdered, the authorities concluded that she was mauled to death by seven guard dogs. All seven dogs were put down, notably much ahead of autopsy results and without a formal investigation. The unfortunate incident would soon be followed by the hardening of Hong Kong’s relationship to dogs. Along with a series of social reforms to make Hong Kong a more liveable city, an anti-dog campaign was launched to eradicate the dog “nuisance”. In 1974 alone, at least 15,000 dogs – many of which were mongrels – were destroyed. Fast forward to 2026, and we are seeing a near replay of events. A 60kg dog that killed two smaller dogs is temporarily safe from “humane” killing, yet the option to put it down remains open. Following the tragic death of a dog-loving citizen mauled by a mixed-breed dog suspected of having pit bull ancestry, some residents have turned to discussing the “beastly” nature of mongrel dogs. In strengthening Hong Kong’s animal laws, policymakers need to be aware that there is no one-size-fits-all fix to human-canine relations. We have to understand that not all dogs want to be “rescues”. No dog is a “good dog” all the time. No dog should be a “bad dog” for being stray, angry or mongrel. What makes one dog happy is not guaranteed to make another dog yap in joy. Boxing mongrels into the anthropocentric label of “bad” will not lead us to a sustainable and healthy coexistence with our canine residents. “Mongrel” is not a behavioural diagnosis, just as “rescue” is not a guarantee that a dog can safely enter every home or facility. We no longer live in the past. Stop flattening dogs into convenient labels. Catherine S. Chan, Department of History, Lingnan University ‘No-kill’ rhetoric doesn’t translate into safety for everyone The horrific death of a woman who was attacked and killed by a dog she was caring for is a devastating reminder of the harm that can be caused by “no-kill” propaganda. According to news reports, the dog involved was available for adoption despite needing training. A volunteer was reportedly paying for the dog to stay at the boarding and training facility where the victim worked until it could be placed in a home. As this sad case shows, not every animal can be rehomed safely. Shelters and volunteer adoption groups must prioritise public safety and animal welfare over padding their “live release” numbers. Adhering to a “no-kill” mandate can lead to dangerous or suffering animals being pushed through the system, with disastrous consequences. The deprivation of being warehoused in kennels for extended periods can cause psychological distress, leading even previously docile dogs to develop aggression. In constant confinement, dogs can start to display repetitive behaviour indicative of mental trauma, such as constant pacing, spinning in circles and chewing on cage bars. Others can become depressed and withdrawn, further reducing their chances of adoption. Cats fare little better. According to Peta’s research in the United States, some facilities instruct people to leave these domesticated animals on the streets, where they might suffer vehicle strikes, transmissible diseases, severe weather, predator attacks and intentional harm by people who consider them a nuisance. A humane sheltering system must not be guided by appealing-sounding slogans but by a determination to protect every animal from suffering, even when the best we can offer is a peaceful release from a world that has failed them. Instead of demonising humane euthanasia and the caring workers who perform it, communities must emphasise sterilisation, adoption and responsible guardianship. They must also support the open-admission shelters that make the most compassionate choice for every animal in need. Jason Baker, president, Peta Asia

title: Wife of British man who died after turbulence sues Singapore Airlines
description: ‘Nothing prepared me for hearing he had died. It was absolutely devastating,’ said Linda Kitchen, who broke her back during the 2024 incident.
content: The wife of a British passenger who died after severe turbulence struck Singapore Airlines (SIA) flight SQ321 in May 2024 has begun legal proceedings against the carrier in Britain, seeking damages after she suffered serious spinal injuries in the incident. Linda Kitchen, 74, broke her back during the flight and has begun High Court proceedings seeking damages to help her access specialist support for her recovery, the BBC reported. Her husband Geoff Kitchen, 73, had also died on the flight. Citing High Court papers, two claims were filed by the Kitchen family, The Independent reported – one by the widow and another brought by her on behalf of her husband’s estate. Court records also showed several other passengers taking legal action against SIA, including Bradley Richards, Jack Jenkins, Hannah Fullerton, Andrew Dawood, Bryan Matthews, and Pauline and Michael Rainey, according to The Independent. SIA on Saturday said it was unable to comment on matters which are before the courts. Kitchen and her husband were beginning a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when SQ321 encountered severe turbulence over Myanmar while flying from London to Singapore. Turbulence became so severe that she thought the aircraft was going down, the woman said, according to the BBC. Her husband fell on top of her during the incident, pinning her against a seat armrest before other passengers helped move him and a doctor performed CPR. She was taken to hospital in Bangkok, where she spent 10 days before being flown back to Bristol. She was also in hospital for about another week in Britain and required significant help after she was discharged, the BBC reported. Kitchen said she learned of her husband’s death two days after the incident. “Nothing prepared me for hearing he had died. It was absolutely devastating,” the BBC reported. She also told The Independent that she wanted to understand the circumstances surrounding her husband’s death. “I feel I owe it to him to at least get some answers,” she said. Anthe Korelidou, a specialist aviation lawyer representing Kitchen, said that the family still has questions about what happened and whether more could have been done to prevent their injuries. The family is awaiting a coroner’s inquest into Kitchen’s death, The Independent reported. Flight SQ321 was carrying 211 passengers and 18 crew members when it encountered severe turbulence over Myanmar on May 21, 2024. The Boeing 777-300ER was diverted to Bangkok, where it made an emergency landing so the injured could receive medical treatment. Kitchen died and dozens of others were hurt. A final report released by Singapore’s Transport Safety Investigation Bureau (TSIB) in May 2026 said Kitchen suffered heart failure and pulmonary oedema, which is a condition involving a build-up of fluid in the lungs. TSIB found that the turbulence was convectively induced and likely associated with a rapidly growing cloud capable of producing significant updrafts and downdrafts. The SQ321 pilots had seen no bad weather on their navigational displays in the minutes before the incident and visual checks indicated a clear flight path. Investigators concluded that it was likely the aircraft’s weather radar did not detect the bad weather before the turbulence struck, although the radar manufacturer said it found no evidence that the system had failed to detect and display weather during the flight. The seat belt sign had been switched on after the aircraft began experiencing turbulence, but severe turbulence struck just 17 seconds later, leaving no time for the flight crew to make a cabin announcement. Rapid changes in gravitational force sent some passengers who were not wearing seat belts airborne before they fell back down. Apart from Kitchen, 56 people suffered serious injuries and 23 had minor injuries, while 149 were uninjured. In June 2024, SIA offered US$10,000 to passengers who suffered minor injuries. Passengers with more serious injuries were invited to discuss compensation based on their individual circumstances and were offered an advance payment of US$25,000 to meet their immediate needs. SIA apologised following the incident and subsequently introduced several measures aimed at strengthening turbulence management. These included enhanced turbulence monitoring tools on crew tablets, updated guidance to flight crews on weather radar under-detection, refresher training for flight crews on turbulence management and in-flight procedures, and additional reminders for passengers to keep their seat belts fastened. This story was first published by CNA

title: Addisu Gobena shatters Sydney Marathon record, Jepchirchir takes women’s title
description: Addisu Gobena claims first World Marathon Major title, knocking almost 90 seconds off previous best time.
content: Ethiopia’s Addisu Gobena shattered the course record to win the Sydney Marathon on Sunday, while Kenyan world champion Peres Jepchirchir put in a commanding performance to claim the women’s title. Victory was the first in a World Marathon Major for 21-year-old Gobena, who came second last year, while Jepchirchir added to her previous triumphs in Boston, New York and London. Gobena made his move with little more than half-a-mile to go to power home four seconds clear of compatriot Chimdessa Debele Gudeta in two hours, four minutes and 42 seconds. Lesotho’s Tebello Ramakongoana was third. The dominant run shattered the course record by almost 90 seconds, with last year’s winner Hailemaryam Kiros dropping from the pace in the dying stages. “I am very happy,” said Gobena, who was a javelin thrower before transitioning to long-distance running, gaining international attention by winning the 2024 Dubai Marathon. “Last year I came second, I learnt from my mistake, and I went back home and I worked on my mistake to perform and break the record today.” The unstoppable Jepchirchir was in a league of her own, crossing the finish line in front of the Sydney Opera House in 2:18:31, nearly four minutes ahead of fellow Kenyan Irine Cheptai and Ethiopia’s Shure Demise Ware. “I was prepared, but I was not sure when I came here if I would win, so I’m so glad and I’m so happy,” Jepchirchir said. “It was so hilly. First half [of the race] was so tough, but the second was better at least. But it was not easy.” In the men’s race, the leading pack had thinned to 15 by the halfway mark, with Gobena, world champion Alphonce Simbu and Kiros among them. Dawit Wolde, Vincent Ngetich and Gobena all attempted breakaways, but they were reeled in by a pack reduced to seven with around four miles to go. It was still the same group at the 25-mile mark, before Gobena and Gudeta made their move, pulling clear with Gobena out-kicking his countryman in the final sprint. Kenya’s Priscah Cherono went out hard among the women, opening a 30-second gap by halfway. But the lead chasers, down to just Jepchirchir and Cheptai, caught the 46-year-old Kenyan with 18 miles gone. Jepchirchir and Cheptai eased clear and the relentless world champion then put her foot to the floor, finishing nine seconds off the course record set by Olympic champion Sifan Hassan in 2025. American Daniel Romanchuk won the men’s wheelchair race, while Switzerland’s Manuela Schar, a three-time Paralympic gold medal winner, took out the women’s. Around 40,000 runners, a record, competed over the picturesque 26.2-mile course through the city from North Sydney, over the Harbour Bridge to the finish line on the forecourt of the Opera House. The race was elevated last year to the seventh World Marathon Major, putting it on a par with London, Tokyo, Boston, Berlin, Chicago and New York in the elite global series.

title: Reviving Kuala Lumpur: can Malaysia modernise without pricing out its past?
description: Urban renewal aims to regenerate the capital’s historic core, but polish and authenticity don’t always share the same street.
content: A yellowing receipt, framed behind glass near the entrance of Abdul Razak Gold House, records an address that no longer officially exists: “63 Ampang Street, Kuala Lumpur (Malaya)”. The shop’s modern glass frontage, polished counters and gleaming bullion cases give little away about its history. But step inside and that simple receipt serves as a small window onto pre-independence Malaysia. For six decades, this family business has reinvented itself in step with the city around it. What began as a modest goldsmith’s counter beneath a row of old shophouses is now a brightly lit jewellery and bullion store. Today, skyscrapers and overhead train tracks loom over the capital’s commercial core, and many of the businesses along Lebuh Ampang – the modern name for Ampang Street – that the shop’s proprietor remembers from his childhood have long since vanished. Mohd Razalie Abdul Rasul, 37, is the newest custodian of Abdul Razak Gold House. He has expanded the business into bullion trading, bought the property next door and is, ultimately, preparing for a handover to the next generation. “My dad is still a mentor, but the way he thinks and I think is totally different,” he said. “We have to think very modern. We have to stay one step ahead.” Their family drama is a microcosm of the soul-searching currently sweeping Kuala Lumpur: how do you hold on to the past while still moving forward? Muddy origins Long before Malaysia existed as an independent nation, a small trading post emerged at the junction of the Klang and Gombak rivers. This geographic meeting point gave the future capital its name, which translates from Malay as “muddy confluence”. Today, those humble riverbank origins stand in sharp contrast with the towering glass and steel of the Petronas Twin Towers and Merdeka 118. Yet cradled beneath this hyper-modern skyline lies Kuala Lumpur’s historic heart. Here, amid old shophouses, traditional temples and bustling markets, the city’s earliest trading streets still endure, even as the tides of modern commerce have slowly drifted away from them. Reversing that decline is the aim of Warisan KL, a heritage-led regeneration programme working to restore landmarks, upgrade public spaces and improve transport links across the old city. Its ambition is to turn heritage into an economic asset without emptying it of the traders who make it feel authentic, or dressing it up as a backdrop for tourists rather than a place where people actually live and work. Tourist footfall is the wrong measure of success, according to Syed Redza Algadrie Syed Hassan, CEO of Prasarana Integrated Development (Pride), a government entity tasked with revitalising Malaysia’s urban public transport network. What mattered more was whether visitors lingered and spent money at local businesses, he said. “The discipline is to let commerce follow authenticity rather than replace it,” Syed Redza told This Week in Asia. “If you over-polish a heritage district, you risk removing the very qualities that made it distinctive and valuable in the first place.” Izwan Ibrahim, CEO of PNB Merdeka Ventures, which oversees the Merdeka 118 precinct, takes a similarly hard line on what counts as success. Growth that comes at the expense of the communities already living in a heritage enclave is not growth worth having, he argues – pointing to the restored Merdeka Stadium, which now hosts not only sports events but also concerts and community programmes, as a case in point. “It is not enough to restore heritage buildings or bring more visitors into an area if the surrounding community does not also see improvements in its everyday environment,” he said. Masjid Jamek, one of the city’s busiest transport interchanges, illustrates the approach: the station has been deliberately positioned as a gateway, funnelling commuters into the historic quarter around it rather than simply moving them through. Pride reports that its pilot projects in transport hubs have generated more than 624,000 social media impressions, while the digital heritage trails on its MyRapid PULSE app drew over 22,600 engagements in the first three months since launch. “The early signals are encouraging,” Syed Redza said. Heritage for show? Not everyone is convinced that physical improvements alone can revive a neighbourhood’s soul, however. “You can’t contract out authenticity or buy it through municipal budgets,” said Azry Bruce Aziz, a Kuala Lumpur-based independent history researcher. For him, what makes a place authentic has little to do with the buildings themselves and everything to do with their function. He points to the hardware stores and Chinese medicinal halls of Jalan Tun H.S. Lee, the gold and textile traders of Lebuh Ampang and the temples, grocers and eateries that still pull people into the city centre. “When planned regeneration focuses purely on surface makeovers, you end up with heritage for show,” he said, warning that “treating historic streets like a pretty backdrop for weekend photos” would only result in higher rents that “kick out the very shops that made the area real in the first place”. Azry is not opposed to the idea of regeneration. Better lighting, pavements, drainage and public space can make a district safer and more inviting, he says – provided the change does not come at the expense of the businesses that already operate there. What concerns him more is the inevitable ripple effects of rising property values, which incentivise landlords to swap out low-margin tenants such as repair shops, tailors and stationery stores for glossier, higher-rent lifestyle brands. “What planning should be doing instead is acting as a protective shield, instead of trying to invent fake charm,” he said. “Top-down planning only works when it protects the real community that’s already there.” Adapting to survive There is a compelling economic case for getting this right. Heritage-led regeneration is about more than just urban renewal or cultural preservation; it can drive tourism’s share of Malaysia’s gross domestic product beyond its current 15 per cent. The commercial returns on such projects tend to be modest, according to Yeah Kim Leng, director of Sunway University’s economic studies programme, but there are other cultural and heritage benefits that do not show up neatly on a balance sheet. “Integrating with local arts, crafts, food and entertainment will be important to maximise tourist spending along with enhancing visitors’ experiences and return visits,” Yeah said. He sees no tension between old landmarks and new ones: Merdeka 118 and the regeneration of Kuala Lumpur’s historic districts can complement each other, both attracting investment into hotels, restaurants, commercial property and transport infrastructure. True success, Yeah argues, is not measured by raw visitor numbers. Instead, it is found in the jobs created, the wages lifted and the living standards raised for everyone the work touches. Back on Lebuh Ampang, Razalie knows this balance all too well, without needing an economist to explain it to him. His family’s business has survived not by staying the same but by adapting – what it sells, how it sells and who it sells to – while holding onto something intangible that has not changed: the trust built up over generations of customers. He hopes his son will one day take the reins, even if he doubts the business will look anything like it does now under his management. “Nothing is going to be easy in the coming years,” Razalie said. “We have to stay one step ahead.”

title: Is Ulaanbaatar worth visiting? What to do in Mongolia’s capital – and beyond
description: From Buddhist temples and cashmere shopping in the city to the Gobi dunes and pristine western peaks, here is how to explore Mongolia.
content: A sprawling metropolis that is home to almost half of Mongolia’s population, Ulaanbaatar is not the most tourist-friendly city in the world. Mongolia’s capital is international travellers’ first point of entry into the country before they move on to the deserts, grasslands, steppes and mountains that make the nation such a popular destination among nature lovers. Most visitors to Mongolia are happy to spend a couple of days in town or skip the place altogether, but Ulaanbaatar still offers pockets of charm, especially in the summer months, when mild temperatures allow for leisurely walks in a place that is not necessarily pedestrian-friendly and lacks an easy-to-navigate transportation system. Where to stay For a city of such scale, Ulaanbaatar has surprisingly few high-end hotels. The most established and the only true luxury property is Shangri-La Ulaanbaatar, located in the heart of town and connected to Shangri-La Centre, a modern mall home to a few luxury boutiques, a great gym with an Olympic-size pool that hotel guests can access freely and plenty of eateries. Spanning 21 floors of a modern skyscraper, the hotel is popular with business travellers and tourists seeking convenience and all the trappings of a five-star property. Its well-appointed 290 guest rooms, familiar to those who have stayed at other Shangri-La properties in Asia, offer expansive views of the city’s concrete jungle and the surrounding mountains. Eateries include Hutong Restaurant and Naadam Bar & Restaurant, which come alive at night, when seemingly every expat and tourist in town shows up to enjoy a variety of dishes and drinks in a fun, happening atmosphere. What to eat Heavy on the meat, Mongolian cuisine relies on the country’s traditional herding culture. Mutton, lamb, beef and goat are popular on menus, as are hearty starches like savoury pastries and dumplings. For a great introduction to the local food, the Mongolian selection at Naadam Bar & Restaurant offers favourites such as beef or lamb tsuivan – chewy noodles with cucumber, carrot, onion and garlic – and mama’s khuushuur, deep-fried dough pastries filled with beef. More adventurous types can also order pan-fried beef liver with onion and mutton tail. The nearby Choijin Temple Restaurant is a great option for Mediterranean dishes with a Mongolian twist. For something more exclusive, those with the right connections can book a table at Highland Park, a private members’ club located at the foot of Bogd Mountain and housed in a sleek chalet with beautiful views of the city. What to do Because public transport is limited, the best way to explore Ulaanbaatar is to book a guided visit with operators such as Gobi Tours. They offer options ranging from day-long group tours to private, tailored visits that cover key sites in town and natural attractions on its outskirts. Ulaanbaatar is home to many Buddhist temples. If you only have time to go to one, the Choijin Lama Temple is very centrally located near the city’s main gathering spot, Sükhbaatar Square. Fans of Genghis Khan should check out the Chinggis Khaan National Museum, situated just off the square, and the Chinggis Khaan Statue Complex, the world’s biggest equestrian statue, which is a relatively short drive from the centre of town, depending on traffic. History buffs should also visit Bogd Khaan Palace Museum, an imperial residence known as “the winter palace of the Bogd Khaan”, a Mongolian king. Outdoorsy types have plenty to see and do in Gorkhi Terelj National Park, home to the very Instagrammable Turtle Rock and one of the country’s most beautiful temple complexes, Aryapala Temple, a Tibetan-style meditation retreat shaped like an elephant in a valley surrounded by mountains. Terelj offers activities such as horse or camel riding and falconry. A bit further from town but also worth exploring, Hustai National Park is a wonderful protected area, where you can admire Mongolia’s Przewalski’s horses (takhi) in the wild. Where to shop Cashmere is to Mongolia what maple syrup is to Canada, so to speak. The country is home to goats whose hair produces prized yarns from luxury brands such as Loro Piana. For something more affordable, you should check out Gobi Cashmere, which has plenty of branches in the city. At its two-storey boutique on Sükhbaatar Square, you can find basics such as crew neck or turtleneck sweaters and cosy blankets. Surprisingly, the brand also makes very cool cashmere shoes such as slip-ons and sneakers that may not be super practical in rainy weather but are fashionable and chic. Peace Avenue, one of the city’s main thoroughfares, is home to many souvenir shops selling everything from gold trinkets to sheep-shaped charms, as well as landmark destinations like the State Department Store. The mall, which isn’t actually state-owned, houses many international and local brands, including a branch of Michel Amazonka, one of the country’s top fashion labels. The brand famously designed uniforms for Mongolian athletes for the 2024 Paris Olympics, which drew a lot of attention on social media. If you’d like to bring back traditional food, you can’t go wrong with pine nuts from HushKhan. The ubiquitous chain makes hand-picked natural pine nuts and organic pine nut kernels, and also sells pine nut-derived products like pine nut oil, which you can use for cooking or drizzle over salads. Further afield If you decide to extend your trip, Mongolia offers extraordinary environmental diversity and unique experiences. Venturing beyond Ulaanbaatar and its immediate surroundings is an expedition in every sense of the word. Booking such excursions with a reputable provider is essential. Outside major hubs, much of the country lacks paved highways, public transport and cellular infrastructure – making independent travel dangerous and logistically impractical. These guided itineraries span a wide spectrum of comfort. Upscale operators offer well-appointed tourist camps with modern creature comforts and transport in luxury SUVs. On the rugged end, immersive homestays welcome you into traditional gers alongside nomadic host families – facilities here are basic, but the hospitality is warm and the experience delightfully authentic. Owing to Mongolia’s vastness, most travellers focus on a single region per trip. The central belt around Ulaanbaatar is lush, with rolling green steppes, roaming herds of livestock and smooth paved routes offering relatively easier access to ancient ruins. The north and west are a realm of jagged peaks above pristine alpine lakes, traditional eagle hunters and noticeably cooler climes even in peak summer. But it is the southern Gobi – often imagined as a boundless, endless expanse – that delivers Mongolia’s most dramatic variations. Beyond its famed sand dunes lie rich subregions featuring dramatic canyon walls, dinosaur fossil beds and otherworldly rock formations. The immense distances and complete absence of paved roads make for a profound escape from civilisation. Whichever direction you choose, Mongolia offers rare encounters with untouched terrain and unforgettable journeys. Additional contributions by Himanshu Bhandari

title: ‘Green miracle’: US teacher returns to China after 26 years to find donation grew into forest
description: ‘You gave the trees life and watched them grow, just as parents take pride in their children,’ says Sakolsky.
content: A retired American teacher has reunited with a Chinese farmer 26 years after their initial encounter, returning to the once-barren sandy landscape transformed by his generous donation into a lush green environment. In 1999, Ronald Sakolsky, now 67, was teaching English in Luoyang, Henan province, central-eastern China, when he discovered Inner Mongolian farmer Yin Yuzhen’s efforts to combat desertification. Inspired by her dedication, he donated US$5,000 to support her mission. The pair first met during a donation ceremony in the Mu Us Desert in 2000. Afterwards, Sakolsky returned to the US, while Yin used the funds to plant over 50,000 trees. Today, vegetation covers more than 80 per cent of the Mu Us Desert, which is one of China’s four major sandy regions. In May, Yin, now 60, reconnected with Sakolsky via video call and invited him back to China to witness the “green miracle” that his contribution had helped foster. Their long-anticipated reunion took place at Ordos Airport on August 23. Yin, with her signature long braid, broke down in tears as she embraced Sakolsky. She later recalled the tears “tasted sweet,” while Sakolsky expressed his gratitude to her and her husband, tears streaming down his own face. “I never thought I would see you again. That in itself is a miracle,” Sakolsky remarked. “It also shows that people from different cultures can keep their promises.” That evening, they explored the city and paused at a musical fountain as “See You Again” played in the background. After singing along, Sakolsky joyfully declared in Chinese: “I am back.” The following day, he admired the fruits and vegetables Yin had cultivated in the desert and visited her home, which had transformed tremendously since the humble mud-brick dwelling of decades before. “If you take care of the Earth, the Earth will reward you,” he observed, adding that after more than four decades of battling the desert, Yin “deserves the very best.” Together, they walked hand in hand into the government-designated “Sakolsky Forest,” where he embraced the trees and planted a friendship tree alongside Yin. “You gave the trees life and watched them grow, just as parents take pride in their children,” he told state-run English-language cable TV, CGTN. For Yin, however, the forest came with a personal cost. She reflected that decades spent nurturing trees had made her a devoted “mother” to the forest, but perhaps less so to her family. Driven by the belief that she would “rather die planting trees than be defeated by the sand,” Yin endured years of hardship alongside her son, who still helps tend the forest. Her commitment consumed so much of her life that she admitted she did not even know her grandchild’s age. Sakolsky sees Yin as the true driving force behind the green transformation. “More than 20 years ago, US$5,000 was equivalent to about 20 years of income for a Chinese farmer,” he pointed out. “She could have used it to improve her own life, but instead, she dedicated it to the trees. Very few people would do that.” He told the SCMP that before meeting Yin, he never considered himself an environmentalist and had minimal knowledge of desertification. Their friendship profoundly reshaped his perspective on humanity’s relationship with the planet. “We only have one Earth. If we don’t take care of her, she won’t take care of us.” After several days together, Sakolsky found that language increasingly felt unnecessary. He reflected that their bond was truly one of the heart. Yin noted another quiet connection: both kept phones filled with photographs of animals, a sign, in her eyes, of their shared deep affection for life. Before leaving the desert, Sakolsky collected a jar of sand to take home, seeing it as both a piece of the forest and a symbol of the ties between ordinary people in China and the US. Yin also presented him with a cross-stitch piece bearing the words “One Earth, One Dream,” along with a pair of handmade insoles embroidered with roses and blessings. During his trip to China, Sakolsky also visited Luoyang. His reunion with Yin resonated with the public. At the Inner Mongolia Museum, visitors quickly recognised and greeted him, as videos of the pair garnered over 120 million views on mainland social media within days. One commenter described their story as “a bond of trust that transcends time and distance,” adding: “Sakolsky sowed seeds of kindness, and Yin nurtured them over decades.” Another wrote: “I’ve followed this story for months, and it is heartening to see it come full circle. In the right hands, US$5,000 can change the world.”

title: Human-wildlife clashes on the rise in China’s Giant Panda National Park
description: Farmers on the giant nature reserve report rising concerns over damage to crops and livestock as well as attacks from wild animals.
content: Friction between humans and wild animals at China’s Giant Panda National Park intensified significantly over the past decade as conservation efforts expanded, a new study has found. Farmers reported increasing losses between 2015 and 2024, stemming from damage to property and crops as well as attacks on humans and livestock. The team behind the study said the issue had become the most prominent challenge facing the park’s administrators. The Giant Panda National Park covers 22,000 sq km (8,500 sq miles), 2½ times the size of Yellowstone in the United States, and officially opened in 2021. Spanning the provinces of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu, the park is now home to more than 1,300 wild giant pandas, 70 per cent of their total population. The park is also home to 8,000 other plant and animal species, including red pandas, deer, migratory birds, golden snub-nosed monkeys, snow leopards and takins. “The Giant Panda National Park reshaped local human-environment interactions, shifting traditional resource-dependence conflicts towards compound conflicts arising from institutional constraints and ecological restoration,” the team wrote in a paper published in the peer-reviewed Chinese-language journal Acta Ecologica Sinica last month. “Human-wildlife conflicts” are defined by the team as incidents that involve attacks on humans, damage to property and the impact on wild animals, including hunting and habitat encroachment. Researchers from Beijing Forestry University and the Shaanxi Academy of Governance said such incidents had “continuously intensified” over the study period, although there were fewer contests over the use of resources. National parks play a critical role in safeguarding global biodiversity, serving as safe havens for species threatened by habitat loss due to human activities. Over the past few decades, China has established dozens of giant panda reserves, setting aside vast tracts of land to safeguard the species after its numbers were depleted by deforestation, habitat loss and human activity. But the study says that when governments introduce protective measures, it can lead to increased tensions with the local community over the economic impact. If they also help increase the number of wild animals in the area, that can lead to more incidents involving humans and wildlife. The regional economy in the area covered by the park is mainly based on resource-dependent industries – such as agriculture, forestry, hydropower and mining. This meant, the researchers said, that local communities faced “varying degrees of conflict between protection and development”. This was “due to restrictions on resource collection, forestry regulations, insufficient alternative industries and the impact of wildlife activity”, they said. The paper used data from nearly 2,400 surveys of farming households in the Sichuan section of the park – which accounts for nearly 90 per cent of its area. The surveys, taken between 2015 and 2024, asked them to indicate the strength of their feelings about different issues on a scale of 0 to 3. They found that concerns about incidents involving wildlife had risen steadily over the period, from an average of 1.147 to 1.949. Meanwhile, the average financial cost to farmers from these incidents increased by 2.7 times. “Regarding human-wildlife conflict, the probability of low-level conflict decreased while the probability of high-level conflict increased,” the team said. They also found that resource-use conflicts – over issues such as collecting firewood and plants, logging, agricultural activity and grazing – had gradually fallen. Meanwhile, concern about industrial development conflicts – which covers restrictions on farmers’ economic activities – peaked in 2021 before dropping back to pre-park levels. Meanwhile, the average farmer’s revenue from ecotourism increased more than tenfold. The researchers also said that while the benefits of wildlife protection were shared, the costs were mainly borne by farmers. To tackle the problem, they called for a shift away from compensating farmers after their property was damaged – which can be a slow process – in favour of better preventive measures such as electronic fences, intelligent infrared monitoring and early warning systems.

title: JD.com’s US$1.3b expansion could test Hong Kong’s footfall-driven retail property model
description: Chinese e-commerce firm builds network of stores and warehouses that analysts say may reduce reliance on footfall for some retailers.
content: JD.com’s rapid expansion in Hong Kong could challenge the property model that has long made the city’s busiest streets and shopping centres its most valuable, analysts say. The Chinese e-commerce giant has invested more than HK$10 billion (US$1.3 billion) in Hong Kong property over the past two years, building a network of stores, warehouses and other assets that analysts said could reduce the importance of footfall for some retailers while increasing the value of logistics hubs and other strategically located sites. The investments are part of a broader push into Hong Kong by JD.com, which in June said it had invested HK$35 billion in the city across retail, logistics, technology and other businesses. For decades, Hong Kong property values have largely been driven by location: the more people passing through a street or shopping centre, the higher the rent it could command. If Hong Kong continues to reduce everything to land prices, rental values and footfall, then JD will be mistaken for just another big tenant Francis Neoton Cheung, Chief Executive’s Policy Unit Expert Group Analysts said JD.com was testing a different model. Its stores, warehouses and logistics facilities were valued not only for the income they generated, but also for their role in a wider network moving goods to customers. JD.com did not respond to a request for comment regarding the investment strategy. Francis Neoton Cheung, chairman of think tank Doctoral Exchange and a member of the Chief Executive’s Policy Unit Expert Group, called JD.com’s expansion a “stress test” for Hong Kong’s traditional property model. “If Hong Kong continues to reduce everything to land prices, rental values and footfall, then JD will be mistaken for just another big tenant,” Cheung said. JD.com’s purchases span warehouses, supermarkets, offices and student housing. The mix should be seen as part of the company’s logistics-driven strategy rather than a simple bet on property, analysts said. “I don’t see JD Property [the company’s infrastructure investment platform] as an important driver for JD.com,” said Chelsey Tam, senior equity analyst at Morningstar. The acquisitions suggested the group remained focused on its core e-commerce and logistics businesses, she added. Hong Kong is also part of subsidiary JD Logistics’ broader international expansion, with the company similarly building out infrastructure in overseas markets, including Europe. Yan Yuejin, vice-president of Shanghai E-house Real Estate Research Institute, said student housing illustrated the wider strategy. While it had no obvious link to JD.com’s core business, it could provide stable rental income and access to a concentrated customer base, he added, creating opportunities to bring the company’s retail, delivery and other services into a residential setting. Over time, logistics facilities and other income-producing assets could also be recycled into a real estate investment trust or another property platform, allowing JD.com to release capital while retaining access to infrastructure, Yan said. “Whether for its own use or operations, the fundamental purpose is to improve JD.com’s supply chain system in Hong Kong,” he said. The potential implications are most visible in retail. Hong Kong retailers were already facing pressure from residents spending across the border in mainland China and the continued growth of online shopping, while the value of some prime street shops had fallen sharply from their peak, according to market data. JD.com’s model separates functions traditionally concentrated in a single store. Yan said shops could serve as showrooms, experience centres or service points, while inventory and fulfilment are handled elsewhere. Retailers selling standardised goods may no longer need a prime location to store inventory, complete transactions and serve customers. “That could reduce the importance of footfall for some retail property,” Cheung of the Chief Executive’s Policy Unit Expert Group said. On the contrary, the same shift could raise the value of industrial and peripheral sites if they connect warehouses with customers and cross-border markets. Analysts cited JD.com’s latest involvement in Hung Shui Kiu as an example of how this model could extend beyond individual properties. The company has won Hong Kong’s first large-scale investment in the mega Northern Metropolis project, along with Sino Land and other state partners. JD Logistics plans to build an automated hub where robots sort goods and autonomous vehicles help move them through a network linking Hong Kong, the mainland and overseas markets. For JD.com, the value of the site lies not simply in what can be built on it, but in what can move through it. By bringing its own logistics flows and business activity, the company could create value in a peripheral area rather than simply paying a premium to locate where that value already existed, Cheung said. He added that the challenge for Hong Kong was whether its planning model could adapt to an economy increasingly organised around the movement of goods, data and services. “Hong Kong has to decide whether it wants to remain a consumer end point or become a supply chain node,” Cheung added.

title: Best Japanese pens, from Pilot Juice Gel to Uni-ball Jetstream and Zebra bLen
description: Our picks include award-winning smudge-resistant ballpoint, precise and smooth rollerball gel pens, and even an easy-to-grip mechanical pencil.
content:
Stationery is arguably very important – especially when it comes to the pen you write with. Whether you are composing an essay or filling out a form, a good pen is crucial to your experience, as it can improve your handwriting and reduce wrist fatigue.
Coming from someone who places great significance on the pens she uses, here are five considered to be the very best.
Pilot’s Juice+ Gel won in the ballpoint pen category at the 2026 Japanese stationery awards. The frosted barrel is an upgrade to the company’s Juice Up Gel Pen and is smooth despite its thin body and even slimmer, ultrafine 0.4mm tip. There is no scratchy feel here thanks to its gel ink glide.
This pen is a great overall pick, especially for heavy, daily use and when you want super neat handwriting. It comes in eight colours, including classic black, blue and red, as well as trendy sakura and mint.
Have you ever felt like you are losing control of your pen? Uni-ball’s classic Jetstream rollerball series, first introduced in 2006, is designed to prevent any wobbling so your handwriting is never crooked.
It also uses a low-viscosity, oil-based hybrid ink that does not smudge, so if you are writing an exam or scribbling in your diary, you’ll be safe from ink marking pages and hands.
Plenty of pens come with a clip, but not many stay secure once you attach them to a notebook or apparel. Zebra’s Sarasa Clip is widely praised for its sturdy binder clip, which makes it easy to slip the pen onto books of any thickness.
It’s a great choice if you work on the go or travel a lot. The pen also boasts a high-performance water-based pigment gel ink and a super comfortable rubber body for great grip. Just note that it is not completely water-resistant.
A pen you have to grip tightly is tiring – and painful. That discomfort affects your writing experience and can even lead to conditions like carpal tunnel. To solve this issue, Pilot’s Dr Grip G Spec is a mechanical pencil with a wide, soft rubber grip that allows you to relax and reduces hand fatigue.
Its Frost line features slightly rough “frosted” grips that ensure nothing slips. This is a great pen – or rather, mechanical pencil – for extended writing, such as multiple exams, revision sessions or lengthy essays.
Do you get distracted by rattling inside your pens? Zebra’s bLen ballpoint pen is engineered to eliminate pen tip vibrations and noise for a smooth, stress-free experience.
In addition, the bLen’s tip is brass-weighted, lowering the pen’s centre of gravity for greater stability. The bLen line won an iF Design Award in 2021 and is best for writing exams and for people who cannot stand the noise pens can make.

title: Being Chinese | A Chinese-American bride says yes to a lucky red dress
description: The cheongsam I wore to my wedding tea ceremony wasn’t just another outfit. It was my way of celebrating my father and my heritage.
content: My wedding plans didn’t begin with a red dress. The idea was to bring the wedding to my dad in his assisted-living facility – a nice one housed in a former hotel in suburban New York, complete with a cinema and a fancy swimming pool. My fiancé and I also made arrangements with the pastor, the DJ and the photographer, as well as a short and sweet guest list, while artificial intelligence (AI) helped us come up with a special cocktail for the occasion. With 60 days to go before the wedding, I thought we were in good shape. “What about the dress?” a good friend asked. What about it, indeed? I had bought not one but two white wedding dresses post-engagement. I’d been through the ritual of being fitted by both a boutique and a national bridal retail chain. I had photographic proof of myself ringing a bell and posing with a “I said yes to the dress!” sign. In Western tradition, white wedding dresses symbolise purity, while the gown has become the centrepiece of the event. Not only have romantic comedies such as 27 Dresses spotlighted the wedding gown, the search for it has also inspired reality television series like Say Yes to the Dress. But because I meant to pay tribute to my father on the big day, it slowly sparked a desire to incorporate our culture. The Chinese dress known as cheongsam or qipao surfaced from memory. I’d attended wedding banquets myself where the garment was a must-have. I dug up lovely photos of my aunt’s wedding in 1960s Hong Kong, showcasing the qipao she and her guests wore – as personalised as a fingerprint, not a single inch of extra fabric. The figure-hugging dress has long evolved from the loose Qing-dynasty robe, and red is traditionally worn for good fortune. As I did more homework, I learned that modern Chinese couples’ preferences have changed: brides increasingly prefer the white dress, or make sure they have two – one white, one red – for dual photo shoots and ceremonies. Suddenly, I wanted to have the best of both worlds too, and began frantically searching for a suitable red dress weeks shy of the wedding. I googled Shanghai Tang, but shook my head at the exorbitant prices. My cousin in Hong Kong WhatsApped me a more practical solution: a link to affordable ready-made dresses, which unfortunately weren’t meant for a Chinese-American with broader shoulders. An XXL dress sent from Hong Kong was a bit snug. I could only suck in, smile and thank my well-meaning relative. Ultimately, after more scrolling and swiping, I found the winner: a Chinese dress from a company run by a Caucasian couple out of Hawaii, who have given a modern-day twist to the cheongsam. Once this dress was settled, the rest of the wedding quickly fell into place. A traditional Chinese tea ceremony was cobbled together at the eleventh hour, with a tea set bought via Amazon. AI proved helpful in providing a script for the tea ceremony. What tea would be sipped and what song would be played during the ceremony? Well, we’d figure it out. Most guests … didn’t necessarily understand the intricacies behind the cheongsam and the tea ceremony. But they would remember the two dresses and the laughter. And what’s a wedding without lucky red envelopes? I filled ours with faux-ancient Chinese coins, red candy and fortune cookies. The menu consisting mostly of Italian-American dishes was offset by noodles for longevity and spring rolls symbolic of gold bars (and therefore wealth). As the finishing touch, my sister and I hung red-stringed jade ornaments on an arbour indoors, between clusters of sunflowers. Then it was time. The DJ cued us in with “Long-Jing Tea Garden”, an instrumental piece that reminded me of westernised Chinese restaurants. Cups of scalding tea were served to elders on both sides. The new mother-in-law was enthralled. “Mmm, this is good, it’s sweet,” she said. “Bottoms up!” my sister quipped, and the room exploded in laughter. Soon afterwards, I dashed into the gym and changed into bridal white. This gown was sequinned and pretty, but at the end of the day, I felt a deeper affinity for the red dress, knowing it was a connection to my father’s roots. And when it was my turn to speak, I had to reference the fortune cookie, an American invention forever associated with Chinese restaurants. Addressing my dad, I said: “Your story and journey have been an inspiration for so many. Like a fortune cookie, you open and speak and a gem of wisdom falls out.” For example, when I received some good news that dispelled a health scare, my dad told me to take it slow. I asked him what he meant and his answer stuck with me: “Spend your time on the things that appeal to you, and steer around the things that irritate you.” Most guests, including my husband’s Irish-American family, didn’t necessarily understand the intricacies behind the cheongsam and the tea ceremony. But they would remember the two dresses and the laughter. For myself the red dress wasn’t simply another outfit. It was a bridge to my father, his homeland and a part of myself I hadn’t realised I wanted to reclaim.

title: Former UN official says Hong Kong’s low fertility offers opportunity. Here’s how
description: Siddharth Chatterjee, former UN resident coordinator in China, outlines proposals to help Hong Kong earn ‘Child Friendly City’ status.
content: Hong Kong’s low fertility rate is an opportunity rather than a challenge and gives the city a chance to become a global leader in building a child-friendly environment, a former UN resident coordinator in China has said. Siddharth Chatterjee, who held the role from 2021 until March this year, said Hong Kong could create a “pioneering blueprint” for others to follow if it could earn the status of a “Child Friendly City” under a UN initiative. While most developing countries and territories are grappling with declining fertility rates, Hong Kong has one of the lowest in the world. Hong Kong recorded just 0.73 births per woman in 2025, with UN data showing the city had the second-lowest fertility rate among 236 jurisdictions, behind only Macau. Despite government support measures to incentivise families to have children, Hong Kong recorded fewer than 30,000 births in a year for the first time on record, according to its midyear population update published earlier in August. But in an interview with the South China Morning Post, Chatterjee, who now serves as an honorary adviser to the Hong Kong Committee for Unicef, said those very challenges could make the city a “model” for others to follow. “That actually presents an opportunity rather than a challenge for Hong Kong to really play a leadership role in transforming itself into a child-friendly city,” he said. “If Hong Kong can solve the ‘child-friendly’ equation within a hyper-dense, high-stress environment, we will create a pioneering blueprint. We can show the world how a mega-city can balance economic intensity with deep, structural compassion for its youngest citizens.” Unicef’s Child Friendly Cities Initiative was launched in 1996 and helps municipalities develop policies that support children’s rights in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. While more than 100 mainland Chinese cities and numerous others across the region are taking part in the initiative, Hong Kong has never formally incorporated it into the city’s governance framework. Unicef called on Hong Kong to include the goal of becoming China’s first internationally recognised Child Friendly City by 2030 in its first five-year plan. The international organisation’s suggestions also included providing at least 18 weeks of statutory maternity leave and introducing legislation to protect workplace breastfeeding rights. Chatterjee said Hong Kong shared the pressures of ultra-low fertility, high living costs and intense academic competition with other countries in the region. But he noted that Singapore, by comparison, had invested “more comprehensively and continuously” in family-support measures. In his National Day address earlier this month, Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong unveiled a series of new pro-family measures, including linking childcare leave to the number of children a parent has and providing up to S$62,000 (US$48,650) in financial support for every eligible child from birth to age 17. Chatterjee said Hong Kong’s “relative lag” was most visible in the “systematic integration of child rights across urban planning and daily policy”, the scale and accessibility of early childhood care, and the depth of mental-health services for children and adolescents. Other recommendations from Chatterjee included expanding subsidised childcare places and establishing a dedicated cross-bureau fund for child and adolescent mental health. Despite the challenges, he expressed optimism that the city could gain recognition status under the initiative before 2030. “I think Hong Kong, the way it’s primed, with this convergence of big data, technology and innovation, can actually leapfrog and become a model for many other cities in the world that are still grappling with this issue,” he said. He also said Hong Kong could be an “education hub for the world”, serving as an alternative to the United States’ Ivy League system, citing the performance of the city’s top universities and current geopolitical developments. During his tenure as resident coordinator in China, Chatterjee led the work of 26 UN agencies in the country. Throughout his nearly three decades of work at the UN, he served in leadership roles in countries facing complex challenges, such as Iraq, South Sudan, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Taking a broader view of the global landscape, Chatterjee said the world was facing a “five-pronged interlocking crisis” of health, climate change, conflict, food insecurity and rising levels of inequality. He added that throughout his career, he had never seen the UN under such stress, and that it needed leadership to make the body “fit for purpose”. “Today we are in a state of such a geopolitical crisis of such proportion, and one country and one individual can actually upend global geopolitics,” he said, clarifying he was “not talking about anybody” in particular. Touching on China’s leadership, he cited a series of global schemes unveiled by President Xi Jinping in recent years, as well as the benefits of the Belt and Road Initiative, as examples. He also pushed back against Western criticism of China’s growing influence in the UN – which has included allegations of reshaping international norms and alleged human rights abuses – saying his time working in the country showed Beijing’s support for the multilateral system. “So the multilateral system needs to get fit for purpose. We need leadership in the UN that makes it fit for purpose,” he said. “I feel that China’s role in this new rebalancing is important.”

title: James Scott, Scotland star who once ‘infuriated’ Celtic, out to reboot career in Hong Kong
description: James Scott aiming to ‘make a name for myself again’ with Supreme Sha Tin following ‘the hardest year of my life’.
content: After a barren time in the Scottish Highlands that he called the “hardest year of my life”, James Scott has pitched up in Hong Kong aiming to “make a name for myself again”. Still only 25, and a former Scotland under-21 striker, Scott is a fine signing for Supreme Sha Tin, the club that drew the fifth-largest turnout of the 12-year Hong Kong Premier League era on Friday. A whopping 4,592 crowd turned out for their Mong Kok Stadium clash with Lee Man, although a 3-0 defeat was not in the script. Scott’s first concern after arriving in the city earlier this month was to avoid the fate of compatriot Calum Hall, who collapsed from sunstroke during a pre-season game following his move to Eastern three years ago. “The heat is totally different from where me and Callum are from,” Scott said. “It’ll take me a wee while to get used to it.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by JS (@_jamesscott_) Drenched in sweat and catching his breath after a goalscoring debut in a 3-1 win over Eastern last week, in front of another bumper crowd of 3,329, Scott joked that he was “too tired to think”. From Glasgow, and a Celtic season ticket holder, a very young Scott was released by his boyhood club and told he “wasn’t good enough”. Disillusioned and discouraged, he stopped playing for a year, until his mother and grandfather, John Gray, who played for Motherwell in the 1970s, formed a youth team to tempt him back to the sport. “It was a hard time and I was upset, but they got me back into loving football again,” Scott said. “I did really well and I owe my mum and grandpa a big thanks for doing that for me.” Soon, Scott had the “weird but good” experience of trialling with Rangers. Celtic came knocking again, too, but influenced by Grandpa John, he joined Motherwell at 13. “It was good to know I should be at that level,” he said. “I knew lots of players had done well for Motherwell and got big moves. “I loved my time at Celtic. I was probably too young at the time and it wasn’t meant to be, but I’d love to play for them one day.” Two years after joining, Scott played in a Scottish Challenge Cup match for Motherwell under-20s against Edinburgh City. “I was too young to understand what was going on, but Motherwell were brilliant doing that for me,” he said. “I’m really glad it happened; I learned lessons that helped me become the player I am today.” A first-team debut followed off the bench at Ross County in April 2018, when Scott was 17. He was just old enough to legally buy a round in the pub when fate decreed that he would make his first senior start at Celtic. Motherwell lost 4-1 and after the match The Times ran with the headline, ‘James Scott’s stunning lack of sportsmanship infuriates victorious Celtic’. His crime was to play on when Celtic felt the ball should have been given back after they had kicked it out to allow midfielder Ryan Christie to receive treatment. Receiving the ball from a throw-in, Scott charged forward to aim a shot that goalkeeper Scott Bain pushed out for Gboly Ariyibi to score on the rebound. Scott’s father was sitting among those baying for blood inside Celtic Park. Delighted to get my first call up!👏💙 https://t.co/hh50MaXFwe — JamesScott (@_jamesscottt_) August 19, 2019 “That moment probably made me a Motherwell legend at the time,” Scott said. “There was a bit of miscommunication on the park. I was still young, there was a lot of noise and when I got the ball, I just got my head down and wanted to do well for the club.” In January 2020, barely a year after he had signed a 3½-year contract extension with Motherwell, whose manager Stephen Robinson called Scott “a very talented boy … I have high hopes for him”, Hull City paid £1.5 million (US$2 million) for the 19-year-old striker. But early in his first training session with the club, Scott injured an ankle and was ruled out for six months. “That injury was the biggest challenge of my life,” Scott said. “Covid kicked in soon after, but I learned from some big names at Hull, and I’m glad I went.” Scott had a good 2021-22 back in Scotland on loan with Hibernian, wrapping up the campaign with a hat-trick in a 4-0 win over St Johnstone, after beginning it by earning the last of his three international under-21 caps. Having played alongside the likes of Lewis Ferguson and Nathan Patterson, who went to the World Cup this summer, Scott said Scotland recognition was “of course” still on his radar, and hoped that “if I do well for a few years, it’ll get my name out there”. Returning to Hull, Scott came under the charge of future Chelsea boss Liam Rosenior. “He was nothing but good to me, but the club had bigger ambitions, and I wasn’t doing so well coming back from injury, so we decided to part ways,” Scott said. After four goals from 36 games, albeit only 14 were starts, Scott swapped Hull for Exeter City in February 2023. Twelve months, four goals and 43 games later, he was borrowed by St Mirren, who kept him in Scotland’s top flight for 2024-25. After a campaign on the periphery, Scott agreed a loan to Scottish Championship team Ross County. “We believe he is a fantastic addition to the group,” Don Cowie, the manager, said. Cowie was gone after three games.
