Scott subsequently had two more permanent bosses, as he drifted to the fringes and his team dropped out of the division. “That was probably the hardest year of my life,” Scott said. “I was uncomfortable because I wasn’t playing, so I wanted to try something completely different, come out of my comfort zone in a different way, and restart my career. “I want to progress and develop as a person, and make a name for myself again.” Already looking at home on the field, Scott is equally settled off it after being joined in Hong Kong by his partner. “When I moved to Hull at 19, I loved experiencing new things,” Scott said. “Coming here, my family and partner were asking how I was so calm. But I love new challenges and I’m really excited. I want to do well, then maybe go to a bigger league, but my only focus now is on doing well for Supreme.”

title: ‘Chilling effect’: Japan’s whistle-blowers weigh high price of speaking out
description: Legal experts and those targeted in such cases say whistle-blowers can face termination, costly litigation and difficulty finding work.
content: Yutaka Kato* knew there would be risks when he reported suspected misconduct by his employer to Japanese authorities. What he did not expect, he said, was a 47.88 million yen (US$300,000) damages claim from that employer – the Japanese subsidiary of US-listed medical device manufacturer STAAR Surgical – along with the prospect of years in court and the uncertainty of whether he would ever return to work. Kato is among a growing number of whistle-blowers in Japan who say laws meant to protect them from retaliation have not stopped companies from pursuing damages claims, dismissals and other actions that can leave them financially drained, professionally isolated and afraid to speak out. His former employer’s claim was dismissed by the Tokyo District Court in December last year but was appealed to the High Court, with a ruling set to be handed down on September 3. Kato has challenged his dismissal in a separate lawsuit, with the High Court ruling in his favour, although the company has appealed to Japan’s Supreme Court. And he admits to being “anxious” ahead of the rulings. “There is no public financial assistance to support my living expenses and the economic burden I face while the litigation continues,” he said. “At present, there is also no clear prospect of my actually returning to work. The company may, of course, have a different view as to the reasons for my dismissal. From my perspective, however, I believe that the dismissal had a retaliatory aspect because I had made whistle-blower reports.” When Japan introduced its Whistleblower Protection Act in 2004, it was expected to protect workers who reported suspected misconduct, including against their own employers. More than two decades later, critics say the law’s limits have become clear in cases where employers argue that their claims concern conduct surrounding a disclosure, rather than the whistle-blowing itself. The Act bars companies from dismissing or otherwise disadvantaging workers on the grounds of whistle-blowing and from seeking damages simply because they suffered losses as a result. But legal experts and those targeted in such cases say whistle-blowers can still face termination, costly litigation and difficulty finding work in the same industry when companies cite related conduct – such as handling internal information – as the basis for action against them. This Week in Asia reached out to STAAR Japan, which declined to comment on Kato’s case as it is “a pending legal matter”. But Kato’s legal representatives claim he was targeted after he filed reports with authorities. Kato said the reports he made concerned suspected improper payments to doctors and the handling of patient information linked to surgical videos involving the company’s intraocular lenses. In a related bribery case, a doctor at Yamato-Takada Municipal Hospital in Nara prefecture was later convicted of accepting payments linked to the use of the company’s lenses and sentenced to 18 months in prison, suspended for three years. Four people linked to the company, including former executives, also received fines in connection with the bribery case. The damages claim against Kato centres on the alleged removal of company information, rather than the act of whistle-blowing itself. Aiko Ohbuchi, a lawyer specialising in corporate law at the Amour Law Office in Tokyo, said companies bringing such claims might not see themselves as exploiting a flaw in the legislation. Article 7 of the Act provides that an employer “may not seek damages from a whistle-blower on the grounds that the employer has suffered damage as a result of the whistle-blowing”, she said. This provision does not, however, expressly cover a whistle-blower collecting and taking out information to make a disclosure. Nor does it specifically prohibit an employer from seeking damages on the grounds that it suffered harm resulting from such conduct. Ohbuchi said she was aware of 12 lawsuits where employers sought damages on the grounds that a whistle-blower collected or took information out of the company, although there were many more cases in which whistle-blowers were “subject to adverse treatment, such as dismissal or disciplinary action”. She said she was confident Kato would prevail in the damages case. “The courts have ruled in favour of whistle-blowers where the conduct was necessary to establish the truth of the matters reported and the method used was reasonable and proportionate,” she said. Amendments due to take effect on December 1 would strengthen the law by expanding protection to freelancers and introducing criminal penalties for dismissal or discipline on the grounds of whistle-blowing, Ohbuchi said, adding that they would also shift the burden of proof in some disputes over dismissal or disciplinary action after a report. While there was “growing awareness of the importance of protecting” those who spoke out, Ohbuchi cautioned that even a clear-cut victory in court might not dissuade firms from similar tactics in the future. Other recent cases have underscored the same broader concern: that litigation itself can deter workers considering whether to report suspected wrongdoing. Nozomi Fukuda, an ex-employee of the company behind Momuri – a high-profile Japanese resignation agency that helps workers quit their jobs – was among former staff who helped bring to light allegations that the agency had improperly referred clients to lawyers in return for fees. Those allegations led to a criminal case against Momuri’s operator, Albatross, and its former president, according to Japanese media and company statements, but the company also pursued civil litigation against former employees over separate claims that included allegedly false statements about harassment. Fukuda told Japanese media that the stress of the case caused her to suffer a cerebral infarction, transforming her life and that of her family. She later divorced her husband. While she continues to feel the effects of her illness, the lawsuit remains unresolved. According to Japanese media, Fukuda has said that had she known in advance the toll it would take, she might have chosen to stay quiet. Kato said he was frustrated by what he saw as a “significant gap” in the protection system that allows companies to sue whistle-blowers and potentially intimidate others considering speaking out. “A very large damages claim can itself impose a significant financial and psychological burden on a defendant and potentially have a chilling effect on that person’s speech and actions,” he said. “If the company ultimately wins and I am ordered to pay around 47.88 million yen, I do not have the financial means to pay that amount. “In that event, I could potentially face a serious financial burden for decades to come.” *Name changed to protect interviewee’s identity

title: South Korea to revise exam rules after AI cheating scandal
description: Five candidates caught using smart glasses to cheat in technical qualification tests within two months.
content:
South Korea is set to revise regulations governing technical qualification examinations following the discovery of five candidates who used AI-enabled smart glasses to cheat over just over two months.
These five incidents, which were reported between May and June, were revealed in information provided to the Human Resources Development Service of Korea by opposition politician Kim So-hee, according to The Korea Herald.
In two of the cases – in Gwangju and Daegu – the candidates were caught because examiners spotted a light or electronic sound emitting from their glasses. In another incident in Mokpo, a candidate was seen pressing a button on a pair of glasses, causing a blue display to appear on the lens.
In Seoul, a camera lens was found embedded in the frame of the glasses worn by a candidate taking an information processing engineer exam, while in Ulsan, a check revealed a lens and display in the glasses worn by another candidate.
All five were penalised for cheating, and three of them were referred to prosecutors.
In June, the incident involving the candidate in Gwangju became the country’s first criminal case, according to the Korea JoongAng Daily. The man in his forties was charged with violating the National Technical Qualification Act. An examiner noticed light reflecting from the lenses of his glasses during the fire protection facilities engineer certification exam.
In May, the Human Resources Department expanded its list of prohibited electronic and communications devices, allowing proctors to remove candidates caught using them and invalidate their scores.
Smart glasses are not explicitly named in the current list of items forbidden in exam halls – which includes electronic or communications devices such as mobile phones, digital cameras and camera-equipped pens.
However, given the pace of technological evolution, the Labour Ministry is planning to use broader language so that new devices can be restricted without the authorities having to constantly change the rules to keep up with the trend.
“It is difficult to revise the enforcement rules every time a new device emerges, so we are considering making the regulations somewhat more flexible so that we can respond more quickly to technological changes,” a Labour Ministry official said.
The public notice process will start in September, and the ministry hopes to complete the revision within the year.
Smart glasses are also causing problems in other major exams, including two during the English for international communication tests in May and three during the Test of Proficiency in Korean (TOPIK) exams last year.
TOPIK administrator, the National Institute for International Education, installed radio-frequency and metal detectors at all domestic test centres in April to catch cheaters.
The Education Ministry is also considering measures to prevent technology-assisted cheating. In June, provincial departments such as the Gyeonggi-do Office of Education and the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education sent circulars to their schools outlining the most popular devices used for cheating and tips on how to spot AI glasses, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported.
A viral clip posted by an internet technology YouTuber in June showed an edge a smart glass user could have over others. In the video, the YouTuber uses a pair of AI glasses to solve all 30 questions in a practice maths test for the college entrance exams, or suneung , in just 18 minutes – scoring 96 out of 100.

title: North Korea’s defence minister dismissed in reshuffle of military leadership
description: No Kwang-chol was also demoted in the ruling party leadership to ‘first vice-director of the Munitions Industry Department’.
content: North Korea’s defence minister has been dismissed as part of a reshuffle of the country’s military leadership, state media reported on Sunday. The “structural reorganisation plans” were decided during a meeting on Saturday led by Kim Jong-un, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said. No Kwang-chol was not only dismissed as defence minister but also demoted in the ruling party leadership to “first vice-director of the Munitions Industry Department”, KCNA said. Kim Song-gi, director of the General Political Bureau of the Korean People’s Army, was named as the new defence minister. Another senior official, defence adviser Pak Jong-chon, was given the position of vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission and named to the ruling party’s Political Bureau. Several other promotions were also announced. In a separate report, KCNA said Kim had lauded scientists, researchers and officials at a ceremony on Saturday for their advances in defence technology, giving them top national honours. The honourees greatly contributed to “resolving scientific and technological problems of epochal significance in developing new combat weapon systems”, KCNA said, without specifying the type of system. A photo released by KCNA showed Kim pinning a medal on a recipient. The nuclear-armed state’s weapons research centre “has recently developed exclusive technologies, to be regarded as an event in strengthening the capability for fighting a war”, it added without giving details. With such technologies, it has shown “the course of unique development of the country’s military and technological capabilities”, it said. In late June, Kim oversaw tests of a new extended-range multiple rocket launcher and artillery system. In Seoul, the government also ⁠unveiled a cabinet ⁠reshuffle on Sunday, ⁠naming Kang Shin-chul, former deputy commander of the South Korea-US Combined Forces Command, as the new defence minister, presidential chief of staff Kang Hoon-sik said in a televised address. The leadership shuffle comes shortly after joint annual drills between South Korea and the US wrapped up. The drills, which are regularly denounced by Pyongyang as preparations for an invasion, were closely watched this year after US President Donald Trump ordered them to be shortened. Trump criticised the drills as provocative towards the North and bashed Seoul for not supporting his war against Iran. The US president also praised North Korean leader Kim, whom he met twice during his first term in office, as he eyes a new meeting, potentially this year. Despite Trump’s overtures, North Korea has shown little sign of reciprocating, firing missiles and condemning the scaled-down drills. Pyongyang has also slammed Washington’s approval of arms sales to South Korea and plans to fund programmes documenting human rights abuses in the North. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Editorial | Hong Kong is right to harness market forces for urban renewal
description: Plot ratio concessions will encourage developers to rebuild older properties, realigning commercial interests with the city’s development needs.
content: Urban renewal is essential, not optional, for a small and densely populated city like Hong Kong. While new buildings continue to mushroom across the districts each year, it is outpaced by the relentless ageing of blocks, many of which have become dilapidated and pose a danger to public safety. In this context, the government’s new five-year bonus plot ratio pilot scheme to expedite redevelopment is not merely a technical tweak to planning rules. It is a much-needed and pragmatic attempt to realign developers’ incentives with the city’s redevelopment needs. This will hopefully enhance building safety, housing supply and the quality of living in Hong Kong. Starting from September, developers can get an extra 20 per cent of gross floor area as a reward for taking on private redevelopment projects in seven designated old districts. Only residential plots of at least 700 square metres (7,535 sq ft) with buildings aged 50 years and above will be eligible. Relevant lease conditions and penalties will be set out to ensure the projects are completed on time. Alternatively, the bonus gross floor area can also be converted into land premium value to offset the land premium payable for the redevelopment project or any land transactions by the developer, including land bidding, lease modification or land exchange projects, in the Northern Metropolis project and other areas in the city within a decade. First announced in the chief executive’s policy address last year, this initiative follows the legislative amendment two years ago to lower the compulsory sale threshold for redevelopment. The measures underline the government’s awareness of the difficulties involved and its determination to accelerate the slow pace of urban renewal. Data compiled by the Legislative Council research office showed that the number of buildings at least 50 years old doubled to 10,200 between 2014 and 2023, and is projected to surge by 138 per cent to 24,300 by 2043. As of 2025, 68 per cent of private buildings were 30 years old or above, with a further 14 per cent due to cross this threshold within a decade. As the design lifespan of concrete is typically 50 years, the city’s ageing building stock poses mounting safety risks. This situation is not helped by the slow pace of redevelopment by the Urban Renewal Authority and private developers. Of the 1,650 private buildings demolished from 2013 to 2022, only about 240 were handled by the statutory body, according to the Development Bureau. Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho was frank in pointing out the challenges ahead. Even though 80 per cent of the redeveloped flats come from private renewal projects, market participation remains sluggish due to acquisition costs and constraints on redevelopment. “It is necessary for us to adopt an innovative and bolder policy to push the market to undertake redevelopment,” she said. For too long, urban renewal in Hong Kong has been hamstrung by a wealth of financial and procedural hurdles. High costs and tight development parameters mean many potential redevelopment projects are still idling on the shelf. Lowering the compulsory sale thresholds earlier was a necessary first step to make acquisition easier. But nothing is more directly beneficial than an instrument that relaxes the maximum development potential for free for developers. Whether the bonus scheme can unlock more new projects in old districts remains to be seen. While the property market is still less than bullish, the approach of offering premium-free gross floor area ought to appeal in a city where every inch of space literally costs a fortune. The alternative ratio-for-land premium arrangement also provides flexibility for developers. Hong Kong cannot afford to slow down on urban renewal as more buildings reach beyond their structural lifespan. While the latest initiative may not necessarily unleash a tower of applications for redevelopment, it at least strives to respond to the market, which hopefully will help more private-led renewal initiatives turn from concept to implementation. With proper safeguards and monitoring, the scheme has good potential to speed up redevelopment and make our homes more liveable and safer.

title: How Hong Kong Gen Z talent agency WPM aims to change city’s ‘stubborn’ creative mindset
description: The founders of Wasted Potentials Management talk about growing their youth-driven talent agency and give one surprising piece of advice.
content: In a city obsessed with efficiency, stock tickers and a rigidly defined path to success, calling your company “Wasted Potentials Management” (WPM) is either an act of self-sabotage or a stroke of genius. For founders Harry Leung, Venus Fan and Jasper Chung it is a tongue-in-cheek reclamation, turning their authenticity into a business model. Founded in 2025, WPM is a youth-driven talent agency that connects Hong Kong’s young underground creatives – ranging from videographers and models to tattoo artists and DJs – with brands hunting for an edge. Its projects include collaborations with Drmers Club, Bape Japan and GQ Hong Kong. WPM currently represents eight creators, with an average age of 22. Besides matchmaking, it also organises pop-ups and events, offers brand consulting and more. The blueprint for the company can be traced to when Leung began to see his home city’s divided culture. Born and raised inside the Cantonese-speaking local school system, he had rarely spoken English in his daily life, let alone immersed himself in Western media or its creative codes. “Growing up like that, it puts you in a box,” he says. “Asian culture kind of always encourages you to be part of the crowd. Be normal like everyone else. But what is normal? In these schools, they want everybody to look the same, act the same, and I was always a bad kid, but I also knew the system was bad for me. I wanted to escape.” At a casual gathering around six years ago, a mutual friend introduced him to Yutaro Chirikiri, a Japan-born, Hong Kong-raised creative who would later become one of the agency’s first signed talents. Until that night, Leung recalls, he had been living with only “half of the culture”, confined to familiar local networks and a world conducted almost wholly in Cantonese. Chirikiri and his circle gave him entry to a parallel Hong Kong – a space shaped by fashion, underground music and global aesthetics that his own upbringing had never exposed him to. Merging local culture with international community When Leung met Chung – freshly returned from a decade in the United Kingdom and already steeped in the world of international streetwear and marketing – and later Fan, who had spent a year and a half running her own one-woman digital marketing operation, the three realised they wanted to build something together. Chung surveyed the loose network of stylish, like-minded friends they had inadvertently gathered and posed a question that would become the agency’s founding logic. “Since all your friends are cool as well,” he remembers saying, “why don’t we just build an international community that also has the local culture in it, and kind of merge it together?” It was an invitation to formalise what they were already doing: bridging two worlds and turning a scattered group of friends into a platform capable of reshaping Hong Kong’s creative economy. For Fan, it made perfect sense. Though she had built everything at her own operation from the ground up – social media management, branding, design, website work – the constant juggling of freelance clients left no room for collaboration. “It was always just me learning, keep learning and keep doing everything by myself,” she recalls. “There’s no getting inspired by someone else. I was good at the work, but it was lonely.” At its core, the collective tries to push a sense of community. That comfort, they believe, is what allows creativity to flourish. “In communities like this, you have other people with you,” Chirikiri says. “You’re connected, you have a community of good people. You’re never alone.” Setting creativity free The life of an influencer might seem like it would be the same whether posting from a flat in London, a studio in Seoul or a cafe in Hong Kong. The internet, after all, is meant to flatten geography. But the team at WPM insists that where you create fundamentally shapes how you create – and in Hong Kong, the conditions are starkly different from those abroad. “Let’s take magazine shoots in the West,” explains Moosa Kalimullah, one of WPM’s talents and a student at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. “They’re a lot crazier, and they’re very bold with it. In Hong Kong, they’re very commercial and they have very strict guidelines.” The team argues that the environment in Hong Kong is one that instinctively tightens the creative leash. The root of the difference, they say, lies in why people make things in the first place. “They’re not creative for the sake of creation, they’re creative for the sake of monetisation,” Kalimullah says. In cities like New York or Paris, they say, there is a societal romantic tolerance for the struggling artist, a cultural permission to experiment without an immediate pay cheque while breeding work that is confrontational and genuine. The city’s infamous status anxiety is compounded by a high cost of living, and the pressure to project financial stability actively punishes the sort of risk-taking that produces bold, unconventional work. “People are so concerned about how they are perceived to other people,” Chirikiri says. Building a business For WPM, that unforgiving climate translated into early indifference from brands. “We just had to sacrifice a lot. We had to do everything for free,” Leung says. “But I think that’s how it works for anything. You have to show evidence that you’re actually able to create something and provide, then you can talk about money.” Those early gigs representing brands and styling or filming shoots as mutual favours eventually built portfolio material that grew along with their company identity. Where the collective once scraped for attention, they now field calls from fashion labels, alcohol brands and lifestyle companies looking to tap into a youth market they can no longer afford to ignore. “I was actually at a business meeting, and someone there approached me and told me her and her friends actually follow WPM stuff,” Chirikiri says. “That felt surreal – like, we’ve been doing this for so long, and to see it actually spreading, to have people recognise what we’re building, that part was really rewarding.” Hong Kong brands, long fixated on traditional advertising, are beginning to recognise that a creator with a genuine community can move product with a credibility that a billboard never will, the team says. The plan is to continue dragging the city forward by showing that a Hong Kong-based creator can still build a sustainable career. “We don’t really need validation from everyone,” Chung says. “We just have to keep making cool things, and that stubborn mindset in Hong Kong people will eventually change.” ‘You have to understand the system before you decide to leave it’ And yet, the team has a surprising piece of advice: try a nine-to-five job first. “Everybody should work, like, at least get into a job to experience how it works before you even say you don’t want it,” Leung says. “You might like it. You never know. You should try everything.” Kalimullah studies quantitative finance and risk management – a “respectable” path by Hong Kong standards – while simultaneously building a career in content creation. “Whichever you like, you can kind of choose,” he says. Chung took a resolutely unglamorous route before co-founding the agency. Back in the UK, he worked in a Chinese restaurant. He resold trainers. He clocked in for retail shifts. Leung had tried cryptocurrency, worked as a junior marketing executive at an alcohol distribution company, and pursued other odds and ends before he found the role he truly loved. “I quit [other jobs] because I think you just can’t be creative like that,” he says. “When you’re a junior [in a company], you basically can’t have an opinion. Everything I said meant nothing. But that experience was important. You have to understand the system before you decide to leave it – and it’s the fastest way to find out who you actually are. “At the end of the day, it’s about doing what you’re actually passionate about.”

title: In Focus | Is the Irtysh River the choke-free Arctic shipping gateway that China needs?
description: A proposed Irtysh route could link China to the Arctic, but political and natural barriers would have to be overcome.
content: As conflicts around the world highlight the vulnerability of global shipping lanes, China and Russia are reportedly weighing the possibility of turning a vast river into an inland cargo route to the rest of the world. At the heart of this ambition is the 4,248km (2,640-mile) Irtysh River, which originates in China’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region and runs through Kazakhstan before flowing into Russia’s Ob River and ending in the Arctic Ocean. To China, this river-to-sea shipping route could offer inland access to the resource-rich and strategically important Arctic. More importantly, unlike traditional maritime chokepoints like the Malacca and Bering straits, the route could avoid Western naval blockades, foreign coastguard surveillance and sanctions by the United States, according to observers. Shipping through the Arctic – the so-called Northern Sea Route – was long impractical due to the thick ice that covered the sea for much of the year. But warming temperatures have gradually made the passage more viable, raising China’s interest in the route. That interest has been compounded by geopolitical tensions. Zhao Long, a senior research fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz were raising prospects for alternative shipping routes. “Both overland transport corridors and maritime shipping lines are facing the impacts of geopolitical conflict and the spillover effects of these conflicts are increasingly long-term and pronounced,” Zhao said. “Therefore, any potential solution that offers additional route options will inevitably gain momentum.” An added advantage is the amount of time saved. Voyages along the Northern Sea Route could go from China’s Ningbo port to Felixstowe in Britain in 20 days, compared to 40 days via the Suez Canal. Chinese freight companies are already seeing the potential. Earlier this month, Chinese carrier Sea Legend Line launched a regular weekly container service along the route, the first of its kind using the Arctic Ocean. Alexei Likhachev, head of Russia’s state atomic energy corporation Rosatom, which manages the Northern Sea Route, said that more than 30 shipments were expected along the route this year. That is up from 14 in 2024 and 24 in 2025, according to news agency Interfax. Likhachev said shipments between Chinese and Russian ports accounted for nearly 15 per cent of all cargo traffic along the route, adding that freight between the two neighbours via the Arctic Ocean “should reach 20 million tonnes by 2030”. But China’s access to the route now relies on the Bering Strait, making it a potential chokepoint for Beijing – and Moscow – in the event of an American blockade launched from Alaska. Separating Russia’s Chukchi Peninsula from the Seward Peninsula of Alaska, the Bering Strait is the only marine gateway between the Arctic and Pacific oceans. At its narrowest point, the strait is only about 85km wide. During the Cold War, both the US and Soviet Union fortified their sides of the strait, which was often transited by submarines collecting intelligence. Marc Lanteigne, a professor with The Arctic University of Norway, said the militarisation of the Arctic had been revived in recent years and that the US was now monitoring Alaskan waters more closely. Since 2015, Chinese and Russian navies have carried out regular patrols in the Bering Strait. In July 2024, for the first time, Chinese and Russian strategic bombers flew over the area, prompting the North American Aerospace Defence Command to scramble US F-16 and F-35 fighters alongside Canadian CF-18s to intercept the formation. In October 2024, the China Coast Guard entered the Arctic Ocean through the strait in a joint drill with their Russian counterparts for the first time, an operation that Chinese observers said at that time had effectively expanded the coastguard’s far-seas operational range. This activity has raised alarm in the US. In July last year, US President Donald Trump signed a budget bill with almost US$25 billion in extra coastguard spending, including almost US$9 billion for new icebreakers and US$300 million for new facilities in Alaska. When the Chinese research icebreakers Xuelong and Xuelong 2 passed north through the US exclusive economic zone and over the extended North American continental shelf in the Bering Sea last month, they were watched closely by both Canadian and the US coastguards for days. This proximity to the US “is why the Northern Sea Route passing through the Bering Strait is never safe geopolitically”, according to Artyom Lukin, a professor of international relations at Far Eastern Federal University in Vladivostok. “If China wants an assured access to the Arctic Ocean, it needs to solve the Bering Strait dilemma. A corridor along the Irtysh River, via China itself, Kazakhstan and Russia, is one obvious solution.” Zhao said that while passing through the Bering Strait remained the most economical option, developing the Irtysh River made sense for contingencies. “If extreme situations arise – such as a total blockage of the strait making it unnavigable, whether due to natural causes, political reasons or security factors – then obviously, you still have a backup plan.” If China wants an assured access to the Arctic Ocean, it needs to solve the Bering Strait dilemma Artyom Lukin, Far Eastern Federal University While landlocked Kazakhstan has long sought to develop the Ob-Irtysh system, the vision gained momentum in 2024 when the country revealed a concrete plan to develop the route. Then last year Kazakhstan approved a blueprint to develop shipping on the river system. Speaking last month at a Russia-Kazakhstan cooperation forum held beside the Irtysh in the city of Omsk, Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow and Astana were working together on plans for the river and aiming “to strike a balanced approach between increasing freight transport, developing water resources and preserving the river’s ecosystem”. Batyrbek Musin, an adviser to the board for development at Pavlodar River Port on the Irtysh, said the three nations were actively considering the new transport corridor. “This strategic issue can take the form of a ‘Water Silk Road’,” Musin said on the sidelines of the forum, according to news portal Russia’s Pivot to Asia. The Chinese government has not made any statement on the proposed route. Kazakhstan hopes to expand its shipbuilding, repair and port facilities to support heavy freight on the Irtysh. The goal is to increase its annual cargo traffic to an estimated 2.5 million tonnes, from the 1.5 million tonnes today. Russia, meanwhile, has designated the Ob-Irtysh system as part of its planned Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor, a broader strategic project aimed at creating shipping routes beyond the reach of Western sanctions. Zhao, in Shanghai, said this project could link Russia’s vast Siberian heartland with the Chinese market. “This aligns with Russia’s need to reduce its transport dependence on Europe under Western sanctions, while also fitting into its broader foreign policy pivot.” But turning the river into a major trade artery will not be easy. Navigating the river system would mean overcoming the harsh Siberian winters that freeze the waterway for up to six months a year, possibly limiting commercial shipping to a narrow summer window. Meanwhile, seasonal low water levels and heavy silting also create shifting sandbars, which would require huge dredging capacity so that large cargo barges would not run aground. As part of its cooperation with Russia, Kazakhstan launched its first dredger, the Irtysh-2503, in April. In addition, getting cargo to and from China’s densely populated coast to remote Xinjiang – especially in the quantities required to make the river route worthwhile – would require further infrastructure investment. Lanteigne said that in expanding infrastructure along the Irtysh River, authorities would also need to balance preserving the waterway as a source of fresh water. Another key challenge for the project would be navigating China and Russia’s subtle tug of war for influence in Central Asia. “Astana has been seeking to diversify its regional friends, including China as well as in the Caspian region, while Russia has been trying to maintain its traditional role as a security guarantor in Central Asia.” Lukin said that making the Irtysh route navigable would require enormous investment and the renewed political support of the three countries. “The total costs could be in the tens, and even hundreds, of billions of dollars. Only China has the resources on such a scale. “But will it commit such huge investments to the project that mostly runs through the territories of Russia and Kazakhstan? Undertaking the Irtysh project requires a whole new level of trust and closeness between China, Russia and Kazakhstan.”

title: This week in PostMag: Hong Kong’s leading tech hub marks 25th anniversary with a focus on the future
description: How legacies are built, from HKSTP’s tech innovation to culinary fusions and Nancy Kwan’s Hollywood impact.
content: How is a legacy defined? Of the many profound, poetic and compelling words that far more eloquent scribes have strung together to capture that notion and its palpable impact, perhaps American songwriter, actor, filmmaker and librettist Lin-Manuel Miranda summed it up best when he penned the following lines, for his hit musical Hamilton: “It’s planting seeds in a garden you never get to see. I wrote some notes at the beginning of a song someone will sing for me.” Legacy is intertwined with that which cannot be bought, cannot be forced and cannot be artificially generated: time. Except, in some cases, there is an opportunity to be part of history in the making and play a pivotal role in shaping the narrative as it’s being told. Consider the rapid, exponential speed of technological development – most game-changing breakthroughs were achieved in the past couple of centuries, and the velocity is only accelerating. We went from digital computers the size of rooms to laptops thin enough to fit into a Manila envelope in a matter of decades. Few people understand this relentless tempo of forward progression better than Cordelia Chung – the new chairman of the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP). Since its establishment, in 2001, HKSTP has grown into the leading start-up incubation ecosystem in the city, driving innovation and technology advancement across the Greater Bay Area and beyond. With the institution’s silver jubilee on the horizon, P. Ramakrishnan dives into the yesterday, the now and the tomorrow of HKSTP to learn more about Chung’s strategic vision and ambitious blueprint for the future, and the operational efforts of HKSTP CEO Terry Wong Ping-sau. Building bridges and sustaining a legacy is not limited to the realm of innovation – it also happens in kitchens, and on the palate. China and India have been immersed in continuous culinary conversations for almost 2,000 years, a flavourful dialogue that was birthed along the Silk Road and through the spice trade. Hei Kiu Au listens in as two chefs put their heads (and hands) together to bring Indo-Chinese cuisine to a Hong Kong audience. Hollywood legend Nancy Kwan Ka-shen knows a thing or two about legacy. After all, she helped transform the Western film industry’s perception of Asian actors at a time when yellowface was still prevalent, in the 1960s. Now in her 80s, Kwan looks back on a life well lived and a career well served, regaling Faye Bradley with anecdotes. Last but not least, in an entirely different setting – but keeping the same pace, and eyes on the prize – Marissa Carruthers dips her toes into the world of long-distance running, at the 11th Angkor Empire Marathon, in Cambodia. Racing in the shadow of ancient temples as mist hugs the landscape is a rather convincing argument for athletic pursuits. Enjoy the read.

title: Creatine for women: benefits for strength, brain health and hormones – without the bulk
description: Long linked with men’s bodybuilding, the supplement is now proven to boost women’s health – even Balenciaga is getting in on the action.
content: Creatine has had a pretty fixed identity for most of its commercial life. It came in enormous tubs, it lived next to things called Xtreme Mass and Hyper Shred, and it was, for a very long time, something men bought before lifting heavy things. Most women never questioned whether it applied to them, and most brands never bothered to suggest that it might. But at some point, searches for creatine for women started climbing, and by 2025, Thorne, one of the supplement industry’s most credible names, had tapped Grammy-winning artist Ciara specifically to make the case that creatine wasn’t just for the guy with the bulk bag. Our body produces creatine naturally, stored in muscle and topped up through food. Women generally have lower total creatine stores than men, around 70 to 80 per cent less, a gap that, according to Dr Mark Kovacs, founder of the Kovacs Institute and former director of the Gatorade Sports Science Institute, “creates a scenario where women may have more room for improvement from supplementation”. That deficit is precisely the point. According to Jarman Gosai, strength trainer and founder of Gym Concoction in Melbourne, that lower starting point actually makes women more responsive to creatine supplementation. “It’s like a phone battery sitting at 30 per cent versus one at 70 per cent: the one at 30 per cent has more room to charge, so the boost from plugging the cord in is bigger,” Gosai says. What creatine is actually doing is replenishing ATP, the body’s primary fuel source, which muscles burn through almost instantly during high-intensity effort. “I usually like to think of creatine as the tool to increase the size of your ‘quick energy backup pool’ – the more you have of it, the longer your muscles will be able to tolerate intense repeated work,” says Marwa Ahmed, certified strength and conditioning expert and founder of The BodyMind Coach. What that usually means is better running times, heavier lifts or faster recovery between repeated sets. The gym case is pretty well-established at this point. But for most women, the hesitation is about what creatine might do to their bodies. The bloating, the bulk, the puffy look; a handful of specific fears tend to come up again and again, and they’ve followed creatine into the women’s wellness conversation for years. Starting with the bulk: building the kind of size typically associated with creatine use in men requires testosterone levels that women simply don’t have. “The low testosterone with the lower creatine baseline means the effects of creatine show up more as better recovery, higher performance or improved mood – more so than visible muscle gain,” says Ahmed. The water retention question is related but different. “Creatine primarily increases water inside the muscle cell, not underneath the skin,” says Kovacs. “This intracellular hydration is actually one of the mechanisms that may contribute to improved muscle function, recovery and adaptation. It is very different from the type of water retention people often associate with feeling puffy.” And the bloating complaints that do exist come almost entirely from loading phases, an entirely optional practice where, instead of taking the standard daily dose, you take around 20 grams a day for a week to saturate muscle stores quickly and get results faster. “Creatine is not particularly water-soluble – less soluble than table sugar, for reference – so at those volumes, some of it sits undissolved in your gut and draws water into your intestines through osmosis,” says Gosai, and that’s where the bloating, the puffiness and the one to two kilos of extra scale weight usually come from. Women who track their cycle and notice their performance dips in the second half of the month aren’t imagining it. During the luteal phase, when progesterone rises, the body’s reliance on carbohydrates for fuel drops and muscles lean more heavily on the creatine-phosphate system. Energy feels lower, workouts feel harder and there’s no obvious reason why. Although the research on whether supplementation can smooth that dip is still in its early stages, it’s pointing somewhere useful. A 2024 study, for example, found that women who got enough creatine through their diet had a significantly lower risk of irregular periods, and given that dietary creatine comes almost entirely from red meat and fish, vegetarians tend to have lower stores than most and may notice more of a difference from supplementing. And for anyone navigating perimenopause who’s noticed their brain suddenly feels like it’s running on low battery, Ahmed points to research showing women tend to have lower creatine levels in the frontal lobe, the part of the brain that handles mood, memory and cognition, with that gap becoming more pronounced as oestrogen fluctuates, “suggesting that creatine production does not stay steady in women as it does in men, and that can be related to hormones”. For something with this much research behind it, creatine is surprisingly easy to overthink. Creatine monohydrate is the one with decades of research behind it, and despite the newer formats (HCl, buffered, micronised), none of them have meaningfully outperformed it. Terry Tateossian, menopause lifestyle medicine coach and founder of Thor, advises her clients, “Take three to five grams a day, every day, of a quality monohydrate, with a meal, for the rest of your life. Don’t load. Don’t cycle. Don’t overthink it.” For women already juggling a supplement routine, Ancient + Brave’s True Creatine+ is female-founded, B Corp certified, and blends magnesium, taurine and vitamin D into the mix, which means one less thing to add to the shelf. While brands like Thorne and Momentous, both NSF-Certified for Sport and independently tested for purity, are the ones to reach for if clinical credibility is the priority. The research on creatine and women is still catching up. There’s more to learn about hormonal variability, about the different life stages, about everything the early studies missed by defaulting to male subjects. But the direction it’s heading is pretty consistent. “Creatine doesn’t build muscle. What it does is increase the capacity to do the work that builds the muscle,” says Tateossian. Turns out that capacity was always there.

title: Opinion | Jason Arday’s death is not just a ‘woke Cambridge’ tragedy
description: In our globalised knowledge system, his death indicts universities, the press, online mobs – and those of us imagining ourselves safely outside culture wars.
content: Three weeks ago, I watched with horror the car crash of Cambridge professor Jason Arday’s public unravelling. You know the story: allegations about plagiarism; then more accusations, headlines and people announcing they had always felt “something was off”. It was less an investigation than a very British public audit involving spreadsheets, screenshots and the enthusiasm normally reserved for catching misbehaving MPs – except far more obsessive. Even after Arday’s death and his family’s request for privacy, journalists camped outside his home. I had heard Arday speak at my university. Less fiery preacher than community worker, he seemed friendly, quietly listening, even awkward. I did not know him, but could not reconcile that man with the monster, martyr and morality play constructed around him. I also had a selfish, perverse thought: what if this happened to me? Ethnic minority academics I spoke to shared the anxiety; several disclosed less public but no less relentless, targeted harassment themselves, by agents backed by insidiously larger legal, financial and networked resources. Many colleagues of colour are afraid that speaking up will draw attention to their own records and private lives. Readers in Asia may cast this aside as a black-and-white drama of the “woke West”. Yet every aspiration to international standards, academic arrival or a place on “the global stage” implicates us. I am a non-white Chinese transnational scholar, albeit privileged, who writes about race and decolonisation. I have produced books, articles and far too many PowerPoint presentations with malapropisms and charmingly primitive infographics. Somewhere are phrases I would now qualify, poorly formatted references, perhaps even an unwise semicolon. I do not equate scholarly slippage with the serious allegations against Arday. But the scrutiny became a fixation that his entire being was fraudulent. Here lies the point: one need not believe him blameless to recognise when inquiry becomes a witch hunt. Cambridge first celebrated Arday as its youngest Black professor. Once allegations emerged, his identity became evidence that diversity appointments and the entire “woke DEI” project in diversity, equity and inclusion were mistakes. Yet double standards are stark: white academics have plagiarised and fabricated, sometimes failing upwards, without becoming arguments about employment. Nobody writes mournfully that centuries of white appointments have gone too far. The story is tidied into binaries: Arday was either an innocent whose critics were racist, or the product of lowered standards for black folk. Both versions are suspiciously self-contained; yet human beings are not, nor are the biased systems they have created in academia and media. Structurally, together – Cambridge, the press and social media commentators – produced conditions in which legitimate questions became trial by spectacle: the university invoked due process while a man accused of no crime was cross-examined mercilessly; newspapers insisted on public interest while producing clickbait; online voyeurs exercised their right to baat guah, gossip. To be sure, investigative journalism cannot be compromised. But these inquiries began with unproven allegations by a disgruntled academic dabbling in suspect research on race science, himself investigated and sacked by Cambridge. Chinese people in Chinese-majority societies do not consider ourselves ‘people of colour’ … But cross even an online border and the racial settings rearrange themselves I feel uncomfortable adding another article to the pile. Yet testimonials from former students emerged only after Arday’s death, when accounts contesting the first attacks were finally heard. The least dishonest response is to admit my complicity. I watched, flustered and angry, refreshing my newsfeed; now I write about why others watched. Why does this matter to “yellow” folk outside black vs white UK politics? Chinese people in Chinese-majority societies do not consider ourselves “people of colour”; Western identity politics should not be exported like an overpriced university franchise. But cross even an online border and the racial settings rearrange themselves. I grew up an ethnic Chinese in Singapore, comfortably in the majority. In Britain I became an international student, ethnic-marginal, part of a model minority. A Chinese physicist is not called a “DEI hire” as a black sociologist might be. Yet I am a middle-aged Chinese woman still mistaken for a PhD student at white-majority conferences; embarrassed colleagues credit Korean skincare. (I’m not Korean.) Chinese academics occupy a peculiar position: welcomed as fee revenue, scientific labour and proof of internationalism, while students writing in English are presumed to be “of course using AI”. This suspicion disrupts the neat typology that black academics are token hires while Asians are hardworking machines. These forms of racism are not equivalent; ranking them into a hierarchy of victimhood helps nobody. What matters is their intersectional asymmetry: how race, gender, nationality and class determine credibility and the right to a mildly observed life. Universities, journals and old-boy groups gatekeep whose authority looks natural and whose mistakes represent an entire race: look how the list of names protesting the suspension of Arday’s whistle-blower skews one way. Arday’s story travelled through that stacked system: a UK scandal became a feeding frenzy, stripped of context; retrofitted into arguments about meritocracy and liberal excess. Cut the cake however you like: there is no clean “side”, only failing and unequal systems. Arday’s death is not merely a “woke people’s tragedy” in Cambridge. It impeaches global knowledge and political systems that market United-Colours-of-Benetton diversity while distributing trust much less evenly. It indicts universities, the press, online crowds, hidden networks – and those of us watching from elsewhere, imagining ourselves safely outside the cultural wars. We are not outside them. We are viewing the car crash from different racial playing fields, clutching our own spreadsheets, track records, naive aspirations, cultural debits and credits – and leaving our coffers open for whoever eventually comes to scrutinise them.

title: A brief guide to choosing the right underwear for workouts, and mistakes to avoid
description: Women’s health experts explain the issues caused down there by sweat and friction during exercise and the best materials for preventing them.
content: Most of us probably would not contemplate going for a run in jeans or tackling a HIIT class in an everyday bra, yet the underwear beneath our gym kit tends to receive considerably less thought. But with sweat, friction and tight-fitting gym clothes all potentially affecting intimate skin, perhaps it deserves more consideration. From moisture-wicking seamless briefs to plastic-free thongs, there are now plenty of pairs designed – or marketed – specifically for exercise, but do we actually need designated “workout underwear”, and could your trusty cotton underwear be doing more harm than good during a sweaty session? Experts explain what happens when we sweat down there, which fabrics perform best and the underwear mistakes to avoid at the gym. Can the wrong underwear cause thrush or a UTI? There is an important distinction between causing an infection and creating conditions that may contribute to irritation. “Tight, sweaty clothing combined with repetitive movement can cause rubbing and irritation of the delicate vulval skin, particularly in women who are already prone to eczema, dermatitis or vulval conditions,” says Dr Nikki Ramskill, women’s health doctor and founder of The Female Health Doctor clinic in the UK. “Thrush tends to thrive in warm, moist environments, so staying in damp, non-breathable clothing for prolonged periods may contribute to conditions that favour yeast overgrowth in women who are susceptible.” But she stresses that sweaty underwear does not directly cause urinary tract infections. “UTIs are caused by bacteria entering the urinary tract, so sweaty underwear itself isn’t a direct cause of a UTI,” Ramskill says. “However, changing out of damp clothing and maintaining sensible vulval hygiene is worthwhile, particularly if you’re someone who experiences recurrent infections.” What happens down there when we exercise? Sweating around the groin is entirely normal, but the combination of moisture, heat, tight clothing and movement can create uncomfortable conditions. “The issue is that this area is already warm and enclosed, so when you add sweat, friction and tight clothing, you can create a damp environment that may irritate the skin,” says Nikkii Behrens, a Pilates instructor and founder of Nikkii Health and Rare Street Pilates in Switzerland. “Fabric makes a difference because some materials hold onto moisture, while others help move it away from the skin and dry more quickly,” Behrens says. “Breathability and fit are just as important as the fabric itself.” That means the underwear that work perfectly well for an ordinary day may not necessarily perform as well during a sweaty spin class. Is cotton always best? Cotton underwear has long been recommended for its breathability, but the gym is one situation where it may not always be the obvious winner. “For everyday wear, breathable cotton is an excellent option, particularly for women with sensitive vulval skin,” Ramskill says. But for exercise, she says, “cotton can absorb a lot of sweat and stay wet, so a well-designed moisture-wicking sports fabric may actually be more comfortable during a sweaty workout”. The keywords she would look for are: “breathable, moisture-wicking, soft and non-irritating”. Pour Moi’s lingerie buyer Emma Woodrow says cotton is hydrophilic, meaning it absorbs moisture rather than moving it away from the skin. “This ultimately leads to that unpleasant ‘damp’ feeling many gym-goers will relate to,” says Woodrow, who is based in the UK. “As such, my main recommended style for working out is synthetic seamless underwear with a cotton gusset.” However, synthetic performance fabrics bring their own environmental considerations. Fabrics produced at scale are often treated with chemicals to help make them softer, brighter, water-resistant and odour-repellent. Among them are PFAS – dubbed “forever chemicals” – which are used for their water-, grease- and heat-resistant properties. These chemicals don’t necessarily sit inertly in fabric. Research published in the scientific journal Environment International suggests some PFAS can permeate the skin barrier and enter the bloodstream, which may give customers another reason to check the label. What about plastic-free underwear? Unfortunately, many moisture-wicking performance fabrics are synthetic, so those trying to reduce their use of plastic-based clothing may prefer natural or plant-derived fibres. For lower-impact workouts when you are not sweating heavily, there may be no reason to abandon the comfortable underwear you already own. “You absolutely don’t need to buy designated workout underwear simply because it’s marketed that way,” Behrens says. “If your everyday underwear is comfortable, breathable, fits properly and works well during exercise, that’s perfectly fine.” For yoga, Pilates, walking and other lower-impact forms of exercise, look for breathable natural-fibre underwear – particularly if reducing synthetic fabrics is a priority. If you sweat heavily, however, bear in mind that natural fibres such as cotton can remain damp for longer, so changing promptly afterwards becomes particularly important. Is seamless really better? If you are constantly attempting to discreetly retrieve your underwear halfway through a squat, the problem may be the cut rather than the material. “For the most part, I’d always pick seamless styles as my preference for the gym,” Woodrow says. “Beyond performance, seamless styles also work best for avoiding visible lines or bunching, since women often work out in leggings or tighter Lycra-material trousers. “After all, it’s tricky to get your best workout in if you’re constantly pulling at your underwear!” But there is no need to throw away anything with a seam. “If you’re someone who prefers lower-impact workouts, such as slower yoga, your regular, most comfortable underwear will do the job,” Woodrow says. “Seamless just earns its place when you’re moving dynamically or sweating a lot!” Ramskill says seams can be the culprit of irritability, too. “Sometimes it isn’t the fabric causing the problem at all, but a seam repeatedly rubbing the same part of the vulva or groin,” she says. Whether you are thinking about your underwear while exercising may be the best way to determine if it is right for you. “Your underwear shouldn’t be something you’re constantly aware of while exercising,” Ramskill says. “If you’re repeatedly adjusting it, it’s digging into the groin, riding up, rubbing, or you’re consistently coming away from exercise with redness, itching, soreness or chafing, it’s probably not working for your body.” The most important bit might be what you do afterwards Whatever underwear you choose, the experts emphasise the importance of not spending the rest of the day in sweaty clothes. Ideally, you should change out of your workout gear “as soon as reasonably possible”, Behrens says. “You don’t need to panic if you can’t change the second your workout finishes, but I wouldn’t recommend spending hours in damp leggings and underwear. “Showering and putting on clean, dry clothing after training helps reduce prolonged moisture, friction and irritation. If you can’t shower immediately, even changing into dry underwear and clothes is worthwhile.” So perhaps skipping a long coffee straight after a workout is the way forward to prevent irritation.

title: Trump steps up stunts as US midterms loom
description: From a row with Canada to proposed talks with North Korea’s Kim, is the US president trying to distract voters from his unpopular Iran war?
content: From trolling Canada about a lake to suddenly talking about Kim Jong-un, US President Donald Trump’s recent distractions speak louder than words. The former reality television star has long been known for his reliance upon a simple tactic: when you don’t like what’s being said, change the conversation. But the 80-year-old’s recent stunts appear to be even more targeted than usual at wrestling the news away from the Iran war and the economy as difficult midterm elections loom in November. “This president specialises in diversions,” said William Galston of the Brookings Institution. The war on Iran is proving a major drag on Trump’s approval ratings, which polls show are consistently in the low 30s, but there is no end in sight to the conflict as it hits the six-month mark. The Atlantic reported that the White House’s strategy was to try to push the conflict into the background, avoiding more military action and focusing on less newsy economic measures against Tehran. One way of doing that is by making people look the other way. On Thursday, Trump called the press into the Oval Office for a stunning announcement: he was signing an order to rename Lake Ontario, on the border with Canada, as “Lake America”. The move followed days of a headline-grabbing trade war with Canada, all reinforcing the “America First” narrative Trump sells to his political base. Democrats blasted what they called a “juvenile” move. “It’s a pathetic attempt at distraction, and it’s working families who are paying the price,” Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said in a statement after the lake announcement. A week earlier, Trump suddenly brought up the prospect of talks with North Korean leader Kim, despite having rarely mentioned the subject since returning to office in January 2025. Trump lavished praise on Kim, whom he met three times in his first term, while bashing US ally South Korea and downsizing joint military drills with Seoul. The billionaire president has also been even more talkative than usual about his makeover of the White House – although Democrats say that makes him look out of touch. On Friday he was posting on his social media platform about “cleaning and regrouting the Granite” at the White House entrance. But at the same time as he seeks to distract voters, Trump is also trying to get them to focus – on himself. After his hand-picked candidates won in a number of primaries ahead of the midterms, the two-time president is apparently convinced that he is the best way to deliver a result for Republicans. “Pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump told Fox News on Wednesday. Trump is also planning to buy television ads about his own record ahead of the elections – when many Republicans fear they will lose control of Congress – using a US$400 million political war chest. The White House has been pushing the message, highlighting this week what it said were “14 recent wins” on everything from suppressing mail-in ballots to stepped-up deportations of migrants. Yet Trump faces major challenges in getting the conversation to where he wants it. The Iran war remains a quagmire for a president who promised not to get America involved in more foreign wars. If oil prices, and therefore the cost of living, remain high then the economy is likely to remain the single biggest issue with voters in the midterms. “It’s hard to change people’s minds when you’re talking about things they’re experiencing directly,” said Galston, of the Brookings Institution. The White House has also lost one of its most powerful messengers, after formidable Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt stepped down, saying she wanted to devote more time to her children. Trump’s own star could dim too as he enters the lame-duck phase of his presidency after the midterms. But he will still be able to stay in the spotlight by creating suspense over whom he endorses as his successor in 2028. Trump has also dropped repeated hints about running for a third term as president himself. That is barred under the US constitution – but a bet against Trump has often proved a risky one.

title: Far-right activist Milo Yiannopoulos deported after immigration arrest in US
description: The British commentator is accused of overstaying in the US then failing to show up for an immigration hearing.
content: British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported back to the UK after his arrest by American immigration authorities, US officials said on Saturday. The US Department of Homeland Security said Yiannopoulos was returned to his home country on Friday after being accused of overstaying after entering the US legally in May 2019. An immigration judge had issued a final order of removal on July 22 after he failed to show up for an immigration hearing, a Homeland Security spokesman said. Yiannopoulos was arrested on Thursday at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Louisiana and detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a Homeland Security spokesman said in a statement. Yiannopoulos and his representatives did not respond to requests for comment. He has not posted on his social media account since Thursday. Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticising feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of US President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. “Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts,” Yiannopoulos wrote on social media last year. The British national has most recently worked for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, who performed in New Orleans on Friday evening. Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the early 2010s as an incendiary writer for the conservative website Breitbart News. He resigned from the company in 2017 after a video of him endorsing paedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologised for the remarks and said he himself was a victim of sexual assault as a minor. Yiannopoulos’ arrest on Thursday comes amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump’s immigration crackdown. Far-right conservative activist Laura Loomer swiftly took to social media to applaud Yiannopoulos’ arrest after years of public feuding between the two personalities. “I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer said. Controversy around Yiannopoulos ballooned in 2017 when he carried out what he called his “Troll Academy Tour” across college campuses nationwide. Fights broke out when some students protested Yiannopoulos’ appearances and accused him of hate speech, while others celebrated him as a champion of free speech. Around that time, BuzzFeed reported on Yiannopoulos’ cosy relationships with self-proclaimed white nationalists. In recent years, Yiannopoulos continued to work in the orbit of conservative activism. In 2022, he was an intern for former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, according to The Washington Post. He subsequently ran the short-lived 2024 presidential campaign for Ye. Most recently, Yiannopoulos has worked as a spokesman for Ye, who has been beset by controversy of his own following antisemitic comments that the rapper has since apologised for.

title: Nepal floods: rescuers send air pipe into tunnel with trapped workers
description: There could be over 100 survivors stuck inside the tunnels, and the breakthrough raises hopes that rescue teams will be able to reach them.
content: Nepali army rescuers broke through to a hydropower tunnel on Saturday and began pumping air and sending a camera inside, raising hopes of reaching workers trapped since devastating floods struck the site three days earlier. Nepal’s government says more than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside tunnels at hydropower projects, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites. Those trapped are among 933 hydropower workers missing since a wall of mud and debris swept down on Wednesday morning, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The US Geological Survey said the disaster on the China-Nepal border was caused by a glacial collapse, with nearly 3,000 people missing and 682 confirmed dead. At Trishuli 3A, army rescue teams using drills broke through on Saturday evening into the upper part of a mud-swamped tunnel. “We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” Nepali Home Minister Sudan Gurung said in a statement. The Ministry of Energy reported that “partial success has been achieved in the drilling operation”, adding that “efforts have begun to try to send a camera and oxygen into the tunnel”. Rescuers continued to work to clear “the mud accumulated inside the tunnel”, it added. Specialised Indian and Chinese tunnel-rescue teams have also joined the effort. India has extensive experience with difficult Himalayan tunnel rescues, including teams of “rathole” miners skilled in being able to crawl into narrow spaces. Initial reports suggested the 100 trapped were in a single location, but Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said that “rescue efforts are going on in multiple tunnel sites”. Shrestha said operations were ongoing “despite the adverse weather and extremely challenging circumstances”. Photographs shared by the disaster office showed workers wading through churned mud and navigating vast boulders left by the floods. Nepal appealed on Saturday for specialised rescue kits, including heavy-lift drones and “technologies that help us locate people alive in the affected areas”. Nepal’s expert mountain rescue teams – used to aiding climbers on the world’s highest peaks, including Everest – are also joining the search for missing people at another damaged hydropower site. “We do similar work on the mountains, with rescue operations for people trapped in risky places so I believe our skills will be useful,” said Tul Singh Gurung, president of Nepal National Mountain Guide Association.

title: Man held after laundry capsules dumped into pond, killing catfish and injuring turtles
description: Hong Kong police arrest 42-year-old suspect after examining surveillance footage of Ma On Shan incident.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a 42-year-old man after he allegedly dumped laundry capsules into a pond, killing a catfish and injuring 30 turtles in Ma On Shan, the South China Morning Post has learned. Police said on Saturday that officers were alerted on Wednesday by a security guard who found a large amount of foam in a pond at a residential estate on Kam Ying Road where turtles were kept. The guard removed the turtles from the pond and cleaned it, the force said. Officers arrested the man on Friday on suspicion of animal cruelty, according to police. A source said the guard alerted police after finding the dead catfish and 30 injured turtles in the pond at the Kam Ying Court estate. Officers examined surveillance footage and found that the suspect dumped laundry capsules into the pond at 4.57am on Wednesday before leaving the scene, according to the source. Investigators identified the suspect based on analysis of the footage and arrested him near his home at 9.15pm on Friday, the source said, adding that the man was granted bail and was required to report to police on October 1. Residents expressed anger over the incident. “Turtles have lives. This was utterly heartless,” a resident said. A boy said: “I’m really sad because those turtles are suffering.” In Hong Kong, animal cruelty is an offence punishable by up to three years’ imprisonment and a HK$200,000 fine (US$25,500).

title: Rise of Asian players Eala, Zheng points to progress on tennis’ diversity at US Open: Pegula
description: American Jessica ⁠Pegula says growth in number of black, Asian players shows sport’s global reach; Coleman Wong to start early Monday morning.
content: American players Jessica ⁠Pegula and Frances Tiafoe said tennis was moving in the right direction on diversity as Tiafoe highlighted increased representation at the top of the game and the financial barriers facing young players. Pegula said the sport’s global reach was one of its strengths, pointing to players from ‌around the world and the varied fan bases they attract. “I think the best part of tennis is there is so much diversity,” Pegula told reporters ahead of the US Open. “Everybody from around the world can play.” Pegula cited representation among black players, as well as the growth of tennis in Asia because of the likes of Alexandra Eala of the Philippines and China’s Zheng Qinwen. “You see talent from all over the world,” she said. “I think it’s honestly one of the most diverse sports.” Eala, who won her first WTA title this month, will start her US Open campaign against American Mary Stoiana, while Zheng came through the qualifying rounds to face Russia’s Kristina Liutova. Hong Kong’s Coleman Wong, meanwhile, also made it out of the qualifiers but faces a daunting first-round opponent in American 20th seed Tommy Paul at around 12.10am on Monday, Hong Kong time. The ‌New York setting of the US Open shares that diversity, Pegula said. “You see a lot of different countries and fans and different types of people come out and support ‌who they love to support,” she said. Tiafoe said representation in the women’s game had been ⁠strong for years and ⁠pointed to an increasing number of players from a range of backgrounds competing near the top of the men’s game. Tiafoe and France’s Arthur ‌Fils made history at the Cincinnati Open last week when they became the first black players to face each other in an ATP 1000 ‌tournament final. “That’s a huge thing,” Tiafoe said. Still, Tiafoe said access remained a major challenge in ‌tennis. “USTA is doing great getting underserved community kids to play the game,” he added. “Obviously, so many things cost; racquets, ⁠strings, coaching, shoes, whatever.” The USTA’s 2026 US Tennis Participation Report said 3.7 million Black Americans played tennis at least ⁠once in 2025, an increase of more than 450,000 players from the previous year. The report also showed broader changes in the demographic profile of US tennis players. Hispanic/Latino players accounted for 19 per cent of participants in 2025, up ‌from 18 per cent in 2024, while Asian/Pacific Islander players accounted for 11 per cent, unchanged from the previous year. While he said the sport was progressing, Tiafoe cautioned that affordability could not be solved quickly. “Yeah, it’s going the right direction,” he said. “It’s not something that’s going to change overnight. Cost is cost, right? It’s got to come from somewhere.”

title: Chinese coastguard has 0.3% chance of using weapons in disputed waters, war game suggests
description: Researchers create AI framework to read unknown vessels’ intentions by identifying them as ‘hostile’ or ‘harmless’ to assess risks at sea.
content: A Chinese coastguard ship is shielding a cluster of fishing boats when several small, fast vessels begin circling – sometimes darting closer, sometimes backing off. Are they just curious fishermen? Or are they probing for a weak spot, trying to lure the patrol ship into a trap? In the real world, a split-second decision could escalate a tense maritime stand-off into something far more dangerous. This is exactly the kind of nerve‑wracking scenario Chinese coastguard researchers have been running inside a computer war game. Their findings, published this month, revealed a surprising number: under the existing rule‑based command system, the simulated Chinese coastguard would resort to lethal weapons only 0.3 per cent of the time. It is a remarkably low risk – but for Beijing, even that chance is too high when the encounters involve sensitive, disputed waters. To push the risk down to zero, the team developed an artificial intelligence (AI) framework that can read a vessel’s intentions like a seasoned mariner reads the sea. The AI does not simply stamp a target as “hostile” or “harmless”; it continuously calculates the odds of multiple possible intentions – from routine fishing to coordinated harassment – and adjusts its response accordingly. In one simulation, the AI‑controlled “red side” coastguard vessel started by assigning a 72 per cent probability that a nearby ship was simply passing through harmlessly. But when three vessels suddenly formed a wedge and began closing in from different bearings, the system flipped its assessment: the probability of “successive probing” jumped to 68 per cent. The AI then ordered a water cannon to deter further advances – a measured, non‑lethal response that stayed well within the rules of engagement. Across dozens of simulated runs, the AI‑powered system never once triggered a weapons‑use violation, effectively reducing the risk to zero. It also cut the overall rate of rule breaches – such as getting too close to another vessel – from 1.2 per cent to 0.8 per cent. By comparison, the older rule‑based system correctly guessed a vessel’s intentions only 68.5 per cent of the time, while the AI reached 89.6 per cent. The secret lies in the way the AI thinks. Traditional systems rely on simple if‑then rules: if a boat crosses a certain line, it is flagged as a threat. The new framework, by contrast, merges radar tracks and other sensor data with a “causal model” – a kind of digital brain that reasons about what a vessel is trying to achieve, rather than just reacting to its movements. In one test, a group of simulated fishing boats pretended to retreat, hoping to distract the coastguard ship. Moments later, vessels from another direction suddenly accelerated in what looked like a collision attempt. The AI saw through the deception, linking the manoeuvre to a likely trick and holding its ground. “Our method generates more rational and flexible opponents and effectively exposes plan weaknesses,” wrote Sun Shengzhi, a professor at the China Coast Guard Academy and the study’s lead author. The academy, which trains officers for the People’s Armed Police Force, published the research on August 10 in the Chinese journal Command Control & Simulation. The war game was built around a “foreign interference during fishing protection” scenario – a thinly veiled reference to the kinds of grey‑zone confrontations that regularly flare up in the South China Sea and other contested waterways. One Chinese patrol vessel guarded fishing boats while four to six simulated foreign vessels carried out low‑intensity harassment and reconnaissance. All sides had to obey constraints: a minimum safe distance of 0.5 nautical miles (0.9km), strict weapons‑authorisation protocols and other operational limits. The central challenge was figuring out what a small, nimble boat really wanted, because in the maritime “grey zone”, hostile probing can look a lot like everyday navigation or fishing. Sun’s team believes the AI framework can do more than just lower the risk of accidental gunfire.
