By linking intention recognition, constrained decision‑making and adaptive opponents into a single system, it makes war games themselves more realistic – exposing weaknesses in current plans and sharpening the decision‑support tools available to human commanders. Future work, the paper said, would extend the approach to more complex, cross‑domain scenarios and explore how humans and AI can make decisions together. Still, the researchers were careful to note that taking the human out of the loop entirely was not the goal. “AI decisions remain aligned with higher‑level strategic intentions and ethical norms would require further research,” Sun wrote.

title: Xi, Putin to meet in Bishkek for Power of Siberia 2 pipeline talks: Kremlin
description: Second face-to-face talks this year to come as leaders of China and Russia visit Kyrgyzstan for Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin are expected to discuss the Power of Siberia 2 project in a meeting in Bishkek on Monday, according to the Kremlin. The meeting in Kyrgyzstan’s capital will be their second face-to-face talks this year, following Putin’s trip to Beijing shortly after a visit there by US President Donald Trump. “The issue will be discussed bilaterally,” Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov was quoted as saying on Friday by Russian news agency Interfax. “It will be discussed not only at the level of the [September 1-4] Eastern Economic Forum [in Vladivostok], but also in the meeting with the Chinese leader, which will take place on August 31.” Ushakov was responding to a question on whether the two sides were going to finalise the agreement over the long-stalled pipeline, a flagship project designed to boost Russian gas deliveries to China and further consolidate ties between the two neighbours. The Chinese foreign ministry said earlier this week that Xi would pay a state visit to Kyrgyzstan starting from Sunday and attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit there. Xi and Putin will join their Central Asian counterparts as well as the leaders of India, Pakistan, Iran and Belarus in Bishkek for the August 31-September 1 summit of the SCO, a Eurasian security bloc marking its 25th anniversary. Founded in Shanghai by six member states to counter terrorism, extremism and separatist movements in the region, the SCO has since expanded to promote economic cooperation and logistical connectivity. It has also emerged as a significant counterweight to the Western-led international order. This year’s summit comes as two SCO member states remain locked in conflicts without an end in sight. As Russia’s war in Ukraine drags on, Iran – an SCO member since 2023 – remains embroiled in a direct conflict with the United States following a sharp rise in regional tensions. The crisis is further threatening global energy stability following Tehran’s decision to restrict passage through the Strait of Hormuz – a critical chokepoint that handles roughly a quarter of the global seaborne oil trade. Iran has vowed to stand firm after the US announced fresh sanctions against 60 entities and individuals around the world, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong in the latest attempt to squeeze the Islamic republic economically after military and diplomatic efforts failed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. On Thursday, Trump also suggested that he might target Chinese banks for their dealings with Iranian entities. Concerns are growing that the latest sanctions could ignite a new flashpoint in US-China ties just weeks ahead of Xi’s visit to Washington. About half of China’s total seaborne crude oil imports in 2025 transited the Hormuz Strait, according to Chinese commodity market intelligence provider JLC. However, China’s vast pipeline network allows it to source oil and gas overland from Russia and Central Asia, mitigating the risk of maritime disruptions. First proposed in 2006, the planned 2,600km (1,616-mile) Power of Siberia 2 pipeline is expected to deliver 50 billion cubic metres (1.77 trillion cubic feet) of natural gas annually to China via Mongolia from the Arctic gas fields of Yamal in Russia. On the sidelines of Putin’s visit to Beijing in May, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said that some contracts for the pipeline were approaching “final agreement” following the summit. Beijing, however, has remained relatively quiet on the matter. China’s first-ranked vice-premier Ding Xuexiang, who oversees the intergovernmental investment and energy cooperation commissions with Russia, will join Putin at the Eastern Economic Forum next week. The international forum hosted annually in Vladivostok focuses primarily on economic integration between Russia and the Asia-Pacific region.

title: Japan probes 39kg of bread dumped in national park
description: The bread was initially believed to have been used as bait for cameras live streaming images of animals, but no such equipment was found.
content: A total of 39kg (85 lbs) of bread was recently dumped along a roadside in a national park in western Japan, prompting police to investigate who discarded it and why. The loaves were left near crash barriers in Daisen-Oki National Park in Tottori Prefecture between August 14 and 20. The incident has prompted the spread of fake images and videos attempting to link the dumping to a sharp increase in bear encounters in Japan over the past year. “When I first heard of the reports, my head was full of question marks,” said Koji Iwaihara, director of the Natural Parks Foundation’s Tottori branch. The bread was initially believed to have been used as bait for cameras live streaming images of animals, but no such equipment was found. The foundation later came to believe the bread had been left to feed animals after 1.3kg of chicken was found in the same area. Bread was also found scattered around the prefecture’s Hakuto coast, but the brand appears to be different from that found in the national park. Neither the bread nor the chicken was poisoned. The prefecture has since installed security cameras in Daisen-Oki National Park, but no further dumping has been reported. “I don’t understand why it was left on the side of the road” as opposed to inside the mountain, said Tottori Governor Shinji Hirai, questioning the theory that the food may have been placed there as bear bait. If that really is the aim, “it may become a dangerous precedent as bears become accustomed to the taste of bread”, he added. AI-generated videos and images showing a bear looking at or eating the bread have spread on social media. The prefectural government plans to ask social media platforms to remove them over concerns that the false content could cause reputational damage. Prefectural police said the perpetrator may have violated a law against illegal dumping or regulations governing national parks.

title: Scientists probe if herpes virus is killing sardines off South Africa
description: Pilchard herpesvirus is a fish virus and poses no known risk to human health.
content: Scientists in South Africa are investigating why masses of sardines have washed up dead or dying along parts of the country’s west and south coast – and if a herpes virus detected in the fish is responsible. The mass mortality of sardines this month has so far stumped the country’s Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, though scientists have come to at least one conclusion: it is the first time that the virus in question – pilchard herpesvirus, or PHV – has been identified in sardines off South Africa. PHV, which was linked to two mass sardine mortality events in Australia in the 1990s, can cause inflammation and thickening of sardines’ gills, which interferes with their oxygen uptake, according to the South African environment department. Sardines and pilchards are the same type of fish, with sardines being the younger, smaller ones. PHV is a fish virus and poses no known risk to human health, the department said, and its detection does not mean that healthy sardines caught commercially or canned sardine products are unsafe to eat. Dozens of sardines taken from affected areas, some dead and some alive, are being examined by scientists at the South African Institute for Aquatic Biodiversity and a local university. In some initial results, dead fish collected from the mass mortality events showed consistently high levels of PHV, the department said in a statement, while live fish that were examined had varied levels of the virus. Scientists have also considered whether harmful algae found in the ocean or unusually cold sea temperatures or low oxygen conditions might be responsible for the sardine deaths, but “the evidence increasingly points to PHV as the leading explanation,” the environment department said. Dalene Vosloo, a biological sciences lecturer at South Africa’s University of KwaZulu-Natal who is not involved in the investigation, said the herpes virus may not tell the whole story and “it remains possible that multiple factors contributed to the mortality event.” Changes in water quality or temperature can make fish more vulnerable to disease, she said. While the investigation continues, the sardine deaths have caused other complications. The Koeberg Nuclear Power Station north of Cape Town on South Africa’s west coast – the only nuclear power station in Africa – had to cut power by 50 per cent at one of its two units after dead sardines clogged a seawater intake, according to the national electricity company that runs the station.

title: What Japan’s coming fighter jet deployment to India means for China
description: The historic move signals Tokyo’s desire to strengthen defence ties with ‘like-minded’ Indo-Pacific powers, analysts say.
content: Japan plans to deploy fighter jets in India for the first time next month, a decision experts say reflects Tokyo’s desire to strengthen security cooperation with “like-minded” countries in the Indo-Pacific region as it ramps up defence spending in response to China’s growing military power. According to a Japan Air Self-Defence Force announcement on Tuesday, Tokyo will conduct a joint training exercise, Veer Guardian 26, with the Indian Air Force between September 9 and 21 in Rajasthan in western India. As part of the joint training, Tokyo said it would deploy three F-2 fighter jets to India, as well as about 110 personnel from the Eighth Air Wing stationed at Tsuiki Airbase in southwestern Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture. “This will be a valuable opportunity to enhance mutual understanding and trust,” said Takehiro Morita, chief of staff of the Japan Air Self-Defence Force. The deployment – Japan’s first involving fighter jets to India – comes on the heels of a visit by Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi to India last week. Koizumi met Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and pledged “to further deepen defence cooperation” through bilateral exercises, aiming to achieve a free and open Indo-Pacific. The strategic message is therefore significant: two major Asian powers increasingly see their respective security theatres as interconnected Jagannath Panda, Indo-Pacific affairs expert The news of the deployment was first reported earlier this month, with Japanese media saying that Koizumi would discuss the F-2 fighter during his visit to India. An unnamed Japanese defence ministry official reportedly told the Asahi Shimbun that the deployment aimed to “serve as a check on China”. A Chinese expert cited by state-backed tabloid Global Times at the time accused Tokyo of trying to turn New Delhi into a “frontline player” in Japan’s geopolitical rivalry with China and its revival of “militarism”. Jagannath Panda, head of the Stockholm Centre for South Asian and Indo-Pacific Affairs at the Institute for Security and Development Policy in Sweden, said that the significance of this year’s Veer Guardian exercise went well beyond a routine bilateral drill. He said Japan’s F-2 deployment to India showed that the two air forces were “gradually moving from political-strategic understanding towards greater operational familiarity”, with China as an “important strategic backdrop”. “India confronts China along the Himalayan frontier, while Japan faces growing Chinese military activity in the East China Sea and western Pacific,” Panda said. “The strategic message is therefore significant: two major Asian powers increasingly see their respective security theatres as interconnected.” Both Japan and India are members of the “Quad” security alliance, along with the United States and Australia. The group is seen as a counterweight to China’s expanding presence in the Indian Ocean and wider Indo-Pacific region. The two countries held their inaugural Veer Guardian joint air exercise in Japan in January 2023, at the Hyakuri and Iruma airbases outside Tokyo. The drills featured India’s Su-30MKI aircraft and Japan’s F-2 and F-15 fighters. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government has pledged to accelerate the country’s military build-up amid growing tensions with China and US pressure on allies to shoulder more of the defence burden. The Japanese defence ministry is reportedly preparing to request a record budget of 8.9 trillion yen (US$56 billion) for the 2027 financial year in an attempt to reach 2 per cent of gross domestic product. In a white paper published earlier this month, Tokyo described Beijing’s external posture and military activities as a “matter of serious concern” for Japan and the international community. It added that China’s activities presented an “unprecedented” strategic challenge. The white paper also said Japan would actively promote bilateral and multilateral exercises “with its ally and like-minded countries” throughout the Indo-Pacific region. Relations between Beijing and Tokyo soured in November after Takaichi suggested that Japan could take military action in the event of an attack on Taiwan. Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo’s International Christian University, said Japan was “actively diversifying” its security portfolio in the face of pressure from both Beijing and Washington. “Deploying F-2s to India signals a mutual recognition that Indo-Pacific stability requires networked deterrence. It’s a pragmatic step to build trust and operational familiarity outside traditional US-centric bilateral frameworks,” Nagy said. “[Japan and India] demonstrate to Beijing that regional powers can coordinate complex air operations, complicating China’s strategic calculus across multiple theatres simultaneously.” Nagy said that Japan increasingly viewed its security through a broader Indo-Pacific lens, and by projecting its presence into South Asia, Tokyo was showing it could be a “credible, stabilising security provider” far beyond northeast Asia. “This reflects a deliberate division of labour. With Washington distracted by the Iran conflict, middle powers like Japan and India are stepping up to anchor regional deterrence.” Liselotte Odgaard, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute in Washington, said Japan’s fighter deployment was primarily aimed at strengthening the strategic partnership with New Delhi as part of a “broader Indo-Pacific balancing strategy”. “The exercise reflects Tokyo’s interest in building security networks among like-minded countries concerned about China’s growing military power and coercive behaviour,” Odgaard said. “It also enables the Japan Air Self-Defence Force to gain experience in long-range deployments, expeditionary logistics and operations far from northeast Asia.” She added that the exercise would contribute to “deeper defence cooperation” that “complements” expanding cooperation in maritime security, defence technology, information sharing and broader Quad-related initiatives. Panda said that India’s growing military partnership with Japan should “primarily be understood through the China factor and the changing Indo-Pacific balance of power”. “New Delhi increasingly regards Japan as a highly trusted strategic and technological partner whose security interests overlap considerably with India’s, particularly regarding maritime security, freedom of navigation, resilient supply chains and concerns over China’s growing military capabilities,” he said.

title: Hong Kong’s Diocesan Boys’ School to become first to offer 3 university pathways
description: Parents should weigh international competitiveness and their child’s individual suitability when choosing curricula, education expert says.
content: Hong Kong’s elite Diocesan Boys’ School is set to offer the International Advanced Level curriculum from 2027, becoming the city’s first school to offer three university pathways if it secures the Education Bureau’s approval. Headmaster Ronnie Cheng Kay-yen made the announcement on Saturday at a Primary One admission talk at its Mong Kok campus, after the school obtained approval from Cambridge International Education and the Hong Kong Examinations and Assessment Authority. “We are now waiting for the Education Bureau’s green light,” Cheng said. “We are going full throttle to offer the Diploma of Secondary Education, the International Baccalaureate and the International Advanced Level. “We have 1,400 secondary students and 900 primary students. Their learning speed, ability and direction are very different. We should strive to find ways so they can find a suitable learning model.” Cheng said Form Three students in the 2026-27 school year, which starts next Tuesday, were expected to opt for the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE), International Baccalaureate (IB) or International Advanced Level (IAL) curricula. DSE is the city’s main university entrance pathway, while the IB and IAL are internationally recognised curricula. The South China Morning Post earlier reported that Hong Kong public universities admitted a record number of students applying outside the local DSE exam system, jumping by 63 per cent from 2,706 in 2019-20 to 4,401 in 2025-26. Meanwhile, the intake of home-grown students taking the DSE exam dropped by 7 per cent, from 12,355 to 11,503 over the same period. Samuel Chan Sze-ming, founder of education consultancy Britannia StudyLink, said parents weighing the three curricula must balance international competitiveness against their child’s individual suitability. He noted that the DSE showed weakness in overseas university applications and was better suited for students who performed well in rote memorisation. “The DSE is newer compared with the IB and A-levels, and it can be seen as more of a spoon-feeding curriculum in overseas university applications,” he said. Chan described the IB as more comprehensive, blending science and humanities through a project-based approach. But he cautioned that its framework required strong time management and self-discipline. “It suits well-rounded students, but not those who struggle to balance different areas,” he said. The IAL was better suited for students who excelled in specific subjects while avoiding weaker areas, Chan said. “It has become a popular choice for students seeking a different route into top local universities through the non-JUPAS pathway,” he said, referring to the centralised system for local students applying to full-time undergraduate programmes. He added that the IAL’s modular structure allowed students to pick subjects that matched their strengths, offering greater flexibility. “If more Hong Kong Direct Subsidy Scheme schools follow the lead of institutions like Diocesan Boys’ School and embrace IAL, I believe Hong Kong will become more internationally competitive,” he said. Currently, non-local curricula are offered at 53 international schools, eight private independent schools and 21 semi-private local schools in Hong Kong. Florence Yu, whose elder son is enrolled in Form Two at the Diocesan Boys’ School, said she was glad to see the school offering more options. “It’s up to him to choose the curriculum, whether he wants to enrol in local [universities] through the DSE, or he wants to challenge himself and try the IB or even IAL. More options are always better,” the mother in her thirties said. But Yu noted that competition for admission into the school’s IB programme was intense. She added that teachers would observe students’ academic performance and personality, and advise them to pick a suitable curriculum, noting that the IB and IAL might better align with overseas universities. Another parent, surnamed Tsang, whose son is nearly five years old, said having more curriculum choices increased the school’s appeal. His wife, surnamed Chau, said it was too early to tell which curriculum would suit her son, as circumstances could differ in nine years, such as the popularity and international recognition of the curricula. She added that her child’s interest in certain subjects, and his language as well as time management skills, would also affect his choice. The Education Bureau said on Saturday evening that it had received the application from the school and was reviewing it.

title: Soldiers’ mutiny rocks Niger capital, but junta says back in control
description: Niger has been ruled for three years by a military junta that has struggled to contain jihadist violence.
content: Mutinying soldiers led armed clashes in Niger’s capital on Saturday, alarming residents, but the ruling junta said it had largely wrested back control after hours of heavy exchanges around some of its most sensitive sites. While the fighting had subsided later on Saturday, the rebel troops were said by a regional security source and an African diplomatic source to be holed up in an airbase near the capital’s airport. Niger’s ruling junta declared, in a statement read on state television, that it “gradually took back control” after hours of clashes. When the fighting broke out, shortly after midnight, soldiers blocked access to the presidential palace and to the national television station, Tele Sahel, which went off the air for just over an hour, before being restored around 10am. “There was an attempt by insurgents from the Nigerien armed forces to enter the presidential palace,” a security source said, adding that “they were pushed back by the presidential guard”. Niger’s defence minister, General Salifou Mody, said in the statement on state television that a group of soldiers held some troops hostage at a barracks in Niamey and opened fire at “certain sensitive sites” in the city, without specifying which ones. “The prompt reaction of the defence and security forces made it possible to contain this heated moment and they gradually took back control of these sites,” he added. Mody’s statement called on the population to “remain calm and freely go about their business”. Niger has been ruled for three years by a military junta led by General Abdourahamane Tiani that has struggled to contain jihadist violence flaring in the west African country for around a decade. “Everything is calm again, we can’t hear any more shooting,” a resident of the Yantala district close to the presidential palace said late on Saturday morning. The gunfire began in the early hours of Saturday morning, prompting the military to issue a statement on its social media pages urging people to stay calm and “avoid sharing unverified information”. “Our defence and security forces have been mobilised for the defence of the homeland,” the statement said. One local resident said that there was “heavy gunfire and explosions” at Base 101 in Niamey, a claim confirmed by several other witnesses. Junta supporters called for “sincere patriots” to demonstrate in support of the authorities. Neighbouring Algeria condemned Saturday’s events and pledged support for the Niamey government. The first shots were heard at about 1am and continued until daybreak, according to a video published by a local journalist filming the area around the airport. Another local resident said he heard “bursts of gunfire” at about 7am adding that the weapons heard “are not the kind that terrorists on motorbikes can carry”. “I went to get credit for my phone. I saw a military vehicle heading towards the base that had to turn back,” he said. Another resident in the west of Niamey said he heard sporadic small-arms fire at about 5am. Videos online showed armoured vehicles deployed to reinforce the neighbourhood near the airport. Niamey airport has been targeted twice this year by jihadists, first by the Islamic State in the Sahel (EIS) in January, then in late June by its rival, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM), the Sahel branch of al-Qaeda. The jihadist groups not only target civilians and the military but are also struggling for dominance over each other in the Sahel, and especially in Niger. Twenty assailants were killed and four soldiers wounded in the January assault, authorities said at the time. In June, at least 11 soldiers and two civilians were killed, as well as 22 attackers, according to the defence ministry. Both attacks were repelled by the army. The EIS and JNIM are also active in neighbouring Burkina Faso and Mali, allies of Niger that are also ruled by military juntas that seized power in coups. The three countries quit the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) bloc, turned their backs on traditional Western partners in the fight against jihadist violence, especially France, and sought closer ties with Russia. Air Force Base 101, located within the international airport complex, is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Africa Corps in Niamey and the command of the unified force of the Alliance of Sahel States, of which Niger is a member with Burkina Faso and Mali. The site is sensitive. Between December and January, it hosted a large shipment of uranium concentrate, which was held up while awaiting export. No movement of the shipment has been identified since.

title: Spud-tacular hotel celebrates potatoes in food, facials and farming
description: Germany’s Potato Hotel offers potato treatments, yoga sessions and work opportunities for young travellers who are looking for a free stay.
content: Guests arriving at the Potato Hotel in northern Germany are greeted by a schnapps served in potatoes-turned-tumblers. After taking a bite from the canapés – potato zucchini rolls and sweet potato pie – it should be clear that potatoes rule all at this cosy refurbished farm to the southeast of Hamburg. While waiting for the room key – adorned with a stone potato – visitors can purchase sacks of freshly harvested potatoes at reception. The rooms, some of which used to be cattle pens, are named after old varieties like Gloria, Hansa and Clivia. Olaf Stehr, who has run the establishment for 30 years, proudly explains that it draws guests from around the globe. Stehr fondly remembers when managers from Japan’s largest chip factory came to stay: “They were delighted. We cooked Japanese-German recipes together.” Angelika Offermann has not travelled from as far as Japan, but she has been to the Potato Hotel an impressive 28 times, or maybe 29 – she cannot remember exactly how many, she says. Offermann, who is from a town roughly two hours away by car, initially came to the hotel – called Deutsches Kartoffel-Hotel in German – with a group of friends. Years later, she still regularly returns to the hotel on her own to enjoy the quiet in the village of Lübeln that counts less than 100 residents. “During the day, I hire a bike, cycle about 20 kilometres [12 miles] and stop somewhere for an ice cream. After that, I relax and look forward to the evening meal,” she says. Many guests are attracted by the tranquillity of the nearby Elbe river, or the many walking trails and cycling routes in the Lüneburg Heath region, with tips often exchanged at the breakfast buffet, according to Offermann. The Potato Hotel was born some 35 years ago, when Stehr’s family began offering getaways for the region’s farmers at their horse farm. Payment could be made in kind, with the Stehrs hoping for hay and straw, which was scarce at the time. But the farmers brought masses of potatoes instead. Since they were unsuitable as horse food, the unique guest house was born. Offermann has made friends with Gabi Hoffmann from Berlin who is staying for five days. “I’ve really been able to relax here,” she says, praising the staff for their attentiveness. Yoga sessions are offered three times a day, alongside a meditation practice in the evening. Guests can also enjoy several potato treatments, including face masks and full-body wraps. Heide Brohzat, who has been in charge of treatments at the hotel for decades, mixes cooked, dark-yellow Princess potatoes with oil and honey to make a face paste, while offering tips for making beauty products at home. Six cooks are in charge of dinner. The main star? Potatoes, of course. The hotel employs a total of 20 people, while also offering work opportunities for young travellers who are looking for a free stay as well as paid-for German lessons. “We always have young people from all over the world, and they’re all forced to communicate in foreign languages,” says Sylvia Methfessel, Stehr’s right-hand woman. “That really brings the team together.” “It’s exciting and educational,” says Dagmar Lach while preparing the evening menu in the kitchen. Next to her, Gabriel, a temporary worker from Spain’s Canary Islands, is peeling buckets full of potatoes. “I like Germany,” Gabriel says with a smile. He does not speak English, but he is learning German every day. Stehr notes that many of his cooks have been working at the hotel for a very long time, including one who has been there for more than 30 years. “It’s actually my second home; I only go back to my flat to sleep,” says chef Lach with a grin. The hotel has 35 rooms. As if the potato theme was not quirky enough, one room is dedicated to the Rolling Stones, in a nod to the nearby Stones Fan Museum. Visitors to the museum get a discount at the Potato Hotel.

title: China’s Middle East policy at a crossroads 6 months into US-Israeli war on Iran
description: Gulf states are rethinking their strategy after coming under attack, but observers say Beijing does not want to commit itself too deeply.
content: Gulf states are making a strategic pivot as the war in Iran drags on into its sixth month, but observers warn that their shift towards self-reliant defence networks could test China’s “involvement without commitment” strategy in the region. The war has forced Gulf leaders to face the reality that neither the United States nor China is able to protect them from attacks by Iran. On Wednesday, the Iranian army warned that any “possible future war” with the United States could spread across the region and target energy and communications infrastructure. In the face of such threats, Gulf states have been seeking new defensive partners. On Thursday, Kuwait signed a military cooperation agreement with Pakistan, which promised to provide training and boost the city state’s defensive capacity. The deal followed Saudi Arabia’s signing of a three-way pact with Turkey and Pakistan, which included a Nato-style clause that an attack on one member would be treated as an attack on them all. Analysts have said that agreement may serve as a precedent for other US-aligned nations seeking greater strategic autonomy. Zhu Zhaoyi, executive director of the Institute of Middle East Studies at the Pangoal Institution, a Beijing-based think tank, said the Iran war was “an imperative accelerator” that had forced neighbouring countries to rethink their position. “Over the past decade, US dominance in the Middle East has steadily unravelled, yet considerable uncertainty remains regarding what a post-American regional order will look like,” he said. “Middle powers such as Turkey, Israel, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates are all exercising greater autonomy and engaging in higher-intensity strategic manoeuvres.” When the US and Israel launched their attack on Iran in late February, the Gulf states had initially hoped that China, one of Iran’s main diplomatic and economic partners, would use its influence to steer Tehran towards a negotiated settlement. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi embarked on a flurry of diplomatic activity, speaking to his counterparts in all six Gulf Cooperation Council member states as well as the foreign ministers of Iran, Israel, Egypt and Turkey. In April, President Xi Jinping also unveiled a four-point peace plan when he met Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the crown prince of Abu Dhabi, in Beijing. But despite these efforts, Iran continued targeting the Gulf states. “The war exposed the gap between China’s influence and its power,” said Naser al-Tamimi, a British-based political analyst and the founder of MidEast Strategia, a consultancy specialising in geostrategy, energy politics and China’s relations with the Gulf. “Beijing has significant economic leverage over Iran and privileged political access in Tehran, but it does not control Iranian decision-making. “Nor is China prepared to expend substantial political, economic or military capital to restrain Iran for the Gulf’s benefit. This matters especially when Tehran believes its regime’s survival is at stake.” He said Beijing saw the Gulf states as important partners for energy, trade and investment, but its core interests were not at stake and it remained guided by a non-interventionist policy. “China is not becoming less important; its role is becoming clearer,” he said. Ahmed Aboudouh, an associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank and head of the China Studies Unit at the Emirates Policy Centre in Abu Dhabi, said China had adopted an approach of “involvement without commitment”. He said: “This position was designed as a risk-mitigation insurance policy, not as a diplomatic offence aimed at gaining more influence.” Tamimi said the Gulf states were looking to strike a balance between their security relationship with the US and economic and diplomatic ties with China – an approach he described as a “deeper shift” from “hedging between great powers to hedging against dependence itself”. This changing dynamic has left China’s Middle East policy, and its ambitions to act as a peacemaker, at a crossroads. In 2023, it helped to broker an agreement to restore diplomatic relations between Iran and Saudi Arabia. The following year, it helped 14 feuding Palestinian factions, including Hamas and Fatah, sign a declaration of unity. But Aboudouh said: “By continuously targeting Gulf states, Iran is effectively undermining Beijing’s model of reconciliation established by overseeing the Iran-Saudi rapprochement agreement in 2023. If it collapses, China’s diplomatic posture may be brought back to square one.” Zhu argued China had to avoid being drawn into regional alliances, saying: “If Beijing is forced to choose sides, it would undermine its narrative as a leader of the Global South. “Maintaining strategic composure between multipolarisation and bloc politics is the central issue Beijing faces in this conflict, as well as a crucial litmus test for the maturity of China’s Middle East policy.”

title: Hong Kong school opens at new Tai Po campus after deadly Wang Fuk Court blaze
description: Nearly 600 Tai Po Baptist Public School pupils to begin new term at renovated campus after months of disruption split across two temporary sites.
content: Nearly 600 pupils and their teachers at a Hong Kong primary school closed after the deadly Wang Fuk Court blaze will be reunited at a newly renovated campus in Tai Po, ending months spent across two temporary sites. Tai Po Baptist Public School, formerly located near Wang Fuk Court, opened its new premises at Fu Shin Estate on Saturday, with pupils, teachers and parents expressing relief at finally having a settled place to reunite. The campus was formerly home to CCC Kei Ching Primary School, and the Education Bureau spent HK$43.6 million (US$5.6 million) refurbishing classrooms, toilets, the assembly hall and basketball court, as well as replacing electrical and air-conditioning systems. Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin officiated at the opening ceremony. “The school has gone through difficulties and, with the collaboration of various parties, has been reborn after the fire,” she said. “The relocation … to its new premises at Fu Shin Estate is not merely a change of location, but also a significant moment for all teachers and students to reunite and embark on a new page together.” The deadliest fire in the city in decades tore through seven of the eight blocks at Wang Fuk Court last November, killing 168 people and displacing about 5,000 residents. Tai Po Baptist Public School, directly opposite the estate, was temporarily sealed off after the fire to support emergency relief efforts. Managers later said they hoped to relocate because the view of the charred buildings could make parents and pupils uncomfortable. From December 2025 to last month, the school’s pupils were split between two host institutions in the district. They attended makeshift temporary classrooms at Tai Po Government Primary School and NTWJWA Christian Remembrance of Grace Primary School. Primary Six pupil Chloe Yang, 12, said she was excited to see the renovated campus and could finally be reunited with her classmates after being assigned to Tai Po Government Primary School during the interim period. “I am so happy to see familiar faces again,” she said. “I was impressed by the new climbing room and basketball court – I love to play basketball – and I look forward to classroom learning.” Teacher Alice Lai said she was glad the school could finally “come back home”, adding that guided tours would be arranged during the first week to help pupils familiarise themselves with the new facilities. She said she still felt sentimental about leaving the campus where she had taught for eight years. “Before the fire, the old campus was full of sunlight and vitality, as the lobby faced the Wang Fuk Court building directly. But when we returned to pack up, we saw the estate after the fire – there was mud and iron bars scattered all over the ground,” she said. The new campus has been equipped with an artificial intelligence sports corridor for interactive exercise, as well as six new multifunction rooms for counselling, speech therapy and play. A Wang Shing House resident surnamed Hung, whose seven-year-old son, Ethan Ching, is entering Primary Two, said she hoped he would enjoy the new campus and its facilities. “I am thankful to the teachers for providing emotional care during the transition, and I arranged more activities for him over the summer holiday to help him forget what happened when the fire broke out,” she said, adding that her son was at home when the fire broke out. Principal Siu Ting said the new campus was equipped with a diverse range of facilities to support whole-person development. The school was also working with universities and NGOs in the hope of establishing long-term partnerships to develop pupils’ soft skills and facilitate learning outside the classroom. She acknowledged that the relocation had affected enrolment, with three Primary One classes this year, compared with four last year. “Moving into a new estate, we need time to build trust with parents, but we hope to work with different organisations to provide more learning opportunities for our students,” she said.

title: China football talent left sat on sidelines as game is ruined, ex-captain Li says
description: Former international Li Weifeng takes aim at the ‘social influence’ he says stops best people from being in position to improve things.
content: Football in China is being run by people without the skill to do so, as those with talent sit on the sidelines, former international Li Weifeng has said in a withering assessment of the game in the country. Speaking during a live stream on social media, Li, who stopped playing in 2015, said the decision to axe head coach Bora Milutinovic, who guided China to their only Fifa World Cup appearance to date in Japan and South Korea in 2002, was a classic case in point. Rather than being rewarded with a contract extension, the Serbian tactician was cut by the Chinese Football Association after the tournament, where his team lost all three group matches against Costa Rica, Brazil and Turkey. A long-serving national team member from 1998 to 2011, Li said that in the environment at the time, those with talent who existed outside the established system could not secure their positions on professional merit alone. The problem according to Li was “not in the individual abilities of players and coaches,” but rather that social connections were a significant influencing factor in who rose to the top. “Without breaking down these barriers, no matter how many managers, coaching teams, or player rosters are changed, the current state of the industry cannot be altered,” Li reportedly said. Asked about the departure of Milutinovic, Li briefly paused for a few seconds, before saying: “Bora is too capable, and he has too many ideas of his own.” While most Chinese social media users appeared to have accepted the distorted culture and suggested it happened in almost every business and sector, there were still some who were hoping for a change. “We won’t change if we don’t acknowledge it, we won’t improve if we don’t change,” one commentator said. “Those senior figures within the industry are accustomed to and benefiting from established patterns – they have become the biggest obstacle to reform.” Others said the 2002 incident was the “biggest scandal” in the history of the Chinese national football team, and that Milutinović was “really tricked” back then. Last week, after Xu Jiayin, founder of the Evergrande Group, was sentenced to life imprisonment, the history surrounding football club Guangzhou Evergrande and the impact they had on Chinese football again became a hot topic. Li revealed an incident when Evergrande, then still playing in China League One, tried to lure him away from Suwon Bluewings in South Korea by faxing him a contract that left the salary column blank. The former Chinese captain, who did not sign the contract, said he was told “to fill in anything, and it would take effect as soon as I did”. It was estimated that Xu had invested a total of 17 billion yuan (US$2.5 billion) in football projects from 2010 to 2011, of which 14 billion yuan was given to the Evergrande team, with three billion yuan more spent on the Evergrande Football School. The annual pre-tax salary of the Evergrande squad in 2018 was also reportedly as high as 1.45 billion yuan. Some social media users suggested that, while Chinese football’s decline began many years ago, it was timely that someone from outside the current system was willing to raise and expose the long-standing issues, such as ultra-high salaries keeping the players in the country instead of playing overseas, and the distorted culture of driving the more able people away. Although one user summed up the feelings of many, writing: “The issue of social circles isn’t something that happened overnight, don’t expect him to change it all by himself.”

title: China-Nepal floods: police officer filmed guiding people away from stricken border post
description: Footage from Gyirong Port in Tibet shows how Huang Peng tried to guide civilians to safety moments before the crossing was destroyed.
content: Video footage taken moments before a catastrophic mudslide hit a border post in Tibet this week shows how one police officer stationed there tried to guide civilians to safety. The clip, which shows the officer trying to direct people away from the police station at Gyirong Port, went viral online in China over the weekend. State broadcaster CCTV said the officer, whom it named as Huang Peng, also rushed into a nearby tourist service centre to tell those inside to evacuate. The 34-year-old, who had served at the border station for 13 years, was on duty when the disaster struck on Wednesday and there has been no word on whether he survived. The landslide was triggered by the collapse of a glacier about 7km (4.3 miles) from the border crossing. The debris was travelling at an estimated speed of 50 metres (164 feet) per second when it struck the crossing, giving people virtually no time to react. Satellite images indicate that all the buildings at Gyirong Port were obliterated by the mudslide and its social media accounts have gone silent. Internet users have flooded previous posts with hundreds of messages praying for the safety of the border team. “Please post an update to let us know you’re safe,” one comment read. The disaster knocked out power and internet and phone signals across the affected area, although telecoms services were restored to one village about 3km from the border on Thursday, according to state news agency Xinhua. Search and rescue efforts continued on both sides of the border on Saturday. Seven people have been confirmed dead on the Chinese side, with 544 missing. At least 675 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal as of Saturday, while over 2,400 remain missing.

title: Driven by ‘deep love’: China family’s 3,500km drive for son’s university marks life milestone
description: Viral story has taken mainland social media by storm, with netizens praising – and deeply envying – the family’s tight-knit bond.
content: A family embarked on a remarkable 3,500km journey from eastern China to the northwestern region of the country to help their son commence his university life, garnering significant attention online and receiving a wealth of good wishes. The boy graduated from high school in Zaozhuang, Shandong province, this summer before being accepted at Xinjiang Second Medical College in Karamay, a prominent city in Xinjiang. His father, surnamed Geng, opted to drive his family in their seven-seater MPV to take the boy to medical school, which is situated 3,500km from their hometown of Zaozhuang. According to a report from the news portal The Cover, the trip involved six family members. In addition to the boy and his parents, his older sister, her husband, and the boy’s grandfather, who is in his 80s, were also aboard. They set off on August 20 and reached the university four days later. To make their journey memorable, the father spray-painted the vehicle’s back window, displaying Chinese characters that read, “Sending son to university; Zaozhuang of Shandong to Karamay of Xinjiang.” This eye-catching message drew public attention along the route, and other drivers often expressed camaraderie, empathising with such devoted parents, Geng noted. Geng, his wife, their daughter, and her husband took turns driving. They made regular stops for safety and occasionally visited tourist spots along the way, as shared on Geng’s social media. Before arriving in Karamay, they first travelled to Urumqi, the capital city of Xinjiang, as the grandfather wished to see his younger brother after decades apart, hindered by travel difficulties between Shandong and Xinjiang. Geng estimated the total cost of the trip at 12,000–15,000 yuan (US$1,800–US$2,200), which included 6,000 yuan for petrol, 3,000 yuan for road tolls, and several thousand yuan for meals and hotel stays. This approach was more economical than flying, which would have cost about 18,000 yuan for six passengers, yet pricier than the train trip, which totalled around 10,800 yuan. “But driving offers convenience. We can bring a lot of luggage and stop whenever we like. More importantly, this journey creates lasting memories,” Geng remarked. He mentioned having to suspend his machine rental business for two weeks to make the trip possible. “Sending my child to register at university is far more important than making money. Beginning his university life is a significant milestone,” he explained, adding that he regretted not having taken his son on trips in the past decade due to his demanding work schedule. In 2017, Geng and his wife also drove to accompany their daughter to study at a university in Qingdao, located about 400km from their home. Geng’s son chose to study clinical medicine in high school. With a mid-level score on the national university entrance exam, he was only able to enrol in a medical school in a remote region like Xinjiang. “I am profoundly moved by my family’s decision to drive such a long distance to support my university journey. Their deep love for me is unmistakable,” said the boy, who celebrated his 18th birthday a few months ago. The story has resonated widely, earning a flurry of praise on mainland social media. “What a happy family! I admire the strong bond they share,” remarked one online observer. Another added: “Kudos to this family! I believe the boy will cherish this trip for a lifetime.”

title: Russian drone strike near Kyiv kills at least 37
description: The strike hit a depot that appeared to have been storing ‘explosive objects’.
content: At least 37 people have died after a Russian drone struck a depot near Kyiv’s western suburbs overnight, sparking a huge fire and explosions, authorities said on Saturday. The depot, near the capital’s western suburbs, appeared to have been storing “explosive objects”, Ukrainian prosecutors said, as President Volodymyr Zelensky suggested ammunition was to blame. “Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions... ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas,” he wrote on social media. Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, sparking fires and sending civilian casualties to record levels. AFP reporters saw a huge column of black smoke pouring over the capital’s western suburbs, as officials reported the facility was still on fire. The blast damaged surrounding residential areas, as well as a care home for the elderly and disabled people, Zelensky said. “Unfortunately, the number of dead in the Bucha district has risen to 37 … Rescuers and all relevant services are continuing their operations at the scene of the tragedy,” Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram. Among the dead was Taras Didych, mayor of the village of Dmytrivska, he added. Ukrainian prosecutors announced an investigation. “On August 28, at around 8.10pm, an unmanned aerial vehicle … fell on or struck the grounds of an enterprise in the town of Myla,” the office of Ukraine’s prosecutor general said. Myla is a town on Kyiv’s western outskirts. “A large-scale fire broke out on the enterprise’s grounds, and detonation began,” it added. The prosecutor’s office specified that its investigation would focus on “the legality of the … storage of explosive objects and materials on the enterprise’s grounds”, as well as whether the company, which was not named, had the “necessary permits and approvals”. Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky expressed regret that a “lesson” had not been learned after a previous deadly attack in July in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, on a munitions depot. That investigation revealed serious failings on the part of the state-owned company, which did not comply with standards despite the proximity of residential buildings. “In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence,” he said on Telegram. “Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again.”

title: Temasek backs Singapore Airlines’ Air India investment amid growing scrutiny
description: News of the funding request prompted a lawmaker from Singapore’s opposition to urge that Temasek’s funds not be used.
content: Singapore state investor Temasek, the ⁠majority shareholder of Singapore Airlines , on Saturday backed the airline’s investment in Air India, as scrutiny grows over its stake in the loss-making Indian carrier. Air India’s request for about US$1.5 billion in fresh equity from owners Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines was ‌first reported by Reuters this week. Singapore Airlines owns 25.1 per cent of India’s second-largest airline, with the rest owned by Tata. News of the funding request prompted Kenneth Tiong, a lawmaker from Singapore’s opposition Workers’ Party, to urge that Temasek’s funds not be used to shore up the Indian carrier. Singapore’s Business Times also ran a commentary arguing that Singapore Airlines could not realistically ⁠exit its Air India stake, with Tata the only plausible buyer. It questioned what its 25.1 per cent holding ‌offered beyond a board seat and a share of the losses, while saying the strategic logic of the investment still held. In a letter to the newspaper ‌responding to that commentary, Juliet Teo, joint head of portfolio development at Temasek Singapore, said ⁠Temasek viewed Singapore ⁠Airlines’ decision to invest in Air India from a long-term perspective and was supportive of it. The letter said the transformation of ‌Air India involved complex, multi-year operational and integration challenges, with outcomes shaped by industry developments and external factors such as airspace disruptions, geopolitical ‌developments and ‌fuel price volatility. “Efforts of this scale take time and are not expected to be linear,” it ‌said. Temasek did not address whether it would support any capital contribution by Singapore Airlines to Air ⁠India. Air India’s multibillion-dollar revamp has been under way since Tata took control of the former state-owned carrier ⁠in 2022. Air India has been hit by Pakistan’s airspace ban on Indian carriers, disruptions from the US-Israeli war with Iran, and the fallout from a crash last year that killed ‌260 people. In the year ‌to March, the airline and its budget unit Air India Express posted combined losses of US$2.33 billion, weighing on Singapore Airlines’ profits. Singapore Airlines said on Thursday its board would carefully consider any requests for additional capital from Air India, taking into consideration the group’s other capital requirements and Air India’s business strategy.

title: Vietnam’s move to end executions for drug trafficking sparks debate in region
description: The proposal has put a spotlight on the different legal approaches against drug trafficking offences in the region.
content: Vietnam is seeking to end executions for drug trafficking under a draft revision to its Penal Code, a notable shift in a country with one of Southeast Asia’s toughest anti-drug regimes. The proposal, presented to lawmakers last week, would remove trafficking from Vietnam’s list of capital crimes. Last year, Hanoi kept the offence on the list during an earlier round of death penalty reforms. If passed, the revised law would leave capital punishment for four crimes: treason, murder, terrorism and illegal narcotics production. For years, several Southeast Asian governments have treated serious drug trafficking as a crime that warranted the death penalty. However, some countries have re-examined their laws, leading to amendments. Malaysia ended mandatory death sentences in 2023. Singapore retains the death penalty for the most serious trafficking offences in which the legal thresholds are exceeded for quantities of various controlled drugs. The issue has led to debates on whether capital punishment still has a place in society, whether judges should have the discretion in sentencing, and how governments can disrupt the drug trade without the death penalty. Hanoi’s gradual reforms Vietnam’s proposal is not an abrupt departure from capital punishment but the latest step in a long-running, incremental recalibration, according to Hai Thanh Luong, a Vietnamese criminologist at Griffith University in Australia. Luong described Hanoi’s approach as “retentionist-but-reductionist”, referring to the state’s steady narrowing of offences punishable by death and retaining the punishment for exceptionally serious crimes. He said the proposal to remove the death penalty for drug trafficking reflected gradual political and legal reforms, doubts over whether executions could suppress drug supply and Vietnam’s deeper integration into global legal and diplomatic frameworks. “The strongest driver [is] Vietnam’s gradual legal and political reforms rather than a sudden ideological shift,” Luong said. The proposal would still allow the death penalty for illegal narcotics production, drawing a distinction between manufacturers – seen as more central to sustaining the drug trade – and traffickers. Luong said the changes would not have a major impact on drug availability. “Drug markets quickly adapt by replacing arrested individuals and shifting routes,” he said. When asked about the different treatment of drug traffickers in Vietnam, Malaysia and Singapore, Luong said that the three countries viewed deterrence, social order and the state’s role in punishment differently, even as they faced similar challenges of curbing drug flows. Singapore’s approach While Singapore retains capital punishment for the most serious drug trafficking cases, it incorporates a broad anti-drug strategy that includes enforcement, education and rehabilitation. Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam has said Singapore’s policy aims to prevent the harm caused by drugs, while imposing severe penalties on traffickers who bring substantial quantities into the country. The city state’s Ministry of Home Affairs said a 2024 survey of 12,000 respondents in six regional cities found that 84.2 per cent believed the death penalty deterred people from trafficking substantial amounts of drugs into Singapore. About 82.5 per cent considered the death penalty a more effective deterrent than life imprisonment, according to the survey. Shanmugam has said the government would reconsider the policy if evidence shows that abolition helps or that the death penalty does not help. Until then, he said, Singapore would “hold the line”. The death penalty is not a certainty under Singapore’s anti-drug laws, as they take into account the role played by convicted individuals in an offence. Eugene Tan, an associate professor at Singapore Management University’s Yong Pung How School of Law, said offenders convicted of trafficking above the prescribed thresholds could receive life imprisonment if they had acted only as a courier. They also had to obtain a certificate from the public prosecutor confirming they had provided substantive help to the authorities in disrupting trafficking activity. Couriers whose abnormality of mind had substantially impaired their mental responsibility could also be sentenced to life imprisonment without a certificate, Tan said. Tan explained that the framework allowed courts to differentiate between degrees of moral blameworthiness, while retaining zero tolerance against serious offences. “The shift to the discretionary death penalty regime should not be misconstrued as letting up on serious crimes such as drug trafficking,” Tan said. This Week in Asia has contacted Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs for comment. Malaysia’s sentencing shift In 2023, Malaysia announced that it was abolishing the mandatory death sentence for drug trafficking, leaving courts to choose between execution and life imprisonment. Ngeow Chow Ying, a Malaysian lawyer and deputy convenor of the Anti-Death Penalty Asia Network, said the change led to a sharp fall in new death sentences. Citing Amnesty International figures, she said Malaysian courts imposed 38 new death sentences in 2023, 24 in 2024, and 15 in 2025. For drug trafficking cases, “courts now weigh aggravating and mitigating factors to decide between death and life imprisonment”, Ngeow said. Mitigating factors could include an offender playing a lower-level role such as a courier or mule, the type of drugs involved and an early guilty plea, Ngeow explained. “Appellate courts, for instance, have commuted death sentences to life imprisonment for young or first-time couriers caught with substantial drug quantities, in recognition of their limited role in the operation,” she said. Even so, inconsistencies in interpretation persisted between different judicial levels in some cases, with High Court death sentences imposed on couriers later set aside by superior courts for life imprisonment, Ngeow said. “This suggests that trial-level sentencing remains uneven and continues to depend heavily on appellate correction,” she added. Law vs enforcement operations For rights groups, Vietnam’s proposal matters because it targets an offence that has contributed to the largest number of death sentences. Chiara Sangiorgio, Amnesty’s death penalty expert, said the latest proposal came after reforms in 2025 reduced the number of offences punishable by death to 10 from 18, alongside judicial guidance that further limited the imposition of capital punishment in some drug cases. “We are hopeful that these reforms will lead to immediate and concrete impact, particularly given that the majority of new death sentences that Amnesty International has recorded in recent years were imposed for drug trafficking,” Sangiorgio said. Amnesty’s preliminary assessment pointed to a decline in new death sentences in Vietnam so far this year following the reforms, according to Sangiorgio. But official secrecy around executions has made it impossible to assess the reforms’ full impact. Amnesty’s preliminary assessment pointed to a decline in new death sentences in Vietnam so far this year following the reforms, according to Sangiorgio. But official secrecy around executions has made it difficult to assess the reforms’ full impact. Amnesty was also concerned that unfair proceedings had led to death sentences and executions in some cases in Vietnam, Sangiorgio said. However, she added that recent developments in other countries suggested that sustained political will could move drug policies towards a humane, evidence-based and health-focused approach. Regardless of the different legal approaches in Southeast Asia, Luong said the most effective way to deal with the scourge was to intensify efforts to cripple drug trafficking operations at their root. “The certainty of detection has more preventive impact than harsher punishments,” he said. “Effective intelligence, cooperation, investigations and harm-reduction efforts are more sustainable than increasing severity alone.”

title: Reality check for China’s carmakers as authorities tell them to focus on quality, not tech
description: Vice-minister says that to ensure safety, new technologies that fail to pass stricter approval procedures will be barred from market.
content: China’s shrinking car market has received another reality check as regulators step in to police the hi-tech offerings that carmakers use to drive sales. A nationwide inspection campaign assessing the quality of Chinese-made cars that was announced this week would see some consumers shelve purchase plans, exacerbating a bearish outlook for the country’s auto sector, dealers and analysts said. Vice-Minister of Industry and Information Technology Xin Guobin told a news conference in Beijing on Wednesday that new auto products and technologies would be barred from entering the market unless they passed stricter approval procedures. “Some reckless innovative designs were installed in vehicles without sufficient testing and verification,” Xin said. “Several incidents attracted public attention due to concerns about the cars’ quality and the safety of autonomous driving technology.” The ministry announced on Thursday that a one-year campaign to review smart driving, product design and the safety of cars would begin soon. “Several accidents and growing consumer complaints have spurred the regulators into action,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “With improved oversight, carmakers will have to shift their focus from making their vehicles more intelligent to ensuring quality.” Three people died in March last year when the Xiaomi SU7 they were travelling in crashed in central China’s Anhui province while its driver-assistance system was operating. The preliminary self-driving system alerted the driver to take control just two seconds before the electric vehicle (EV) crashed into a barrier at high speed. The crash prompted Chinese authorities to tighten their oversight of early-stage autonomous driving technologies. Xinhua reported last month that a rising number of complaints about EV battery quality had been received by various public information platforms this year. Xin told reporters at Wednesday’s news conference that those issues were serious and could not be ignored. He pledged to enhance monitoring of carmakers’ designs and production to safeguard consumers’ interests. Analysts said China’s carmakers and automotive suppliers were at the vanguard of EV technology and production, buoyed by government support and consumer appetite for innovation. Nearly all of the roughly 100 carmakers in China have been developing new technologies, such as self-driving systems and digital cockpits, to lure consumers in the world’s largest automotive and EV market. But Paul Gong, head of China car research at UBS, said intense price competition amid the constant rolling out of new models had become an “enemy within” for the country’s auto industry. Dozens of carmakers with similar products were embroiled in “involution” as they fought for market dominance, he said in May. The term refers to intense ­competition that erodes sustainable growth and makes profits elusive. Overall car deliveries in mainland China, including petrol-powered vehicles and EVs, plunged by 20.9 per cent year on year in July to 1.46 million units, data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed. EVs sales, which accounted for 65.1 per cent of last month’s total, fell by 3.9 per cent year on year, extending their decline to a seventh consecutive month as fading government incentives and weaker consumer demand weighed on the market. Between January and July, Chinese carmakers delivered a total of 5.67 million EVs to domestic customers, down 12.5 per cent from a year earlier, according to the CPCA.

title: 10 years, 1,800 survey sites: inside China’s hi-tech push to map linguistic diversity
description: New Hunan Museum hall showcases major Chinese dialects and more than 100 ethnic minority languages, including Mongolian, Tibetan and Uygur.
content: Speak a few sentences of your hometown dialect into a microphone at a museum in central China, and a machine will pinpoint exactly where you are from. The interactive voice-recognition booth is among star attractions at a new language resources hall that opened on Monday at the Hunan Museum in Changsha. The hall showcases recordings and other language materials from Chinese dialects, minority languages and oral culture collected over the past decade. The compilation from more than 1,800 field survey sites nationwide reflects Beijing’s broader initiative to turn the vast digital archive of the country’s linguistic diversity into a public cultural resource. The recordings represent 10 major Chinese dialects and more than 100 ethnic minority languages, including Mongolian, Tibetan, Uygur and Zhuang, according to Chen Xuliang, deputy Communist Party secretary for the museum. More than 30 language-related cultural relics are also on display. “Digital technology is helping to bring the results of language preservation research out of databases and into public cultural spaces,” Chen was quoted as saying by state news agency Xinhua. Visitors can listen to local dialects, folk songs and recordings of some endangered languages, while interactive exhibits allow them to explore linguistic developments in China. Materials showcased at the exhibition hall are the result of a decade-long national language survey. The state-led initiative, called the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China, was launched by the Ministry of Education and the State Language Commission in 2015. It leverages modern technology to collect and document China’s regional languages, dialects and oral heritage into a large, continuously expanding multimedia database. Beijing has in recent years stepped up efforts to preserve and make greater use of the country’s linguistic and cultural resources. A policy document issued in December urged stronger support for language museums, calling for efforts to turn linguistic resources into drivers of cultural development and advocating for their integration into everyday life. A national plan for cultural heritage development followed in July, also calling for greater use of digital technology and wider sharing of digital resources held by museums and cultural institutions. The policies align with China’s drive under President Xi Jinping to promote “cultural confidence” – one of the “Four Confidences” he introduced in 2016. It refers to confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Beijing sees “cultural confidence” as vital to national cohesion and creativity, as well as a key driver of soft power and global competitiveness. The Changsha exhibition hall is also serving as a pilot for the planned China Language Resources Museum, expected to be built at the city’s Malanshan Video Cultural and Creative Industrial Park. While China boasts a highly diverse linguistic landscape of more than 100 languages and numerous dialects, efforts to preserve minority languages have often been at odds with Beijing’s campaign to promote Mandarin as a common language. Beijing claims the two goals can coexist, while critics argue that the growing emphasis on Mandarin in education and public life risks weakening the use of minority languages and eroding ethnic minority cultures and identities.

title: Hongkongers can use either ID or home return permit at revamped Huanggang Port
description: Security chief Chris Tang reveals arrangement after massive drill at border crossing, which could open next month.
content: Hongkongers can present either their identity card or home return permit at the revamped Huanggang border checkpoint instead of both documents under the latest agreement with mainland Chinese authorities, the security minister has revealed. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung announced the measure after a drill at the crossing involving more than 20,000 civil servants on Saturday. “Under our latest agreement with the mainland, for e-channel entry to the mainland and returning to Hong Kong, you can use the Hong Kong identity card or the home return permit for both ways, whichever you prefer,” Tang said. The interchangeable use of Hong Kong identity cards and home return permits at the crossing will apply to both Chinese and non-Chinese residents holding a valid mainland travel permit. However, Tang reminded residents that they should still carry a valid mainland permit with them, despite not having to use it at the checkpoint. Saturday’s drill was the largest so far, with more than 20,000 civil servants taking part to simulate peak stress on the building’s capacity. Huanggang Port is expected to be able to handle 200,000 passenger trips per day and is the first checkpoint to use a “joint clearance” model. Passengers only need to undergo departure and arrival clearance at a single checkpoint and present one travel document at either automatic or manual counters, instead of passing through separate counters. Sources previously said the revamped crossing between Hong Kong and Shenzhen could open as early as next month. All 90 clearance lanes on the Hong Kong departure side – both automatic “joint clearance” machines and manual counters – as well as in the arrivals hall, were tested on Saturday. Saturday’s drill also involved 300 vehicles testing the “joint one-stop” clearance lane. Drivers only needed to present their identity documents at one machine so that five departments in Hong Kong and Shenzhen could approve their clearance and record their biometric data and temperature. Through the lane’s “integrated information collection device”, Hong Kong’s Customs and Excise Department, Immigration Department and Department of Health can confirm clearance on their side. At the same time, Shenzhen’s immigration and customs authorities can carry out the equivalent task. Following the drill, Tang said the exercise had achieved its purpose, as operations inside the checkpoint remained orderly even with a record number of civil servants taking part. “Overall, it has been very smooth. We will conduct an internal evaluation afterwards and have a joint meeting with Shenzhen authorities to look at the safety and smoothness of operations to determine when the checkpoint can be opened,” Tang said. The security minister said a test simulating 20,000 passengers – twice as many as in the previous drill last Saturday – passing through the checkpoint in an hour was staged, with the longest wait to cross the border remaining under 15 minutes. For the one-stop vehicle lane, Tang said drivers could pass through the clearance gate in around a minute. However, Tang noted that Wi-fi connectivity was still an issue inside the building. He said some crowded areas lacked a signal on Saturday, which was not a problem in the test with 10,000 participants last week. Saturday’s drill began with a simulation of heavy passenger flow arriving by public transport. The Transport Department commissioned 300 buses and minibuses to take part, picking up passengers from various terminals and intermediate stops across urban areas before arriving at the checkpoint. Passengers were then directed to escalators inside the building to head straight to the departure hall on the fifth floor. Meanwhile, private cars and cross-border buses arrived at the one-stop vehicle clearance lane on the first floor of the complex. While passengers had to get out of vehicles for immigration clearance, drivers remained inside and crossed the border using the integrated information collection device.

title: Macroscope | Global debt crisis will mean higher taxes – or worse
description: Bond markets are in revolt in response to rising government debt, meaning urgent change is needed in how national priorities are financed.
content: Taxpayers everywhere should brace themselves. Their taxes could soon rise unless there are fundamental changes in the way that increasingly unsustainable government debt in the United States, Japan and beyond is financed. This can be done, but it will involve tough political decisions. Attempts by national leaders to boost defence and other spending in the wake of a profligate borrowing boom make a crisis inevitable. While stock markets continue to ride high, the stress in key global bond markets is beginning to show through as a warning signal to investors. An insufficient proportion of income and savings in major countries is being directed into financing public spending on defence, health, infrastructure, climate change remediation and other priorities. Governments normally turn to borrowing to plug the gap between tax revenue and spending, but bond markets around the world are in revolt, as shown by rapidly rising yields on sovereign bonds. Frederick Kempe, president of the Washington-based think tank Atlantic Council, wrote on August 25 that converging recent events – the US national debt hitting a record US$40 trillion, the new “economic D-Day” campaign against Iran and the US-Canada trade war – posed threats to US global leadership. The inverse of rising bond yields is falling bond prices. This applies especially to long-term bonds, and so governments are forced to issue increasing amounts of costly short-term debt, raising their already lofty debt service ratios. People should understand that, in addition to facing higher tax bills, a greater proportion of their savings should go into financing public investment. Currently, too much of people’s discretionary savings go into the stock and bond markets, where money is often directed into fashionable investments such as artificial intelligence (AI). Fund managers competing to achieve maximum returns will follow a herd mentality rather than pursue the public interest. Leaders of the US and Japan – two of the world’s leading economic powers – seem intent on ignoring the reality of the situation. Their government debt-to-GDP ratios have soared to 248 per cent in Japan’s case and 122 per cent in that of the US. US President Donald Trump appears set upon waging wars that are costly in terms of money, infrastructure and human lives. His capricious behaviour is plunging the country’s finances into steadily deeper debt and destroying the willingness of external creditors to continue underwriting his excesses. Meanwhile, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is determined to pursue her 370 trillion yen (US$2.3 trillion) stimulus package. Coupled with her decision to pursue a two-year reduction of the country’s consumption tax on food, this is simply asking for trouble. Takaichi appears to be on course for her own “Liz Truss moment” and a similar political fate to Britain’s shortest-lived prime minister, who was forced out of office after just 44 days. Truss’ plan to tackle Britain’s cost of living crisis hinged on slashing taxes while borrowing heavily, spooking markets and sparking a collapse in the British pound. How can governments overcome the influence of bond market vigilantes other than by drastically raising taxes, cutting spending – or both? The first step would be to reduce the role of the global asset management industry. Its assets derive from contributions from pension funds, life assurance companies and numerous other institutional investors, as well as from individual investors through myriad mutual funds, investment trusts, exchange-traded funds and other savings and investment schemes. Asset managers in the private sector might well be intelligent and caring individuals, but as a group they all too often feel compelled to follow the herd. They need to compete with one another to show the best financial return on investments, and this in turn lures them into making excessive investment in popular sectors such as AI and other hi-tech fields. Investment in essential social areas is neglected, leaving governments to step in to cover the shortfall. If the role of existing investment institutions is going to be reduced, how should private savings be directed into essential public investments currently being overlooked? The answer from planned economies appears to be doing so via state investment vehicles. Market economies have yet to find similar success amid their growing fiscal predicaments, yet their champions still cling to the belief that their finances are managed more efficiently through private sector channels. Governments in market economies need to establish specialist state financial institutions to better direct public savings into areas of key social importance, even if this does mean raising taxes to cover the cost of staffing such institutions. It also implies the need for more innovative thinking on the part of governments by employing economists and financial specialists in newly created institutions rather than leaving the matter to amateur politicians. The treatment for this debt crisis might be painful, but the cure will be worth achieving.

title: Green day: Hong Kong horticultural therapist’s relaxing urban farm experiences
description: Linda Lee’s urban farming experience days mix hydroponics, plant care, mindfulness and crafts.
content: When Linda Lee was young and living in the heart of Hong Kong’s urban metropolis, her father found peace in a small cluster of greenery in their flat. He stood in the corner each day, tending to each pot.
