When he smoked, he always turned to blow the smoke onto the plants, which would absorb the chemicals, he said, leaving clean air for Lee and her mother. Lee’s father was a tough character. He did not talk much, or have many friends. But Lee saw something in his face relax whenever he tended to his “garden”. Each time Lee starts her day as a horticultural therapist, she remembers him. Today, Lee works at Farmacy, an urban farming organisation using hydroponic technology – where plants grow in a water and mineral solution instead of soil – to create mobile farms and farm labs in Hong Kong. These spaces are usually compact, indoor, climate-controlled environments. Lee leads urban farming experience days around once a month, a time when participants can drop their usual worries and engage all five senses in the greenery in Farmacy’s headquarters in Shau Kei Wan. When visitors step into the premises on the 20th floor of a commercial building, a distinct floral smell greets them that emanates from the vast hydroponic farm that they will soon become acquainted with. Lee starts by taking the guests through a brief mindfulness practice, designed to bring them into the space and return their attention to their breathing. Lee says the grounding process can look a little different indoors than it would in a nature-filled environment. “If you go out in nature, I would recommend people take off [their] shoes and step on the grass, hug the trees a little bit … but here in the indoor environment, you can just relax, make yourself feel safe and comfortable,” Lee says. Next, she either takes participants on a tour of Farmacy’s vertical farm or gives a short presentation on hydroponic farming. To enter the urban farm, guests must wear special sanitation outfits and step through an air shower, which works to sanitise people before entering. From there, participants move to the “hands-on planting and caring” section of the event, where the guests prepare their own planters or crops. Participants choose from a series of tactile activities. Lee says the overarching theme is horticultural therapy, “which is about using the plant as the medium or the base to connect with the person”. “That builds the sense of responsibility, patience and the sense of purpose,” Lee says. The list of hands-on activities includes plant rubbing – an artistic technique that captures the texture of different leaves by placing them underneath a piece of paper and shading over it with crayons or pencils – and seeding arts. Visitors can also try aromatherapy. There is also an option for a farm-to-table experience, where participants work together to create a simple meal with fresh produce from Farmacy. Lee says groups have made everything from Vietnamese spring rolls to pizza and tacos with parsley, basil and mint. Kindness, intention, connection and sharing After the activities, participants slow down for a “kindness and intention” section, where they can choose an intention or a wish for themselves or their plant. “It creates an emotional bridge: nature becomes a mirror for resilience,” Lee says. A “connection and sharing” time concludes the experience, where participants are invited to share their takeaways with the group. People often share feelings of connection and pride in their work, Lee says. “Some people just say that they completely forgot about what they did, but they just enjoyed that moment,” she says, adding that this is the most important part of the workshop – the opportunity to “forget about the world for a while”. “They just immerse themselves into their fingers, their nose, their eyes and [their] taste,” Lee says. “So all [these] body senses within themselves lead them back to their focus.” In addition to the urban farming experience days, Lee leads a myriad of workshops and programmes throughout the community. She brings greenery and fresh life to corporate offices and local classrooms. Farmacy also refurbishes unused classrooms as urban farm labs, according to community programme lead Alison Lee. The farm labs provide two purposes: to decentralise farming, allowing for local produce rather than importing produce from mainland China or overseas, and to help out local communities, especially in lower-income areas. “We would love to have hubs that provide really fresh veggies for people within the community,” Alison Lee says. Linda Lee has seen the benefits of horticultural therapy for many different segments of the community. In schools and social settings, she has seen people become more focused and confident. In corporate settings, she sees a decrease in stress levels and an elevated mood. Horticulture therapy is most beneficial when it is used as “supportive care”, she says, meaning that it can be used alongside medical treatments. It can be helpful for anxiety and burnout, social challenges, low mood, and trauma-informed care. In Linda Lee’s personal life, working with plants is a connection to her father since his death. “He’s still alive to me, to be honest, whenever I’m doing all this gardening – just anything related to planting, to just looking, growing small pots of plants,” she says. Today, her mother tends to the same garden in the corner of their family’s flat. “They are my mom’s companions now, you know … so that she doesn’t feel lonely, and she feels [supported], and she’s feeling more alive because they are growing,” Linda Lee says. “They are like evergreen.” Her father may have died, but his presence lingers in the leaves of the little corner garden.

title: Europe drought drives demand for Chinese water-saving goods as EU trade tensions grow
description: Chinese makers of low-flow taps, garden gear and insulated drinkware are seeing European orders surge as heatwaves and drought reshape demand.
content: After the intense European heatwave beginning in late May fuelled a surge in imports of Chinese air conditioners, drought across the continent is now driving unexpected overseas demand for Chinese-made water-saving hardware. In Yiwu – a city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province known as the world’s small-goods capital – Liu Junming has spent more than two decades exporting kitchen and bathroom hardware. He said exports of taps and showerheads had risen unusually sharply this summer. Taps bound for Europe totalled fewer than 2,000 units per month this time last year. That figure has now surged to about 10,000. Liu said he had done little to court European customers: rather, they had sought him out. “Most of our new buyers are from the UK, Spain and Italy. They stumbled across my product posts on social media and placed orders straight away,” Liu said. “Water-saving products were what they were actively seeking.” Beneath the export boom lie Liu’s revamped product offerings. This year, he reworked his product line to introduce low-flow taps for overseas customers. According to him, the fixtures can cut water consumption by 50 per cent over comparable periods of use. He is not alone in riding this export wave. A Zhejiang company specialising in garden-watering gear has also seen strong sales growth, state broadcaster China Central Television reported this week. Its equipment can reduce water use by 70 per cent per watering session, and its production capacity is fully booked until 2027 by orders from the UK, France, Germany and Spain. Behind the red-hot demand for Chinese-made water-saving goods lies pervasive drought across Europe. Germany’s Low Water Information System recorded extremely low water levels at 44 per cent of measuring stations on the Rhine and 78 per cent of those on the Danube by the end of July. And those arid conditions have persisted into August. The Danube has plummeted to historically low levels this month, according to a report last week by Politico. Against that backdrop, water-use restrictions have become commonplace across Europe. France was under water restrictions across nearly 70 per cent of its territory amid record summer heat, France 24 reported on August 11. In the UK, 10 water companies had announced hosepipe bans prohibiting water use for gardens, washing cars and filling swimming pools, the BBC reported on August 17. According to Water UK, the country’s water industry trade association, Portugal, Spain and Ireland have also introduced similar water restrictions. “Water-use restrictions and official calls for conservation have made European consumers more receptive to water-saving products. They have also long been environmentally conscious, creating a natural fit between their priorities and my offerings,” Liu said. This year’s brutal heatwave has created fresh commercial opportunities for Chinese manufacturers. Shanghai-based Solidware designs and manufactures stainless-steel drinkware. Zhang Bin, its general manager, said the company had long prioritised thermal-insulation performance, but this year’s weather events had opened up new avenues of thought. “Repeated heatwaves and drought have reshaped local consumer markets. Drinkware that combines cold-retention and environmentally friendly features has become a new consumer trend, so we moved quickly to upgrade our product line,” Zhang said. Buoyed by its newly introduced products, the company’s export volumes rose more than 20 per cent year on year from January to mid-August. The export boom in these small-ticket goods comes as Chinese manufacturers closely watch rising trade tensions between China and the European Union. Brussels has given Beijing until October to deliver “tangible results” on reducing trade imbalances, after imposing a levy on low-value parcels and opening several anti-subsidy investigations. The bloc’s trade deficit with China reached €359.8 billion (US$418.8 billion) last year, or nearly €1 billion (US$1.2 billion) a day. According to Chinese customs data, China and the EU were each other’s second-largest trading partners in 2025, with bilateral goods trade rising 6 per cent year on year to 5.93 trillion yuan (US$882.3 billion).

title: China-Nepal floods: Hong Kong groups rally to aid victims as government pledges HK$50m
description: City’s Nepalese community and other charities step up fundraising efforts, while Chief Executive John Lee vows swift processing of relief funds.
content: Hong Kong’s Nepalese community and other local organisations have launched fundraising drives to support those affected by deadly flash floods at the Himalayan nation’s border with the Tibet autonomous region, as the city government earmarked HK$50 million (US$6.38 million) to support relief efforts. In a social media post on Saturday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the HK$50 million would come from the Disaster Relief Fund and that its advisory committee would process applications swiftly. “I express my deep condolences for the victims and extend my heartfelt sympathies to those affected and the families of the victims,” he said. The Hong Kong Jockey Club also announced it was donating HK$20 million to support ongoing relief efforts, while the Macau government said it would donate 30 million yuan (US$4.5 million). The club added the Institute for Disaster Management and Reconstruction, a collaboration between Polytechnic University and Sichuan University established in the wake of the deadly 2008 quake in mainland China, was also taking part in rescue efforts. On Wednesday, a huge wall of mud and rock collapsed into a river along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet, triggering catastrophic flooding. Seven people have been confirmed dead on the Chinese side, with 544 still missing as the rescue operation passes a critical 72-hour window. In Nepal, at least 675 have died and nearly 2,500 are missing. The Hong Kong Red Cross on Saturday issued an emergency appeal to support immediate humanitarian needs for those affected by the floods. It also allocated HK$200,000 to support ongoing relief efforts. World Vision Hong Kong, the local branch of the international Christian humanitarian aid organisation, issued a call for donations across its social media channels. Speaking to the South China Morning Post from Kathmandu, Isaac Anup Rana, World Vision International Nepal’s field operations director, said conditions in the disaster zone were “very difficult”. He said communication was difficult due to a lack of electricity, while aid workers were also facing difficulties accessing the area as many roads were blocked and bridges were destroyed in the flood. “It is really heartbreaking to see the situation here,” he said. “Everything is destroyed … and the people are really traumatised because of what they experienced recently.” He said his team had allocated US$100,000 while they were aiming to reach 1,000 households as part of their “first wave” of support. He also thanked Hongkongers for their “very generous” contributions to the organisation over the years. Hong Kong’s 30,000-strong Nepalese community has also begun organising fundraising events across the city. “As Nepalese living abroad, we feel a strong responsibility to support people back home,” said 28-year-old Soyena Dhakal, who was born and raised in Hong Kong. Dhakal, who works in finance, serves as president of the Hong Kong chapter of the Federation of International Nepali Youth Entrepreneurs, a global network with chapters across the world. The group is currently directing its members, of which there are more than 100 in Hong Kong, to donate to the Nepalese government’s official relief fund. “For us, the priority is making sure people in the community are aware of the different ways to contribute,” she said, adding that the organisation was also considering different options to provide support. The cocktail bar Orchard in Central, tied to the local Nepalese community, will host a fundraising event on Monday, in which 100 per cent of the sales will be donated to the fund operated by the country’s government. Alex Pun, the 40-year-old founder of the bar who has lived in the city since 2003, said he was encouraged to host the event after witnessing the response from the wider Hong Kong community in the aftermath of the flood. “It’s a very emotional thing when the people who live in Hong Kong text me personally just to check on me and my family,” he said. Pun said it was quite a hard time for all Nepalese people. He wanted people in Nepal to know they were not alone and had the support of those living abroad. “I’ve been living away from home for like 20 years … but the connection with the home country is always there,” he said. “We Nepalese people know that this is the moment to show some unity and compassion.”

title: South Korean court rules banging on ceiling, calling to complain considered stalking
description: A woman is fined US$1,400 for repeatedly striking the ceiling with a backscratcher and calling her upstairs neighbour through the intercom.
content: A woman in her fifties has been fined for repeatedly banging on her ceiling with a backscratcher and contacting her upstairs neighbour over noise, with a South Korean court ruling that her actions amounted to stalking. The Chuncheon District Court fined the 55-year-old woman, identified only as A, 2 million won (US$1,400) for violating the Act on Punishment of Crimes of Stalking, according to legal sources on Saturday. The court also ordered her to complete 40 hours of a treatment programme for stalking offenders. A was accused of stalking her upstairs neighbour on nine occasions between March 17 and May 11 last year at a residential complex in Chuncheon, Gangwon province. Her actions included repeatedly striking the ceiling with a backscratcher and calling the upstairs flat through the building’s intercom system. According to the investigation, A had been asking the neighbour, a woman in her forties identified as B, to keep the noise down since January last year. When the problem remained unresolved, A repeatedly contacted B directly through the intercom to complain. B asked A not to contact her directly over the noise and instead raise any complaints through the management office. During the trial, A denied that her actions constituted stalking, arguing that they were within a socially acceptable range of conduct aimed at finding a solution to the noise problem and that she had no intention of stalking B. The court rejected her argument. “Considering the circumstances that led the defendant to complain, as well as the methods and frequency of her actions, they were objectively sufficient to cause anxiety or fear in the other person,” the judge said. The court said A’s conduct could not be regarded as having a legitimate reason or falling within the bounds of socially acceptable behaviour. This article was first published by The Korea Times

title: King Haakon VIII takes throne as Norway mourns death of King Harald
description: The 53-year-old takes over a monarchy hailed for its modernity and modesty but which has been beset by a string of recent scandals.
content: Norway’s new King Haakon VIII on Saturday addressed Norwegians for the first time since taking the throne, paying tribute to his 89-year-old father who died the day before. “Above all, you were a person who always stayed true to your values and commitments,” Haakon said of the late King Harald V in a televised speech. The new regent said it had been a “powerful and moving experience” to see the thousands of Norwegians who had gathered since Friday outside the Royal Palace in Oslo with “flowers, tributes and candles”. “We are in mourning, yet at the same time it brings comfort and strength that so many are grieving together with us,” the 53-year-old said. Visibly moved, he also noted that his father and mother, Queen Sonja, would have celebrated their 58th wedding anniversary on Saturday. “Happy wedding anniversary, dear Mum,” he said, choking back tears. Flags flew at half mast on Saturday as scores of Norwegians flocked to the palace, adding flowers to the masses already on the ground after more than 20,000 people paid their respects Friday. The late king enjoyed massive support, despite the slew of scandals that dogged his family in the final stretch of his 35-year reign. Haakon thanked his father for being “a good dad” to him and his sister Martha Louise, and acknowledged that he now faced a “great task himself”. “He constantly reminded us in the family that each of us must do things in our own way. Find our own form. Be ourselves,” Haakon said. “Now it is my turn,” he declared. Tributes have poured in from European monarchies and world leaders, including US President Donald Trump who hailed the memory of “a strong, proud, and greatly respected man”. Earlier on Saturday, King Haakon held audiences at the palace with the leaders of the Church of Norway, parliament and supreme court. He also received Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store for a viewing of the late king’s casket, which was brought to the palace from Oslo University Hospital Friday evening. Store was seen speaking informally to mourners outside the palace earlier on Saturday, weaving through the crowds and shaking hands. A national period of mourning has been declared. No date has been set for the late king’s funeral. King Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in parliament on Tuesday. City halls across Norway set out condolence books on Saturday for the public to write personal messages. Oslo Mayor Anne Lindboe, who had called off her own wedding on Friday due to the king’s death, was the first to write a message in Oslo’s City Hall. “Dear King Harald, you didn’t need a crown to be a king. Thank you so much for everything you have done for our city. We will never forget you,” she told reporters she had written. One of the first members of the public to write a message after the mayor, Unni Zetterquist Thorsen, 68, said she had thanked the late king for his “patience and strength through difficult times in Norway”. King Haakon and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit, are not expected to be crowned in a ceremony – Norway abolished coronations in 1908. But, like his father and grandfather before him, the new king could choose to have his reign blessed during a ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906. King Harald was widely seen as the embodiment of an open and tolerant Norway, and praised for leading a monarchy that was modern and modest. Harald had been in hospital in Oslo since August 17, suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells that leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. The regent faced mounting health problems in his final years, forcing him to scale back his official schedule. The past year has been a turbulent one for the Norwegian royal family. Queen Sonja, also 89, was briefly admitted to hospital in May due to heart problems. New King Haakon’s wife Mette-Marit is under scrutiny for her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In June, Mette-Marit’s son from a relationship before her marriage to Haakon, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes, a sentence that is under appeal. Suffering herself from a serious lung disease, Mette-Marit, 53, underwent a lung transplant in July.

title: US envoy’s Kashmir ‘part of India’ remark rattles Pakistan ties
description: Whether a slip or a calculated trade tactic, Sergio Gor’s remark upended decades of studied American neutrality on Kashmir.
content: Seven words, spoken almost in passing on a recent afternoon in Srinagar, have set off a diplomatic tremor across South Asia. “This is an important part of India,” Sergio Gor told reporters on August 19, during the first visit by a US ambassador to Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in six years. Within hours, Pakistan had summoned the top American diplomat in Islamabad, Natalie Baker, to deliver a formal protest. Kashmir, a disputed Himalayan region claimed in full by both India and Pakistan, has been the casus belli for no fewer than three wars between the nuclear-armed arch-rivals, as well as numerous other skirmishes and border stand-offs since their independence and partition in 1947. India now administers the populous central and southern Kashmir valley, while Pakistan controls a western portion of the region known as Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan. Washington’s long-standing official line has been that Kashmir’s status remains unresolved and should be settled bilaterally. In New Delhi, Gor’s remark was welcomed by some as a sign that the United States might be edging closer to India’s position. For Islamabad, it had the look of Washington abandoning decades of studied neutrality on one of the world’s most combustible border disputes. Pakistan’s foreign ministry called Gor’s statement “irresponsible” and “factually incorrect”, while an Indian foreign ministry spokesman told local media in response that he saw “no reason to comment on Pakistan’s frustration”. Slip or strategy? Analysts were divided on how much weight the US envoy’s comment should carry, but few who spoke to This Week in Asia thought it was accidental. Vivek Mishra, deputy director of strategic studies at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi, read it as “subtle messaging” aimed squarely at Pakistan: a reminder that Washington’s support was not unconditional. He said Jammu and Kashmir’s trajectory had been “largely peaceful and development-oriented” in recent years, contrasting it with this summer’s unrest in the Pakistan-administered part of the region, where security forces have clashed violently with protesters demanding governance reform and relief from inflation. India revoked the decades-old special autonomy of the part of Kashmir it administers in 2019, bringing it under the direct control of the central government. This move was initially followed by protests and intense security lockdowns, but has since led to a boom in domestic tourism and infrastructure spending. A deadly militant attack in Indian-administered Kashmir last year that Delhi blamed on Islamabad triggered a four-day conflict involving direct cross-border missile and air strikes from which the region has been slowly recovering. For Priyajit Debsarkar, a London-based South Asia analyst, Gor’s remark was more than a diplomatic slip. He framed it as a “change of stance by a senior American representative” that showed Washington was “probably not happy” with the ceasefires in the US-Israel war on Iran that Pakistan had helped broker. Debsarkar suggested that it was “only natural that the US should do a course correction” by acknowledging India’s position “especially in the security paradigm of cross-border terrorism” – noting that the two countries “have a lot of confluence of values, trade and people-to-people contact”. Gor’s dual role as special envoy for South and Central Asia lent the remark added weight, he said. But not every Washington watcher is convinced. South Asia analyst Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council think tank cautioned against reading too much into the remark – attributing it instead to Gor’s own “one-man mission to strengthen a sputtering relationship” since arriving in Delhi in January. “By saying Kashmir is an ‘important part of India’, he was giving it a handsome compliment,” Kugelman wrote in the Indian Express newspaper. Gor’s visit and his suggestion that the US might downgrade its travel advisory to Kashmir – praising authorities for making “some incredible steps in keeping this area safer and making it more safe” – were welcomed by some as an American vote of confidence in the region’s recovery. Mishra predicted it would “boost business sentiment”, regardless of what it did or did not mean for US foreign policy. Yet some of the same analysts who saw intent in Gor’s words were also careful to frame them as an adjustment in tone, not doctrine. Harsh Ramaswamy, an independent political commentator, suspects there is a transactional layer beneath the diplomatic one. Officially, nothing has changed. There has been no formal statement from the US State Department and India’s foreign ministry declined to engage directly with Pakistan’s protest. Ramaswamy said Gor’s remark might have been Washington testing the political waters on Kashmir even as it worked on a very different negotiation: a bilateral trade deal that the ambassador said in June was just steps away from completion. Gor had been consistently upbeat about ties since taking up his post, Mishra said, though progress on a deal was slower than his optimism suggested. “We have been hearing that a trade deal is around the corner,” Mishra said, but “the Trump administration has not been budging from some negotiating points and neither has India”. What is clear to observers is that both sides appear to be working to repair a relationship bruised by trade friction and by Washington’s recent warmth towards India’s regional rival. Gor announced on Monday that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio would return to India in October, his second visit since May – a trip Mishra believes could be laying the diplomatic groundwork for a long-awaited visit to India by President Donald Trump himself. Neither Rubio nor Trump has made any such visit to Pakistan in an official capacity.

title: Several ride-hailing firms express interest in Hong Kong licences: minister
description: Transport chief Mable Chan expresses confidence in operators, saying they are capable of meeting requirements laid out for licences.
content: Several ride-hailing firms have expressed an interest in offering services under the new regulatory regime in Hong Kong, one day after the government opened licence applications setting out nine requirements, the transport chief has revealed. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said on Saturday that two to three firms had expressed an interest in offering ride-hailing services, emphasising that operators were capable of meeting the requirements. “Just one day after our announcement, at least two to three platform operators have expressed an interest in running the ride-hailing services. I hope they can apply soon,” she told a radio programme. “We will hold a briefing session in mid-September to communicate directly with interested applicants. We expect the first batch of applicants can be approved in early December.” Her bureau announced nine key requirements on Friday for offering ride-hailing services under the new regulatory regime, with applications for licences closing on October 30. Among the nine conditions, operators must have a proven track record of providing lawful services in cities with populations of more than 7.5 million and handling more than 100,000 daily orders in at least two locations. Operators must also submit audited financial reports for the past three years. They must have capital of at least HK$50 million (US$6.4 million), at least HK$30 million in bank deposits and a HK$30 million credit line. Chan said authorities had not set a quota for the licences, adding candidates would be selected based on merit. “As long as the platform operators meet the requirements, then it will be OK for us,” she said. She explained that the requirement for a track record of handling more than 100,000 daily orders was necessary as Hong Kong was an international city with many tourists, and operators should be able to serve different kinds of customers. “Our survey also indicated that the daily demand for ride-hailing platforms in Hong Kong was about 110,000 trips, so the requirement is really basic. Some operators said they could cope with it. “We don’t favour any parties. Those with local or overseas experience can apply as they can form a joint venture with others.” As for ride-hailing drivers, she said the response was overwhelming, with more than 9,000 applicants registered for a new combined test for taxi and ride-hailing services. The written test will take place in September. Chan said authorities would set up a ride-hailing data management system to store the information on vehicles, drivers and the trips to ensure operational smoothness. The government earlier set a quota of 10,000 for ride-hailing vehicles. In Hong Kong, apart from Uber, Singapore-based Tada, Amap and Didi Chuxing currently serve the market. Amap is operated by Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the South China Morning Post. Both Uber and Didi have said they would apply for the licence.

title: AI can make China’s political language sound more threatening, scholar warns
description: Professor Li Yan says human expertise is vital to retaining context in AI translations of Beijing’s policy ideas for overseas audiences.
content: China is being urged to use human translators to refine AI renderings of its political messaging, amid concerns that literal translations could make Beijing’s language sound more threatening abroad. An article in a state-affiliated academic newspaper said the country should strengthen its translation capacity and guard against AI-generated distortions to improve how its policies and intentions were understood overseas. As artificial intelligence (AI) takes on more translation work, human translators should work alongside the technology, according to Li Yan, a professor at Xian Fanyi University. “The value of translation goes far beyond language itself,” Li wrote in an article published on Wednesday in Chinese Social Sciences Today, a newspaper run by the Beijing-based Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. “In the AI era, a country’s translation capabilities have become a core measure of its cultural soft power and ability to participate in global governance.” Li called on Chinese translators to strengthen their ability to refine AI translations according to context, audience and purpose. She cited the Chinese idiom taoguang yanghui, widely used since the 1990s to describe Deng Xiaoping’s foreign policy approach: keeping a low profile internationally, avoiding confrontation, and prioritising domestic stability and development. Yet in English-language discourse, the phrase is often rendered as “hide your capabilities, bide your time” – a formulation that some overseas observers interpret as a deliberate effort to mask China’s long-term ambitions until it is strong enough to challenge the United States militarily, politically and economically. Without identifying a specific model, Li said AI had rendered the idiom as “hide brightness, nourish obscurity”. She warned that, taken literally, the translation could fuel perceptions that China was concealing a secret strategic agenda. “Recasting it as ‘maintain humility while building strength’ could convey our country’s diplomatic principles of peaceful development and proactive engagement.” Li also called on translators in the AI age to develop the practical skills needed to recognise, analyse and interpret culturally specific symbols, metaphors, references to history and political ideas. She pointed to a hallmark slogan from the 1980s that guided China’s reform drive, mozhe shitou guohe, often translated as “crossing the river by feeling the stones”. Translating it as “exploratory reform with incremental steps”, and dropping the imagery, could help foreign audiences better grasp the political-economic concept, Li said. Her recommendations come as Chinese government departments and academics place growing emphasis on translating political catchphrases and culturally specific concepts – an effort some frame as part of a wider contest over international narratives and public opinion. In the AI era, a country’s translation capabilities have become a core measure of its cultural soft power and ability to participate in global governance Li Yan, Xian Fanyi University Experts have warned that such translations shape both the messages Beijing sends abroad – where imprecision can raise the risk of miscalculation amid intensifying strategic rivalry with Washington – and overseas understanding of China’s domestic and foreign policy thinking, with consequences for its global image. Meanwhile, the challenges of translation have repeatedly complicated high-stakes diplomacy, particularly where languages and political cultures diverge sharply. In a report published last October, the prominent US think tank Rand Corporation accused a number of influential China experts – all proficient in Chinese and reliant on Chinese-language sources in their arguments – of introducing a “hawkish” distortion into their translations and interpretations of Beijing’s terminology. Stefan Messingschlager, a historian and political scientist at Helmut Schmidt University in Hamburg, similarly argued in an article published last September that Western governments had continued to misread Beijing, although they possessed armies of Chinese speakers and AI translators. He argued that what was missing was independent, context-rich expertise: people capable of decoding China’s history-laden signals and puncturing bureaucratic groupthink. In her article this week, Li warned that China must guard against cultural misreadings, lapses in logic and value-laden bias when AI translates its political terminology. Still, she urged Chinese translators to actively embrace AI tools while developing the skills to work effectively with them and manage the risks they present. Li also proposed introducing interdisciplinary courses in China covering AI translation technology, human-computer interaction design and the digital humanities. A note accompanying the article said the piece formed part of an ongoing research project supported by China’s National Social Science Fund.

title: China leverages short-video ecosystem, lower costs to carve out lead in AI video
description: Models from Alibaba, MiniMax and ByteDance currently dominate benchmark rankings on industry evaluation platform Artificial Analysis.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence companies are carving out a distinct lead over their US rivals in video generation, leveraging vast short-video ecosystems, looser copyright rules and aggressive pricing to dominate an arena where compute alone does not dictate success, analysts say. While US tech giants such as OpenAI and Anthropic continue to lead in frontier closed-source large language models (LLMs), Chinese firms are emerging as some of the most formidable competitors in the AI video generation battleground. Models from Chinese firms including Alibaba Group Holding, MiniMax and ByteDance currently dominate benchmark rankings on industry evaluation platform Artificial Analysis. Alibaba’s Wan 3.0 ranks first on Artificial Analysis’ text-to-video leaderboard with audio, ahead of second-placed Google Gemini Omni Flash. A version of MiniMax H3 post-trained by US platform fal ranks third, followed by the original open-weight H3 and ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0. Together, Chinese models occupy eight of the top 10 positions. Chinese models also lead across several related categories, including image-to-video and video editing, based on blind user comparisons using identical prompts. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Industry analysts attribute China’s video AI momentum to a combination of proprietary training data, rapid iteration cycles, and strong domestic demand for short-form digital content. While both the US and China have major social media platforms that can provide data and distribution, “Chinese companies like ByteDance have made video generation more of a priority”, said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L Thornton China Centre. “ByteDance has created a positive flywheel, turning AI-generated short form video into a real industry,” Chan said. Early hits signalled strong viewer demand, driving ByteDance to double down on the technology and transform it into a lucrative business line. Domestic downstream commercial demand has provided additional tailwinds. “China’s short-drama and AI-generated comic-drama industries have developed rapidly, with Chinese production teams also supplying content for overseas markets,” said Wang Zebin, an investment manager at private equity firm JG Investment. Analysts said diverging approaches to copyright risk have also created a distinct playing field. US AI developers faced “much more potential risk and liability” over intellectual property, according to Chan. In contrast, comparatively flexible copyright enforcement in China gave domestic firms more runway to test and commercialise their models, Wang said. The practical impact of these differing standards was highlighted by Shenzhen-based AI enthusiast Cecilia Huang, who noted that Google’s Gemini rejected her request to render a photo into a Ratatouille character for a 15-second video on copyright grounds, whereas ByteDance’s Doubao fulfilled the request. ByteDance did not respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. In response to allegations that it used copyrighted content to train Seedance 2.0, ByteDance told the South China Morning Post in February that it “respects intellectual property rights” and was “taking steps to strengthen current safeguards as we work to prevent the unauthorised use of intellectual property and likeness by users”. Open-weight Chinese developers are also competing aggressively on cost. MiniMax’s H3, which can generate 15-second 2K videos with stereo sound, is one-third the cost of mainstream competing products, according to the company. It was subsequently made available through ByteDance’s Dreamina creative platform, granting it access to global creators. According to Artificial Analysis estimates based on default API settings, generating one minute of 1080p video costs around US$7.80 via MiniMax H3, compared to US$6 for Google’s Gemini Omni Flash and US$9.07 through ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0. Meanwhile, effective commercial prices for Chinese models are often discounted heavily through enterprise agreements, with Wan 3.0 and Seedance 2.0 trading at substantial markdowns on their headline rates. This technical and pricing edge is translating into top-line revenue. Kuaishou Technology said its Kling AI video-generation platform generated more than 850 million yuan (US$118 million) in second-quarter revenue, up over 200 per cent year on year. By June, Kling AI’s user base had topped 100 million globally, up about 67 per cent from late 2025, while its enterprise client roster expanded by roughly 67 per cent to nearly 50,000 businesses, according to Kuaishou. Kling 3.0 1080p Pro version ranks ninth in Artificial Analysis’ text-to-video leaderboard for audio.

title: Singapore to auction luxury goods, properties from US$2.4 billion money laundering case
description: Island-wide raids in August 2023 uncovered millions of dollars earned from an illicit gambling ring run by Chinese suspects.
content: More than 1,000 luxury items and 80 real estate properties forfeited in Singapore’s S$3 billion (US$2.4 billion) money laundering case would go under the hammer from September 7, audit firm Deloitte said on Saturday. The properties will be auctioned by SRI, Edmund Tie & Company and Knight Frank, while auction house Hotlotz will handle the luxury goods, comprising jewellery, watches and handbags. Some selected properties will also be offered for sale through an expression of interest process run by List International Realty, outside the auction process. The assets will be sold in phases between September and mid-2027. Deloitte said the composition and number of items in each phase were still being finalised and could change as authentication and preparatory work continues. Deloitte was appointed by the Singapore Police Force in July 2025 to manage and realise the non-cash assets forfeited in the case. The case emerged after island-wide raids in August 2023 uncovered millions of dollars earned from an illicit gambling ring based in Southeast Asia. The 10 offenders, all originally from China although some held other citizenships, have since been convicted and deported after serving their sentences. Exclusive viewing Hotlotz said it would hold 15 online auctions of the luxury items from September to May 2027. The firm does not accept commission or telephone bids, and does not hold traditional in-room auctions. Catalogues for the first two auctions will be released at 10am on September 7, when online bidding also opens. The first auction, closing at 4pm on September 20, will have handbags and accessories from brands including Chanel, Louis Vuitton and Christian Dior. The second, closing at the same time on September 27, features jewellery pieces from makers such as Graff, Bulgari and Van Cleef & Arpels. The two auctions will include over 300 handbags and accessories and over 250 jewellery pieces, with a presale estimate of between S$2.9 million and S$3.9 million. Catalogues for subsequent auctions would be released closer to each sale, and would include Hermes handbags and watches from Patek Philippe, Richard Mille and Rolex, Hotlotz said. The auctions are open to participants globally, though bidders must register and pass compulsory identity verification checks before taking part. Approved bidders can book a viewing slot at Le Freeport, a high-security storage facility in Changi where the items are kept. Viewing is strictly by appointment, and walk-ins are not allowed. Hotlotz said appointment slots were limited and assigned to registered participants on a first-come, first-served basis. Hotlotz founder and chief executive Matt Elton said the case’s global profile would draw added attention to the auctions, but that he was keeping sensationalism at bay. His aim was to “sell everything in the fairest, most transparent way and offer it to the widest market”, he said. “At the end of the day, I try to avoid the sensationalism. My job is to sell these items. My job is to understand what they are, to put them into the market at the correct price, and to be very objective about how we talk about them,” he said. “I’m trying not to be knocked off my perch by the kind of stories around it.” Elton said transparency was key, including making sure bidders knew where the items came from. Starting prices were benchmarked against other auctions rather than original retail or secondary-market prices, he added. This article was first published by CNA

title: US families hold out hope for relatives lost in Nepal floods
description: About 90 Americans are among those unaccounted for, according to the US State Department.
content: Mukti Patel has huddled with family and friends at her parents’ Richmond, Virginia, home since her dad, sister and two other relatives went missing in the catastrophic flash floods along the Nepal-China border. She knows the hotel they were staying in was swept away. But as she shared memories of them on Friday, she caught herself. “I shouldn’t talk in past tense yet,” she said. “We don’t know anything.” As rescuers continued pulling survivors from the mud, family members of some of the more than 2,000 people missing in the disaster were still holding out hope – however dim – that their loved ones survived. On a Zoom call Thursday night, some family members wanted to know if they could reach the site and whether a relative might be trapped inside an air pocket, said Sanket Pandey, managing director of Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company. The tour group, which has an office in Baltimore, had organised a two-week excursion to the region with 40 guests and seven tour guides. All of them were now missing, Pandey said. Their families are desperate for any information. “It’s really difficult to have nothing,” he said. Patel’s family was in the Himalayan Glacier group when the floods struck on Wednesday, killing hundreds of people and leaving more than 2,000 missing. About 90 Americans are among those unaccounted for, according to the US State Department. Patel, 27, said her dad, Umesh Kumar, 56, had wanted to make the trip for many years and travelled through India to Nepal, where he was joined by her sister, Akanksha, 32, and her sister’s husband, Ishan, 32. Ishan’s mum, Shilpa, 59, was also on the trek. Ishan and Shilpa Patel have dual Canadian and US citizenship while Umesh Kumar and Akanksha Patel are Canadian citizens. Akanksha Patel is a psychiatrist who wants to break stigma around mental health problems, according to her sister. “Everything I’ve done in life has been off the blueprint of my sister,” Mukti Patel said between tears in a phone interview. “There’s no ounce of meanness in her.” Her father was a joyous person who helped victims of the Covid-19 pandemic, and her brother-in-law, an orthopaedic surgeon, had brought great happiness to her sister’s life, she said. Ishan Patel turned 32 on Wednesday, and the family called to wish him a happy birthday. That was their last contact. Mukti Patel said she would like more countries to help the rescue and recovery efforts. Flood epicentre Jiwan Jyoti, who has US citizenship, also was travelling with Himalayan Glacier and was listed by the group as missing. They had stopped in Timure, Nepal, before they were set to leave for a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others, her long-time friend Manmeet Singh Meet said. Jyoti, a 50-year-old from Lexington, Massachusetts, called her family from breakfast on Wednesday as she was preparing to cross into Tibet. Meet said Jyoti “hung up the phone at around 8.40am local time in Nepal, and then I think around 8.45am, this flash flood came, and then our world turned upside down.” He later heard from mountain guides that the hotel where Jyoti had been staying – and where her location was last recorded on the Find My iPhone app – was destroyed. Now Meet says he is losing hope that his best friend of 15 years will be found alive. “She was essentially almost in the epicentre over there,” Meet said. Vaasavi Unnava, a 31-year-old PhD student, thought her parents had already crossed into Tibet with the same tour group when she saw reports about the flood. “I was not really that worried, but I just sent them a text like to be sure,” she said. The WhatsApp message never delivered. Her father, Hanumantha Rao Unnava, and mother, Vasundhara Unnava, had set out on a retirement trip and were most excited to go spend two months in India with family after hiking Mount Kailash. The couple from Woodland, California, are among dozens of US citizens missing in the flood. “They were so, so excited. My dad was talking about finally getting to spend time with his mother,” she said. Until recently, her father was the dean of the Graduate School of Management at the University of California, Davis, for 10 years, and her mother lectured at the university, she said. Unnava described her dad as “disciplined and duty-bound” but also “a big joker.” She described her mom as “spontaneous and playful” and “the smartest woman I’ve ever met”. She takes solace in knowing that “they have just changed so many people’s lives for the better”.

title: Hong Kong legal sector welcomes making bay area practice scheme permanent
description: Scheme opening up Guangdong cities to Hong Kong lawyers in 2020 is enshrined in Lawyers Law, strengthening cross-border flow of services.
content: Hong Kong’s legal community has hailed a move by mainland China to make permanent a pilot scheme allowing lawyers to practise in Greater Bay Area cities, predicting the demand for such cross-border legal services will continue to grow. Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok said on Saturday that amendments passed by the country’s top legislative body the previous day would further accelerate the development of the bay area and the lawyers already providing services under the trial scheme had contributed to the building of the rule of law. “The national 15th five-year plan outline calls for deepening the construction of the [bay area] and accelerating the development of an international first-class bay area,” Lam said, referring to the national blueprint for economic and social development between 2026 and 2030. The Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress passed the amendments to the Lawyers Law on Friday, and they will take effect on September 1. The pilot scheme, launched in 2020, ran for three years and was extended for another three years in 2023. According to the Department of Justice, more than 650 Hong Kong and Macau lawyers have obtained the necessary licences to provide legal services in the nine Guangdong cities on specified civil and commercial matters to which the mainland laws apply. The Bar Association welcomed the passage of the amendment and expected the number to qualifying members to continue to increase. Law Society president Roden Tong Man-lung said the statutory recognition of the regime would encourage more Hong Kong lawyers to offer cross-border legal services. “It also strengthens Hong Kong’s role as an international legal and dispute resolution services centre under ‘one country, two systems’,” Tong said, referring to the principle governing ties between Hong Kong and the mainland. The society also suggested exploring the possibility of a professional indemnity pilot scheme to strengthen client protection. To qualify, lawyers must pass the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area Legal Professional Examination, organised by the State Council’s judicial administration department, and obtain a mainland qualification to practise. They will then be allowed to handle specified legal matters in Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Foshan, Huizhou, Dongguan, Zhongshan, Jiangmen and Zhaoqing in Guangdong province. The State Council’s judicial administration department sets the exam’s enrolment requirements, the application procedures for practising and the scope of permitted practice. Legislator Thomas So Shiu-tsung, also a former president of the Law Society, hailed the latest move. “This further solidifies the initiative for further integration of legal talents across the bay area region,” So said. He added that the scheme had been popular with Hong Kong lawyers as the bay area was a huge market. Barrister and former lawmaker Eunice Yung Hoi-yan, a qualified bay area lawyer since 2020, said she expected mainland enterprises’ demand for Hong Kong legal services to increase with the regularisation of the scheme, as well as the operation of the International Organisation for Mediation headquartered in Hong Kong. Yung said she was hopeful more Hong Kong lawyers could obtain the qualification although some might find the exam hard. “The exam is not easy. There are written papers as well as interviews, and they are in [simplified] Chinese or Mandarin,” she said. “Some Hong Kong legal practitioners may find the test difficult because we are used to using English here.” The qualifying examination is open to permanent residents of Hong Kong and Macau who, among other requirements, must have five years’ experience and be able to write in simplified Chinese and have professional proficiency in spoken Mandarin.

title: China-Nepal floods: 9 Chinese tunnel experts sent to aid rescue in race against time
description: Move follows direct request from Kathmandu, Beijing says, as more than 100 people remain trapped inside multiple hydropower tunnels in Nepal.
content: China has sent nine specialist tunnel rescuers to Nepal to help with emergency operations following a direct request from Kathmandu, as search teams race against time to find survivors from Wednesday’s devastating floods. Seven people have been confirmed dead on the Chinese side, with 544 still missing as the rescue operation passed a critical 72-hour window. In Nepal, at least 675 have died and nearly 2,500 – hundreds of them foreigners – are missing. Five of the Chinese tunnel experts were flown in by helicopter from Gyirong county in Tibet, state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday. They arrived in the afternoon to join rescue operations at a hydropower plant in the border region. The five were “urgently dispatched at the request of the Nepalese government”, China’s Ministry of Emergency Management said on Saturday evening. According to local authorities, more than 100 people remain trapped inside multiple hydropower tunnels and Nepali army teams are drilling in an “extremely challenging” rescue bid. Four more Chinese tunnel experts were also urgently sent to support the rescue efforts, the ministry said. Rescue operations are also in full swing on the Chinese side of the border. On Saturday morning, engineers and workers started clearing away mud and debris using excavators and heavy earth-moving machinery in an effort to reopen the route to the Gyirong Port border checkpoint. The final stretch of the national highway leading to Gyirong Port has been severely damaged, with mud up to 2 metres (6.6 feet) deep burying sections of the route, while parts of the roadbed have been completely washed away. Overnight rain since Friday further hindered repair work. As of Saturday afternoon, rescuers had cleared the road to within roughly 1.5km (0.9 mile) of Gyirong Port’s hardest-hit zone, state broadcaster CCTV reported. Meanwhile, heavy-lift drones have been deployed to airdrop rescue equipment and crucial supplies to frontline teams, providing vital support to sustain search and rescue operations. Tibet’s military command has deployed two helicopters into the flood zone to deliver emergency supplies – including food, medical kits and rescue gear. Advanced laser-video artificial intelligence monitoring equipment had been deployed at the disaster sites, CCTV reported. The sensors can detect sub-millimetre shifts, providing timely alerts for rescuers to evacuate. The alert is crucial for on the ground work as Wednesday’s debris flow created a barrier lake, which forms when a natural dam of landslide debris blocks a river. The lake, which CCTV said spanned around 100,000 square metres (1.08 million sq ft), equivalent to 14 standard football pitches, is being monitored by radars and drones. There were fears of a potential breach after the barrier lake first formed, but the immediate threat appears to have passed. The latest update from China’s hydrology monitoring authorities on Saturday night said the blockage had largely been washed away, allowing the river to flow naturally and easing the threat of a sudden outburst. Many of the Chinese frontline workers involved had taken part in another rescue operation in July last year, when the region was hit by a mudslide that washed away a bridge, CCTV reported. At the all-but-destroyed Gyirong Port checkpoint, about 70 firefighters were carrying out a comprehensive sweep in a search and rescue effort, it said. Meanwhile, Chen Hongqi, a senior engineer from the Ministry of Natural Resources, warned there was a risk of secondary disasters. He told CCTV on Friday that an even larger water tower of about 120,000 square metres was forming near the collapsed glacier that triggered the disaster, and an ice sheet hanging from a nearby cliff had also fractured. “Ice, unlike rock, is essentially rootless and lacks a structural anchorage, which makes hazard evaluation exceptionally difficult. We must rely on detailed surveys before making further rescue decisions,” he said. The first rescuers arrived at the scene on Friday afternoon and so far two villagers have been found alive in rubble near the Gyirong border checkpoint, according to Tibet’s emergency bureau. But at the border crossing itself, there was no sign of any survivors. Liu Maolin, the rescue team leader, said the checkpoint building had been completely destroyed by a mudslide. The China Meteorological Administration warned that Gyirong county would see light rainfall and temperatures as low as 8 degrees Celsius (46 degrees Fahrenheit) over the next three days. Each of the firefighters had been equipped with a 72-hour self-sufficiency kit containing food, water, thermal gear and medical supplies, Liu told CCTV. The first two to three days after natural disasters are usually the critical window for finding survivors. Liu said advance scout units were sending real-time GPS coordinates and road conditions to the main search teams and their support teams to help them map out the best possible routes to take. On Saturday, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu sent his condolences to the victims and announced that the city government had set aside HK$50 million (US$6.4 million) from the Disaster Relief Fund to support the search and rescue operations. On the same day, the Macau government announced it would donate 30 million yuan (US$4.5 million). On Friday, Nepal agreed to allow foreign emergency teams to help with its rescue efforts in the face of intense pressure from governments whose citizens remain missing. The Nepalese government had previously said it was capable of handling the rescue operation and Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told Reuters on Saturday that the country needed help in specialised ⁠and technical areas rather than search and rescue operations. According to the Nepal Tourism Board’s latest records, 517 foreigners from 31 countries remain missing, including 178 from India, 65 from the United States, 53 from Ukraine, 35 from Australia and 33 from Britain.

title: How Hong Kong is vital in Patrick McDowell’s ready-to-wear expansion
description: Worn by the Princess of Wales, Lady Gaga and Keira Knightley, the fashion designer explains how Hong Kong is a key part of his plans.
content: At 30, Patrick McDowell already has the résumé of designer lore: winner of the 2025 Queen Elizabeth II Award for British Design, guest speaker at the United Nations on sustainability in fashion, and celebrity clients that include Lady Gaga, Keira Knightley and Sarah Jessica Parker. Now the London-and-Venice-based British fashion designer has turned his attention to Asia, where he will speak at Hong Kong’s Fashion Summit (HK) conference at the Hong Kong Palace Museum on September 3. McDowell first came to the city at 17, having financed the journey by making bags and selling them to friends. Hong Kong struck the teenager from Wirral near Liverpool as “an amazing washing machine of the whole world in one place”. It remains a fitting image for a city that excels at ideas, textiles, capital and speed. “I respond really well to that,” McDowell says. “I like working very quickly, and I like that kind of immediacy in Hong Kong.” Over a decade on, he returns with a consequential retail foothold at Joyce Boutique, whose racks have long offered a regional test of fashion’s next proposition. McDowell’s proposition is, at first look, a tricky one: occasionwear with a conscience; romance with traceability; a sustainability programme that has to survive the inconvenient demands of a business. But among fashion’s ever-revolving crop of bright young things, the formula seems to be working. The royal accolades have helped. Catherine, the Princess of Wales, who presented him with the Queen Elizabeth II Award for British Design last year, wore a custom McDowell coat dress to the Order of the Garter service this year. Rendered in English rose silk damask woven by Stephen Walters, Britain’s oldest silk weaving company, the buttery-yellow look offered a polished argument for British craftsmanship and design. “It’s really special that she’s using her voice to support younger British talent,” McDowell says. Hong Kong’s role in ready-to-wear shift But the more consequential part of McDowell’s story may be unfolding far from Windsor. His Asian expansion is not simply a hunt for new customers with a taste for British occasionwear. It is changing the machinery of his business. When McDowell began considering ready-to-wear, he returned to Hong Kong, where he met luxury fashion retailer Joyce and Hong Kong-listed apparel manufacturer High Fashion, which has operations in places including mainland China. “That was when we began those seeds of relationships,” he says. The city made a swift practical case for itself. “As a Brit in Asia, it’s certainly a bit easier in Hong Kong because we share the language,” he says, adding that many business systems feel familiar. But its appeal is cultural, too: “a real melting pot of different people and places”. For its first seven years, McDowell’s eponymous brand was chiefly a made-to-order business: occasionwear with the patience, craft and implied permanence of an heirloom. The brand’s characteristic drama derives in part from Liverpool, which has a “very glamorous, very colourful, very bold sense of style”, McDowell says. “People really dress up, even if it’s just a small dinner.” In September 2025, the label introduced its first wholesale ready-to-wear collection at London Fashion Week, then moved to four annual collections, including pre-collections. “We were able to do that through this Hong Kong manufacturing partnership, basically,” McDowell says of High Fashion. “It was really important … that we expanded from the beginning in a way that was scalable and proper.” The word “scalable” does not summon romantic swathes of chiffon or a champagne-soaked front row. For an independent designer, however, it can mean the difference between a spirited London atelier and a business that survives beyond its first burst of attention. The fashion industry has an impressive appetite for discovering talent and a less dependable habit of underwriting its survival. McDowell knows that all too well. Before receiving the Queen Elizabeth II Award, he says that things were so tough, he had thought about closing the business down. Once the award was announced, though, “interest was through the roof”; press and clients followed, providing a huge boost and “almost a seal of approval for people to buy from us”. The skill level in China is so high … and often can’t be found anywhere else in the world today Patrick McDowell, designer McDowell still works with specialist British makers on bespoke pieces, for which he often sources heritage fabrics, deadstock and next-generation materials, including mycelium-based hides and Amazonian bio-leather harvested without harming trees. Yet High Fashion gives the label the technical capacity and supply-chain visibility that sustainable ready-to-wear requires. “Silk is the fibre that I love the most, and that we use the most,” McDowell says. High Fashion, he explains, is a specialist in the material and owns the silk process from the farm that grows the silkworms all the way to the places that make the clothes. That degree of vertical integration is unusual, he says, and includes work on natural coatings that can make silk washable, as well as next-generation silk developments. It also challenges a persistent but lazy Western shorthand around Chinese manufacturing. “There’s this kind of myth of ‘made in China’ that now just isn’t true. The skill level in China is so high … and often can’t be found anywhere else in the world today,” he says, adding, “I’ve seen where the fabric is printed. I’ve seen where the knits are knitted. I’ve seen where the clothes are stitched together.” Alongside that is an openness to experimenting with new ways of working with designers. “Without that openness, we wouldn’t have a business, really.” He says that it is always difficult to align sustainability and growth. His answer is proximity and restraint: natural fibres where possible, small runs and first-hand knowledge of the supply chain. “Even though we are kind of scaling, we’re scaling from, like, one of one to 10 of one.” The clothes, however, must earn their place before their credentials enter the conversation. “The most important thing is that the pieces feel and look amazing and make people feel amazing,” he says. “Then, you can build in other sides of your business.” An ethical garment that nobody wants to wear is hardly a revolution. In retail, a collection cannot rely on the explanatory scaffolding of an interview, lookbook or report. “The pieces have to kind of stand on their own and really convince people that they’re great,” McDowell says. Joyce’s in-house alterations offer a small but meaningful continuation of his bespoke roots. His grandmother, who taught him to sew, remains a touchstone. “She always wanted things to be good quality and wanted them to last,” he says. “She bought the best she could, even though she didn’t have much money.” That ethic informs clothing intended not merely to be owned but to accumulate a life: “You’re usually wearing our pieces to a wedding, a party, a celebration or a lunch; something that holds memory. Then that piece becomes the memory of that thing.” It is also a shrewd proposition for luxury consumers seeking distinction beyond the mega-brand. The typical McDowell client demands “things that are more unique and individual and interesting … perhaps something her friends don’t have because she already has all she wants from big brands anyway.” He says Patrick McDowell is very much a British brand with a British style. Still, he is encouraged that the work travels: “People appreciate the craftsmanship and the style.” The royal endorsement has only helped make the case that heritage, luxury and circularity can coexist. Hong Kong offers more than a route east. It is a proving ground where British craft, Chinese production, international retail and impatient business culture meet. For this Liverpudlian designer, whose work joins sustainability, silk and ceremony, it may be precisely the washing machine in which a small fashion label becomes a global business.

title: Japanese expansion and global domination next on NFL’s radar, Asia chief says
description: Ex-rugby boss Brett Gosper says Japan is a ‘market of interest’ as American football seeks to be ‘top 3 sport’ in countries it operates in.
content: The NFL plans to expand into new international markets, including Japan, as it seeks to build on growing interest outside the United States, the league’s head of Europe and Asia-Pacific Brett Gosper said. The league’s 2026 regular season, which begins on September 10, will feature ‌a record nine international games across seven countries, up from seven the previous year. “Japan is a market of interest at the moment. There is a good following, good participation in that market as well … and a lot of sporting fans and an affinity with American sports like baseball and so on,” Gosper told Reuters. The former CEO of World Rugby, however, did allude to a potential limitation with scoring a touchdown in some Asian markets. “Sometimes some of the markets are ⁠more challenging to grow because they’re not on the US game schedule or match window time schedule and therefore more challenging hours ‌in Asia,” Gosper said. The NFL has exported its sport to territories like the United Kingdom, Brazil, Spain and now Australia, which will host the first of the nine international games on September 11 ‌in Melbourne involving five-time Super Bowl champions San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams. The objective it appears within ⁠the NFL ranks is to ⁠have more games internationally. “The commissioner outlined this, there’s a possibility that over the next coming years, we could build to a point of 16 games internationally outside ‌of the US – that potentially by 2030, that’s something that he’s mooted as a possibility,” Gosper, a former rugby player, said. Gosper believes the recent increases in international ‌games ‌benefit fans in the US and abroad. “Those increases in international games have usually come and been accompanied by a movement of ‌a game from pre-season into the main season so [US] fans don’t feel like they’re losing a game to overseas, they have ⁠still a high volume of games in their market. “So, for the moment, we see excitement around this, whether it be in ⁠the States or outside of the States.” According to the NFL, the UK is home to more than 17 million fans, with the country having hosted 42 games since 2007. What furthers fan interest is the visibility of talent ‌from markets where the NFL is ‌seeking to establish a strong footprint. “We’ve seen that effect with Jordan Mailata, particularly in Australia,” Gosper said. “A lot of fan growth, which we can attribute to the interest that he’s engendered through the [Philadelphia] Eagles.” The NFL’s long-term goal is a clear one. “Our objective … in 10 years would be to see ourselves rated very highly as a top three favourite sport in the countries that we operate in,” Gosper said.

title: Malaysian police arrest 7 Yemeni men in Kuala Lumpur after dangerous road stunt goes viral
description: The men reportedly told police that they leaned out of the cars and sat on the windows for fun while celebrating a friend’s wedding.
content: Seven Yemeni men were arrested in Malaysia after they allegedly performed dangerous stunts while travelling in two vehicles along Jalan Sungai Besi early on Friday. Kuala Lumpur Traffic Investigation and Enforcement Department chief Mohd Zamzuri Mohd Isa said the incident, which occurred at about 12.30am, came to light after a video of the incident went viral on social media. He said preliminary investigations found that both vehicles were travelling along Jalan Sungai Besi towards Jalan Bukit Bintang when the passengers allegedly leaned out of the vehicles and sat on the windows. “All seven individuals were Yemeni men aged between 23 and 26,” he said in a statement on Saturday. “Five of them are students at a public university in Kedah, while the other two are university graduates.” Arabian Nights in KL: Dangerous Midnight Parade on the Highway by u/whusler in malaysia Mohd Zamzuri said police questioning found that the stunts were performed simply for fun while celebrating a friend’s wedding. He added that all seven men involved were detained for further investigation before being released on police bail. The case is being investigated under Section 336 of the Penal Code for committing a rash or negligent act that endangers the life or personal safety of others. Those convicted face up to three months’ imprisonment, a fine of up to 500 ringgit (US$120), or both. Mohd Zamzuri also urged anyone with information or witnesses to the incident to assist investigations by contacting the Tun H S Lee Traffic Police Station or any nearby police station. This article was first published by The Star

title: Why some Wang Fuk Court owners have refused buy-back deal even as deadline nears
description: While acquisition price for flats at fire-ravaged estate is seen as generous, about 3.5 per cent of homeowners have not accepted offer.
content: As the deadline approaches for homeowners to accept the Hong Kong government’s deal to buy back their flats at fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court, some who refuse to sell have said the offer cannot make up for the loss of their property and communal bonds. With the clock ticking to the August 31 cut-off date, the South China Morning Post spoke to six residents determined not to sell their homes at the devastated Tai Po estate, even though experts say the government’s offer is generous and compulsory acquisition would result in a lower price. The six residents are among the 3.5 per cent of homeowners – about 70 people – who have not accepted the offer, under which the government will buy flats at HK$8,000 (US$1,020) or HK$10,500 per square foot, depending on whether the land premium has been paid. Vincent Ho Kui-yip, a former president of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors, described the acquisition price as a “generous offer”, noting that Wang Fuk Court was more than four decades old. The proposed price exceeded recent transaction levels for other Home Ownership Scheme flats in the same district, he added. Pre-fire estimates by the institute put the market value of flats in the eight-block estate at about HK$6,000 to HK$8,000 per square foot. Owners can use the cash to buy a flat on the open market or join a special sales programme for a subsidised home, using cash or a flat-for-flat exchange. While most owners opted to accept the offer and move on, some of the holdouts said they were not waiting for a better deal but for the chance to return to the homes they were forced to flee. Among them was Lucia Cheung, a 40-year-old resident of the worst-hit block, Wang Cheong House, who lost both parents in the blaze. Cheung said that between obtaining death certificates, digging through ashes for keepsakes and calming her traumatised son, she was exhausted. “I do not have any energy to deal with the buyout. I did not even open the letter of acceptance [sent by the government],” she said. “Some families of the deceased do not want to go back any more, and I respect that. But I cannot let it go. My parents are gone. I cannot bear that the proof of their existence is gone too.” Her working-class parents, first-batch owners in the 1980s, poured their savings into the flat and raised her son there after she married and moved out, she said, calling it “our ancestral home”. Cheung said the government offer could leave her roughly HK$1 million short of the value of a comparable two-room flat in Kai Tak or Fanling near the MTR, after accounting for price differences, renovations and stamp duty. With much of the family’s cash savings burned in the fire, she said the shortfall was a heavy burden with her husband as the sole breadwinner. The deadliest fire in the city in decades tore through seven of the eight blocks last November, killing 168 people and displacing some 5,000 residents. The government announced in February it would spend about HK$6.8 billion to acquire the flats in the seven blocks. In June, it extended the buy-back offer to the only unaffected block, Wang Chi House, adding another HK$1 billion to the scheme’s cost. It also ruled out on-site redevelopment. Another resident, Shirley Keung, in her thirties, said she moved from nearby Kwong Fuk Estate into Wang Kin House with her parents and three siblings a few years ago. As Wang Kin House was less damaged than some other blocks, Keung said she was pinning her hopes on a building inspection report, waiting to see if repairs were possible. “I will wait for the report to tell me whether my building is truly unfit for living. Then I can make a well-informed decision,” she said. “If it can be repaired, I am willing to share the cost.” Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said last Sunday that the government’s offer was already 30 per cent above the pre-fire value and would not be negotiated, as in a private sale. He acknowledged that some residents felt it was insufficient but warned that compulsory acquisition would yield substantially lower compensation. Another Wang Kin House resident, Mabel Wong, said she was not bargaining for money but for the right to return home. “We only ask to return to a home that is nowhere else, and no amount of money can replace,” she said. Ross Leung, 33, bought his Wang Chi House flat with a mortgage that he is still repaying. “You cannot measure all units with the same price. My unit has a sea view and was bought at a higher price,” he said, arguing that the government’s offer was 20 per cent lower than the price he paid for the flat. “Why are we not allowed to return? Instead we are thrown into a scheme where residents have to fight each other for scraps, desperately competing for a comparable flat,” he said. “Resorting to compulsory acquisition will be a loss not just for Wang Fuk Court, but for Hong Kong, which prides itself on a private property market and rights.” A retiree surnamed Wong from Wang Kin House moved to Guangdong province after being displaced. He bought a flat across the border before the fire and chose to stay there for a better living environment. Wong said he was prepared for the worst if legislation for a forced sale drove prices down, with his life savings to fall back on. “I will not sell even if the price drops to zero. This entire buyout is unfair,” he said. A Wang Chi House resident surnamed Xiong, 58, bought her 10th-floor flat in 2003. A confinement nanny, she said she was too drained by the disaster to continue working, and her husband was being treated in a psychiatric hospital because of the fire. “I am willing to pay for repairs, but that option was never raised,” she said. “This is worse than the 44 hours I waited for the fire to die down. Then I still had hope I could return home. Now that hope is wiped out.”

title: China tests GJ-21 stealth drone as Sichuan Type 076 warship carries out sea trials
description: Social media clips show naval combat drone over Liaoning province while Beijing’s catapult-equipped drone carrier prepares for deployment.
content: China’s GJ-21 large stealth attack drone has been spotted on flight tests this month, as the country’s first Type 076 amphibious assault ship – the vessel that will launch the drone – enters its final sea trials. The GJ-21, the naval variant of the GJ-11 stealth attack drone, first appeared at China’s Victory Day parade in September last year and has made rare public appearances since then. Computer-generated footage aired by state broadcaster CCTV in July showed how it would be launched from the Type 076 Sichuan – China’s most advanced amphibious assault ship and the world’s first drone carrier. A Chinese social media post on Thursday showed the GJ-21 flying over a highway service area in the northeastern Chinese city of Huludao in Liaoning province. Another post dated August 19 had shown the GJ-21 flying over the same service centre, although from a different direction. The two videos, which the South China Morning Post has geolocated, appear to be flight tests of the GJ-21. However, it is not clear when they took place. The drone was also spotted in a third video posted online on Thursday that showed the GJ-21 flying at a different angle from the first video.
