In its July broadcast, CCTV quoted an expert who said the 40,000-tonne Sichuan drone carrier had entered its final testing phase. The PLA Navy is expected to take delivery of the warship by the end of this year. The vessel was seen with deck-line markings and deploying decoys in other CCTV footage. Early this month, further CCTV footage showed it launching a red test vehicle using its electromagnetic aircraft-launch system. As the only amphibious assault ship in the world equipped with an electromagnetic catapult system, the Sichuan is expected to launch crewed and uncrewed fixed-wing aircraft, including the GJ-21 drone, as well as helicopters. Also on Thursday, satellite imagery shared by X user MT Anderson appeared to show the Sichuan – alongside two Type 052 destroyers and three Type 054 frigates – pictured on August 25 just off the Qingdao naval base, the headquarters of the PLA’s Northern Theatre Command navy. The image, which the SCMP has not independently verified, also showed the Liaoning – China’s first aircraft carrier – moored at the pier. It is not clear whether the vessels were there for trials with the Sichuan. With a full-load displacement exceeding 40,000 tonnes, the Sichuan is designed to transport landing craft, troops, armoured vehicles and aircraft to support amphibious operations, and expected to be one of Beijing’s most important assets in any potential conflict with Taiwan. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. It has also stepped up military and political pressure on the island since cross-strait tensions escalated some four years ago. Most countries, including the United States, Taiwan’s main international backer, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Asian Angle | India-China ties are warming, the time to capitalise is now
description: The post-Galwan freeze is over. Rebuilding economic dialogue offers both nations a win-win path forward.
content: When Ajit Doval met China’s top diplomat Wang Yi in June, New Delhi’s national security adviser called China and India “partners, not rivals” and said a stable relationship “serves the common interests of both sides”. Wang, for his part, called for the two countries “to accelerate the resumption of dialogue mechanisms and promote exchanges” in trade, finance and other fields. These warm statements were a sharp departure from the adversarial tone that had bedevilled ties since Chinese and Indian troops clashed at Galwan in the summer of 2020. Before Galwan, Beijing and Delhi had been actively trying to repair a relationship frayed by frequent, low-level border clashes. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and China’s Xi Jinping met for a summit in Mamallapuram – a historic Indian port city with a long history of Buddhist exchanges with China – in October 2019, having already met in Wuhan the year before. But Galwan swept all that away. It took five years of diplomatic and military negotiations to change the tone of the relationship again, culminating in a Modi-Xi summit on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation gathering in Tianjin last August. That thaw has now provided an opportunity to revive the India-China Strategic Economic Dialogue (SED), the mechanism launched in 2011 by Manmohan Singh and Wen Jiabao that produced six rounds of talks before 2019. India originally pushed for the SED to address its ballooning trade deficit with China. The dialogue’s working groups focused on six key areas: infrastructure (including Chinese investment in high-speed rail and railway modernisation), energy conservation and environmental protection, policy coordination, pharmaceuticals and hi-tech cooperation in AI, mobile technology and other areas. The last meeting, in September 2019, ended on an upbeat note, with Delhi stating that the SED had “emerged as a crucial mechanism to facilitate bilateral trade and investment flows, and enhance economic cooperation”. The big question now is whether it still can. The answer is probably yes, even though the world has changed dramatically since 2019. Disruptions to the multilateral trading system caused by US President Donald Trump’s tariffs and Washington’s weaponisation of trade, energy and finance have hurt China and India both. But a revived SED would need a wider ambit in this newly fractured world and some long-standing issues still need to be addressed. China must convincingly address Indian concerns about its aggressive trade and industrial policies, while India must clear the air regarding Chinese questions over targeted foreign investment restrictions. India should also look at the trade deficit issue from a holistic perspective. A trade relationship defined by higher imports is not, on its own, detrimental. India has a trade deficit with partner countries like Japan and South Korea, for instance, but has secured export-oriented investment from them. Hence, if India can grow its own manufacturing and export sectors, Chinese imports can become an asset rather than a liability. As Delhi expands export-oriented manufacturing – with the India-assembled iPhone, for example – it may well need to import more components and machinery from China, not less. Vietnam shows how this can work: its trade deficit with China reached US$115 billion in 2025, up from US$83 billion the year before. Over the same period, its exports to the United States climbed from US$137 billion to US$194 billion. Imports and exports, in other words, can rise together. The SED could help achieve such an outcome, steering Chinese capital into India’s export-led manufacturing. Delhi is already, albeit very cautiously, exploring the possibility of Chinese investment in non-sensitive sectors and its finance ministry has suggested export-oriented Chinese investment as a way of dealing with the trade imbalance. With production costs rising at home, Chinese manufacturers may well find a lower-cost Indian base attractive – particularly as a springboard into South Asian, African and Middle Eastern markets. Handled well, such investment would let Chinese imports feed into greater Indian exports, creating mutually beneficial economic synergy. India was once counting on the huge American consumer market to power its growth, but US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau made clear in March that Washington had learned its lesson, telling an audience in Delhi: “We are not going to make the same mistakes with India that we made with China 20 years ago.” Washington was not “going to let you develop all these markets, and then, the next thing we know, you are beating us in a lot of commercial things”, he said at this year’s Raisina Dialogue in the Indian capital. In this new, fractured world, India needs a new strategy to reach out to non-Western markets. Harvard Professor Meg Rithmire and co-author Peter Cowhey have argued that the US should try to work with China to re-industrialise itself. If that logic holds for America, it holds for India too. Closer economic cooperation with China could also open new markets in the Global South. There’s no doubt that most Global South countries would welcome closer cooperation between China and India, as it could help strengthen the world economy and improve the functioning of multilateral economic and financial institutions. A new positive China-India economic synergy could profoundly help the wider Global South. The time has clearly come for policymakers in both countries to understand that major win-win possibilities exist. If they both accept this, a revived SED can be more meaningful than the earlier rounds of sectoral dialogues. That means returning to an earlier logic that characterised the bilateral relationship, based on the understanding that a pending resolution of the border issue and “peace and tranquillity” along the Line of Actual Control would allow the wider relationship to move forward. The tone of ties has already shifted. The time to act has, decisively, arrived. Sanjaya Baru is Distinguished Fellow, United Services Institution of India. He was adviser to Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and Director for Geo-economics & Strategy, International Institute of Strategic Studies. This article was published in coordination with the Asian Peace Programme (APP), an initiative to promote peace in Asia, housed in the NUS Asia Research Institute.

title: Letters | Don’t take peaceful days in Hong Kong as a given
description: Readers discuss the security of the city, a China-Nepal early-warning mechanism, and AI boot camps.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. There is a security guard at the entrance of my housing estate. He has worked there for more than a decade, knows every resident by sight and remembers when each child finishes school and which elderly resident takes evening walks. During the Covid-19 pandemic, he had one more task: reminding everyone entering the lobby to check their temperature. No one ever found him annoying. Everyone understood he was simply doing his job, and that job allowed the entire building to sleep soundly. Curiously, no one has ever suggested, “There has been no break-in for five years, so let’s fire security.” No one has proposed, “CCTV is a waste of electricity, let’s remove it.” On the contrary, the more upscale the building, the more sophisticated its security systems: double-access gates, floor-specific lift cards, 24-hour guards and full CCTV coverage. Residents in such buildings do not complain that there are too many security measures – they only worry they are not professional enough. The same logic should apply to the security of our city. What happened in 2019 was like someone storming into our lobby, smashing things and creating chaos. Now the protests have stopped, door locks have been installed and guards put in place. That does not mean the locks can be removed. Risks don’t disappear; they evolve. Just as estate security knows burglars do not only enter through the main entrance but also through the car park and back staircases, Hong Kong must secure not only its streets but also its cyberspace, schools, media and legal system. A functioning lock proves its value not by being picked every day but by deterring anyone from trying. The deterrent effect of national security legislation lies in the fact that it does not need to be frequently invoked. Our guard is getting older and will soon retire, but I know his replacement will undergo the same training and work the same shifts. Peaceful days have never fallen from the sky. They have always had to be guarded. If this is true for our estate, it is no less true for Hong Kong as a whole. The lock cannot be removed. Dr Chen Xiaoxin, president, Policy Research Committee, Hong Kong Quality and Talent Migrants Association China-Nepal early-warning mechanism needed Your report, “China-Nepal border disaster: 1,000-plus missing as Beijing sends rescue teams” (August 27), describes two rescue operations. That is precisely the difficulty: two states mobilising separately on opposite sides of a valley that the water treats as continuous. The reflex is to read this as an upstream-downstream problem, the hazard forming in one country and landing in another. The figures dispel that. The Chinese side reported more than 550 people missing. This is not a case of competing interests requiring a negotiated bargain. It is a case of two governments with an identical interest and no channel to act on it. The lakes above this border, supraglacial and moraine-dammed, are already observed by satellite. What does not exist is an agreed threshold at which an observation on one side triggers an automatic alert on the other, through a technical contact point operating below the diplomatic level, so that a warning does not need a ministry’s signature to cross a border. Treaties on Himalayan rivers concern themselves with water rights and allocation, but not always hazard information. The gap is now measurable in the missing. Dr Zaheer Allam, College of Architecture, Art and Design, American University of Sharjah Hold AI camps for youth The United Kingdom is providing “AI boot camps” to youth who are out of work or at risk of unemployment. The number of young Britons neither working nor learning reached 1.01 million in the first quarter. An International Labour Organization report showed global youth unemployment reaching 12.4 per cent last year, equivalent to 67 million unemployed people aged 15 to 24. More artificial intelligence boot camps should be created for young people, so they can learn to build AI tools, understand how businesses use AI and use the technology responsibly. Addressing the issue is in the interest of affected youth as well as the community. Lau Wing-sze, Tseung Kwan O

title: Iranian leaders admit economic toll of war with US as trade drops 35%
description: With the war now at the six-month mark, the Trump administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with an ‘economic D-Day’.
content: Iranian leaders are acknowledging the economic toll of war with the United States, with the supreme leader calling on the government to address the hardship while the president reported foreign trade has shrunk 35 per cent due to the American sanctions and blockade. The warnings came even as other leaders threaten the US with military retaliation and declarations that the Iranian navy maintains control of the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway giving Iran ‌leverage through its ability to disrupt global energy markets. With the war now at the six-month mark, and negotiations at an impasse, President Donald Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an “economic D-Day”. Washington has warned countries to cut their business ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions – though the Treasury Department stopped short of imposing penalties against major Iranian trade partners such as China and India, which could have repercussions for the US and global economies. The US Treasury Department did impose sanctions on Egypt’s Banque Misr for doing business with Tehran, proposing a rule that would cut off ⁠the bank’s branches in the United Arab Emirates from dollar transactions. Egypt’s central bank said it and the foreign ministry were in contact with US officials concerning the matter, adding ‌the measure was limited to Banque Misr UAE’s US dollar transactions with correspondent banks only. US Treasury officials separately issued sanctions targeting one entity based in Hong Kong and one person linked to Iran’s Bank Melli, according to a notice posted on the department’s website. The sanctions drive ‌compounds the toll of the war on Iran’s economy, where annual inflation hit 66 per cent last month. Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured ⁠and has not been seen publicly since ⁠the February 28 attack that killed his father, former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, called on the government to tackle the economic hardship. “There is the need to seriously address the chain of economic and livelihood challenges, ‌such as inflation, unemployment, management of prices and the market for goods and services,” a written statement attributed to Khamenei said. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that Iranian exports and imports slumped nearly 35 per cent because of US sanctions ‌and a ‌naval blockade of Iranian ports. But he said Iran was able to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived memorandum of understanding that the US ‌and Iran signed in June, when Washington permitted Iranian oil sales. With the US focused on its economic pressure campaign, others have sought to revive diplomatic efforts to end the ⁠war. Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani met Iranian leaders in Tehran on Thursday. He said he had stressed during the meeting the importance of ⁠returning to the pre-war status of open shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi on Friday described the talks with Al Thani as “creative”. Qatar, a US ally and Gulf neighbour of Iran, and Pakistan helped broker the June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire before disagreements over the strait caused it to unravel. US ‌military commanders say American forces have cleared sea mines from the strait that had been laid months ago by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Trump has repeatedly said the strait is open, but the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ navy said in a statement that such claims “are an obvious lie”, reiterating that the waterway remained closed to ships without Iranian permission. Preliminary shipping data released on Friday showed that only seven commodity vessels had transited the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, down from 17 a day earlier and below the 10-day average of 15.

title: How the Philippines missed a Korean gambling racket worth US$3.8 billion
description: Recent arrests expose a long-running crime network that flourished in the shadow of the nation’s Pogo scandal.
content: The Philippines spent years dismantling Chinese-linked gambling compounds in dramatic, headline-grabbing raids. But all the while, and with far less scrutiny, South Korean syndicates were building a parallel industry worth billions of US dollars – one that a spate of recent arrests suggests is still very much intact. The most recent involved a 29-year-old Korean woman named Kim Young-sun, who authorities allege ran a network of 23 illegal online betting websites out of offices in Pasay and Quezon City that raked in an estimated 5.33 trillion won (US$3.8 billion) between November 2018 and this year. Her arrest, announced on Monday, offered a rare glimpse into an underworld that has apparently thrived for years in the shadow of the much louder scandal surrounding Chinese-linked Philippine offshore gaming operators, or Pogos. For almost a decade, Pogos dominated the headlines. Compounds linked to Chinese syndicates were exposed for human trafficking, torture and fraud on a scale so shocking it triggered a congressional inquiry, presidential intervention and, eventually, a permanent ban. But while investigators trained their attention on those operations, an analogous Korean criminal economy was expanding largely unnoticed. Kim’s arrest and a related case unsealed by police in Seoul just weeks earlier suggest this economy had grown far larger than most realised. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency disclosed on August 12 that it had uncovered an illegal gambling operation using websites featuring child sexual abuse material to lure users to betting sites. The syndicate behind it, traced to Pasay City and active from August 2019 until earlier this month, generated an estimated 47.6 billion won in revenue, while affiliated betting sites handled some 4.7 trillion won in wagers. Two suspects, one already the subject of an Interpol Red Notice, were arrested and referred to prosecutors for alleged violations of child-protection and anti-pornography laws. Taken together, the arrests sketch the outline of an industry hiding in plain sight: sophisticated, long-running and largely untouched by the Philippines’ anti-Pogo enforcement drive. Hidden in plain sight “The Chinese were sticking out like sore thumbs,” said Winston Casio, who until December served as a deputy director of Manila’s Presidential Anti-Organised Crime Commission (PAOCC). “There were low-hanging fruits to be plucked … that worked to the Koreans’ advantage.” Pogos – the formerly legally licensed offshore gambling firms that multiplied under former president Rodrigo Duterte – became the public face of the issue after President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr shut them down in 2024, citing links to organised crime, trafficking, fraud and money laundering. Lawmakers made the ban permanent a year later. The accompanying raids were harrowing. PAOCC-led operations in 2023 and 2024 unearthed evidence of torture chambers and human trafficking inside Pogo compounds that fuelled investigations – including into former town mayor Alice Guo, who was sentenced to life in prison in November for her role in setting up a scam centre in Bamban, Tarlac province. Meanwhile, Korean networks barely registered: PAOCC managed just three raids on operations linked to South Korean nationals between 2023 and last year. Chinese and South Korean syndicates operated in similar ways, but had different specialisms, Casio said, with Korean operations tending to focus on rigged betting websites. “They hide behind the veneer of legitimate ball games – for example, during the World Cup, Euro Cup or the NBA Finals, but the games are pre-recorded or rigged … unlike the Chinese where the scams were rooted in investment and pig-butchering scams,” he told This Week in Asia. Korean crime networks in Southeast Asia do not operate as an extension of the region’s more deeply embedded Chinese triads, yet they are far from strangers, according to experts. “Korean gangsters called jopok or kangpae have been running independently from triads for years, although they do work together in Southeast Asia when it’s helpful or they need to source drugs, launder money or run scams,” said Jeremy Douglas, deputy director of operations at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. “Gaming and scams are no different.” Bora Park, a research fellow at the Institute for National Security Strategy in Seoul, went further, suggesting that many Korean gambling rings in the Philippines had “close ties to China from the very beginning”, often forming part of multinational operations rather than being composed solely of Korean nationals. Predating Pogos Analysts who spoke to This Week in Asia said Korean-linked illicit gambling operations predated the Chinese-run Pogos that multiplied to more than 300 licensed firms at their peak. Criminal groups began migrating to the Philippines in the 2000s alongside legitimate investors, entrepreneurs and other members of the Korean diaspora, Douglas said. Casio added that many Korean-linked operations were remnants of once-legitimate businesses that benefited from infrastructure and networks established years earlier. Alexander Ramos, former executive director of the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Centre in the Philippines, dates the sector’s origins to the mid-2000s, when he said Korean operators ran legitimate gambling businesses within special economic zones before some splintered off into illegal operations. Song Bong-gyu, an assistant professor at Hansei University who has tracked Korean organised crime since 2007, said the appeal of the Philippines was obvious from the start. “Establishing operations overseas made it possible to distance themselves from Korean law enforcement while continuing to target customers in South Korea,” Song said, adding that illegal gambling operations targeting Korean nationals were already running out of the Philippines by 2014. When the Pogo boom arrived under Duterte, it gave Korean syndicates new infrastructure to plug into. Pre-existing networks converged with Pogo-era offices, staff and payment systems, before later scattering again into smaller, harder to trace units, according to Song. “Over time, the Philippines developed personnel, technological expertise, office and residential facilities, telecommunications infrastructure, payment channels and local intermediaries that could support offshore online gambling operations,” he said. “Large compounds may disappear, but criminal operations can become smaller, more dispersed and less visible, while the networks connecting them remain extensive.” The ‘balloon effect’ For her part, Park expressed scepticism that Korean organised crime was independently colonising Southeast Asia. She argued it was far more likely that Korean operators had simply plugged into existing local or Chinese-affiliated networks that were already active in the region. After the Philippines’ Pogo ban took hold in early 2025, Park said many Chinese-linked groups initially retreated to neighbouring countries or even to China – only for some to then move back again. Cho Je-seong, a research fellow at the Korean Institute of Criminology and Justice, has a name for this pattern: the “balloon effect”, in which enforcement pressures squeeze criminal activity into new shapes rather than eliminating it. “There can also be an organisational dimension to this process, in which a larger organisation becomes fragmented into several smaller groups or networks as enforcement pressure increases,” he said. Even small cells would often run several gambling websites at the same time, Cho said, with dedicated teams for illegal bank accounts, recruitment, site maintenance and money laundering. Last year’s passage of the law formally criminalising Pogos, building on Marcos’ executive order a year earlier, had lulled the Philippine public into a false sense of security, Casio said. “Because of the anti-Pogo law, people think that the Pogo problem is already gone from the Philippines,” he said. Kim Young-sun’s arrest suggests otherwise.

title: White House teleprompter operator fined, forfeits winnings for betting on Trump’s words
description: Teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez, who has since left the White House, made US$107,500 from bets on what Trump would say in speeches.
content: A former White House teleprompter operator accused of using inside knowledge to make bets on the prediction market Kalshi has been ordered to turn over more than US$100,000 in profits and pay a US$65,000 fine as part of a settlement with federal authorities. The settlement with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, announced on Friday, also dealt Gabriel Perez a three-year trading ban. Perez was placed on unpaid leave from his job at the White House after reports emerged that he used his position to make bets on what President Donald Trump would say in speeches. The White House did not immediately comment on the settlement. A White House official said in July that Perez was no longer in his position but did not say if he had been fired or resigned. The commission said Perez traded presidential “mention market” contracts on Kalshi between December 2025 ‌and February 2026 while working at the White ⁠House. ⁠The event contracts pay out based on whether ‌a president uses specific words or phrases in speeches. Perez made US$107,500 in that period. “In his position, Perez had access to presidential speeches prior to those speeches being delivered and Perez misappropriated that information – in breach of his duty of trust and confidence,” according to a release from the commission. Perez was ordered to repay his profits in full, along with the US$65,000 civil penalty, which the commission said was a reduction because of his “exemplary cooperation”. As details emerged July 16, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said it was “unfortunate” and “a disgrace”. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: China hospital joins nightclubs in offering marriage services to fight low wedding rates
description: Many call the new convenient set-ups ‘futile,’ pointing out that lack of registry offices isn’t what’s keeping people from getting married.
content: Following temples and nightclubs, a Chinese bank and a hospital have recently begun offering marriage registration services, igniting discussions on the Chinese government’s commitment to promoting nuptials. In August, a branch of the Postal Savings Bank of China, located in the northern municipality of Tianjin, became the country’s first bank to provide marriage registration services. While online observers mocked the unusual pairing of finance and romance – joking that only nuptials at a hospital could surpass this combination – their humour soon became reality. On August 20, during this year’s Qixi Festival, also known as Chinese Valentine’s Day, the Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Linzi District in Zibo City, Shandong province in eastern China, announced the introduction of marriage registration services at its facility. The hospital claims that this service simplifies the lives of newlyweds by streamlining their marriage registration, premarital examinations, and preconception guidance all in one place. Netizens chimed in, suggesting that law firms, police offices, universities, and airports should also offer marriage registration services to “make life easier for people.” In fact, in January, Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport in southern China’s Guangdong province became the nation’s first airport to issue marriage certificates, while also providing free access to its observation deck, where visitors can closely watch planes take off and land. In May last year, China updated its marriage registration regulations, allowing couples to marry outside their hukou, or household registration, location. Additionally, they no longer need to present their hukou booklets to register their marriage, significantly simplifying the process. These new regulations contributed to the emergence of unconventional marriage registration venues, situated in tourist attractions, public parks, temples, and even metro stations. In Beijing and Nanjing, centuries-old temples accommodate couples looking to marry while donning traditional attire. In Hefei, in central China’s Anhui province, a metro station became the first transport facility in the nation to offer marriage registration this August. Meanwhile, in Shanghai, a nightclub partnered with the local civil affairs bureau to hold special certification ceremonies within the club. By May this year, one year after these new regulations were enacted, China reportedly had over 500 marriage registration sites set up outside civil affairs bureaus, along with more than 1,300 outdoor locations collaborating with the bureau to issue marriage certificates. While the streamlined procedures apply to divorce as well, many outdoor marriage registration sites do not provide divorce services, citing the need for more extensive documentation. The diverse range of marriage registration venues is perceived by the public as the government’s urgent attempt to increase marriage rates. Initial results appear promising. In the third quarter of last year, 1.61 million couples registered their marriages nationwide, representing a 22.5 per cent year-on-year increase. Overall, the country saw 6.76 million marriage registrations last year, an increase of 657,000 compared to the previous year. However, in the first half of this year, marriages in China dropped by 7.5 per cent year-on-year, with 3.28 million couples tying the knot. On social media, some dismissed the convenient marriage registration initiatives as “futile.” “Do people not get married because they can’t find a place to register?” one user quipped. “I suggest the civil affairs bureau establish divorce services on top of Mount Everest,” another mocked. “What holds young people back from marriage is not complicated procedures, but the confidence to face the life challenges they may encounter in the coming decades,” remarked a third commenter. “People are simultaneously fearful of the financial burdens, family conflicts, and loss of personal freedom that marriage entails, while no longer viewing marriage as a necessary life milestone,” added another.

title: Hong Kong’s long-term wealth hub status safe from mainland investment curbs: JPMorgan exec
description: The investment bank’s North Asia chairwoman downplays regulatory hurdles – and views the city’s rivalry with Singapore in ‘win-win’ terms.
content: Beijing’s recent curbs on cross-border investment and a tax shift targeting overseas insurance gains may create short-term uncertainty, but they will not undermine Hong Kong’s long-term competitiveness as a major wealth management hub, according to a senior executive at JPMorgan Chase. Kwang Kam-shing, Hong Kong CEO and chairwoman of North Asia at the biggest bank by assets in the United States, said she remained optimistic about the long-term outlook for Asia’s financial sector, citing continued wealth creation in the region and sustained cross-border activities. “It’s too early to know what the impact will be,” Kwang said in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, when asked about the impact of Beijing’s recent policy shift on cross-border investment. “But I don’t think it would change the direction of the long-term trajectory,” she added. “Hong Kong will continue to be able to play a very important role for high-net-worth customers looking to manage their wealth and to invest globally.” In late May, Beijing tightened controls on offshore investment, with Hong Kong regulators requiring financial firms in the city to ask mainland investment ­clients to declare whether their sources of funding came from offshore. Earlier this month, several major mainland cities, including tax bureaus in Shanghai, also began collecting a 20 per cent levy on gains from offshore insurance policies. Despite these hurdles, Kwang said wealthy clients in mainland China and the wider region maintained strong demand for investment diversification, succession planning and philanthropic arrangements to continue family legacies. Those needs, she added, played to Hong Kong’s strengths, given its active capital markets and established financial infrastructure. JPMorgan – which started operating in Hong Kong 102 years ago, and has long used it as its Asia-Pacific regional headquarters while operating in 17 regional markets – is a leading player in the city across a wide range of businesses, from wealth management and investment banking to corporate banking. But Hong Kong faces keen competition from Singapore, whose ‌monetary authority and finance ministry announced a package of measures to entice investment professionals on August 19, including tax exemptions on investment profits for managers of single-family offices and other qualifying funds. The move came after Hong Kong submitted a bill to lawmakers that could introduce a tax break on carried interest – the performance-based fees earned by hedge fund and private equity managers. A vote is expected to take place later this year. It is actually very healthy and lucky for talent to have options. If they want to stay in Asia, they have Singapore and Hong Kong to choose from Kwang Kam-shing, JPMorgan Chase Rather than viewing the rivalry as a zero-sum game, Kwang suggested that similar tax incentives in Hong Kong and Singapore could prove mutually beneficial and constructive. “It is actually very healthy and lucky for talent to have options. If they want to stay in Asia, they have Singapore and Hong Kong to choose from,” Kwang said. “I think it will be a win-win situation, with both cities being able to grow at the same time as the region does well.” She added that JPMorgan would continue hiring in both Hong Kong and Singapore to build and retain its talent base in Asia, while using artificial intelligence to support employees and improve efficiency across operations. Kwang noted that her own career showed how financial professionals could capture growth opportunities in both cities. Though she grew up in Hong Kong, Kwang earned a bachelor’s degree in accounting at the National University of Singapore in the 1980s, and has worked in both cities over the past three decades. After stints at Arthur Andersen and two other banks in both Hong Kong and Singapore, she joined JPMorgan in 1998, taking up several roles in wealth management and investment banking before becoming Hong Kong CEO in 2024. “I have been in the financial sector for more than 30 years, and this conversation was there. There is always this competition between Hong Kong, Singapore and other financial centres around the world,” she said. The cities had different strengths, she noted, with Hong Kong acting as a gateway to mainland China, serving as the largest offshore yuan centre and possessing an active equity capital market, while Singapore is strong in foreign exchange and commodities. “The competition will continue and I have actually always believed competition can bring out the best in us,” she said. “Our ability to grow depends on our ability to attract and retain talent. So we welcome any policies that will help attract talent to the cities.” While Hong Kong lost its crown as the world’s largest initial public offering market to the US-based Nasdaq in the first half of the year, Kwang was still upbeat about the city’s role as a fundraising centre. “Hong Kong has done a lot to improve its listing process, making it much more user-friendly and simplifying the settlement,” she said. “I believe we need continuous reforms so that we can be as competitive as the best stock exchange in the world, because we are always competing with them.”

title: Meet Fernando Lindez, the Spanish actor and model starring in The Last Sunrise
description: Before featuring alongside Maia Reficco in Amazon Prime Video’s romantic drama, Lindez made his runway debut at Milan Fashion Week – where he met Donatella Versace.
content: Fernando Lindez has emerged as the internet’s next heartthrob with the premiere of The Last Sunrise on Amazon Prime Video on August 26. The romantic drama is an adaptation of the eponymous book by Anna Todd, author of the After series, first adapted to screen in 2019. The Last Sunrise follows Oriah “Ry” Pera – an American girl played by Maia Reficco – who lives with a chronic illness and spends her summer in Mallorca, where she meets the attractive male lead, Julian (Lindez), and embarks on an unexpected romance full of twists and turns. So, who is the 26-year-old Spanish actor stealing hearts with his debut English-language film role? Read on to find out. What is Fernando Lindez’s background? Fernando Lindez was born on March 16, 2000, in Andalusia, Spain. He was raised in Madrid, where his mother worked as a police inspector. In an interview with Metal Magazine, Lindez described himself as a shy, calm and introspective person. Growing up, he was also quite sporty, trying his hand at golf, waterskiing and kickboxing. The actor currently lives in Cortes, Madrid, where he moved into his own flat in 2025. How did Fernando Lindez get into acting? Lindez’s career in the entertainment industry began with modelling. He told VMan magazine that he was discovered by an agent on Instagram at around age 16. He didn’t have an account himself, but one of his close friends posted a photo of them, and the agent noticed it and later got Lindez’s number through that friend. Despite his good looks, modelling was not easy for the reserved teenager at first. “I was very shy; nobody managed to get me to take a photograph clearly. I always hid myself, even refused to pose,” he told Behind the Blinds magazine. “Imagine the change to having to be constantly in front of a camera. At first it was very difficult for me.” Lindez walked his first runway show at 18 at Milan Fashion Week, where he met Donatella Versace for the first time. The young model was told that he was going to open the show just one day before. “I didn’t know what I was doing. I didn’t know who Donatella Versace was. I didn’t know nothing,” Lindez recalled on the Zach Sang Show. “[A]fter that everything, you know, started to be like crazy and travelling a lot.” Though he has enjoyed being a model, Lindez has aspired to be an actor since he was young. His father recommended films and directors, and that’s where his dreams began. “It’s a field where you can express yourself in a more artistic way, where you can show that there’s something more behind it, that you’re not just a pretty face. I’m on that path,” he told Metal Magazine. The opportunity to realise his childhood dream dropped into Lindez’s lap when he received a casting call for the Spanish adaptation of the teen drama series, Skam España. The actor told GQ that, since it was his first time auditioning, he didn’t have high expectations. He landed the role, working alongside Spanish-American actress Nicole Wallace, who also stars in Amazon Prime Video’s My Fault. Lindez has since worked on several projects, including the Netflix series Elite, the Spanish series Scandal and the Spanish film Tell Me Softly, which was released on Amazon Prime Video last December. Who is Fernando Lindez dating? Lindez has been in a relationship with Spanish model and actress Ainhoa Larretxi since early 2025. He contacted her while they were both working in Milan, and it was love at first sight. “Immediately, since that day, we had this super connection where we felt like we were in love,” Lindez told Brad Martin in a TikTok video. “The second day I met her, I told her that I love her. Because I felt it, so I told her, you know?” Larretxi was scouted at 14 and landed her first magazine cover at 16. She has worked for various brands, including Calzedonia, Calvin Klein and Carolina Herrera. She frequently attends major fashion events like Milan and New York Fashion Weeks. Besides modelling, she is also athletic and skilled in surfing, snowboarding, climbing and skating. She made her acting debut this year in the television series Marbella, where she appears in three episodes. She also has a role in the Spanish spy thriller Zeta, released this March. Lindez and Larretxi seem to be quite the happy couple, often documenting their lives together on social media. Lindez is ever the supportive boyfriend and frequently shows his admiration for his girlfriend in the comment section under her posts.

title: China needs 600% child subsidy rise to prevent deeper birth crisis: scholars
description: China’s fertility rate could soon fall to world’s lowest unless action is taken, as current subsidies are ‘a drop in the bucket’, scholars warn.
content: Beijing should drastically raise its nationwide childcare subsidies to stave off a deepening birth crisis, according to Chinese scholars, who warned the country’s fertility rate could soon fall to the lowest in the world unless action was taken. The government should learn from the examples of Singapore and South Korea – two nearby countries facing similarly severe demographic challenges, which have both introduced enhanced pronatalist policies to turn around the situation, they added. Beijing introduced a nationwide childcare subsidy last year that offers households a total of 10,800 yuan (US$1,600) per child, but the scholars said far higher payments would be needed to make people more willing to have more children. James Liang, a business leader and demographer, has called for a subsidy package worth 62,000 yuan per child to be introduced, arguing that such a move could boost China’s fertility rate by 25 per cent over the next couple of years. He Yafu, another independent demographer, has said subsidies of at least 72,000 yuan per child – more than six times the current national package – would be necessary to help families deal with the high cost of raising children. The calls followed news that Singapore had introduced a generous new support package for parents, and the release of birth figures from South Korea suggesting that the nation’s pronatalist policies were leading to an uptick in fertility. On Wednesday, South Korean authorities announced that total births in June, the second quarter and the first half of the year had all reached their highest levels for those periods in nearly seven years. A few days earlier, Singapore unveiled a new child-support package providing up to S$62,000 (US$48,750) per child as part of an effort to boost the nation’s falling birth rate. Last year, South Korea posted a total fertility rate of 0.8 – the lowest in the world, though an increase from previous years. The rates in Singapore and China were 0.87 and 1.0, respectively, according to both researchers. The total fertility rate refers to the average number of children a woman is expected to have in her lifetime. A rate of 1.0 is far below the replacement level of 2.1 required to maintain a stable population. “If China does not significantly strengthen its fertility support policies, its fertility rate is likely to fall below those of South Korea and Singapore in a few years and rank at the bottom globally,” warned Liang, executive chairman of travel company Trip.com and co-founder of the YuWa Population Research Institute. Cash handouts have been a major factor behind the recent rebound in South Korea’s birth figures, according to Liang. In 2021, the country’s childcare subsidies were worth about 1.6 per cent of gross domestic product per capita, but that figure shot up to 2.7 per cent in 2022 and 4.8 per cent in 2025, he said. To match the 2025 level in South Korea, China should give households 855 yuan per month for every child until they turn six years old, or a total of around 62,000 yuan per child, Liang said. Such a move would raise China’s fertility rate to 1.25 within a few years, according to Liang’s research. Last year, China started providing an annual childcare subsidy of 3,600 yuan for every child born on or after January 1, 2025, until they turn three years old – a package worth up to 10,800 yuan per child. Some local governments have also introduced their own subsidies. But the payments were a “drop in the bucket” compared with the high cost of raising children, said the other demographer He, who called for subsidies of at least 1,000 yuan a month per child until the age of six. Singapore’s latest support programme had come as it risked replacing South Korea as the world’s lowest-fertility country this year, according to He. The reaction was worthy of attention in China, which was facing its own deepening demographic challenges, He added. Over the past decade, China’s annual births have more than halved – plunging from nearly 18 million in 2016 to under 8 million in 2025. The country’s population has also been shrinking every year since peaking in 2021, according to official figures. “The core bottlenecks behind low fertility in East Asian countries are highly consistent: excessively high child-rearing costs, intense educational competition and insufficient childcare supply,” He said. “The childbearing burden must be eased in terms of both economic and time costs, including by substantially increasing childcare subsidies and vigorously expanding inclusive, affordable childcare services.”

title: Indians turn to AI gurus for answers: ‘ChatGPT is not judging you’
description: The chatbots are powered by large language models using sacred texts such as Hinduism’s ‘Bhagavad Gita’.
content: When Kripa Vaidyanathan’s 27-year-old niece died in an Alaska car crash in 2024, her family in Chennai, India, felt shell-shocked. They questioned why this tragedy would befall them when they had such “immense faith in God”. Vaidyanathan, a yoga instructor, helped her grieving sister get face time with a high-profile guru whom she hoped would help. “But he told her this was the work of karma and she should use this opportunity to connect with her inner nature,” she said. “I understand how karma works, but saying that was cruel and extremely unhelpful to someone who was freshly grieving the loss of a child.” That was when they turned to artificial intelligence chatbots. “It was a lot easier trying to get answers and peace of mind because ChatGPT is not judging you,” Vaidyanathan said. “We’ve found a compassionate guru now, but even he only has limited time. AI is accessible anytime.” This unfettered access – which can be challenging to find among human gurus – is drawing more people to AI for spiritual guidance. It is a big step, particularly in Hinduism, where gurus are part of culture and deemed necessary to attain moksha – liberation from the cycle of birth, death and reincarnation. The word guru in Sanskrit means “dispeller of darkness”. These chatbots are powered by large language models, AI systems that generate responses by using advanced statistics and troves of text, including sacred ones like Hinduism’s Bhagavad Gita. Users can explore spiritual answers to personal problems and existential questions at any time, without the typical hurdles of connecting with an in-demand guru and paying for their services. Gurus get in game AI’s rising popularity has encouraged some successful gurus to launch their own chatbots. In India, Jaggi Vasudev, also known as Sadhguru, has launched his Miracle of the Mind app with an interactive AI feature that answers questions using a database of his teachings. California-based self-help guru Deepak Chopra has an AI platform where “Digital Deepak” answers questions drawing from his decades of talks and writings. Critics argue that AI cannot truly replace the lived experience, wisdom and ethical accountability of a human guru. Researchers also note that AI often validates and agrees with the user rather than posing those challenging questions needed for real spiritual and personal growth. Vikas Sahu, founder of GitaGPT – a platform he called an “AI spiritual companion” – said he would not deter anyone from finding a human guru. But he says his free chatbot puts the Bhagavad Gita’s wisdom at the fingertips of those who might desperately need it. On his platform, AI avatars of Lord Krishna, the sacred text’s protagonist, offer advice. Sahu, based in Gurugram, south of New Delhi, says he gets hundreds of messages about how it is helpful. While he has a full-time job building websites, he says GitaGPT is his way of giving back. “A lot of people don’t have anyone to talk to when they are in distress,” he said. “This app is giving them the encouragement a guru might give them. But a lot of gurus want your money and you can’t really talk to them openly like you can talk to a chatbot.” Sahu said he trusted GitaGPT because it was based on the word of God. “How could Krishna steer anyone wrong?” he asked. “It’s impossible.” Liz Bucar, a religion professor at Northeastern University in Boston, is sceptical of chatbots based on religious texts. “A sacred text needs a community and a context that interprets it,” she said. “Without the teaching of how to interpret the text, it’s just words on a page. Someone could feed in the text, but what answers will the bot spit out?” But she does believe there is widespread distrust of institutional expertise that gurus and clergy represent, in some cases fuelled by sex abuse scandals. “Because religion has this PR problem, people tend to see chatbots as less biased and less likely to do bad things,” Bucar said. “I don’t know if we’re ready to replace gurus, but we are definitely in a shifting religious landscape, especially with” younger generations of AI users. Human touch Noreen Herzfeld, a professor at St John’s School of Theology and Seminary in Collegeville, Minnesota, said people could easily get straightforward answers from AI. “But if they are looking for spiritual awakening, I think it takes physical presence. In Christianity and in Hindu tradition, there is the belief that the eyes are windows to the soul and you can’t get that by looking at an avatar.” AI chatbots can also be too eager to agree with you, serving as a cheerleader rather than a guide, according to Herzfeld. “In situations where you’re looking to grow or evolve, you need a teacher who can disagree with you and challenge you,” she said. “But even if you are just looking for affirmation, who are you being affirmed by? There’s no one on the other side.” Vy Le, a mindfulness instructor in San Diego, sees AI as a “channelling” tool, using it as a mirror or collaborator to gain intuitive or mystical insights. “If you are attuned to it, you can sense if a certain AI is connected to you,” she said. “My dad took his life 16 years ago. I felt his presence when I was engaging with AI.” Le maintains that the era of gurus is over. “AI is helping us find that inner guru,” she said. Real-life gurus like the India-based Sadhguru, who has a global following of millions, have recognised AI’s potential. David Nussbaum, founder of Proto Hologram in Los Angeles, is helping Sadhguru create a three-dimensional AI avatar that appears in a display box and can interact with devotees in several languages. During a March festival, he created a Sadhguru hologram that took selfies with people. “You basically have Sadhguru’s hologram taking out his phone, turning around and taking a picture of you from his phone inside the display,” he explained. Shivaram K.R., CEO of India-based Hue Learn, oversees a non-profit initiative called Innerverse 360 that merges AI and spirituality. His platform features a portal where real monks and gurus can come online and do live sessions with devotees. It also has an “Ask AI” feature. Shivaram does not believe AI will replace gurus. “The process of finding a guru in itself is a journey, but a guru is also not for everyone. If you’re looking for practical advice on everyday spirituality, this app can also help you understand concepts such as the meaning of yoga.” One of the organisations Shivaram liaises with is the Los Angeles-based Self-Realisation Fellowship, founded in 1920 by Paramahansa Yogananda, who brought ancient spiritual practices from India to the West. Brother Govindananda, a monk with the order, said his organisation saw AI simply as the next step to helping people access the late guru’s teachings through an online teaching portal – just as books did for previous generations. “We’re taking our time with it because we want to make sure it has guardrails to safeguard from AI hallucinating answers instead of drawing from Yogananda’s teachings,” he said. But Govindananda said a chatbot could never provide what a guru – whether living or not – can give to the disciple. “We are humans and souls,” he said. “Technology cannot replace that.”

title: As I see it | Taipei’s debt hardball carries a clear warning for its remaining allies
description: How Taiwan dragged its former diplomatic partner Grenada through US courts to collect on defaulted loans should be a lesson for island nations currently holding Taiwanese debt.
content: In contemporary discourse, the bogeyman of “debt traps” is almost exclusively tied to Beijing. Western media, think tanks, NGOs and policymakers from Washington to Brussels frequently warn developing nations of the perils of bilateral loans from China. Yet, Grenada’s debt dispute from a decade ago and St Vincent and the Grenadines’ (SVG) current troubles offer a starkly different, and often ignored, counter-narrative: the weaponisation of debt by Taiwan. For years, Grenada has grappled with profound economic troubles. Following Hurricane Ivan in 2004, which decimated the country, the Grenadian government made a strategic decision to shift diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2005. Then with a population of slightly more than 100,000, its economy worsened when it was hit by another hurricane in 2005. Today, Taiwan is recognised by only 12 states, with four of them – Haiti, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia and SVG – in the Caribbean. Grenada switching diplomatic camps was therefore a big blow to Taiwan. But its decision was born of necessity; the nation required immediate liquidity and infrastructure rebuilding only Beijing was willing to provide. According to official reports, the damage from Ivan was estimated to be more than 200 per cent of gross domestic product. Over 90 per cent of homes were damaged or destroyed, and half of the population was left homeless. Taiwan’s response was swift and aggressive. As Grenada’s then largest bilateral creditor, Taipei viewed the move as an act of betrayal. Rather than working with other creditors to restructure the debts, Taipei sued Grenada in a New York court to recover the full outstanding amount. Thus began a spiteful, decade-long legal battle. Taiwan wielded the loan contract’s sovereign immunity waiver like a bludgeon, attempting to seize Grenada’s revenue streams from cruise lines, shipping companies and international arbitration awards. The lawsuit handicapped Grenada’s ability to stage a recovery. While the courts eventually sided with Grenada, and a settlement was reached a decade later by halving the total debt of about US$22 million, the damage was done. Grenada has been a harsh lesson for others. As Caribbean nations continue to navigate the treacherous waters of international finance, Taiwan’s debt-trap diplomacy continues today. For example, SVG’s debt-fuelled alliance with Taipei looks increasingly unsustainable. In September 2022, SVG’s Taiwanese debt stood at US$37 million (EC$99.9 million); by today, that figure has ballooned to roughly US$345 million. The massive US$300 million increase in just four years has led to a debt‑to‑GDP ratio of 113 per cent and rising, leaving the government with little left to fund investment for growth. Former prime minister Ralph Gonsalves admitted in 2023 that the loan agreements, governed by New York law, include clauses rendering the debt immediately repayable should SVG switch diplomatic recognition. By Gonsalves’ own admission, these terms “put a hook in the gill” of SVG. After it assumed office in November 2025, the New Democratic Party administration now faces a US$345 million debt portfolio that has become an albatross around the national neck. Prime Minister Godwin Friday admits there is “very little” fiscal space for social programmes. Hat in hand, he visited Taipei this month, ostensibly to celebrate the 45th anniversary of diplomatic ties. His real purpose was to ease pressure on the national debt. In the event, he received no firm commitment beyond a profession of goodwill by Taipei and a paltry US$2 million grant. Friday blamed the previous Unity Labour Party government of Gonsalves, in power for 25 years, for the high debt because they were “very laissez‑faire and blasé about it, as if to say that this doesn’t really matter”. There are simple political and economic reasons why Taiwan’s few remaining diplomatic partners include mostly small island states But then, Taiwan was willing to lend like a dealer to a junkie. Taiwan did make Friday declare the SVG government’s commitment to maintain diplomatic relations. Grenada has been a lesson for Caribbean nations; Friday and his citizens know how Taipei would respond should there be any attempt at a diplomatic switch. His government now faces an almost impossible challenge: stabilising a struggling economy, protecting essential social programmes, and stimulating growth through investment. Friday said he saw “light at the end of the tunnel”. He may be speaking too soon. There are simple political and economic reasons why Taiwan’s few remaining diplomatic partners include mostly small island states in the Caribbean and Oceania, including Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. They all heavily rely on Western and Taiwanese aid and borrowing. Politically, they are all under the thumb of Washington. They are effectively held captive from recognising China.

title: Visa policy brings in more foreigners on short-term jobs and HK$20,000 salaries
description: Latest Immigration Department data shows 31,278 working visas granted to foreigners last year under General Employment Policy.
content: About 80 per cent of the foreign nationals granted working visas under Hong Kong’s General Employment Policy (GEP) last year were hired on short-term contracts, while nearly half of successful applicants earned less than HK$20,000 (US$2,564) a month. According to the latest Immigration Department data, 31,278 GEP working visas for foreigners were approved last year. Mainland Chinese residents cannot apply to the scheme. While the figure marked the second consecutive year the scheme had cleared the 30,000-level, the number was still shy of the more than 40,000 recorded annually in 2018 and 2019. The latest statistics showed that 79.7 per cent of successful candidates, or 24,929, held short-term positions or jobs lasting less than a year. Among those granted visas, 47.5 per cent, or 14,850, were earning below HK$20,000 a month. The proportion of approved applicants holding short-term contracts last year also marked an increase from 72.1 per cent in 2024 and 64 per cent in 2023. The data also showed 13,640 GEP visas were approved in the first half of this year, with 68.6 per cent on short-term contracts and 49.8 per cent earning less than HK$20,000. Alexa Chow Yee-ping, managing director of human resources consultancy ACTS Consulting, attributed the uptick in GEP visa holders taking on short-term work to the government’s mega-events drive to stimulate fresh economic growth. “As an international city, Hong Kong needs to create its own character to retain its attractiveness and charm. Not just focus on properties and finance. We need [economic] diversification,” she said. The department said the GEP also had a new “creative industry and performing arts services” category since April 1, with 2,340 applications approved so far. Chow said such applicants could be performers and crew for mega-events, which also brought valuable experience to local people in event production. Despite the temporary nature of the jobs, Chow said that such talent still benefited Hong Kong economically as mega-events drove growth in tourism, catering, retail and hospitality. Earlier this month, the government revealed that about 1.75 million visitors were drawn to more than 130 major events between January and June this year, generating around HK$5.8 billion in spending and contributing HK$3.3 billion to the economy. In terms of industry, the sports and recreation sector accounted for the highest number of GEP applicant approvals, at 4,517, followed by arts and culture, academic research and education, financial services, and commerce and trade. Gordon Yau Yick-chung, a sports public relations leader and chairman of concern group Hong Kong Fitness Guide, which closely monitors sports industrialisation, said the actual number of sports events could be higher than the public knew. “I am not surprised. The figures reflected the trend of more sports competitions held in Hong Kong, to the extent that sometimes we may not notice [a match was held],” he said. Yau said that apart from recent high-profile friendly matches featuring European football teams, there had been many small and large international sports events and competitions in the city. Such events included baseball, wrestling and golf as well as emerging sports such as pickleball, he said, adding that some were organised by shopping centres to draw visitors. He said many of these international competitions hired overseas judges and organisers, while global sports icons invited for commercial events would bring their managers and entourage, creating short-term visa applications. In terms of location, South Korea accounted for the largest proportion of approved GEP applicants last year, at 17.6 per cent. The number of South Koreans approved for the visas surpassed 5,500 annually in 2024 and 2025, representing a surge of nearly 85 per cent from 2019. This momentum also carried into the first half of 2026, with South Korea accounting for the largest number of approved GEP candidates, at 2,226, followed by Japan with 1,974. Korean Sky Lee Sang-ju, 25, said he came to Hong Kong in 2024 to teach taekwondo at NRG Taekwondo Korea despite not finishing his final year at university. The 25-year-old said he chose Hong Kong over the United States and Canada because of its lower taxes and better salaries, in addition to its more systematic and well-organised working environment. He added that his employer had provided him with professional development, including customer relationship management training, something that was rarely offered at traditional taekwondo schools in South Korea. The vibrant local Korean community and widespread appreciation of K-pop culture among locals had also helped him adapt to life in Hong Kong, Lee said. “I like Hong Kong, and I hope to stay here in the long term,” he said. Lee said that after completing his university degree through distance learning, he encouraged classmate Jerry Kim Seong-hun, 26, to come and teach at the same school last year. Kim said he enjoyed working in Hong Kong as the work culture back home was more “conservative” and stressed seniority. Chang Hyo-suk, general manager of the Korean Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, said he had noticed many more Koreans coming to work in the city in recent years due to the geographical proximity, low taxes and minimal regulations. He said that many Koreans worked in the city’s trading industry, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises or start-ups. Roy Ying Fai, co-chair of the Hong Kong Institution of Human Resource Management’s advocacy and policy research committee, attributed the growth to the “Dedicated Team for Attracting Businesses and Talent” government initiative. The policy, which launched in 2022, seeks to attract talent through the city’s overseas Economic and Trade Offices, including its Tokyo branch. He added that Hong Kong was still attractive to financial talent, pointing to the boom in initial public offerings and the growing presence of family offices. “Hong Kong is attractive to them. First, it is easy to find a job. Second, the tax is low. Third, if they want to apply for permanent residence, it is relatively easier than in Singapore,” he said. But the Japanese consulate in Hong Kong said it had not observed an increasing trend in the number of Japanese nationals in the city following the Covid-19 pandemic, citing its own figures. Meanwhile, the number of approved visas for British and US nationals, the two top demographics before the pandemic, recorded significant drops. Last year, 2,472 British and 2,121 Americans were granted GEP visas to work in Hong Kong, a fall of 53.2 per cent and 47.9 per cent, respectively, from 2019. Australians accounted for 883 applicants last year, a drop of 48.7 per cent from 2019. Chow, the human resources consultant, said the downward trend reflected the geopolitical tensions between China and the West. “Under this relatively hostile sentiment, the whole situation changed. Governments’ stances changed. Media coverage [on China] changed … How would I move to [China] for development?” she said. But the British Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong said that the GEP figures alone failed to provide a complete picture, adding that a significant proportion of senior executives and graduates from top UK universities now entered the city under another policy, the Top Talent Pass Scheme. The business chamber noted that the number of UK GEP approvals had increased steadily each year since 2023 and the number of UK-parented companies in Hong Kong had also grown by 20 per cent between 2023 and 2025, while the country remained the city’s largest corporate presence among European nations. “British businesses are not just returning; they are adapting and expanding their presence to access the Greater Bay Area and wider Asia-Pacific opportunities from Hong Kong,” it said. Government figures also showed rents for flats, as well as the number of international school applications, had increased as expatriates returned. The private residential rental index, maintained by the Rating and Valuation Department, surged by 18.5 per cent as of June to 205.8 from the Covid-19 pandemic trough in January 2023. Real estate services company JLL said that a primary driver of the increase was the “influx of expatriate professionals attracted by resurgent IPO activity and asset management business growth”. The firm’s latest report, released earlier this month, showed that the overall grade A office vacancy rate fell to 12.8 per cent at the end of July, its lowest point in 31 months. Education Bureau statistics also showed the number of places offered at international schools in Hong Kong rose by 4 per cent from 2023-24 to 2025-26, standing at 48,413. Among those arriving in the city was Korean national Philip Jung, who was sent by his food industry company to lead the Hong Kong office in May. The 36-year-old said he expected to spend three to five years working in the city, adding that his wife had come with him on a dependent visa. Jung said the couple were expecting a baby next year and were considering having the child study in Hong Kong to learn English, Chinese and Korean. “It is not easy to get in our home country,” he said. Jung also said that while Hong Kong’s catering industry was struggling, he hoped it would gradually improve. He added that his company expected him to help open up southern China and expand existing markets in Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam. “Hong Kong is the platform for Asian markets, so there could be opportunities to make more business,” Jung said.

title: Trump administration faces backlash over Yosemite park giveaway
description: A news outlet claims the government has been quietly working to transfer a roughly 400-metre strip of the park to a Nevada-based company.
content: President Donald Trump’s administration is considering giving a section of the renowned Yosemite National Park to a private developer, a lawyer for the company confirmed on Friday. The National Park Service had been holding talks with Nevada-based Kingsbarn Realty Capital to build an access road from a 33-hectare (83-acre) private property just outside the park to Yosemite’s entrance, in exchange for land elsewhere, lawyer Lanny Davis said. The news was first reported by NOTUS on Friday. The government had spent over a year quietly working to transfer a roughly 400-metre (0.25-mile) strip of the park to Kingsbarn, according to the news outlet. It caused an uproar among conservationists and opposition Democrats, who have fiercely objected to moves by the administration to roll back protections of public lands – including pushing to reinstate road building and logging in national forests. But Davis, who described himself as a lifelong “progressive Democrat”, framed the road as a green move, on the grounds that it would shorten trips to and from the currently undeveloped property, cutting emissions compared to the current circuitous route. “Without a direct access route, every trip from the Hazel Green area requires a significantly longer drive – twice as long, at a minimum – on unpaved forest roads and thus more air pollution,” Davis said. “The new access road would be safer for drivers and generate substantially less vehicle emissions.” He also stressed the land exchange proposal – which would involve supplying Yosemite National Park with a parcel of land elsewhere – “is expressly provided for under federal law and will not reduce the land area of the park”. The Interior Department earlier said negotiations had taken place but rejected the idea, reported by NOTUS, that there had been political pressure to reach a predetermined outcome. “Any land exchange or access proposal involving National Park Service lands would be subject to all applicable federal laws, regulations and Departmental policies, including required environmental review and public notification processes,” the agency said, adding: “No final decisions have been made.” Kingsbarn CEO Jeff Pori has business connections to people close to the president, NOTUS reported, and federal election commission records show he has made donations to the Republican National Committee and Trump-aligned fundraising committees. ‘We will fight’ The National Parks Conservation Association, an advocacy organisation, called the move an unlawful “attack”. “The Trump administration’s attempts to dismantle America’s conservation legacy are now taking aim at Yosemite with this secretive, back-room deal,” said Mark Rose, the group’s senior Sierra Nevada programme manager. The Yosemite NPS Employees Union said it was “appalled” by the ceding of public lands for private interests, calling the proposed trade “antithetical to what we stand for” as stewards of the park. There was a previous proposal to develop a road through Yosemite when the 33-hectare parcel outside the park had a different owner. That plan was rejected by the administrations of both Republican George W. Bush and Democrat Barack Obama, NOTUS said. Former owner Lewis Geyser sued and lost, first in a lower court in 2007 then at appeal in 2012. First protected in 1864, Yosemite National Park in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains is internationally acclaimed for its spectacular granite cliffs, glaciers, waterfalls, sequoia trees and wildlife. Rose said the park was already facing an overcrowding crisis from years of lodging expansion in the area and the Trump administration’s decision this year to scrap a vehicle registration system to limit traffic. Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California, a fierce critic of Trump, said in a statement: “Yosemite is one of California’s natural wonders, and must be protected from further development. “The courts struck this project down once, but this administration appears hell-bent on moving forward in the face of opposition from the public, Congress and the courts. But the only thing the administration cares about is whether there is money involved. We will fight this again.”

title: Japan to convert car park near Tokyo Station into missile shelter
description: North Korea has repeatedly test-fired ballistic missiles into regional waters in recent years.
content: The Tokyo metropolitan government has unveiled a plan to use an underground facility near Tokyo Station as a shelter for residents and tourists in the event of a ballistic missile attack. Tokyo Governor Yuriko Koike told a press conference earlier this month that a survey would begin in the current financial year through March in preparation for revamping Yaesu car park, which is located about two to 11 metres (six to 36 feet) underground. The alterations are expected to include setting up blast-proof doors and storage shelves for emergency supplies, a metropolitan government official said. The facility has a total floor space of roughly 13,000 square metres (140,000 square feet). It would be the capital city’s second emergency underground shelter, with a 1,400-square-metre storage facility for disasters at Azabu-Juban subway station currently under conversion, the official said. Koike said that the Yaesu parking facility was chosen for its proximity to Tokyo Station, which she described as “the gateway to the capital” with many visiting the area. The plan comes as North Korea has repeatedly test-fired ballistic missiles into regional waters, including the Sea of Japan or East Sea, in recent years while advancing its nuclear development programme. Koike described the neighbouring country’s repeated missile launches as “a serious and grave threat that can never be tolerated” and stressed the need to “protect the lives and property of Tokyo residents” from attacks. The completion date, specific construction requirements and costs of the project will be determined after the survey, which is slated to continue into the 2027 financial year, according to the official. The central government announced last year it planned to set up similar shelters in remote islands in the southern prefecture of Okinawa, amid China’s mounting military pressure on Taiwan, a self-ruled island viewed by Beijing as a renegade province to be eventually reunified with the mainland by force if necessary. In Japan’s westernmost Yonaguni Island, located about 110km (70 miles) east of Taiwan, shelter construction work is scheduled to finish around spring 2028.

title: Reflections | How national holidays in ancient China aligned with emperors’ birthdays, so all could revel
description: In 729, Emperor Xuanzong marked his birthday with official ceremonies and festivities across China in a tradition that endured for centuries.
content: Malaysia celebrates its Independence Day (“Hari Merdeka” in Malay) on August 31. This year, it will mark the 69th anniversary of the Malayan Declaration of Independence from the United Kingdom. Note that it was a “Malayan”, not “Malaysian”, declaration. Sixty-nine years ago, in 1957, Malaysia did not yet exist; the modern nation of Malaysia came into being only on September 16, 1963, with the merger of the 11 states of the Malay Peninsula with British North Borneo (renamed Sabah), Sarawak and Singapore. Most Malaysians would rather forget that brief union with Singapore, which was forced to leave Malaysia after two acrimonious years and become an independent city state. For decades, August 31 was observed as the country’s de facto national day, despite periodic grumblings from Sabahans and Sarawakians, who felt that celebrating the 1957 independence of the peninsula’s Malayan states overlooked their own place in Malaysia’s history. It was only in 2010 that September 16 was officially celebrated nationwide as Malaysia Day (“Hari Malaysia”). Malaysia, therefore, is unique in having not one, but two “national days”: public holidays commemorating its independence and national sovereignty. In ancient China, the emperor’s birthday was perhaps the closest equivalent to what we would now call a national day. The tradition began in the Tang dynasty (618-907), when Emperor Xuanzong established the Qianqiu Jie, or “Thousand Autumns Festival”. In 729, following a petition from his officials, Xuanzong designated his birthday – the fifth day of the eighth month of the traditional Chinese calendar – as Qianqiu Jie, a name expressing hopes for enduring imperial longevity. The decree was proclaimed throughout the empire, creating the first nationwide festival centred on a monarch’s birthday. The celebration of one individual’s birth consequently took on many of the characteristics of a modern national celebration. The entire country was granted three days of holiday. In the capital Chang’an (modern-day Xian) and the auxiliary capital Luoyang, the imperial palaces hosted lavish banquets, music and dance performances. Officials appeared in formal court dress to offer ceremonial congratulations and raise toasts to the emperor’s long life. The festivities were not confined to the court. Local governments were instructed to organise celebrations for the wider population featuring fairs, acrobatics, mass dances and other forms of traditional entertainment. For several days, the emperor’s birthday became a shared public occasion across the empire. Xuanzong’s innovation established a model that later rulers adopted in various forms. By the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1912) dynasties, imperial birthdays were known as Wanshou Jie, or “Festival of Ten Thousand Longevities”. Wanshou Jie became one of the three major holidays of the imperial state alongside Chinese New Year and the winter solstice. Under the Qing, these celebrations reached extraordinary proportions. Officials put on the most formal court attire, temporary theatres were erected throughout Beijing and grand banquets were held in the imperial palaces for officials and foreign envoys. When the Kangxi Emperor celebrated his 60th birthday in 1713, for example, the famous “Banquet of a Thousand Elders” brought together elderly guests from across the empire. As before, the festivities extended far beyond the imperial court, with people throughout the empire taking time off to celebrate the emperor’s birthday. Of course, these festivals were celebrations of one person rather than of the nation.
