Yet they possessed many of the features we associate with a modern national holiday: a legally recognised public holiday, nationwide festivities, elaborate official ceremonies and participation extending throughout society. Malaysia’s dual national days make the country an interesting starting point for thinking about how nations choose to mark important dates. The answer is not always as straightforward as it might seem: sometimes the date celebrates independence from foreign colonisers, sometimes the creation of the country itself, and in imperial China, it was simply the emperor’s birthday.

title: Henrik Stenson’s place in golf history secure, but knows LIV Golf will merit a mention
description: The much-accomplished Swede, who will chase his first Macau Open in October, says the breakaway league did at least help shake up the sport.
content: Major winner, Olympic silver medallist, Ryder Cup star and briefly captain, and latterly LIV golfer, Henrik Stenson’s decades in the game come with the sort of CV that merits hall of fame discussion. Like everyone, the Swede wonders what he will be most remembered for, and while his association with the Saudi-backed team competition will be a significant part of that legacy, there is a hope it will not be a defining one. That might be wishful thinking. As a former co-captain of the Majesticks GC team, Stenson will forever be asked his opinions on the league, its future and how it too will be judged when the history of this era of the game is written. Stenson described the past several years as “turbulent”, although he acknowledged any view depended “on what lens you look through”. Even so, the changes made by the PGA Tour, DP World Tour and the growth of the Asian Tour might all be said to have been a direct result of LIV's emergence. “I know LIV has been very popular in many parts of the world,” he told the South China Morning Post. “It’s brought top-class golf to areas that have been starved of that and had huge receptions and success. “It’s definitely changed the game. I can fully understand that some of the golf fans felt like it got split up, and some of their favourite players went left, and some of the players went right, and they didn’t get to see everyone compete and so on. “I don’t have the answers to what’s going to happen next. I will follow it like everyone else, but it was certainly a shake-up, and shake-up comes with good things and some bad things.” Before the loss of funding, staff jobs and the expectation that any LIV 2.0 will be a shadow of its former self, the league was scheduled to return to Hong Kong Golf Club in 2027 for a fourth time. Sources in the city said there had been no substantive discussion yet as to whether February’s tournament will go ahead as planned, although scepticism was the overriding feeling among those in the know. A tie for 50th at Fanling last year was indicative of Stenson’s final season with LIV, and ended a Majesticks career that did not mirror what had gone before. Whichever tour he has been a member of, the 50-year-old has played, competed and won almost everywhere in the world, except, as it turns out, Macau, something he will put right playing-wise when the Asian Tour rolls into town in October. Having served his penance for having been allowed to return to the PGA Tour and DP World Tour, Stenson is slowly getting back into the swing of things. A senior PGA Champions Tour start in Detroit this week in the Ally Challenge followed a missed cut in the Danish Golf Championship, his first DPWT event since January 2023. The SJM Macau Open will be another step on that road to returning to full-time golf and the chance to “shake off some rust”. “There is definitely some work to do to get into good form, and also keeping in mind that when I went on that break, it wasn’t like I was playing my best golf by any means at that time,” Stenson said. “So, I’m kind of realistic and knowing that we need to do some work, and it might take a while to get into good form, but I still feel like I’ve got good potential and a good game when I’m doing the right thing.” Any wins from now will only add to the already impressive CV, but asked how history might judge a career that includes 22 professional victories, and the 2016 Open champion points to an eponymous foundation that works with disabled golfers and junior players, and the fact “I really try to give back”. “I spent a lot of time and effort in doing that, and golf is a great game in that sense,” Stenson said. “I think it’s probably one of the best, if not the best, sports in giving back to charities to different initiatives all around the world. “That doesn’t matter if you’re playing on LIV, you’re playing on PGA Tour, on the DP World Tour. So, we [players] are all great at giving back, I think that’s the thing. We should all take pride in that and be remembered for it.” The phrase “growing the game” became synonymous with the start of the LIV experiment. Taken at face value, it backs Stenson’s belief that golf’s community work is unrivalled, though others might take issue with that. “We do a lot to promote the game outside of competing, and we all made different choices on where we saw opportunities and where we wanted to play on different tours,” he said, before adding that “we all did what we felt was right at the time and tried our best”.

title: Inside Thailand’s bid to wire the world’s AI revolution
description: Malaysia has the chips. Vietnam has the assembly lines. But Thailand’s humble circuit boards help keep the AI boom alive.
content: In the rush to build an AI future, semiconductors are the silicon rock stars that soak up all the applause. Yet behind the curtain, an unglamorous stagehand is doing much of the heavy lifting. Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the copper-laced panels inside every mobile phone, car key fob, digital camera and data-centre server rack on Earth. Without them, even the most advanced AI chip would be useless, unable to process even a single line of code. This year alone, more than 1 million square metres (10.8 million sq ft) of PCBs will roll out of WellTek Electronics’ factory in Ayutthaya – just one company’s contribution to Thailand’s scramble for an edge in the global tech supply chain. “They are essential to our daily life. They are in all electronics you are using,” said WellTek founder Jennifer Deng, who established the Thai subsidiary of her China-based Jiangxi Welgao Electronics in Ayutthaya two years ago. Thailand is now Southeast Asia’s No 1 producer of PCBs – often described as the nervous system of modern electronics, channelling essential signals through increasingly complex arrays of semiconductors, resistors and capacitors – and the fifth largest in the world. Deng’s US$75 million WellTek plant, built in under a year, is the first of two planned for Ayutthaya, a major Thai industrial zone once dominated by Japanese carmakers and global electronics giants, now being rewired for the artificial intelligence age. Circuitous success Malaysia may lead the field in lucrative semiconductors and Vietnam in electronics assembly, but PCBs give Thailand its competitive advantage in Southeast Asia’s race for tech relevance. Its rise in this niche owes as much to the trade wars triggered by Washington as it does to the smart timing of Thai authorities in welcoming global companies seeking new bases away from the tariff line of fire. “The market demanded movement to Thailand,” Deng told This Week in Asia from WellTek’s Ayutthaya headquarters, where workers in crisp company polo shirts hustled down corridors beneath posters bearing the mantra “Conscience and Altruism”. Over the next few years, Deng not only wants to build a second factory but treble output to more than 3.6 million square metres (38.8 million sq ft) of PCBs per year. Thailand’s existing PCB industry gave it a head start over rivals, she said, explaining that “Europeans and Americans all requested we are outside of China, and our main partners are here in Thailand.” Narit Therdsteerasukdi, secretary general of Thailand’s government-run Board of Investment, told an investor forum on Wednesday that the country was at a “turning point”. Investment in the PCB and electronics component sector topped US$10 billion over the past three years, he revealed, calling this proof of how Thailand should pivot its economy. “We need to restructure our economy … and the electronic industry, especially PCBs, is a very good example [of how to do it],” he said. “The key question is where do we go from here?” For Narit, the country’s future growth depends on climbing the value chain, backed by a higher-skilled workforce trained for the AI age. Printed fortunes PCBs are a rare success story in a decade of patchy industrial policy that has left Thailand a regional growth laggard. Many of the ideas floated to accelerate growth through new manufacturing chains and a splurge of foreign investment have been delayed, watered down or scrapped entirely on contact with the reality of delivering big infrastructure projects in a politically febrile kingdom. Trade dispute and fuel-price spikes from distant wars have further hurt an economy that expanded just 2.4 per cent last year – a relative crawl compared with Vietnam’s 8 per cent. Yet around 60 per cent of all new investment into Southeast Asia’s PCB industry has flowed into Thailand since 2023, according to the Thailand Printed Circuit Association. Phutana Daoruang, the association’s general manager, said Thailand already had the PCB infrastructure, built up by a dozen or so Taiwanese firms, when Donald Trump’s first presidency fired the starting gun on companies fleeing US tariffs. Thailand’s location and logistics networks, tax breaks, industrial estates and skilled workforce allowed the new factories to plug straight into electronics clusters like Ayutthaya, with the upgraded deep-sea port at Laem Chabang – a two-hour drive away – providing a maritime gateway to China. “We pitched to compete with Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam as the fundamental infrastructure was already here,” Phutana told This Week in Asia. “Thailand is quite suitable, we are quite strong in logistics and electricity supply is stable – especially compared with Vietnam and Malaysia.” There are now around 50 PCB companies in the country, forming a sector that meets a modest 5 per cent of world demand but is eager to capture more of a global market forecast to reach US$100 billion in the coming years. The ambition is to export eight to 10 times more PCBs than Thailand currently does – reaching roughly US$18 billion to US$25 billion in trade volume and a 20 per cent global market share. Lofty as that sounds, it may not be impossible given the trillions of dollars flowing into data centres that need increasingly complex layers of PCBs. “It’s quite complicated and uses very specialised material,” Phutana said of PCB manufacturing. “Thailand has the fundamentals to do it.” Running hot AI has changed the stakes for PCB manufacturers. A PCB destined for use with an AI accelerator card – roughly the size of a sheet of A4 paper – is a very different beast from the boards that are found inside car key fobs. Densely layered with winding copper traces that resemble an illuminated cityscape from above, these boards must survive extreme heat and power loads while shuttling vastly more data at far higher speeds, providing the physical foundations for the AI chips crunching numbers across the region’s data centres. Thailand has attracted billions of US dollars of data-centre investment in recent years on the promise of booming AI demand – so much, so fast that the capital is arriving well ahead of the physical buildout of centres themselves. But data centres are voracious consumers of water and electricity while creating comparatively few jobs, and domestic critics argue that beyond a handful of landlords, Thailand risks getting the environmental costs without the economic rewards. Delta Electronics Thailand, the local arm of the Taipei-headquartered “grid to chip” manufacturer that became the first company on the Thai stock exchange to be valued above US$100 billion in February, is now eyeing a bigger prize – the power and cooling systems that keep those centres humming. In the Thai electronics world, Delta is the gatekeeper to the big data-centre contracts – and as it grows, Thailand and its PCB makers are desperate to keep it on side. “Thailand is moving beyond cost competitiveness towards higher-value industries,” Delta said in a statement, pointing to “advanced engineering talent, energy infrastructure readiness and supply chain depth” as the areas that, with “continued progress” and “pro-business policies”, could give the country a lasting regional edge. Not everyone shares that confidence. Analysts the world over have grown increasingly nervous about an AI investment bubble and what its bursting might do to countries that have calibrated their industrial strategy on the boom continuing. Even Delta admits to being “mindful” of “tariff uncertainty, engineering talent gaps, supply chain constraints, intensifying competition in AI infrastructure” and the difficulty of scaling manufacturing “while maintaining quality and profitability”. Down on the factory floor, the constraints are more immediate. PCB manufacturing demands “a crazy amount of water each day”, according to Thailand Printed Circuit Association chief Phutana – and it needs to be “high purity”, competing directly with the needs of households and other industries. “The next wave of investment is there. Everyone in AI servers and data centres is looking for new land to expand their facility.” he said. “The customers cannot wait.” Layered on top of water constraints is a supply squeeze on laminates – the non-conductive, rigid base material that forms the physical foundation of circuit boards – and essential chemicals, a knock-on effect of the US-Israel war on Iran disrupting imports. Thailand’s Board of Investment says it is exploring ways to free up more water and power, but critics argue the country is sprinting ahead of its own capacity to sustainably keep pace. Somnuck Jongmeewasin, research director at environmental monitor and advocacy group EEC Watch, said automation had killed the jobs case for hosting PCB plants at all. Relocation incentives meant most equipment was imported, he said, with little technology transfer or upskilling of local workers – turning Thailand into an “assembly line” for foreign capital rather than a genuine beneficiary. “The factories that come here don’t use as much labour as they used to,” he said. “If they come from Chinese capital, they barely hire Thai workers at all. Blue collar [workers] are Myanmar, white collar are Chinese.” Despite the scepticism, there is a more hopeful reading – one rooted less in job numbers than in opportunity. Thailand’s education system produces precious few science, technology, engineering and mathematics graduates each year and PCBs may be one of its rare growth industries suited to hiring them. “Thailand faces a severe shortfall in meeting the surging demand for PCB and electronics workers,” said Panisa Harnpathananun of the National Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation Policy Council in Thailand. She estimated the sector would need roughly 225,000 high-skilled workers over the next five years, against the around 1,100 electronics engineers Thai universities produced in 2024. “This deficit is driven by an ageing population and a structural educational mismatch,” Panisa said. Plans are afoot to close that gap, including a “sandbox” scheme to fast track engineering degrees and proposals to retrain redundant car industry workers for PCBs and semiconductors. In a country short on other engines of growth, Panisa said PCBs might offer “the most critical opportunity and the strategic careers” its graduates were likely to find.

title: Our cheat sheet for the best things to do in Hong Kong, August 29-September 12
description: Treat your fur baby to an Afternoon Dim Sum Paw-ty at Sichuan Verandah, have a night on the tiles with Hutong’s mahjong-inspired cocktails, suit up for the Ultra Heroes Exhibition 2026 at the Incubase Arena and get your fungi on at the Yunnan Wild Mushroom Feast by Man Ho Chinese Restaurant x Tuber Umberto Bombana.
content: DO THIS Afternoon Dim Sum Paw-ty On September 6, from 3pm to 5pm, four-legged friends can join their paw-rents at Sichuan Verandah for afternoon delights. While humans tuck into a six-course set menu, pups can enjoy a basket of gourmet “doggy dim sum”. After the meal, head to the adjoining Garden Terrace for fun and games, including a Best-Dressed Dog contest with toy prizes from Wooffoo, photo ops, an etiquette class for canine dining and a mini market. 2/F, West Tower, Hyatt Centric Victoria Harbour Hong Kong, 1 North Point Estate Lane, North Point. For tickets, click here DRINK THIS Hutong Hutong is turning mahjong night into a liquid adventure with 16 new cocktails and mocktails. Allow your senses to be enthralled across four chapters – Qi, Cheng, Zhuan, He – as the experience begins with the drawing of a mahjong tile to reveal your drink. Qi (shuffle the tiles) encapsulates the fizz of excitement at the start of a game; Cheng (draw a tile) emulates the mystery; Zhuan (form the hand) blends East-meets-West flavours; and He (win the hand) finishes the set with a triumphant conclusion. Our pick is the Gentle South Wind, a non-alcoholic option of cold-brewed jasmine tea with lychee and yuzu. 18/F, H Zentre, 15 Middle Road, Tsim Sha Tsui SEE THIS Ultra Heroes Exhibition 2026 Suit up to save the world with your favourite Ultraman heroes this summer. Incubase Studio brings Eiji Tsuburaya’s renowned tokusatsu special-effects television and film franchise to Hong Kong’s Incubase Arena with “Ultra Heroes Exhibition 2026”, running until September 13. Revel in the nostalgic line-up of original Ultraman “super suits”, and see a 270-degree immersive view of “Heroes Assemble”, the centrepiece of the official “Ultraman Exhibition” currently touring Japan – a tribute to the “aliens of justice” who have been saving the world for 60 years and counting. B1/F & B2/F, Chong Hing Square, 601 Nathan Road, Mong Kok. For tickets, click here EAT THIS Man Ho Chinese Restaurant x Tuber Umberto Bombana For the ninth edition of the Yunnan Wild Mushroom Feast, available until September 20, Man Ho Chinese Restaurant and Tuber Umberto Bombana are presenting an “epicurean symphony of nature’s bounty”. Prepare for a gastronomic adventure led by chefs Jayson Tang and Keith Yam, featuring highlights such as Chinese noodles braised in a secret termite mushroom and beef gravy sauce, and steamed abalone and morel mushrooms with foie gras. Save room for an earthy dessert: a walnut pastry topped with hazelnut cream and porcini mushrooms. 3/F, JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, Pacific Place, Admiralty

title: Gazans warned against flying kites amid tensions with Israel
description: Children’s play deemed hazardous as fears of renewed conflict escalate in the region.
content:
Parents in Gaza have been cautioned against allowing their children to fly kites in the conflict-stricken territory, following Israel’s warning of a strong reaction should Hamas reignite its strategy of sending incendiary kites across the border.
A statement released earlier this week by local popular committees, which include members from various NGOs and charities operating displacement camps and shelters in Gaza, conveyed this warning.
The announcement was ‌coordinated with Hamas authorities, a source in the militant group said.
“We are working tirelessly on the ground and doing everything possible to stop this practice, not to restrict the childhood of our children, who have already been deprived of the most basic rights to play and live in safety, but to protect their innocent lives,” said the statement.
In 2018, Gazans sent incendiary balloons and kites over the border, causing fires across hundreds of acres of open fields and farmlands, in what they said was a protest at the Israeli blockade of the Hamas-controlled enclave.
In the past month, several kites that were not ⁠reported to be carrying incendiary materials were spotted drifting from Gaza into Israel, alarming Israelis who live in the nearby villages, which came under attack in the October 7, 2023, ‌Hamas-led assault that sparked the war.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Hamas that unless it stopped immediately, “those responsible” for launching kites, balloons or drones towards Israel would be targets of assassination and that areas from which they are sent would be ordered to ‌evacuate.
Umm Mohammed, a mother from Gaza City, said she was worried that her son could ⁠be hurt.
“Every summer, my kid, Ahmed, 10, ⁠and the kids in the street fly those kites to entertain themselves, but I will not allow him to, not any more,” she said.
A senior Israeli defence official said Hamas was trying to provoke Israel by encouraging ‌Gazans to fly kites across the border.
A Hamas official said the group has complained to ceasefire mediators that “Israel was making fake pretexts to continue the war on Gaza”. Israel complained to US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, which ‌oversees ‌the implementation of the 2025 Gaza ceasefire deal, about the kites, according to a second Israeli official.
“All militant activity in Gaza must stop, including the flying of kites. We ‌have conveyed this message directly through the established mechanism,” said an official of the Board of Peace.
“Israel, too, must comply with the ceasefire; military action cannot extend beyond responding ⁠to genuine and imminent threats,” he added.
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim slammed the Board of Peace for characterising children’s play as militant activities.
“What utter audacity! Is it even ⁠conceivable that attempts to appease the war criminal Netanyahu have reached the point of framing innocent children’s activities as armed operations, at a time when Netanyahu continues his daily killing and destruction despite the agreement?” Naim said.
An October 2025 ceasefire halted major fighting, but it didn’t end Israeli attacks.
An Israeli air strike killed ‌one Palestinian on Tuesday in the Mawasi area ‌of Khan Younis, in the south of the enclave. The Israeli military said it had targeted a militant, without further information.
Later, another Israeli air strike killed at least three people in the vicinity of a school housing displaced families in Jabalia in northern Gaza, doctors said. The Israeli military didn’t immediately comment.
More than 1,280 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect in October, according to Gazan health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed.

title: Your Voice: Hong Kong in WWII, volunteering and data centres (online letters)
description: This week, students reflect on the city’s resilience during the Second World War, taking part in a music therapy programme at a paediatric hospital and AI.
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form .
Venus Cheng Yee-lam, St Mary’s Canossian College
Our history class recently finished a unit on Hong Kong’s experience during the Second World War, and the lessons I’ve taken away have stayed with me far more than any textbook chapter.
Before learning about this period, I only thought of WWII as a distant, global conflict, something that happened far away from Hong Kong. But reading first-hand accounts, such as diaries from residents, interviews with survivors, and stories of everyday life under the Japanese occupation, showed me how deeply the war touched this city.
I was especially moved by the stories of ordinary people’s resilience. When food and supplies ran low, neighbours shared rice and vegetables, even when they barely had enough for themselves. Shop owners hid medicine and food for refugees, risking severe punishment if caught. Students who were forced to leave school formed secret study groups, passing on lessons to younger children so their education wouldn’t stop. These acts weren’t grand, heroic gestures, but small, quiet acts of courage that kept hope alive.
What struck me most was how the war changed Hong Kong’s sense of community. People who had never spoken to each other before worked together to help the sick, protect the vulnerable, and rebuild their lives after the occupation ended. It made me realise that resilience isn’t just about surviving hard times; it’s about looking out for one another, even when things feel hopeless.
Today, when we face challenges like the housing crisis, climate change, or even the stress of school life, these lessons still matter. The war taught us that a community is strongest when we stand together. It showed us that even small acts of kindness can make a huge difference to someone who is struggling. And it reminded us to never take peace and stability for granted, because we know how quickly they can be taken away.
As young people growing up in Hong Kong, we have a responsibility to carry these lessons forward. We can learn from the courage of those who came before us, and use that strength to build a better, more caring city for everyone.
Xu Yimeng, Wuhan Britain-China School (Wuhan)
I am writing to share my sincere reflections on a music therapy volunteer programme at a local paediatric hospital, where I witnessed the quiet bravery of young patients with tumours aged three to seven.
The two-hour activity featured interactive rhythm games, group singing and lyric rewriting, with every moment filled with gentle warmth. Beneath this cheerful atmosphere lies a poignant truth: every child participated wholeheartedly, with thin IV lines fixed to their arms as they clapped and swayed with faint trembles. Most had lost their hair to chemotherapy, leaving lingering surgical scars across their bare scalps – silent proof of their gruelling fight against illness.
While rewriting the lyrics to Flying Fireflies , the children disregarded rhyme and polish. Replacing the original line “As long as you are by my side”, they simply filled in the blank with their most genuine wish: “As long as you are happy”. This makes me realise that adults often overvalue technique and polish, gradually losing the pure sincerity children naturally hold. For these young patients, happiness resides in the smallest blessings: company, laughter and simple gifts.
Medical treatment heals physical wounds, but it cannot ease their long-term loneliness. I sincerely call on the public to provide tangible care for children with chronic illnesses. Teenagers can join volunteer programmes to accompany and comfort them. Meanwhile, charitable foundations and social organisations replace stereotyped sympathy with equal respect and provide targeted support within their capacity. I believe even tiny kindness can brighten a fragile childhood.
Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots such as Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT need data centres to operate. The centres contain computer servers used for data storage, analytics, and streaming.
Generative AI has its perks: it can collect information and make life more convenient. However, do the harms outweigh the benefits?
We’ve survived centuries without AI – it’s not fundamentally necessary for human existence. In addition, AI data centres are damaging the environment and depleting the resources required for survival.
First, data centres cause immense noise pollution, creating a constant hum. According to the Environmental Health Project, data centres generate noise levels that may exceed 90 decibels – a unit used to measure sound loudness. This exceeds the 85-decibel limit for safe hearing. Additionally, there will be increased light pollution – disrupting the natural rhythms of the body at night for those nearby – and air pollution.
Data centres don’t just impact those who live nearby. One of the biggest arguments against AI data centres is their reliance on fresh water to cool their servers. A report from the Environmental and Energy Study Institute found that a large data centre can use up to five million gallons of water (189,270,000 litres) daily, equivalent to the water use of a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. There are already 5,426 data centres in the United States, which means these centres use billions of gallons of fresh water every year.
In a world where more than two billion people live in countries with water scarcity, can we afford to waste so much water on AI data centres? Benjamin Sovacool, a professor of earth and environment and the director of the Institute for Global Sustainability at Boston University, has said: “There will be no water by 2040 if we keep doing what we’re doing today.”
A 2040-doomsday countdown doesn’t sound great, does it?

title: Lyas on why his La Watchparty is on Madonna’s and Charli XCX’s fashion week itinerary
description: Denied entry to Jonathan Anderson’s Dior debut, Elias Medini held a watch party at a Paris bar – now he also runs events in New York, London and Milan.
content: The drinks are flowing, cigarette smoke hangs in the air and the music is thumping on a late night during Paris Men’s Fashion Week on a hot night in June. “It” girls Charli XCX and Gabbriette, along with the eternal diva, Madonna, arrive at the function ready to party as flashing strobe lights signal it’s time to dance. This isn’t your average rave though. This is La Watchparty, the community-first cultural phenomenon kick-started by 27-year-old content creator Elias Medini, known to his 488,000 Instagram followers as Lyas. “Of course, you see that and think, ‘What the f*** is happening in my life?’” Medini leans back into his chair, a sheepish grin settling on his face as he considers how the decidedly anti-establishment event he originally threw together on a whim and funded himself has rapidly evolved into something the establishment now clamours to be a part of. The set-up started out simple enough: denied entry to Jonathan Anderson’s highly anticipated debut show for Dior Men in mid-2025, Medini decided to host a watch party for it instead, bringing his own TV to his regular bar in Paris to livestream the event. The parties have only got bigger and better since. Medini has brought the concept to New York, London and Milan, and now boasts an ambitious schedule rivalling that of fashion month itself. “But I think I stay grounded,” he muses. “I don’t know if I do. Maybe other people could tell you more.” If staying grounded involves staying true to oneself while being lauded by the masses, the hundreds of fans who crowd Medini’s events in search of a good show and a good time would surely attest to that. And if La Watchparty was born out of the desire to open up an industry that inspires the fear of missing out, I, for one, felt a different kind of FOMO watching Charli and Madonna co-host the latest Watchparty after-party from the environs of my own home. How does Medini manage to balance the high-profile, highly exclusive energy of an event like that without compromising on the all-inclusive aims of La Watchparty? The answer may lie in how he carries himself. Away from the spotlight and dressed in a plain T-shirt, the Medini dialling into this interview is noticeably less imposing than the Lyas I observe on my Instagram feed mingling with celebrities and offering the occasional very hot take on the season’s latest fashions. The very French nonchalance and signature red lipstick, however, are there. The same level of authenticity is there no matter where he is. “It changed a lot in my personal life since I do not have a second for myself any more,” Medini says of La Watchparty’s evolution into a big-ticket event that is increasingly attracting corporate sponsors like MAC Cosmetics and even participation from the luxury brands being streamed. The powers that be, from Bottega Veneta to Chanel, have given their blessing, while La Watchparty participants have been invited to real runway shows by Willy Chavarria and Zomer. Still, Medini strives to keep La Watchparty unpretentious and “open to everyone”. “I realised there was a lack of community in the fashion industry, a lack of space for the passionate to meet – everything is on a guest list, everything is quite elitist,” says Medini, who always considered fashion his safe space, growing up an outsider in a family obsessed with football. His parties are first-come, first-served affairs, with free entry and free drinks. “There, you can share your thoughts with people who think alike, without being scared of being blacklisted.” Going back to the very first Dior watch party that started it all, Medini, already an established commentator online, might not have been scared to leave a bad review for Anderson’s predecessor Maria Grazia Chiuri – but he was a little scared he might not be invited back to Dior shows again. In an interview with The New York Times, he described being dismissed from his fashion correspondent role at Interview magazine in the aftermath and explained how, ironically, it was his designation as an “influencer” that precluded an invite. Today, he’s back on good terms with Dior. But the lines are even more blurred as he juggles double duty as a critic with his own agenda and an entrepreneur who has to answer to brands, hosting watch parties for others while being jetted off to attend shows himself. “I always stay true to my editorial vision – I cover what I want to cover,” Medini says with a shrug, seemingly unfazed by the pressures and potential conflicts of interest. “Same with La Watchparty. Sometimes there are brands I don’t want to show [and] we just don’t show them. That’s freedom.” He expresses gratitude for fellow creator-commentators who have supported him since the beginning, such as Beka Gvishiani of Style Not Com, but throws shade at the Vogue magazine empire, which he accused of copying his La Watchparty concept earlier this year. “The main people who always look down on me are working at Condé Nast,” he says. Is it any surprise that Medini and the new vanguard of fashion tastemakers taking social media to fresh heights are increasingly wielding more clout than established editors? “Those big magazines are so scared of losing their power that they’d rather steal and gatekeep what they have, the crumbs of power they have left,” Medini says. “It’s a shame. They have to go to Amazon to get money now, but at least you have the name. You could bring new people in to bring fresh ideas [but] you just steal them – which strategically is very dumb. Are they dumb or are they feeding on this controversy to stay in conversations? I don’t have that answer.” I remark that as a fashion media veteran himself, Medini must be familiar with how those who reach the pinnacle of our industry seem accustomed to closing the door behind them. “That’s good,” he quips, scrambling to write the phrase down. “I myself might have, in the beginning, fallen into that, and thought you have to gatekeep access to stay relevant or look like you belong,” he admits. But Medini says exclusive events that feel increasingly out of touch with reality, like “Vogue France’s yoga retreat on a luxury yacht in Cannes”, were a rude awakening. Like many young people of his generation, Medini has grown disillusioned with corporate money grabs. “That’s what Vogue is now,” he concludes. “People are going to lose interest and every sense of respect towards these big brands that don’t speak to them any more. We don’t think it’s a sign of the times. It’s celebrities and [wealthy] tech people who suck each other’s d***s while the world is burning.” All of which raises the question: are there any truly authentic voices left in fashion? Medini praises designer Duran Lantink, for one. “It’s hard to be punk at a very established corporate house, so I’m here to support uncompromised voices – and whether it’s good or not, what he’s doing is challenging the status quo,” Medini says. “No one else is doing that. Everyone is staying safe with the investors and CEOs.” None of fashion’s seemingly inherent power imbalances have stopped Medini – a regular kid who grew up just outside Normandy, in northern France – from succeeding on his own terms and making fashion fun with a capital ‘F’. “It would take more to dissuade me,” he laughs. “If I don’t get invited [to a show], it’s OK. At least I’ve opened the door for a new generation, for who I was 10 years ago.” For someone whose first big break in fashion came from partying with the former editor-in-chief of GQ France, La Watchparty is a real full-circle moment. It’s also where you’ll find fashion’s “real fans”, Medini says, because “[in] the front row, no one gives a f***. Most of them want to go home. But the people outside, they would kill to be [there].” La Watchparty also feels like Medini’s tribute to the people who have made his vision possible, who “allowed me to have a voice”, he says. “It’s [PR expert] Lucien Pagès, [who] introduced me to [Saint Laurent creative director] Anthony Vaccarello. [Fashion editor] Carine Roitfeld. [Fashion designer] Stefano Pilati, who told me to wear red lipstick. Madonna, who allowed me in her apartment when no one opened that door for me. Charli XCX, who put me in a music video.” Though Medini never felt quite at home watching sport with his family, he fondly remembers the “collective energy” the pastime inspired. Could an industry built on exclusivity ever feel as inclusive as the NBA Finals watch parties that swept New York this summer, or as intense as World Cup fever? Medini seems to think so. The question we should be asking instead is whether La Watchparty could ever become bigger than a fashion week itself. It’s already the week’s main event for many.

title: Trump says US has deal with Venezuela for control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves
description: The US president faces mounting pressure to address high petrol prices as Iran war hits a six-month milestone with no conclusion in sight.
content: President Donald Trump on Friday said the US had entered an agreement with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of the South American country’s oil reserves. Trump in a social media post announced the agreement he said was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez. “The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Trump said. The announcement of the deal comes nearly nine months after the US military at Trump’s direction carried out an operation to capture Venezuela’s president Nicolas Maduro and spirit him to the US to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges. Trump faces mounting pressure to address high petrol prices as the war in Iran reaches a six-month milestone with no conclusion in sight. The US has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026. In the days following Maduro’s ousting in January, Trump floated the idea of US oil companies returning to Venezuela to tap its oil reserves. Trump has argued that Venezuela stole US oil when former Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez moved decades ago to nationalise hundreds of foreign-owned assets, including those owned by American oil companies. Venezuela has one of the largest oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil in the ground. That is about 17 per cent of the world’s supply, according to the US Energy Information Administration. Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela’s soil are largely mapped and known, experts say. But because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1 per cent of the world’s oil.

title: Editorial | China-Nepal border flash flood must galvanise climate change cooperation
description: While relief and rescue operations are the first priority, the tragedy should not only spark attention to early warning systems but also to longer-term solutions.
content: The human catastrophe resulting from the flash flood and mudslide on the Nepal-China border continues to unfold. The search for answers has already begun. But the safety of survivors, rescue of victims and relief operations are paramount. President Xi Jinping’s directives to emergency responders and dispatch of Premier Li Qiang to the border to oversee operations are evidence of that. The immediate cause of the disaster remains the subject of debate. But there seems little doubt of the involvement of climate change in the separation of a large chunk of rock and ice from a high-altitude Himalayan glacier before it slid into a valley more than a kilometre below and triggered the lethal torrent. Accelerated melting and receding of glaciers is linked to global warming. The Himalayas are especially vulnerable because their steep slopes have a large amount of permafrost – rock and soil sometimes frozen for centuries – which can start to melt with rising temperatures. Even a minor earthquake can accelerate destabilisation. This is not only happening in the Himalayas. One recent incident, in particular, illustrates the importance and urgency of developing early warning mechanisms. In May last year, a large part of the Birch glacier in the Lotschen valley of the Swiss Alps became detached and triggered a catastrophic rock-ice avalanche that obliterated most of the village of Blatten. Thanks to prior surveillance and hazard assessment, the local population had been evacuated just nine days earlier. Scientists warn that without reliable early warning systems, such incidents could happen elsewhere with catastrophic results. The current tragedy unfolded on Wednesday morning when a massive landslide triggered a fast-moving debris flow. According to state broadcaster CCTV, the torrent was travelling at up to 200km/h (124mph) and generated a wall of water as high as 15 metres (50 feet) when it slammed into the Gyirong Port border checkpoint between the Tibet autonomous region and Nepal. Ordering all-out search, rescue and relief operations, President Xi said that the most urgent task was doing everything possible to find missing individuals, evacuate residents at risk and treat the injured to minimise casualties. Meanwhile, there is debate about early warning systems. While these systems can be useful, and have helped in some cases including the one in Switzerland last year, there are limitations at this stage, given the number of variable factors. After this devastating tragedy, China and other nations can be expected to speed up research into and deployment of these technologies. But the long-term solution is to combat climate change. Unfortunately, globally, the political will to do so is weakening rather than strengthening. Countries like the United States are turning their backs on the issue. Even Europe is distracted by other issues. Regionally, China has been trying to strengthen its economic and people-to-people ties with Nepal. This disaster is a blow to that effort, having destroyed many border-connecting points. But it can also be turned into an opportunity. As the threat of glacier melting and mudslides rises, China can provide rescue and disaster relief not only to its people but also to those affected in Nepal. It can also help Nepal rebuild and reconstruct the border facilities. In the longer run, China is also in a position to help Nepal – and other countries bordering the Himalayas – to build a surveillance and communication system to guard against these kinds of disasters. Hopefully, the threat to all from global climate change will help countries find common ground on which to work together and build mutual trust. Hundreds of people from more than two dozen countries have been reported missing on both sides of the China-Nepal border. Such an international roll-call is a reminder that climate change is a global issue requiring cooperative solutions from rich and developing countries alike. Apart from scores of Chinese nationals on the Nepalese side, tourists and pilgrims unaccounted for included Americans, Indians, Australians, Britons and Canadians, to name a few nationalities. Sadly, amid prayers for the missing, the death toll can only go up.

title: What is hepatitis B? The viral infection 1 in 20 Hongkongers has, with many unaware
description: Hepatitis B is a viral liver infection that can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. A vaccine exists, but many don’t know they are infected.
content: David, who is in his forties and works in finance in Hong Kong, does not remember a life without hepatitis B, a viral infection of the liver. “I have been a … carrier for as long as I can remember,” he says. “I found out early on as a child since I was born with it – my mother is a carrier, too.” David’s experience is far from unusual in Hong Kong. According to Dr Loey Mak Lung-yi, a specialist in gastroenterology and hepatology, mother-to-child transmissions account for more than 90 per cent of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) cases in the city. About 410,000 people in Hong Kong have hepatitis B, according to the government’s Viral Hepatitis Action Plan. Alarmingly, 40 per cent are completely unaware of their infection and 70 per cent are not receiving appropriate medical follow-up care. Or as Hong Kong-based general practitioner Dr Wong Sze-man puts it: “When you take transport during rush hour and see 20 people, one of them is infected and is a silent carrier of the virus.” The fact that so many people living with chronic hepatitis B infection are unaware of the condition puts David – who has known his hepatitis status his whole life – in an ironically fortunate position. He has had regular blood tests for years, and consults a doctor every three to six months. He takes medication to keep the condition in check and looks out for warning signs, such as if he experiences abnormal levels of fatigue or his skin or eyes turn yellowish. Aside from his regular checks, David makes sure he eats a balanced diet and exercises regularly. Hepatitis B is just another manageable part of his life and not his whole life – his choices around diet and exercise are “very much a lifestyle choice instead of doing these consciously to keep the disease at bay”. Hepatitis B is the ‘most deadly’ variant Wong says that hepatitis B is an ongoing concern, particularly in endemic regions like Hong Kong. It is generally considered the most deadly of all the hepatitis variants because it often goes undetected. It accounts for roughly 1.1 million deaths a year globally, mostly from cirrhosis and liver cancer that develop slowly, years or decades after chronic infection takes hold. In Hong Kong, chronic hepatitis B infection is the leading cause of liver cancer, which is the city’s fifth most common cancer and third leading cause of cancer death. Hepatitis B is nearly 100 times more infectious than HIV and about 10 times more infectious than hepatitis C. It can survive outside the body on surfaces for at least seven days and still cause infection. It is also very sneaky: it can hide in your liver cells for life. Even people who successfully fight off the infection can technically still carry a dormant trace, which may reappear with a vengeance if their immune system is suppressed – such as if they are undergoing chemotherapy treatment for cancer. “The challenge … is its silent progression and patients can feel completely fine for decades while the virus silently replicates,” Wong says. “Around 15 per cent to 40 per cent of untreated chronic hep B carriers will eventually develop liver complications such as cirrhosis [liver scarring] and hepatocellular carcinoma [liver cancer].” A feature of chronic HBV infection is that it can lead to liver cancer without apparent damage in livers without cirrhosis. One of the most important measures to reduce liver cancer deaths related to chronic HBV infection, says Mak, is regular surveillance, with an ultrasound scan and blood tests every six months to detect early liver cancer. This will allow for treatment aimed at curing it, such as resection – surgically removing a diseased part of the organ. The Hong Kong government has started a “Hepatitis B co-care scheme”, says Mak, and encourages eligible people to receive free-of-charge screening at District Health Centres and subsidised management in primary care settings. In addition, the Liver Foundation – an NGO that promotes liver health awareness and helps prevent liver diseases – launched its Hepatitis Testing Express service in 2024 to provide free screening to all Hong Kong citizens. There is still a lot of stigma around hepatitis because of a lack of education. Many myths prevail, for example that hepatitis is only ever the result of drug and alcohol use rather than – as Mak is at pains to point out – much more often a mother-to-child infection. Another myth is that the hepatitis C form is a “death sentence”. While that might have been nearly true once, modern oral antivirals cure more than 95 per cent of hepatitis C infections within two to three months. “If you feel fine, you can’t have hepatitis” is also untrue. In fact, chronic hepatitis B and C are notorious for being symptomless for years or decades while quietly damaging the liver. This is a big reason why global death tolls stay so high despite available treatments: people just do not know they have it. Wong’s 6 golden rules for liver protection Vaccinate: Check your antibodies for hepatitis A and B, especially before travelling. Practice hygiene: Never share razors, toothbrushes or nail clippers. Ensure safe piercings/tattoos: Confirm single-use, sterile equipment is used. Watch food and water overseas: Avoid raw shellfish, tap water, and unpeeled fruits and vegetables in endemic areas. Practice safe sex: Use barrier protection. Moderate alcohol: Avoid excessive drinking or unverified herbal supplements that strain liver function. From A to G: the medical detective story behind hepatitis The word “hepatitis” comes from the Greek “hepar/hepat” for liver and “itis” for inflammation, so “liver inflammation.” It is a description of the condition, not a specific virus – several unrelated viruses (and other causes like alcohol, autoimmune disease or toxins) can all cause that inflammation. Five types of the hepatitis virus affect humans: A, B, C, D and E. A sixth, G (GBV-C), is sometimes listed but, as Mak says, it is not a well-recognised entity as it does not seem to cause disease in humans. Confusingly, the A, B, C, D and E do not reflect their order of discovery. Before any virus was isolated, doctors recognised two clinically distinct forms of hepatitis: one spread through contaminated food and water, the other through blood. In 1947, British hepatologist Dr Frederick “Frank” O. MacCallum named these “hepatitis A” and “hepatitis B”, years before either virus was actually pinpointed. So when American geneticist Dr Baruch Blumberg identified the “Australia antigen” in 1967 while researching unrelated genetic blood markers, it inherited the name hepatitis B, once confirmed as the culprit behind serum hepatitis. Hepatitis A was identified in 1973 by American virologist Dr Stephen Feinstone at the US National Institutes of Health. Italian doctor Mario Rizzetto identified hepatitis D in 1997 as a “defective” virus that could only infect people who already had hepatitis B. Hepatitis E was identified in 1983 after Russian virologist Dr Mikhail Balayan deliberately infected himself with a suspected sample to prove it caused disease; like hepatitis A, it is caused by consuming undercooked foods and unclean water. Hepatitis C came last, in 1989, having spent years as a placeholder diagnosis – “non-A, non-B hepatitis” – until British scientist Michael Houghton’s team finally isolated it from infected blood. Blumberg won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1976 for his work in identifying hepatitis B. He went on to develop the first hepatitis B vaccine, which he and his colleague, Irving Millman, refused to patent. World Hepatitis Day marks Blumberg’s birthday, July 28. His decision not to restrict licensing of the vaccine proved an especially important and altruistic move as hepatitis B is by far the most widespread of the chronic, blood- and sexually-transmitted forms. title: US Treasury sanctions Hong Kong-based firm over Iran money laundering ties
description: Kameng Trading Ltd allegedly acted as front company to help Iran’s Pedram Pirouzan Exchange House access international financial system.
content: The United States announced sanctions on a Hong Kong company on Friday for allegedly helping launder funds for a sanctioned Iranian exchange house, the latest Chinese entity to be targeted as part of Washington’s expanded efforts to squeeze Iran’s financial sector. The development comes as Washington has in recent days slapped new Iran-related sanctions on various Chinese entities, prompting Beijing to vow retaliation just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to the US. Hong Kong-based Kameng Trading Ltd acted as a front company to help the Iranian entity Pedram Pirouzan Exchange House, also known as Opal Exchange, access the international financial system, the US Department of the Treasury said. “Treasury promised to sever every economic lifeline Tehran has left and finally end the threat of the Iranian regime,” said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, referring to a new operation called “Economic Outcast” announced on Monday that expands secondary sanctions on entities in jurisdictions deemed to be supporting Tehran. Kameng was incorporated in July 2024 and has its registered office in New Mandarin Plaza in Tsim Sha Tsui, according to Hong Kong’s Companies Registry. Musthafa Azheekkodantakath, an Indian passport holder with a correspondence address in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, is listed as the company’s only shareholder and director. The US Treasury imposed sanctions in May on Pedram Pirouzan Exchange House, describing it as a “leading sanctions-evasion facilitator” in Iran that uses an “extensive network” of front companies to support Iranian banks and the Tehran government. The Treasury also announced on Friday that it has sanctioned a Dubai-based branch manager of Iranian bank Bank Melli, which has been accused of facilitating billions of dollars’ worth of transactions through accounts controlled by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Qods Force. Tehran condemned the new sanctions on Friday, describing the US actions as “state terrorism”. “US sanctions against Iran, by virtue of both their nature and their consequences, constitute a flagrant violation of the UN Charter,” Iran’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement. The Chinese embassy in Washington said the new sanctions amount to “economic warfare” that will disrupt the global economic and financial order. “China has made clear on many occasions its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council,” the spokesman said in a statement. The US Treasury last year issued an advisory accusing Hong Kong of being a “key jurisdiction” for Iranian money laundering operations, including revenue generated through the illicit sale of Iranian oil. It said that Iranian actors were setting up front companies in Hong Kong that bank with mainland China-based financial institutions. Earlier this week, the US imposed sanctions on nearly 60 Iran-linked entities and trading partners spanning digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong. The move sparked anger in Beijing, which vowed to “take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its rights and interests”.

title: UK far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos arrested by US immigration
description: A supporter of Trump’s crackdown on migrants, the controversial commentator is accused of overstaying in the US.
content: US immigration officials arrested controversial British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos on Thursday in New Orleans, according to the Department of Homeland Security. Immigration officials announced on Friday that Yiannopoulos was arrested at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport and accused him of overstaying after entering the United States legally in May 2019 through New York. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal on July 22 after Yiannopoulos failed to show up for his immigration hearing, a DHS spokesman wrote in an email. “He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a spokesperson for DHS wrote in an emailed statement. ICE’s online detainee locator does not say where Yiannopoulos is being held but directs family and legal representatives to the agency’s office in Alexandria, Louisiana, a deportation hub for international flights. Representatives of Yiannopoulos did not respond to a request for comment. It is unclear whether he has legal representation. The British national has most recently worked for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, who is scheduled to perform in New Orleans on Friday evening. Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticising feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of US President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. “Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts,” Yiannopoulos said on social media last year. Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the early 2010s as an incendiary writer for the conservative website Breitbart News. He resigned from the company in 2017 after a video of him endorsing paedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologised for the remarks and said he himself was a victim of sexual assault as a minor. Yiannopoulos’ arrest on Friday comes amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump’s immigration crackdown. Far-right conservative activist Laura Loomer swiftly took to social media to applaud Yiannopoulos’ arrest after years of public feuding between the two personalities. “I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer said on social media. Controversy around Yiannopoulos ballooned in 2017 when he carried out what he called his “Troll Academy Tour” across college campuses nationwide. Fights broke out when some students protested Yiannopoulos’ appearances and accused him of hate speech, while others celebrated him as a champion of free speech. Around that time, Buzzfeed reported on Yiannopoulos’ cosy relationships with self-proclaimed white nationalists. In recent years, Yiannopoulos has continued to work in the orbit of conservative activism. In 2022, he was an intern for former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, according to The Washington Post. He subsequently ran the short-lived 2024 presidential campaign for Ye. Most recently, Yiannopoulos has worked as a spokesman for Ye, who has been beset by controversy of his own following antisemitic comments that the rapper has since apologised for.

title: In Focus | Can Beijing’s gateway plan for Tibet survive geopolitics and natural disasters?
description: Beijing hopes trade will stabilise Tibet, but friction with India and the looming Dalai Lama succession are hampering its efforts.
content: On the windswept plains just south of Tibet’s second-largest city, the towering smart inspection systems and automated cargo gantries of a brand-new international land port gleam under the plateau’s high-altitude sun. Official road maps predict the multibillion-yuan project in Shigatse will process up to 300 trucks daily by the end of 2030 – loading cargo off trains and onto the trucks that will take goods to their final destination. It will also allow the authorities to carry out customs checks away from the region’s international borders, which straddle the Himalayas. However, on a quiet afternoon when the SCMP visited in late June, the Shigatse International Land Port processed just five trucks, according to Tenzin Namgyal, general manager of Shigatse Chengyou Supply Chain Management Co, the port’s operator. The port is key to Beijing’s plans to transform Tibet into a southward-facing geoeconomic “bridgehead” by building up the region’s economic connections with South Asia. But analysts say that achieving this goal will require overcoming extreme geography and navigating political tensions, which are set to rise with the looming reincarnation of the Dalai Lama. The vulnerability of this remote, high-altitude corridor was seen this week when deadly landslides and flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border, causing widespread devastation. The disaster underscores the challenges of China’s long-term “southbound strategy” – a billion-dollar geopolitical lifeline that Beijing is determined to build through the brutal terrain of the Himalayas. The vision When it opened in August 2024, the Shigatse land port cut the time that cargo takes to travel from China’s coastal regions to Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, from 45 to 15 days. According to Tenzin Namgyal, the port had attracted 160 enterprises, generated 2,500 jobs and facilitated some 120 million yuan (US$17.8 million) in trade by mid-June this year. The government’s increasing focus on Tibet’s trade potential is a sharp contrast from how Beijing has approached the region in recent decades, seeing it as a restive frontier where security always came first. The winds of change began at the 7th Central Tibet Work Forum in 2020, which was chaired by President Xi Jinping. While Xi emphasised national security and “combating separatist activities”, he also called for major infrastructure projects to be completed. The 14th five-year plan – which covered the country’s economic and social goals from 2021 to 2025 – called for Tibet to be built into an “important channel for opening up to South Asia”. “Developing Tibet as a premier gateway to South Asia is a top-level strategic decision within the Belt and Road Initiative,” said Zhang Shigao, director of the Institute of Contemporary Studies at the state-run China Tibetology Research Centre, arguing that this pivot would unlock vast market potential, drive economic growth and deliver shared benefits to both China and South Asia. Sun Yong, director of the West China Frontier Research Institute, said Beijing’s concept of “national security” had expanded from a singular focus on military defence to an “interconnected network of defence, ecology, culture and development”. “The ultimate baseline for long-term frontier defence is the stabilisation and enrichment of the borderlands,” said Sun, also former Communist Party chief of the Xizang Academy of Social Sciences. Xizang is the official Chinese name for Tibet. By elevating the livelihoods of frontier ethnic minority communities – including the Monpa and Lhoba populations in the disputed Zangnan, or Arunachal Pradesh, area – economic development had replaced the obsolete “economy versus security” binary to become recognised as a vital pillar for long-term border stability, he said. This playbook might sound familiar to those who have followed government policy in Xinjiang, another autonomous region to the north that has been riven by ethnic tensions and alleged human rights abuses, which Beijing stridently denies. In the past 13 years, the vast, landlocked region’s historic trading connections with Central Asia and Europe have been revitalised, positioning it as the “core area of the Silk Road Economic Belt” initiated by Xi in 2013. Nepal’s counterweight While Xinjiang bordered on eight countries about which China has “few security concerns”, Tibet’s situation was totally different, said Barry Sautman, a specialist in China’s ethnic minorities and professor emeritus at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. “Most of its external border is with India, which continues to contest its frontiers with China; Nepal, which is friendly to China, but not politically stable; and Bhutan, effectively India’s protectorate, with no formal diplomatic relations with China,” he said. Tibet also shares a relatively short, remote border with Myanmar. Sun noted that while China-Europe freight trains gave Xinjiang access to a vast market, Tibet’s infrastructure capacity was far weaker, as was consumer demand in its neighbouring countries. Last year, while Xinjiang saw over 10,000 transcontinental trains, Tibet saw a mere 12 freight trains travel from coastal Yiwu to Shigatse, carrying a total cargo value of just 230 million yuan. Tibet’s foreign trade data has also experienced a dramatic boom-and-bust cycle. From 4.87 billion yuan in 2019, total trade value peaked at a record high of 12 billion yuan in 2024, but plunged to 8.5 billion yuan last year, customs data show. Among Tibet’s four neighbours, Nepal is most willing to tango. The landlocked nation shares a 1,400km (870-mile) border with Tibet and observers say it views Beijing as an indispensable counterweight to reduce its economic dependence on New Delhi. The country has historically been hit by multiple devastating, months-long economic blockades imposed by India, most notably in 1989 and 2015, which cut off supplies of fuel, medicine and food. In 2018, China announced that it would build what it calls a trans-Himalayan multi-dimensional connectivity network with Nepal – involving railways and communication links – as part of the Belt and Road Initiative. Currently, with six border crossings with Nepal – five in Shigatse – China is the country’s second-largest trade partner after India. Nepal remains Tibet’s uncontested primary trading partner, seeing its share of Tibet’s total foreign trade rise from 40 per cent in 2024 to 46 per cent last year. But Ivan Lidarev, a research fellow at the Institute of South Asian Studies at the National University of Singapore, doubted that trade via Nepal would reshape Chinese access to South Asia. He pointed out that Nepal was an unstable country with a population of just 30 million, a nominal GDP of about US$46 billion and a relatively small middle class. He remained sceptical of Tibet’s ambition to serve as a “massive economic bridgehead” to South Asia. “There are far easier, faster, and significantly cheaper alternatives, such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor through Xinjiang, or traditional maritime shipping routes connecting Chinese ports directly to southern India and Bangladesh,” Lidarev argued. One of the biggest obstacles for road transport was fluctuating costs, according to Tenzin Namgyal. Sun attributed the difficulty of trading with Nepal to seasonal weather disruptions, poor local infrastructure and geopolitical friction, which made the land port’s “capacity utilisation fall drastically short of its normalised operational targets”. Amit Ranjan, another research fellow at the NUS Institute of South Asian Studies, said: “It will take time to transform the infrastructure status of Nepal. The reasons for such are many, including delay in effective implementation of the projects.” The reality has been laid bare by the China-Nepal cross-border railway, a key project of the Belt and Road Initiative linking Tibet’s Gyirong county with Kathmandu. Costing an estimated US$2.75 billion for the 72km Nepalese stretch alone, the line and its many bridges and tunnels run through a rugged and seismically active landscape where the impact of this week’s floods has yet to be determined. The project has also met political inertia and social unrest in Kathmandu, especially after pro-China prime minister K.P. Sharma Oli left office late last year and was replaced in March by the populist, China-sceptical Prime Minister Balen Shah. “An expected June 2026 feasibility report has been stalled by uncooperative Nepalese politicians, delaying realistic completion estimates past 2035,” according to Sun, who has run a social media account tracking the railway project alongside Nepali scholars since 2022. The Nepalese loophole One bright spot in trade with Nepal has been electric vehicles, which an official from Shigatse’s propaganda department called a “highly popular star product”. Gyirong Port, which was devastated by the recent flash floods, is Tibet’s main foreign trade port and handles one-third of China’s trade with Nepal. Since 2023, it has been a major hub for exporting Chinese EVs to Nepal. Last year, 12,938 Chinese-made EVs poured into Nepal, marking a 6.8 per cent jump since 2024, when the land port started operations. Most of these vehicle exports, however, were re-exported to India by Nepali middlemen, taking advantage of a free-trade deal, Tenzin Namgyal said. This provides Chinese carmakers with a back door into an Indian market protected by strict regulatory hurdles and prohibitive 70 to 125 per cent tariffs, though it remains unclear how traders bypass supposedly strict rules-of-origin criteria. “We’re using Nepal as a stepping stone; our main focus is still India for its large population and underdeveloped infrastructure,” Tenzin Namgyal said. Lidarev warned that the Nepalese loophole was highly vulnerable to an Indian clampdown. He said the trade only persisted because its current volume was small; if it grew, New Delhi would likely restrict goods from Tibet, pressure Kathmandu, or reconsider the trade deal. He added that encouraging a massive increase in border trade would entrench Chinese economic influence in North India, undermine Indian producers and even weaken the “Make in India” manufacturing initiative championed by the Narendra Modi government. Tensions with India From the perspective of Chinese planners, India remains the economic prize in South Asia. But observers say commercial ambitions must be guided through a complex and fragile stabilisation between Asia’s two nuclear-armed giants. According to Lin Minwang, vice-dean at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, Beijing’s grand vision for Tibet’s South Asian corridor has been consistent for three decades and reflects a “strategic patience”. The overarching blueprint was a multi-generational gamble designed to “plug directly into India’s vast 1.4-billion-population market whenever a structural diplomatic pivot occurs”, said Lin, who is also deputy director of the university’s Institute of South Asia Studies. However, Lin acknowledged a profound deadlock since 2020, driven by border restrictions in the wake of frontier clashes between the nations and New Delhi’s continued wariness about opening up to China. While Beijing issued about 200,000 visas to Indians in 2025, New Delhi issued a mere 2,000 visas in 2024. Although India lifted its five-year ban on Chinese tourist visas in July 2025 – which drove a 63 per cent rebound in business travel – volumes remain far below pre-pandemic peaks due to strict financial requirements and background checks. Lin added that New Delhi was actively neutralising Nepal’s potential as China’s “proxy corridor” by refusing essential overflight rights for Nepal’s newly built, Chinese-constructed international airport, rendering it virtually non-operational. “Frankly, the actual economic and trade space is indeed not large right now,” Lin said. “The risks are manageable, and we must maintain a degree of optimism, but overinflated expectations are unrealistic.” Lidarev noted that India opposed opening its “underdeveloped, minority-populated, poorly integrated and security-sensitive borderlands” – especially its troubled northeast – to Tibetan trade. “While there is an internal debate in India about gradually relaxing investment restrictions for Chinese firms, this does not encompass the border areas.” Sautman said the deadlock was fuelled by animus among India’s elite over a staggering 6-1 merchandise trade deficit against Beijing. As a result, less hostile diplomatic rhetoric has yet to translate into real, on-the-ground cross-border commercial interchanges. However, recent high-level diplomacy indicates a thaw may be under way, including when the two sides resumed cross-border trade through the Lipulekh Pass and Nathu La Pass after a six-year suspension. In June, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged Ajit Doval, India’s national security adviser, to speed up the resumption of dialogue mechanisms. That month, India’s new ambassador to China paid his first visit to Tibet to review arrangements for Indian pilgrims following Beijing’s restoration of access to the sacred Mount Kailash after a five-year hiatus. Hours before the devastating cross-border floods struck, Beijing and New Delhi announced eight measures to further ease cross-border tensions, including steps to keep talks about cross-border trade and pilgrimages moving. Hundreds of pilgrims are thought to be among the victims of the floods. But unfreezing crossings does not guarantee a trade spike. Lin pointed out that when the Nathu La Pass last reopened after a closure, in 2006, trade between Tibet and India was strangled by the latter’s rigid passport and visa restrictions, dashing hopes of greater economic integration. Interior hurdles Restrictions do not just come from foreign governments. For ordinary businesspeople in Tibet, getting cross-border trade moving can prove next to impossible despite Beijing’s goals. Xizang Zanggangdise Agricultural Products Technology Development Co is government-mandated to spearhead exports to South Asia and the Middle East, targeting a 320 million yuan annual pre-tax output. General manager Phuntsok Dondrub said the company – which makes soy sauce and vinegar – had already boosted the local economy, creating 209 jobs and increasing agricultural incomes by 5 per cent for over 2,000 households. But, despite securing a 1 million yuan export order to Kathmandu in June, the firm found getting its paperwork in order a challenge. “Obtaining a passport and visa is still quite difficult locally within Tibet,” he said.

title: Opinion | US-China AI rivalry needn’t preclude cooperation
description: Forcing countries to choose between the US’ and China’s initiatives would be counterproductive to global AI governance.
content: Artificial intelligence (AI) poses risks that do not respect national borders, from cyberattacks and misinformation to system malfunction and potentially dangerous misuse. In a geopolitically charged world, does greater incompatibility between countries make AI safer? UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres offered a clear answer at the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance: “When countries align on how to test systems, measure risk and assign responsibility, safety travels with the technology.” By contrast, “a patchwork of incompatible rules raises costs, divides the world – and protects no one”. Yet just as AI creates an unprecedented need for cooperation, geopolitics threatens to pull the world apart. China established the World AI Cooperation Organization (Waico) last month with 29 founding members. Besides AI cooperation and governance, it aims to help developing countries bridge the AI divide. The United States, meanwhile, has developed the Pax Silica initiative around AI, technology and supply-chain security. Both initiatives overlap but do not primarily seek to address the same problems. Waico can promote development and cooperation while strengthening China’s influence in global AI governance; Pax Silica can address genuine concerns about critical technologies and supply-chain resilience while consolidating a US-centred network of trusted partners. Because these initiatives come from fierce competitors, an analytical problem arises when geopolitical rivalry is treated as sufficient to explain their entire meaning. Indonesia joined Waico while engaging in Pax Silica discussions; Kazakhstan joined both. The US is reportedly preparing to tell countries that participation in initiatives deemed incompatible with the American framework could lead to exclusion. Must international AI cooperation reproduce geopolitical blocs? Conflict between countries arises from commercial, strategic and political interests, but perceptions matter too. Once a country is seen primarily as a strategic adversary, cooperation may be read as bloc-building, regulation as political control and ambiguous actions as evidence of hostile intent. This is not merely theoretical. A Carnegie Endowment for International Peace paper warns against dismissing Chinese AI regulations because of the Communist Party being in power or viewing them primarily through geopolitical competition. The picture is complicated: political and information control matter, but policymakers are also responding to AI’s social, economic and ethical consequences. Geopolitical differences can coexist with areas of policy convergence. A 2025 study of US and Chinese AI governance examining more than 40 policy and corporate governance documents found overlap including in system reliability, algorithmic transparency and the use of AI to enhance safety. The analytical mistake lies not in identifying political motives but in treating political motives as exhaustive explanations. Consider human control. At the World AI Conference in Shanghai, Chinese President Xi Jinping called for AI to remain under human control while discussing risk prevention and opposing abuse. Less than two weeks earlier, the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance included “robust human oversight” among the governance priorities. Yet the same language can be interpreted very differently: Xi’s call, for example, has been read as referring to control exercised by Communist Party institutions. This resemblance in language does not necessarily mean the Chinese and UN approaches have the same motivations, objectives or implementation mechanisms. But neither does institutional difference prove that their underlying policy concerns are fundamentally different. We need to ask what problems a policy seeks to address and how it functions within its institutional environment. A country’s political system should be understood through its history and culture, and form part of the context through which a policy is interpreted – not judged against assumptions about what the system ought to be, with those assumptions used to predetermine what a policy must mean. Communist Party leadership is a central feature of China’s institutional environment. But recognising its importance is different from using it as an all-purpose explanation. An AI policy may reflect political considerations, technological safety, economic development, national security – or several objectives simultaneously. Journalists, think tanks and academics have a responsibility: neither to minimise genuine differences nor manufacture common ground, but to identify both accurately and distinguish evidence from inference. The choices of Indonesia and Kazakhstan suggest another possibility: participation without alignment. Countries can engage with different technological ecosystems and retain room for independent policy choices. Forcing them to choose may harden precisely the divisions global AI governance needs to bridge. The Chinese expression “he er bu tong” means harmony without uniformity. Countries shaped by different histories, cultures and circumstances need not share political systems, values or strategic interests to cooperate.
