AI will not wait for geopolitical rivalries to subside. If AI is to serve humanity rather than deepen geopolitical divisions, governments must cooperate across differences. Those who analyse international affairs have a role too: not to overlook disagreements, but to take care not to enlarge them through assumptions – and to recognise common ground where it exists. The views expressed here are the author’s own.

title: China-Nepal floods: rescuers pull out survivors caked in mud as toll climbs
description: Nepal has reversed an earlier decision and says it will allow foreign teams and experts to help with rescue efforts.
content: Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that killed 676 people and left nearly 3,000 missing. The rescue efforts included a team that rappelled into a severely damaged checkpoint area on the Chinese side of the border between the two countries. Rescuers were on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that formed high up in the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods on Wednesday. Experts warned that the lake, created after a glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was starting to overflow. Nepal’s army was deployed to help rescue more than 100 people believed trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower plant located in the country’s worst-hit district. Like elsewhere in the disaster zone, their work was complicated by thick layers of mud that covered the site. The rappelling rescue team descended into the once-bustling border-crossing area from wooded mountain slopes, the state broadcaster China Central Television said. “As far as I can see, it’s nothing but debris,” rescue official Zou Mingqi told state media. The area where travellers went through border control to enter or leave China has been flattened to a muddy area, according to satellite images. The floods have killed 579 in Nepal, the country’s disaster-management authority said Friday. Nepali police later put the number of deaths at 553. There was little information on survivors on the Chinese side, where the death toll rose to seven on Friday as state media showed evacuations of villages and leaders’ efforts to direct the relief response. More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Meanwhile, the number of people who were unaccounted for in the country nearly doubled to 1,924 as more local residents were added to the tally. China’s state media said 554 people were missing on the Chinese side. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak. In other developments, Nepal on Friday reversed an earlier decision and said it would allow foreign teams and experts to help with rescue efforts, apparently under pressure from other countries, especially those whose citizens are unaccounted for, a leading English-language newspaper, The Kathmandu Post, reported. Nepali police issued a fresh alert on Friday after receiving information that a dam on the Tibet side had burst. Security personnel and rescue and relief workers were told to stay on high alert and move to a safe location if necessary. It was unclear if the dam bursting was related to flooding concerns over the lake that formed after the initial flash floods. Chinese broadcaster CCTV said the newly formed lake, located more than 10km (six miles) from Gyirong Port, the hard-hit border crossing with Nepal, sits at an elevation of 2,950 metres (9,680 feet). Nepali and Chinese authorities earlier warned of more flooding from the lake, which was already overflowing. Rescuers heading to the disaster zone were ordered to stop temporarily on Friday due to concern the lake would release more water and debris, and people in potentially affected areas were urged to move to safer ground. Monitoring data from the Chinese Ministry of Water Resources later showed that the lake had dwindled in size. The water level dropped by 10 metres (32 feet) from the high point on Thursday morning, the state broadcaster said. Some 680 rescuers eventually reached the Gyirong area by foot and via rafts. Some were dropped down from drones flown to the area, CCTV footage showed. “Anyone, anyone?” rescuers yelled, according to footage by the broadcaster. It was not immediately known how many people were at the border checkpoint building when the floods hit. In Nepal’s Rasuwa district, Nepali army rescuers struggled to help more than 100 people believed to be trapped by thick mud in a tunnel that’s part of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project. The army said it had rescued 350 people from the tunnel so far. Video from the scene showed rescuers helping a man covered in mud out of the tunnel by pulling and pushing. “It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud,” Army spokesman Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet said. Nepal’s disaster-management authority said 3,253 people had been airlifted by helicopter from the disaster area. The search-and-rescue efforts have been supported by an outpouring of financial support from neighbouring countries, including small, poorer countries like Sri Lanka, said Kanni Wignaraja, the United Nations development agency’s regional director for Asia and the Pacific. “Sri Lanka has its own huge fiscal problems, but it has just sent US$1 million immediately to the Nepal government,” Wignaraja said. Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as magnitude 5.2. The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal. Customs officer Karbir Gaire was among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with China, where some 1,500 people had lived. Gaire reached his office around 8am on Wednesday and was working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake. “Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us,” he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family. “We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us.” Fifteen of Gaire’s colleagues are missing. “It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don’t call it a flood. It was a tsunami.” Nepal’s tourism board has said that among the missing are more than 500 foreigners. Some of the missing may have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others. Indian spiritual guru Jaggi Vasudev, also known as Sadhguru, said in a social media post that 77 people returning from Mount Kailash with groups organised by his Isha Foundation were at the immigration centre in Gyirong when the flooding struck. Vishnuram Ramaswamy, who works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry, said that he spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on that pilgrimage Wednesday morning. It was a highly anticipated trip, something his mother had always wanted to do, he said. “This was the last we spoke to them,” he said. “They have been unreachable since.”

title: Trump orders creation of US ‘Space Academy’, amid rivalry with China
description: The institution, which will train civilian and military recruits, will be modelled on the famous military school at West Point.
content: US President Donald Trump on Friday announced the creation of a “Space Academy” to train future civilian and military recruits for an arena where the United States faces rivalry with China. Speaking at Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre in Houston, Trump said the institution would be modelled on the famed US military academy at West Point. “It’s called the US Space Academy. That’s a big deal,” Trump said as he signed an executive order creating the new school. “It’ll serve both the United States Space Force as well as Nasa and the civilian space flight industry, and it’ll attract, train, and graduate the very best of our nation.” Trump has credited the US Space Force, the sixth branch of the US armed forces, with an important role in the recent American military operations in Venezuela and Iran. He did not say where the new academy would be built. The US president also presented the Congressional Space Medal of Honour to the crew of Nasa’s Artemis 2 mission, which flew past the moon in April. Outer space has become an increasingly strategic domain for global powers in the military and technology fields. The US is competing with China in the race to land astronauts on the moon before 2030, more than 50 years after humans first walked the lunar surface. Trump last week pledged a “golden age” of space in a push to launch more rockets, including to Mars and the moon.

title: As Iran war hits six-month mark, Trump says he’s ‘not in a hurry’
description: The president’s ‘little excursion’ in the Middle East grinds on, despite his earlier promise to voters to keep the US out of ‘endless wars’.
content: President Donald Trump arrives at an awkward moment for his presidency on Friday as the US-Israel war against Iran reaches the six-month mark, a notable milestone for a conflict that the Republican leader repeatedly assured Americans would be a “little excursion” lasting a matter of weeks. The war is not over, though Trump claims that through bombs and blockade, he has already devastated Iran’s leadership, military and economy. And this week his administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure – rather than military action – to try to finish off Iran. The shifting strategy centres on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran. The turn to using sanctions as the cudgel of choice comes as the administration weighs diminished munitions stockpiles after months of war, sparking concerns that the prolonged conflict could undermine US military readiness in other parts of the globe. As the conflict grinds on, Trump’s talk of finding a quick end to the war also appears to be fading. He stressed this week that he’s “not in a hurry” to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continues making the case that the Islamic Republic’s leadership is on the ropes. “They’re not paying their troops. They’re in deep trouble. They have very little capacity,” Trump told reporters Thursday. “We don’t want to speak to them. We’re not looking to meet or anything,” he said. It is unclear how – or if – Trump will address the six-month anniversary of a conflict that has already cost the US more than US$37.5 billion and done damage to his popularity ahead of critical November elections for his party. The president is spending Friday in Houston, where he will honour the Artemis II Nasa crew for their 10-day mission around the moon earlier this year. On its face, the moment is complicated for the “America First” leader who fiercely criticised his White House predecessors for wasting American taxpayer money and US troops’ lives in Middle East conflicts and vowed on the campaign trail to keep the military out of “endless wars”. But Trump has bristled at suggestions that this war – in which no American troops have deployed into Iran – can be compared with the years-long wars in Iraq and Afghanistan in which more than 7,000 Americans were killed. His Republican predecessor, President George W. Bush, was widely mocked for a 2003 speech aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln under a White House-produced banner that read “Mission Accomplished”. It came to symbolise a premature declaration of victory for the Iraq War, which would go on for nearly nine more years. More than two decades later, there are still US troops stationed in Iraq. Trump’s war has stretched on far longer than he told Americans it would. It didn’t stop him from sharing a social media post this week declaring “MISSION ACCOMPLISHED 2026”. The AI-generated image features Trump against a backdrop of US fighter jets, a warship and American flags above smaller images of Bush and former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in an Israeli strike in the opening salvoes of the war. Trump has consistently emphasised that the US and Israel campaign has been devastating for Iran’s navy and air force. Iranian officials have said the country has suffered US$270 billion in direct and indirect damage. Israeli military strikes in the first weeks of the war wiped out much of the theocratic government’s leadership structure, including Khamenei. But Iran has found leverage through its own strikes in the critical Strait of Hormuz, where relatively few vessels carrying oil and liquefied natural gas are risking passage. Trump again declared Thursday that the “Strait of Hormuz is open,” saying 24 vessels passed through a day earlier. That is a fraction of the roughly 130 vessels that passed through the vital waterway daily before the war began. Mediators Qatar and Pakistan continue to press for a diplomatic off-ramp from the two sides. Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, was in Tehran on Thursday to discuss a proposed plan between Iran and Oman to boost traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. But in Washington, Trump has shown little interest in getting back to the preliminary deal reached in June that aimed to reopen the strait and launch talks about Iran’s nuclear programme. That deal fell apart within weeks after Iran started attacking ships. At the same time, Trump says the US effort to economically choke off Tehran is working, with a US naval blockade preventing Iranian oil from making it to market as the trickle of vessels carrying oil from other Gulf nations passes through. “We have control and we have the blockade,” Trump said. “Iran is not getting anything. Nothing is going through.” There is no doubt that the strikes combined with decades of international sanctions have battered Iran, said Aarathi Krishnan, a geopolitical risk analyst at Raksha Intelligence Future. But as Trump tries to turn to a new chapter in the war, Krishnan argues the Republican may be misguided in concluding that more pressure on Tehran – which has spent decades adapting to international economic sanctions – will produce the political outcome he wants. Indeed, Iran’s economy in the run-up to the start of the war was mired in surging inflation, according to the International Monetary Fund. National income per person had fallen from about US$8,000 in 2012 to $5,000 in 2024, according to World Bank data. But Tehran has also shown resilience, selling discounted oil and establishing opaque shipping and financial networks, Krishnan said. “This administration has completely underestimated the Iranian resolve,” Krishnan said. “This is not new to the Iranian regime.” Richard Goldberg, who served as a senior adviser on Iran at the National Security Council during Trump’s first White House term, argues that Iran now finds itself in “uncharted waters” if the administration follows through with a truly biting campaign to pressure Iranian trade partners. “What we should be seeing is an attempt to seal off every escape hatch the regime has left,” said Goldberg, who is now at the Foundation for Defence of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. “Use the economic power of the United States to layer a naval blockade with an air and land embargo while dropping the hammer on anyone who gives the regime access to hard currency – whether that’s in the Middle East, China or even Europe.” But it remains to be seen how far the administration is willing to go. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week unveiled a campaign the White House calls “Operation Economic Outcast”, but only issued warnings to nations to cut trade and has yet to announce any secondary sanctions. Bessent told reporters the administration wanted countries to have a chance to shift away from Iran before it was too late – and acknowledged there was economic risk to the US, too, in moving ahead. The Treasury Department announced on Friday that it was taking steps that could lead to eventually severing Banque Misr, Egypt’s second-largest bank, from the US financial system. The department accused the bank of serving as an economic lifeline to Tehran’s leadership. China, which is Iran’s biggest trade partner and oil buyer, responded earlier this week to the Trump administration’s broad threats of going after countries and firms that still do trade with Iran by expressing its opposition to “illegal unilateral sanctions”. Pressed on Thursday about why he was not already sanctioning Chinese banks, Trump offered a cryptic response. “Who said I’m not? You don’t know if I’m doing it,” Trump said. “I don’t have to announce everything, do I?”

title: Warsh signals US Fed may need to raise rates if above-target inflation lingers
description: This was the closest he has come to acknowledging interest rate hikes may be needed to ease price pressures.
content: The US central bank will “have work to do” if policymakers are not confident that underlying inflation is returning to its 2 per cent target, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said on Friday in remarks that acknowledged financial conditions do not appear restrictive and marked the closest he has come to acknowledging interest rate hikes may be needed to ease price pressures. “Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. ‌Otherwise, we have work to do. That’s our job … our mandate … and our charge to keep,” Warsh said in remarks prepared for delivery to the Fed’s Jackson Hole economic symposium in Wyoming. The remarks drew applause from an audience of global central bankers hungry for more than the vague promises to deliver price stability that have been a feature of Warsh’s previous remarks. Markets also heard the message, raising bets on a rate hike next month that had previously been priced in as more of a long shot. While much of the 16-page address focused on large issues, like the influence of artificial intelligence, that Warsh feels will be critical in the long run, it also included some key acknowledgements – including that “short-term interest rates are the predominant tool to achieve the dual mandate”. Notably, Warsh said the recommendations of five task forces he has commissioned to study longer-term issues “will come later and have no bearing on decisions we make in the current policy conjuncture. But I believe that for future policy challenges, this intellectual investment ⁠today will leave us far better prepared”. He did not directly address recent market interventions by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent but did say that the Fed “needs clear market signals, as unfiltered ‌as possible”, to set proper monetary policy. But it was his comments on inflation that arguably went the furthest to meet what some had seen as a gap in Warsh’s remarks at his first two press conferences. “Progress over the past two years has been modest,” Warsh said of inflation readings ‌that by the Fed’s preferred Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index remained at 3.7 per cent on an annual basis as of July. Recent data “do not tell me that underlying ⁠trends have meaningfully improved”, he said, with about ⁠half of the items in the PCE basket of goods and services increasing at more than a 3 per cent annual rate, below the ratio seen during the Covid-19 inflation surge but above the pre-pandemic norm. Traders moved to price in about ‌even odds of a rate hike at the Fed’s September 15-16 meeting after the remarks, up from about 40 per cent earlier on Friday, and the 2-year Treasury yield rose to its highest level in about a month. Stocks slightly extended gains. Warsh did not suggest a timeline for rate hikes, and explicitly said his remarks should not be taken as “forward guidance” or even as the more explicit “reaction function” investors and ‌Fed analysts have suggested he provide – neither of which he feels would be appropriate or possible to accurately provide. But they do amount to his most detailed comments yet on where the Fed stands ⁠in its efforts to return inflation to the 2 per cent target after more than five years above it. He noted, in another elaboration, that he currently sees inflation expectations as anchored, though ⁠they must be “closely minded”. “It’s the Fed’s job to make sure that inflation expectations do not get unanchored,” Warsh said. He also said that not only does the economy appear resilient, but that given current market interest rates, and a Fed short-term policy rate unchanged since December, “credit and loan markets are showing few signs of policy restraint”, comments that ‌could lay the groundwork for arguments in favour ‌of a rate hike if inflation persists. Ahead of Warsh’s speech, investors saw a roughly one-in-three chance the central bank would raise rates next month. A hike at or by the December 8-9 meeting was given more than a 90 per cent probability, according to data from the CME Group’s FedWatch Tool. There was sentiment at the July meeting to tighten policy, with three policymakers dissenting from the decision to keep the policy rate steady in the current 3.5 per cent to 3.75 per cent range, where it has been since December. Key unemployment, job growth and consumer inflation data for August will be released early next month. Questions about Warsh’s approach have intensified amid US President Donald Trump’s continued calls for lower interest rates. While Trump has continued to defend Warsh, whom he appointed, the president has criticised other Fed officials for supporting higher rates. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Philippine tennis trailblazer Alexandra Eala poised to bring fervent following to US Open
description: Eala’s growing fan base, improving game – she won her first WTA title this month – could make her one of the main attractions at final major.
content: Philippine tennis trailblazer Alexandra Eala has emerged ⁠as one of the ⁠sport’s fastest-rising players after a ⁠breakthrough season, and her growing fan base and improving game could make her one of the main attractions at the United States Open. Former world No 4 Mary Joe Fernandez said the scale and intensity of ‌support for Eala had become increasingly apparent over the past year, recalling packed practice sessions at the Miami Open and vocal crowds at recent tournaments. “Her following, the fans that just come to watch her not just play her match, but to watch her practise, is off the charts,” ESPN commentator Fernandez told ⁠reporters on a conference call this week. “It’s just gotten bigger and bigger everywhere she ‌goes. “It’s almost like she’s playing a Billie Jean King Cup match when she’s out there,” she added. “Every point is loud. Every point ‌she wins, it feels like she’s won more than a point.” Eala claimed ⁠her first WTA ⁠title with a victory over Jessica Pegula in Washington this month and the 21-year-old’s triumph showed she ‌was worthy of all the attention. “She was outstanding in Washington,” Fernandez said of Eala, who also beat Elina ‌Svitolina and ‌Naomi Osaka en route to the title. “Her game is really good. She backs ‌it up. “She’s improved tremendously … She’s getting better and better.” Now ranked 18th in the world, ⁠Eala is the highest-ranked Filipino and Southeast Asian player in WTA history, and her ⁠rise presents an opportunity for the WTA to build interest in the Philippines and among its large global diaspora, Fernandez said. Fellow ESPN commentator Patrick McEnroe ‌said US Open organisers ‌should ensure Eala gets time on one of the tournament’s larger courts. “The USTA better make sure they put her on big courts,” McEnroe said. “I think the crowd is going to be wild for her. It’s going to be a great story.”

title: BYD posts US$1.2 billion profit in second quarter on surging global demand
description: The Chinese EV giant beat market estimates in the second quarter, as booming exports helped offset a prolonged decline in the domestic market.
content: China’s electric vehicle (EV) giant BYD saw its earnings jump 30 per cent in the three months from April to June, ending a five-quarter losing streak as buoyant overseas sales and premium models enhanced its net margin and profitability. The Shenzhen-based carmaker, also the world’s largest EV builder, posted a net income of 8.2 billion yuan (US$1.2 billion) in the second quarter, up 30 per cent year on year. The quarterly performance beat a consensus estimate of 8 billion yuan in a Bloomberg survey of analysts. Revenue dipped 3 per cent to 194.6 billion yuan. The second-quarter data was derived by comparing figures in its interim earnings report, published on Friday, with its first-quarter results, according to its Hong Kong stock exchange filings. “BYD’s quarterly profit would boost the Chinese auto industry’s confidence despite weak sales at home,” said Ivan Li, a researcher at Loyal Wealth Management in Shanghai. “They could increase sales abroad, banking on their technological and production strength.” From April to June, BYD recorded sales of 471,091 vehicles outside mainland China, up 82.5 per cent year on year. On the mainland, carmakers’ average net profit margin per vehicle is only about 5,000 yuan (US$744), according to Nick Lai, head of auto research for Asia-Pacific at JPMorgan. But the margin in overseas markets could be four times higher at 20,000 yuan, as Chinese cars are often sold at higher prices abroad, he added. For the first half of 2026, BYD reported its first interim earnings drop in six years, as the firm’s strong second-quarter performance failed to offset a big fall in the preceding three months. Net profit for the first half of the year reached 12.3 billion yuan, down 20.5 per cent from a year ago. Revenue fell 7.1 per cent to 344.8 billion yuan. BYD said the profit decline resulted from weaker domestic demand and higher raw material costs, which outweighed a 67.8 per cent surge in overseas sales. “Consumers remained cautious about automobile purchases,” BYD said in the report. “Sustained price increases in bulk commodities, raw materials and chips further squeezed the profit margins of carmakers, testing the overall industry profitability.” BYD’s first-half car sales worldwide slumped 15.7 per cent to 1.81 million units. Buoyed by technological advances and pricing advantages, Chinese-developed EVs have reported sizzling overseas sales this year, but higher revenues abroad were still not enough to help most of China’s carmakers generate a net profit. Among the nearly 30 Chinese carmakers that only make EVs, only BYD and Stellantis-backed Leapmotor were profitable in the first half of the year. Their counterparts struggled to break even, battered by high research and development costs and price competition that ate into their profit margins. EV deliveries in China dropped 3.9 per cent to 951,000 units in July, data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed, extending their decline to a seventh consecutive month amid fading government incentives and weaker consumer demand. During the first seven months of 2026, Chinese carmakers handed over a total of 5.67 million EVs – comprising pure electric and plug-in hybrid cars – to domestic customers, down 12.5 per cent from a year earlier, the industry consortium added.

title: The ‘Asian water tower’ is starting to wobble, computer simulations show
description: The Tibetan Plateau is losing stability, a study suggests, as a catastrophic flash flood hit on the Nepal-China border.
content: “Asia’s water tower” is heading towards a more unpredictable and unstable future, according to a new study measuring the Tibetan Plateau’s stability. The study, published on August 21 in Nature Communications, examined the entropy of the region to gauge how much chaos or disorder was building up in a complex system. The results were released just days before a catastrophic flash flood struck the Nepal-China border, killing hundreds and leaving a trail of devastation along the way. Chen Xiaosong, a physicist at the school of systems science at Beijing Normal University and lead author of the study, said on Thursday that from now to the end of this century, “the increase of soil water and the intensification of glacier melting [in the Tibetan Plateau] will constantly trigger such geological disasters”. Countries along the Himalayas could also face greater risks. “India will definitely be affected, but the specific impacts still require further analysis and research,” he added. Chen’s team examined the plateau’s soil moisture system from 2000 to 2024, which is closely linked to the water and climate patterns affecting nearly two billion people across South and East Asia. The researchers found that the plateau became more stable as it became wetter. “Our analysis found that entropy declined while soil moisture increased and the plateau became wetter.” But that trend is projected to reverse. “From 2025 to 2100, entropy starts to rise and the system becomes more disordered,” said Xie Yiran, the study’s first author. The projected rise in entropy is accompanied by declining soil moisture, weaker hydrological buffering and stronger regional contrasts. Lower entropy means soil-moisture variability is concentrated in a few coherent patterns, while higher entropy means it is spread across more competing patterns and the system becomes more disordered. “Traditional methods treat entropy as a core quantity, but it is difficult to calculate the entropy of complex systems directly,” Chen said. “Our entropy method can describe the overall properties and collective behaviour of a complex system and can even serve as an early-warning signal.” Xie said the approach differed from conventional climate indicators because “it does not look at a single location or the average of the whole region, but at how different parts of the system coordinate with one another”. From 2000 to 2024, soil moisture across the plateau increased significantly, with about 57.5 per cent of the region showing significant wetting and only 8.1 per cent showing significant drying. Over the same period, soil-moisture entropy declined significantly, indicating that the system became more organised, with the decline accelerating after about 2018 as the plateau became wetter. But the model predicts that the plateau’s present wetting-driven buffer may not last under continued warming by the end of this century. The study’s implications extend beyond the plateau because changes in its soil moisture can influence the South Asian monsoon, downstream river basins and extreme precipitation, while major river systems across South and East Asia support nearly two billion people. The system is also influenced by El Nino and La Nina, with Tibetan Plateau soil-moisture entropy lagging El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) entropy by about six months. ENSO is a climate cycle with two opposite phases: El Nino, the warm phase marked by above-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific, and La Nina, the cool phase marked by below-average temperatures in the same region. Recent strong ENSO events can therefore have delayed effects on the Tibetan Plateau and surrounding regions, with the soil-moisture response lagging the climate signal by about six months. During El Nino, shifts in the Walker circulation trigger atmospheric anomalies that alter moisture transport across the plateau, changing regional precipitation and soil-moisture differences. The Walker circulation is a large-scale atmospheric overturning cell over the equatorial Pacific. “The result is a ‘see-saw’ between the western and southwestern Tibetan Plateau, with stronger regional contrasts associated with higher entropy,” Xie added. The researchers found that precipitation is the main driver of this spatial contrast, with snowfall and spring melt particularly important in the west and monsoonal rainfall dominating the southwest. The six-month lag reflects the accumulated response of the hydrological system, as soil moisture responds to precipitation after about one month while snowmelt and seasonal freeze-thaw processes can delay the signal further. The ensemble showed a significant breakpoint around 2052, after which the dominant soil-moisture mode declined at more than twice its previous rate and the contrast between western and southwestern regions increased sharply. The authors therefore describe the result as a heightened risk of instability in a complex system rather than proof of an inevitable tipping point.

title: Hong Kong authorities to get tough on careless dog owners during special operations
description: Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department also says it seized fighting dog in Stanley earlier this week and may prosecute owner.
content: Hong Kong authorities will take enforcement action against dog owners who fail to keep their pets under control during special operations taking place on Sunday and the following weekend in response to a spate of canine attacks. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) also said on Friday that it seized a fighting dog at a restaurant in Stanley two days earlier after conducting an inspection in response to a complaint. It said that it would prosecute the owner if there was sufficient evidence of wrongdoing. The AFCD added that it would conduct special operations on Sunday and the following weekend. “During the special operations, [department] officers will step up inspections and enforcement at public places where dogs congregate,” a spokesman said. “If dog keepers are found not to have properly controlled their dogs in accordance with the legal requirements, the [department] will take immediate enforcement action without warning in advance.” Under the Rabies Ordinance, it is an offence to leave a dog unleashed in public areas or at any place from which it may wander into a public space. Offenders can be fined HK$10,000 (US$1,275) upon conviction. The department also confirmed it had seized a fighting dog after the owner wrote on social media that authorities had taken the 10-year-old canine. He also claimed that the animal did not legally count as dangerous. Under Hong Kong law, pit bull terriers, dogo Argentino, Japanese Tosa, fila Brasileiro and their crossbreeds are classified as fighting dogs. In a Facebook post, the AFCD said: “The department’s vet identified and confirmed the dog as a pit bull terrier, a classified fighting dog. To safeguard public safety, the vet conducted an observation and temperament assessment of the dog and confirmed it could be returned to the owner after being neutered. “The department is investigating the case. If there is sufficient evidence of a legal breach, it will initiate prosecution.” The department added that it had instructed the owner to arrange for the animal to be sterilised under its supervision and undergo training. The Dangerous Dogs Regulation states that fighting canines must be neutered by a registered veterinary surgeon. Owners are also required to obtain a valid desexing certificate. Fighting dogs must be securely muzzled and held on a leash not longer than 1.5 metres (feet) at all times in public places, in addition to wearing special collars. Under the same regulation, any dogs weighing no less than 20kg must be secured in public with a leash of up to two metres. Anyone who fails to comply faces a maximum penalty of three months in prison and a HK$25,000 fine. On Wednesday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu promised to review laws governing dangerous dogs and the related penalties in response to the string of dog attacks. Only a week before Lee made the pledge, the 33-year-old owner of a pet training facility was mauled by a mixed-breed fighting dog registered as a mongrel. She was discovered dead nearby shortly after the attack. Earlier that same week, a 60kg mixed-breed dog killed a miniature poodle and a bichon frise in separate attacks near Yoho Mall in Yuen Long. Two further attacks were reported this week. The attacks took place as authorities push to make the city more dog-friendly. From July 9, canines were allowed to enter restaurants holding a relevant licence under a government scheme. More than 980 restaurants held the dog-friendly venue licence as of early August.

title: China moves to stabilise property sector with ‘stronger-than-expected’ policy package
description: The measures aim to shift China’s vast property sector away from a presales model, as Beijing strives to stabilise market downturn.
content: Beijing has unveiled a package of measures to shift home sales in China’s vast property market away from a presales model, in a stronger-than-expected push to stabilise a property downturn that has weighed on consumer demand for years. A notice released on Friday laid out reforms to China’s home sales system, telling local governments to prioritise completed-home sales. It was jointly issued by the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, the Ministry of Natural Resources and the National Financial Regulatory Administration (NFRA). Two other documents released the same day dealt with property sector financing. The central bank and the NFRA set out new rules on development loans, while the securities regulator said it would support listed developers in mergers and restructurings. “The policies announced today are stronger than what the market expected,” said Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management. China’s sluggish domestic demand was “to a large extent” caused by the troubled property sector, he said, adding that the measures suggested policymakers recognised the urgent need to stabilise the market. The housing notice called for the “vigorous and orderly” roll-out of completed-home sales. Projects on newly transferred land, as well as those on land already sold but without a construction planning permit, should prioritise the completed-home sales model, it said. Projects already holding permits were also encouraged to adopt it. Presales will remain, but under tighter rules. Where they continue, individual buildings must be topped out before units can be sold, and buyers’ down payments, mortgage proceeds and other purchase funds must all be placed in supervised accounts. To help developers deal with the funding pressures that come with the shift to completed-home sales, the notice also called for greater financing support and a lead-bank system for property projects, with one bank designated for each project to provide development loans or lead a lending syndicate. The central bank and the NFRA set out the terms, requiring development loans to match a project’s construction and sales cycle and to run no longer than five years for presale projects and seven years for completed-home and commercial projects. Mortgage loans will also be released later under the new rules: after a sale is registered for completed homes, and only after a project is registered as complete for pre-sold ones. Buyers would “get the home first, then repay the loan”, a central bank official said in comments published alongside the document. The maximum mortgage term was extended to 40 years from 30. The housing notice further told local governments to shorten approval times and roll out a “certificate on handover” system, ensuring homebuyers get their ownership papers the day they move in. Chinese developers saw their share prices rise in Hong Kong on Friday. China Vanke closed 2.5 per cent higher at HK$2.49, Country Garden 2.6 per cent higher and Yuexiu Property 2.2 per cent higher, while Sunac China Holdings jumped 10.7 per cent.

title: Unmanned electric aircraft makes maiden flight in Hong Kong
description: Flight marks collaboration between mainland Chinese firm EHang, local transport operator Kwoon Chung Bus Holdings and tech hub Cyberport.
content: An unmanned electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft made its maiden demonstration flight in Hong Kong on Friday, as the city pushes to develop a low-altitude economy, with the government aiming to complete drafting relevant legislation by 2027. The flight marked a collaboration between mainland Chinese autonomous aerial vehicle firm EHang, local transport operator Kwoon Chung Bus Holdings and the city’s technology hub, Cyberport. The flight took place at Cyberport in Pok Fu Lam. Kwoon Chung, which earlier revealed plans to buy 30 eVTOLs from EHang for more than HK$70 million (US$9 million), intends to deploy some of them for passenger and logistics services in Hong Kong. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said Hong Kong boasted a common law system and civil aviation regulatory standards that were fully aligned with international standards.” “Mainland low-altitude enterprises conducting risk assessment flights in complex airspace within the city’s ‘Regulatory Sandbox X’ for the low-altitude economy can generate data and regulatory experience that can be directly translated into templates applicable worldwide,” she said. A regulatory sandbox is a space where software or new technology can be tried out in a pilot scheme or test environment. EHang’s flagship model, the EH216-S, carried a robot and conducted multiple sorties along predetermined routes, with public demonstrations set to continue until Sunday. Chan said the successful flight marked “a key step” towards eVTOLs operating in Hong Kong. She added that the government was collecting data through the regulatory sandbox to draft relevant civil aviation legislation for non-traditional aircraft, such as eVTOLs weighing more than 150kg. “[The government] aims to complete the drafting of this legislation by 2027, thereby laying a solid safety foundation for the future commercialisation of passenger transport and the realisation of the Greater Bay Area air corridor,” she said. The three parties signed a memorandum of understanding in 2024 to leverage their respective expertise to advance research and applications in Hong Kong of eVTOL aircraft, which was selected as one of the government’s Sandbox X pilot projects in April. Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun, who leads a working group on developing the low-altitude economy, said more than 140 projects had become permanent since the sandbox scheme launched in March last year. Wong said commercialisation of such projects was under way, covering areas including infrastructure surveys, the hoisting of materials, building monitoring and management, and the cleaning of external walls. EHang chief operating officer Zhao Wang said the first public flight of the EH216-S in Hong Kong marked a “vital validation” under the sandbox model, serving as a practical test of the company’s technical standards and safety systems within the city’s regulatory framework. The low-altitude economy refers to economic activities in airspace below 1,000 metres (3,281 feet), including goods delivered by drones and passenger flights using eVTOL aircraft.

title: Fifa was bashed for 2-year World Cup idea but could it solve netball’s existential crisis?
description: Hong Kong set to end 24-year wait to compete in global tournament but some in sport fear overexposure will water down flagship product.
content: When he began banging the drum for the football World Cup to be staged every two years, Arsene Wenger was taken aback by the “emotional” response to his proposal. The chief of global football development for Fifa, Wenger was rounded on by fans’ groups, coaches and European governing body Uefa, whose president, Aleksander Ceferin, related “grave concerns” over a plan that risked “diluting” the competition. Noises over holding a biennial finals have quietened amid a shift to vaster, overblown World Cups, with a very real possibility that 64 teams could play in the 2030 edition. Still, the monolithic football beast time and again proves that it can withstand the worst excesses of its more grasping administrators. Other less popular sports are condemned to existing in existential crises. In its quest to futureproof a sport that inhabits an “increasingly complex landscape”, netball borrowed from Wenger’s playbook and has chosen to stage a World Cup every two years instead of every four from 2027. On the face of it, World Netball’s decision has its merits. The Commonwealth Games, which every four years provides the platform for one of netball’s marquee tournaments, is seemingly withering on the vine, while the sport is engaged in an ongoing battle for Olympic Games inclusion. “These decisions allow us to control our destiny, and it’s positive news for everyone,” Fiona Harold, the World Netball CEO, said following last year’s announcement. “As the international federation, it is our job to sustain and grow the game over the long term.” Nonetheless, there are respected netball folk who believe overexposing the sport’s flagship product is short-sighted, threatens to create a closed shop of elite teams, and is reflective of administrators who are asleep at the wheel. Hong Kong will end a 24-year wait to compete in the global tournament next year, after reaching the final of their home Asian Championships this month. There are fears inside the local association over familiarity breeding contempt, according to sources, and those are shared elsewhere. Alison Akinrinlola is an expert on all things netball, a sport she calls a “sleeping giant”. A former England player, she was the brains behind Netball Aid, the charity match set for its second edition this year after attracting more than 5,000 fans and generating 6 million social media views for its 2025 launch. In 2024, Akinrinlola co-founded Birmingham Panthers, the franchise in England’s Netball Super League that last year sold a significant stake to Knighthead Capital Management, the billionaire firm that, along with American Football great Tom Brady, owns Birmingham City Football Club. More recently, Akinrinlola was appointed head coach of Nigeria, after the African country relaunched its national team with a view to claiming a podium finish at the 2030 Commonwealth Games. “The finances don’t exist for a World Cup every two years,” Akinrinlola told the South China Morning Post. “Without big sponsors, Nigeria can’t afford to go to a World Cup every two years. Teams will drop out, and you’ll end up making it more exclusive.” Concerns abound at the sport’s summit, too. With twin daughters, Tori and Mali, who last year played for Jamaica in the Netball World Youth Cup, Akinrinlola is aware that the world’s No 4 nation is financially stretched. “They’re trying to get the funds together for the Horizon Series [in England in November], after being in Scotland for the Commonwealth Games [where they claimed silver], and there’s a World Cup next year,” Akinrinlola said. “I know the struggles that are there. A World Cup every four years gives you time to plan, prepare and save.” Hong Kong typically have to scratch around for competitive matches, given the sport’s puzzling absence from the Asian Games, and the city team’s ineligibility for the Commonwealth Games and Southeast Asian Games. With minimal help from elsewhere, Hong Kong, China Netball got proactive in initiating the East Asian Cup last year, while a camp in Perth allowed players concerted preparation for the recent Asian Championships, where a thrilling semi-final victory over Malaysia sealed that World Cup passage. “We felt privileged to have that opportunity, in Perth,” key player Zenia Wong said. “We usually juggle so much, but it was just netball. The competition was on a different level and we learned how to recover and play day in, day out.” Hong Kong’s recent success has already engendered a demonstrable uptick in netball interest in the city. For next month’s two-day Netfest event, the curtain raiser for the new campaign, 50 junior teams have already registered, compared with the 25 that competed 12 months ago. “Netball’s a sleeping giant,” Akinrinlola said. “If I were in charge of World Netball, I’d be asking, ‘what do you need to get netball off the ground in Nigeria [and other smaller nations]?’. Give us courts, posts and equipment, then everything else will fall into place.” Also the founder of AP Saints, who are in the English third tier and boast a comprehensive youth programme, after beginning with seven girls 17 years ago, Akinrinlola staged Netball Aid at seven weeks’ notice last year. Featuring a number of celebrities in the image of Soccer Aid, including one unnamed star she said would single-handedly sell out Birmingham’s 15,600-capacity Utilita Arena, it will return in November. Along with needing intangible qualities such as bravery and passion, converting netball’s huge participation numbers into fandom and commercial growth required “getting in front of people so they buy into your vision”, Akinrinlola said. “I’ve always been more successful speaking to people,” she said. “Netball is a long-term investment; we’re not quite there yet, because we haven’t got the right people behind the sport. “We need commercial people in those governing bodies. We need people in the governing bodies who love people.” Netball’s first failed attempt to join the Olympic movement came way back in 1967. It is pushing hard to be included in Brisbane in 2032, and by the end of last year, World Netball’s “Back the Bid” petition had gathered more than 115,000 signatures. Nonetheless, Akinrinlola feels the sport is still not sufficiently inclusive, given its low profile in English state schools. In Hong Kong, netball is prominent in English Schools Foundation institutions and international schools, but is included on the PE curriculums of only around 20 local primary and secondary schools More positively, Akinrinlola believes the introduction of a men’s netball World Cup from 2029 will aid the sport’s Olympic quest. “I don’t know if getting into the Olympics will make a difference to the grass roots,” Akinrinlola said. “Right now, there’s not enough of a foundation for netball to build on to where we want it to go. I think that goes back to who’s playing, and it not being inclusive enough.”

title: China strips former generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli of top military positions
description: Zhang and Liu have been under investigation since January for alleged failures of discipline.
content: Beijing has formally removed former senior officers Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli as members of China’s supreme military command. The two generals have been under investigation for alleged discipline violations since January and were officially stripped of their positions on the Central Military Commission (CMC) at a meeting of the National People’s Congress’ Standing Committee on Friday. As the CMC’s senior vice-chairman, Zhang was the highest-ranking uniformed officer in the Chinese military. Liu was chief of the CMC’s Joint Staff Department. Zhong Shaojun, the former director of the CMC’s General Office, and Ju Qiansheng, the former commander of the PLA’s Strategic Support Force, were also removed from their positions. The announcement was the first sign that the pair may be investigated for possible corruption. A commentary by the PLA Daily in January said Zhang and Liu had betrayed the trust of the Communist Party and undermined the party’s absolute control of the military as well as the reputation of the armed forces. Both Zhang and Liu are decorated veterans and took part in People’s Liberation Army campaigns against Vietnam in the late 1970s. Their sudden downfall left the country’s top military command with only two members, Chinese President Xi Jinping and vice-chairman Zhang Shengmin, who is in charge of disciplinary affairs within the armed forces. It also sends a stark message about Xi’s zero tolerance for lapses in party discipline and political purity. In a separate case, Jiang Chaoliang, former banker and Hubei’s party chief during the initial Covid-19 outbreak, received a suspended death sentence for corruption on Friday. He accepted more than 746 million yuan (US$111 million) in bribes, state news agency Xinhua reported.

title: Uzbekistan tests US-China AI rift with bid to join rival tech bloc
description: Tashkent eyes Pax Silica entry as Central Asian nations resist growing pressure to choose between Washington and Beijing in the AI race.
content: The Central Asian country of Uzbekistan has approached the United States about joining Pax Silica, Washington’s flagship initiative on artificial intelligence (AI) supply chains, a month after signing up for China’s own global grouping, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Uzbekistan’s ambassador to the US, Furqat Sidikov, said Tashkent had formally notified the US State Department in a diplomatic note last week requesting to join the US-led initiative. “Now, the US should confirm. We are ready to sign,” he said in Washington on Thursday. Sidikov added that countries should have a “chance to be part of any kind of international cooperation”, and that drawing red lines around participation would be “counterproductive”. “This gives us opportunities, and it’s good competition,” he said. In an email response to the South China Morning Post on Saturday, the State Department said it would not comment on “private diplomatic discussions” but welcomed the “growing interest” in the initiative. “We welcome growing interest in the pro-growth principles reflected in Pax Silica and the AI Opportunity Statement, including support for innovation, private-sector-led development, and a secure and resilient global technology ecosystem,” a State Department spokesperson said. The developments come as countries face growing pressure to choose between Washington and Beijing in the race for AI dominance, with both powers promoting competing visions to shape the technology’s standards, supply chains and strategic partnerships. Kazakhstan, also in Central Asia, is the only nation so far with membership in both Pax Silica and Waico. Reuters reported on August 14 that Washington planned to warn partners they could not join both Pax Silica and China’s rival AI framework, citing an internal draft. Earlier this month, a US State Department official told the SCMP that Washington was “actively engaging with global partners to advance responsible, pro-innovation, pro-growth AI development, both bilaterally and through multilateral forums”. The 24-member Pax Silica aims to build AI supply chains independent of China, covering critical minerals, semiconductors and logistics. While the programme does not explicitly target China, one of its key objectives is to reduce “coercive dependencies” – a phrase widely understood to mean Chinese dominance in rare earths and other minerals essential to semiconductor production. Pax Silica architect Jacob Helberg, who serves as US undersecretary of state for economic affairs, said last month that while China had pursued a state-led approach, the US and its allies were leveraging “incredible companies that build transformative products that people really love”. “We realise that the US government is not set up in a way to compete with the Chinese tit-for-tat on that same basis,” Helberg told the SCMP in an exclusive interview. “We decided to lean into that strength and leverage the innovative, creative capacity and dynamism of our private sector,” he said. Waico, which describes its mission as advancing “AI for good and for all”, was launched by Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shanghai last month during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, with 29 founding members. The grouping has since expanded, adding nine more members. Xi called it a “major move by China to answer the call of the Global South and unite the international community together to promote vigorously AI development and governance”. “It will be an important milestone in the history of AI development,” he added. Uzbekistan has large reserves of gold, copper, uranium, tungsten and molybdenum. Officials say new mines and processing plants could produce up to 28 types of critical minerals, including rare earths and rare metals. The country has also made a US$4.2 billion minerals programme a key part of its industrial policy through 2030. American tech companies offer cutting-edge AI chips and AI models. China, in turn, offers open-source models that are significantly cheaper than American ones. And we would like to have access to both Bobur Khodjaev, Uzbek official China already has a strong presence in Uzbekistan, with foreign direct investment reaching about US$10.7 billion as of the middle of last year, according to the Eurasian Development Bank. China’s pipeline of projects in the country spans energy, mining and potential data centres, and its proximity to Central Asia makes it a difficult partner to displace. US President Donald Trump’s administration is seeking a bigger role in the region. In February, the US and Uzbekistan signed an agreement on critical minerals and rare earths, which was followed by a Development Finance Corporation (DFC) investment framework and a proposed joint holding company. For Washington, dual membership in Waico and Pax Silica clashes with the latter’s mandate, which aims to keep critical minerals, processing and transit routes inside a trusted, China-free chain. Middle powers see the opposite challenge. They cannot build a full AI stack alone, and they do not want to treat AI as a loyalty test. “As a developing country, we want to have access to all available technologies,” said Bobur Khodjaev, an aide with Uzbekistan’s presidential administration, speaking at the Silk Road Finance and Technology Forum in Tashkent this week. “American tech companies offer cutting-edge AI chips and AI models. China, in turn, offers open-source models that are significantly cheaper than American ones. And we would like to have access to both,” he added. Ken Moriyasu, senior fellow at the Washington-based Hudson Institute, said it was “unrealistic” to expect countries such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to make an “exclusive geopolitical choice between American and Chinese technology”. “Their entire foreign policy is built around avoiding precisely that kind of dependence,” he said, stressing that Washington must find a way to protect “genuinely sensitive” technologies without turning technological safeguards into a geopolitical loyalty test. Moriyasu contended that the larger strategic objective was not to make Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan choose America. “It is to make sure they always have a choice – and that they never have to choose China exclusively,” he said. Kazakhstan is the live test, and the region is watching. The country “shares an enormous border with China. No government in Astana can pursue a serious strategy based on excluding Beijing,” Moriyasu said. Political scientist Zamir Karazhanov told The Times of Central Asia that Astana was “probably closer to the Chinese approach at the moment” on open source and keeping AI out of bloc politics. “Kazakhstan also does not want AI to be used as an instrument of politics, and on this point, we agree with China,” he said. “I think an attempt to pressure Kazakhstan would be unsuccessful,” he said, adding that Washington could not easily squeeze a country that held minerals it needed. Indonesia is running a parallel hedge. While the country has signed on to Waico, Indonesian Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto has insisted Jakarta is still “involved in the development of Pax Silica” and that the two groupings “should not be pitted against each other”. Malaysia is also a founding member of Waico, despite its deep US semiconductor ties. A Chatham House paper on sovereign AI from February argued that middle powers could not match the US or China in capital, computing power or talent, so they must choose where to compete, where to partner and where to accept dependence. “The critical question is not whether to depend on other nations for AI, but on which nations, to what extent and on what terms,” it said.

title: China’s radar satellites capture sharp images of glacier collapse site in Nepal
description: Swift commercial response highlights how Chinese space surveillance capabilities are expanding beyond military and government circles.
content: Within hours of a devastating glacier collapse on the China-Nepal border, a Beijing-based satellite company had already redirected six of its satellites to survey the disaster zone. The high-resolution radar images they captured revealed a massive collapse site near a remote mountain pass. Unlike optical sensors, radar signals can pierce through haze and cloud, mapping terrain changes with high precision even in the rugged Himalayan plateau. The swift commercial response also underscores a broader trend: China’s space surveillance capabilities are rapidly expanding beyond military and government circles to private enterprises that can operate with greater flexibility and transparency. The disaster struck on Wednesday, when a large section of glacier on the Nepal side broke away – triggering a massive rock and ice avalanche that unleashed deadly flash floods downhill. The surge devastated communities along the China-Nepal border and beyond, leaving more than 400 people dead and over a thousand missing across both nations. It also caused severe damage to the Gyirong Port border checkpoint in Shigatse, in China’s western Tibet region. In the immediate aftermath of the disaster, Beijing Minospace Technology activated its “Dongpo” satellite constellation – built in partnership with state-owned commercial aerospace firm Huantian Intelligence – to image the affected area. According to a company representative, the Dongpo-11 satellite provides 0.5-metre (1.6-foot) high-resolution optical imagery, while the Dongpo-15 to 19 are all metre-class synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites capable of continuous, round-the-clock monitoring in any weather. By combining optical and SAR observations, the constellation was able to see through the region’s persistent cloud cover and challenging topography, delivering precise data on terrain shifts at the collapse site. The company told the South China Morning Post that satellite imagery captured before and after the disaster was submitted on Thursday through the National Earth Observation Science Data Centre, where experts were analysing the materials.

title: China’s chip supply chain ‘safer’ as self-sufficiency push gains traction, says top planner
description: Beijing will leverage its ‘whole nation’ approach under the 15th five-year plan to achieve breakthroughs in core technologies, official says.
content: China’s semiconductor supply chain was much “safer”, the country’s top economic planner said on Friday, signalling progress in the country’s chip self-sufficiency drive amid mounting pressure from US export controls. The supply chain security of the domestic chip industry had “significantly improved” this year, with home-grown chipmaking equipment and materials growing steadily, marking a transition from “isolated technological breakthroughs” to “full-chain industrial synergy”, Li Chao, spokeswoman for the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), said at a press briefing on Friday. Beijing would leverage its “whole nation” approach under the 15th five-year plan – covering 2026 to 2030 – to achieve decisive breakthroughs in core technologies, Li said. The latest claim from Beijing underscores the country’s accelerated efforts for chip self-sufficiency, as it seeks to cushion its tech sector against expanding US export controls. In the latest move, Washington is mulling new restrictions on Chinese tech imports, including a proposed prohibition on the sale of cars with connected-vehicle technology linked to China and a ban on imports of Chinese humanoid robots and power inverters. Chinese chip companies are riding a historic wave of artificial intelligence hardware demand amid an agentic AI frenzy. China’s integrated circuit exports nearly doubled in the first seven months to US$216 billion, according to official data unveiled earlier this month. Li also attributed the boom to China’s breakthroughs in sectors including power semiconductors, compound semiconductors, advanced packaging technologies and memory chips, as the country sees capacity utilisation rates at domestic foundries exceed 90 per cent. Globally, the semiconductor industry is also experiencing a surge in demand for AI chips. Driven by the intense need for memory, bandwidth and power in data centres, global shipments of AI application-specific integrated circuits were expected to reach 10.5 million units in 2028, edging out the forecast for 10.1 million general-purpose graphics processing units, according to a report last week by research firm Omdia. Despite the aggressive push into frontier technologies, the state agency warned of a potential bubble in the booming robotics and embodied AI sectors. Cautioning domestic players against “blindly following trends”, Li stressed that robotics development needed to remain “orderly and healthy” and “rooted in local strengths”. To ensure sustained growth, NDRC said it would focus on practical deployment by establishing physical training grounds and pilot testing bases. These facilities aimed to resolve the industry’s bottlenecks, including “data hunger”, by constructing high-quality real-world data collection systems, according to Li.

title: 2 dead in school attack near Berlin
description: A 19-year-old German man was detained and is being held in police custody.
content: One of the two people killed in an attack at a school near Berlin was a 30-year-old nursery worker, police said on Friday. It had previously been reported that the man who was killed in Thursday’s attack was the caretaker. A woman and a man were killed in the violent incident at a school in the small community of Gosen-Neu Zittau on the southeastern edge of the German capital. The school site houses a primary and secondary school, as well as a nursery. A 19-year-old German man was detained and is being held in police custody. According to media reports, the woman is believed to have been the suspect’s ex-girlfriend. The police said the crime was linked to a relationship and confirmed that the woman was aged 18. Hours after the incident, police were leading pupils and parents out of the school playground, with some in tears. Emergency counsellors were at the scene to provide support to pupils, teaching staff and relatives. Some were still in the sports hall late in the afternoon; they were provided with drinks and later collected by their parents. A police spokesman said some pupils might still be interviewed. In the evening, around 100 children and adults gathered with flowers and candles for a memorial service. Most of the attendees still looked shocked and people wept. Some laid down soft toys, others embraced. The attack occurred on the campus of a privately run school surrounded by woodland and lakes on the outskirts of Gosen-Neu Zittau, a small town of around 3,500 residents in eastern Brandenburg, on the border with Berlin. The Docemus campus houses a grammar school, a secondary school and a technical college, at a site designed to promote shared learning and emphasises flexibility between the different kinds of school.

title: Opinion | US and China must team up to keep maritime trade routes free and safe
description: The Strait of Hormuz crisis shows neither state benefits when key waterways can become instruments of political pressure or economic coercion.
content: With the end of the 60-day US-Iran memorandum of understanding, tensions in the Strait of Hormuz have flared again. The crisis in the strait highlights how the security and stability of key international waterways are becoming an increasingly urgent global concern. Over the past decade, major maritime routes have been affected by regional armed conflicts, geopolitical tensions and growing security risks. These disruptions have exposed a vulnerability in the global trading system: a key international waterway need not be formally “blocked” for shipping to become constrained. A strategic international strait may remain legally “open” while ships face military threats, attacks, higher insurance premiums, sanctions-related risks, forced re-routing or arbitrary conditions for passage. In such circumstances, the question is no longer simply whether the waterway is “open” or “closed”, but whether ships can pass through it safely, predictably and at a reasonable cost. This distinction matters significantly to both China and the United States. Global trade and energy transport depend on a limited number of key waterways, particularly the English Channel, Strait of Malacca, Strait of Hormuz, Panama Canal and Suez Canal. Disruption in any of these chokepoints can quickly spread through global markets by raising freight and insurance costs, delaying supply chains and driving up energy prices. China is particularly dependent on maritime transport for its trade and energy supplies. The Strait of Malacca is a major gateway for China’s trade with the Middle East, Africa and Europe, while the Strait of Hormuz is critical to energy flows. That is why China keeps emphasising that, for the Strait of Hormuz, “ensuring unimpeded passage serves the common interest of the international community”. The US is also deeply embedded in the global maritime system. Although its energy structure and trade patterns differ from China’s, disruptions to key international waterways impose economic costs too, while increasing the resources Washington must devote to protecting global maritime security. For both China and the US, the continued availability of key international waterways is not merely a regional security issue. It is a basic condition for a functioning global economy. The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz suggests that the traditional distinction between an “open” and a “closed” waterway may no longer be sufficient. A key international waterway can remain formally “open” while becoming increasingly difficult or expensive to use. Military threats can deter commercial vessels. Armed attacks can force ships to seek alternative routes. Sanctions and compliance risks can make certain voyages commercially unattractive. Higher insurance premiums can have a similar effect. More worrying is the possibility that political or military non-state actors like the Houthis may attempt to impose explicit conditions on passage, such as fees, permits or selective, even discriminatory restrictions. If such practices become normalised, the principle of free and non-discriminatory passage could gradually be hollowed out without any formal declaration of a “closure” or “blockade”. The Strait of Hormuz illustrates the danger. Recent concerns over possible restrictions and charges for passage have highlighted how quickly a key international waterway can become entangled in a broader political confrontation. The recent Red Sea attacks show another dimension of the problem: non-state armed groups can disrupt international shipping even without exercising formal control over the waterway. These developments should concern both China and the US. Neither state benefits from a world in which key international waterways can become instruments of political pressure or economic coercion, even from a non-state actor like the Houthis. Undoubtedly, China and the US have profound differences over security, geopolitics and the international order. Nevertheless, cooperation to ensure free passage in key international waterways does not require the two states to resolve these broader disputes. There are areas in which their interests overlap: maritime safety, search and rescue, protection of commercial shipping, maritime information sharing, anti-piracy efforts and prevention of marine pollution. These are practical issues with relatively low political sensitivity. In this regard, China’s experience in the Gulf of Aden is particularly relevant. This month, the navy dispatched its 49th escort task force to the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia. Since December 2008, Chinese naval forces have taken part in international anti-piracy operations and escorted thousands of commercial vessels. As a result, over the years, China has accumulated substantial experience in long-distance escort operations and maritime security cooperation. For China and the US, strategic competition should not prevent cooperation where their fundamental interests coincide. Indeed, maintaining the free passage through key international waterways could become a concrete area where the two states can pursue practical cooperation while continuing to disagree on broader global issues. The objective need not be a new bilateral maritime security alliance. Nor should either state seek special “control” over any strategic international waterway. The more modest and realistic goal is to prevent critical maritime chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb from becoming permanently unsafe, prohibitively expensive to use or subject to arbitrary conditions set by coastal states like Iran and Oman, or armed groups like the Houthis. In an increasingly fragmented international environment, keeping key international waterways open is a shared interest for both China and the US. These two major powers may not agree on many issues concerning the future of the international order, but both have a high stake in ensuring the world’s maritime arteries remain safe, predictable and accessible to commercial shipping. With the leaders of both countries set to meet in Washington next month, this specific common interest deserves greater attention.

title: HKEX Tech 100 adds Pony AI, WeRide in index revamp targeting AI stocks
description: The revision is designed to help the tech index recover from an underwhelming first half by tapping a new generation of Chinese AI firms.
content: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) will add 10 companies – including autonomous-driving firms Pony AI and WeRide – to its Tech 100 Index as part of a quarterly reshuffle that increases the benchmark’s exposure to artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies. Other additions include AI drug-discovery specialist Insilico Medicine, printed-circuit-board maker Victory Giant Technology, enterprise AI company Beijing Haizhi Technology and AI data-intelligence provider Mininglamp Technology. The 10 companies are rounded out by data infrastructure company Shenzhen Xunce Technology, robotics firm OneRobotics (Shenzhen), digital-twin specialist Beijing 51World Digital Twin Technology, and semiconductor player Montage Technology, according to a statement issued by HKEX on Friday. Meanwhile, 14 constituents will be removed from the index, including Alibaba Health Information Technology, Ganfeng Lithium Group, JD Health International, Bilibili and NetEase Cloud Music. The changes will take effect on September 14, according to the statement. The reshuffle follows an overhaul of the Tech 100 methodology announced earlier this month, which HKEX said would broaden the benchmark’s exposure to “emerging technology trends, including opportunities across the AI value chain”. The index, launched last year by HKEX, was designed as a broader gauge of technology to reflect the “depth and diversity” of innovative companies listed on the exchange. It covers 100 large- and mid-cap companies eligible for Southbound Stock Connect – which allows mainland investors to trade Hong Kong-listed stocks – across six themes: AI, biotechnology, electric vehicles and smart driving, information technology, internet and robotics. The revision of the gauge came as investors increasingly questioned whether Hong Kong’s existing technology benchmarks were keeping pace with the rapid emergence of a new generation of Chinese AI companies. The criticism has centred particularly on the Hang Seng Tech Index, whose largest constituents remain established internet and consumer-technology companies even as investor interest has shifted towards AI models, semiconductors, autonomous driving and robotics. The Hang Seng Tech Index, which tracks 30 major tech companies listed in Hong Kong, has fallen 16 per cent so far this year, lagging global peers despite the surge in AI-related stocks. The HKEX Tech 100 Index has dropped 13 per cent this year.

title: Germany jails man, 81, for life over murder of tourist 30 years ago
description: The case remained unsolved for decades. A breakthrough was only achieved after old DNA traces were analysed using new technical methods.
content: An 81-year-old man has been sentenced to life imprisonment in Germany for the murder of an American tourist more than 30 years ago, the presiding judge at Koblenz Regional Court, Rupert Stehlin, announced on Friday. The court also found that the offence was of a particularly serious nature. In doing so, the bench concurred with the unanimous assessments of the prosecution, the representatives of the joint plaintiffs and the defence counsel. The defendant had admitted to the offence in general terms at the start of the trial. The court considers it proven that, in September 1994, the man tied up 24-year-old Amy Lopez, sexually assaulted her and killed her with nine stab wounds. He is alleged to have lured her into a secluded, derelict building. Children playing in the area found the body shortly after the crime. The case remained unsolved for decades. A breakthrough was only achieved after old DNA traces were analysed using new technical methods. These were traced to the 81-year-old, who was subsequently arrested at the end of February 2026 in a care home in the Koblenz area.

title: Why Malaysia’s push for 15 million Muslim tourists is no sure thing
description: With disruption to long-haul flights, Malaysia may not draw more Muslim visitors at the expense of the travel hubs in Dubai and Doha.
content: Malaysia sees an opening in the Gulf travel disruption caused by the Iran war, pitching itself as a Muslim-friendly destination for travellers seeking halal food, prayer facilities and family-focused holidays. But such gains could be limited because the conflict has not only weakened tourism within the Middle East, but also affected long-haul flight routes that Malaysia depends on to draw Muslim tourists, according to analysts. The push comes as the six-month-old war continues to disrupt travel across the Gulf, where Dubai and Doha have long served as major destinations and aviation gateways for travellers moving between Europe, Asia and Africa. “This crisis, this problem … we turn [it] into opportunity,” Mohammad Faisal Abu Suaib Khan, director general of Malaysia’s Islamic Tourism Centre, told This Week in Asia on Thursday. “When the Middle East shuts down, people still want to travel. They still need an option where they can go,” he said, describing Malaysia as a natural substitute because of its established Muslim-friendly tourism ecosystem. Dubai International Airport, the world’s busiest hub for international passengers, handled 31.5 million travellers in the first half of this year, down 31.3 per cent from the same period in 2025, according to Dubai Airports. Aircraft movements fell 32.1 per cent over the same period.
