Flight cancellations, re-routing and soaring jet fuel prices have rippled well beyond the region, with major carriers including Lufthansa, British Airways and Singapore Airlines remaining cautious about restoring some services. On Tuesday, Finnair announced the suspension of Dubai flights for the coming winter season because of continued instability. Dubai Airports CEO Paul Griffiths said passenger volumes had nevertheless been climbing after two months of severe disruption, telling the Associated Press that “the trajectory now is universally positive”. Malaysia has not escaped the fallout. Tourism Minister Tiong King Sing said on Monday that 4,111 scheduled flights to the country were cancelled in the first half because of geopolitical tensions in West Asia, with cancellations rising from just nine in February to 1,419 in June. Seat capacity from West Asia fell from more than 1 million in the first half of last year to 806,532 in the same period this year, including a decline of more than 20 per cent in capacity from Europe routed through West Asian hubs. Closer to home Almost two-thirds of Malaysia’s population is Muslim, with Islam accounting for 63.5 per cent of the population in the country’s 2020 census. Halal food is widely available, while prayer rooms are common in shopping centres, airports and tourist attractions. The country again topped the Mastercard-CrescentRating Global Muslim Travel Index this year, scoring 82 out of 100 and finishing ahead of Indonesia, Turkey and Saudi Arabia, with the latter three tied for second place. There were 196 million Muslim international arrivals worldwide last year, up 11.3 per cent from 2024, with annual expenditure from these travellers forecast to reach US$310 billion by 2030. Malaysia received a record 9.7 million Muslim visitors in 2025 and wants to raise that figure to 15 million by 2030, according to the tourism ministry. But industry data on the diversion of Gulf tourists to the country in recent months is not as clear-cut. Fazal Bahardeen, founder and CEO of Muslim travel consultancy CrescentRating, said there had been “no significant shift of Gulf travellers to Malaysia”. Instead, the disruption is changing how Muslim travellers choose destinations. “Travellers are opting for shorter trips rather than cancelling,” Bahardeen told This Week in Asia. “Proximity now matters as much as price.” Muslim travellers from Asia, excluding those from the Gulf, were increasingly travelling within East Asia and Southeast Asia, he said, with Malaysia picking up travellers who might previously have considered the Gulf or Turkey. That could favour Malaysia in the short term, but the Middle East contributed relatively few – albeit high-spending – tourists to Malaysia, meaning the impact on overall arrivals was likely limited, Bahardeen said. Apart from Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and the Philippines are increasingly competing for Asian Muslim travellers. These “novelty” destinations offered something Malaysia, for all its established Muslim-friendly infrastructure, had to contend with, Bahardeen said. Hub trouble But the bigger risk Malaysia may face is from the decisions of airlines rather than tourists, according to industry experts, who warn that the Middle East conflict could weaken the long-haul connections on which its tourism industry depends. Bahardeen said travellers from Europe, Britain, Africa and the Middle East were heavily reliant on connections through Dubai and Doha to reach Malaysia. His firm’s data showed Doha-Kuala Lumpur was the busiest route logged by international users of the HalalTrip mobile app last year, followed by Dubai-Kuala Lumpur, while Jeddah-Kuala Lumpur ranked fourth. “If the disruption is short term, it favours Malaysia. If prolonged, it does not,” Bahardeen said. The Strait of Hormuz – which carried about a fifth of the world’s oil supply before the war – remains severely disrupted despite US efforts to clear mines and diplomatic attempts to restore normal shipping. Ship-tracking services estimate traffic remains at just 5 to 15 per cent of normal volumes. Malaysia has also been expanding direct links with the Gulf. Last month, Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh Air made Kuala Lumpur its first scheduled destination in Southeast Asia, with three weekly Boeing 787-9 flights. Tourism Malaysia has called Saudi Arabia a “high-yield” market. Aviation analyst Shukor Yusof of Endau Analytics said Malaysia had been popular with Arab Muslim travellers long before the war and would remain so, but cautioned against treating the disruption as a simple contest in which Kuala Lumpur gained at Dubai’s expense. “The situation in the Gulf is not exactly a zero-sum game,” he said. “Malaysia has been a favoured destination for Muslim travellers from the Arab world long before the Iran conflict. This will continue.” Shukor said Malaysia should also look further afield for growth, pointing to Central Asia and Russia as “untapped regions” that Malaysia Airlines and the wider tourism industry could pursue. Malaysia launched the fifth edition of Islamic Tourism Month on Thursday, with a revamped online platform allowing travellers to browse and pay for hotels, tours, spas, restaurants and other Muslim-friendly products in one place. The month-long campaign begins on September 1 and forms part of the country’s Visit Malaysia 2026 drive, bringing tourism businesses, government agencies and communities together to market Muslim-friendly experiences to domestic and international travellers.

title: China and Russia agree to boost competitiveness of Arctic shipping route
description: Economist says appeal is likely to grow as traditional routes, such as the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz, become riskier.
content: China and Russia have signalled their willingness to boost the competitiveness of the Arctic shipping route, which is set to become more important as traditional routes between Asia and Europe remain vulnerable to disruption. Transport Minister Liu Wei and Alexey Likhachev, the director general of Rosatom – the Russian state nuclear company responsible for managing the Northern Sea Route – pledged in a video meeting on Thursday to strengthen cooperation on the route. Liu’s ministry said he expressed hopes that China and Russia would focus on “expanding the scale of shipping … and continuously enhancing the competitiveness of the Arctic shipping route to contribute to the economic and trade development of both countries, as well as the stability of regional logistics supply chains”. Likhachev said Russia was willing to enhance port services for vessels transiting through the route and deepen training for polar crew members, the ministry said. The North Sea Route – spanning Russia’s Arctic coast from the Barents Sea to the Bering Strait – used to be mostly impassable, but the melting of polar ice due to climate change and advances in icebreaker technology are making it more accessible. “Its appeal is likely to grow as traditional routes, such as the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, become riskier,” Alicia Garcia-Herrero, a senior fellow at Bruegel, a think tank based in Brussels, said in a report released on Monday. She is also French investment bank Natixis’ chief Asia-Pacific economist. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz – a vital waterway which in peacetime handled around one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas flows – has largely come to a standstill in the six months since the US-Israeli war on Iran began, prompting governments to re-examine their trade routes and supply networks. Xinhua reported this month that the Arctic route had begun regular commercial operation, with Chinese shipping company Sea Legend launching a weekly summer service connecting China to European ports including the Netherlands’ Rotterdam and Britain’s Felixstowe. It said the route nearly halved the typical 40-day transit time for shipments via the Suez Canal, adding that the service would transport heat-sensitive goods such as energy storage units, power batteries and photovoltaic modules. Garcia-Herrero said that while planned volumes remained relatively small, partly because Arctic vessels would only be a fifth the size of the container ships that passed through the Suez Canal, the service’s fixed schedules and pricing would allow Arctic transits to be integrated into supply chains. Other nations are looking to tap into the Arctic passage too, with South Korea dispatching its first trial container ship to test the route on Saturday. In the long term, China planned to maintain stable operations along the route for four months every year, Xinhua reported.

title: Gong Zizheng, who led China’s planetary defence project, dies at 61
description: Described as warm, generous, unassuming and deeply devoted to his work, Gong was a pioneer of space debris research.
content: Gong Zizheng, a pioneer of space debris research and a key figure in China’s planned asteroid defence mission, has died at 61. A top government adviser and prominent leader in international space debris organisations, Gong died on Saturday after a battle with illness, according to Chinese media reports. No further details were given. On social media, one of Gong’s colleagues at the China Academy of Space Technology remembered him as a prolific scientist deeply devoted to his work, a warm and gentle person, and a generous mentor who readily shared his knowledge and guided younger scholars. A fellow space debris researcher who worked with Gong in his final years said he was devastated to hear the news. “I had known since last October that he was seriously ill and understood how grave his condition was, but never imagined we would lose him so soon,” he said. The researcher described Gong as practical, down-to-earth and unassuming, despite his standing in the field. He recalled meeting Gong for the first time – Gong arrived on a small folding bike and told him that he cycled so much he had worn out several bicycles. Born in December 1964, Gong graduated from the National University of Defence Technology in Changsha with a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1986. He earned a doctorate in explosion mechanics from the Beijing Institute of Technology a decade later. After completing postdoctoral work at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Gong spent time at Caltech and the Carnegie Institution for Science in the United States as a visiting scholar. He joined the China Academy of Space Technology in 2006, where he went on to lead work on protecting spacecraft from orbital debris. He played a key role at that time in drawing up the country’s national blueprint and project guidelines for tackling the problem of space debris. Among the technologies Gong worked on was using lasers to clean up space junk. His team studied how a laser mounted in orbit could repeatedly zap debris to gradually knock it into lower orbits and eventually send the space junk burning into the atmosphere. In 2020, Gong called for China to build a national near-Earth asteroid defence system. The country is now preparing for its first planetary defence mission before 2030, aiming to slam a spacecraft into an asteroid at more than Mach 26 – fast enough to alter its path around the sun or even break it apart. In one of his last known public appearances, Gong gave a popular science lecture to students at a Beijing high school in May 2025, speaking about China’s space programme and encouraging young people to pursue their own dreams of exploring the cosmos.

title: How the Nepal flash flood unleashed a wave of anti-China misinformation
description: Scientists still don’t know what caused the glacier collapse but that hasn’t stopped a torrent of claims about Chinese construction.
content: To scientists, the cause of this week’s deadly flash flood on the border between China and Nepal is clear: a glacier high on the Nepal side of the Himalayan range collapsed, sending catastrophic amounts of water and debris downstream. Initial uncertainty over the cause of the event fuelled a wave of misinformation on social media, some of which pinned the blame for the event on Chinese-built infrastructure in the region. But a war of information over China’s activities in the region continued to brew online even after Beijing and Kathmandu agreed on the scientific analysis. When news of the flood broke, social media users began to speculate whether the cause of the event was natural or the result of human activity, with suggestions that the disaster had originated from the Chinese side of the border. Some posts claimed that the flood was caused by the collapse of a Chinese dam in Tibet, while others blamed it on mega infrastructure projects in the region. The social media account Nepal Correspondence, which claims to be a Nepal-based platform for investigative journalism, said in a post on Wednesday that the flash flood was caused by Chinese construction in the Himalayas. “This is not only a purposeful ecological disaster but is cruel too,” the post read. In another post on the same day, Tunku Varadarajan, an Indian-British journalist, said: “China will be the death of everyone and everything downstream of it. Literally, and metaphorically.” In a preliminary assessment on Wednesday, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said the cause was a sudden release from a Tibetan river that had been blocked by an avalanche, Nepali news portal Republica reported. Another report by the Kathmandu Post on Thursday, citing a technical report from the Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research, also said a flood had entered Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River from the Tibetan side. However, satellite analysis later pointed authorities in Nepal and China – and further abroad – to a glacier collapse in Nepal, rather than Chinese infrastructure, as the cause. The analysis indicated that the glacier collapse occurred on the Nepalese side of the mountains, near the Langtang Lirung peak. Daniel Shugar, an earth scientist and associate professor at the University of Calgary, told The Guardian on Thursday that initial analysis showed a large chunk of ice at 5,200 metres (17,060 feet) above sea level had collapsed vertically, falling around 1.2km (0.74 miles) into the valley floor. “This ice and rock then flowed into a river, turning into the devastating debris flow and flash flood that we see in the CCTV footage at the border,” said Bethan Davies, the chair of glaciology at Newcastle University, told the Science Media Centre on Thursday. That same day, China’s Ministry of Natural Resources confirmed that the deadly mudslide was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal. Some initially believed that the ice-rock avalanche had been caused by an earthquake, as the impact of the avalanche was so strong that it registered on seismographs as a magnitude 5.2 tremor. Brahma Chellaney, an Indian geostrategist and columnist, referred to the earthquake claims in a social media post on Wednesday, saying that a moderate seismic event could trigger a cascading disaster. He also linked the dangers to Chinese construction. “This will renew global attention on China’s folly in persisting with the construction of the world’s largest dam in the middle of the Himalayan seismic zone,” he said, adding that its plan to build the dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in Tibet was a “water bomb in the making”. In another post on Thursday, Chellaney wrote: “It is now clear that the Nepal disaster was caused by a natural trigger … but amplified by Chinese hydrological modifications and infrastructure footprint along the Tibetan side of the border. “In other words, China’s upstream actions did not cause the glacier failure but contributed to the disaster’s severity and cascading impacts downstream.” Scientists are still not sure exactly what triggered the initial glacier collapse, but catastrophic events like this have happened elsewhere in the region, including a glacier collapse and avalanche in India’s Chamoli district in 2021. Shugar told Associated Press on Friday that clearer satellite images indicated the bedrock underneath the glacier might have also collapsed, which could explain the glacier collapse. But that has not prevented a blame game over early warnings. Republica quoted NDRRMA spokeswoman Shanti Mahat as saying the authority only learned about the disaster after the flood had reportedly already swept through Gyirong Port. She said that a lack of timely information on the Tibetan side made it impossible to issue an early warning in Nepal. Parshuram Kaphle, a Nepali journalist, echoed the sentiment in a social media post on Wednesday, saying China had “significantly undermined us”. “By failing to provide early warning of such a massive disaster, we suffered immense loss of human life,” Kaphle wrote. Ouyang Chaojun, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told state broadcaster CCTV that the debris flow was moving at about 40-50 metres per second (131-164 feet per second). “Furthermore, because the debris flow reached the Gyirong border crossing in a very short time – only about 7 minutes – there was no time for evacuation,” he added. Hydrologist Hannah Cloke, a professor at the University of Reading, told the Science Media Centre that high up in the valley near the source of the flood, early warnings were “exceptionally difficult, no matter how advanced the technology”. The centre quoted a number of scientists as saying that while it was not known whether climate change was behind Wednesday’s collapse, warming was exacerbating the risk of catastrophic mountain failures and flooding due to melting glaciers, thawing permafrost, and increased meltwater run-off. “A warming environment can make these kinds of events more common or likely,” Davies said. Ouyang said that following the mudslide, some of the other slopes in the region had become unstable, making monitoring the region essential. Concerns have been raised over a newly formed barrier lake upstream from Gyirong county that was formed by the landslide, which CCTV said on Friday was holding the equivalent of 1,000 Olympic swimming pools of water.

title: Who is Garrett Clark? Meet the Good Good co-founder at the centre of a golf ad controversy
description: Intended as a parody of the film Obsession, the ad was accused of normalising violence against women – and led to Callaway severing ties with the YouTube channel.
content: On August 21, a 56-second advertisement sent shockwaves through the golf world. Promoting the Callaway x Good Good Quantum Driver, the video showed Garrett Clark – co-founder of YouTube channel Good Good – shoving golfer and content creator Alexis Miestowski to the ground before warning her, “Do not touch my new driver.” The backlash was swift, with critics accusing the brand of normalising violence against women. The ad, intended as a parody of the 2026 film Obsession, was rapidly pulled from all platforms. Callaway, one of the world’s largest makers of golf equipment, which approved the ad before it went live, quickly issued an apology. “That approval should never have happened,” Callaway CEO Chip Brewer wrote in a statement. By August 26, Callaway announced it was ending its partnership with Good Good Golf entirely – pledging US$1 million in donations to organisations fighting violence against women. The commercial fallout spread rapidly. Dick’s Sporting Goods and Golf Galaxy pulled Good Good merchandise from their shelves and digital platforms. Golf Channel first postponed and later cancelled the premiere of its Big Break x Good Good reality show reboot, while Good Good pulled its title sponsorship of an upcoming PGA Tour event in Austin, Texas. PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp called the situation “fluid”, describing Good Good’s initial response as “disappointing, a bit defensive and late”. Meanwhile, Clark issued a personal apology in an eight-and-a-half-minute video on August 26, calling the skit “super dumb” and admitting his “skin was crawling” and he was “cringing” the moment he saw it. He also urged viewers to stop sending hate to Miestowski, the woman creator featured in the controversial clip. But who exactly is Garrett Clark – the man at the centre of the Good Good controversy? What is Garrett Clark’s background? Good Good was founded in 2020 by Garrett Clark, Matt Scharff and Stephen Castaneda. It became one of the world’s most popular sports channels on YouTube, credited with bringing golf to a younger, more diverse audience. As of Friday, Good Good has over 2 million subscribers, while Clark’s personal channel, GM Golf, has surpassed 1.4 million. What did Garrett Clark do before Good Good? A Kansas City native, Clark was home-schooled and began playing golf at age 13, later joining the team at Christ Preparatory Academy as a freshman. His passion for the sport soon led him to compete in junior tournaments. A dedicated fan of golfers and content creators the Bryan Bros, Clark started his first YouTube channel at just nine years old – which initially had nothing to do with sports – before launching GM Golf to post trick shots and practice highlights. By late summer 2019, Clark’s channel had garnered 150,000 subscribers. It was then that he approached his father – a financial adviser – about dropping out of school to pursue full-time content creation. His father, Jerry, in turn, challenged him to earn US$60,000 from YouTube. “Well, he made that in a heartbeat. I said, ‘Son, you need to drop out of school immediately because you’ve got lightning in a bottle right now. College can wait.’” Jerry told Golf.com in 2020. Clark’s career has taken off since. In March 2025, Good Good raised US$45 million in funding through Creator Sports Capital – with NFL legend Peyton Manning among the investors. Who is Garrett Clark dating? Clark is in a relationship with professional golfer Marissa Wenzler, who is also a content creator in the Good Good orbit and hosts her own YouTube channel, Marissa Wenzler Golf. Wenzler, 25, turned professional in June 2024 and competes on the Epson Tour. A University of Kentucky alumna, she holds a bachelor’s degree in finance and a master’s in kinesiology and health promotion.

title: Uncertainty over CATL lithium mine restart could fuel price volatility: analysts
description: The latest hold-up has yet to meaningfully roil lithium carbonate prices but the impact may be felt during the fourth-quarter.
content: Restart schedules for the Jianxiawo lithium mine in Yichun, Jiangxi Province operated by CATL – the world’s largest lithium-ion-battery producer – are now facing fresh uncertainty. Analysts said the development could fuel volatility in lithium prices in the fourth quarter since the mine – the world’s largest single‑deposit lepidolite mine according to Yichun city – represented roughly 4 to 5 per cent of global supply when operating at full capacity. Local environmental regulator Yichun Ecology and Environment Bureau said on its website on Wednesday that it had removed the public notice signalling proposed acceptance of the environmental impact assessment report for the CATL project. The move has cast doubt over the timeline for a return to production since the operations were suspended in August 2025 when its original mining permit expired, according to CATL. Market participants had earlier expected the mine to resume operations in late September, following its receipt of a safety-production permit on June 29 which cleared a critical regulatory hurdle, records from government platform Credit China show. The latest hold-up had yet to meaningfully roil domestic lithium carbonate prices but the impact may be felt during the fourth-quarter, according to analysts. “A number of lithium mines are going through mining-license conversion procedures,” said Xiao Jiaying, an analyst with Shanghai-based Orient Futures. “Together with the Jianxiawo episode, this leaves the fourth-quarter supply outlook more uncertain and will continue to fuel price swings.” There is broad market agreement that lithium carbonate demand remains firm Lou Jiahao, Cinda Futures Extracted from hard-rock ores and salt flat brines, lithium can be processed into lithium carbonate, a vital raw material deployed across downstream consumer markets such as electric vehicles and drones. Lou Jiahao, an analyst with Hangzhou-based Cinda Futures, said in an August 9 research note that domestic lithium carbonate stockpiles had fallen to multi-year lows. “There is broad market agreement that lithium carbonate demand remains firm,” he said. “If demand posts a 5 per cent month-on-month increase as forecast, alongside the current pace of inventory drawdown and unresolved risks surrounding the Jianxiawo lithium mining project, prices could stage a strong rebound.” Lithium carbonate futures contracts traded on the Guangzhou Futures Exchange have risen more than 30 per cent year-to-date, with prices holding above 150,000 yuan (US$22,312) per tonne. The price rebound in lithium and its related products has delivered tailwinds for industry participants. Tianqi Lithium, the Sichuan-based global heavyweight in lithium-ion battery materials, on Thursday reported record‑high revenue and profits in the first half. In the six months ending June, it generated over 12.2 billion yuan in revenue, marking a 153 per cent year-on-year increase. Net profit attributable to equity shareholders surged an eye‑catching 4,925 per cent to 4.2 billion yuan. According to the firm, the soaring earnings stemmed from growth within the new-energy industry that drove demand for its flagship lithium products.

title: MTR Corp to deploy a world-first use of skidding method for Hung Shui Kiu station
description: Station sections to be built beside the operating Tuen Ma line and skidded into position to shorten construction time, but network disruptions are expected.
content: Hong Kong’s rail operator will use a skidding method – the first worldwide for a heavy-rail project – to build Hung Shui Kiu station, helping to overcome time constraints and ensure completion by 2030. The MTR Corporation said on Friday that the station structures, each weighing about 10,000 tonnes, would be assembled from prefabricated components at worksites on either side of an operational viaduct. They would then be skidded into their designated positions alongside the operating Tuen Ma line. Hung Shui Kiu station, located between Tin Shui Wai and Siu Hong stations on the Tuen Ma line, will serve the future Hung Shui Kiu/Ha Tsuen New Development Area in the Northern Metropolis megaproject. It will also be Hong Kong’s first station built on an operational railway viaduct. “This innovative construction method significantly reduces the need for works during non-traffic hours, greatly reduces construction risks and secures project progress,” said Carl Devlin, the corporation’s capital works director. He referred to the daily “golden two hours” during the non-traffic period, when the rail line is available for repairs, maintenance and other works. “However, service adjustments are required and inevitable for adopting this method. Drawing on our experience from previous railway projects, we will undertake careful planning and do our utmost to minimise the impact on passengers,” he said. Services at Tuen Mun, Siu Hong and Tin Shui Wai stations will be affected by skidding procedures carried out on both sides in the latter part of the first quarter and the third quarter next year, respectively. The MTR Corp said it would announce detailed arrangements after completing its assessment of the impact on services. Political party the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment and Progress of Hong Kong urged the MTR Corp to cautiously handle disruptions affecting commuters travelling between Tuen Mun, Yuen Long and Tin Shui Wai. It called on the corporation and the Transport Department to disclose details of the service suspension one month in advance, and to provide sufficient feeder buses and staff to help commuters.

title: China’s CXMT posts massive 870% revenue surge as ‘aggressive expansion’ pays off
description: China’s leading DRAM chipmaker outperforms its own forecasts in its first financial results since a blockbuster Shanghai listing.
content: Chinese chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) reported a sharp surge in first-half revenue on Friday, as the firm released its first financial results since becoming China’s most valuable publicly traded company in a blockbuster Shanghai listing last month. The Hefei-based firm – China’s leading maker of dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) products – posted revenue of 150.31 billion yuan (US$22.4 billion) for the six months to June, up 873.64 per cent year on year, according to a filing with the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Net profit attributable to shareholders reached 77.61 billion yuan, reversing a loss of 2.33 billion yuan in the same period last year. The results were well above CXMT’s pre-initial public offering guidance, which forecast first-half revenue of 110 billion to 120 billion yuan and net profit of 50 billion to 57 billion yuan. Revenue exceeded the top end of that range by about 25 per cent, while attributable profit was about 36 per cent higher. The earnings boom has been fuelled by skyrocketing demand for memory products from the artificial intelligence industry. CXMT said global DRAM supplies remained tight and prices continued to rise in the first half, a supply shortage that it expected to persist in the coming months. The company has also benefited from expanding production and an improving product mix as it ramps up output of newer products including DDR5, which is increasingly used in personal computers, workstations and servers. DDR-series revenue reached 69.47 billion yuan in the first half, accounting for 46.3 per cent of CXMT’s main business revenue, up from 31.9 per cent in 2025. CXMT said its latest LPDDR6 chip – capable of speeds of up to 12,800Mbps – had been sent to key customers for validation as the company accelerates preparations for mass production. It marks the first time a Chinese DRAM maker has entered the commercialisation race for a new LPDDR generation at roughly the same time as global industry leaders. China’s domestic DRAM producers are gaining global market share as they expand capacity faster than overseas rivals. UBS estimates Chinese suppliers’ share of global DRAM shipments will rise from about 7 per cent in 2025 to 8.4 per cent this year and 9.4 per cent in 2027. “We don’t think the impact of more aggressive expansion by Chinese suppliers will be as severe as some investors fear,” said Jimmy Yu, head of China technology research at UBS Securities, on Thursday. “We still expect the DRAM upcycle to last until the second quarter of 2028.” Morgan Stanley, which initiated coverage of CXMT with an overweight rating this week, estimates the company will reach monthly production capacity of 300,000 wafers this year, equivalent to about 13 per cent of global DRAM wafer capacity and 11 per cent of global bit shipments. It expects capacity to rise to 500,000 wafers per month by 2028. The bank forecasts CXMT’s full-year revenue to reach 388.9 billion yuan in 2026, suggesting a significant further acceleration in the second half if that estimate is met. Morgan Stanley expects the company’s earnings growth to be supported by rising output, strong memory pricing and greater exposure to higher-value products including DDR5, server DRAM and high-bandwidth memory. The rapid expansion comes despite a persistent technology gap with overseas rivals. UBS estimates Chinese DRAM manufacturers remain around two to three technology generations behind leading global suppliers, while larger die sizes leave domestic producers with a cost disadvantage. The bank nevertheless expects capacity additions by Chinese firms to be absorbed by rising demand over the next two years rather than cause a global supply glut. CXMT’s shares fell 0.88 per cent on Friday to 58.6 yuan, giving the company a market capitalisation of about 3.98 trillion yuan. The stock has risen more than 576 per cent from its IPO price of 8.66 yuan. Morgan Stanley this week set an 88 yuan price target for CXMT, implying 18.5 times estimated 2027 earnings, compared with 4.4 times for global memory peers. The bank said the premium reflected CXMT’s faster growth, capacity expansion, China’s memory localisation drive and exposure to rising demand from the country’s AI infrastructure sector.

title: Hong Kong launches first regional mediation platform for medical disputes
description: New Healthcare Dispute Resolution Centre online platform provides both virtual and face-to-face services for patients and doctors.
content: Hong Kong has launched the first regional mediation and arbitration platform dedicated to medical and healthcare services as part of the city’s efforts to resolve local and cross-border disputes and strengthen its bid to become an international legal services hub. The Healthcare Dispute Resolution Centre, a non-profit organisation set up in 2024, announced its new online platform on Friday, providing both virtual and face-to-face services for patients and medical practitioners to settle conflicts through mediation and arbitration. “Disputes, whether they are related to medical errors, patient rights or contract issues, often turn into litigation that takes time, incurs high costs, and goes toe to toe. Litigation not only harms the relationship between patients and healthcare providers, but also wastes precious public resources,” centre chairman Samuel Kwok Po-yin said at the launch ceremony. “As cross-border use of medical services becomes more frequent, the new website and platform will become a hub for resolving medical and healthcare disputes in Hong Kong and in the Greater Bay Area.” The bay area refers to Beijing’s initiative to link Hong Kong, Macau and the nine Guangdong cities into an economic powerhouse. Kwok said that, compared with court litigation procedures, mediation and arbitration would take less time and cost less, while cases would be kept confidential and dealt with based on professional knowledge. Currently, complaint cases against healthcare professionals are generally handled by the statutory Medical Council of Hong Kong. Between 2020 and 2025, the council completed 263 cases by inquiry, with more than 75 per cent concluded within five years. Eleven cases took between 10 and 15 years. The platform is backed by the eBRAM International Online Dispute Resolution Centre, a non-profit company supported by the Asian Academy of International Law, the Law Society of Hong Kong and the Hong Kong Bar Association. The platform is also supported by the Hong Kong International Medical Mediation Centre, which offers services through its 30 branch offices around the world, including in mainland China, Singapore and the United Kingdom. Alan Ng Wai-lun, founder of the Cancerinformation.com.hk Charity Foundation, said he would adopt a wait-and-see attitude towards the platform and hoped it could help resolve medical disputes objectively and quickly. He added that patients often struggled through lengthy complaint processes, citing the example of a 15-year delay in the Medical Council’s handling of a complaint against a paediatrician, Dr Sit Sou-chi, who was found guilty of professional misconduct over a blunder that left a boy permanently disabled in 2009. The case led to proposals to reform the council, including increasing its proportion of lay members, cutting the complaint-handling process from 42 to 29 months, and making the inquiry time frames public.

title: Dutch court jails man for life over role in Rwanda genocide
description: He had prevented Tutsis from escaping and threw a grenade into the crowd.
content: A Dutch court on Friday handed a life sentence to a 66-year-old man for his role in the massacre of 3,000 Tutsis during the 1994 Rwanda genocide. During the violence that took place in April 1994, terrified victims sought refuge in a football stadium in Mbazi, southern Rwanda, only to be systematically slaughtered. The judge said that the man, identified as Eugene N., prevented Tutsis from escaping the stadium and threw a grenade into the crowd. The court said he was also involved in attacks preceding the stadium massacre, when houses were looted and set on fire. “Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families,” the court said. His actions were committed with “genocidal intent”, said the presiding judge handing down the verdict. He was convicted of war crimes and the crime of genocide. At hearings in June before the District Court of The Hague, prosecutors had urged a life sentence, saying that N. was “personally involved” in the killings. “If the horrific crimes of the suspect – in which not one but an estimated 3,000 innocent people were literally slaughtered, in which the suspect personally threw a grenade into a stadium … do not deserve a life sentence, then what does?” one prosecutor asked the court. The 1994 Rwandan genocide claimed the lives of an estimated 800,000 people over the course of three months. According to UN figures, most of the victims were part of the Tutsi minority in Rwanda. The suspect had denied the charges, saying he himself was a victim who had lost dozens of his own relatives in what he described as “those horrific events”. N.’s lawyers had urged an acquittal on all counts, saying their client in fact did “everything to prevent the genocide”. “The case has torn his scars open again. He is a broken man,” said one of the defence lawyers during the trial. According to local news agency ANP, the defence said they will “almost certainly appeal the charges”. At the time of the massacres, N. held a position of responsibility in the community, said the court, overseeing around 1,000 people in Mbazi. “The suspect was a man who was held in high regard and he must have been aware of his role and the influence he had as a local authority,” said the court. “Instead of staying on the sidelines, the defendant committed multiple severe crimes,” added the court. The court said he watched from a road as his men stormed into houses of Tutsis, setting them ablaze. He was, however, acquitted of the charge of incitement to genocide. N. fled to the Netherlands in 1998. Rwandan authorities issued an international arrest warrant for him in 2014. However, according to Dutch law, he cannot be extradited as he has obtained nationality in the Netherlands. Dutch prosecutors opened their own investigation in 2020 and have since interviewed dozens of witnesses in Rwanda. N. was arrested in 2024. European courts have tried and convicted several dozen people involved in the Rwanda genocide under the principle of universal jurisdiction, which allows them to hear the most serious crimes even if committed abroad.

title: BOCHK posts higher profit as lower credit costs offset margin pressure
description: Bank beats forecast with HK$23.74 billion profit, helped by reduced credit costs and stronger fee income from wealth and insurance.
content: Bank of China (Hong Kong), one of the city’s three note-issuing banks, reported a 7.1 per cent year-on-year increase in first-half net profit, as lower impairment charges and a wider net interest margin helped offset continued pressure on lending margins from falling Hong Kong interbank rates. Profit attributable to shareholders came to HK$23.74 billion (US$3 billion) for the six months to June 30, or HK$2.2453 per share, according to a stock exchange filing on Friday. The result beat analysts’ average estimate of HK$22.94 billion. BOCHK’s net interest margin, including income from foreign exchange swap contracts, stood at 1.57 per cent, versus 1.54 per cent a year earlier. “We will further optimise our management in Southeast Asia and build a leading regional headquarters,” said Sun Yu, vice-chairman and chief executive of BOCHK, at a press conference on Friday. Sun added that BOCHK would actively support national strategies and Hong Kong’s development, while striving to “continue creating enhanced value for shareholders and stakeholders”. Credit costs also eased during the period, supporting the lender’s bottom line after elevated impairment charges in recent years. For the first half, the net charge of impairment allowances came to HK$2.38 billion, down 26.9 per cent from about HK$3.26 billion a year earlier, with the impaired loan rate at 0.89 per cent, versus 1.02 per cent at the end of June 2025. Hong Kong lenders have navigated a broader transition as monetary policy pivots away from the elevated rate environment that had previously bolstered margins, while commercial real estate exposures in Hong Kong and mainland China continue to demand close monitoring. To mitigate margin pressure, lenders industry-wide had narrowed cost-to-income ratios and leaned further into fee-based business, according to a KPMG review of Hong Kong’s banking sector published in June, even as credit quality across the sector remained broadly stable. Net fee and commission income fell 5.8 per cent to HK$5.98 billion, mainly because commission income from insurance and trust and custody services declined 40.5 per cent and 22 per cent, respectively. The decline was partly offset by stronger wealth management activity. Commission income from funds distribution and funds management increased 55.1 per cent and 78.2 per cent, respectively, while credit card commission income rose 12.2 per cent amid a recovery in local retail spending. The bank’s insurance business also recorded stronger sales, with the value of standard new premiums increasing 27.9 per cent year on year to HK$18.96 billion, while its contractual service margin rose 23.6 per cent from the end of 2025. The lender continues to broaden its offshore yuan offerings, tapping the city’s role as the leading renminbi deposit pool outside the mainland to secure a bigger share of outbound capital and trade. “We are leveraging Hong Kong’s position as the primary offshore renminbi hub to capture growing capital flows from mainland enterprises expanding overseas,” Sun said. He added that the bank would continue to expand its suite of cross-border trade settlement and treasury management products to solidify its market-leading position in the regional renminbi business. The board declared an interim dividend of HK$0.8188 per share, up from HK$0.58 in the first half of 2025. It also approved a three-year shareholder return programme for 2026 to 2028, including plans to distribute additional shareholder returns of no less than HK$10.5 billion over the period. The results come after BOCHK completed its five-year strategic plan, with return on average shareholders’ equity reaching 13.18 per cent in the first half of 2026, compared with 12.86 per cent a year earlier. BOCHK’s shares closed up 2.27 per cent at HK$50.97 on Friday before the announcement, while the benchmark Hang Seng Index was flat.

title: Review | Chinese violin virtuoso Zhang Aozhe, 18, makes magical Hong Kong debut
description: The Premio Paganini winner played Beethoven, Mozart, Vivaldi and more with flawless technique in a show that deserved a higher turnout.
content: At the tender age of 18, Zhang Aozhe, the 2025 winner of the Premio Paganini International Violin Competition’s top prize, has just made his Hong Kong debut. This should have been a major attraction, but from my observation, the seats at the City Hall Concert Hall were about half empty. Was the low attendance due to the summer holidays, or was it a case of insufficient publicity? It was difficult to tell, but the truth is that many people, including frequent concertgoers, missed a show that deserved more appreciation than it received from a small audience that included many children. Zhang was born in Hefei, in China’s Anhui province, in 2008, and recorded his first solo album at 14. His wins at the 2025 Premio Paganini International Violin Competition – where he took the Gold Prize and Best Paganini Concerto Performance Prize – are his most distinguished accolades to date. Previous winners of the competition include Salvatore Accardo and Gidon Kremer. The recital programme in Hong Kong was a mix of works for solo violin, sandwiched by two sonatas for piano and violin. The pianist was Xie Beini, associate professor of piano at the Shanghai Conservatory of Music. The concert began with an articulate and spirited performance of Mozart’s “Sonata in A major, K. 305”. The lightness one usually expects in the first movement was missing, however; the tone was as serious as Zhang looked on stage. In fact, he seldom made eye contact with the audience throughout the show. The stage was all Zhang’s when it came to the next set: Ysaye’s “Sonata No. 5” and two caprices by Paganini. Zhang’s interpretation of the sonata was magical. One distinct feature of the piece is its abundance of overlapping lines and layers. Zhang showed his intuition for the contrapuntal texture, and his performance was poetic and full of dynamic contrasts. Paganini’s works are noted for being intensely difficult. Of course, Zhang’s technique was near perfect. With these two caprices (“No 7” and “No 24”), both comprising multiple sections, he showed delicate phrasing and showcased the full spectrum of musical expression. Next, Zhang and Xie took on Beethoven’s grand “Kreutzer Sonata” – the longest, most complicated and symphonic among Beethoven’s 10 violin sonatas. The two musicians showed a good understanding of the form, the starkly contrasting musical ideas and the subtle dynamic changes, and delivered the piece with a broad range of expression. Although some audience members were thrilled by Zhang and Xie, the applause was generally polite, save for one or two shouts of “Bravo”. The duo instantly returned with a free and witty encore of Kreisler’s “Tambourin Chinois”, which the audience loved. The second encore was Gershwin’s “Bess, You Is My Woman Now” from the 1935 opera Porgy and Bess. While others might have been tempted to overplay the piece’s blues and spiritual influences, Zhang showcased his flawless technique and the velvet-like sound – especially at the high positions on the lowest G string – of his 1937-made Ansaldo Poggi violin. The final encore was special. Three young violinists – Evangeline Wong (15), Eleanor Wong (12) and Jamie Wong (13) – joined Zhang in the first movement of Vivaldi’s “Concerto for Four Violins in B minor”. While leaving City Hall, I felt lucky to have been in the audience. The three Wongs were even luckier. How lovely, even life-changing, to share the stage with a Premio Paganini Competition winner! They all played very well. Jamie was also Xie’s page-turner. I have never seen the job so nicely done by a youngster in full concert attire. “The Magic of Violin – International Violin Competition ‘Premio Paganini’ Winner Aozhe Zhang Violin Recital”, Hong Kong City Hall Concert Hall. Reviewed: August 25.

title: ‘Never sell love for money’: China actress Jing Tian hits back at crypto mogul Justin Sun’s claims
description: While their relationship timeline is unclear, Sun proposed in January and sent a 30- million-yuan (US$4.5 million) ‘bride price’ to her parents.
content: A Chinese cryptocurrency tycoon is suing an actress and her parents to recover a bride price of 30 million yuan (US$4.5 million), then revealed details of their relationship online while the actress urged that the dispute be left to the courts. Justin Sun, 36, founder of the blockchain platform Tron, has an estimated net worth of US$8.5 billion, according to Forbes. On August 27, Sun published a post titled “My Girlfriend Jing Tian,” recounting their relationship and touching on surrogacy and the bride price. He labelled the account “fictional,” waived copyright, and invited its circulation online. Jing, 38, who starred in From Vegas to Macau and Police Story 2013, has more than 26 million followers on Weibo. Sun wrote that his interest in Jing dated back to 2007, when she was the face of a major Chinese instant-messaging platform and he had just entered university. It remains unclear when the pair began dating. In January, Sun proposed and transferred 30 million yuan to Jing’s parents as a “bride price,” he wrote. He alleged that Jing later sought a Hong Kong property registered in her name and US$50 million to have a child for him through surrogacy. Uncertain whether to pay, Sun consulted the AI-powered coding assistant Claude Code, which advised against the transfer. The couple split soon after and lost contact. He revealed to mainland media that he routinely consults AI on major business decisions but was unsettled by its advice regarding his relationship. Sun also described the article as an outlet for his personal emotions and sought to separate the dispute from his business. On the same day, Sun’s lawyer, Zhang Qihuai, disclosed that a court had accepted a lawsuit seeking the return of the 30 million yuan from Jing and her parents. The case has yet to reach a substantive hearing, and no final ruling has been issued. Zhang also clarified that the lawsuit concerned only the bride price and made no reference to surrogacy. Amid mounting online speculation, Jing’s studio stressed that the dispute would be handled through legal channels, adding that an entertainer’s reputation was both “a livelihood and a vulnerability.” Jing responded on Weibo on August 28, admitting to “poor judgment in men and insufficient wisdom” but insisting she “would never trade love or her soul for money.” She reaffirmed her faith in the law and her belief that justice and fairness would ultimately prevail. “Time will prove everything,” she wrote. The SCMP has contacted both Sun and Jing for comment but received no response by the time of this article’s publication. Lawyer Li Zhenwu, who has more than 706,000 followers online, cautioned that bride- price disputes often take unexpected turns and should be settled in court rather than on social media. He characterised Sun’s article and media appearances as “a well-prepared battle for public opinion.” “From a legal perspective, Jing’s cautious approach to the judicial process reflects a respect for the rule of law that deserves recognition,” Li added.

title: Could the China-Nepal disaster spur a safety rethink for a flagship rail project?
description: Gyirong in Tibet is the start of a planned train line to Kathmandu and in an area prone to dangerous glacial lake floods.
content: This week’s devastating floods on the China-Nepal border could be a catalyst for joint early-warning systems, particularly in relation to a proposed rail link between the countries. Rescuers were still struggling on Thursday to reach Gyirong Port in the Tibet autonomous region where a mudslide struck a day earlier, following flash floods from Nepal. The port is the region’s main foreign trade gateway, which handles a third of China’s trade with its neighbour. Gyirong is also one end of a multibillion-dollar trans-Himalayan project connecting Tibet with Kathmandu. The project was proposed in 2016 but bad weather, poor local infrastructure and geopolitical friction have resulted in little progress. In 2018, the project was folded into China’s Trans-Himalayan Multi-Dimensional Connectivity Network of rail and communication links with Nepal as part of the Belt and Road Initiative. Researchers on both sides of the border say the location of the disaster highlights the need for a joint approach to hazard management, particularly on such infrastructure. They underlined that need in a social media post on Thursday on the “China-Nepal Railway and South Asia Exchange”, a social media account that has brought Chinese and Nepali researchers together to track the railway project since 2022. In the post, Balmukunda Regmi, a professor at Nepal’s Tribhuvan University, noted that the middle Himalayas was the most vulnerable area in the world to glacial lake outburst floods. “The August 26 mountain flood is no isolated incident,” Regmi said. “Although the landslide at Gyirong Port was directly triggered on the Nepalese side, it reveals a fundamental scientific truth: hydrological disasters on both sides of the Himalayan watershed are deeply coupled.” To prevent such disasters, Regmi said, China and Nepal should team up to establish an automated, real-time early warning system for such floods at high-risk glacial lakes. As the effects of climate change have intensified across the Himalayas, China, Nepal and neighbouring South Asian nations such as India have already set up cross-border mechanisms to monitor fragile glaciers and prevent downstream disasters. Regional research platforms – such as the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development – enable joint scientific expeditions and share data to identify high-risk glacial lakes across the Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali river basins. But Yang Rongtao, an associate researcher at the West China Frontier Research Institute, said border management needed to be updated to cover joint action on such hazards. He said border management between the two countries was still subject to the 1963 Boundary Protocol designed mainly for static frontier demarcation, such as placing boundary markers and defining territorial lines across their shared 1,400km (870-mile) frontier. The framework treats transboundary rivers as static territorial lines rather than dynamic, high-risk ecological systems, leaving both nations without protocols to manage modern climate-driven hazards. To address this vulnerability, Yang argued for the protocol to be upgraded to a dedicated, modern disaster-prevention treaty that formalised real-time data sharing and joint risk management across the Himalayas. Cheng Fei, another associate researcher at the West China Frontier Research Institute, said cross-border hydrological assessments should be included in feasibility studies for the proposed 72km Gyirong-Kathmandu railway. Landslide zones and high-risk lakes along the route should be avoided or the focus of “reinforcement”, Cheng said. Beyond physical geology, experts cautioned against the “politicisation of disasters” in international public debate. Di Fangyao, a professor from the Xizang Minzu University’s Centre for South Asian Studies, said physical infrastructure challenges could be co-opted into geopolitically sensitive talking points about regional safety and water security. One example of this was the scepticism in India over China’s massive hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo River, which becomes the Brahmaputra in India. The dam, expected to be the world’s largest hydroelectric project, has caused serious concern about the impact on the river, which is a vital water source for millions of people. China has tried to reassure India over the plan, with Wang Lei, chargé d’affaires of the Chinese embassy in India, pledging Beijing “will not try to benefit at the “expense of its neighbours”. The Sunkoshi Marin Diversion Tunnel Project is another major cross-border infrastructure project. Built by Chinese firms Covec and China Railway No 2 Group under the Belt and Road Initiative, the 13.3km tunnel diverts water from the Sunkoshi River to the arid Marin River region, irrigating 122,000 hectares (301,500 acres) of farmland in Nepal’s Terai Plains and generating 28-31 megawatts of hydropower. Di said the project was a testament to the kind of mutually beneficial engineering that defined China-Nepal cooperation. Wu Xi, a professor from Southwest University of Political Science and Law, said transparency was key to countering scepticism. “When disasters strike, false causal chains claiming that Chinese infrastructure causes Himalayan imbalances quickly emerge,” Wu said. “Science-based, institutional transparency between both governments is the strongest response.”

title: How Singapore investors are lured by foreign-stock scams
description: Analysts say real overseas stocks, trading platforms and chat groups can give scams a veneer of legitimacy.
content: For more than a month, Aaron* thought he and his wife were learning how to trade stocks. Only later would they realise the lessons were part of the trap. The Singaporean business owner had found a group of self-styled investment experts on Facebook, claiming to offer foolproof tips and guaranteed returns. Soon, he and his wife, who were dabbling in stocks for the first time, were spending about two hours every other day in a WhatsApp group chat with dozens of other participants, taking lessons from a “professor” who sent lengthy messages and documents on how to judge bullish markets, analyse market conditions and identify stocks with high potential. Through private messages, another purported expert told Aaron which stock to buy, when to buy it and when to sell, promising quick returns each time. The couple did not know then that they were being drawn into a scheme that bears all the hallmarks of what analysts call a pump-and-dump scam. In such schemes, fraudsters artificially inflate the price of a company’s shares by generating buying interest, then sell their holdings after the price rises, leaving other investors exposed when the stock falls. After making profits from two stocks under the guidance of the self-styled experts, the couple were told to prepare as much money as possible for a stock with “high potential” that “did not come by often”. “They would say, if you put in one million, you’d get back three million within a month, and if we didn’t, they’d put their heads on a chopping board,” Aaron said. He took a bank loan to buy S$650,000 (US$512,000) worth of shares in CMBC Capital – a financial services firm listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange – and noticed that its price started to decline soon after. The experts’ WhatsApp accounts also disappeared. Aaron was left scrambling to repay the bank loan after losing more than S$500,000. “I still have employees to pay and a family to feed,” he said. “We are left trying to pick up the pieces because no one is here to help us recover our losses.” Hong Kong stocks ‘ideal’ Singaporeans have been falling victim to pump-and-dump scams for years, as a scam scourge plagues the city state. Analysts say that fraudsters would typically operate with stocks listed on foreign exchanges to increase their chances of success. Trading on recognised foreign exchanges allows victims to independently identify the existence of the company, which could create a strong sense of perceived legitimacy and increased confidence, said Whistine Chai, founder and principal psychologist at behavioural risk intelligence firm ForenSights. “They may not realise that the person promoting the stock may have a vested interest in generating buying interest and driving up its price for their own benefit,” she said. Hong Kong-listed stocks were a natural target for scammers preying on Singaporeans due to several factors such as cultural and time zone similarity between both cities, said Gloria Yu, an assistant professor of finance at the Singapore Management University. The Hong Kong stock exchange, as in many markets, hosts stocks with low free float and active retail participation, features scammers can exploit to discuss coordinated buying, she added. Victims are also drawn in by low-cost online trading platforms such as Moomoo and Tiger Brokers in Singapore, which make buying foreign stock easier. “The ideal asset is one the victim knows just well enough to feel comfortable with but not well enough to verify,” Yu said. “For Singapore, Hong Kong stocks sit precisely at that point.” In August 2021, the Singapore Police Force warned the public of a resurgence in pump-and-dump scams. Four months later, it conducted a joint investigation with the Hong Kong police into a syndicate suspected of operating such scams using shares listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Nine people in Hong Kong and one in Singapore were arrested, and assets totalling over HK$70 million (US$9 million) were frozen. Hong Kong police said it did not maintain figures for losses incurred in cross-border pump-and-dump scams. This Week in Asia has asked the Singapore police for comment. Sounding the alarm After realising he had fallen prey to a scam, Aaron filed a police report, and contacted CMBC Capital and Moomoo – which he used to buy the shares – in a last-ditch attempt to recover his money. Singapore police told This Week in Asia the report had been lodged and they were looking into the matter. Legal provisions in Singapore allow certain securities offences to be pursued even when part of the conduct occurs overseas or involves stocks listed on an international market. CMBC Capital announced on Tuesday that it had received reports from individuals alleging its name might have been used in investment scams. The suspicious activities had been conducted without its knowledge, consent or authorisation, it said. It also said it had not independently concluded that its shares were manipulated, and had reported the suspected activities to Hong Kong authorities. Aaron, who said he had yet to hear from Moomoo and CMBC Capital, said he felt he had little recourse. This Week in Asia has contacted CMBC Capital and Moomoo for comment. As scam operations become increasingly sophisticated with technological advancements, victims are often left to bear losses when the scammers are not arrested, according to analysts, who urge collective measures across all parties involved. “Our whole mental model of what a scam looks like needs to be changed,” Chai said. “We often associate scams with unauthorised transfers and fake websites and accounts, but increasingly, scammers can exploit real institutions and legitimate infrastructure.” Individuals should verify the investment and the person recommending it separately, while platforms could implement measures such as warnings that remind investors to do so before completing the trade, she said. Yu said that brokerage platforms had the “clearest edge” in stopping ongoing scams, as they could spot abnormal trading in real-time and act directly. “The caveat is incentives,” she said, noting that brokers may hesitate to implement aggressive anti-scam measures as false alarms could frustrate customers and push them towards competing platforms. But as scams involve multiple parties – victims, brokerage platforms, social media and messaging platforms, listed companies and authorities, Yu urged coordinated effort. “The failure is in the ecosystem, not in any one node.” *Name has been changed to protect the interviewee’s identity

title: Hong Kong lawyer warns against doxxing after AIA employee suspended over mall brawl
description: Internet users identified and circulated employee’s personal details, including her name and profession after viral play-area brawl.
content: A lawyer has warned internet users in Hong Kong against exposing personal information of others on social media or risk committing the criminal offence of doxxing, after an insurance firm suspended an employee allegedly involved in a brawl at a Kwun Tong shopping centre. Insurance service provider AIA on Thursday reportedly suspended an employee who was linked to a viral dispute among three women at a children’s play area the previous day. The trio were charged with fighting in a public place, while the AIA staff member’s elderly mother faces an additional count of common assault. The woman and her 68-year-old mother were seen in a viral video of the brawl at APM mall in Kwun Tong on Wednesday, with internet users screen-grabbing and sharing their faces. Internet users also exposed and widely circulated the 34-year-old woman’s personal details, such as her name, her profession, and details of her social media accounts such as LinkedIn, Facebook and Instagram, as well as the address of the AIA office where she worked. Lawyer Vincent Chong Yip-fung warned that social media users risked committing the criminal offence of doxxing by disclosing others’ personal information and causing them harm. “There’s a chance that those who disclosed the mother’s background could fall foul of doxxing as the disclosure had caused specific harm to the mother, including psychological harm,” he said. He advised social media users to refrain from disclosing other people’s personal information. “People can comment on a particular incident. No need to expose others’ personal information as law enforcement will handle it,” he said. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data said it had not received any complaint in relation to the matter and would not comment on the case because it involved judicial proceedings. The three women were involved in a brawl in a children’s play area in the atrium of the shopping centre on Wednesday. A dispute reportedly erupted between a boy and a five-year-old girl in the play area, prompting his grandmother to get involved. Investigators said they believed that the girl’s mother initially slapped the grandmother, who then struck back at the woman and her daughter.

title: Chinese robot maker Micbot looks to woo Aramco while chasing Hong Kong IPO
description: AI-powered quadrupeds, designed for extreme conditions and hazardous sites, are undergoing tests in China as Micbot awaits Aramco’s mass-procurement decision.
content: A Chinese robotics firm is accelerating its overseas strategy, with a fleet of AI-powered industrial quadrupeds being primed for Saudi Aramco facilities, while revving up its bid for a listing in Hong Kong next year. Heavy-duty, explosion-proof robots from Micbot are tipped to join similar products from other suppliers at oilfields, petrochemical bases and mines operated by Aramco, according to Micbot’s chief marketing officer, Huang Ziyan. Unlike consumer-focused companies that make educational desktop units or agile companion robots, Micbot’s products are intended to replace humans in extreme, demanding or dangerous industrial settings, Huang said in an interview. Featuring a stout, low-centre-of-gravity chassis with a wheeled-leg design for carrying heavy payloads, its products are engineered to withstand strong magnetic fields, high temperatures, extreme dust, and wet or submerged conditions. Micbot, based in Zhejiang province, asserts that its core competitiveness is anchored in comprehensive “four-in-one” protection – antimagnetic, explosion-proof, waterproof and freeze-resistant – tailored for some of the most challenging oil and gas production conditions at Aramco and in the broader Saudi Arabian market. Micbot added that Aramco executives and technicians had paid four visits to its research and development centre in Zhejiang since February, and that Micbot’s products had been optimised with Aramco’s input and were undergoing rigorous tests in China, with the first batch of shipments to Saudi Arabia expected in September or October. Aramco will then provide feedback, before a decision on mass procurement is made by the end of the year, according to Micbot. [W]hile other robots may be seen as replacing human workers, ours are purpose-built for extreme, high-risk operations Gu Jufeng, Micbot co-founder Specifically, its explosion-proof robots can be fitted with gas sensors and infrared thermal imagers for continuous, autonomous inspection. They can detect leaks or early fire indicators in real time and issue immediate alerts, according to the company. “The difference in our products is that, while other robots may be seen as replacing human workers, ours are purpose-built for extreme, high-risk operations at petrochemical plants, mines, electrolytic aluminium facilities and other hazardous environments to keep workers out of harm’s way,” Micbot co-founder Gu Jufeng said in an interview. Additionally, Aramco’s mining operations may become a new proving ground for Micbot’s products, as Saudi mines face a combination of challenges, including high temperatures, sandstorms, complex terrain and a harsh desert environment. The robotics developer said its products stood out in Aramco’s initial selection due to designs featuring full-terrain adaptability for sand and gravel, high-payload capacity for exploration equipment, and a wide temperature tolerance. The units are driven by a vision-language-action architecture and reinforcement learning, enabling autonomous navigation without the need for continuous human remote control. A Beijing-based agent representing Aramco confirmed the oil giant’s cooperation programmes with Chinese start-ups but did not comment further. Aramco runs an R&D centre in Beijing and has throughout the years stepped up ties with China – one of its largest overseas markets – including with Chinese tech companies. Domestically, Micbot in June also announced a partnership with Sunho Group, a state-owned coal-mining and aluminium-processing company based in Henan province, to automate safety inspections deep underground. China’s burgeoning robotics industry, touted by state media as the epitome of Chinese tech and manufacturing upgrades, has seen a flurry of fundraising and overseas market expansions in recent months. Unitree Robotics saw its shares surge during the trading debut of its blockbuster initial public offering in Shanghai last week, though prices have since retreated amid market concerns over bubbles. Regardless, Micbot executives appeared optimistic. The application scenarios for robots, coupled with the proliferation of artificial intelligence, will expand as the sector moves from flashy demonstration to practical deployment, they said. They also revealed in Hong Kong this week that the company aimed to submit its listing application to the city’s bourse, eyeing an IPO in 2027. Other contenders in the field, including Deep Robotics, Leju Robotics, AgiBot, X Square Robot and LimX Dynamics, are among the Chinese robot makers pursuing public listings.

title: Meituan snaps losing streak with profitable June quarter though Douyin threat looms
description: Revenue for the quarter rose 14.4 per cent year on year to 105 billion yuan, beating the consensus estimate of 101 billion yuan.
content: On-demand delivery giant Meituan swung back to profitability in the second quarter as China’s price war in food delivery cooled, allowing the company to scale back subsidies and target higher-value customers. Beijing-based Meituan posted an adjusted net profit of 2.5 billion yuan (US$372 million) for the June quarter, snapping a three-quarter losing streak according to its earnings report on Friday. The figure beat average analyst forecasts of 340 million yuan compiled by Bloomberg. Revenue rose 14.4 per cent year on year to 105 billion yuan, beating the consensus estimate of 101 billion yuan. Revenue and adjusted net loss for the first half came in at 196 billion yuan and 2.4 billion yuan, respectively. Meituan’s Hong Kong-listed shares closed flat at HK$77.50 on Friday ahead of the earnings announcement. The latest results come amid Meituan’s effort to curb promotional spending following a year of intense competition with rivals including JD.com and Alibaba Group Holding, which had used aggressive subsidies to capture market share. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. As market subsidies receded, Meituan had been paring back support for low-value orders to redirect resources towards high-value users and larger orders, Huatai Securities said in a recent research note. The company’s local commerce division – its main revenue generator spanning domestic food delivery and in-store services – recorded an operating profit of 5.7 billion yuan for the quarter, a 52.3 per cent growth year-on-year buoyed by an optimised subsidy strategy and spending on higher-value orders, according to Huatai Securities. The performance serves as a litmus test of whether Meituan can leverage a calmer competitive environment to drive sustained profitability while financing new growth engines. While rivalry in China’s food delivery sector appeared to be levelling off, Douyin – the Chinese sibling of TikTok – was emerging as a potent challenge to Meituan’s in-store business, according to Li Chengdong, founder and chief analyst at e-commerce consultancy Dolphin. The in-store business generates revenue by selling customer vouchers for dining, tourist attractions, entertainment and other local services. Douyin posed a “structural, long-term threat” to Meituan’s operations by leveraging its organic and high-frequency user engagement to siphon traffic away from Meituan’s transaction platform, Li said. Douyin remains one of China’s most engaging digital platforms, counting over 1 billion monthly active users as of March, according to April data from traffic analytics firm QuestMobile. By using short-video algorithms and live streaming sessions to convert online viewers into offline customers, Douyin is aggressively courting restaurant chains and offering heavily discounted meals, posing a significant challenge to Meituan on both the merchant acquisition and consumer retention fronts, Li said. On the post-earnings call on Thursday, Meituan chief financial officer Chen Shaohui acknowledged the increased rivalry in the in-store business, but said the competitive landscape had evolved and the market was much bigger. He explained that the company’s authentic customer reviews accumulated over the years, as well as a strategy of not going after subsidy-driven and low-quality orders, would help it fend off rivals. To offset domestic headwinds, Meituan is expanding overseas and scaling up its artificial intelligence footprint. Global expansion through its Keeta platform, paired with AI investments, could provide room for long-term valuation growth, Guotai Haitong Securities analysts wrote in a research note last month. The brokerage expected Meituan to enter more international markets, while its work on proprietary AI models, autonomous delivery and embodied robotics could pivot the firm from a transaction platform into a tech-driven services company. Meituan founder and chief executive Wang Xing said on the call that the company’s AI mindset was less about competing on model capabilities and more about leveraging AI to reshape the company and strengthen its core businesses. Separately, specialised AI agents were rolled out across restaurants, hotels and in sectors such as retail, medical, health and travel to help merchants with their daily operations, according to Wang. “We aim to become a digital co-pilot for merchants on our platform,” he said. Meituan’s research and development expenses increased by 22.5 per cent to 7.7 billion yuan in the second quarter, primarily driven by higher corporate-level investments in AI, according to the company.

title: Bangladesh confirms Chinese J-10CE jet deal, citing Rafale kill in India-Pakistan clash
description: Dhaka’s decision to buy the fighters shows that views on Chinese weapons are shifting and the market is opening, military expert says.
content: Bangladesh has for the first time confirmed a long-expected deal to buy Chinese 4.5-generation J-10CE fighters, pointing to the jet’s combat performance against Rafale jets in last year’s India-Pakistan conflict. One military expert said it was a sign that the global perception of Chinese weapons was shifting and the market would gradually open. Zahed Ur Rahman, information and broadcasting adviser to the prime minister of Bangladesh, said on Tuesday that a draft proposal to buy the Chinese J-10CE had been submitted to the Ministry of Finance and Armed Forces Division for final approval, according to the website of the Press Information Department (PID) of Bangladesh on Wednesday. The draft proposal also includes the purchase of Chinese attack helicopters, VIP transport helicopters and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems, according to the PID, the government’s official news distribution wing. “Subject to necessary budgetary allocation in the current fiscal year, this procurement will be executed immediately; otherwise, it will roll over into the next budget cycle,” it said. Bangladesh’s current budget year runs from July of this year to June of next year. Rahman said Bangladesh had “paid attention” to the conflict between Pakistan and India in May of last year, when Pakistan reportedly used J-10CE fighters equipped with active electronically scanned array (AESA) radars and PL-15 long-range air-to-air missiles to shoot down Indian Rafale fighters. “There is a recent real-world experience in a combat situation … So, Bangladesh has paid attention to that and, hopefully, we are moving very well in this path,” he said, according to video footage of the press briefing. “Compared with Rafales of similar quality, or European variants such as the Eurofighter Typhoon, the price of Chinese fighter jets is comparatively much lower. But I repeat, it performed better in head-on combat.” The Business Standard said Dhaka was set to spend US$2.3 billion to buy 20 J-10CE fighters, citing a report from the Armed Forces Division. The Bangladeshi newspaper reported that the cost of each fighter rose from a base price of US$62.7 million to nearly US$115 million after accounting for training, logistics, construction and other related expenses. Fu Qianshao, a Chinese military analyst and former air force officer, said the J-10CE was the cheapest option among several medium-weight fighters including the US-made F-16 and the Dassault Rafale from France. “In my personal view, the J-10CE offers the best overall performance. It uses an [AESA] radar with a relatively large aperture, giving it long-range detection, strong multi-target tracking and engagement capabilities,” Fu said. He added that the J-10CE had been upgraded to a semi-stealth fighter from a non-stealth platform, as it was coated with radar-absorbing materials. Bangladesh is China’s second-biggest arms buyer after Pakistan, which was the first country to order J-10CE fighters from China. Dhaka is seeking to modernise its ageing fleet. It has 36 F-7MG fighters in service, according to a report by aviation publisher FlightGlobal. The F-7MG is a derivative of China’s J-7 series designed for Bangladesh. The South Asian country also has trainer aircraft from China, including the K-8, along with Chinese tanks, vessels and missiles. “Bangladesh buying the J-10CE is a natural choice, and the only limiting factor now is their budget,” Fu said. “Now that they have publicly made this statement, it shows their mind is made up.” “Through real-world combat, people are gaining a new perspective on Chinese-made weapons,” Fu said, adding that the market would gradually open up and continue to expand. He said it would be hard to open the warplane market, now dominated by the US and Europe, but Chinese missile exports – especially short- and mid-range missiles – could be quite promising.

title: Philippine Roblox ban call sparks wider debate over children’s online safety
description: The online gaming platform has been blamed for the rise in school shootings and child sexual exploitation cases in Southeast Asia.
content: Roblox has become a flashpoint in Southeast Asia’s debate over child safety online, as officials scrutinise whether young users are being exposed to harmful subcultures on the gaming platform. But analysts warn that it might just be a convenient scapegoat for wider failures in how children are protected online and offline. Most recently, Roblox has been linked to the August 18 school shooting in the southern Philippine city of Zamboanga, where a Grade 9 student brought two firearms to a private school, live-streamed the attack and killed one schoolmate before taking his own life.
