Authorities were quick to identify the cause. The suspect was a “Roblox fanatic”, Zamboanga Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso said. Characterising the attack as a “case of desensitisation to violence” linked to the games children play online, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla called for a total Roblox ban on August 20. Remulla had said a day earlier that authorities had a “great degree of confidence” that Roblox had influenced the shooter’s actions, even as they had yet to conduct a forensic examination of his devices. “Roblox in itself is not a dangerous game. It is the chat group … that is where the coaxing happens, where the radicalisation takes place.” Roblox, which reported 123 million average daily active users globally in the second quarter of this year, is not a single game but an online platform built around user-created virtual worlds, play and chat – features that safety advocates say can make it easier for children to encounter strangers or be drawn into harmful communities. Online games have been scrutinised as a potential pathway for radicalisation since a Tacloban school shooting that killed three students in June. One of the suspects was found to have been an avid GoreBox player – prompting the cybercrime unit to block access to the violent game while investigators assessed its role in the attack. Roblox blocks On Thursday, Philippine officials met Roblox executives in Singapore to discuss measures to protect Filipino children from online harm. After the meeting, Department of Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda said Roblox had agreed to strengthen child-safety protections for users in the Philippines – including age verification, parental controls, faster removal of harmful content and closer cooperation with law enforcement. Roblox has said it has “advanced safeguards and robust safety policies” to protect users, such as filters to block the sharing of personal information, age checks before users can access chat, AI detection systems, safety teams, reporting tools and cooperation with law enforcement. This Week in Asia has contacted Roblox for comment. The platform has also been tied to concerns over grooming and exploitation. On June 30, the National Bureau of Investigation arrested a 19-year-old man in Pampanga province for allegedly persuading minors to engage in sexual activity and send sexually exploitative images in exchange for Robux, Roblox’s digital currency. Concerns over Roblox-linked content have also surfaced in Singapore. In May, authorities detained a 14-year-old boy who they said had been preparing to carry out a mass-casualty stabbing attack at his secondary school after becoming self-radicalised online. Singapore’s Internal Security Department said the boy, then aged 12, had encountered first-person shooter games on Roblox that recreated real-life school shootings, including the 1999 Columbine attack, before moving on to more violent content elsewhere online. In Indonesia, Roblox has said it will introduce additional content and communications controls for players under 16, after the country moved to restrict children’s access to high-risk digital platforms in March. Australia’s eSafety Commissioner on August 20 secured a court-enforceable undertaking requiring Roblox to strengthen protections against child grooming, sexual exploitation and abuse after the regulator said testing showed adults could still contact children despite earlier safety measures. Ban or better safeguards? Experts warn that bans risk pushing these dangers into less visible areas, leaving deep-seated safety failures unaddressed. Ysrael Diloy, a child protection and online safety specialist with the non-profit Stairway Foundation, said authorities should distinguish between saying a platform carries risks and saying it caused a violent incident. “If a child involved in a serious incident was using Roblox, then that online activity should absolutely be looked at,” Diloy said. “Investigators should find out what the child was doing there, who the child was talking to, and whether there was any harmful influence. But the conclusion should come from evidence.” He warned against starting with the name of a platform and trying to make everything fit around it, but added that platforms attracting millions of children “should also accept that they have a very high responsibility to make those spaces safer”. While the concern around Roblox is valid, not every new platform is a threat, according to Munira Mustaffa, executive director of Chasseur Group and a senior fellow of Verve Research. “We risk repeating the same mistake we did with TikTok back in the early 2020s,” she said. “It’s the same conversation all over again. Tomorrow will be a new platform but the same debate. It will never end unless we understand what exactly is the problem and what we are countering.” Paco Pangalangan, a fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Carr-Ryan Centre for Human Rights, said bans should not be the default response. “If our concern is adult strangers contacting younger users on Roblox, a ban doesn’t make those users disappear. It only pushes them into less visible and less regulated spaces,” he said. “If governments want platforms to be accountable for what happens on them, they need enforceable design obligations that reduce harmful behaviour and keep platforms inside the reach of regulators and parents.” One safeguard that is often cited is age verification, but that has its own risks too. “Sometimes [platforms will] ask you to upload like a government ID or things like that,” said Carl Javier, executive director of ethics organisation Data and AI Ethics PH. “That’s a new privacy layer that needs to be protected by the company that you’re uploading it to.” He also cautioned against the one-size-fits-all approach, saying extremist behaviour and sexual exploitation were distinct kinds of harm, with different types of perpetrators and victims. “The tools we have are trying to address both. But they’re such different ways of attacking.” Platform accountability should be specific, evidence-based and proportionate, Diloy said. “Roblox should be held responsible for risks that happen on Roblox. Telegram should be held responsible for risks that happen on Telegram,” he said. “But none of these platforms should become an easy explanation that stops us from looking at everything else happening in a child’s life.”

title: Malaysian man kills wife, 2 children and self over love scam
description: Police say the distraught husband left a note blaming US$61,000 in scam debts and his wife’s ongoing contact with a fraudster.
content: A 48-year-old Malaysian man is believed to have killed his wife and their two young children before taking his life at a Kuala Lumpur flat, in a case police said might have been linked to losses from an alleged online love scam purportedly involving the woman. Initial police investigations found a note left by the man, blaming his actions on the scam, which had left the family with US$61,000 in losses and debt, police said on Friday. The 48-year-old father wrote that he was distraught over his wife’s purported relationship with a scammer and claimed she had continued trying to contact the scammer despite the family’s financial losses, said Kuala Lumpur police chief Fadil Haji Marsus. In the note, police said the man felt her actions had gone too far and that he was ashamed in front of their children. “The note was found on the dining table after the man fell to his death from their Desa ParkCity flat building on Thursday,” Fadhil said. His “wife is a housewife while the murder suspect works as a director in a family-run business”. Police received a report on Thursday afternoon that a man had fallen from the unit, which led police to forcibly enter the family’s flat with help from fire rescue personnel. Police found the 47-year-old wife, her nine-year-old daughter and seven-year-old son dead in separate rooms. “All three victims were found with severe injuries to their necks,” Fadil said. At the scene, police recovered a knife and glove believed to be used in the killings in the master bedroom drawers at the flat located in an upscale neighbourhood. Police have not confirmed the precise location where the incident took place. This Week in Asia spoke to several security guards who said the man fell from the 33rd floor of the NorthShore Gardens building near Central Park, a public park, in the upscale Desa ParkCity area. “We heard about the man falling from the building around 3.30pm on Thursday,” said the security guard, who declined to be named. Fadhil said a postmortem examination was conducted on Friday on the girl, with findings showing a 5cm wound on her neck. Two more postmortem examinations on the wife and son are expected to be concluded later in the day. “The postmortem examination of the suspect is expected to be conducted tomorrow [Saturday] after the Kuala Lumpur Hospital forensic team visits the scene tomorrow morning,” he said. The case is classified as murder under Section 302 of the Penal Code. Earlier this year, Malaysian police reported several other cases of murder and murder suicides said to have involved family members. On January 16, a 34-year-old doctor was charged with killing his 37-year-old wife and his four-year-old son in their home in Johor earlier in the month, where the wife was found with slash wounds on her neck while the child had bluish marks on his face believed to be caused by smothering, according to the state’s police. In early February, a couple aged 54 and 52 were found dead in a bedroom with multiple stab wounds, with the case classified as a murder suicide and police citing a domestic dispute as the motive. On February 17, a 32-year-old security guard allegedly slashed and killed his 55-year-old mother, 28-year-old wife and two daughters aged three and four before taking his own life in Taman Cherating Damai in Kuantan, Pahang. Police believe the motive for the killing was financial pressure. Women, Family and Community Development Minister Nancy Shukri said on February 17 that the government had noted a worrying trend of familicide cases, with six recorded so far in the year, pledging to strengthen the role of local social support services to help those experiencing emotional distress. “It has become urgent for us to expand counseling services through the local social support centre,” Nancy was quoted by the New Straits Times newspaper on the same day. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Goal of Tiananmen vigil group an ‘empty slogan’, not actual plan: defence lawyer
description: Stated goal of ending Communist Party rule reflected ex-leaders’ beliefs, but there was no actual plan to oust government, defence says.
content: The stated goal of leaders of the now-disbanded group behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen vigil to end one-party rule was an “empty slogan”, and they never incited anyone to overthrow the Chinese government, their defence lawyer has told judges. The court heard on Friday that the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan, former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were merely expressing their belief in the pursuit of freedom and democracy by advocating an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China. Last week, Lee, 68, and Chow, 41, were convicted of inciting public hatred towards the Communist Party, while 74-year-old Ho earlier pleaded guilty to the same charge. They were accused of using the annual vigils commemorating Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in June 1989 to attract supporters and instigate them to take action to oust the ruling party. Submitting oral mitigation at West Kowloon Court on Friday, defence counsel Erik Shum Sze-man, representing Lee and Ho, said bringing an end to one-party rule was an “empty slogan”, and that the alliance had never made concrete plans to realise the goal. “Over the past 30 years, not a single person was incited by the alliance’s promotion to undermine the party. The Communist Party has been consistently stable over all these years, fulfilling its duties,” Shum said. Founded after the 1989 crackdown, the alliance organised annual candlelight vigils in Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to mark the event and call for accountability and democratic reforms across the border. It held its last vigil in 2019. Shum said the alliance’s stated goal of ending Communist Party rule was “theoretical and conceptual”, and that there was no clear evidence showing that anyone had taken action to subvert mainland authorities following the annual vigils. Chow, a barrister by profession, told the court that she did not commit any wrongdoing by hoping to build a democratic China, and that expressing her beliefs through the alliance’s events was once deemed lawful. Justice Alex Lee Wan-tang said he understood the trio wished to achieve their goals, but that their beliefs would not be condoned if they contravened the law. He told Chow: “In criminal law terms, that means you lack remorse as you hold fast to your beliefs.” Shum asked the court to consider the fact that Lee and Ho did not anticipate that their participation in the alliance over the years would violate the national security law, which came into effect in June 2020. He submitted that the illegality of their actions was not evident before the present court’s judges ruled that the alliance’s advocacy had undermined the fundamental system of China under its constitution. Their judgment last Friday noted that Article 1 of the Chinese constitution, amended in 2018, described the party’s leadership as the “defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics”. But Shum said that applying the constitution to a national security trial in Hong Kong introduced a new legal perspective that had no precedent in the city. Inciting subversion in Hong Kong carries a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment under the national security law. Any company or organisation that commits an offence under the law can be fined, with no limit on the amount. Shum appealed for a lenient sentence for his clients that amounted to no more than five years in prison. While the presiding judges on Friday did not set a date for sentencing, they said it would be scheduled within two weeks.

title: Chinese rescuers reach checkpoint destroyed by deadly flash floods along Nepal border
description: Footage taken at Gyirong Port in Tibet shows scenes of utter devastation following disaster that killed hundreds of people.
content: Beijing promised to send emergency aid to Nepal on Friday as Chinese rescuers battled through hazardous conditions to reach the border checkpoint hit by deadly flash floods this week. The disaster left five dead and 558 missing in Tibet’s Gyirong county, while Nepal reported 579 dead and 1,924 missing as of 7pm on Friday. Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a message of condolence to his Nepalese counterpart, Ram Chandra Paudel, following the devastating mudslides, state broadcaster CCTV reported. Xi also chaired a meeting of the Politburo that promised to send “urgent emergency assistance” and offered “international rescue cooperation” with Nepal, state news agency Xinhua reported. “Search and rescue operations face extreme difficulty due to the high-altitude, frigid environment, steep valleys, volatile weather and lingering geological hazards from surrounding glaciers and glacial lakes,” the Politburo said. Despite these hazardous conditions, the first team of 21 firefighters and a rescue dog reached the worst-hit area of Gyirong checkpoint around 5pm on Friday, according to state media. Video footage released by China Fire and Rescue showed the first responders crossing the muddy terrain on foot and scrambling up slopes to search for survivors and calling “is anyone there?”. The footage showed that structures near the border crossing had been completely destroyed, with the ground choked by mud and rock. A massive boulder – standing more than twice the height of a human – blocked the road. Other rescue teams travelled along the flooded waterways in inflatable boats, while high-capacity drones dropped firefighters in the disaster zone. The Politburo ordered the strict monitoring of a lake formed by debris from the landslide near the Gyirong Port border crossing, which has started to overflow. CCTV said the lake was thought to have grown by around 25 per cent on Friday, swelling to more than 2.5 million cubic metres of water, the equivalent of 1,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Friday’s Politburo meeting, which began with a moment of silence for the victims, called for a “scientific and well-targeted” search and rescue plan to find all those still missing. Such a public act of mourning by China’s top leadership is unusual, typically occurring only during major national disasters or official state commemorations. The last time this happened was in April 2020, when Xi and other top leaders observed a moment of silence at the leadership compound at Zhongnanhai to honour victims and frontline workers who died during the Covid-19 pandemic. The Politburo also called for better international cooperation on border disaster management, the proper resettlement of displaced residents and strict site management to protect emergency workers. The meeting also ordered a “full-scale screening of disaster hazards to mitigate lingering risks”, and called for “an urgent inventory of glaciers and glacial lakes across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau” alongside enhanced real-time monitoring to better identify disaster risks. The Politburo also called for better emergency response mechanisms by establishing “linked upstream and downstream warning networks” and enforcing strict evacuation measures, including designated escape routes and temporary shelters for vulnerable communities. It also ordered a targeted expansion of fire and engineering response forces in vulnerable high-altitude and border regions, including “upgraded response capabilities” when electricity supplies, roads or communication networks were cut off. Meanwhile, international concerns are mounting over the scale of the loss. US President Donald Trump said there were “50, maybe 60” Americans missing and pledged to offer Nepal “any help they need”. “We are sending aid, and we’ve spoken to the leadership, and we’ve let them know anything they know we’ll have,” he said. On Thursday, the Nepalese authorities released a list of 537 foreign nationals missing in the wake of the floods, including 178 Indian citizens, 65 Americans, 53 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 35 Australians and 33 Britons. Premier Li Qiang, who arrived in Gyirong on Thursday to direct rescue responses, inspected the disaster-hit area and called for measures to prevent further disasters. According to Xinhua, he also called for prompt disease controls and said all information about casualties and relief operations must be released in an open and transparent manner. Meanwhile, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said that official assessments from both countries had concluded the disaster “originated from a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal”. China’s Ministry of Natural Resources released dramatic before-and-after 3D imagery of the Gyirong debris flow, showing how buildings, bridges and roads had been completely erased. “Upon slamming into the main Gyirong Zangbo riverbed, the high-velocity debris flow surged nearly 3km [1.8 miles] upstream against the natural current,” Guo Zhaocheng, a senior remote-sensing engineer from the ministry, told CCTV. He said the destructive power of this event was far in excess of last year’s flooding that sent a wall of water surging down the Bhotekoshi River, destroying the Nepal-China Friendship Bridge at Gyirong and killing 17 people. “The collapse originated at an altitude of approximately 5,140 metres [16,900 feet], whereas Gyirong Port sits at around 1,800 metres – a massive drop of nearly 3,300 metres within just 20km,” Guo said. The debris flow took only seven minutes to reach the border crossing, travelling at an estimated average speed of 50 metres per second, Guo said. The disaster followed repeated warnings from scientists that climate change is destabilising the high Himalayas, especially its permafrost. This frozen mixture of rock, soil and ice acts as a type of natural glue that holds mountain sides together, but as it starts to thaw, the risk of catastrophic landslides increases. Scientists have warned that such accidents may become more frequent as a result of global warming. Last year, the Swiss village of Blatten was largely destroyed by torrent of ice, mud and rock when a massive section of the Birch Glacier collapsed. The village’s 300 or so residents had been evacuated weeks before the disaster, which killed one local man.

title: Opinion | The end of history? No, the world’s thermodynamic bill is coming due
description: When energy, technology, money and power are linked, governments can’t escape the laws of nature.
content: How do you explain what Charles Dickens called “the best of times” and “the worst of times”? We live with massive societal inequalities. The rich have never had it so good, and the middle class has rarely been so discontented. We are suffering through years of heatwaves, and wars in Europe and the Middle East. Stock markets are at record highs while bond markets are creaking under rising interest rates. Are we seeing the effects of imperial overreach or simply overstretched asset valuations? There is a consistent theme across centuries and civilisations. Societies thrive when their values, economies and institutions remain anchored to physical reality, but they decay when elites drift into self-referential systems of paper wealth, prestige and power. Climate change, fossil fuels, water, food and energy are anchored physically to the laws of thermodynamics. Meanwhile, human perception and agency – the willingness to intervene in human affairs and nature – can be detached from reality by ego, hubris and euphoria. There are three laws of thermodynamics. First is the law of energy conservation: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed. The second involves entropy: in any spontaneous process, the total entropy, or disorder, of the universe will always increase. The third involves absolute zero: as the temperature of a system approaches absolute zero, the entropy of the system approaches a minimum constant value. This means absolute zero cannot be reached. Strictly speaking, the laws of thermodynamics do not apply to human social systems. Human perceptions or valuations can be inflated or understated, while human agency changes the game. Just as artificial intelligence models hallucinate, people’s perception or valuation of assets goes from mild inflation to periodic hallucination and great crashes. The view that the Soviet system collapsed because it violated the “hard budget constraint” originated with Hungarian economist Janos Kornai. He saw market economy firms go bankrupt when they consistently lost money. This imposes discipline and drives efficiency. In the Soviet socialist system, state-owned enterprises and governments operated under “soft budget constraints” because the state would bail out losers. This continued until the state itself became bankrupt, defaulted or collapsed. Hard budget constraints are thermodynamic limits on fiscal excesses. Cambridge political economist Helen Thompson was among the first to draw parallels between the geopolitics of war and energy, highlighting that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is really about food, energy and rare earth minerals. Political, military, financial and social power run on energy. Without energy or money, the system declines or stops. Western historians have argued that empires rise through creative adaptation and shared purpose, then rot as elites become self-serving, overextending militarily while their economic core hollows out. As complexity increases, new laws and bigger bureaucracies cost more money, resources or energy than the system can bear. When elites fail to respond to crises as there are no more surpluses left, the system collapses. These insights are not uniquely Western. The 14th century Arab scholar Ibn Khaldun captured the full life cycle in a single concept: asabiyyah, or shared cohesion and purpose. Empires rise lean, grow fat on luxury and bureaucracy, then starve as taxes crush the productive base and elites lose the will to adapt. Ancient India’s Kautilya, also known as Chanakya, put it bluntly in the Arthashastra: wealth is the foundation of power. Surplus comes first; everything else follows. Paper prestige cannot feed an army or sustain an empire. Chinese traditions frame the challenge as alignment with nature. Do not force what cannot succeed: act with reality, not against it. With the experience of the rise and fall of many dynasties, pragmatism becomes a survival strategy: test small, adjust, scale and never mistake names for substance. Across all these traditions, one lesson remains: moral order and physical order are one. Hard budget constraints, justice and shared purpose are not luxuries; they lower enforcement costs, sustain trust and conserve energy. When the moral anchor fails, thermodynamic collapse follows. Today, the global order displays late-stage symptoms. Governments are running debt burdens that outstrip real output, and meanwhile financial engineering outpaces productive engineering. Narratives and memes amplify faster than facts while markets value acceleration over substance. We are not witnessing the end of history. We are essentially watching the thermodynamic bill come due. Every financial transaction, every institution, every army runs on real energy and resources. Dickens’ novel David Copperfield summed it up best: “Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen and six, result happiness. Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure twenty pounds ought and six, result misery.” Humans prosper when we stay grounded in reality. We fall when we believe hubris can rewrite the laws of nature. Markets that are concentrated and overstretched in valuation are fragile, and their bursting will have systemic implications. Facing such reality is not a policy choice but admitting the hard knocks of life.

title: Who is King Haakon? What to know about Norway’s new monarch
description: Haakon takes the crown following his father’s death, and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra becomes heir apparent.
content: Crown Prince Haakon became Norway’s king on Friday after the death of his father Harald. Here are some ⁠facts about the new 53-year-old monarch. Early years The new king was born Haakon Magnus on July ⁠20, 1973, and went to a state primary school, as is expected of royals in the egalitarian Scandinavian nation – though his secondary school was private. He joined the navy before studying politics at the University of California, Berkeley and, later, development studies at the London School of Economics. Haakon developed an early love of music and surfing. He has said that if he were not a ‌royal, he would have aspired to be a pro surfer on the World Tour. A marriage tangled in scandal He met his wife Mette-Marit Tjessem Hoiby in a bar at a music festival in 1999 in the southern Norwegian city of Kristiansand. The fact that she was a commoner and a single parent, with a son from a previous relationship, initially triggered a media furore. Two decades later, the US Justice Department released extensive email correspondence between Mette-Marit and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. At the same time, her first son Marius Borg Hoiby, 29, – now Haakon’s stepson – was ⁠standing trial for rape and domestic violence, charges he denied. In June, Marius Borg Hoiby was found guilty of two out of four counts of rape and ‌one count of domestic violence and sentenced to four years in prison. Both he and the prosecution have appealed the sentence. Haakon stood by his wife through it all. He said he wanted to support his stepson, but released a statement ‌expressing sympathy with the alleged victims and said Hoeiby should face the judicial system like any other citizen. What will his royal name be? The new king will tell ⁠the government which name he has chosen at an extraordinary council of state in the early days of his reign. He is widely expected to keep his name – as his father did before ‌him – and so become King Haakon VIII of Norway. He could also choose another. Norway’s royal family has no surname. Who is next in line? Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, 22, is now heir apparent. She ‌is ‌in line to become Norway’s first female head of state since Queen Margrete I ruled over Norway, Sweden and Denmark at the turn of the ‌13th and 14th centuries. Since reforms introduced in 1990, it is the oldest child, male or female, who prevails in the line of succession. After Ingrid Alexandra ⁠comes Prince Sverre Magnus, 20. He caused a sensation aged 11 with his “dabbing” dance move on the royal balcony during the national day parade in ⁠2017. Hoiby is the oldest child in the family, but not in the royal succession. A European lineage Haakon is Norway’s fourth king since the country gained full independence from Sweden in 1905. His great-grandfather – Norway’s first king in the modern era – chose the title Haakon VII to evoke ‌the six, much earlier, King Haakons from ‌the medieval era, when Norway was independent. From the late 14th century until 1814, the country was ruled from Denmark, followed by Sweden until 1905. The Norwegian royal family has family links to other European monarchies. Haakon VII was the brother of the king of Denmark when the Norwegian parliament formally asked him to take the crown. Haakon VII’s wife, Queen Maud, was a daughter of Britain’s King Edward VII. That makes the new Norwegian king the great-great-great grandson of Britain’s Queen Victoria.

title: 5 new Hong Kong cafes and coffee shops to try in September 2026
description: A home-grown cafe returns to Kwun Tong, a Wan Chai pawn shop gets a caffeine kick and new spots open in IFC Mall, Sai Ying Pun and Tai Hang.
content: This month, Hong Kong’s cafe scene welcomes the return of a decade-old favourite to its original neighbourhood, as well as new establishments in Sai Ying Pun and Tai Hang. Several new openings blend concepts, including a coffee shop set up in a former pawn shop and a cafe collaboration with a cult car-tuning company from Japan. Here are five new coffee shop openings to visit in Hong Kong this September. 1. How Dept How Dept – which now has branches in Hysan Place, K11 Art Mall and other malls – started life as a furniture-showroom-cum-cafe hidden in an industrial building in Kwun Tong. Now, it returns with a new location on the same street it occupied a decade ago. The ground-floor space at The Angle mall looks out over the bustling streets, while the upgraded menu includes snacks such as Sichuan spicy beef nachos and mains such as cheese egg rolls with dried sakura shrimp and salmon roe. There is also an extensive coffee selection. Shop G01, G/F, The Angle, 98 How Ming Street, Kwun Tong 2. Coffee Boats x Project House @ Chun On Pawn Shop Coffee Boats was founded in late 2025 as a social enterprise supported by Caritas Hong Kong to empower youth and women from marginalised communities through work opportunities and training. Its coffee beans are sourced directly from farmers and roasted by professionally trained women from Caritas Hong Kong’s Healthy Neighbourhood Kitchen Project. Coffee Boats has held various small pop-ups and events across Hong Kong. Now, its most ambitious project yet sees it collaborating with charity One Bite Social to take over the historic Chun On Pawn Shop in Wan Chai. The takeover runs until December 19, with 20 per cent of the revenue to be donated to Caritas Hong Kong, which has also trained young people to operate the cafe. G/F, 91 Wan Chai Road, Wan Chai 3. Brown Heart A humble operation with a small menu, Brown Heart is the latest in a string of coffee shops to occupy its corner spot near Sai Ying Pun MTR in recent years. The food is simple but bursting with flavour, with signature sandwiches including burrata; Parma ham and green grape with truffle balsamic glaze; and crabmeat and mentaiko with mascarpone cheese, basil and cheddar. The matcha espresso latte is a good choice for those who cannot decide between coffee and matcha. 176 Queen’s Road West, Sai Ying Pun 4. Pop Beans An unusual coffee pit stop has landed inside the new Tai Hang store collaboration between cult Japanese car tuner Liberty Walk and Hong Kong model car brand Pop Race. Pop Beans cafe offers motorheads a prime spot to refuel on caffeine while perusing the latest racing merch and custom builds. G/F, China Tower, 1-9 Lin Fa Kung Street West, Tai Hang 5. Urban Coffee Roasters The home-grown roastery has opened a second outlet in Central following its Hollywood Road location. The IFC store features four branch-exclusive coffees, including a fruity single-origin Ethiopian bean with notes of passion fruit, blood orange and grape; and a Geisha blend with notes of flowers, honey and tangerine. The Geisha coffee is also crafted into a gelato for the perfect pairing. To celebrate the new opening, guests who sign up as UCR members can get a free upgrade to the Geisha blend with any coffee purchase from August 28 to 30. Shop 1032, 1/F, IFC Mall, 8 Finance Street, Central

title: Macau tycoon Lawrence Ho’s family office expands into space sector in de-SPAC deal
description: The business combination with Singapore-based Astrum Space could set the stage for a New York Stock Exchange debut by the end of the year.
content: Black Spade Capital, the family office of Macau casino billionaire Lawrence Ho Yau-lung, has announced its third “de-SPAC” deal through a merger with a satellite communications firm, a move granting it access to the space technology sector. Under the agreement, Singapore-based Astrum Space will combine with special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Black Spade Acquisition III, or BIII, at an equity value of about US$1 billion. The combined entity, Astrum Space Company, would seek a listing on the New York Stock Exchange, according to a press release published on Thursday. “Over the years, the space sector has evolved into one of today’s most dynamic industries and continues to play an increasingly important role in everyday life,” said Dennis Tam, executive chairman of the board and co-CEO of BIII, in the statement. “This partnership with Astrum reflects our belief in the power of enabling technologies to create meaningful impact.” Founded in 2023, Astrum is developing a next-generation satellite-to-device (S2D) broadcast network for the Asia-Pacific region. The company operates a wholesale business model targeting mobile network operators, broadcasters, governments and enterprise clients. Zhou Qingzhi, Astrum’s founder, promised financial backing of up to US$168 million to support the firm’s operations, investments and financial activities, including its satellite development milestones, according to a Thursday document filed by the company to the US Securities and Exchange Commission. The proposed combination with BIII is expected to strengthen our ability to execute our commercialisation strategy and expand strategic partnerships across the region Michael Do, Astrum Astrum currently operates its own in-orbit GEO satellite and is developing the NEASTAR-1 satellite for a planned launch in late 2028 or the first quarter of 2029. The company’s shareholders are projected to own over 80 per cent of the combined entity after the transaction, which is expected to close by the end of this year, pending regulatory and shareholder approvals. “The proposed combination with BIII is expected to strengthen our ability to execute our commercialisation strategy and expand strategic partnerships across the region,” said Michael Do, president and CEO of Astrum, in Thursday’s statement. In January, BIII raised US$150 million through its initial public offering in the United States. The Hong Kong-based firm previously stated that it was targeting a business combination at the intersection of entertainment-related enabling technology and digital financial infrastructure, according to the press release. BIII is the third SPAC by Black Spade Capital, the private investment arm of Ho, who serves as chairman and CEO of casino operator Melco International Development. Black Spade Capital’s first SPAC, Black Spade Acquisition, completed a merger in 2023 with Vietnamese electric vehicle maker VinFast – often dubbed “Vietnam’s Tesla” and founded by the country’s richest man, Pham Nhat Vuong – valuing the automobile company at about US$23 billion. Its second SPAC completed a merger with media and entertainment company The Generation Essentials Group.

title: MiniMax expands Alibaba cloud pact as compute needs surge for training and inference
description: Chinese AI firm burns through two-thirds of its cloud budget by June, forcing a dramatic increase in its Alibaba deal ceiling.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence firm MiniMax has raised the three-year purchase ceiling on its cloud computing deals with Alibaba Group Holding by 220 per cent to US$1.2 billion, underscoring surging demand for computing power among the country’s top AI developers. The Shanghai-based company planned to spend up to US$300 million on Alibaba Cloud services this year, nearly triple its original US$115 million cap, after burning through two-thirds of its budget by the end of June, according to its Hong Kong stock exchange filings on Wednesday. Under the updated agreement through 2028, MiniMax’s annual spending limits on Alibaba Cloud services will jump from US$125 million to US$400 million for 2027, and from US$135 million to US$500 million for 2028. In a separate revision, MiniMax expanded its application programming interface (API) service budget with Alibaba, raising the 2026 cap from US$650,000 to US$7.5 million, an over tenfold increase. This brings its three-year API spending ceiling to US$62.5 million, a nearly 20-fold jump from previous limits. The aggressive revisions reflect MiniMax’s expanding compute needs for both model training and live inference. Known for its M-series large language models, the H3 video-generation model and popular consumer app Hailuo AI, MiniMax this week reported a 283 per cent surge in first-half revenue to US$116.6 million, driven by a 700 per cent leap in enterprise sales. Founder and CEO Yan Junjie said on Wednesday the firm’s coming models – including M3.1, M3 Pro and H3.1 – were “nearly completed”. To support its expansion, MiniMax raised HK$16 billion in July via a share placement and convertible bond issuance, earmarking about 80 per cent of net proceeds for AI infrastructure and model development through 2027. The revised deals highlight an industry-wide shift in China’s generative AI landscape from foundational model training to scaling compute-heavy inference workloads driven by agentic AI. China’s model-as-a-service market was projected to handle 40,000 trillion token calls by 2026, according to projections by research firm IDC. Alibaba reported a 45 per cent revenue increase in its cloud and AI businesses for the quarter ended June, its fastest growth in 22 quarters. The firm also began commercial-scale deployment of its Zhenwu M890 AI processor earlier this month. MiniMax said in its filing that Alibaba cloud service procurement accounted for about 30 per cent of its total research and development expense of US$253 million last year, a ratio it expected to maintain as it scaled infrastructure to support future operations. The company’s procurement of Alibaba products, it added, could ensure “secure, stable and efficient underlying infrastructure and cloud service support with high scalability and flexibility”, supporting the smooth running of its core business and the development of foundation models. Beyond its deep Alibaba cooperation, MiniMax has also been establishing its own computing infrastructure. During the earnings call this week, Yan said MiniMax was building an “independent and controllable” computing cluster – complete with high-bandwidth networks, dedicated lines, servers and storage – to serve as a core technology going forward. The company had started using domestically made AI chips, which would account for a larger share of its computing power from the fourth quarter of this year, he said. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: Truce in DR Congo offers US mining foothold while Chinese firms dominate output
description: Washington could secure access to crucial eastern coltan deposits, though analysts say Beijing’s entrenched infrastructure leaves American investors trailing.
content: A peace plan agreed between the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Rwanda-backed M23 movement last weekend could open the rebel-held Rubaya coltan deposit and other parts of mineral-rich eastern Congo to US investors. But observers say that even a lasting settlement would leave the United States far behind China, whose companies have spent decades building mining assets, relationships and supply chains across the country. The peace road map followed five days of talks and set out steps and timelines for negotiations under a US-brokered framework reached last year. The two sides also agreed to establish a mechanism for investigating ceasefire violations, although parties remain divided over sanctions on M23, the release of detainees and the timing of political reforms. The Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus, or EJVM+, carried out its first ceasefire-monitoring mission in eastern Congo this week with support from the UN mission MONUSCO. Massad Boulos, the US senior adviser on Arab and African affairs, called it “an important step from commitments on paper to pursuing peace on the ground”, saying effective monitoring could “build confidence, protect civilians” and help create the conditions for lasting peace. Kai Xue, a Beijing-based corporate lawyer who advises on foreign direct investment and cross-border financing, said peace in the DR Congo would pave the way for capital from China, the US, the Gulf states and India to work together to “ensure the copper century in Congo”, referring to an expected period of rising global copper demand. The Trump administration has secured preferential access for US companies to selected Congolese mineral assets, including in Rubaya, one of the world’s richest coltan deposits. Coltan is a source of tantalum, a heat-resistant metal used in electronics, aerospace technology and defence equipment. America First Global, chaired by Trump ally and former campaign fundraiser Gentry Beach, is seeking rights to the site alongside Swiss commodities trader Mercuria. But Rubaya remains under the control of M23 rebels, who use taxes from its mineral trade to help finance their operations. Chris Berry, head of US-based advisory firm House Mountain Partners, said a ceasefire alone would not make Rubaya an attractive investment. M23 would need to withdraw, and US investors could require government support such as a guaranteed minimum price. “A ‘lasting ceasefire’ would need to migrate to a withdrawal in order to properly balance risk and reward here,” Berry said. US-backed investors are also expanding their presence in southern Congo, where major Chinese companies have vast copper and cobalt operations. The US has been pushing to curb China’s dominance of DR Congo’s critical minerals sector. In 2024, the Biden administration reportedly urged Congolese state miner Gecamines to block a US$1.4 billion takeover of Chemaf SA by Norin Mining, a unit of China’s state-owned Norinco group, fearing it would deepen Beijing’s control over strategic copper and cobalt supplies. Under Trump, Washington then backed the acquisition of the same assets by US firm Virtus Minerals. Berry said it was still early days for the US in the DR Congo, with the Virtus deal only one example of a Western presence in the country. “It’s a good start but nowhere near comparable to the Chinese presence in the [DR Congo],” Berry said, adding that Chinese companies already operated mines, had invested heavily and had commercial relationships and supply chain links in the country. “For the southern copper and cobalt belt, peace would remove a big cloud hanging over the country and region. “It would encourage large Chinese mining companies to keep on making major investments and build infrastructure, leading to double-digit growth in output year after year.” Chinese companies also have gold interests in the conflict-hit east, including the Chinese-backed Twangiza mine, which M23 seized in May last year. “In South Kivu, small-scale Chinese mining operators have created something of a wild west,” Xue said, referring to poorly regulated gold mining in the conflict-hit province. He said peace could reset the sector and allow more established companies to enter. China and the DR Congo deepened formal mining cooperation in March by signing a memorandum covering geological data sharing, investment protection, local processing and compliance monitoring. Berry said the timing appeared to be a response to Washington’s growing involvement and reflected Kinshasa’s attempt to extract better terms by balancing the two powers. “Both the US and China are after the same thing – the resources – so the DR Congo has some real leverage here regarding the terms of any deal it wishes to strike with the Americans and the Chinese,” Berry said.

title: Japanese rugby officials roll back on proposed restrictions on certain foreign-born players
description: Top domestic competition Rugby League One will allow certain players with Japanese nationality, but who were born elsewhere, to qualify.
content: Rugby officials in Japan on Friday said they had reached a settlement to allow players with Japanese nationality, but who were born elsewhere, to qualify for the top eligibility category in the domestic competition, Rugby League One. Under proposed rules changes that were to go into effect when the league opens in December, players with Japanese passports, but who were born outside Japan and not educated there during childhood, would have had their eligibility restricted. In a statement on Friday, Japan Rugby League One said it decided “to revise certain requirements”. It said players who acquired Japanese nationality before the end of May 2025 would be treated on a par with native-born players. Twenty-four players affected by the proposed rules change – all with Japanese passports but born elsewhere – filed a suit in a Japanese court and pushed for the rollback. Among them was Timothy Lafaele, who starred for Japan in the 2019 World Cup, which was held in Japan. The proposed rules had specified that players had to live in Japan for “at least six of nine years” of junior school and junior high school to qualify for the highest category of eligibility. “League One takes seriously the feedback received regarding this system change, as well as the fact that prior explanations and communication with all relevant parties were insufficient, and will reflect this in the future management of the league,” it said in a statement. Many players born in countries like Australia and New Zealand move to Japan at a young age in search of a rugby career. The group of players who mounted legal action included several who helped Japan stun Ireland and Scotland on the way to the World Cup quarter-finals in 2019. It was the first time an Asian country had ever reached the last eight. How the immigration debate touches rugby Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been pushing tougher policies on immigration and foreigners. Many Japanese complain of struggling with stagnant salaries, rising prices – and some link it to a surge in foreigners to sustain a shrinking workforce as Japan’s population declines. Many sports bodies across the globe consistently bend eligibility rules for commercial reasons, or to gain a competitive edge. And changing eligibility rules often faces pushback, particularly when local players seem to be sidelined. Japan rugby officials have said the player pool of Japan-born players is shrinking, and limiting foreigners would help boost it.

title: Japan police to roll out body-worn cameras nationwide in 2027 after trials
description: The National Police Agency has requested US$1 million to deploy 2,000 cameras to verify questioning and gather evidence.
content: Japanese police will expand use of body-worn cameras nationwide from next financial year after trials showed they were effective in providing evidence and verifying that investigative procedures were followed appropriately, the National Police Agency said on Friday. The agency has requested about 170 million yen (US$1 million) for the year starting April 2027 to cover related costs for around 2,000 cameras. Trials began in September last year in 13 prefectural police departments, covering community affairs, traffic enforcement and crowd control operations. Trials were conducted for community affairs in Tokyo, Osaka and Fukuoka prefectures until November. Footage was used as evidence in a case of obstruction of official duties, in which a Fukuoka prefectural police officer who had intervened to mediate a dispute – while the incident, including police questioning, was being recorded – was kicked by a man. In another case, a suspect in drug-related cases claimed to have been forcibly taken in for questioning, but video footage confirmed that there were no issues. While Niigata, Aichi and Kochi prefectural police conducted trials in traffic enforcement operations for six months, supervisors used footage on around 160 occasions to check whether procedures for catching traffic offenders had been done by the book. Some drivers who were stopped by police said they thought it was good that cameras recorded questioning, according to the agency. Year-long trials for crowd control in public places, such as event venues and railway stations, are being conducted by police in nine prefectures, including Hokkaido and Hiroshima. In more than 10 cases during the three kinds of trials, people showed resistance to being filmed. When officers were unable to gain consent even after explaining the purpose of the recording, they handed the matter over to an officer not wearing a camera, the agency said. Police considered introducing cameras amid cases in which the appropriateness of street questioning and traffic enforcement was called into question. “Video footage provides an objective and accurate record of when something happened, who was involved and what they did,” an agency official said, stressing the usefulness of the cameras.

title: Shares in Chinese MLCC makers rise as AI lifts sales and profits
description: CCTC and Guangdong Fenghua have reported strong first-half results as AI data centre demand drives MLCC orders and a global pricing upcycle.
content: China’s top makers of multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) – ubiquitous components known as the “rice of the electronics industry” – saw their shares rise on Friday after reporting ballooning first-half sales and profits amid soaring demand linked to AI. Shenzhen-listed shares of Chaozhou Three-Circle Company (CCTC) and Guangdong Fenghua Advanced Technology, two of the country’s largest MLCC makers, gained nearly 1 per cent and 3 per cent, respectively, in morning trading. CCTC’s Hong Kong-listed shares rose more than 4 per cent. The rally followed strong first-half earnings reported on Thursday. CCTC’s revenue surged 55 per cent to 6.4 billion yuan (US$952.3 million), while its net profit jumped 56 per cent to 1.9 billion yuan. On the same day, domestic rival Guangdong Fenghua said its net profit for the first half of 2026 rose 74 per cent year on year to 290.3 million yuan. Sales increased 26 per cent to 3.5 billion yuan. CCTC attributed the increase in sales to improving market sentiment and a recovery in MLCC prices. For the second half of 2026, CCTC said it would step up its push into high-end MLCCs for the server and automotive sectors, seeking breakthroughs in – and mass production of – ultra-high-capacitance, large-format products. Guangdong Fenghua also highlighted its shift towards higher-end products. The company said it had made progress in developing and scaling up production of several such products, “centring around high-growth segments like AI computing and automotive electronics”, according to its interim report. This marks a departure from the company’s previous practice of limiting price adjustments to distributors and signals that the MLCC industry has officially entered an upcycle TrendForce MLCCs have become increasingly sought-after amid the rapid buildout of power-hungry data centres to support AI’s expanding computing needs. Yet the high-end MLCCs used in AI servers and data centres remain dominated by Japan’s Murata Manufacturing, the world’s largest producer, and South Korea’s Samsung Electro-Mechanics (SEM), both of which have been inundated with orders and are operating at or close to 95 per cent of capacity. SEM has taken the lead among major global MLCC makers by raising fourth-quarter prices for standard MLCCs used in consumer electronics by an average of 25 to 30 per cent, according to a TrendForce report published on Thursday. The move was intended to curb demand for consumer-grade MLCCs and free up capacity for higher-end products, the report said. Prices for AI-server-grade MLCCs, meanwhile, were expected to rise by an average of 10 to 20 per cent. “This marks a departure from the company’s previous practice of limiting price adjustments to distributors and signals that the MLCC industry has officially entered an upcycle,” TrendForce wrote. In July, SEM said it would focus on supplying cutting-edge MLCCs for AI applications after reporting second-quarter revenue of 3.5 trillion won (US$2.5 billion), up 24 per cent year on year, and net income of 315.7 billion won, up 143 per cent. Murata raised its full-year operating profit forecast by 13 per cent to a record high of 430 billion yen (US$2.7 billion) for the financial year ending March 2027, buoyed by AI server demand. It reported a 21 per cent increase in revenue to 502.3 billion yen, and a 64 per cent jump in net profit to 81.4 billion yen in the June quarter.

title: Hong Kong’s revised heat stress warning system may lack rest provisions: experts
description: Work breaks triggered by higher alerts are also not protected by law, legislator says.
content: Hong Kong’s outdoor workers could still lack adequate rest under the revamped heat stress warning system, a lawmaker and a construction industry representative have said, adding that work breaks triggered by higher alerts are not protected by law. The response followed the Labour Department’s announcement on Thursday that it had updated the Heat Stress at Work Warning system to better safeguard workers, after the mechanism was criticised for not triggering higher-tier alerts during record-breaking temperatures earlier this month. Lawmaker Lam Chun-sing, chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong and Kowloon Labour Unions, said on Friday that the department should consider extending rest periods to workers with moderate workloads under the system’s highest-level black warning, so that street cleaners could be covered. “Aside from modifying the triggering mechanism, the threshold requirements for the highest heat stress warning signal remain high,” he said. Lam cited that all non-essential outdoor workers were required to stop working regardless of their workload when either the No 9 or 10 typhoon warning was issued. The total duration when highest heat stress warnings were active in any given year could be even less than when the highest typhoon signals were in effect, he said. “During such severe conditions [of extreme heat], allowing work suspension to cover workers of moderate workload, such as street cleaners, will offer them much better protection,” Lam said. He said that whether the revamped system provided sufficient rest periods under high heat stress would require further review by the department. “We still need to see how things work in practice, as workers’ real experiences on the ground can be different from scientific data,” he said. The heat stress warning system has three levels – amber, red and black – which alert employers and staff to the severity of heat stress when working outdoors or indoors without air conditioning. The system relies on the Hong Kong Heat Index, which factors in air temperature, humidity, wind speed and solar radiation to measure heat stress. When the amber warning is active, employers are advised to arrange additional rest periods for affected workers. Workers with “very heavy” workloads should suspend their duties under the red alert, while those with “heavy” workloads should do so under the black warning. But the suspension does not cover workers with “light” or “moderate” workloads, who should still work under the highest warning, but are advised to be given longer rest periods. The department earlier estimated that under the revamped system, which took effect on Friday, the red warning could be issued four to seven days a year, while the black alert could be triggered one or two days a year. The estimate amounted to about 10 affected days for some workers. Citing a guideline by the Hong Kong Construction Association, Lam said the industry also recommended a blanket, site-wide suspension of all work when a black heat stress warning was issued, regardless of the trade or workload intensity. Lawrence Ng San-wa, permanent honorary chairman of the Hong Kong Construction Sub-Contractors Association, said that 10 affected days annually would have a limited impact on most construction projects, except for individual cases where work clashed directly with the 10 days. On August 9 this year, when the Observatory logged the highest temperature reading at its headquarters since records began in 1884, only one out of the 10 monitoring stations recorded an index reading of more than 32, according to figures obtained by the South China Morning Post. Before the adjustments to the heat stress warning system, amber, red or black warnings were issued when index readings at the King’s Park Meteorological Station or four of the nine other monitoring sites reached 30, 32 or 34, respectively. The amber alert could also be triggered when the Observatory issued the extremely hot weather special alert. From Friday, if the special alert is active, the warning can escalate to red or black if the King’s Park station or two of the other nine monitoring sites record index readings of 32 or 34. If measured temperatures reach 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) across at least 40 per cent of weather stations, the index threshold for the red or black warning will drop to 30 and 32. But the department did not take the advice from leading meteorologists that the system should adopt the international wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) index, which puts more weight on direct sunlight exposure. Lam urged authorities to reconsider the WBGT measurement. “Direct sunlight combined with high perceived temperatures makes the work [of outdoor workers] significantly tougher,” he said. Despite the new changes, the heat stress warning system also remains an advisory guideline. But Lam urged authorities to monitor employer compliance and consider legislation. Ng, representing construction subcontractors, said appropriate rest for workers could reduce health risks and was “ultimately a positive thing” for projects. He echoed Lam’s views on the point of legislation, urging authorities to consider making work suspension for construction workers during the black heat stress warning signal a statutory requirement rather than a guideline. “In reality, it is very difficult for subcontractors to decide whether to suspend work,” Ng said, noting that delays in projects could result in financial penalties from contractors’ clients.

title: Bitcoin rally and Alibaba share purchases: the numbers moving markets
description: Alibaba shares, bitcoin, Hong Kong second-hand home prices and Shein’s IPO plans in spotlight this week.
content: Bitcoin and gold rallied this week as the size of America’s sovereign debt continued to haunt global financial markets. Meanwhile, Alibaba Group Holding’s top executives and founder Jack Ma bought back shares, and Shein announced plans for a smaller Hong Kong initial public offering than previously expected. Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week. Founder, executives buy over HK$800m of Alibaba shares Alibaba founder Ma, chairman Joe Tsai and CEO Eddie Wu Yongming collectively bought more than HK$800 million (US$102 million) worth of the company’s Hong Kong-listed shares within days. Ma accounted for more than HK$600 million of the purchases, while Tsai and Wu spent a combined HK$202 million, signalling confidence in Alibaba – owner of the South China Morning Post – as it steps up its push into artificial intelligence. Bitcoin climbs above US$80,000 Bitcoin climbed past US$80,000 for the first time in three months this week. The rally, which took bitcoin above US$80,900 on Tuesday, came as Washington’s efforts to curb elevated Treasury yields boosted appetites for alternative assets such as cryptocurrencies. Hong Kong’s lived-in home prices fall 0.46 per cent Hong Kong’s lived-in home prices index slipped to 321.5 in July from 323 in June, Rating and Valuation Department data showed on Thursday. It was the first decline in the index, which tracks the prices of second-hand homes, in 16 months. Shein seeks up to HK$13.85b in Hong Kong IPO Fast-fashion giant Shein is seeking to raise as much as HK$13.85 billion (US$1.76 billion) in its long-awaited Hong Kong initial public offering, reviving a listing plan first contemplated four years ago. The company is offering 279 million shares at HK$47.60 to HK$49.50 apiece, with trading expected to begin on September 1, according to a stock exchange filing on Monday.

title: More Chinese regions are raising minimum wages, but will it help boost consumption?
description: Guangdong, Shanxi and Xinjiang have announced plans to introduce increases of 10 per cent or more in the next few months.
content: As more Chinese provincial-level regions raise minimum wages, economists say the increases could encourage lower-income workers to spend more, but were unlikely to significantly boost consumption or the broader economy and could add to the cost burdens faced by smaller firms. The provinces of Guangdong and Shanxi and the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region announced this month that wage increases of around 10 per cent or more would be implemented later this year. The increases far outpace their rates of gross domestic product growth last year – which ranged between 3.9 per cent and 5.5 per cent – and are double 2025’s national GDP growth rate. Sheana Yue, an economist at Oxford Economics, described the moves as “part of a broader rebalancing towards household income”. The adjustments were “targeted at lower-income workers, who tend to have a relatively high propensity to consume”, she said. Guangdong has planned the largest increase, with its minimum monthly wage to be 2,040 yuan (US$304) from next month – 16.6 per cent higher than at the start of this year. Resource-rich Shanxi and the far-western region of Xinjiang followed, with both planning to raise their monthly wage floors by about 10.3 per cent from October. The adjustments will see Shanxi’s minimum wage rise to 2,150 yuan and Xinjiang’s to 1,930 yuan. Chongqing municipality and Sichuan province, both in southwestern China, have published draft proposals to raise minimum wages by more than 7 per cent to 2,360 yuan from December. Many of the regions missed their GDP growth targets last year, with Guangdong – whose economy grew just 3.9 per cent against a target of about 5 per cent – planning the most striking wage increase relative to its economic performance. All of the mainland’s 31 provincial-level regions have increased or announced plans to increase monthly minimum wages since last year, with more than half opting for double-digit rises, according to calculations based on government data. In recent years, Chinese policymakers have repeatedly called for higher household incomes as a way to boost domestic consumption. In the first half of this year, per capita real disposable income increased 4.2 per cent, but real consumer spending rose only 2.7 per cent, according to government statistics, underscoring the gap between income growth and household spending by cautious consumers. China’s current weakness in consumption reflects broader concerns about employment, income expectations and household wealth Sheana Yue, Oxford Economics China’s first five-year plan dedicated to consumption, published last month, called for the use of diversified channels to boost household incomes and the steady raising of minimum-wage standards. However, economists have questioned how much of that extra income will actually translate into spending. “Minimum-wage workers are only a subset of households, and China’s current weakness in consumption reflects broader concerns about employment, income expectations and household wealth,” Yue said. “A wage increase cannot by itself resolve those issues.” She said she expected the impact on household spending to be marginal, with minimum-wage increases unlikely to give national economic growth a meaningful lift on their own. Alex Muscatelli, director of economics at Fitch Ratings, also said that, viewed in isolation, the increases would not provide “substantial upside” to the consumer spending outlook. Yue and Muscatelli both said the higher labour costs from the wage increases could be another burden for employers, many of whom were already struggling with weak domestic demand and shrinking margins. “For companies, particularly labour-intensive and low-margin private firms, the immediate effect is an increase in labour costs at a time when profitability and cash flow are already under pressure,” Yue said. Muscatelli said there would be “pockets of small firms where the impact may be felt”, but he expected the impact on firms’ profitability to be limited, given the gaps between minimum-wage levels and average earnings. Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research, said China’s minimum-wage standards were equivalent to just 25 to 30 per cent of average monthly earnings, well below the international benchmark of about 40 per cent, and that meant “there is still substantial room for future hikes”. Some local governments in regions such as Shanghai, Jiangsu, Hunan, Guangdong and Sichuan have also intensified scrutiny of social security contributions this year, compounding the cost pressures on smaller firms, according to Chinese media reports.

title: Norway’s King Harald dies at 89 after 35-year reign
description: Son becomes King Haakon VIII following the death of Europe’s oldest reigning monarch.
content: Norway’s King Harald has died aged 89, the palace said on Friday, his 53-year-old son Crown Prince Haakon automatically succeeding him on the throne. “It is with deep sadness that we announce that His Majesty King Harald passed away today. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, August 28 at 6.35am,” it said in a statement. The flag at the royal palace in Oslo was lowered to half mast. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said he had received the news with “deep sorrow”. “An entire nation mourns, and at the same time remains profoundly grateful for a long life devoted to Norway,” he said in a statement. “King Harald loved Norway. And Norway loved its king.” The government later announced a period of national mourning until the king was buried. Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, King Harald had been in hospital in Oslo since August 17 suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. The royal family had rushed to his bedside on Thursday as the palace announced that Harald’s condition was “extremely serious”. His wife Queen Sonja, Haakon and his wife Mette-Marit and their adult children spent much of Thursday at his bedside, with media reporting that Haakon kept vigil overnight. The public streamed to the palace in central Oslo for a second straight day on Friday, laying flowers on the ground and huddling in groups. Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne in 1991, has had multiple health problems in recent years, forcing him to have a pacemaker fitted and to scale back his official schedule. But he always ruled out abdicating, arguing that he took a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament. Neighbouring Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf called him “an outstanding representative of his country. He gave ‘All for Norway’”, referring to Harald’s royal motto. Denmark’s King Frederik meanwhile called the late monarch “an extraordinary man”. The British King Charles III said he mourned the death of his “dear cousin”, hailing Harald as a “towering figure”. Harald was also king when the Oslo Accords between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) were negotiated in the 1990s, and Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he was “deeply saddened” by his passing. The past year has been a turbulent one for the Norwegian royal family. In February, King Harald was hospitalised for an infection and dehydration in Tenerife, where he was on a private trip with Queen Sonja. His wife, also 89, was briefly admitted to hospital in May due to heart problems. Haakon’s wife Mette-Marit is under scrutiny for her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Documents published in January in the United States revealed her sustained and at times intimate correspondence with Epstein between 2011 and 2014, at a time when the American financier had already been convicted. Mette-Marit’s son from a relationship prior to her marriage to Haakon, Marius Borg Hoiby, is also in the spotlight as a result of his legal troubles. He was sentenced in June to four years in prison for two rapes and 32 other charges, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed the verdict. Suffering herself from a serious lung disease, Mette-Marit, 53, had to undergo a lung transplant in July. The royals remain broadly popular with the Norwegian public, in large part to Harald’s unifying status and his unassuming, modest lifestyle.

title: Meet Lorenzo Musetti, the Italian tennis star gearing up for his comeback at the US Open
description: Sidelined by a leg injury earlier this year, the Tuscan-born player recently shared the court with Roger Federer for a special practice session at Arthur Ashe Stadium.
content: Lorenzo Musetti, who missed the French Open and Wimbledon with a leg injury, is set to make his comeback at the 2026 US Open. The main draw runs from Sunday to September 13 at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in New York. The 24-year-old Italian is currently ranked No 14 in the ATP singles rankings, having reached a career-high No 5 after finishing as runner-up at the Hong Kong Tennis Open in January. Here’s what we know about Lorenzo Musetti. What is Lorenzo Musetti’s background? Born on 3 March 2002 in Tuscany, Italy, Lorenzo Musetti is the son of a marble producer and a secretary. He started playing tennis at age four, and at eight, he met coach Simone Tartarini, who has since shaped him into a world-class player known for his bold, high-risk shots. “A really important turning point came when Lorenzo was 14,” Tartarini told the ATP last year. “That’s when I made the decision to invest in him professionally and financially. I left my tennis club and started travelling the world with him to help him grow.” How did Lorenzo Musetti get injured? During his Australian Open quarter-final match against Novak Djokovic in January, Musetti felt a tweak in his upper right leg at the beginning of the second set. As he played through the pain, it worsened, leading him to eventually concede the match. He had won the first two sets and was trailing in the third when he took a medical timeout. “At the end, when I took the medical timeout, to stay three minutes, I sat, and when I started to play again, I felt even more and was getting higher and higher the level of the pain,” Musetti told the press at the time. But the story didn’t end there. When Musetti faced Casper Ruud at the Italian Open in May, the pain struck again – this time in the front part of his left thigh. Musetti ended up losing to Ruud 6-3, 6-1. View this post on Instagram He later took to Instagram to announce the results of his medical tests. “After yesterday’s match, I underwent medical examinations which revealed a rectus femoris injury, requiring several weeks of rest and recovery,” Musetti wrote. “Unfortunately, this means I won’t be able to compete in Hamburg and Roland Garros – news that is incredibly hard to take.” He also thanked the home crowd for their support. “A huge thank you to the Rome crowd for your incredible support: that’s exactly why, despite not being 100 per cent, I chose to step on court and give everything I had in my home tournament. I’ll keep you updated.” Who is Lorenzo Musetti dating? Musetti is in a relationship with graphic designer Veronica Confalonieri. The pair went Instagram-official in 2022 and share two sons: two-year-old Ludovico and nine-month-old Leandro. Confalonieri is a regular presence in the stands, frequently cheering on her partner during major matches. The couple are not currently married.

title: Nepal army races to rescue 100 trapped in hydropower tunnel after flash floods
description: Helicopter teams are operating in high-risk conditions following a glacial collapse that inundated the Trishuli 3A project.
content: Helicopter rescue teams were working on Friday to rescue around 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower project in Nepal swamped by a devastating flood two days earlier. “Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet said. “Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people with what they need,” he added. The prime minister’s office said in a statement that the army had been working in tough conditions. “A Nepali Army team has successfully rescued 350 workers and locals who were trapped in the tunnel a while ago facing extremely risky and challenging conditions amid adverse weather and rapid floodwaters,” the statement read. “The army is still working to safely evacuate more than 100 people trapped in the same tunnel.” It did not give further details about the nationalities of those rescued or trapped. Devastating floods near the border with China this week have killed at least 579 people in Nepal, its disaster authority said on Friday. More than 1,400 people are missing, including hundreds of foreigners. The scale of destruction from devastating floods in Nepal’s northern border region was becoming clearer on Friday, with roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure destroyed and survivors describing scenes of extraordinary devastation. Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed. “There were at least 400 workers at the site,” Dev Shrestha, who was airlifted from the site where he was working, said after his rescue. “More people died than were rescued.” Worker Buddha Tamang said he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck – but he had managed to get out and reach help. “I survived as I was in the tunnel,” said Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours. “The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away.” Another worker, Arjun Kumar Tamang, spoke of “massive damage” at the hydropower site where he had been. “I don’t know how many people died but the force of the water swept everything away,” he said. The US Geological Survey said the disaster on Wednesday was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris. Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses. The destruction has severed vital links across a mountainous region where roads and bridges are often the only routes. The damage also extended to Nepal’s key hydropower sector, with several projects – both operating and under construction – hit hard. The US Geological Survey said the disaster – the deadliest for Nepal since a 2015 earthquake – was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris. In addition, Indian authorities recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be victims of the devastating floods, officials said on Friday. Authorities are working to identify the bodies, and the seven bodies in India are not included in the overall toll.

title: Will Australia be locked out of top scientific research by shunning Chinese universities?
description: Observers say Canberra is starting to align with Washington on security policy after it cut partnerships with two institutions from China.
content: Australia’s decision to axe partnerships with two Chinese universities has raised concerns that Canberra is moving to align with Washington on research security policy. The decision came after the United States expanded its restrictions on research entities from China. One analyst warned that Canberra’s latest move would not hinder Chinese progress, but it could leave Australia locked out of top-tier scientific research. The Australian National University confirmed in a statement that it would comply with Foreign Minister Penny Wong’s order earlier this month to end its teaching partnership with Shandong University on national security grounds. ANU said the university took “risks associated with foreign interference, national security and international engagement seriously”. Earlier, The Australian reported that Wong had also cancelled a research collaboration between the University of Queensland and the Chinese Academy of Sciences to develop pain relief from a native plant, also citing security concerns. Canberra’s directive came after the Pentagon added Shandong University to its list of foreign institutions deemed to pose national security threats.
