Chen Hong, director of the Australian Studies Centre at East China Normal University in Shanghai, said the axed deals suggested Canberra was starting to move in lockstep with Washington on research security. “The US defines which Chinese institutions pose a risk and Australia re-examines its own partnerships through the lens of allied security,” he said. “It signals a shift towards replacing project-level risk assessments with institutional blacklisting, and replacing academic judgment with political discretion.” The ANU joint venture with Shandong University offered undergraduate programmes in biology, chemistry, mathematics and physics. The pain relief research was part of a broader collaboration between the state of Queensland and the CAS, with funding from both sides. Chinese students enrolled in the SDU-ANU Joint Science College could study in China for three years before doing a two-year stint in Canberra. Chen noted there were growing political risks facing joint projects between China and Australia, particularly in sensitive “dual-use” sectors such as artificial intelligence, quantum technology, advanced materials, biotechnology, data science and autonomous systems. That view was echoed by James Laurenceson, director of the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney. He said Wong’s directive sent a clear political message to academia, prompting Australian universities and individual researchers to “proactively steer away from collaborations with China”. According to Chen, Canberra’s alignment with Washington created regulatory barriers for Chinese institutions in Australian academia while extending trust to its Five Eyes partners – an intelligence alliance with the US, Britain, Canada and New Zealand. “If this trend continues, when selecting partners, Australian universities may no longer prioritise those who possess the strongest research capabilities, but who is deemed strategically most trustworthy,” Chen said. Laurenceson described the axed partnerships as “relatively low risk” and questioned whether Australian researchers could easily switch to US-aligned allies for such projects. He said policy-driven disruptions would do little to slow China’s technological rise, given that the country was leading the way in key fundamental research. “If we deliberately cut ourselves off from China, the inevitable consequence will be that in a growing field Australia will be locking itself into a second-rate scientific research ecosystem,” Laurenceson said. Responding to the cancellations, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian hit out at what he called “overstretching the concept of national security” and politicising or weaponising normal scientific, educational and academic exchanges. Neither Chen nor Laurenceson expected a total collapse in education and research ties between Australia and China given their deep institutional roots. An Australian Department of Education report in June said China had approved three joint institutes and eight joint programmes with Australia this year – up from two institutes and one programme in 2025. That took the total to 22 active joint institutes and 101 joint programmes by May. Notably, nearly 80 per cent of the newly approved partnerships are in fields related to digital and information technology, advanced manufacturing and engineering, and environmental sustainability and ecology. Australia and China have mended ties under Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s Labor government after a prolonged period of tension over issues including political meddling allegations, a ban on Huawei 5G, Canberra’s push for an investigation into the origin of Covid-19, and trade. According to Laurenceson, the government’s veto of joint university projects suggested political trust between the nations remained low, but he said it was unlikely to derail the broader stabilisation agenda or trigger fallout in areas like trade.

title: China Life’s revenue surges as top insurer ramps up investment in AI, chips and biotech
description: Company pledges long-term support for tech-innovation after revenue jumps 81 per cent and net profit soars 228 per cent.
content: China Life Insurance, the country’s largest life insurer, has posted record highs in its first-half results, and says it will scale up investments in technology-related sectors while seeking to become a long-term partner for innovative enterprises. The Shanghai- and Hong Kong-listed insurer recorded revenue of 434.3 billion yuan (US$64.6 billion), up 81.5 per cent year on year, according to interim results released on Thursday. Net profit surged more than 228 per cent to 134.5 billion yuan. The company, the world’s largest life insurer by market value, attributed profit growth to business development with risk control, progress in product and business diversification, refined asset allocation and robust investment returns. “Investment in areas related to new quality productive forces represents a key growth driver best positioned to deliver differentiated returns, and there lies broad potential for future investment and layout,” vice-president Liu Hui said at a press briefing in Beijing on Friday. “Our investment portfolio includes ChangXin Memory Technologies. Next, we will increase investments in sectors such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors, healthcare, biotechnology and new-generation infrastructure.” China Life had accelerated deep-level integration of new technologies such as AI large models into its business scenarios, according to the company. Its investments in technology finance surpassed 1 trillion yuan during the half-year period, while investments in new quality productive forces exceeded 540 billion yuan. Premiums from new policies reached 180 billion yuan, up 11.6 per cent year on year, according to its earnings report. The board proposed an interim cash dividend of 3.58 yuan per 10 shares, totalling 10.12 billion yuan, a 50.4 per cent increase year on year.

title: Chinese power stocks slump after US grid ban: is the sell-off warranted?
description: Sungrow and Sieyuan shares fell sharply after Washington’s order, but analysts say markets may be overlooking enforcement hurdles and strong global demand.
content: Chinese power equipment stocks have tumbled after the United States moved to bar certain foreign-made grid equipment and related software, but some analysts believe the sell-off may have been excessive, with enforcement still uncertain and Chinese firms able to offset the impact in other markets. Sungrow Power Supply, a major Chinese inverter maker, slumped 12.24 per cent on Thursday after US President Donald Trump signed an executive order a day earlier, declaring a national emergency and barring certain foreign-produced bulk-power equipment and associated software from being bought or installed in the US. Also on Thursday, Sieyuan Electric, which is listed on Shenzhen’s main board where daily price movements are capped at 10 per cent, hit its maximum limit with a 10 per cent fall. Despite the sharp equity-market reaction, analysts said investors might have overestimated the potential fallout. Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, a think tank under the Ministry of Commerce, said the direct impact would not be as severe as markets feared, though the ban “clearly touches a lot of companies”. Its real-world effect, he noted, would depend on how strictly Washington enforced the order, as US officials would need to weigh the restrictions against potential disruptions to the American economy and end users. From a purely commercial standpoint, the long-term financial impact of this ban on Chinese companies will be fairly limited Wu Xinbo, Fudan University “We’ve seen similar playbooks before – for instance, when restrictions were placed on DJI drones. In reality, many US users couldn’t simply abandon or replace that equipment overnight,” Zhou said. “I believe the market sentiment has, at times, exaggerated the actual impact. How this plays out in practice remains to be seen.” As of 11.30am on Friday when the domestic A-share market closed for lunch, Sieyuan had fallen a further 6 per cent, while Sungrow was down 1.24 per cent. The South China Morning Post reached out to both companies by phone, but neither had responded at the time of publication. Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, stressed that the US was only one among many markets for Chinese firms. The Belt and Road Initiative, he noted, continued to drive infrastructure development worldwide, ensuring exports of electrical equipment despite any direct impact of Washington’s policy shift. According to Chinese customs data for the first seven months of this year, US-bound shipments of electrical transformers, static converters and inductors accounted for 8.6 per cent of China’s total exports in the category by value, while storage batteries also accounted for just 9 per cent. “From a purely commercial standpoint, the long-term financial impact of this ban on Chinese companies will be fairly limited,” Wu said. “The actual commercial damage isn’t nearly as severe as people think. That is why I believe the market exaggerated the fallout.” The White House directive comes amid growing scrutiny of foreign-made hardware used in critical infrastructure, particularly products from China. According to the order, Trump stated that certain foreign actors were “increasingly creating and exploiting vulnerabilities” in the nation’s bulk-power system, describing the situation as an “unusual and extraordinary threat”. In response to the move, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian said Beijing consistently opposed “overstretching the concept of national security to suppress foreign companies”, urging the US to provide a fair, just and non-discriminatory environment for businesses from all countries. The presidential order followed a July decision by the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to add foreign-produced power inverters and advanced robotic devices to its “Covered List”. The commission argued such inverters introduced “additional vulnerabilities which compound as inverter-based resources proliferate on the US grid”. Responding to the FCC move, China’s commerce ministry said robots and power inverters were “normal international goods” and that all sides, including the US, benefited from trade. It warned that if Washington persisted with the move, “China would resolutely take countermeasures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.

title: Waves of attacks in Thailand’s deep south leave  villagers trapped in a cycle of fear
description: Coordinated arson attacks, bombings and gunfire heighten mistrust in Narathiwat as Bangkok seeks to revive peace talks.
content: Security guard Ni-arfan Doloh was taking a routine photograph for his nightly report on Saturday when five masked men carrying rifles emerged from inside a government office in Thailand’s southern Narathiwat province. “I was shocked,” said Ni-arfan, 25, recalling how they led him and another guard behind the Chang Phueak subdistrict office, instructed them to sit with their hands behind their backs, and promised no harm would come to them. The masked men then set fire to the building, one of at least 78 incidents in a coordinated wave ‌of arson, bombings and other attacks across four provinces in Thailand’s insurgency-hit deep south last weekend, injuring three people. No group has claimed responsibility, as is the case with most attacks in the predominantly Muslim and ethnic Malay provinces bordering Malaysia, where a slow-burning insurgency waged by separatist movements has killed more than 7,800 people since violence flared in 2004. Confined mostly to Thailand’s deep south, the violence has rarely intruded into the idyllic beaches and glimmering temples that make the country one of the world’s top destinations for millions of tourists each year. But it has long shaped life in these rural provinces, dotted with rubber plantations and fishing communities, and the recent spate of attacks has heightened fear and mistrust, even as Bangkok seeks to revive peace talks. The latest targets included government buildings, businesses and ⁠convenience stores, vehicles and pylons, while an explosion damaged railway tracks and disrupted train services. Two hours after the office was torched, Solae Doloh and his three friends were riding back home from ‌a camping trip along a nearby road when they suddenly came under fire. Solae said he was hit in the stomach by gunfire that appeared to come from a military helicopter circling overhead – an account backed by another witness and a village headman who was in the area. “I stopped my motorcycle and lifted both my arms,” ‌said Solae, 21, speaking with a bandage over his stomach. “They shot us in the first round, but didn’t hit anyone. After we went on, they came around to the ⁠front and shot at us again.” The Thai military ⁠has vehemently denied that its troops fired from the helicopter. A regional commander told reporters that the aircraft was surveying the area. Village headman Nuseng Lateh, 61, said he recognised the group as they passed by the burning office before the shooting, adding that they had ‌previously gone through a security checkpoint, where no weapons had been found on them. Police are investigating the shooting, and local lawmakers and community representatives have also called for an independent inquiry to determine how Solae was shot. “Deep down, I hope we will receive justice but ‌I’m afraid they ‌will accuse us of being insurgents,” said Hasan Toema, 27, one of Solae’s friends. Despite living through repeated bouts of violence, the shooting has deepened a sense of insecurity among some residents, including Solae’s older brother, ‌Matohae Doalo. “I don’t want to go out anywhere alone,” the 27-year-old said. “This happened to my brother, so I am afraid it will happen to me, too.” Since the middle of the last century, separatist ⁠groups have fought against the Thai government in three predominantly Malay-Muslim provinces of Pattani, Yala and Narathiwat that were once part of the independent Malay sultanate of Patani. Peace talks between the Thai government and insurgent ⁠groups to end one of Southeast Asia’s long-running conflicts began under Malaysian facilitation in 2013 but have repeatedly stalled, yielding little tangible progress. The weekend attacks came as Thailand sought to revive talks with the Barisan Revolusi Nasional, the main separatist group fighting in the region. Bangkok’s chief negotiator Thanut Suvarnananda said this month that the Thai government wanted to move beyond trading concessions for reducing ‌violence and instead address underlying political grievances. Thanut declined to ‌comment and the BRN has not responded to questions. In a previous round of violence on July 22, when suspected insurgents killed five paramilitary rangers and wounded six civilians, 10-year-old Habib was playing outside his home, next to a military checkpoint. A stray bullet during an exchange of fire passed through his leg, fortunately without striking any major arteries or bones, but covered his limb in blood, his mother, Na, said. More than a month later, Habib becomes anxious when he sees soldiers or large groups of people and struggles to sleep, said Na, giving only one name. “I feel frightened by what happened,” she said. “I worry about how we are supposed to continue living because incidents occur every day.”

title: Iran’s supreme leader remains unseen 6 months after war began
description: Reportedly disfigured in air strikes, Mojtaba Khamenei is said to delegate daily authority while holding final say.
content: Six months after the air strikes that began the war and propelled ⁠a badly wounded Mojtaba Khamenei into the role of Iran’s supreme leader, he remains entirely unseen and unheard by Iranians – a vacuum at the heart of his country’s leadership. Questions over his condition and role are growing increasingly fraught, with Iran facing critical decisions over a war that has set the Middle East aflame while trashing the country’s already fragile economy. Iranian officials and other senior sources in the country say Khamenei remains in control, ruling from the shadows for security reasons as he recovers from disfiguring wounds while delegating broad daily authority to a coterie of top figures. But with no photograph, video or ‌audio message released since his appointment a week into the war, Iranians are ever more sceptical about his position in an Islamic Republic in which the leader’s voice is meant to be absolute. “The question is no longer whether Mojtaba is alive, but whether Iran still has a functioning supreme leader,” said Alex Vatanka of the Middle East Institute in Washington. Khamenei’s only messages to the Iranian people have come via a handful of written statements read aloud by news broadcasters and he was even missing from the extravagant week of funeral rites for his father last month. Top officials and other insiders attribute Khamenei’s absence to assassination fears and say he holds frequent meetings with top figures, receives all major reports and takes the final decisions on every important issue. President Masoud Pezeshkian said on August 10 that he had held a seven-hour meeting with Khamenei. But even among the Islamic Republic’s most hardline supporters, doubts ⁠are creeping in. “We need to hear our leader’s voice, or see any sign that he is there on top and leading the country to give us more confidence,” said a member of the Basij volunteer militia in Qom, the seminary ‌city at the heart of Iran’s theocratic state. While the Basij member, who requested anonymity to discuss such a sensitive subject, said he believed Khamenei was indeed still making key decisions, the lack of even a photograph was damaging morale and not in Iran’s interest. Among Iranians who oppose the ruling hierarchy or want broad reforms, the message is blunter. “How do we know that ‌Mojtaba has not been killed?” said Shahrokh, a pro-reform businessman in Tehran who also requested anonymity. “It is not logical that there is not a single sign proving he is alive, let alone evidence that ⁠he is involved in decision-making,” he added. Iran has weathered six months of war with its most powerful enemies to emerge battered but still standing. Its political system has held. Its military retains the ability to choke off global energy supplies and strike US Gulf allies. The clerical establishment has shown it can absorb the loss of ‌a supreme leader and senior commanders without collapsing, maintaining a political and military chain of command loyal to their theocratic ideology. But Iran’s economy is buckling under the cost of the conflict and a months-long blockade of its oil exports, which has cratered the rial currency, risking a resumption of the mass protests that authorities ‌crushed in ‌January by killing thousands of demonstrators. Meanwhile the ruling establishment has reorganised around a clear imperative: preserve the state, restore deterrence and stop the economic fallout from destabilising the country. The Revolutionary Guards, long a powerful force, grew in influence from the ‌start of the war and remain central to strategic thinking at the top of a reconfigured ruling system around the Supreme National Security Council, the sources said. That upper echelon includes the top Guards commanders as well as senior political figures such as ⁠Pezeshkian and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. Several senior sources reached by Reuters in Iran said Khamenei was in fact holding meetings with those top figures, was fully involved in deliberations and has the final say on all major questions. A senior ⁠Iranian official said only a small number of officials retained direct contact with Khamenei in person and that no details of him had been published for fear of leaking information that could allow the US to target him. His health is meanwhile improving significantly, said a person close to Khamenei’s inner circle, describing him as sharp and involved in decision-making. “Despite all the pressures, services to the people have not stopped. Our foreign policy ‌line is unified and our decisions are coherent. All of this ‌shows the supreme leader is in charge,” a second official said. Even before the war, Khamenei preferred a back room role as his father’s top aide, shunning public attention. His wounds in the early hours of February 28, when Israel and the United States launched their war with air strikes that killed his late father, disfigured his face according to senior sources. But now elevated to a role seen as conferring divine guidance, and at the country’s moment of greatest crisis since the 1979 revolution, such considerations look unconvincing. “A genuine deal with Washington requires Mojtaba’s unmistakable approval and so does any decision to sustain a long and costly conflict with the United States,” said Vatanka. “His prolonged absence has created a dangerous situation in which rival factions can all claim to know what the leader really wants,” he added.

title: Storm travel chaos as Typhoon Saudel makes double landfall in China
description: US embassy urges American citizens to stay clear of affected coastal and storm zones and track local news for updates.
content: Typhoon Saudel made landfall in the eastern Chinese province of Zhejiang on Friday morning, disrupting flights and ferry services across major urban centres, including the industrial hub of Ningbo and the economic powerhouse of Shanghai. Ningbo Lishe International Airport suspended all flight operations from 11.30pm on Thursday. Even though services resumed at 11am on Friday, some 16 inbound and 28 outbound flights were cancelled for the day. In the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou, a base for private enterprise, 197 flights were grounded on Friday. In neighbouring Shanghai, the Shanghai Passenger Ferry Company announced ferry routes were suspended from 9am on Friday, except for the Changxing-Hengsha river crossing. Major air carriers such as Air China and China Southern Airlines have offered free rebooking or full refunds for passengers flying to and from affected hubs, including Shanghai, for travel between Thursday and Saturday. According to the National Meteorological Centre, Typhoon Saudel made landfall along the coastal area of Yuhuan in Taizhou, Zhejiang, at about 8am, with winds of up to 126km/h (78 miles per hour) near its centre. After briefly moving out to sea, the typhoon’s centre made a second landfall at Wenzhou at about 9.10am. The forecaster has maintained a red typhoon warning, the highest level in China’s four-tier system. Following typhoons Bavi and Dolphin, Saudel is the third to make landfall in Zhejiang this year, equalling the province’s 2004 record of three typhoon landfalls in a single year. It is also the seventh typhoon to strike mainland China this year. According to the forecast, Zhejiang and Fujian provinces will bear the brunt of the heaviest rainfall, with localised extreme downpours. Moving further inland, the typhoon will bring strong winds and heavy rainfall until Monday across regions, including the manufacturing powerhouse of Guangdong province and the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. Weather authorities are urging people in affected areas to take precautions against potential flash floods and landslides. Education authorities in Zhejiang’s capital, Hangzhou, have directed schools and tutoring institutions to suspend classes and cancel outdoor events. Meanwhile, the city’s iconic West Lake scenic spot has been temporarily closed to visitors. In the popular coastal tourist hub of Xiamen in Fujian, all ferry services have been suspended. In a rare move, the US embassy in Beijing issued a weather warning on Thursday night, urging American citizens to stay clear of affected coastal and storm zones and to track local news coverage for updates. The National Climate Centre has said that the active typhoon season and prolonged wind and rain in China since summer are linked to a brewing El Nino event marked by an unusual warming of surface waters in the tropical Pacific Ocean. Saudel closely follows Typhoon Narra, which made its third landfall in Wuchuan, Guangdong, on Wednesday. Before hitting Guangdong, Narra lingered over the Beibu Gulf for days, dumping heavy rain across Hainan, Guangdong and Guangxi. Guangxi is still reeling from the impact of Narra as it braces for another round of heavy downpours between Saturday night and Monday. According to state broadcaster CCTV, by August 23 heavy rainfall had caused widespread flooding across several areas of Guangxi, affecting 61,000 residents and displacing 54,000. Chongzuo in Guangxi, a city known for its dramatic waterfalls and karst limestone peaks, emerged as one of the worst-affected areas. Floods submerged homes and cropland while knocking out power and communications across multiple townships. According to local media, authorities were racing to clear mud and debris, carry out disinfection and epidemic prevention, repair damaged infrastructure and inspect for safety hazards so that normal life and order could be quickly restored. Meanwhile, helicopters dropped essential supplies, such as bottled water and bread, to stranded residents.

title: China’s commercial space sector expands global footprint with Thailand deal
description: GalaxySpace describes mission as first turnkey satellite export to a Southeast Asian customer by a Chinese commercial space company.
content: Beijing-based GalaxySpace’s deployed what it called China’s first turnkey satellite export to Southeast Asia this week, underscoring the country’s efforts to boost its influence in the space industry overseas amid competition with Elon Musk’s SpaceX. GalaxySpace said it launched the Lingzhi-09 Thailand CubeSat aboard a Long March-6C rocket – alongside six other satellites – from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Centre in Shanxi province on Tuesday. Developed for Thailand’s Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA), the CubeSat satellite will collect remote-sensing data for land, agriculture and ecological applications, and also support practical training for Thai university students. The mission marked the first time that a Chinese commercial space company had developed, launched and deployed a complete satellite in orbit for a Southeast Asian customer as a packaged solution, showing the sector’s ability to provide integrated services spanning satellite delivery, operations and training, the company said. GalaxySpace, China’s first commercial space sector unicorn – a start-up valued at US$1 billion or more – provided GISTDA with an integrated package covering the spacecraft, ground system and personnel training. Thai personnel were trained in China, while GalaxySpace later sent teams to Thailand to help build and test the ground system, it said. Chinese commercial space companies were moving from “exporting products” towards “exporting services and ecosystems”, turning satellite technology into an end-to-end service offering for overseas markets, said Yang Kuan, an associate professor at Beijing Institute of Technology and deputy director of its Institute of Aerospace Policy and Law, in an interview with the Beijing-based Financial News. The overseas push comes as China’s commercial space sector ramps up satellite constellation deployment and overseas expansion in a challenge to SpaceX’s Starlink project. Shanghai-based SpaceSail, which just completed a record funding round for China’s satellite sector, has secured approval to provide satellite communications services in Brazil while also exploring markets including Malaysia, Thailand and Kazakhstan. Geely-backed Geespace has conducted satellite communications trials with telecoms operators in more than 20 countries across the Middle East, Africa, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, South Asia and Latin America. Still, the industry’s ability to export satellites hinges largely on a constraint closer to home: rockets and affordable launch capacity. An industry expert who declined to be named said China’s satellite manufacturing sector was relatively mature, but the shortage of cheap launch capacity was holding it back. Some Chinese launch services can cost around US$20,000 per kilogram, compared with roughly US$2,700 to US$3,000 per kilogram for SpaceX’s reusable Falcon 9, according to a report by the Mercator Institute for China Studies that was published in February. However, the two countries’ gap in reusable rocket development appears to be narrowing. Private rocket maker LandSpace successfully recovered the first stage of its Zhuque-3 rocket on land this month, marking China’s first successful ground-based recovery of an orbital-class booster. The achievement followed last month’s successful sea-based recovery of the first stage of a state-developed Long March-10B using a net. Founded in 2018, GalaxySpace had launched more than 40 spacecraft by early this year, Peter Huang, the company’s general manager for international business development, told Bloomberg in February. Thailand was part of GalaxySpace’s broader push into overseas markets, he said, adding that the company was working with telecoms and space companies in Thailand and other countries to validate its technology and find “real world use cases”. GalaxySpace has also begun preparations for an A-share listing this year, joining a dozen commercial space firms including LandSpace, Galactic Energy and Spacety seeking to tap China’s capital markets.

title: US surgical robotics firm eyes Hong Kong listing to power push into mainland China
description: Noah Medical expects to file application as early as next year, joining surge of tech listings tapping city’s international fundraising pool.
content: SoftBank-backed surgical robotics company Noah Medical has begun preparations for a Hong Kong initial public offering, joining a wave of cutting-edge technology firms tapping the city’s international fundraising pool. The US-headquartered company aimed to raise more than US$100 million and planned to file its listing application as early as next year, according to founder Zhang Jian. “We want to expand our business in [mainland] China, and Hong Kong – as an international financial centre with a globally recognised stock exchange – is the natural choice for our listing,” Zhang said in an interview on the sidelines of MedTech World Asia in Hong Kong on Thursday. The company plans to expand sales of its surgical robots in top-tier and emerging mainland cities, such as Hangzhou, capital of China’s eastern Zhejiang province. Hangzhou’s Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital is a target customer, following regulatory approval from China’s drug regulator in November last year. Currently, 90 per cent of the company’s revenue is generated in the United States, where its surgical robots have treated about 15,000 patients. SoftBank Vision Fund, Lenovo Capital and Incubator, and HSG were among its investors, according to private market data tracker Tracxn. Saudi Arabia’s state oil giant Saudi Aramco, American-Irish medical device maker Medtronic, Japanese precision technology provider Olympus and Primavera Capital also supported the company, Zhang said. Noah Medical was valued at around US$571.5 million as of September 2025, according to market intelligence provider Forge Global. Founded in 2018, the company develops surgical robots that reach internal organs such as the lungs through natural orifices like the throat, avoiding incisions. The robots sell for about 10 million yuan (US$1.5 million) per unit in China, with patients paying about 10,000 yuan per operation. “Bleeding is localised and minimal, as the procedure avoids cutting through skin and tissue,” said Zhang, who earned a master’s degree and a mechanical engineering PhD at Columbia University specialising in medical robotics. “Patients typically do not need to stay in hospital overnight, many can go home the same day or after just one night. And they are left with no body scarring.” Noah Medical launched the most advanced version of its surgical robotics platform, Galaxy II, this month. It allowed doctors to toggle between high-definition digital tomosynthesis and cone-beam CAT scanning mid-procedure, rather than being locked into one imaging method throughout, according to the company. The Hong Kong stock exchange has received about 420 listing applications this year, bringing the total number under review to 793, according to its website.

title: Hormuz deal presses pause on Iran conflict, but fears of ‘forever war’ remain
description: Tehran is likely to stick to its guns in the hopes that the US midterms will bring about a Republican defeat, analysts say.
content: A diplomatic push by Oman, Pakistan and Qatar is widely expected to yield another pause in the Iran conflict, but there remains little prospect of a stop to what analysts fear has already become a “forever war”. On Monday, Iran and Oman agreed in principle to a temporary maritime route for ships travelling through the Strait of Hormuz. This could lead to the easing of the tit-for-tat blockades imposed by Iran and the US if President Donald Trump’s administration accepts it. Regional mediators frame it as part of a “phased” process of confidence-building measures envisioned under the Islamabad Declaration, signed by both sides in June. Analysts, however, are sceptical about the chances of a breakthrough, saying the mediation efforts are primarily aimed at preventing a feared region-wide escalation. “The current trajectory signals an interregnum, but the likelihood of further escalation still looms large,” What Is Iran? author Arshin Adib-Moghaddam said. Both sides currently wanted to prevent “yet another military escalation”, said the co-director of the Centre for Iranian Studies at SOAS University of London. “The only variable that can’t be logically and rationally predicted is Donald Trump’s ability to stay consistent, as he has been incredibly unstable and irrational as a president.” With the pivotal midterm elections on November 3 approaching, the Republican president’s administration switched the focus of the war from military action to imposing secondary sanctions against Iran’s trading partners on Monday – just hours after the Iran-Oman deal was announced. “After President Trump and the overwhelming might of the US military dismantled Iran’s military capabilities and crippled its nuclear programme, America is entering the endgame with the single greatest financial offensive ever mounted against an adversary,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said, describing the measures as the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran. Trump, meanwhile, claimed that the US Navy had successfully demined navigation channels in the Hormuz strait. “There is a Zero Tolerance policy on mine placement in full force and effect,” he posted on his Truth Social platform on Monday. This contrasted with the agreement between Tehran and Muscat to “implement a joint project to clear the strait of mines”. Ebb and flow Having already endured sanctions since 2018 and the destruction of much of its industrial base during the first phase of US-Israel attacks in April, Tehran has stuck to its guns. “Our principle is understanding and resolving issues through interaction and negotiation, but at the same time, we will stand firm against economic pressures, as we have done so far and will continue to do,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Wednesday, according to state media. Concurrently, the Revolutionary Guards asserted that Hormuz was under its control, with vessels attempting to exit via a US-organised route hugging Oman’s coast continuing to come under Iranian fire. “If America does not accept our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened under any circumstances,” the Guards said. Rhetoric notwithstanding, it appeared from the comments by Trump and Bessent that the US “is pivoting away from threats of renewed military action to a new phase of economic pressure”, said Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, Middle East fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy. This corresponds with the overall ebb and flow of the conflict, now at its six-month point, according to Guy Burton, author of China and Middle East Conflicts. “We have seen a recurring pattern of military confrontation followed by periods of deliberation, dialogue and diplomatic outreach,” the Brussels-based academic said, calling it a “forever war” in which military action and diplomacy occur simultaneously. Instead of a resolution, a pause “may simply represent another period in which both sides reassess their positions before the next round of confrontation”, he said. Regional mediation efforts continued on Thursday with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani – who is also the emirate’s foreign minister – visiting Tehran to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. This engagement with the pro-negotiation faction of the Islamic Republic, led by parliamentary speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, was preceded on Monday by negotiations between Pakistan’s influential Chief of Defence Forces Asim Munir and Mohsin Razaee, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council – the leader of Tehran’s hardliners, who are opposed to talks with the US. Eye to midterms The US is not the only one with an agenda heading into the midterms. The Iranian leadership had “every interest in seeing the Republican Party defeated”, said political scientist Ali Alfoneh, author of Political Succession in the Islamic Republic of Iran. So it would use its remaining resources to stay afloat until November 3 – and preferably until the new Congress convenes in January. By then, Tehran “hopes” that a Republican defeat, a disputed election result, and Trump’s possible refusal to accept that result could push the US into political chaos or even a constitutional crisis – “providing Iran with a much-needed reprieve”, said Alfoneh, a senior resident scholar at the Washington-based Arab Gulf States Institute. Iran “has an incentive” to keep regional tensions – and consequently oil prices – high before the midterms, thereby contributing to a Republican loss, he said. Burton, who has taught international relations at universities in Iraq, the United Arab Emirates and the West Bank, agreed that Iran “appears increasingly interested not simply in surviving the conflict but in imposing political costs on Trump”. If Tehran can give Trump “a sufficiently visible ‘bloody nose’”, it may calculate that this will damage his political standing and potentially the Republican brand ahead of the midterms. This suggests there may be “little incentive for Trump to make a major strategic concession” like conceding control of Hormuz under the Iran-Oman framework before the elections. US economic pressure and military action were “likely to coexist for some time”, Burton added. Washington was effectively “putting multiple instruments on the table in the hope that one of them will eventually create a viable diplomatic off-ramp”, Burton said. The danger was that, without a clear political settlement, this would produce an intermittent conflict and economic confrontation that “is not quite a conventional war, but not peace either”. Periodic flare ups could become “a new status quo”, Ulrichsen said, because each party to the conflict “appears to think it has the upper hand and can outlast the other”. Under such circumstances, Alfoneh said regional mediators now confronted “an unenviable set of possibilities”: pushing to implement the Islamabad Declaration, “becoming targets themselves” – or “facing both outcomes simultaneously”.

title: South Korea backs Trump’s North Korea outreach, but warns against being sidelined
description: Seoul insists any diplomacy between Washington and Pyongyang must yield nuclear progress and preserve joint defence readiness.
content: South Korea supports US President Donald Trump’s efforts to resume dialogue with North Korea, ‌but aims to ensure its security posture is not weakened and that Seoul is not sidelined, according to South Korea’s national security adviser. Seoul believed the resumption of talks between the US and North Korea should focus on progress on the North Korean nuclear weapons issue and must not undermine the country’s security readiness, Wi Sung-lac told reporters on Friday. “One point to keep in mind is ⁠the need to coordinate with the United States to ensure that any resumption of US-North Korea dialogue leads ‌to substantive progress on the North Korean nuclear issue, alongside efforts to establish a peace regime on the Korean peninsula,” Wi said. To achieve these aims, policy coordination and ‌communication between South Korea and the United States were more important than ever, he said. Wi ⁠cited Trump’s order earlier ⁠this month to substantially scale back major joint military drills between the two allies, saying the US president was signalling a willingness ‌to engage with North Korea. At the same time, Seoul should ensure it was not “sidelined” in Washington’s efforts to restart talks with Pyongyang, Wi said. Trump ‌cited ‌in part Seoul’s refusal to offer help in the Iran war for cutting short the Ulchi Freedom ‌Shield drills this month and said it sent a wrong message to North Korea. Trump has been seeking ⁠a new summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. The two met three times in 2018 and ⁠2019. South Korea, Japan and the United States will conduct joint military drills from September 9 to 11 to test readiness against North Korea’s missile and nuclear weapons threats, South Korea said ‌on Friday. Wi said South Korea ‌was seeking to deepen cooperation with Washington on a range of issues that had sometimes caused friction between the allies. These included South Korean investment in the US agreed under a trade deal, the treatment of US-listed e-commerce firm Coupang, security cooperation, intelligence sharing and the transfer of wartime operational control, he said.

title: Ride-hailing platforms seeking Hong Kong licence must have handled 100,000 orders a day
description: Uber and Didi among platforms submitting applications, with both saying criteria are reasonable and that they will roll out measures to help drivers.
content: Hong Kong authorities have opened licence applications for ride-hailing platforms under a new regulatory scheme, requiring operators to have a proven track record of providing lawful services in cities with populations of more than 7.5 million, while handling over 100,000 daily orders in at least two locations. Announcing the licensing terms on Friday, the Transport Department said eligibility criteria also included using technology such as facial recognition for due diligence checks to ensure vehicles were driven by their registered owners with valid permits. “By introducing the regulatory regime for ride-hailing services, we aim to require platforms, vehicles and drivers providing these services to obtain relevant licences and permits, providing members of the public with safer and compliant choices for point-to-point transport,” a department spokesman said. “To ensure that ride-hailing platforms possess the operational capability to provide platform services, we will impose specific requirements regarding booking management technology, experience in operating ride-hailing platform services, financial proof and capital investment.” Under the new regulations, applicants must be Hong Kong-registered companies with permanent executive staff and an office in the city. An operator’s most senior executive must have a university education and experience in transport management, and must primarily live in Hong Kong. Interested operators must submit audited financial reports for the past three years. They must have capital of at least HK$50 million (US$6.4 million), at least HK$30 million in bank deposits and a HK$30 million credit line. Operators will also be required to submit data on every trip to the government at specified intervals and in prescribed formats. The data must be stored in Hong Kong. They must maintain a proper and efficient standard of service and may not offer cross-border services. Authorities also stressed that operators must comply with the city’s national security laws. Applications for operating licences will close on October 30. They will be vetted by an assessment committee comprising representatives from the Transport and Logistics Bureau, the Digital Policy Office and the Transport Department. Approved licences will be valid for a maximum of five years, with an annual licence fee of HK$1.2 million. Legislative Council transport panel chairman Ben Chan Han-pan said the threshold on personnel, operating experience and financial resources should not be set too low or too high, arguing that an overly low bar could bring in too many platforms and spread resources too thinly. “If the threshold is set too high, it could deter platform operators from entering the market altogether,” he added. Chan said the financial requirement was the main consideration and was not unreasonably high given the annual licence fee of HK$1.2 million. The number of platforms should be kept at an appropriate level, as too many operators could fragment the pool of 10,000 licensed vehicles, he said. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan earlier outlined the timetable for the regulatory regime, with the first batch of platform licences expected to be issued from late November. Licensed platforms would be given nine months to meet the new regulatory requirements before they are fully enforced on August 22 next year, Chan told Legco in July. The government has also launched a combined written test for taxis and ride-hailing vehicles to allow interested drivers to prepare and apply for a vehicle and driving permit in the fourth quarter of this year. Most legal provisions governing the sector took effect on August 3 with ride-hailing service permits capped at 10,000 vehicles. The government said the quota would be subject to review. The transport minister revealed last weekend that more than 7,500 people had applied for the new written test, calling the number a “very good and positive” sign. She also said more ride-hailing platform operators from mainland China and Southeast Asia had approached the government about entering the market, but did not identify the companies or reveal how many were involved. Uber already operates in Hong Kong, while mainland platforms Didi and Amap also offer local booking services. Amap is operated by Alibaba Group Holding, which also owns the South China Morning Post. Geely-backed CaoCao, the mainland’s second-largest ride-hailing operator, signed a strategic partnership agreement with Octopus in June aimed at operating licensed services in the city. Singapore-headquartered Grab is Southeast Asia’s largest ride-hailing platform and operates in more than 900 cities across eight countries. Other major mainland operators include T3 Chuxing and Meituan’s mobility platform, but neither has an established presence in Hong Kong. Uber said on Friday that it was preparing to apply for the licence, adding that its global experience and work with Hong Kong’s taxi sector demonstrated its readiness to operate under the new regime. The company said it had doubled its support team to help drivers through the transition. This included guidance on licensing requirements and written-test preparation. Didi also confirmed that it would submit an application, with a spokesman saying the requirements were “pragmatic and reasonable” and would help platforms prepare for future operations. He added that the company had introduced support measures for drivers, including partnerships with several training institutions to offer course discounts and help prospective drivers prepare their applications. Didi also said it would provide 24-hour customer service and a rapid response mechanism for handling safety incidents, as well as strengthen its compliance management and user protections in line with the Transport Department’s requirements. Ben Chan said the transport panel would visit Beijing in early September to study how ride-hailing platforms were regulated and operated there. He said members wanted to understand the problems that platforms encountered in their operations, what policy support might be needed and how regulators supervised the sector, given Hong Kong had no experience with such a regime. The delegation would also look at autonomous driving, road maintenance and transport management and planning, he added.

title: US visa interviews on hold; China slams fresh sanctions over Iran: SCMP’s 7 highlights
description: From catastrophic flash floods at the China-Nepal border to a sacked Malaysian academic, here are top stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from this week’s news across Hong Kong, mainland China, the wider Asia region and beyond that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. The path to America is narrowing. Here’s what that means for legal immigrants US green card interviews are on hold worldwide, student and work visas are subject to new restrictions, and citizenship is under fresh scrutiny. The SCMP breaks down what the latest US immigration crackdown means for people planning to study, work or settle in America. 2. China vows to safeguard interests after ‘Economic D-Day’ sanctions over Iran ties China has condemned fresh US “Economic D-Day” sanctions imposed on Chinese entities over their ties to Iran, pledging “all necessary measures” to protect its interests. 3. China-Nepal flash flood: death toll rises to 392, over 1,000 missing Rescue teams struggled to reach the site of a massive Himalayan mudslide and flash flood on the China-Nepal border as the toll from the disaster rose to 392 dead, with more than 1,000 missing. 4. Islamic university sacks professor who claimed Malays could fly A Malaysian Islamic university has formally distanced itself from an academic whose viral claims about ancient Malay civilisation – including that Malays could fly and taught the Chinese “flying kung fu” – have drawn ridicule from historians. 5. China sends archaeologists to South America to trace ancestral links Chinese archaeologists are heading to South America for the first field project on the continent in search of ancestral bonds between ancient Chinese and native American civilisations. 6. Jack Ma buys HK$600 million of Alibaba shares, signalling AI confidence: sources Alibaba Group Holding founder Jack Ma has bought more than HK$600 million worth of the company’s Hong Kong-listed shares on consecutive days, according to people familiar with the matter, a show of confidence in the firm’s long-term prospects for artificial intelligence. 7. 2 arrested in Hong Kong fight over elderly woman slapping girl Hong Kong police have arrested two women on suspicion of assault at a shopping centre in Kwun Tong, with a viral clip showing a fight breaking out after a five-year-old girl was shoved and then knocked to the ground.

title: Meet ‘Boston’ singer Stella Lefty’s boyfriend, viral country star Vincent Mason
description: Inspired by John Mayer, the rising musician co-wrote ‘Something to Lose’ with Lefty and joined her to perform the track at Lollapalooza 2026.
content: Singer-songwriter Stella Lefty’s country-pop single “Boston”, which went viral on TikTok before its official release in March, peaked at No 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart this week, sitting just below Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas”. On Monday, the 24-year-old announced her first tour days after she released her debut album Long Way Home. The tour will kick off on January 9 in Detroit, and span 18 cities including a fitting stop in Boston on January 17. The album features 14 songs totalling 38 minutes, including her pre-release single “Something to Lose”, a stand-alone track Lefty recorded in collaboration with her boyfriend, Vincent Mason. So, who exactly is the 25-year-old artist featured on Lefty’s debut album, and how did the pair meet? What is Vincent Mason’s background? Born in Roswell, Georgia, Mason wrote his first song after enrolling at the University of Mississippi. He soon transferred to Lipscomb University in Nashville – the “Music City” his mother insisted he move to for his musical aspirations, as he told Atwood Magazine last year. The budding country musician ultimately dropped out of school altogether. But the risk paid off: Mason is now preparing for his second headlining tour, “There I Go”, which launches September 3 and spans 17 cities across the US. His song went viral on TikTok In 2024, Mason’s single “Hell is a Dancefloor” gained momentum on TikTok three months after its release, paving the way for his signing with Interscope Records/Music Soup and a partnership with Music Corporation of America. The country singer released his debut album, There I Go, last November, featuring 14 tracks heavily inspired by John Mayer – who, Mason told The Hollywood Reporter, was “the reason I started making songs”. The album brings an emphasised intimacy to the modern music landscape, with its single “Damned if I Do” reaching No 94 on the Billboard Hot 100 in May. After playing major festivals like Stagecoach, Rock the South, and Calf Fry this year, Mason also joined Lefty during her Lollapalooza set to perform their duet. How did Stella Lefty and Vincent Mason meet? The musical couple’s love story started in a very modern way: Mason dropped Lefty a line on Instagram about his thoughts on her single “Thinking About You”, Lefty shared on The BobbyCast interview podcast last month. “I don’t think he was looking for love,” Stella said. The romance sparked nonetheless, and the couple has been together for about six months now.

title: ‘Find your own room’: Japan says no more space, money for ballooning Asian Games numbers
description: Athletes already staying in a cruise ship and shipping containers, but with new sports added, organisers say there is no budget to house more.
content: Japanese organisers have told late additions to next month’s Asian Games to find their own accommodation, saying they don’t have the money or space to deal with ballooning competitor numbers. About 15,000 athletes and officials were initially expected at the Games, which are being held in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from September 19 to October 4. That was already more than the Olympics, but the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) last week put the number at 17,000 – 11,000 athletes and 6,000 officials. There is no dedicated athletes’ village, with organisers instead relying on a cruise ship, temporary wooden containers and hotels. In March, the OCA added teqball and padel to the sporting programme. Organising committee president Hideaki Omura told reporters that they had “neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements” for extra participants. “The host city agreement specifies a delegation of 15,000 people,” Omura, who also serves as the governor of Aichi Prefecture, said this week. “We have not set aside a budget for any more than that. There is simply nowhere for them to stay.” Organisers have opted for temporary athlete accommodation to cut costs, hiring the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena for the event. Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes will stay on the ship, while a further 2,000 athletes and officials will stay in the shipping container-style huts. The rest will be in hotels, including in Tokyo, where swimming, diving and equestrian events will take place. Reports this week said the local organising committee had asked the OCA to reduce the number of participants. “If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements,” Omura said. AFP has repeatedly contacted the OCA for comment. Nagoya mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who serves as acting chairman of the organising committee, said on Wednesday that it was “difficult to accommodate this number, both in terms of time and physical capacity”. “From a cost perspective we are operating on a tight budget and it is difficult,” he said.

title: He’s worked with Jackie Chan, Jet Li. Martial artist Alfred Hsing’s rise in film
description: After leaving a financial career, the wushu champion became a fight coordinator, stuntman and actor working with some of film’s top stars.
content: Behind every action film – be it a biopic on wing chun kung fu master Ip Man or a Hollywood sci-fi flick – there is someone who choreographs the fight sequences and coordinates the stunts. Los Angeles-based actor and martial artist Alfred Hsing has been one of these masterminds for more than a decade. The 42-year-old worked as a member of the official Jackie Chan stunt team on the 2015 historical epic Dragon Blade and served as Jet Li’s assistant in 2010. More recently, he performed stunts in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey (2026) and was the action choreographer for Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender, a new film sequel to the fantasy-adventure Nickelodeon animated show that came out in July. Hsing conceptualised the latter film’s action design, including choosing the weapons and abilities for Katara, Zuko and the other characters. After the artists finalised the scene boards, he choreographed the fight sequences and captured the moves on camera to provide a reference video for the animators. “At its core, I feel that Avatar: The Last Airbender [the original animated show, which ran from 2005 to 2008] is like a wuxia [film],” Hsing says. “You know, you have these travelling heroes learning [martial arts] skills and also sharing moral lessons. So I always felt it connected to me and my upbringing.” Many concepts in the animated series also directly reference Eastern mythology. In the TV show, characters bend the natural elements water, earth, fire and air by performing the martial art associated with each: tai chi, hung gar, northern Shaolin kung fu and baguazhang (a practice that emphasises circular footwork and fluid hand movements), respectively. But Hsing takes artistic liberty, adding his own creative twists to these movements and sprinkling in his own technical flair. How Hsing got into the movie industry “I didn’t know what my plan was out of college,” says Hsing, who now has hundreds of film credits under his belt – as an actor, stuntman, action coordinator and choreographer. Before that, he was grinding away in the corporate world. The son of Taiwanese immigrants, Hsing was raised in the San Francisco Bay Area, where he began training in Shaolin kung fu and wushu in his teens, quickly earning medals in national competitions. He recalls growing up watching martial arts films, including those of Jackie Chan and The Karate Kid. “When I was growing up, there was a stereotype that all Asians know kung fu … but the funny thing is that if you got to me, it’d be like, ‘Yeah I do know it,’” Hsing says. He studied economics and computer specialisation with a minor in East Asian languages at the University of California, Los Angeles from 2001-06. When not studying labour market and financial trends, he attended drama classes at the university. While a student, he even interviewed Stephen Chow Sing-chi when the Hong Kong star visited the campus. After Hsing graduated, he landed jobs at financial institutions KPMG and City National Bank, but soon quit the industry and committed himself to martial arts. He remembers weighing his options at the time and thinking: “If I take the risk into the unknown, then I can risk greatness.” In 2009, he made the United States Wushu A team. “That meant I could compete at the World Wushu Championships, which is an IOC [International Olympic Committee] recognised event,” he says. That same year, he became the first American male to bring home a gold medal at the championships. A ‘crazy crash course in filmmaking’ Hsing was promptly thrown into the world of martial arts cinema. He worked as an assistant to Jet Li from 2010 to 2011, following him from Hong Kong to Beijing to Singapore, and acted opposite him in the 2011 fantasy action film The Sorcerer and the White Snake. It was also during this period that Hsing studied acting at the Beijing Film Academy. Not long after, he was on Jackie Chan’s stunt team for the 2015 martial arts film Dragon Blade. Hsing also appeared as a stunt double alongside Michelle Yeoh in Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022), trained Jennifer Tse Ting-ting for her stunts in Europe Raiders (2018) and acted in Steven Spielberg’s Ready Player One (2018). Despite working with so many A-list stars, Hsing says Chan and Li are the only two actors he recalls feeling truly star-struck by. “Those two people had such a deep impact on my youth when watching these films, and they were the few people of heroic representation [of Asians] in the West,” Hsing says. “Growing up as a second-generation Asian-American at that time – and even now – there aren’t many true big stars or just, like, people that you can model yourself after.” Hsing describes Chan and Li as a “yin and yang”. They are both driven by their shared ferocious desire to achieve excellence, but he notes that Chan was the extroverted mentor while Li wielded a quiet, focused determination. Hsing also met Hong Kong icon Donnie Yen while working in the US as a stunt coordinator for Ip Man 3 (2015) on the fight scene between Yen’s character and Mike Tyson’s. On that project, he also briefly studied under Yuen Woo-ping, a Hong Kong martial arts choreographer and director who served as an action choreographer or adviser on multiple Ip Man films, Kung Fu Hustle (2004) and Kill Bill: Volume 1 (2003). Recalling these projects, Hsing feels like he “had this crazy crash course in filmmaking” in which he saw the differences between Western and Eastern action films. Eventually, in 2019, he moved back to the US. More recently, Hsing starred in the Academy Award-nominated film Train Dreams (2025) as Fu Sheng, a Chinese railroad labourer in the US Pacific northwest during the early 20th century. Recapturing the magic of martial arts cinema In recent years, martial arts cinema has not been able to match the widespread popularity it achieved during its heyday in the 1980s and 90s despite more calls for Asian representation in Hollywood. “We need a new wave. I’m not saying there’s none, but not too many have really stepped into that forefront. So, you know, I volunteer to help,” Hsing says, laughing. These films require people who can “truly act and have the gong di – the martial arts fundamentals” in which they can shoot footage that feels authentic with minimal stunt doubles and cuts. But Hsing understands that it may be hard to recreate some of that past magic, as martial arts films used to spend months perfecting just single fight sequences. “In that golden era, there was this meticulousness to get the shot perfect because there’s this [idea] that film lasts forever … obviously that was before CGI and AI,” he says. Looking to the future, Hsing hopes to write and direct his own projects and has already written a few action scripts. “I mean, I didn’t go through 20 years or more of learning martial arts [and] being on the greatest martial arts sets … to not synthesise that information and put it out in my own way,” he says. In the coming months, Hsing’s fight choreography will be seen in another Avatar universe sequel animation, the TV series Avatar: Seven Havens. Perhaps because Hsing wears many hats in the film industry, Bryan Konietzko – one of the creators of the original Avatar: The Last Airbender series – jokes that Hsing is “the avatar” since he mastered bending each element. But for those who are curious, Hsing chuckles: “If I weren’t Avatar Alfred, I think I might be an airbender. I can be spontaneous – go with the flow.”

title: How typhoons and extreme weather could undermine Taiwan Strait combat readiness
description: This year’s storms and record temperatures highlight how climate conditions can disrupt military planning and operations.
content: The record heat and extreme weather seen across East Asia this summer have prompted warnings that climate change will be an increasing challenge for military planners focused on potential flashpoints such as the Taiwan Strait. Besides the risks to both troops and equipment, typhoons and other storms could also damage critical infrastructure and disrupt training, as well as divert personnel and resources towards emergency relief. Although militaries may be able to adapt in peacetime, they may have less flexibility in times of war, where extreme weather could have a direct impact on combat operations. Armed forces are adapting to the challenge in different ways. For example, Japan and the United States have formally incorporated climate risk into their assessments of force readiness, bases, equipment and supply chains, while Taiwan has folded climate-related disasters into its mobilisation and resilience planning. The Philippines is expanding facilities under its defence cooperation agreement with the US, some of which are specifically designed to strengthen its disaster response and ability to carry out humanitarian relief operations. Meanwhile, mainland China’s public response has focused heavily on tactical adaptation. This summer, mainland Chinese forces continued testing how extreme heat affected their operations. For example, in the southern region of Guangxi, a People’s Armed Police unit pushed drones to their limits in high temperatures, according to China Military Online. Meanwhile, a People’s Liberation Army Air Force unit analysed how personnel and equipment performed in high temperatures and explored specialised maintenance procedures for extreme conditions. Environmental factors are already imposing real-world trade-offs. Earlier this month, Typhoon Dolphin hit Okinawa at a time when US forces at Kadena Air Base were carrying out a readiness exercise. The approaching typhoon, which prompted the evacuation of more than a million people in eastern China, meant personnel had to prepare helicopters and tankers for the storm while simultaneously supporting the readiness exercise. The previous month, a series of typhoons struck mainland China, causing widespread flooding across vast swathes of the country that prompted the PLA to send personnel, vehicles and other equipment to help with relief efforts. Typhoons have also repeatedly disrupted Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang exercises. They forced parts of the 2023 and 2024 drill to be cancelled or halted prematurely, while Typhoon Danas diverted some forces towards disaster recovery at the start of the 2025 edition. Extreme conditions also have a direct impact on both servicemen and women and the uncrewed systems that play an increasingly important role in modern warfare. The US Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine has found that as well as having a physical impact, heat stress can also impair cognitive functions such as attention and memory. Meanwhile, Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said planners would have to account for different conditions when deciding what equipment to use. “For example, the cheap componentry and light weight of many smaller variants of unmanned systems make them susceptible to extreme temperatures and high winds,” Bosack said. Storms can also sharply curtail military activity. When Typhoon Gaemi struck Taiwan in July 2024, the PLA aerial activity around the island fell from 22 aircraft in the July 2023-24 period to zero for three consecutive 24-hour periods, before flights resumed. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Most countries, including the US, Philippines and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but many are opposed to any attempt to take it by force. The impact of extreme weather on military operations would be amplified in wartime, when commanders may not be able to wait for conditions to improve. Several analysts highlighted the ways in which it could affect any large-scale assault on Taiwan, where tensions with the mainland have been steadily rising. In 2020, a peer-reviewed Chinese study found statistically significant long-term increases in wind speeds and significant wave heights in the Taiwan Strait, based on simulations covering 1988 to 2017. “While improvements in PLA capabilities may have reduced some of these seasonal constraints, they have not eliminated the underlying physical challenges,” said Christopher Sharman, director of the China Maritime Studies Institute at the US Naval War College, speaking in a personal capacity. PLA amphibious forces, he added, were working to improve their ability to operate in poor weather, at night and under other degraded conditions. Sherri Goodman, secretary general of the International Military Council on Climate and Security, pointed to modernised amphibious brigades, larger amphibious ships, civilian vessels and improvements in transport and logistics as examples of how Chinese capabilities had evolved. But Goodman, a former US deputy undersecretary of defence for environmental security, also warned that while better capability could widen a weather window, “it does not eliminate the window”. K. Tristan Tang, a non-resident fellow at the National Bureau of Asian Research, said extreme weather would affect forces on both sides but the impact would probably be greater on the PLA because it would have to project and sustain forces across the strait. “Severe weather would not necessarily make those operations impossible, but it could reduce their effectiveness and make coordination considerably more difficult,” Tang said. For Goodman, the scale of the operation presents a further problem. Moving a large force would require not only troops and vehicles but also a continuing flow of fuel, ammunition and other supplies across contested waters and onto beaches or through ports. “An invasion is not won by getting the first troops ashore. It is won by sustaining them,” she said. James Holmes, a professor at the US Naval War College, argued that harsher conditions could favour Taiwan as the tactical defender, provided its own military remained operational. “Anything that afflicts the aggressor only enhances that advantage,” he said. Taiwan would face vulnerabilities of its own. Tang said that damage to the island’s ports or airfields could seriously hamper its operations, although it could also deny the PLA infrastructure it might hope to use after securing a foothold. Goodman offered a broader qualification, arguing that the effects would depend on where vulnerabilities emerged across the different forces involved and their ability to recover. “Climate change does not automatically favour one side. It imposes costs and creates vulnerabilities across the battlespace,” she said. “The important question is where those vulnerabilities occur, how concentrated they are and how quickly each side can recover from them.” That shifts the question from exposure alone to how well militaries can absorb disruption. Measures such as redundancy, dispersal, hardened infrastructure, rapid repair and alternative logistics routes could help forces continue operating when parts of their networks are damaged. “Resilience is not simply disaster preparedness. It is warfighting capacity,” Goodman said. “The military that can fight through disruption – and recover fastest from it – will have an advantage.”

title: China-Nepal floods: debris lake the size of 1,000 Olympic pools in breach danger
description: Nearly 500 confirmed dead as frantic hunt for survivors continues and barrier lake threatens to overflow.
content: The death toll from catastrophic flash floods and mudslides at the Gyirong Port border crossing between China and Nepal continued to rise on Friday, as concerns grew that a lake formed from the debris could breach, triggering further flooding. As of Friday afternoon, five people were confirmed dead and 558 missing on the Chinese side of the border, with 469 dead and nearly 1,000 missing in Nepal. The tragedy unfolded on Wednesday morning when a massive Himalayan landslide triggered a fast-moving debris flow that swept down from the border area, leaving widespread devastation in its wake. According to state broadcaster CCTV, the torrent was travelling at up to 200km/h (124mph) and generated a wall of water as high as 15 metres (50 feet) when it slammed into the checkpoint. Satellite images released on Thursday by state news agency Xinhua showed extensive mud and debris burying the checkpoint at Gyirong county in the city of Shigatse and its surrounding residential areas. The Nepal-China Friendship Bridge was washed away, while large deposits of silt altered the river channel and surrounding terrain, obscuring roads and parts of original structures. Affected facilities included customs staff quarters, homes, a parking area, police station compound and an immigration inspection building. Critical transport infrastructure was also severely damaged. Meanwhile, concerns are growing over a newly formed barrier lake created by the massive landslide near the border, upstream from Gyirong, where water levels continued to rise. The state broadcaster said in its update at noon on Friday that the barrier lake was holding more than 2.5 million cubic metres of water – the equivalent of 1,000 Olympic swimming pools. The figure is also 25 per cent higher than the 2 million cubic metres recorded as of Thursday morning. Earlier on Friday, CCTV reported that the barrier lake had already begun to overflow, forcing a temporary pause in ground rescue operations at the site while teams awaited further directions from command headquarters. According to Xinhua, China’s Ministry of Water Resources has said that expected rainfall could add another 3 million cubic metres over the next three days to the lake, near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers. The prospect of so much extra water raised the risk of a breach in the barrier lake that could trigger further flooding at Gyirong Port and downstream areas, the ministry warned. The state broadcaster said on Friday morning that the barrier lake had already begun to overflow, forcing a temporary pause in ground rescue operations at the site while teams await further directions from command headquarters. China’s National Immigration Administration said late on Thursday that it would suspend issuing electronic border-management permits for travel to Shigatse in the Tibet autonomous region, effective midnight on August 28. Authorities strongly advised existing permit holders against travelling to the area. Chinese Premier Li Qiang arrived at the checkpoint on Thursday afternoon to direct disaster relief efforts and visit emergency responders.

title: ICE agents in US to be equipped with pain-delivering electric shock gloves
description: Agency says gloves will be used in ‘high-tension environments’, like managing detainees and controlling crowds.
content: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement has awarded a US$16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks, saying officers would use them to control detainees and protesters who resist. ICE moved forward with the purchase despite opposition from civil rights advocates and Democratic members of Congress, who said ICE officers cannot be trusted to use them appropriately. A notice published in a federal database Thursday said ICE entered into a no-bid contract to purchase the gloves from Compliant Technologies LLC, a Kentucky-based firm that manufactures them. The deal includes acquiring 6,000 of the devices along with support equipment and services over the next six months. Civil rights advocates have said ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. ICE published the notice hours after a group of US senators, led by Democrat Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, urged the agency to cancel its plan to buy the gloves. In a letter to ICE’s acting director Thursday, Cortez Masto and 15 of her colleagues in the Democratic caucus questioned ICE’s need for the devices. “The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant scepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause,” the letter said. The senators were the latest to express opposition to the plan, which became public this month when ICE published a notice outlining its intent to purchase thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for officers and investigators. The devices are normal patrol gloves until an officer presses a button to activate the electrical mode. They must be applied directly to someone’s skin to produce a shock that causes pain, which is promoted as a way to gain compliance from people who are resisting. They have been used by some local jails and police departments in recent years. ICE’s notice said officers would use them in “high-tension environments”, including while making arrests, transporting combative detainees and responding to civil disturbances outside detention facilities. “It will be used when a subject is actively or passively resisting and an officer needs to gain control quickly to prevent injuries to both parties,” the document said. It said that the shocks would help “maintain control over inmates and prevent aggression or escape attempts”, allow officers to handcuff people hiding their hands, and assist in crowd control. The goal would be to avoid using “more severe force”, including firearms. The notice said the gloves would be used with “approved policy, training, and accountability standards”, but it did not elaborate. Cortez Masto and the other senators said in their letter that the device “presents substantial risks if deployed during civil arrests – even more so if it is deployed without clear limits, appropriate training, and comprehensive oversight”. They said ICE must make public details about how officers will be trained and how use of the gloves will be documented and reviewed internally to avoid misuse. ICE’s parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, reacted defiantly Thursday to critics of the purchase. “Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from any safety equipment is despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers,” the agency said in a statement.

title: South Korea, Japan and US set joint drills despite Trump cuts
description: The three countries will proceed with the multi-domain Freedom Edge exercise near Jeju Island.
content: South Korea said on Friday it would hold joint military exercises with the United States and Japan in September, after Washington scaled back annual drills with Seoul in an apparent bid to encourage dialogue with North Korea.
