The three countries would conduct the North Korea-focused Freedom Edge exercise from September 7 to 11 in international waters east and south of South Korea’s Jeju Island, Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said. “This exercise is a defensive drill conducted annually by the three countries to respond to North Korea’s nuclear and missile threats and safeguard peace and stability in the region,” the JCS said in a statement. The multi-domain exercise is expected to include maritime missile defence, air and air-defence drills, anti-submarine warfare and cyber defence, according to Seoul’s Yonhap news agency. Pyongyang had previously slammed the trilateral drill as a “reckless show of strength” that showed its adversaries’ confrontational stance against it. It also said the drill contained a US intention to lay siege to China and exert pressure on Russia. Freedom Edge was first held in June 2024 following an agreement reached by the leaders of the three countries at their Camp David summit in 2023. “This premier multi-domain exercise will continue to reinforce our shared values, enhance our shared interoperability and further strengthen our defence partnerships to ensure peace and stability throughout the Pacific,” said a spokeswoman for the United States Pacific Command, Yonhap reported on Wednesday. The announcement comes after US President Donald Trump this month ordered the countries’ annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises cut from 11 days to five. Trump at the time said the drills were “very insulting” to North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and said Kim had been “very well behaved”, as Washington sought to revive dialogue with Pyongyang. South Korea said on Monday the United States had cancelled another joint exercise, the biennial Ssangyong drills, due to constraints on force availability caused by the war with Iran. Despite Trump’s overtures, North Korea has shown little sign of reciprocating, firing missiles and condemning the scaled-down drills, as well as Washington’s approval of arms sales to South Korea and plans to fund programmes documenting human rights abuses in the North. Pyongyang had previously said it would not resume diplomacy with the US unless it dropped its demand for a North Korean denuclearisation as a precondition for talks. Since his earlier diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019, Kim has boosted his military and diplomatic credentials by enlarging his nuclear arsenal and aligning with Russia over its war against Ukraine. With greater leverage now, experts say Kim would likely aim to win big US concessions like an international recognition of North Korea as a nuclear state and sweeping sanctions relief in return for a partial surrender of his nuclear arsenal. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Letters | Fix Hong Kong’s healthcare silos with link workers
description: Readers discuss bridging medical and social welfare, why Hong Kong must change, and an epic road trip.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong faces profound structural challenges related to the rising prevalence of chronic diseases among the ageing population, and the associated problems of loneliness and the burden on caregivers. As the government prepares its inaugural five-year plan, this moment offers a vital opportunity to reform the city’s health and medical system to tackle the interlocking challenges. Since 2011, Health In Action has witnessed that grass-roots families struggle not only with illness but also with housing, financial strain, access to healthy food, caregiving, social isolation and health literacy. Social determinants of health are estimated to account for a substantial proportion of health outcomes, often more than half, depending on the model and population studied. Residents simply don’t know where to access or how to navigate existing resources because public services operate in silos. The lack of coordination pushes them back into the Hospital Authority system, deepening avoidable demand and long-term fiscal pressure. Future primary healthcare must evolve from siloed operations into a cross-disciplinary system capable of addressing the full spectrum of community needs. We submitted a paper to the Hong Kong government, urging it to leverage the five-year plan to introduce social prescribing as a cornerstone policy tool to bridge medical and social welfare and make the best use of social capital – community stakeholders. Social prescribing goes beyond simply referring citizens to community activities. The client journey begins with holistic needs being identified by professionals, followed by trained link workers setting goals, identifying resources and providing continuous connection before progress is reviewed. Social prescribing can take place in the established system composed of District Health Centres, community pharmacies and community living rooms. Alternatively, when a patient is discharged from hospital, a joint medical and social assessment could be used to create a care plan for a link worker to follow while coordinating the relevant services and health empowerment listed in the prescription. Implementation does not require a new or unwieldy bureaucracy. Instead, we can build upon existing foundations through pilot programmes. Health In Action and other NGOs have piloted social prescribing in the local community. The Hong Kong government can use these efforts as a reference. The five-year plan offers a forward-looking framework for enhancing the use of existing resources in the community. By ensuring vulnerable groups receive timely and coordinated support through a new workforce of link workers, Hong Kong can evolve towards a sustainable health future that cultivates well-being. Social prescribing should be recognised not as an adjunct, but as a core strategy for a more equitable, coordinated and human-centred healthcare system. Dr Fan Ning, founder and executive director, and Ruby Leung, senior community dietitian, Health In Action Hong Kong must change, survive, excel I refer to the letter, “Reinventing Hong Kong does not require amnesia” (August 21). Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule in 1997. Before the handover, Hong Kong was a British colony; now, it is a city in China. Isn’t it logical to change? Change can revitalise a city as it keeps abreast of inexorable technological progress. We must change, lest we lag behind. Our neighbour Shenzhen, thanks to its unceasing efforts to change, has transformed from an obscure city into one of China’s top cities. Shenzhen’s economy is now as robust as Hong Kong’s, if not more so. It serves as a classic example of how change can bring prosperity. In this rapidly changing era, we must change, survive and excel. Yu Mei-mei, Yuen Long A journey of strength and love The story of Liu Peijin’s love and support for his disabled wife is beautiful, the very best of humanity (“‘Die on the road, not in hospital’: Chinese man takes paralysed wife on epic road trip”, August 18). We are reminded that in the face of adversity the greatest strength we have is the love we share with the person we choose to spend our lives with, be that interracial, LGBTQ or mixed-faith. Love is the foundation of happiness, achievement, mental health stability and friendship. As Liu has shown, love is the journey of our lives. Mark Peaker, The Peak

title: Malaysia moves Anwar’s National Day speech indoors as haze spikes
description: Choking cross-border air pollution from Indonesian wildfires forces the Malaysian prime minister to relocate his National Day address.
content: Choking haze has forced Malaysia to move its leader’s annual National Day speech to an indoor venue from a public square, the communications ministry has said, underscoring the severity of cross-border pollution from severe wildfires in the region. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, due to address the country on August 30 on the eve of Independence Day celebrations, will speak from a convention centre in the administrative capital Putrajaya instead of at Kuala Lumpur’s Merdeka Square, a historic open area where independence was declared. Kuala Lumpur briefly had the world’s most polluted air late on Thursday, according to IQAir, and was second worst after Delhi on Friday morning with an air quality index score of 169. The Malaysian capital and surrounding suburbs are blanketed by haze that mostly originates from forest fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra in Indonesia, which is investigating those responsible. Decisions regarding the traditional open-air parade will be made after taking into account views from the health and meteorology officials. The parade is typically held on the morning of August 31 at Merdeka Square, but the meteorological department said in a statement on Thursday that haze would persist at the capital until Independence Day. Malaysia has used diplomacy to try and solve the transboundary haze issue, with Anwar seeking regional action through Association of Southeast Asian Nations mechanisms. Arthur Joseph Kurup, minister of natural resources and the environment, has previously said Malaysia had permission from Indonesia to cross into its border areas’ airspace to carry out cloud-seeding. Malaysia’s Kuching city, in Sarawak state on the Malaysian side of the Borneo island, has also previously ranked as having the most polluted air in the world, as smoke from Kalimantan, Indonesia’s part of Borneo, drifts across the border. The meteorological department also warned that Sarawak’s air quality could cross into very unhealthy levels through August 31.

title: US judge blocks rule implementing Trump plan to curb mail-in ballots
description: A Trump administration appeal is expected as both parties battle for control of Congress in the midterms.
content: A US federal judge on Thursday blocked the US Postal Service from implementing core parts of a new rule it adopted at President Donald Trump’s direction that would tighten mail-in voting requirements ahead of the November congressional elections. US District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston issued a temporary restraining order ‌at the behest of Democratic-led states and voting rights groups after the US Supreme Court on Monday issued a ruling that led to the lifting of earlier injunctions blocking Trump’s plans to restrict mail-in voting. That decision led to a frantic effort by dozens of Democratic state attorneys general and voting rights groups including the League of Women Voters to renew their legal fight and secure an order that would prevent the USPS from enforcing a rule ⁠that was allowed to take effect on Wednesday. The restraining order Talwani issued will remain in place while she considers whether ‌to issue a longer-term preliminary injunction blocking the rule. The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Barack Obama, plans to consider whether to do so during a September 3 hearing. Under the rule, ‌states must supply the USPS with lists of mail ballot recipients, and all outbound and return ballot envelopes ⁠must bear unique bar codes. ⁠The USPS, under the rule, may refuse to deliver ballots that do not comply with the new standards or are associated with voters who do not ‌appear on the lists. It issued the rule to implement an executive order the Republican president signed in March after years of Trump calling for tighter rules on ‌voting by ‌mail and pushing the false claim that his 2020 presidential election defeat to Democrat Joe Biden was the result of ‌widespread voter fraud. All 50 states allow for some form of mail-in voting, with 29 allowing voters to ask to cast ⁠ballots that way without providing a reason and eight conducting their elections entirely by mail. During the 2024 election, the USPS ⁠says it processed nearly 100 million ballots, and about 30 per cent of voters nationwide cast ballots by mail, according to the states. They argue the new federal restrictions risk disenfranchising voters and would unduly burden states in the weeks ‌running up to the election, forcing ‌them to buy new envelopes and equipment, establish new systems and train staff. The plaintiffs argue the USPS lacks authority to issue the rule and by issuing it usurped the authority states and Congress were given under the US Constitution to regulate elections. They contend the rule also undermines the USPS’ role as a neutral mail carrier and violates federal laws protecting voters’ rights.

title: Japan to expand security aid to 12 Indo-Pacific nations
description: Tokyo has more than doubled its security assistance programme to US$114 million in a strategic push.
content: Japan plans to provide defence equipment and other supplies to the armed forces of at least 12 like-minded countries under its Official Security Assistance programme in the current financial year, up from eight countries the previous year, people familiar with the matter said on Thursday. The military of Kenya, which sits on the western Indian Ocean, is expected to be a first-time recipient under the programme, with the Japanese government seeking to strengthen maritime security cooperation, particularly in surveillance and monitoring, amid China’s growing assertiveness in the Indo-Pacific region. Japan selects recipient countries each financial year. The government has allocated about 18.1 billion yen (US$114 million) for the security assistance programme in the year ending March 2027, more than double the roughly 8 billion yen set aside for the last financial year. In July, the foreign ministry decided to provide Cambodia’s military with communications equipment and patrol boats. Japan also plans to work with Australia to help Fiji build military facilities. Other countries being considered for help include the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Sri Lanka, as well as Vietnam, East Timor and Palau. Japan is considering supplying completed defence equipment, excluding items defined under Japan’s Self-Defence Forces Law as weapons intended to kill or destroy. To date, Japan has mainly provided dual-use equipment and supplies to foreign militaries, including patrol boats and coastal surveillance radar systems. The government also hopes that greater use of Japanese-made equipment will help expand the country’s defence industry overseas.

title: Chinese battery giant CATL spreads investments in search of new growth drivers
description: World’s largest producer of lithium-ion batteries for EVs and energy storage systems has committed over 17 billion yuan to non-battery deals.
content: From data centres to hydropower stations, Chinese battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) is placing investment bets on prospective growth engines following the electric vehicle (EV) boom, according to analysts. Since June last year, at least seven CATL-led equity deals involving a total of over 17 billion yuan (US$2.5 billion) have been announced in non-battery industries. The sectors involved span humanoid robots, state-owned hydropower stations, artificial intelligence data centres (AIDCs) and large-language-model developer DeepSeek. The equity investments by Fujian-based CATL seemed primarily strategic, similar to its earlier playbook of forming joint ventures with carmakers and investing in EV start-ups, said Yang Jing, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. “As the incumbent leader, sustaining market share and margins requires identifying new high-growth frontiers early and capturing first-mover advantages,” she said. “AIDC’s high-growth, high-barrier characteristics position it as a potential ‘third growth curve’ alongside EVs and energy storage systems.” Yang said CATL’s investments related to data centres could help cement its dominance in the post-EV era if the centres’ use scaled up energy storage demand as projected. CATL is the world’s largest producer of lithium-ion batteries for EVs and energy storage systems. But it is facing weakening demand for electric cars in China – the world’s largest automotive market – and intensifying competition with domestic rivals for energy storage orders in overseas markets. In May, Nasdaq-listed VNET Group, a Chinese third-party provider of neutral data centres, said two CATL-affiliates would acquire up to 38.1 per cent of its shares for US$942 million, becoming its largest shareholder. This month, Shenzhen-listed Hangzhou Zhonhen Electric, which supplies power supply systems for data centres and vehicle charging, said that it planned to sell a 49 per cent stake in the business to CATL for 4.09 billion yuan. In June, CATL and affiliates committed 5 billion yuan in the latest round of fundraising by Chinese AI company DeepSeek. CATL also led a 1.1 billion yuan fundraising round in Beijing-based robot start-up Galbot in June last year, and a year later it said a Galbot robot model using its batteries had been used on a production line. Lucas Zhang Liutong, director of Hong Kong-based consultancy WaterRock Energy Economics, said investments in humanoid robot makers could help CATL develop next- generation batteries to capture future demand growth. Globally, battery-powered humanoid robots are projected to require 6,000 gigawatt-hours of electric power a year by 2035, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie, which is based in the United Kingdom. One GWh is enough to power about 100 average American households for a year. From November to last month, CATL also took stakes in three joint ventures with state-owned enterprises for three clean energy projects in southwestern and western China. It contributed 670 million yuan to the Yagen II Hydropower Station on the Yalong River in Sichuan province, 360 million yuan to the Danba Hydropower Station on the Dadu River, also in Sichuan, and 528 million yuan to a project aiming to develop sources of clean energy in the Tibet autonomous region’s upper Lancang (Mekong) River basin. Zhang said the projects could provide CATL with affordable green power, reducing its carbon footprint to meet European Union regulations and its decarbonisation target. CATL chairman and CEO Robin Zeng Yuqun said at a news conference on August 17 that the company regarded carbon neutrality as “not only a mission, but also a capability developed through practice, and, above all, a tremendous opportunity for growth”. CATL said in a statement issued the same day that it aimed to neutralise emissions throughout its value chain, from mining to cell manufacturing, by 2035. Zhang said CATL might also be able to become more extensively involved in industrial estates targeting zero carbon emissions, because battery energy storage systems were a critical part of such initiatives.

title: Why Filipino migrants are rethinking their futures in Japan
description: The weak yen, rising costs and uncertainty over immigration rules have made staying long term in Japan difficult for foreign workers.
content: When Japan’s embassy in the Philippines extended applications for healthcare jobs on April 15, the pitch was straightforward: 50 positions for nurses and 300 for care workers in Japan, a three- to four-year placement, free Japanese-language lessons in both countries and a daily allowance during training. On social media, the post’s attractive terms drew widespread interest from Filipinos – a reminder that Japan is still urgently recruiting foreign labour even as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s administration, amid growing political pressure over foreign residents, moves to make it harder for migrants to settle long-term. The need is especially acute in care work: Japan will require about 2.72 million care workers by financial year 2040, roughly 570,000 more than in 2022, according to Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare estimates, while one think tank projection has warned the country could be nearly 1 million foreign workers short by then if current inflows continue. For the Filipino care workers, nurses and other professionals who came to Japan seeking greener pastures, the contradiction has become personal: the country needs them, but high living costs, a weak yen and uncertainty over immigration rules make it harder to imagine staying long-term. Job Galutan Andawey, a licensed nurse from the Philippines working as a carer in Kanagawa prefecture, is in his sixth year in Japan after arriving through the Japan-Philippines Economic Partnership Agreement, a treaty that includes career placement and language training programmes for nurses and care workers. “I chose Japan because I was influenced by Japanese culture. I dreamed of working here in Japan since I was little,” Andawey told This Week in Asia. But as time runs out on his work visa, the Filipino nurse is having second thoughts. “The cost of living is getting expensive while the salary is stagnant. And with the increase in visa fees and not much aid coming from the company, it is hard to save up,” Andawey said, adding that he was considering moving to Europe or the Middle East if he could not remain in Japan. Merrychris Urcales, a carer in Kagawa prefecture who came to Japan on a special skilled worker visa in 2024, said finding a job had been “relatively easier compared with other types of work because there is a high demand for carers in Japan”. But the weak yen and rising costs made saving difficult, and Urcales said she would need to consider other countries that might offer “better opportunities and a higher income”. For some workers, concerns over the yen’s declining value outweigh anxiety over immigration policy changes and reports of anti-foreigner sentiment, according to Alyssa Manalo, a PhD student at Hiroshima University who researches Filipino migration. “These changes do not seem to be as significant” for carers, assistant language teachers and those on special skilled worker visas, Manalo said. “For newer migrants who have their families in the Philippines, they generally just want to finish their contracts, save money, and return to the Philippines … they were more concerned about the declining yen than about changes in immigration policies or anti-foreigner sentiment.” The low exchange rate made it harder for migrant workers to send the same amount of money home, Manalo said. For those who have already spent years adapting to the country, however, Japan’s tighter immigration policies have increased the sense that long-term settlement is becoming harder. “They made it easier to come here, but made staying more difficult,” Kevin*, an engineer from the Philippines who has lived in Tokyo for 10 years, told This Week in Asia. The challenges are not lost on Catherine Ogalesco, a licensed care worker who first came to Japan nearly nine years ago to work in a factory. Ogalesco said she saw no problem with tougher language requirements, as she believed preparing for life in Japan required fluency. But she took issue with the proposed increase in the income threshold for permanent residency applications from 3 million yen (US$18,830) annually to 5.75 million yen, or 479,000 yen in monthly household income. “I think it is unfair especially for single households like myself, and for foreign workers in Japan in fields such as nursing care, factories, hotels and agriculture, where workers are sorely needed … how many foreign workers earn that much? Probably less than 20 per cent,” Ogalesco said. “With those rules, they are already excluding us from the possibility of applying for permanent residency.” The policy changes have also unsettled students and white-collar workers. Manalo said she had hoped to remain in Japan to pursue an academic career researching Filipino migrants, but was now re-evaluating her options. “Part of the proposed law would require foreign nationals to have Japanese proficiency, and I’m not that good at speaking Japanese,” said Manalo, who is on a scholarship programme. She said her last visa extension cost 6,000 yen, but the proposed guidelines would mean she might have to pay up to 50,000 yen depending on the length of the extension. Language requirements are also a source of anxiety for Amanda*, a software programmer who moved to Japan in 2022. Her company sponsored her language training until she passed level 3 of the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, a condition for full-time employment, but has since asked her to continue studying towards the advanced-intermediate level 2. “Even at level 3, I still don’t feel confident in my language skills … I’m getting anxious at the possibility of being asked for a level 2 certification just so I can keep my job,” Amanda told This Week in Asia. She considered moving to a larger company for better prospects but said the shifting climate made her more cautious. “I’m afraid of applying for other job positions as it might put my visa renewal at risk next year,” she said. Despite the policy changes, foreign residents described reports of rising anti-immigrant sentiment as the views of a minority amplified by the political climate, rather than a universal experience. “I live in a rural area of Japan, and I have not experienced any forms of racism or discrimination. As long as you follow Japanese etiquette and rules, I personally don’t think Japanese people will say anything bad to you,” Manalo said. Ogalesco remains undeterred by the changing rules. “Even with the changes, I would still choose to stay and work here in Japan. Here, I feel safe and financially comfortable.” Manalo is hopeful that Japan’s growing reliance on foreign workers will push the government to reconsider its approach as the country continues to grapple with labour shortages and an ageing population. “Japan is already becoming more dependent on foreign workers, particularly in sectors such as caregiving, construction and agriculture,” she said. “At some point, Japan needs to be more open to migrants, especially in care-related work where the demand for workers will continue to grow.” *Names changed to protect interviewees’ identities

title: In Focus | Xi’s crusade against corruption has gone well beyond economic crime
description: Wider campaign is now increasingly about how officials use their power, whether they toe the line, and what they do in their private lives.
content: The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the fourth part of an accompanying series, Yuanyue Dang and William Zheng delve into the broader reach of the campaign. While economic crimes are often seen as the target of President Xi Jinping’s crusade against corruption, the campaign has become much wider. Thirteen years since it began, it is now increasingly about how officials use their power, whether they toe the line, and what they do in their private lives. The South China Morning Post analysed the findings of hundreds of disciplinary investigations conducted by the anti-corruption watchdog from 2013 to 2025. The findings suggest that Xi’s campaign has expanded from economic corruption to a broader effort to reshape how the bureaucracy is run. While bribery is still the legal foundation for cases to enter the court system, political loyalty, discipline, policy implementation and cadre management have become part of how corruption is defined and punished in China. The SCMP analysis looked at the cases of 423 cadres who were “centrally managed” – meaning senior officials who reported directly to the Central Committee of the ruling Communist Party. Cadres at this level are overseen by the party’s personnel agency – the Central Organisation Department – which is responsible for administration, assessment and recommendations on who is in and who is out. Most cadres in the analysis were ranked at deputy provincial or ministerial level or above. A small number were slightly lower in rank but headed financial institutions, state-owned enterprises or other key organisations. The findings analysed were released by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection after an investigation and most cases were then passed to judicial authorities. They are not court judgments and do not provide a complete account of the evidence held by investigators, but are more like a public explanation from the authorities as to why an official crossed a red line. ‘Political sin’ The anti-corruption campaign was launched after Xi became China’s top leader in 2013. Beijing has said there would be “no forbidden zones, full coverage and zero tolerance”. As the campaign has rolled on, the CCDI has released longer statements on its investigations, mainly to include political-related accusations. Economic crimes have remained part of nearly every case. But these cases now include allegations involving “improper” banquets, resisting investigation, and issues around policy implementation, use of power and political risk. Of the 423 cases reviewed, 93.4 per cent of the officials were accused of using their positions to seek benefits for others. Some 88.7 per cent were accused of taking bribes, and 67.1 per cent were accused of accepting cash or gifts. These were the three most common allegations. Economic corruption and integrity violations accounted for 52.4 per cent of the allegations from 2013 to 2017 – about five years after the party congress when Xi became leader. In the next five years to 2022, they made up 43.2 per cent of the allegations, and in the period from 2023 to 2025 it was 46.4 per cent. This does not mean bribery has become less important in the campaign, rather that the party’s definition of corruption is now broader. Qian Jingyuan, an assistant professor of political science at Boston College, said this reflected the dual nature of the campaign. “From Beijing’s perspective, corruption has been viewed not just as an economic crime, but also as a political sin,” Qian said. “Thus, public announcements must emphasise the political nature of an official’s wrongdoing before the economic aspects, while the latter often constitute the substantive basis for the criminal indictment.” Power and conduct To assess how the campaign has changed over time, the SCMP analysis divided the cases into three periods in line with the party congress cycles, according to the year the CCDI released its findings. There were 159 cases from 2013 to 2017; 124 from 2018 to 2022; and 140 from 2023 to 2025. From 2013 to 2017, 18.9 per cent of cases contained allegations involving political security or political risk. The CCDI accusations included seeking political patronage, forming cliques and factions, damaging the political environment, saying one thing while doing another, associating with political swindlers and engaging in superstitious activities. There was a jump in these cases – to 64.5 per cent – in the period from 2018 to 2022. They fell slightly to 59.3 per cent in the period from 2023 to 2025. The language used in these allegations is in line with the Regulations on CPC Disciplinary Action – or rules of conduct within the party – which underwent a major revision in 2015. Six forms of discipline are listed: political, organisational, integrity, “mass” discipline governing relations with the public, work and personal conduct. As political allegations have increased, there have been fewer occurrences of specific claims like forming cliques or making improper comments about the central leadership. Deng Yuwen, a former deputy editor of Study Times, the official newspaper of the Central Party School, said that reflected a move away from dealing with questions of political alignment and towards more detailed scrutiny of administrative conduct. “After the major political cliques like [those of former public security vice-minister] Sun Lijun have been brought down, Beijing’s effort went into the details of how the senior cadres use their power, and their conduct,” Deng said. “Systematic power abuse will lead to systematic economic and social risks. Abusive official conduct will accumulate social discontent. Both are dangerous for the legitimacy and the long-term rule of the Communist Party.” When an official’s political loyalty is questioned, they are often also accused of concealing personal matters, lying during interviews, or resisting investigation, according to the SCMP analysis. These allegations appeared in 48.4 per cent of cases in the 2013-17 period. That jumped to 82.3 per cent from 2018 to 2022, and reached 88.6 per cent in the 2023-25 period. This has coincided with an expansion of the supervisory system. China amended the constitution in 2018 to establish supervisory commissions at every level and enacted the Supervision Law. The commissions – which work with discipline inspectors – extend oversight from party cadres to all officials who exercise public power. An expanded detention system known as liuzhi replaced the party’s largely informal shuanggui disciplinary system. The way anti-corruption bodies publish their investigation findings and their format has also become more standardised since the law took effect. Qian from Boston College said the campaign had brought “both greater institutionalisation of cadre supervision and more personalised control”. Toeing the line As the campaign has progressed, the clearest shift in the CCDI’s investigation notices can be seen in their direct assessments of governance. In the 2013-17 period, only 23.9 per cent of cases involved allegations of failure to implement central decisions, other governance problems, departures from the “new development philosophy”, abuse of power, and interference in market, judicial and law enforcement activities. That proportion rose to 53.2 per cent in the period from 2018 to 2022, and hit 73.6 per cent from 2023 to 2025. These governance issues are now in the disciplinary rules after they were again revised, in 2023. The latest version says officials can be punished for violating political discipline if they express support for central decisions but fail to implement them, carry them out half-heartedly, or dilute or circumvent them. The rules now also include – under problems with governance performance – any departures from the “new development philosophy” and “high-quality development” as well as wasteful “vanity projects”. Qian said the sectors targeted by anti-corruption investigators were increasingly connected to the party’s governance priorities. He cited the more intensive scrutiny of financial and banking officials as Beijing sought to guard against “systemic risk”. “Apparently the central leadership has used anti-corruption as a means to enforce its policy agenda and incentivise the officials’ governance outcomes by targeting specific sectors,” he said. That view was echoed by Jiangnan Zhu, an associate professor with the University of Hong Kong’s Department of Politics and Public Administration. “The concept of corruption in the Chinese party-state is broad and dynamic,” Zhu said, adding that it could change with the leadership’s governing priorities. But she said there had been a consistent theme in the anti-graft campaign from the start: improving governance while strengthening party control. Path to jobs Another new focus as the campaign has gathered pace is how cadres are selected for jobs. Cases involving irregularities in personnel selection and appointments or post-retirement misconduct rose from 39 per cent in the first period (2013-17) to 60 per cent in the latest period (2023-25). Inspectors are now looking at bribery that has already occurred but also the entry, promotion and exit of cadres. They aim to break corrupt chains formed through money and private networks and to continue supervision once officials have retired. In Zhu’s book, Bribery as a Third Path to Power? Political Selection in China Beyond Performance and Patronage, she described the buying and selling of public sector jobs as “personnel corruption”. She wrote that this type of corruption allowed money to replace competence and loyalty in determining who could enter or rise through public office, ultimately causing “the privatisation of public power and deinstitutionalisation of meritocracy”. Zhu said Xi’s anti-corruption campaign had a focus on the networks formed through the buying and selling of posts because they could develop into power bases beyond the central leadership’s control. Her research found that explicit cases of buying and selling official positions have fallen sharply since 2017, suggesting the campaign had reduced these activities and helped the party regain control over personnel selection. Officials’ personal and family lives have also become part of cadre supervision. Across the entire sample analysed by the SCMP, 49.2 per cent of officials were accused of improper family conduct, failing to supervise or educate relatives, or involvement in family-based corruption. This accountability framework extends a senior official’s responsibility to their family, subordinates and political networks. Whether a cadre is loyal, reports personal matters truthfully, selects personnel appropriately, keeps family members and those around them under control, and implements central policy can now appear alongside bribery allegations. But analysts cautioned that this does not point to comprehensive changes to the party-state system. “I do not see clear evidence that the campaign itself is reshaping the general structure of the party-state bureaucracy,” according to Qian. He said the campaign had brought large-scale personnel changes, altered promotion standards, performance evaluations and officials’ incentives, and established new institutions intended to tighten control over the bureaucracy. But he said the broader centralisation of power and strengthening of party leadership could not be attributed entirely to the campaign. The SCMP analysis also suggests that the party is changing the standards it uses to assess the performance of officials. That was expressed more directly in a party-wide education campaign on “correct” governance launched by the Central Committee earlier this year. It identified a number of problems that needed to be corrected, including short-sighted decision-making, falsification, blind expansion and “vanity projects” that waste labour and money. Assessment of governance must also include the implementation of central decisions and “high-quality development”. Economic growth and policy outcomes remain important in the evaluation of cadres’ performance. But there is now greater weight given to political loyalty, integrity, control over subordinates and family members, and the ability to carry out central directives. “As the scope of ‘corruption’ has broadened, some officials would rather choose to ‘lie flat’ and may be reluctant to experiment with policies that could potentially cross the lines drawn by higher authorities,” Qian said. For Beijing, this means the next phase of the anti-corruption campaign will involve not only continuing to identify problems, but also finding the line between control and encouraging initiative. “Finding a balance between enforcing discipline and incentivising officials’ performance and innovation remains an important task for the central leadership,” Qian said.

title: Bend over backwards until you break? Student film on cost of people-pleasing
description: ‘As You Wish’ explores the dangers of always prioritising others; a psychologist explains why teens are especially susceptible to this.
content:
When does empathy cross the boundary into people-pleasing?
A Hong Kong student film, As You Wish , explores the mental health impact of constantly putting others’ needs above your own.
Produced by Sonakshi Shrivastava, Rachell Lee and Jayne Lau, all 17-year-old students at King George V School, the short film follows a teenager, Alice, who struggles to say no to others.
“[People-pleasing] is tied to anxiety, fear of conflict and self-worth,” said Sonakshi, who played the film’s main character. “Alice isn’t weak. She’s empathetic , but she hasn’t learned boundaries yet.”
Rather than examining Alice’s conflict with her peers through dialogue, the filmmakers chose to focus on her psychological spiral and the idea that the only one who can get Alice out of her troubled state is herself.
Jayne, the main cinematographer and one of the directors, noted: “Alice thinks she’s irreplaceable because she does absolutely everything for everyone. But in reality, the moment she stops producing, the moment she falters, she’s completely discardable.”
In April, As You Wish was featured in the PKX Teen Arts & Film Festival in New York, which showcases international teen films and visual art exhibits.
In March, the film took home awards for best sound design and best actress at the third Babel Film Awards’ Open Competition, which showcases student filmmakers across Asia. The annual event is hosted by Hong Kong-based Babel Film Workshop, a film and media arts education provider. As You Wish is available to stream on Babel Slate, an online space for student filmmakers.
Hong Kong-based therapist Elizabeth Jung Rowlinson, who practises at Your Relationship Clinic, explained that people-pleasing “involves prioritising the needs and desires of others over one’s own”.
Signs of this include having difficulty saying no, excessively apologising when it is not your fault, avoiding conflict and taking responsibility for others’ negative moods.
Rowlinson explained why adolescents would be particularly prone to people-pleasing. Teenagers’ brains are hypersensitive to social rewards and peer approval, especially as they become more independent from their families.
“Saying yes frequently, not wanting conflict and constant worry about fitting in has to do with wanting to identify [with others] ... The teen brain views peer judgment as a physical threat,” the therapist said.
The film uses mirrors to show Alice’s gradual breakdown and reflect her conflicting states.
“Alice’s mirror self is like a repressed part of herself that knows the danger of being a [people-pleaser],” said Rachell, another director and the main sound designer.
“I think we all have a part of ourselves that sees our flaws clearly, but whether or not we dare to face [them] is another question.”
The film also explores people-pleasing’s emotional consequences for Alice through sound design and lighting.
Rachell noted how small, everyday sounds in the film’s background – a coffee machine, an alarm and typing on a keyboard – become more amplified as the story progresses.
“Overlapping common household sounds ... created the sense that [Alice’s] regular world was crashing down on her,” Rachell explained.
Jayne added: “It is suffocating by design because that’s exactly what it feels like to live in that head space.”
She also noted that the lighting reflected how someone who is struggling will have their view of society distorted.
The lighting progressed from a warm “golden hour glow” at the start of the film to a “poisonous green” as Alice began to burn out, Jayne noted.
The colour change, in addition to the blurred fishbowl lens, was meant to illustrate how this internal fatigue warps one’s perception of the world.
The film lacks a typical resolution, reflecting the danger and helplessness of burnout .
“By regularly and long-term placing other people’s [needs] above your own, one could start to feel neglectful or resentful,” Rowlinson warned, adding that it could cause a person to lose their personal direction and passion.
For those struggling with people-pleasing, Rowlinson suggested keeping a logbook that tracks feelings and the reason for these emotions, which will help address the pattern of behaviour.
She also suggested setting healthy boundaries by examining your values and definition of friendship.
Having boundaries doesn’t mean automatically saying no; instead, they are about knowing your limits and voicing them out.
Sonakshi said she hoped the film would encourage students to examine and establish their own boundaries.
“The hidden cost of kindness should not be at your own expense,” she emphasised.
“If As You Wish starts even one conversation about that, then it’s done its job well.”

title: White House construction cited in Trump helicopter close call with airliner
description: Radio problems kept air traffic controllers from hearing calls warning that Marine One was getting ready to take off.
content: Construction work at the White House was a factor in the US presidential helicopter passing too close to a passenger plane in the skies over Washington earlier this month, investigators said Thursday. The close pass happened on August 4 after President Donald Trump took off on Marine One from a temporary site on the Ellipse, outside the grounds of the White House, during the construction of a permanent helipad inside the grounds. The White House and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) have both said that Trump was never in danger. In their preliminary report, investigators at the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) cited FAA estimates that the presidential helicopter and an Envoy Air passenger plane were separated by 1.3km (0.82 miles) horizontally and about 215 metres (700 feet) vertically when the incident happened – less than the required minimum separation of 2.4km (1.5 miles) and 152 metres (500 feet). The NTSB is working to “calculate and confirm” those distances and is continuing its investigation. Investigators found that air traffic controllers at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport did not receive the first radio transmission signalling the presidential helicopter’s imminent departure and “the second attempt was broken and completely unreadable”. “There was not adequate line of sight to ensure communications between the radio transmitter/receiver sight and The Ellipse, where (Marine One) was temporarily operating from while construction was ongoing at the White House,” the report said. In January, a collision between a passenger plane approaching the same airport and a US Army Black Hawk helicopter killed 67 people.

title: Opinion | A Chinese cook in the Middle East serves up a very different anti-war film
description: Upending Hollywood’s ‘saviour-hero’ convention in war films, a tale about a humble chef offers a quiet, distinctly Chinese perspective.
content: This summer, Chinese anti-war film Once Upon a Time in the Middle East has dominated the mainland box office. The film implicitly answers the question: what happens when a story about international conflict is told, not through the sights of an assault rifle, but through a gentler lens? It offers a fundamental restructuring of cinematic narrative paradigms, one that challenges decades of Hollywood inertia. For nearly a century, mainstream international anti-war cinema has been heavily anchored in the Western hero’s crucible. From The Hurt Locker to American Sniper, classic Hollywood conventions have framed global conflict through a distinct lens: military intervention, the combatant’s moral angst or the intervention of a solitary “saviour” imposing order on local chaos. While these films often critique the horrors of war, they inadvertently reinforce a paternalistic dichotomy – reducing local populations to passive victims who form the backdrop to the agency of foreign soldiers. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East dismantles this formula. Its protagonist, Xu Fu, is neither an elite mercenary nor a geopolitical agent. He is an ordinary Chinese cook earning a living abroad to pay off debt. When war erupts around his small restaurant, he neither picks up a weapon nor delivers lofty ideological speeches. Instead, he simply keeps the cooking stoves lit. By centring a civilian whose primary act of defiance is feeding people, the film shatters the Western “saviour” archetype. It reframes anti-war drama from a spectacle of military prowess to a quiet testament to human endurance. This shift has ignited a fresh debate about global storytelling: can international cinema move past the binary of conqueror vs victim to build narrative tension around the preservation of daily life? Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’s narrative is rooted in Chinese history. The protagonist’s name, Xu Fu, brings to mind the alchemist sent overseas by Emperor Qin about 2,200 years ago. Yet while the ancient Xu sailed to seek imperial immortality, the modern Xu travels simply to earn a living. He represents generations of Chinese migrants who built roads, manned kitchens and quietly endured hardships in foreign lands. The true weight of the film lies in how it articulates a distinctly Chinese world view – translating ancient philosophical concepts into grounded, accessible visual storytelling. In the film, the repeated phrase “eat well” transforms from a mundane greeting into an immovable moral anchor. When artillery shatters city streets and dust flies through broken window frames, the sizzle of hot oil in Xu’s wok becomes a counterweight to destruction. The aroma of food rising through war-torn ruins reawakens the most fundamental human desire for life and stability. This visual metaphor reflects a core element of the Chinese philosophy of safety: security is not an abstract geopolitical concept enforced by military deterrence but something tangible, found in quiet streets, accessible meals and unbroken daily routines. Protecting the dinner table protects the baseline of human existence. Rather than portraying foreign lands as alien or hostile spaces needing order imposed from without, the film frames the restaurant as a crossroads of cultures. Serving people of diverse ethnic and political backgrounds, the restaurant becomes a sanctuary amid chaos. This mirrors the classic ethos of Chinese wisdom, seeking harmony without forcing uniformity. The film avoids advocating ideological alignment. Instead, it shows that when people sit down to share a meal, artificial divisions dissolve. Lasting peace is built not by erasing differences through force, but by respecting diversity and finding common ground in shared humanity. The film’s most poignant arc involves the rescue of 23 orphans. When warned that “they are not your children”, the protagonist simply answers: “They are still children.” This moment captures another aspect of Chinese wisdom – extending care for one’s children to those of others. In a world where hundreds of millions of young people live under the shadow of armed conflict, the film stresses that safeguarding children is safeguarding the future itself. It posits a security concept rooted in empathy rather than zero-sum competition, arguing that true stability can only grow when the causes of hatred are replaced by basic human care. The fascination with the film suggests audiences are hungry for alternative perspectives on global challenges. By pairing rich, serious themes with human warmth and accessible storytelling, the film highlights the maturing capabilities of China’s film industry – not just in technical production but also in narrative confidence. As international conflicts continue to dominate headlines, this film offers a vital reminder: peace is not a gift granted by force, but a shared responsibility cultivated through empathy, dialogue and mutual respect.

title: Expanded Mid-Autumn Festival lantern show to light up Hong Kong. Here’s what to see
description: International Lantern Spectacular, organised by Hong Kong Tourism Board, among the city’s efforts to entice locals and visitors alike.
content: A more international and upgraded lantern show is set to light up Hong Kong’s Victoria Park during the Mid-Autumn Festival next month, as part of the city’s efforts to entice locals and tourists alike. The International Lantern Spectacular, organised by the Hong Kong Tourism Board, will be held at the Causeway Bay park between September 17 and 27, complementing other festive activities such as the Fire Dragon Dance in the nearby Tai Hang neighbourhood. To help readers get into the spirit of the festival, the South China Morning Post lists the latest additions to this lantern extravaganza. Did someone say lanterns? A highlight of the show is the World Lantern Boulevard, which will showcase more than 3,000 distinctive lanterns from 20 countries and regions, such as South Korea and Brazil. The moment visitors walk through the park’s main entrance, they will be greeted by the sight of “Shadowlight”. The eight-metre-tall lantern, inspired by the city’s iconic banyan trees, is the work of master artisans from Nanjing and features a colourful array of lights. The event will also include four tailor-made giant Qinhuai lanterns, also made by Nanjing artisans. Nanjing’s Qinhuai lantern craftsmanship is known internationally and included on China’s national list of intangible cultural heritage. Another highlight, “Lotus Fish”, features rows of giant lotus leaves in neat formation, accompanied by brightly coloured carp that shine against the backdrop of a concrete forest. What about local heritage? Over at the park’s Hill Knoll Pavilion, more than 400 classic handcrafted Hong Kong lanterns are set to go on display. Their designs pay tribute to local tradition and include household favourites such as rabbit, star fruit and goldfish lanterns, while evoking the city’s colourful, signature Lantern Street in Yuen Long’s Tai Kiu Market. So why the upgrade? Lanterns are a visual tradition of the Mid-Autumn Festival – a time when family and friends reunite, gaze at the moon and enjoy mooncakes. This year’s festival falls on Friday, September 25, with the following day marked as a public holiday. The Tourism Board said the upgrade was part of its vision to connect local culture and festive experiences with tourism-related offers. “By combining local festive culture with tourism and spending experiences, the board aims to attract more visitors to Hong Kong to experience first-hand the appeal of Asia’s events capital, where local traditions meet global cultures, and to drive the tourism economy,” said Anthony Lau Chun-hon, the board’s executive director. What other festive activities are nearby? The board is teaming up with charitable organisation Po Leung Kuk to hold a charity sale at the park to offer specially made mooncakes from Hong Kong and the mainland between September 17 and 20. The Leisure and Cultural Services Department will also host its annual Mid-Autumn Lantern Carnival at the park. Just a few minutes’ walk from the park, locals and tourists can catch the Tai Hang Fire Dragon Dance, when a 67-metre-long beast of legend made from 12,000 burning incense sticks will be carried down the famous neighbourhood between September 24 and 26. The board is also set to unveil further details about citywide promotions and activities to mark the festival.

title: Chinese cinema offers noon nap service with flat seats to boost lunchtime business
description: For a monthly subscription fee of about US$6, patrons can enjoy a rejuvenating nap in two designated screening halls on any weekday.
content: A cinema in northwestern China has gained attention on social media for its unique noon nap service, offering adjustable seats for workers to relax during their lunch breaks. This popular initiative at Lumiai Cinema in Xian, Shaanxi province, has been operational since April last year, according to Jimu News. Priced at 39.9 yuan (US$6) for a single membership and 59.9 yuan for a double pass, the monthly subscription allows patrons to enjoy a rejuvenating nap in two designated screening halls on any working day. A manager from the cinema, known by her surname Xu, shared with the media that the noon nap service was launched to boost the occupancy rate of its screening halls, as attendance tends to be low on weekdays. The cinema has designated two halls featuring a total of 76 adjustable seats, which can be reclined flat, allowing customers to rest from 12pm to 2.30pm. Complimentary blankets, coffee, and other beverages are provided, whereas disposable earplugs and eye masks are available for a nominal fee of 5.9 yuan each. Customers are requested to silence their mobile phones, and if they need to make or receive calls, they should step outside the napping area. In adherence to a policy aimed at maintaining a pleasant atmosphere, patrons are required to keep their shoes on in the sleeping area, as highlighted by the promotional poster for the service. Most of the seats are located in the Leisure Screening Hall, which is favoured by customers for its more spacious seating options ideal for napping. The other venue, dubbed the Massage Seat Hall, features massage chairs that can also be reclined flat. For customers who snore, the cinema staff will gently advise them to use the Massage Seat Hall, where fewer individuals rest due to the narrower seating arrangement. A 33-year-old man, surnamed Guo, who works nearby, mentioned that he has subscribed to the noon nap service for four months. “In the past, I would nap at my workstation, but it was never restful. Now, I come here for a break every working day,” he stated. “The Leisure Hall is dark and clean; I can lie down comfortably, making it easy for me to fall asleep,” Guo added. Wittily branded as the “lying flat plan,” the noon nap service taps into a popular trend in China, referring to the younger generation’s inclination to adopt a minimalist approach to life. The manager noted that more than half of the seats are utilised for the noon nap service on most days. The story has captured the attention of mainland social media. “Workers truly need this. It’s affordable. I hope it gains traction across the country,” commented one internet user. Another added: “What a creative solution! The cinema can benefit financially from this as well.” Taking a midday nap is a prevalent practice in China, believed to be advantageous for health. A survey published by the China Sleep Research Society in March found that over 70 per cent of Chinese people enjoy an afternoon nap lasting at least 30 minutes.

title: The path to America is narrowing. Here’s what that means for legal immigrants
description: Experts advise green card and other visa applicants to stop assuming that following the rules guarantees a smooth way to stay in the US.
content: US green card interviews are on hold worldwide, student and work visas are subject to new restrictions, and citizenship is under fresh scrutiny. Here’s what the latest US immigration crackdown means for people planning to study, work or settle in America. Why did the US cancel immigrant visa interviews? US embassies and consulates around the world have postponed immigrant visa interviews so that officers can train on a stricter “public charge” test: whether an applicant is likely to rely on public benefits. The freeze came days after a federal judge struck down a separate 75-country visa block built on the same idea. The State Department emphasises that officers must apply the test “comprehensively and consistently”. The factors themselves are not new: age, health, family size, money, education, skills and job prospects. What has been added is the instruction to apply them more aggressively, including by issuing public charge bonds in some cases. Sarah Pierce, director of social policy at Washington-based think tank Third Way – who is also a former US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) analyst – said the Donald Trump administration “chose the most disruptive possible way to roll this out”. Charles Kuck, an Atlanta immigration lawyer who last year represented more than 100 students against the administration, said officers were being trained “on how to deny cases under public charge rules”. Family applicants would find it “much harder to immigrate”, he said, adding that the change would also hurt diversity lottery applicants. Does this cancel my green card petition? A cancelled interview does not usually erase an approved petition or a priority date. “State is postponing the interview; it has not announced that these underlying approvals are being revoked,” Pierce said. “The real harm is delay” for people who have already booked flights, sold homes or attended medical examinations. “State has not said when normal scheduling will resume,” she said. Diversity visas generally must be issued by the end of the financial year, which for the US government is September 30. Make sure the National Visa Centre has a working email, phone number and mailing address for you. Does the pause affect non-immigrant visas? No. This freeze applies to green-card interviews abroad. H-1B, student and tourist windows are not part of it. However, the public charge provision could legally apply to non-immigrants too, Kuck noted, while adding that “as of right now, it only appears to be applying to immigrant visa holders”. That does not mean those visas are easy to obtain. Pierce said that much of the H-1B agenda was “forward-looking”: the proposed US$103,000 fee is not in force yet and a new lottery is not the problem for people already selected. The people most exposed are those who still need a stamp outside the US, according to Pierce. What is the public charge test? Officers weigh age, health, family, money, education, skills and sometimes past benefits. A proper I-864 affidavit of support was normally enough in family cases, unless there were “unusually significant concerns”, she said. While Pierce would not call the new push “a legal blanket ban”, she warned that the danger was that aggressive implementation “begins functioning like one for certain populations”. Kuck’s worry is the vacuum. “There is no guidance in the statute,” he said, which “allows for a great deal of mischief”. What should I do if my visa interview was cancelled? If the appointment is gone, the petition usually is not. Kuck’s advice is to stay put unless you already hold a work visa that lets you return and keep the job. Most people who received the cancellation email are not in this position. “They should remain in their home country until the interview is reset,” Kuck said. Can the US revoke an petition after it is approved? “A consular officer does not simply get to overrule USCIS,” Pierce said. If the interview turns up fraud, a big change in facts or a clear error, the officer can send the file back. USCIS then decides. Her advice to applicants is to know what was filed in your name and “don’t guess when an officer asks about something you don’t know”. Family cases are hard to unwind, because “somebody is either a spouse or not a spouse”, according to Kuck. Employment files get more second guessing. Many returned petitions were later reapproved, he said. Should I leave the US to stamp my visa? If you already have lawful status, do not travel unless you must. “No one should leave the United States unless they have an emergency need to travel,” Kuck said. Pierce’s test was the same. “Think harder before international travel if returning depends on a new visa,” she said. An approved O-1 petition was not a reason to fly out for a stamp. What documents should visa holders carry in the US? Carry proof of status: the green card, or an I-94 plus an I-797 or employer letter. Keep copies where family can reach them, Pierce said. “This administration has dramatically increased the volume and aggressiveness of immigration enforcement, which makes the consequences of bureaucratic mistakes much higher.” Workers flying in should carry pay stubs and a job letter, Kuck said. People with no lawful status, including those on a 240-day extension after an H-1B has ended, or those with only a pending green card or asylum case, should not travel. What is changing for F-1 students? New arrivals lose open-ended duration of status. They get a fixed date, generally up to four years, plus a 30-day grace period, down from 60. Students already in the US on September 15 can usually keep the old terms until they leave and come back. Travel can switch the clock. “Work with your foreign student adviser,” Kuck said. How can OPT students avoid unlawful presence? Do not overstay. Put the end date on a calendar and “do not take any chances of leaving even one day late”, Kuck said. A tidy record in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System will not save you if the I-94 has expired. The advice is to track the I-94, I-20, EAD and any pending filing, and act before the earliest date. What if an H-1B worker is laid off? The law still offers 60 days, but Kuck advised not to trust it. “Legally, they still have the 60 days. Yeah, but in reality, they have none.” File to change status before the job ends. Pierce said that people who already held valid H-1B status inside the United States were less exposed than those who needed a stamp abroad. Can the US take away citizenship? Only through a narrow civil case, and it is still rare – the Justice Department says it has filed 123 such cases since 20 January 2025, which is a record. “The government cannot simply strip citizenship from a naturalised American because it later decides that person is undesirable,” Pierce said. It must show citizenship was illegally procured or obtained by hiding a material fact. What had changed was “the government’s appetite for reopening old files”, she added. Many of Kuck’s clients used a second identity after an old deportation order. “If you were deported under a different name, you should be very worried.” What about the citizenship of children born there? The United States cannot take away citizenship of children born in the US because of their parents’ immigration status, the Supreme Court ruled in June. Denaturalising a parent is a separate process and does not, by itself, revoke the citizenship of a child who was a citizen at birth. In Trump vs Barbara, the court held that children born in the United States to parents who were in the country unlawfully or only temporarily “are citizens at birth”. “Birthright citizenship is fundamentally different from naturalisation,” Pierce said. A citizen at birth did not “procure” naturalisation, so the government “cannot simply use the denaturalisation process to retroactively turn that person into a non-citizen”. Kuck pointed out that children and spouses were not automatically stripped of their citizenship when the government was targeting visa fraud. Are green card holders safe to travel? The ones at risk will be those on the way back to the US who are residents convicted of a crime after they received the card, according to Kuck. “No one else needs to worry about it.” Long trips can still raise old abandonment questions. Carry the card. Who is safe, and who is at high risk? “The vast majority of people who follow the rules, they’re fine. That’s 99 per cent,” Kuck said. The heat is on old fraud, a second name or no status. Pierce offered a different caution: following the rules no longer means a calm process. “Build in more time. Expect more scrutiny.” Highest risk: prior fraud, travel without status, diversity visa deadlines and family applicants who look poor under a tougher public-charge screen. Is legal immigration to the US still possible? Yes, but it will be slower, with more scrutiny. “There is no doubt that this administration is engaged in a systematic attack against legal immigration,” Pierce said. Asked what she would tell people, Pierce said: “I would tell them to stop assuming that following the rules guarantees a smooth process.” The agenda “is not confined to illegal immigration. It has made a deliberate choice to make legal immigration harder as well.” Kuck’s advice was to keep a backup plan for now. “This episode will rest in the ash heap of history soon enough.” Until interviews resume, treat a cancelled date as a delay, not a dead case. This article is for general information only and is not legal advice. Readers should consult a qualified immigration lawyer about their own case.

title: AI use on 1823 platform will cut frustration but data safeguards needed: experts
description: Hong Kong lawmakers say enhanced AI could speed up complaint handling, but expert warns agentic systems pose privacy and automated error risks.
content: Deploying artificial intelligence on Hong Kong’s 1823 complaint platform will reduce public frustration and strengthen governance, but authorities must also guard against privacy leaks, lawmakers and an expert have said. They described the AI measures announced on Thursday as a step in the right direction, saying the technology could reduce residents’ waiting times and help direct cases to the appropriate departments. “In the past, residents often complained that their cases were assigned to the wrong authorities,” technology-sector lawmaker Duncan Chiu said, noting that complex issues – such as fallen trees on boundaries between private and public lands – frequently led to interdepartmental confusion. “If AI can guide phone operators to ask a few more targeted questions to gather better clues, it can lead to much clearer triage and save residents significant time.” The Digital Policy Office, which operates Hong Kong’s 1823 inquiry and complaint platform, said on Thursday that it would expand its use of artificial intelligence to help staff transcribe residents’ calls, summarise emails and log information in its system. It said it would also use AI to triage complex and urgent cases for experienced staff to forward to the relevant departments, while collecting and summarising emerging district governance issues identified through residents’ complaints. The office said the move aimed to enable staff to devote more time to resolving complex cases and better addressing residents’ needs. Chiu said the enhanced AI capabilities would help ensure complaints were directed to the correct departments from the outset, addressing a long-standing source of public frustration. He also explained why Hong Kong had taken so long to deploy AI on the platform. While the roll-out of such tools might appear late, Chiu said the underlying technology was complicated. Few large language models could reliably transcribe Cantonese, particularly given its range of accents and the mixing of Cantonese with English. “There are many accents in Cantonese and may sometimes mix with English or other languages,” he said. “If residents talk about some landmarks, such as when one says ‘the golden flower in Wan Chai’, would the AI know where it is? These all need training.” Chiu was among 67 lawmakers who visited Beijing during the summer and toured the 12345 Citizen Hotline Service Centre, which uses big data and AI to dynamically route complaints to authorities, with time frames set for resolving issues. He said that while 1823’s technological initiatives could match about 80 per cent of Beijing’s platform capabilities, the main differences lay beyond technology. Beijing’s success relied on top-down administrative mandates requiring departments to resolve assigned complaints within strict 14-day deadlines, as well as a fully integrated and centralised cross-departmental database, he said. Hong Kong authorities might need to consider whether adopting the same approach would be cost-effective, he added. Lawmaker Johnny Ng Kit-chong said expanding the use of AI was a good starting point for authorities. He added that AI could be used more widely in governance, such as by monitoring departments’ progress in following up on residents’ complaints and using computer vision to analyse photos and videos submitted by residents. “For example, after some time, AI could produce some content urging the relevant departments to take action, following up until the complainant was satisfied with the result,” he said. Michael Chau, a professor of innovation and information management at the University of Hong Kong, agreed that expanding AI use on the 1823 platform was a step in the right direction. He said the system’s effectiveness remained to be seen, but incorporating AI could significantly shorten the time residents waited for responses. “Now, with 1823 combining the use of AI and human involvement, I expect it to perform better than solely relying on either as it could balance reply efficiency and quality,” he said. Alongside the expanded use of artificial intelligence at 1823, the office said it would pilot agentic AI in the fourth quarter of this year. Agentic AI refers to technology that can act autonomously on users’ behalf to carry out various tasks. Chau said the trial was in line with industry trends, as many commercial firms were also testing AI agents to automate workflows and free workers for higher-level tasks. However, he warned that the technology carried greater risks, particularly involving data privacy and potential errors when AI agents operated with more autonomy. “Since agentic AI is more automated than standard AI, the level of human supervision will decrease,” Chau said, noting that government work involved handling a lot of sensitive data. He called for a mechanism to prevent data breaches and unintended actions by AI agents. Chiu also backed the government’s plan to trial agentic AI, describing it as a logical and timely step amid the technology’s “explosive” growth. He added that rapid technological advances over the past year had already addressed early concerns over data privacy and security, and said he was confident the government could safely use AI agents to transform administrative workflows.

title: Road from China talent factory to pickleball glory paved with tears and cheers for Kong
description: Kong Lingwei wanted to be a tennis star, but somewhere in Wichita she swapped her racquet for a paddle and has never looked back.
content: A natural gift for tennis felt more of a curse than a blessing for Kong Lingwei when, at the age of 10, she was sent away to Guangdong Ersha Sports Training Centre. “It was pretty sad, and I cried a lot,” Kong said. “But I knew I wanted to be a professional tennis player, so I had to hide my emotions and be strong.” Christened the “cradle of champions”, Guangdong Ersha’s alumni, including diving star Quan Hongchan, delivered eight gold, two silver and two bronze from the 2024 Olympics. Since opening 72 years ago, the talent factory has produced more than 120 world champions. In Kong, it nurtured the first individual from mainland China to earn a full-time living from pickleball. The singles world No 16, and ranked third in Asia, Kong is poised for an assault on three titles from the US$1.1 million Hang Seng Bank Hong Kong Slam in October. “Really good at running and other sports, and very athletic”, as a child in Hunan province, Kong zeroed in on tennis after a coach alerted her parents to their daughter’s potential following a school event. “They told me to give it a shot and it went from there,” Kong said. Growing up, she admired Maria Sharapova, the Russian who was separated from her mother for two years after moving to the USA at 7 to aid her own tennis ambitions. “I first liked her because she was gorgeous, but later I learned she’s much more than that,” Kong said. “She’s focused and worked so hard, and [her example] helped shape who I am today.” Just as five-time grand slam champion Sharapova emerged from her difficult sporting baptism to flourish, Kong survived a “very tough period of time” after going it alone so young to “learn how to be independent and strong”. The classroom took a back seat to the tennis court and in 2015, aged 17, she began competing on the ITF Asia Tour. Faring moderately four years later, as she juggled tennis and a sport training degree from the South China University of Technology, and keen to add English to her proficiency in Mandarin, Cantonese and Korean, Kong took herself to Wichita State University in Kansas. “I was depressed for my first three months,” she said. “I’d been in a major city in Guangzhou and now I was in the middle of nowhere. I was thinking, ‘what have I put myself into? Where is this place?’ I wanted to transfer, but I began to bond with my teammates and coach [with the university tennis team, the Shockers], and I chose to stay.” Living in the USA, where between 2020 and 2025 pickleball participation reportedly grew 479 per cent to 24.3 million players, Kong steadily “fell in love” with the sport. Kong completed her sport management master’s ahead of time in 2023, allowing her to break ground as the first mainland Chinese pickleball professional. In her final tennis tournament that year, an ITF event in Wichita, she earned just US$50 after losing in the first qualifying round. As an example of her increased earning power with a paddle, when she won both the women’s and mixed doubles titles at the recent PPA Asia 500 Ho Chi Minh City Open, Kong pocketed US$5,500 for one week’s work. A brand ambassador for sports equipment companies Kumpoo and Ianoni, she spent time last year playing in the USA’s Major League Pickleball for New York Hustlers, the franchise whose owners include basketball superstar LeBron James. “Witnessing how fast the sport was growing in the States, I knew it would be possible to play professionally, and I think it will soon be as big in Asia as in the US,” Kong said. Troubled over the fact she is “pushing 30”, the 28-year-old is preparing to “back down from singles” next year to manage the multitude of injuries she is carrying. “I know a lot of people, especially in the States, who think pickleball is for old people and is not professional, but when you reach this level you appreciate it requires the same athleticism as tennis and other sports,” she said. In addition to practice and playing, Kong has three 90-minute gym sessions every week. She is “very strict with my diet, eating clean and avoiding sugar”, other than the occasional bubble treat. Where Sharapova was her tennis idol, Kong now admires the “passion and loudness” on court of American pickleball world No 2 Anna Bright. “I’m like that, too,” she said. “I play better when I’m pi**** … when I’m loud. I don’t try to copy her, but watching her compete helps me find who I really am on court.” Kong claimed her Ho Chi Minh City mixed doubles crown playing for the first time alongside Jack Wong Hong-kit, the poster boy of Hong Kong pickleball who has climbed to world No 16 and is Asia’s top-ranked man. “He’s the most-loved player in Asia, so I thought ‘I’d better not screw this up’,” Kong said. The pair will link up again at Kai Tak Arena in two months. “She’s very positive on court and gives me lots of energy,” Wong said. “Her enthusiasm really helped us through the long matches. “Pickleball has blown up in China but at the moment it’s more of a leisure activity. I’d love to see them have more professional players.” Kong has been followed into the full-time ranks by Long Yufei, the 27-year-old world No 22, but the next best mainland China woman is amateur Anni Xie at 110 in the global standings. In last week’s Shenzhen Open, Kong partnered Selina Turulja of Australia to women’s doubles silver. “A few years ago, my parents knew about pickleball only because I played, they had no desire to pick up a paddle,” she said. “Now, when I go back, all my family are playing. In Shenzhen, the fans were crazy, shouting my name and cheering me on.
