I could never have imagined that happening.” Now based in California, Kong thinks she will keep going for at least three more years, leaving her little time for her favourite downtime pursuits of “hiking, going to the ocean, and cooking Chinese food with friends and family”. “I want to play for as long as my body allows, but when I finish I will definitely do something pickleball-related,” she said. “I started out just wanting to have fun and seeing what I could achieve, but watching more of the younger generation begin in the sport, I’m very honoured to be a pioneer for pickleball.”

title: Hong Kong home prices end 13-month upswing as tax fears weigh on demand
description: Housing rally stalls in July as tax risks curb demand, analysts say, raising doubts over market’s near-term outlook.
content: Hong Kong’s lived-in home prices fell 0.46 per cent in July, halting a 13-month upswing, according to the latest official data. The index tracking second-hand homes slipped to 321.5 in July from 323 in June, Rating and Valuation Department (RVD) data showed on Thursday. It was the first decline in 16 months, following a drop in April last year. Prices were flat that May, then climbed steadily for 13 months starting in June. “As residential property prices have increased by 7.3 per cent year to date, further upside is expected to be limited in the short term,” said Eddie Kwok, executive director for valuation and advisory services at CBRE Hong Kong. “The residential market is likely to enter a consolidation phase in the coming months.” Since the trough in March last year, when prices had lost more than 28 per cent from their September 2021 peak, the index had recovered 13.37 per cent by June, data showed. “Corrections in the Hong Kong stock market may affect investor sentiment, while controls on outbound investment from mainland China could reduce capital flows into Hong Kong’s property market,” Kwok said. “Taken together, these factors are expected to dampen investment demand.” The decline comes as Beijing’s crackdown on offshore wealth stirs concerns about the potential impact of a 20 per cent personal income tax on certain returns earned by mainland residents from offshore assets, including Hong Kong insurance policies. The biggest worry is the uncertainty about the degree of retroactivity of global taxation for individuals Karl Chan, JPMorgan Chase If it applied to property income, mainland demand for Hong Kong homes and commercial real estate assets could slow, analysts said. Mainland buyers accounted for 29 per cent of home sales volumes and 37 per cent of value in Hong Kong, based on the frequency of pinyin surnames, according to JPMorgan Chase. While most of these buyers were living in Hong Kong and had “genuine demand”, the biggest worry was the “uncertainty about the degree of retroactivity of global taxation for individuals,” which had implications beyond property-related taxes, said Karl Chan, head of Hong Kong property research at the US investment bank, in a report this week. “Theoretically it includes all other types of income [for example, salaries] earned outside mainland China.” Chan added that while there was “no explicit mention of retroactivity in the event of non-compliance”, the latest guidance required unpaid taxes on trust assets since January 2023 and trust income before 2026 to be settled within 90 days to avoid penalties. “Thus, a three-year period seems to be the potential time frame,” Chan said, adding the exact implementation rules remained unclear. A worst-case scenario of retroactivity covering 20 years could hit savings and cash flows of mainland Chinese individuals in Hong Kong, he said. “Another concern is the lack of clarification or clear rules about mainland Chinese buying properties in Hong Kong. If there ends up to be some clarification, it could be a clearing event for investors,” Chan said. If not, the overhang could persist, he added. Joseph Tsang, chairman of JLL Hong Kong, said mainland buyers have recently been “one of the key sources of demand”. Following Beijing’s announcement it would tighten tax enforcement on offshore assets, “some buyers have adopted a wait-and-see approach towards the property market while awaiting details of the measures,” he added. “This led to a decline in residential sales in June and July.” Tsang said he expected the measures to continue weighing on home prices and transaction volumes in the short run. However, even if taxes were eventually imposed on purchases of overseas properties, this would primarily increase acquisition costs for mainland buyers. “The market is expected to gradually absorb the impact of such policies, and their long-term effect on Hong Kong’s residential market is limited,” he said. Tsang forecast mass-residential prices would rise 5 to 10 per cent this year, with most of the gains already realised in the first half. In the leasing market, rents were set to continue climbing, supported by demand from non-local students and returning expatriates. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s home rents set another high in July, rising by 0.77 per cent from June, according to RVD data.

title: Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Cats musical returns to Hong Kong, with a Cantonese twist
description: With a flash of whiskers and the timeless anthem of ‘Memory’ in the air, the Jellicle cats take over Hong Kong for a ‘purr-fect’ comeback.
content: Once a year, the Jellicle cats gather for their annual ball, and this year, Hong Kong is the stage. Andrew Lloyd Webber’s record-breaking musical Cats is touring the world once more, making a stop in the city for the first time since 2018. With a dramatic set, dynamic choreography and fur-ocious costumes, alongside a local surprise to ground the production, this promises to be a captivating spectacle. Cats’ latest residence in Hong Kong is a testament to the show’s enduring appeal. More than four decades after its 1981 West End debut, in London, the musical has been staged in 54 countries and reached over 77 million fans worldwide. While Hong Kong has hosted international tours of Cats since 1994, the current cast brings fresh energy to the Xiqu Centre’s Grand Theatre. More show dates were added following an overwhelming audience response, extending the limited run to September 13. At the heart of this musical legacy is a simple yet mystical story. Cats chronicles a tribe of felines, the Jellicles, gathering for the annual Jellicle Ball, where Old Deuteronomy, the group’s leader, decides which of them will ascend to the Heaviside Layer and be reborn into a new Jellicle life. Each cat takes the stage to tell their tale and prove their worth. Based on T.S. Eliot’s Old Possum’s Book of Practical Cats, an anthology of whimsical poems published in 1939, Webber’s original score and Gillian Lynne’s energetic choreography form the backbone of the experience. Chrissie Cartwright, associate director and choreographer, and resident director Matt Krzan protect the creative vision, staging and movement language of Cats in its international productions. In the 2026 rendition, Cindy-Ann Abrahams, the “Best Actress in a Musical” winner at the 61st Cape Town Theatre Awards, in July, keeps the “Memory” alive as Grizabella the Glamour Cat, leading a seasoned performing company that also stars Dylan Janse van Rensburg as the rebellious Rum Tum Tugger and King B as the wise Old Deuteronomy. A highlight is when the cast performs a portion of “The Moments of Happiness” in Cantonese, tailor-made for the Hong Kong audience, for a local touch that ensures the show feels personal to the crowd, even after 45 years. It’s no wonder Krzan feels paw-sitive about the show’s reception: “We absolutely love being in Hong Kong. Hong Kong has welcomed our Jellicle cats with open arms and we’re completely smitten with the city. You might even say it’s the cat’s whiskers.” Whether it’s your first time seeing Cats or your fifth, prepare to leave humming “Memory”, dancing down the street and wondering how you might become a Jellicle cat yourself. Cats. Until September 13. Grand Theatre, Xiqu Centre, 88 Austin Road West, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tickets from HK$388

title: US base dispute hangs over Japan’s Okinawa governor election
description: The LDP is mounting an all-out campaign to unseat the incumbent, wagering cash promises can quiet anti-base opposition.
content: Okinawa’s governor election next month is set to be a major test of whether Japan’s ruling party can win over voters from a prefecture that has long opposed its security agenda and the heavy US military presence on its islands. A victory by Genta Koja, the Liberal Democratic Party-backed candidate, would likely help smooth ties between Okinawa and Tokyo and weaken resistance against the planned relocation of the US Marine Corps’ Futenma base within the prefecture, according to analysts. Such an outcome would boost efforts by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s LDP to convince Okinawans that closer cooperation with Tokyo can deliver stronger economic support. The LDP is preparing to go all out to support Koja in the election scheduled on September 13, according to Japanese media reports. The ruling party hopes the 42-year-old will replace incumbent governor Denny Tamaki, an independent politician backed by the All Okinawa coalition, which includes the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan and the Social Democratic Party. Koja, a former vice-mayor of Naha, the capital of Okinawa, is also backed by other parties including Komeito and the Democratic Party for the People. “We’ll help Koja realise his election pledges with all our strength,” said Yasutoshi Nishimura, chairman of the LDP’s election strategy committee, at a rally for Koja’s candidacy in Urasoe, a city in Okinawa, on August 20. Announcing his policy agenda on August 14 in Naha, Koja pledged to double prefectural income and achieve an average economic growth rate of 7 to 8 per cent over his four-year term. However, he did not mention the controversial project to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma base to the Henoko district in Nago city. The relocation has dragged on for years due to fierce opposition from residents, who demand that the base leave Okinawa rather than move to another part of the prefecture. They say that Okinawa bears an unfair burden of hosting the most American military facilities in Japan. Japan is seeking the relocation to reduce safety and noise hazards in a densely populated urban area, while keeping the US military presence in Okinawa. Raymond Yamamoto, an associate professor at Aarhus University, said the election centred around Okinawa’s relationship with the central government. Tamaki represents the continuation of the All Okinawa coalition, which has resisted the relocation and challenged Tokyo’s security agenda. “Koja, by contrast, is backed by the LDP and seeks to restore a more cooperative relationship with the central government,” Yamamoto said. “His candidacy can be seen as an alternative to Tamaki’s confrontational approach towards Tokyo.” Yamamoto noted that the LDP had struggled to win the Okinawan governorship for over a decade. The last time a candidate backed by the LDP won an election in the prefecture was in 2010, when Hirokazu Nakaima, a businessman and former public servant, won re-election. The US military presence in Okinawa has become increasingly important for Japan as it seeks to boost its defence of its southwestern islands amid rising regional tensions, according to Yamamoto. “A victory would send a strong national signal that the LDP has returned to political dominance under Takaichi’s leadership,” Yamamoto said. Ra Mason, an associate professor of international relations and Japanese foreign policy at the University of East Anglia, said given the LDP’s tactics to “win at all costs” in local elections, Koja could potentially unseat Tamaki. With half of the facility in Henoko having been built, the “damage” was already done, said Mason, author of Okinawa: Great Power Competition and the Keystone of the Pacific, with the issue having been “relegated to a symbolic struggle”. “An LDP-affiliated prefectural governor will likely serve to enable further fortification and militarisation of the Okinawan islands and the Ryukyu Island chain,” Mason said. Okinawa is the largest island of the Ryukyu Islands, a chain stretching southwest from Kyushu to Taiwan. One of the biggest challenges Koja faces is whether he can persuade Okinawans that his links to the LDP will lead to higher investment in the prefecture that benefits ordinary citizens living there, instead of just large companies, according to Mason. “[These entities] have historically sucked profits back to stakeholders on the Japanese mainland.” Consistently ranking last among Japan’s 47 prefectures for annual average income, Okinawa has almost double the mainland’s unemployment rate and the highest rate of non-regular employment. Benjamin Ascione, a lecturer at Waseda University’s Graduate School of Asia-Pacific Studies, said these indicators would favour Koja, who had argued that closer cooperation with Tokyo could deliver greater economic benefits. Ascione said the LDP was in a strong position in the election as it had devoted significant time and resources to win over voters, adding that Koja had a good chance of winning given that legal opposition to the Henoko relocation plan appeared to have run its course, with Okinawa losing almost all its lawsuits against Tokyo over the move. “This significantly alters the significance of a vote for Tamaki as he no longer has an effective legal mechanism to prevent the central government from proceeding with the Henoko plan,” he said. The fragmentation of the All Okinawa coalition opposing the relocation and the shift in attention towards cost-of-living issues would also put Koja in good stead, Ascione said. “Even if Tamaki wins, he would have a visibly weaker and more divided coalition,” he added. Calling it premature to call Koja the clear favourite, Ascione said: “The race remains competitive, with neither candidate having established a decisive lead.” Okinawa hosts about 25,000 American service members across 31 US military facilities, making it a key hub for Washington’s power projection in the Pacific. Japan and the US have been holding talks on cost-sharing to maintain the American military presence in the country. Having Okinawans on board over the US military issue would help soothe tensions between the prefecture and Tokyo, according to Ascione. “However, from an alliance-management perspective, the effect would be primarily symbolic as it would not fundamentally alter Washington’s broader demands on Japanese defence spending and burden-sharing,” he said.

title: How to recognise when self-optimisation has gone too far
description: Quest for perfection can lead to stress and depression, and social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram create unrealistic expectations.
content:
Self-optimisation is everywhere in modern life. And why not? Who doesn’t want to become better? Live more healthily? Work more productively?
But many self-optimisers take their work on themselves to extremes and end up the worse for it. Instead of just going for a jog, they draw up the perfect training plan for a half-marathon, with optimal running shoes, the right amount of carbs per workout and a sophisticated recovery programme.
They strive to improve their score on the sleep quality index, and simply eating a balanced diet isn’t sufficient. Everything has to be high in protein, macronutrient intake is tracked, and micronutrients are added via dietary supplements.
Indeed, the quest to become the best version of yourself can devolve into constant performance pressure. This can lead to stress, fatigue, and feeling that you still haven’t done enough.
“Essentially, a propensity for perfectionism is always problematic,” said Dr Nathalie Claus, a psychotherapist in the University of Bremen’s Department of Psychology in Germany.
It’s especially unhealthy, she said, if you set unrealistic goals, such as, “I mustn’t make any mistakes.” It’s also harmful to be inflexible in your goals and standards, or to see yourself as a failure if you don’t live up to them.
“Self-optimisation becomes a problem if your own actions make you suffer,” said Sarah Pritz, a cultural sociologist and teaching assistant in the Department of General Sociology and Sociological Theory at the Technical University (TU) of Berlin in Germany.
Instead of enhancing their well-being, rigid self-optimisers are constantly under stress, emotionally and physically exhausted or perpetually dissatisfied. This can result in depression and sleep disorders.
The boundary between healthy continuous self-improvement and obsessive self-optimisation is often fuzzy, according to Claus. The former involves self-care; you’d like to change something about yourself for the better.
“It’s no problem so long as you remain flexible,” she said. “In other words, if you allow yourself on some days not to self-optimise and be perfect.” A possible warning sign that you’re overdoing it is neglecting certain needs, such as social contact, to achieve a particular goal.
“Mostly adolescents and young adults are affected by self-optimisation,” Pritz noted. They’re very active on social media, where they constantly compare themselves with each other.
On platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat, ideals quickly become the norm more than the exception: slim, toned, wrinkle-free men and women with no visible blemishes and who seem to have their lives under control. This can encourage unhealthy, unrealistic imitation.
Achievement-oriented people are at greater risk of taking self-optimisation to extremes, Pritz said, as they tend to assess their self-worth by measurable results. An example is university students, who continually endeavour to improve their academic performance in response to competitive pressure and societal expectations.
One reason it’s so hard to quell the urge to keep improving yourself, Claus said, is because it’s mainly the product of societal pressure “to perform and be productive, otherwise you’re a burden to society”. Many people strive for perfection to bolster their self-esteem, and fear of failure is a driver too.
Difficult though it may be, it’s possible to hop off the self-optimisation treadmill. Pritz recommended questioning societal norms. Ask yourself: are the ideals you’ve adopted truly worth striving for?
Claus said it may be worthwhile to prioritise self-acceptance over giving in to performance pressure. She added that you should also recognise what’s likeable about yourself beyond achievement.
Don’t demand perfection from yourself in all things, remarked Pritz. “Good can be enough – it doesn’t always have to be superlative.”
Another tip: Delete any fitness or productivity apps installed on your smartphone that measure performance and suggest improvements. Instead, accept your capabilities and carefully listen to your body and its needs.
“It’s also important to talk about the adverse effects of excessive performance pressure and obsessive self-optimisation with others, such as family members and friends,” Pritz added. This can help you treat yourself better.

title: Editorial | HKEX’s role crucial as Hong Kong helps build future of global finance
description: The city’s stock exchange is set to attract hi-tech mainland manufacturers looking to raise funds even as it forges partnerships overseas.
content: The latest record-high profit results from the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) are more than just a fiscal milestone, they signal a market resurgence. Technological and financial trends on the mainland are aligning with those of the city. Witness the spectacular initial public offering (IPO) of Unitree Robotics on the tech-focused Star market of the Shanghai Stock Exchange. The humanoid robotics pioneer’s shares soared 460 per cent on their first day of trading. Market insiders now speculate that a secondary listing in Hong Kong is only a matter of time. The city is positioning itself as a key gateway for the next generation of hi-tech firms from the mainland. China currently commands 97 per cent of global humanoid robot shipments, according to Morgan Stanley, which has projected a significant increase in annual production. Deliveries are expected to grow from 12,000 units in 2025 to 50,000 this year, reaching 446,000 units by 2030. The nation’s undeniable lead in humanoid robotics, coupled with rapid advances in semiconductor manufacturing and artificial intelligence, is at the heart of this shift. As these mainland manufacturers eye public listings, Hong Kong stands as the natural beneficiary, poised to become the premier venue for such capital-raising efforts. This is a profound opportunity for our IPO business, but one that requires strategic navigation. To fully capitalise on this momentum, HKEX must execute with precision. As HKEX’s CEO Bonnie Chan Yiting has indicated, the introduction of new investment products is a critical next step. These could be modelled after existing “Connect” cross-border investment programmes such as those for stocks, bonds and ETFs. However, success will hinge on clear timelines and seamless collaboration with mainland regulators and other financial authorities. The precedent set by the successful Stock Connect and Bond Connect schemes provides a blueprint for expanding these channels, potentially broadening the scope to include more sophisticated IPO-focused products. Furthermore, the recent regulatory shift allowing mainland insurers to invest in Hong Kong ETFs represents a watershed moment. This month, the National Financial Regulatory Administration expressed support for mainland insurers investing in Hong Kong through ETFs via schemes such as Stock Connect. Such initiatives are likely to boost southbound market inflows in coming months, as Hong Kong market inflows reached a one-month high of HK$14 billion on August 18. HKEX data already shows a 22 per cent increase in ETF turnover this year, with average daily turnover hitting HK$40.6 billion through July. The infusion of massive insurance capital from the mainland into our financial markets is, quite simply, big news. It will reinforce the depth and liquidity of our market and underscore the vital importance of the cross-border financial links we have cultivated. In all this, HKEX is key. Its latest record second quarter net profit increased 21 per cent to HK$5.38 billion while first-half net profit rose 24 per cent to HK$10.57 billion. Crucially, IPO growth and increased stock turnover drove financial performance. Yet, as we embrace this mainland-driven growth, we must remain mindful of the bigger picture. While the IPO pipeline is flourishing, Hong Kong’s strength has always been its role as a global connector. We should look to partnerships beyond our borders – such as the latest example established by the mutual cooperation agreement between the Hong Kong and Malaysian stock markets – to ensure a balanced ecosystem. Bursa Malaysia will be the 21st stock exchange recognised by HKEX, clearing the way for Malaysia-listed companies to pursue secondary listings here. The Malaysian bourse will be the fourth recognised in Asia, after those of Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand. Encouraging Asian and other regional companies to pursue secondary listings here is not only a boon for our local exchange but a testament to Hong Kong’s enduring status as an international financial hub. The path forward is clear. By leveraging our deep expertise in cross-border connectivity and fostering innovation both in mainland technology and international partnerships, Hong Kong is not just observing the future of global finance – we are actively building it.

title: Profile | How Josie Ho rejected her billionaire heiress destiny for punk rock and indie filmmaking
description: Macau casino magnate Stanley Ho’s eighth child has built her own legacy as a musician, award-winning actress and movie producer.
content: This is the 84th instalment in a biweekly series profiling major Hong Kong pop culture figures of recent decades. Josie Ho Chiu-yee has spent her career dismantling assumptions and forging her own identity through unbridled creativity. When it came to pursuing a music career, the daughter of the late Macau casino magnate Stanley Ho Hung-sun rejected the easy path of Cantopop ballads and blockbuster fluff, instead favouring 1980s-inspired punk rock and genre movies. Today, at age 51, Josie Ho is perhaps best known for championing independent cinema – 20 years ago, she founded the production company 852 Films to back edgy projects spanning from Hong Kong to Hollywood. “I needed to make sure I knew how much I could earn by myself, with my own hands. That’s why I kept working so hard,” Ho told the South China Morning Post’s PostMag in 2014. “It’s very important because one day those things might be gone and you might have to come out and make a living yourself.” Escaping the gilded cage Ho was born in 1974 into a massive business empire centred on gaming, real estate, shipping and hospitality in Macau and Hong Kong. She is one of 17 children of Stanley Ho, who was one of Asia’s richest men with a personal fortune estimated at HK$50 billion upon his retirement in 2018. Her mother was Lucina Laam King-ying. A rebellious youngster, Josie often sneaked out of school to watch films at the cinema with friends and reportedly began clubbing at age 12. Unsurprisingly, she was drawn to the performing arts rather than the family business. “Even at eight years old I dreamed about being a singer,” she told PostMag. “I was hanging around with my sister [Pansy Ho Chiu-king] a lot and she happened to have a lot of popular singers as friends, like Anita Mui [Yim-fong] and Danny Chan [Pak-keung].” Mui, in particular, became Josie Ho’s hero; seeing a modern, independent woman thrive in the industry inspired her to rebel against the traditional “ladylike” expectations of her wealthy background. But her father was not pleased when it came out that Ho wanted to join the entertainment industry. The turning point came when her singing at his Macau beauty pageant attracted the attention of Virgin Records. To prevent Ho from being sent back to university in Los Angeles, Pansy orchestrated a dinner to convince their father to support her showbiz ambitions. “Pansy was the only one in the family who didn’t think I was crazy,” Ho said in a 2008 New York Times interview. “She knows that if I don’t do this, I would not fit in anywhere else. It is my way to express myself.” Ho signed her first music contract in her father’s office when she was 18. In 1994, she released her debut album, Rebel, with Capital Artists. Knowing her family name would follow her, she chose a self-referential title for her 1996 follow-up, Ho Ka Suk Lui (“The lady of the Ho family”). A shift to the alternative Ho’s tenure with Capital Artists was short-lived; in 1997, she was reportedly dropped for singing off-key during a major performance. Amid a subsequent music hiatus filled with clubbing, she befriended influential hip-hop group LMF and met hip-hop artist Conroy Chan Chi-chung, whom she would later marry. These connections influenced her musical trajectory. When she returned in 2003 with her album Sickid, she showed her reverence for rock music by leaning into a darker, noisier sound. In the late 2000s, she formed the alternative rock band Josie and The Uni Boys, which injected elements of electronic and emo music into her repertoire. “Now I don’t care about the market,” she told the SCMP in 2008. “I just do what I want to do in music. I think rock means free spirit. Rock music doesn’t necessarily have to be very loud or angry, but it has to be individualistic and personal.” Ho also pursued acting, making her feature film debut in 1994. Her breakout role came in the 1999 action thriller Purple Storm, in which she played a Khmer Rouge militant and performed her own stunts. Her star rose higher four years later when she played a prostitute in the sex comedy Naked Ambition (2003), a role that earned her the best supporting actress prize at the 2004 Hong Kong Film Awards. The 2004 lesbian drama Butterfly, in which she played a married teacher navigating repressed desires, earned her a best actress nod at the 2005 Golden Bauhinia Awards. She then played the daughter of a mobster (Tony Leung Ka-fai) in The Drummer, which in 2008 became the first Hong Kong production to compete at the Sundance Film Festival. Despite proving herself as a serious actor, Ho has admitted to feeling underrated and has expressed frustration that her family’s high profile often overshadowed her artistic efforts. She even trained with Zuni Icosahedron, an experimental theatre company in Hong Kong, to broaden her skills. Taking control behind the lens In 2006, she co-founded the production company 852 Films with Chan and her manager, Andrew Ooi. The goal was to back international indie films and generate the complex roles she felt the mainstream industry was unwilling to offer her. The company’s first production, the 2010 slasher Dream Home, remains one of the most disturbingly gruesome films in contemporary Hong Kong cinema. Ho and Chan were inspired to make it after watching the outrageously gory cult classic Riki-Oh: The Story of Ricky (1991). Directed by Pang Ho-cheung, Dream Home earned Ho a best actress nomination at the 30th Hong Kong Film Awards and the best actress prize at Spain’s Sitges Film Festival for her role as a woman who goes on a killing spree to lower local property values and secure a flat. She later merged her interests in filmmaking and music by producing Finding Bliss: Fire and Ice (2019), a documentary that followed Josie and The Uni Boys on a trip to the rugged landscapes of Iceland. Around the same time Josie was recognised with a lifetime achievement award at the 2022 Hawaii International Film Festival, Chan suffered a near-fatal ruptured aorta. Josie halted her work commitments to serve as his primary carer during a prolonged recovery. An uncompromising path More recently, she has returned to nurture her dual loves for music and cinema. In February 2025, she headlined the Dragon Rock Concert in London, leading Josie and The Uni Boys in a showcase of Hong Kong rock. On the filmmaking front, she has two titles ready to launch: director Mike Figgis’ psychological thriller Mother Tongue, in which she plays an acclaimed actress attempting to reconnect with a daughter she gave away; and The Mage, a Hong Kong crime/horror movie directed by Danny Pang Fat in which she also stars. For decades, she has received occasional advice from her siblings to retire from entertainment. But whether defying expectations surrounding her family’s business empire or resisting the 1990s pop machine, her stance remains uncompromising: retreating is not an option. As she made clear to Edmund Lee, now the SCMP’s film editor, in a 2010 interview, her life’s objective has always been “to be an outstanding performer”. “If I weren’t a performer, there would be no point of me living,” she added. “I’d be living dead, a zombie. I hope that when I’m old, people will only say one thing: ‘I remember a certain scene of a certain movie, in which that Josie Ho touched me very deeply.’ I can then die without regrets.” Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Tiger, Futu post strong overseas gains after Beijing clampdown stalls mainland growth
description: Brokerages shift to Southeast Asia, US and Europe amid Beijing’s stepped-up drive to root out illegal cross-border securities activity.
content: Tiger Brokers and Futu Holdings, two of the region’s largest online brokerages, posted robust second-quarter growth as they expanded overseas to absorb Beijing’s toughest crackdown yet on illegal cross-border stock trading. UP Fintech Holding, parent of Tiger Brokers, reported on Wednesday that revenue rose 31.4 per cent year on year to a record US$182.3 million. Net income attributable to shareholders, however, slipped to US$39.4 million from US$41.4 million a year earlier. Chairman and CEO Wu Tianhua said the “great majority” of the 32,600 new funded accounts in the quarter came from Singapore and Hong Kong, lifting total accounts 10.3 per cent year on year to 1.32 million. Client assets also climbed 16.7 per cent to US$60.7 billion. “To streamline users’ compliance procedures and reduce tax declaration complexities, we rolled out a dedicated tax reporting tool under our Hong Kong, Singapore and New Zealand regulatory licences,” Wu said in an exchange filing, adding that Tiger also rolled out fractional share trading for Singapore-listed stocks and index options trading in Hong Kong. Hong Kong client assets grew almost 30 per cent quarter on quarter after Tiger stepped up offline client-acquisition campaigns, while assets in the US jumped nearly 50 per cent and those in Australia and New Zealand rose more than 30 per cent. Futu, which reported last week, posted revenue of HK$7.2 billion (US$918 million), up 35.6 per cent, and net income attributable to the shareholders of HK$3.64 billion, up 41.6 per cent. Funded accounts expanded 33.6 per cent to 3.84 million, led for a third straight quarter by Malaysia, with Hong Kong and Singapore also among the top contributors. The strong results come two months after mainland Chinese authorities escalated a long-running campaign against unlicensed cross-border brokerages to root out illegal securities activity and curb unauthorised capital outflows. On May 22, the China Securities Regulatory Commission fined Tiger, Futu and Longbridge Securities a combined 2.2 billion yuan (US$327 million) and ordered a two-year wind-down of remaining mainland operations. Mainland accounts have been barred from making new purchases or deposits since June 12. Stripped of their original growth engine, Tiger and Futu have restructured their business models to capture retail investors across Southeast Asia, North America and Europe. In July, Futu obtained a licence from Thailand’s securities regulator to launch its Moomoo platform, extending an overseas footprint that already spans Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia. The brokerage also broadened its global product suite, launching prediction markets in the US in June and securing regulatory approval in Hong Kong for a virtual-asset financing service through its proprietary platform PantherTrade, according to its earnings statement. Disclosures made earlier this year showed that mainland Chinese investors made up about 13 per cent of Futu’s funded accounts as of the first quarter, while Tiger reported mainland assets comprised roughly 10 per cent of its total at the end of last year. Neither brokerage disclosed updated metrics on mainland account exposure in their latest earnings statements.

title: Talks are ‘only way out’ on Iran, Beijing says as Trump hints at Chinese bank bans
description: Latest salvo from US president adds pressure to already fragile US-China ties before expected summit in Washington.
content: Beijing has pushed back suggestions that Washington might sanction Chinese banks over their commercial links with Tehran, casting fresh uncertainty over next month’s summit. The Chinese foreign ministry stressed on Friday that dialogue and negotiation were the “only viable way out” regarding Iran. “China’s position opposing illegal unilateral sanctions is consistent and clear,” ministry spokesman Lin Jian said. The comments followed US President Donald Trump’s hint on Thursday that such sanctions could be on the table for Chinese lenders – something that the US has so far avoided. Asked why the US had not sanctioned Chinese banks for their dealings with Iranian entities, Trump said: “Who said I’m not?” “Well, I don’t have to announce everything, do I?” Earlier this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new sanctions against 60 entities and individuals around the world, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong, and demanded “immediate action” from nations maintaining economic and commercial ties with Iran. “Let me be clear: any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking,” Bessent said on Monday. The administration dubbed the new actions “Economic D-Day”. The measures were part of the administration’s attempt to put further economic pressure on Tehran after military strikes and diplomatic negotiations failed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or bring the six-month conflict to an end. While the latest sanctions targeted a broad network of mainland Chinese and Hong Kong-based procurement, financial and shipping intermediaries, Washington stopped short of blacklisting major Chinese banks and refiners. The Chinese embassy in Washington also said that “China will do everything necessary to firmly safeguard its rights and interests”. “Economic warfare and maximum pressure provide no solution,” embassy spokesman Liu Chang said. The US Treasury Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. With just weeks to go until Chinese President Xi Jinping visits the US, Trump’s remarks add another layer of complexity to already fragile US-China ties. Both sides are seeking to insulate the summit from broader tensions while continuing to ratchet up economic and diplomatic pressure on each other. Washington and Beijing have continued to impose sanctions, tighten export controls, expand blacklists and target companies, creating a growing list of disputes that could complicate efforts to maintain a stable backdrop for the talks. Pressure is building on Capitol Hill, particularly from hawkish members of the House Select Committee on China. Politico reported on Wednesday that multiple committee members spoke out in favour of sanctions, including Darin LaHood, a Republican congressman from Illinois, who argued that any country propping up Iran economically, China included, must face consequences. He called bank sanctions a deterrent signal to Beijing and others. But some lawmakers, especially those from districts hit by China’s past agricultural and rare earth retaliation, remain wary of provoking Beijing further. Haley Stevens, a Democratic congresswoman from Michigan, told Politico that accountability needs strategy behind it, given China’s demonstrated willingness to weaponise its rare earth dominance. Some experts are signalling the same alarm. Dennis Wilder, who served as the National Security Council’s director for China under president George W. Bush, tweeted that sanctioning major banks like Bank of China would amount to a “nuclear economic weapon”. Even without formal Treasury action, big international banks might start pulling back from their Chinese counterparts on their own, wary of drawing US regulatory scrutiny, Han Lin, China country director at The Asia Group, told The New York Times – a shift towards broader caution in dealing with Chinese financial institutions. China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, accounting for more than 80 per cent of the country’s total oil exports in 2025, according to data from analytics firm Kpler. “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions,” Bessent said when asked about the possibility of the US imposing secondary sanctions on Chinese banks over their commercial links with Iranian entities. He added that Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests” to halt their engagement with the Iranian regime, but did not identify the countries he had contacted. But on Thursday, Trump said that “there’s not a lot to speak to” and that he had no interest in engaging with other countries. “We don’t want to speak to them. We’re not looking to meet or anything. The strait is open.” On Tuesday, the Chinese foreign ministry said Beijing’s cooperation with Tehran was conducted “within the framework of international law and should not be disrupted”. Economic wars and maximum pressure were “not the solutions”, ministry spokesman Lin said.

title: Peter Cullen, voice of Optimus Prime and Eeyore, dies at 85
description: In his role as the Autobot leader in the Transformers cartoon, Cullen struck a nerve with his authoritative baritone.
content: Peter Cullen, a prolific voice actor who enlivened scores of television series, specials and films, including Optimus Prime in the syndicated 1984 series Transformers and Eeyore in the Winnie the Pooh cartoon franchise, has died. He was 85. His agent, Kevin Motley, said Cullen died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles. “His family asks that you honour his remarkable legacy by serving your communities and leading others with compassion, integrity, and loyalty and always remember ‘be strong enough to be gentle’,” a family statement said. Cullen’s career spanned from being an announcer at the groundbreaking late-1960s comedy and variety series The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour and joining comedy sketches for Sonny & Cher to voice acting in The Smurfs and multiple G.I. Joe iterations. But he struck a nerve as Optimus Prime. While the original cartoon ran just a few years, it left an indelible mark on pop culture, with a toy line, spin-off cartoon series and comics produced over the next two decades. That culminated in the launch of a multibillion-dollar, live-action film franchise in 2007 by Michael Bay. Before his audition, Cullen knew only that he would be reading for the part of a truck, though giving voice to a vehicle did not seem that crazy. “You’re always auditioning for something in animation that’s a little off of the norm,” Cullen said in 2019. When Cullen read about the heroic Autobot leader that turned into a red cabover semi-trailer, he thought about his older brother, who had served as a US Marine in the Vietnam war. “He was my hero, and he certainly was the mainstay behind the character,” Cullen said. “I just did an impression of Larry, and he’s still alive in my mind today because every time I do Prime, there’s my brother Larry.” Cullen’s authoritative baritone as Optimus Prime also appeared in 2009’s Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen through Dark of the Moon, Age of Extinction, The Last Knight, Bumblebee and Rise of the Beasts in 2023. His thoughtful, almost operatic lines would be quoted for decades by children and adults alike: “I am Optimus Prime, and I send this message to any surviving Autobots taking refuge among the stars: We are here. We are waiting,” he said in the first film. In another, he intoned: “Fate rarely calls upon us at a moment of our choosing.” Other highlights from Cullen’s prolific career include voicing Eeyore across various Winnie-the-Pooh projects, including Disney’s The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh television series that aired from 1988-91, as well as voicing the villainous KARR opposite KITT in the 1980s NBC series Knight Rider, and lending his pipes to King Kong in the Jeff Bridges-led King Kong remake in 1976. “Optimus is my favourite character because it’s been so well received and it’s had such an effect on so many people,” Cullen told The New York Times in 2008. “Because of that, I hold it closer than any other character I’ve done – outside of maybe Eeyore, who’s had a considerable effect on younger children too.” One of Cullen’s strangest jobs had no words at all: He provided the clicking sounds for the main alien creature in Predator, which he said he based on the sounds of a dying horseshoe crab. Cullen received a lifetime achievement award at the Children’s & Family Emmy Awards in 2023 and was nominated for a Daytime Emmy for voicing Optimus Prime in 2011. Cullen would attend conventions around the country to meet with fans from multiple generations, often getting teary. He said parents sometimes got more excited than their children meeting him. “I expect that I will run into a father with his son, and the father will more than likely get choked up,” Cullen said before MegaCon Orlando in 2019. “And then I get choked up, and then the kid is saying ‘What are these two grown men getting choked up about?’ ” Cullen is survived by his four children, Angus, Claire, Pilar and Clay.

title: US urged to use Beijing playbook to secure Chinese tech transfers
description: Experts say Washington should target areas where cutting-edge Chinese technological know-how could be welcomed, then applied to help US.
content: The United States should take a leaf out of Beijing’s industrial playbook and strategically open up specific sectors to Chinese investment while ensuring that technology transfers occur, US industrial policy and supply chain experts said at an event on Thursday. The assessment comes as Washington mulls new broad restrictions on Chinese technology, including a proposed prohibition on the sale of cars with connected-vehicle technology linked to China and a ban on imports of Chinese humanoid robots and power inverters. However, merely shutting out Chinese technology from the US without a clear strategy to boost domestic competitiveness would not guarantee that the US catches up in areas where China now has a clear lead, the experts said at an online panel organised by the Quincy Institute, a Washington think tank that advocates for a less militarised American foreign policy. Instead, Washington should target areas in which cutting-edge Chinese technological know-how could be welcomed, then applied to help the US catch up, possibly through joint ventures and technology licences. “China is overly paranoid about the US, and I think the US is overly paranoid about China,” said Jake Werner, director of the East Asia programme at the Quincy Institute. “But China has figured out a way to incorporate American business and technology in its advanced sectors … What is stopping us from doing basically the same thing is my rhetorical question.” The question of how the US should treat Chinese technology has been the subject of heated debate in Washington in recent years as China has come to dominate cutting-edge areas such as electric vehicles and batteries. While US national security hawks have advocated strict bans to address risks associated with Chinese technology, including surveillance and supply chain vulnerabilities, some moderate voices are calling for the US to welcome some Chinese involvement in the industry to lower costs for US consumers, promote US innovation, and bolster US competitiveness. Susan Helper, former chief economist at the US Department of Commerce during Barack Obama’s second presidency, said on Thursday’s panel that Beijing “brilliantly” opened up the Chinese economy in the past to learn from European and American multinational companies, suggesting the US could do the same. Still, she warned that an “extreme openness” to Chinese technology would also backfire without adequate protections for US workers and arrangements that maximise technology and process-knowledge spillovers while containing security risks. Such arrangements could include local supplier requirements and regulatory walls that force Chinese firms to build local capacity in the US in sensitive areas such as data storage, preventing them from relying only on suppliers at home, said Jonas Nahm, an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies. “All of those things can be done, and what’s interesting to me is when you go to China, and you see how they did it, a lot of it is exactly that,” he said. A key uncertainty, however, is whether Beijing would allow it to happen, even if Washington moves towards such a strategy. In recent years, Chinese authorities have increasingly erected barriers on outflows of Chinese technology in strategic sectors, such as the recent intervention in Meta Platforms’ acquisition of Chinese-founded AI start-up Manus. New regulations coming into effect next month also codify exit bans on Chinese citizens suspected of violating export controls and technology transfer rules. “If the relationship continues to be so acrimonious as it has been, I think that window for learning might be sort of closing at some point,” said Nahm. “And it’s also really hard in Washington today to have a conversation about where [national security risks] apply, where it does not apply and, where it does apply, what do we do about it?”

title: Exclusive | Chinese executives may join Xi’s US trip, as trade truce extension ‘almost certain’
description: Inclusion of business leaders in delegation is under discussion and one-year deal agreed in Busan is likely to be extended, sources say.
content: Chinese and US officials are discussing whether business leaders will join President Xi Jinping’s delegation to the United States next month, as the two sides prepare to extend a one-year trade agreement reached in Busan last October, according to people familiar with the talks. The negotiations come as Xi is expected to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington on September 24. Trump travelled to Beijing in May with a large group of top American CEOs, including the heads of Tesla, Apple, Nvidia and Boeing. In a meeting with US ambassador to China David Perdue in Beijing on Wednesday, Foreign Minister Wang Yi called for both sides to implement the leaders’ consensus, manage differences and remove obstacles to high-level exchanges, so ties could become “stable, healthy and sustainable”. Perdue said Trump and Xi had provided “important strategic guidance” and described Trump’s May visit to China as “very successful”. Washington was ready to strengthen communication, advance cooperation and prepare for “important high-level interactions in the next phase”, he said, calling for a constructive and stable relationship based on “respect and reciprocity”. Trump’s envoy later wrote on social media that the meeting was part of preparations for Xi’s visit. Against that backdrop, four people with knowledge of the discussions said the inclusion of Chinese business leaders was being negotiated, with the idea framed around reciprocity after the US executives joined Trump in May. Accounts differed as to which side was driving the request, and a final decision had yet to be reached. Two sources said Beijing was eager to bring business leaders, noting that many Chinese companies remained interested in investing in the US. One of the sources said the discussion pointed to China’s interest in accelerating talks on the stalled Board of Investment, one of the key announcements from the May summit. Another source said Chinese companies covered by the Board of Trade agreement could be part of the delegation, as the pact directly related to their business interests. The Board of Trade was another important outcome from the summit in Beijing, and efforts to get it up and running are in the final stages, focusing on identifying non-sensitive sectors and products eligible for tariff-reduced trade capped at US$30 billion for each side. Another person close to the talks said a delegation could potentially help with a shift from confrontation towards managed economic competition and allow Chinese and US business leaders the space to build ties alongside the political summit. A separate source, however, said the delegation was requested by Washington. The business delegation and trade talks are unfolding in parallel, with both sides looking for concrete outcomes from the September summit as they manage broader trade and investment ties. There is a broad understanding that the trade truce agreed in Busan, South Korea in October 2025 will be extended, according to sources. The two sides at the time agreed to reduce some US tariffs on Chinese goods, suspend additional US restrictions on Chinese-affiliated companies, pause certain Chinese rare earth export controls for a year, and secure Chinese commitments on American soybeans and fentanyl precursors. Sources said an extension of the Busan trade deal was likely or “almost certain” as both sides wanted it despite recent retaliatory measures and actions by the US Federal Communications Commission, but they disagreed over its duration. Beijing preferred an extension that ran through the end of Trump’s presidency while Washington was seeking another one-year deal, one source said. The source added that Beijing, in negotiating a longer extension of the trade pact, sought stability and wanted to “lock in” what it viewed as a favourable agreement. Another person familiar with the talks said the Trump administration was “playing coy” over the duration of the extension to create an impression of leverage. Given the current state of the discussion, the agreement is set to be extended for one year, according to another source. One source said US concerns over rare earth supply flows could be addressed through dialogue and that the Busan deal was not expected to be given prominence during the Xi-Trump talks. Low-level tit-for-tat measures involving export controls and targeted actions against companies are likely to continue; however, concerns about miscalculation remain. The Federal Communications Commission last month banned the import and sale of new foreign-made robotic devices and power inverters, sectors in which China is a global leader. Washington also added over 40 Chinese companies to its Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act entity list the same month. Beijing retaliated by tightening export controls on drones and sanctioning seven American firms. Another person said the agreement could be extended quietly or folded into a broader economic understanding, allowing both sides to preserve the existing trade framework without making it the centrepiece of the Xi-Trump meeting. But Washington, according to another source familiar with the discussions, was not seeking any major breakthrough when the two leaders meet next month. Sources also indicated that the impending US tariffs on excess industrial capacity against 16 economies, including China, were unlikely to adversely affect Xi’s visit. Washington has conveyed to Beijing that the additional tariffs imposed under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act are simply replacing the import levies that the US Supreme Court struck down in February. Last month, the Trump administration imposed tariffs of 10 to 12.5 per cent on goods from 60 economies under its forced labour probe, with China facing the 12.5 per cent rate. Beijing opposed the move but did not retaliate. Both sides are actively attempting to insulate the September meeting from the near-regular actions spanning multiple sectors, seeking to prevent existing and new disputes from derailing broader efforts to stabilise bilateral ties ahead of the summit.

title: Opinion | Why Southeast Asia isn’t buying the US’ offer of ‘flexible realism’
description: Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby talked up US partnerships with Asean nations during his trip to the region, but Washington’s actions contradict its ‘Asia first’ rhetoric.
content: In arguably his most important foreign trip, Elbridge Colby, US undersecretary for defence policy, visited key Southeast Asian capitals this month. In a speech in Manila, the Pentagon policy chief extolled America’s “flexible realism”, which he said serves “the practical, concrete interests of regular Americans” and echoes Southeast Asian nations’ commitment to “pragmatism, an openness to dialogue, respect for counterparts, proud nationalism, and a focus on economic prosperity”. Amid the United States’ growing unpopularity, and deepening doubts over its wherewithal due to the festering conflict in the Middle East, Colby sought to reassure his hosts by emphasising how the Trump administration views Asia as being of “paramount importance” strategically. He stressed the US commitment to preserving a “favourable balance of power” to ensure the region remains “free of hegemony”. He dismissed criticisms of American foreign policy as “the cheap talk of the cognoscenti”. Colby described his host, the Philippines, as a “model ally” and highlighted the deployment of American coastguard forces amid rising tensions in the South China Sea. He carried a similar message of reassurance and strategic sympathy to Jakarta, where he hailed a “partnership founded on mutual respect and deeper cooperation” in a meeting with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, while pushing for expanded defence relations in Thailand and Cambodia. Through burden-sharing, mutual capacity-building and diplomatic reciprocity, Colby essentially argued, the United States was in a historic position to reassert its leadership and strategic primacy in the region. By all indications, however, Southeast Asia remained sceptical of American strategic commitment. Battered by US tariffs and the energy shock of the ill-conceived Iran war, there is widespread discontent with Washington’s foreign policy. Moreover, key regional states have doubled down on their strategic cooperation with China. The US has yet to provide its closest Southeast Asian ally, the Philippines, with sufficient military and economic assistance despite mounting challenges. Colby is no ordinary apparatchik. A scion of the American strategic elite, the Ivy League-educated strategist has enjoyed support across key constituencies within the Republican Party. This includes the more nationalist-populist wing represented by Vice-President J.D. Vance, who personally pitched for Colby’s Senate confirmation last year. Blessed with keen political instincts, Colby has also imbibed the “Make America Great Again” ethos. During his Manila speech, for instance, he wasted no time in lambasting previous administrations for a supposedly “hollow, merely symbolic engagement” with Asian allies and “rhetorical pressurisation without adequate material strength and resolve”. Aside from serving as an architect of the first Trump administration’s defence strategy, which embraced a new era of great power competition, he also shaped America’s strategic posture with his “strategy of denial” thesis. Central to his vision is the idea that Asia is the primary theatre of competition in the 21st century, with China as the pre-eminent and pacing threat to American hegemony. Allies, therefore, should be active partners rather than vulnerable dependencies. His vision of flexible realism, however, seems unrealistic. To begin with, the Trump administration’s actions seem to contradict the “Asia first” rhetoric: military adventurism in Latin America, a devastating war in Iran, and a quagmire in Ukraine. And Colby’s trip concluded just as the Pentagon was forced to redeploy the US Navy’s only US aircraft carrier in the region, the USS George Washington, to replace the overstretched USS Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East. In fairness, the Pentagon has sought to expand its military footprint in Asia in the past year by deploying troops, aircraft and missile systems to war games such as the Balikatan exercises. For the first time, it deployed its most cutting-edge missile system, the Dark Eagle long-range hypersonic weapon, with China in its range. Yet, Beijing has become more assertive across the East and South China seas in recent months. Beijing seems to have gained strategic momentum in Southeast Asia. The Indonesian navy conducted a major drill with Beijing near Taiwan, while the Malaysian leadership is now openly supporting Beijing’s position on Taiwan. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has also cast the deepening Philippine-US military cooperation in the South China Sea as a threat to his country’s interests. “As a neighbouring country closely affected by claims over Sabah, we are somewhat concerned with the tension,” he said last week. “Our basic defence capabilities must be strengthened.” Unquestionably, the Philippines represents the rare bright spot for American defence strategy. President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr has approved an expanded US military presence on Philippine soil, including the establishment of rotational presence in and deployment of weapons systems to strategic facilities facing both Taiwan and the South China Sea. Still, the Philippines has yet to receive high-grade weapons systems nor has it secured desperately needed US-made fighter jets after years of stalled negotiations. Filipinos welcomed Colby’s announcement of the deployment of four US coastguard cutters for joint patrols in Philippine waters. But China’s increased deployments to and harassment of Philippine naval forces in the South China Sea have exposed the limits of the Philippine-US alliance. Despite being America’s “model ally”, Manila has been slapped with two rounds of double-digit tariffs in the past year. Years of negotiations for a US-Philippines free trade agreement have yet to show any breakthrough. Meanwhile, civil society groups and experts vociferously oppose Washington’s only major new economic initiative, Pax Silica, due to concerns over energy-intensive data centres, extractive investments and a lack of technology transfer. With the Marcos administration entering its twilight years in office, there are also concerns over the future direction of Philippine-US cooperation. Overall, Colby’s “realism” is struggling against the rough texture of geopolitical reality in Asia.

title: Trump’s new US mail voting rules take effect as states warn of midterm disruption
description: Trump-ordered requirements could let the Postal Service reject non-compliant ballot mailings; opponents seek emergency court intervention.
content: New US restrictions on mailed ballots took effect on Thursday, leaving state and local election officials racing to comply – or persuade a federal judge to intervene – weeks before millions of ballots are due to be sent to voters ahead of November’s midterm elections. The US Postal Service rules require election authorities to assign unique bar codes to outgoing and return ballot envelopes, submit voters’ names, addresses and corresponding bar code information through a new federal portal, and obtain a review of their envelope designs. The agency can refuse to accept an outgoing batch of federal election ballots if officials have not met the requirements, raising concerns that administrative or technical problems could prevent eligible voters from receiving their ballots. The US Postal Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The requirements were adopted in response to an executive order signed by US President Donald Trump in March as part of his campaign to impose federal citizenship-verification and election-integrity measures. The Postal Service said the changes would improve its ability to track individual ballots, increase the visibility of election mail as it moves through the postal system and help law enforcement identify potential fraud. Opponents contend that Trump is using the Postal Service to assert authority over elections that the US Constitution assigns principally to the states and Congress. Democratic attorneys general from 23 states and Washington, along with Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, filed a renewed lawsuit in Boston on Wednesday seeking to block the final rule. Voting rights organisations have filed a parallel challenge and asked for immediate relief. US District Judge Indira Talwani has scheduled a September 3 hearing on whether to issue a preliminary injunction, although the challengers are also seeking a temporary restraining order that could halt the rule sooner. The litigation has taken on added urgency because some jurisdictions will begin sending ballots in September. Lower courts had previously blocked the Trump administration from implementing the mail-voting provisions. The US Supreme Court lifted one of those injunctions on Monday, concluding that the states’ initial lawsuit had been filed before the Postal Service completed its rule making. The justices did not decide whether the president or the Postal Service possesses the legal authority to impose the requirements. Once the rule was finalised, the states and voting rights organisations returned to court, arguing that their challenges were no longer premature. Misunderstanding at any point in the life cycle of a mail ballot … could have marked effects on a voter’s ability to participate National Association of State Election Directors The non-partisan National Association of State Election Directors (Nased) had warned during the rule making process that the timetable could force election offices to make potentially destabilising changes to critical voting systems at one of the busiest points in the election calendar. Nased represents election directors in all 50 states, Washington and five US territories. Its members are career public servants rather than elected officials, and the association said its objections concerned implementation rather than the merits of Trump’s executive order. In comments submitted to the Postal Service in July, the association said compliance could require hurried changes to voter-registration databases and election-management systems, which are commonly placed under a “code freeze” before elections to prevent outages, cybersecurity problems and other disruptions. Because those systems can also contain information used in electronic poll books and to manage voting districts, an unintended problem in one part of the system could affect other election operations, the association warned. Nased also raised questions about whether there would be sufficient time to train postal employees and officials in more than 8,000 state and local election jurisdictions. “Misunderstanding at any point in the life cycle of a mail ballot, from envelope design to delivery, could have marked effects on a voter’s ability to participate,” the organisation said in its July comments. Election offices often purchase envelopes from six months to more than a year before a federal election, according to Nased. Jurisdictions that previously used generic bar codes – or none at all – may have to reprint their supplies to include the uniquely serialised bar codes required by the new rule. Those bar codes allow each outgoing and return envelope to be tracked individually. The Postal Service says they can be generated with free online tools and printed using commonly available equipment. Election administrators told Nased, however, that implementing the system could require changes to their voter databases and the use of commercial printers capable of producing reliably scannable bar codes. The Postal Service said in its final rule that its mailpiece-design specialists generally aim to return feedback within two business days. Nased had reported that jurisdictions previously experienced waits of three to six weeks and sometimes received conflicting guidance about the same envelope design. Under the new process, election officials or authorised vendors must upload information appearing on the outside of each ballot envelope to the Federal Ballot Mail Portal before presenting outgoing ballot batches to the Postal Service. USPS also says information in the portal will not be publicly available and will be protected through encryption, multifactorial authentication and restrictions limiting access to authorised users. The new verification takes place before outgoing ballots enter the postal system. Once an outgoing mailing is accepted, the Postal Service says it will not intercept or delay individual ballots because of the rule. Voters can continue returning completed ballots through residential postboxes, blue collection boxes or postal retail counters. USPS says returned ballots will be processed under its existing procedures, although it encourages voters to use the return envelope supplied by their election authority. Ballots sent to US military personnel and civilian voters living abroad under the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act are expressly excluded from the rule. The exemption applies to eligible Americans voting from China, Hong Kong and other overseas locations. Mail voting has become an increasingly contentious political issue since the 2020 presidential election, when its use expanded sharply during the coronavirus pandemic. Trump has repeatedly alleged that widespread mail voting enables fraud, although documented cases remain rare. The US president voted by mail in Florida’s August 18, 2026, Republican primary. Palm Beach County records showed that he requested the ballot in late July and returned it on August 13. The White House confirmed his mail vote, saying that he primarily lives in Washington and that Trump supports exceptions for travel, illness, disability and military service while opposing universal mail voting.

title: US air traffic controllers left work early before fatal crash. The FAA wants them fired
description: Two pilots died after their Air Canada Express plane collided with a fire truck at New York’s LaGuardia Airport in March.
content: The US Federal Aviation Administration is taking steps to fire two air traffic controllers determined to have left their shifts early before an Air Canada Express plane collided with a fire truck at New York’s LaGuardia Airport in March, according to people familiar with the matter. The moves are in keeping with a broader push by the Trump administration to crack down on controllers leaving shifts early or abusing sick leave, said the people, who asked to remain anonymous because the information is not public. “The FAA is committed to holding employees accountable, and we will not compromise the safety or efficiency of the National Airspace System,” the agency said in an emailed statement. The regulator said it was meanwhile staffing up its controller workforce through hiring. So-called early shoves are a long-standing, informal practice where supervisors give controllers permission to leave early during slow periods, while still giving them full pay. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Thursday that the agency was conducting a broader review of alleged timecard fraud and was moving to fire the two controllers. “When a small percentage of individuals take advantage of the American taxpayer, unfairly add additional work to their fellow controllers and impact the airspace – we have no choice but to act,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement. “We will not tolerate fraud, and we are taking appropriate action to hold folks accountable and prevent unlawful practices from disrupting the travelling public.” The two pilots on the Air Canada Express plane died as a result of the crash shortly after landing at LaGuardia on March 22. The aircraft, which took off from Montreal, was carrying 72 passengers and four crew. The plane hit a Port Authority of New York and New Jersey fire truck after touching down shortly before midnight and came to a standstill about halfway down the runway. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association, the union that represents controllers, said it was actively discussing the allegations with FAA leadership. “We believe those discussions are the appropriate forum for addressing the matter,” the association said. A representative for the National Transportation Safety Board said the case is still under active investigation.

title: Harvard and MIT scholars head to Canada, as Carney offers millions
description: 48 researchers were poached from the US, where policy changes have left scientists feeling unsupported.
content: Canada has awarded 64 global scholars with C$504 million (US$362 million) in funding to relocate their work to Canadian universities and advance projects in areas such as health and artificial intelligence. Some 48 of the researchers were poached from the US, including from elite institutions such as Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The other 16 researchers are coming from 12 other countries, including the UK, Germany, China and Japan. “While certain countries are cutting research and turning their back on academic freedom, we’re doubling down on science and we’re doubling down on research,” Industry Minister Melanie Joly said in Vancouver on Thursday. Canada’s effort to lure top research talent contrasts with recent US federal funding cuts that, combined with tightening immigration policies and clashes between the Trump administration and top-tier universities, have led some scholars to look for opportunities elsewhere. Joly noted that 23 of the research chairs are also Canadians returning home. The announcement is part of an initiative Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government unveiled last year to boost Canadian universities, earmarking C$1.7 billion over 12 years to recruit more than 1,000 researchers. The bulk of that money – C$1 billion – was dedicated to attracting as many as 100 world-leading research chairs to schools across the country. Robert Asselin, chief executive officer of U15 Canada, which represents the country’s leading research universities, said the government’s ability to attract these scholars reflects the strength of Canada’s post-secondary institutions. He also said policy changes in the US left scientists feeling less supported, helping Canada’s effort to attract them. “That was absolutely a reason why they wanted to come to Canada. So we seized the opportunity, and I’m really happy this happened,” Asselin said. Among the new research chairs is Sara Seager, a renowned planetary scientist whom the University of Toronto already announced would be leaving MIT to return to her alma mater. Canada has also signed MIT professor James LeBeau, a materials scientist. Brian Kuhlman, a researcher from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, whose work was referenced in connection with the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, will be joining the University of British Columbia as a research chair. Also heading to UBC is Curtis Huttenhower, a professor of computational biology and bioinformatics at Harvard whose research focuses on the intersection of microbes and human health. The Canadian government also promised last year an accelerated immigration pathway for H-1B visa holders after the Trump administration decided to charge US$100,000 for the visas. It has yet to roll out that programme. Other major world economies are also seeking to attract top scholars open to leaving the US. The European Union has also launched its own €500 million (US$583 million) initiative to attract global researchers and scientists. The new research chairs will receive funding over eight years to work on projects in priority fields set out by the Canadian government, including in health, advanced digital technologies and the environment. “New chairs and their teams will advance transformational research projects that can be applied and/or commercialised by connecting with receptors in industry, government and society, while also developing the next generation of highly qualified personnel,” the government said about the initiative last year. The government is set to announce the next round of chairs in the coming months.

title: Trump orders Lake Ontario renamed ‘Lake America’ as US-Canada trade war escalates
description: Canadian leaders dismiss move as ‘foolishness’ and ‘rhetoric’ as US president targets northern neighbour over trade.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he was renaming Lake Ontario to be known as “Lake America” in the United States, as he escalated his trade war with Canada. The Republican president signed an executive order directing the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the US geographic naming service. Trump cannot force Canada to follow along, however. Trump has been floating the idea of the name change in recent days as the US announced it was imposing 50 per cent tariffs on US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down. Trump has been needling America’s northern neighbour since he returned to the White House last year, suggesting the ally with whom the US once had warm relations should instead be absorbed as the 51st state. Canada responded to Trump’s import taxes this week by imposing retaliatory tariffs on US$20 billion worth of American goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment. Trump, who signed the order as he was sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, had a large sign behind him propped on a stand with a map of the Great Lakes. Over Lake Ontario, in big red letters, the map read “Lake America”. On the other side of the president was another map with the words, “MAKING THE GREAT LAKES EVEN GREATER”. The lake is one of multiple Great Lakes that the US and Canada share borders along. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, invoking the lake’s indigenous roots and noting that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he said on social media. Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston dismissed Trump’s move in a social media post, writing: “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy”. There is no single international body that determines names of international bodies of water and Trump has wide latitude over how the US government recognises geographic places and landmarks. Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has traded insults with Trump, this week brushed aside the prospect of Trump changing the lake’s name as “a lot of rhetoric”. The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word oniatarí:io, which means “lake of shining waters”. The province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake. Trump said that while his action was not meant to send any particular geopolitical message, “Canada’s been ripping us off for a long time” on trade and military issues. “They wanted to be treated like a state and they’re not a state,” the president said. “We just can’t do that any more.” “We love the people of Canada,” Trump added. “I don’t think their representatives do, an appropriate job. Maybe they’ll change. I really don’t know. It doesn’t make much difference.” The move is reminiscent of his move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”. Trump scribbled his name with a Sharpie pen on the executive order, then held it up for the cameras, offering: “And we filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else”. “We’ve notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So, we’ve done everything that you have to do,” he said. “And this is official, effective immediately.” The executive order Trump signed shows that the changes are, in fact, are supposed to be made within 30 days. He also suggested his push to rename bodies of water may not be finished. “So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean,” Trump said. “So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them.”

title: Shackled Tate brothers ask to be released from jail during extradition fight
description: The influencer duo were arrested in Miami to face rape and sex-trafficking charges from the UK.
content: Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate stood in the witness box in federal court on Thursday and said they could not adequately defend themselves from criminal sex charges if they had to remain in a Miami jail while fighting extradition to the UK. During nearly two hours in a Miami courtroom, the Tates, in shackles and tan jail jumpsuits, denied under oath criminal accusations across multiple countries, blasted their critics and described their brash online personas that exude wealth and excess as characters and not their true personalities.
