The hearing ended after eight hours without a decision from US Magistrate Lauren Louis, and the brothers headed back to jail. Prosecutors said the Tates are liars who exaggerate all the time. Assistant US Attorney Abbie Waxman told a judge that Andrew Tate was accused of choking and holding victims and raping them while Tristan Tate was accused of human trafficking, money laundering and violence against minors. The brothers also face sex crime charges in Romania and prosecutors said they have contacted witnesses in that case and talked about it on video. “They promote incredible violence against women consistent with the allegations against them,” Waxman said. Andrew Tate said he was innocent, could not work with his Romanian lawyers while in jail in America and feared his absence would mean an unfair life sentence in Eastern Europe. “If I lose a fair fight I can take it,” he said. Lawyers for the Tates are asking Louis to allow them to be freed from custody at least until an extradition hearing can be held on their UK rape and trafficking charges. They have remained in a federal detention centre in Miami since they were arrested July 18. Their lawyers argued that their high profile and active social media presence make it nearly impossible for them to flee. The UK’s request was out of line because their criminal case in Romania is going first. Romanian officials have let them remain free until the proceedings conclude and they have not tried to flee and are complying with all court restrictions. The judge reminded defence lawyers that she had to follow US laws, but she did ask them to report to her by Monday on what would happen if the Tates missed a hearing in Romania. No date for an extradition hearing has been set. The UK has until mid-September to provide evidence to the State Department. Prosecutors said the brothers appeared to have money and had bragged about multiple passports. The Tates said their claims of wealth were largely exaggerated to boost their social media personas. They said luxury items like the US$50 million yacht or US$2.1 million Aston Martin car seen in their videos did not belong to them. But prosecutors showed a passport for “Vladimir Scorpius” from Mexico with Tristan Tate’s date of birth and photo. They said it had a real Mexican identification number. They also told the judge the brothers had shown no evidence the luxury boat or cars were rented or borrowed. The Tates have become among the world’s most polarising internet personalities by promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. Andrew Tate, 39, has said women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and shared graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. Tristan Tate, 38, has worked with his brother on multiple businesses, including the production of online webcam pornography. On his way into court Thursday, defence lawyer Joseph McBride told reporters he had not heard of a case where the judge had allowed someone out on bail while awaiting an extradition hearing. But while the odds were not in their favour, McBride felt that the truth was. He called them innocent, good men who have never run from the law. In court, Tristan Tate was called to the stand on Thursday and said he could not prove he was innocent if he was kept in jail. “I need to clear my name. I need to take part in these proceedings, I can’t do that from the secure housing unit,” he said. Both brothers also complained of conditions at the Miami jail. Tristan Tate said there were ants and the only toilet in his cell was where anyone walking by could see him. He said he had lost 14 pounds (6.4kg) eating mostly junk food in the nearly six weeks he had been in custody. Prosecutors said prisoners were fed three balanced meals a day. They did not have access to scales, and medical records showed the brothers had gained a few pounds. Andrew Tate testified that people were confusing him with a character he played online. He said people who accuse him of attacking women or supporting human trafficking are taking his comments out of context. “On the internet, you have to shake people out of apathy,” he said. The former professional kick-boxers, who have dual American and UK citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of US President Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers should not expect any help from the president.

title: Brazil’s rare earths will not loosen China’s magnet grip this decade, researchers say
description: Despite vast reserves, Brazil lacks the processing capacity and commercial plants needed to turn its own raw materials into magnets.
content: Brazil will not be able to make rare earth magnets from its own raw materials before 2032, the coordinator of the country’s main magnet pilot plant said on Wednesday, leaving China’s near monopoly on the technology intact for years to come. Andre Luis Pimenta de Faria, who runs the plant for Senai, the research and training arm of Brazil’s national industry confederation, told a public policy panel at Exposibram, the country’s largest mining congress, that first batches could come by the end of 2028, but only using imported inputs. “If we look at the full picture of everything needed to produce a permanent magnet, we are talking about a more distant horizon, maybe 2032–2035,” Faria said. The plant runs on Asian process technology chosen when it was designed, and buys abroad the processed ore it feeds into its furnaces, Faria said. Brazil also makes no electrolytic iron, a high-purity input very different from the ore it ships overseas, despite being one of the world’s two largest iron ore exporters. Pablo Cesario, chief executive of the Brazilian Mining Institute, called even that timetable optimistic and put the average gap between a proven reserve and first production in Brazil at 17.2 years. “This is a 10 or 15-year game. And in those 10 or 15 years the others are running too,” he said. The contest over Brazilian ore Those timetables matter because permanent magnets made from rare earths drive the motors in electric vehicles, wind turbines, industrial robots and precision weapons, and China produces roughly 90 per cent of the world’s rare earth permanent magnets. In April 2025, Beijing imposed export controls on seven medium and heavy rare earths and the magnets made with them, disrupting supply to carmakers in Europe, the United States and Asia. Brazil holds the world’s second largest rare earth reserves after China, and the contest over who gets access to them has already reached the presidential campaign. Ronaldo Caiado, then governor of the state of Goias and now a presidential candidate, signed a critical minerals memorandum with Washington in March, and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva accused him and other opposition figures of preparing to “sell Brazil”. The state is home to Serra Verde, which says it is the only miner outside Asia producing the full set of magnet rare earths at scale, and in April the American company USA Rare Earth agreed to buy it for US$2.8 billion. The transaction could redirect the mine’s output from Chinese refiners to American ones. That contest is a fight over ore rather than over industry, because Brazil refines almost nothing of what it mines and has no commercial magnet plant of its own. Asked by the South China Morning Post whether Brazil could diversify its partners while Beijing controls the processing technology, and whether the alternative was alignment with China, Cesario said he had put that question directly to Chinese officials. “They are open to us. They do not see us as enemies, they see us as partners,” he said. Faria added the export restrictions were a strategy Brazil had to work around rather than protest against. “We can kick and scream, we can cry, but it is a strategy of the Chinese government,” he said, arguing the disruption had pushed manufacturers worldwide to look for suppliers outside China. A bill stuck in the Senate Brazil has no legal framework for converting any of that demand into binding contracts. The bill written to supply one has been stuck since May, when the lower house approved it and sent it to the Senate, where it stalled amid friction between Lula and Senate president Davi Alcolumbre. Senators are expected to take it up during a week of priority votes starting on Monday. If approved, this legislation would create a national critical minerals policy and a fund to guarantee financing for mining projects, but the fight is over a third element, a council attached to the presidency. Mining companies say the proposed council would have a say over offtake agreements – the long-term supply contracts that underpin mine financing – and over changes in company ownership. Cesario said that leaves too much discretion in the hands of the executive. Mining companies say the proposed council would have a say over offtake agreements “If we scare off foreign investors, or any other investor, the sector locks up,” Cesario said. Those powers would land hardest on Chinese companies, which have been taking stakes in Brazilian lithium and rare earth projects. If the council carries them, Brasilia would hold a veto over supply deals and over future acquisitions of the sort agreed at Serra Verde. Where the industry fears too much state control, the foreign ministry complains of too little direction. Mauricio Lyrio, its secretary for climate, energy and environment, told the panel in a recorded message that Brazil faced “almost a universal courting” from countries seeking rare earth partnerships, and that it had no framework for deciding which offers to accept. Until it has one, Lyrio said, Brazil should “pick the ideal partner for each individual mineral rather than react to proposals from abroad”, citing what he called the country’s ecumenical diplomatic tradition. That approach is already being tested away from both Washington and Beijing. Luis Gonzaga Trabasso, who coordinates Magbras – a magnet project involving 28 companies and seven research institutes – said the group was bidding into a European raw materials partnership programme, with talks under way with Germany, Sweden, Switzerland and Norway. Jorge Boeira, an analyst at the Brazilian Industrial Development Agency, said none of those routes changes the underlying arithmetic, because the gap Brazil is really trying to close is one of planning time. Beijing “set up a government office dedicated to rare earths in 1975, decades before anyone treated the sector as strategic”, Boeira said. “They had 50 years to build the chain they dominate today, in mining, in refining and downstream,” the analyst added. Faria borrowed that same date to place Brazil on the clock. “We are setting up the framework now because we know we have potential,” he said.

title: US Patriot missile shortage in Europe ‘beyond critical’ due to Iran war, officials say
description: In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault, Nato could be forced ‘to take punch after punch in the mouth’.
content: The US military is experiencing a “beyond critical” shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe largely driven by US President Donald Trump’s war with Iran, an American defence official in Europe and a Nato official said, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in Nato countries to a potential Russian attack. The US defence official said the most concerning shortfall involves Patriot missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles. The Nato official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots among American and Nato forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters. In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on, for example, a military headquarters or power plant, Nato could be in a similar position to Patriot-starved Ukraine and be forced “to take punch after punch in the mouth”, the US defence official said. In Europe, the American military “definitely” does not have enough Patriots to stop any possible sustained ballistic missile attack and would have “very limited” capability to defend against a single ballistic missile strike or a stray Russian missile that goes off course, the US official said. It illustrates the cascading fallout from Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran, a conflict that reaches the six-month mark on Friday. US missile stocks in Europe have been moved to the Middle East, where US and Gulf allies have fired off significant numbers of interceptors, including Patriots, to thwart Iran’s drones and missiles. Some of those attacks have killed and wounded American troops. Though a Russian ballistic missile attack against Nato countries is not imminently expected, CIA Director John Ratcliffe went to Moscow this week to warn Russia not to attack, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump played down the significance of the rare and secretive trip, saying it was “sort of semi-routine”. European and Nato officials say Russia could be in a position to attack countries in the alliance by 2030. Patriot stockpiles are projected to rebound by then. In the meantime, Russia’s war in Ukraine could hinder its ability to carry out any missile attack on Europe as it would be a challenge for Moscow to fight an air war on two fronts. The Patriot missile shortage is most acutely felt in Ukraine, where officials are begging for more air defence support and where previous US transfers also have drawn down some supply. Kyiv says only US-made Patriots can stop Russia’s advanced ballistic missiles, which increasingly are getting through Ukrainian defences, including as part of a barrage overnight into Thursday. The US supplied hundreds of Patriot missiles to Ukraine over the course of the 4½-year-long conflict, but the Iran war was the tipping point for shrinking inventories, said Ed Arnold, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a military think tank in London. The supply to Ukraine was planned for and reasonably measured, he said, whereas stocks in the Middle East have been unexpectedly and quickly drained, exposing supply chain constraints. The US military in Europe also is grappling with critical shortages of the Army Tactical Missile System, or ATACMS, a medium-range ballistic missile designed to strike behind enemy lines, the two officials said. But the overall munitions picture in Europe is less dire than on air defences alone because some European militaries have their own offensive missiles, such as the Taurus and Storm Shadow, which are both long-range air-launched bunker-busting missiles. US Army Colonel Martin O’Donnell, a senior Nato military spokesman, said it is “simply not the case” that the number of Patriot missiles in Europe is beyond critical. Nato, he said, is able to “block punches” and has enough air defence munitions available to defend itself as well as to donate to Ukraine. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement Thursday that claims of US munition shortages “are false”. “We have everything required to strike at the time and place of the president’s choosing,” Parnell said. “Across multiple combatant commands, we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests.” The dearth of Patriot interceptors in Europe would leave few alternatives for shooting down Russia’s more advanced ballistic missiles, which can be combined with swarms of inexpensive drones to overwhelm defences, experts say. Ukraine and some allies already use systems that can destroy slower-moving drones without expensive missiles. But ballistic missiles are a challenge because they dive steeply towards targets at more than five times the speed of sound, leaving little time to stop them. The Patriot system tracks the missile, predicts its path and launches within minutes, all while carrying out complex calculations to ensure the interceptor finds its target. One Patriot battery can only cover a limited area: for example, a small military base but not a whole city. One alternative could be France and Italy’s SAMP/T NG air defence system. France has promised to speed up the delivery of the system – the upgraded version of the current SAMP/T – to Ukraine, which the manufacturer says is better able to counter ballistics. The new iteration, however, has not yet been battle tested and the current version of the SAMP/T has a smaller range than the Patriot. While US and European militaries have warships that can serve as mobile air defence, they may be too far from a target to protect it and could risk getting sunk. Ukraine has received Patriots from American and European stockpiles since Russia’s 2022 invasion, with the US providing about 600 of the interceptors during the Biden administration, said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel who is now senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington think tank. But the greatest expenditure has been during the Iran conflict, which has used up 65 per cent of US Patriots, amounting to roughly 1,500 of the nation’s 2,330 interceptors, CSIS says. About 600 missiles, including those destined for Europe, should be made this year, with a production goal of 2,000 Patriot missiles a year set for 2030, Cancian said. Nato says Europe’s first Patriot missile production facility is expected to open in Germany in September, with deliveries possibly beginning early next year. The first deliveries should go to countries that have already placed orders, including Germany, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain, the US defence official said. But for now, that means some countries, such as Germany, have bought expensive Patriot systems but are in the “ridiculous” position of not having any ammunition to fire from them, said Arnold of the London think tank. Germany’s defence ministry said it does not comment on stockpiles. Moscow is unlikely to be able to carry out a sustained air assault on a Nato target while it launches almost nightly attacks on Ukraine, Arnold said. Ukraine’s recent strikes into Russia also have exposed weaknesses in Russia’s air defences, which could prompt Putin to think twice about provoking a retaliatory attack. “The uncomfortable truth is possibly the best air defence that we have is Russian constraints,” Arnold said.

title: Uefa targets Fifa’s Infantino with criminal complaint over failed World Cup investor plan
description: Uefa pursues legal action against the Fifa president in Switzerland for alleged financial misconduct in the collapsed investment scheme.
content: Uefa is preparing a criminal complaint against Fifa president Gianni Infantino in Swiss courts for possible financial mismanagement over his failed plan to sell future World Cup profits to private investors. Uefa said on Thursday it filed documents in a Manhattan court requesting discovery of potential evidence from the New York investment fund, Thrive Capital Management, founded by Joshua Kushner. Uefa also filed a request in a southern Florida district for authorisation of discovery “in a foreign proceeding” against Fifa itself, which has offices in the Miami suburb of Coral Gables. Thrive and Kushner were to be the anchor investors intending to pay Fifa US$4.2 billion for a 20 per cent stake in a subsidiary that would run the football body’s commercial events, including the World Cup. “Uefa and its counsel are contemplating a Swiss criminal proceeding against Infantino and possibly other Fifa officials for criminal mismanagement under Article 158 of the Swiss Criminal Code,” Uefa’s lawyers said in a 56-page document seen by Associated Press. The document suggests the US$4.2 billion figure could be a “fraudulently off-market price promoted by Infantino for his own benefit”. Infantino dropped the sell-off plan on August 1 after a furious backlash by global football leaders, including Uefa. Uefa first threatened to take legal action on August 3 when it warned Fifa against destroying or hiding any “relevant materials” related to the plan. “Infantino claimed that the plan would ‘unleash the commercial potential and opportunity that Fifa has’,” Uefa lawyers told the courts. “In truth, it was a vehicle for Infantino and that small circle to acquire a permanent stake in and otherwise profit from Fifa’s most valuable assets to the detriment of Fifa, its members, and other parties within the football family. “Under the terms Infantino announced, those investors stood to acquire a permanent financial interest in Fifa’s commercial arm for US$4.2 billion, implying an absurdly low enterprise value of only approximately US$20 billion, a figure that was neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer.” Spokespeople for Fifa and Thrive have been approached for comment.

title: Foreigners jostle to secure UK residency rights before rules tighten
description: The proposed reforms to a scheme offering permanent residency would double the qualification period from five to 10 years.
content: The United Kingdom has seen a spike in the number of migrants applying for citizenship and permanent settlement ahead of a planned government clampdown. Government data shows what appears to be a rush to secure residency rights in response to changes announced by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood that would force migrants to wait longer before they can gain them. The Home Office said 199,628 people were granted settlement, giving them the right to live, work and study in the UK permanently, in the year through June 2026. Most granted indefinite leave to remain can then apply for citizenship after 12 months. These figures represent a 24 per cent increase from a year earlier and the highest number since 2010. Over the same 12 month period, 245,520 people were granted British citizenship. Although that was slightly lower than a year earlier, the number of citizenship applications surged 17 per cent to a record 315,224. There was a 44 per cent increase in the number of citizenship applications refused. The proposed reforms to indefinite leave to remain, which offers permanent settlement rights and a route to citizenship, would double the qualification period from five to 10 years and are controversial among members of the governing Labour Party. The government is currently consulting on the proposals for stricter settlement rules and new Prime Minister Andy Burnham is under pressure from Labour MPs to reconsider whether to push ahead with the changes, first announced under his predecessor Keir Starmer. Migration is a difficult political topic for Burnham, who also faces pressure from parties on the right over the issue. The Conservatives and Reform UK parties have suggested they would remove settlement rights from people who currently have it. The UK continued to see a rise in the number of Americans applying to remain in the country. More than 9,400 US nationals applied for British citizenship, either through registration or naturalisation, over the last year. But the US remains behind India, Pakistan, Italy, Nigeria, Romania and Poland in the list of nationalities seeking citizenship. Nuni Jorgensen, researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said the increase in citizenship applications reflects rising migration with a particularly sharp jump among European Union nationals, pointing to a sudden change in people’s desire to become British. “The data do not tell us why, although it is possible that government and opposition party debates about restricting rights or removing people without citizenship may have played a role,” she said. “Research suggests that uncertainty can encourage migrants to secure their status by applying for citizenship.” The figures also showed a sharp fall in the number of asylum seekers being housed temporarily in UK hotels, a flashpoint for community tensions in recent years. The figure stood at 16,021 at the end of June, down 50 per cent year on year and the lowest since data was first reported in 2022. Mahmood said in a statement that the Labour government is “restoring control” of the contentious asylum system.

title: Hong Kong officer charged over indecent messages to suspect’s friend
description: Man, 32, charged with misconduct after allegedly contacting a friend of a suspect and sending her indecent texts and images.
content: A Hong Kong police officer has been charged with misconduct after allegedly sending obscene messages and photos to a woman friend of a suspect in a criminal investigation. Officers from the New Territories South regional crime unit detained the 32‑year‑old man in Tuen Mun on August 20, a police spokesman said on Thursday. During an investigation into a case in May last year, the officer from Kwai Tsing police district allegedly contacted a friend of one of the suspects and sent her indecent texts and images. The woman reported the incident to police later that month. Following inquiries, the officer was charged with one count of misconduct in public office. He is expected to appear in Sha Tin Court on Friday. The officer has been suspended from duty. A police spokesman said the force attached great importance to officers’ conduct and would not tolerate any unlawful behaviour. It would deal with any such misconduct seriously, he added.

title: Infantino doing ‘great job’ World Cup star Suker says, tells Hong Kong ‘be more like Croatia’
description: Ex-Real Madrid striker Davor Suker made honorary president of Eastern District, tells city’s players to train like China’s table tennis heroes.
content: Soon after he joined the Hong Kong football association 2½ years ago, the now outgoing technical director John Morling pointed to the success of Croatia and asked, “why can’t that be us?” With a population just shy of 4 million, Croatia have reached one World Cup final and two semi-finals in the past 28 years. Now, Davor Suker, one of the stars of their 1998 run to the last four, is poised to share some of his country’s secrets with Hong Kong: population 7 million, world No 156 and as far away as ever from qualifying for a World Cup, even if it is expanded to 64 teams. The former Real Madrid and Arsenal striker, who is a Fifa ambassador and leapt to the defence of president Gianni Infantino on Thursday, Suker has been made honorary president of Hong Kong Premier League club Eastern District. While his appointment left a few people scratching their heads, Suker said he had grown friendly with Eric Fok Kai-shan and Timothy Fok Tsun-ting, the current and former chairmen of the Football Association of Hong Kong, China, over his nine years as head of the Croatian Football Federation. During Suker’s tenure, which finished in 2021, his country reached the 2018 World Cup final. “My job is as a Fifa ambassador, we need to help each other, and with my experience in the dressing room, on the pitch and in administration, I can support this big club in Hong Kong,” Suker said. “In Croatia, we’re small, but in football we’re so big. If you train well, and work hard 24-7, the results will come. I think Hong Kong can one day reach a World Cup … but they need to train like China trains for table tennis. “We don’t have the money in Croatia, but we’re excellent at researching and finding hungry young players. Selling Luka Modric [to Tottenham Hotspur] earned Dinamo Zagreb £16.5 million [US$22.5 million]. There’s so much information today, it’s easy to copy systems in a good way.” Suker will attend Eastern District’s opening game of the campaign at BC Rangers on Sunday, and return again next month. In March, he staged the inaugural Davor Suker Youth Football Tournament in Macau, and last year the 58-year-old was a guest at the World Football Summit in Hong Kong. The scorer of 45 goals in 69 Croatia appearances, Suker said he would also help identify and recruit players from Europe for Eastern District. “I’m not getting any money, I can see it’s a family club and I’m so happy to be part of it,” he said. “I know the clubs and the league, and it needs the support.” After travelling with instructions from Infantino to pass on his best wishes to Eastern District’s players and staff, Suker said he believed the Swiss had “done a great job” helming Fifa and deserved to be re-elected for another four-year term. Infantino is more vulnerable than at any time of his 10-year tenure ahead of the global governing body’s presidential election in Morocco next March after he tried to sell off the World Cup. “I voted for him in 2016 and I hope in Morocco we can celebrate the victory of Gianni Infantino,” Suker said. “I see people writing bad things, but he transformed Fifa and did a really good job for [Croatia], too. I wish him all the best and he will do another great job in his next term.” Goldberg Ko Chi-chiu, the Eastern District vice-president, said Suker would also use his “personal network and experience to help us build up a youth system”, while helping the club place talented players in Europe. They will also hire some Croatian coaches to work with their youth teams. In their first top-flight campaign last season, Eastern District were one of only three clubs to average four-figure home attendances. Ko is aiming to add 20 per cent to the gates this term after adding more quality players over the summer, despite keeping the budget pegged not far above HK$5 million. A former Hong Kong goalkeeper, Ko said: “With me and Alex [Chu chi-kwong, sporting director] we have two guys who know a lot about Hong Kong football. We know everything won’t go smoothly but this is our first step. We have time and patience. If this works, great. If not, we’ll come back and go down another road.” Elsewhere, it appears that Fifa have adopted a rip-it-up-and-start-again approach to their new Asean Cup. According to the global governing body’s website, “Challenge Division” hosts Hong Kong will now face Laos instead of higher-ranked Myanmar in a group that also features lowly Brunei. The city team are scheduled to play Laos at Kai Tak Stadium on September 27, with Brunei their opponents at the same venue three days later. The prize for the group winner will be an October 3 final clash with one of Myanmar, managed by former Hong Kong boss Jorn Andersen, Cambodia, and Timor-Leste. Mong Kok Stadium matches between Laos and Brunei, and Myanmar and Timor-Leste, are set to launch the competition on September 24. The Football Association of Hong Kong, China, who are set to lose Morling to their UAE counterparts, have remained tight-lipped over Fifa Asean Cup arrangements.

title: US singer Post Malone delays Hong Kong concert, sparking fan complaints
description: Concert organiser Live Nation Hong Kong says September 16 show at Kai Tak Stadium has been postponed.
content: American singer and rapper Post Malone has postponed his coming Hong Kong show, prompting complaints from disappointed fans in mainland China who said they had already booked holiday leave and hotels. Announcing the decision on social media on Thursday, concert organiser Live Nation Hong Kong said the September 16 show at Kai Tak Stadium had been postponed. The statement, which gave no reason for the move, outlined full refund arrangements for fans who bought tickets through official platforms. Original ticket prices for the 31-year-old singer’s show at the 50,000-seat stadium ranged from HK$699 (US$90) to HK$3,199. The news left fans frustrated, with many complaining on social media platforms. “I’ve already applied for my holiday leave and booked my hotels,” a user on popular mainland social media platform RedNote wrote. “They just said ‘postponed’ in a single sentence, zero concern for our flight tickets and hotel bookings,” another user added, with some questioning whether ticket sales had underperformed. The abrupt schedule change is not an isolated incident, as Post Malone has delayed or cancelled other shows on his world tour. Earlier this year, the artist pushed back multiple dates during the North American leg of the “Big Stadium World Tour”, citing the need for extra time in the studio to finish his album. But seat charts reportedly showed up to 75 per cent of tickets remained unsold at some major stadium venues in Texas and Florida. The Asia and Australasia legs of the tour have also faced widespread disruptions. In addition to Hong Kong, postponed stops include Kaohsiung, Singapore, Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, Manila, Seoul and Yokohama, as well as cities in Australia and New Zealand. Tour organisers have not announced a specific reason for the broader regional postponement. Affected ticket holders are being offered refunds and rescheduled dates have not yet been confirmed. Post Malone last performed in Hong Kong in September 2023 at AsiaWorld-Expo during his “If Y’all Wasn’t Here, I’d Be Crying” tour. His most-streamed song, the 2018 hit “Sunflower” with US rapper Swae Lee and taken from the Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse soundtrack, has amassed 4.4 billion plays.

title: Why climate extremes will not stop expansion of China’s nuclear power industry
description: Technological advances alongside planning for increasingly severe weather events are more likely to help the rapidly growing sector.
content: While extreme weather is disrupting nuclear power generation in some parts of the world, it is unlikely to derail China’s rapid expansion in the sector, according to an industry specialist. The unusually hot and dry summer has disrupted reactors across Europe, forcing units to shut down from France to Romania, as river levels have fallen and water temperatures risen. France – where nuclear accounts for around 70 per cent of electricity generation – had a record shortfall of more than 20 per cent in its nuclear-based capacity, with outages linked to drought, extreme heat and an invasion of jellyfish, Le Monde reported on August 11. Nuclear facilities require large quantities of reactor-cooling water. However, unlike Europe’s reactors – which are mainly built along rivers – China’s nuclear power plants have been constructed along the coast. Using open seawater for cooling makes Chinese reactors less vulnerable to droughts and heatwaves, according to Francois Morin, China director of the World Nuclear Association, an international industry body. While coastal areas faced a range of threats associated with extreme weather, including storms and rising sea levels, China had a good understanding of typhoons and they did not pose a serious threat to its nuclear reactors, Morin said. “Like earthquakes, typhoons can be managed through appropriate design and engineering measures,” he said on July 29. The Lufeng project, under construction in the southern province of Guangdong, is a typical example of how extreme weather factors are incorporated into China’s nuclear safety planning. Located in Shanwei, on China’s eastern coast, the project’s six third-generation nuclear technology units will consist of four Hualong One and two CAP1000 pressurised water reactors. The domestic Hualong One was co-developed by the state-owned China National Nuclear Corporation and China General Nuclear Power Group, while the CAP1000 is a localised version of the American company Westinghouse’s AP1000. According to a report published by Jinan Times in late July, the effects of extreme weather were taken into account from the earliest stages of the Lufeng project’s design, with its location frequently exposed to typhoons, torrential rain and storm surges. The site is designed to withstand the ground motion associated with a 10,000-year earthquake while its flood defences are expected to be able to handle rainfall levels of events with a one in 1,000 chance of occurring. The nuclear-island structures had also been designed to withstand winds of up to Force 17 – a level of strength associated with super typhoons, the report said. Zhang Min, head of the project’s safety protection department, told the newspaper that a comprehensive early-warning and emergency-response system had also been established. These included standardised procedures for dealing with extreme weather and practical emergency exercises for responding to exceptionally strong typhoons, according to the report. The project has already withstood several powerful typhoons, including Typhoon Ragasa in September last year. Overall, its operations had remained safe and controllable, with risks kept in check and no safety incidents reported, the article said. According to Morin, in addition to engineering safeguards and emergency preparedness, China’s technological advances could help its nuclear expansion better withstand the effects of climate change – and eventually lay the groundwork for inland reactors. While China’s nuclear buildout centres on the Hualong One and CAP1000, Beijing is also promoting next-generation reactor designs that require less water and are safer. Unlike mainstream pressurised-water reactor technology, China’s leading fourth-generation high-temperature gas-cooled reactors do not use water as their main coolant. A fast-neutron-reactor demonstration project is also operating in Xiapu county on the eastern coast of Fujian province. Such reactors typically use liquid sodium or lead as a coolant. As early as 2011, China’s National Climate Centre was warning that, before nuclear energy could help address climate change, nuclear power plants themselves could become highly vulnerable to its effects. In an article published that year, the centre noted that while the International Atomic Energy Agency recommended designing nuclear power plants to operate for 100 years, climate models disagreed on what conditions might arise during that period. It remained uncertain how plants would be operated over such a long lifespan, the article said, adding that some newer reactor designs required less water but the operating costs of these systems could be prohibitive. “The bottom line is that nuclear power must adapt to climate change while also taking measures to mitigate the effects. This is a major challenge,” it said. Despite connecting its first nuclear power plant to the grid in 1991, decades after Western pioneers, China is today building reactors faster and at a lower cost than its peers, with the State Council approving 10 or more reactors annually since 2022. The country is set to overtake the United States as the world’s largest nuclear power operator by installed capacity within five years, as current projects reach completion. Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

title: China and Iran sanctions: what US moves mean for Beijing, and its retaliation options
description: Washington’s new measures seen testing a recent bilateral detente with Beijing, and room for escalation remains, threatening trade, payments and supply chains.
content: The United States has imposed sweeping sanctions on nearly 60 Iran-linked entities, spanning digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping, as Washington seeks to “sever every economic lifeline” that sustains Tehran. Beijing denounced the measures, with the Chinese foreign ministry calling them “illegal unilateral sanctions” and vowing to “take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its rights and interests”. With the fresh sanctions complicating an already delicate diplomatic detente, we examine the Chinese entities targeted, delineate Beijing’s red lines and assess the potential economic countermeasures that China’s leadership could utilise if tensions escalate. How do Washington’s new sanctions on Iran affect China? More than a dozen Hong Kong- and mainland-based entities and individuals were named in the latest round of sanctions, primarily for helping to procure sensitive goods or for shipping Iranian oil. This included Hong Kong-based Sweet Ocean, which the US alleged had acted as an intermediary for the acquisition of sensitive equipment, such as laser optics, bound for the heavily sanctioned Malek Ashtar University in Iran. Other Hong Kong-based firms, including Feili Co, Minvur and Feisu, allegedly transferred capital to Sweet Ocean and acted as front companies to facilitate payments for Iran’s “shadow banking” networks. Also on the list were Hong Kong-registered Riqueza and China-based Lilimoon Navigation, which US authorities accused of owning foreign-flagged ships transporting Iranian crude to China – Tehran’s biggest oil buyer. Washington also signalled a readiness to deploy secondary sanctions on countries that refuse to cut economic ties with Iran. “Every country will be given a defined timeline to shut down the Iran-related activity we have identified. If they fail to act, Treasury will act,” the US Department of the Treasury said in a statement. Where does the escalation risk lie for Beijing? Analysts suggest that Washington remains wary of jeopardising the stability brokered during US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May and ahead of President Xi Jinping’s planned trip to the US next month. Still, Beijing’s red lines are well defined. “Harsher US actions – for example, targeting large Chinese banks or companies – will certainly invite a harsher response,” said Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, noting how such moves would cut off affected major Chinese entities from the US financial system. However, Xu added that if sanctions remained confined to smaller companies, Beijing’s pushback was likely to be symbolic. While the US has thus far refrained from targeting Chinese financial institutions facilitating the Iranian oil trade, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, when asked about non-compliant Chinese banks and shipping companies, warned that “no one is above the reach of US sanctions”. Cui Shoujun, a professor at Renmin University of China’s School of International Studies, said Beijing’s core objectives were to safeguard national energy security, protect economic interests of Chinese enterprises, and prevent the US from infringing upon China’s economic sovereignty. Despite the sanctions, some analysts said they expected China to maintain its crude intake from Tehran, even as US naval pressure has limited the supply flow. [China] also retains the trump card of rare earth export controls Xu Tianchen, Economist Intelligence Unit What are China’s options for economic retaliation? Should tensions boil over, China could move to enforce a blocking order, instructing companies to disregard US sanctions, Xu said. Beijing first deployed this regulatory lever in May, striking back against US sanctions on Hengli Petrochemical (Dalian) Refinery, a subsidiary of a private chemical giant, for buying Iranian oil. “It also retains the trump card of rare earth export controls – the existence of which is the very reason the US won’t go too far,” Xu added. Cui similarly noted that China could tighten enforcement and impose strict end-user and end-use reviews on key strategic minerals and rare earths involved in advanced manufacturing, thereby restricting the flow of these materials to certain US defence and hi-tech-related entities. He added that, to mitigate risk, Beijing could be accelerating the expansion of its Cross-border Interbank Payment System to reduce reliance on US dollar clearing networks by increasing bilateral local-currency settlements.

title: Bosnian Serb commander and war criminal Ratko Mladic dies in prison
description: The 84-year-old, who oversaw the 1995 Srebrenica slaughter, was serving a life sentence for genocide and war crimes.
content: Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military chief dubbed the “Butcher of Bosnia” for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, has died, Serbian state broadcaster RTS reported on Thursday. Mladic, 84, who had suffered several strokes in recent months, was serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity after overseeing the Srebrenica slaughter, Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since second world war. Serbian state officials and Mladic’s family had appealed for his release due to his failing health, but those calls were rejected by The Hague tribunal. He was the military face of a brutal trio, led on the political side by ex-Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic and former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, as the former Yugoslavia descended into carnage after the fall of communism. The 1992-95 war left around 100,000 people dead and 2.2 million displaced. The most infamous atrocity was committed in Srebrenica, where Serb forces under Mladic’s command executed 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys who had sought shelter in what was meant to be a UN-protected enclave. Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al Hussein described Mladic as “the epitome of evil” after his conviction. But most Serbs continued to revere him. “He only defended his people,” Bosnian Serb veteran Ljubo Tomovic said. “To convict him would be a disgrace and a sin,” he said before Mladic’s 2021 verdict. Mladic pushed the image of himself as “a simple man” chosen to protect his people. “Fate put me in a position to defend my country that you Western powers had devastated with the help of the Vatican and the Western mafia,” he told his appeal hearing in 2020. Yet he oversaw a siege of the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo, for more than three years, his snipers and artillery shells killing thousands of men, women and children in the streets and in their homes. And video footage from Srebrenica shows him reassuring a 12-year-old Muslim boy shortly before his soldiers massacre thousands of civilians. At roughly the same time, he is seen returning to a deserted Srebrenica, telling the camera: “We give this town to the Serb people as a gift.” Mladic formed a Serb nationalist triumvirate with Karadzic and Milosevic that unleashed a wave of ethnic killing in a bid to redraw the map of the region. While Karadzic was the ideologue and Milosevic the wily politician, Mladic was the soldier and his metier was waging war. Mladic had barely drawn breath before his life was indelibly marked by conflict. He was born during second world war in Kalinovik in eastern Bosnia – most accounts say in 1942, but Mladic told the tribunal he was actually born in 1943. His father was killed at the bitter end of the war, fighting for Marshal Tito, the leader who managed to knit together the multi-ethnic state of Yugoslavia and suppress simmering enmities. By most accounts, Mladic always wanted to be a soldier. He left for army training in Belgrade in the early 1960s, becoming an officer by the age of 22 and ascending to be commander of the Bosnian Serb forces in the war. Although he was revered by his men, former Yugoslav army spokesman Ljubodrag Stojadinovic once described him as “narcissistic, conceited, vain and arrogant”. During the war, he baffled international negotiators with rambling diatribes on Serbian history. In the closing days of the war, close allies questioned his mental faculties. “I respected General Mladic as a soldier and a man,” the late former Montenegrin president Momir Bulatovic told a 1990s BBC documentary. “But after three years of war, he’d lost contact with reality.” Mladic was dismissed from his post after being indicted in 1995, but he evaded capture for another 16 years. At first, he led a life of luxury, pampered by the Serbian military, but the pressure on him mounted after Milosevic fell from power in 2000. He was finally arrested in May 2011 at his cousin’s country house in northern Serbia. His daughter Ana killed herself in 1994 at the age of 23, with some accounts saying she could not bear the shame of the crimes committed by her father, though Mladic’s family dispute this. His last request before being transferred to the court was to visit her grave. During all this time, his reputation grew, his wartime leadership immortalised in murals around Republika Srpska – the Serbian entity within Bosnia. “I think that this verdict propelled general Mladic straight into a legend,” said Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik after his life sentence was upheld. “Serbs know that without him our people would have suffered much more.” Others disagree. “Wherever their army came, wherever their boot stepped in, they committed genocide,” said Munira Subasic, president of one of the Mothers of Srebrenica associations.

title: Hong Kong arts figures, fans pay tribute to Yayoi Kusama after her death at 97
description: West Kowloon arts hub chief Bernard Chan and AllRightsReserved founder Lam Shu-kam among those expressing sadness at Japanese artist’s death.
content: Hong Kong fans and cultural figures have paid tribute to Japanese avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama following her death at 97, saying her legacy will inspire generations to come. Among those expressing sadness on Thursday were West Kowloon Cultural District Authority board chairman Bernard Chan and local design studio AllRightsReserved. Adrian Cheng Chi-kong, former CEO of developer New World Development, shared a photo of himself with Kusama taken in Japan in 2022. Kusama, known for her signature polka dots and pumpkin sculptures, died on August 14 at a hospital in Tokyo from multiple organ failure. Her studio and Tokyo’s Yayoi Kusama Museum confirmed the news on Thursday. Chan said the West Kowloon art hub’s M+ museum had been honoured to host the “Yayoi Kusama: 1945 to Now” exhibition, which ran from November 2022 to May 2023. “A moment I will treasure forever was travelling to Tokyo in March 2023, to thank her in person,” Chan said in a social media post. “Spending an hour in her presence was a deeply moving experience I will never forget. She was a singular, visionary force whose art reshaped how we see the world and touched millions across the globe. “Rest in peace, Kusama-san. Your infinite light and spirit will continue to inspire generations to come.” AllRightsReserved founder Lam Shu-kam recalled the studio’s collaboration with the late artist in 2007 for the “Yayoi Kusama: Dots Obsession. Soul of Pumpkin” project at the Harbour City shopping centre in Tsim Sha Tsui. It was Hong Kong’s first large-scale outdoor exhibition of her works, curated by the design company. “Her iconic pumpkin and infinite dots invited audiences into her extraordinary artistic universe,” Lam said. “Thank you, Yayoi Kusama, for the inspiration and creativity you shared with the world. Your legacy will continue to live on through generations.” Actress Ivana Wong Yuen-chi said in a Facebook post: “Thank you for your art, your life, and your devotion. You have opened countless minds, freed soul after soul, and allowed spirits to find hope and comfort in the infinite … Rest in peace, Queen of Polka Dots.” Art critic Lau Kin-wai said Kusama’s works were very popular among younger generations because her motifs of dots and pumpkins presented a simple, colourful world. “Her works are no doubt highly commercial. They showed a colourful world with a soothing effect,” he said. One fan wrote on social media: “She views our entire planet as just one solitary dot among billions of stars in the vast cosmos … By covering everything in dots, she creates a sense of universal unity where everyone is connected as a whole.” The M+ exhibition on Kusama was popular, drawing 280,000 visitors. With more than 200 works on display, the show marked the largest retrospective of Kusama in Asia outside Japan at the time. The popularity of the show prompted the authority, which manages the West Kowloon arts hub, to curate and export it to the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao in Spain in 2023 and the Serralves Museum in Porto, Portugal, in 2024. A spokeswoman for M+ said that it was “deeply privileged” to have featured Kusama in its inaugural special exhibition following the modern art museum’s opening in 2021. The exhibition across the three venues – Hong Kong, Spain and Portugal – had attracted about 1.65 million visitors in total, she noted. “Kusama’s spirit and her art will continue to resonate far beyond her lifetime,” she said.

title: Fosun rebounds after property clean-up with core focus on growth, innovation
description: Profit attributable to shareholders rose 160 per cent to 1.72 billion yuan in the six months through June.
content: Fosun International is emerging from a painful clean-up of its property portfolio with a sharper focus on pharmaceuticals, insurance and tourism, betting that years of asset sales and debt reduction have cleared the way for a return to growth. The group swung back to stronger profitability in the first half, helped by the absence of the heavy impairments that weighed on 2025 earnings. Chairman Guo Guangchang said in a statement on Thursday that the company had completed a systematic process of “repairing the roof on a sunny day”. “Over the past few years, Fosun has steadfastly advanced its business streamlining and core business-focused strategy,” Guo said. “Fosun has now returned to a growth trajectory and is well-positioned to accelerate its growth going forward.” The rebound comes after Fosun reported a 23.4 billion yuan (US$3.48 billion) loss in 2025, with property-related impairments accounting for about 55 per cent of the provisions. The group has since sold noncore and non-strategic assets to raise cash and reduce leverage, including more than 12 billion yuan of disposals in the first half of this year. Profit attributable to shareholders rose 160 per cent to 1.72 billion yuan in the six months through June, while industrial operating profit increased 17 per cent to 3.69 billion yuan. Revenue was stable at 86.96 billion yuan, indicating the improvement was partly from last year’s low base rather than a broad-based acceleration in demand. The restructuring has nonetheless given Fosun more room to concentrate on businesses it considers to have stronger long-term prospects. Overseas operations now account for more than half of group revenue, while pharmaceuticals, insurance and tourism are emerging as the main pillars of the next phase. Innovation is central to that strategy. Fosun invested 4.2 billion yuan in technology during the period and said its pharmaceutical business had seven innovative drugs approved for 20 indications in domestic and overseas markets. It is also using artificial intelligence in drug discovery, clinical development and other parts of its healthcare operations, while expanding AI applications across tourism and insurance. Globalisation is the other major growth lever. Fosun operates across more than 40 countries and regions, and overseas revenue increased 5.3 per cent in the first half. Its pharmaceutical business continued to expand internationally, while insurance operations in Portugal and China delivered stronger earnings. Guo said Fosun would continue to pursue “innovation-driven and global development” in sectors where it has competitive advantages. “Going forward, we will continue to advance innovation-driven and global development in industries where we have established competitive advantages,” he added. “With a clear path ahead, we are confident that we can steadily restore annual profit to the 10 billion yuan level.” The recovery is not without challenges. Some businesses remain under pressure, including baijiu maker Shede Spirits, whose profit fell sharply as weak consumption and high inventories continued to weigh on the industry. In June, Fosun broke ground on the redevelopment of the former Shaw Brothers movie studio in Clear Water Bay, after paying HK$2.18 billion (US$278 million) in land premium in 2024, when Hong Kong’s property market was still under pressure. The HK$10 billion project is planned to include more than 800 luxury units and about 215,000 square feet of commercial space, with sales potentially starting in late 2027 or early 2028. “We must always grit our teeth and pull through during difficult times,” Guo – who makes only rare public appearances – said at the groundbreaking ceremony in June.

title: India’s missile tech transfer to firms signals defence self-reliance on track
description: Despite the forthcoming transfer from a state agency, Indian firms are still years away from being able to make advanced missiles.
content: India is turning to its private industry to help produce missiles, hoping a wider manufacturing base can cut its import dependence while boosting its defence export capacity and deterrence against Pakistan and China. But India’s push towards self-reliance in defence manufacturing is still a distant goal, according to analysts, citing its missile supply chain’s heavy reliance on imported components, while private firms have yet to prove that they can soon build complex weapons. On Tuesday, Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh approved the transfer of technologies developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), the research and development wing of the country’s Ministry of Defence, for all conventional missile systems to Indian defence companies for domestic production. The move is part of New Delhi’s Aatmanirbharta (self-reliance) campaign aimed at strengthening its defence manufacturing sector and reducing its dependence on overseas suppliers. Gaurav Kumar, a researcher at the United Service Institution of India, a defence think tank, said the national objective would take many years to achieve, citing the complexity of missile production. “A missile is one of the hardest things to build. It packs propulsion, electronics and software into a small tube, and everything has to work perfectly. India’s private firms have the money and the factories, but they’ve never built a full missile on their own,” Kumar said. Walter Ladwig, a senior international-relations lecturer at King’s College London, said a key challenge was how quickly private firms could build “sophisticated missiles reliably and at scale” after absorbing the technological transfer. “Transferring a design is one thing, establishing qualified production lines, suppliers and quality control is another, and some imported components will probably remain in the supply chain,” he said. However, if private firms could progress from making basic components for public-sector producers to incorporating more advanced designs, it would signal a milestone in India’s defence-industrial model, Ladwig said. Rahul Wankhede, a research analyst at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses in New Delhi, noted that firms such as Tata Advanced Systems were already supplying parts for the Akash and MRSAM air defence systems, and the Pinaka artillery weapon system. With time, these firms could develop the capability for “certified, repeatable, high-volume production”, he added. If India’s private sector could bridge gaps in areas such as advanced propulsion technologies, semiconductors and other electronics components, it would show DRDO’s technological transfer is a successful launchpad towards the objective, according to Wankhede. Kumar said that Indian companies could eventually move beyond conventional missile production towards manufacturing long-range and nuclear-capable missiles such as the Agni, citing the likes of Larsen & Toubro, Bharat Forge, Tata Advanced Systems and Adani Defence & Aerospace as potential beneficiaries. However, Kumar called on the Indian government to commit to regular and large orders from the private sector to achieve its self-reliance objective. “Without that, the new production lines sit idle. So for now, India still leans on the state firm Bharat Dynamics and on imports. Give it five to 10 years of steady orders, and private industry can seriously cut the import bill,” Kumar said. Rahul Rawat, a researcher at the Observer Research Foundation think tank’s Strategic Studies Programme, said that while India’s private defence sector had performed well in production and exports in the past few years, it still relied heavily on overseas suppliers for core components and raw materials. “This weak link needs to be bridged effectively to synchronise domestic demands and intentions to become a major global defence-industrial player,” Rawat said. Weapons supply during conflict The minister’s announcement comes as recent conflicts show how weapons can be quickly expended, underscoring the importance of a country’s defence manufacturing sector. Citing India’s four-day conflict with Pakistan last year, Kumar said: “India needs to make them faster and in bigger numbers so it doesn’t run short in a longer fight. China is the harder problem. It can keep fighting for weeks. So India needs mass, not just good missiles, and more factories help with that.” Ladwig said the conflict highlighted the need for India to build advanced weapons in sufficient quantities. “The important shift is from possessing sophisticated indigenous missile technology to having the industrial capacity to manufacture it in quantity. This [defence ministry’s initiative] should eventually make it easier for India to build larger missile inventories and replenish them more rapidly,” he added. Ladwig said that Delhi’s latest defence initiative would not help India narrow the gap with China in terms of production capacity, given Beijing’s much larger defence-industrial base. According to Wankhede, India should not attempt to match China’s “enormous defence-industrial ecosystem”. Instead, it should focus more on closing the industrial gaps that would allow it to produce weapons more efficiently and replenish inventories faster, he added. The move to transfer more defence technologies will also help boost the country’s competitiveness in defence exports, with analysts citing the success of the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile system co-developed by India and Russia. In recent years, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines have placed orders to buy the BrahMos from India, with Thailand reportedly exploring the system to boost its military capabilities. Despite the success of BrahMos, India still has a long way to go before it can become a major weapons exporter, according to Kumar. According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, India was not listed among the top 10 global arms exporters and was the world’s second largest arms importer between 2021 and 2025. “Defence exports have hit a record. More factories mean India can promise buyers faster delivery, a strong selling point in Southeast Asia, where countries want a choice beyond China and Russia. None of this shifts the balance this year,” Kumar said.

title: Alibaba pushes into South America’s AI market with launch of Brazil data centres
description: The Chinese tech giant is rapidly building AI infrastructure in emerging markets amid an intensifying US-China tech rivalry.
content: Alibaba Group Holding has launched its first data centres in South America, as the Chinese technology giant ramps up its artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout in emerging markets amid an intensifying US-China AI rivalry. The Hangzhou-based company announced on Thursday that its new Brazilian venture would operate two data centres offering local enterprises secure cloud infrastructure and a suite of “agentic AI services”. “Brazil is one of the world’s most dynamic digital economies and a new market central to Alibaba Cloud’s expansion in Latin America,” said Allen Guo, Alibaba Cloud’s general manager for the Latin America region and vice-president of international business. Alibaba launched its first data centre in the Latin American market with the opening of a Mexico facility in early 2025. With its entry into Brazil, Alibaba Cloud now has a presence in 106 “availability zones” across 31 regions, according to the company. The move underscores Alibaba’s rapid AI infrastructure buildout outside mainland China, as the firm seeks new growth markets amid a fierce US-China AI race. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. With the new local infrastructure and its growing partner ecosystem, Alibaba Cloud aimed to power Brazilian enterprises’ AI capabilities and connect them to the company’s global network, Guo added. The venture gives enterprises, start-ups, developers and public institutions in Brazil direct access to a full portfolio of cloud services running on local infrastructure, engineered for the low latency, resilience and data governance that mission-critical workloads require, according to the company. Alibaba said it was also partnering with Brazilian technology providers to help local enterprises scale AI capabilities. Local partners include Insi, one of the largest tech solution providers in the country, as well as 4Linux, which specialises in open-source software and enterprise IT services, according to the company. While US tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft expand in North America, Chinese firms are focusing on leveraging competitive pricing and open-source models to win over the rest of the global market. In June, Alibaba announced the launch of its first data centres in France, as it continued to expand its footprint in Europe amid growing calls on the continent for data sovereignty. It also launched its third data centre in South Korea earlier this month. The company has set aside massive capital for its AI infrastructure buildout, with a three-year commitment to invest 380 billion yuan (US$56.5 billion) on AI infrastructure announced in February 2025. Half of that capital had already been invested by the end of June, the company confirmed last week. The entry into Brazil also came a day after Alibaba’s launch of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next – a multimodal preview of its next-generation Qwen4 AI model, which features 125 billion parameters for its main model, with 6 billion parameters active per token, according to the company. Alibaba said revenue for AI cloud and compute services – a new reporting segment covering its cloud and chip businesses – had reached 48.4 billion yuan in the second quarter of 2026, with revenue growing at its fastest pace in 22 quarters.

title: US lawmakers condemn right-wing podcast’s calls for Chinese-American internment
description: Members of Asian-American congressional caucus warn the ‘dangerous and unacceptable’ rhetoric fuels discrimination and violence.
content: Asian-American lawmakers in the US Congress have condemned a right-wing podcast that called for the forced internment of Chinese-Americans during a hypothetical war with Beijing, warning that such rhetoric fuelled hate against the community. The joint statement was released by congresswomen Grace Meng, chairwoman of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (Capac), and Judy Chu, Capac’s chairwoman emerita, as well as congressman Ted Lieu, vice-chairman of the House Democratic Caucus. The backlash was sparked by comments made on Timcast IRL, a pro-Trump video podcast with 2.77 million subscribers on YouTube hosted by commentator Tim Pool. During an episode posted on August 14, social media influencer Ian Crossland openly floated the idea of wartime confinement. “If there was a war between the Chinese and the Americans, and the Chinese landed in, like, Alaska and started coming through Canada, what – do you think we should intern all the Chinese-Americans we can find? Because it kind of seems like we should,” Crossland said. Crossland claimed he did not want to implicate all Chinese-Americans because “that’s horrific”, but proceeded to question their allegiance. “How can you tell where their allegiances are? And how do you know if their allegiances will or won’t flip if the tide of war starts to change?” he added. Kevin Smith, another guest on the podcast, questioned whether such forced confinement would be possible today. “I don’t think you could do that now because I think while they were interning the Japanese, a lot of people probably didn’t know what was happening,” Smith said. “You can’t do stuff like that now – with social media and stuff, there’d be protests outside of each one of them.” The lawmakers slammed the “dangerous and unacceptable” rhetoric, calling it an insult to millions of loyal citizens. “These comments invoke centuries-old racist tropes that cast Chinese-Americans as perpetual foreigners and question their loyalty to the United States,” the lawmakers said in the statement on Wednesday. “Such rhetoric fuels discrimination and violence against Chinese-Americans and those perceived to be Chinese, and contributes to a climate in which one in five Americans are currently concerned about Chinese-Americans posing a threat to US society.” “To call for a return to one of the darkest chapters in US history – the incarceration of more than 120,000 American citizens of Japanese descent during World War II – is dangerous and unacceptable,” they added. “This kind of rhetoric has no place in our country and we condemn it in the strongest possible terms.” During World War II, the US government forcibly incarcerated more than 120,000 people of Japanese descent, most of whom were US citizens, in camps across the country. Decades later, Washington officially recognised the internment as a grave injustice driven by racial prejudice and war hysteria, issuing a formal government apology and financial reparations to survivors. Podcast host Pool posted a screenshot of media reports covering the controversy on social media on August 18. Reposting it, Crossland acknowledged the discussion: “It is true. The concept was discussed. I cannot undo that now.” The controversy underscores a broader, unsettling reality for the Chinese diaspora in the United States, which finds itself increasingly caught in the crossfire of geopolitical tensions and domestic politics. According to this year’s “State of Chinese-Americans Survey” – released by the Committee of 100 and the National Opinion Research Centre at the University of Chicago – 55 per cent of Asian-Americans regularly encounter assumptions that they are foreign. Unlike other racial or ethnic groups, US-born and foreign-born Asian-Americans are perceived as outsiders at nearly equal rates, a persistent stereotype that researchers say inflicts severe psychological distress on the community, according to the report. The survey also highlighted the direct link between political discourse and anti-Asian sentiment, with about 54 per cent of respondents stating that China-related rhetoric from US President Donald Trump negatively affects how Chinese-Americans are treated in the country.

title: China and Nepal built an early warning system for melting glaciers in Himalayas. Does it work?
description: Wednesday’s deadly ice-rock avalanche on high-altitude Tibet border highlights glacial instability in region vulnerable to climate change.
content: Chinese scientists have developed a cross-border early warning system with counterparts in Nepal to monitor Himalayan glacial lake outburst floods. The system has issued timely alerts over the past several years, effectively preventing casualties. But on Wednesday, a high-altitude ice-rock avalanche took everyone by surprise. The debris flow hit a river in Nepal, generating a devastating flash flood that swept all the way down to Gyirong county in the Tibet autonomous region in China. Some specialists say the disaster was triggered by glacial rock collapse. It remains unclear whether the China-Nepal early warning system had detected an anomaly before this disaster or issued an alert. But coincidentally, a paper published on Wednesday by the project team highlighted several of China’s recent successes. “These include the Himalayan glacial lake monitoring network established under the second Qinghai-Tibet scientific expedition, as well as early warning systems for ice avalanche disasters in the Yarlung Tsangpo River’s Sedongpu area and for the Cirenma Co glacial lake in the cross-border China-Nepal basin,” the team wrote in the paper for the peer-reviewed Journal of Glaciology and Geocryology. “Together, these systems have successfully issued seven early warnings [including one at the China-Nepal border last year],” they said, without specifying the latest case. The South China Morning Post has contacted lead author Wang Weicai and the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) for comment. “High-altitude ice-rock avalanches release enormous energy and are far more destructive than typical glacial lake outburst floods,” a glaciologist from a research institute in Chengdu, Sichuan province, told the Southern Weekly on Thursday. Kang Shichang, a mountain hazards expert with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, pointed to the challenges of early warning systems along transnational terrain. “In theory, detecting an ice-rock avalanche upstream could give about 20 minutes of warning. But monitoring equipment is limited at that area, and the source of the disaster is on the Nepalese side. By the time sensors pick up anything unusual, the mudslide may already be on its way,” Kang told The Paper on Thursday. The Tibetan Plateau and its surrounding areas are home to more than 100,000 glaciers. With global temperatures rising, these are melting at an accelerating rate, bringing a host of climatic and ecological consequences. The most visible manifestation of this trend is the growing frequency of glacial lake outburst floods. In 1981, the Cirenma Co glacial lake on the China-Nepal border burst, destroying the China-Nepal Friendship Bridge and claiming more than 200 lives in the Himalayan country. From 2011 to 2020, there were more than 15 such floods per year on average – three times the rate from 1981 to 1990. Chinese Qinghai-Tibet expedition findings published in 2025 identified 1,256 high-risk glacial lakes in the region – 182 of which posed an extremely high danger of outburst flooding. A research team with CAS’ Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research began work in 2017 to build the multidimensional, cross-border disaster warning system. Using satellite remote sensing, ground-based monitors and field observations, the team established a preliminary network to successfully identify and issue alerts for potential disasters. Xu Baiqing, deputy director of the institute, told a conference in Nepal in May that the early warning system continuously tracked changes in glacial lake area, water levels, glacier dynamics and the surrounding weather. On July 7 last year, patrols along the Boqu River in Tibet’s Nyalam county noticed the water had turned cloudy – a clear warning sign of a possible glacial outburst or mudslide. They reported it immediately, and local authorities quickly evacuated downstream residents. The next day, a 0.68 sq km (680,000 square metre) glacial lake on the Purepu Glacier in Gyirong county ruptured. The resulting outburst flood triggered a deadly cross-border mudslide that destroyed the China-Nepal Friendship Bridge, over a kilometre of highway and four hydropower stations. At least 18 people were killed and scores of others were reported missing. The incident occurred in part because the lake that burst had not been designated as a key monitoring target by the early warning system, Xu told the Kathmandu meeting. “It also highlighted the inherent challenges of these events, which are highly sudden and can have enormous cross-border impacts, leaving downstream areas with extremely limited time to respond once an outburst begins,” he added. While the exact cause and full impact of the latest disaster have yet to be officially confirmed, what is clear is that climate change is rapidly increasing the region’s vulnerability. Temperatures in the Himalayas are rising at more than twice the global average. Warmer weather is causing surface meltwater to seep through cracks deep into the glaciers, undermining their stability, while existing glacial lakes continue to expand. A study published last December by Zhang Guoqing and others from the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research warned that without intervention, the intensity of glacial lake outburst floods in the Himalayas was projected to rise by more than 27 per cent.

title: Hong Kong parents to get alerts over teens’ self-harm searches on Instagram
description: Meta Platforms rolls out alerts to help parents intervene when teenagers repeatedly search for self-harm-related content as part of wider safety measures.
content: Meta Platforms has started sending out alerts to parents whose children repeatedly search for content about suicide or self-harm on Instagram as part of broader efforts to strengthen online safety for young users. Parents supervising a teen’s account can receive notifications by email, text message, WhatsApp or Instagram, depending on the contact information available. They will also be directed to expert resources on how to approach potentially sensitive conversations. Philip Chua, Meta’s Asia-Pacific general manager for product public policy, said on Thursday the company wanted to balance protecting teens and allowing parents to intervene when necessary. “We think that the balance here is delicate, but the balance here should be supportive of a parent,” he said, adding that Meta already directed users searching for sensitive topics to resources including The Samaritan Befrienders Hong Kong. The global technology conglomerate said the alerts, which began rolling out this month, would be triggered by repeated searches for terms including “suicide” and “self-harm”, as well as phrases promoting such acts or suggesting that a user wants to hurt themselves. Instagram requires users to be at least 13 years old to create an account, while Meta’s Teen Accounts safeguards apply to those aged 13 to 17. Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger and Threads, this week agreed to pay up to US$18 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits brought by nearly all states in America. The suits alleged that Facebook and Instagram were deliberately designed to addict children and that Meta had misled the public about the risks they posed to young users. The company denied wrongdoing, and the settlement remains subject to judicial approval. As part of the agreement, Meta will introduce significantly tighter safeguards, including a default two-hour daily limit for teenagers; restrictions on access between midnight and 6am without parental permission; limits on notifications during school hours and stronger age-verification measures. Asked whether the settlement could spur stronger safeguards elsewhere, including Hong Kong, Chua said it had given Meta “an opportunity to set an industry standard” for age-appropriate design in the US. “We are looking forward to more conversations in Hong Kong with the regulators as well as with industry partners to really make sure that the age-appropriate experience is one that is right for Hong Kong teens,” he said. The company also announced a broader package of measures for Hong Kong parents and educators, including a digital safety toolkit it plans to distribute through more than 150 family service units and 1,300 primary and secondary schools, reaching more than 35,000 carers. It will also train about 100 parent-teacher association representatives under a “Digital Parent Navigation” programme, while promoting interactive educational materials on screen time, cyber safety and healthy digital habits. Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data Ada Chung Lai-ling said protecting children online was a shared responsibility among parents, educators, social media operators and other parts of society. She said her office had held more than 100 anti-doxxing talks at schools, reaching more than 30,000 students.
