It was also working with overseas privacy regulators to examine how online platforms protected children’s data. “In this area, our work is only ongoing,” Chung said. “There is no point at which it ends.” Technology and innovation sector lawmaker Duncan Chiu, who had earlier raised the possibility of restricting children’s social media use in the legislature, cautioned against relying on blanket bans. “I don’t believe one law can change everything,” he said, arguing that children would find ways around restrictions and that platforms, schools and parents all needed to play a role. Andy Chan Ying-kit, supervisor at the Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups, also said parental intervention should not begin with punishment when children encountered trouble online. “First, deal with the emotions, then deal with the problem,” he said. Chan added that parents should preserve evidence, avoid blaming children who may themselves be victims and seek professional counselling support if needed. Meta said its Teen Accounts protections had already been fully rolled out across Facebook, Instagram and Messenger in Hong Kong. They include age-appropriate content restrictions, limits on contact with strangers and reminders after 60 minutes of daily use. Parents can also impose additional time limits or block access during certain hours. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Crypto slump, AI boom overshadow CZ’s bullish pitch at Hong Kong’s Bitcoin Asia
description: Capital, talent and public attention have moved from crypto to AI, leaving the digital asset industry feeling ‘smaller’, says organiser.
content: Anxiety over the booming AI trade and bitcoin’s uncertain future is overshadowing this year’s Bitcoin Asia conference in Hong Kong, as a lingering crypto slump dampens enthusiasm despite a star appearance by Binance founder Zhao Changpeng. Zhao, known in the industry as “CZ”, struck a bullish tone during his highly anticipated appearance on Thursday. Speaking to a large crowd, the 48-year-old billionaire entrepreneur drew applause and cheers by declaring that bitcoin “will for sure become more important than gold”. “I think bitcoin will overtake gold pretty soon,” he added. The former Binance CEO also commended the United Arab Emirates for having “the most progressive crypto regulations”, while noting that Hong Kong was “moving pretty quickly” compared to a “little bit more conservative” Singapore. His optimism stood in stark contrast to the prevailing mood at the conference. “Psychologically, I think this has been one of the hardest bear markets we’ve had, because this time it wasn’t just the price of bitcoin that took a hit,” said Brandon Green, CEO of conference organiser BTC, during his opening address. “This time, the bitcoiners’ ego also took a hit.” Capital, talent and public attention had moved from crypto to artificial intelligence, leaving the digital asset industry feeling “smaller”, Green noted. Bitcoin Asia – the regional edition of one of the world’s largest cryptocurrency events – debuted in Hong Kong in 2024 at the invitation of the local government, which continues to position the city as a digital asset hub. However, this year’s gathering appeared to lack the buzz of last year’s edition, which featured Eric Trump, the second-born son of US President Donald Trump, promoting his American Bitcoin venture. While the younger Trump hailed China as “a hell of a power” in crypto during the 2025 event, a senior Hong Kong official from the city’s Securities and Futures Commission and legislator Johnny Ng Kit-chong pulled out at the last minute amid rising US-China trade tensions. Ng returned to the conference stage this year, touting Hong Kong as an “undisputed premier hub for bitcoin and the Web3 ecosystem in Asia” while praising the industry’s “incredible resilience” through “short-term volatility”. Earlier this week, bitcoin broke above US$80,000 for the first time in three months following a downturn that wiped out nearly half its value earlier this year. However, analysts cautioned against viewing the rebound as a definitive bull market return. On Thursday, bitcoin remained nearly 37 per cent below its record high of US$126,000 set in October. Compounding market uncertainties, surging demand for AI computing power has driven several bitcoin mining firms to pivot towards computing infrastructure. Canaan, for instance, a Hangzhou-founded and Singapore-headquartered mining giant, is expanding into energy-related compute infrastructure, according to Leo Wang, vice-president of capital markets and corporate development. “The future of bitcoin may become increasingly narrow,” Wang said on the sidelines of the event. He pointed to bitcoin’s once-every-four-years “halving” events – programmed code updates that cut miner rewards in half to control inflation – which naturally reduce token production and thin out mining participation. Wang believed that while the industry would not disappear, the era of hyper-growth and windfall profits was over. Still, he reaffirmed that bitcoin remained Canaan’s core business.

title: Macroscope | Bond market revolt signals fading confidence in US economic leadership
description: From surging debt to trade wars with Canada, self-harm has been the main consequence of Trump’s reckless policy decisions.
content: Two years ago, the prospect of a trade war between the United States and Canada, two of the world’s most closely integrated economies, would have been unthinkable. However, US President Donald Trump’s recklessness and capriciousness know no bounds. Last week’s breakdown in negotiations between the North American neighbours, which triggered the imposition of US tariffs of 50 per cent on a wide range of Canadian goods, showed the degree to which Trump’s trade policies are vindictive, politicised and self-defeating. According to Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has responded in kind by announcing levies of up to 50 per cent on hundreds of US goods, the White House changed the terms of the deal at the eleventh hour. US negotiators insisted Ottawa renounce its promotion of French as a coequal language with English and agree to measures that would restrict its ability to strike trade deals with other countries. Although Canada’s economy – which sends more than 70 per cent of its exports to the US – will bear the brunt of a full-blown trade war, the US will suffer, too. Canada is the second-largest US trading partner after Mexico, while the two nations’ automotive supply chains are deeply integrated. Trump’s threat to raise tariffs on Canadian cars and automotive parts to 50 per cent poses a huge risk to the US car industry and its supplier network. Self-harm has been the main consequence of Trump’s protectionist and highly expansionary fiscal policies. While the entire world is contending with the geopolitical and economic fallout from Trump’s second presidency, the biggest casualty – and the one that matters most to global markets – is the management of the US economy. Last year, the Taco acronym, which stands for “Trump always chickens out”, was popular among investors, many of whom believed Trump’s bark was worse than his bite. While equity investors continue to be dazzled by the boom in artificial intelligence, bond markets are in a less forgiving mood this year, partly because of the inflationary impact of the energy shock and the dramatic increase in debt issuance by the leading technology companies. However, the main reason yields on long-term bonds have risen sharply is the lack of credibility in US economic policy. Barks can be just as damaging as bites, especially when they are menacing and incessant. The uncertainty created by Trump’s policies has reached a dangerous tipping point as the White House becomes more concerned about a sharper and disorderly sell-off in bond markets. The rise in the 30-year US Treasury yield from 4.8 per cent on June 24 to 5.3 per cent on August 17 – its highest level since 2007 – unnerved Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to such an extent that he intervened in the debt market in an effort to reduce some of the upwards pressure on long-dated bond yields. The unexpected decision by Bessent on August 19 to double the Treasury’s planned purchases of outstanding 10- to 30-year debt showed how far the Trump administration is willing to go to manipulate bond markets by artificially suppressing yields. It also underscored the lack of credibility and acute tensions in US policymaking. First, by seeking to push down long-dated bond yields, Bessent is making debt issuance less predictable and politicising the Treasury. Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman said that, far from being a credible treasury secretary, Bessent has become “a consummate Trump sycophant”. Even hedge fund billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller, who mentored Bessent in his early career as a trader, said he should not be fiddling with interest rates. Second, Bessent’s intervention has shone a spotlight on the causes of the surge in bond yields. Last week, America’s public debt hit a record US$40 trillion, with half the rise occurring in the last decade. As the debt burden swells, investors are starting to demand a higher premium to hold Treasuries. “The bond market’s message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter,” Citadel Securities said. Third, by meddling in bond markets, Bessent has put Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh in a tighter spot. Already facing criticism for ditching forward guidance on the likely trajectory of interest rates, Warsh wants markets to play a stronger role in shaping expectations for monetary policy and has welcomed the rise in bond yields, which helps the Fed quell inflation. It is bad enough that two of the world’s most important policymakers strongly disagree when it comes to the signals from bond markets. It is worse that the growing tension between the Fed and the Treasury is mainly attributable to the mismanagement of the US economy, which has been much more severe since Trump’s return to the White House. The Taco narrative was deeply flawed. The uncertainty and unpredictability that pervade Trump’s presidency are damaging in themselves. Bond markets are sending a message that the US must attend to its self-inflicted wounds.

title: Himalayan glacier collapse hits crucial China-Nepal trade route as casualties mount
description: Tragedy at Gyirong hub lays bare climate risks along fragile mountain corridor.
content: The catastrophic flash floods and mudslide that devastated the Gyirong Port crossing along the China-Nepal border on Wednesday have dealt a heavy blow to China-Nepal trade and imperilled Kathmandu’s push to cut reliance on Indian transit routes. However, if Beijing and Kathmandu are to proceed with ambitious infrastructure projects, they are expected to take environmental factors into consideration and adjust their construction methods accordingly, one expert said. Chinese officials confirmed three deaths and said more than 500 people, including 260 foreign nationals, remained missing on Thursday. Nepal said more than 900 people were missing, including 517 foreigners, and at 5pm Thursday its official death toll was 359. China’s Ministry of Natural Resources said on Thursday that the deadly mudslide was initially triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse inside Nepal that rapidly evolved into a high-velocity debris flow. According to Guo Zhaocheng, a senior engineer at the Aero Geophysical Survey and Remote Sensing Centre under the ministry, the collapsing ice rushed down the channel at high speed, swept up vast glacial moraine, or scraped rock, and evolved into a debris flow before hitting Gyirong Port and surging downstream into Nepali territory. Gyirong Port serves as the strategic anchor connecting China and Nepal. It handled nearly 30 per cent of total trade volume between the two in 2024, and is a primary overland entry point for Indian pilgrims travelling to Tibet. Some 280 Indian pilgrims remain missing after the disaster, according to India’s foreign ministry. Gyirong is one of three international gateways along the 1,415km (879-mile) Himalayan frontier between Nepal and China, where it operates alongside Purang and Zhangmu to handle both passenger travel and cross-border commerce. All six major overland crossings on this border lie within China’s Tibet autonomous region, with the other three functioning exclusively as commercial trade points. “This massive mudslide has severely affected Gyirong port and will inevitably hit trade between China and Nepal hard,” said Liu Zongyi, director of the Centre for South Asian Studies at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies. “Nepal imports far more from China than it exports, so its dependence on the Chinese economy remains significant. “Establishing road and rail links with China is essential for Nepal if it wants to alter its economic trajectory and geopolitical landscape,” Liu said, highlighting the broader stakes for Kathmandu. “To transform itself from a landlocked country into a land-linked one, connectivity with China is indispensable.” At the centrepiece of these infrastructure ambitions is the proposed China-Nepal railway, which is currently undergoing feasibility studies. Designed to extend from Shigatse through Gyirong directly to Kathmandu, the megaproject aims to drastically reduce transit times and freight costs across the Himalayas. Zhang Li, deputy director of the Fudan Institute of Belt and Road & Global Governance, said the disaster would cause short-term disruptions to the operation of Gyirong Port, the preliminary geological survey work for the China-Nepal railway, and the cross-border movement of materials and personnel. However, “they will not change the overall direction of China-Nepal connectivity and cooperation”, he asserted. “On the contrary, they will prompt both sides to adopt more refined and meticulous approaches in railway route selection, disaster monitoring and early warning systems, as well as the disaster-prevention standards for the China-Nepal power interconnection project.” Yet the physical realities of the terrain present formidable obstacles. Liu cautioned that the rail link remained a long-term plan. “The geological conditions along the route are extremely difficult. If the railway is built, it would have to rely heavily on tunnels.” “These projects are strategic and especially significant for Nepal, as they are crucial for reducing its dependence on India. If construction proceeds in the future, environmental factors will be taken into account and construction methods adjusted to make them more scientific and more rational,” Liu said. In a push to boost trade with China, the Nepalese government has pledged to start construction on the Tokha-Chhahare Tunnel. Connecting Tokha in Kathmandu to Chhahare in Nuwakot, the project lies along the vital Kathmandu-Rasuwagadhi transit corridor and could cut bilateral transport costs by up to 50 per cent, according to local media. Expanding cooperation beyond transit, the two countries are also working to construct a 16km, 220kV power transmission line connecting Nepal’s Chilime region to Gyirong. The landmark initiative is designed to enable two-way electricity trading and optimise seasonal grid balance. China’s deepening footprint along the Himalayan crest continues to draw scrutiny from India – Nepal’s largest trading partner by a wide margin – which strongly opposes the railway initiative. New Delhi’s fears that a modern rail and road link stretching from Tibet to Kathmandu brings Chinese logistics closer to the Siliguri Corridor – the narrow, strategic strip of land connecting mainland India to its northeastern states. By using landlocked Nepal’s economic reliance on Indian transit routes, New Delhi has historically deployed formal and informal restrictions to maintain geopolitical leverage. Providing Nepal with an alternative overland trade route through China threatens to undermine India’s historical transit monopoly and diplomatic clout over Kathmandu. The disaster follows a recurring pattern of environmental shocks along the fragile corridor. In July last year, a glacial lake outburst about 35km upstream in Tibet sent a wall of water surging down the Bhotekoshi River, destroying the Nepal-China Friendship Bridge at Gyirong, halting border traffic for months and leading to 17 deaths. Researchers from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), alongside partner organisations in Nepal and China, are assessing whether a high-altitude ice-rock avalanche was the initial trigger for the disaster. “The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time most probably triggered by an ice avalanche [that] blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist for ICIMOD, said in a statement. According to the US Geological Survey and preliminary assessments by earth scientists, the disaster could have been triggered when a collapsing glacier set off a violent chain reaction that caused a powerful surge of water and debris down narrow mountain gorges into the valley. Meanwhile, earth scientists are issuing cautions about climate-driven destabilisation of the high Himalayas. The United Nations reported that Nepal has lost nearly a third of its ice cover in just over 30 years, with glacial loss accelerating 65 per cent faster over the past 10 years than the previous decade. Rising temperatures are actively thawing the region’s permafrost – the centuries-old frozen soil and rock anchoring the steep mountain faces. As the structural binder thaws, massive rock and ice formations will become unstable, turning routine slope failures into catastrophic torrents downstream.

title: Iran endures 6 months of US strikes as Trump’s war goals hit ‘dangerous impasse’
description: ‘I don’t think the administration is any closer to finding a way out of this,’ an ex-diplomat says, as Tehran bets time is on its side.
content: The Iran war has reached its endgame: a costly stalemate. Six months after US and Israeli ⁠forces attacked Iran, killing its supreme leader and maiming his son and successor, the Iranian government is under economic siege, but it still holds power and believes it has time on its side. A threat by US President Donald Trump to impose crippling new sanctions on Iran faces a fundamental problem: Tehran is betting he will not take the final step to break the stalemate – aggressively enforcing secondary sanctions on the countries keeping its economy afloat, foremost among them China and India. Washington’s latest measures, announced on Monday, mark a new phase in the conflict that began on February 28, shifting the battlefield from missiles and air strikes to Iran’s oil revenues, banks and trading partners. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the ‌United States will cut off the financial lifelines sustaining Iran’s economy, while a US-led naval blockade restricts Tehran’s oil exports and access to hard currency. “The [Trump] administration is groping in a sort of desperate fashion to try to find a pathway out of this,” said Aaron David Miller, a former US diplomat and senior fellow at Carnegie Endowment. Bessent invoked the 1944 D-Day landings in France during second world war when he unveiled the sanctions, but Miller said: “To me, this isn’t D-Day. It’s Desperation Day. I don’t think the administration is any closer to finding a way out of this.” Michael Knights, head of research at Horizon Engage, a New York-based strategic advisory platform, said the blockade may prove more consequential than the sanctions themselves because Iran’s immediate challenge was no longer how to survive economic pressure but how to break out of it. Tehran has spent decades adapting to sanctions and endured previous “maximum pressure” campaigns without altering its behaviour, he said. Mounting economic pressure, he said, may increase Iran’s incentive to raise the cost of the confrontation for its adversaries by pressuring ⁠Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia, to push Washington towards a diplomatic off-ramp. Knights said Iran could increasingly adopt the model used by its Houthi allies in the Red Sea: periodic attacks, intermittent negotiations and a prolonged campaign of disruption short of all-out war, potentially targeting shipping, ports, energy infrastructure ‌or other critical assets to make the conflict increasingly costly for Gulf states to tolerate. Washington rejects that assessment and says the balance of power is in its favour. “The Iranian economy is in free fall and the regime’s military has been decimated,” US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in response to questions for this article. “President Trump holds all the cards, and we are cutting off every financial lifeline the regime has remaining.” Alan Eyre, a former US diplomat who worked on Iran, questioned whether Washington has the international support and bureaucratic machinery to make the sanctions stick. He said that unlike the multilateral campaign preceding the 2015 nuclear deal between ⁠Tehran and major powers, which curbed Iran’s nuclear programme in exchange for lifting ⁠sanctions, the latest measures rely on public threats rather than sustained diplomacy with allies and trading partners. Iranian officials dismiss the US strategy as a replay of a playbook that has already failed. One senior Iranian official said that countries such as China would not stop cooperating with Iran simply to serve US interests. Some political analysts say the strategy faces ‌a deeper flaw: from North Korea to Russia and Iran itself, sanctions have rarely forced governments to abandon goals they view as existential for their survival. The senior Iranian official said Tehran believes Washington’s broader objective is to fuel domestic discontent in the hope that economic hardship could eventually translate into political unrest, but that the “maximum pressure” campaign failed during Trump’s first term and would ‌fail again. “If ‌the pressure increases, Iran’s approach will change too,” he said, adding that Gulf Arab governments understood that squeezing Tehran further could put them at greater risk as well. For Iran’s rulers, the biggest threat may not be economic pain itself. It may ‌be the risk that worsening hardship again spills into mass unrest, according to insiders and an Iranian official. Annual inflation reached 66 per cent in July, while consumer prices were 87.9 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to Iran’s Statistical Centre. Food prices rose 128 per cent year on year. President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged the ⁠severity of the squeeze last week, saying: “Our problems have multiplied several times over, while our income has also fallen.” Economic grievances have repeatedly erupted into nationwide protests in recent years. In January, demonstrations over economic hardship were crushed by the Revolutionary Guards and the Basij militia, with thousands killed. The ⁠appointment this month of Hossein Taeb, a main architect of previous crackdowns, to lead the Basij was one of the clearest signs yet of official concern about renewed unrest, a former reformist official said. The Basij, a paramilitary force affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards, has repeatedly been deployed by Iran’s clerical rulers to suppress protests. That points to a paradox at the heart of Washington’s strategy: sanctions may deepen Iran’s economic damage without forcing its rulers to change course. The leadership has historically answered domestic unrest with ‌repression and external pressure with threats of retaliation abroad. For the Gulf ‌states, the calculation is especially fraught. They prefer economic and diplomatic pressure to another round of war, but fear an outcome that enables Iran to declare victory while retaining the ability to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global oil supply route that Tehran has effectively blocked, pushing up global oil prices. Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Centre, said Gulf governments are unconvinced that sanctions alone can rapidly alter Iran’s behaviour, given the leadership’s resilience and ability to maintain internal control. Significant political change or the collapse of Iran’s theocratic leadership, he said, is unlikely to come quickly. The result is a “dangerous impasse” if mediated talks fail to produce a breakthrough. Washington wants Iran to abandon its leverage over Hormuz without conceding Tehran a role in managing the waterway, Iran wants the US naval blockade lifted without appearing to surrender, and Gulf states want the conflict contained without letting Iran emerge as the victor.

title: ‘Strong signal’: South Korea raises rates again to fight inflation, rising home prices
description: Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun-song says the pre-emptive moves aim to help ‘reduce the costs to the economy’.
content: South Korea’s central bank has raised interest rates for a second straight month, with analysts saying its semiconductor boom has given policymakers room to confront inflation, a weak won and rising home prices, but at the cost of a deeper squeeze on indebted households and small businesses. The Bank of Korea (BOK) lifted its benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage point to 3.0 per cent on Thursday, a month after an identical increase took it to 2.75 per cent in July. The latest move brought the rate to its highest level since February 2025 and signalled a central bank willing to accept some damage to domestic demand to contain broader financial risks. Households with housing-related loans, small businesses and other borrowers are expected to feel the pressure most acutely. But with semiconductor exports and investment driving stronger-than-expected growth, economists said the BOK had decided the greater danger lay in moving too slowly. The Monetary Policy Board made that priority clear in its statement, saying: “It is important to prevent inflationary pressures from becoming widespread through pre-emptive action, and it is also necessary to continue paying attention to financial stability risks. “The board will decide the timing and pace of further increases in the Base Rate while assessing trends in inflation and the domestic economy, as well as financial stability.” BOK Governor Shin Hyun-song described the consecutive July and August rate increases as “a step outside convention” intended to send “a strong signal” about the central bank’s determination to stabilise financial markets. The rate increase came as the BOK sharply upgraded its economic growth forecasts for both this year and next, citing robust semiconductor exports and investment. It now expects the South Korean economy to grow 3.3 per cent in 2026 – up from its previous forecast of 2.6 per cent – and 2.9 per cent in 2027, up from 2.1 per cent. The central bank said the domestic economy continued to grow strongly, led by exports and investment, while improving income conditions supported a gradual recovery in consumption. It expects robust growth to continue as semiconductor exports and investment remain strong. South Korea’s external accounts have also benefited from the semiconductor boom. The country recorded a cumulative current-account surplus of US$191.01 billion in the first six months of 2026, the largest half-year surplus on record and roughly four times the US$47.87 billion surplus recorded during the same period in 2025. “By controlling inflation expectations through pre-emptive measures and responding early before price increases spread, we can ultimately reduce the costs to the economy,” Shin said. He also expressed concern about continued rapid increases in housing prices in the Seoul metropolitan area. Although price growth has slowed in some parts of Seoul, overall housing costs across the capital region have continued to rise at a high pace, and household loans have also increased. Shin acknowledged that “it is unreasonable to control housing prices solely through interest rates”, but said the latest rate increase would help ease the upward trend. The weak won against the US dollar is another factor behind the BOK’s move to raise rates. The currency had fallen to around 1,550 won per dollar in late June, its weakest level in 17 years, but has since recovered to the upper 1,300-won range. “The won-dollar rate has stabilised to a large extent, but historically, the won is still very weak,” Shin said, adding that a stronger won would help curb inflation by lowering import prices. Economics Professor Song Heon-jae of the University of Seoul said he was surprised by the back-to-back rate increases. “Through the rate increases, the central bank is seeking to stabilise the financial market, even if it may hurt households and small businesses saddled with debts and other borrowers,” Song told This Week in Asia. South Korea’s household credit balance topped 2,000 trillion won (US$1.45 trillion) for the first time in the second quarter of 2026, driven by rising housing transactions and debt-financed investments. Younger households are particularly exposed to the effects of higher borrowing costs because of their leveraged investments in equities and housing. “Financial authorities are confident that robust exports led by semiconductors would be enough to make up for the increases’ negative impact on domestic demand,” Song said. Inflation remains another major concern. Consumer prices rose 3.1 per cent year on year in May and 3.2 per cent in June before easing to 2.8 per cent in July. Although the July figure was the lowest in three months, it remained above the BOK’s 2 per cent target. The BOK expects inflation to remain above its target for a considerable period as elevated cost pressures pass through to consumer prices and stronger incomes gradually boost demand. It forecasts headline inflation at 2.7 per cent this year and 2.3 per cent next year. High economic growth can add to inflationary pressure as rising incomes increase demand. The BOK has therefore emphasised the need to act before price increases become more broadly entrenched. The rate increase could also support the won by narrowing the interest-rate gap between South Korea and the United States as a smaller differential can reduce incentives for investors to move funds into dollar-denominated assets. Economics Professor Kim Sung-hyun of Sungkyunkwan University said the growth trend was likely to continue into next year, citing long-term semiconductor contracts and strong demand for products from Samsung and SK Hynix. “The government and the central bank are giving priority to stabilising the financial market through the rate increases, even though it would slow economic growth somewhat and increase the burden on borrowers, including the government,” Kim said. Hur Jung, an economics professor at Sogang University, said the won’s recent appreciation against the dollar could prove temporary, partly because of increased foreign-currency supplies from major semiconductor exporters such as Samsung and SK Hynix. “However, there will soon be a great demand for dollars when South Korea starts implementing its promised US$350 billion investment in the US, driving the exchange rate higher again,” he said. At the same time, the government was pursuing an expansionary fiscal policy to stimulate economic growth and address income disparities, despite inflation concerns, Hur said. “Under these circumstances, the bank is likely to raise the rate again by another 0.25 percentage point sometime in the coming six months,” he said. The BOK’s latest decision highlighted the “difficult balance” facing South Korean policymakers: keeping inflation and housing-market risks under control without undermining domestic demand, Hur added. Economics Professor Kim Gwang-suk of Hanyang University said inflation was likely to ease towards 2 per cent, while the central bank could seek to maintain its benchmark rate between 3.25 per cent and 3.5 per cent in the foreseeable future. “The rate increases will help curb rising housing prices. But they will put greater burdens on those relying on debt, while causing no major impact on large companies that are enjoying the export boom,” he said.

title: Hong Kong expands AI sandbox with projects that include banks, securities and insurance
description: Regulators select 36 use cases involving dozens of financial institutions and tech partners to test AI use in onboarding, payments, claims and customer service.
content: Hong Kong’s financial regulators have selected the first batch of projects for an expanded generative artificial-intelligence (GenAI) testing programme spanning banking, securities, insurance and pensions, as the city explores the use of more autonomous AI agents in financial services. A total of 36 use cases were selected for the first cohort of the expanded GenAI Sandbox++ programme, according to a joint statement on Thursday by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), Insurance Authority and Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority. The projects involve 30 financial institutions and 27 technology partners, with participants including Ant Bank (Hong Kong), WeChat Pay Hong Kong and HSBC Life (International). Technical trials are expected to begin later this year on a platform managed by Cyberport’s Artificial Intelligence Supercomputing Centre, the statement showed. The first cohort will focus on “agentic AI” – systems capable of carrying out tasks and making decisions with a greater degree of autonomy, and the trials will cover end-to-end processes including customer onboarding, payments, insurance claims and customer interactions, according to the statement. HKMA chief executive Eddie Yue Wai-man said that the programme would foster partnerships between a wider range of financial institutions and technology companies, helping Hong Kong strengthen its position as an international financial centre and innovation hub. “These partnerships are unlocking the potential of agentic AI to create new opportunities. Through the GenAI Sandbox++, the HKMA will continue to promote cross-sectoral and ecosystem collaboration,” Yue said in the statement. And SFC CEO Julia Leung Fung-yee said: “The financial industry’s exploration of agentic AI marks a pivotal step forward in developing a future-ready Hong Kong market, where greater system autonomy is underpinned by sound governance and clear accountability.” The Sandbox++ was launched in March as an expansion of the GenAI Sandbox initiated by the HKMA and Cyberport in 2024, bringing together Hong Kong’s four financial regulators and extending testing to securities and capital markets, asset and wealth management, insurance, mandatory provident funds and stored-value facilities. The initiative continues to focus on three key areas – risk management, fraud prevention and customer experience – while exploring the use of AI to monitor and mitigate risks created by other AI systems.

title: China keeps yuan in check as PBOC resists sharp rise against weaker US dollar: analysts
description: Compared with a more than 2 per cent decline in the US dollar index since late July, the yuan gained less than 1 per cent against the dollar.
content: As the US dollar weakened amid recent US Treasury market interventions, analysts noted that the Chinese yuan had strengthened by a smaller margin, highlighting Beijing’s caution over allowing a sharp appreciation in the currency. Compared with a more than 2 per cent decline in the US dollar index since late July amid two US Treasury interventions – a joint US-Japan currency intervention to support the yen and the Treasury’s move to expand long-term bond buy-backs – the yuan has gained less than 1 per cent against the dollar, according to a note issued by Gavekal Dragonomics on Wednesday. “The response of the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) to these unusual interventions from the US has been telling,” He Wei, a China economist at the Beijing-based research firm, said in the note. Rather than seizing the opportunity to push the currency higher, He said the PBOC resisted market pressure for appreciation, with the Chinese currency even “achieving some depreciation in trade-weighted terms”. “That reaction confirms the PBOC’s turn to a more cautious stance on the currency in 2026, and suggests the renminbi will probably not move a lot more in coming months.” On Thursday, the PBOC set the yuan’s midpoint, or the daily fixing rate, at 6.7840 per US dollar, slightly weaker than 6.7829 a day earlier. The level was also weaker than the offshore yuan, which traded at 6.721 per US dollar at midday on Thursday. For much of the past few weeks, global markets have been closely watching how US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been navigating a bond rout that pushed long-term US Treasury yields to multi-year highs. After a rare joint US-Japan intervention in late July amid the yen’s slide – a move many analysts saw as partly aimed at limiting selling pressure on US Treasuries – the US Treasury last week followed up with plans to at least double the size of some long-end bond buy-backs. Gavekal’s He said that after a sharp single-day drop in the US dollar index following the buy-back announcement, the PBOC strengthened the yuan’s daily fixing by just 46 pips, far less than the 219-pip strengthening after a similarly sized decline in the US dollar index following former Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell’s dovish speech in August 2024. “The central bank’s tolerance for a stronger currency thus appears to be fading,” He said. He added that if the US dollar weakened further, the PBOC would probably tolerate only a gradual appreciation of the yuan against the dollar, while keeping the pace slower than the appreciation of other currencies, so that the effective exchange rate weakens. But some analysts said the cautious approach did not signal a shift away from Beijing’s broader preference for a stable currency with room for gradual appreciation. Cliff Zhao, chief economist at CCB International in Hong Kong, said central bank caution on daily fixing was not a rejection of reasonable yuan appreciation, but an effort to prevent sentiment from overheating and to keep the exchange rate broadly stable. Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, shared a similar view, saying the approach was a way for the PBOC to manage short-term volatility. “The central bank does not oppose yuan appreciation, as a stronger currency can make yuan-denominated assets more attractive and support the internationalisation of the yuan. But it is usually wary of rapid appreciation,” he said. Xu added that modest yuan appreciation was the most likely scenario for the rest of the year, as concerns over the fiscal sustainability of developed economies weighed on their currencies, while the recent stronger macro policy support underpinned the yuan.

title: China vice-premier signals reform to reshape central-local finances amid funding pressure
description: Ding Xuexiang discusses a fiscal reset through expanded local discretion, bigger outlays from the central government and scientific fiscal management pilots.
content: Against a backdrop of softened economic growth and slumping land-transfer proceeds that are squeezing local coffers across China, the nation’s top-ranked vice-premier has cast the spotlight on reforms to realign fiscal ties between the central and local governments. During an inspection tour of Anhui province on Tuesday and Wednesday, Ding Xuexiang attended a symposium on “pilot scientific fiscal management” programmes, and Xinhua reported that the vice-premier said Beijing would “increase local governments’ discretionary fiscal resources” – a policy objective written into China’s 15th five-year plan (2026 to 2030). The central government will also increase its share of national fiscal outlays while directing more funding to national strategic priorities and strengthening basic livelihood safeguards, Ding reportedly said. During his stay in Anhui, Ding also visited a county-level finance bureau to inspect a scientific fiscal management pilot scheme and grass-roots fiscal operations, according to Xinhua. Ding’s visit came at a time when none of China’s provinces can fully finance their spending with locally generated fiscal revenue, according to a July research note from Guizhou-based Huachuang Securities. It said the average provincial fiscal self-sufficiency rate stood at 55.9 per cent in the first quarter of this year, and that such revenue-spending gaps were made up through central-to-local fiscal transfer payments. And the note singled out Shanghai as a particular case in point. The city has long ranked among China’s strongest provincial-level fiscal performers, regularly posting a fiscal surplus. Yet, even Shanghai swung into a shortfall in the first three months of 2026, as year-on-year revenue growth stood at 2 per cent while expenditures surged 20 per cent from a year earlier. Since local governments bear direct responsibility for local development, they ought to be granted greater discretionary fiscal powers Ye Yongqing, tax lawyer In a mid-August press release, Tang Zaifu, an official with the Ministry of Finance, pointed out that the situation was normal under the existing fiscal system. “The central government has ramped up fiscal transfer payments, so local governments can still achieve overall fiscal balance,” Tang said. Some analysts noted how the vice-premier’s remarks underscored that realigning central-local fiscal relations remained one of Beijing’s top priorities. “With the 14th five‑year plan having already set out a systemic framework, the 15th five‑year plan lays out concrete operational steps,” said Ye Yongqing, a tax lawyer with Beijing-based Anli Partners. “It indicates that the structural gap between local governments’ revenues and spending has grown substantial.” Ye also noted that the increased priority given to this reform stemmed from a longer-than-anticipated property downturn, which has crushed land-transfer proceeds and related tax receipts. “That has gradually laid bare local governments’ revenue shortfalls,” he said. Figures from the finance ministry show that land‑transfer proceeds totalled 977.8 billion yuan (US$145.5 billion) from January to June, marking a year-on-year decline of 31.5 per cent. “Reliance on central-to-local fiscal transfer payments naturally suffers from efficiency shortfalls and limited transparency. Since local governments bear direct responsibility for local development, they ought to be granted greater discretionary fiscal powers,” Ye added. For years, consumption tax has been levied predominantly at the production stage, with all proceeds accruing to the central government Lu Zhe, economist Some analysts also identify the consumption tax – levied across 15 categories, including alcohol, automobiles and cigarettes – as a key policy lever to address the imbalance. Finance ministry data shows domestic consumption tax reached 867.3 billion yuan (US$129.04 billion) in the first half of this year, making it China’s fourth-largest source of tax revenue, trailing value-added tax, corporate income tax and personal income tax. “For years, consumption tax has been levied predominantly at the production stage, with all proceeds accruing to the central government,” said Lu Zhe, chief economist at Suzhou-based Soochow Securities. He proposed shifting collection downstream to the wholesale or retail stage and steadily devolving the related revenue to local governments, arguing that the move would “both bolster local fiscal receipts and further incentivise local authorities to improve the consumption environment”. China has overhauled central-local fiscal arrangements before. The landmark tax-sharing reform of 1994 came after years in which the bulk of tax revenue accrued to local governments, leaving Beijing chronically short of fiscal resources. This time, some say, the challenges to turning the tide appear more daunting. “Back then, China’s economy was at the start of a fresh upward cycle,” Ye noted. “Pushing through reform is far easier when growth is accelerating.” Meanwhile, the available policy levers appear more limited. Beyond the consumption tax, property tax was once seen as another key tool to broaden local revenue streams. To date, it has been piloted only in Shanghai and Chongqing. “Several years ago, authorities sought to expand the property-tax pilot to more cities,” Ye recalled. “But the pandemic struck, and the real estate market weakened sharply in 2021. The reform now appears to have been put on hold indefinitely.”

title: Hong Kong retirees’ living costs grow 3 times city’s average on more northbound travel
description: Travel costs surged by 10 points over the six-year period, the highest among all items, followed by food, dining and cross-border transport.
content: Hong Kong retirees are facing living cost growth nearly three times the city’s average over the past five years, mainly driven by the strong demand for northbound travel, according to a new report. The findings came from the first edition of the Hong Kong-Macau Retirement Expense Index, a gauge reflecting retiree inflation, conducted jointly by the Institute of Financial Planners of Hong Kong (IFPHK) and YF Life Trustees. The index rose to 131.6 in 2026, up from 127 in 2023 and 100 in 2020, marking an annualised growth rate of over 5 per cent from November 2020 to May 2026, the institute and the insurer said in a statement on Thursday. The figures from 2023 and 2020 were based on surveys done by IFPHK, which excluded Macau. Travel between Hong Kong and mainland China was restricted during Covid-19, and only opened fully after February 2023. In comparison, Hong Kong’s composite consumer price index inched up only about 1.8 per cent per annum over the same period, according to official data. “Following Covid, the frequency of retirees travelling abroad and commuting between (the city and) mainland China has increased significantly, leading to substantial growth in transport and accommodation expenses,” said IFPHK CEO Paris Yeung at a briefing on Thursday. “Together with food prices and dining-out costs, these all constitute key components of retirees’ daily consumption,” Yeung said. In June, 304 Hong Kong retirees were surveyed about their monthly spending. Aged from 55 to 74, they had a monthly personal income of at least HK$20,000 (US$2,551) before retirement and had not received means-tested social security or charitable support. According to the data collected in 2020 and 2026, the gauge for travel costs surged by over 10 points over the six-year period, the highest among all items, followed by food, dining and cross-border transport. However, the city’s retirees spent less on housing, with the corresponding gauge decreasing by 7.9 points. As a result, Hong Kong retirees’ monthly cost of living rose about 2.65 per cent to HK$15,090 on average this year from HK$14,700 in 2023. Notably, the average spending of retirees in Macau amounted to 10,408 patacas (US$1,289) in this year’s survey, 33 per cent lower than in Hong Kong. The Macau findings were based on a separate survey conducted in June of 100 local retirees aged 55 to 74. While Macau’s retirees also favoured northbound travel in recent years, Yeung said it was not appropriate to compare the two readings given the differences in cost of living and lifestyle habits between the two cities. Meanwhile, unpredictable medical costs and inflation were the top two concerns in Hong Kong, according to 51 per cent and 41 per cent of surveyed retirees, respectively. Worries about running out of savings ranked third, given that the retirement life of Hong Kong residents could last 20 to 30 years, said Yeung. “The 2026 data clearly shows that while retirees desire active lifestyles, they are heavily squeezed by medical inflation and the fear of outliving their wealth,” said Alvin Tse, CEO of YF Life Trustees. “To bridge this gap, retirees must shift away from viewing retirement savings as a static lump sum.”

title: 3 women charged over Hong Kong play-area brawl, police say grandmother was hit first
description: Force says dispute began over basketball attraction and investigators believe girl’s mother slapped 68‑year‑old first.
content: Three women have been charged after a brawl broke out in a children’s play area at a Hong Kong shopping centre. Police disclosed details of their investigation on Thursday, revealing they suspected that a 68‑year‑old woman seen in a viral video slapping a young girl had been struck first. The dispute took place in the atrium of the APM shopping centre in Kwun Tong at about 4.45pm on Wednesday. Footage widely circulating online appears to show the elderly woman, who was visiting the play zone with her 34‑year‑old daughter and grandson, forcefully shoving a five‑year‑old girl before slapping her, causing the child to lose her balance and fall. The girl’s mother, also 34, then rushes forward to confront the younger woman, leading to further scuffling. At one point, the boy’s mother confronted the girl’s mother while holding an umbrella, saying: “You cannot leave.” Two men intervened at different stages, with one confronting the elderly woman and shouting: “Did you just hit a child? I saw you.” Police stepped in and later arrested all three women. Further details have emerged, with a force source revealing the boy and the girl had argued over use of the basketball attraction. Investigators said they believed that the girl’s mother initially slapped the grandmother, who then struck back at the woman and her daughter. A spokesman said all three were charged with fighting in a public place, while the elderly woman faces an additional count of common assault. The girl and the two younger women were taken to United Christian Hospital for treatment of minor facial injuries. All three are due to appear in Kwun Tong Court on September 3. Following the dispute, the boy’s mother was suspended by her employer, insurance provider AIA. A company spokesman said on Thursday that AIA held its advisers to strict standards of professional conduct and did not condone any form of violence. “The firm has mechanisms in place to properly handle such matters,” he said. “The individual concerned has been temporarily suspended, and AIA will follow up on the incident appropriately.” The case is being handled by the police’s Kwun Tong district investigation team.

title: Hong Kong to launch free AI courses with tech giants Google, Microsoft for SMEs
description: Productivity Council collaborating with tech giants to roll out free training, boosting business adoption under HK$50 million initiative.
content: Free courses coordinated by the Hong Kong government will leverage the expertise of tech giants such as Google and Microsoft to help boost the adoption of AI by businesses for content creation, data analysis and workflow efficiency. The Hong Kong Productivity Council on Thursday announced the launch of the programme targeting industries such as education, healthcare, manufacturing, retail and logistics as part of the government’s HK$50 million (US$6.38 million) “AI for All” initiative. “Currently, over 90 per cent of businesses in Hong Kong are small and medium-sized enterprises [SMEs] and comprise the most important part of the city’s economic development,” Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong said. “Therefore, how we can help SMEs transform and upgrade through AI to enhance their competitiveness is an important direction within the AI for All initiative.” Council deputy chairman Emil Yu Chen-on said the courses would go beyond teaching employees to use artificial intelligence, calling them “a future-facing talent investment” that also ensured the technology was used safely. “It’s to … truly transform AI into productivity and competitiveness,” he said. “We can provide actionable, replicable, and expandable AI application areas that cater to the needs of different industries.” In addition to the council, the city’s two tech hubs, Cyberport in Pok Fu Lam and the Hong Kong Science Park in Pak Shek Kok, are leading the implementation of the “AI for All” initiative. Under its umbrella, more than 200 activities will take place over two years and are expected to benefit 50,000 people. The council’s AI push will focus on helping businesses “rapidly adopt AI technologies”, with a focus on practical applications of generative AI for content creation, data analysis and workflow efficiency. The council will also provide hands-on experience in AI application development and implementation to improve integration of solutions into real business scenarios for different industries. Courses will also cover human resources and leadership to help organisations understand AI talent management and application trends to prepare for future workforce needs. Additionally, the council’s “AI BiteClass” can be accessed by elderly residents and underprivileged communities. The council’s programme, “AI with HKPC – Business Empowerment”, started last week at the Hong Kong Computer and Communications Festival, but details for future courses were yet to be announced. A council spokeswoman said the course instructors would be drawn from various industries with AI project and solution development experience, including Google, Microsoft, Tencent Holdings, Huawei Technologies, Amazon Web Services and others. The council added it would provide free one-on-one consultations to encourage SMEs to make the most of government funding to upgrade and transform their businesses by assisting them with the identification of appropriate schemes and applications. Most of the courses will take place at the council’s base in Kowloon Tong, while select ones will take place online through the government “iAM Smart” system.

title: Park So-yeon breaks through esports glass ceiling, first woman to play for South Korea
description: Park So-yeon will represent her country in survival horror game Identity V at Asian Games in Japan next month.
content: Park So-yeon is set to become the first woman to represent South Korea’s national team in esports and wants to pave the way for more in the male-dominated world of competitive gaming. South Korea is an esports powerhouse and Park has been chosen to compete in survival horror game Identity V at the Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from September 19 to October 4. The 23-year-old Park, the only woman in South Korea’s team of 36 esports competitors heading to Japan, said she wanted to “go all out and have no regrets”. “Since I am the first I feel a great responsibility to pave the way for other women athletes who love playing games as much as I do,” said Park, who majored in taekwondo in college. South Korea’s formidable team will be spearheaded by superstar gamer Lee Sang-hyeok. Better known as Faker, he was part of the South Korea team that won gold in League of Legends at the 2023 Asian Games in China’s Hangzhou. “Since the South Korean people have high hopes for the esports category I want to fulfil that hope and give them back pride and honour,” he said. “I will do my very best in my role to ensure that our team wins the championship and brings back the gold medal.” South Korea won two golds, one silver and one bronze at the 2023 Asian Games, when eSports made its debut as an official medal event. They were second in the medals table behind China. The number of esports events has risen for this year’s Asian Games, with 13 different games being used in competition.

title: 18 new Hong Kong restaurants, bars and bakeries to try in September 2026
description: There’s a whole host of new eating and drinking experiences to enjoy in September. Here’s our comprehensive list of recommendations.
content: From contemporary Hokkien cooking and charcoal-fired French grills to glamorous Italian hospitality, new openings in Hong Kong this September promise to bring a diverse array of flavours. Read on to find out more. 1. Hokkien House Helmed by Levi You, winner of the Michelin Guide Fujian’s Young Chef Award in its inaugural 2025 edition, Hokkien House puts a contemporary take on Fujian’s coastal and mountainous flavours. The menu transforms classic regional ingredients, homestyle traditions and street foods into refined dishes, including pan-fried oyster cake with pickled radish and oyster soup, Fuzhou drunken pork ribs, and mangrove mud crab glutinous rice. 21/F, H Queen’s, 80 Queen’s Road Central, Central 2. Il Presidente Il Presidente promises to bring the glamorous golden era of Italian hospitality to Duddell Street in Central. Launched by executive chef Marcello Scognamiglio, also behind Wan Chai’s popular Trattoria Felino, the restaurant focuses on elevating recognisable regional comfort foods. Highlight dishes include indulgent house-made agnolotti all’ossobuco (pasta with veal shank); a giant ricotta and spinach cannelloni; and a decadent stuffed veal chop. The meal is completed by a theatrical churned gelato experience at the table. Shop M2, 13 Duddell Street, Central 3. Aoi By Kaiyo A playful, modern take on Japanese izakaya dining has officially opened at K11 Musea in Tsim Sha Tsui. The comprehensive menu at Aoi By Kaiyo features over 100 dishes, including fresh sashimi, charcoal-grilled items and Kansai-style sukiyaki. Diners can enjoy premium uni (sea urchin), toro sushi Napoleons and customisable seafood DIY wrap sets. Shop 406, 4/F, K11 Musea, Tsim Sha Tsui 4. 180º Modern Fire Grill Hora Hospitality Group, which runs French gastronomy concepts Babette and Chouchou, is expanding its portfolio with 180º Modern Fire Grill on Wyndham Street in Central. This new concept focuses on rustic cooking with a French touch. The menu emphasises rigorous, smoke-kissed execution, featuring premium charcoal-grilled selections, harissa popcorn chicken, lamb shoulder skewers, and rich cast iron pot bone marrow rice. Yu Yuet Lai Building, 43-55 Wyndham Street, Central 5. Canton Library Aqua Restaurant Group, behind venues including Aqua, Hutong, The Chinese Library and Dim Sum Library, has unveiled Canton Library in Tsim Sha Tsui. Led by executive chefs Junno Li and Leung Kwok-wa, the restaurant serves modern Chinese cuisine celebrating Lingnan coastal traditions. The hot kitchen spotlights premium seafood using time-honoured southern Chinese techniques, while the modern dim sum menu transforms nostalgic comfort food into new creations. 29/F, One Peking Road, Tsim Sha Tsui 6. Yukkuri This popular Kowloon City cafe has brought its signature Japanese antique aesthetic to a quiet corner of Hysan Place in Causeway Bay. Diners can look forward to dishes such as thick-cut grilled beef tongue paired with zucchini, and a deeply savoury black sesame curry pork slice with soft cabbage, all served with dashi-infused Japanese rice or silky udon. Shop 328, 3/F, Hysan Place, Lee Garden, 500 Hennessy Road, Causeway Bay 7. Chiu San This new Kennedy Town opening debuts Hong Kong’s first fusion of Chiu Chow and Japanese cuisine, served as contemporary teishoku (traditional Japanese set meals). The menu features stone-grilled USDA prime beef short rib with a rich satay-teriyaki sauce; salt-grilled yellow croaker roasted over an open flame; and a crispy, flash-fried pomegranate-shaped chicken dumpling. Each set includes comforting staples, artisanal tamagoyaki and wagashi desserts. Kin Liong Mansion, 16 North Street, Kennedy Town 8. Quan Quan brings refined contemporary Chinese fine dining to Central. Helmed by chef Justin Yang, the first runner-up of Chinese reality cooking show The Divine Dish season one, the eatery specialises in elevated Fujianese cuisine from his ancestral hometown of Quanzhou. Diners can expect creations such as Fujian old wine drunken crab, Rongcheng sweet and sour pork, and red rose grouper with chicken oil and sand shallots. 5/F, CCB Tower, 3 Connaught Road Central 9. Haedam Haedam is a new Korean restaurant in Tsim Sha Tsui that specialises in traditional Busan-style seaweed and kelp soups. Each order of signature soup, such as the oyster seaweed soup, includes freshly cooked Korean hot stone pot rice, grilled mackerel, crispy seaweed and six exquisite side dishes for a full and satisfying meal. M/F, 46-48 Granville Road, Tsim Sha Tsui 10. Fello Award-winning bartender Shelley Tai of Mius has launched Fello, her highly anticipated second venue in a two-storey space on Wyndham Street. The menu features signature drinks such as the spicy Fello paloma and the pineapple basil smash, which are ideally paired with elevated bar bites, including a tsukune chicken burger and ikura shrimp sando. 43-55 Wyndham Street, Central 11. Pocofino Philippines-based brand Pocofino has opened a cosy takeaway shop in Wan Chai. The menu features Italian master chef Matteo Minante’s Neapolitan pizzas certified by the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana – an official designation from Naples, Italy, guaranteeing that the pizzas strictly adhere to centuries-old traditional Neapolitan methods, equipment and specific ingredients. The menu also features Hong Kong-exclusive sweet fritta (fried pizza) in local egg tart and durian flavours. 8 Ship Street, Wan Chai 12. Tate Chef Vicky Lau has reopened her restaurant in a grand two-storey residence in Sheung Wan. Designed by Chris Shao, it incorporates custom furniture and bespoke artisanal ceramics made with local clay. The refreshed menu blends Chinese seasonality with classical French techniques in inventive ways, with reimagined signature dishes, including an upgraded Ode to Lobster and Ode to Crab. 68 Lok Ku Road, Sheung Wan 13. Cafe Landmark The iconic Cafe Landmark returns to the Landmark Atrium after a complete design and culinary transformation. Reimagined with the rustic elegance of Tuscany, the open-air restaurant introduces a new menu blending French foundations with Japanese accents. Diners can enjoy elevated signatures like Boston lobster spaghetti, an upgraded dessert trolley and a new cocktail menu. Shop 107-108, 1/F, Landmark Atrium, 15 Queen’s Road Central, Central 14. Draft Land The draft cocktail bar has expanded to open its first branch in Kowloon. Operating as a dual-concept lifestyle destination, the space is a Nodi cafe from 8am to 5pm, then serves Draft Land’s signature cocktails on tap. The Tsim Sha Tsui location also features branch-exclusive coffee-infused cocktails and an elevated snack menu by chef Logan Hester. Shop G5&6, No 8 Minden Avenue, Tsim Sha Tsui 15. Abebe Bakery South Korea’s celebrated Abebe Bakery is making its Hong Kong debut on Mody Road in Tsim Sha Tsui this September. Known for connecting Jeju Island’s local heritage with artisanal baking, the shop features iconic cream-filled doughnuts and innovative cream buns layered with chewy glutinous rice cakes. Shop W, 37 Mody Road, Tsim Sha Tsui 16. Mother Pearl Mother Pearl has opened a new two-storey flagship store in Central. The ground floor provides daytime fuel such as espresso creations and sugar-free vegan gelato. Meanwhile, the first floor features the Crafted Bar, where guests can enjoy premium cocktails infused with ancient botanicals alongside decadent bites like caviar-topped tea eggs. 24 D’Aguilar Street, Central 17. General Provisions by Alfred’s General Provisions by Alfred’s is a premier all-day artisanal destination located on the third floor of The Landmark’s Gloucester Tower. It bridges the gap between modern retail and refined dining by offering gourmet ingredients, speciality coffee and exclusive artisan gifts. Shop 303, 3/F, Landmark Atrium, 15 Queen’s Road Central, Central 18. Madé The artisanal French madeleine boutique Madé has soft-opened on the slopes of Central. Founded by a French couple, the specialised atelier serves premium madeleines made with French ingredients. Prices begin at HK$98 (US$12.50) for a box of three pieces. The permanent selection showcases six inventive flavours: the signature classic, the choc-o-holic, matcha white chocolate, black sesame, egg tart core and lemon. 54 Lyndhurst Terrace, Central

title: Russia lashes out at UK, France over Ukraine missile technology transfer
description: Moscow warns of potential strikes on British military targets, urging London to change its stance on supporting Kyiv.
content: Russian ⁠foreign ⁠ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova ⁠said on Thursday that Russia could strike British military targets inside and outside Ukraine ‌in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles. Zakharova called on Britain to back off what she called London’s hostile ⁠stance on Ukraine, which she said ‌risked taking the conflict to an entirely new level. She ‌had told the same Moscow ⁠news ⁠briefing earlier that Britain and France were “playing with ‌fire” by supplying sensitive missile technology to Ukraine. Britain ‌announced on ‌Monday it would allow ‌Kyiv access to classified technology to ⁠start its own production of Storm Shadow ⁠long-range cruise missiles, capable of carrying out strikes deep within ‌Russia. France ‌has already given its assent to licence the technology for the European missile. Also on Thursday, the ⁠Kremlin ⁠dismissed US media reports that Russia could attack a Nato member state and that the ‌purpose of US CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow this week had been to warn Russia against such a move. Asked ⁠to comment on the reports, Kremlin ‌spokesman Dmitry Peskov said: “A lot of this kind of ‌scare-story material is being published right now. ⁠Of ⁠course, it has nothing to do ‌with reality and nothing to do with the ‌intentions ‌of the Russian Federation.” Earlier on Thursday, ‌the head of Russia’s SVR ⁠foreign intelligence service said he had held ⁠a “working-level meeting” with Ratcliffe and that they had discussed unspecified ‌and sensitive matters ‌falling within the remit of their respective intelligence services. Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov on Thursday said that talks between Ukrainian and ⁠Russian ⁠teams could be held ⁠in September and include US representatives. Budanov said Ukraine ‌was aiming to revive the talks, with further developments likely next month. The US-led peace talks stalled this year as Ukraine refused Russian demands to cede more territory and ⁠as Washington became increasingly preoccupied with the conflict ‌with Iran. “I’m hoping for that, yes, and American ones too, of course. We ‌can’t do without them,” Budanov told ⁠Ukrainian ⁠media Novyny Live, when asked whether this meant direct talks between ‌Ukrainian and Russian negotiators. Zelensky said recently that Ukraine ‌saw a window ‌of opportunity for US mediation until ‌the end of next summer and has drafted ⁠one page of ideas with US and European officials ⁠to be presented to Moscow. The last round of trilateral Ukraine-Russia talks involving US ‌representatives took ‌place in February. Ukrainian and Russian representatives have only had separate talks with the US team since then.

title: Flights, ferries cancelled in Shanghai and Shenzhen as Typhoon Saudel closes in
description: Saudel is forecast to make landfall on Friday morning, becoming the seventh typhoon to hit the mainland this year.
content: The coastal Chinese province of Zhejiang is battening down for the approach of Typhoon Saudel, with flights cancelled across the area. The eastern province is home to a number of major commercial centres, including the industrial hub of Ningbo, the port city of Zhoushan, and Wenzhou. Ningbo Lishe International Airport said flights in and out of the facility would be suspended from 11.30pm on Thursday. In Wenzhou, 90 flights were cancelled, while 22 flights were grounded in Zhoushan. According to the National Meteorological Centre, Saudel is expected to make landfall along the coast between Sanmen county in eastern Zhejiang and Xiapu in southeastern Fujian province between early Friday morning and noon as a typhoon or severe typhoon. If Saudel hits Zhejiang directly, it will be the third to make landfall there this year, equalling the province’s 2004 record of three typhoon landfalls in a single year. The province took direct hits from Typhoon Bavi in July and Typhoon Dolphin earlier this month, both of which brought fierce winds and torrential rain to the region. Saudel would also be the seventh typhoon to strike the Chinese mainland this year. The typhoon is centred over waters about 335km (208 miles) east of the Zhejiang city of Wenling, with winds of up to 144km/h (89mph) near its centre. A forecaster at the Zhejiang Meteorological Bureau told local media that Saudel was moving slightly faster than the previous two typhoons before entering the East China Sea. Its intensity was similar, while its impact would be shorter. The province is on an orange alert, the second-highest in China’s four-tier weather warning system. Saudel is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds across eastern and southern China, affecting manufacturing powerhouse Guangdong and Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. The approaching storm has also prompted authorities to suspend transport services elsewhere. Shanghai Ferry Company announced the suspension of all passenger ferry routes on Thursday and nearly 20 high-speed trains from Shenzhen to Nanjing, Xiamen, Shanghai, and Hangzhou were cancelled. Multiple high-speed train services within Zhejiang and Fujian provinces have also been halted. Major ports have also ramped up safety measures, with nearly 800 commercial vessels in Ningbo waters moved to shelters and all passenger ferry services stopped. Ningbo-Zhoushan Port, the busiest port in the world by cargo tonnage, fully suspended container operations on Wednesday. In Wenzhou, the government on Wednesday updated its typhoon emergency response to Level 2, the second-highest level in China’s four-tier emergency response system. It has halted all outdoor group activities, classes, work, business operations and public transport. Scenic spots and tourist attractions across affected coastal areas have also been closed to the public.

title: Viral China maths genius’ new workbook sells 26,000 copies in 4 days, sparking mixed reactions
description: Wei’s venture into supplementary education prompts criticism that he is profiting from his fame at the expense of his academic reputation.
content: A famous Chinese mathematician known for his dishevelled genius image recently began selling workbooks for primary and secondary school students, which were quickly sold out within days. Wei Dongyi, 35, is an associate professor in the Mathematics Department at Peking University. He gained instant fame in 2021 after a vox pop on the Peking University campus. In the video, he appears dressed simply, carrying a 1.5-litre plastic bottle of water and a bag of steamed buns. In the clip, he shared that he has studied at Peking University since his bachelor’s degree and is now a teacher there. Although he comes across as introverted, he remains unfazed, a characteristic later described by his admirers as typical of genius. Wei’s remarkable past was uncovered by curious onlookers. The mathematician from Shandong province in eastern China was a mathematics prodigy. He earned international recognition in his field by winning two gold medals at the 49th and 50th International Mathematical Olympiads, achieving perfect scores in both. As a result, he was affectionately dubbed “God Wei” by his followers. Since 2010, Wei has pursued his studies at Peking University up to the postdoctoral level. He also declined opportunities to study abroad, modestly attributing it to the difficulty of English. Last year, Wei registered social media accounts to thwart impersonators claiming his online identity. On August 18, Wei posted his first video in 14 months, introducing his method for solving a primary school maths problem. It was later revealed that this was a promotional video for his newly published workbooks – one aimed at primary school students, priced at 39.8 yuan (US$6), and another for junior secondary students, priced at 49.8 yuan. Wei serves as the editor-in-chief of these workbooks. The commercial nature of this move raised questions about the authenticity of the account. However, Peking University later confirmed that it was indeed Wei’s account, leading parents to swiftly buy the workbooks – 26,000 copies sold in just four days – prompting the account to remove the product listings without explanation. Nonetheless, store staff indicated that the books would continue to be available through specialised bookstores. Wei’s foray into the supplementary education market has sparked mixed reactions. Some criticised him for potentially profiting from his fame at the expense of his academic reputation, while others supported him and pleased to see him take a more “down to earth” stance. “I do not think Wei seeks to profit from his fame. He would have been wealthier long ago if that were his intention,” one commenter stated. “We should thank ‘God Wei’ for his willingness to teach children,” remarked another. “I hope my child can embody God Wei’s spirit on their learning journey,” said a parent who bought a workbook.

title: Singapore MP opposes Temasek funding for Air India amid US$1.5 billion plea
description: ‘If Singapore Airlines wants to continue its bet on Air India, it should do so on its own two feet, and not on Temasek’s,’ Kenneth Tiong says.
content: A Singapore opposition lawmaker has urged that state investor Temasek’s money not be used to shore up Air India, after the Indian carrier had asked owners Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, which Temasek majority-owns, for US$1.5 billion. Kenneth Tiong, a member of parliament for the opposition Workers’ Party, said ‌in a social media post on Wednesday that because Singapore Airlines owns about 25 per cent of Air India and Temasek in turn owns most of the Singapore carrier, the request was “not only a question for private shareholders”. “I will not support, nor expect, any future use of Temasek’s funds to prop up Air India via Singapore Airlines. If Singapore Airlines wants to continue its bet on Air India, it should do so on its own two feet, and not on Temasek’s,” ⁠he said. “Whichever of the two writes the cheque, it will have a significant impact on Temasek,” he added, without elaborating further. Singapore’s Ministry of Transport, Temasek, ‌Air India, Tata Sons and Tiong did not respond to emails seeking comment. A Singapore Airlines spokesperson said its board would carefully consider any requests for additional capital from Air India, weighing the group’s other capital requirements and ‌the Indian airline’s business strategy. Tiong said he had also filed a question for oral answer in parliament on September 8, asking the ‌transport minister whether losses from and the carrying amount in Singapore Airlines’ foreign associates have been assessed against its ⁠capacity to provide essential transport ⁠services. The comments bring political scrutiny in Singapore to what has been a commercial decision for Singapore Airlines. Its 25.1 per cent stake in Air India has weighed on its ‌earnings as the Indian carrier’s losses widened during a multibillion-dollar turnaround that Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran has said could take up to a decade. Air India and its budget arm ‌Air ‌India Express posted combined losses of US$2.33 billion in the year to March, more than double the previous year. Singapore Airlines has booked ‌its share of those losses. Air India is expected to continue requiring capital infusions in the coming years, a source familiar with the matter ⁠said earlier this week. It is not the first time the city state’s flag carrier has been queried about future funding for ⁠Air India. Ahead of its annual general meeting last month, the Securities Investors Association (Singapore) asked whether the Singapore Airlines board had set capital allocation limits for Air India and under what circumstances it would approve additional capital. In a written response ‌on July 17, Singapore Airlines did ‌not provide a limit. The company said its board would carefully consider any requests, taking into consideration its other capital requirements and Air India’s business strategy. Air India has been hit by Pakistan’s airspace ban on Indian carriers, disruptions to its international network from the US-Israeli war with Iran, and the fallout from a crash last year that killed 260 people.

title: Unitree’s stock slump since IPO stokes fears of a bubble in Chinese humanoid robotics
description: Even after the sell-off, Unitree’s market value is more than four times the top of the range indicated by lead underwriter Citic Securities.
content: Shares in Chinese robotics star Unitree Robotics rebounded on Thursday following five straight days of losses that erased nearly half of its market value, although it did little to cool fears of a Chinese humanoid robot bubble. The stock rose nearly 4 per cent to close at 615 yuan on Thursday, giving the company a market capitalisation of 248.8 billion yuan (US$37 billion), after touching a record low of 571 yuan on Wednesday. That low marked a 48 per cent drop from its peak of 1,100 yuan on its August 19 debut, wiping out 200 billion yuan in market value. “Given that level of uncertainty, Unitree’s high valuation is probably not justified,” said Dong Chen, chief investment officer for Asia at Bank J. Safra Sarasin, citing the stock’s lofty price-to-earnings ratio and the difficulty in staying ahead in an “infant level” industry where competition was intensifying. The Hangzhou-based company opened 629 per cent higher when it debuted on Shanghai’s Nasdaq-style Star Market last Wednesday. The market exuberance contrasted with the demeanour of founder Wang Xingxing, who was poker-faced at the bell-ringing ceremony. As mainland China’s first listed humanoid robot maker, Unitree’s debut was closely watched as a valuation benchmark for a clutch of highly valued, private embodied-AI unicorns seeking an initial public offering. Leading players such as Galbot already command valuations of more than 20 billion yuan, although few have matched Unitree’s record of revenue-generation and mass production. Unitree said last week that it had cumulatively produced about 18,000 bipedal humanoids across multiple models as of July, while its first quarter revenue rose 68.5 per cent year on year to 423 million yuan. An early Unitree investor, who asked not to be identified, told the South China Morning Post before the IPO that his team had stopped looking at robotics deals because companies had become too expensive and homogenous, while commercial deployment remained far off. Embodied AI remains a long-term growth story, but some of the recent hype has been driven by investor FOMO and a wave of specialist funds launched after the sector was elevated to a national priority, the person said.
