Still, one stock’s performance is not enough to declare an industry-wide bubble, Chen said. “Based on this company alone, I would be reluctant to call the sector a bubble.” Earlier this month, Citic Securities, the IPO’s lead underwriter, gave Unitree a valuation of 50.6 billion yuan to 55.9 billion yuan six to 12 months after listing, Reuters reported, citing a report sent to bookbuilding investors. Even after the sell-off, Unitree’s market value at Thursday’s midday break was more than four times the top of that range. Ying Zhang, an economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said the listing had put the commercial potential of China’s robotics boom in the spotlight, but demand remained a key hurdle. “Widespread adoption is currently hindered by financial constraints, such as high upfront and maintenance costs, and technical limitations, such as short battery life, which make it difficult for manufacturers to justify the investment,” Zhang said in a report based on a recent field research in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province. China’s current push into advanced technology was intended to drive industrial upgrading and reinforce supply-side competitiveness, Zhang added. The next test would be whether sectors like robotics could develop commercially viable uses. Additional reporting by Xinmei Shen

title: Hong Kong lowers heat stress warning system thresholds after calls for revamp
description: Labour Department says updates include automatically raising alert level when temperatures in multiple parts of the city reach 35 degrees.
content: Hong Kong labour authorities have unveiled changes to the system that sends out warnings to workers about overexertion during very hot weather, reducing the threshold so higher-tier alerts can be issued more easily following intense criticism of the mechanism. The Labour Department said on Thursday that two new conditions would be introduced to the Heat Stress at Work Warning system starting on Friday. The system has three warning levels – amber, red and black – which alert employers and staff to the severity of heat stress if they are working outdoors or indoors without air conditioning. The first change will lower the threshold for triggering a higher-tier warning if the Observatory has already issued the extremely hot weather special alert, ensuring a quicker response. The second change will automatically raise the warning level by one tier – from amber to red, or from red to black – when measured temperatures generally over Hong Kong reach 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) or higher. The revamp follows criticism over a lack of higher alerts earlier this month, when the city grappled with record-breaking temperatures. “We expect this new arrangement will continue to give timely warning alerts to workers working under heat stress caused by high humidity and poor air circulation, as well as trigger earlier and higher warnings to scenarios of abnormally high temperatures, especially for workers working outdoors,” Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui Chark-shum said on Thursday. The current warning system relies on the Hong Kong Heat Index, which factors in air temperature, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation and hospital admission figures to measure heat stress. Amber, red or black warnings are issued when index readings at the King’s Park Meteorological Station or four of the nine other monitoring sites reach 30, 32 or 34, respectively. The amber alert can also be triggered when the Observatory issues the extremely hot weather special alert. Under the revamped system, if the special alert is active, the warning can escalate to red or black if the King’s Park station or two of the other nine sites record index readings of 32 or 34. If measured temperatures reach 35 degrees across at least 40 per cent of weather stations, the index threshold for the red or black warning will drop to 30 and 32. According to Labour Department guidelines, employers are advised to arrange additional rest periods for affected workers when the amber warning is active. Workers with “very heavy” workloads should suspend their duties under the red alert, while those with “heavy” workloads should do so under the black warning. On Thursday, the department estimated that in the future, the red warning could be issued four to seven days a year, while the black alert could be triggered one or two days a year. Kevin Wong Chi-ching, a senior occupational hygienist with the department, said the red warning would have been issued on August 9, when the Observatory logged a record-breaking peak temperature of 36.9 degrees at its Tsim Sha Tsui headquarters, under the revamped system. He added the red and black alerts would have gone out on August 8, when maximum temperatures in some parts of the city exceeded 38 degrees. However, Ivanhoe Chang Chi-ho, the department’s deputy commissioner overseeing occupational safety and health, noted that heat stress risks on August 9 were actually lower because humidity and wind speed indicators were more favourable. Despite calls from former Observatory leaders, the department decided not to adopt the wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) index, an internationally recognised measurement of outdoor heat stress affecting the human body. Wong said the localised index was better suited to Hong Kong because it reflected the city’s hot, humid conditions. But Lam Chiu-ying, a past Observatory head, still urged the government to adopt the WBGT index. “The baseline metrics of the Hong Kong Heat Index remain unscientific and stand as a key shortcoming to be addressed. I hope it can be solved by next summer,” he said. Lam added that the government should mandate rest times and mitigation measures under heat stress warnings, improve heatstroke compensation and address potential issues from extended construction work. The Labour Department said it would step up inspections in the future, particularly at high-risk workplaces, and take enforcement action. The department said it had conducted 13,342 inspections and issued 602 warning letters as of July. It added that heatstroke was now considered a work injury and employers were liable to pay compensation under the law. But any move to classify heatstroke as a statutory occupational disease, making it easier for workers to claim compensation for work-related cases, would depend on factors such as the strength of the link between the illness and the occupation, the department said. Labour authorities recorded 132 suspected cases of heat stress-related work injuries from 2022 to July this year, with most leading to compensation or out-of-court settlements. The Association for the Rights of Industrial Accident Victims said it believed the revamped mechanism could improve the warning system’s sensitivity and more easily trigger higher-tier alerts. “The government should continue to monitor the actual situation and whether it matches the wet-bulb globe temperature index. It should review the mechanism in a year,” it said. The association also urged the government to go a step further by introducing a suspension policy for certain work under the black warning and classifying heatstroke as an occupational disease.

title: Meet the late Dolly Parton’s lifelong best friend and assistant, Judy Ogle
description: Having known the ‘Queen of Country Music’ since childhood, Ogle founded The Dolly Archive and was even rumoured to be romantically involved with the ‘Jolene’ singer.
content: Dolly Parton’s family, fans and public figures have expressed grief over her death at 80 on Tuesday, following a brief cancer battle. National flags across the US are flying at half mast for a week as ordered by President Donald Trump in honour of the “Queen of Country Music”. Jane Fonda, Parton’s co-star in the 1980 film 9 to 5, shared a long tribute on Instagram on Wednesday to remember the star. “I know that millions are mourning and I want to say this – more than anyone I have ever known, Dolly will always be with us because she was so present, so powerful, so generous and playful that she is woven into all our lives and hearts forever,” her post read. View this post on Instagram Miley Cyrus, Parton’s goddaughter, also recalled the precious moments she shared with the country music legend, adding that one of their last conversations was about music. “What I KNOW is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong,” she wrote. Of all those mourning the loss of the musical icon, few will feel Parton’s absence more deeply than her best friend, Judy Ogle. How long had Dolly Parton and Judy Ogle been friends? Both Tennessee natives, Parton and Ogle were childhood friends and grew up together. In a 2019 interview with The Sun, Parton revealed she and Ogle were friends for 64 years, making their friendship a seven-decade-long one at the moment of Parton’s passing. In the same interview, the superstar said they were “like sisters” and that their opposite personalities suited each other. “She was very quiet, I was very outgoing. So we made perfect friends. We went all through school together,” Parton said. Ogle was Parton’s assistant, too After Parton and Ogle graduated from secondary school, they went on separate paths for a while – the former moved to Nashville to pursue her music career, while the latter joined the US Army to support her family. The two reconnected soon after Ogle completed her military service. Joining Parton in Nashville, she eventually became the singer’s personal assistant and touring companion. “We picked right up where we left off,” Parton shared on The Big Interview with Dan Rather in 2014. In the 1970s, Ogle also started The Dolly Archive, collecting and preserving every photo, article and costume piece connected to the artist’s life and career. On National Best Friends Day in June this year, Parton celebrated her enduring friendship with Ogle on Instagram: “I’ve always had a little bit of Tennessee with me at every point in my career, thanks to my best friend, Judy Ogle. She travelled with me, worked as my assistant and was there for anything I needed. We had so many adventures and so many laughs – and I can’t imagine my years on the road (or my life) – without her!” Were Dolly Parton and Judy Ogle romantically involved? Seeing how close Parton and Ogle were, some fans speculated that the two were romantically involved. Parton, who was married to Carl Thomas Dean for close to 60 years before he passed away last year, squashed the rumours in a 2012 interview with Nightline. “Judy, my friend, they just think that you just can’t be that close to somebody,” Parton said. “Judy and I have been best friends since we were like in the third and fourth grade. We still just have a great friendship and relationship, and I love her as much as I love anybody in the whole world, but we’re not romantically involved.” Parton was a long-standing advocate for LGBTQ rights, first publicly supporting the community through her 1991 song “Family”, in which she encouraged families to accept their relatives regardless of their sexual orientation. “I have a huge gay following, and I’m proud of them,” the star told The New York Times in 2016.

title: Zhipu AI shares jump as viral Ox Alpha model revealed as GLM-5.3-Flash on Chinese chips
description: Model shows China can scale AI on domestic chips, setting a usage record as Beijing pushes to cut reliance on US hardware.
content: China’s Zhipu AI has launched its latest open-weight model, GLM-5.3-Flash – previously code-named Ox Alpha – saying that the system ran entirely on a cluster of 100,000 domestically produced chips during a high-profile stealth trial. The announcement followed a week of heavy traffic on artificial intelligence model marketplace OpenRouter and agent platform OpenCode, where the model processed 62 trillion tokens before its formal release on Wednesday, according to Zhipu. On OpenRouter, the system processed more than 11 trillion tokens in its first three days, making it the platform’s biggest launch to date. Zhipu’s shares closed more than 12 per cent higher at HK$1,160 in Hong Kong on Thursday. The deployment marks a significant test of China’s ability to handle large-scale global inference workloads on home-grown hardware, as Beijing seeks to reduce reliance on advanced processors from US market leader Nvidia amid tight export controls. During its preview, Ox Alpha rapidly surged to the top of global usage rankings. According to OpenRouter data on Thursday, the model ranked first among coding systems on the platform, accounting for 10.3 trillion tokens, or nearly 31 per cent of its total weekly volume. To overcome the lower memory capacity and bandwidth of individual Chinese chips compared with top-tier Nvidia graphics processing units, Zhipu – which operates internationally under the Z.ai brand – said it built a specialised inference engine that split processing stages into independently managed computing pools. The firm said these architectural adjustments tripled end-to-end serving performance from its initial baseline, bringing hardware efficiency and per-token costs on par with mainstream Nvidia accelerators. The claims have yet to be independently verified. While Zhipu did not name specific chip suppliers for this cluster, it has previously collaborated with top domestic semiconductor developers, including Huawei Technologies, Cambricon Technologies and Moore Threads. Cambricon said on Thursday it had achieved “Day 0” compatibility to serve GLM-5.3-Flash. Moore Threads said it also achieved “Day 0” support for the new model. Featuring 320 billion total parameters, GLM-5.3-Flash activated just 18 billion per request to reduce computing overhead, according to Zhipu. It is also the first model in the GLM-5 series to natively process visual information alongside text. Benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis gave the model a score of 57 on its Intelligence Index, placing it 10th globally and third among open-weight models, trailing Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B. Zhipu is touting aggressive pricing to win over international developers, offering GLM-5.3-Flash at 1/10th the rate of standard GLM-5.3 – dropping to 1/20th under a limited promotion. It claimed the new model cost about 1/40th as much as Anthropic’s Opus 4.8 at comparable intelligence levels. Despite heavy traffic during the free trial, early developer feedback was mixed. While users praised the model’s ability to debug complex code – a community test showed that it solved 28 per cent of 175 LiveCodeBench problems – others reported occasional hallucinations, dropped tasks and sluggish generation. Artificial Analysis similarly noted that GLM-5.3-Flash’s output speed trailed the industry average. Zhipu has released the model weights globally and integrated GLM-5.3-Flash across its application programming interface, ZCode platform, and GLM Coding Plan. The launch coincides with intensified competition in China’s open-source ecosystem. On Wednesday, Alibaba released Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a multimodal preview of Qwen4 that it said activated 6 billion of its 125 billion parameters to similarly drive down inference costs. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Additional reporting by Xinmei Shen

title: Opinion | How Shenzhen can win the ‘AI for science’ race
description: Rather than copy the research-focused models of Beijing and Shanghai, the tech hub must leverage its industrial depths to become a premier lab for experimentation and deployment.
content: The next big competition in artificial intelligence is over science. The question is shifting from who has the largest model to who can use AI to shorten the discovery cycle: forming a hypothesis, running simulations, designing an experiment, operating equipment, collecting results and learning from them. The United States made that shift explicit. The Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission aims to bring together 17 national laboratories into an integrated discovery platform to double the productivity and impact of US research and innovation within a decade. This year, the programme announced a partnership with Japan, reinforcing the idea that AI for science is becoming infrastructure and a network, not simply another model. China is moving in the same direction but increasingly through cities. Beijing’s 2025 plan calls for common scientific-intelligence infrastructure, at least 10 high-quality scientific databases, more than 10 million users and at least eight benchmark applications by 2027. Shanghai’s “Hundred Teams, Hundred Projects” initiative offers support for up to 70 per cent of approved investment, capped at 50 million yuan (US$6 million). The race to harness AI for science is no longer merely national. This creates both an opportunity and a trap for Shenzhen. The opportunity is obvious: AI could become a new source of scientific productivity and industrial growth. The trap is copying what other cities are doing. Shenzhen should not try to become Beijing with more hardware, or Shanghai with a different set of industry labels; it should build around its own comparative advantage. The first advantage is the structure of its innovation economy. Shenzhen invested 245.31 billion yuan in research and development in 2024, the highest R&D intensity among Chinese cities. Strikingly, companies accounted for over 93 per cent of that spending. Those figures describe a city where research, engineering and commercial deployment sit unusually close together. This matters in the AI-for-science drive because the hard part isn’t only inventing an algorithm, but turning it into a reliable scientific tool. The second advantage is even more distinctive: scientific discovery does not end when a model predicts a molecule or proposes a material. Samples have to be prepared, instruments operated and experiments repeated. The US Genesis Mission’s work on AI-driven autonomous laboratories combines robotics, edge AI, real-time analysis and intelligent feedback for this reason. Shenzhen has an extraordinary physical technology base. It produced 194,900 industrial robots and nearly 8 million service robots last year, alongside large volumes of drones, servers, integrated circuits and 3D-printing equipment. They can become tools with which AI performs science. That is where Shenzhen can take a genuinely different path. Instead of treating robotics as one more AI-for-science application, the city should turn robotics and laboratory automation into a shared experimental layer for different fields. The third advantage is that Shenzhen increasingly has the scientific assets to connect to this engineering base. Guangming Science City operates major facilities for synthetic biology, brain research and materials genomics that have served more than 200 universities, research organisations and companies, as well as logged more than 330,000 hours of equipment use. The ingredients are there. The missing piece is how to make computing, AI models, robots and scientific instruments work as one system. So what should Shenzhen do? First, it should stop thinking in terms of separate AI platforms for every scientific discipline. Build a shared city-level foundation for computing, scientific data, model access, simulation, experiment scheduling, equipment interfaces and traceability. Let biology, materials, energy and other fields build specialised layers on top. Second, make automated experimentation the city’s signature capability. Shenzhen should select areas where it has both scientific facilities and industrial depth – for example materials and synthetic biology – and demonstrate a complete loop from AI prediction to real experiments to data feedback. Success should be measured by whether experiments become faster, cheaper and easier to reproduce. Third, design for interoperability from the beginning. Common interfaces, data formats and testing methods should be developed alongside the technology. Where they work, they can become local or industry standards and eventually compete for international adoption. Finally, Shenzhen should make these tools usable beyond the city. Make models, software, experimental interfaces and validation methods portable so outside laboratories can use them while keeping sensitive data locally. Shenzhen has spent decades learning how to turn engineering into products that travel. AI for science gives it a chance to do the same with scientific capability. China’s cities are going to spend heavily on AI for science. Shenzhen does not need to spend in exactly the same way. Beijing’s plan builds on its concentration of national research institutions. Shanghai is mobilising large teams and domain projects. Shenzhen’s strongest opportunity is complementary: become the place where AI moves from prediction to experimentation, where fragmented scientific resources are turned into a reusable system. The key measure of success should not be how many AI-for-science centres Shenzhen creates. It should be whether a biologist, a materials scientist or eventually an outside laboratory can use the same Shenzhen-built tools to move from an idea to an experiment and back again. If Shenzhen can achieve that, it will have built something much harder to copy.

title: 5 of the best things to do in Hong Kong this weekend, August 28-30
description: From a Wagyu challenge and cosmic musicals to clothing swap, meditation and Harry Potter, there’s plenty to do in Hong Kong this weekend.
content: The weather’s looking a bit dicey again this weekend, but there will still be plenty of events happening around town. There’s a Wagyu challenge, a musical with cosmic themes, a clothing swap and a beginner’s meditation class to keep you busy. If you are looking to learn something new, explore the galaxy, test your intuitive meat-weighing skills or upcycle your wardrobe, there’s a wide variety of options available. 1. “Golden Cut” Wagyu Challenge On Friday, August 28, Wagyu Yakiniku Jun is hosting a “Golden Cut” Wagyu Challenge for meat lovers across Hong Kong at 7.30pm. At Wagyu Yakiniku Jun’s branches in Tsim Sha Tsui and Causeway Bay, guests can observe the chef’s knife skills up close, while each table has one opportunity to guess the weight of a special “Golden Cut” of A5 Wagyu. The table that guesses the exact or closest weight will receive the entire portion of beef. Shop 3, 1/F, Hilton Towers, 96 Granville Road, Tsim Sha Tsui; 7/F, HDH Centre, 8 Pennington Street, Causeway Bay 2. Space Fantasy This weekend marks the debut of Space Fantasy, an original musical by the City Chamber Orchestra of Hong Kong, written by Leanne Nicholls, with music by Luna Pan and Miles Brown. A cosmic adventure suitable for all ages, it features the theremin, the only musical instrument in the world that produces music with no physical contact from the player. It creates an otherworldly sound, and it has frequently been heard on soundtracks for science fiction films. The musical will be held at the Tsuen Wan Town Hall Auditorium on Saturday (3pm and 7.30pm) and Sunday (3pm). Tickets are priced at HK$600, HK$400, HK$250 and HK$120, with a discount available for students, senior citizens aged 60 and above, comprehensive social security assistance recipients and those with disabilities along with their accompanying minder. Click here to learn more about the event. 72 Tai Ho Road, Tsuen Wan, New Territories 3. Golden Hour: Swop & Shop On Sunday, The Hive in Sai Ying Pun is hosting a full-day clothing swap. Guests can bring preloved pieces to earn Hive credits and revamp their wardrobe, without the environmental impact of buying brand-new clothes. It is a chance to detox and refresh your wardrobe, without breaking the bank or contributing to consumerism. To participate, you can select a spot in advance through Swop’s official website, and bring up to 10 clothing items to swap out at your assigned time. Once you receive the credit for the items, you can browse the racks of other members’ renewed fashion finds and use your Swop credit to purchase them. Tickets for general sale cost HK$128, and the arrival slots are hourly from 11.00am to 4.00pm. Click here to learn more about the event. The Hive, G/F, 5-13 New Street, Sai Ying Pun 4. Free meditation class This Saturday, Sahaja Yoga Hong Kong is hosting a free meditation course for beginners. The course will cover an introduction to Sahaja Yoga Meditation, as well as an introduction to the subtle energy system and the chakras. The session will also include an introduction to meditation in the home, and a question and answer section of the class. The class is free to attend and will be taught in Cantonese, but guests can request English or Mandarin interpretation when they register. Click here to learn more about the event. Flat L, 8/F, Winner Factory Building, 55 Hung To Road, Kwun Tong, Kowloon 5. 25 Years of Magic: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone On November 4, 2001, a movie premiered that would change the world. Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone (also known as Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone), the first of eight films based on the bestselling books by British author J.K. Rowling, was unveiled at London’s Odeon Leicester Square cinema. As young actors Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint stepped out into the spotlight, it was the start of Potter movie mania, a magical cinematic journey that launched careers, spawned franchises, opened theme parks and influenced a generation of children’s Halloween costumes. Relive the beginning of boy wizard Harry’s time at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry with this special 25th anniversary re-release in Hong Kong, which also features 10 minutes of behind-the-scenes content never before screened in cinemas. 25 Years of Magic: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone is in cinemas now.

title: Dovish or Hawkish? Markets await Warsh’s Jackson Hole debut for rate, policy clues
description: Investors are watching closely for shifts in interest-rate and monetary policy during Friday’s symposium.
content: Investors are gearing up for Kevin Warsh’s first speech as chair of the US Federal Reserve at the central bank’s annual economic policy meeting, looking for any clues on monetary policies that will affect assets. Warsh is due to address the three-day Jackson Hole symposium on Friday, and indications from him on the US interest-rate outlook would be significant for stocks and bonds, which experienced pressure recently amid rising Treasury yields and Washington’s intervention to cap long-end yields. Dovish rhetoric from Warsh would act as a tailwind for stocks, as well as short-dated bonds, easing expectations about financial tightening, boosting risk appetite and keeping AI infrastructure investments at a relatively low funding cost. A hawkish stance would weigh on equities, particularly AI stocks with elevated valuations that have already priced in years of explosive growth. “Warsh’s speech at Jackson Hole is going to be an important tone-setting event,” said Zhang Shuming, an analyst at Orient Securities. “That will sway the movements across various assets. Most investors may opt to be on the sidelines before his speech.” A subdued reaction to Nvidia’s stellar quarterly results underscored that traders were refraining from big bets before Warsh’s high-stakes speech. The Hang Seng Index dropped 0.3 per cent on Thursday and the CSI 300 Index rose 0.9 per cent. Warsh, who took over the helm of the Fed in May, has been criticised by Wall Street for altering his predecessors’ approach to market communications. He favours the argument that the market should do more of the job of responding to economic data, rather than depend on the Fed for policy guidance. Goldman Sachs and Citigroup predicted that Warsh would likely strike a dovish tone in his speech due to moderate recent inflation data. Core personal consumption expenditure, a gauge preferred by the Fed for inflation, which excludes food and energy, rose by an in-line 0.2 per cent from a month earlier in July, pointing to a sign of disinflation. “We still see risks as balanced dovish,” Citigroup said in a note this week. “Warsh has generally avoided commenting on recent data, but that means any acknowledgement of the last two months of cooler core inflation data would be particularly notable.” The likelihood that the Fed would leave the benchmark interest rate unchanged at its interest-rate meeting next month was about 62 per cent, according to analysis by CME Group, compared with 18 per cent a month ago. Bank of America said in a report this week that Warsh’s focus on discussing price stability and bringing inflation back to the 2 per cent target in his speech would signal a hawkish tone, while a stress on structural issues such as productivity or demographics would indicate a dovish stance. “The big issue is not the absence of forward guidance but the lack of specification of a reaction function,” said Erik Weisman, chief economist and portfolio manager at MFS Investment Management. “Specifically, Chair Warsh needs to highlight the factors he considers when he decides the course of policy. Without a credible set of potential responses to incoming information, the promise of price stability rings hollow.”

title: Amid ‘super’ El Nino worry, Li Qiang vows ‘all necessary measures’ to secure autumn harvest
description: During an inspection tour in northeastern China, Premier Li says advanced tech can protect crop yield.
content: Premier Li Qiang has stressed the importance of national food security during an inspection tour of China’s most important grain-producing provinces, as a growing number of global investment banks warn that El Nino and regional conflicts could trigger a prolonged and more widespread global grain crisis. The country’s No 2 political figure visited the northeastern provinces of Heilongjiang and Jilin, which together generated nearly a fifth of the country’s grain output last year. During the three-day tour that began on Monday, Li visited farms, research institutes and agricultural companies, inspected soybean, corn and rice crops, and repeatedly stressed the need to secure a strong harvest. “The autumn harvest accounts for the bulk of China’s annual grain production, and crops are now at a critical stage,” Li said, calling for better field management, stable supplies and prices of agricultural inputs, and stronger policy support to secure a bumper harvest. Li also reiterated Beijing’s long-standing emphasis on food self-sufficiency, invoking the oft-repeated line that China must “keep its rice bowl firmly in its own hands”. The coming autumn harvest typically accounts for about three-quarters of China’s annual grain output, making it critical to the country’s efforts to feed its 1.4 billion people and reduce its reliance on imports. However, frequent extreme weather, combined with disruptions to commodity and fertiliser shipments related to the Middle East conflict, has added pressure to global food production this year. Li said China must build on its strong summer harvest, ensure stable supplies of grain and other key agricultural products, and “take all necessary measures to secure a bumper autumn harvest”. He also called for wider use of advanced breeding technologies, high-end farm machinery and artificial intelligence, as well as stronger disaster preparedness to protect crops from droughts and floods. His remarks come as extreme weather and disruptions to commodity and fertiliser shipments have been weighing on global food production, heightening Beijing’s concerns over domestic supplies and exposure to volatile international markets. The Middle East conflict, an escalation in the Russia-Ukraine war and extreme weather – including heatwaves across the northern hemisphere and a potentially strengthening El Nino – are tightening supplies and pushing up grain prices, HSBC said in a report. Prices for wheat, corn, barley and rice were collectively 22 per cent higher year on year as of July, according to the bank on Tuesday. “Having strong supplies and stocks going into this year has helped keep prices from spiking higher, but the buffer is now starting to be run down quickly,” HSBC economist Jamie Culling warned. The report followed a warning from JPMorgan that another global food crisis could emerge next year, especially as war-related disruptions to fertiliser supplies coincide with a potential “super” El Nino. The bank expects global food inflation to accelerate from about 2.8 per cent in the first half of 2026 to an annualised rate of around 5 per cent in the first half of 2027. Combined with an energy shock, the pressures could add about 0.6 percentage points to global headline inflation and slow the expected easing in prices, it said.

title: What China can do to secure trade routes in its coming high-seas struggle with US
description: Di Dongsheng argues it could take three decades for China to dominate access to ports, straits, canals and shipping lanes around the world.
content: China should forge a national consensus on “regaining mastery of the oceans” and direct overseas investment returns into defence spending to brace for sea-power competition with the US, according to a prominent Chinese academic. Di Dongsheng, associate dean of Renmin University’s school of international studies in Beijing, warned on Tuesday that as economic ties between the United States, the dominant maritime power, and China, which relies heavily on sea-bound trade, shifted towards competition, the era of open oceans could be drawing to a close. “We must prepare for struggle in a coming contest over sea power and the security of shipping routes,” Di wrote in a note on his social media channel. He argued it could take about three decades for China to secure dominance over and access to ports, straits, canals and shipping lanes around the world in a step-by-step process. “Before then, the possibility that a portion of [China’s] import and export trade relying on maritime transport would come under threats, or even partial shocks, still warrants close attention,” he said. Di noted that Beijing had gained the “upper hand” in last year’s tariff and sanctions wars, forcing US President Donald Trump into a temporary compromise. However, his research indicated that the White House remained unconvinced and he said some viewed Washington as actively targeting China’s vulnerabilities and waiting for the right moment to act. “One of China’s obvious soft spots is the maritime routes,” Di said. He described geopolitical events since the second half of 2025 around the Panama Canal, Greenland and the Strait of Hormuz as “a series of warning signals that the openness of the seas is tending towards an end”. Several natural deepwater ports, especially those China has heavily invested in recent years, such as Ream Naval Base in Cambodia and the Port of Chancay in Peru, Kyaukphyu in Myanmar and Gwadar in Pakistan, could become “potential focal points of geopolitical struggle in the future”, he said. His warning comes amid growing debate over where the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran and the Hormuz crisis could take the strategic rivalry between the world’s two largest economies. Some observers have read Trump’s repeated calls to take control of Greenland, a semi-autonomous territory of Denmark, the unfolding diplomatic contest between Beijing and Washington over the Panama Canal, and the abduction of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January as Washington’s strategic moves to constrain Beijing’s strategic space and global footprint by controlling key international trade and energy nodes. Di wrote the US was unlikely to fully block Chinese shipping, but would tighten control over key nodes and create a calibrated tension, “like holding a knife and repeatedly waving it back and forth around sensitive areas such as your throat, leaving you worried and anxious”. Pushing back against the view that China did not need to compete with the US head-on at sea and could instead turn to developing overland routes linking Asia, Europe and Africa, Di said such an approach “would probably be nowhere near enough to solve the problem of foreign trade channels”. He said annual freight by weight on the China-Europe Railway Express matched about two days’ throughput at Ningbo, the world’s busiest port by cargo volume, and the entire service could be shut down if a single country along the rail line blocked the route, whereas sea-bound trade could switch to alternative routes during emergencies. Di said China should upgrade both the quality and quantity of its naval abilities as foundations of maritime power while building supply bases across the world through long-term diplomatic and military efforts. Although China’s navy had surpassed the US in the number of ships, its total tonnage had not yet overtaken Washington’s. The US alliance system and about 800 overseas bases must also be factored in, he said. While China’s naval equipment was “pulling ahead of the US” at a technical level, there remained “a gap in experience and capability”, Di added. “[We] need to shape a series of new national consensuses,” he wrote. “The future of the Chinese nation does not lie only in East Asia. Peace and respect cannot be bought through retreat and conservatism. Only by embracing, taming and regaining mastery of the oceans does the Chinese nation have a future.”

title: Hong Kong to expand AI use on 1823 platform to vet public inquiries by end of year
description: Digital Policy Office also says it will explore using agentic AI from fourth quarter, automating certain tasks to free up staff for other duties.
content: The operator of the Hong Kong government’s 1823 platform will expand the use of AI within the year to transcribe, summarise and triage residents’ inquiries, freeing frontline staff to handle more complicated cases. The Digital Policy Office also said on Thursday that it would start exploring the application of agentic artificial intelligence from the fourth quarter this year and study how it should be expanded to other departments “with a safe and controlled approach”. The government’s 1823 public inquiry service platform received more than 7.5 million submissions from residents last year, with 4.1 million resolved by automated services such as its AI text and audio chatbots. Acting commissioner for digital policy Daniel Cheung Yee-wai said the platform would extend its use of AI to help staff transcribe residents’ calls, summarise emails and log submissions into its system by the end of the year. Cheung said the expansion would enable staff to dedicate more time to solving complex cases and better address residents’ needs. “Our goal is to elevate the service quality so that residents can receive the service or answers they need. Cutting manpower demand is not our objective,” he said. Simon Lam Kwok-wai, the office’s assistant commissioner for contact centre and change management, said he expected the technology to shorten handling times for calls and emails by 15 per cent and 30 per cent, respectively. An AI-powered triage system would also help identify urgent and complex issues, and refer them to a dedicated team of 1823 staff, who would in turn dispatch messages to the relevant departments, he added. Lam said this could help slash the time for assigning inquiries and complaints to the correct departments from up to two days to just a few hours. The system would also summarise inquiry and complaint data to identify emerging issues in each district and flag them to relevant departments. The move was announced after Hong Kong lawmakers visited the 12345 Citizen Hotline Service Centre during a visit to Beijing in July. The centre uses big data and AI to refer complaints to relevant authorities and set reply deadlines, prompting lawmakers to study proposals for improving 1823. An investigation by the ombudsman in 2024 found that the 1823 platform could not effectively solve cross-departmental complaints or those with unclear delineation of responsibilities. An independent committee investigating last November’s deadly Tai Po fire also found that some residents complaining about the use of combustible materials at the Wang Fuk Court housing estate were passed from pillar to post after 1823 failed to assign them to the correct department. Cheung acknowledged that the platform still had room for improvement and said the office had been helping departments to coordinate in resolving complex issues. “So with the assistance of AI, we expect the time for processing such complex problems will be greatly [shortened],” he said. According to Cheung, among all inquiries and complaints received by the platform in 2025, hundreds of cases needed 1823’s coordination of different departments. Only two complaints could not be resolved by the process and had to be handled by the Task Force on District Governance chaired by Deputy Chief Secretary Warner Cheuk Wing-hing, he added. Deputy digital policy commissioner for data governance Ng Ping-chung said authorities would also pilot the use of agentic AI starting from the fourth quarter this year, referring to technology that can autonomously trigger actions within embedded systems. “We will automate some tasks with agentic AI to relieve government staff from heavy and repetitive administrative matters, so they can focus more on issues that require their professional judgment,” he said. Ng added that the trial would start within the Digital Policy Office, exploring how the technology could “bring value across workstreams” before expanding the practice to other government agencies. “We want to make sure [we] start with a safe and controlled approach to test agentic AI,” he said.

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing explores merging GEM with main board, source says
description: The bourse operator is exploring creating a chapter listing rule to absorb 300-plus firms from the GEM board.
content: Bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) is exploring merging the GEM board with its main board by creating a new chapter of its listing rules, according to a source familiar with the discussions. The proposal to create Chapter 18D, which would be a core part of the second phase of the review of the listing regime, would be subject to a public consultation by the end of the year, the source told the South China Morning Post. Merging it with the main board was an option to reboot the poorly performing GEM, the source said, as the second board was seeing minimal turnover and fewer new listings. “There have been studies on reforming the GEM for a long time, as the second board did not really work well in terms of allowing smaller-sized companies to list,” the source said. “Allowing these smaller players to list in a specific chapter … may be a better option,” the source said. Since its 2018 reform, HKEX has introduced new specific chapters of listing rules, tailored to different companies’ needs, for firms that could not meet general requirements. The chapters include 18A, for pre-revenue biotechnology, 18B for special purpose acquisition companies and 18C for large technology companies without revenue. The proposal for a Chapter 18D would allow newly established, small-sized companies that could not meet the profit requirement to list, the source said. The existing 300 or so firms on GEM may be grandfathered in to join the main board under the new chapter. “The new chapter to replace the GEM would widen the scope of the listed companies at the HKEX, while it would also help the smaller firms to get funding. The reform would help to improve the overall market diversity and also benefit the real economy,” the source said. A spokesman for HKEX said the exchange was exploring further new measures related to its listing regime. “HKEX is pleased to have implemented the first phase of the listing framework competitiveness review, which drew strong market support and enhanced Hong Kong’s attractiveness as a premier fundraising destination,” the spokesman said in a statement. “Building on this progress, we will continue to explore additional measures to strengthen the attractiveness of our listing framework to ensure it remains fit for purpose, and will share updates as appropriate in due course,” he said. The GEM, formerly known as the Growth Enterprise Market, was established in 1999. GEM does not have a profit requirement, while the main board requires a company to make at least HK$80 million in the three years before its listing. As of Thursday, the GEM included 306 firms with a combined market capitalisation of HK$78 billion (US$9.9 billion) – far below the figures for Hong Kong’s main board, which comprises 2,455 companies with a market capitalisation of HK$47.05 trillion. On Thursday, turnover on the GEM was just HK$125 million, about 0.05 per cent of the turnover on the main board. In the first half of the year, the GEM only saw one new company listing, which raised US$9.62 million. The main board, by contrast, hosted 79 new listings that raised a combined US$26 billion – the second-highest total in the world, behind only the Nasdaq. “With only one or two GEM IPOs every year, against a very active main board market, it shows the GEM is not adequately serving start-ups and other smaller growth companies,” said Stephen Law Cheuk-kin, president of the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants (HKICPA) and a private-equity investor. “Hong Kong needs a genuine GEM board reform rather than a cosmetic rebranding,” he added, noting that several previous reforms to the GEM had not worked. To be successful, any reforms to the GEM would need to give the board a clearer purpose, with proportionate admission criteria, a proper disclosure and compliance regime, better liquidity arrangements, and a clear pathway for companies to graduate to the main board, according to Law. “If a new chapter within the main board can achieve those outcomes, it would be better than preserving a separate GEM label that has lost market momentum,” Law said. Tom Chan Pak-lam, honorary president of the Institute of Securities Dealers, also supports the proposal. “It is a sensible evolutionary move that acknowledges GEM has not worked well as a stand-alone board for small and medium-sized enterprise fundraising,” Chan said. “GEM’s problems were never purely structural. Liquidity has been poor, while many GEM-listed firms have struggled with profitability and interest from both retail and institutional investors has been limited.” But Chan said simply relocating existing GEM companies to a new chapter of the listing rules would not be enough to attract investors and encourage research analysts to cover the board. Proper regulation and promotion would be needed to attract start-ups to raise funds via the new mechanism, he added. Chan said the exchange would need to make sure the new listing chapter 18D had a balanced regulatory approach to attract listings from quality small companies.

title: Japan to probe popular animal cafes amid hygiene, welfare concerns
description: A WWF Japan survey has found that some shops keep endangered species while others have inadequate hygiene management.
content: Japan plans to look into popular animal cafes, where visitors can interact with anything from cats to capybaras, following concerns about hygiene and the creatures’ welfare, authorities said on Thursday. Japan has hundreds of the cafes where campaigners say animals are sometimes kept in cramped spaces, and that their popularity encourages the capture and illegal trade of rare wildlife. A fact-finding survey will begin as early as next month, starting with obtaining basic information such as the number of establishments and what animals they keep, according to an environment ministry official. The ministry would examine whether they complied with relevant laws, including whether animals had enough space and how often cleaning took place, the official said, without wishing to be named. “We may then do on-site inspections if we find facilities that appear to be breaching rules” stipulated by the animal welfare law, he said. The decision to launch the survey followed recommendations by members of an expert panel about animal welfare. Animal welfare groups have long been alarmed by the cafes, where visitors can pet and play with a dizzying array of animals including micro-pigs, hedgehogs, owls and snakes. A 2025 survey by WWF Japan said that some kept endangered species listed on the Red List of the International Union for Conservation. They also included species covered by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, which regulates international trade in wildlife. Some shops had inadequate hygiene management without prompting visitors to wash hands after contact with animals, while “microbiological testing detected pathogenic bacteria in multiple facilities”, the report said. What may appear charming to visitors can be stressful and unnatural for the animals Laila Imai, campaign coordinator in Asia for Peta “Whether the animals are otters, capybaras, raccoons, owls, reptiles, or other wild species, these businesses are built around close encounters that prioritise customer entertainment over the animals’ needs,” said Laila Imai, campaign coordinator in Asia of animal welfare group Peta. “Many are subjected to constant handling, noise, flashing cameras, and interactions with strangers throughout the day,” Imai said. “What may appear charming to visitors can be stressful and unnatural for the animals forced to live that way.” Some animal cafes act as adoption centres, helping to find new homes for rescued cats and dogs.

title: Philippines’ rising military pensions risk triggering budget ‘time bomb’
description: The surge in pensions may weaken the country’s push to buy modern military assets to strengthen its deterrence.
content: The Philippines’ push for military modernisation is being squeezed by a ballooning pension bill for its troops as fears mount over its ability to finance newer ships, aircraft and other defence assets. The Department of National Defence has proposed spending 142.95 billion pesos (US$2.3 billion) on military and uniformed personnel (MUP) pensions in 2027, out of a total proposed defence budget of 324.6 billion pesos. The planned pension budget is 7 per cent higher than the 133.91 billion pesos allocated in the 2026 General Appropriations Act amid increasing calls for Manila to review the pension system. While civilian workers typically contribute a part of their salaries to state fund systems, military and uniformed personnel are not required to make pension contributions, which are drawn from the national budget. Proposals to legislate reforms to the armed forces’ pension system have long languished in Congress, with lawmakers warning that it is unsustainable. The debate comes as the Philippines faces growing pressure from the US to spend more on its military. Funds for the military’s modernisation programme next year are set to rise by 10 billion pesos to 50 billion pesos from 2026, which the Department of Budget and Management said was part of efforts to “enhance the military’s capabilities to protect the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity”. But the proposed pensions were nearly triple the amount set aside for the military upgrade, former finance undersecretary Cielo Magno said in an interview with The Philippine Star on Monday. While it was important to compensate the troops fairly, “we must also confront the trade-off: resources consumed by an ever-growing pension bill are resources we cannot use to modernise our armed forces, strengthen territorial defence and fund other essential public services”, Magno said. Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr pushed back on the criticism, saying only 49.6 per cent of the total pension budget was earmarked for military retirees, while the rest would be for “other security services”. “Therefore, to equate the total MUP pension to the AFP [military] modernisation is not accurate as a comparison indicator,” he said in a statement on Monday. Teodoro also defended government-funded pensions for the country’s troops, saying they continued to contribute to national security efforts even in retirement. Soldiers on active duty should get their pensions funded by the national government because of their national security responsibilities, he added. “Our soldiers address a variety of missions 365 days a year without any breaks. Our force structure is extremely lean,” Teodoro said. “Given the fact that they must keep watch over 7,600-plus islands and 2.4 million sq km of maritime area on a purely national government basis and do services for other government entities including [local government units] … their pensions should be national-government derived.” Teodoro said discussions over budget allocations should take into account the total resources devoted to defence, adding that with “worldwide vulnerabilities”, nearly all countries “have made the conscious decision to increase defence spending in large adjustments”. “We cannot be immune to this,” he added. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore in May, urged Washington’s partners to spend at least 3.5 per cent of their gross domestic product on defence. But Manila said it would struggle to meet the target despite higher annual defence spending. “We are a low-income country that has so many other development needs. We are in a catch-up mode, investing in defence capabilities and modernising our armed forces,” Arsenio Balisacan, the country’s chief economist, said in July. Growing financial burden The pensions debate highlights the recurring tug of war between budget constraints and political pressures, according to analysts. “Military pensions have long been a problem, and to me, it points to deeper structural problems in our budget,” said a security analyst, who asked not to be identified. The analyst said the problem was compounded by Manila’s constant push to ensure loyalty from the military. In 2018, former president Rodrigo Duterte raised the base pay of troops by 58.7 per cent. Because pensions were tied to current salaries, authorities said the move created huge financial pressures for the government. In 2023, then finance secretary Benjamin Diokno warned of an “imminent fiscal collapse”, with pension payments expected to reach 1 trillion pesos by 2035. Retired military and uniformed personnel were on average receiving eight times the pensions that civilian workers were entitled to through their contributions, Diokno said. Magno told The Philippine Star that calls for structural pension reform had been “repeatedly deferred”. Chester Cabalza, president and founder of the Manila-based International Development and Security Cooperation think tank, warned of the adverse impact of higher pension payments on the country’s military modernisation, with the “fiscal time bomb” ticking for taxpayers. He said the debate over pensions was linked to motivating the military to “become more patriotic” amid a tussle among the region’s major powers. Meanwhile, the unnamed security analyst said the defence budget’s priority should be strengthening military hardware and called for a revamp of the pension system. “Force restructuring can be done first, which would include identifying whether the number of MUPs and the positions are still appropriate given our current defence priorities,” he said. Calbaza argued that pensions for military personnel should be aligned with those for civil servants. He called for new troops to contribute to their pensions and local governments to partly finance pensions of uniformed personnel, such as police and prison personnel and firefighters. “True defence requires balance,” he added.

title: Shanghai aims to quintuple tax-free merchandise sales to foreign tourists within 5 years
description: Inbound visitors are considered a low-cost initiative to address the nation’s consumption figures.
content: When British actor Tom Holland and his actress wife Zendaya arrived in Shanghai late last month to promote Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the celebrity couple’s sightseeing excursions and shopping expeditions grabbed even more headlines than the blockbuster itself. From dining at a local noodle shop to wearing affordable Chinese apparel brands, the A-list pair spent a day exploring the city, reigniting online buzz in China over the growing trend of foreign tourists visiting and spending in the country. Attracting foreign consumers has become a key strategy for China to stimulate its slowing economy. As the country’s gateway city, Shanghai holds natural advantages in this arena, which are reflected in its officials’ ambitions. In its latest five-year plan for international trade, the municipal government set a target to nearly quintuple tax-free merchandise sales to inbound visitors. The city, positioned as an international consumption hub, recorded 4.28 billion yuan (US$636.8 million) in tax-refund sales last year, and aimed to increase that figure to around 20 billion yuan by 2030, according to the plan released on Tuesday. The plan outlined measures to foster an environment hospitable to spending by visitors from abroad, including simplifying the tax-refund process for departing tourists, optimising multilingual signage and expanding foreign card payment services, currency exchange facilities and luggage storage services. Shanghai’s push aligns with a broader national strategy. Over the past few years, Beijing has rolled out visa-free policies for dozens of countries, leading to a surge in inbound tourist arrivals and a significant boost to spending. Liu Simin, a veteran tourism researcher and a director of the Beijing Tourism Society, said this approach was of strategic importance to China. “While overall tourist numbers have picked up over the past two years, tourist spending has yet to return to pre-pandemic levels in 2019,” he said. “With tourism product supply remaining relatively stable, the arrival of foreign visitors essentially functions as on-the-ground exports – a low-cost way to offset weak domestic demand.” Attracting tourists to experience China first-hand through consumption was both more cost-effective and persuasive, Liu said, than spending on overseas advertising to promote China’s image. Chinese authorities have not released specific figures for national tax-free merchandise sales in 2025, but said the figure nearly doubled from 2024. Sales last year alone were roughly equivalent to the total accumulated over the decade from 2015 – when the tax-refund policy was first implemented – through 2024, the Ministry of Commerce said in a press conference in May. As China’s top destination for inbound tourists, Shanghai received 5.31 million overseas visitors in the first half of this year, up about 28 per cent year on year, figures from the municipal government showed. These visitors generated 2.3 billion yuan in tax-refund sales, a 58 per cent increase from a year earlier. Beneath the growth in external demand is persistently sluggish domestic consumption. Despite Shanghai’s surging inbound tourist spending, official figures suggested that the city’s total retail sales of consumer goods grew only 0.7 per cent year on year in the first half of this year. Nationwide, this number stood slightly better at 1.3 per cent. The Study Times, a newspaper affiliated with the Central Party School of the Communist Party of China, warned that despite the strong momentum in inbound tourism, tourists’ share of shopping expenditure remained low, and though tax-refund consumption had posted substantial growth, it had yet to achieve economies of scale due to a low base. “China’s inbound consumption market is now entering a period of concentrated policy dividends,” it said in a commentary in March, urging the industry to seize the opportunity to build a globally appealing consumption ecosystem for international visitors.
