Singapore’s authorities had reported compliance in earlier cases involving online platforms, Nuurrianti said. “Many of these capabilities are not being developed entirely from scratch,” she said. “Major platforms already have different forms of spam detection, unknown-sender filtering, blocking, group privacy controls and scam warnings.” Mahmood said scams should also be understood within a wider transnational criminal ecosystem, which could include offences such as human and drug trafficking, increasing the incentive and urgency for companies to cooperate. “Scams in isolation might not be a huge policy priority for companies, but when you look at it more holistically, it’s connected to illegal operations around the world and that’s something companies take very seriously,” he said. A regional model? Singapore’s expanded requirements may set a precedent for Southeast Asian countries to adopt a similar framework to tackle scams, given the scale and cross-border nature of online fraud, according to Ysa Marie Cayabyab, an associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore. “Southeast Asia has a highly connected digital environment, but this leaves us exposed to a wider range of scams and vulnerabilities,” she said. Neighbouring countries have also started placing more responsibility on platforms to stop online harm. In June, Malaysia implemented rules requiring online service providers to include safeguards that limit account registration and ownership by users under the age of 16, and to implement stronger content governance. Thailand in May introduced requirements for social media platforms to verify the identity of advertisers before publication, in a bid to prevent online crimes. In March, Indonesia started enforcing a social media ban for under-16s to shield some 70 million children from the threats of online pornography, cyberbullying and internet addiction. Cayabyab said, however, that effectiveness would vary considerably across the region. “Differences in digital literacy, regulatory capacity, platform penetration, languages, and patterns of online behaviour mean that a measure that works well in Singapore may not translate directly elsewhere,” she said. But a regional approach would still be useful, she said, urging greater information sharing among governments and platforms, such as common standards for identifying suspicious behaviour and faster mechanisms to act on red flags. Lam urged coordination and cooperation between Southeast Asian nations, citing a precedent case which resulted in positive action. In January, Indonesia and Malaysia temporarily blocked or restricted access to the Grok AI chatbot operated by Elon Musk’s xAI amid growing concern internationally over sexualised images, while officials in the Philippines also signalled action. Within the month, xAI imposed new restrictions limiting image editing.

title: China-Nepal flash flood: 392 dead and over 1,000 missing, including hundreds of foreigners
description: Premier Li Qiang at scene after ice-rock avalanche triggers disaster leaving hundreds of tourists from around the world unaccounted for.
content: Rescue teams struggled to reach the site of a massive Himalayan mudslide and flash flood on the China-Nepal border as the toll from the disaster rose to 392 dead, with more than 1,000 missing. As of Friday morning, three people were confirmed dead and 558 missing on the Chinese side, with 389 dead and at least 644 missing in Nepal. “Nearly 100” Chinese nationals were missing on the Nepalese side, foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said in Beijing on Thursday. The Chinese embassy in Nepal was working with local authorities to further verify the information, he added. Those missing on the Chinese side include 260 foreign nationals, according to an official update on Thursday morning from Shigatse, the city in China’s Tibet autonomous region that administers the Gyirong border checkpoint. Chinese Premier Li Qiang arrived at the checkpoint on Thursday afternoon to direct disaster relief efforts and visit emergency responders. The Nepal Tourism Board said that among the missing from the disaster were 540 foreign nationals from more than two dozen countries. About 178 of them are from India, 65 from the United States, 35 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Malaysia has confirmed that 55 of its citizens are among the missing. A spokesman for the Nepal Tourism Board earlier told Associated Press that 133 of the missing tourists were Indian pilgrims. Chinese authorities have mobilised more than 1,500 rescue personnel, including firefighters, soldiers and engineering teams, according to the Ministry of Emergency Management. Vice-Premier Zhang Guoqing had arrived at the scene to direct operations but a newly formed barrier lake was complicating rescue efforts, China’s state broadcaster CCTV reported earlier on Thursday. The disaster started in Nepal and hit Gyirong county in Shigatse at around 10.30am on Wednesday. Guo Zhaocheng, a senior remote-sensing engineer from China’s Ministry of Natural Resources, said the disaster was triggered by the collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. The falling ice mass surged downstream, becoming a debris flow and striking the Chinese port facilities, Guo told CCTV. Initial assessments by Nepalese officials pointed to a possible earthquake-triggered collapse of a glacier’s lower section, which may have unleashed the devastating floodwaters. The impact of the glacial avalanche was so immense that it released energy equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, registering on seismographs as a strong tremor. However, the US Geological Survey confirmed that no tectonic quake took place. The area sits alongside a key pilgrimage corridor leading to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar, which draw hundreds of devotees from India and beyond each year, especially during the warmer months. Rescue operations at the stricken port are facing critical roadblocks. According to CCTV and the Shigatse military sub-command, a barrier lake about 2.5km (1.6 miles) from the port and choked with mudslide debris nearly 1.5 metres (5 feet) thick, is severely hampering heavy equipment access. The barrier lake, located at the confluence of a river in Nepal and another in China, posed a risk of triggering secondary landslides, China’s Ministry of Water Resources warned. The water ministry said the lake was already holding about 2 million cubic metres of water, and it had “begun to overflow”. Another 3 million cubic metres was expected to flow into the lake over the next three days, posing a “high risk of a dam breach”, the ministry told CCTV, adding that conditions could worsen with heavy rain on the way. The ministry has sent specialists to the site to monitor the barrier lake. Rescue personnel told Chinese media outlet The Paper that draining the barrier lake was the top priority as only then could crews safely clear nearly 3km of sediment jammed upstream of the port. Meanwhile, continuous rain forecast for the next three days poses a critical threat of secondary disasters, including landslides, rockfalls and flash floods, according to Chinese weather officials. Engineers from China’s Ministry of Natural Resources have also underscored the risks posed by the treacherous terrain – including a vertical plunge exceeding 3,000 metres from icy glacial summit lakes to the valley floor below. The disaster has completely cut off road access and severed local power and communication networks, with five base stations down, according to CCTV. Rescue teams remain unable to establish direct contact with the core port area. Apart from the 1,500 emergency management personnel, 248 workers from central state‑owned enterprises, along with more than 120 units of heavy machinery, Mi‑171 helicopters and a Y-20 transport aircraft have been sent for aerial reconnaissance and logistics, according to CCTV. Dozens of telecoms workers and power grid staff are also at the scene in an effort to restore connectivity. Beijing has allocated 120 million yuan (US$17.8 million) in emergency relief funds for Tibet, as well as 100 million yuan for infrastructure restoration, according to the Ministry of Finance and the National Development and Reform Commission. With the barrier lake threatening to breach and unstable slopes overhead, rescue teams were waiting for conditions to stabilise before entering the core zone, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported. Military engineers were working through the worsening weather to clear blocked roads, the report said.

title: Letters | Hong Kong should study the mainland gig worker insurance model
description: Readers discuss labour protection for delivery riders, and a new era for India-Bangladesh relations.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Labour protection for delivery riders remains controversial in Hong Kong. Critics cite higher corporate costs and potential impacts on catering businesses, yet the rights and safety of riders cannot be sidelined. When Deliveroo left Hong Kong in 2025, 200 full-time staff received severance pay, but 12,000 self-employed riders were left with nothing. Some injury claims became unenforceable once the platform closed. This is not an isolated case: commercial insurance offered by local delivery platforms frequently provides compensation far below the statutory standard set by the Employees’ Compensation Ordinance. The draft bill on injury compensation for digital platform workers is a welcome step, but legislation alone cannot close the gap. Mainland China’s dual model – combining government safeguards with proactive corporate responsibility – is mature and worth studying. Under the mainland’s pilot occupational injury insurance programme for workers in new forms of employment, platforms pay only a small premium per order, allowing costs to flex with demand and fit the volatile gig economy. By June, nearly 30 million workers nationwide had joined the programme. Government-run administration also streamlines claims, reducing disputes and delays. Corporate responsibility is equally important. The experience of JD.com shows that worker welfare is not merely a cost but a long-term investment and responsible behaviour. This approach delivers three measurable gains. First, its S&P Global corporate sustainability rating was the highest among Chinese retail firms, helping lower financing costs and strengthening brand trust. Second, lower rider turnover improves service quality, with the company leading the industry with a user satisfaction score of 95 in 2025. Third, proactive investment also reduces compliance risks and sets benchmarks for competitors. Clearly, firms can and should go beyond minimal legal requirements. Labour protection is not a luxury but a win-win for companies, riders and society. In the meantime, the Hong Kong government should look into adapting lessons from the mainland while also considering supportive measures such as tax incentives for businesses and issuing stakeholder guidelines. A sustainable economy rests on protected worker rights and collaboration among various stakeholders. Legislation provides the baseline, but corporate responsibility is the true engine of sustainable progress. Chen Zihan and Liao Xiru, students, and Dr Chris Cheung, lecturer, Wu Jieh Yee School of Interdisciplinary Studies, Lingnan University India-Bangladesh ties must look beyond Hasina India and Bangladesh share one of South Asia’s most consequential relationships. Their 4,096km border, shared rivers, trade, energy links and security interests make stable cooperation indispensable. Yet rebuilding trust now requires New Delhi to recognise that Bangladesh’s political landscape has fundamentally changed. Over 15 years, India developed exceptionally close ties with Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League government. That cooperation produced gains in connectivity, border management and security. But relations between two states cannot remain anchored to one leader or party. Governments change; geography and national interests do not. Many Bangladeshis believe India still views their country through a “Hasina-centric” lens. Diplomacy depends not only on official intentions but also on public confidence. That confidence will remain difficult to restore if Indian territory is perceived as a platform for political activity by Bangladesh’s former leader. Bangladesh’s expanding engagement with China should not automatically be interpreted as hostility towards India. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s June visit to China advanced discussions on trade, investment, infrastructure, the Teesta River and a proposed China-Myanmar-Bangladesh economic corridor. Dhaka is also strengthening relations with Japan, the United States, Europe and the Middle East. Such diversification is normal for a sovereign state seeking economic opportunity and strategic flexibility. Nor can Bangladesh afford an anti-India foreign policy. India remains its most important neighbour. Equally, an India-centric foreign policy would constrain Bangladesh’s sovereignty and options. A prolonged estrangement would damage both sides. Bangladesh needs cooperation on water, trade, energy and border management. India needs Bangladesh for access to its northeast, Bay of Bengal strategy, regional connectivity and security. The way forward is neither nostalgia nor a contest over which country would suffer more. India should engage Bangladesh as a sovereign society. Dhaka, in turn, should pursue cooperation without surrendering strategic autonomy. A durable foundation of this relationship is built on geography, sovereign equality, mutual interest and the aspirations of both peoples. Shahidul Alam Swapan, Geneva

title: Japan’s sumo chiefs trim tour dates, demand air con to beat summer heat
description: Japan sweltered through its hottest summer on record last year and parts of the country have hit 40 degrees in recent days.
content: Sumo chiefs are planning measures to beat Japan’s increasingly punishing summer heat, including avoiding venues that do not have air conditioning and lightening the load on weary wrestlers. Japan sweltered through its hottest summer on record last year and parts of the country have hit 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in recent days. Hakata ward in the southwestern city of Fukuoka on Wednesday saw the temperature hit 40.4 degrees, caused by hot, moist air from a typhoon flowing into the surrounding region, the Japan Meteorological Agency said. Across the nation, 246 of 914 observation points reported 35 degrees or higher during the day, crossing the threshold of “extremely hot”. When the mercury tops 40 degrees, it is classified as “cruelly hot”. Like elsewhere, human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of dangerous weather in Japan, scientists say. The weather agency expects high temperatures will continue for about a month, advising people to stay hydrated and avoid heat sickness. Sumo wrestlers have been in action throughout August, taking part in a gruelling annual summer tour that sees them perform at venues all around the nation. Tour chief Takadagawa, who goes by one name, told reporters that changes would have to be made to protect their safety. “We can’t do it in places that don’t have air conditioning in summer,” he said this week. Wrestlers held exhibitions this month in at least one venue that had no air conditioning around the ring or in the changing rooms, local media said. Takadagawa, a former wrestler who is now a stablemaster, said sumo chiefs also planned to reduce the number of annual tour dates, starting from next summer. “The schedule has been 90 days until now but we are looking to reduce it to around 70,” he said. “To reduce the physical strain, we will have wrestlers stay in the same place for nearby venues and incorporate two- or three-day tournaments. “We won’t make them undergo excessive travel,” Takadagawa added. Japan experiences about 1,300 heat-related deaths annually. Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi died in Japan earlier this month after being taken to hospital with symptoms consistent with severe heatstroke. Authorities have adjusted the timing of several cultural and sporting events in recent years because of the heat. Additional reporting by Kyodo

title: Singapore police raid iron ore trader Radiant World over fake document claims
description: Law enforcement has targeted the iron ore trader as US authorities also probe transactions following complaints over invalid invoices.
content: Singaporean police raided the local office of iron ore trader Radiant World last week and questioned some of the firm’s employees, according to people familiar with the matter, part of an investigation into the company’s transactions after some counterparties raised concerns about allegedly falsified documents. Several major commodity traders have cut ties with the company amid concerns that it provided invoices or other documents to its banks that were not valid. The Singapore police said that investigations were ongoing and further details were not available. Radiant World declined to comment in response to questions for this story. The company separately said: “The company is engaging with the relevant authorities, and it would not be appropriate to comment further while those processes are ongoing.” It said it would not litigate the company’s affairs through the media. The Singapore police confirmed it was looking into Radiant World last Thursday, saying that reports had been lodged against the trader, without indicating who had made the complaints. The US Justice Department and Commodity Futures Trading Commission are also investigating transactions involving Radiant World and its creditors. Radiant World has not been accused of wrongdoing and investigations do not always lead to charges. The company has previously denied wrongdoing and said that it conducted its business to the highest commercial and legal standards. Commodities broker Marex Group has frozen all Radiant World’s accounts following allegations that the iron ore trader used invalid invoices to raise funds, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: China’s Akeso says cancer drug beat AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi in phase 3 trial
description: The biliary tract cancer trial is the latest breakthrough for Akeso’s ivonescimab, which has also shown promise in treating some lung cancers.
content: Chinese biopharmaceutical firm Akeso announced on Wednesday that its immunotherapy drug had outperformed AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi in a head-to-head phase three trial for biliary tract cancer. The result represents another breakthrough for Akeso’s ivonescimab – which has already been licensed by the US firm Summit Therapeutics in a multibillion-dollar deal – as China’s biopharmaceutical industry increasingly looks to compete on the global stage. The Chinese trial tested ivonescimab and chemotherapy against AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi (durvalumab) plus chemotherapy on a total of 682 patients with advanced biliary tract cancer – a particularly deadly form of cancer with a five-year survival rate of less than 5 per cent, according to a Nature study. The results showed that patients taking Akeso’s novel drug lived longer than those using the AstraZeneca treatment, the company said in a Hong Kong stock exchange filing released a day ahead of its interim results. The study marks the first positive phase three study for ivonescimab in gastrointestinal tumours, potentially opening the door for the drug to be used in a “broader range of solid tumours”, said Xia Yu, Akeso’s founder, chairwoman and CEO. However, Akeso has yet to disclose the exact survival figures from the trial, which the Zhongshan-headquartered company is expected to present at a coming conference. Ivonescimab has already shown promise as a treatment for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), receiving initial approval from Chinese regulators. The drug’s licenser, Summit, is also applying for approval to use ivonescimab to treat NSCLC in the United States. Akeso has launched a string of trials to test ivonescimab on other forms of cancer, including colorectal cancer and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. The moves come as China’s biopharma firms increasingly look to compete directly against global giants such as AstraZeneca. The British-Swedish firm generated more than US$6 billion in revenue last year from sales of Imfinzi, up 28 per cent year on year. If things go smoothly, Akeso should be able to begin marketing ivonescimab as a treatment for biliary tract cancer in China relatively soon following the successful trial, according to analysts. “Typically, it takes about a year from a successful phase three trial to market launch, once a company files its regulatory application for a specific indication,” said Zhang Jialin, head of China healthcare research at Nomura. But Tony Ren, head of Asia healthcare research at Macquarie Capital, cautioned that the trial would not necessarily open up a big new market for Akeso, as advanced biliary tract cancer was “a rare disease”. Akeso’s shares rose nearly 7.5 per cent to HK$101.20 on Thursday, extending Wednesday’s rally and bucking the broader market. The benchmark Hang Seng Index slipped 0.34 per cent. Akeso first drew comparisons to artificial intelligence start-up DeepSeek’s disruptive rise after ivonescimab beat Merck’s Keytruda in a phase three advanced lung cancer trial in September 2024. The result stunned global oncology circles by showing a Chinese drug developer could outperform a Western blockbuster in a head-to-head study. The trial found ivonescimab cut the risk of disease progression or death by nearly half compared with Keytruda.

title: Nvidia ships first H200 chips to China, but forecasts no data-centre computing revenue
description: AI chipmaker upbeat on global demand, saying it expects revenue to grow by about 70 per cent in 2028 financial year.
content: Nvidia has confirmed its first shipments of H200 data-centre processors to China under a new US licensing scheme, ending a months-long lockout. However, the sales accounted for less than 1 per cent of the company’s US$89 billion data-centre revenue in its second quarter, which ended on July 26. The H200 disclosure marked a shift from the previous quarter, when Nvidia said it had made no shipments of Data Centre Hopper products to China. Although Washington approved H200 exports in January, Beijing initially restricted purchases as it promoted home-grown alternatives, before allowing selected Chinese AI companies to buy limited quantities from last month. The US chip giant’s US$108 billion third-quarter revenue forecast continued to assume no data-centre computing revenue from China. Despite the muted contribution from China, Nvidia struck an upbeat tone on global demand. The company said it expected revenue to grow by about 70 per cent in its 2028 financial year, describing the forecast as supply constrained. CEO Jensen Huang said actual demand was “much greater than 70 per cent”, adding that Nvidia’s available supply allowed it to confidently forecast growth at that level. “The unconstrained [growth] would be a lot higher,” Huang said in an earnings call webcast on Wednesday, adding that the company had secured significant capacity but still needed “a lot more”. He said hyperscalers represented only about half of the opportunity, with the remainder coming from enterprises, neo clouds and sovereign AI projects. As demand surges, Nvidia is also taking a more active role in helping artificial intelligence companies finance the infrastructure needed to buy and deploy its chips, prompting concerns over so-called “circular financing”. “We know some will call this circular financing. We see it differently,” chief financial officer Colette Kress said during the company’s earnings call on Thursday morning in Asia after the US market close, arguing that Nvidia’s investments were backing companies with rapidly expanding demand whose growth was increasingly limited by access to computing infrastructure rather than customers. Nvidia had invested nearly US$50 billion in frontier AI laboratories and recently partnered with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR on financing platforms designed to mobilise more than US$500 billion of third-party capital for AI infrastructure, Kress said. We get paid twice, once on the hardware sale and again through the share of rental revenue Colette Kress, Nvidia chief financial officer The company had introduced revenue-sharing arrangements with AI cloud operators that saw it provide a take-or-pay commitment on part of a facility’s capacity and a minimum revenue guarantee that could help the operator secure financing. In return, Nvidia received a share of revenue generated above that threshold, she said. “We’re not making loans in this model,” Kress said. “We get paid twice, once on the hardware sale and again through the share of rental revenue.” The third-quarter revenue forecast followed another record quarter. Nvidia reported second-quarter revenue of US$96.2 billion, up 106 per cent from a year earlier and ahead of analysts’ average estimate of US$92.5 billion, according to Bloomberg. Revenue from AI clouds, industrial and enterprise customers jumped 138 per cent year on year to US$40.3 billion. Nvidia shares rose 4.71 per cent in after-hours trading following the results. Nvidia also disclosed a major expansion of its partnership with Amazon Web Services (AWS), which will deploy an additional 2 million Nvidia GPUs from the current quarter through to the second quarter of the 2029 financial year. AWS will also deploy Vera central processing units, including some integrated with Rubin systems. The next major growth driver is expected to be Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform. Production shipments began early this month, and the company said it had already received purchase orders from every major hyperscaler, AI cloud provider and system manufacturer. Nvidia said it expected Rubin to account for about 20 per cent of data-centre revenue in the third quarter and expected it to mark the fastest product ramp-up in the company’s history. Supply, however, was expected to remain a bottleneck through to at least the end of the 2028 financial year. Nvidia said sharply higher memory prices would also put pressure on profitability, with gross margin expected to fall from 74 per cent in the third quarter to between 71 and 72 per cent in the fourth quarter before recovering to 72 to 73 per cent in the 2028 financial year as price increases took effect.

title: Hong Kong remains most international city in Asia, widening lead over Singapore
description: City leads in business, connectivity and talent diversity but trails rivals in technology investment, Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce finds.
content: Hong Kong has widened its lead over Singapore as Asia’s most international city, buoyed by gains in innovation and ideas, but still trails in attracting technology investment, a leading business chamber study has found. The Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce’s annual Asian Cities Internationality Index, released on Thursday, ranked Hong Kong first among 11 Asian cities with 74.6 out of 100 points in a measure of seven key areas. Its lead over Singapore widened to two points, up from 0.2 points last year. Hong Kong retained first place in business and economy, scoring 78.6 points. It ranked second in quality of life, infrastructure and connectivity, and human capital diversity. The city rose from fourth to third place in innovation and ideas. It also remained third in government and legal systems for business, and fourth in cultural interaction, for the second consecutive year. Chamber chairman Jacob Kam Chak-pui said Hong Kong performed well in research and innovation exchanges through its universities and scientific work, and in attracting leading global professionals through talent admission schemes. “So in these two areas, we are doing well and can continue to build on them,” he said. However, Hong Kong had to step up its efforts in securing private investment for technology innovation, Kam said, adding that with traditional investment funds remained cautious because of the higher perceived risks. “A new start-up finding investors and securing funds elsewhere is relatively easier than in Hong Kong,” he said. Kam cited Shanghai, which has set an explicit goal of cultivating 100 unicorns by 2027 and introduced policies to speed up progress. “Over the past decade, we have witnessed the emergence of about 20 Hong Kong unicorns, demonstrating the city’s tremendous capability in nurturing world-class innovative enterprises,” he said. “Looking ahead, Shanghai’s ambitious goal-setting serves as a powerful inspiration for Hong Kong to further boost its momentum.” Kam said broader social acceptance of innovative technology was another crucial area. Asked how cultural interaction could be improved, he said the city should strengthen its overall atmosphere, cultural appeal and diversity for visitors, international businesspeople and expatriates through activities held throughout the year, alongside established signature events such as the Hong Kong Sevens rugby tournament. “Mega-events [should not] only be at Kai Tak [stadium]. As Hong Kong embraces the ‘tourism is everywhere’ initiative, we invite businesses to explore new investment opportunities and enhance the variety and diversity of cultural and entertainment events,” Kam said. “For mega-events, [it should give] the impression to visitors of the entire city that they are not just watching one sports match, but have related or other entertainment choices before and after. “This can boost the competitiveness of our overall cultural interaction.” Singapore retained second place with 72.6 points. Seoul rose to third, overtaking Tokyo, which fell to fourth, followed by Shanghai, Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur. The study, conducted by independent research firm Ipsos, combined 60 per cent hard data from authoritative sources with 40 per cent soft data from an online survey conducted in February and more than 10 in-depth qualitative interviews, according to the report. The survey involved 1,111 executives across the 11 cities, split evenly between local residents and foreign executives who had lived and worked in the city for the past two years. All respondents also had experience of living, working or doing business in at least three of the selected cities. Among other recommendations, the report said cities should develop sector-focused policies linking trade and logistics, align urban planning with affordable housing and green spaces, attract international research talent, and advance the digitalisation of government and judicial processes. Kam said the study aimed to help raise Asia’s overall competitiveness, as its economies are projected to account for about 60 per cent of global gross domestic product growth, underscoring the region’s growing economic significance. Allan Zeman, chairman of Lan Kwai Fong Group, said the 50,000-seat Kai Tak Stadium was a game-changer that had attracted more international events, while the M+ contemporary art museum and the Hong Kong Palace Museum had also strengthened the city’s cultural appeal. Zeman said Hong Kong’s high degree of safety remained a key factor in attracting foreign capital and talent but was often overlooked. He added that the city’s financial services sector was thriving, accounting for 27 per cent of GDP, while geopolitical tensions could prompt hundreds of family offices from the Middle East to establish operations in Hong Kong. Zeman also said the city was benefiting from mainland China’s rapid advances in electric vehicles and robotics, driven by long-term planning and government support. “As China gains more and more popularity and more and more confidence from other countries in the world, Hong Kong can only get stronger and stronger,” he said.

title: Bears and pest control: how Japan is spending its departure tax windfall
description: Critics say the funds are being channelled into projects with limited direct benefit to travellers and question how the money is being spent.
content: Billions of yen from a higher departure tax that Japan plans to use to support tourism are being channelled into projects that critics say offer limited direct benefit to travellers, including measures to prevent bear attacks and eradicate an invasive beetle. The Japanese government expects to raise 130 billion yen (US$817.7 million) in the 2026 financial year from the International Tourist Tax, after increasing the levy last year on anyone leaving the country through an airport or seaport. The cost of leaving Japan for foreign tourists and Japanese travellers alike rose from 1,000 yen to 3,000 yen per person on July 1. During political debate on the increase – when a figure as high as 5,000 yen was discussed – the government emphasised that the additional funds were needed to address problems linked to chronic overtourism in some parts of the country. The government said additional spending would go towards promoting Japan as an overseas destination and developing large resort facilities. The industry expressed hope that funds would also be used to hire more tourism staff in rural areas, train guides, improve multilingual signage and information, and upgrade tourism websites. But an investigation by the Asahi newspaper found that billions of yen had been allocated to measures to reduce bear attacks in rural communities and a scheme to eradicate an invasive beetle species that preys on native trees, including cherry trees. Besides countermeasures against bears and insects, money from the departure tax has also been earmarked for a facility to preserve manga artwork, a new centre where important cultural properties can be restored and an exhibition hub for murals from the ancient Takamatsuzaka Tomb in Nara prefecture. An additional 16.4 billion yen has been set aside to reduce the cost of obtaining a Japanese passport, part of a campaign to encourage more Japanese people to travel abroad by cutting the application fee by 7,000 yen. “The bear control measures sound very much as if they are primarily spending for a domestic audience and are good political capital for the government,” said Ashley Harvey, a travel marketing analyst who has worked in Japan’s travel sector for more than 15 years. “Obviously safety is important, but I doubt very much that a tourist from New York is going to be basing his decision on whether to come to Japan or not on the likelihood of being eaten by a bear,” he told This Week in Asia. Nevertheless, an Environment Ministry official justified using 6 billion yen from the tax by telling the Asahi that foreign hikers could be attacked by bears. The ministry has been contacted for further comment. There have been 55 reported injuries in bear attacks across Japan since the start of the financial year on April 1, with a record six fatalities. Two foreigners were among those injured. About 60 per cent of the incidents happened in mountain forests, with the remainder occurring on farmland or in suburban areas. Questions have also been raised over the 600 million yen allocated to efforts to eradicate insects that damage cherry trees, with the ministry saying it is important to protect the trees because many foreign tourists visit Japan specifically during cherry blossom season. The report also pointed out that using tourism tax income for campaigns against bear attacks and insects eased pressure on the national budget, as previous funding had come from the government’s general revenue allocation. “I’m half-and-half on the way this money is being spent,” said Yuuki Bando, owner of the Bang-Do travel guiding business in Tokushima City, on Shikoku island. Bando lauded the campaign to protect cherry trees as “positive” but said the government’s plans were not explained clearly to tourism industry players. “I had not heard about the ways the money is being spent previously, and it is a problem if the government changes its plans without notifying the industry,” she said. Bando called for better signage and information in different languages to encourage more foreign visitors to her region, but said that despite the government’s windfall, “I have not noticed any greater spending on tourism infrastructure here.” Harvey said he feared bureaucratic inefficiencies at the local level would consume a large portion of the money earned through the higher tax, meaning less would be available where it was most needed. “It’s not really a question of how much the government brings in; it’s a question of the methodology behind how it is spent,” he said. Local governments’ tourism departments cannot directly spend on promotion efforts – a legal constraint designed to increase transparency and prevent companies from receiving favourable treatment. Instead, local authorities have to operate through destination management organisations, which inevitably take a cut of the funds that would otherwise go directly into the tourism sector, according to Harvey. “There are inbuilt inefficiencies and ineffectiveness in the way the system operates here, with more layers of companies involved just making everything more complicated, time-consuming and expensive,” he said, adding that streamlining processes and dramatically reducing the bureaucracy would arguably be the best way of spending the government’s tax windfall.

title: Rectangular watches are back, from Cartier to Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet
description: Driven by a revival in classic elegance, rectangular cases are capturing a new generation of collectors looking beyond standard round sports watches.
content: Rectangular watches have long occupied a unique spot in horology. Less ubiquitous than round exemplars, these cases are home to some of the industry’s most enduring designs. Now, as dressier watches continue to outperform sports models, the shape is moving further into focus. According to a new report from Chrono24, an online marketplace for luxury timepieces, demand for rectangular cases rose 9.3 per cent year on year in 2025, suggesting buyers are increasingly looking beyond their rounded brethren. “The growing demand for rectangular cases is driven by a broader market shift towards classic elegance and understated luxury,” says Kana Mackie, who is responsible for Chrono24’s Asia-Pacific business. “Buyers are increasingly looking for distinctive silhouettes that stand out from the standard round sports watch.” The origins of the rectangular case shape can be traced back to the early 20th century, as wristwatches began replacing the pocket variety. World War I accelerated that shift, as soldiers and officers needed practical timepieces they could check at a glance. As production increased, so did experimentation with different case shapes. A round wristwatch, of course, made total sense as it not only followed the silhouette of the pocket watch, but also proved easy to seal against water and dust. A rectangular case, on the other hand (pun intended), benefits from a streamlined look that is more closely aligned with the shape of the wrist. The most famous rectangular timepiece is no doubt the Cartier Tank. Designed by Louis Cartier in 1917 and first released in 1919, it took its name from the military tanks then appearing on the Western front. Seen from above, the tank’s rectangular body and parallel tracks were translated into the watch’s case and brancards, resulting in a design unlike that of any of the round watches that had come before. The shape also found its natural home in the art deco period of the 1920s and 30s, when symmetry and geometric lines transformed everything from architecture to jewellery design. In 1931, Swiss watchmaker Jaeger-LeCoultre added another icon to the rectangular line-up with the Reverso. Originally designed for polo players, its swivelling case enabled the dial to be flipped, protecting the crystal from mallet and ball impacts. Rectangular cases also posed a new challenge inside the watch. Early wristwatches often used rounded movements, which fitted neatly into round cases but left unused space inside rectangular ones. Watchmakers responded by developing rectangular movements that fitted the case properly, rather than placing a round calibre inside and leaving empty space at the corners. Today, models like the Tank and Reverso continue to drive growth in the rectangular watch category, with demand for the Tank up 17.4 per cent in 2026 compared with 2025, while the Reverso is up 8.7 per cent, according to Mackie. Beyond these established rectangular veterans, she says, demand for references like IWC Schaffhausen’s Novecento, Patek Philippe’s Twenty-4 and the Cartier Tank Américaine has more than doubled over the past year. Demand for rectangular watches is concentrated around the 1980s, where buyers are drawn to the neo-vintage look; and the 2010s, where the attraction is more minimal and modern. “New releases from the past two to three years play a comparatively smaller role,” Mackie notes. “The current momentum is clearly built on established silhouettes rather than fresh launches.” So who’s buying them? According to Mackie, buyers under 30 are 33 per cent more likely to choose a rectangular watch than those aged 50 to 60, suggesting the shape is finding a younger audience. Demand has also historically been strongest in Europe, particularly in the UK and France, though Mackie says the trend is now picking up in the US. At auction, the market tells a similar story. Jonathan Darracott, global head of watches at Bonhams, says rectangular watches are “far more accepted and appreciated than they were a decade ago”, with Cartier continuing to lead the category. “More than 100 years after its introduction, the Tank has seen a strong resurgence in both popularity and value,” he says, pointing to models such as the Bamboo and Tank Allongée, as well as the Tank Basculante, which he describes as “probably the most rectangular watch, with a case made of three swivelling rectangular frames”. Brands are now leaning back into that history. Audemars Piguet is the latest watchmaker to revive an iconic rectangular model with the Neo Frame Jumping Hour, which takes its inspiration from a 1929 model, placing a jumping-hour display and sector dial inside a compact rectangular case. German maker A. Lange & Söhne, meanwhile, has returned to the shape with the Cabaret Tourbillon Honeygold, a 50-piece limited edition with a rectangular case and dial made in the brand’s proprietary Honeygold, with black-rhodiumed surfaces and a tourbillon with stop seconds. For Eric Wind, a vintage watch dealer and owner of Wind Vintage in Palm Beach, Florida, the appetite for rectangular and uniquely shaped watches is part of a wider broadening of collector taste. “Collector interest in rectangular and shaped watches has increased significantly in the last few years,” he says. “I think part of it is the appeal of old-world glamour. Hollywood actors from the 20s through the 40s often wore rectangular watches.” He doesn’t anticipate the momentum stopping any time soon, either. “It has been great to see the vintage and modern watch markets widen and deepen across all aspects,” Wind says. “I expect interest in rectangular watches to continue growing, and values for the best examples to also increase.”

title: South Korean ex-spy reveals toll of secret missions to North: ‘treated as expendable’
description: Agents work in isolation and the surveillance never stops, a former agent trained to infiltrate North Korea reveals.
content: In 1984, Ha Tae-jun, then 24, spotted a notice recruiting for a special unit at the Military Manpower Administration office in central Seoul’s Yongsan district. The notice was scrawled on the wall in marker, with little explanation. Ha applied, and his life was changed forever – training as a South Korean operative for covert missions into North Korea. “About a month after submitting background check documents, they said I’d passed and told me to meet at a cafe near my house,” said Ha, now 66 and president of the Association of Bereaved Families of Special Mission Agents. At the time, he had no idea it would be three years before he saw home again. Taken to a safe house on Mount Cheonggye in Seongnam, Gyeonggi province, he passed a fitness test and got into a car, believing it would take him home. Instead, the car took him to another safe house in Sokcho, Gangwon province, operated by the Headquarters of Intelligence Detachment, a South Korean military unit that trained and dispatched agents on covert infiltration missions into North Korea. The next morning, he woke up surrounded by North Korean military uniforms, with every weapon in sight made for use by hostile forces. From that day, his life took an unexpected path. According to Ha, four people were assigned to each agent. He lived in a villa with an officer, a non-commissioned officer and two enlisted men, one handling daily chores, the other monitoring him as a training assistant. Constant surveillance One of the most important principles they operated under was, ironically, keeping him in the dark. That way, if he were captured in North Korea, he would have nothing to tell them. “I didn’t even know the names of the people I lived with, only surnames like Kim, Lee or Park, or nicknames like ‘big teacher’ and ‘little teacher’. I was trained only for the operation I’d carry out in the North, nothing else.” Training began at 6am with a 4km (2.5-mile) run. Twice a week, he ran 12km of mountain terrain in an hour, carrying 25kg of sand, 1kg weights on each leg, and his rifle. Because operations took place at night, infiltration drills were concentrated after dark. He was also drilled in Morse code, used to stay in contact with headquarters after crossing into North Korea. Agents trained in isolation, being kept apart so they never met. Trainees learned North Korean dialect and trained in skydiving and scuba diving, since a single agent had to operate on land, sea and air alike. Every piece of equipment at the safe house, down to the firearms, was not South Korean. Unlike the way South Korean films often portray the training of agents who infiltrate North Korea, there was no beating or verbal abuse, Ha said. “The instructors spoke politely, because with weapons right there, pointing a gun the wrong way during training could turn deadly.” But the hardest part mentally was the surveillance. “Once you go in, you can’t come out. They tell you it’s for two or three years, but that’s just talk. The state controlled us with no rule of law, and everyone knew the contract meant nothing.” Once you go in, you can’t come out Ha Tae-jun, former agent The surveillance did not end with his discharge. Every time he moved and had a home phone installed, he would get a call asking if the move went well. To him, it meant he was still being watched, and knowing that made him instinctively withdraw. That caution carried over to the operations themselves. Asked whether he had ever gone into North Korea, Ha said: “No comment.” He added that no one who crossed over after the South-North joint statement on July 4, 1972, would ever tell. In that statement, the two Koreas agreed on principles for unification and pledged to stop sending armed agents into each other’s territory. Licence to kill The training reshaped more than what he could say. Learning to kill without hesitation, steal and blow things up turned Ha’s personality cruel. Three years of isolation ended with his discharge. To his family, he had simply vanished and reappeared. “I went to my sister’s house. She and her husband asked where I’d been all this time without a word,” he said. “Just as I was trained to say, I told them I’d been out on a deep-sea fishing boat.” Not long after, more trouble surfaced. One day, police showed up and tried to handcuff him. At the station, it turned out he had been considered a long-term missing person. During his years as an agent, he had also never once attended reserve forces training. “If you skipped reserve forces training, you got hit with heavy fines. I later looked at my training record card, and for years there was a record of me being indicted.” That indictment record made his return to society far harder. A month after he got a job at Samsung Electronics, the general affairs office showed him the record and asked for an explanation. He could not give one and was fired. “The state abandoned the promise of a stable job to people who had their whole future ahead of them,” Ha said, adding that most former agents, like him, ended up with criminal records and could not find proper work. In 2004, a law providing compensation and recognition for former infiltration agents was passed, but Ha said it was not enough. “There should have been a fact-finding committee to determine how much we contributed and suffered, but none existed. Bereaved families don’t know whether their father, child or sibling went on an infiltration mission. The state didn’t notify them for decades whether the person was dead or alive. It treated us as expendable.” For Ha, what the state owes its agents is more respect and sincerity. “In the United States, people are given the highest respect the moment they put on the uniform. Is that really true in South Korea? The state needs to properly carry out the work of finding the bereaved families of North Korea infiltration agents.” This article was first published by The Korea Times

title: Opinion | Wanted in Hong Kong: the theatrical equivalent of a hawker centre
description: Raze Hong Kong Stadium, which has outlived its purpose, and build a theatre village in its place to establish the city as a global cultural powerhouse.
content: On a Saturday evening, Causeway Bay crackles with its famous retail energy, yet by 9 o’clock the streets begin their nightly death. There is nowhere magnetic to spill into – no late-night jazz den, immersive dinner theatre or playhouse humming with an experimental musical. Nearby, the 40,000-seat Hong Kong Stadium squats in silence while the catering rooms of the Happy Valley racecourse sit largely empty on non-race nights. This dead zone between one of the world’s densest shopping districts and a historic sporting valley is a failure of urban imagination. The remedy is hiding in plain sight: demolish the obsolete stadium and replace it with a dense, dining-infused cluster of at least 20 small to medium-sized theatres, physically linked to both the racecourse and the Lee Garden retail corridor. International producers of first-run musicals routinely bypass our city. The hottest Broadway and West End transfers increasingly open in Shanghai or Shenzhen. The issue is simple: venue supply rather than audience taste or ticket pricing. Hong Kong’s cultural infrastructure remains trapped in a binary: a few cavernous halls or shoebox black boxes. What every world city has – and what we lack – is the theatrical equivalent of a hawker centre: a dense, walkable precinct of contrasting performance spaces, each with integrated food and beverage options. Happy Valley’s stadium site is the only plausible venue. With the Rugby Sevens migrating to Kai Tak, the concrete bowl has lost its purpose. Raze it, and in its place build a theatre village of deliberately contrasting venues, clustered around a lantern-lit central piazza. Picture a doorway leading to a sumptuous 800-seat Cantonese opera house that evokes the lost glory of the original Lee Theatre – the fabled Percival Street venue that was the spiritual home of Cantonese theatrical tradition right in Causeway Bay’s heart. A new Lee Theatre within the cluster would reclaim that heritage. Next door, a 1,500-seat Broadway-calibre musical theatre would compete for first-run productions that currently head north. Across the courtyard, a 400-seat jazz and cabaret supper club could host late-night vocalists, while a thrust-stage drama theatre, sprung-floor dance house, dedicated children’s theatre, indie live-house and black-box Cantonese comedy studio would complete the mix. Twenty-plus distinct venues turn a single-destination evening into a multi-night draw. A tourist might have dim sum at the Cantonese opera on Friday, take in a Broadway musical on Saturday afternoon and enjoy a negroni-fuelled jazz set that night – all without calling a taxi. Every venue must integrate dining and drinking into its architecture. When performance and gastronomy are inseparable, a full sensory journey ensues. Shenzhen can build shiny multiplexes inside shopping centres, but it cannot fabricate the heritage-infused, walkable, alfresco atmosphere of a Happy Valley theatre quarter – provided we build it. The physical linkage makes this vision economically irresistible. Lee Garden Five and the Hysan-Swire ecosystem already channel a wealth of high-spending visitors daily. An air-conditioned, art-lined pedestrian spine must extend directly from Lee Garden Five along Hysan Avenue and Leighton Road, pulling that footfall naturally towards the theatres. On race nights, the Jockey Club’s superb restaurants and members’ boxes can absorb the overflow seamlessly. Ticket packages combining a race day buffet with a post-race musical will become a unique selling point. On non-race nights, those same Jockey Club catering facilities could transform into pre-theatre supper clubs, jazz brunch venues or late-night dessert bars serving the theatre crowds. The entire valley should pulse as one integrated entertainment ecosystem, ending the absurdity of two great institutions staring silently at each other. The government must zone the stadium site for a cultural and entertainment cluster, mandating a minimum number of small to medium-sized theatres, compulsory food and beverage integration and a design brief that compels physical linkage with both the racecourse and the Lee Garden extension. Land release will be the catalyst. Once the footprint is available with a clear cultural zoning, developers, the Jockey Club and international theatre operators will invest because Causeway Bay’s guaranteed footfall curbs the proposition’s risks. Venues bring investment, and investment creates the fresh, layered experiences that keep a city alive after dark. For too long, Hong Kong has believed a single flagship venue can anchor its cultural identity. To compete with Shenzhen, we must stop playing the scale-and-cost game and instead offer something algorithm-optimised malls cannot replicate: a dense, character-rich, dining-infused cluster where Cantonese opera, Broadway musicals, jazz cabarets and experimental theatre hum side by side. Tear down the silent coliseum. Build the 20 stages. Let Causeway Bay’s crowds flow into Happy Valley, and let the Valley sing back every single night.

title: Taiwan man wins lawsuit but gets jailed for using robot vacuum to record wife’s affair
description: Court rules that marital obligations do not override individual’s right to privacy, sentencing husband to five months in prison.
content: A man in Taiwan who used a robot vacuum cleaner to gather evidence of his wife’s affair won a civil lawsuit but was subsequently sentenced to prison for invading her privacy. A recently released court ruling, reported by local media, disclosed that the man, whose identity remains confidential, got married in 2021. The couple lived with his parents and only visited their holiday home during holidays. In September 2023, the man discovered a used toothbrush at the holiday home, heightening his suspicions. After reviewing surveillance footage from a parking garage, he identified an unknown man who had previously driven his wife home. Three months later, he remotely activated the home’s robot vacuum cleaner via its mobile application, planning to use its built-in audio feature to communicate with his wife. However, the live feed captured his wife in an intimate encounter with another man. Seeking evidence for a legal claim, he began recording the footage. The video showed his wife changing clothes, embracing her alleged lover, and moving around the house unclothed, while her partner was seen lying on the sofa. Shortly thereafter, the husband used the footage as evidence to sue his wife and her lover for infringing on his marital rights, seeking NT$2 million (US$68,000) in damages. The court determined that their relationship had surpassed the limits of ordinary friendship and ordered the pair to pay the husband NT$500,000 in compensation. However, this civil victory did not protect the husband from legal repercussions regarding how the evidence was obtained. The wife subsequently counter-sued, accusing him of recording private footage without her consent. The man contended that the video had already been accepted by the civil court and that his actions were “legally justified.” Nonetheless, the court rejected his defence, ruling that marital obligations do not supersede an individual’s right to privacy. It determined that the recording was deliberate. Furthermore, any lights or voice alerts from the robot vacuum were deemed insufficient to establish that the wife was aware she was being recorded or had consented to the capture of the footage. The man was ultimately sentenced to five months in prison and fined NT$150,000 for unlawfully recording private images. Under Taiwanese law, secretly recording or disclosing another person’s private activities or intimate information without authorisation can result in a sentence of up to three years in prison and a fine of up to NT$300,000. The case has garnered widespread attention on social media. One online commenter noted: “The husband is a victim in some respects. He lost his marriage and also his freedom.” Another remarked: “While proving infidelity can be challenging, there are legal avenues available, including chat histories, hotel receipts, and financial transactions. Seeking justice must always adhere to the boundaries of the law.”

title: Hong Kong cancels rainstorm warnings, afternoon school sessions go ahead
description: Observatory cancels amber rainstorm warning at 10.15am, about an hour after downgrading it from red.
content: Hong Kong’s weather forecaster cancelled its rainstorm warnings on Thursday, following spells of heavy rain that led to the suspension of morning and whole-day schools, with afternoon classes allowed to proceed. The Observatory issued the red signal – the middle level in a three-tier system – at 5.05am, and soon after also sent out a special landslip advisory for Po Toi Island due to heavy rain. The forecaster downgraded the red alert to amber at 9.20am and then cancelled that one at 10.15am. The Education Bureau announced that classes at all morning and whole-day schools were suspended. But afternoon classes proceeded as usual. The Home Affairs Department opened temporary shelters for residents affected by the adverse weather. The forecaster warned earlier in the morning that heavy rain could trigger flash floods, with flooding occurring or expected around watercourses. “Residents living in close proximity to rivers should stay alert to weather and should consider evacuation if their homes may become flooded,” it said. The weather throughout the rest of Thursday is forecast to be mostly cloudy, with heavy showers and squally thunderstorms. The rain is expected to gradually ease off, while temperatures are likely to peak at about 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit). The forecaster also said that Tropical Cyclone Saudel would edge closer to the coast of Fujian and Zhejiang provinces in mainland China on Thursday and Friday. “Under the influence of its outer subsiding air, the weather will become very hot over southern China in the latter part of this week,” the Observatory said, warning that the high temperatures could trigger further showers. Saudel is a name provided by the Federated States of Micronesia and refers to the guards of the legendary ruler of the country’s Pohnpei Island. The Observatory predicted that the weather would remain unsettled over the next couple of days, with rainfall expected on Friday and Saturday.

title: China launches world’s first 100kW bamboo-built floating solar farm off Shandong coast
description: The experimental platform is part of a broader push to replace steel and plastic components with more environmentally friendly materials.
content: China has launched the world’s first 100-kilowatt (kW) floating solar farm built with bamboo frames, offering a more environmentally friendly approach to offshore energy. The floating solar platform, named Jilin-2, is made of composite bamboo tubes and pipes. It has been deployed at a demonstration base off the coast of Yantai in the eastern province of Shandong. It will supply power to an integrated hydrogen, ammonia and methanol production project, manufacturer Yantai CIMC Raffles Ocean Technology Group announced in late June. “Compared to conventional steel or [high-density polythene] structures, the bamboo-based design significantly reduces marine environmental impact,” CIMC Raffles said. The new platform builds upon an earlier 10kW prototype called Jilin-1 from 2023. Jilin-2 was developed by the CIMC Offshore Engineering Research Institute, CIMC Raffles’ research arm, as well as China Forestry Group Corporation and Beijing Forestry University. CIMC Raffles said its next step was to build a megawatt-level bamboo-based project and to promote the global adoption of green marine materials. Across China’s vast coastline, offshore solar farms are being built to help meet the country’s dual carbon goals of reaching peak emissions by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2060. In December, a one-gigawatt (GW) offshore solar farm – the world’s largest – was brought online off the coast of Dongying in Shandong, according to state-owned developer CHN Energy. Conventional offshore solar farms are built using sturdy steel or plastic frames along with buoyant floats. In 2023, China launched an action plan to replace plastic with bamboo, and has included the initiative in its latest forest and grassland conservation plan released in July. Bamboo is a fast-growing, giant woody grass naturally found across Asia, Africa and Central and South America. It is used as a building material because it is lightweight, flexible, durable and strong. The new solar platform uses bamboo-wound pipes as a core support, as well as “sea bamboo pipes” – fibre-reinforced wood-bamboo composite pipes developed by Beijing Forestry University that provide buoyancy and load-bearing support. Qi Chusheng, a professor at the university, told the official forestry trade newspaper China Green Times that the wood and bamboo materials were modified to allow them to withstand high humidity, corrosion, salt spray and ultraviolet radiation. He said that these renewable materials could be processed into high-value, durable engineering materials, offering ways to reduce reliance on conventional high-energy-consuming materials, according to a report in the paper on August 12. The platform will be monitored to see how the sea bamboo pipes perform in terms of long-term durability, environmental adaptability and fatigue, which will provide technical support for the use of wood-bamboo composites in offshore power plants, marine energy islands and marine ranches. Marine ranches are areas of the ocean that are managed as underwater farms to cultivate marine life while restoring ecosystems. China has been developing them to promote food security through sustainable seafood production methods, according to a paper published in the Bulletin of the Chinese Academy of Sciences last year. China is increasingly adopting bamboo-based materials for innovative projects, including anchoring shifting sand to halt desertification in its arid northern regions.

title: In Focus | As Hong Kong faces more heatwaves, what must be done to make the city more resilient?
description: From supporting vulnerable residents to revamping laws and public spaces, experts say city must adopt comprehensive climate resilience strategy.
content: Yung, an elderly Hong Kong resident, has spent hours hanging out at a neighbourhood shopping centre in Kwai Chung all summer. But he has not been going there to shop, instead taking refuge from the sweltering heat in the mall’s soothing air-conditioned arcade. The retiree, who lives in a 100 sq ft subdivided flat with his wife, is reluctant to use the air conditioner for long periods to avoid a hefty electricity bill, despite the hot and stuffy weather in recent weeks. “There have been more instances this year when I have felt dizzy, with a tightness in my chest, inside my flat,” said Yung, who is in his seventies. He turns on the air conditioner at night for about an hour before going to sleep, but often awakes at around 1am, covered in sweat. Yung is among many underprivileged residents whose health and sleep cycles have been disrupted by extreme heat, as Hong Kong recorded a scorching 36.9 degrees Celsius (98.4 Fahrenheit) at the Observatory’s headquarters in Tsim Sha Tsui on August 9, the highest since records began in 1884. His experience underlines questions about the city’s climate resilience, as heatwaves are predicted to occur more frequently and to affect larger areas surrounding the Pearl River Delta, including Hong Kong, by 2040, according to a study published in a scientific journal in May. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu highlighted the worsening situation at a recent consultation session for the city’s first five-year plan, to be unveiled next month, pledging to improve urban management and unite efforts to tackle extreme weather events and disasters. Community organisations, weather experts and urban planning professionals said strengthening the city’s heat-stress warning system, improving urban designs and shifting the mindset of policymakers were key to helping residents adapt to the new normal and making extreme weather less unbearable. Heatwaves triggered as early as April by 2040 Intensified heat stress from Hong Kong’s hot and humid climate was “a risk projected to worsen”, said Jimmy Fung Chi-hung, chair professor of the environment and sustainability division at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST). In July, an 11-year-old boy died after presenting with symptoms of heatstroke, including vomiting and fainting, at the end of a 400-metre (437-yard) training run at Tseung Kwan O Sports Ground. Fung warned that the city would face more frequent and prolonged heatwaves by 2040. Heatwaves are typically defined as prolonged periods of excessively high temperatures, often with severe consequences for human health, ecosystems and infrastructure. In Hong Kong’s urban areas, the median daily temperature during heatwaves typically hits a high of about 33 degrees. Citing his study published in the journal Weather and Climate Extremes in May, Fung said his research team found that heatwaves would become more frequent and extensive in the 2040s, with such occurrences beginning as early as April. To make their predictions, researchers studied local weather patterns using data from 18 global climate models from countries including Australia, Canada, Germany, the United States and China. Fung said the core heatwave season would also last longer, with extreme heat on a near-daily basis between June and August in most years. By the 2090s, the main heatwave season would further lengthen, starting earlier in May and extending to cover some days in September. Fung projected that the number of days in a year repeatedly affected by heatwaves would jump from an annual average of 14 days in the 2010s to 101 in the 2040s. Such days are estimated to occur across at least eight out of 10 years for each decade, marking the transformation from what was once a peak summer hazard into a “persistent warm-season threat”, Fung said. Is extreme heat a natural disaster? Unlike typhoons and rainstorms, which Hong Kong authorities manage with pre-event preparation, emergency response plans and cross-department protocols, extreme heat is not classified as a natural disaster and there is currently no comparable action plan to mitigate its impacts, according to urban climate expert Professor Ren Chao of the University of Hong Kong (HKU). Yet the urgency of the problem was underlined by an HKU paper in 2024, which estimated that the 18 heatwaves recorded in the city between 2014 and 2023 had each produced about 93 “excess deaths”, resulting in 1,677 additional fatalities over that period. Currently, the Observatory’s heat-related alerts include a special advisory for temperatures reaching 28 to 32 degrees, a very hot weather warning for temperatures reaching 33 degrees, and “prolonged heat” and “extremely hot” special alerts. Once a very hot weather warning is issued, government departments remind the public and employers to be mindful of health risks and open temporary heat shelters. The city also has a Heat Stress at Work Warning system, which requires employers to arrange additional rest periods for workers. However, the formula that triggers the warnings is now being reviewed as the record temperatures earlier this month exposed its failure to reflect the extreme conditions. Ren said the government should thoroughly consider factors related to extreme heat and build them into their policy formulations. Where are heat shelters? Ren called on the government to study the potential challenges facing residents of each district under climate change, then devise corresponding design solutions and strategies to mitigate them. For more immediate measures, pop-up cooling community centres or heat shelters remained essential, she said. Alongside eight community centres opening for heat refuge during operating hours, the city currently runs 19 temporary heat shelters converted from community halls whenever the very hot weather warning is in force. These 19 shelters will run overnight if the warning is still in force at 4.30pm. Between August 5 and 13, the warning was issued for more than 204 hours, and the 19 shelters served between 160 and 250 residents each day. But Kwai Chung resident Yung said he was not familiar with the government’s initiatives and had not heard of the nearest shelter, located in Kwai Shing Community Hall. In any case, it would take him half an hour to get there, which he said was “simply too far”. Terry Wong Chi-ho, senior manager of local emergency response at Hong Kong Red Cross, called for more shelters at more convenient locations, especially in densely populated areas such as Yau Tsim Mong and Kowloon City, where heat-related risks are the highest. “While districts like North and Yuen Long … are hotter during daytime with fewer shades, Yau Tsim Mong and Sham Shui Po are the two districts most affected by hot nights, due to the heat island effect,” he said. The charity has been working with labour groups, churches, non-profit organisations and small shops to free up spaces as pop-up cooling stations, especially in these high-risk areas, allowing residents to replenish their water supplies and cool down. “Users need not just physical space, but also to be able to eat inside, charge their mobile devices [and] take a shower,” he said. Ultimately, residents preferred cooling down in the sanctuary of their own homes, so authorities could consider providing home appliances and heat subsidies, Wong said. A subdivided home tenant in his eighties, surnamed Chan, who lives in a 100 sq ft flat in Mong Kok, found the heat slightly more bearable at home after the Red Cross provided him with a cooling mattress topper and circulation fan. Along with a wall fan, the equipment helped cool down his body and improve ventilation, as Chan kept his windows firmly shut due to rodent infestations in nearby areas. “I dare not open the windows as the rats could come in,” he said. In Singapore, the government offers quarterly rebates to residents living in eligible public housing to offset their utility bills. It also provides climate vouchers of up to S$400 (US$315) for families to buy energy and water-efficient appliances. Green pockets, urban shade and street fans Revamping Hong Kong’s greening strategy, as well as its building and street designs, could also mitigate heat and offer shade to the public and outdoor workers, urban planning experts said. Although 70 per cent of Hong Kong is covered by green spaces, residents were surrounded by only about 35 per cent of greenery within 500 metres of their home on average, according to data collected in 2020 for a HKU-led study. Bin Chen, an assistant professor at HKU’s division of landscape architecture who led the research, said efforts should focus on providing smaller and more distributed greenery to improve everyday exposure, such as street trees and shaded routes connecting homes with community facilities. But according to Anthony Cheung, vice-president of the Hong Kong Institute of Urban Design, the city’s existing design and building rules and approval procedures do not facilitate building more canopies, covered walkways and footbridges, which can mitigate the discomfort for residents on very hot days. Under the Buildings Ordinance, balconies and canopies cannot extend beyond three metres or 10 per cent of the street width, whichever is shorter. Cheung said building designs under the rule could not provide sufficient shade for pedestrians to seek shelter from the sun and rain. He added that only covered walkways connecting a building’s main entrance to the site boundary and main entrances between buildings could be exempted from gross floor area calculation. By contrast, Singapore mandated covered walkways in all developments in designated key areas. Cheung acknowledged the government’s attempts to incentivise private developers to build sheltered pedestrian links, including footbridges, by waiving land premiums under certain conditions. However, he noted that approval for the scheme, launched in 2017, was a “very long process” and proposals were subject to different tests to assess their public benefit. He also pointed out that scattered developments in certain neighbourhoods, such as Mong Kok, were an obstacle to building an extensive shaded network, and the government might at best consider building covered walkways on major streets. Cheung, who is also a director of architecture firm Ronald Lu and Partners, suggested installing energy-efficient facilities in Hong Kong to cool the environment. He cited the example of Air Tree, a tree-like structure designed by his company’s scientific arm, Behave, that provides greenery and shade while using solar panels to power fans. In Japan, cooling mist systems have helped cool down commuters at bus stops and visitors at parks and plazas during record-breaking heatwaves. A Japanese firm also sells the Do Hiemon Box, a “human fridge” kept at 15 degrees, which offers outdoor workers quick relief from the heat. Theresa Yeung, president of the Hong Kong Institute of Planners, said the city should replace concrete structures with permeable materials to ease increased flooding that came with more frequent rainstorms triggered by global warming. She proposed installing stormwater storage tanks beneath small parks and adopting nature-based solutions such as Rotterdam’s water plazas in the Netherlands. Designed like a storage tank, such facilities are generally used as public spaces and retain rainwater to manage the drainage load on sewage systems during storms. Acknowledging the financial cost of such proposals, Yeung suggested that authorities could leverage market forces to implement climate-resilient designs in new development and urban renewal projects. She said the Development Bureau’s bonus plot ratio scheme, to be launched next month, was a timely introduction. The scheme will grant developers redeveloping old residential buildings in seven designated districts an extra 20 per cent of gross floor area or an equivalent premium value to offset payment in the redevelopment or any land transactions in the city. It encourages developers to provide socially beneficial facilities and adopt planning that benefits the broader community. Yeung suggested that the government mandate climate-resilient designs in relevant residential projects and eventually expand the scope to commercial buildings. “Climate-resilient designs not only help the government but also residents by protecting their properties and assets,” she said. The bureau said the government required public works projects to incorporate greening elements in their planning and development stages to deliver quality landscape. The Buildings Department said it had been supporting the development of a sustainable built environment by imposing relevant requirements, and would continue to review and propose revisions to building standards as needed. The Drainage Services Department said locating stormwater storage facilities beneath recreational space was a practical application, such as those underneath Tai Hang Tung Playground and Happy Valley Recreation Ground. Taking urban resilience forward To develop the best policy solutions and infrastructure support, experts said the government and society at large must first adopt the right mindset. Leung Wing-mo, a former assistant director at the Hong Kong Observatory, said every resident and institution should adopt a “forward-thinking mindset” to build the city’s climate resilience. The case of tenant Chan, who faced rodent infestations and heat stress, showed that social and environmental issues rarely occurred in isolation, he said. “We hope the government can take a comprehensive approach [in tackling extreme heat], taking into full consideration the environmental issues that cover air pollution, extreme heat and ventilation altogether,” Leung said. Winston Chow, an urban climate professor at Singapore Management University’s College of Integrative Studies, said urban resilience should be a priority for governments in the face of increased risks to people, economies and infrastructure. As early as 1991, Singapore included climate adaptation strategies in its long-term planning. In 2010, the National Climate Change Secretariat was formed under the Prime Minister’s Office to develop and implement policies and strategies to tackle climate change. “The strategy is not based on one governmental agency or department. These sorts of issues cut across different ministries, and they are coordinated by the Prime Minister’s Office,” Chow said. He said the approach was helpful as the office coordinated issues among government agencies and departments, which often did not communicate or convey their interests and concerns to one another. He also stressed the importance of public education, which helped generations of Singaporeans support government policies. Herman Yiu Kwan-ho, programme officer at Hong Kong’s CarbonCare InnoLab, noted that education and outreach were essential to empowering residents to tackle the heat. Simple home-based remedies such as reducing clutter by removing old cardboard or clothing promoted better air circulation and cooled spaces, while using insulated curtains and cleaning one’s air conditioners regularly also improved energy efficiency, he said.
