Wong from Red Cross said extreme heat could cause heatstroke, hospitalisation or even death, but so far insufficient statistics had been compiled to identify definitive trends. “We believe that the general public still underestimates the impact caused by this extreme heat,” he said. “Extreme hot weather is a type of disaster … [It] not only [causes] discomfort, but is also an invisible killer.”

title: Prudential sees new business profit growth slow, announces US$300m share buy-back
description: New business profit increases 8 per cent to US$1.38 billion in first half as market braces for potential fall in number of mainland visitors.
content: British insurer Prudential announced a US$300 million share buy-back, to be completed by December, as it reported an 8 per cent increase in new business profit for the first half of the year. The buy-back and slower profit growth came amid market concerns over a potential pullback in mainland Chinese visitors to Hong Kong that could test the performance of insurers in one of their largest markets. New business profit – a key metric tracking the future profitability of newly written life insurance policies – rose to US$1.38 billion in the six months ended June 30, the company said on Thursday. That matched analysts’ estimates. The financial results showed a lower growth rate than in the first half of 2025, when new business profit surged 12 per cent to US$1.26 billion. In the first half of this year, adjusted operating profit increased by 9 per cent to US$1.81 billion, or 58.4 US cents per share. Annual premium equivalent sales – a major sales indicator combining regular and single premiums – rose 3 per cent to US$3.42 billion, up from US$3.29 billion recorded in the same period last year. “We remain focused on delivering long-term savings, health and protection solutions in our markets, meeting customer needs and supporting the societal aims of regulators and governments alike,” Prudential CEO Anil Wadhwani said in the earnings statement. “The strength of our performance is giving us the capacity to invest in long-term growth opportunities while increasing returns to shareholders. Today, we have announced a further $300 million buy-back to be completed by 18 December 2026.” Prudential declared an interim dividend of 8.88 US cents per share, compared with the 7.71 US cents payout per share in the first half of 2025. The share price of Prudential remained flat at HK$110.60 as Hong Kong trading began at 9.45am, following the announcement on Thursday morning, performing better than the broader Hang Seng Index, which fell 0.3 per cent to 25,579. After the press conference, the share price dropped 1.5 per cent to close on Thursday at HK$109. Hong Kong, traditionally Prudential’s major engine of growth and its biggest single market, saw annual premium equivalent (APE) sales shrink by 6 per cent to US$1.02 billion in the first half. This represented 30 per cent of its total APE sales from its markets across Asia and Africa. The new business profit in Hong Kong rose by 7.6 per cent to US$581 million in the first half. The city’s insurance sector is facing headwinds in its mainland visitor sales amid Beijing’s tightened controls on offshore investment in late May, with financial firms now requiring investment clients to declare if their source of funding is outside mainland China. Earlier this month, several major mainland cities, including tax bureaus in Shanghai, started collecting a 20 per cent levy on gains on offshore insurance policies. Prudential said its sales to mainland Chinese visitors in Hong Kong were subject to robust customer identification and source of funding controls. “While it is too early to assess whether recent commentary regarding the enforcement of existing rules will affect the buying behaviour of mainland Chinese customers ... the fundamental drivers of demand have not changed, they remain very solid,” Anil Wadhwani, the CEO of Prudential said in the briefing. “We remain confident in the structural growth prospects of our Hong Kong business,” Wadhwani added. The insurer, whose Hong Kong businesses are split roughly equally two ways between the city’s market and the market for mainland visitors and international buyers, conducted a survey in June which showed mainland visitors continued to visit Hong Kong to purchase insurance policies for investment diversification and protection needs. In mainland China, Prudential’s joint venture with Citic, Citic-Prudential Life, recorded a 21 per cent increase in annual premium equivalent sales to US$461 million, though new business profit dropped by 4 per cent as two near‑term factors squeezed volumes and margins. First, newly prescriptive banker‑expense rules forced immediate compliance across dozens of bank partners, disrupting established bancassurance sales flows and reducing second-quarter volumes. Second, a shift in product mix towards lower‑margin or transitional offerings compressed reported new business profit. However, Angel Ng, Prudential’s regional CEO for Greater China, customer, wealth and product, maintained that pipeline and non‑product opportunities should help restore margins in the second half. “These adjustments hit second-quarter volumes and margins, but they also create a stronger foundation for longer-term growth in the China market,” Wadhwani added. Meanwhile, key Southeast Asian markets, including Singapore and Malaysia, delivered a partial buffer, growing sales by 12 per cent collectively.

title: South Korea hands police more power even as dead bodies expose the lies
description: Fabricated calls and erased files kept two deaths hidden. Now, a force prone to cover-ups is inheriting unchecked authority.
content: On a farm up in the hills of South Korea’s Jeju Island, investigators this week uncovered what a mother had spent three months fearing they would not find: the body of her daughter. Jang Mi-ran, 37, vanished without a trace in May. Police records would later show her case had been quietly closed without anyone ever verifying if she was alive. It was the second such discovery in a matter of days. The first was the skeletal remains of a man in his sixties, found on Saturday after his family warned officers he had spoken of suicide and left his children a farewell message. Both cases had passed through the hands of the same officer, identified only by his surname Bu, who allegedly told worried relatives he had personally traced and spoken to the missing individuals – conversations investigators say never took place. What began as a local scandal on the southern resort island has since turned into a far larger debate, on whether South Korea’s national police force is fit to inherit the sweeping investigative powers it is about to receive. A president’s rebuke “The recent breakdown in police discipline and irresponsibility in public safety matters have become serious problems,” President Lee Jae Myung told a cabinet meeting on Tuesday in response to the scandal, demanding the creation of a dedicated government body to police the police. He spoke days after signing into law revisions to South Korea’s Criminal Procedure Act that will, from October, strip prosecutors of their remaining investigative powers and hand much greater authority to the police – the culmination of a decades-long campaign to cut the prosecution service down to size. “Going forward, the police may exercise the greatest power among government agencies,” Lee said, noting that people were deeply concerned about the change. “Power, when concentrated, always creates problems. The level of responsibility should be strengthened to match the extent of the authority.” He acknowledged the public’s “scepticism” about whether the country’s police were equipped to wield such extensive authority responsibly – scepticism that has only grown as more details of the Jeju cases have come to light. “Problems involving police discipline are not something that started yesterday or today,” Lee said. “Given the sheer size of the police force, problems can arise in many places, but we need both preventive measures and solutions.” For the president, the failures were structural. “The police are a hierarchical organisation in which following orders is extremely important and command responsibility is therefore crucial,” he said. “If a frontline officer is at fault, can the matter really end with disciplining that individual? If so, what is the command structure for? … Those who have the authority to command must also naturally bear responsibility commensurate with that authority.” It’s high time for this country to overhaul the police Choi Jin, Institute of Presidential Leadership Compounding matters is a second scandal that unfolded in Gwangju, where a police inspector was arrested in July on suspicion of destroying evidence during the investigation of a high-profile murder whose suspect happens to be the son of a senior police official. “These incidents reveal the shocking laxity in police discipline and accountability,” Choi Jin, head of the Institute of Presidential Leadership, told This Week in Asia. “It’s high time for this country to overhaul the police, focusing on enhancing accountability and oversight, improving command and control, and strengthening investigative capabilities.” Fabricated calls Public anger has only grown since details of the Jeju disappearances began to emerge in mid-August. Jang’s boyfriend reported her missing in May. Yet he says when he asked for updates, Bu told him she had been found and spoken to, but did not want her whereabouts shared That was a fabrication, investigators allege: phone records show no such call was ever made. Bu is accused of instead deleting Jang’s file from the missing-persons system altogether, apparently to keep his unresolved-case count low. An autopsy on the body recovered from the Jeju palm farm on Monday confirmed it was Jang. Police believe the circumstances suggest she may have taken her own life following a dispute with her boyfriend – the same dispute that had preceded her initial disappearance. The man in his sixties suffered an almost identical fate. His family had explicitly warned police he was suicidal, but Bu allegedly closed that case too – again after supposedly claiming contact had been made. The man’s remains were only located after the case was reopened. Bu has since been placed under arrest and all four officer in his chain of command at Jeju Seobu Police Station have been suspended pending further investigations. It has since emerged that Bu was previously investigated over an alleged bathroom intrusion and questioned in connected with suspected domestic violence, fuelling questions about how he remained on frontline duty. ‘Painful reform’ Analysts say the case reflects a structural blind spot rather than a single officer’s failures. Lee Keon-su, a professor in Baekseok University’s Department of Police Science, pointed to a loophole: under current police rules, missing adults were typically treated as “runaways” – a category with non of the urgency reserved for cases involving people with intellectual disabilities or dementia. “Sloppy initial responses, such as the false closure of Jang’s disappearance case, are entirely possible occurrences within the current system,” he said. Bae Sang-hoon, a psychological analyst with more than 20 years’ experience in criminal profiling , argues that the fix must come from outside the chain of command itself. “A system must be established to allow a third-party agency to look into and monitor police investigations into missing-person cases,” he said. Political scientist Jhee Byong-kuen of Chosun University traced the deeper malaise to internal culture. He said promotion decision that hinged on the goodwill of superiors created fertile ground for exactly the kind of corner-cutting alleged in Jeju. “Transparency and oversight are the two key words for police reform,” Jhee said. The issue has since migrated to the National Assembly, South Korea’s parliament. Han Byung-do, floor leader of the ruling Democratic Party, told a parliamentary meeting on Tuesday that “painful reform” was needed. “The police are now at the final test of whether they can regain the public’s trust,” Han said. For a force about to inherit more power than it has held in decades, the pressure is on to rebuild that relationship.

title: Hong Kong preschoolers to get complimentary dental check-ups for launching soon
description: Over 70 per cent of kindergartens enrol in a programme promoting early oral health awareness.
content:
Starting next month, preschoolers in Hong Kong will have access to complimentary dental check-ups, with over 70 per cent of the city’s kindergartens already registered for this new government programme.
The Department of Health revealed on Monday that the Outreach Oral Health Programme for Preschool Children will kick off on September 1. The initiative aims to promote good oral hygiene practices and prevent tooth decay from an early age.
Under the scheme, dental teams from 23 participating service providers will visit kindergartens across all 18 districts once each academic year, offering pupils aged 32 months or older free oral screenings and risk assessments.
“Children usually have a full set of milk teeth by the age of three. The period between the ages of three and six is the most crucial time to protect these teeth,” said Dr Kitty Hse Mei-yin, consultant in charge of the dental service at the department.
“At this stage, children love to eat, which makes reinforcing dental care and oral hygiene extremely important.”
Hse said that conducting examinations in a familiar school environment helped ease young children’s anxieties.
“With the encouragement of teachers and the support of peers, they view it as a routine school activity, making it much easier for them to accept,” she said.
As part of the preventive treatment, medical teams will also apply sodium fluoride varnish to healthy teeth to strengthen them and prevent cavities. For children who already have tooth decay, teams will apply silver diamine fluoride to control the condition.
The teams will also issue screening reports to parents, offer individualised dental care advice for children with decayed teeth and provide referrals for eligible students in need.
Service providers began contacting kindergartens in June to schedule visits for the 2026-27 academic year. As of Sunday, providers had reached out to 890 of Hong Kong’s 949 schools, with 680 agreeing to participate – representing 71.7 per cent.
Hse said that most of the remaining institutions already had existing dental care arrangements in place, while others were facing closure or relocation.
She added that providers would continue to follow up with non-participating kindergartens, noting that schools could join at any point during the term.
Free oral health workshops for kindergarten teaching staff will also be held by the dental teams to help them deliver oral care messages to their students.
“The proportion of children with tooth decay experience has remained high over the past decade, meaning a large proportion of five-year-olds still face the threat of dental decay,” said Dr Alex Chau Man-him, senior dental officer in oral health promotion at the department.
According to the department’s 2021 Oral Health Survey, 41.6 per cent of five-year-olds in Hong Kong experienced tooth decay, with an average of 1.8 affected teeth per child.
The survey revealed that most of these cavities went untreated, with half of affected children having four or more decayed teeth.
Only about a quarter of parents had ever taken their five-year-olds to see a dentist, with nearly half of those visits prompted after dental problems had already developed.
With funding support from the Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust, the dental school of the University of Hong Kong has previously organised an oral health project and offered free check-up services to the city’s kindergartens since the 2019-20 school year.

title: The Hong Kong law trainee taking her skills on the netball court into the city’s courtrooms
description: Part of the city’s team that qualified for next year’s Netball World Cup, Zenia Wong sees comparisons between her sport and legal career.
content: For many, equating playing netball and studying to become a lawyer is a bit like comparing apples and oranges, unless you are an elite athlete and you see a direct correlation between the two. Part of the Hong Kong squad that has qualified for next year’s World Cup, for Zenia Wong, the problem-solving nature of her sport and working with a team from different backgrounds provides a direct link between the two. “I knew my strengths of being quite analytical and practical, as well as loving to solve problems that sort of fit a legal career,” she said. “That’s also why I like netball in some way – because it’s such a tactical sport. I love it when I see the set play, and I can figure out the holes in other people’s games. The idea of things being a puzzle always interests me. “I like to work with people, in a team, from different departments or offices; it’s quite special to meet people from different backgrounds and work together. I think that’s sort of the same in netball. I have my role, you have yours, and together we achieve a bigger goal.” And after success on the court, the University College London (UCL) and University of Hong Kong law school graduate will continue to work towards becoming one in court. Wong begins a two-year training contract at an unnamed international law firm in her home city next month, although she has yet to decide in which area of the profession she will specialise. “Your mind is your greatest strength, but it can also be your greatest enemy, and that’s something I’ve experienced myself,” she said. “There have been games where I think we have won as a team, or me personally have contributed to that because I was strong mentally, and actually because I was in some way fitter physically, I was able to be strong mentally. “It’s so easy to be influenced by what other people say to you, and there will always be negativity – whether self-imposed or from others. Ultimately, self-confidence and inner strength are what carry you through; that’s what I learned in recent years as I reached elite competitive levels, where everyone possesses elite speed and skill.” Wong, who balanced academics and sport during Covid, as well as dealing with a left-hand injury that sidelined her for months just when she broke into the UCL first team, said the final five minutes of the semi-final against Malaysia was maybe “one of the most stressful times of my life”. “What differentiates you in those last moments is your courage, mental strength and unwavering belief in yourself,” the 23-year-old said. As much as netball has now been an integral part of her life, Wong was a “music kid”, singing in a choir and attaining grade eight in piano while also practising oboe, an instrument that built up her lung capacity and made her a better athlete. Still a niche sport with about 2,000 people playing in Hong Kong, netball came into Wong’s life when she switched from a local primary school to an international school, where “sport was a very big part of school life”. Still, at the start, it was nothing more than a means to make more friends for a young girl thrust into a new environment. “It made me come out of my comfort zone to speak more English, and to try something new. I think I’ll always be grateful that I did that,” she said. “It opened a lot of doors for me, made me more outgoing and comfortable being with people. I think netball has helped me a lot with my confidence as a person.” The unique rules, including no dribbling and emphasis on working with teammates, fascinated Wong, but those were not the only reasons she fell in love with the sport. “I am an only child, so I became quite independent growing up,” she said. “I never experienced the idea of a team. I never got that feeling of responding to others and actually communicating with others growing up. “And netball is so inclusive; we all have different assets to bring. If you have speed, you need height, creativity and strength. I think that it genuinely is a team sport because one person can’t do it alone, so being a part of a team, especially with so many young girls, is quite a powerful thing.” From playing an extracurricular sport at school to joining the city’s development and youth programmes, Wong was the only player in the team who came through the entire Hong Kong pathway across different age levels. Her journey in those regional academies as a young teen led to her international debut with the under-21 squad, and ultimately landed her a spot as the youngest member of the senior team. Reflecting on her rise, Wong called it “special and quite fast” to achieve so much in just over a decade. Wong said her biggest growth as a player came from trying out for and making the UCL team during her two years in London. “It was life-changing for me as a netball player because it threw me into the deep end,” she said. “I think playing in a different style and playing against players who were taller, faster and stronger really challenged me. “We played twice a week, and sometimes trained three times a week. We would travel to Oxford, Manchester or Bath to play against all the universities in the United Kingdom. Every day of my life really was dedicated to netball and law, but I would never have had it any other way.” On the night that Hong Kong women’s team qualified for the World Cup in Sydney next year, Wong, a wing attack by trade, was running onto the ball and holding the team together as a centre. Her vocal performance at Kai Tak Arena, where she was threading passes into the goal circle and making herself heard over a deafening crowd, led her friends to compare her to Arsenal and England midfielder Declan Rice. “It’s the first tournament I’ve actually realised how loud I can be,” Wong said. “I grew up playing as a wing attack, that’s kind of like the playmaker, so it’s my job to see the attack and to direct that play. “My recent transition to centre was a little different, but one that I think was quite fitting for my personality because I need to read off the other players.” The last time Hong Kong played in an international event, in 2003, Wong was only 10 days old. Now she is part of the team carrying the dreams of the netball community. “In netball, I found a home not just with my 12 players and my coaches, but I also found a home in the people that I get to interact with through a coaching or volunteer capacity. “My goal is not just to be a better player, but also to make sure that, as my teammate Gessy [Li Ga-wing] always says, I hope the next time someone asks me, I wouldn’t need to explain what netball is.”

title: 5 everyday objects with surprising origin stories
description: Did you know chainsaws were intended for use in childbirth and tattoo needles were invented by Thomas Edison?
content:
Most objects you see today are used for the purpose they were designed for – or at least, something in the same realm. But others were created for surprisingly different reasons. From chainsaws to high-heeled shoes, check out these items that are used for very different reasons than when they were invented.
The history of high-heeled shoes dates back to 10th century Persia – modern day Iran – where they were primarily worn while horse riding to lock the rider’s feet in the stirrups and provide stability, especially when using weapons. In 17th century Europe, heels were a symbol of aristocratic status and masculinity, but they came to be seen as women’s footwear in the 18th century.
The chainsaw was originally created to assist in childbirth and is now used to cut down trees. The current adaptation is electric and much larger, but the idea of using a smaller, manual device to cut through a person’s body without anaesthesia is still hard to fathom.
In the 1780s, the tool was used to amputate parts of the body and cut out diseased bone sections. Additionally, to assist in difficult childbirth, the chainsaw was used to cut through the mother’s pelvic bone and cartilage faster in cases where a baby had become trapped.
What is now a great item to fidget with was created as a textured wallpaper in the 1950s. The design didn’t take off, however, as consumers found the plasticky bumps unappealing. If you think about it, those walls would have become an interactive toy, eventually losing their bubbles. The creators soon realised that bubble wrap had far bigger potential in the shipping industry as a protective packaging material.
During World War I, Kleenex crepe paper was developed as an absorbent material for use inside gas mask filters to trap poisonous vapours. After the war, the company adapted that crepe paper to create women’s sanitary products. Later, it began making facial tissues for removing make-up and face cream, marketing the tissues as disposable handkerchiefs.
The tattoo needle was meant to be an electric pen.
You may be wondering, “What is an electric pen?” That’s because the invention, created by Thomas Edison in 1875, never took off as intended.
The design was adapted by tattoo artist Samuel O’Reilly in the 1890s to invent the first-ever electric tattoo needle, revolutionising the industry and keeping the original electric pen design in use.

title: Colombia mulls locking up dangerous criminals on prison ships
description: Humanitarian watchdogs warn that this form of incarceration breaches human rights.
content: Colombia’s new hard-right government wants to use prison ships adrift at sea to lock up people it considers highly dangerous criminals, a defence ministry source said on Wednesday. President Abelardo de la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to come down hard on armed groups in Colombia, the world’s largest cocaine producer. The US-backed millionaire campaigned on a pledge to bomb guerrillas and build so-called “mega prisons” in the style of El Salvador’s leader, Nayib Bukele. During a security council meeting, the president asked for the prison ship proposal to become a reality, the source said. The Colombian Navy is in charge of seeing the project through, the source added, without providing further details. Prison ships supposedly prevent detained people from escaping and limit contact with dangerous individuals and the rest of the world. Humanitarian watchdogs warn that this form of incarceration breaches human rights. Colombian ex-leader Alvaro Uribe in 2007 sent drug leaders aboard prison ships in the Atlantic and Pacific before their extradition to the US. De la Espriella also wants to forge ever closer ties with the US and Israel to achieve his security goals. On August 12, Colombia authorised joint US bombardments on its own soil as part of its crackdown on drug trafficking.

title: Editorial | Consortium that won Northern Metropolis plot shows way forward
description: The joint venture comprising mainland heavyweights and a Hong Kong developer indicates that a diversified model could be the way to go for the mega-project.
content: The HK$1.03 billion (US$132 million) tender for 10.5 hectares in the Northern Metropolis is a landmark in Hong Kong’s development. A consortium comprising five mainland state-owned and private companies as well as local developer Sino Land has been awarded the first batches of land in the pilot area in Hung Shui Kiu. The mainland partners will diversify the financial risks and help Hong Kong align with national goals under the 15th five-year plan. The transaction sets a good example for structuring complex, multifaceted urban development. On the face of it, the land premium does not reflect a project of this scale. Viewed in isolation, the figure understates the underlying economics, but the true financial commitment is staggering, with the total investment projected to reach HK$16.8 billion. This highlights the complexity of the project. The consortium is taking on multibillion-dollar responsibilities for infrastructure development and land formation, costs that would otherwise be borne by the government. By shouldering them, with Beijing’s support, the developers are demonstrating long-term commitment and confidence in the Northern Metropolis project. Even though the land premium looks low, this is still a significant signal from the market, given scepticism about how enthusiastic developers would be about the project. Critics questioned whether the private sector – and specifically major mainland enterprises – would put real capital behind such a long-term, visionary government initiative. On a massive, multifaceted development such as this, a consortium of local and mainland groups has proved to be the way to go. The tender answers doubts, despite a challenging macroeconomic environment. As Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho rightly noted, these enterprises have cast a tangible “vote of confidence” in the Northern Metropolis. The willingness to absorb high infrastructural costs and commit billions to a multi-year timeline speaks volumes about recognition of the project’s strategic value. Mainland Chinese enterprises are now set to be key players in projects in the Northern Metropolis, a 30,000-hectare mega-development close to the city’s border with the mainland, destined to become an economic powerhouse and housing hub. Real estate experts say more flexible tender arrangements and other terms may be necessary if more companies are to take part in future bids. Meanwhile, the joint venture between subsidiaries of state-backed developers China Merchants Land, China Resources Land (Overseas), China Overseas Land & Investment and CTG Investment, mainland e-commerce giant JD.com and Hong Kong developer Sino Land is a blueprint for the future. The Development Bureau said the consortium would carry out site formation works on three plots of residential land and build more than 3,000 flats. It would also form a site earmarked for company and technology park developments and build a smart logistics centre, with JD.com taking part as a strategic enterprise. JD.com will occupy at least 15,300 square metres, around 30 per cent of the facility’s gross floor area, in 55 months. The consortium will return two enterprise and technology park plots and a government, institution or community site to the authorities by 2028 after completing site formation. The outcome of the tender is a reminder that the value of major land disposals of this kind should not be judged solely by the land premium but also by the long-term economic benefits of diversified, forward-thinking development. Massive, multifaceted projects like the one at Hung Shui Kiu require a diverse range of expertise, from traditional real estate development to modern logistics and commercial planning. The consortium approach allows corporate giants to pool financial resources, share risks and coordinate expertise such as local real estate experience with deep industry knowledge in logistics, e-commerce and cross-border operations. By uniting a local property stalwart with mainland industry leaders to share risks and rewards, this project establishes a diversified development model. It sets a practical example for how future phases of the Northern Metropolis – and similar large-scale urban initiatives – can be successfully tendered, funded and built.

title: This 1,080 sq ft Singapore flat is a layered sanctuary that gradually reveals itself
description: Blending privacy and comfort, Leena Interior Design Studio transformed a public housing unit into a couple’s ideal home.
content: When the front door of this flat in Singapore’s Pinnacle@Duxton swings open, nothing of the interior is visible: an L-shaped foyer blocks the line of sight, while a low platform compresses the space before it opens out into an expansive living area. Interior designer Leena Goh considers this the first “layer” of several in the 46th-floor, 1,080 sq ft (100 square metre) public housing unit. There are a few more to be found across the flat, introduced to allow it to reveal itself gradually. Privacy, unsurprisingly, was the priority. Another was to ensure a clear separation between the public and private zones – an important consideration for Goh when designing homes. “I believe that good planning should carry that complexity so daily life can remain simple,” says Goh, who runs her eponymous practice, Leena Interior Design Studio (Lids), in the city state. “Every design decision was measured against one question: does this make living in the home feel more intuitive and effortless?” In addition to carefully composed layers, she also drew on framed views and overlapping spaces from her bag of interior tricks. This came after a significant reconfiguration of the floor plan – which included walls coming down – to fulfil the lifestyle needs of the flat’s occupants. Her client, Steve Tan, a Singaporean software design director, remembers an instant connection with Goh when they met in 2023. After he had bought the apartment, he decided to renovate it and interviewed more than 20 interior designers that same year. “She made an effort to find out about my wife and me and what we envision our home to be before she even started sketching any layout or offering solutions,” he says. Completed in 2009, the seven 50-storey-high towers that make up the Pinnacle were then Singapore’s tallest public housing. By the time of Tan’s purchase, the development was already showing its age. But he was undeterred. Its excellent downtown location and panoramic southeast views towards the shophouses and skyscrapers of Tanjong Pagar and Chinatown won him over. Fortunately for Tan, his instincts paid off. In creating the brief with Goh, Tan explained that he and his wife had hybrid work arrangements. Additionally, he wanted a dedicated space for his musical hobbies: playing the keyboard and electric guitar. The living room, he told her, would be for watching films on a large screen and light workouts. Occasionally, they planned to host social gatherings. “He was very clear that he wanted a home that felt generous despite its footprint,” Goh says. “That immediately shifted the conversation from creating more rooms. We then removed unnecessary boundaries and focused on designing a layout with a seamless flow when all the doors are open.” Previously enclosed, the now-open kitchen was moved from beside the guest bathroom to just by the foyer. The dining area and living room are organised in front of it. Floor-to-ceiling windows opposite the kitchen island are broken up by a bar counter that also multitasks as a standing desk. Because her clients needed only a bedroom and a study, three bedrooms became two, allowing the living room – where the couple spend most of their waking hours – to expand by almost 60 per cent. The main bedroom was also enlarged, just enough to accommodate a bed, dressing table and walk-in wardrobe. With the extra space, Goh could introduce built-in display shelves and storage cabinets on most walls. Sometimes, when I am designing, I also want to redefine how people use a space Leena Goh, interior designer The sofa, Tan says, is one of his favourite parts of the apartment. When not busy admiring the view out the window and watching cars drive down South Bridge Road, he catches up on the latest action flicks projected onto the 100-inch screen or plays his PlayStation 5. That same vantage point gives him a view of the framed doorway that leads to the rooms. Wrapped in a continuous oak finish, it stands as the layer between the communal and private areas. “When I sit and look at the dividing wall and portal, the use of a single material to clad it makes it feel harmonious and comfortable,” Tan says. Beyond, a vestibule leads to three areas: the study, the en suite bedroom and the guest bathroom. Each has a door that can add layers to the flat, with the former two using pocket doors to save space. The layout also reduced unnecessary circulation spaces, Goh says. The original floor plan had a corridor running half the length of the flat, which felt like a waste. By absorbing it into the surrounding rooms instead, she was able to increase the apartment’s usable footprint. Elsewhere, practical constraints were folded into the plan, too: the raised platform at the entrance, for one, conceals a repositioned sewerage pipe. Part of the reclaimed corridor is now a walk-in wardrobe in the bedroom, which also accommodates a queen-sized bed and a pair of bedside tables. “They have the big living room where they spend most of their time,” Goh says. “Sometimes, when I am designing, I also want to redefine how people use a space.” A restrained colour and material palette was applied to the flat to reinforce the way the home is organised and experienced. Only three principal tones are used: oak, light grey and dark grey. Oak forms the foundation, used on the engineered wood floor and as a laminate on most vertical surfaces. This includes the carpentry for the kitchen, where the widest panel is, in fact, the door for the Civil Defence Shelter – commonly called a bomb shelter – which doubles as a storeroom. Such shelters have been a mandatory feature in Singapore residences since 1997. Light grey serves as a secondary colour, providing moments of visual pause. It features in the carpentry above the hob and sink, as well as in the Silestone quartz cladding that wraps the island. The hue is also on the perimeter and structural walls, while dark grey is used in the bathrooms. “The consistency I feel when I walk around my home is calming,” Tan says. Special mention has to go to the dining and coffee tables, constructed entirely from the bark of the Malaysian Rain Tree. The maker, Dad’s Woods from Goh’s hometown of Penang, Malaysia, is run by its second-generation owner. “I like how they work with us to customise designs for our projects,” Goh says. “We chose this solid wood because of its yellow and gold tones that complement the oak well.” It has been two years since Tan and his wife moved into their very private flat. He admits that while he is constantly drawn to the new and novel, he has never tired of the design. “I still have the same contentment and peace today as when I first started living here. They’re wonderful feelings to have for a home.” Kitchen Lids designed the kitchen, with an island clad in Silestone quartz from Cosentino. Dining table designed by Lids and made by Dad’s Woods. Chairs from Taobao. Flowerpot VP1 pendants by Verner Panton from &Tradition. The widest panel conceals a door to the Civil Defence Shelter. Living area Display shelf, bar counter and window seat all designed by Lids. Sofa from Prelude Living. Beanbag from Taobao. Coffee table designed by Lids and made by Dad’s Woods. Carpet from Proof Living. Main bathroom The main bathroom is accessed from the bedroom via a walk-in wardrobe. Main bedroom Beside the main bedroom is a walk-in wardrobe designed by Lids. Butterfly stool by Sori Yanagi from W. Atelier. Bed from Taobao. Bedside lamp from Astro Lighting. Guest bathroom Cabinetry designed by Lids. Basin from Bathworld Singapore. Tap from Rigel. Entrance Elevated platform designed by Lids and built with engineered oak. Light switches by Legrand Singapore. Study Display shelf designed by LIDS. Work chair from Taobao. Above are lights from Million Lighting. Tried + tested A stand-alone console covered in oak laminate was customised for a projector, sound bar, subwoofer speaker and PlayStation 5. Careful measurements ensured each appliance fits snugly, with cables neatly stored out of sight and connected to power sources in the floor. Rather than a plain rectangular box, the console takes on an angular form, with a vertical cut-out in the base that continues the framing narrative of the flat and makes it feel lighter.

title: China’s robotics IPO wave gains steam as 2 more firms eye Hong Kong listings
description: The two start-ups plan to launch IPOs as early as next year, as Hong Kong becomes a key launch pad for China’s rapidly scaling robotics industry.
content: Another two Chinese robotics start-ups have confirmed plans to launch initial public offerings in Hong Kong as early as next year, boosting the city’s role as a prime fundraising hub for China’s fast-growing technology sector. The two Hangzhou-based firms – both founded by former executives at Alibaba Group Holding – are part of a wave of Chinese embodied artificial intelligence start-ups looking to go public as the industry rushes to scale up production. Infiforce Technology Group, the developer of a cognitive system for robots known as “AtomBrain”, is raising capital ahead of a potential Hong Kong listing, according to company founder Isabella Bai. “We are aiming for [a listing in] 2027, and preparation is currently under way,” said Bai, a former Alibaba vice-president. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Bai noted that industry financing and research and development spending were moving at a rapid pace, but declined to disclose specific targets or investor details. Founded in 2023, Infiforce completed a new funding round of nearly 1 billion yuan (US$149 million) earlier this month and recently secured overseas orders, including a 1,000-unit contract in Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile, UDeer.ai, another Hangzhou-based embodied AI firm, is also planning a Hong Kong IPO, according to the company’s founder. “We are launching our IPO process, including restructuring red-chip structures and corporate shareholding reforms,” founder Robin Chen told the SCMP on the sidelines of a tech summit in Hong Kong on Wednesday. “Once these steps are completed, we plan to submit our IPO application in the first half of next year. Hong Kong is our first choice, but our teams are simultaneously evaluating A shares as well,” added Chen, who previously led robotics research at the Damo Academy, Alibaba’s in-house research initiative. Founded in 2023, UDeer already mass produces autonomous cleaning robots that use large-model reasoning to identify and remove litter – such as fallen leaves, waste paper and cigarette butts – rather than blindly sweeping entire areas. “Our revenue target for 2026 is around 300 million to 500 million yuan, aiming for around 1 billion yuan in 2027,” Chen said. The company’s shipments are expected to hit the high thousands this year and reach around 50,000 units next year, according to Chen. In the medium-to-long term, UDeer aimed to develop serving robots with arms capable of handling soft or irregular items like takeaway bags and performing complex interactive tasks such as retrieving order slips, he added. The two start-ups join a wave of robotics companies going public in Hong Kong. However, Puhua Capital – a venture capital firm that mostly invests in hard-tech and embodied intelligence start-ups – has warned that valuations are becoming overheated. “Overall, valuations are currently on the higher side due to capital clustering, with 80 per cent to 90 per cent of market capital concentrated in the top 10 per cent to 20 per cent of tracks,” said Shen Qinhua, founding partner of Puhua Capital. “Embodied AI has been one of the hottest tracks since early last year, and valuations have surged rapidly – it’s clearly a bit overblown right now.” Shen said this year was the “first year of mass production” for the embodied AI industry, but noted that companies and the market still needed time to digest the current high valuations. For Chinese tech firms, going global was no longer optional, but essential, he added. Over the past two years, Hong Kong has become a crucial gateway for Chinese firms looking to raise funds and expand overseas, according to Shen.

title: Bill Gates warns of AI’s impact, urges the US and China to cooperate
description: Tech titan argued on Wednesday artificial intelligence needs significant limits or else the harm to humans will outweigh any potential good.
content: Cooperation between the United States and China is required to manage the unprecedented societal impacts of rapidly advancing artificial intelligence (AI) technology, Bill Gates wrote in a new essay published on Wednesday. The call to action comes as the billionaire philanthropist and tech titan warns that AI is ushering in “one of the most turbulent times in human history”, which could either become “the greatest equaliser ever invented, or the worst source of injustice”. “[The] countries that host the leading AI developers and control critical parts of the supply chain should begin meeting now to set up shared norms, before competitive pressure makes it harder for them to cooperate,” he wrote. “Building the framework I’m talking about will take years, which is why we need to start now.” In the 6,000-word essay, the Microsoft co-founder said world leaders are not adequately preparing for the transition to the AI era, which he believes differs from past technological transitions because of the pace of AI progress and the scale of its potential impacts. “This time really is different,” he wrote. In recent years, concerns that rapid AI progress is outpacing societies’ ability to manage its impacts have prompted experts to call on the US and China, the two leading AI superpowers, to slow research and development. The two countries are set to hold talks on AI governance next month during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US, though it remains unclear what will be discussed. Gates wrote in his essay that, while he supports a global slowdown in AI development in theory, he does not believe it is likely to happen due to existing geopolitical and economic incentives “to go full speed ahead”. Instead, world leaders should start by convening experts to identify gaps in institutional preparedness, he wrote, highlighting three main areas where AI risks are most urgent: labour displacement, AI-enabled crimes and surveillance, and impacts on children and human relationships. Gates noted that China has “gone the furthest” so far to implement safeguards for children using AI, citing Beijing’s recent restrictions on AI companion apps that foster emotional dependence among minors. In the section on blue-collar jobs, Gates wrote that many Americans do not realise how rapidly robotics is advancing because “much of the advanced work” is being done in China. “I think ‘smart’ robots will begin to compete with people on some physical tasks – in the construction and hospitality industries, for example – by the end of the decade.” The US and China previously agreed in 2024 to keep humans, not AI, in control of nuclear weapons. That remains the only high-level agreement between the two countries on the development and use of AI, as they compete fiercely to develop frontier AI models and robots. However, recent high-profile incidents such as the hacking of software systems by cutting-edge AI models developed by US companies have raised expectations that Washington and Beijing may agree to cooperate on issues of shared concern, such as terrorist misuse of AI systems. Reuters reported on Wednesday that Gates is working to finalise a meeting with Xi in China, tentatively in November, where he plans to raise his concerns about AI impacts. Gates last met with Xi in 2023, when he was the first foreign business leader invited to meet the Chinese president following the pandemic.

title: In Focus | Is ‘resource curse’ to blame in regions hit harder by Xi’s anti-corruption campaign?
description: China’s past CCDI annual plenums stress intensifying efforts to combat corruption where ‘power, funds and resources are concentrated’.
content: The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the third part of a series accompanying the data project, William Zheng looks at the relationship between rich regional resources and corruption. Beneath the desolate Gobi Desert and sparsely populated mountains of China’s less developed regions lie abundant mineral resources, ranging from coal, the most basic fuel for China’s economy, to critical minerals needed for cutting-edge industrial machinery and state-of-the-art military products. These regions are not only rich in natural resources critical to the world’s second-largest economy, but also appear to be fertile ground for deep-seated corruption. Research by the South China Morning Post shows that China’s resource-rich and border regions have been the hardest hit in the country’s decade-long corruption crackdown, as Beijing tries to avoid succumbing to regional “resource curses”. The SCMP research examined every detention notice, investigation conclusion and career path of “tigers”, or high-ranking officials, released by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) – China’s top anti-corruption and political supervision agency – from 2013 to 2025. It shows that China’s mineral-abundant regions, including Jiangxi, Liaoning, Inner Mongolia, Shanxi and Hebei, top the chart for the most senior officials sacked for corruption in that period. The research also finds that the highest per capita toll is among the leadership of regions receiving the highest per capita financial support, including the country’s largest ethnic minority autonomous regions. Observers say the results suggest Chinese regions with rich natural resources or that receive large sums in financial support from the central government are more susceptible to so-called rent-seeking, thus drawing fire from anti-graft fighters in Beijing. The numbers Jiangxi province, which is immensely abundant in natural resources, especially rare earth minerals and tungsten, was home to the highest number of senior corruption crackdowns, with 15 tigers, according to the tally. Among them was Su Rong, the former Communist Party boss of several provinces, including Jiangxi. He was sentenced to life in prison in 2017 for taking more than 116 million yuan (US$17.3 million) in bribes in exchange for granting promotions, government contracts and land rights, making him the highest-ranking official taken down during the early years of the anti-corruption fight. Mainland Chinese media reported in 2014 that Su’s wife had also dabbled in Jiangxi’s mineral resources, land transfers and real estate development. Su’s conviction triggered a domino effect within the regions he previously governed, particularly Jiangxi, where a sweeping purge followed, leading to the arrest or demotion of dozens of local officials in his network. Liaoning – which has the country’s largest reserves of iron ore, magnesite and boron, as well as large deposits of critical minerals for modern manufacturing and clean energy, such as vanadium, zinc, molybdenum and manganese – ranked second with 14 deputy provincial or higher-ranked officials facing corruption investigations. Like Jiangxi, Liaoning also saw the downfall of its party boss, Wang Min, who served in the position from 2009 to 2015. On July 7, 2014, after its first investigation of Liaoning, Beijing’s inspection team reported “prominent problems”, such as “leading cadres interfering in project bidding, land and mineral resource transactions”. Wang was removed the following year and investigated in 2016. He was handed a life sentence in 2017 for taking 146 million yuan in bribes, embezzlement and dereliction of duty. Beijing’s inspectors also said they unearthed vote-rigging in Liaoning’s legislature in 2014. Some 523 of 619 deputies in the province’s people’s congress were implicated in the scandal, either by taking bribes or allowing the vote-rigging. Inner Mongolia, Shanxi – which is also among China’s leading coal-production zones – and Hebei, the country’s foremost ferrous metal hub, tied for third, each with 13 tigers hunted down. Actions in Inner Mongolia were roundly criticised under the unprecedented “looking back 20 years” anti-graft initiative launched by Beijing in early 2020. Under the initiative, the resource-rich autonomous region – home to more than a quarter of China’s coal reserves – became the central target because of an extraordinary concentration of wealth and a frenzy in the resale of state-owned mineral resources at artificially low prices, as well as illicit rent-seeking opportunities in coal and other mining sectors. Before the push, the region saw the downfall of a string of top officials in the late 2010s, including Yun Guangzhong, the former party secretary of the capital, Hohhot, former regional security boss Xing Yun and deputy government chairman Bai Xiangqun, revealing a deeply entrenched, multi-decade network of government-business collusion. Under the initiative, Beijing issued an unprecedented retrospective order to Inner Mongolia: audit every single coal mining transaction, lease and regulatory approval stretching back to 2000. In a campaign review in November 2021, authorities investigated more than 730 corruption cases in Inner Mongolia’s coal sector alone, with 1,023 officials facing investigations and more than 52 billion yuan of the economic losses recovered. Earlier in Chinese President Xi Jinping’s anti-graft push, Shanxi was the first coal economy shaken up by graft fighters from Beijing. During China’s “Golden Decade of Coal” from 2002 to 2012, when coal mining firms gained tremendously from skyrocketing coal prices, Shanxi produced about a third of the nation’s coal. However, the energy boom turned the province into the epicentre of what the Chinese anti-corruption body called “avalanche-style corruption” – a state of total institutional decay where entire government networks were co-opted by private mine owners, known as the “coal bosses”, or mei laoban in Chinese. State media said the nexus between local mine inspectors, police, county officials and mine owners created a lethal moral hazard. When fatal mine explosions or cave-ins occurred, local officials routinely helped private mine owners cover up casualty information, aided by hush money and forged reports, to prevent being shut down by the central government. By 2014, Beijing said graft in Shanxi was no longer about individual bad apples, with the CCDI sending teams to Shanxi with unprecedented authority. What followed was a historic near-complete downfall of a provincial political establishment: Beijing almost effectively removed Shanxi’s entire top leadership and parachuted in external replacements to clean house from the top down. In 2014, seven incumbent or former senior officials from the top provincial leadership were removed, an extremely high number for any province during the anti-corruption drive, ranging from the province’s top economic officials, party affairs chief, top anti-graft fighters and heads of the largest cities in the province. Ling Zhengce, the elder brother of former Chinese presidential aide Ling Jihua, was brought down from his post as the vice-chairman of Shanxi province’s political advisory body the same year. Wang Rulin, who was parachuted into Shanxi in 2014 as provincial party boss to clean up the mess, said in March 2015 that the sweeping anti-corruption fight resulted in nearly 300 vacancies at the deputy municipal level and above. There is no sign that the CCDI will lessen its pressure and attention towards resource-rich provinces. During the past five CCDI annual plenums, the national gathering of Xi and China’s top disciplinary officials has repeatedly stressed their intensifying efforts to combat corruption in areas where “power, funds and resources are concentrated”. ‘The resource curse’ In keeping with a phenomenon known as “the resource curse” or “paradox of plenty”, abundant resources do not guarantee better growth, more equitable income distribution and clearer government, according to Alfred Wu, associate professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy in Singapore. While such a concept was mainly discussed at the national level – countries with plentiful non-renewable natural resources such as oil, gas, gold and minerals tend to experience less economic growth and worse governance than countries with fewer resources – it could be applied to regions or provinces within the same country, Wu said. In a resource-rich region, the local government tended to fund itself by collecting “rents”, royalties or revenues directly from mining companies in contracts involving large amounts of money, and the local leading officials could have a strong influence, he added. “The easiest way to get rich in a resource-cursed province isn’t to build a great business with a great invention or a new technology; it’s to secure a government contract. That encourages rent-seeking and shifts the region’s brightest minds to political plundering.” Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at the National Institute of Strategic Studies at Tsinghua University, said the campaign not only shattered the unspoken “safe landing” rule in which officials were not prosecuted for past corruption after retiring, but also marked the first time the CCDI had targeted entire critical industrial supply chains. “The total-cleansing model pioneered in Inner Mongolia’s coal sector has since been replicated across other strategic areas, including the financial sector, the national healthcare apparatus and the judicial-security complex,” Xie said. Xie also noted that despite Xi naming environmental protection as a top priority in his policy metric, in Inner Mongolia, corrupt officials routinely turned a blind eye to massive, illegal open-pit mining operations that caused severe desertification and ecological destruction, while local cadres falsified environmental audits to keep the coal revenue flowing. “By breaking the political stranglehold of the coal money, Shanxi finally began shifting its monoculture economy away from pure mine extraction, redirecting state investment towards clean energy transitions, like solar, hydrogen, coal-bed methane, hi-tech manufacturing and cultural tourism,” he said. “That’s unimaginable without the crackdown.” Border and minority regions The SCMP analysis found that the Tibet autonomous region, Qinghai, Hainan, the Ningxia Hui autonomous region and Inner Mongolia had the highest number of corruption cases relative to their population size. Some of these regions are also among the biggest per capita recipients of central government financial support – measured in transfer payments from Beijing. China’s central government transfer payments to provinces are massive fiscal allocations – consistently exceeding 10 trillion yuan annually – used to bridge regional fiscal gaps, helping poorer regions gain parity in basic public services such as education, healthcare, and social security. They also include targeted funds for specific national policies and infrastructure projects, helping cash-strapped local governments fund their development needs. According to data released by the Ministry of Finance, Tibet received 74,700 yuan per capita in transfer payments in 2025, far exceeding other regions. This figure was 2.55 times that of second-ranked Qinghai’s 29,300 yuan per capita, with Xinjiang ranked third on 20,170 yuan. The other top regions with high per capita transfer payments were Ningxia, Heilongjiang, Inner Mongolia, Gansu, Jilin, Hainan and Guizhou – all border provinces that are less developed. Besides Qinghai and Ningxia, the remainder received more than 10,000 yuan transfer payments per capita. Singapore’s Alfred Wu said management of the large transfer payments had long been a problem in China, particularly in less developed regions where a few top officials could dictate the use of this massive amount of money. “Since 2015, the State Council started a series of reform measures aiming at reducing wastage and strengthening supervision. But even with that, we still see corruption cases where local officials in less developed provinces frequently embezzled or misappropriated funds intended for poverty alleviation, agricultural subsidies, basic medical care and basic social security,” he said. China’s border and autonomous regions with large minority populations have also been home to the downfall of a string of their ethnic-Han party bosses and ethnic-minority government heads in the past few years. The most prominent downfalls include that of Ma Xingrui, a Politburo member and the former party boss of Xinjiang in April and, in 2024, the former party chief of Tibet Wu Yingjie, who had spent 47 years in the autonomous region. In July last year, Wu was sentenced to death, suspended for two years, after pleading guilty to accepting 343 million yuan in bribes. More ethnic minority government heads are facing corruption investigations. In January 2025, Qizhala, the ethnic-Tibetan former chairman of the Tibet autonomous region, was investigated, followed a few months later in May by a probe into Lan Tianli, the ethnic-Zhuang chairman of Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. In July, Liu Hui, the ethnic-Hui former chairwoman of Ningxia Hui autonomous region, came under investigation for alleged corruption, just as Qizhala was being expelled from the party. A Chinese political scientist who declined to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter, said the anti-corruption campaign in border and minority regions, such as Xinjiang, Tibet, Inner Mongolia, Guangxi, and Yunnan, had given Beijing “opportunities to put in place trusted top officials to carry out the new ethnic policies”. “Many Xinjiang and Tibet officials facing investigation were accused of being ‘two-faced’, meaning they publicly echo Beijing’s directives but privately sympathise with local religious movements, protect local traditions against assimilation, or show ‘softness’ in enforcing hardline security measures,” the political scientist said. “Removing these Janus-faced officials allowed Beijing to put in place a slew of iron-fisted tough administrators to carry out Beijing’s ethnic integration plan.” Beijing named and shamed former Xinjiang education chief Sattar Sawut and justice department chief Shirzat Bawudun in 2021 as typical “two-faced” officials. Sawut was deemed to have taken advantage of the Han officials who were not proficient in the Uygur language to publish local textbooks “detrimental to national unity and ethnic solidarity”. Bawudun was accused of “using his security and justice position as cover” and having “planned and carried out separatist activities”. Both were charged with separatism and each was handed a suspended death sentence in 2021.

title: US seizes Chinese hacking platforms targeting Nasa, Fed and Senate
description: Justice Department says QTFY targeted US critical infrastructure on behalf of China’s security ministry and military.
content: The Justice Department and the FBI said on Wednesday that they seized two Chinese state-sponsored online platforms that targeted US critical infrastructure and other critical networks, including Nasa, the Federal Reserve and the US Senate. According to court documents, the seizures involved a group known as “QTFY”, operated by China-based Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Co, which created and ran the QScan and QTRouter sites. “State-sponsored malicious hackers preying on America’s critical infrastructure will be stopped and prosecuted,” said US Attorney General Todd Blanche in a statement. “Federal law enforcement investigated and disabled [China’s] malicious software, the latest in a series of technical operations to dismantle indiscriminate hacking activities sponsored by the People’s Republic of China [PRC].” QTFY allegedly offered computer hacking services for a fee to its clients, including China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) and the People’s Liberation Army, according to court documents in the Southern District of California. The Chinese embassy in Washington said the Chinese government opposes and combats all forms of cyberattacks. “We urge the US side to stop using cybersecurity issues to smear or discredit China,” the spokesman said. Other reported victims of the QTFY hacking operations included the Department of Energy, Department of Justice, Department of Health and Human Services and the National Institutes of Health, as well as hospitals, telecommunications providers, power companies, financial institutions and defence contractors. “We’re taking the fight to PRC-sponsored cybercriminals to protect the critical services Americans rely on every day,” said US Attorney Adam Gordon for the Southern District of California. In reality, however, the transnational nature of threats, the relative anonymity of foreign individuals involved and the ease in creating and moving sites make it difficult to prosecute and otherwise counter cyberhacking operations, analysts said. Another concern: the Trump administration has cut staff and budgets significantly at US agencies responsible for fighting these threats, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation, National Security Agency (NSA), Federal Communications Commission and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA. “The CISA workforce has been cut by nearly a third, and the scope of the agency has been reduced, leaving the US more exposed to adversarial cyber threat actors,” said the Washington-based non-partisan New Lines Institute in an October 2025 report. “National cybersecurity infrastructure cannot become a casualty to partisanship.” As outlined by the Justice Department on Wednesday, QTFY’s hacking services, such as QScan and QTRouter, tended to work in tandem. QScan would scan and automatically infect thousands of smart devices worldwide – such as video doorbells, fitness trackers and heart rate monitors – that were then added to the QTRouter network of devices it controlled. QTRouter, in turn, would operate as an “obfuscation network”. That allowed QTFY and other “malicious cyber actors” to conceal the Chinese origin of their activities by making communications appear to originate from computers outside China, the agency said. QTFY’s malicious cyber activities dated back to at least 2018, according to an FBI affidavit, which said QTFY, also known as QT and QTCYBER, tended to hire former PLA employees who used their connections to gain business and sign contracts. The move to seize and make inoperable QScan and QTRouter was justified, the court said, given that money-laundering laws were violated to pay for the US sites and because the seized domains were hard-coded into both the QScan and QTRouter malware, which were used for such essential tasks as communication and authentication. China has frequently denied accusations of state-sponsored cyber hacking, rejecting them as “unfounded” and “a smear”. Western intelligence agencies and cybersecurity firms, including Microsoft, Mandiant and CrowdStrike, have identified a number of Chinese state-backed threats, however, including Volt Typhoon, reportedly sponsored by the People’s Liberation Army Cyberspace Force and Salt Typhoon allegedly sponsored by MSS. In its 2025 report, New Lines said Salt Typhoon was in US telecoms networks at least since 2023 and possibly as far back as 2019. “One of the most troubling and unique elements of the Salt Typhoon campaign is that its persistence model relied on having access to the supply chain on the most fundamental level,” the group said. “Given enough time, this access provides the group with data on just about any person or entity residing in the US that it seeks to target. Data has been exfiltrated on over 1 million users, including senior US officials.” Analysts said Beijing often focuses on deniability. “Chinese intelligence agencies appear to be under pressure to meet ever higher levels of performance. In response, they are intensifying their operations and diversifying sources and methods,” said Matt Brazil, a senior fellow with the Jamestown Foundation. “Chinese agencies, particularly the MSS, increasingly use commercial consulting arrangements, third-country intermediaries and, as the FBI tells us, online platforms, to find recruitable targets and minimise the risk of detection. But they still employ traditional spying methods when person to person contact is needed.” US President Donald Trump appeared to defend China’s cyber hacking activities recently. “You don’t think we do that to them? We do,” he told Fox in June. “That’s the way the world works. It’s a nasty world.” But analysts pushed back. “Critical differences exist between what we and they do. US government computer network operations seek a clearer picture of foreign capabilities and intent. That is, a form of intelligence collection,” said William Hannas, a lead security analyst at Georgetown University and former CIA official. “Chinese hacking, directly or through its proxy networks, besides intelligence gathering, aims to gain commercial advantages, exfiltrate proprietary technology, gain leverage over institutions and individuals,” he added. In a related development, Trump on Wednesday signed an emergency order keeping some foreign-made transformers and other critical energy equipment out of the nation’s electric grids on national security grounds. In signing the order, Trump warned of “certain foreign actors” who are “increasingly creating and exploiting vulnerabilities in the United States bulk-power system” without mentioning China by name.

title: Opinion | As the US and China compete over AI, Asean must secure strategic autonomy
description: Asean’s choice is not between technological dominance and isolation but between dependence and agency.
content: International relations has long measured power through familiar instruments: military capability, territory, energy, capital and control of trade. The digital revolution added information to that equation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is taking the transformation further by turning information into a strategic capability that can shape economies, governments and societies. For the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), the central question is no longer whether Southeast Asia will participate in the AI revolution. The more consequential question is whether Asean will possess enough control over the infrastructure, knowledge and systems behind AI to shape its own future or whether it will have to rent intelligence from others. Southeast Asia is rapidly becoming an important physical centre of the AI economy. Data centres are expanding and investment is flowing into digital infrastructure. The International Energy Agency expects electricity demand from data centres in Southeast Asia to more than double by 2030. Malaysia and Singapore are emerging as major regional hubs, while Indonesia and Thailand seek to capture a larger share of the digital infrastructure boom. However, beneath this expansion lies a strategic paradox: Asean might provide the land, electricity, connectivity, markets and physical infrastructure for the AI economy while depending on external powers for advanced chips, foundational models, cloud platforms and technological standards. This marks a subtler dependency: states retain sovereignty while increasingly relying on foreign AI systems to run critical functions. This matters because Asean’s traditional concept of strategic autonomy was developed in a world where states could diversify their economic and diplomatic relationships without necessarily having to choose their technological architecture. That assumption is becoming less secure. The United States and China are developing competing technology ecosystems. Reuters reported earlier this month that Washington was preparing to encourage countries taking part in its Pax Silica initiative to choose between competing US and Chinese AI frameworks. Meanwhile, China is expanding AI engagement with Southeast Asia through training, infrastructure, research and industrial applications. For Asean, technological pluralism is essential. It must cooperate with multiple powers while avoiding dependence on any single AI ecosystem or strategic alignment. This is where the idea of intelligence dependency becomes important. Technological dependency means relying on another country for technology, but intelligence dependency goes further. It means relying on external systems to process information, predict outcomes and assist in decisions that increasingly affect how societies function. Whoever controls those systems possesses a form of structural power that is less visible than military coercion but is more deeply embedded in everyday governance. Therefore, Asean needs to move from AI adoption to intelligence resilience. This does not mean trying to manufacture every chip or build a frontier model in every member state. That is unrealistic. Instead, strategic autonomy means maintaining alternatives: regional computing capacity, trusted data systems, multilingual AI models, cybersecurity capabilities, local technical expertise and interoperable standards. China-Asean cooperation could become particularly important. The inauguration of the China-Asean Artificial Intelligence Industry Innovation Centre in Beijing in May marked a further institutionalisation of cooperation in AI development and applications. China’s strengths in manufacturing, digital infrastructure and large-scale AI deployment offer Asean valuable opportunities, but the objective should not be to replace dependence on American technology with dependence on Chinese technology. China could support Asean’s AI capacity through research, training, infrastructure and technology transfer, fostering mutual interdependence rather than technological patronage. The same logic applies to the wider Islamic world, particularly the Gulf. The US, China, the Gulf and Asean possess complementary strengths and could become centres of strategic agency rather than consumers of competing technological ecosystems. However, there is a physical constraint that policymakers cannot ignore. AI requires enormous quantities of electricity, cooling and infrastructure. Southeast Asia’s data centre boom is already raising concerns over water and energy consumption. For Gulf countries, AI development depends on balancing technological capacity with sustainable energy and water resources to avoid new vulnerabilities. Asean should respond through an AI strategic resilience framework built around four pillars: computing capacity, data capacity, human capacity and institutional capacity. It should support regional research centres, trusted data-sharing mechanisms, independent testing of high-impact AI systems and common standards for AI infrastructure. Major foreign data centre investments should also be assessed against energy, water, cybersecurity and local skills-development requirements. The strategic objective should be simple: open to all, dependent on none. The emerging contest is not simply a race between American and Chinese AI. It is a contest over who controls the infrastructure through which societies think, calculate and make decisions. Asean and the Islamic world should not become passive arenas in that competition. They possess too much capital, energy, human talent and market power to remain mere consumers. The coming decade will determine whether Asean remains an AI consumer or gains the technological agency to shape the emerging global order. The choice is not between technological dominance and isolation but between strategic dependence and strategic agency.

title: Trump declares ‘Mission Accomplished’ in Iran, as conflict drags on
description: US president’s claim evokes George W. Bush’s premature declaration about the US invasion of Iraq in 2003.
content: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday declared “Mission Accomplished” in Iran even as the unpopular and costly war drags on with no end in sight and no sign that the US is close to achieving any of the lofty goals he set for the conflict. Trump posted an image of himself along with Iran’s slain former supreme leader Ali Khamenei against a stylised landscape background of punishing US air and missile attacks. “Mission Accomplished 2026”, a caption reads. The slogan evokes former president George W. Bush’s infamous premature declaration of “mission accomplished” in Iraq, a conflict that continued for years afterwards. Trump even includes a photo of Bush in the image with the caption “Mission not accomplished 2001-21”. Democrats trashed Trump for what they called a tone-deaf “mission accomplished” claim with Senator Chuck Schumer calling the president “delusional” for saying he has won anything in the Iran fight. “Trump started a war with no plan, no mission, and no idea of the consequences, like sky-high gas prices,” Schumer told the Daily News. “He’s made the world more dangerous, driven up our costs, and he’s put American lives at risk every step of the way.” A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed Trump’s handling of Iran is supported by just 31 per cent of American voters, and his failure to end the conflict on terms that show a clear victory could cost Republicans at the ballot box in the November midterm elections and beyond. A big chunk of his own base opposes the war, which some see as a clear violation of his campaign pledge to end overseas entanglements. Trump’s claim of victory comes without any apparent movement on key war aims he set out, like permanently ending Iran’s nuclear programme, preventing Tehran from attacking neighbours and funding terror proxy groups. Trump vowed to engineer regime change but Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba Khamenei, took power after his father’s killing and the regime appears little changed and more firmly entrenched in power than ever. Most Republican strategists believe Trump should focus on kitchen table issues like tax cuts and the fairly resilient US economy rather than trying to put a positive spin on the Iran war, which has caused the price of fuel to skyrocket. Trump himself is badly underwater in polls, with less than 40 per cent of the American voters approving of his performance in the White House, raising the question if he will drag down congressional Republicans to defeat especially if he focuses on unpopular issues like Iran. Non-partisan analysts predict Democrats will retake control of the House of Representatives and have a decent chance of flipping the Senate, though they would need to win daunting races in several red states to do so.

title: 50 years after first landing in Hong Kong, the LPGA Tour is back and bigger than ever
description: Golf’s best expected to head to Clear Water Bay in March for Futu Ladies World Championship and a prize purse that is the richest in Asia.
content: The last time the LPGA Tour was in Hong Kong, Concorde arrived at Kai Tak Airport for the first time, the famous floating restaurant Jumbo Kingdom was just weeks old, and Clearwater Bay Golf and Country Club was still drawings in a course designer’s sketchbook. Nearly 50 years since Judy Rankin held off Hisako Higuchi to win the Colgate-Hong Kong Open in November 1976, the Tour announced its return to the city with the Futu Ladies World Championship, a US$3.4 million prize fund and multi-year partnership as part of a renewed Asian spring swing. The Clear Water Bay club will stage the 78-player tournament next March, the final leg of a three-event stop in the region, following on from the Honda LPGA Thailand and the HSBC Women’s World Championship in Singapore. A double announcement in Boston on Wednesday ahead of the FM Championship, and then at the Hong Kong venue little more than 12 hours later confirmed an event organisers hope will attract the best in the world. Among them will be Hong Kong’s Tiffany Chan Tsz-ching, the first professional from the city to earn a spot on the women’s Tour.
