Undergoing a tough time recently, Chan has been handed a wild card for the course she calls home. “This event checks every box we look for - a championship-calibre course, a market ready for the Tour, a perfect fit within our spring Asia swing, and partners who share our vision,” Chris Madsen, the LPGA’s managing director for the Asia-Pacific, said. Backed by Hong Kong fintech company Futu Holdings and global investment and trading platform Moomoo, the tournament is being organised by Asia-based sports and entertainment company SMK. An initial agreement will see the tournament in place for five years, with the potential to extend that should it prove a success. “Starting with the best purse, best course, and best partners, SMK endeavours to provide world-class lady golfers an unforgettable Asia experience in the inaugurated 2027 Hong Kong LPGA tournament,” Sum Huang, CEO of SMK, said. The Futu Ladies World Championship will be held from March 4 to 7.

title: Two German airport workers die of malaria from mosquito on plane
description: Six workers in total were infected with malaria tropica – the most dangerous form of the disease – at Frankfurt Airport.
content: Two workers at Frankfurt Airport have died from malaria after being infected by mosquitoes believed to have arrived in Germany on aircraft from malaria-endemic regions, airport operator Fraport and city health authorities said on Wednesday. The first death occurred in early July, the Frankfurt city health authority said, adding that the cause was established only after the patient died. The second death occurred in August, it said. The health authority said a total of six workers had been infected with malaria tropica – the most dangerous form of the disease – at work. The other four people infected are now recovering well and have all been treated, the authority said. In mid-July, the Robert Koch Institute (RKI) had initially confirmed an outbreak of four malaria cases among airport workers. “The individuals affected fell ill between July 4 and 6, 2026,” the RKI wrote in its Epidemiological Bulletin. “It is assumed that the infection was transmitted by an infected Anopheles mosquito imported by aircraft.” The Anopheles mosquito is also known as the nail or marsh mosquito. Fraport said mosquito traps had been set up and mosquitoes had been caught, which were now being examined in a laboratory, a spokesman said. “The mosquito is probably already dead,” said Peter Tinnemann, head of the Frankfurt health authority. “There is no likelihood of person-to-person spread. The risk to the Frankfurt population is negligible.” Malaria is a life-threatening disease transmitted by mosquitoes, according to the Foreign Ministry. “Particularly in at-risk groups, the disease can lead to coma and death. Protection against mosquito bites and the taking of preventive medication can prevent the disease.” The RKI said “very rare” airport malaria occurs when an infectious mosquito is imported on an aircraft or in luggage, with infection then taking place on the plane, at the airport or in its immediate vicinity. The last such case was documented in 2023, also at Frankfurt Airport, the institute said. Doctors treating people who work at or near airports with intercontinental connections – both passenger and cargo flights – should consider airport malaria as a possible diagnosis, particularly in summer, in cases of unexplained fever with no travel history, it said. Frankfurt health authority doctor Regina Ellwanger Berry also stressed that airport malaria was so rare that it did not feature among the standard differential diagnoses used by doctors for patients with no travel history. “Malaria is highly treatable if you know that it is malaria,” she said.

title: Tim Curry, famed for Rocky Horror Picture Show, dead at 80
description: The UK actor appeared in numerous films, often as an over-the-top villain, and was nominated three times for a Tony Award.
content: Tim Curry, the baritone-voiced British actor who pranced to movie fame as a singing, lingerie-clad “sweet transvestite” in the 1975 ⁠cult classic The Rocky Horror Picture Show, has died at ⁠the age of 80, his manager said on Wednesday. A cause of ⁠death was not immediately given, but Curry had been in ill health for some time. He died peacefully on Tuesday at his home in Los Angeles, his manager said. Curry appeared in numerous films, often as a hammy villain, was nominated three times for a Tony Award for Broadway roles, and performed voice work in many animated films and television shows. But his best-known role was Dr Frank N. Furter, which came in his debut film, the outrageous, crowd-pleasing horror-comedy-musical The Rocky Horror Picture Show, co-starring Susan Sarandon and Barry Bostwick. “I’m not ‌much of a man by the light of day. But by night I’m one hell of a lover. I’m just a sweet transvestite from transsexual Transylvania,” Curry sang in one scene as he strutted around with garish eye shadow and lipstick, in a skimpy black outfit complete with black stockings and garter belt. In a 1975 television interview, Curry noted the risk of having his career defined by such an outlandish role – a prescient worry, as it turned out. “When I read it, I just thought it was very, very witty and funny,” Curry said, although he confessed to some initial reluctance. “I mean, I was hesitant in that, if it worked, it might be ⁠a difficult thing to shake off. But, really, I’ve always thought that it [a part] wasn’t worth doing unless you took a risk,” Curry said. Among his other films were Charlie’s Angels (2000), Muppet Treasure Island (1996), The ‌Shadow (1994), The Three Musketeers (1993), Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992), Clue (1985), Legend (1985) and Annie (1982). Curry did much of his best work on stage. He was nominated for a Tony, Broadway’s top honour, in 1981 for his role as Mozart in Amadeus, a tale of the great composer’s interaction with jealous rival Salieri. ‌ Curry was also nominated for a Tony in 1993 for My Favorite Year and in 2005 for his role as King Arthur in the zany Monty Python’s ⁠Spamalot. Possessing a rich baritone voice, he was ⁠in demand as a voice actor for animated films and television shows. He won a Daytime Emmy Award in 1991 for his voice work on the animated Peter Pan & the Pirates. With his sinister grin and menacing laugh, ‌Curry was frequently cast in Hollywood films as a villain – sometimes with comic overtones, which let him deliver the type of over-the-top performances for which he was famed. “I do love those roles – they’re always the best written,” Curry told interviewer Andrew ‌Kay in ‌2011. He conceded that some of his films were mediocre, singling out 1995’s Congo, a tale of diamond mines and killer gorillas. “I was really very bad in it,” Curry said. “I ‌won a Razzy award for one of the worst performances of the year – and I richly deserved it, too.” Curry was born in the English village of Grappenhall, Cheshire, on ⁠April 19, 1946. His father, a Royal Navy chaplain, died when he was 12. His mother was a school secretary. Curry studied drama at Birmingham University. In 1973, he landed the ⁠part of Dr Frank N. Furter in the original London stage version of The Rocky Horror Show. He performed the play in New York and Los Angeles before it was made into a film, renamed as The Rocky Horror Picture Show. The film was not an instant hit but won a cult following in midnight screenings ‌in New York and elsewhere, with audience members ‌often dressing up as Rocky Horror characters. Curry withdrew from a British stage production in 2011 due to ill health. In 2013, his agent said that he had suffered a stroke but was recovering “in great humour”. From then on he used a wheelchair and reduced his workload. In 2024, he did, however, return to the big screen, appearing in the horror film Stream. Curry, who lived in Los Angeles, never married and had no children. A composer and a singer, Curry also performed with his own rock band and released a handful of albums.

title: US critical minerals proposals to Brazil go unanswered as China looms
description: A US diplomat says Brasilia has not responded to two overtures, even as a US-backed rare earth acquisition in Brazil nears completion.
content: Brazil has not answered two American proposals to formalise cooperation on critical minerals, a senior US diplomat said at Latin America’s largest mining fair, leaving Washington without a bilateral deal as it races to build rare earth supply chains outside China. Matthew Lowe, economic counsellor at the US embassy in Brasilia, said Washington invited Brazil years ago to join the Minerals Security Partnership, a US-led grouping that coordinates investment in mineral supply chains, but never received a response. A draft framework agreement sent in February also went unanswered. “We’ll probably have to wait till the election, no matter what happens,” Lowe told the audience in Belo Horizonte on Tuesday, referring to Brazil’s presidential vote in October. Lowe was speaking at Exposibram, the conference run by the Brazilian Mining Institute, alongside officials from France, Canada, Australia and Britain, most of whose governments have signed the kind of agreement Washington cannot get from Brasilia. The five spent the session describing how they intend to loosen China’s grip on mineral processing without once naming China. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earths after China, a resource base that brought the five to a fair in the Brazilian interior. Rare earths are a group of 17 metals that are common in the ground and difficult to separate from one another, and they sit inside the wider category of critical minerals that also covers lithium, nickel and cobalt. Lowe came closest to naming China when he turned to separation, the chemical step that splits mined ore into the individual metals used to make magnets, and where China does close to 90 per cent of the world’s work. “A lot of us are developing the technology from scratch because it’s controlled by the one country that has really been doing rare earths, and that’s a joint problem that we all share,” he said. Benjamin Gallezot, France’s interministerial delegate for strategic minerals, said the choke point lies in refining rather than in mining, and described a market shaped by “some dominance of some country or some restriction”. Asked whether building that capacity outside China is realistic, he said Brazil had the energy, the workforce and the permitting to do it. “There is nothing magic about processing,” Gallezot said. USA Rare Earth expects to complete a US$2.8 billion takeover of the Brazilian miner Serra Verde within days, once its own shareholders vote on Friday. On Monday it finished raising US$1.55 billion for a company set up by US government agencies and private investors, which will buy the whole of the mine’s output for 15 years at guaranteed minimum prices. Serra Verde runs the Pela Ema mine in the central state of Goias, which entered production in 2024, and is the only operation outside Asia producing all four of the rare earths that go into permanent magnets. Those magnets sit inside electric car motors, wind turbines, drones and guided weapons, and no substitute performs as well. Pela Ema also yields dysprosium and terbium, the two heavier elements that stop a magnet losing its strength when it gets hot and which most Western projects cannot produce at all. The geology explains the difference, because the metals there sit loosely in soft clay near the surface rather than locked inside hard rock, the same formation that underpins southern China’s dominance in the heavier elements. Beijing put USA Rare Earth on its export control list on June 22, alongside MP Materials and eight other American firms, barring Chinese companies from selling them equipment with both civilian and military uses. China called the move retaliation for Washington’s expansion of its own list of Chinese firms it accuses of military links. For all that, the mine at the centre of the deal still depends on China, because Serra Verde had committed Pela Ema’s output to Chinese processors under 10-year contracts. It renegotiated last December and cut almost eight years off the term, but the half-finished product is still shipped to China to be separated into individual metals. Left-wing deputies have asked the Brazilian courts to annul the sale, which the country’s antitrust authority cleared this month. The US embassy has meanwhile pursued agreements at state level, signing a memorandum with Goias in March that Lowe said “became a bit of an issue” because critics questioned whether a governor may strike mineral deals with a foreign power. It hopes to try again elsewhere once the election is over, he said. Lowe also criticised the bill now before the Brazilian Senate, which would let a new presidential council and the mining regulator approve or block changes in the control of companies holding mineral rights. “That’s fine as long as it’s apolitical and predictable, but it cannot be done in a way that is susceptible to a change every four years with every new government,” he said. The bill passed the lower house in May and is on the agenda for the last sitting week before voting begins in October. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth term, said last week that the Senate would advance the law to defend the national interest. “We will not allow anyone from outside to come here and exploit our mineral resources, because we want their processing and transformation to happen here,” Lula said. Carlos Eduardo Braga Filho, who runs Brazilian operations for the cobalt and nickel processor Jervois, made the case for keeping processing in the country at a panel across the hall the same afternoon. “You can’t take a mine to another country, but processing you can. So why do it here? You have to create value, you have to be competitive,” Braga Filho said, speaking in Portuguese. He then named China directly, something none of the five diplomats across the hall had done. “I want to have rare earths here, but I want to have rare earths to sell to China. We may end up deciding yes, but that is not the path we have understood to be the best,” he said. His own plant shows how far that ambition sits from the ore, because the refinery Jervois is restarting in Sao Paulo will run on imported raw material when it opens next year with a capacity of about 12,000 tonnes of nickel a year. Almost all the nickel Brazil digs up is the grade that goes into stainless steel rather than the grade batteries and specialist alloys need. Flavio Moraes da Mota of the state development bank BNDES said it is backing 12 critical minerals projects worth 35 billion reais (US$6.8 billion) in rare earths, nickel and lithium. Chinese companies had filed no rare earth exploration applications of their own in Brazil as of June, according to an analysis of regulator records by the Associated Press and Reporter Brasil. China Nonferrous Metal Mining bought the tin producer Mineracao Taboca in 2024 and has said it will study the rare earth potential of its Amazon operation.

title: 2 arrested in Hong Kong fight over elderly woman slapping girl
description: Viral footage shows elderly woman shoving and then slapping girl at shopping centre, before another woman retaliates.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested two women on suspicion of assault at a shopping centre in Kwun Tong, with a viral clip showing a fight breaking out after a five-year-old girl was shoved and then knocked to the ground. The fight took place at the atrium of the APM shopping centre at around 4.45pm on Wednesday as a crowd of parents and young children gathered around a play area. A source said one of the suspects, aged 68, was visiting the play area with her 34-year-old daughter and grandson. A dispute reportedly erupted between the boy and a five-year-old girl over use of the installation, prompting his grandmother to get involved. In the clip, an elderly woman can be seen forcefully shoving a girl and then slapping her, causing the child to lose her balance and fall. Another woman then rushes forward to confront the first woman and strikes her. At one point in the footage, the boy’s mother confronts the other mother and says: “You can’t leave.” Two men intervene at different points in the scuffle, with one confronting the boy’s grandmother and shouting: “Did you just hit a child? I saw you.” Police later arrived at the scene and arrested the older woman and the girl’s mother, also aged 34, on suspicion of assault or assault occasioning actual bodily harm. They added that the girl and the two younger women were taken to the nearby United Christian Hospital to treat minor facial injuries. The force’s Kwun Tong district investigation team is handling the case.

title: In a small Virginia town, distrust of Big Tech hampers Trump’s AI push
description: Controversy over first data centres in Danville typifies ongoing debate with concerns over secrecy, distrust and China’s influence.
content: The front page of the Danville Register & Bee, a local newspaper in southern Virginia with a circulation of fewer than 4,000, carried an unusual headline. “LEADER: CHINA BEHIND THE MISCONCEPTIONS”, it read, above a photograph of two homes dwarfed by a data centre behind. The leader in question was Vic Ingram, chair of the Danville-Pittsylvania Regional Industrial Facility Authority (RIFA), a local body jointly established by the city of Danville and neighbouring Pittsylvania County to promote economic development in one of the poorest parts of the state. Ingram had just helped secure what officials described as the biggest economic development project in southern Virginia’s history: a proposed data-centre campus at Berry Hill, a 3,500-acre (1,400-hectare) industrial site about 16 kilometres (10 miles) outside Danville. But some residents were questioning the project at public meetings and on social media over its environmental impact, power requirements, and the secrecy surrounding its approval. As the chorus of discontent grew louder, Ingram told the local newspaper in June that much of the “propaganda” online against the area’s first-ever data centres was driven by the “Communist Chinese”. Other supporters of the project have also invoked China in response to local resistance, portraying the data centres as essential to America’s ability to compete with Beijing in artificial intelligence – an increasingly common refrain of US President Donald Trump as data centres become increasingly unpopular nationwide. Three-quarters of Americans now oppose having a data centre built near them, up from 42 per cent just a year ago, according to Heatmap. Danville residents, however, say they do not need China to tell them what to think. Their concerns are rooted in distrust of local officials, a history of broken investment promises and an opaque decision-making process, they say. The dispute is the latest chapter in Danville’s complicated relationship with China. After the collapse of its textile industry, the city turned to Chinese manufacturers to help revitalise its economy, but that turned into disappointment when those investments failed to materialise. Now China is being used to justify Danville’s latest economic gamble and discredit those who question it. A failed China strategy To understand why the Berry Hill project has generated such intense debate, residents say it is necessary to understand what Danville has lost and its relationship with northern Virginia. The city used to boast one of the biggest textile plants in the southeastern US, Dan River Mills, which employed over 18,000 people at its peak. In the 2000s, manufacturing in the industrial town all but disappeared as textile jobs went overseas, mainly to China. When the mill closed in 2006, thousands lost their jobs, throwing the city into a tailspin that has lasted almost two decades. “We’ve gone through some hard times socially, but when that mill closed, that was the hardest time economically,” said Frank Leist, a local entrepreneur. Desperate to secure Danville’s next big economic driver, local officials turned to the big economic opportunity at the time: China. In 2013, officials devised “The China Strategy” – an initiative to recruit Chinese companies to set up manufacturing plants in the area. They paid a Pittsburgh consulting firm US$150,000 as part of the strategy, according to official records. The initiative seemed to bear fruit at first. City council announcements at the time hailed the arrival of Chinese companies like furniture company GOK International, which pledged to invest US$12.5 million and employ 300 locals. None of those deals materialised, says Jonathan Travis Hackworth, a local historian. GOK failed to honour a US$1 million grant from a state economic development body. Danville was left to foot the bill. Further disappointment followed in 2023 when officials sought to make Berry Hill the home of Ford Motor’s new US$3.5 billion battery plant, which licensed its technology from Chinese battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL). The plant eventually went to Michigan after then-Virginia governor Glenn Youngkin removed Berry Hill from consideration, citing concerns about CATL’s involvement. RIFA’s Ingram shared a post on Facebook after Youngkin’s intervention questioning whether the United States should “refuse to do business with any company simply because they have ties to China”. Three years later, Berry Hill is again at the centre of a politically charged debate in Danville involving China – this time as a reason to support the proposed investment rather than reject it. Another enormous promise Shannon Kelly, a local reporter at the Chatham Star Tribune, said the area’s recent history of failed economic development looms large over the data centre debate. “I don’t think anyone is against data centres on principle,” she said. “Rather, many people have concerns or some trust issues with local officials.” A major point of contention has been the use of non-disclosure agreements among officials and Colorado-based Stack Infrastructure, the company behind the project, during the early stages of the approval process. When it was first disclosed in March that SAC III, a company that shares the same address as Stack, would be acquiring land at Berry Hill, officials would not say what the land would be used for, citing non-disclosure agreements. Only a month later did they confirm that Stack would build a “hyperscale” data centre – a new generation of data centres marked by their enormous scale – promising US$100 billion in investment and 2,500 jobs over 30 years. At almost 3,000 acres, the project surpasses the 1,100 acres bought by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI for its Colossus supercomputer in Tennessee as well as Facebook owner Meta Platforms’ initial 2,250-acre acquisition for its Hyperion campus in Louisiana. “It all feels very sneaky, like we don’t have all the information,” said Kelly. “Residents feel like there’s a lack of transparency in these talks.” Supporters say non-disclosure agreements are standard for economic-development negotiations because they protect commercially sensitive information and prevent land speculation. But the Coalition for the Protection of Pittsylvania County, one of the principal groups questioning the project, has accused data-centre companies of using such agreements “to keep the public in the dark” until projects are too advanced to stop. The South China Morning Post contacted the coalition and other opposition groups, but none agreed to speak on the record. One resident cited the fact that the SCMP is a Chinese outlet as the reason for declining to speak. China’s return to the debate As local opposition has grown, including an online petition with around 900 signatures calling for greater community input, some supporters began tying residents’ concerns to China. In his newspaper interview, Ingram accused residents of buying into Chinese propaganda because “it looks very believable”, citing a report into Chinese influence operations released in June by US AI giant OpenAI. However, the OpenAI report claimed only that online accounts “likely originating from China” were trying to influence US public opinion, with “no evidence” that they had succeeded. Ingram did not respond to multiple calls and emails requesting evidence that Chinese propaganda had swayed residents, whom he has also labelled the “anti-growth crowd” and “low-information voters” on social media. According to Bethany Allen, head of China Investigations and Analysis at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, it is an “age-old ploy” for officials anywhere to dismiss opposing voices by tying them to foreign actors. She notes that such accusations of foreign influence in the US mirror how Beijing levels the same charge against anti-government voices in China. Ken Larkin, Danville’s city manager who supports the data centres, says he is not aware of China influencing the local opposition. He notes that securing a buyer for Berry Hill has become a top priority for local officials following several missed opportunities in recent years, with more than US$217 million spent on preparing the site since it was acquired in 2008. ‘Playing it by ear’ For Leist, the entrepreneur, the worry is that politics elsewhere once again dashes Danville’s economic hopes. Though Virginia is known as having the most data centres in the world, with more than 600, most are concentrated in northern Virginia, where some of the richest counties in the US are. Over the past year, northern Virginia residents’ growing complaints about living next to data centres have led to calls to rebalance the state’s policy towards the industry. While Virginia’s latest budget, approved in June, retained a controversial sales tax exemption that has made the state a prime destination for the industry, it nonetheless introduced a new electricity consumption tax for data centres. Stack has said it will proceed as long as the sales tax exemption remains. Still, Leist says that economic inequality has been a neglected issue in Virginia’s data centre debate, with most people arguing over environmental and geopolitical issues. “My entire life, northern Virginia has always stopped southern Virginia from being great,” he said. “Now northern Virginia is against data centres, and it’s like, we haven’t had our chance to benefit from it yet, so why are you trying to block it now?” Tensions remain high because the Berry Hill project could still fall apart. Officials have touted a headline figure of around US$737.8 million for Stack to purchase the land at Berry Hill – almost triple the annual budget of the entire county – but the money is split over multiple instalments and the company retains the right to pull out, according to the land sale agreement. Leist describes feeling “backstabbed” by local officials when news first broke in March about the data centres, after years of being told that Berry Hill would be home to a manufacturing plant. He has since come around to it, as much in hope that Stack keeps all its promises as in fear that Danville – where empty tobacco warehouses and boarded-up shopfronts sit as quiet reminders of the last two decades – misses out again on the next big industry. “For me, I support the data centres because I know that that’s the next step in our technology phase,” he said. “But I’m more of a ‘let’s play it by ear’ at this moment in time.”

title: Hong Kong lawmaker urges firms to expand into emerging markets amid US visa pause
description: Jonathan Lamport tells SCMP the local business community is closely monitoring whether business visa processing, approvals will be affected.
content: Hong Kong companies should accelerate their expansion into the Middle East, the Asean bloc and Central Asia to reduce their exposure to geopolitical risks, a lawmaker has said, as the US moved to disrupt immigrant-visa appointments worldwide. Jonathan Lamport, the representative for the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce (HKGCC) in the Legislative Council, said the visa uncertainty reinforced the need for companies to broaden their overseas presence beyond traditional Western markets. “The business sector cannot put all its eggs in one basket,” he told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday. “While we will continue to maintain our relationships with traditional markets like the US and Europe, we must also accelerate our strategic expansion into emerging markets such as the Middle East, Asean and Central Asia.” The Association of Southeast Asian Nations comprises the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor. The commercial sector lawmaker said the local business community was closely monitoring whether the disruption would affect the processing and approval of business visas. The worldwide pause, first reported by the Financial Times, applies to appointments for immigrant visas, which allow recipients to live permanently in the United States, rather than temporary business and tourist visas under separate non-immigrant categories. But in a reply to the SCMP, the US State Department used broader language, with a spokesman saying “appointments for visa services” would be adjusted as officers underwent training at embassies and consulates worldwide. The department did not specify whether the scheduling of non-immigrant visa interviews would also be affected. Most non-immigrant visa applicants, including those seeking temporary business visitor visas, are generally required to attend an in-person interview with a consular officer, with limited exceptions for certain renewals. “Normal economic and trade exchanges are in the mutual economic interests of both sides,” Lamport said. “We sincerely hope that regular business activities and people-to-people exchanges can remain smooth and unobstructed during this period.” Lamport said he believed the HKGCC would contact the US consulate in Hong Kong to seek information on the latest visa processing timelines, allowing companies to make timely adjustments and budget for business trips, exhibitions and contract signings. The US State Department spokesman said Washington had been updating its guidance and training on assessing whether applicants were likely to become dependent on public benefits. “In early August, we launched a global training initiative at all of our embassies and consulates worldwide,” he said. “To accommodate this in-depth training, appointments for visa services will be adjusted.” The department did not disclose how many appointments had been affected in Hong Kong or when normal scheduling would resume. It said embassies and consulates would communicate any changes directly to applicants. “The Trump administration is protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants,” the spokesman added. The disruption comes as US President Donald Trump intensified restrictions on legal and illegal immigration during his second term. A US federal judge on Friday struck down a separate administration policy suspending immigrant-visa issuance to applicants from 75 countries, ruling that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had exceeded his statutory authority. The administration had argued that nationals of those countries presented a high risk of becoming dependent on public resources. Washington this week also proposed making permanent a US$103,265 fee for H-1B visas, which are used by American employers to recruit highly skilled foreign workers. A federal judge blocked the temporary version of the fee in June, while the administration is appealing that decision. The State Department has also expanded online-presence reviews across a range of visa categories, requiring applicants including skilled workers, students and exchange visitors to make their social media profiles public. The HKGCC separately declined to comment on the appointment changes.

title: Meta to pay US$18 billion and limit teen access to settle US addiction case
description: Landmark deal imposes new safety limits on Instagram and Facebook for teens as company calls on TikTok and YouTube to follow.
content: Meta agreed to pay a coalition of US states as much as US$16.7 billion and to impose sweeping new limits on how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram, according to a court filing on Wednesday that ends a landmark trial in California. The settlement, which a federal judge quickly approved, resolves claims by 29 states that Meta deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users, misled the public about the risks and unlawfully collected data from children under 13. Texas reached a separate agreement with Meta, which increased the total payout to around US$18 billion. The changes to how young people use its apps go further than anything Meta has accepted before, and follow years of criticism from parents and experts over the effects of the world’s biggest social media platforms on children. Anger over the impact of Instagram and Facebook – as well as rival apps like Snapchat and TikTok – has driven the spread of age limits and school phone bans around the world. Meta still faces thousands of additional personal injury claims and litigation from school districts. The case by the 29 states was among the most far-reaching, with Meta warning that a courtroom loss could have exposed it to more than US$1 trillion in penalties. “Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms – and will do it within months,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement. He called the outcome “real change, real transparency, and real enforceable protections for children”. The agreement will apply only to teenagers in those signatory states, with no effect internationally. The filing states that the agreement does not amount to an admission of liability or wrongdoing by Meta, which has consistently denied the allegations. The most far-reaching provisions are not financial. Meta has agreed to a long list of new safeguards that will substantially change how the apps work for young people. One change is an automatic nighttime block that locks teenagers out of Facebook and Instagram between midnight and 6am local time. Teenage accounts will also be capped by default at two hours of cumulative daily use across Meta’s apps, though time spent messaging or watching long-form video does not count towards the limit. Meta framed the deal as a template for the rest of the industry and pressed its competitors to match it. “Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution,” said C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer. “We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away.” Should competing platforms adopt equivalent commitments, the overnight lockout would widen to 10pm through 7am and the daily allowance would fall to 60 minutes per app, capped at two hours in total. Compliance would be policed for 10 years by an independent auditor chosen jointly by Meta and the states and paid for by the company. The settlement payment schedule provides for 10 annual instalments. California, the largest recipient, is due US$1.5 billion to US$2.1 billion over the decade, followed by New York with up to US$1.13 billion. The settlement ends the trial in its second week. Instagram boss Adam Mosseri took the stand on Tuesday and admitted he touted newly launched safety tools for teens without disclosing low adoption rates from early testing several years ago. Other witnesses testified over the past week that Meta knew the tools were not effective and even that they were “designed to fail”. Meta Founder and Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg had been expected to testify as well. “Meta is now facing the same ugly truth as the makers of Agent Orange, asbestos, and other dangerous products. If you’re liable at all, the lawsuits will keep coming and coming,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell University. “Settling with the states is a way to try to limit Meta’s overall exposure and get some of the biggest and most dangerous plaintiffs to go away,” he said.

title: China vows payback for US Iran sanctions, testing stability ahead of Xi-Trump summit
description: Beijing warns economic pressure will fail; semi-official Track 1.5 dialogue targets risk control before Chinese president visits US.
content: Beijing has vowed to retaliate against Washington’s expanded Iran sanctions targeting Chinese entities, threatening a clash that could erode recent stability in the US-China relationship and become a new flashpoint weeks before President Xi Jinping visits the US, according to observers. But they say that efforts on both sides, such as this week’s Track 1.5 dialogue, could serve as a check on tensions and allow each side to understand the other’s concerns. The US on Monday announced fresh sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, including entities in mainland China and Hong Kong, in its latest push to squeeze Iran economically after months of military strikes and diplomatic talks failed to resolve the six-month conflict. On Tuesday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian dismissed the sanctions as “illicit” with “no basis in international law”, saying the US move would heighten tensions and disrupt the global economic and financial order. “Economic warfare and maximum pressure provide no solution,” he said. “China’s cooperation with Iran is conducted within the framework of international law, thus should not be disrupted.” Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said it was not clear if the latest sanctions would directly affect Xi’s planned meeting with Trump but that the sanctions development was “becoming a new risk point” ahead of the summit. “The key may lie in whether the US expands secondary sanctions to major Chinese banks. If it’s limited to individual companies and intermediaries, both sides may still be able to keep the disagreement contained,” he said. “But if it touches China’s core financial institutions, the situation could become quite different.” Xi is expected to visit Washington next month – his first state visit to the US in more than a decade – for talks with Trump. Sun said that if the US doubled down on its secondary sanctions on Iran to target key Chinese financial firms, the summit risked becoming an exercise in “damage control” rather than a platform to promote stability and produce results, which would be a setback to the “hard-won momentum of stability” in US-China ties. Song Guoyou, deputy director of Fudan University’s Centre for American Studies, said the latest US move exposed Washington’s dilemma. On one hand, the ongoing conflict with Iran was causing serious problems at home, pushing the Trump administration to escalate pressure on Tehran. But on the other hand, its relationship with Beijing mattered too, he added, suggesting that the US was unlikely to risk large-scale sanctions against China. “This is because the Sino-US trade war that began last year has proven that no matter what kind of sanctions the US adopts, including secondary sanctions on Iran, it cannot truly make China back down,” he said. According to Song, the US sanctions could “indeed become a significant new factor affecting Sino-US relations”. “China will certainly defend its economic interests, and in a legitimate and reasonable manner. Therefore, in future Sino-US interactions, the Iranian issue and the US economic sanctions against Iran … will become a new uncertainty,” he said. The two sides have in recent weeks traded tit-for-tat measures that analysts earlier said could cloud the Chinese leader’s landmark visit to the US. Washington last month added dozens of Chinese firms to its Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act entity list and banned the import and sale of new foreign-made robotic devices and power inverters – sectors in which China is a global leader – prompting retaliatory sanctions from Beijing days later. Zhu Junwei, director of Chinese think tank Horizon Insights Centre, said Washington’s moves were likely aimed at building up bargaining chips ahead of next month’s summit. She said they were unlikely to derail the summit itself but could shape its outcomes. But even with signs of rising tensions, observers say recent dialogue could help soothe some concerns between the two sides. Beijing on Tuesday hosted the third US-China Track 1.5 Dialogue, a semi-official mechanism established in 2023 to bridge official diplomacy and non-governmental exchanges between the two countries. Liu Haixing, head of the Communist Party’s International Department, told attendees – Chinese and foreign representatives from local governments, think tanks and universities as well as members of US strategic and business communities – that China and the US should work towards “normal stability with controllable disagreements”. Zhu said the dialogue was beneficial in keeping lines of communication open between both sides, even though it was not clear how much influence the American attendees had over the Trump administration. Sun, from Tsinghua University, said such dialogues could serve as a “guardrail” amid escalating tensions but he cautioned against overstating their impact. “The greatest value of this type of dialogue isn’t to resolve major policy disagreements like sanctions on the government’s behalf, but to help both sides more accurately understand each other’s red lines and policy logic,” he said. “Especially on an issue like Iran secondary sanctions, the US and China can easily end up with misaligned perceptions … This is where unofficial and semi-official channels can discuss things more candidly.”

title: China’s steel sector must avoid US rust belt’s fate: party journal
description: Trade barriers, oversupply and falling export prices are squeezing steel producers as the Qiushi Journal warns against letting the industry contract.
content: As geopolitical tensions intensify, China’s steel sector – the world’s largest – is facing trade-restrictive measures in overseas markets and shrinking margins, but the country must strive to avoid the mistakes of America’s rust belt, according to an article in the Communist Party’s top theoretical journal. The piece, published in the latest issue of the Qiushi Journal and written jointly by the journal and the China Iron and Steel Association, argued that China should not allow its steel sector to contract in an attempt to redirect more resources towards emerging industries. “Lessons from America’s rust belt remain a sobering reminder,” the article said. “The de-industrialisation of traditional industries will inevitably trigger a chain of repercussions, including regional economic recession, job losses and sluggish innovation.” The rust belt refers to a swathe of the United States that experienced severe industrial decline in the late 20th century. Local economies were once heavily anchored in iron and steel production, carmaking, coal mining and raw-material processing. Industries that underpin national economic security “must never be allowed to undergo market-driven liquidation or passive contraction”, the Qiushi article said. Profit margins for domestic steelmakers remain depressed Yu Jiayi, Orient Securities China has held the world’s top spot in crude-steel output for three decades, the article noted, adding that the country’s production exceeded 960 million tonnes in 2025, accounting for more than half of global output. The sector has evolved from being “barely capable of manufacturing” into a full-fledged system offering the broadest product range, superior quality and competitive pricing, the article said. However, it also acknowledged that the sector has faced mounting headwinds, both internal and external, in recent years. From 2020 to June this year, Chinese steel goods were subject to more than 110 trade-remedy investigations. Trade-restrictive measures have expanded from low-end offerings such as construction steel to high-value-added grades for new-energy vehicles, aerospace use and embodied intelligence, according to the article. It highlighted Washington’s Section 337 investigation targeting carbon-steel and alloy-steel goods that Chinese firms sell in the US, alleging that the investigation was “dealing a direct blow to China’s exports of high-end steel products”. Wang Guoqing, a researcher at the Beijing-based Lange Steel Research Centre, said on Wednesday that trade frictions in the steel sector were poised to “become the new normal”. “Developed economies will deploy an array of instruments to shield their domestic steel industries, one example being the UK’s nationalisation of British Steel, which was previously owned by a Chinese group,” she said in an interview. “This is the global business environment that Chinese steelmakers will face over the long term.” Another growing concern is squeezed export profit margins, with domestic oversupply and cutthroat price competition persisting. In 2025, the average export price for Chinese-made conventional steel products stood at just US$694 per tonne, an 18 per cent drop from 2020. That stems from “slowing infrastructure construction across Southeast Asia and the Middle East”, the Qiushi article said. Yu Jiayi, an analyst at Shanghai-based Orient Securities, wrote in a Sunday report that some Chinese producers are scheduling planned maintenance shutdowns defensively to limit losses. “Currently, profit margins for domestic steelmakers remain depressed,” Yu said. “Oversupply is set to persist over the near and medium term.” Wang noted that de-industrialisation in the US rust belt sparked a host of socioeconomic woes, and that preserving foundational industries did not mean retaining backward capacity. “The goal is to sustain the industrial foundation, not keep outdated production capacity. China’s push for steel-industry upgrading marks a fundamental difference from the US experience,” Wang added.

title: Iran and Oman reach Hormuz deal, but reopening hinges on US compliance
description: The Revolutionary Guards said the waterway ‘will ‌not be opened under any circumstances’ if Washington failed to accept the demands.
content: Iran and Oman have reached agreement on their share of the Strait of Hormuz and its revenues, but the vital waterway will not be reopened if the US does not accept their conditions, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday. Iran and Oman have held on-and-off talks for weeks ‌about controlling traffic through the strait, which handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February. Most shipping has since been shut down, driving global energy prices higher, as Tehran and Washington have tried to assert control over the channel, imposing separate blockades. “The Strait of Hormuz belongs to Iran and the country of Oman … We have been in negotiations with Oman for about a month, and we have reached results that are acceptable to both sides,” Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said in comments published by Iranian state media. “In these negotiations, agreements have been reached regarding the ‌share of each country in the waters of the strait and the share of Iran and Oman in its revenues,” Mohebbi added. The IRGC accused the US of seeking to obstruct the negotiations between ‌Iran and Oman and said this had caused the agreement to be delayed. “If the United States stops obstructing ⁠and returns to the agreement, ⁠we can open the Strait of Hormuz within the framework of the agreement reached … If the United States does not accept our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will ‌not be opened under any circumstances,” Mohebbi said. Though active hostilities between the US and Iran have largely subsided in recent weeks, diplomatic efforts to reach a peace ‌deal have ‌stalled, and continuing attacks on ships mean passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains perilous. Iran announced a blacklist on Sunday ‌of 45 ships in an apparent effort to stop ship-to-ship transfers used by Gulf energy producers to evade the Iranian blockade. Some companies plan ⁠to stop using vessels added to the blacklist, sources said. In an effort to tighten pressure on Iran’s economy, the US ⁠earlier this week threatened to punish countries that continue to do business with Iran, but said it would not impose penalties immediately. The sanctions did not feature Chinese financial institutions suspected of easing oil exports from Iran that the US blockade ‌has cut. Iran denounced the US effort ‌to isolate its economy as an act of “gross lawlessness”, expressing confidence that many countries would not join the pressure campaign. Oil prices fell for a third day, dropping more than US$2 a barrel to a two-week low, following signs of renewed efforts to seek a mediated end to the war that began on February 28 with US and Israeli strikes on Iran.

title: Why US visa pause could have ‘real consequences’ for Asian applicants
description: Observers warn the pause ‘risks months of cascading delays’ for Asian countries with large numbers of pending applications.
content: Asian workers and families already facing years-long waits for US visas could be pushed deeper into uncertainty by a global pause on immigrant visa appointments, as President Donald Trump’s administration tightens legal immigration through new screening and higher costs, experts warn. The US State Department on Tuesday said it had launched a global training initiative for consular officers at all US embassies and consulates, and that immigrant visa appointments would be adjusted to accommodate it. The department did not specify the scope or duration of the training, beyond saying it was intended to help officers screen out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on US public benefits and ensure they were evaluated “comprehensively and consistently”. Immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates have begun receiving notices that their appointments are being rescheduled, with new dates to follow, according to reports. The disruption has left applicants uncertain not only about when they will be interviewed, but also whether documents tied to existing appointment dates – including police clearances, medical checks and financial records – will need updating. For Asian applicants, experts say, the impact could be especially acute in countries with large visa pipelines and already crowded consular calendars. “It’s not clear if this is being handled embassy by embassy or centrally. The Asian countries with the largest number of pending applications will likely be hit the hardest,” said Russell A. Stamets, a partner at the New Delhi-based law firm Circle of Counsels. Srinivasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at the Indic Researchers Forum, said the immediate hit for Asian applicants was cancellation notices and open-ended waits, as no restart date was given. “In high-volume places like India, the Philippines and Vietnam, where family queues already stretch years, this is unlikely to be a few days’ blip. It risks months of cascading delays as slots get rebooked amid heavier screening. India, with its massive skilled and family pipeline, stands especially exposed and will feel the backlog first,” he said. The appointment pause announcement came a day after the Department of Homeland Security proposed a new US$103,265 fee for H-1B petitions subject to the annual cap – a move that could sharply increase the cost of hiring skilled foreign workers and is expected to hit Chinese and Indian professionals particularly hard. Immigrant visas cover permanent migration, including family reunification and some employment-based categories, while H-1B visas are temporary skilled-worker visas. Experts said the US moves suggested employment-based applicants could face particular scrutiny, even as family cases risked being swept into broader appointment delays. “It’s possible that employment-based applicants will be treated differently than simple family reunification applicants. Taken together with the renewed push to add at least US$100,000 per visa for employment-based visas, there may be further implications for this type of applicant,” Stamets said. Balakrishnan warned employment-based applicants would face “real consequences”, including postponed interviews, stalled careers, frozen job offers and prolonged uncertainty for highly skilled talent America still needs. Washington’s move implied that family reunification cases from the Philippines, Vietnam, China and especially India would be among the hardest hit because those categories already dominated immigrant visa caseloads and waiting lists, Balakrishnan said. Hoang Lan Anh, an Australia-based academic who has studied Vietnamese overseas migration, said US-bound Vietnamese applicants were concentrated mainly in student, skilled or employment-based visas and family sponsorship. “Because these applicants – particularly student and skilled-visa applicants – tend to come from middle- and upper-class backgrounds, I wouldn’t expect this pause to trigger major economic shocks for the applicant pool itself, in the way a similar disruption might affect lower-income labour migrants elsewhere,” Anh said. But the sudden halt could still significantly disrupt individual plans for study, work or family reunification, she said. “These are not abstract inconveniences, but plans people have built their lives around, sometimes over years.” The consequences could be especially acute for family-sponsorship visas, which Anh said were often the outcome of years or even decades of planning, saving and coordination across generations. “When processing queues are suddenly frozen, the immediate fallout is less about a single missed deadline than about the collapse of a whole scaffold of interdependent decisions built around an expected timeline,” Anh said. “Families lose not just time, but also the ability to plan with any confidence at all.” Those planning costs could quickly become financial ones if the pause lasts long enough for immigration documents to expire. A Philippines-based immigration lawyer and lecturer, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, said the costs could be especially burdensome for family-based applicants because many documents required for US immigration cases were valid only for limited periods. “Many US immigration requirements are supported by documents that are valid for only six months or other limited periods,” the lawyer said. “As a result, the reopening itself does not provide relief from document validity requirements, and affected applicants may be required to obtain and submit updated documentation at their own expense.” Stamets agreed, saying: “Since the entire thrust of the administration’s immigration policy is to make immigration more difficult and expensive except for a favoured few classes and categories of people, I would anticipate that any time-sensitive documentation will need to be updated.” The larger concern, Balakrishnan warned, was that the pause could be followed by a “permanently slower, more subjective process that could reshape legal immigration from Asia for years”. Administration versus judiciary The training is explicitly tied to public-charge screening, a US immigration law assessment of whether an applicant is likely to depend on certain government benefits. That rationale has also placed the appointment pause in the middle of a wider legal and political fight over the Trump administration’s immigration agenda. “A pause like this rarely translates into a short, contained disruption. Consular sections typically batch and schedule interviews weeks or months in advance, so even a brief suspension forces a backlog that takes far longer to clear than the pause,” said Amritraj Kaushal, an advocate in India’s Supreme Court. Vivek Mishra, deputy director of strategic studies at the Observer Research Foundation, said the latest move appeared to be part of a showdown between the administration and the US judiciary. A federal judge on Friday struck down a ban on visas for immigrants from 75 countries, finding it was contrary to law and outside the statutory authority of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The State Department had paused the issuance of immigrant visas from almost 40 per cent of the world’s nations in a move that it said would prevent the entry of people who would “take welfare and public benefits”. The Philippines-based lawyer said the shift from a country-specific suspension to a worldwide training pause “appears to be an attempt to sidestep” the federal court ruling that barred nationality-based discrimination. The State Department would still have to comply with the court’s ruling, but a legal block on the 75-country policy might not prevent consular officers from applying stricter scrutiny to otherwise eligible applicants, the lawyer said. Mishra called the visa pause a “doubling down” by the US administration. “They are saying we are going ahead with a broader mandate this time. They are giving the alibi that consulates need training, which might be true.” He predicted the US would issue new guidance and standard operating procedures to its embassies, resulting in more stringent visa checks. “If they see what they consider as a red flag, it will reduce your chances of a visa,” he said. Even if appointments resume, experts say the larger concern is that applicants could return to a system in which officers have wider discretion to reject cases under public charge and other screening rules. Additional reporting by Vincent Tan and Sam Beltran

title: AI server boom fuels record supply crunch for the ‘rice of electronics’
description: UBS data shows a major squeeze on MLCCs, setting the stage for what some believe could be the longest demand cycle in the sector’s history.
content: Global inventories of multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) – tiny components dubbed “the rice of the electronics industry” – have dropped to a record low as the industry grapples with surging demand from artificial intelligence infrastructure. Worldwide distributor inventory volume for the components – which act as electrical buffers in circuit boards and are increasingly used in massive volumes in high-performance servers – declined 8 per cent by August 9 compared with four weeks earlier, extending a downward trend, according to a Wednesday report by UBS Evidence Lab. MLCCs have emerged as the latest AI-driven investor darling following memory chips and optical modules. With average unit prices continuing to climb, the total value of distributor inventory jumped 10 per cent over the same period, the UBS report showed. Year-on-year data to the end of July showed a 13 per cent rise in the unit price index, distributor volumes plunging 22 per cent and inventory value up 6 per cent. “We believe supply-demand tightness could start with AI-related and distributor channels and then spread to the overall market,” wrote UBS analysts led by Shingo Hirata in the report. Inventory levels at major manufacturers followed a similar trend to distributors. By August 9, Japan’s Murata Manufacturing and South Korea’s Samsung Electro-Mechanics (SEMCO) saw volume declines of 8 per cent and 20 per cent, respectively, compared with four weeks earlier. While these leading MLCC producers have expanded manufacturing capacity, the output has struggled to keep up with soaring demand as the sector enters what Goldman Sachs called the “largest and longest” cycle in its history – fuelled by the intense computing loads required by modern data centres. Citrini Research projected that demand for AI server-grade MLCCs was likely to grow by about 80 per cent annually. Asset managers on Wall Street are racing to bet on new hardware bottlenecks in the broader AI supply chain. On Wednesday, Defiance ETFs launched the first US-listed exchange-traded fund (ETF) specifically targeting MLCCs and passive electronic components powering AI infrastructure. “The market has spent three years pricing the chips. CAPA is about what powers them,” said Sylvia Jablonski, chief investment officer of Defiance ETFs, when referring to the fund, which tracks major MLCC companies including Japan’s TDK Corporation, Murata and SEMCO. “Capacitors are the least appreciated layer of the AI buildout ... we believe the companies supplying this layer sit at a structural demand inflection,” Jablonski said in a statement.

title: Family seeks help after Hongkonger held in Philippines despite finishing jail time
description: Family of Tang Lung-wai says he remains in prison and still faces lengthy administrative procedures before deportation.
content: The family of a Hong Kong man imprisoned in the Philippines for more than two decades has appealed to city authorities for help after he remained in custody despite a court in the country recently ruling he had finished serving his sentence. Tang Lung-wai was arrested in the country in July 2000 for the possession of methamphetamine, also known as Ice, and placed on remand. He was later convicted in 2011 and sentenced to 40 years in prison. While the court recently ruled that his sentence was now considered served after taking into consideration a good conduct time allowance, Tang’s family said he remained in prison and faced lengthy administrative procedures before he could be deported. In a decision handed down by the Muntinlupa City Regional Trial Court on July 30, which was also seen by the South China Morning Post, Judge Abraham Joseph Alcantara ordered Tang’s release and transfer to the country’s Bureau of Immigration “for immediate deportation without further proceedings, all in accordance with the law”. The court ruled that, as of July 5, Tang had technically served 40 years, one month and thirteen days in prison when factoring in his good conduct allowance. “He has already served the maximum period of detention, making his immediate release warranted,” Alcantara said. The court also said an inaccuracy in prison records previously showed that Tang had only served 39 years and four months. Tang’s petition for habeas corpus, which applies to “all cases of illegal confinement or detention in which individuals are deprived of liberty”, was subsequently granted. His elder brother, Billy Tang Lung-piu, said he was worried about Tang’s personal safety in prison. “I am very anxious. I don’t know if there is any accident before his release,” he said. He said that even after Tang was released from prison, he would need to undergo a lengthy administrative process at the Bureau of Immigration before his deportation, including a medical check and a confirmation of his identity. Billy Tang said he contacted the Hong Kong Immigration Department last week, with an officer telling him that authorities were waiting for the Chinese embassy in the Philippines to inform them of his brother’s actual release date. He urged the Hong Kong government to send an officer to Manila to follow up on his brother’s case and expedite his release. In a reply to the South China Morning Post, the Immigration Department said that upon receiving the latest updates on the case, it would provide practical assistance on the deportation arrangements. It added that it would continue to render assistance according to the wishes of Tang and his family members. A spokesperson for the Philippine consulate in Hong Kong said it had taken note of the family’s concerns and would convey them to “the relevant Philippine authorities through the Department of Foreign Affairs as soon as possible”. In 2018, then-city leader Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor wrote to Rodrigo Duterte, the country’s president at the time, to urge him to push immigration authorities to hasten their search for records believed to prove Tang’s innocence. The next day, Tang’s family members received crucial immigration records. While the records suggested that Tang was not in the Philippines during the period that local police said he was under surveillance, he lost his final appeal against his conviction in 2020.

title: Asian Games organisers looking to reduce numbers as registrations exceed target
description: Aichi-Nagoya officials ‘are in talks with ‌the Olympic Council of Asia for a solution’ after number of athletes, officials exceed 15,000.
content: Asian Games organisers in ⁠Japan said ⁠on Wednesday ⁠they were looking to reduce the number of participants at next month’s event after athlete and official registrations blew ‌past the projected 15,000. The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) said last week entries had risen to around 17,000, including 11,000 athletes and 6,000 officials, for the Games, scheduled to be held in Nagoya and the ‌Aichi region from September 19 to October 4. Figures for the 2023 Games were about 12,000 athletes and 5,000 officials, making it the largest Games ever, and bigger than the Paris Olympics. “It ‌is true that the number of registrations ⁠has exceeded 15,000 and we are trying to ⁠trim the excess numbers,” the organising committee told Reuters. “We are in talks with ‌the OCA ‌for a solution.” Reuters has contacted the OCA for comment. Japan’s Kyodo news agency said the local organising committee had asked the OCA to address the surge in numbers. The organising committee told AFP that they would “prefer not to comment on the details of our discussions with the OCA”. “We are sharing information with the OCA, the event organiser, regarding the registration status of the various national teams, and are holding regular discussions with them regarding arrangements such as accommodation for the teams,” a spokesperson said. AFP has contacted the OCA for comment. The overshoot in numbers could strain ‌accommodation plans for the Games, which will ⁠not ⁠feature a traditional athletes’ village. Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes will stay on the Costa Serena cruise ship, which features 571 cabins, seven swimming pools, eight restaurants and nine bars. Officials are confident that the plan will not be disrupted by Japan’s typhoon season, which is usually in full swing in September-October. A further 2,000 athletes and officials will stay in wooden shipping container-style huts in Nagoya’s Garden Pier area while the rest will stay in hotels. That includes in Tokyo, where swimming, diving and equestrian events will take place. The Games will bring together 45 countries and regions for 16 days of world-class competition across 43 sports and 71 disciplines, with 1,407 medals to be awarded across 469 events. The 2023 Hangzhou Games involved 40 sports and 61 disciplines.

title: Could the delay to China’s moon mission ease pressure on Nasa?
description: Postponement of ‘especially ambitious’ Chang’e-7 no surprise to space specialists, but the US agency will not be celebrating.
content: China’s delay of a high-stakes mission to hunt for water ice near the moon’s south pole may slow its lunar ambitions, but is unlikely to change the bigger contest with the United States over who can build a lasting presence on the moon, according to space experts. No reason was given when Chang’e-7 was postponed until next year, just hours before Sunday night’s scheduled lift-off, though a major tropical storm was approaching the launch site. Chinese space authorities said only that the mission did not “meet the launch requirements” and, by Monday evening, the rocket had been rolled back to its assembly building. Space security strategist John Sheldon, a co-founder of the London-based consultancy AstroAnalytica, said space professionals in the US would certainly not be celebrating the delay. “The same variables that caused the Chang’e-7 postponement can just as easily happen – and have happened – to US lunar missions.” However, politically it could ease some pressure on Nasa, Sheldon said. A later Chang’e-7 launch pushed back the prospect of another successful Chinese moon landing, avoiding – for now – some of the “media and political angst” that could generate in Washington. Svetla Ben-Itzhak, a space security researcher at Johns Hopkins University in Washington, said she was not particularly surprised by the delay, because “space is hard”. While all lunar missions were complex, Chang’e-7 was “especially ambitious”, Ben-Itzhak said, with its combination of orbiter, lander, rover and a hopper designed to investigate permanently shadowed regions. China’s earlier Chang’e-5 mission – which collected samples from the lunar surface in 2020 – was also delayed for years because the Long March 5 rocket was not ready, she noted. “So this is not necessarily about missions always launching on time, but about pursuing missions sequentially and in a sustained manner,” Ben-Itzhak said. “So far, China’s broader lunar programme has done so, with an exceptionally high rate of mission success.” The Chang’e-7 mission has unusually narrow launch windows because it relies mainly on solar power. The spacecraft needs to touch down near the start of a roughly three-month period of near-continuous sunlight to maximise its time for exploration. At least two potential launch windows are available next year, around spring and autumn, according to a scientist involved in the mission who spoke on condition of anonymity. That meant Chang’e-7 could be delayed from six months to a year, the scientist said. Sunlight will also be critical for the mission’s navigation and autonomous hazard avoidance systems during the descent to the moon’s surface. The lunar south pole is riddled with craters, steep slopes, ridges and deep pits, while the low angle of the sun leaves much of the terrain either hidden in shadow or washed in glare, making safe landing sites difficult to identify. The southernmost successful lunar landing to date has been India’s Chandrayaan-3, which touched down at a location some distance from the pole itself in 2023. Two US commercial missions have landed closer, but both tipped over. The Chang’e-7 delay might give the US space agency a chance to reach the south pole region first. Blue Origin’s uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lander, carrying two Nasa instruments, could launch as early as the first half of next year, potentially putting it on a similar timeline to the Chinese mission. Ben-Itzhak noted that the Chang’e-7 mission was very important to China’s longer-term ambitions, as the next step in a much larger, sequential lunar programme. With Chang’e-8, which will focus on resource utilisation, the mission will set the stage for a basic version of the planned International Lunar Research Station by 2035. “The more meaningful competition is over which country can translate individual missions into a sustained presence in lunar and cislunar space and build a broader international coalition around its vision for lunar exploration and governance,” she said. A one-year delay, therefore, did not mean that China was suddenly “losing” this competition, she said. “What it does illustrate, however, is that neither the American nor Chinese lunar timetable should be treated as fixed.” The concept of cislunar space – which refers to the region between the Earth and the moon – has become increasingly relevant in recent years, especially for the military sector. title: No gym needed? Scientists in China develop self-exercising muscle grafts
description: The team says ‘myografts’ could provide health benefits to those who cannot exercise easily, such as bedridden people.
content: Scientists in China have created a self-exercising muscle graft that might allow bedridden people to gain the benefits of working out without any physical exertion. With just an injection of muscle cells below the skin, the cells self-assembled into muscle grafts, which not only improved whole-body muscle mass in mice but also led to improvements in bone density, endurance, liver function and cognitive health. The “myografts” could provide the health benefits of exercise to patients with age-related conditions such as Alzheimer’s and osteoporosis, and future applications could even extend to those who just want to build muscle without hitting the gym. “While the complete safety and [pharmacological] profile of autologous myografts remains to be established in human trials, our mouse preclinical studies constitute a noteworthy first step in this direction,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Ageing on Wednesday. “In a sense, we’re distilling the best part of exercise out … and avoiding all the negative effects of exercise, whether it’s the stress on the heart or the stress on your joints,” said study author Ng Shyh-Chang, a professor and principal investigator at the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Zoology. Moreover, the team found that the myografts could be used as a living biofactory to produce targeted therapeutic proteins within the body, including compounds such as GLP-1, which is used to manage diabetes and as a weight-loss tool. During exercise, skeletal muscle can secrete hundreds of kinds of proteins that help give working out its multi-organ benefits, but also plays a role in suppressing factors related to ageing, such as the loss of bone density and muscle mass. Exercise is known to address both metabolic and degenerative diseases associated with ageing and obesity. But the people who are most in need can also be those who have the most trouble with physical movement. “It turns out that the people who need exercise the most are also the folks who cannot exercise the most,” Ng said. “So we need some way to mimic exercise to get them started, to get their basic health going before they can actually do the exercise that they need to do.” Ng said his team initially tried to transplant lab-grown muscle organoids into mice. Organoids are miniature, artificial versions of real organs designed to mimic their natural counterparts. However, early efforts failed because the three-dimensional cell structures were too large for nutrients to diffuse properly, causing them to die. “Then my students decided, why don’t we just go back to the basics. Why don’t we just put the cells under the skin and let them form the organoid slowly under the skin,” he said. The sheer amount of good factors it’s secreting exceeds what you can get from acute exercise for just one hour Ng Shyh-Chang, professor This was achieved using myocytes – specialised cells that make up muscle tissue – that were derived from mouse muscle stem cells. Once transplanted into the skin along with a supportive gel scaffold, these cells self-organised into mature myografts capable of long-term spontaneous contractions without any physical or neural input. “We found that subcutaneous myograft transplantation ameliorates many problems associated with ageing, including muscle atrophy, osteoporosis, chronic inflammation, liver damage and metabolic dysfunction,” the team wrote in the paper. The myografts were able to improve muscle mass across the bodies of ageing and obese mouse models, leading to better outcomes in strength and mobility tests. Ng said they were still trying to understand what was being secreted by the myografts to offer all these benefits, but the fact that they constantly contracted might play a role. “It’s contracting non-stop, 24/7, so it’s persistently secreting the good beneficial factors into the bloodstream,” he said. “The sheer amount of good factors it’s secreting exceeds what you can get from acute exercise for just one hour.” He said the muscle fibres assembled were also younger or immature, which could allow them to secrete higher concentrations of beneficial factors than older, mature muscles. Over time, the grafts gradually mature and integrate with local blood vessels, all while remaining stable with no tumour-like growth. When asked about the potential for over-exercise, Ng said his team had not seen signs of toxicity or negative health impacts so far, though he noted that clinical trials were necessary to confirm safety. The team is considering trials with intensive care unit patients. Once safety and efficacy were confirmed, they planned to test the myografts in broader patient populations, Ng said. He noted that while the grafts were implanted shallowly in mice for easy visual tracking, human skin was thicker. He added that the transplant site would be chosen carefully so that the movement of the grafts was not obvious.

title: Prince Harry and Meghan back in UK after 6 years, beginning a new chapter
description: The couple will not return to royal duties while their children, Archie and Lilibet, look forward to starting school in Britain next month.
content: Prince Harry and his family arrived back in Britain on Wednesday, the BBC reported, days after it was revealed the couple were relocating six years after quitting royal duties and moving to the United States. Last week, Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, surprised even their close family when it was disclosed that they would move back from California to somewhere ‌outside London for what was described as an extended period of time. Their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, will start school in Britain in September. Precise details about where they will be based or the school the children will attend are being kept private. However, they will not be living in a royal residence or carrying out official duties. The BBC said they had landed in Britain after flying in from California privately on Wednesday. There was no immediate comment from Harry’s spokesperson. The couple left for the US in 2020, stepping down from official royal duties to chart ⁠independent careers, but they never left the headlines, as Harry accused the royals of neglect, the tabloid press of ruining his life and the government of failing to ‌provide enough security for him to ever return home. King Charles only found out about their return days before the decision became public, and the couple will remain non-working royals, as was agreed with the late Queen Elizabeth. Harry and his father’s relationship has ‌improved in recent months, with the Duke’s family visiting Britain last month, allowing Charles to see his grandchildren for the first time since 2022. But ⁠Harry is still barely on speaking ⁠terms with his brother, the heir-to-the-throne Prince William, and with other senior royals also distrustful of Meghan, the potential for future family disagreements played out in the media spotlight remains. Harry married Meghan Markle at Windsor ‌Castle in 2018, amid hopes that his union with the former actor would reinvigorate the historic institution for a new generation. But it was not long before cracks in their relationship with the rest of the royal ‌family began ‌to emerge. Two years later, they announced they would step down from official duties and move to the US, saying they wanted to leave behind the “toxic” press scrutiny ‌they faced in Britain. They settled in the wealthy seaside enclave of Montecito, near Santa Barbara, California, a home they will maintain. The reason for their change of ⁠heart is unclear. Some commentators have speculated that their business ventures have struggled, saying their appeal in the US is waning and the return might boost their earning ⁠power. The announcement of their return came a day before a London court ruling meant Harry could be liable to pay millions of dollars to the publisher of the Daily Mail after a failed privacy lawsuit.
