Media reports have said Meghan is in talks about a return to acting, although neither ‌her representatives nor those involved with the mooted ‌television drama have commented, and it was later reported the offer had been withdrawn because of a backlash. Meanwhile, Harry has always been clear he wants his children to spend more time in Britain and to see their grandfather, especially given the 77-year-old monarch is still undergoing treatment for cancer. “It’s really worth remembering this might not be some terribly cynical move or some desperate move, it might be a very human move – ‘I want to be near my dad’,” a former senior royal aide said.

title: Hong Kong customs seizes HK$11m of suspected sex pills, cancer drugs at warehouse
description: Officers arrest two people during raid at Sheung Shui site, confiscating more than 400,000 alleged controlled pharmaceutical items.
content: Hong Kong customs officers have seized suspected men’s sexual health pills and cancer treatment drugs worth more than HK$11 million (US$1.4 million) in a Sheung Shui warehouse, arresting two people. Inspector Shirley Woo Suet‑yi of the syndicate crimes investigation bureau at the Customs and Excise Department said on Wednesday that officers had noticed a rising demand for controlled pharmaceutical products in recent weeks. Investigators launched the probe early this month and identified an industrial space in Sheung Shui believed to be linked to smuggling activities. On Tuesday, customs officers raided the warehouse, which had been used to repackage and store the drugs. More than 400,000 suspected controlled pharmaceutical items were seized, with an estimated street value exceeding HK$11 million. A 56‑year‑old woman who received the goods and a 51‑year‑old man employed as a handyman were arrested at the scene. Both held two‑way permits issued by mainland China to enter Hong Kong. Authorities believe most of the drugs originated from South Asia, although the exact source remains under investigation. More than 60 per cent of the haul consisted of erectile dysfunction drugs, alongside cancer treatments and other pharmaceutical products. Many of the seized products were labelled as containing substances classified as Part 1 poisons under Hong Kong law. There were also fertility treatment drugs and HIV management medications among the seized items. Inside the warehouse, officers also found large quantities of cardboard boxes and adhesive tape used for repackaging. Investigators believed the drugs were intended to be smuggled to various destinations. Woo said investigators were determining whether a larger criminal group was behind the operation. She added the raid had intercepted the drugs at the source, preventing them from reaching the market. Tony Chan Hon‑wah, Department of Health senior pharmacist, said most of the seized drugs could only be taken under a doctor’s instruction and dispensed by registered pharmacists at licensed premises. He urged people not to buy or consume medications of unknown origin, warning that selling controlled drugs illegally through online platforms, instant messaging apps or social media carried criminal liability.

title: Opinion | The security-obsessed global economy needs its own Helsinki process
description: Cold War rivals used ground rules to make competition more transparent, bounded and predictable. Today’s weaponised trade needs the same ambition.
content: Forty years ago, the Stockholm Document turned the political promise of the 1975 Helsinki Final Act into a more practical system of confidence-building. Amid the Cold War, Europe’s East and West did not disarm, abandon deterrence or begin to trust one another. Instead, they agreed that military competition could be made safer through prior notification, observation, information exchange and verification. The lesson was modest but durable: adversaries do not need trust to reduce uncertainty. That logic is now needed beyond the military sphere. Today’s world is not divided into Cold War-style military blocs. Yet in trade, technology, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and supply chains, increasingly security-oriented economic networks are forming around the United States and China. Export controls, sanctions, investment screening, industrial policy and resource restrictions are turning interdependence into a potential source of vulnerability. For three decades, globalisation rewarded concentration. Firms sourced from the cheapest producer, countries specialised and supply chains were designed around “just in time”. That system lowered costs, but it also created chokepoints. Once governments began to regard dependence as a national security risk, the organising principle changed. Efficiency gave way to resilience; “just in time” increasingly became “just in case”. Some redundancy is rational. Gulf states amid the Iran war have built oil pipelines that can bypass vulnerable maritime chokepoints. European governments are trying to restore domestic capacity for critical medicines and pharmaceutical ingredients. Countries are stockpiling food, energy and strategic materials, while firms diversify suppliers and duplicate production. These measures buy security, but at a price. The problem is that one country’s resilience can look like another country’s preparation for decoupling. The second country then localises production, restricts exports or builds alternative networks, confirming the first country’s original fears. Each step may be rational in isolation; collectively they create a geoeconomic security dilemma in which everyone pays more to insure against everyone else. The answer is not to return to “hyper-globalisation”. Nor is it realistic to abolish sanctions, export controls or industrial policy. Economic security is now embedded in statecraft. The more useful question is whether governments can place limits around their use. The aim should be to reduce the costly redundancy driven by a fear of arbitrary geopolitical disruption. A geoeconomic Helsinki process should begin with a narrow floor for essential civilian functions. Basic medicines are an obvious case. China and India have become major upstream suppliers of antibiotics and pharmaceutical ingredients, while Western firms and financial systems control other critical medical technologies, services and transaction channels. Food and fertilisers provide another case: interruptions can rapidly become humanitarian crises. There is precedent. In 2022, World Trade Organization members agreed that food bought by the World Food Programme for humanitarian purposes should be exempt from export prohibitions or restrictions. The principle is important: states may retain economic security tools while accepting that certain civilian needs should remain outside geopolitical coercion. That principle could be widened carefully. A first basket might cover basic food, designated essential medicines, emergency agricultural inputs, clean water supplies and the payments, insurance and shipping services necessary to deliver them. Protection should extend to functions: a legal exemption for medicine is meaningless if banks refuse the payment, insurers will not cover the shipment or transport providers fear secondary penalties. None of this requires Washington, Beijing or other key actors to surrender their most valuable strategic leverage A second basket should establish geoeconomic confidence-building measures. Governments introducing major restrictions affecting protected civilian functions could provide advance notice where possible, state the purpose, scope and expected duration of the measure, identify humanitarian exemptions and provide a channel for emergency consultation. Other states could request clarification when an unusual disruption occurs. Regular reviews could distinguish temporary emergency measures from open-ended coercion. None of this requires Washington, Beijing or other key actors to surrender their most valuable strategic leverage. Advanced semiconductors, military-relevant artificial intelligence, rare earths and other highly dual-use goods are unlikely candidates for an initial agreement. The Helsinki approach succeeded precisely because it began with limited rules that made behaviour more predictable. The bargain must also be reciprocal. China and other major producers could accept restraints on politically motivated disruptions of designated essential physical supplies. The United States and its partners could guarantee that sanctions, financial controls, insurance restrictions and technology rules do not obstruct agreed humanitarian flows. The objective would not be to de-weaponise economic statecraft, but to civilise it. What such rules would create is bounded certainty: even during a severe political crisis, governments and firms would know that some essential channels should remain open. Middle powers have a particular interest in such rules. They are often connected to both US- and China-centred economic networks and bear large costs when competition becomes systemic fragmentation. Asean members, Gulf countries, India, Switzerland, Brazil and others need not form a third bloc. Their more consequential role may be to preserve cross-system connectivity and turn functional multilateralism into institutional guardrails. There are useful efforts to organise thinking about this new landscape. The Helsinki Geoeconomics Society’s New Helsinki Process is developing a Helsinki Manual on Corporate Geoeconomics, mapping economic-security regulation and corporate responses across trade, investment, finance, industrial policy and technology. The next step is to ask whether the Helsinki logic can move from understanding geoeconomic competition to stabilising it. The original Helsinki process did not end the Cold War. The Stockholm Document did not make Nato and the Warsaw Pact trust each other. They made parts of rivalry more transparent, bounded and predictable. The global economy now needs the same ambition: decide what must remain outside the battlefield, and build rules that make the rest of the competition less dangerous and costly.

title: Before Xi’s India visit, China and India agree on 8 steps to ease border tensions
description: Sources and experts caution against overplaying expectations, saying offers on the table fall well short of a breakthrough or grand bargain.
content: After two years of a cautious thaw, China and India are heading towards a pivotal test: can the relationship move beyond managed optics to meaningful engagement? President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are expected to cross paths next week at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Sources expect a short, tightly managed encounter on the sidelines of the August 31-September 1 summit that would set the stage for the main event – in India. The Chinese foreign ministry confirmed on Wednesday that Xi would attend the SCO summit, while Modi is also expected to participate. The fuller sit-down is planned for New Delhi from September 12-13, when Xi is expected to attend the Brics summit with a reported delegation of around 400. This will be the Chinese leader’s first visit to India in seven years and both sides are working hard to churn out deliverables. Beijing has not officially confirmed Xi’s India visit, saying only that China attaches importance to Brics cooperation and supports India in hosting the summit. The disputed China-India border is expected to be high on the agenda when Xi meets Modi in the Indian capital, alongside trade, investment and people-to-people ties, including visas, according to people familiar with the negotiations. On Wednesday, New Delhi and Beijing gave that track a more detailed script. Eight-point consensus after Doval-Wang talks India’s Ministry of External Affairs and China’s official Xinhua News Agency on Wednesday released matching “eight points of outcomes and consensus” from the 25th round of Special Representatives talks on the boundary question, held in Beijing on Tuesday. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, Beijing’s special representative on the boundary question, co-chaired the 25th round of talks on the Himalayan border dispute with Modi’s principal security adviser and confidant, Ajit Doval. The list does not settle the Himalayan boundary. It does lock in a work plan: keep the frontier quiet, create new working groups, add military communication channels, and keep pilgrimage, border trade and river talks moving, with the next Special Representatives round parked in India in 2027. In his opening remarks, Doval told Wang that the latest special representatives’ talks on the boundary question were “very important, particularly in the wake of the Brics summit to happen shortly”, referring to the grouping of major emerging economies. Modi and Xi had already given “clear and positive direction” to the relationship at the Kazan Brics summit in October 2024 and the Tianjin SCO summit a year ago, Doval added. The return of “normalcy”, Doval argued, was “a direct result of both sides maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas”. The Indian foreign ministry later said the talks were “candid and in-depth” and that both sides agreed to keep seeking a political settlement “in the context of their overall and long-term interests”. According to a read-out from the Chinese side, Wang told Doval that both sides should “place the border issue in its proper place within bilateral relations”, while urging that they “maintain forward momentum without pausing, regressing, or veering off course”. Ahead of the border talks, Doval met Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng in Beijing. According to China’s state news agency Xinhua, Doval said the two countries, home to the world’s largest populations and among its fastest-growing major economies, were facing a “historic opportunity” to deepen cooperation. The deliverables: border, trade, investment, visas Sources say that when Xi sits down with Modi in New Delhi, the deliverables on offer are likely to be incremental, not a grand settlement. “Delimitation”, or agreeing on paper where the boundary runs rather than simply managing troops along the Line of Actual Control – the disputed China-India border – could be among the issues discussed. Both the Indian embassy in Beijing and the Chinese foreign ministry used the term in referring to the talks between Doval and Wang. In a social media post, the Indian embassy said that the two sides discussed making “progress on boundary delimitation”, while the read-out from Beijing said they discussed “advancing boundary delimitation negotiations”, alongside border management, improving institutional mechanisms, and cross-border cooperation. The Indian ministry, however, used the broader formulation of seeking a “political settlement of the boundary question”. On Wednesday, the two sides announced that they had agreed to establish an expert group on boundary delimitation and a working group on border management under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on China-India Border Affairs (WMCC). They will begin by agreeing on their respective terms of reference, with a mandate to pursue an “early and substantial harvest” on delimitation and border management. The two sides also agreed to add two meeting points for senior military commanders and two new border defence hotlines in the eastern and central sectors, while committing to use existing diplomatic and military channels to address incidents along the LAC and reduce the risk of misunderstanding or miscalculation. They also agreed to hold expert-level talks on trans-border rivers in September, including discussions on hydrological data sharing and renewing relevant memorandums of understanding. At the 24th special representatives’ round in New Delhi last August, Doval and Wang agreed to set up an expert group under the WMCC to explore an “early harvest in boundary delimitation”. The strategy prioritises the less contentious stretches and putting off Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh – which Beijing calls Zangnan or “south Tibet” – for later. The economic track, however, could offer more tangible wins. Under newly relaxed Indian rules, investors from countries sharing a land border with India – including China – can acquire non-controlling stakes of up to 10 per cent without government approval, barring specific restricted sectors. A Xi-Modi summit could deliver political momentum to efforts to boost trade and investment and address the glaring trade deficit. While tourist visas and direct flights have resumed, the return of Chinese journalists to India remains the last major piece on the negotiating table. On visas, New Delhi has moved more slowly than Beijing, and sources said any restoration was expected to be tightly controlled and reciprocal, not a blanket move. Managing expectations Zhu Yongbiao, dean of the school of politics and international relations at Lanzhou University, described the Wang-Doval talks as a “positive signal” but called for sober realism without high expectations, noting that concrete actions from India mattered far more than its rhetoric. On the border issue, Zhu remains considerably less optimistic. He expects the situation at best to “freeze or revert to the prior status quo”, and that “breakthrough progress remains unlikely”. Substantive breakthroughs were unattainable without a “sober, objective shift” in India’s “self-perception” and regional strategy, he added. Manoj Kewalramani of the New Delhi-based Takshashila Institution said: “Anyone looking for a breakthrough on difficult issues like the boundary is likely to be disappointed. “A joint read-out would be noteworthy, but is very unlikely. The last two times that Modi and Xi have met, there has been no joint statement.” He noted that although the two sides agreed in October 2019 to establish a high-level economic and trade dialogue, the initiative was derailed first by the pandemic and later by their deadly 2020 border stand-off. “So some sort of new, formal mechanism for trade, investment and green energy technologies might be useful,” Kewalramani said, while ruling out any grand bargain. “This is not the moment for grand bargains for either side,” he said. “What one can pursue is stability and building some linkages between the two countries that can serve the narrow basket of common interests.” Antara Ghosal Singh of the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi said that for India, a successful meeting would mean a stable border, secure upstream manufacturing supply chains, greater leverage in negotiations with the United States and more room to advance “Make in India” – a national initiative to become a design, innovation and manufacturing hub. For China, she said, high-level contact with India could weaken US efforts to check and balance Beijing. According to Singh, two key factors drive India’s stance – its deep supply-chain dependency on China and the unpredictability of Trump 2.0. For China, she said the critical challenges were domestic economic headwinds, export dependence and deteriorating ties with major trade partners, from the US and European Union to India. “Overall, the conditions are ripe in both New Delhi and Beijing for a deep reset in bilateral ties,” she said. “But both sides will be seeking to maximise their gains while reducing concessions. Surely, it is going to be a difficult negotiation.” This week’s China-India talks reflected a broader thaw following tensions stemming from a clash in Ladakh’s Galwan Valley in 2020, in which at least 20 Indian soldiers were killed. China said four of its soldiers died in the fight, which triggered a prolonged military and diplomatic stand-off along the LAC. Relations began to improve after the two sides reached an understanding in October 2024 to resume patrolling in parts of their disputed border. Apart from the resumption of direct flights and visa arrangements, steps to restore broader exchanges have included the revival of the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, the annual pilgrimage to Tibet for Indian nationals. Last year, Modi met Xi on the sidelines of the August 31-September 1 SCO summit in Tianjin – the Indian leader’s first visit to China in seven years. The two leaders said China and India were development partners rather than rivals and agreed that the boundary issue should not define the broader relationship.

title: As US threatens ‘D-Day’ for Iranian economy, how will China’s oil supply be affected?
description: As northern hemisphere prepares for winter, analysts say latest US sanctions would not deter China from purchasing Iranian oil.
content: While new sanctions from the United States threaten to choke Tehran’s oil exports, analysts say the measures might not do much to stop China, Iran’s largest buyer, from continuing to buy Iranian crude, though the naval blockade has limited its flow. Washington has targeted shipping, alongside four other sectors, under its “economic D-Day” campaign against Iran, aiming to disrupt the Middle Eastern country’s crude revenue. Most of exported Iranian oil flows to independent Chinese refiners located in eastern Shandong province, known colloquially as teapots. “Beijing has made clear … that China continues to defend its ties with Iran, suggesting that the Chinese government does not plan to direct teapots and financial institutions to cut off the Iranian oil trade,” said Xu Muyu, a crude oil analyst at trade-intelligence firm Kpler. She added if Washington introduced further punitive measures targeting major Chinese entities, this might change Beijing’s stance, but doing so would risk escalating tensions ahead of a planned summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month. Chim Lee, a senior analyst at the Economist Intelligence Unit, noted that Washington was likely to prioritise stability and refrain from crossing potential red lines for Beijing, including avoiding blacklisting major Chinese firms from the US financial system. The US has so far refrained from targeting Chinese financial institutions that are facilitating the Iranian oil trade. However, when asked about non-compliant Chinese banks and shipping firms, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that “no one is above the reach of US sanctions”. China’s foreign affairs ministry on Tuesday called the US measures “illegal” and “unilateral”, and vowed to safeguard its own interests. It added that China’s cooperation with Iran was conducted within the framework of international law and “should not be interfered with or undermined”. There is currently limited Iranian crude available for sale, Xu noted, and no laden Iranian tankers had managed to break through the US blockade as of last week. “That already partially achieves Washington’s goal of exerting economic pressure on Tehran,” Xu said. Chinese imports of Iranian crude currently stand at around 800,000 barrels per day, down from 1.3 million barrels per day in May, according to Kpler data. The decrease was partly due to rounds of US blockades, and partly due to data delays caused by the increasing difficulty of tracking Iranian tankers, Xu said, meaning the numbers were harder to verify. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is back at a near standstill as the war nears its six-month mark. No vessels exited the waterway on Monday, according to the market intelligence firm Argus Media. While authorities in Iran and Oman have outlined a plan for a temporary shipping route through the strait, Tehran has said that the waterway would remain closed until Washington followed through with its previous commitments, including lifting the naval blockade. The prolonged disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping lane for both oil and gas, threatens to tighten energy supplies for some countries in the coming months as winter nears. Europe, for instance, would find it difficult to manage natural gas storage through the winter if exports from the Gulf remain constrained, and if prices did not rise enough to discourage competition from Asian demand, analysts from Goldman Sachs wrote in a note on Sunday. Under Kpler’s assumptions that the US and Iran would not see a resolution to the crisis this year and that China’s crude buying would not return to pre-war levels, the global average crude deficit would stand at around 1.4 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, Xu said.

title: ‘Massive casualties’ after flash floods, landslide strike China-Nepal border
description: An unknown number of people are also missing as rescuers search the rubble of a border checkpoint in Tibet’s Gyirong county.
content: Dozens of people were dead and hundreds of others – many of them foreign tourists – were missing on Wednesday night, hours after massive flash floods and landslides engulfed a border area between China and Nepal. Chinese state media reported that the disaster struck Nepal at around 9am, spilling over into Gyirong county in the Tibet autonomous region, causing “major casualties and missing persons” at a border checkpoint in the county, which is administered by the city of Shigatse. Footage circulating online showed a landslide descending on the Gyirong Port checkpoint in seconds as people on the ground fled, before mud and debris obscured the camera. The South China Morning Post could not independently verify the video. Gyirong Port is Tibet’s main foreign trade port and handles the vast majority of China’s trade with Nepal. Quoting a rescue command centre in Gyirong, state broadcaster CCTV reported that by 8pm three people were dead and 265 were missing after the landslide in the county. Shanghai-based news outlet The Paper quoted Nepalese police as saying 97 people had been killed and 54 rescued in Nepal. In Nepal, 384 tourists and travellers were missing – 93 Nepalese and 291 foreigners, according to the Nepal Tourism Board. The board said the missing foreigners included citizens from India, Australia, the United States, Britain and the Netherlands. The nationalities of 111 individuals had yet to be confirmed. The Kathmandu Post quoted Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, a professor at Kathmandu University and climate researcher, as saying that an ice avalanche falling into the upstream section of the Lhende Khola River might have created a surge of water sweeping downstream, causing a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi River. Kayastha noted that the initial assessment was based on preliminary findings between Nepali and Chinese scientists. Meanwhile, Nepal’s disaster management agency said it had received similar findings, but emphasised that the assessment was initial and that official efforts remain focused on search and rescue. Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered local authorities to “spare no effort” in the search and rescue mission, evacuating residents, promptly treating the injured and minimising casualties. Xi also called for monitoring and early warning systems to be strengthened, and prevention of secondary disasters. Soldiers and personnel from the People’s Armed Police, a paramilitary law enforcement agency, had arrived at the scene for emergency rescue and disaster relief operations. The authorities have closed the road leading to the Gyirong checkpoint for the next seven days. Footage spreading online captured the aftermath of the landslide, showing roads covered in mud and heavy debris washing down a river. State-owned construction and emergency response firm China Anneng Construction Group sent 200 emergency personnel as well as geologists and engineers to the site, with 100 more on standby for deployment, according to state news agency Xinhua. The team deployed to the disaster zone brought construction machinery and advanced equipment, including reconnaissance drones, 3D laser scanners and life detectors, the report said. China’s embassy in Nepal had activated its emergency response mechanism and checked on Chinese nationals and enterprises in the disaster zone, the mission said in a statement. It also called on the Nepalese government to conduct full-scale rescue operations. China Newsweek reported that about 60 Chinese personnel were working for the Tibet Tianlu construction company on a highway repair and improvement aid project near the port when the disaster struck. A family member of one employee was quoted as saying that the company’s office was just 3km (1.9 miles) from the customs building at the port and he had lost contact with his wife and the entire team. More than 10 Chinese workers employed on other construction projects were also living in nearby low-rise factory buildings, which were all swept away, the man said. China is Nepal’s second-largest trading partner, accounting for roughly 16.9 per cent of the country’s total trade. It is also a major source of imports for the Himalayan country. China allows trade and transit through six border points, five of which are in Shigatse, the second-largest city in Tibet. However, disruptions caused by flash floods earlier this year had left hundreds of vehicles stranded and contributed to a 24 per cent drop in electric-vehicle imports in Nepal’s financial year ending in mid-July, local media reported. In 2018, China announced that it would build what it calls a Trans-Himalayan Multi-Dimensional Connectivity Network with Nepal – involving railways and communication links – as part of the Belt and Road Initiative. For Nepal, this network could be a lifeline. The landlocked nation has suffered multiple devastating, months-long economic blockades imposed by New Delhi – most notably in 1969, 1989, and 2015 – which choked off vital supplies of fuel, medicine and food. For this reason, Kathmandu views Beijing as an indispensable strategic counterweight to its southern neighbour. Nepal joined the Belt and Road Initiative in 2017, but progress on related projects has been slow, constrained by weather disruptions, poor local infrastructure and geopolitical friction. A cornerstone project, the proposed Rasuwagadhi-Kathmandu Rail Line that would connect Gyirong with Kathmandu, remains at the planning stage.

title: Hong Kong Hyrox tickets go on sale Thursday – you might have only 30 minutes to book a spot
description: Registration for public opens on Thursday, after two-day affiliate presale sees strong demand, with allocations selling out in minutes.
content: Public registration for the AIA Hyrox Hong Kong 2027 fitness race opens on Thursday at 6pm local time, following a 48-hour affiliate presale that saw local gyms report fierce demand and the selling out of ticket allocations in minutes. The event, scheduled for January 7 to 10 at AsiaWorld-Expo, has been extended to four days to accommodate surging demand. Since debuting locally in 2022, the mass-participation fitness event has drawn almost 20,000 participants to its standard race format combining 1km running segments with functional workout stations. Demand during the 48-hour early access window, for members of Official Hyrox Training Clubs, which opened at 6pm on Tuesday, triggered an immediate rush among gym-goers across the city. At Coastal Fitness in Tin Hau, a 200-ticket presale allocation vanished almost instantly. “The demand during the affiliate presale was extremely strong,” Isabelle Wolfe, general manager at Coastal Fitness, said. “We had 200 available tickets and they all sold out in about 20 minutes. It was really cool to see.” Wolfe noted that members set alarms and waited online early to secure their spots, reflecting Hyrox’s growing status as a key fixture on Hong Kong’s athletic calendar. “In the beginning, it was mainly the more competitive athletes from our gym taking part, but now we’re seeing a huge increase in everyday members who are looking for a new challenge and a clear goal to work towards,” she said, adding that doubles and relay formats have made competitive fitness far more accessible. The scramble was equally evident at other affiliate venues. At a Kennedy Town branch of a major 24-hour fitness chain, where each location received a 50-ticket allocation for its members, a queue began forming outside three hours before Tuesday’s early access started. “People came over at around 3pm to line up even though they knew registration started at 6pm,” a gym staff member said, noting that staff handed out queue tokens at 5.30pm to maintain order. By 5pm on Wednesday, only eight of the branch’s 50 spots remained, before the gym announced on its official social media account 20 minutes later that all allocations were completely sold out. “Compared with last year, it’s even more exaggerated this year because it’s become so popular,” the staff member said, adding that her branch drew a diverse mix of local residents, mainlanders and expatriates. She also warned of the physical risks involved if gym-goers competed without sufficient conditioning. “The injury risk is relatively high because some of the required movements are quite dangerous,” she said, comparing the race’s physical strain to running a marathon. “If you haven’t done proper training, it’s easy to get injured.” The 2027 event will feature open and elite individual divisions, doubles and four-person relays across men’s, women’s and mixed categories, catering to participants of all fitness backgrounds, including adaptive athletes.

title: China’s CNOOC rakes in record first-half profit on high oil prices amid Iran war
description: China’s largest offshore oil and gas producer saw net profits jump over 23 per cent in the first half amid turbulence in the Middle East.
content: China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC), the nation’s largest offshore oil and gas producer, saw its net profit jump 23.4 per cent to a record high in the first half of the year, as higher oil prices and increased production boosted earnings amid the Iran war. The company’s net profit rose to 85.8 billion yuan (US$12.7 billion) in the six months ended June, up from 69.5 billion yuan a year earlier, according to an exchange filing on Wednesday. Revenue increased 16.9 per cent to 242.7 billion yuan, also a record high for any interim period, the filing showed. CNOOC’s oil and gas sales rose 20 per cent to 206.1 billion yuan during the period, while net production increased by a more modest 3.7 per cent to a record 398.7 million barrels of oil equivalent. Both domestic and overseas production reached record highs, according to the company. “In the second half of the year, we will stay focused on our annual production and operation targets, spare no effort to increase reserves and production, intensify research on core technologies, steadily grow our new energy business, further tap the potential for quality and efficiency enhancement, and strictly uphold the bottom line of safety and environmental protection,” said Zhang Chuanjiang, the company’s chairman, in the interim report. The firm declared an interim dividend of HK$0.94 per share, up 28.8 per cent from a year earlier and the highest since its listing. Its shares had fallen 0.8 per cent to close at HK$24.92 in Hong Kong ahead of the earnings release. The strong interim results came amid a turbulent period for global energy markets, as escalating conflict in the Middle East and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz sent oil prices sharply higher. Brent crude, which started the year at around US$61 a barrel, surged above US$100 in March and traded as high as US$115 in the second quarter, before retreating as ceasefire talks raised hopes of a recovery in oil flows through the key waterway. Higher oil prices also lifted earnings at China Petroleum & Chemical Corporation, or Sinopec, although the impact was more mixed because of its much larger refining and fuel-marketing businesses. Sinopec, the largest oil refiner in China, reported over the weekend that its net profit had jumped 19.3 per cent to 25.6 billion yuan in the first half, while revenue had increased 2 per cent to 1.4 trillion yuan. It said in its interim report that geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East had caused international crude prices to fluctuate sharply, with the average spot price of Brent crude jumping 29.1 per cent year on year to US$92.60 per barrel in the first half. Sinopec said it responded to the Middle East conflict by increasing crude purchases from non-Middle Eastern sources and adjusting its procurement pace. But high oil prices had also weighed on domestic fuel consumption, contributing to a 28.6 per cent year-on-year decline during the period in operating profit at its marketing and distribution business, it added. Separately, Sinopec bought back 2.33 million of its Hong Kong-listed shares for HK$10.98 million on Wednesday, at prices ranging from HK$4.69 to HK$4.72 per share, according to an exchange filing.

title: China targets hi-tech pillars by 2030 to fuel economic growth
description: Beijing bets on next-generation manufacturing – and stricter industrial oversight – to secure its economic strategy.
content: Beijing has vowed to develop emerging industries such as 6G and robotics into new drivers of economic growth by the end of the decade, while pledging renewed efforts to curb cutthroat competition in the domestic automotive industry. Vice-minister of Industry and Information Technology Xin Guobin outlined plans through 2030 to develop a range of hi-tech industries as new pillars of the economy and sources of future growth, from next-generation 6G communications and quantum technology to brain-computer interfaces and nuclear fusion. “We will focus on developing new quality productive forces and integrating technological and industrial innovation to promote high-quality development,” Xin said at a press conference hosted by the State Council Information Office on Wednesday. As part of the efforts, the ministry said it planned to accelerate the commercialisation of artificial intelligence in manufacturing, with officials highlighting embodied AI – systems that allow robots and automated machines to perceive, learn from and interact with their environment – as a crucial area of development. Liu Yulin, head of the ministry’s information and communications development department, said next-generation 6G communications would be a “top priority”. The ministry would fast track core technology research, run technology trials and develop industry standards to prepare for eventual commercial roll-outs, Liu added. The comments come as Beijing pushes to sustain growth through technological self-reliance and industrial upgrading amid mounting economic challenges. Domestically, sluggish consumer spending, a prolonged property sector slump and industrial overcapacity in sectors like electric vehicles (EV) continue to weigh on the economy. Internationally, China is navigating intense competition in advanced technologies and foreign scrutiny of its booming export sector, including clean energy products. Addressing the domestic EV industry, Xin, the vice-minister, noted that “irrational competition remains a prominent issue” despite the sector’s growing global influence. “We must also clearly recognise that the current development of the industry faces a series of problems,” he said. Xin pointed out that some manufacturers had rushed new vehicle designs to market without sufficient testing and validation, drawing public concern over product quality and safety following several high-profile incidents involving driver-assistance and automated features. “These problems cannot be ignored or avoided and must be addressed more forcefully during the 15th five-year plan period,” Xin said. The push for stricter oversight comes as Chinese regulators move to ban retractable car door handles, following a fatal incident last year in which a driver was trapped inside a burning vehicle as bystanders failed to open the doors. China also saw its largest car recall to date last week, targeting hidden door handles that can be difficult to locate and open in an emergency. The sweeping recall includes 2.98 million China-made and imported vehicles from US EV maker Tesla and 400,000 from its Chinese rival Xiaomi. In a Tuesday note, economists at ANZ Research wrote that while the rapid rise of China’s “new economy” – particularly clean technology – appeared impressive, “it is not sufficient to offset the domestic property weakness”. “Industrial advancement is critical to China’s potential growth. But institutional reform is needed to avoid overcapacity in targeted sectors and manage a volatile growth profile,” they added.

title: So long, West? Why South Asian students are rethinking where to go for university
description: Rising costs, visa restrictions and better regional choices drive a shift towards domestic undergraduate study before going abroad.
content: For years, South Asian students – particularly from India – treated an overseas undergraduate degree as the default springboard to an international career. That assumption is now changing. Students across the region are still drawn to prestigious Western institutions, but tightening visa restrictions, rising costs and uncertain post-graduation job markets in countries like the United States are prompting families to rethink their options. Experts say more are choosing to complete their first degree closer to home. The shift represents a recalibration rather than a retreat from global ambitions: undergraduate study at home or within Asia, followed by postgraduate study abroad. Many students are also turning to regional alternatives as international institutions establish branch campuses in India and other countries such as Singapore and Japan gain traction, according to the Cambridge Destination Survey 2025-26, released on Monday. According to the report, 53 per cent of South Asian respondents now prefer remaining in their home countries for undergraduate studies before pursuing postgraduate degrees abroad. Rod Smith, group managing director at Cambridge International Education, told This Week in Asia that South Asian students undertaking Cambridge school-level qualifications previously viewed the curriculum as an automatic pathway to undergraduate study in Australia, the US, Canada or the UK. “But actually over the last five years plus that pattern has been changing and actually has been accelerating,” Smith said. “There’s probably more students [who] stay on in India than travel overseas, even with their international qualifications.” The survey noted that students “increasingly view domestic or regional universities as viable launch pads for international careers and postgraduate study”. At the same time, traditional study-abroad hubs face growing competition from Singapore, Dubai, South Korea, Japan and Malaysia, alongside European destinations including the Netherlands, Germany and Ireland. Applications to US universities from Indian undergraduates dropped 15 per cent in the 2025-26 cycle, according to a report released by the non-profit organisation Common App on Tuesday – one of the sharpest country-specific declines and a clear reversal after years of growth. Arjun Seth, founder of New Delhi-based education consultancy EdBrand, which guides students and young professionals applying to university programmes abroad, said interest in studying overseas remained high, but visa restrictions in the US had dampened enthusiasm. Historically, overseas education for Indian students was concentrated at the postgraduate level due to cost constraints, Seth said, as four-year undergraduate degrees cost considerably more than one- to two-year master’s programmes. “They think that if they study for one to 1½ years overseas they can get a job globally, which is not true now,” he said, adding that the US had remained the most popular destination despite declining interest among students. Though the UK had also benefited from this trend, sluggish economic growth and a tough job market had weighed on students’ choices, he said. Despite the growing interest in universities in places like Singapore and Dubai, Seth said their total intake was a fraction of the millions of Indian students entering higher education each year. Expanding regional choices The shifting education landscape also reflects the growth in “high-quality options” in India, according to Smith. Following India’s 2023 policy allowing foreign universities to open independent campuses, the UK’s University of Southampton launched operations in Gurugram, within India’s National Capital Region. The Cambridge survey said the shift among Indian students partly reflected growing interest in private Indian universities such as Ashoka, Krea and Flame. India now has 52 universities in the QS World University Rankings 2027 edition – up from 14 in 2015 – a 271 per cent increase in little more than a decade. The country is now the fourth most represented higher education system globally after the US, UK and China. “There is still a huge need for many more collective philanthropy-based universities which are run by professionals and the Indian diaspora,” Seth said, adding that the demand for high-quality education still outstrips supply. Other South Asian nations are adjusting their policies to retain local talent. Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are actively updating policies to welcome foreign education providers and transnational models. Md. Habibe Millat, president of the Global Centre for Democratic Governance in Canada, who previously held a prominent faculty role in Bangladesh’s university education sector, said the trend was part of a broader shift across South Asia. “In Bangladesh and across South Asia, more families are considering strong universities at home or elsewhere in Asia for undergraduate study, while reserving Western universities particularly for postgraduate and specialised education,” Millat said. “The quality and diversity of higher education in Asia have improved significantly, particularly in medicine, engineering, technology, and business. Students now have credible regional alternatives that can offer good academic standards at a much lower cost.” He added, however, that genuinely high-quality university places in Bangladesh remained scarce relative to demand. Nevertheless, he said rising tuition fees and living costs in traditional Western destinations were major considerations for students, as securing scholarships had become increasingly competitive and lengthy visa processing and uncertainty were discouraging applicants. “Families are now looking beyond university rankings and considering security, employment prospects, visa accessibility, and whether students will feel welcome in the destination country,” Millat said.

title: MiniMax revenue surges 283% but remains behind pace to meet forecast amid crowded AI race
description: Despite soaring revenue and enterprise growth, MiniMax’s results underscore the fierce competition with US and Chinese AI labs.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence firm MiniMax on Wednesday posted a 283 per cent surge in first-half revenue to US$116.6 million, powered by a 700 per cent jump in its enterprise business, though top-line growth remains off pace to hit full-year analyst forecasts. Revenue for the six months ended June 30 accounted for roughly 32 per cent of the US$363.77 million expected by analysts for the full year 2026, according to estimates compiled by Bloomberg. The company reported full-year revenue of US$79 million for 2025. The top-line growth was largely driven by MiniMax’s enterprise-facing business. Revenue from its Open Platform and other AI-based enterprise services jumped more than 703 per cent year on year to US$73.9 million from US$9.2 million. This segment accounted for 63.4 per cent of its total revenue, expanding from just 30.3 per cent a year earlier, reflecting growth in paying users and enterprise customers, according to MiniMax. Revenue from other AI-native products also doubled. On the bottom line, total loss for the period narrowed 11 per cent to US$358 million. However, adjusted net loss expanded 111.2 per cent to US$293 million from about US$139 million a year earlier, the company said. Gross profit grew more than five-fold to US$20.8 million from US$3.7 million, as gross profit margin increased to 17.9 per cent from 12.1 per cent in the same period a year earlier, according to MiniMax. Shares of Hong Kong-listed MiniMax closed up 1.13 per cent at HK$303 on Wednesday ahead of the earnings announcement. Founded in 2021, Shanghai-based MiniMax is known for its M-series large language models (LLMs), its latest H3 video-generation model and popular consumer apps such as video-creation tool Hailuo AI. The company said in May that its annual recurring revenue (ARR) – a key metric that projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period – reached about US$300 million, doubling from February. In August, the firm’s ARR rose to US$800 million, driven mostly by improvements in model capabilities, said Yan Junjie, MiniMax’s founder and CEO, in an earnings call on Wednesday. Enterprise customers contributed to 80 per cent of MiniMax’s August ARR, according to Yan. The company’s total token consumption in July increased 20-fold from January, he added. MiniMax and Beijing-based Zhipu AI, China’s first two publicly traded LLM developers, saw valuations soar after blockbuster initial public offerings (IPOs) in January, but both now trade at a fraction of their peaks. MiniMax has fallen about 77 per cent from its all-time high of HK$1,330 in March, while Zhipu AI, known internationally as Z.ai, closed at HK$1,030 on Wednesday, about a third of its record high of HK$2,980 in June. Following a July plunge partly triggered by its post-IPO stock lock-up expiry, Yan pledged to forgo his salary until the company achieves artificial general intelligence – in a bid to boost morale. Both firms face intense rivalry from Chinese AI model developers such as Moonshot AI and DeepSeek while striving to catch up with US frontier labs including Anthropic and OpenAI. MiniMax’s latest LLM, the M3, launched in June, had “yet to establish a clear advantage on either capability or cost-performance”, leaving it “vulnerable to stronger models at one end and DeepSeek’s historically aggressive economics at the other”, JP Morgan analysts wrote in a note earlier this month. The coming M3.1 model would be a “key test” of whether its LLM could “regain relevance on the capability-cost frontier”, JP Morgan analysts Olivia Xu, Alex Yao and Daniel Chen said. On Wednesday, Yan also teased MiniMax’s next models – including M3.1, M3 Pro and H3.1 – saying they were “nearly completed”. M3.1 is designed to balance stability, quality and efficiency for “wide adoption on a large scale”, while M3 Pro will scale to 3 trillion parameters and deliver improvements in inference efficiency, according to Yan. MiniMax currently has enough computing power for the training and inference for its M3 Pro and video models, according to Yan. The company was building an “independent and controllable” computing cluster – complete with high-bandwidth networks, dedicated lines, servers and storage – that would serve as a core technology going forward, he said. He added that the company had started using domestically made AI chips, and that domestic processors would account for a larger share of its computing power from the fourth quarter of this year.

title: PwC International must face trial of Evergrande scandals claims: Hong Kong High Court
description: Liquidators seek claims of about 38 billion yuan from PwC International for Evergrande audit failures.
content: The liquidators of collapsed developer China Evergrande Group have won a legal victory against PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) International, indicating that the firm and two other units of the accounting giant would need to jointly face the largest corporate lawsuit claims in Hong Kong, according to a court judgment on Wednesday. Deputy High Court Judge Patrick Fung Pak-tung rejected the application by PwC International to be dismissed from the lawsuits involving claims by the liquidators of China Evergrande Group. In his ruling, the judge said PwC International “did owe a duty of care” to China Evergrande Group, as the liquidators’ lawyers had pointed out that PwC International had the power to control and govern its member firms. As such, it should not strike out the international firms from the lawsuit without a trial, the judge said. “There are factual matters in dispute which should be explored by cross-examination at trial,” he said. The ruling means that PwC International, alongside PwC Hong Kong and PwC China, would need to jointly face the lawsuits filed by the liquidators of China Evergrande Group. The liquidators are seeking approximately 57.9 billion yuan (US$8.6 billion) in total from PwC Hong Kong and PwC Zhong Tian, of which approximately 38.1 billion yuan is also claimed against PwC International, the judgment paper said. Evergrande’s liquidators, Tiffany Wong and Eddie Middleton of Alvarez & Marsal, filed the lawsuits against the trio in early 2025, but PwC International later tried to strike itself out of the claim. In a hearing in May in the High Court, the liquidators’ lawyers said PwC International failed to check on the work of its members in Hong Kong and China over Evergrande’s audit, but PwC International’s lawyers argued that it only coordinated the accounting firm’s global network from London and did not itself provide audit or advisory services. The liquidators on Wednesday welcomed the court decision. “The decision does not determine the ultimate merits of the claims, which will be decided by the court in due course,” the statement said. “The liquidators will continue their duties to investigate the affairs of China Evergrande Group and pursue recoveries for the benefit of creditors.” Hong Kong’s High Court ordered Evergrande to be wound up in January 2024, appointing Wong and Middleton as joint liquidators after the company failed to present a viable restructuring plan for its more than US$300 billion in debt. Last week, the Shenzhen Intermediate People’s Court handed down a life sentence to Evergrande’s founder, Hui Ka-yan, the billionaire founder also known as Xu Jiayin, following a high-profile trial for financial fraud and mismanagement. On Friday, a court in southern China’s Guangdong province formally accepted a bankruptcy-liquidation petition against China Evergrande Group’s main onshore unit. Hong Kong regulators have already taken enforcement action against PwC over its audits of Evergrande, but multiple lawsuits remain active. Besides the claims against the PwC units, the liquidators are also seeking a judicial review against the Securities and Futures Commission’s settlement with PwC Hong Kong to pay HK$1 billion (US$128 million) in compensation to minority shareholders of Evergrande, out of concerns that it could affect the creditors’ chance to get compensation.

title: No lead poisoning cases found among children after infant formula scare
description: Officials say all 237 children are healthy after consuming Friso batch flagged by Macau authorities.
content: Hong Kong health authorities have confirmed that no child has shown signs of poisoning after drinking a batch of infant formula found to contain excessive levels of lead. The Department of Health gave an update on Wednesday, a month after Macau authorities alerted the public that a batch of Frisolac Prestige Stage 1 infant formula, manufactured by the Dutch company Royal FrieslandCampina, might contain lead levels exceeding permissible limits. The department said its dedicated hotline and the maternal and child health centres had received 762 relevant inquiries. Health officers provided advice on switching infant formula and referred 446 babies and young children to public hospitals for assessment and follow-up. Among them, 237 had undergone clinical assessments. “Results indicated that their overall health is good and that none have shown signs of lead poisoning,” the department said. The rest were either pending assessment or the parents had decided not to proceed with check-ups, it added. The hotline will cease operations at 6pm on Friday as the number of inquiries in recent weeks declined. The department advised parents to seek medical advice if their children were feeling unwell. The Centre for Food Safety, which ordered the recall of the product, said it had stepped up surveillance of lead content in powdered infant and follow-up formula in the market. No cases have been found to exceed Hong Kong’s statutory standard for lead so far. Macau authorities flagged safety concerns in late July after some samples from a batch contained 0.2mg/kg of lead – 10 times the maximum legal limit of 0.02mg/kg for such goods. The Dutch maker of Friso insisted that the product was safe and said third-party quality testing had found that their products complied with Hong Kong and Macau standards.

title: Singapore’s future island plan stirs concern over reefs and old fishing grounds
description: The plan to merge three islands could be another example of nature, memory and maritime heritage giving way to development, activists say.
content: Few have spent as much time in the waters surrounding Singapore’s southwestern islands as fisherman Hamzah Mohamad, 71. The former resident of Pulau Sudong has been fishing, primarily by setting up bubu – wire fish traps in Malay – in the rocky coral reefs surrounding Sudong, Bukom and Semakau for more than half a century. He knows the underwater reefs by heart, what the wind changes mean for visibility and which fish species are in season. But the seascape he has long known may be set for another transformation. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced plans on Sunday to form a new island in the coming decades for industry, energy and defence needs by merging islands including Semakau, Bukom and Sudong, similar to how Singapore joined smaller islands through land reclamation to create the energy and chemicals hub Jurong Island. Delivering his National Day Rally speech, Wong said: “Jurong Island shaped our economy for the last fifty years. This new western island can help shape Singapore for the next 50 years and beyond.” Wong framed the proposal as part of Singapore’s long-term approach to land use, saying the city state had to plan over decades to create options for future generations while balancing development with green spaces, biodiversity and heritage. The proposed western island, he said, could support advanced manufacturing, new power generation infrastructure and defence needs, while a new link would connect Jurong Island with the future island. For former islanders, environmental groups and marine advocates, the long-term plan has raised questions over how Singapore can balance future land needs with coral reefs, access to fishing grounds and its remaining maritime traditions. The islands were once home to hundreds of residents who made a living mainly as fishermen and had to relocate to mainland Singapore in the 1970s when their islands were earmarked for redevelopment. Sudong has since become a military live-firing zone with an airstrip, while Semakau was joined with the smaller island of Pulau Seking to form a landfill and Bukom houses an oil refinery. Since 1991, there have been proposals to increase the land mass surrounding the three islands under Singapore’s long-term plan from the Urban Redevelopment Authority. In the 2011 edition of the plan, the islands were earmarked for “possible future reclamation”. As of the latest plan dated 2022, the islands were not merged. Former islanders, non-governmental organisations and environmentalists said they were concerned about what the project could mean for coral reefs and their former home, with some telling This Week in Asia they feared it could become another example of nature, memory and maritime heritage giving way to development. The Straits Times quoted Huang Danwei, director of the National Institute for Marine and Ocean Sciences, as saying reefs in Pulau Hantu and Semakau dated back about 8,000 years and that there was “no mitigation” for reefs directly buried by land reclamation. A Ministry of National Development spokesman told This Week in Asia that the government recognised the biodiversity value of the western islands and their surrounding waters, and was studying the plans carefully to prepare ahead and create options for the future. He said “technical studies” would be conducted to guide the development plans, including the reclamation profile. Feasibility studies, site investigations and surveys, as well as engineering and environmental studies, would also be undertaken to better understand possible development options and their preliminary impact on biodiversity and hydrodynamics. The government would “engage stakeholders early” and consider their feedback before launching the studies and work. Their knowledge and expertise would be tapped to assess potential biodiversity impact and identify measures to avoid and mitigate effects where possible, he added. Firdaus Sani, founder of non-governmental organisation Orang Laut SG, told This Week in Asia that the indigenous orang pulau, or island people, and orang laut, or people from the sea, communities felt overlooked and helpless about whether they could still have access to the southern waters. “If you were to look at it from a different perspective of indigenous associations outside Singapore, indigenous spaces and viewpoints might be treated more seriously. Now it seems like the priority is more an economic one, as we’re not even consulted about the plans, which is a shame,” he added. Han Jok Kwang, 72, a former resident of Bukom and a business development adviser, was concerned about the sea life surrounding the islands, having spent his first 16 years on the island. “My level-headed brain is telling me that humans need to take care of humans, but I worry about the rich marine life there,” said Han, whose grandmother was a resident of neighbouring Semakau. “It’s a very big project, and it’ll probably take so long to build that nobody will be upset any more by the time it opens,” he added. End of bubu fishing? Several former residents from Sudong, like Hamzah, regularly take boats out to fish in the area surrounding their former homes using the bubu traps, traditionally made using materials such as bamboo or rattan, to earn an income – a vanishing trade in modern Singapore. Firdaus said: “What happens to the community’s livelihood? What happens to history, memory, waterways that we remember and that we know, and some of the places that we deem sacred? Some of the islands also have deep roots to these spaces, more than a physical sense. There are a lot of these things that have not been considered.” If the islands and surrounding waterways were reclaimed, the fishing grounds would disappear as well, he said. “It’s literally erasing an entire fishing and maritime culture that we still have a connection to. It’s the only thing that they had left.” While their origins are unclear, bubu traps are an indigenous craft practised by the early Malay and local islander communities like the orang laut for generations, long before Singapore’s independence in 1965. Maritime communities throughout Southeast Asia also use the device for fishing. At West Coast Park, Hamzah and other former islanders have built makeshift shelters over the years along a fenced-up beach area where they keep their bubu traps and moor their boats. He and his brother, Ahmad Sah Mohamad, known in the community as the Sudong brothers, spend most days under their shelters weaving their bubu traps and make a weekly pilgrimage to the waters around Sudong to collect their catch and replace traps – a traditional way of life that has been passed down through generations. They are not allowed to go near the island or land as it is a restricted area. “Once this place is gone, I’ll have to learn almost everything again because I know these places so well, and how the water is like here and what kind of fish are in season here. I don’t know if there will be other coral reefs we can go to,” Hamzah said. The retired contractor hopes the waters remain open for fishing as he relies on it for income, and that there will still be rocky coral reefs in the area for him to place bubu traps. “I don’t know what I’ll do if the area is closed off. If I have to go somewhere else, it has to be somewhere with coral reefs because that’s the only way you can really place a bubu,” Hamzah said. Orang Laut SG’s Firdaus said he was not hopeful about prospects for the traditional fishing practice. “The truth of the matter is I don’t know. We could continue to try, as a way of preserving cultural heritage, but it’s not going to be truly a living heritage. It’s really going to be how museums are – static and remaining in the past,” he said.

title: AI boom, profit surge fuel China’s ambitious chip assembly buildout
description: Chinese chip packaging firms launch multibillion-dollar expansion drive after logging triple-figure profit growth on surging AI demand.
content: China’s leading semiconductor packaging and testing companies have launched a multibillion-dollar capacity expansion drive, as they ride a surge in artificial intelligence demand, stellar first-half profit growth, and Beijing’s urgent push for tech self-sufficiency. In the first half of the year, China’s three leading outsourced chip packaging companies – Jiangsu Changjiang Electronics Technology (JCET), Tongfu Microelectronics and Huatian Technology – announced capacity expansion investments exceeding a combined 15 billion yuan (US$2.2 billion). Packaging and testing are the final steps in chip manufacturing. The fresh capital is aimed at scaling the firms’ high-end advanced packaging for AI accelerators, after the companies reported robust earnings growth in the first six months of 2026. JCET, China’s largest packaging and testing firm, saw its net profit surge 79.4 per cent year on year to 845 million yuan, while revenue hit a record 19.5 billion yuan on strong computing electronics sales, according to its earnings report last week. In June, the firm unveiled a 7.8 billion yuan plan for a sprawling new advanced packaging and testing facility for high-end AI chips in Shanghai’s Lingang area, with phase one scheduled for completion in the second half of 2028. Meanwhile, Tongfu Microelectronics – slated to release its latest earnings results on Friday – has forecast a first-half profit surge of up to 337 per cent year on year, driven partly by its strategic partnership with US semiconductor firm Advanced Micro Devices’ next-generation processors. The Chinese company recently received regulatory approval for a 4.2 billion yuan private share placement, and plans to allocate 888 million yuan to add 849,600 wafers of annual memory chip capacity. Huatian Technology, based in northwest China’s Gansu province, reported last week a 259 per cent profit jump in first-half profit to 813 million yuan. It announced a 3 billion yuan investment in May for a Nanjing facility designed to produce 430 million memory chips annually. The capacity race reflects how advanced packaging – including 2.5D, 3D stacking and chiplet architectures – has shifted to centre stage as physical limits slow traditional silicon scaling under Moore’s Law. China’s domestic champions are also receiving a further boost from Beijing’s drive for technological self-reliance. “The value of advanced packaging can reach tens or even hundreds of times that of traditional packaging, driving a revaluation across the industry chain,” analysts at mainland brokerage China Securities wrote in a recent research note. They highlighted that in Nvidia’s B200 AI processor, the combined cost of CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) packaging and testing now rivalled advanced node wafer manufacturing itself. With Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s CoWoS capacity tightly constrained, outsourced chip assembly and test providers are benefiting from strong pricing power. The momentum extends to smaller domestic players. SJ Semiconductor raised 5 billion yuan via an initial public offering on Shanghai’s Star Market to fund 3D multi-chip integration projects, while Forehope Electronic announced in June a 10.3 billion yuan investment for its phase-three facility in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. Globally, major players in chip packaging and testing have also set aside massive capital to solidify their positions amid the rapid expansion wave. ASE Technology Holding, the Taiwan-based industry leader, in July raised its 2026 capital expenditure budget to US$10.5 billion – up from the US$8.5 billion target set in April.

title: China makes officials liable for environmental damage for life
description: Revised personnel rules tie performance to eco-impact more closely as the country shifts gear from growth to sustainability.
content: China has reminded its officials of their lifelong responsibility for serious environmental damage on their watch, tying green efforts more closely to performance assessments in the country’s push for higher-quality growth. The conditions and potential disciplinary action were outlined in revised rules released on Tuesday by the Communist Party and the State Council, China’s cabinet. Under the rules, officials will be held to account for serious environmental damage “regardless of whether they have been transferred, reassigned, promoted, left their jobs or retired”. The Central Organisation Department, the party body overseeing personnel appointments, said that despite “historic” and wide-ranging changes, underlying and longer-term pressures on environmental protection had yet to be fundamentally eased. The changes are linked to President Xi Jinping’s “new development philosophy” and are part of China’s push to build what it describes as an “ecological civilisation”. Both concepts feed into an environmental protection policy framework meant to shift China away from a growth model focused on quantity towards one that prioritises quality and sustainability. More broadly, China is aiming to realise the “dual carbon” goals of reaching peak carbon emissions before 2030 and carbon neutrality before 2060. As such, the revisions signal a continued move away from GDP-focused cadre evaluations, and come as local leadership changes are being rolled out across China. Those transitions will culminate at the national party congress next year, when the focus is expected to be on changes at the upper echelons as well as endorsement of a fourth term for Xi. The lifelong responsibility rules have been in the works for some time and are based on a trial process in 2015. They were revised by the Politburo Standing Committee in July and take effect immediately. The revisions have widened the scope of accountability. While the 2015 version of the rules focused on party and government officials, the revisions extend the framework to leaders of state-owned enterprises and their affiliated organisations, as well as those at public institutions and development zones. Officials overseeing these institutions can be disciplined if they approve projects that violate environmental laws or cross ecological “red lines”, fail to properly regulate polluting businesses, mishandle major environmental incidents or neglect problems identified by environmental inspectors. They could also be held accountable for failing to advance green development and carbon goals, or allowing environmental problems in their areas of responsibility to persist or recur. As well as a renewed focus on the environment, the revised rules reflect Xi’s priority this year to promote a “correct view of political performance”, with greater emphasis on tangible results for the public rather than short-term economic gains. Since March, Xi has repeatedly called on officials to create achievements that can stand the test of “practice, the people and history”. On Monday, he described the effort as a “long-term task”, urging officials to make “scientific” decisions, deliver concrete results and work for the benefit of the people. One notable change in the revised rules is that while any punishment should be strict, it should factor in the circumstance of each official. “Accountability for ecological and environmental damage by party and government officials should be within clear policy boundaries, with authorities accurately determining responsibility and making accountability decisions based on factors including the historical causes, nature and severity of the damage, the response and handling, the consequences and impact, and efforts to recover losses, so as to prevent accountability from becoming generalised or simplistic.” The revised rules also drop “an order to make a public apology”, which was among the accountability measures in the 2015 version.

title: Philippines eyes drones and ‘system of systems’ to boost asymmetric defence
description: Manila plans to use drones as force multipliers, but analysts warn building a credible deterrence network will require multi-year investment.
content: Facing a far larger Chinese military presence at sea, the Philippines is looking to drones not as a substitute for warships and aircraft but as a relatively low-cost way to make its forces harder to find, suppress and outmanoeuvre, analysts have said. The administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr has focused on expanding the military’s drone fleet as part of its external defence strategy. Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr told lawmakers on Tuesday that Manila also needed to secure communications, artificial intelligence and operational networks to integrate unmanned systems into military operations. During a House appropriations committee hearing on the Department of National Defence’s proposed budget, Teodoro said the initiative would be funded through a proposed 50 billion-peso (US$810 million) allocation for military modernisation in 2027, a 25 per cent increase from this year’s budget. “We have to integrate the capabilities and have proper working procedures in using them,” Teodoro said. “We currently have a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles, which provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance services for us. As we mature on the cycle, then we can acquire more.” Acquiring drones was not the main challenge, he said, the more sensitive issue involved the systems they carried and the capabilities those systems could provide. “Initially, we have to have the connectivity and the network capabilities to operate them as real time as possible … Connectivity and the security of connectivity is paramount for us,” he added, noting they were in “close contact” with several countries with drone expertise. Analysts said Manila’s shift towards asymmetric external defence and integrated operations increased the strategic importance of acquiring low-cost, high-utility drones and strengthening its cyber capabilities. “Drone development entails sustainable effort on subsidising local research and development, optimising technology transfers and building indigenous capability,” Chester Cabalza, president and chief executive of the Manila-based International Development and Security Cooperation think tank, told This Week in Asia. “The Armed Forces of the Philippines is looking to Ukraine’s development of an indigenous drone capability as a model. Rather than relying solely on expensive conventional hardware, locally produced drones could support asymmetric maritime deterrence, with aerial and maritime drones serving as force multipliers.” South China Sea concerns Justin Kyle Malarayap, a visiting assistant professor at Arellano University in Manila, said the Philippines was building networks to support drone operations in preparation for a potential South China Sea contingency. “As we’ve seen recently, the Philippines has been interacting with Ukraine, the US and Japan to build these networks and capabilities to improve Philippine joint military operations,” he said. Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and chief executive of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a Canadian foreign policy think tank, agreed that drones could serve as force multipliers. She said the significance of Teodoro’s disclosure was that Manila was treating drones as part of a “system of systems” connecting unmanned platforms with sensors, secure communications, command-and-control networks, ships, aircraft and land-based missile systems. “That is consistent with the Philippines’ broader Comprehensive Archipelagic Defence Concept. The lesson from Ukraine and other recent conflicts is that a drone is only as valuable as the network behind it,” Nadjibulla said. The archipelagic concept is Manila’s framework for shifting its military focus towards external defence across the country’s territory, maritime zones and approaches. Manila and Kyiv are reportedly in discussions to advance an October 2025 initiative to pursue drone co-production, a proposed partnership that could combine Ukraine’s battle-tested technology with the Philippines’ transition towards a more agile, technology-driven defence posture. The Philippine military currently operates unmanned systems across all three service branches for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and emerging combat missions. The army uses Elbit THOR and commercial DJI drones, while the air force operates Hermes 450 and 900 platforms. The navy and marine corps deploy ScanEagle drones for maritime surveillance and are developing unmanned surface and underwater systems. In April, the air force and its government and industry partners also unveiled locally developed autonomous, loitering and armed drones for reconnaissance and precision-strike missions. Discussing Manila’s drone expansion, Teodoro said the priority was integrating the systems into military operations, including the secure communications and network capabilities needed for effective use. Multi-year investment Building that integrated architecture, however, requires sustained funding. Nadjibulla said the proposed allocation was insufficient to develop the full defence network Manila ultimately needed, adding that credible deterrence would require multi-year investment rather than the occasional acquisition of individual platforms. “It can build a significantly better and operationally useful network in the near term. The priority has to be resilience and redundancy. Partners can substantially accelerate that process,” Nadjibulla said. Philippine allies such as the US, Japan and Australia were coordinating investments in sensors, information-sharing systems and cybersecurity, while Canada was providing maritime domain awareness capabilities such as “dark vessel detection”, Nadjibulla said. “The Philippines does not need technological parity with China. It needs sufficient awareness, resilience and distributed capability to complicate Chinese military planning and strengthen deterrence by denial,” she said. However, achieving such capabilities will require Manila to make difficult spending decisions. Malarayap said persistent financial constraints were forcing the government to prioritise military projects based on their demonstrated combat effectiveness and evolving threat assessments. Yet he was optimistic that Manila could build the communications and operational networks needed to make unmanned systems effective in a near-term conflict. The Philippine military was prioritising communications systems to improve its response to natural disasters and security contingencies, and thereby boost archipelagic logistics, Malarayap said.
