Cabalza was more cautious, saying Manila’s AI-enabled surveillance and command-and-control capabilities were limited, but increased defence funding could help the armed forces address those gaps. “This is a David vs Goliath scenario of UAVs. While military armaments are key to war success, strategy places the best part in its execution. The world has not yet seen a sea battle of swarming UAVs,” Cabalza said. For Nadjibulla, unmanned systems could help offset the advantage of China’s much larger fleet but could not eliminate it, and that disparity was precisely why drones and other unmanned platforms made strategic sense for the Philippines. “China will retain an overwhelming numerical advantage in ships and aircraft, so Manila cannot realistically compete platform for platform,” Nadjibulla said. “Drones offer a relatively inexpensive way to generate persistent surveillance, distribute sensors across a very large maritime area and make Philippine forces harder to find and suppress.”

title: Chinese wife, 90, inspires millions by preserving Alzheimer’s husband’s dignity
description: Story provides China youth with a fresh perspective on growing old, defined by mutual respect and deep devotion.
content: A 90-year-old woman in Beijing is devoted to caring for her husband with Alzheimer’s disease, determined to safeguard not only his health but also his dignity. Wen Bo and her husband, who is two years older, first met as secondary school classmates. After several years of long-distance courtship, they married in 1960. Together, they raised two sons and embraced an active lifestyle for decades, engaging in activities like swimming and walking, as well as taking occasional trips throughout China and abroad. Their lives took a turn in 2023 when Wen’s husband began to experience memory loss and incontinence, ultimately receiving a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease. Rather than burden their sons, who are busy with their own families and careers, Wen chose to become her husband’s full-time carer. According to reports from mainland media, the couple rely on a domestic helper for cooking and household chores, while their children visit whenever possible. As his condition progressed, Wen’s husband struggled to remember his medication, experienced a decline in mobility, and ceased asking about his grandchildren. Determined to provide the best care, Wen taught herself about Alzheimer’s through books and online resources, dedicating each day to cognitive exercises with him, including maths problems, puzzles, and painting, alongside some physical training. Thanks to her efforts, her husband’s condition has deteriorated at a slower pace. When they go out, he can still operate his electric wheelchair independently and occasionally reminds Wen to take a break. Wen has chronicled her caregiving journey in diaries shared on RedNote, garnering support from millions of netizens. On August 23, she recounted that her husband completed an arithmetic test, taking a bit longer than usual but only making one mistake. Worried he might forget her name, Wen reminds him every night before bed to call her for help whenever he needs it. “He has to remember my name. I am his wife. I should be the last person he forgets,” she expressed in an interview. Wen also encourages him to engage in simple household tasks, patiently allowing him to complete them at his own pace. She firmly believes that people with Alzheimer’s should not be defined by their illness. “Self-respect, a sense of existence, and the feeling of being needed are essential for individuals with Alzheimer’s disease,” she stated. In one post, she mentioned that she would consider hospice care if her husband’s condition significantly worsened. For China’s younger generation, Wen and her husband’s story presents an alternative vision of ageing, centred on dignity, autonomy, and companionship. Their journey unfolds against the backdrop of China’s rapidly ageing population, which surpassed 320 million individuals aged 60 and older by the end of last year, representing over one-fifth of the total population. One online observer remarked: “Grandma Wen’s posts always bring me comfort. She shows me what an ideal later life could look like: being with the person you love while living independently.” Another noted: “I used to fear not knowing how to care for my ageing parents, but her experiences have provided me with valuable guidance and increased confidence for the future.”

title: Frustration in China as US freezes green card interviews worldwide, citing ‘training’
description: The cancelled appointments mark the latest squeeze in a tightening vice on legal immigration during Donald Trump’s second term.
content: People in China reacted with frustration and disbelief after American consulates around the world began cancelling immigrant visa interviews – the latest setback for applicants waiting to enter the United States legally. A post by an immigration agent on the Chinese social media platform RedNote claimed that the US consulate in Guangzhou had abruptly cancelled all immigrant visa interviews on Tuesday. According to the agent, who declined to be named because they were not authorised to speak to the media, multiple clients scheduled for interviews later this week were notified via email that their appointments had been cancelled and would be rescheduled at a later date. The agent said visa appointments scheduled for late September remained unaffected for now, though applicants were advised to monitor their emails for updates. “It’s not just Guangzhou; similar situations have also been reported at other consulates around the world,” the agent said. Internet users shared their experiences, with one saying the notification came when he was already at the consulate. Another said he arrived in Guangzhou only to find his interview had been cancelled. While single-day disruptions occasionally happen around major holidays such as Christmas, the agent noted that a widespread, multi-week cancellation of this scale was entirely unprecedented. In a statement to the South China Morning Post, a US State Department spokesperson did not deny that visa interviews had been cancelled en masse, saying US President Donald Trump’s administration was “protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants”. The spokesperson confirmed that a “global training initiative” had been launched at every US embassy and consulate since early this year. The department representative said that visa appointments would be “adjusted” as officers underwent training to screen applicants at risk of becoming a “public charge”, or those the Trump administration considers likely to rely on public benefits. The Financial Times first reported that applicants who had already secured interview slots – some after months or years of paperwork, fees, medical exams and travel plans – received emails saying their appointments had been cancelled or postponed. They were told a new date would come later, but they were not given a time frame. It is the latest squeeze in a tightening vice on legal immigration during Trump’s second term. The administration first froze immigrant visa issuance for nationals from 75 countries in January, citing concerns over applicants becoming a public charge. A federal judge last week struck down that policy, ruling that it went beyond US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s authority. Days later, immigrant visa interviews themselves were pulled from consular calendars worldwide – not through another country-specific ban, but under the banner of “training”. Earlier this month, the State Department said certain immigrant visa applicants might be required to post public charge bonds. If the US government believes an applicant might become dependent on government benefits, the applicant could be required to post cash as security. Since January, official Trump administration accounts have promoted mass visa revocations, a crackdown on so-called birth tourism, and a simple message: a visa is a privilege, not a right. Immigrant visas cover permanent residence cases processed overseas, including family- and employment-based green card applications. For many applicants, the interview is the final consular step before they can join a spouse, parent or employer in the US. Tourist, student and temporary work visas operate on separate tracks, but those categories, too, have faced increased scrutiny, denials and delays. The tightening is reflected in official numbers. According to State Department data, the refusal rate for B-visa applicants from India rose from 16 per cent in 2024 to 22 per cent in 2025. The visa covers short-term visitors travelling to the US for tourism and business. Refusal rates are even higher for applicants from Nigeria, Bangladesh and Pakistan. An analysis of US State Department data by educational services firm Shorelight showed that F-1 student visa refusals reached a decade high of about 35 per cent last year, and 61 per cent for Indian applicants. Denials of H-1B skilled worker petitions remain low at around 2 per cent, though applicants have faced delays in getting their physical visa stamps processed at US consulates due to additional vetting and cancelled interviews.

title: Obituary | Zheng Fengrong, first Chinese female athlete to break world record, dies aged 89
description: The high jump pioneer won numerous awards for her achievements and served as vice-president of the Chinese Athletics Association.
content: Zheng Fengrong, a high jump legend and the first Chinese female athlete to break a world record, died on Tuesday aged 89. While there has been no official confirmation, state broadcaster CCTV Sports shared a tribute video across its digital platforms. Born in Jinan, Shandong province in 1937, she joined the national athletics training team in 1953. She later served as vice-president of the Chinese Athletics Association, a deputy to the Third National People’s Congress, and a member of the fifth, sixth and ninth National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference. In 1954, she won the women’s high jump title at the National High School and College Games. Three years later, Premier Zhou Enlai made a special October trip to watch the Sino-Soviet Athletics Friendship Tournament at the Beijing Institute of Physical Education and met Zheng. And less than a month later at a Beijing athletics meet on November 17, she cleared 1.77 metres to break the world record of 1.76m held by American athlete Mildred McDaniel, becoming the first Chinese woman to set a world record. The Associated Press reported at the time that “a 20-year-old Chinese girl has warned the world track and field with a powerful jump in Beijing that the 600 million Chinese will not forever be backward athletes”. She was affectionately praised as “a swallow announcing the arrival of spring for Chinese sports”. On June 26, 1963, at Nanjing’s Wutaishan Stadium, she surpassed her personal best by clearing 1.78m. Zheng was awarded the title of Master of Sports in 1956 and received the Sports Honour Medal from the National Sports Commission in 1959. In 1987, the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) awarded her its 75th Anniversary Gold Medal of Merit. In 1994, she was named one of the 45 Sports Heroes of the 45th Anniversary of the Founding of the People’s Republic of China, and a year later she received the Olympic Order in Silver from the International Olympic Committee. After retiring, she remained active in sports, having served as vice-president of the Chinese Athletics Association since 1979. In 1980, she joined a Chinese sports service company, working behind the scenes on major events including the Beijing Marathon, the Hong Kong-Macau Rally and the Yangtze River Expedition. Zheng’s husband, Duan Qiyan, was also a high jumper. Bound by a shared passion for sport, the couple were married for more than 50 years. Their love for and commitment to sports deeply influenced their grandchildren, who went on to show remarkable athletic talent. Zheng was the grandmother of Nina Schultz (Zheng Ninali), China’s first naturalised track athlete, and Ty Schultz (Zheng Enlai), a naturalised player for China’s men’s ice hockey team. On Zheng’s 80th birthday, her grandson Ty expressed his desire to renounce his Canadian citizenship to represent China at the 2022 Winter Olympics, wearing the No 77 jersey to commemorate his grandmother’s historic record. “My childhood dream was to become an athlete like my grandmother. She was my idol, and I hoped I could reach her level,” he once said. A year later, upon turning 20, her granddaughter Nina, who had trained in athletics from an early age, submitted a declaration to the IAAF expressing her intention to represent China at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics. “My grandmother never had the chance to compete in the Olympics. I want to help her fulfil her dream,” she once said. Nina won the women’s heptathlon at the 14th and 15th National Games. She reached her career peak at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games by taking the gold medal in heptathlon. In 2024, a knee injury ruled her out of the Paris Olympics, leaving her unable to fulfil her wish of realising her grandmother’s Olympic dream. According to a social media post by actor Zang Jinsheng, Zheng died of cancer, and her memorial service will be held in Beijing on Saturday.

title: Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan, policy address to be unveiled on September 16
description: Hong Kong’s leader says releasing blueprints together will show how the five-year plan sets direction and the policy address implements it.
content: Hong Kong’s leader will deliver the city’s first five-year plan and his annual policy address on September 16, stressing that presenting the blueprints together will help residents better understand how they are deeply connected. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced the move on Wednesday after he visited residents from lower-income households and inspected community services at Un Chau Estate in Sham Shui Po district to gather public views. Lee said unveiling the five-year plan and then his policy address shortly afterwards would help residents better grasp how they complemented each other in defining the vision for Hong Kong’s future. “The five-year plan draws the eyes of a dragon, while the policy address draws the entire dragon … but the public may not fully understand how they work together,” he said. “If the public can look at the two documents together, they will see how the five-year plan sets the directional requirements and guidance and how the policy address formulates policies and implements the direction of the blueprint.” He added that the policy address would formulate measures and set out indicators for implementing the five-year plan, based on the international environment, economic forecasts and the latest developments. Lee said that he would present both documents at the Legislative Council on September 16, before attending a question and answer session with lawmakers the following day. While Legco was originally scheduled to resume general meetings in October after the summer recess, he said the legislature would hold a special session for his presentation. A government source underscored that the two documents were “deeply interconnected and hard to separate”, echoing the leader’s point that delivering them on the same day would help the public understand how they worked together. “It definitely will not be an hours-long readout of the full five-year plan, followed by the policy address. That would be overwhelming,” the insider said. “The chief executive is likely to deliver summaries of both, followed by elaborations on various occasions. Detailed arrangements are still being discussed internally.” The source added that ministers would host briefings in the days after both blueprints were revealed to explain the various plans and policies. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said releasing the two blueprints together highlighted their relationship and would help focus public attention. “During the formulation of the five-year plan, the government described Legco as a close partner and involved it from the beginning,” Lau said. “To announce the plan in Legco underscores their partnership, and answering questions from lawmakers can strengthen interaction between the two branches.” The government has concluded its two-month public consultation for the five-year plan, while consultation on the policy address is ongoing. Earlier on Wednesday, Lee visited Un Chau Estate as part of public consultations for the policy address. He used the occasion to pledge to ease burdens on older people and their carers to support ageing in place. “Enabling elderly people to live healthily and with dignity in familiar communities is an important direction of our elderly care policy,” the leader said in a social media post after the visit. “My team and I will continue to promote the integration of medical care, rehabilitation, community support and technology applications, so as to reduce the burden on the elderly and their carers.” During the one-hour visit, Lee spoke with residents, toured a centre for the elderly and tried out a stationary bike at the estate. Accompanied by Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau and Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen, Lee met an elderly resident surnamed Chan at the centre. The 88-year-old told Lee that she was hospitalised with pneumonia earlier, and was arranged for a follow-up at an ambulatory care centre after her discharge. She commended the centre’s comfortable environment and short waiting times for check-ups, saying these had aided her recovery and eased the pressure on her family to accompany her to appointments and provide care. Lee also inspected the call centre for the government’s 1823 public inquiry hotline and instructed staff to adopt artificial intelligence and other technologies to enhance efficiency. The city leader previously met more than 200 residents and district representatives selected by authorities for two town hall meetings to gather views on the policy address and the five-year plan. The plan aims to better align local development with efforts under the national blueprint for 2026-2030, while providing direction and strategic guidance for the future. It will outline the city’s vision for the Northern Metropolis megaproject, the advancement of innovation and technology, and the development of finance, shipping and trade. Lee earlier said the city needed to strengthen urban management to ensure better handling of natural disasters and public complaints. He also said at the time that the five-year blueprint would create more quality jobs for young people and help them move up the housing ladder. Analysts suggested that Lee’s decision to meet elderly residents indicated that their care would be among the priorities outlined in the five-year plan and the policy address, noting nearly a quarter of the city’s total population was aged 65 or older last year. The national 15th five-year plan also covers several key livelihood issues, with addressing an ageing society among the priorities. It proposes measures to improve elder care, promote smart ageing and boost the silver economy. Lau described the rapidly ageing population as a pressing challenge, saying the two blueprints could not sidestep the issue as it risked undermining societal and economic development. Lawmaker Peter Douglas Koon Ho-ming agreed that the demographic shift was a long-standing challenge and said it required better coordination among bureaus. “It is related to housing, healthcare, social welfare and the silver economy. The entire policy needs a clear [plan] in the five-year blueprint,” he said. Acknowledging that many elderly people live in cramped flats, Koon said better housing and other supporting measures were needed to facilitate ageing in place.

title: Chinese navy fires new radar-absorbing YJ-18A anti-ship missile in sea trial, expert says
description: Black radar-absorbing finish on upgraded ship-launched weapon would improve penetration and visual camouflage over deep water, say analysts.
content: China has tested a new variant of the YJ-18A anti-ship cruise missile bearing a black stealth coating, according to specialists who say the advanced finish on the ship-launched missile will improve its penetration ability. The coating was highlighted in footage released by state broadcaster CCTV on Saturday, which showed an extreme-performance test of a new type of anti-ship missile fired from a navy ship’s vertical launch system in unknown waters. China’s most active-duty shipborne missiles are painted in lighter colours, such as grey or white. Specialists identified the missile as a variant of the YJ-18A, Yingji or “Eagle Strike”, an anti-ship missile that cruises at subsonic speed before making a supersonic terminal attack, often equipped on the 7,500-tonne Type 052D and 12,000-tonne Type 055 destroyers. “Despite complex and severe sea conditions, the test team precisely captured the missile’s flight parameters,” CCTV reported. Although the footage was previously shown in early July, the black coating was only pointed out in the most recent broadcast. “The total amount of data collected during the test was several times greater than originally planned, providing detailed and reliable data to support further improvements to the weapon system,” CCTV said, referring to the YJ-18A. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military commentator and former People’s Liberation Army instructor, said the black coating was a type of stealth coating with strong radar-wave-absorbing properties, reducing the amount of radar energy reflected back to enemy radar and making the missile harder to detect. Song said the black coating also served another purpose. “Don’t assume that the sea is always blue; in fact, the colour of the deep sea can be quite dark, even approaching black. So it provides both radar stealth and visual camouflage by matching the colour of the sea,” he said. According to Song, the video showed that the missile was launched and then quickly performed vector manoeuvring, allowing it to begin sea-skimming flight as quickly as possible. By lowering its flight altitude, it reduced the likelihood of the missile being exposed and detected. Vector manoeuvring means the missile rapidly changes its flight direction after launch. “What matters most for an anti-ship missile is its ability to penetrate enemy defences,” Song said, adding that there were two ways to do this: through stealth and through high-speed flight – and the YJ-18A combined both. “In its terminal phase, it can penetrate defences at supersonic speed while also employing stealth. Maintaining stealth throughout its flight can further improve its ability to penetrate enemy defences, particularly when striking large surface vessels,” Song said. The CCTV report said the People’s Liberation Army Navy had made advances in its weapons and equipment, with batches of new missiles undergoing trials at sea-based test ranges. The original YJ-18, derived from the Russian 3M-54E submarine-launched anti-ship missile system, has a range of 540km (335 miles). It has a cruise speed of 966km/h (600mph), and when approaching a target, its warhead can accelerate to Mach 3 speed, according to China Daily. The YJ-18A made its first public appearance in 2019, and the YJ-18C variant for land attacks was revealed at the September 3 Victory Day military parade last year. The YJ-18C reportedly improved its radar cross-section through multifaceted stealth design to as low as 0.005 square metres (0.05 square feet), similar to that of a seabird. In March, a black US Tomahawk land-attack cruise missile was seen for the first time in strikes on Iran, The War Zone military news site reported, saying that its black coating made it harder to spot while skimming low over the water.

title: Meet comedy icon Eddie Murphy’s son Myles, who is following in his father’s footsteps
description: The rising stand-up comedian, who recently performed a set in New York, is the second child of the Saturday Night Live alum and his ex-wife Nicole Mitchell Murphy.
content: Legendary comedian Eddie Murphy’s son is following in his father’s footsteps and has entered the comedy scene. Myles Mitchell Murphy, the third of four sons among Eddie’s 10 children, recently made a surprise appearance at the West Side Comedy Club in New York, where he delivered a stand-up set. After his set, the 33-year-old sat down with comedian Jeffrey Gurian, who shared stories about the comedy icon that Myles had never heard before. In 1980, when he was only 19, Eddie Murphy got his big break on Saturday Night Live and has since become one of the most beloved comedians in the US. Now, it seems his son is ready to take on the mantle. But what else do we know about the next rising Murphy comedian? Read on to find out. He comes from a big family Eddie Murphy was known for his series of romantic relationships early in his career, and he has 10 children with five different women. Myles was born on November 7, 1992, to Murphy and his then-wife, model Nicole Mitchell Murphy. Apart from their second-born Myles, Eddie and Nicole share four more children: Bria, Shayne, Zola and Bella. Eddie also has three children – Eric, Christian and Angel – with former girlfriends. He shares two other children, Izzy and Max, with his current wife, Australian model and actress Paige Butcher. Eddie’s children range in age from seven to 37. “I never knew I would have 10 kids, but now it’s the best thing ever. If you can afford that many kids, you should have as many kids as you can afford. That is fun,” Eddie told People last year. “My children are all decent people. I don’t have one rotten one, and I would like to think that they got some of that from me,” he continued. When did Myles Murphy get into comedy? Myles started running an Instagram page dedicated to his stand-up comedy sets this January. According to Page Six, he works as a screenwriter during the day and has been performing for less than a year. “Performing comedy was something he’s always wanted to do, and he’s performed in several of the clubs in [Los Angeles],” an insider told Page Six. Not only did the crowd like Myles’ jokes, but they appreciated his good looks, too. “He got up, did his set, and he’s really good,” the insider added. “Though everyone remarked how handsome he was.” Who is Myles Murphy married to? Myles is married to his long-time partner, Carly Olivia Fink. The couple have been together since at least 2012, and Myles proposed to her in 2022, which she documented in an Instagram video. They tied the knot on September 9, 2023, in a private ceremony in Beverly Hills. Myles and Carly have two daughters: Evie Isla Murphy, born July 2, 2019, and Zuri Liv Murphy, born October 30, 2024. While Myles keeps his personal life private, he seems like quite the family man, often posting photos on Instagram of himself spending time with his wife and daughters.

title: Chinese hotpot chain Haidilao bets on takeaway, new brands, lower-tier reach for growth
description: Takeaway emerges as Haidilao’s fastest-growing segment as it diversifies its formats, expands into lower-tier markets despite a soft economy.
content: China’s largest hotpot chain Haidilao International Holding has seen takeaway emerge as its fastest-growing segment, with demand for single-serving meals like rice-bowl sets surging, amid positive revenue and profit growth in the first half. Takeaway revenue for the Hong Kong-listed group reached 2.05 billion yuan (US$305 million) in the first six months, surging 121.2 per cent year on year. The segment accounted for 9.2 per cent of total revenue, up from 4.5 per cent a year earlier, according to its interim results released on Tuesday evening. Still, the upbeat results came against a weak macroeconomic backdrop and fierce competition in the catering sector of the world’s second-largest consumer market, analysts said. “China’s restaurant industry is highly fragmented – chains hold roughly 20 per cent of the market versus around 40 per cent globally. That means a well-run chain like Haidilao can still gain share even in a soft macro environment,” said Ivan Su, director of equity research at Morningstar. “I expect Haidilao to deliver growth over the coming years because it has operational and supply chain advantages that give it better reach into lower-tier cities than most hotpot peers.” Over the six-month period, the group posted total revenue of 22.34 billion yuan, up 7.9 per cent year on year. Net profit rose 0.5 per cent to 1.77 billion yuan. The Haidilao brand’s dine-in customers spent an average of 97 yuan, little changed from a year earlier. It reported slow new-store openings in the first half, with faster expansion planned in 2027, including new restaurants in shopping malls in higher-tier cities and in the mass market in lower-tier cities, according to its earnings report. Haidilao operated 1,389 restaurants as of June, including 1,267 self-operated outlets in mainland China, and 23 in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan. The period saw 32 closures due to outdated facilities and underperformance. Following the return of founder Zhang Yong – a Singaporean citizen – as CEO in January, the group has ramped up investment in new growth initiatives. It has continued to expand its multi-brand business, spanning burger, sushi and street-style eateries. Revenue from this segment reached 1.27 billion yuan, jumping 113 per cent year on year. For the group’s other brands, the total number of restaurants rose to 183. The food-stall hotpot and sushi business formats were ready for large-scale replication and would be scaled up in the second half, the group said. It would also strategically pursue high-quality asset acquisitions to further diversify its catering portfolio. Beyond domestic multi-brand expansion, Haidilao continues to grow its overseas footprint. The brand operated 127 overseas restaurants as of March. Its first overseas store opened at Singapore’s Clarke Quay in 2012, but closed in August last year. It has expanded in markets including the US, the UK, South Korea, Japan and the United Arab Emirates. Shares of Haidilao jumped 7.3 per cent to HK$12.25 on Wednesday. Its share price has declined about 14 per cent this year.

title: Who is the late Dolly Parton’s sister, Rachel – co-author of their family cookbook?
description: The youngest of the 12 Parton siblings went on tour with the late Grammy-winning superstar known for ‘Jolene’, ‘The Bargain Store’ and other great country hits.
content: Revered worldwide as the “Queen of Country Music”, Dolly Parton passed away on Tuesday at age 80 after a brief battle with cancer. In honour of the superstar, US President Donald Trump ordered national flags across the country to fly at half-staff for a week. With a career spanning over six decades, Parton was an 11-time Grammy Award winner. She was married to her lifelong partner, Carl Thomas Dean, for nearly as long – until his passing in 2025 at age 82. View this post on Instagram Parton’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, released a statement on the singer’s Instagram account, mourning the loss on behalf of the Parton and Owens families, the latter being the late star’s maternal side of the family. Seaver also shared that the announcement was something that his aunt had asked of him “years ago”, admitting that, despite imagining the “heaviness of this moment”, he “[hasn’t] truly felt it until now”. In October 2025, Parton’s sister Freida sparked concern when she posted on Facebook that Dolly “hasn’t been feeling her best” and asked fans for prayers. The country icon quickly addressed the speculation in a video, assuring fans she was “not dying” and joking that she “ain’t done working” yet. At the time, Parton attributed her health issues to a kidney stone and the emotional toll of losing her husband. In 2024, Parton released a cookbook alongside her younger sister and lookalike, Rachel Parton George. Good Lookin’ Cookin’ serves as a tribute to the Parton family kitchen, featuring recipes inspired by the sisters’ late mother, Avie Lee Owens. “Dolly cooks quite a bit like our mother,” Rachel told The Hollywood Reporter when the book was released in September of that year, adding that it offered an opportunity for the sisters to “share memories and recipes”. Well, what’s cookin’, good lookin’? It’s our new cookbook! I wrote this book with my sister, Rachel, who might just be the best cook I know. If you’re like us, you believe that good food and good times are the next best thing to pure love. So take a journey with us, into the… pic.twitter.com/V2hYsqDFY1 — Dolly Parton (@DollyParton) March 6, 2024 Reminiscing about their family, Rachel said: “We often talk about mama, and then we’ll start talking about our aunts, our grandmothers, our dad, some of our brothers.” From cooking alongside the country music star to growing up as the youngest Parton sibling, here is a closer look at Rachel Parton George’s life. How big is the Parton family? The youngest of 12 siblings, Rachel Parton was born on August 31, 1959 – the same year her iconic sister released her debut single, “Puppy Love”, at age 13. Their parents, Avie Lee Owens and Robert Lee Parton Sr., raised the family in Locust Ridge, nestled in the Great Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee. The Partons grew up in a musical home Music was a way of life for the Parton family and for the youngest of the Parton clan it was just as ingrained. “Singing was like breathing at home,” Rachel once told People, reminiscing about how the siblings would spend their time “concocting songs”, their mother later transcribing the tunes for the whole family to sing after supper. She was Dolly Parton’s backing vocalist After eighth grade, Rachel left school to join Dolly on the road, supporting her sister with make-up, styling and backing vocals. “We’ve always gotten along really good … it was a joy all the way around to work on something creative together,” the late music legend previously told Allrecipes. Stepping into the spotlight herself, Rachel appeared in the television sitcom adaptation of 9 to 5, inspired by the eponymous 1980 film starring Dolly, Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda. Beyond acting, Rachel embraced her musical roots as the lead singer of Honey Creek – a band co-founded with her late brother, Randy – while regularly performing alongside her family’s musical ensemble. Who is Rachel Parton married to? In 1976, Rachel met husband-to-be Richard Dennison, who had been hired as Dolly’s pianist. According to People, they were hitched in 1979 but later divorced, though the exact date of their split isn’t known. Rachel eventually remarried, this time to Eric Wilson George, to whom she remains wed. Additional reporting by Varvara Rodchenko

title: Opinion | China’s multilateral pitch is finding an audience
description: Beijing’s push for global cooperation is clearly self-interested, but even US allies in the West can see the benefits of multilateralism.
content: As Washington increasingly turns away from the multilateral order it once helped build, Beijing is emerging as an advocate of international cooperation and rules-based stability. For some, the real surprise is that China’s rise is not challenging the world order but that its interests align with preserving it. When I met Foreign Minister Wang Yi in the corridor of a congress centre in Myanmar, he had just finished addressing more than 50 foreign ministers, emphasising the need for a multilateral, cooperative approach to our shared future. It was 2017, and the message was what you would expect in a ceremonial speech. Few in that hall could have imagined that less than a decade later, serious Western leaders would regard China as one of the foremost advocates of the international order. The years that have passed since then have left the world more volatile than it has been in decades, and the behaviour of its strongest actor has not worked in favour of stability. The United States, the chief architect of the post-war order and once the proud protector of international law, has been showing signs of losing its edge in more areas than it can peacefully accept. Washington’s increasingly erratic behaviour on the international scene has been met with disbelief by even its allies. There is a vacuum forming in global leadership. US withdrawals from a multitude of international organisations and US President Donald Trump’s tariff war against practically half the world made this obvious lately. The US is not isolating itself – it is as active internationally as ever. But instead of building coalitions and upholding well-established standards, it acts without any multilateral constraint, disintegrating said standards across the board. While Europe is weighed down by structural problems and its lack of a common voice, the Global South is gaining momentum. Still, China is not rushing to take the vacated spot of a global hegemon. On the contrary, it is calling for an end to this world order that has long been defined by domination. In Beijing’s view, the future is written through multilateral cooperation, respect for the international legal order and finding win-win solutions to all major global dilemmas. Beijing is not alone in the push for a multilateral global order. Western leaders such as French President Emmanuel Macron or Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez have reaffirmed multilateralism, and many seem to agree that Washington can no longer be treated as a global compass. This does not sit well with the US, whose pre-eminence on the global stage is now challenged. China is not simply the leading country in trade. According to the Australian Strategic Policy Institute’s Critical Technology Tracker, China now leads the US in 69 of 74 fields, and Washington appears to be countering this by building a “China threat” narrative. Critics of this modern Chinese multilateralism might argue that Beijing is only doing this out of self-interest. Of course it is, and that is a good thing; that means we know it is genuine. It is the logical consequence of becoming the world’s largest trading nation, deeply integrated into global supply chains and dependent on stable markets. China benefits more from predictable rules than from instability. In other words, Beijing’s commitment to multilateralism is convincing precisely because it aligns with China’s long-term national interest. It is interest-driven, just like it was interest-driven when the US stood for these values. The difference is that when diplomacy seemed too tedious, Washington used military interventionism. Beijing’s strategic culture prefers economic and diplomatic instruments. Just see the list of wars on one side and the comparative lack thereof on the other. Some in the West have long judged China through their own standards of governance styles, perhaps without sufficient context or insight into China’s past decades and believing a little too easily American narratives. Time is on the side of China, whose leaders can afford to follow generational strategies instead of brief election terms. One thing at least seems clear for the neutral spectator: today’s global challenges – from climate change to demographic tendencies, from extremism to inequality – are screaming for multilateral measures. There is no hegemon or form of dominance that will get us through these times in a sustainable manner.

title: ‘Smart’ diabetes probiotic; Chinese missile AI with 90% accuracy: 7 science highlights
description: From a proposed South China Sea robotic fortress to HIV cases at Wuhan port, here are some highlights from SCMP’s recent science reporting.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage on science from the past two weeks to help you stay informed. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Chinese team aims to put ‘smart’ diabetes probiotic on US shelves within 2 years Chinese researchers have engineered a probiotic that could make diabetes care as simple as drinking a cup of yogurt or swallowing a capsule. 2. Chinese missile AI tracks F-22, F-35-like heat signatures with over 90% accuracy The F-35 and F-22 may be among the world’s most advanced stealth fighters, but they cannot hide one thing: heat. When heat-seeking missiles lock onto aircraft, fighters release flares to confuse infrared sensors and break missile tracking. 3. Electrochemist Liu Jiawei moves from Singapore to Hong Kong to start her own lab For materials scientist and chemist Liu Jiawei, moving to Hong Kong supported her pivot into launching her own research group. After a decade immersed in Singapore’s research ecosystem, Liu sought a transition that would keep her closer to family in mainland China while maintaining an international, high-standard research environment. 4. Chinese coastguard proposes turning South China Sea isles into robotic fortress The South China Sea’s contested islands could be transformed into autonomous, robotic fortresses, according to a defence proposal by the Chinese coastguard. The plan, which was detailed in a Chinese-language journal supervised by the state-run China Shipbuilding Industry Corporation, envisions a maritime landscape defended by a coordinated swarm of machines instead of soldiers. 5. China’s drone production capacity can only meet 60% of war demand: study Even when fully mobilised, China’s industrial system would only be able to meet 60 per cent of the country’s military demand for drones in a conflict, according to a rare study looking into the expected effects of a sudden war. 6. International students account for most HIV cases detected at Wuhan port: study International students accounted for more than half of the HIV infections identified among individuals entering China through the city of Wuhan over the past few years, although the number of cases remained low, according to customs data. 7. Chinese stem cell therapy restores heart function in 90% of trial patients A hospital in east China has used reprogrammed stem cells to treat severe heart failure, with 90 per cent of patients showing significant recovery in heart function after the novel therapy.

title: Amos Food plans Hong Kong listing to expand global sweets empire
description: The confectionery firm’s Peelerz gummies have become a viral sensation on TikTok. Now, it aims to raise funds to expand its overseas presence.
content: Chinese confectionery giant Amos Food is seeking a listing in Hong Kong, as the firm looks to capitalise on the viral popularity of its sweets brands by ramping up investment in its overseas operations. Shenzhen-based Amos – known for its Peelerz peelable gummies and TastySounds music lollipops – has seen its sales soar over the past few years, especially in North America, where its sweets have become a sensation on the TikTok short video platform. The firm’s listing application, submitted to the Hong Kong stock exchange in April, remains under regulatory review, with the company yet to publish a post-hearing information pack or receive approval to launch the offering. “It is the latest case in which Hong Kong plays a key fundraising role in Chinese firms’ going-global drive,” said Ivy Chu Dang, an assistant professor of marketing at the University of Hong Kong Business School. “Hong Kong’s international capital market can help Amos reach a broader pool of global investors, particularly those familiar with cross-border consumer businesses and overseas growth strategies,” she added. “A successful listing could strengthen the company’s financing capacity and corporate-governance transparency, supporting its expansion in markets such as the United States while improving its distribution network and brand building.” Amos posted revenue of 2.78 billion yuan (US$410 million) in 2025, up 77 per cent from a year earlier, according to its listing application. Net profit more than tripled to 600 million yuan, from 198 million yuan in 2024 and 137 million yuan in 2023. More than 77 per cent of the company’s revenue came from overseas markets last year, as Amos expanded its sales network to more than 80 countries and regions. The company was China’s largest confectionery maker by global retail sales value over the period. North America was its largest market in 2025, generating 52.7 per cent of total revenue. Amos said it had established strategic relationships with major global retailers including Walmart, Costco, Sam’s Club, Target and 7-Eleven, covering product development, distribution and end sales. A new Chinese brand should not only be liked by Chinese consumers, but should also become a Chinese brand loved around the world Ma Enduo, Amos Food Amos has yet to confirm its fundraising target for its Hong Kong listing. JPMorgan, Bank of America Securities and China Merchants Securities International are serving as joint sponsors and overall coordinators. The company plans to use the proceeds to expand manufacturing capacity in China and overseas, deepen its distribution and marketing presence in North America and Europe, invest in research and product development, upgrade its digital systems and pursue potential acquisitions. Beyond selling its own brands, Amos operates an original design manufacturer business, developing and producing third-party branded confectionery for retailers and consumer companies. The model provides Amos with market feedback that it can use to track consumer preferences and refine its own products. Amos’ third-party branded products generated 614 million yuan of revenue in 2025, accounting for 22.1 per cent of total sales, down from 37.2 per cent in 2023, as Amos’s own brands became a larger contributor. The company’s founder, Ma Enduo, has said his ambition is not merely to manufacture products for overseas brands, but to build a Chinese confectionery name recognised by consumers worldwide. “A new Chinese brand should not only be liked by Chinese consumers, but should also become a Chinese brand loved around the world,” he told the Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, adding that Amos’ mission was to become “the world’s messenger of sweetness”. To diversify its production base, Amos is building its first overseas factory in Vietnam. The plant is designed to have an annual capacity of 13,300 tonnes and is expected to begin operations in late 2026. Amos said the project would support its “China plus one” manufacturing strategy and strengthen the resilience of its global supply chain.

title: Brain-tech push gains pace as China draws up standards and firms challenge Neuralink
description: Dozens of guidelines are coming, covering medical, industrial and consumer users as emerging neural technology moves towards wider adoption.
content: China is drawing up an extensive set of standards for brain-computer interface technology, seeking to accelerate the commercialisation of a field in which Chinese start-ups are increasingly competing with Elon Musk’s Neuralink for global leadership. Under draft guidelines released by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), Beijing aims to formulate or revise more than 40 standards by 2028 and encourage at least 100 companies to adopt them. It also plans to lead or participate in the development of more than 10 international standards. By 2030, China aims to have developed more than 80 standards, creating a comprehensive framework for the domestic industry while increasing its influence over global rules for the emerging neural technology. Brain-computer interfaces allow the mind to communicate directly with external devices. Their potential uses range from restoring movement and speech in people with disabilities to controlling computers, industrial machinery and consumer electronics. China has identified brain-computer interface technology as one of six “industries of the future” under its 15th five-year plan, as the country looks to nurture domestic competitors in a field where Neuralink is widely regarded as the commercial front runner. Domestically, China has leading neural-tech firms such as Neuracle, which has won approval for an implanted system that helps paralysed patients regain hand movement, as well as StairMed and NeuroXess, which focus on invasive implants and the interpretation of neural signals, and BrainCo, which develops non-invasive devices and brain-controlled prosthetics. Additionally, the municipalities of Beijing and Tianjin, along with Hebei province, have launched a joint initiative to strengthen the brain-computer technology supply chain, focusing on electrodes, chips, systems and algorithms. On Wednesday, Tianjin’s market regulator said the initiative was designed to promote closer regional cooperation and support industry development. The MIIT said on Tuesday that the technology was entering a critical stage of commercialisation and broader adoption, making common standards essential to “guide innovation and ensure the industry’s orderly development”. Its proposed framework spans hardware, software, data, products, commercial applications and safety, establishing common benchmarks for technologies that draw on fields as diverse as neuroscience, semiconductors, artificial intelligence and clinical medicine. The draft divides products using the technology into six categories: medical devices, industrial production, consumer electronics, personal health, scientific research and integrated applications. It proposes technical standards for uses ranging from industrial control and hazardous operations to brain-controlled gaming and immersive virtual and augmented reality. For hardware, the guidelines cover the safety and durability of implanted electrodes, the accuracy and energy efficiency of chips and other components, and the reliability of equipment used to monitor, stimulate and communicate with the brain. Common standards should make research findings easier to compare, improve compatibility between hardware and software Citic Securities Citic Securities said in a research note on Wednesday that clearer standards should make neural technologies easier to evaluate and integrate across the supply chain, benefiting companies with strong technological, manufacturing and testing capabilities. Medical applications are given particular attention in the framework, which covers both implanted and non-invasive systems designed to diagnose neurological conditions, support rehabilitation and restore functions such as movement, speech and vision. Potential applications include the treatment of epilepsy, Parkinson’s disease, strokes, spinal cord injuries and depression. Products classified as medical devices would remain subject to existing laws and regulatory requirements, the ministry said. The guidelines also address how brain data should be stored, shared and analysed, while seeking to ensure that different devices, algorithms and software systems can work together. “Common standards should make research findings easier to compare, improve compatibility between hardware and software, and reduce the cost of connecting technologies developed by different companies,” the Citic Securities note said. The brokerage added that clearer benchmarks for product design, safety testing and clinical evaluation could also improve cooperation among companies, hospitals and testing institutions, helping turn experimental neural systems into products suitable for clinical use. China’s brain-computer technology industry is expected to be worth between 10 billion yuan (US$1.49 billion) and 14 billion yuan by 2030, according to estimates by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology.

title: Shein set for Hong Kong stock listing amid controversies and competition
description: The fast-fashion giant eyes a US$27 billion valuation while facing scrutiny and challenges.
content:
Shein, the Chinese-founded retailer that harnessed social media to chart a meteoric rise in the global fast-fashion industry, will debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange next month in a long-awaited listing that values the group at close to US$27 billion.
Here’s what you need to know about the clothing giant, which has faced allegations of labour and environmental abuses as well as regulatory scrutiny abroad.
Shein’s main competitive advantage lies in its ability to offer a staggering variety of items on its platform – backed up by hyper-efficient product development and supply chains.
Customers love the firm’s massive catalogue of ultra-cheap items at a time when inflation has shrunk purchasing power around the world.
The firm moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022 – a move analysts say was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.
But it still benefits from China’s unique combination of a huge low-cost textile manufacturing sector and a highly sophisticated e-commerce logistics network.
The company tracks users’ search data and social media trends to generate designs with a high likelihood of attracting demand – often appearing to simply copy from other brands.
The rapid growth achieved by Shein was driven in large part by its success in marketing its products on social media – particularly on the short-form video app TikTok.
As internet usage worldwide peaked during the pandemic, the firm developed a strategy that enlisted small-scale video bloggers and ordinary social media users to represent the brand in exchange for free products and cash.
It quickly built a loyal following of customers in the US and elsewhere, with many taking part in a trend of posting videos of their “Shein haul” of new clothes online.
But that strategy has also bred controversy, with a sponsored factory tour for a group of Western influencers in 2023 sparking a strong backlash for glossing over alleged labour violations.
Today, Shein’s challenges are compounded by increasingly tough competition from rival low-cost e-commerce giant Temu.
Like other fast-fashion giants including H&M and Zara, Shein has faced allegations of underpaying and overworking textile workers at its factories.
The firm has also been accused of obscuring its production processes from the public eye.
In 2024, the European Union added Shein to its list of digital companies that are big enough to be subject to stricter safety curbs.
Another hurdle arose in February of this year, when the European Commission launched an investigation into the firm’s compliance with the Digital Services Act.
Areas assessed by the probe include the firm’s systems for preventing the sale of illegal products, risks associated with its “addictive design” and the transparency of its content recommendations, the Commission said.
Others say the company’s super-cheap products and frenzied online marketing encourage a culture of overconsumption to the detriment of the environment.
A ranking last year by US-Canadian campaign group Stand Earth placed Shein tied for last place on a list of over 40 major fashion brands in terms of their environmental practices.
In the boldest move yet globally to curb the rise of fast fashion, France is set to impose per-item fees on Shein, Temu and other platforms deemed by the legislation to engage in “ultra-fast fashion”.
The tsunami of parcels generated by low-cost e-commerce giants has also been dealt a fresh blow by the scrapping of US tax exemptions for individual shipments valued less than US$800.
Shein says it conducts regular third-party audits to ensure fair wages and that its on-demand model avoids overproduction, thereby “dramatically reduces waste”.

title: Nepal flash flood kills at least 157, leaves hundreds of tourists missing
description: The overspill from the Bhotekoshi River caused power cuts, damaged roads and power projects near the country’s border with Tibet.
content: A huge wall of mud ⁠and rock collapsed into a river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and China’s Tibet on Wednesday, triggering catastrophic flooding on the Nepali side that killed scores of people and left hundreds of tourists missing. In a still-unfolding disaster, verified videos showed dozens of people swept away at the border, with authorities on both sides fearing far higher casualties and massive destruction. Houses, roads and power projects were washed away in Nepal, while officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border land crossing in the county of Gyirong. “It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us. As it got closer, ‌it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud,” said Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor, who was being treated at a small hospital. “Four or five hours later, a helicopter came to rescue me. My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud. She’s gone.” Another survivor described being saved by clinging to a mango tree as he watched the house where he had been working disappear. Initial reports from Nepali officials suggested an earthquake in the area could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger the floods. As darkness fell, authorities continued the grim task of recovering and trying to identify bodies. Some 157 bodies had been recovered so far, Nepal police said late on Wednesday. Officials at Nepal’s tourism ministry told media outlets that ⁠over 400 tourists are missing, of whom around 340 are foreigners. Sunil Sharma, a Nepal tourism board spokesman, told Associated Press that 133 of the tourists were from India on a pilgrimage. He said 47 of the missing tourists were from the US, ‌34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 24 from Canada. A US State Department spokesman said: “The State Department is aware of Americans impacted by the floods in Nepal and is closely tracking the situation.” Canada was also closely following the situation, said Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on social media, calling the floods “absolutely devastating”. The region lies on a popular route to Kailash Manasarovar in Tibet, a site ‌visited annually by hundreds of Hindu pilgrims from India and elsewhere, particularly at this time of year. China’s state broadcaster said three people were killed and 265 missing in Gyirong. It said the toll ⁠was still being verified and rescue efforts were ongoing. South Korea separately ⁠said that eight of its nationals working on a hydropower plant were missing. Security footage captured on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border showed many people fleeing before a torrent of rock, mud and water destroyed buildings and vehicles and took many lives. The German Research Centre for ‌Geosciences said there was a 4.4-magnitude quake around seven minutes before the time shown on the security footage time-stamp. Locals from the affected areas of Nuwakot and Dhading were seen gathering outside a Nepali army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members. Police were recording the names of the missing just ‌outside the ‌barracks gate, using mobile phone flashlights as their only source of light as the area remained without electricity due to damaged hydropower infrastructure. In the affected areas, houses, trees and vehicles were submerged or buried in mudslides. Helicopters hovered overhead all day in the ‌area bringing in survivors. An initial study of Planet Labs satellite imagery indicated that a landslide of ice and rock triggered a debris-laden flood in the Lhende River, about 20km (12 miles) northeast of the Nepal-China Rasuwagadhi border crossing, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction ⁠and Management Authority said on social media. Rescue helicopters could not land in Nepal’s affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa, with a population of about 50,000, officials said, with the river flowing above its normal course. Television ⁠images showed collapsed homes, floating cars and a metal bridge being washed away, while witnesses told Reuters the waters engulfed entire villages. “There is devastation everywhere we look,” said Tula Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa. “The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing.” China’s official Xinhua news agency said the mudslide hit the Gyirong port, cutting roads, communications and power links in the Shigatse ‌region near the border. A rescuer interviewed by Chinese state broadcaster ‌CCTV said they had been trying to establish contact with the Gyirong border port but “so far there haven’t been any results”. All roads leading to the border crossing had been “completely destroyed” after a preliminary inspection with a drone, the rescuer added. With the deluge of muddy water sweeping down from an estimated nearly 2,000 metres (6,560 feet) above sea level, flood alerts were issued in the populous northern Indian states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, which border Nepal and where several rivers flow down the mountains into the plains. Authorities in Bihar said they had evacuated about 5,000 people from six districts and planned to evacuate a total of 10,000 to 12,000 people.

title: Zelensky urges China to use its diplomatic weight to end Russia’s war with Ukraine
description: Kyiv releases Chinese president’s Independence Day greeting as top envoy urges broader Black Sea security cooperation.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged China to play a “strong diplomatic role” to help end the war between Russia and Ukraine, bolstering his call by highlighting national day congratulations from Chinese President Xi Jinping. “We count on further cooperation and on China playing a strong diplomatic role in bringing Russia’s war against our country to an end,” the Ukrainian leader wrote on social media on Wednesday. “Peace can be our shared achievement.” In his posts, Zelensky attached copies of Chinese and Ukrainian versions of a letter Xi sent to congratulate Ukraine on its Independence Day. It is the second consecutive year Beijing has sent Kyiv such a public congratulatory message following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Beijing has not published the latest letter. Xi and Zelensky last spoke during a phone call in April 2023. “China-Ukraine friendship serves the fundamental interests of both peoples. China is ready to work with Ukraine to continue upholding the principles of mutual respect and equality and mutual benefit to promote the long-term, healthy and stable development of bilateral relations,” Xi said in the letter posted by Zelensky. More than four years into the Russia-Ukraine war, ground fighting continues and the humanitarian crisis is worsening, with no major diplomatic breakthrough in sight. China’s position on the conflict has remained under close international scrutiny, while its closer partnership with Russia has been seen as a major stumbling block in its efforts to mend ties with the European Union amid its strategic rivalry with the United States. China has repeatedly affirmed that its relationship with Russia is not directed at any third party and that it consistently supports a political settlement of the war through dialogue and negotiations. “Dialogue and negotiations are the only viable way to resolve the Ukraine issue,” Fu Cong, Beijing’s permanent representative to the United Nations, told a Security Council session on Monday. He said China had maintained “close communication with the parties concerned”. In an article published on the Ukrainian embassy website on Sunday, Kyiv’s top envoy to Beijing, Olexander Nechytaylo, urged China to play “a more active role” in advancing the peace process, protecting global food security, restoring a reliable grain corridor in the Black Sea and guaranteeing freedom of civilian navigation. “Ukraine is convinced that China has sufficient international weight, political authority, and diplomatic tools to make its contribution to bringing peace closer, more tangible,” he wrote. “We are open to a substantive dialogue with China on ways to achieve a just peace. Such a dialogue must be based on realities, international law and respect for the legitimate interests of the Ukrainian people.” In a note posted on social media on August 18, Ding Xiaoxing, a research professor at the Beijing-based China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, wrote that neither Russia nor Ukraine was likely to achieve a complete military victory in the long run. The “spirit of Anchorage” – a vague claim of progress said to come out of a summit between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, in Alaska a year ago for a settlement – appeared to have failed, he said. “[That process] over-relied on unilateral mediation by major powers, ignored the core interests of all parties and lacked a binding mechanism”, added Ding, who also serves as deputy secretary general of the academic committee at the think tank affiliated with the Ministry of State Security, China’s top intelligence agency.

title: Where an izakaya owner in Hong Kong goes for Japanese food, noodles and congee
description: Clement Wong is a fan of comfort food, and has a few regular Hong Kong haunts for Italian, Chinese and Japanese dishes.
content: Clement Wong is the co-founder of lamb-focused izakaya concepts Mt Yotei and Kyanbasu. He spoke to Andrew Sun. I love to try all types of food, whether it’s fine dining or street food, regardless of its origin. Growing up, I was fortunate to travel and study abroad, which gave me the opportunity to learn about different cultures – and at the heart of every culture, I believe, is its food. But my all-time favourite is still my grandma’s cooking – always warm, heartfelt and delicious. When I eat out, I tend to stick to a few spots specialising in comfort foods. My father’s office was in Sheung Wan and Sang Kee Congee Shop (7-9 Burd Street, Sheung Wan. Tel: 2541 1099) was the place he would take me for fish belly congee. The fish is incredibly fresh, with an almost silky texture. Mak’s Noodle (77 Wellington Street, Central. Tel: 2854 3810) does the best wonton noodles in Hong Kong, but it is pricey. The savoury dried flounder broth is superb, and each wonton is perfectly sized with just the right amount of filling. Dieci (B/F, 29-31 Gough Street, Central. Tel: 9077 2629) does family-style Italian cuisine that is simple, comforting and delicious. Ankôma (16/F, Cubus, 1 Hoi Ping Road, Causeway Bay. Tel: 2981 1688) is a Japanese-inspired French restaurant led by the very talented Frankie Wong – who was given Michelin Guide Hong Kong and Macau’s Young Chef award in 2025 – with great attention to detail. The food is innovative, well balanced and elegantly finished. Torikaze (43-45/F, Forty-Five, Gloucester Tower, Landmark Atrium, 15 Queen’s Road Central, Central. Tel: 3501 8585) is my favourite yakitori spot. The skewers have a strong, smoky charcoal flavour and are grilled to perfection by Matsui-san and his team. I would take visitors to Right Tea-rific (Shop D, G/F, Harvard Commercial Building, 105-111 Thomson Road, Wan Chai. Tel: 6805 1818), which elevates classic cha chaan teng dishes with a refined touch and premium ingredients – such as using Ranou eggs from Japan for their sandwiches and egg tarts. For dinner, it has to be hotpot. Big JJ Seafood Hotpot (Basement, Landmark Prince’s) is my top choice, thanks to its fresh ingredients, great atmosphere and excellent wine selection. For a splurge, Cristal Room by Anne-Sophie Pic (44/F, Forty-Five. Tel: 3501 8580) offers great views, paired with excellent interior design, outstanding food and a top-notch service team. It’s my go-to for both celebrations and formal business dinners. I visit Shanghai at least twice a year to catch up with friends and to savour hairy crab. I had a memorable meal at Ling Long (105, 1/F, Waldorf Astoria Hotel, 2 Zhongshan Dong Yi Road, Huangpu, Shanghai. Tel: +86 21 2329 0313). I really enjoyed how they smartly and subtly incorporate different seasonal Chinese ingredients, presenting them in a refined and elegant way. In Tokyo, Hakunei (4-9-11 Nishiazabu, Minato-ku, Tokyo. Tel: +81 90 8946 3919) is a modern French fine-dining restaurant, headed by incredibly talented chef Dai Hayashi. His cooking achieves a perfect balance between textures and flavours. They also boast an excellent wine list, featuring a selection of rare Japanese wines.

title: Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh City plans low-emission zone to clear downtown air
description: Vietnam’s business hub aims to phase out petrol and diesel transport from central areas by mid-2027, starting with buses and delivery fleets.
content: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam’s commercial ⁠hub, is proposing ⁠to gradually restrict ⁠petrol- and diesel-powered vehicles from its downtown area from mid-2027, as part of a planned low-emission zone (LEZ), according to state-run Thanh Nien newspaper. Under the proposal, the ‌city would pilot the LEZ from July 2027 in its core downtown area and the new Thu Thiem urban area, covering roughly 930 hectares (2,300 acres), Thanh Nien reported, citing city authorities. From early 2029, the LEZ will expand to within the ⁠city’s Ring Road 2, an area that already ‌restricts heavy trucks and sleeper buses from the inner city during certain hours. The new ‌timeline is later than a previous proposal, in which the ⁠implementation of ⁠the LEZ was set to begin early this year. The revised plan adjusts the ‌scope and some milestones to align with the launch of green transport infrastructure and ‌give residents and ‌businesses more time to switch vehicles. Buses are the ‌first group required to convert, and will need to use electricity ⁠or clean energy when entering the LEZ starting in 2027. Motorcycle-taxi drivers ⁠and delivery riders will follow, while other categories such as taxis face later deadlines. The proposal remains subject to ‌further review before ‌it is formally approved. Hanoi said in June it also planned to phase out petrol-powered ride-hailing motorbikes from low-emission zones, beginning with voluntary restrictions and moving to a ban from January 2027.

title: North Korean athletes ‘determined to bring joy’ to Kim Jong-un at 2026 Asian Games
description: The delegation of about 100 people would be smaller than the one sent to the Hangzhou Games in 2023, where the country won 11 golds.
content: North Korea will send about 100 athletes to compete across 14 sports at the Asian Games in Japan next month, a senior official said, aiming to “bring joy to Marshal Kim Jong-un”. The nuclear-armed state suspended participation in international sporting competitions during the Covid pandemic but returned at the Asian Games in China in 2023, and also took part in the Paris Olympics. The team for the regional Games in Nagoya and the Aichi region include two Japan-based ethnic Koreans competing in women’s football and karate, Ko Chol-ho, secretary general of North Korea’s Olympic committee, said. “Our delegation will send more than 100 athletes to compete in 14 sports, including men’s and women’s football, weightlifting, boxing and wrestling,” Ko told Choson Sinbo, a pro-North Korean publication based in Japan, during an interview in Pyongyang. “We are making every effort, driven by a strong desire to live up to the expectations of our country and people by achieving even greater results at the upcoming Games,” the official said, in remarks published Tuesday. He noted that the delegation would be smaller than the one sent to the Hangzhou Games in 2023 but said he hoped it would win more medals. Authoritarian North Korea won 11 golds last time, half of them in weightlifting. The official said that morale among the athletes was high for the event, which runs from September 19 to October 4, and they were motivated to win for their leader. “Our athletes are training tirelessly every day, determined to bring joy to Marshal Kim,” he said.

title: Monk remanded after alleged theft of Monkey King statue from Hong Kong temple
description: Court documents state that Zha Jianxin, a Shenzhen-based two-way permit holder, allegedly took the statue from Lung Mo Temple on August 24.
content: A mainland Chinese Buddhist monk has been remanded in custody after allegedly stealing a statue of the Monkey King, a deity famed in classic Chinese novel Journey to the West, from a Hong Kong temple. The 57-year-old, Zha Jianxin, appeared in West Kowloon Court on Wednesday after being charged with one count of theft involving the statue belonging to Lung Mo Temple in Tsuen Wan. The statue, valued at HK$2,000 (US$255), depicts Sun Wukong, the mythological Monkey King from the 16th century novel. In Chinese culture, the character is often seen as a symbol of resilience, rebellion, transformation and spiritual growth. Court documents state that Zha holds a two-way permit and lives in Shenzhen. He allegedly took the statue from the temple on August 24. Zha did not apply for bail at the hearing but told Magistrate Amy Chan Wai-mun he wished to make a phone call to a fellow monk. His lawyer said the defendant was due to help a friend by chanting sutras but could not because of the case. The magistrate granted the request and ordered Zha to remain in custody. The next hearing is scheduled for September 23.

title: Indonesia opens its skies to Malaysian rainmakers as haze crisis deepens
description: Joint cloud seeding efforts offer immediate relief from the haze, but experts warn fire prevention at source is the real battle.
content: Indonesia and Malaysia have agreed to share the skies amid a haze crisis that has closed nearly 600 Malaysian schools and erased much of the Kuala Lumpur skyline from view. The Petronas Twin Towers, usually visible for miles around, have been swallowed by a grey shroud as wildfires that continue to rage across Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan on the island of Borneo. Authorities from both countries are coordinating operations along their shared Bornean border, with Malaysia’s environment minister confirming that Jakarta has granted permission for joint cloud-seeding operations to tackle the worsening transboundary haze. Malaysia’s national disaster management agency and its meteorological department are scheduling work in border areas, with operations to be coordinated by the Indonesian military. Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Arthur Joseph Kurup said in a statement on Monday that 16 areas in Malaysia had recorded unhealthy air pollutant index (API) readings as of 10am on August 26. He warned that the El Nino weather phenomenon was expected to intensify by October, coinciding with the southwest monsoon, adding that both nations had pledged to step up preventive measures and early firefighting efforts. “Malaysia stands ready to extend assistance to the Republic of Indonesia at any time, should it be required for immediate firefighting efforts,” Kurup said. In Malaysia, API readings between 0 and 50 indicate good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy and above 300 is classed as hazardous. Three locations in Sarawak state had logged API levels above 160 as of Wednesday. In Peninsular Malaysia, Negeri Sembilan state reached 162, Kuala Lumpur and Cheras recorded 159, and Putrajaya registered 158. Another 52 areas remained at moderate levels, with only Kangar in Perlis and the Langkawi archipelago in Kedah recording good air quality. On Friday, nearly 600 schools in Sarawak were forced to close as pollution reached “very unhealthy” levels, affecting almost 200,000 pupils. View on Threads Malaysians took to social media to vent their frustration, posting side-by-side photos comparing clear views of the capital’s landmarks with the smog-choked skyline, while urging employers to reinstate work-from-home arrangements from the pandemic era. “It’s OK to allow work from home and online classes for a while instead of forcing people to inhale haze,” one person wrote. Others complained of sore throats and other illnesses caused by the smog. “The Twin Towers are gone from my view, and my throat hurts,” another user wrote. Indonesia has been battling severe wildfires across multiple provinces since earlier this month. Dozens of people suspected of starting some of the blazes have been arrested. Prabowo’s promised crackdown Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has vowed firm action against corporate offenders found responsible for the fires. “We will go after them if they are proven guilty. We will penalise them according to the law,” he told reporters in Palangka Raya, Central Kalimantan. The president flew to West and Central Kalimantan on Saturday to assess the destruction and coordinate emergency responses. Indonesian forest ministry data shows more than 2,000 square km (770 square miles) of land burned between January and July, with nearly 950 square km (366 square miles) affected in last month alone. Six provinces – including Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra and parts of Kalimantan on Borneo – have been designated priority zones for emergency response, with fires also breaking out in Java, Papua and Nusa Tenggara. Thousands of personnel, water-bombing helicopters and cloud-seeding aircraft have been deployed nationwide. Indonesian police have named 72 arson suspects, 14 of them in Kalimantan, and four companies in West Kalimantan are now under investigation over land burning. Under Indonesian laws passed in 1999 and 2009, deliberate burning carries penalties of up to 10 years in prison and heavy fines. Regional climate experts argue that Asean’s consensus-based approach continues to limit the effectiveness of regional responses, despite the bloc adopting a legally binding transboundary haze agreement two decades ago. The Association of Southeast Nations signed the Asean agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution in 2002 and it came into force a year later, but Indonesia – the main source of regional smog – did not ratify the pact until 2014. “Haze does not respect national borders, and neither should our response,” said Renard Siew, a climate change adviser at the Malaysia-based Centre for Governance and Political Studies, welcoming the cross-border move. While cloud seeding could help induce rainfall under the right atmospheric conditions, Siew said it could not replace fire prevention at the source. “Prevention must become the priority rather than responding only when the haze has already crossed borders,” he said, urging Asean to leverage the transboundary agreement signed more than two decades ago.

title: Shellfish thieves in Australia make off with 400,000 oysters worth US$250,000
description: The oyster farm, which lost a third of its stock, says it will not be able to replenish in time for Christmas.
content: Australian police said on Wednesday they were on the hunt for thieves who made off with hundreds of thousands of oysters. The molluscs have an estimated total value of A$350,000 (US$250,000) and were lifted from an oyster farm near the town of Taree, north of Sydney, New South Wales police said. Over 300 bags, containing 400,000 oysters, were stolen. Police are urging the public to come forward with any information they might have about the theft, which they said happened “earlier this year” but was reported to them only on Tuesday. Oysters are a staple of brunch menus and seafood buffets across Australia, with local varieties famed for their rich, creamy flavour.
