Oyster grower Ryan Freeman told national broadcaster ABC he had lost a third of his stock. “We probably get through 35,000 to 40,000 dozen at Christmas time. That’s why the thieves would have targeted them because they’re not going to be far off, they’re going to be able to sell them this Christmas,” he said. “It’s going to have a massive impact.” There was not enough time to look for more stock, he told the broadcaster. “It takes three to four years to grow a Sydney rock oyster,” he said. “I understand everyone is [having] it tough, but I don’t believe stealing and taking from someone else is going to help someone else; all you’ve done is take someone else out for a small reward and high risk,” he said. “It’s going to take us a few years to recover and all they’ve done is put us back another two to three years.” Additional reporting by SCMP’s Asia desk

title: China’s BeiDou satellite navigation system covers 90% of ‘key industry’ uses: ministry
description: 39 pilot cities added 2.96 million BeiDou positioning terminals in first half of this year, up 30 per cent year on year.
content: China’s BeiDou satellite navigation system – its home-grown alternative to the US-run Global Positioning System – has been adopted in about 90 per cent of “key industry” applications nationwide, according to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. In a social media post on Wednesday that also reposted a report by state broadcaster CCTV, the ministry said BeiDou’s comprehensive application penetration rate across key industries had reached about 90 per cent. Further detail on which sectors constituted “key industries” was not provided. In its post, the ministry said it had launched a pilot programme in 2024 to promote the large-scale application of BeiDou across the Chinese economy. In the first half of this year, 39 cities taking part in the pilot programme had added 2.96 million BeiDou stand-alone positioning terminals, up about 30 per cent from the same period last year, the ministry said. It added that several cities had achieved 100 per cent adoption of BeiDou in specific areas, including shared bicycles, taxis, government vehicles and agricultural machinery. By the first half of this year, 39 pilot cities had deployed more than 12 million BeiDou-enabled stand-alone positioning terminals, the ministry said, with more than 7.2 million in consumer applications, over 4.6 million in industrial manufacturing and more than 1 million in integrated innovation. The post quoted Li Xiayu, an engineer at the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, as saying that while BeiDou’s application continued to deepen in sectors including transport, public safety and smart agriculture, the system was also expanding rapidly into consumer products. BeiDou positioning had “basically become standard” in smartphones, smart wearables and in-vehicle terminals, Li added. The ministry said more than 98 per cent of the 133 million mobile phones shipped in the domestic market in the first half of this year supported BeiDou positioning. By the end of last year, cumulative shipments of domestically made BeiDou-compatible chips and modules had reached nearly 2.6 billion units, while more than 2.2 billion BeiDou-enabled terminals and other products were in use nationwide. While BeiDou has established a dominant position in the Chinese market and is deeply integrated into domestic infrastructure, Beijing is also pushing for wider international adoption to offer an alternative to Western-led systems like GPS and the European Union’s Galileo. The BeiDou system recently completed a comprehensive upgrade, Xinhua reported late last month. The upgrade focused on replacing older satellites with newer, third-generation models and realigning their orbital paths to allow more comprehensive global coverage, according to a document released by the China Satellite Navigation Office in late March. BeiDou’s overseas users are currently mostly concentrated in countries taking part in the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s infrastructure-forward strategy for regional connectivity. For instance, the system is used for ship navigation and port scheduling in the Middle East, and in the agricultural and transport sectors in Central Asia.

title: Hong Kong man loses HK$2.8 million in investment scam, among 50 cases in past week
description: Fraudsters conned victim in his sixties into investing in fraudulent ‘recyclable waste project’ by energy giants in Hong Kong, mainland China.
content: A Hong Kong man has lost more than HK$2.8 million (US$357,000) in an online investment scam in which fraudsters claiming to be employees of electricity companies duped him into investing in a “recyclable waste project”. Police also said on Wednesday that the force had recorded 50 investment scams in the past week, with the total losses exceeding HK$30 million. The force said the man, who is in his sixties, became acquainted with one of the scammers on Facebook. The fraudster claimed to be an employee of CLP Power, one of Hong Kong’s electricity suppliers. The scammer said the company was collaborating with the State Grid Corporation of China, a state-owned electricity supplier, on a “recyclable waste project”, describing it in messages without providing any official websites. The victim then transferred HK$1.5 million to different bank accounts on the scammer’s instructions. “When the victim raised doubts, the fraudster kept on boasting that the project had a high return, displaying a handwritten statement that no deception was involved and a picture of a forged Hong Kong identity card to reassure the victim and induce him to transfer another HK$1 million,” police said. Later, another fraudster claiming to be a State Grid employee contacted the victim on WhatsApp and sent him images of a forged staff card and a fake HK$9 million cheque, claiming the project had yielded profits. The scammer demanded further payments from the man before he could receive the “dividends”, which led the victim to believe he had been scammed. According to the force, the man lost more than HK$2.8 million to the scammers. Police said residents should verify the identities of company employees through official channels before making investments and should not disclose sensitive personal data to others, including those claiming to be “internal employees” of any organisation. “Never trust investments claiming ‘high returns with zero risk’ [and] never transfer money to unknown personal bank accounts,” it added.

title: At least 14 newborns die in Pakistan hospital fire triggered by air-con fault
description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has directed authorities to conduct an immediate investigation into the fire at the state-run hospital.
content: At least 14 infants were killed ‌in a fire at a state-run hospital in Pakistan’s capital of Islamabad on Wednesday, the prime minister said, with local media blaming the tragedy on a fault in the air conditioning system. The blaze started around 7am at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, on the third floor of the hospital’s ⁠mother and child health ward, said broadcaster Geo TV, which put the death toll ‌at 15. Islamabad chief commissioner Sohail Ashraf said on social media that rescue teams, specialists, police and himself “immediately reached the site and controlled the fire”. “Give me my child,” Javeria, who lost her newborn, said outside the hospital, where ambulances had gathered. “I want justice.” The incident ‌is among the deadliest hospital fires in recent years in the country, ⁠where government healthcare ⁠is subsidised but facilities are under-resourced and overburdened while watchdogs have frequently criticised state-run facilities as mismanaged. There were ‌16 newborns in the ward when the fire broke out, one of whom was rescued, Geo reported. Prime ‌Minister ‌Shehbaz Sharif’s office said he had directed authorities to conduct an immediate investigation. The ward ‌was cordoned off, a witness said. Mudasir, another parent who also lost ⁠his child, said all doors of the ward, except one, were shut and that ⁠there was “no fire security” in the ward. Javeria and Mudasir both gave only their first names. There was no immediate comment from the hospital or authorities ‌on the incident. Centrally located in Islamabad, the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, where former prime ‌minister Imran Khan was ‌briefly treated last week, is one of the main public hospitals in the city of around 1.1 million people. Fires in large buildings are frequent in Pakistan, often due to poor safety laws and building codes as well as lax enforcement. In January, more than 65 people were killed in a shopping centre fire in the port city of Karachi. At least 11 people were killed in another shopping centre fire in Karachi in 2023. In 2021, at least 16 workers died after a factory fire in the same city. In 2012, at least 250 labourers died at a garment factory in Baldia Town, in western Karachi, when a fire engulfed the facility. The building had no fire escape. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: China dividend stocks back in vogue as AI trade fizzles out and bond yields fall
description: Shanghai bourse dividend index shows growth of 4.1 per cent for energy, banking and transport industry stocks, beating AI’s 0.2 per cent loss.
content: Chinese investors have been seeking shelter in dividend stocks in the wake of a global rout on technology stocks, with a handful of old-economy companies beating chipmakers and artificial intelligence hardware manufacturers. The Shanghai Stock Exchange Dividend Index of 50 high-dividend stocks from the energy, banking and transport industries has risen 4.1 per cent this month, trouncing a 0.2 per cent decline in the chip-heavy Star Market 50 index. If the momentum holds up, it will extend the outperformance of the dividend index to a second consecutive month. The gauge jumped 13 per cent in July, while the tech index slumped 26 per cent for its biggest monthly decline on record. The disparity underscores broader trends, as local investors turn cautious about the AI trade and defensive in positioning outsized gains, seeking safer bets to place their investments as some headwinds against technology stocks still lingered. Meanwhile, dividend stocks have also become more attractive after China’s worse-than-expected July economic data rapidly drove sovereign bond yields lower on expectations about further policy easing. “The rebound in dividend stocks is a result of more visible interim results, repair of excessive declines and a rebalancing of investment styles after the tech rout,” said Zhao Yang, an analyst at Sealand Securities. “The gains are concentrated on resources companies, such as coal and petrochemicals.” The dividend index of the 50 stocks on the Shanghai exchange is dominated by traditional industries. The coal and oil sector accounts for 32 per cent of the weighting, followed by the banking industry with a 29 per cent representation and transport with 14 per cent, according to the fact sheet posted on the website of the Shanghai bourse, the index compiler. The biggest constituent is Cosco Shipping, with a 5.08 per cent weighting. Coal producer Yankuang Energy ranked second with 3.33 per cent, followed by Shanghai Zhonggu Logistics with 3.31 per cent. The dividend index now returns an average of 4.08 per cent in the dividend yield, its fact sheet showed. That compares with 1.682 per cent for the yield on China’s 10-year government bond, currently trading around a one-year low. Still, the gauge has trailed the Star Market 50 index this year, rising 10 per cent versus the 22 per cent gain in the benchmark of tech stocks. After July’s turbulence, Chinese tech stocks have been diverging from their US counterparts in performance. While US tech stocks have recouped most earlier losses to close in on their record highs, the Star Market 50 index is revisiting an August low after a brief rebound on unease over faster supply of new stocks. CCSH Corporation, the parent of NAND flash maker Yangtze Memory Technologies Corporation, is close to selling initial public offering shares in Shanghai, with the size likely to surpass the 66.6 billion yuan (US$9.9 billion) listing by ChangXin Memory Technologies as the biggest flotation on the Star Market. Meanwhile, Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the South China Morning Post, has announced plans to raise HK$80 billion (US$10.2 billion) in a Hong Kong share placement to fund its AI expansion. “With the market style leaning defensive and cautious, dividend assets with low volatility and high dividend yields are expected to hold the edges,” said Chen Xiao, an analyst at Ping An Securities.

title: Who was Dolly Parton’s late husband Carl Thomas Dean, whom she was with for over 60 years?
description: The country music legend, who passed away at age 80, met the Nashville native as her career began to take off, and they famously had an “open” marriage.
content: Beloved country singer Dolly Parton, known for her timeless songs “Jolene”, “I Will Always Love You” and “9 to 5”, sadly passed away on August 25 at age 80. The musician faced autoimmune and kidney issues before her death and was admitted to the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville last Friday, per People. Parton’s nephew and her security head, Bryan Seaver, also shared news of her passing in a video on Instagram. The type of cancer was not specified. On the day she was admitted to the hospital, Parton told People about her recent health decline. “As I’ve shared in video messages throughout the past year, I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn’t pay attention to when I was watching over Carl,” she said. “[I]t’s not like I haven’t been through hard times with my health.” Parton’s late husband, Carl Thomas Dean, passed away in March 2025 at age 82. The couple met when Parton was 18 years old, and were together for 60 years. Parton shared her struggles with dealing with the death of her husband, who had kept a low profile compared to his superstar wife. “I’ll always miss him, of course, and I’ll always love him,” she told Today in an interview two months after his passing. “He was a great partner.” Here’s everything we know about the country singer’s late husband, Carl Thomas Dean. How did Dolly Parton meet Carl Thomas Dean? The love story between Dolly Parton and her one and only husband of nearly six decades, Carl Thomas Dean, could have come straight out of a country romance ballad. The pair met for the first time in 1964 at the Wishy Washy Laundromat on Parton’s first day in Nashville. She was 18, and he was about four years older. They dated for two years before tying the knot in 1966. This is when the singer’s career started to take flight with the release of her debut album Hello, I’m Dolly in 1967, according to her new Channel 5 documentary, Dolly Parton: In Her Own Words. What’s the secret to their lasting marriage? Parton and Dean were together for over 60 years. With plenty of other celebrity romances on the rocks, how did they do it? According to the Grammy award-winning singer’s 2017 book Dolly on Dolly, Interviews and Encounters, having an “open” marriage has contributed to their success. “Men are my weakness. Short, fat, bald or skinny – I’ve had crushes on some very unusual men, but Carl knows I’ll always come home and I’m not having sex with these people – I’m just flirting and having fun,” she said. “He’s not jealous and I’m not jealous of him. He knows I flirt. He flirts too,” she added. The country star clarified, however, that there was nothing sexual about their external encounters: “Yes, it’s an open relationship, but not sexually and I would kill him if I thought he was doing that. He would shoot me too. At the end of the day we love each other madly.” What did Carl Thomas Dean do? Per Stylecaster, Dean was a Nashville native working as an asphalt businessman when he met Parton. He was rarely seen in the public eye and kept a very private relationship with his country superstar wife. Did Parton and Dean have any children? Although they had been married for over half a century, Parton and Dean never had any kids together. “I know this sounds like a selfish, awful thing to say, but I’m almost glad I never had children,” Parton previously told Mojo magazine. “I worry myself to death about my little nieces and nephews and grandnieces and grandnephews.” “My husband and I, we just think of ourselves as each other’s child,” she continued. “He’s my only child, and I’m his only child.” Was Dolly Parton related to Miley Cyrus? Parton and Miley Cyrus were not biologically related, but the country star was the Disney alum’s godmother. According to a 2023 interview on The Howard Stern Show, Parton became close to the “Wrecking Ball” singer via her dad, Billy Ray Cyrus. “We just got to be good friends because he’s a Kentucky boy, I’m from Tennessee,” Parton said. “And he said … ‘We’re having a girl, and you’ve got to be her godmother!’ And I said, ‘Well, I’d be honoured.’ So actually, Miley and I took over from there. We just stayed very, very close through the years.” Additional reporting by Alexa Vernice Pacis

title: ‘Squeezed further’: calls for SME energy subsidies as Hong Kong power fuel surcharges soar
description: Industry leader urges relief for Hong Kong SMEs and household consumption vouchers to ease pressures and support local businesses.
content: Small and medium-sized businesses need subsidies to cope with soaring electricity costs as fuel surcharges imposed by Hong Kong’s two power suppliers have risen by up to 78.5 per cent due to the Middle East war, an industry leader and a lawmaker have said. HK Electric, which mainly supplies Hong Kong and Lamma islands, announced its fuel clause charge would increase by 5.9 per cent to 60.7 HK cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in September. The company has raised the charge every month since June, citing the impact of the war on global energy prices. Since March, shortly after the war began, the charge has increased by 78.5 per cent. HK Electric’s average net tariff will rise to 188.6 cents per unit in September, up by 16.4 per cent from 161.9 cents in March. In Hong Kong, the total billed to users, or the net tariff, comprises the basic tariff plus the fuel clause charge. CLP Power, which serves customers in Kowloon, the New Territories, Lantau and other outlying islands, also announced on Tuesday that its fuel cost charge would rise to 45.1 cents per unit in September. Its surcharge has increased by 15 per cent since March, from 39.2 cents per unit, in six consecutive monthly rises. The average net tariff will be 146.3 cents per unit of electricity in September, up by 4.2 per cent from 140.4 cents in March. Those prices include the average basic tariff of 101.2 cents per unit. Pamela Mak Mei-yee, honorary president of the Hong Kong Small and Medium Enterprises Association, said that while electricity costs were inevitable for every shop owner, absorbing rises would prove difficult. “Once costs keep rising, and merchants find it difficult to fully pass the increase on to customers, profits will naturally be squeezed further,” she said. Mak called on the power companies and authorities to offer time-limited support for smaller, high-consumption businesses, such as fuel-cost rebates, instalment payment options and subsidies for energy-saving equipment. She also suggested issuing consumption vouchers to eligible households for use at specific local shops, which would ease the economic burden on residents while boosting business in the catering, retail and services sectors. In the longer term, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) should be supported in upgrading their air-conditioning, refrigeration, lighting and power-management systems to reduce the impact of future energy price fluctuations on their operations, Mak said. The Brent crude benchmark was at US$86.80 on Wednesday morning. Despite a 1.96 per cent decline compared with the day before, the price remained higher than the US$72 recorded in late February, shortly before the war began. To ease high electricity bills, the two utilities have introduced rebate and relief schemes, as households face higher air-conditioning costs after a summer with an unusually high number of very hot days. The government earlier rolled out diesel and liquefied petroleum gas subsidy schemes, but these applied only to vehicles and vessels – not to commercial electricity users. They ended in June and July respectively. Lawmaker Ray Wong Wing-wai said that while the latest electricity fee increases were not especially high, attention should remain focused on the wider energy issue. “For the industrial and business sector, the most troublesome thing is the constant back-and-forth of hikes and cuts to electricity bills – it actually makes it harder for them to keep their costs under control,” he said. “This is something we take quite seriously.” Wong said SMEs in industries with high electricity consumption, such as laundries and food manufacturers, were likely to be hit the hardest. Running a food factory was already difficult and higher power bills significantly increased their costs, he added. He said one laundry business reported that electricity costs, which previously accounted for 5 to 8 per cent of its overall expenses, now represented about 13 to 14 per cent. Wong urged the government and power companies to offer targeted subsidies for commercial users, while businesses should also adopt energy-saving tools and solutions, drawing on mainland China’s experience. He noted that data centres would be built in the Northern Metropolis, generating substantial waste heat that could potentially be recovered for power supply. Lawmaker Jonathan Leung Chun said many Hong Kong restaurants had gross profit margins of less than 10 per cent and could not readily pass higher costs on to consumers given they were spending less. He said the prices of sundry goods, such as tissues, had increased because of higher transport fees, while rising labour costs had also put pressure on the sector. “I have seen that the profitability of many different restaurants is not ideal,” he said. “If the cost further goes up, it will definitely be difficult [for the restaurants].” Leung added that the biggest problem was not a dramatic rise in electricity costs but businesses’ already limited capacity to absorb them. Any additional expense, he said, risked becoming “the final straw”. Additional reporting by Lam Ka-sing

title: Hong Kong police officer suspected of accidentally discharging firearm at base
description: Police say single round believed to have been fired at West Kowloon Regional Emergency Unit’s base, but no one was hurt.
content: A Hong Kong constable is suspected of discharging his service firearm accidentally at a police base in Mong Kok, the force has said. Police said on Wednesday the officer was loading a round into his weapon at the West Kowloon Regional Emergency Unit’s base at 11.01pm the previous day. A single round was believed to have been fired. No one was injured. Police stressed that the force had strict regulations covering the use of firearms and that an investigation was under way. In May, an officer accidentally fired a single round when she was loading her semi-automatic pistol in a designated loading area on Concorde Road in Kai Tak, with no injuries reported. In June last year, an officer’s semi-automatic firearm was accidentally discharged at the force’s headquarters in Wan Chai while he was unloading the weapon in a designated area. No one was hurt.

title: South Korea scrambles jets after Russian military planes enter air defence zone
description: This is the second incursion in weeks since over 10 Chinese and Russian military jets entered the zone in late June.
content: South Korea said on Wednesday it had scrambled fighter jets in response to Russian military aircraft entering its air defence zone, the second such incursion in weeks. The relationship between the countries has worsened since South Korea joined Western sanctions following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and since Moscow built stronger ties with North Korea. Seoul’s defence ministry said multiple Russian aircraft had entered and then left its air defence identification zone over the East Sea, also called the Sea of Japan. “South Korea’s military detected the Russian aircraft before they entered the zone and deployed Air Force fighter jets to prepare for any contingency,” it said, without giving details. The Russian aircraft did not violate South Korean airspace, it said. An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area where countries require foreign aircraft to identify themselves for security purposes. Military aircraft are generally expected to notify the relevant country before entering its zone, although there is no legal obligation to do so. In late June, more than 10 Chinese and Russian military aircraft entered South Korea’s air defence zone. Beijing’s defence ministry said at the time that Chinese and Russian forces had conducted a “strategic air patrol” over the Sea of Japan, the East China Sea and the western Pacific Ocean. Russia’s defence ministry said the patrol was part of normal military cooperation plans and “not directed against third countries”. But South Korea still lodged protests with Beijing and Moscow and demanded measures to prevent a recurrence.

title: Hong Kong’s John Lee vows to review laws on dangerous dogs after string of attacks
description: City leader says public education should be strengthened to prevent further attacks, after two more cases emerge.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has pledged to review the laws governing dangerous dogs and the related penalties after a woman and another pet were injured following a string of similar cases. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Wednesday acknowledged public concerns over the spate of dog attacks and said education would need to be strengthened to prevent further cases. Authorities would strictly enforce the law against any owners who failed to control their pets, he added. “The dog owners’ responsibility is very important. If a dog is in a public place, the owner must keep it under proper control to ensure it does not harm or disturb others,” Lee told the media after visiting low-income residents in Sham Shui Po district. He also said the government would examine whether current laws on dangerous dogs and related penalties were sufficient. The Environment and Ecology Bureau and the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) earlier announced a review of the legal definition of fighting dogs and related regulations. The announcement was in response to the mauling of the 33-year-old owner of a pet training facility by a mixed-breed fighting dog registered as a mongrel last week. She was discovered dead nearby shortly after the attack. Earlier that week, a 60kg (132lbs) mixed-breed dog killed a miniature poodle and a bichon frise in separate attacks near Yoho Mall in Yuen Long. Two further attacks were also reported this week. In the first case, a woman called police after being bitten by a dog in Kennedy Town at 11.09pm on Tuesday. The force said the woman had been bitten on her left foot by a female mongrel being walked by a man. It remained unclear if the dog was on a leash. She was taken to Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam for treatment of the bite, which had caused bleeding and swelling, police said. The AFCD said it was reaching out to the victim and the dog owner as part of its investigation. Police also said on Wednesday they had received a report from a woman the previous afternoon that her dog, a nine-year-old Malinois, had been attacked by other canines, leaving it with head injuries. The case was referred to the AFCD, which said it had contacted the animal’s owner to gather more information. “If there is sufficient evidence that persons concerned had violated laws, the AFCD will initiate prosecution,” it said. A Facebook user, Terrance Chan, said on Tuesday that a family member had taken his dog to the Tai Lam Chung Catchwater near Allway Garden in Tsuen Wan for a walk at around 9.30am when they encountered a woman with four other dogs, which were unleashed. “Suddenly, three of the black medium-to-large dogs charged forward and attacked our dog, causing serious injuries to multiple areas of its head,” he wrote. Chan added that the woman refused to provide contact details or cooperate in making a police report and fled the scene. The post, which included photographs of his dog’s wounds, said this was “not the first time this woman has failed to properly control her dogs in the vicinity”. Under the Rabies Ordinance, it is an offence to leave a dog unleashed in public areas or at any place from which it may wander into a public space. Offenders can be fined HK$10,000 (US$1,275) upon conviction. Additionally, the Dangerous Dogs Regulation states that dogs weighing no less than 20kg must be secured in public with a leash of up to two metres (6.56 feet). Those who fail to comply face a maximum penalty of three months’ imprisonment and a HK$25,000 fine. There were 237 dog attack reports in Hong Kong in the first quarter of this year, according to the AFCD. The city recorded 891 dog attack reports last year, up from 805 in 2024.

title: DeepSeek nears pre-IPO funding round as 2027 market debut takes shape: sources
description: Landmark round to lift Chinese start-up’s valuation to US$74 billion and set the stage for a Shanghai Star Market listing, sources say.
content: DeepSeek is nearing the completion of a new funding round valuing the company at about 500 billion yuan (US$74 billion) before investment, as the Chinese artificial intelligence start-up moves closer to a potential listing on Shanghai’s Star Market, according to people familiar with the matter. The company was seeking to raise about 50 billion yuan in the round, which was expected to close before the end of August, according to one person. Investors included incumbents from the company’s last fundraising round, such as local venture funds Monolith and Shixiang Capital, and Chinese battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL), another source said. New investors in talks included CPE, Legend Capital and Stony Creek Capital – a semiconductor-focused private equity firm historically linked to Zhu Yiming, chairman of chip giant ChangXin Memory Technologies and founder of memory chip designer GigaDevice, the source added. Funds backed by GigaDevice and Hefei state investment vehicles were also involved. The sources requested anonymity as they were discussing private information. The latest funding round comes as Hangzhou-based DeepSeek has started preparing for a potential initial public offering on Shanghai’s Nasdaq-like Star Market. The company could file for an IPO as early as the end of the year, eyeing a public market debut in 2027, two sources said. DeepSeek, Monolith, Shixiang Capital, CATL, CPE, Legend Capital and Stony Creek Capital did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Wednesday. After shaking the global AI industry with its low-cost and high-performance models, DeepSeek faces intensifying challenges from local and global competitors. It has recently raised prices for access to its application programming interface amid aggressive price competition among Chinese AI companies. Other major developers – including Zhipu AI, Alibaba Group Holding, Tencent Holdings and Baidu – have also raised prices this year, reflecting a broader shift away from using discounts to win users and towards monetising increasingly costly AI services. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. That shift reflects mounting computing and infrastructure costs across the sector, as Chinese AI firms search for ways to profit from the burgeoning technology. DeepSeek is also looking to expand its teams and computing infrastructure as competition intensifies, with a reported plan to add about 1 gigawatt to its computing capacity.

title: Deadly Shah Alam brawl reignites Malaysian gang violence fears
description: Dashcam video showing a man being rammed by a car during an armed street fight has triggered a murder inquiry.
content: Malaysian police are investigating a killing near Kuala Lumpur as murder after a man rammed by a car died following an armed brawl in broad daylight that was caught on camera – footage that has stirred fresh alarm over brazen street violence in the country. The fight, in which several men were filmed slashing at one another, broke out at around 2pm on Tuesday in the Taman Alam Megah neighbourhood of Shah Alam, police said. One local man has been arrested in connection with the case. Shah Alam police chief Assistant Commissioner Sarudin Samah said surveillance footage showed a group of men fighting before the confrontation escalated. “CCTV footage showed a group of men fighting before they began slashing at one another,” he said in a statement on Tuesday. “A blue Perodua Alza was also seen hitting one of the suspects, who died at the scene.” Police have not identified the dead man, describing him only as one of the individuals believed to have been involved in the fight, nor have they disclosed a motive or confirmed any gang-related connection. Sarudin said the detained man was assisting with the investigation and that police had opened a murder inquiry under Section 302 of Malaysia’s Penal Code. The offence carries the death penalty or a prison term of between 30 and 40 years, plus a minimum of 12 strokes of the cane if the death sentence is not imposed. The police chief urged the public not to speculate while investigators worked to establish what triggered the fight. A one-minute dashcam clip that circulated widely on Malaysian social media after the killing shows several people rushing from vehicles to attack a man lying on the road, before another vehicle makes a U-turn and strikes a second man, who is then set upon by others. The footage drew online comparisons with nearby Klang, a port city in Selangor long associated with gang activity. Shah Alam is the state capital of Selangor, adjoining Kuala Lumpur. “Even Shah Alam has become Colombia,” one social media user wrote, while another called the violence “open air murder”. The killing comes less than two weeks after a separate armed confrontation in Shah Alam. On August 13, a 38-year-old man suffered serious hand injuries after being slashed with a machete near a petrol station in Sri Muda. Police said two male suspects were believed to have used objects resembling firearms during the clash. Other public attacks have drawn similar attention this year. Tong Wee Sheng, 38, was chased and repeatedly slashed in March with parangs – machete-like knives – in Tangkak, southern Johor state, before dying from his injuries. Three men were charged with his murder in May. None of the cases is known to be connected, but the latest footage recalls a spate of gangland-style violence across the Klang Valley last year, when four men were killed in three separate shootings over eight days in June – including a killing in broad daylight in Klang – that prompted police assurances the situation was under control.

title: China’s coastal regions on high alert as Typhoon Saudel cancels flights, ferries
description: With a weakening Narra continuing to dump torrential rain, the east and southeastern provinces prepare for another battering.
content: Airports in China’s Zhejiang and Fujian provinces remained on high alert for potential delays and cancellations as Typhoon Saudel approached landfall on Wednesday, after multiple flights were cancelled in Taiwan and Hong Kong. Saudel, which entered the East China Sea early on Wednesday morning, prompted the cancellation of 16 flights at Taiwan’s Taoyuan International Airport. Affected carriers included Peach, China Airlines, EVA Air, Starlux and Thai Lion Air. Hong Kong Airlines fully cancelled its HX658/HX659 flights between the city and Okinawa in Japan, while HK Express rescheduled its Okinawa-bound services to August 27 in response to the weather system. If it does make landfall on the Chinese mainland, Saudel would be the seventh typhoon to do so this year. Previous ones, including Bavi, brought torrential rain and floods. The National Meteorological Centre forecasts that Saudel will make landfall between Thursday night and Friday morning along the coast from Xiangshan in eastern Zhejiang, to Fuqing in southeast Fujian province. Zhejiang province has raised its emergency response to Level 3 – the third highest of four levels – and closed all coastal scenic areas, evacuating more than 4,100 tourists from island resorts. More than 90 passenger ferry routes in Zhejiang had also been suspended because of gale-force winds as of 10am on Monday, according to the Zhejiang Maritime Safety Administration. The impact on regional shipping has been severe. Local media reported that in the city of Taizhou, all 18 passenger ferry routes had been suspended, 32 maritime construction projects halted and 67 associated vessels relocated to safe waters. In Ningbo, 22 passenger routes have been suspended and 39 offshore construction projects fully halted. Wenzhou has suspended all 13 coastal passenger routes, with 24 offshore engineering projects shut down. Across the province, work has stopped at 146 offshore construction projects and 527 associated vessels have been moved to safe anchorages. More than 3,300 fishing vessels are now sheltered in ports. Meanwhile, Typhoon Narra made its third landfall at around 11am on Wednesday, arriving in Wuchuan in Guangdong province, southern China, with Force 6 winds before rapidly losing strength. In southwest Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, the impact on maritime traffic has been equally severe. The Beihai to Weizhou Island route – the region’s busiest passenger ferry link – has been completely suspended. A total of 78 coastal water projects across Guangxi have been shut down, with all construction vessels and personnel evacuated from the water. The Qiongzhou Strait has been fully closed to roll-on/roll-off traffic since Tuesday, with ports including Xinhai, Xiuying and the southern railway link in Hainan’s capital Haikou shutting the gates. The suspension is expected to last through to Wednesday afternoon. Despite Narra’s weakening, its residual circulation continues to dump torrential rain across Guangxi, Guangdong and Hainan after days of non-stop downpours. Local authorities have urged residents in affected areas to monitor official forecasts and prepare for potential mountain torrents, urban flooding and other secondary disasters.

title: RTHK editor gets 160 hours of community service for upskirt video
description: Chong Tak-yin, 57, pleaded guilty to unlawful recording of intimate parts after police found an upskirt video on his phone.
content: A Hong Kong court has ordered a civil servant at public broadcaster RTHK to complete 160 hours of community service after he admitted taking upskirt footage of a woman in public. Chong Tak-yin, an assistant chief assignment editor in RTHK’s Chinese news and current affairs division, was sentenced on Wednesday at West Kowloon Court after pleading guilty to one count of unlawful recording or observation of intimate parts. The 57-year-old told arresting officers the offence was “a momentary lapse of judgment” driven by sexual impulse when he filmed the woman in a skirt in Mong Kok on November 14 last year. According to court documents, patrolling officers spotted him suspiciously following the woman. A stop and search found a video on his phone showing the woman’s lower body. At an earlier hearing, defence counsel Joe Chan Wai-yin said Chong was married with two sons and earned about HK$90,000 (US$11,480) a month as the family’s sole breadwinner. He had initially intended to plead not guilty but changed his mind before trial, saying he wanted to set a good example for his children by owning up to his mistake and accepting the consequences. A probation officer’s assessment noted that Chong had sought professional help, found the risk of reoffending to be low and described the incident as a one-off. Magistrate Jeffrey Sze Cho-yiu accepted the recommendation to impose a community service order. The South China Morning Post has contacted RTHK for comment.

title: The high quality, low risk reason Premier League clubs are buying Japanese
description: Ten players from Japan are registered with teams in England’s top tier, with more expected to make the move before the transfer window closes.
content: A record number of Japanese players are in the Premier League this season, with clubs attracted by their proven quality, value for money and the “very little risk” involved in signing them. Ten players from Japan were registered with top-tier English teams when the campaign kicked off last weekend and more are potentially on the way before the transfer window closes. Zion Suzuki was the highest-profile arrival with his switch to Aston Villa, with former Arsenal defender Takehiro Tomiyasu returning to London with Crystal Palace, midfielder Hidemasa Morita joining Hull City and Daizen Maeda swapping Celtic for Ipswich Town. They join an established group of the countrymen already in the top flight, including Brighton’s Kaoru Mitoma, Liverpool’s Wataru Endo and Palace’s Daichi Kamada. Fifa-registered agent Joel Pannick of CAA Base told AFP that English clubs have “increased confidence that signing a Japanese player is a good move to make”. “There aren’t many examples of clubs signing Japanese players and having issues with their adaptation, with their personality, with their integration into the squad, with discipline,” said Pannick, who has about 60 Japanese players on his books. “The risk element that teams previously feared, this fear of the unknown, has gone because with each example of a successful Japanese player it gives more confidence,” he added. Also in the Premier League are Ao Tanaka (Leeds), Kota Takai (Spurs) and Tatsuhiro Sakamoto (Coventry). Midfielder Tanaka, who has played 41 times for Japan, joined from German side Fortuna Dusseldorf for just £3.3 million (US$4.5 million) two years ago. Japanese players in England have come a long way since Junichi Inamoto signed for Arsenal in 2001 and left for Fulham a year later without making a league appearance. There have been successes along the way, with Shinji Kagawa, Shinji Okazaki, Takumi Minamino and Endo all picking up league winner’s medals. Suzuki, 24, will become the first Japanese goalkeeper to play in the Premier League if he makes his debut after joining Villa from Italian side Parma last week. Veteran Japanese football journalist Yoshiyuki Osumi says he is “10 or 20 years ahead of his time for a Japanese goalkeeper”. “If he can play in the Premier League as a goalkeeper, I think that would have a big impact on Japanese football,” Osumi said. Suzuki’s transition to the Premier League will be helped by the fact that he can already speak English. Not all of his compatriots have had that ability in the past, but more are realising that being able to communicate is crucial to succeeding in Europe. Pannick said his client Maya Yoshida started a culture change when he captained Japan ahead of the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. Yoshida, who spent almost eight years at Southampton, would insist that any player who sat at his lunch table must speak in English. “To get this more worldly mentality is something that he was very keen to emphasise to the players,” Pannick said. “This current generation of starting national team players or squad players at the World Cup, almost all of them now will speak English to a pretty good degree.” Most Japanese players will spend playing time in Belgium, the Netherlands, or Portugal before making the step up to the Premier League. The Championship has become another popular staging post, and there are currently eight Japanese players in England’s second tier. Post-Brexit changes to work permit rules have forced English clubs to look beyond Europe for signings. Osumi said an overall improvement in the level of Japanese players had allowed them to thrive in the Premier League. But the journalist believed a change in the nature of the league has also made it easier for them to adapt. “The Premier League has become more tactical, and there are more teams that play as a coordinated unit,” he said. “That kind of football is something Japanese players find very easy to adapt to.”

title: As more expats flock to Hong Kong, luxury home rents poised for further upswing
description: The top source of foreign finance executives moving to Hong Kong is coming from Europe and the US, says relocation firm.
content: Hong Kong’s growing number of expatriates is boosting the city’s residential property leasing market with luxury rents likely to rise by about 5 per cent this year and continue their upswing in 2027, according to property consultancy JLL. The private residential rental index by the Rating and Valuation Department had surged by 18.5 per cent as of June to 205.8 from the Covid-19 pandemic trough in January 2023, which was 173.6, marking the first sustained breach of the 200 threshold. “Hong Kong’s residential leasing market has entered a renewed expansion cycle in 2026,” JLL said in a statement. “A principal driver is the influx of expatriate professionals attracted by resurgent [initial public offering] activity and asset management business growth. This influx is rooted in a broader financial-sector resurgence.” Relocation firm Dwellworks Hong Kong also disclosed that Europe and the US were the top sources of finance executives flocking into the city. Last year, the Hong Kong stock exchange led IPO fundraising globally with HK$285.8 billion (US$36.46 billion) and this momentum continued into the first half of this year with proceeds of HK$210.2 billion, just second to the Nasdaq. Listings of mainland Chinese companies for internationalisation consequently translated into staffing needs across sponsoring, legal, audit and compliance functions. Data from the Census and Statistics Department showed that employees in the financial sector – excluding insurance – and professional and business services rose by about 5,300 in 2025, and increased a further 3,800 to 554,600 in the first half of 2026. The data is based on the three-month moving average of employed persons in the sectors. Likewise, wealth management has emerged as a second engine of demand with Hong Kong replacing Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth centre worth US$2.95 trillion in 2025. Financial services visas granted to foreign nationals jumped 16.9 per cent to 2,343 in 2025 on an annual basis, the most since 2022. In the first quarter of this year, 678 of such visas were granted, representing around 29 per cent of the previous year’s total, according to data compiled by JLL and based on Immigration Department’s figures. “While overall volumes remain below pre-pandemic levels, the pace of growth is the strongest seen in the past three years,” said Joyce Lam, director of operations at Dwellworks. “Our data shows that most relocation initiations originate from the financial sector. In terms of geographic origin, finance-sector transferees typically relocate from Europe and the US, with additional demand coming from Singapore and Japan.” Meanwhile, in the retail industry, relocations “are primarily driven by assignments from Europe, while arrivals in the technology sector are mainly from mainland China and have been gaining momentum since the second half of 2025”, Lam said. Next year, relocation demand is also tipped to rise by at least 10 per cent, she added. Given the rising relocations, some districts are more favoured by expatriates such as those close to their offices, international schools and those that fit their budget, according to JLL. Norry Lee, senior director of projects strategy and consultancy at JLL in Hong Kong, said expatriate housing demand had become “more geographically diverse” as more companies had moved to East Kowloon and West Kowloon over the last few years. “While expatriates have traditionally concentrated to reside in areas such as Central/Soho, near Kowloon Station, South West Kowloon, Discovery Bay and Tung Chung, demand is increasingly shifting towards districts including Kai Tak and Tseung Kwan O, particularly for newer residential developments, penthouses and town houses,” he said. The Hong Kong government’s proposal to grant tax breaks on carried interest, the performance fees earned by hedge fund and private equity managers, is also likely to strengthen the city’s appeal to fund managers, family offices and investment professionals whose pay includes carried interest or performance-based fees. “The resulting inflow of senior finance professionals and high-net-worth individuals is likely to support demand for luxury residential leasing,” said Cathie Chung, senior director of research at JLL in Hong Kong. With some serviced flats converted into student housing and vacancy rates in the residential leasing market remaining low, an intensified competition for expatriates’ accommodation was likely, she said, carrying “implications for occupiers, relocating professionals and landlords alike”.

title: Ming dynasty work shows how Chinese understood the world in the 1600s
description: Scholar Zhang Huang set out to document heaven, Earth and humanity in vast compendium described as a ‘visual summary of Chinese culture’.
content: Long before the digital age, a Ming dynasty scholar made it his mission to map human knowledge from a Chinese perspective. The result was an encyclopaedia spanning 127 volumes known as the Tushu Bian, or Compendium of Illustrations and Texts. The work – published in 1613 – was compiled by Neo-Confucian scholar Zhang Huang and drew on more than 200 printed sources across several decades to document the concepts of heaven, Earth and humanity. “His goal was to gather all the illustrations and texts an educated person needed to understand the world,” information designer Paul Kahn, who analysed the encyclopaedia, wrote in his book Mapping Knowledge Across Time: Seven Books That Visualised the World. “The result was too costly to print during his lifetime. It was eventually carved on woodblocks and printed after his death,” Kahn wrote. Kahn compared the Tushu Bian with six other books that described the world from the perspective of Euro-Mediterranean culture. “The Tushu Bian was chosen because it is an enormous visual summary of Chinese culture from the period when Asia and the West were interacting,” he wrote. In an interview, Kahn said the Chinese work’s depiction of the Grand Canal and major rivers set it apart from the others. The Grand Canal is a vast waterway system that runs from Beijing southward across the Yellow River to canals and tributaries merging with the Yangtze River near the modern-day city of Yangzhou. “In all of the European books, there are many examples of understanding river and maritime networks and showing how people travel from one continent to another,” Kahn said. “For example, there are several reproductions of the Danube River network that covers all of central and northern Europe. “In all of those cases, they are represented as networks and lines connecting one place to another. But in the Tushu Bian, the rivers are represented as continuous, detailed descriptions of every place on the river.” Unlike modern maps that use a bird’s-eye view or a north-south orientation, the Tushu Bian often presents these rivers horizontally, flowing from right to left, regardless of cardinal directions. “Orientation is based on convention,” Kahn said. “What you see is based on what is in your mind. If your mind has certain conventions that north should be at the top, and you look at an image, you do not recognise what you are looking at because it is not matching your expectations.” He noted that there was more flexibility in today’s mobile phone map applications. “They can change the representation if they are well designed … to meet the needs of the person who is using it,” he said. The Tushu Bian also described the human body as a channel for the primordial qi – energy inherited from one’s parents – to connect heaven and Earth, with detailed diagrams of human organs. “There is no representation of the human body as connected to the natural world or as a microcosm in the other books, with the exception of the Catalan Atlas,” according to Kahn. He said the world atlas from the 14th century “includes a human figure with each of the parts of the external body, not showing the internal organs”. “It shows this figure that is related to astrological information and numerical instructions” on when to perform bloodletting, a common medical procedure at the time. In the Tushu Bian, one diagram shows internal organs contained in a pear-shaped outline, with the spinal vertebrae portrayed as bones. Another diagram renders the spine as a sequence of connected circles linked to the head. The view is from the side, which Kahn said might have been done to show the spine and spinal column. “Within that tradition, the location of different parts of the spine is correlated with different parts of the organs, and so I think that was why they did it that way.” According to Kahn, Zhang gathered information for the Tushu Bian that could benefit his students, but it was also a resource that could be used to prepare for the imperial examination – the selection process for government workers. “An aspiring candidate might spend decades preparing for the exam,” Kahn wrote. “The people who tried and failed to pass the exam made up much of the literate population.” The Tushu Bian makes no mention of the seven naval expeditions led by Admiral Zheng He between 1405 and 1433. It depicts the world through a collection of maps centred on the Chinese Empire, with limited representation of surrounding “tribute” countries. “The greatest detail of the outside world is devoted to places where the Chinese were defending against invasions,” Kahn wrote in his book. He told the SCMP: “These amazing gigantic maritime expeditions that had happened during the same dynasty, not that long before, are completely ignored. I would interpret that to mean that he is making decisions about what the people that he wants to see this should be paying attention to.” Kahn noted the need to evaluate where information comes from – whether it is a historical visualisation or the AI-generated content and deepfakes of today. “One lesson that we are learning over and over again is to try and understand the source of the material and become critical in terms of how you judge what you see based on [whether this] is an eyewitness account or someone’s story about a story they heard from someone else,” he said. Kahn gave the example of the Atlas Historique, which was published in Amsterdam in the 18th century and featured illustrations of the Mughal Empire in India. They were copied directly from the personal art collection of an Italian diplomat. Dutch United East India Company traders had brought the works to the Netherlands from India and China. “He had essentially a museum of paintings that were made in India, and the people who did the Atlas Historique went to the museum and they copied them. In this case, they were copying something that was much more authentic,” Kahn said. “When you look at them compared to the images that they created of people in Japan and China, you can see that they are much less European looking,” he said. “The lesson is when you look at a whole range of images like this, try to become sensitive to what is it about the image that represents some kind of authenticity or closer to the source.”

title: Letters | Why Hong Kong needs special courts for drug offenders
description: Readers discuss Hong Kong’s approach to drug-related cases vis-a-vis New York’s, and dog owners’ duty to the community.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. As Hong Kong grapples with drug addiction, it must prioritise rehabilitation over deterrence. Hong Kong has long boasted a deterrent approach. According to Section 8 of the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, mere possession or use of a dangerous drug can mean up to seven years in jail. Unlike New York, which legalised personal cannabis use in 2021, cannabis remains illegal in Hong Kong. Indeed, Hong Kong remains one of the few common-law jurisdictions which use a strict mathematical approach in sentencing drug trafficking offences. Still, deterrence fails to address the multi-factor nature of drug offending. It also lets anarchical apprehension fester. Neighbourhood poverty, unemployment and psychiatric challenges loom large. Although anti-drug campaigns – such as the recent anti-etomidate campaign starring Aaron Kwok – are laudable, they are woefully insufficient, especially for those who use drugs to ward off disruptive hallucinations or smuggle them to stay financially afloat. I handle numerous drug cases as a criminal defence lawyer in New York. I represent clients at several of the 141 “drug courts” within the state, including specialist “opioid courts” which have been dubbed “problem-solving” courts. Eligible defendants – for example, those with no history of violent convictions – are offered the opportunity to undergo court-based screening for a treatment programme. Interviews are conducted by court-appointed medical professionals. They proffer clinical recommendations, such as whether screened defendants should receive in- or outpatient treatment. Interested defendants need not confirm their participation until they have attended an orientation session. The treatment programme features an extended period of supervision. This assuages public safety concerns. Defendants may be required to submit regular urine samples, attend group or individual therapy sessions and work with medical specialists on their health issues. They are dissimilar to Hong Kong’s addiction treatment centres, which are significantly curtailed by logistical constraints. Defendants can also maintain their professional commitments simultaneously, thus easing their reintegration into society. Nevertheless, they must attend court periodically for their progress to be appraised. Specialist judges recognise the risk of relapse. Instead of chastisement, they offer practical solutions for ameliorating compliance. Court formalities are often eschewed in favour of direct interactions between judges and defendants, creating a collaborative atmosphere. In exchange for programme completion, the sentence gets drastically reduced. This improves employment outcomes. Drug offenders are not villains. They are injured souls deserving of our compassion. How we treat them speaks volumes about our society. Alexander Clevewood Ng, New York Dog owners have a duty to protect the community Recent dog attacks in Hong Kong have highlighted a public safety problem that can no longer be ignored. Just last week, a large unleashed dog in Yuen Long killed two small pet dogs within 20 minutes. The same dog was involved in an earlier attack on another dog a month before. Even more alarming, a 33-year-old woman was fatally attacked by a large dog while working at a licensed pet boarding facility in Ta Kwu Ling. The issue is not that dogs are inherently dangerous; rather, too many are inadequately trained, improperly supervised or allowed to roam without leashes in public spaces. Parks, pavements, housing estates and workplaces should not become places where residents fear for their safety. The time for action is now. Existing leash regulations must be rigorously enforced, with all dogs kept on a leash no longer than two metres (6.6 feet) in public areas. Dogs with a history of aggression and certain large breeds should be required to wear muzzles in crowded places. First-time owners should be required to put their dogs through mandatory training in obedience and socialisation before obtaining a licence, while licence renewals should require proof of responsible ownership. Penalties for negligence must also be strengthened, including substantial fines and possible suspension of ownership rights when uncontrolled dogs cause injury or death. Public education campaigns, better reporting systems for dangerous dogs and more designated dog exercise areas could further reduce risks while promoting responsible pet ownership. By combining stronger enforcement, better education and greater accountability, Hong Kong can ensure its streets and public spaces remain safe and welcoming for the two-legged and four-legged. Adeoti Joy, Yuen Long

title: ‘I want to survive’: Malaysian commando adrift in South China Sea for 15 hours
description: The seaman was the last of six navy special forces personnel to be rescued after they missed their landing site and ended up in the sea.
content: “I want to survive.” That was uppermost in Senior Seaman Michael Coccon Johen’s mind while he was drifting in the South China Sea, hours after a free-fall parachute training exercise went wrong. Johen, 27, was one of six Malaysian navy special forces personnel who landed in the sea on August 12 after missing their designated landing site at Pulau Layang-Layang, off Sabah’s coast. It happened during the drill’s second jump at 4.30pm, when a sudden change in weather severely affected visibility. “We were about 10km (six miles) away from the island when we jumped from the helicopter. From 9,000 to 4,000 feet (2,700 to 1,200 metres), we were still moving towards the island,” Johen told the media at state Deputy Transport Minister Henry Harry Jinep’s service centre in Bau, Sarawak, on Tuesday. “But from that point on, our parachutes stopped moving forward because the wind changed suddenly. So we landed in the sea at about 5pm.” Thanks to his training, he did not panic but waited for help from the navy’s safety vessels. However, the vessels could not reach them because the waves were too high. “After about an hour, I kicked off my shoes and retrieved the compass from the parachute to check the bearings to the island,” he said. “I could see the island at a distance and decided to swim towards it. I could also see a lot of navy ships searching for us, but it was getting darker.” Johen, who was wearing a life jacket, kept swimming but the waves were against him, pulling him away from the island. At about 10pm, he saw a flare set off by a fellow commando to attract the attention of the search-and-rescue helicopters. “My five colleagues were all rescued that night, the last one at about 11pm. I was the only one still in the sea. I could see a faint light from the island and that motivated me to keep going. I kept trying to reach the island until about 5am, but I didn’t seem to get closer,” he said. “I realised I needed to rest. I tried to sleep but the waves kept crashing over my face. I must have swallowed a lot of seawater. Finally I covered my face with my hat and I was able to sleep until about 7am.” When he woke up, he could see a navy vessel to his right but it was still quite far away. He decided to rest again and this time he was woken by the sound of the vessel, which was now closer to him. “I started swimming towards the vessel. All I could think of was that I had a chance to be rescued. Finally the crew saw me and pulled me aboard.” That was at 7.55am the following morning, after he had spent 15 hours in the sea. He was brought to the hospital in Kota Kinabalu and discharged after two days. Johen, from Kampung Bogak Sejinjang in Sarawak, attributed his survival to his training and the prayers of his loved ones. “What I was most afraid of was that the rescuers would not be able to find me, because it’s very difficult to search in the open sea,” he said. “I also thought about my loved ones. Usually, before each jump, I will inform my mother and my wife, but this time I didn’t because of poor connectivity.” He thanked the navy for rescuing all six personnel, adding that he would continue to make jumps after this incident. Johen’s wife, Law Lee Eing, said she could not sleep the whole night after hearing the news that the team was missing. “The next morning, I received a call that my husband was missing. Shortly after that, another call came saying that he had been rescued, which was such a relief,” she said. Jinep said Johen’s survival resulted from his determination, courage, mental strength, and commando training. “I hope he will be a role model to the younger generation,” he said. This article was first published by The Star

title: Terror as Malaysian roller coaster fails mid-ride, 10 injured
description: A top official points to metal fatigue as police and the theme park operator face a backlash for delayed comment on Saturday’s incident.
content: A roller coaster malfunction at a major theme park on the outskirts of Malaysia’s capital city injured 10 people on Saturday, the operator confirmed after coming under fire for what critics called a prolonged silence over the incident. Authorities said on Monday that the riders had suffered minor injuries after the ride abruptly stopped, leaving them stranded. The incident sparked a flurry of complaints across Malaysian social media, with numerous posts sharing videos purportedly showing the malfunction and demanding accountability from the park’s operator. Sunway Lagoon, which operates the theme park in Subang Jaya where the malfunction occurred, confirmed on Tuesday “the incident involving an attraction” and said its immediate priority was the welfare of those affected. “We are working closely and fully cooperating with all relevant authorities as they conduct a thorough investigation into the incident,” the company said in a statement. “We remain firmly committed to maintaining the highest standards of safety across our attractions and facilities, and to ensuring the well-being and confidence of all our guests.” The statement followed comments hours earlier from Jeffrey Cheah, founder of parent group Sunway, who also confirmed the incident to local media. “In my view, the incident may be attributable to metal fatigue,” Cheah was quoted as saying by the New Straits Times. It came as online anger grew, fuelled in part by police initially withholding the theme park’s name, giving only its location. Dozens of posts quickly named it as Sunway Lagoon, Subang Jaya’s only large-scale park with roller-coaster rides. Several videos said to show the incident from different perspectives soon went viral, including a series of clips showing a couple enjoying the ride moments before it violently juddered to a halt, followed by footage of them stranded with other riders and their eventual rescue. One social media user also shared pictures she said were from the scene, along with a set of Sunway Lagoon wristbands, claiming her husband and children were among the 22 people on the ride. “Received call from my husband [saying] they [were] stuck and injured – made my heart stop,” wrote the user, known as nurul_aizam, adding that bystanders were left shaken after hearing a “crazy loud sound”. Opened in 1993, Sunway Lagoon is located about a 30-minute drive from Kuala Lumpur and features more than 120 attractions across seven zones, including a water park and amusement park, according to the company’s website. Other recent incidents Exact visitor figures are not publicly available, but Malaysia’s theme parks typically draw millions of visitors every year, according to industry estimates. Serious incidents are uncommon, though authorities have reported two deaths at amusement parks in recent weeks. The most recent came last month, when an 18-year-old student died after falling from the 68th floor of Komtar Tower in Penang state. The victim was found wearing a wristband from a theme park operating at the top of the building. In June, a four-year-old boy died in hospital after he was found unconscious at a water theme park in Sungai Buloh, Selangor state. Police said preliminary investigations showed he fell after leaving the pool area. Separately, on Saturday, a 46-year-old woman developed a blood clot in her head and another sustained a concussion after apparently slipping from an inflatable raft on a water slide at a resort theme park in Ayer Keroh, Melaka. Authorities did not name the theme parks involved in any of these earlier cases.

title: US introduces high fee for H-1B visas, impacting foreign skilled workers
description: New US$103,265 charge raises hiring costs, particularly affecting Chinese and Indian professionals in technology.
content:
The US has introduced a new fee of US$103,265 for H-1B visa applications, a decision that could significantly increase the expenses associated with hiring skilled foreign workers, particularly affecting professionals from China and India.
This proposal comes at a delicate moment in US-China relations, when visa issues have long been a point of contention, and as Beijing enhances its initiatives to attract global technology talent amid escalating competition between the world’s two largest economies.
The US Department of Homeland Security proposed the additional fee on Monday for every H-1B petition subject to the annual numerical cap of 85,000 visas. That figure includes the 20,000 visas reserved for people holding US master’s degrees or higher. Employers would pay the new charge when filing a petition, on top of existing fees.
Universities and certain non-profit or government research organisations would be exempt.
The new measure would also go further than an earlier one. A US$100,000 fee imposed by presidential proclamation in September 2025 mainly targeted new H-1B arrivals from overseas.
The US$103,265 charge would apply more broadly, including to cap-subject petitions filed for people already in the US seeking a change of status.
That means the new policy could have an impact on many international students working in the US under Optional Practical Training.
The administration’s proposal follows a major legal setback over the previous H-1B fee.
In June, a US court in Massachusetts struck down the earlier US$100,000 fee. In a case brought by California and 19 other states, the court ruled that the payment amounted to an unlawful tax that only Congress could authorise.
The administration appealed and sought a stay, but the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit declined to pause the ruling.
DHS is now pursuing a different legal approach through formal rule-making. Rather than presenting the charge as an entry restriction, the department is framing the new fee as a cost-recovery measure.
Officials say the fee could generate about US$8.8 billion a year – money that would help fund immigration adjudication, security vetting, fraud detection and related operations that are currently paid for by taxpayers.
The administration also argues that the high cost would encourage companies to hire and train American workers instead of depending on foreign labour.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance endorsed the proposal, writing on social media that “if an American corporation needs workers, it should hire and train Americans”.
Chinese nationals are the second-largest group of H-1B beneficiaries after Indians, accounting for roughly 12 per cent of approvals in recent years.
That translates into some 46,000 to 49,000 petitions annually, with Chinese H-1B professionals heavily represented in technology, engineering, artificial intelligence and semiconductors.
Indians account for roughly 70–71 per cent of approvals in recent years with about 283,000 to 284,000 petitions annually.
For employers, a six-figure upfront payment – particularly one required without any guarantee that a petition will ultimately be approved – could make sponsoring Chinese and Indian professionals far less attractive.
The effect could be especially significant for Chinese professionals already in the US, many of whom entered the country as students before moving into technology and engineering careers.
Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian declined to comment on the proposed new visa policy during Tuesday’s press conference.
Visa access has long been a contentious issue between Washington and Beijing.
Chinese students and researchers have faced heightened screening, shorter durations of stay and accusations involving national-security risks. Beijing, meanwhile, has repeatedly complained about what it describes as harassment and the politicisation of academic and professional exchanges.
The latest H-1B proposal adds another layer to that dispute.
It also arrives as Washington and Beijing compete for the same pool of highly educated workers in fields increasingly viewed as strategically important, including artificial intelligence, advanced engineering and semiconductors.
China has responded by making a concerted effort to bring talent home.
Domestic AI and semiconductor companies are offering aggressive equity packages and high cash compensation to attract and retain top professionals. Local governments in Beijing, Shanghai and other technology hubs are also offering settling-in subsidies, housing support and tax incentives.
Data already show rising numbers of Chinese students and professionals returning home, with US visa uncertainty among the factors driving the trend.
The talent battle is part of a much larger technology rivalry.
In mid-July, Chinese President Xi Jinping travelled to Shanghai for the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, delivering a high-profile speech presenting China as a champion of open-source AI and global cooperation.
Xi described AI development as a “symphony of global collaboration” rather than a solo performance by any single country. He also hit out at the “overstretching” of national-security concepts to restrict technology sharing.
For years, the US has benefited from its ability to attract international students, engineers, researchers and technology specialists. China is now seeking to strengthen its own pull, offering financial incentives and improved support to persuade skilled workers to return.
The US$103,265 H-1B fee is not yet in force.
A 30-day public comment period will follow formal publication in the Federal Register. After that period, the administration could move to finalise the rule.
Legal challenges are widely expected, meaning the proposal could face another lengthy battle in the courts.
But for Chinese professionals and the US companies that depend on their skills the announcement already sends a powerful signal.

title: Writing the rulebook? China to steer world’s first solid-state battery standards
description: As next-gen EV tech accelerates, the global standard agency’s nod could allow Beijing to export its domestic testing benchmarks worldwide.
content: A Chinese-proposed international standard for automotive solid-state batteries has been approved as a new work item by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) – marking the first of its kind for the advanced power systems and the nation’s latest effort to shape rules in emerging industries. Led by China, with input from technical experts in France, Japan, South Korea and other countries, the proposal outlined application guidelines, items and conditions for testing rechargeable lithium-ion solid-state batteries used in electric vehicles (EVs), according to an official statement by the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR). The governmental agency said the framework would draw on domestic research and development benchmarks to standardise testing specifications for solid-state batteries, which are widely viewed as the next frontier for EV power systems. While EVs on the market today mostly run on liquid-electrolyte lithium-ion batteries, solid-state alternatives are only beginning to see early, limited commercialisation. Beyond cars, their enhanced stability and performance across extreme temperatures have positioned them as promising power sources for emerging sectors, including humanoid robots, drones and electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. Announced by the SAMR last week, the China-led proposal comes amid intensifying global competition in advanced technologies, as major economies increasingly leverage standard-setting to secure long-term industrial influence. “When Chinese products go to an overseas market, they will more easily meet the requirements – there will be few major changes in parameters, production processes and so on,” said a veteran Chinese researcher on international standardisation, who spoke on condition of anonymity. This would place China in the position of setting benchmarks that others followed, she noted. Both Europe and Japan have pursued similar strategies to secure early leadership in emerging technology standards, spanning domains from telecommunications to new materials, the researcher added. “Every country has clear strategic ambitions – no one is hiding it.” China has accelerated its standards architecture in recent years alongside broader global interest in solid-state batteries. In July, the country enacted the world’s first national standard for automotive solid-state batteries using quantitative performance metrics to draw clear technical boundaries between all-solid-state, mixed solid-liquid and liquid batteries. Separately, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released 10 draft industry standards for public comment last month. Yang Chaoxing, a battery analyst at market intelligence provider Shanghai Metals Market, wrote in a research note on Monday that initiating an IEC-level framework signalled the industry had reached a “tipping point”. Standards were no longer optional as carmakers worldwide developed solid-state batteries, he added. “That means China’s testing methods and evaluation systems could become the global default – and that’s worth more than how many batteries it sells,” Yang noted, adding that the rules could also help drive domestic industrial upgrading and accelerate market consolidation by weeding out outdated manufacturing capacity. But while the standards could help establish testing protocols, complex manufacturing and financial hurdles remained, Yang added. “Standards are a catalyst for industrialisation, not a cure-all,” he warned.

title: How a 150kg teacher lost 66kg after being told he might not live to 30
description: Hong Kong-based Paul Goodson suffered from sleep apnoea and binge eating disorder before a diet overhaul, running and Hyrox changed his life.
content: Watching Paul Goodson conquer Hong Kong’s gruelling trail runs and blaze through Hyrox arenas, it is hard to imagine that nine years ago he was trapped in an obese body that was failing him. In 2017, at the age of 29, Goodson weighed 150kg (330lbs). Sleepless nights drove him to the doctor. The verdict was devastating – severe sleep apnoea and a warning that he might not live to see 30. Compounding the crisis was another diagnosis – binge eating disorder (BED). He would regularly gorge on food and then feel a sense of loss of control. “That moment was a reckoning,” Goodson says. For the London-born geography teacher, it kicked off a journey that would take him to Brazil and his current home in Hong Kong – and transform him into a Hyrox competitor and endurance runner. He shed 66kg over the next five years, his weight dropping to 84kg. He has kept close to that weight since.
