Now 38, Goodson’s sights are set on two 2027 events: the London Marathon in April, and qualifying for the Hyrox World Championships in Hong Kong in June. He describes what it took to go from a couch potato in the UK to an elite competitor in Hong Kong. “When I weighed 150kg, any exercise was painful. My earliest big wins were simply going for short walks, one to two kilometres,” he says. He followed his doctor’s recommendation to join the UK-based weight-loss support group Slimming World in 2018. “The emphasis was on eating plans, weekly check-ins and peer support,” he says. “The eating plan emphasised consuming balanced, whole foods rather than severe calorie restriction. We met weekly and the sessions focused on shared recipes, motivation and troubleshooting weight loss hurdles.” How binge eating disorder made losing weight hard Suffering from binge eating disorder made the shift especially difficult for Goodson. “I didn’t know that I was suffering from BED till I went to the doctor,” he says. “I always felt like I had to be eating. I was never full.” Before, he would eat sugary cereal for breakfast, and cheesy chips, pizza or fried chicken nuggets for lunch. “Dinner was the healthiest meal, because my mum cooked it,” Goodson says. “I drank multiple fizzy drinks a day. When I went off to university, things became worse as there was no one to monitor me. I didn’t know when to stop. I knew what it meant to eat healthily, yet I refused to do it.” The roots of his struggle ran deep. Towards the end of primary school, he says, he felt his parents turning more attention to his four siblings and that he could get away with being “sneaky” and consuming more sugary treats. Gradually, as he became large, his friends made fun of him. “I decided to embrace it because I could eat whatever I wanted without consequences.” He adds: “Despite seeing the damage I was doing to my own body, I felt no guilt and continued binge eating because people loved me no matter what or how much I ate.” That mindset shifted when he joined the support group and began focusing on whole foods. “I made sure I had a combination of protein, carbohydrates and fat,” he says. “I cut out sugar and replaced fizzy drinks with water. Whenever I felt hungry, I first drank water.” Starting his journey towards fitness When he took up his first international teaching post in Sao Paulo, Brazil in 2019, he stuck with eating healthier and has done so ever since – swapping sugary treats and fast food for balanced, protein-rich meals and whole foods, substituting water for fizzy drinks and allowing for the occasional slice of pizza. While teaching in Brazil, he lost 50kg through diet changes and taking up running via the Couch-to-5k app, which is about getting people off the sofa and moving. Covid-19 lockdowns briefly stalled his progress, but moving to Hong Kong in August 2021 offered a fresh start and enabled him to lose the final 16kg by May 2022. “Once I lost weight, running was possible,” Goodson says. Running played a big role. “When I arrived in Hong Kong, I saw how popular it was,” he says. “There are so many run clubs – different abilities, genders, intensities – something for everyone. I wanted to be part of the fun.” He joined three clubs and now trains six times a week. “Wazup is fabulously friendly – along Victoria Harbour on Wednesday evenings and Bowen Road on Saturday mornings. Dop is more vigorous, pushing you to your limits at Aberdeen Sports Ground on Tuesdays, or offering a casual zone two run along the harbour on Sundays,” he says, referring to a slow, comfortable, aerobic-base training pace that sits at roughly 60-70 per cent of participants’ maximum heart rate. “Just Keep Moving is excellent for intervals at Tamar Park every Thursday,” he adds. “They mix bodyweight exercises with 700-metre [0.4-mile] and 1km runs, ending with 100 glute-busting squats against the backdrop of Kowloon’s harbour lights.” When Goodson was at his lowest weight, in the summer of 2022, he went to London for an abdominoplasty – a “tummy tuck” to remove excess fat and loose skin. “With all the weight I lost, my skin became loose, and I didn’t feel comfortable in my body,” Goodson says. “The surgery tightened my skin and gave me renewed confidence. I could go to the beach without feeling conscious of how I looked.” Beyond the clubs, Goodson loves the trails. His favourites are the Twin Peaks in Tai Tam Country Park and the 70km Lantau Trail. “Twin Peaks always ends with a sweet reward in Stanley, whereas the Lantau Trail ends with a well-earned pizza at Mui Wo.” He complements running with HIIT and spin classes. “HIIT guarantees a phenomenal sweat,” he says. Goodson averages 40km a week, splitting mileage between midweek runs and weekend long runs. In January 2024, he ran his first marathon, the Standard Chartered Hong Kong Marathon. A year later, he completed his second, shaving more than 20 minutes off his time to finish in 3 hours, 28 minutes, 42 seconds. In 2026, he added his first official half marathon to the list. After the 2025 marathon, Goodson tore his Achilles tendon – a 2cm (0.8-inch) injury that forced him to pause and reflect. “I didn’t allow myself enough rest before returning to training for Hyrox,” he says. “I learned the hard way that, although exercise is fun, our bodies need to be carefully maintained.” Entering the ‘exhilarating’ world of Hyrox Goodson got involved in Hyrox after seeing the excitement in fellow gym-goers. “I remember people at my local gym talking about the first Hyrox event to be held in Hong Kong in November 2022,” he says. “Despite improving my running and building strength, the idea of running 8km and completing eight gruelling stations of cardio and weighted exercises scared me. “The hype was exhilarating. I regretted not participating once I witnessed the smiles, laughter and camaraderie of the participants.” He made sure to sign up for the next one, and has since completed 21 races in 18 events in Hong Kong, mainland China, Japan, Taiwan, Thailand and Singapore. Goodson says that the Hyrox race atmosphere stays with you from the first event. “The electric atmosphere, [the] EDM beats … the inevitable fatigue – lactic acid flooding the legs, testing every athlete’s grit. And the spectators – family, friends and strangers alike, whose cheers deliver a surge of energy no gel can match,” he says. For Goodson, the Hyrox experience in Taipei in March 2026 was a high point: in the Pro Singles category, he crossed the line with a new personal best of 1 hour and 10 minutes. “The triumph was tempered by reflection,” he says. “Poor wall balls reminded me that resilience is not just about finishing, but about striving to improve.” The rewards for Goodson have been tangible. His heart rate is lower, his sleep is uninterrupted and leg pain that once plagued him is gone. His transformation has touched those closest to him. For Christmas, his younger sister Caitlin gave him a custom book cataloguing all his Hyrox races. He now channels that support to friends and strangers who reach out for advice. “I’m a big advocate of having a sense of community as the key to success,” Goodson says. “The moment you are determined to make a physical change, no obstacle can stop you.” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Chinese worker develops severe muscle breakdown after manager punishes her with 200 squats
description: After finishing the punishment, Yang was left unable to stand properly and struggled to walk.
content: A Chinese woman developed life-threatening muscle breakdown after her company forced her to perform 200 squats as punishment for unfinished work. The young woman, surnamed Yang, recently moved to Hangzhou in eastern China’s Zhejiang province and began her first job as a financial consultant at a loan assistance company in June. The role was essentially a telesales position. Her team manager, surnamed Zhang, required each team member to make 200 calls, invite one client, and secure one client expressing intention to collaborate every day. On July 28, after failing to complete her work quota, Yang was given the choice to either perform 100 squats or pay 50 yuan (US$7) for each unfinished task. Having completed neither task, she opted to perform 200 squats to keep her job, stating: “I have no money.” She recorded videos of herself doing the squats in batches at various locations throughout the office building as proof for her supervisor. In the footage, after completing the last few squats, she was unable to stand up properly and staggered while walking. She reported feeling severe pain in her legs. However, due to her financial situation, Yang did not seek medical attention until five days later when her urine turned dark. At the hospital, she was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis, a serious condition where damaged muscle tissue breaks down rapidly, releasing its components into the bloodstream. If present in large quantities, these components can harm the kidneys and potentially lead to life-threatening kidney failure. Yang’s diagnosis revealed that her creatine kinase level exceeded 16,000 U/L, whereas a level of 1,000 U/L is typically sufficient for a diagnosis of rhabdomyolysis. Fortunately, Yang did not suffer from kidney failure. The doctor advised her to rest and avoid strenuous exercise. Yang stated that she spent 1,400 yuan (US$210) on treatment. Furthermore, as her condition prevented her from working or completing her punishment, she resigned on July 30. Yang believed the company was intentionally managing her out by imposing unrealistic targets. She contacted Zhang and demanded reimbursement for her medical fees, transport costs, and 15,000 yuan (US$2,200) in compensation for personal injury, to cover her living expenses for 75 days as her condition would not allow her to search for a new job soon. Zhang rejected her demands and suggested she take legal action. Yang sought assistance from a local conflict-resolution TV show. Speaking to the reporter, Zhang admitted to violating labour laws but insisted that the issue had nothing to do with the company. Zhang indicated he could not accept the amount of compensation Yang requested. Yang registered her case with the labour inspection unit responsible for overseeing the company, and the staff assured her they would investigate the matter. According to labour law, if an employer insults or physically punishes employees, the responsible personnel may face detention for up to 15 days. “Zhang should be detained for 15 days,” insisted an online observer. “The young lady should recognise that no job is more important than her health,” remarked another.

title: Singapore court hands Amos Yee 4 new charges for posts on race, child porn
description: This brings the online commentator’s total number of charges to seven – including three for dodging national service.
content: Singaporean online commentator Amos Yee Pang Sang on Wednesday received four fresh charges linked to posts he made about race and children. This brings his total number of charges to seven, including three for allegedly dodging national service. According to charge sheets, the 27-year-old allegedly promoted feelings of disharmony between racial and religious groups in Singapore in two blog posts in April. In the posts, he allegedly discussed racial discrimination, commented on crimes and sentencing, and suggested that members of certain races should protest to hold another race accountable. On May 27, he uploaded a video in which he allegedly commented on racial discrimination and the reasons for the number of inmates from a certain race. He also suggested that members of that race protest. Yee is accused of making an indecent communication by publishing an article titled “Why Sex with Babies is Bad” on June 30. He was also charged with making an indecent communication over videos made in 2021 while he was outside Singapore. The videos were titled “Free Speech for the Pedophile”, “Why Child Pornography Should Be Legal” and “Why Pedophilia Is Alright”. In the videos, he labelled himself as an “advocate” for “child porn” and “baby porn”. Asked if Yee had any position on the new charges, Yee’s lawyer, Divanan Narkunan, said the new charges were served yesterday and he was in the middle of taking instructions. The prosecution offered bail of S$15,000 (US$11,800), on conditions including that Yee must not post anything online concerning his views on paedophilia, or anything inciting ill feelings between racial groups. Yee attended court with his mother but did not address the court. X took down the video published in May after police issued a direction requiring it to do so. Police also directed Yee to remove the posts from his blog. Yee was originally charged with national service enlistment offences after being deported to Singapore from the United States in March. He was set to plead guilty to the NS-related charges in September, but the hearing has been vacated as of Wednesday and refixed for a pre-trial conference on September 18. Defaulters can be jailed for up to three years or fined up to S$10,000, or both, per charge. For promoting racial disharmony, an offender can be jailed for up to three years, fined, or both. For making indecent communication likely to cause alarm under the Protection from Harassment Act, an offender can be fined up to S$5,000. This article was first published by CNA

title: Meet Mikayla Demaiter, the hockey player-turned-model dating golfer Bryson DeChambeau
description: Previously linked to Lilia Schneider, the two-time US Open champion is now dating the Canadian influencer dubbed the ‘world’s sexiest hockey player’.
content: US professional golfer Bryson DeChambeau is dating 26-year-old Mikayla Demaiter, according to Us Weekly. DeChambeau was previously rumoured to be dating Lilia Schneider. But earlier this month, fans of the golfer noticed that in a photo Demaiter posted, the Canadian model was wearing a guest pass for a LIV Golf event in New York, while a Crushers GC cap – the team DeChambeau captains – could also be seen in the background. “They are both pretty private when it comes to relationships,” a source told Us Weekly. According to the insider, the relationship is fairly new, but DeChambeau and Demaiter seem happy together. A model and influencer with a massive social media following, Demaiter is nicknamed the “world’s sexiest hockey player”. Here’s what we know about the latest girlfriend of the two-time US Open champion. What is Mikayla Demaiter’s background? Mikayla Demaiter was born on May 14, 2000, in Ontario, Canada. She played ice hockey in the Provincial Women’s Hockey League, and was a goaltender for the Bluewater Hawks. Demaiter had a promising season from 2018 to 2019, playing 20 games. She retired from the sport in 2019 due to a knee injury and moved on to modelling. She now has 3 million followers on Instagram and 1.2 million followers on X. Despite her retirement, the former goalie occasionally shares photos and clips of herself returning to the ice in her hockey gear. She has a bookish side Demaiter attended Western University and majored in occupational therapy and disability studies, per her Instagram Stories. The model revealed that from a young age she has had a passion for outer space, ancient Egypt and dinosaurs, and has even taken an online astrophysics course. She is also an avid reader, sharing book recommendations such as 1984, Man’s Search for Meaning and Eragon on social media. She is an animal lover Last September, Demaiter purchased over 20 hectares of land, where she has since been enjoying rural life. The animal lover shares her home with six dogs, two cats and two horses. Two of her dogs, Georgie and Willie, are disabled, having been born with the double merle gene that causes deafness and blindness. Demaiter explained on Instagram that merging her university studies in disability with her love for animals felt like “destiny”. Her long-term goal is to turn her property into a non-profit animal rescue, with plans to create a mental health programme for veterans who will be granted unrestricted access to the animals.

title: Huawei, HP settle disputes with multi-year Wi-fi patent cross-licensing deal
description: Huawei has been pushing for the monetisation of its patent portfolio to generate returns on its investments in research and development.
content: China’s Huawei Technologies and US personal computer giant HP announced on Wednesday that they had reached a deal to license each other’s Wi-fi patents. The two companies signed a multi-year global patent cross-licensing agreement, which granted HP the right to use certain Huawei Wi-fi patents on its PCs for a fee. “This agreement is a strong testament to Huawei’s persistent independent innovation in cutting-edge fields in information and communications technology,” said Alan Fan, Huawei’s chief intellectual property (IP) officer, in a statement. “Through patent licensing, Huawei shares its innovation with the industry, particularly in the area of standardised technologies.” The agreement came after Huawei filed a lawsuit against HP in 2025 over Wi-fi 6 patents, but the disputes were resolved in November last year after the American PC maker became a licensee of the patent pool of Italian intellectual property management firm Sisvel, gaining access to some of the contested patents. “This is a standard-essential patent licence covering Wi-fi technology – something used broadly across the industry and routine for companies whose products connect to Wi-fi,” HP said in a statement on Wednesday, adding it did not indicate a deeper strategic or commercial partnership with Huawei. Standard-essential patents cover technologies required in products to comply with technical industry standards, such as Wi-fi and 5G. Huawei has been pushing for the monetisation of its vast patent portfolio spanning from telecommunications to audio and video technologies, as it seeks to generate returns on its continuous investments in research and development. The Shenzhen-based firm invested 192.3 billion yuan (US$28.6 billion) into research and development in 2025, accounting for nearly 22 per cent of its total revenue, according to Huawei’s annual report. One of the world’s largest patent holders, Huawei had 165,000 active granted patents in its portfolio as of 2025. In 2022, Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei urged the company’s IP team to step up efforts to turn its vast pool of patents into revenue via “reasonable pricing” and to “generate an appropriate return” on the R&D investments. Huawei has expanded the influence of its IP through over 260 licensing deals with major global tech firms including Nokia, Samsung and Amazon, alongside domestic smartphone rivals like Oppo, Vivo and Xiaomi, according to the company. The firm generated more than US$630 million in patent licensing in 2024, according to Huawei. Since it was founded, the company has paid out nearly three times the amount of royalties it received. In June, Huawei announced that it would start charging royalties for its Wi‑fi 7 technologies, the newest wireless standard, with the rate set at US$0.5 per unit. A key player in Wi-fi licensing, Huawei’s patent licensing deals covered 1.6 billion devices globally by the end of 2025, the firm said.

title: Japan expands Fukushima soil recycling project to Sendai, Saitama
description: The government has already reused the soil at 12 sites in Tokyo since July last year, including the prime minister’s office.
content: Japan’s Environment Ministry says it plans to reuse soil collected in decontamination work near the disaster-stricken Fukushima Daiichi nuclear complex at national government branch offices in Miyagi and Saitama prefectures. The government has already reused the soil at 12 sites in Tokyo since July last year, including the prime minister’s office and other buildings in the Kasumigaseki district. Excluding demonstration projects in Fukushima prefecture, the expansion to the cities of Sendai and Saitama will mark the first reuse of the soil outside Tokyo. The government aims to further expand the soil’s reuse to other branch offices in Japan to reduce the total amount of soil that eventually needs to be dealt with. As of the end of July, about 14.46 million cubic metres (510 million cubic feet) of removed soil and other waste had been placed at an interim storage facility near the nuclear complex. The Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant, hit by a powerful earthquake and tsunami in 2011, suffered fuel meltdowns at three of its nuclear reactors, releasing radiation into the atmosphere. The government aims to recycle 75 per cent of the soil with relatively low levels of radioactivity for use in public works, but the outlook for achieving that target remains uncertain, with only 2 cubic metres to be used in the two cities. While the timing has yet to be decided, the soil will be used in plantings at a government building in Sendai’s Aoba ward, and in flower beds at a government building in Saitama’s Chuo ward. Sendai Mayor Kazuko Kori said at a press conference on Tuesday that as the soil was also being used at the prime minister’s office, “I don’t think it will be a problem”. Meanwhile, Saitama Governor Motohiro Ono and Saitama Mayor Hayato Shimizu have asked the government to disclose information such as monitoring test results and proceed only after obtaining residents’ understanding. Okuma Mayor Jun Yoshida and Futaba Mayor Shiro Izawa, whose towns host the interim storage facility, separately expressed hope that the move would contribute to progress towards final disposal outside the prefecture. The expansion beyond Tokyo was “a new step, and I want to help people in regional areas further understand its safety”, Environment Minister Hirotaka Ishihara said at the press conference. The soil waste currently at an interim storage facility near the crippled Fukushima nuclear plant must by law be moved outside the prefecture by March 2045. But with the search for final disposal sites making little progress, the government hopes that expanding soil reuse to regional branch offices will help win public understanding. According to a road map for final disposal outside Fukushima prefecture drawn up in August last year, the government will begin selecting candidate disposal sites around 2030 and make the selection around 2035.

title: Opinion | Why Asimov’s Foundation series still resonates in the AI era
description: Social engineering: why Elon Musk, Nobel Prize winners and cult leaders are all obsessed with Asimov’s Foundation.
content: Elon Musk called it a fundamental catalyst for SpaceX. Nobel laureate Paul Krugman credited it with shaping his career. Newt Gingrich made it required reading for his congressional staff, and even Japanese cult leader Shoko Asahara was reportedly inspired by it. Isaac Asimov’s Foundation was published as a book series 75 years ago this week, and it has lost none of its relevance or poignancy today. Unlike Frank Herbert’s Dune, which is evocative, poetic and elegantly composed, Asimov’s style was functional, unadorned and populated by stock characters. However, Foundation remains a seminal masterpiece of science fiction because of its conceptual ideas and philosophical daring. In the twilight of a once-mighty Galactic Empire, mathematician Hari Seldon develops “psychohistory”, a revolutionary science that uses statistical mechanics (big data) to predict human behaviour and social development. Realising the Empire’s collapse is inevitable and will plunge humanity into tens of thousands of years of dark ages, Seldon creates a master plan to keep the flame of civilisation alive, shortening the coming anarchy to a single millennium. Under the guise of compiling all human knowledge into the Encyclopedia Galactica, Seldon establishes the First Foundation on a bleak planet at the outer edge of the galaxy. Lacking natural resources, the First Foundation nonetheless thrives on the strength of innovation – specifically its monopoly on miniaturised nuclear power. Over centuries, it navigates a series of political and social crises predicted by Seldon, known as “Seldon Crises”. Combining technology, economic leverage and an advanced military, the First Foundation steadily shepherds and coerces its larger, technologically backward neighbours towards galactic unification. The plan is nearly shattered by the arrival of the Mule, a charismatic mutant with hypnotic mind-control abilities. Because psychohistory relies on mass statistics, it fails to account for a single unpredictable individual capable of subjugating millions of followers at will. The Mule effortlessly conquers the First Foundation, proving that technological and economic dominance are useless against mental manipulation. The galaxy is saved only by the mysterious Second Foundation – a hidden group of telepaths Seldon secretly established as the ultimate guardians of his plan. Using “mentalics” – a blend of telepathy, emotional manipulation and cognitive control – these caretakers subtly steer history from the shadows. Their masterclass in psychological warfare neutralises the Mule and convinces the First Foundation that the mentalists have been destroyed. By appearing defeated, the Second Foundation preserves its anonymity, continuing to secretly guide humanity towards a restored empire. When Asimov began writing Foundation 85 years ago, he was capturing the cutting-edge intellectual currents of his era: mathematical determinism, the quantification of social sciences and the rise of central planning in governance. Economists such as John Maynard Keynes argued that macro-level human behaviour could be managed through top-down intervention, while Jan Tinbergen and Ragnar Frisch were building the first econometric models. Seldon’s psychohistory was essentially macroeconomics and public administration pushed to their absolute logical extreme – individual chaos smoothed out by the predictable behaviour of billions. At the same time, Asimov also foresaw the limits and dangers of this naive optimism. The Second Foundation served as an allegory for covert social engineering, arriving just as mass media technologies such as radio and television entered everyday life. Edward Bernays, nephew of Sigmund Freud and father of modern public relations, argued in his 1928 book Propaganda that an “invisible government” must consciously manipulate the subconscious minds of the masses to maintain democratic stability. The world witnessed the darker side of that theory with the rise of Adolf Hitler and totalitarian propaganda in the 1930s. Today, algorithmic micro-targeting, data mining and behavioural profiling enable social engineering on a scale of which Bernays could only have dreamed. Deepfakes, voice cloning and AI conversational agents have made psychological manipulation faster, cheaper and harder to detect. The Second Foundation reflects this “deep state” concept – an unseen elite that ensures the masses retain the illusion of free choice while subtle interventions guide them towards a predetermined outcome. Most intriguingly, in the later sequels, Asimov merged his Robot and Foundation universes into a single grand narrative, bringing artificial intelligence to the centre stage. It is revealed that an ancient robot has been the ultimate puppet master for more than 20,000 years, quietly orchestrating human destiny. Seldon’s plan was actually an instrument of AI control. Centuries before the Foundation was established, human society developed a deep, subconscious fear of AI. Bound by the Three Laws of Robotics – which strictly prohibit harming humans or allowing them to come to harm through inaction – robots realised that protecting humanity from its own self-destruction required covert manipulation. To fulfil their prime directive, the machines retreated to the shadows, initiating a multi-millennial era of “benign” mind control that built the very fabric of human history.

title: Trump pick Darline Graham wins election despite struggling over Taiwan question
description: The political newcomer wins Republican Senate nomination after failing to answer questions about South China Sea issues.
content: South Carolina Senator Darline Graham won the Republican nomination in seeking a full term on Tuesday, overcoming a rocky moment in last week’s debate, when she struggled to answer questions about Taiwan and the South China Sea. Graham, a political newcomer, was appointed to the seat in July following the unexpected death of her brother, Lindsey Graham, one of the Senate’s most senior and influential Republicans. Backed by US President Donald Trump, she was required to contest a special primary to secure the party’s nomination for a full term. According to results released on Tuesday at 9pm, Graham won 52.4 per cent of the vote, defeating Representative Ralph Norman in the run-off and will advance to the November election. South Carolina is a Republican stronghold, and whoever wins the Republican nomination is widely expected to win in November. Graham and Norman advanced from an earlier August primary in which neither candidate won more than 50 per cent of the vote, forcing Tuesday’s run-off. The campaign was not without geopolitical drama. During last week’s debate, Graham was asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the United States. She appeared unprepared for the topic, first asking the moderator to repeat the question, then acknowledging that she was not an expert on national security. “I am not that informed on national security,” she said, after a pause. “But I do support the military.” The moment drew widespread press and social media attention, with critics questioning whether she has the experience and qualifications to serve as a senator. It also highlighted a sharp contrast with her late brother, who spent decades building a reputation in Washington as a prominent foreign-policy hawk. On the same debate stage, Norman gave a more detailed answer, calling Taiwan “a definite ally” and highlighting the island’s semiconductor industry. Norman has also been a strong Trump supporter. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Graham later said in multiple interviews that she is not a polished career politician and had “tripped up” on the Taiwan question. She doubled down on her argument that her focus is on South Carolina voters’ concerns rather than geopolitical issues. “People in South Carolina are more worried about making ends meet,” she said on a FOX TV interview. “They’re concerned about a lot of other things other than Taiwan.” Graham also said China “scares” her, describing Beijing as an enemy and a military and economic threat to the United States. The Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office in Washington said Taiwan enjoys strong bipartisan support in the United States and that “Taiwan-US relations continue to develop steadily”. The office said it would continue to further deepen the partnership. The South China Sea dispute is also resurfacing in Washington, with this year’s defence spending bill containing provisions on the issue. Beijing’s maritime claims overlap with those of Vietnam, the Philippines and other neighbours, fuelling disputes over fishing grounds, energy reserves and shipping routes. China has rejected a 2016 international tribunal ruling favouring Manila. After the debate stumble, Trump rushed to Graham’s defence, describing her as “smart” and “terrific.” “She was being honest,” Trump said to reporters last week. “She’s gonna do what the military wants, and really what the president wants.” On Monday, Maga Inc., the super PAC backing Trump and his allies, poured nearly US$830,000 into Graham’s campaign for voter outreach through calls and text messages. Graham’s victory also underscores Trump’s influence among Republican voters ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, as Republicans seek to maintain control of Congress. Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a doctor who previously ran for Congress and lost, in the November general election.

title: Netflix K-drama Mousetrap: Ryu Jun-yeol leads slick but sluggish mystery thriller
description: Ryu Jun-yeol stars as a novelist with severe anxiety whose life is turned upside-down in this enigmatic if slow-moving thriller.
content: Lead cast: Ryu Jun-yeol, Sul Kyung-gu, Lee Kyu-hyung Netflix Korea releases major new Korean dramas year-round, but it has quietly made a habit of reserving August for some of its most daring offerings – shows such as Mask Girl (2023), The Frog (2024) and Aema (2025), which deliver a cocktail of stylish thrills and generally arrive on the streaming service under a veil of mystery. That tradition continues this year, as South Korea looks forward to winding down one of its hottest summers on record, with the release of the enigmatic thriller Mousetrap. Starring Ryu Jun-yeol (Reply 1988) and Sul Kyung-gu (Hyper Knife), the series follows two very different men whose lives are manipulated by the same veiled figure. Based on the webtoon Deuljwi (whose title has been translated as both “Field Mouse” and “The Rat Trap”) by Ludovico, the series stars Ryu as Je Moon-jae, a man with severe anxiety who never leaves his sleek, sky-high flat in the middle of Seoul. Moon-jae – whose full name sounds like “my problem” in Korean – makes his living as an anonymous author of mystery novels. He is so secretive that his property and bank accounts are all held in the name of his school classmate Son Su-hyeon (Mu Jin-seong, Typhoon Family), who works as an accountant. Consisting of daily treadmill runs, premade meals and medication, Moon-jae’s life is calm and orderly. It is also, by his own admission, a little dull. He tends to gaze wistfully out of the window, lamenting the unbroken routines of the lives unfolding below him and daydreaming about a change. He gets far more than he bargained for one day, beginning with a banking application that no longer accepts his fingerprint login. What at first seems like a minor glitch soon snowballs into a major crisis: he wakes up to a real estate agent demanding he vacate his property, he is frozen out of all his accounts and somebody has even changed his registered fingerprints. He has become, to all intents and purposes, a ghost. Moon-jae winds up out in the bustle of the city with nothing but his pyjamas, slippers and a phone he is unable to use. Things only get worse when No-ja (Sul), a former enforcer who seems to think Moon-jae owes him a substantial amount of money, marches up to the bewildered writer and swings a baseball bat at his head. Meanwhile, homicide detective Park Soon-yong (Lee Kyu-hyung, Uncle Samsik) is investigating a series of deaths involving unidentifiable bodies. During this investigation, he receives an anonymous tip pointing him towards Moon-jae and No-ja. Aside from a brief mention of a traumatic childhood incident to justify Moon-jae’s introverted adulthood, Mousetrap largely dispenses with place-setting before launching into its mystery. It is a bit like yanking away the tablecloth and smashing the dishes before we have had a chance to see what was being served. With a show like this, it is a given that things and characters are not going to be exactly as they seem. However, since we don’t know much about Moon-jae to begin with, his current predicament fails to land with the impact it might, and the questions and secrets that begin bubbling up to the surface similarly fall a little flat. Somewhere in Mousetrap there is a compelling mystery, but what is missing is the contrast necessary to throw it into sharp relief – the narrative’s various set pieces and twists pile up on one another rather than bounce off each other. With too much mystery and too little narrative tissue, the story feels slow at first. This is also down to the staging of the show. The direction of Kim Hong-sun (Money Heist: Korea – Joint Economic Area) is slick but at times spins its wheels in simple scenes that feel unnecessarily drawn out – a look out the window that conveys a single detail captured from too many angles, for instance. The series does warm up a little after its slower opening episodes, when Moon-jae and No-ja are forced to team up to unmask the person ruining their lives. Though details about the characters – particularly Moon-jae – remain thin on the ground, we begin to learn about them through the way they react to and treat each other. As the story begins to lift the lid ever so slightly on its mystery, it deliberately evokes Park Chan-wook’s Oldboy through its use of music and memory, alongside a villain who increasingly feels like Yu Ji-tae’s iconic revenge architect in Park’s film. Mousetrap’s ambitious nod to this classic revenge thriller is admirable, but it also raises the bar to a level its opening salvo struggles to graze, let alone surpass. Mousetrap will start streaming on Netflix on August 28

title: China rushes to develop Moderna-style cancer vaccines amid market frenzy
description: Chinese biotech firms are already working on more than 100 cancer vaccines. Now, many are seeing their shares surge amid Moderna’s breakthrough.
content: A group of Hong Kong-listed biotechnology companies have seen their stock prices surge in the wake of Moderna’s breakthrough cancer vaccine trial, as the Chinese companies push forward with similar vaccine programmes. The companies – from Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals to Li Ka-shing-backed CK Life Sciences – already have a slew of cancer vaccines in development. “China is moving quickly and has already built a large pipeline of more than 100 cancer vaccine programmes,” said Cui Cui, head of healthcare research for Asia at Jefferies. “The next challenge is how to replicate Moderna’s breakthrough in other tumour types, as melanoma alone is not a big market,” Cui added, referring to the severe form of skin cancer Moderna’s vaccine treats. An estimated 2.58 million people died of cancer in China in 2024, according to the latest data from the country’s National Cancer Centre. It also remains to be seen whether the companies can manufacture personalised vaccines quickly and at a reasonable cost, according to the analyst. Markets reacted with euphoria after Moderna and Merck announced last week that their personalised mRNA vaccine had cut the risk of melanoma returning or spreading in a phase three trial of about 1,140 patients – a first for an mRNA cancer vaccine. mRNA-based approaches are more agile and cost-efficient compared with traditional methods that rely on growing cells or proteins Bruce Liu, Simon-Kucher The excitement has also rippled across China, with Shanghai-based Everest Medicines seeing its shares in Hong Kong rise 34 per cent over the past five days. CK Life Sciences, a unit of Li Ka-shing-backed CK Group, has also jumped more than 11 per cent. “The therapeutic cancer vaccines are intended to treat people that have cancer,” said Dr Melvin Toh Kean-meng, CK Life Sciences’ vice-president and chief scientific officer. “The purpose of the vaccine is either to prevent the cancer from coming back after the tumour has been removed, or to actually treat the cancer even though it’s still there.” “When it is injected into a patient, it triggers the patient’s immune system to have an immune response, usually in the form of a T cell response. The T cells will then be able to attack the cancer cells and kill the cancer cells,” he added. “Sometimes a vaccine can also trigger an antibody response, and that can also help to control the tumour growth.” Both CK Life Sciences and Moderna are developing therapeutic vaccines. But unlike Moderna’s personalised approach, CK Life Sciences is developing “off-the-shelf, non-personalised vaccines” using circular RNA, according to Toh. “We think that’s the part that will make it more widely accessible, rather than very specific to individual patients,” he said. The firm’s most advanced asset was expected to enter clinical trials by late 2027, he added. Personalised cancer treatment involves doctors taking a tumour sample from the patient to identify key mutations or neoantigens, and then creating a personalised vaccine that is injected back into the patient, according to Bruce Liu, a senior partner at consulting firm Simon-Kucher. The treatment comes with a steep price tag. Beijing-based Likang Life Sciences, which has developed its own personalised mRNA vaccine candidate, estimates its treatment would cost less than 100,000 yuan (US$14,900) for a six-dose course. Founded in 2019, the company has raised US$27.42 million, according to market data provider Caplight. In China, most cancer vaccine candidates are still in the very early stages of clinical development, as “the field remains at an early stage overall”, according to Cui. Firms including Shanghai Regenelead Therapies – a subsidiary of Jiangsu Hengrui – as well as Hangzhou Newanjin Biotechnology and Likang Life Sciences have started phase two trials for personalised mRNA cancer vaccines, according to a report by Zhongtai Securities released on Monday. Other companies including Akeso – which the report dubbed the DeepSeek of China’s biotech industry – Youcare Pharmaceutical Group and Everest Medicines have entered phase one trials, Zhongtai Securities added. “The technology has entered human trials at some leading Chinese biotech companies and has shown commercial value in treating pancreatic cancer,” said Stella Ling, the founder of JingYuan Consulting and a pharmaceutical industry veteran. According to Liu of Simon-Kucher, “mRNA-based approaches are more agile and cost-efficient compared with traditional methods that rely on growing cells or proteins”.

title: Why Philippine, US forces tried to ‘scope’ a Chinese-linked steel plant in Mindanao
description: US embassy says American military personnel wanted to assess Sanjia Steel’s premises as a potential site for next year’s Balikatan exercises.
content: Philippine military officials said on Tuesday that Filipino and US personnel had tried to access a closed Chinese-linked steel plant in Mindanao as part of planning for a future naval facility and joint military exercises, extending a dispute that had already drawn protests from Beijing over Manila’s handling of Chinese workers at the site. Sanjia Steel Corporation, which leases 22.6 hectares (56 acres) inside the government-run PHIVIDEC Industrial Estate in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental province, now sits beside land Manila considers strategically important for its military expansion in northern Mindanao. At its regular briefing on Tuesday, the Armed Forces of the Philippines confirmed that some of its personnel, along with US soldiers, had attempted to “scope” Sanjia’s premises on August 19. The team left after being told it lacked the written authorisation required to enter the premises, according to the US embassy and local reports citing a police blotter. The US embassy said its military personnel had accompanied members of the Philippine armed forces and staff from the PHIVIDEC Industrial Authority, which operates the sprawling industrial zone. The US soldiers, the embassy said, wanted to assess “its potential for use in bilateral military exercises”, but a lack of any prior written authorisation meant “the team moved on to other site visits as planned. At no point was entry insisted upon”. The Philippine team had a separate purpose, said retired rear admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, a spokesman for the armed forces. “If you look at the situation in Tagoloan, it is close to a future projected site for development for a naval base. It is close to Lumbia Airport, an EDCA site. It is close to other critical government infrastructure,” Trinidad said. EDCA refers to the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement, which allows US personnel to be present on a rotational basis at agreed Philippine military facilities and lets the Pentagon maintain logistics hubs under the 1951 Mutual Defence Treaty and related agreements, including the Mutual Logistics Support Agreement. After the briefing, armed forces personnel explained to This Week in Asia the reason for the visit. Navy deputy spokesman Lieutenant Colonel Vladimir Cabrera said US forces went to Sanjia as part of a “site survey” for next year’s Balikatan, or shoulder to shoulder, military exercises with the Philippines and other nations. He said this did not mean Sanjia itself would be used for Balikatan, but that “the whole area”, including Sanjia, could be affected by the training exercises and accompanying civil-military operations. Military spokeswoman Colonel Francel Margareth Padilla said a Philippine-operated naval facility was going to be built inside the 7,400-acre PHIVIDEC Industrial Estate, where Sanjia was a tenant. The planned naval base “is really projected to be an EDCA site” and would be part of the Comprehensive Archipelagic Defence Concept, the armed forces’ pivot towards external and territorial defence after decades of focusing on internal security and the local communist insurgency, Padilla added. A source who spoke on condition of anonymity said turning the future naval base into another EDCA site “makes sense” since Lumbia Air Base, located about 30km (19 miles) from PHIVIDEC, was already a declared EDCA site. Lumbia used to be a civilian airport until the Philippine Air Force took over in 2013 and upgraded its facilities. The source noted that the planned naval facility would front Macajalar Bay, a natural deepwater bay with depths that can accommodate submarines. According to the Environmental Management Bureau, Sanjia operated its own wharf along Macajalar Bay, where scrap metal imported from Japan and China was offloaded. Sanjia was organised in 2018 and became fully operational inside PHIVIDEC in 2021, with a declared investment of 800 million pesos and annual production capacity of 600,000 metric tonnes of steel. Earlier reports identified Chinese businessman Tony Yang as among Sanjia’s incorporators and chief stockholders, although the company has said he has since divested and is no longer a shareholder, director, officer or beneficial owner. Tony is the elder brother of Michael Yang, a former economic adviser to then president Rodrigo Duterte. Tony Yang was arrested in September 2024 amid investigations into illegal gaming operators and accused of identity and immigration-law violations. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources ordered Sanjia to close in June and cancelled the facility’s environmental compliance certificate, citing findings by nuclear experts from the Philippine Nuclear Research Institute that uranium-238, thorium-228 and thorium-232 had been detected in imported scrap metal used to make steel bars. The plant had already been at the centre of a China-Philippines row in May, when an inter-agency raid led by the Presidential Anti-Organised Crime Commission and the National Bureau of Investigation, and attended by Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, resulted in the arrest of 69 Chinese nationals and one Filipino, according to Philippine reports. Philippine authorities accused the workers of immigration, labour and other violations, while the Chinese embassy said 70 Chinese workers had been detained and objected to what it described as discriminatory and selective law enforcement. Embassy spokesman Ji Linpeng said on August 16: “Teodoro has recently spared no effort to stage anti-China activities. His real purpose is to destabilise and sabotage China-Philippines relations, pushing the Philippines to the forefront of confrontation with China, and create continued tensions and conflicts, all to serve his own ulterior political agenda.” Trinidad said the embassy’s statements were part of what he described as foreign information manipulation and interference activities meant “to shape the information space [with] false narratives” intended “to divide us as a people … and ultimately advance their own interests”. Beijing sanctioned Teodoro and members of his immediate family in June, barring them from mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau, and prohibiting Chinese organisations and individuals from transactions or cooperation with them. Teodoro rejected the accusations and said he was “under no obligation to answer questions from any foreign government or embassy”. He also noted that the PHIVIDEC Industrial Authority, which runs the estate, was under his supervision as defence chief.

title: China event asks if Apec’s rules can close growing AI gap between rich and poor
description: Conference hears that the bloc’s flexible structure could help in developing a fairer regulatory system.
content: A “widening” AI gap between advanced economies and developing countries has sparked calls to use the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation framework to develop an open, fairer and culturally sensitive governance system. Although the technology is often hailed as a great leveller in an era of sluggish economic growth, a conference held in southern China last weekend heard that many Global South countries lacked the critical infrastructure and talent required to harness artificial intelligence effectively. Speakers at the event warned there was a risk innovation could largely benefit a few countries and businesses, and proposed a range of solutions, including joint programmes and taking full advantage of Apec’s flexible structures. Chung Chul, president of the Korea Economic Research Institute, said the economic gap was “widening, not shrinking” and an “inclusive” framework designed to tackle this problem “cannot be treated as a residual outcome. Instead, it should be something considered beforehand, not just after innovation.” He said this principle should be fundamental to any form of technological cooperation and innovation, adding: “So the central policy question is not whether Apec should use AI but whether the region can scale innovation without widening the gap.” Figures from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development indicate the global AI landscape and its rule-making processes are heavily concentrated in the hands of a small group of nations and roughly 100 corporations. Fewer than one third of developing countries have a national AI strategy, a figure that drops to just 12 per cent among the least developed nations. The UN body also said 118 countries, mostly from the Global South, did not play a role in major international AI governance forums. The event, hosted by the Institute of Public Policy at South China University of Technology, heard there was also a risk these countries would be marginalised culturally. Hans d’Orville, a former assistant director general for strategic planning at Unesco, said AI systems were often trained on data sets that carried inherent linguistic and cultural biases. “AI is not culturally neutral; it is reshaping culture at all levels and in all areas,” d’Orville said. He warned that without responsible governance and cultural consideration, AI could reinforce existing biases and inequality, hinder cultural diversity and undermine local identities. “The world urgently needs to … introduce development-focused AI regulations to prevent the widening of the digital divide,” he said. The conference also heard that Apec’s flexible nature could be used to establish an inclusive, open form of AI governance. Chung proposed setting up joint training programmes, public-private partnerships and knowledge-sharing networks to help ensure all members of the bloc were able to integrate AI into their economies. “The objective is not to make every economy develop identically, but to ensure that every economy has a credible pathway to participate in AI-empowered growth,” he said. Chung also urged policymakers to make use of Apec’s pathfinder mechanism, which allows members to set preliminary rules to move forward on a specific policy issue without full participation from the rest of the bloc. He also told the event that Apec’s regulatory sandboxes – which allow restrictions on members testing new technologies, products and business models to be relaxed – should be used to test cross-border data flows and AI governance. He said these real-world cases could then serve as a guide when setting up regulatory frameworks. Chung also called for measures to get a clearer picture of how well-prepared regulators, businesses – especially small and medium-sized enterprises – and workers were for the advent of AI. “We shouldn’t just look at cutting-edge models or how many data centres we have, but evaluate whether people can use them widely,” he said.

title: In Australia, Disney’s Ooshies send Woolworths whooshing ahead of Coles
description: The major grocers are fighting to lure shoppers at a time when cost-of-living pressures and discount scandals are fuelling consumer anger.
content: Ooshies were not just fun to collect – the tiny plastic Disney figurines were powerful enough to move sales between Australia’s supermarket giants. Woolworths Group said on Wednesday that Australian food sales jumped 7.6 per cent in the first eight weeks of the 2027 financial year, with its Ooshies promotion contributing an estimated 1.5 to 2 percentage points of growth. That accelerated from 4.6 per cent sales growth in the 2026 financial year. Chief rival Coles Group felt the other side of the craze. It said a day earlier that supermarket sales rose almost 4 per cent and it gained market share in the year through June, but growth slowed in July amid a “competitor’s collectibles campaign” – a reference to Ooshies. Woolworths’ supermarkets had “a very strong start” to the financial year, Jefferies analysts Michael Simotas and Naveed Fazal Bawa wrote in a note, “with solid underlying growth compounded by the Ooshie benefit”. The numbers underscore the financial stakes behind what might look like a mere promotional gimmick. The country’s dominant grocers are fighting to lure shoppers at a time when some of Australia’s most vaunted consumer brands are confronting growing public scepticism over pricing. Coles and Woolworths have become lightning rods as cost-of-living pressures and discount scandals fuel anger over whether customers are getting a fair deal. The duopoly has also faced scrutiny from regulators and lawmakers over its pricing practices and market power. Efforts to draw customers have ranged from Ooshies to cookware promotions at Woolworths and Coles and the treasure-hunt appeal of Aldi’s cult Special Buys aisle. The promotions offer supermarkets a way to generate excitement and loyalty – and give shoppers a reason to choose one chain over another beyond price. Ooshies are small collectible figurines that Woolworths gave shoppers in mystery packaging with qualifying grocery purchases, typically featuring characters from franchises such as Disney’s Moana and Marvel’s Spider-Man. Shoppers received one for every A$30 (US$22) spent, encouraging repeat shops as families and collectors tried to complete sets, trade duplicates and hunt for rarer characters. The limited-edition promotion became a retail phenomenon before stocks ran out earlier this month. The craze spilled beyond market aisles and playgrounds onto social media, where collectors posted unboxing videos and showed off their hauls. “Multiple signs point to Ooshies driving a significant divergence in sales trends between Woolworths and Coles since its launch in mid-July,” Citigroup analyst Adrian Lemme wrote in a note earlier in August. Still, he cautioned against reading too much into the boost: “We are cautious to overreact to what is essentially six weeks of elevated trading.”

title: Mainland Chinese firms share risks to deliver Northern Metropolis success: analysts
description: Analysts stress that future tenders will require greater flexibility and longer bidding windows to encourage more competition.
content: Mainland Chinese enterprises will play a key role in developing Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis by sharing financial risks and helping align the megaproject with national strategy, according to real estate and political advisers. Their analysis followed the award of the blueprint’s first pilot area in Hung Shui Kiu to HSK New Development, a consortium led by five mainland giants and local developer Sino Land on Monday. Pledging an investment of HK$16.8 billion (US$2.14 billion), the consortium will develop sites totalling 10.5 hectares (25.9 acres) at a low land premium of HK$1.03 billion. It beat the only competitor, a stand-alone bid from Henderson Land Development. The mainland contingent comprises four state-backed developers – China Overseas Land & Investment, China Merchants Land, China Resources Land (Overseas) and CTG Investment – with decades of experience, alongside e-commerce and technology titan JD.com. Jeffrey Lam Kin-fung, chairman of the board of directors of the Hung Shui Kiu Industry Park Company – a government vehicle created to drive the district’s development – noted that pooling top players across real estate, construction and hospitality would accelerate development. “Each of the six companies has a special role to play, which will contribute to the holistic development of the Northern Metropolis,” he said. While analysts attributed the participation of mainland heavyweights to national priorities, technical expertise and familiarity with the local market, real estate advisers stressed that future tenders would require greater flexibility and longer bidding windows to encourage more competition. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said mainland firms would emerge as key players in the Northern Metropolis, a 30,000-hectare mega development close to the city’s border with the mainland set to be transformed into an economic powerhouse and housing hub. “Beijing has encouraged mainland Chinese companies to participate and help transform and upgrade Hong Kong’s industry development. They also have more experience in promoting and planning new quality development forces,” he said, referring to China’s growth model focused on technological breakthroughs and industrial upgrades. “While Chinese firms can help Northern Metropolis development better align and serve national development strategies, they can also organise their businesses in Hong Kong, the mainland and overseas.” He added that it was unrealistic to expect a major influx of investment from the West into the Northern Metropolis amid geopolitical tensions, noting that Western countries too needed investments for development. Lau Chun-kong, chairman of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors’ land policy panel, said the consortium had “formidable financial strength” and an edge across a range of services. He noted that Sino Land had solid cash flow in Hong Kong’s real estate sector to support the pilot area in Hung Shui Kiu, which is envisioned as a future high-end professional services and logistics hub. Under the tender terms, HSK New Development will carry out extensive site formation across the 10.5-hectare area, retaining three residential plots totalling 2.6 hectares to deliver more than 3,000 private flats. According to the consortium, the residential sites will feature over 100,000 sq ft of commercial space, incorporating smart retail concepts and unstaffed supermarkets. The master plan prioritises natural ventilation and optimal sunlight exposure, backed by renewable energy installations and advanced carbon-reduction technologies. All parking spaces will provide electric vehicle charging capabilities alongside smart access control and automated parking systems, while individual homes will be equipped with smart systems driven by artificial intelligence (AI). The consortium will construct a smart logistics hub on a one-hectare enterprise and technology (E&T) plot, with JD.com required to operate at least 15,300 square metres (161,458 sq ft) – roughly 30 per cent of the gross floor area – within 55 months. The facility will also feature hi-tech logistics operations, including autonomous delivery systems. The consortium will return two E&T plots and a government, institution or community site to the authorities by 2028 after completing site formation works. It will also develop a 1.44-hectare open space and build a footpath and a pedestrian street for the government in phases by 2030-33. Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at Colliers, noted that pooling diverse capital sources mitigated risk, following the local property market downturn. “Eventually, it is a relatively long-term project … It involves [industry], residential and infrastructure development. Having various sources of capital and having companies to supplement one another can minimise the risks,” she said. Lee also said she believed mainland firms would play a key role in future pilot projects, noting that the four state enterprises had long operated in Hong Kong while JD.com had steadily built up its local presence. She said established players had a stronger grasp of the local market than newcomers, while geopolitical factors also worked in their favour. “A long-term investment in Hong Kong by American and European businesses remains an uncertainty given the geopolitical developments in recent years,” she added. To accommodate the needs of different enterprises, Lee suggested that the government could allow phased industry development in future pilot area projects. She noted that nascent enterprises might require smaller floor areas while technology firms would be reluctant to share facilities with other competitors. Hannah Jeong, head of valuation and advisory services at CBRE Hong Kong, highlighted that while the land premium was relatively low at HK$1.03 billion, the estimated development cost was HK$16.8 billion, due to requirements to form extensive sites and build facilities beyond residential homes. She noted that while the model remained financially viable, profit margins would be slim. “The residential profits are expected to fund and support the broader innovation-focused development,” she said. She suggested lengthening the tender period for future pilot areas beyond six months. “Given the complexity of these developments and the need to combine technology operators, investors and residential developers, the market requires adequate time to establish the right partnerships and formulate viable business models,” she said. Jeong said that some enterprises had earlier expressed interest in the pilot area but were unfamiliar with the tendering process, noting that mainland firms often had slower decision-making processes. She also urged the government to promote tenders more actively to non-local companies. The government is expected to roll out pilot areas in the future innovation hub in San Tin and the border commerce district in Fanling North, though updated tender dates for the projects – originally set for 2025 and 2026 at the earliest – have yet to be announced. Additional reporting by Jess Ma

title: Hong Kong primed for T20 Asia Cup India cricket clash, stars atoning for 2024 heartbreak
description: Leading all-rounder Kary Chan ready to treat every ball ‘like it’s my last’ two years after locking herself away following qualifying failure.
content: After Hong Kong stumbled at the final 2024 Asia Cup qualifying hurdle, Kary Chan Ka-ying spent five navel-gazing days hiding from the outside world. “I can still remember the pain in my heart … I kept asking myself, ‘what if I’d done something differently?’” Chan said. Two years later and rather than being cooped up indoors, Chan is with her teammates preparing for a Women’s Twenty20 Asia Cup in Dubai where Hong Kong have the redoubtable task of facing Thailand, Pakistan and mighty India. Chan was among the players who spent a short time in hospital after illness swept through the camp during their ongoing preparation trip to Sri Lanka, but it would take more than a bout of bellyache to dampen enthusiasm over the city team’s return to the tournament after 14 years away. In 2012, proficient all-rounder Chan was a wide-eyed 15-year-old who “wasn’t even given a chance to run water onto the field … I sat next to the coach to learn”. “From then, playing in the Asia Cup became one of my life dreams,” she said. Ironically, Chan’s ability to realise her long-term goal stems partly from Hong Kong’s close-run thing in 2024, alongside their progress to the semi-finals of the previous year’s T20 World Cup qualifying. Those efforts earned the women’s team entry to the Hong Kong Sports Institute (HKSI)’s individual athletes support scheme. Among 12 players currently receiving financial backing, Chan has forgone her coaching jobs, including one with the China men’s team. “I can really concentrate on doing my best for Hong Kong,” she said. “I’m thinking about cricket training when I wake up and when I go to bed.” Around half of the city women’s squad are full-time. The men’s contingent do not receive HKSI backing, leaving roughly 80 per cent of them to supplement their cricket with part-time work. In Tanuja Lele, Chan and her colleagues have a strength and conditioning coach who Mamatha Maben, the head coach, credits with “making a huge difference to the way our players perceive fitness”. They train for five-to-six hours a day, with individual running and gym programmes complementing one-to-one and team practices. “They’re beginning to think like athletes, although there’s a long way to go,” Maben said. Appointed nine months ago, former India all-rounder Maben said the Asia Cup would allow her world No 23 team to “see what cricket is all about at the highest level”. Hong Kong twice beat Tanzania, ranked No 20, in a recent quadrangular series but in Thailand, Pakistan and 50-over world champions India, they have the planet’s 12th, eighth and third-rated teams waiting for them in Dubai. “When they get this exposure it’s easier for me to take them up the ladder,” Maben said. “Sometimes, it’s difficult to make them understand the work required, and the sacrifices you have to make, to play quality cricket. This will open their eyes.” The captain for around five years before passing the baton to her “idol”, Natasha Miles, in 2024, Chan said being freed from leadership duties had been “amazing … you just need to focus on your game and not think too much, although I’m always there to help Tash”. Miles is steeped in Hong Kong cricket. Her father, Rodney, is a former president of the local association. Her late mother, Anita, was at the vanguard of establishing Hong Kong’s first women’s league in 2004. Two years later, Natasha Miles was in the party for the city women’s first international series in Pakistan. Although she “moped for a day or two” after Hong Kong failed to reach the last Asia Cup, Miles believes in hindsight that narrowly losing the decisive match to Thailand was “a blessing in disguise”. “We probably just weren’t ready … we had to work out how to come back and really throw some heavy punches,” said Miles, who credits the HKSI support with allowing her to “play more cricket than at any time in the past 10 years”, despite ending her 15-year association with English county Middlesex 12 months ago. In 2022, Miles, 37, and her father launched the Anita Miles Foundation, aimed at promoting “the full and equal participation of women and girls in all aspects of cricket in the Hong Kong community”. Every year, the foundation provides fully-funded overseas scholarships for two Hong Kong cricketers. One of the 2025 beneficiaries was Chan, who played for Aldershot Cricket Club in England. She began in the sport at 14 after a coach visited her school as part of a development programme. Although enormously encouraged that the domestic structure has grown from “three or four teams playing all season” to 23 sides competing in four divisions, Miles said it would be “unrealistic” to think that Hong Kong’s Asia Cup exploits will immediately translate into greater local interest in the sport, because “I know how long it takes to embed the grass roots”. “But having incredible players like Kary and [right-arm medium pacer] Alison Siu Mei-wai who are local-born Chinese and performing at that level is going to be huge for the game,” she said. “You look up to the people who look like you, so it’ll be a big deal, and it’ll help investment and interest. “We want development across the board but we have a couple of [domestic] teams full of Chinese girls, which is incredible.” Miles enlisted the help of a friend who regularly plays golf with Mahela Jayawardena to arrange for the silky-smooth former Sri Lanka batting champion to deliver a pep talk to the Hong Kong squad while they were in the country. The thrust of Jayawardene’s message was that against their superior opponents in the Middle East, Hong Kong must “take away the names of their opponents and focus on the ball”. Drawn in an identical group in 2012, the city team were rolled for 15 and 24 by Pakistan and India, respectively, and handily beaten by Thailand. A former Lancashire Thunder teammate of India’s superstar captain Harmanpreet Kaur, Miles said: “If we put the ball in good areas, throw ourselves around in the field and bat with fearlessness, the result doesn’t matter. “If India have that good day and tank us, it is what it is, but if we deliver our skills we’ll always be in the hunt.” So giddy with excitement after Hong Kong won their ACC Women’s Premier Cup quarter-final against Japan to qualify, Chan double- and triple-checked that the victory had stamped her team’s Asian Cup ticket. They begin against Thailand on Friday. One of only seven women to have claimed more than 150 T20 international wickets, Chan said: “I can’t wait for this moment to come. We’ll treat every ball like it’s the last of our careers.”

title: What is really behind Japan’s planned cabinet shake-up?
description: With voters anxious over inflation, swapping cabinet faces offers a convenient distraction from economic pain.
content: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi remains in a strong position despite a poll showing falling support for her administration, ahead of an expected cabinet reshuffle to bolster her coalition government. A new cabinet could help the government win over voters, reward ruling Liberal Democratic Party lawmakers and win the support of junior coalition partner Ishin no Kai, analysts have said. Takaichi is expected to embark on such a move in mid- or late September, according to reports by Kyodo News and other Japanese media, citing government and ruling party sources. If confirmed, it would be Takaichi’s first cabinet reshuffle since taking office last October as she potentially eyes another term as LDP president in the 2027 party leadership election. The timing of the reshuffle is likely to be determined by her schedule in the coming weeks. Her government plans to adopt a tax reform package, including a consumption tax cut for food in mid-September, while Takaichi is expected to attend a UN General Assembly session in the United States later that month. “A personnel reshuffle is likely after [the adoption of] the tax system reform package,” an LDP source reportedly said. A Yomiuri Shimbun survey released on Monday shows the cabinet’s approval fell to 56 per cent – the lowest since it took office in October – from 57 per cent in the previous survey last month. The cabinet’s approval rating peaked at 73 per cent in the newspaper’s survey in December. Among the reasons cited for the decline were frustration over persistent inflation, including rising energy costs, and public scepticism of the government’s economic measures. Voters were also said to be anxious about the government’s debt and funding gaps tied to the proposed consumption tax cuts on food. Rintaro Nishimura, a Tokyo-based senior associate in the Japan practice of The Asia Group strategic advisory firm, said Takaichi might be hoping that a “fresh-look” cabinet could help stem the decline in approval. “This is a common practice used by prime ministers to shift the focus away from the stale political situation and put the attention on the new faces joining the cabinet. Public approval is critical to Takaichi’s hold over the LDP, especially given her lack of political foundations within the party,” he said. “If lawmakers smell blood, the criticism will become more open.” At least 70 LDP lawmakers who have served around three to five terms in office are aspiring to become part of the cabinet, either as minister, minister of state or parliamentary vice-minister, according to Nishimura. Takaichi would likely not undergo a major overhaul of the cabinet, he said, with key members including Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara likely to stay put. “Takaichi could use the reshuffle to bring in new lawmakers, thus fostering a sense of loyalty among these lawmakers ahead of next year’s presidential election.” While they might not be household names, “having the rank-and-file on your side doesn’t hurt”, Nishimura said. Toru Yoshida, a professor of policy studies at Doshisha University, said the reshuffle could involve a member of the Japan Innovation Party, also known as Ishin no Kai. According to Yoshida, an Ishin lawmaker is likely to be added to the cabinet. “As the LDP does not have the majority in the upper house, and as Komeito went out, it is crucial for the government to have a reliable partner to get bills passed,” Yoshida said. The LDP and Ishin formed a coalition agreement in October, with the smaller party cooperating with the Takaichi administration from outside the cabinet. That same month, Komeito ended its 26-year partnership with Takaichi’s party following slush-fund and corruption scandals involving LDP lawmakers and differing values on security and diplomacy. Yoshida said Takaichi would have to compromise with Ishin to prevent the smaller party leaving the ruling coalition, citing the proposal for a second capital city. “The party was established at first instance for that purpose, and it won’t do any good to stay in the coalition if they aim to be a larger political force,” he added. The proposal to designate a backup capital city was passed last month, aiming to maintain core government and administrative functions in the event of Tokyo being incapacitated by a major natural disaster. Osaka-based Ishin has long backed the proposal and pushed for the city to serve as a secondary economic and administrative hub. The approval of the relevant bill in the Diet was a key promise made by the LDP to secure Ishin’s backing for the ruling coalition. Mikitaka Masuyama, a political-science professor at the National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies, said a key focus of any cabinet reshuffle would be the post of LDP secretary general, currently held by Shunichi Suzuki, the brother-in-law of the party’s influential vice-president and former prime minister Taro Aso, whose backing would be crucial for Takaichi’s party leadership election next year. If Suzuki were to hold on to the role, it would be seen as “maintaining the status quo and pursuing a path of unity within the party”, Masuyama said. Suzuki has faced internal and public backlash for endorsing LDP candidates previously implicated in political fund scandals, which critics say has undermined the party’s credibility. According to Nishimura, Suzuki has been struggling with policy coordination between the party and the government as well as with opposition parties. “Suzuki is an offering to Aso, but there could be negotiations with Aso to give him something else in place of the secretary general role. Takaichi does need someone more capable in that role,” he said. Key positions up for grabs would likely include the internal affairs and communications minister; economy, trade and industry minister; and minister of state for economic and fiscal policy, Nishimura said. These positions are currently held by Yoshimasa Hayashi, Ryosei Akazawa and Minoru Kiuchi, respectively. Hayashi has expressed an interest in running for LDP president, so he could be left out of the next cabinet, Nishimura said. “He is not particularly loyal to Takaichi and not in a ministerial position that absolutely needs continuity or him in that role,” he said. Akazawa, meanwhile, is a “leftover” from the previous administration, according to Nishimura – tasked with implementing a US-Japan investment agreement as part of their tariff negotiations As Akazawa was not “Takaichi’s pick”, he could be on his way out, he said, although lingering uncertainties over the bilateral trade ties could persuade the prime minister to keep him in her cabinet. “We are seeing in the news that he may be travelling to Washington early next month. That could be his last job or a sign that he is likely to stay put,” he added. Having Kiuchi stay in the cabinet “wouldn’t hurt”, as he was a “loyalist” and one of the chief architects of Takaichi’s economic agenda, Nishimura said. “Kiuchi would be effective even without the ministerial role, which is not exactly a prominent role given no ministerial staff is attached to him, so replacing him wouldn’t necessarily mean he has fallen out of favour,” he added. “He could actually be taken out to help Takaichi on the party side as a key policy decision-maker.”

title: ‘Born to Fly’ documents Hong Kong-born Rahul Sharma’s world record 566km run across Sri Lanka
description: Soon after Rahul Sharma began looking for a suitable challenge, he became the fastest man to run the length of Sri Lanka. A new documentary follows his record-breaking feat.
content: In January 2025, Rahul Sharma ran his first marathon, in Mumbai, India. Months later, he learned of British ultra-endurance athlete William Goodge, who ran across Australia in 35 days, a journey of 3,800km (2,361 miles). It was all the encouragement the then 24-year-old needed to up his game. Within weeks, the Melbourne-based exercise physiologist had rallied two of his best friends and decided on a goal: he would run 566km (352 miles) from Point Pedro, the northernmost point of Sri Lanka, to Dondra Head, at its southern tip, in six days. None of the trio – Sharma, Ali Khajeian and Ben Lawson – knew the first thing about ultra-running. But that wasn’t going to stop them. “I try my best not to be cocky, but it’s just not who I am,” Sharma admits in Born to Fly, a newly released documentary that charts his Sri Lanka run. “I have a big head.” But why Sri Lanka? “We didn’t want to follow a blueprint. We wanted to find a country that had never been done before,” says Sharma. Sri Lanka it was then, although, it is not strictly true that no one had attempted it previously; in 2023, Irishman Chris Rickard, assisted by two friends on bicycles, ran a slightly longer route between the same two points in Sri Lanka, in just under 12 days. Born and raised in Hong Kong, Sharma played cricket from a young age, and represented the city’s under-19 team. He stepped away from the sport after a series of injuries. Having moved to Australia, he started running to help in his recovery from the injuries, and the activity quickly became something more all-consuming. Challenging himself to run the length of a country wasn’t just a vanity project, though.
