Driven by a childhood friend’s battle with leukaemia, Sharma aimed to raise A$20,000 (US$13,100) for the Children’s Cancer Institute (CCI), a Sydney-based research organisation. Eventually, the dates were set: December 24 to 30, 2025. Lawson, 25, a journalism major who lived with Sharma while the latter trained, liaised with sponsors, the media and the CCI. He also worked closely with Sharma’s coach to ensure that the runner was getting the optimal amount of nutrients, hydration and rest in between training sessions. Lawson came to know Sharma inside out. But as the day neared, both Sharma’s friends, who had helped map out his entire journey, had to pull out of the actual trip to Sri Lanka for personal reasons. “It was a hard conversation and, honestly, I didn’t think that Rahul would have that level of understanding,” says Khajeian, who, like Lawson, nevertheless stayed involved in the project, and would direct and produce Born to Fly. “I know internally he was crashing out. But on the outside, he was very understanding and very mature. It just brought us closer to each other.” Sharma brought in another friend, Mohammed Abdullah, a Sri Lankan who happened to be in the country at the time. “Rahul is like an older brother figure to me, so this project was important to me because it was important to him,” says Mohammed. Lawson passed on elaborate spreadsheets to Mohammed for use in tracking Sharma’s heart rate, meals and water intake during his attempt. Meanwhile, Khajeian promised to stay awake in Melbourne, which is four-and-a-half hours ahead of Sri Lanka, to instruct Mohammed and the videographers on capturing the right shots for social media and the planned documentary. “He’s very artistically gifted,” Sharma says of Khajeian, 23, who has a degree in finance and is behind several of the social-media reels made for Ebb&Flo, the Australian running club started by Sharma. “I always told him that it was my dream to buy him out of a corporate job because he’s just too gifted to be sitting at a desk.” Finally in Sri Lanka, Sharma spent almost every waking minute of the six days of the attempt on his feet, stopping only to eat and sleep for three hours per night, initially, in a camper van with a malfunctioning air-conditioner. While he ran, his entourage, which included Mohammed, a physiotherapist, two cameramen and the driver, followed in the camper van. With temperatures soaring, the conditions were brutal. “I blacked out on the second day. I have no memory of it,” Sharma says. At one point, he tried to remove his socks only to discover the rubber grips had melted and fused to his skin. They had to be cut off with scissors. Mohammed and Lawson, who were monitoring Sharma’s heart rate and pace, the latter remotely from Australia, suggested he finish in seven days instead of six. “There was a lot of colourful language,” Sharma recalls. “I was just lashing out at the team, telling them it was not an option.” Lawson, Khajeian and Mohammed understood their friend’s frustration. “One of the things we have become very good at as a group is separating our relationship as colleagues from our relationship as friends,” says Lawson. “So I knew that Rahul’s anger at me wasn’t a personal attack on me.” From day three, Sharma slept during the day and ran through the night and early morning, to beat the heat. But the challenges kept coming. An old injury returned in his left knee, becoming “the worst physical pain” he ever felt, he says, akin to two knives stabbing into his Achilles tendon with every step. Painkillers could only do so much, so Sharma and his physiotherapist fell into a different rhythm: every five minutes, he would stop, get restrapped and sprayed down to dull the pain, then continue to run. “My physio had sleepless nights. My whole team was working so hard for me to be able to run,” Sharma says. Mohammed even blacked out from the stress at one point on the final day. “It would’ve been selfish of me to stop or slow down.” Before his sixth and final day, Sharma was told by his father that several priests were praying for him. “Son, tomorrow you will fly,” he told Sharma over the phone, words that would inspire the title of Khajeian’s documentary. Spiritually revived, Sharma’s pace picked up on that last day. Born to Fly’s most affecting moment is when Sharma arrives at Dondra Head. He collapses, bursting into tears as loved ones gather around him. “It wasn’t just the physical pain,” he explains. “I put my team through hell. I didn’t see my friends, but they still came to support me. I hadn’t seen my dad in nine months. We raised money for cancer. We did all of this, and for it to just finish in six days …” Six days, 13 hours and 22 minutes, to be exact – a time that earned Sharma recognition by the World Book of Records as the “fastest man to run from northernmost point to southernmost point of Sri Lanka”, all 566km of it. He also succeeded in raising the A$20,000 for the CCI. Khajeian, who says it took him more than a month to put the two-hour documentary together, has been especially inspired by Sharma’s feat: “It has made me realise that the only thing standing between me and my goals is myself.” Says Sharma, “I don’t know how fulfilled I would be if I was still playing cricket. I never got that feeling of, ‘This is what I was born to do.’ With running, everything just feels right.” His next goal is to tackle a 1,000km route in Nepal. “I’ve done one world record at 24. It’ll be two at 25, if I’m eyeing to be the greatest of all time.” Eventually, though, “I want to build a brand or open clinics through which I can help the community”, says Sharma. “If I can choose to have a world record within eight months, you can choose to do the same in any walk of life.”

title: Ocean temperature hits record high as ‘super’ El Nino forms
description: Higher temperatures contribute to rising sea levels and increase the chance of extreme weather events.
content:
Researchers have recorded the highest temperature ever measured in the world’s oceans, as climate change combines with a powerful El Nino in the tropical Pacific.
The global average sea-surface temperature hit a record 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 Fahrenheit) on August 22, according to Europe’s Earth observation agency Copernicus, which has been tracking the metric daily since 1979. The previous single-day record of 21.09 degrees was measured in March 2024.
“El Nino is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming,” said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus’ European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.
“As ocean temperatures continue to rise, the risks to marine ecosystems and coastal communities also increase,” she said.
Higher ocean temperatures contribute to sea level rise and increase the chance of extreme weather events, as warmer water transfers more heat and moisture to the atmosphere, intensifying storms and heat on land. Warmer oceans also have a reduced capacity to absorb carbon dioxide.
Record temperatures have already been measured in isolated areas of the world’s oceans including the western Mediterranean Sea as well as at the Earth’s poles, driven mainly by man-made climate change. Copernicus expects the trend to continue, with ocean temperatures now being supercharged by El Nino.
The August record is particularly worrying because global ocean temperatures are typically highest in March and April, after the Austral summer, Copernicus said.
Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at Britain’s national weather agency, told the BBC on Friday: “We are expecting the biggest El Nino for over a century, peaking at something over 3 degrees - that is unheard of in modern climate records”.
This means Pacific water would heat up more than 3 degrees above the norm in the coming months.
Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Review | The Dog Stars movie review: Ridley Scott’s post-apocalyptic thriller doesn’t always work
description: Jacob Elordi, Margaret Qualley and Josh Brolin survive in a present-day America where an influenza pandemic has decimated the population.
content: 3/5 stars From Mad Max to The Walking Dead and the recent 28 Years Later films, the post-apocalypse has long been fertile ground for filmmakers, even before Covid-19 made us all feel like we were heading in that direction. Veteran filmmaker Ridley Scott finally jumps on the bandwagon with The Dog Stars, a handsome-looking adaptation of Peter Heller’s 2012 novel that works only in fits and starts. Set in a present-day America where most of the population has been wiped out by an influenza pandemic, the film stars Jacob Elordi as the tightly wound Hig, a former civilian pilot in the before times. Like most, he knows loss and is nursing grief after the death of his wife and unborn child. Now living in Denver alongside Josh Brolin’s sharpshooting survivalist Bangley, he is merely existing day by day, desperate for word of anyone else out there. Piloting an old 1956 Cessna (fuel does not seem to be a problem in this world), Hig is the equivalent of a flying doctor, making trips to the deserted city centre where he distributes much-needed medical supplies, notably to a Mennonite community (featuring Benedict Wong). Yet after a clash with scavengers leaves him bereft, he decides to venture further afield – and trace a garbled message he received over the airwaves. After an engine malfunction, his journey initially leads him to a suspicious rancher father, Pops (Guy Pearce), and his more receptive daughter Cima (Margaret Qualley), a trainee doctor with her own pain to salve. What happens next is best left unspoilt, but Scott – fresh off the back of Napoleon and Gladiator II – has not lost his touch when it comes to staging thrilling battles. One particular adrenaline-driven nocturnal sequence goes full-on Rambo: First Blood. While The Dog Stars does not come close to HBO’s expansive adaptation of the video game The Last of Us – perhaps the pinnacle of all post-apocalypse tales – it certainly borrows from its aesthetics, with its beguiling shots of a dilapidated downtown Denver. From posters that read “You loot. You die” to abandoned buildings with foliage creeping up the walls, the work by production designer Chris Seagers and the VFX team is exemplary. There is also a great late-stage cameo from Allison Janney, again too juicy to spoil, but the film does suffer from an all-too-convenient, slightly too happy final act. While the older actors – Brolin and Pearce – are spot on as granite-jawed patriarchal figures, the pairing of Elordi and Qualley feels too movie-star clean-cut. Their desire to find human connection in a shattered world may be sincere, but it is not convincing. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Chocolate’s bean-to-bar boom, from Asian-inspired flavours to single-origin cacao
description: Artisanal brands like Marou, Dandelion, Pump Street and Fossa are among the makers championing traceable cacao, bold flavours and small-batch craft.
content: Most factory visits can border on dull, but a recent discovery in an industrial building in Hong Kong’s Wong Chuk Hang area left a sweet taste in my mouth. Home to Conspiracy Chocolate, the space hums with the steady churn of cocoa bean grinders and chocolate-enrobing machines, while vats of molten chocolate fill the room with the scent of freshly baked brownies. If Willy Wonka were to set up shop in the city, then this would be his playground. Launched in 2018, Conspiracy Chocolate may be Hong Kong’s first bean-to-bar brand, but it’s one of many independent makers that are transforming the world of chocolate. While it remains a hugely successful food category globally, the industry is undergoing a renaissance as consumers are moving away from mass-produced confectionery towards small-batch, artisanal products. “Chocolate has been in human consumption for more than 5,000 years but over the last 200 years it’s become heavily industrialised,” explains Amit Oz, co-founder of Conspiracy Chocolate. “Customers have also become more educated, particularly regarding quality, which is driving more conscious food decisions. These align with the rise of bean-to-bar chocolate brands, which offer a better product without the guilt associated with health and sustainability concerns,” he says. Mass-produced chocolate tends to include fillers, artificial preservatives, vegetable oil and minimal levels of cocoa (in the US, a chocolate bar can contain as little as 10 per cent cocoa). In contrast, many independent brands focus on celebrating the cocoa bean, which boasts a flavour complexity that is often compared to that of wine or coffee. “In our case, we make chocolate with only two ingredients, which means we have to find the best beans in the world and process them extremely carefully,” explains Todd Masonis, co-founder of San Francisco-based Dandelion Chocolate. “Every harvest and every origin is different: some are fruity, some nutty and some chocolatey. You can taste the terroir and nuance of each bean,” he says. It’s common for independent makers to source their beans directly from farms in countries in Africa, South America and Asia. Each region is known for its distinct flavour profiles, so these artisan bars have a distinctive edge over mass market counterparts. For example, Peruvian beans have earthy, fruity and spicy notes, while Ecuador’s are floral, nutty and complex. The bold and fruity beans of Vietnam are also popular and are being celebrated by Asian brands like Vietnam-based Marou Chocolate, which will be opening a boutique in Hong Kong later this year. “In the traditional chocolate world, beans are shipped halfway across the globe to be processed into something anonymous. We do the opposite,” says Marou co-founder Vincent Mourou. “Making our chocolate in Vietnam gives us incredible control over flavour. We can adjust a fermentation batch, experiment with a new terroir, all within days. That proximity and the independence to be adventurous with our recipes allows us to create something truly distinctive and delicious. Sustainability isn’t separate from our product; it’s part of our flavour strategy.” Of course, selecting the perfect bean is just part of the story. Most of these brands control the entire production process from “bean to bar”, creating a transparent and traceable supply chain, which is a major plus for conscious customers. “Consumers today don’t just care about how products taste, but also about how they are made and where they come from. Ethical sourcing is therefore not separate from quality – it is part of it,” says Yilina Leong, co-founder of Singapore-based Fossa Chocolate. “We work with suppliers who prioritise transparency, fair compensation and long-term relationships with farming communities. While certifications can be useful, we also value direct relationships and traceability because they allow us to better understand how the cacao is produced, and ensure quality and sustainability standards are upheld,” she adds. Controlling production from roasting to refining also allows these brands to create daring and innovative flavour combinations, many of which pay tribute to the cultural identity of where they are from. Conspiracy Chocolate has launched products featuring Asian-inspired flavours such as salted duck, oolong tea and Sichuan peppercorn, while other items, such as its chocolate mooncakes, pay tribute to Hong Kong. Fossa also highlights Singaporean tastes such as Nanyang kopi, satay sauce and rojak. Other makers have also created novelties that appeal to different consumer tastes, including chocolates made from plant-based milks, with less sugar or with wellness-inspired ingredients like adaptogens. “We approach chocolate almost like a culinary ingredient, often incorporating unexpected flavours, textures and local inspirations while still maintaining a strong focus on the quality of the cacao itself,” says Leong. “At the same time, we ensure the products are balanced and sophisticated enough to resonate internationally. Good flavour storytelling is universal, and that’s what keeps people coming back.” 5 bean-to-bar brands to savour Conspiracy Chocolate, Hong Kong Celebrating cacao beans from a single farm in the Dak Lak province of Vietnam, Conspiracy Chocolate boasts products ranging from bars – many made in collaboration with local tastemakers and chefs – to confectionery such as pralines and bonbons. They highlight their compostable consumer packaging and zero-waste production, which results in other delectable items such as cocoa husk tea. Dandelion Chocolate, USA Dandelion is one of the oldest bean-to-bar brands, being founded in 2010 in San Francisco’s Mission District, where it still boasts a factory and retail space offering tours and a cafe. Their chocolate appeals to purists, with most of its bars made from just two ingredients: cocoa beans and sugar. Look out for its stunning packaging, which features patterns silkscreened onto handmade paper from Jaipur, India. Fossa Chocolate, Singapore Founded in 2017 by Jay Chua, Charis Chia and Yilina Leong, Fossa started out as a home kitchen experiment before becoming one of Singapore’s most popular chocolate brands. Known for its small-batch chocolates, it features bold and unconventional flavours, most of which are inspired by Asia – think fragrant teas, local spices and nostalgic desserts. Marou Chocolate, Vietnam The brainchild of two Frenchmen, Marou Chocolate combines French flair with a Southeast Asian soul. Made exclusively from Vietnamese beans using French techniques, their range includes single-origin tablets, snack bars, chocolate-covered fruit and even grocery items. They have 25 retail boutiques in Vietnam, some featuring cafes, and a Marou Academie, which offers pastry and chocolate classes. Pump Street Chocolate, UK This award-winning brand was established by father-and-daughter team Chris and Joanna Brennan and is still family-run. Although they offer a range of products, their bestsellers are their baking-inspired chocolate bars, which pay tribute to their heritage – they started out as a bakery before branching into chocolate. Popular ingredients include sourdough, rye, sea salt and croissant crumbs.

title: US starts returning staff to some Middle East missions after Iran war evacuations
description: US move signals lower risk of immediate regional escalation, though select missions will cap capacity at 75 to 85 per cent.
content: US President Donald Trump’s administration is starting to send staff back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated ‌or downsized amid tensions with Iran, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters. The posts in Lebanon, Israel, Saudi Arabia and Baghdad, Iraq, are among those where staff will return, the sources said. Family members will also be allowed to return to the US post in Riyadh, they added. The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will initially ⁠operate below full capacity. Some embassies will initially operate at no more than 85 per cent of authorised staff levels, the ‌sources said. The return of some staff is expected to start as early as this week, one of the sources said. The United States pulled out staff from embassies across ‌the Middle East after joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28. Some embassies in Gulf ⁠Arab countries such as ⁠Saudi Arabia and Kuwait came under fire from Iran, forcing the latter to temporarily close. Since then, heavy fighting has subsided even though a ‌US naval blockade of Iranian ports persists and the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil and commodities shipping, remains shut with diplomatic efforts to ‌end the ‌war stalled. A US State Department representative told Reuters in an emailed statement that the department continuously reviews ‌the security posture of its diplomatic missions worldwide. “Based on our latest assessment, we are adjusting our staffing posture at certain ⁠posts in the Middle East to ensure we can continue advancing US foreign policy objectives while protecting the safety ⁠and security of our personnel,” the spokesman said. The New York Times earlier reported the return of diplomats and the easing of emergency measures and said embassies in Jordan, Oman, Kuwait and Qatar were also ‌expected to restore higher staff ‌levels, citing an internal document. US embassies in Israel, Jordan and Oman would ultimately return to full staffing, while missions in the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Lebanon would initially be capped at 85 per cent staffing. Posts in Iraq, Kuwait and Bahrain would be limited to 75 per cent, the newspaper added.

title: Editorial | As China’s humanoid robots make strides, practical use is the next frontier
description: Recent competitions in Beijing and Hong Kong have showcased how far these machines have come. Now, it’s time to pivot to the strategy for their deployment.
content: The world has been captivated by the rapid evolution of robotics. From humanoid machines shattering athletic records to the intricate, precision-focused manoeuvres – whether kung fu fighting or tennis playing – in international competitions, we are witnessing a technological shift that transcends mere entertainment. The recent spectacle of humanoid robot games in China, which captured global attention over the weekend, shows the speed at which innovation is advancing. Meanwhile, Hong Kong successfully hosted the Asia-Pacific Broadcasting Union Robocon 2026, the region’s premier university-level robotics competition. The nation is at the forefront of this technology, which increasingly combines robotics with artificial intelligence (AI). But the true measure of this progress lies not in these machines’ performance for entertainment but in their integration into the fabric of our daily lives. The second World Humanoid Robot Games, held at Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, has transformed from a mere curiosity into a rigorous laboratory for testing the boundaries of machine autonomy. With over 2,000 robots competing across 51 events, the scale of this competition suggests we are witnessing the dawn of a new era in embodied intelligence. The Tien Kung robots have effectively dismantled human benchmarks, finishing the 400-metre race in 38.15 seconds – crushing the human world record of 43.03 seconds – and clocking a 100-metre sprint at 9.39 seconds, outpacing human record-holder Usain Bolt. These machines are demonstrating agility and speed that command serious attention. However, the games also provided a necessary reality check. The chaotic nature of the football matches, where robots collided with teammates, shows we are still in the early, messy stages of robotics development. These machines are operating at their limits, and the margin for error remains razor-thin. Behind the spectacle lies a critical engineering challenge. As competition shifts from remote control to full autonomy, high-speed, continuous networks like 5G-advanced have become indispensable. Furthermore, the power demands of combining movement with on-board AI computing are pushing battery technology to breaking point. As Huawei Technologies executive David Li noted, this energy bottleneck is driving a shift towards cloud-based processing, making robust network connectivity the backbone of the next generation of humanoid innovation. The Hong Kong competition, which showcased the ingenuity of 16 university teams, was more than just a display of skill. The theme, “Kung Fu Quest”, demanded that robots demonstrate precision, tactics and strategic cooperation – qualities that are essential in the real-world deployment of automation. It was heartening to see Hong Kong’s students secure top honours and demonstrate that the city remains a formidable centre for nurturing young talent and hi-tech innovation. However, the event should also be viewed through the lens of governance and efficiency. As Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po has rightly noted, the application of AI and robotics must extend into government services and public infrastructure. We are already seeing the benefits of this, from specialised machines assisting in disaster response, such as flood and typhoon management, to the broader push for AI integration across various administrative functions. There is a basic lesson from both the global humanoid games and our local Robocon success: technological marvels with practical application. New competitions included not only table tennis and kickboxing but scenario-based events to cover tasks in industrial production, hotels, homes and logistics. We must pivot from the novelty of manufacturing robots to the strategy for their deployment. For Hong Kong to maintain its competitive edge as an international innovation hub, we need to translate these technological breakthroughs into practical solutions that improve governance, boost efficiency and enhance the quality of life for people. The future of technology lies not just in what robots can do but in what they can help us achieve together. Advances on the mainland are helping to position Hong Kong to take advantage of intelligent machines that will define the coming decades. The future is already automated.

title: Was Mr Hong Kong ‘bad taste’ or ‘great’? Critics and contenders on controversial pageant
description: Slated for objectifying men, TVB’s male beauty contest couldn’t match Miss Hong Kong’s longevity. But will it ever return?
content: From 2005 to 2011 – and again in 2016 – Hong Kong broadcasting company TVB bet on a male pageant to score more than just a win with its female viewers. Modelled loosely after the Miss Hong Kong Pageant, a beauty contest that the station took over in 1973, Mr Hong Kong effectively also served as a star-scouting vehicle for recruiting male talent while offering hopefuls with bulging muscles and big smiles the promise of fame. But unlike Miss Hong Kong – the 2026 finals will take place on August 30 – Mr Hong Kong ran out of steam in just six years. After a brief return in 2016, the event was quickly suspended indefinitely. TVB teased a 2021 revival, but the contest never materialised, and many title winners left the industry within a few years. Perhaps Mr Hong Kong was unintentionally camp and misunderstood by viewers, or maybe, with its salacious attempts at comedy that took precedence over selecting stand-out talent, it was simply a bad knock-off of the Miss Hong Kong contests. It has been a decade since the show was shelved, but one question remains: why did Mr Hong Kong fail to emulate Miss Hong Kong’s longevity? ‘Filled with scenes of screaming and fondling’ For a start, the male pageant was filled with more in-your-face dirty slapstick moments than its sister competition. One incident that caused a media stir occurred during the 2008 contest, when actress Christine Ng Wing-mei pretended to require an oxygen mask after touching a contestant. The following year, the female audience members and guest celebrities were given a “look but don’t touch” rule. In 2009, the Mr Hong Kong pageant became the target of a moral campaign. Members of Hong Kong’s Parents for the Family Association (PFA), together with the California-based Organisation for Justice and Equality and the Hong Kong Men’s Concern Group, lodged public complaints against Mr Hong Kong with the Equal Opportunities Commission. According to records from the PFA, the allegations followed that “the programme was filled with scenes of screaming and fondling, sexually provocative acts by the female judges … giving the impression that the contestants were reduced to objects for female viewing and molestation”. Complainants believed this was a possible breach of the Sex Discrimination Ordinance. The PFA was also concerned about the show’s international viewership in the United States and Canada and believed it “might lead people to believe that Chinese men and women are all lustful and lack inner virtues”. The PFA further wrote in a 2010 online statement that this “also constitutes racial discrimination – or even indirect racial defamation”. In 2010, then-president of the PFA Howard Lai complained about the show to the now-defunct Hong Kong Broadcasting Authority, claiming that the “programme hostess did not give sufficient time for the contestants to express different views” and that the “contest puts emphasis on the appearance of the contestants”. When asked by the South China Morning Post, Lai says he was not, in principle, against the contest, but was concerned about the perceived indecency and sexual discrimination in the show and wanted to implement changes that could “promote a positive and virtuous masculinity” in Hong Kong. The PFA – which formally dissolved in 2022 – never filed any similar complaints against the Miss Hong Kong contest, which some viewers today may argue is similar in its sexual discrimination or objectification. Notably, Miss Hong Kong has historically invited male and female judges to the show, and male judges do not have a segment in which they can touch the candidates. “As an impression, bad taste and indecency did exist occasionally in the Miss Hong Kong Pageant shows,” Lai says, adding that “Miss Hong Kong has a much longer history than Mr Hong Kong. I am not inclined to compare them as it is like to compare an apple with an orange.” Though the Broadcasting Authority ultimately dismissed the complaints, they left a mark. TVB began to tighten the leash on its judges, instructing them to avoid exaggerated reactions. Male judges and guest celebrities featured in the 2011 contest, and a pageant staple – the swimsuit round – was abandoned in the 2016 edition. Did the Mr Hong Kong contestants feel exploited? When TVB actor Joey Law Tin-yu competed in the 2008 contest, there were only female judges and an all-female audience present. Law has had a steady stream of work in TVB projects since his 2008 victory in the contest’s youth division; unlike Miss Hong Kong, contestants could win in either the youth or mature division, with the overall winner selected from both groups. “I really didn’t see it as a problem,” Law says, who believes the all-female audience of his year added a lively atmosphere to the show. “Men rarely shout ‘Oh yeah!’ when seeing another shirtless guy, even if they think ‘Cool, man!’” he says, laughing. Rather than feeling uncomfortable with the judges or audience, Law remembers only feeling discomfort about his own physique. He grew up feeling that he was perceived as “delicate, with a soft voice, and not the very ‘manly’ or tough type”, but feels that the Mr Hong Kong contest helped him develop confidence and confront his anxiety. Law even compares his experience on the show to the fun of a “summer camp”. For 2011 Mr Hong Kong winner Clayton Nicholas Li, the valuable lesson he learned after the show is that “fame … is not easy”. The now 39-year-old does say, however, that he “had a great time” as a Mr Hong Kong title winner. Li left Hong Kong nearly a decade ago after working as a TVB actor in the years following his victory. “I was 24 when I competed, but now I’m in Toronto … pursuing photography and videography,” he says. He now runs his own film and photo studio, Diractor Productions. Li prepared a floating-table magic trick as part of his act for his talent segment – a surreal scene that perhaps captures the show’s unresolved tension and identity crisis. Was this a search for the next leading man, or was it a comedy sketch with six-pack abs? Why were Miss and Mr Hong Kong so different? Miss and Mr Hong Kong were never designed to be the same show, says Tsang Sing-ming, TVB’s former deputy director of publicity, who handled the 2010 complaints. “Miss Hong Kong contestants carried a clear purpose and duty – promoting Hong Kong’s image – and were even supported by organisations like the Hong Kong Trade Development Council,” Tsang says. With a decade having passed since the last edition of Mr Hong Kong – during which time discussions about gender equality have become more prominent – is there space for the competition to return? Law believes that TVB should bring back Mr Hong Kong and recommends that young talent audition for such shows. “When I started, I had no concept of becoming an actor or singer … step by step, I discovered my interests, understood myself better,” he says. Tsang says if TVB were to bring it back, they could host Mr Hong Kong every few years for special occasions rather than as an annual tradition. “It could be like the World Cup or Olympics,” he says. Perhaps, when the contest was running, TVB inadvertently turned the pageant into a self-parody in which the contestants were “in on the joke” in a way some viewers were not. To revive it today in a different social context, Mr Hong Kong will have to rethink how it can escape the limbo between the aspirations of Miss Hong Kong and the campy unpredictability of a variety show. Before returning, Mr Hong Kong must figure out what kind of “man” it is trying to sell.

title: Super-rich losing millions as some Hong Kong trophy homes sell at painful discounts
description: Under-pressure owners are cutting prices to exit Hong Kong’s luxury property market, with some homes losing more than HK$100 million in value.
content: Hong Kong has seen a string of cut-price deals for super-luxury homes in recent months, with financially pressured owners accepting eye-watering losses to exit the market even as demand for trophy homes remains strong. Among the latest examples is the sale of a Bel-Air luxury house for HK$138 million (US$17.6 million), about HK$37 million below the price the former owner paid for the property in 2018. The 3,792 sq ft house in Pok Fu Lam was bought for HK$175 million in 2018 by Shie Thomas, according to Land Registry records. Shie reportedly has ties to the Hong Kong export firm Tak Fi International, and is also listed as a racehorse owner by the Hong Kong Jockey Club. An agreement to sell the property for HK$138 million was signed in June between the property’s latest owner, Shie Serena She-wing, and a buyer named as Chen Dongqiong, with the assignment registered on August 18. The transaction represents a more than 20 per cent loss on the 2018 purchase price. Land Registry records also show the property was mortgaged to Dah Sing Bank in 2022, with a rental assignment subsequently registered in favour of the bank. The Bel-Air sale is not an isolated case. Several high-end houses and flats have recently changed hands well below their previous purchase prices, showing that a revival in luxury home sales in Hong Kong has not necessarily helped every owner recover their equity. At The Morgan on Conduit Road, a nearly 4,000 sq ft home with a private terrace sold for HK$190 million, a painful 45 per cent below the HK$344 million paid by the previous owner in 2018, according to Land Registry records. A sale agreement for the property was signed on August 3. In June, an 8,855 sq ft duplex at Mount Nicholson sold for about HK$550 million, down 7.3 per cent from the HK$593 million paid by the seller back in 2017, Land Registry records show. The seller was listed as Chen Jiarong, who is reportedly affiliated with Shenzhen developer Kingkey Group. However, there appears to have been a drop in the number of high-profile bank-owned luxury homes selling at a loss this year, according to Glen Ho, Deloitte’s national turnaround and restructuring leader. The city’s residential property market had generally been more stable than the commercial sector, with more buyers returning in the first half, reducing the pressure on banks to dispose of homes quickly, Ho said. “Some residential assets may also be handled more discreetly because of issues such as unauthorised building works,” he added. The number of bungalow transactions – excluding HK$100 million-plus internal transfers – rose 8.6 per cent in the first half of the year compared with the previous six months, according to Centaline Property. The value of those transactions reached a combined HK$17.19 billion, up 4.4 per cent from the previous six months and the highest first-half total since 2021, data from the property firm showed. Trophy homes in sought-after developments can still command nine-figure prices, even as individual properties continue to sell at discounts. While Hong Kong’s overall luxury property market has slowed in the second half amid external headwinds, including Chinese tax changes and tighter capital controls, several big-ticket transactions were still recorded in August at projects such as CK Asset’s 21 Borrett Road and K&K Property’s One Stanley.

title: Hong Kong’s property, financial markets face test under cross-border anti-corruption law
description: For decades, Hong Kong has drawn affluent Chinese wanting to build up their wealth through stock listings or asset acquisitions.
content: China’s deliberation on its sweeping cross-border anti-corruption law may ripple through Hong Kong’s financial and property markets, as Beijing seeks harsher punishments for corrupt officials and broadens its scrutiny of the massive pool of wealth transferred overseas. Hong Kong remains in focus after the draft law was submitted on Tuesday to the standing committee of the national legislature for deliberation, analysts said. The law was “designed to give mainland authorities a clearer statutory basis for pursuing corruption cases with an overseas element, strengthening international cooperation and supporting the recovery of illicit assets held abroad”, said Karen Cheung, a partner at law firm HFW. “High-value assets, including luxury goods and prime property, together with complex corporate and trust structures, may come under closer scrutiny where they become relevant to mainland corruption investigations,” she said. For decades, Hong Kong has drawn affluent Chinese wanting to build up their wealth through stock listings or asset acquisitions, with the city’s equity, property and even luxury-goods markets prospering on the inflow of mainland funds. The city was also home to branches of major Chinese financial institutions, state-owned industrial giants and private firms eyeing global expansion. Hong Kong’s financial resilience may now face a test as Chinese President Xi Jinping escalates his campaign to fight corruption within the ruling Communist Party. The unprecedented cross-border anti-corruption law comes on the heels of a tax crackdown on offshore trusts and insurance policies, a move that triggered a plunge in shares of insurer AIA Group on concerns over shrinking demand from mainland investors. State media said the new law would improve the government’s ability to crack down on corruption overseas and fortify the “toolkit” used to retrieve illegal assets and deal with cases related to cross-border corruption. China handed down punishments to 983,000 officials for corruption last year, with the number of penalized senior officials three times that of 2013, according to data compiled by the South China Morning Post. The financial sector has become a focus of the crackdown as top leaders place great emphasis on the importance of capital markets in the nation’s technology self-reliance drive. Yi Huiman, former chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), was investigated for disciplinary breaches in September last year and later removed from Party membership and his public post. In July, former CSRC vice-chairman Fang Xinghai, seen as a reform-minded official who liaised between the regulators and foreign investors, was also put under investigation. For Hong Kong, the repercussions of the law enforcement could be far-reaching, with mainland capital holding sway over the city’s pillar industries. The recovery in the local property market largely hinged on mainland Chinese buyers, who accounted for as much as 33 per cent of transaction values for residential homes, according to an estimate by UBS Group. Meanwhile, the boom in initial public offerings (IPOs) was driven by Chinese companies seeking to tap foreign capital. Hong Kong’s home prices rose an average of 7.9 per cent in the first half, the biggest increase for the six-month period since 2019. Separately, IPO proceeds in the same period surged 84 per cent from a year ago to US$26.4 billion, ranking only behind the Nasdaq that absorbed the mega listing of SpaceX. “Wealthy mainland buyers tend to become more cautious whenever Beijing widens the enforcement spotlight around offshore money,” said Stephen Innes, a managing partner at SPI Asset Management. “That could mean slower decisions on luxury property and less conspicuous spending on watches, jewellery and other high-end goods. Markets often react to the fear of scrutiny well before the rules are actually tested.” The new law, coupled with China’s intensified oversight of offshore assets, comes against the backdrop of accelerating capital outflows, increasing fiscal stress and growing funding needs for the tech industry. At the same time, Chinese capital drove offshore wealth in Hong Kong to an all-time high of US$2.9 trillion last year, overtaking Switzerland as the world’s largest such hub, according to Boston Consulting Group. “These developments point to a shift towards stronger tax compliance and regulatory oversight of offshore wealth and cross-border capital, rather than a reversal of China’s broader opening-up agenda,” Barclays said in a report on Tuesday. “The objective appears to be better monitoring and management of cross-border financial activities while continuing to support strategically important outbound investment.”

title: US man kills 8 relatives, including 4 children, at family dinner
description: Gunman sets home on fire and dies of self-inflicted wound following shooting that wiped out four generations.
content: A man killed eight of his relatives, including four children, as they gathered for Sunday dinner at a home outside Billings, Montana, weeks after his parents asked him to move out, a family member told Associated Press. Brad Ireland, whose former wife and two children were among the dead, identified the shooter as 44-year-old Alan Smith. Smith’s parents, who were also killed, had asked him to move out, but he returned on Sunday and opened fire, Ireland said. The victims represented four generations of the blended family, ranging from a great-grandmother in her 90s who used a wheelchair to a 7-year-old girl, according to Jennifer Mercer, a neighbour and family friend who set up an online fundraiser to help cover funeral costs and other expenses, and was authorised to release these details. Police responded to the home on Sunday evening and heard gunshots coming from out back, just before the house was completely engulfed in flames. Investigators confirmed Tuesday there were eight victims, including four children, and that the suspect had suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound and later died. The investigation has been complicated by concerns about the structural integrity of the house after the fire burned it to its foundation, said Jeff Stovall, a spokesperson for the Billings Police Department. Firefighters fought the blaze until around 1am Monday, according to Billings Fire Department Chief Matt Hoppel. The home is in a subdivision outside of city limits that’s not required to have fire hydrants. Efforts to fight the fire were delayed until the site was secure, allowing the blaze to tear through the home. Among those killed were Ireland’s ex-wife, Megan Ghekiere, and their two children, Owen Ireland, 13, and Chloe Ireland, 7. Also killed were Ghekiere’s two stepchildren with her current husband: Landon Ghekiere, 15, and Charlotte Ghekiere, 12. “The one thing we do know is that Charlotte was the hero,” Mercer said. “Charlotte called 911 and she tried to save her family. And that’s something the family does want out there”. She described the family as “very loving and close”, and said the children all got along and that their parents remained amicable even after divorcing. “I feel like our entire community is devastated, even people that never knew any of them,” Mercer said. The Smith family was originally from the Seattle area. Ireland said that after he and Megan Ghekiere divorced six years ago, she moved to Montana with their children. That’s where she met the man who would become her second husband, Adam Ghekiere, who was working and not at the home when the shooting occurred. Her parents, Dana and Barb Smith, soon followed, buying a house in Billings near their daughter’s home. Evelyn Smith, Dana’s elderly mother, lived in a nearby retirement community, Ireland said. Alan Smith moved in with his parents in Montana and stayed with them for years before being asked to move out a couple weeks ago, Ireland said. He unexpectedly returned to the home on Sunday evening, where the Smiths had gathered for a weekly family dinner. Alan Smith killed his grandmother, his parents, his younger sister and the four children before setting the house on fire, Ireland said. He tried to flee before being confronted by law enforcement, he said. “There were many red flags and many people spoke out,” said Ireland, who lives in Arizona. “No one listened.” Alan Smith was a “hermit” who spent most of his days in his room on his computer, Ireland said. “No one knew what he did in there 24/7,” he said. Alan Smith had attended Eastern Washington University but had been unable to find or hold a job. A search of criminal records in Montana and Washington found no record Alan Smith had ever been arrested or charged with a crime. Ireland said that to his knowledge Alan Smith had never been violent, though he could be verbally abusive. Friends of the victims have set up two GoFundMe accounts to raise money on behalf of Adam Ghekiere and his ex-wife, Erica Schneider. Adam Ghekiere, who works at the airport in Billings, said that he heard over a dispatch radio about an active shooting. After calling each member of his family, he raced across town to the Smith home. When he got there, the house was ablaze, and two hours later, he learned his wife and children had been killed. His children weren’t supposed to be there because family dinner was usually on Friday, he said. “I don’t think he expected my kids to be there,” Ghekiere said, referring to his brother-in-law. “Monster isn’t even enough to describe what he did.” Ghekiere said police confirmed his daughter, Charlotte, was the one who dialled 911 from inside the house. “I keep hearing her quote to me every time I would say ‘I love you’ and she would say ‘I love you more,’” he said. The shootings were the 22nd mass killing this year, according to a database maintained by the AP and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University. Fifteen of those have stemmed from domestic disputes, which is higher than the average of about 50 per cent of US mass killings, said James Alan Fox, a criminologist at Northeastern University who manages the database. The Montana shooting is the deadliest in the US since April, when a Louisiana father fatally shot eight children, including seven of his own, and shot and wounded his wife and another woman.

title: Sikh separatist says FBI, Canadian police warned him of new credible death threat
description: Gurpatwant Singh Pannun says he remains ‘unfazed’ following fresh warnings from US and Canadian authorities.
content: A prominent Sikh separatist said Tuesday that the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have warned him that he faces a new credible threat to his life even as a man from India faces sentencing later this year for a 2023 death plot against him. Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, general counsel for Sikhs For Justice, said he was warned by FBI agents who visited him August 12 that he should not travel until the threat is resolved, and, if he does, the agency should be notified in advance of his plans. He said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police warned him by telephone on Tuesday, though neither law enforcement agency gave any details about the plot that was uncovered. Messages seeking comment from both law enforcement agencies were not immediately returned. Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen, said he was warned according to the terms of a “Duty to Warn” law in the United States that obligates US intelligence and law enforcement agencies to notify individuals when they discover credible and specific threats of murder, severe bodily harm or kidnapping. The new threat comes as Nikhil Gupta, a man from India who pleaded guilty to federal conspiracy charges in February, awaits a November 20 sentencing in Manhattan federal court for plotting in 2023 with others to assassinate Pannun. The FBI has said Gupta was directed by an Indian government employee to carry out the killing. When Gupta tried, he unwittingly communicated with an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a hitman. Federal sentencing guidelines call for Gupta to spend at least two decades in prison. Pannun, who advocates for the creation of the sovereign Sikh state and is considered a terrorist by the Indian government, said in a phone interview Tuesday that he was “unfazed and undaunted” by the attempts to silence him. “I’m not afraid of their death threats,” he said, though he added that he hoped that the administrations of President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney would confront Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi over threats to US and Canadian sovereignty. “The Modi government is proceeding under the Trump administration without fear of any consequences,” he said. Pannun has described himself as a Sikh human rights lawyer who is campaigning to turn Punjab into a place where “all religions will have equal rights”. He said “Duty to Warn” advisories were issued by Canadian law enforcement officials to Hardeep Singh Nijjar, the ex-head of the Canadian chapter of the Khalistan Referendum, in the weeks before he was assassinated on June 18, 2023 in Surrey, British Columbia. Pannun said the continued threats give him courage and confidence that his campaign and outspokenness is working. “I’m going to continue, even at the cost of a bullet,” he said.

title: ‘Fascinating and shocking’ book about Putin’s private life wins prize
description: Exiled Russian journalists awarded Prix Strasbourg for taboo-breaking work based on hundreds of interviews with witnesses who later vanished.
content: A taboo-breaking book about Vladimir Putin’s rise to power and private life, written by two exiled Russian journalists, won a newly established French literary prize on Tuesday. The book, titled The Tsar in Propria Persona: How Vladimir Putin Deceived Us All, draws on more than two decades of investigative reporting by journalists Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin. The work won a newly established literary award called the Prix Strasbourg awarded by EBRA, France’s largest regional newspaper group, and its parent company, Credit Mutuel Alliance Federale. The book is due to be published in France next month. It reads “like a spy novel”, the jury said, describing the book as a “fascinating and shocking work about a figure who is himself fascinating and shocking”. “It is the result of several hundred interviews with witnesses, some of whom later disappeared under tragic circumstances.” Badanin is the founder and editor-in-chief of Proekt, an investigative media outlet created in 2018. Both Badanin and Rubin, his deputy at Proekt, live in the United States after coming under pressure in Russia. Badanin said the authors wanted foreigners to read the book and learn “actual facts” about Putin and the system he had built. “The message we wanted to convey with this book is as follows: there is no need to invent anything about Putin. Instead, learn how things really are. That is horrifying enough,” he said. “Only a genuine understanding of the facts can help us make sound assessments, respond effectively, and plan for the future of relations between nations.” When the book’s Russian edition was published last year, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) said that Badanin and Rubin broke a Kremlin-imposed taboo about Putin’s private life “at great personal risk”. The book “contrasts the official image of the Russian president, now in his 26th year in power, as a leading defender of traditional values against Western decadence with the reality of his private life – where extramarital affairs, nepotism, and connections to organised crime reign”. Launched in 2026, the prize seeks to distinguish itself through its substantial endowment, with €20,000 (US$23,000) awarded to the overall winner and €55,000 distributed across all categories. Other prizewinners include Haitian author Thelyson Orelien and French journalist Marion Dubreuil.

title: As I see it | Africa knows who its true friends are – and they’re not in Washington
description: China’s sustained engagement across the continent stands in stark contrast to a US approach driven purely by strategic utility.
content: The gaffe at last month’s Aids 2026 conference in Rio de Janeiro, where a US State Department presentation displayed a map of Africa with every country mislabelled, serves as more than a source of embarrassment. It was a potent symbol of the distance between Washington’s rhetoric and its real stance regarding the African continent. Earlier this year, Nick Checker, a senior US State Department official, spoke of “resetting” US relations with Africa, pivoting away from dependency and towards mutually beneficial partnerships. Yet, as the mislabelled map suggests, the actual engagement often feels disconnected, chaotic and transactional. Washington’s policies towards Africa have long been a study in contradiction. While American officials try to put the focus on what they call China’s debt traps, the US often pursues a policy defined by punitive tariffs, restrictive visa policies and selective interventions. Whether it is feuding with regional powers such as South Africa, intervening in their domestic affairs, or remaining largely silent on humanitarian crises, the US approach usually prioritises strategic utility over genuine partnership. This pattern echoed throughout the Cold War era. Washington’s support for many brutal and corrupt regimes was often dictated by narrow geopolitical interests rather than the aspirations of African citizens, and this continues to this day. Contrast this with the recent history of China’s engagement. The results are visible in the roads, railways, ports and telecommunications infrastructure that are reshaping African economies. In Nigeria, struggling farmers are benefiting from a high-yield rice strain called Gawal R1. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, Beijing has provided rapid medical aid to contain an Ebola outbreak. According to a youth survey of 16 countries by the South Africa-based Ichikowitz Family Foundation, 95 per cent of respondents aged 18 to 24 viewed Beijing as an ally. This sentiment is mirrored in Pew Research Centre data, which charts a steady decline in favourable perceptions of the United States alongside an increase in support for China. This shift is not limited to physical infrastructure. In the digital realm, African tech users are increasingly bypassing American services in favour of Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models. These systems offer greater customisability and lower costs, supported by Chinese firms that provide the computing power and engineering know-how necessary to integrate with local needs. By establishing government-focused data centres and international AI pacts, China is securing a technological foothold that American companies, too focused on high-cost, proprietary solutions, have failed to capture. Economic pragmatism is also driving this divergence. As trade between Africa and China expands, the yuan is rapidly becoming a major trading currency. Financial institutions across the continent are integrating with China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System to facilitate direct settlements, while nations such as Libya explore issuing panda bonds to fund reconstruction. Large lenders such as Johannesburg-headquartered Standard Bank are moving to reduce reliance on the US dollar, viewing these ties as a necessary strategy to build alternative financial infrastructure and hedge against the volatility of US-led sanctions. The US has long viewed Chinese activities in Africa through its own neo-imperialist lens. While Washington exploits the continent when necessary and ignores it at other times, Beijing has consistently maintained deep partnership, cooperation and aid, almost since the modern nation’s founding in 1949. The Asian-African Conference in Indonesia in 1955, better known as the Bandung Conference, marked a major milestone, allowing China to break out of Western isolation and build ties across Asia and Africa. Under Mao Zedong, Beijing gave unequivocal ideological and material support to the decolonisation of Africa, helped unite anti-colonial leaders and advocated for national sovereignty. Premier Zhou Enlai used the summit to present China as a peaceful, reasonable leader by laying down the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. Beijing never looked back. The strong ties forged with newly independent states helped China take its seat from Taiwan at the United Nations in 1971. The Bandung Conference effectively launched the Non-Aligned Movement of newly independent nations. As China grew wealthy, those developing economies received sustained and continuing support. The US, by contrast, was unmitigatedly active, especially during the Cold War, in attempting to subvert social-democratic governments and movements in Africa, all the while exploiting its natural resources. Good international relations are built on presence, consistency and tangible results. While the US grapples with mislabelled maps and ideological grandstanding, China has been building the infrastructure of the future in partnership with African nations. It is time for observers to stop asking who African nations align with and start listening when they tell us who they believe their friends truly are.

title: Trump says China is driving anger at US data centres. These residents disagree
description: Community living near AI facility in Virginia reports invasive levels of noise, fumes and gas turbines – and it’s not Chinese propaganda.
content: On the tree-lined streets of Sterling, northern Virginia, Lindsay Shaw’s home sits across from an industrial neighbour that has consumed the past several years of her life: a data centre. When Shaw sits outside, she can hear its constant hum. At night, the security lights blaze through her window, making it harder to sleep. Gas turbines, diesel fumes, and 24/7 industrial noise have choked Shaw’s neighbourhood since the data centre moved in. Meanwhile, in Washington, US President Donald Trump is among those attributing community pushback in places like Sterling to foreign influence from China. “It’s not China telling us anything. It’s not Russia telling us anything,” Shaw said. “It’s truly living next to it is what it is.” Shaw came to this view gradually. She did not initially oppose the project. Shaw and her husband had worked in cybersecurity and understood the need for data centres to power cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence. Their concerns only emerged after the facility was approved, when eight gas turbines were added to power it while it awaited a connection to the electrical grid – a process that can take years. It was not until it was up and running that the constant noise, occasional smoke and nightly lights came. Mounting claims that China is to blame for data centre pushback in the US are fuelled by comments from Trump, Republican lawmakers and technology-industry advocates who allege that Beijing is funding or amplifying campaigns intended to slow America’s development of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Several reports tied to the US tech industry, released in the past year, have claimed to find evidence that China is attempting to manipulate US debates over AI and technology policy. But the reports do not establish that Beijing created or meaningfully drove the widespread local pushback. In Sterling, much of the opposition predates the allegations and centres on residents’ direct concerns about noise, emissions and broken promises. The dispute highlights an important distinction in the increasingly politicised US-China AI race: foreign actors may try to exploit genuine domestic grievances without creating them or significantly shaping their impact. Critics say failing to make that distinction allows politicians and industry groups to portray grass roots opposition as foreign interference – and potentially avoid addressing the legitimate concerns of US residents. “It’s just completely unrelated to China – China is just a useful weapon to bash your domestic enemy with,” said Bethany Allen, head of China Investigations and Analysis at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), who researches China’s overseas influence operations. “It’s just removed from reality.” Opposition to data centres is so organic and widespread at both local and national levels that Allen considers it “literally impossible for anyone to have created that through an astroturf campaign”. Not everyone shares that view, however. [Trump] blames everything on China … I don’t take any of it seriously Jessica Medeiros, Sterling resident ‘A big part of it is China’ Just a forty-minute drive away from Sterling in the nation’s capital, Trump remains focused on winning the increasingly competitive race against China to lead the world in AI. While visiting California earlier this month, the president alleged in an interview that Beijing was fuelling community resistance against AI infrastructure in the US. “A big part of it is China,” Trump told Fox News. “Look, whoever wins the AI race is going to win AI … It’s bigger than maybe anything that has happened for literally hundreds of years. The communities that are giving us a hard time, a lot of people think that’s China-oriented.” When Jessica Medeiros, one of Shaw’s neighbours, heard what Trump said, she was in disbelief. A juvenile pretrial officer, she says the data centre near her house has caused her to be diagnosed with dry eyes. Instead of China, she says she is focused on everyday quality-of-life issues. “He blames everything on China, you know, anything that doesn’t go his way or doesn’t pan out,” Medeiros said of Trump. “I don’t take any of it seriously.” An issue of intent over impact The local residents’ experiences do not, on their own, disprove claims of foreign influence, however. Experts say China’s influence operations are often difficult for ordinary people to identify because they mask the origins of their content. One of the main groups alleging Chinese influence is the Bitcoin Policy Institute (BPI), a Washington-based think tank, which has released two reports since May accusing China of trying to slow the US data centre buildout by funding US climate nonprofits and protests. The reports acknowledge legitimate concerns among Americans about data centre impacts on energy, water use and grid capacity, but argue that Chinese-funded actors are amplifying those concerns. House Republicans cited the BPI report in June when they called for an investigation into foreign influence on domestic data centre opposition. According to ASPI’s Allen, the BPI reports are examples of how certain US industry interests are weaponising Chinese influence claims to smear local grass-roots opposition. She points out that BPI is not purely a research organisation focused on Chinese influence operations, but rather an advocacy group for the cryptocurrency industry. BPI disputed that characterisation in an email to the South China Morning Post. Allen said that a similar report released in June by ChatGPT maker OpenAI was better because it focused on Beijing’s intent rather than impact and acknowledged that Chinese influence operations latch on to existing, genuine concerns. OpenAI said it had banned two clusters of ChatGPT accounts, likely originating in China, for posing as Americans and making claims online that data centres were increasing electricity prices for American families, but concluded that there was “no evidence” of this having shifted public opinion. Responding to questions from the SCMP, BPI’s head of research Sam Lyman, a former aide to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, acknowledged that “most opposition to data centres in the US is indisputably organic, and many Americans have sincere concerns about data centres that deserve to be heard”, while adding that evidence of Chinese influence remains “indisputable”. The data centre capital of the world The showdown over data centres is playing out with particular intensity in the northern Virginia county where Sterling sits – Loudoun County, which has the most data centres per capita in the world. One of the wealthiest areas in America, the county’s big houses, access to nature and proximity to Washington have long attracted residents wanting a certain quality of life. Since the 2000s, an extensive underground fibre optic network and permissive land use regulations have given rise to “Data Centre Alley” there, with around 250 data centres in an area only slightly larger than Hong Kong and over 100 more in the works. While the influx of tech companies has delivered massive tax benefits for the county – an estimated US$1.3 billion this financial year – it has also riled up residents who say that the companies have reneged on initial promises about their facilities having minimal impacts on the local quality of life. In Sterling, for example, residents complain that the data centres rely on noisy, polluting gas turbines and diesel generators. But Vantage, the Colorado-based company behind the data centre across from Shaw and Medeiros’ homes, had consistently told local residents and officials during the initial stages of the approval process that the facility would be powered by the local electrical grid, according to Sterling district supervisor Koran Saines. After final approval for the data centre was given in March 2023, Saines said Vantage learned from the energy company Dominion Energy that it would not receive an immediate connection to the grid and subsequently amended its site plan to include gas turbines as an alternative power source. He said the turbines were added through an administrative amendment, without returning to the county Board of Supervisors for a vote. The facility now also has backup diesel generators, the source of the black smoke. “The high-pitched sound is coming from the gas turbines that run the data centres on a daily basis,” Saines said, though he noted that the “average” of the noise readings local officials have taken near the site has never exceeded the legal maximum level of 55 decibels – equivalent to the sound of moderate rainfall. Mark Freeman, Vantage’s vice-president of global marketing, said that the VA2 campus complies with all state and federal emissions requirements and local noise ordinances. Freeman said Vantage had maintained ongoing engagement with residents and officials during all stages of VA2. Dominion Energy has not publicly stated when it will connect the Vantage data centre to its grid. Vantage told residents on Monday in a tense town hall meeting that the company was now looking at 2040 to be connected to the grid, after years of not disclosing a timeline. ‘Folks are experiencing this’ Working at the Virginia Conservation Network, one of the state’s main advocacy groups calling for stricter oversight of the data centre industry, Fatima Kamara has seen the community impact of the data centre buildout and thinks the China claims are “definitely a narrative”. “What is happening is that when foreign actors are building resentment, they typically are doing it around things that folks can’t experience themselves,” she said. “But in this case, folks are experiencing this first-hand. They don’t need a foreign actor to tell them to feel badly about it.” One of the main resident concerns is environmental and long-term health impacts. An analysis by researchers working with the Piedmont Environmental Council estimated annual public-health damages ranging from US$33 million to US$63 million. The researchers had previously estimated damages of up to US$99 million, but the figure was reduced after Virginia’s Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) claimed the findings had “overstated the actual emissions from VA2” by using the facility’s maximum permitted emissions. In Sterling, residents remain dogged by problems with the data centre with no solution in sight. There has not been a single day in the past 16 years when a data centre was not under construction in Loudoun County, with data centres lined up along the highway and even cemeteries surrounded by data centres, the immovable holdouts of an ever-changing landscape. For Shaw, the core issue is that data centre companies like Vantage will say they comply with regulations, while their impacts – recurring black smoke, constant whining noise and the year-round lights – have changed the fabric of the community. “It’s like your neighbour who gets his lawnmower out at 8:01. Is he [doing things] by the book? Yes. Is that a good neighbour on a Saturday morning? Probably not,” Shaw said. Shaw says they want to warn other Americans about their experiences and encourage them to ask the right questions before one is built across the street. “I’ve been living with this, thinking this was normal. And it’s not,” she said, as yet more of the data centre’s whistle seeped through her thick windows. “I don’t know what normal is any more.”

title: US Secret Service says it is aware of Iranian video threat to Barron Trump
description: Iranian state TV airs video claiming tracking of US president’s 20-year-old son and offering US$10 million bounty for his killing.
content: The US Secret ⁠Service is aware ⁠of a video ⁠broadcast by Iranian state television discussing a potential plot to assassinate US President Donald Trump’s youngest son, a spokesman said on ‌Tuesday. “The US Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees. “Out of concern for operational security, we ⁠do not discuss matters of protective intelligence,” Secret Service spokesman Nate Herring wrote in an email. A three-minute video broadcast by Iranian state television ‌discussed a potential plot to assassinate Barron Trump, ⁠20, ⁠claiming that he was being monitored and alleging that a US$10 ‌million bounty had been offered for his killing. The United States and ‌Iran have ‌kept up hostile rhetoric during a nearly six-month-old ‌war started by the US and Israel in ⁠February. Reuters reported earlier this month that the US ⁠has received several warnings from Israel over the past year that Iran intended to assassinate Trump, according ‌to officials, including ‌before a secret Air Force One ruse in Turkey. Trump has described himself as “number one on the kill list for Iran”. Since the US assassination of Iran’s Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iranian media have on multiple occasions circulated content threatening the president and family members. The assassination came at the start of the war in Iran that Trump launched alongside Israel. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Fire at Russian gas chemical complex leaves 6 Chinese dead, 9 more missing
description: Dozens injured as authorities investigate safety breaches at massive joint-venture site in Russia’s far east.
content: Six Chinese nationals were killed and nine ‌more are missing after a fire broke out at a gas chemical complex in Russia’s far eastern Amur region, the plant said on Wednesday. A total of seven people died and 152 people were treated for injuries, including 36 ⁠who were rushed to hospitals, the plant said on the Telegram ‌messaging app on Wednesday. The fire, which broke out on Tuesday, was extinguished, it added. An emergency services ‌plane had arrived to transport the injured to other hospitals ⁠in Russia. The ⁠complex, which bills itself as one of the world’s largest polyethylene and polypropylene ‌producers, is a joint project of Russian company Sibur and Chinese oil and gas ‌company Sinopec. ‌It has yet to begin operations and was preparing for ‌production start. Russia frequently relies on foreign labour, including workers from China, ⁠for the construction of large industrial and infrastructure projects. Russia’s Investigative Committee ⁠said it was investigating the incident as a potential breach of industrial safety regulations and was working to establish ‌the cause of ‌the fire. The Amur Gas Chemical Complex is expected to produce 2.3 million metric tons of polyethylene and 400,000 tons of polypropylene per year.

title: Asian shipper pays record US$5.3 million for Panama Canal access
description: Demand to pass through waterway soars after Iran war upends global trade routes, leaving ships facing 11-day wait.
content: A shipper needing to transit the Panama Canal bid a record US$5.3 million to secure its spot, according to people familiar with the matter. South Korea-based SK Gas Ltd agreed to pay the sum to travel the canal on September 1, said the people, who could not be identified as the information was confidential. The fee, determined through an auction run by the canal authority this week, breaks the previous high of US$4.6 million set earlier this month, also paid by a shipper controlling a South Korean vessel. Demand to urgently pass through the waterway has soared after the Iran war upended global trade routes, particularly to Asia. Wait times at the canal have grown to as long as 11 days for vessels that arrive at the waterway without reservations, according to Argus Media. The Panama Canal Authority has also tightened restrictions on the number of slots starting in September, as well as on how much cargo ships can carry due to likely drought conditions in the region. The winning auction bid allows the G. Spirit, a liquefied petroleum gas tanker, to travel northbound through the canal. As of Tuesday, the ship was shown positioned on the Pacific side of the waterway, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. SK Gas did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Panama Canal Authority, through a spokeswoman, declined to provide comment on the record-high auction price. The canal said in a statement that most of the vessels use a reservation booking system. Recent auction results have reflected “significantly stronger demand”, showing higher prices than the median auction price paid before February of around US$55,000. The El Nino weather pattern brewing in the Pacific is another factor in shippers’ rising willingness to pay for reservations. El Nino is likely to bring severe drought to Panama, which would threaten the freshwater levels of the canal and shipping availability.

title: Dolly Parton, US country music legend and cultural icon, dies at 80
description: Prolific songwriter of ‘Jolene’ and other hits transcended generations, genres and politics over a six-decade career.
content: Dolly Parton, the country music star who rose from grinding poverty in Tennessee to become a rhinestone-studded cultural icon with hits like “Jolene” and “9 to 5”, has died at 80, her family said on Tuesday. Parton was more than a singer – she wrote 3,000 songs, acted in major Hollywood films and donated millions of dollars to charities in her home state and beyond. She was also an accomplished businesswoman, with her interests spanning from her popular Dollywood theme park to cosmetics, pet apparel, baking mixes and even a truck stop. “Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus,” her nephew Bryan Seaver said in a video announcing her death on social media. He said the multiple award-winning artist – known for her glittering style, curvy figure and larger-than-life blonde wigs – had “opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians, and dreamers from every walk of life”. Parton died after “a brief battle with cancer,” her representatives told US media. Parton had recently spoken about unspecified health challenges. Her husband Carl Dean died last year. A small private funeral service will be held, People magazine said, citing the singer’s representatives. US President Donald Trump ordered flags lowered across the United States, and New York’s Empire State Building was to be lit in pink at 9.25pm – a nod to Parton’s hit song and movie 9 to 5. The news sparked a rare moment of unity in a country often bitterly at odds over Trump’s presidency, the war against Iran and cultural issues. “May her legacy live on through her songs, the lives she touched, and the countless artists she inspired. There will never, ever be another one like her,” the Grand Ole Opry, America’s temple of country music, said on social media. Her co-stars from 9 to 5, which sparked her soundtrack smash when it came out in 1980, expressed shock. Oscar winner Jane Fonda said she was “devastated” while Lily Tomlin said only: “No words”. Trump called Parton’s passing a “true loss for millions of people”. “There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” he posted on his Truth Social network. Democratic former president Bill Clinton called her “one of a kind”. Born in 1946 as one of 12 children in rural Tennessee, Parton headed for the country music capital Nashville right after graduating from high school. By 1967, at age 21, she was among the most recognised figures in American music, having joined Porter Wagoner’s syndicated country music television show that broadcast her voice and face into millions of US homes. During a prolific career that spanned six decades, Parton penned some 3,000 tunes. They included “Jolene”, “Coat of Many Colors” and the iconic ballad “I Will Always Love You”, which became an international success for Whitney Houston. Releasing 49 studio albums and more than 100 compilation and collaboration albums, she earned the title of “queen of country music”. Never one to play down her striking looks, Parton essentially wrote the book on how a woman can rule the airwaves in a male-dominated industry, ultimately becoming an American treasure with songs covered by everyone from Shania Twain to Sinead O’Connor. “Instant Sainthood,” Jack White, who covered “Jolene” with the White Stripes, wrote on Instagram. Last year, Parton postponed a series of Las Vegas concerts, citing ongoing health concerns. In May, she cancelled them altogether, sparking new fears. In videos posted to her social media accounts, she said that while treatment for an unnamed illness was going well, she was not ready to perform. Just last week, she said in a statement to People magazine: “I still have so many things I want to achieve, so I’m gonna keep on working as long as I can to see everything come to life”. “She brought so many people together, we will all miss her so much,” said Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger.

title: Canada hits US goods with tariffs of up to 50% as trade war escalates
description: Ottawa targets about US$20 billion in US products and unveils billions in assistance after negotiations with Washington collapse.
