description: As security deal shakes up calculations for the US, China and Russia, a regional order shaped by regional states is no longer unthinkable.
content: The Mecca security pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan stipulates that an armed attack against one shall count as an attack against all three. Yet the real message is directed at the United States: if being an American ally offers no immunity against attack, there is little point in waiting for Washington to honour its security guarantees. That there has been no official White House statement casts some doubt on whether Donald Trump is really “very happy to see that Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have recently, and finally, signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement”, as the US president wrote on social media. “It shows that the Middle East is coming together and how countries will finally be able to defend themselves in a more meaningful way.” Superficially, the needs of the three nations are complementary: wealthy Saudi Arabia lacks military capacity, Turkey harbours ambitions across Eurasia and nuclear-armed Pakistan seeks financial support. Their strengths fit neatly together, cemented by a shared Sunni faith. But it is too early to argue that the Middle East is coming together. The concept of “middle power” may be in vogue after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called for middle power solidarity amid great power rivalry in his landmark Davos address. Yet neither Pakistan nor Turkey, plainly middle powers, are strictly Middle Eastern countries, despite ambitions to extend their influence. And the major powers will not walk away. America’s role in the Middle East might shrink in the long term but a new regional security architecture is unlikely to be short of its presence. The European Union, for instance, has talked about strategic autonomy for over a decade. The Ukraine conflict, however, exposed the hollowness of that ambition, as European security still fell back on American leadership and Nato’s military umbrella. Besides, eroding US influence in the region runs counter to Israel’s interests. Even if Washington were inclined to step back, Tel Aviv would go to great lengths to drag it back into the fray and cling tightly to its American backing – notwithstanding the fact that Israel’s killings in Gaza have shifted public opinion across sizeable segments of the US population, including young Jewish communities. Beijing has not issued a formal statement on the pact either. It should view the agreement with cautious approval. China has a long-standing preference for locally led security frameworks and supports regional powers in assuming greater responsibility for their stability. The pact complements its push for common and comprehensive security. In recent years, as China’s clout has grown, voices have increasingly called for Beijing to step in as a security guarantor. Voices are strongest in the Middle East, in part because China is the only major power that has friendly ties with all nations in the region, including Israel. But this diplomatic balancing act was sustainable partly because regional powers did not have acutely hostile relations with one another before the Gaza war. Should armed conflict erupt, China would find itself squeezed between opposing sides asking for support – a parallel to its predicament over the Russia-Ukraine war. Russia’s role in the Middle East has shrunk, but it is far from being pushed out of the picture. Ukraine-related obligations have tied down plenty of its energy and other resources, yet Moscow can still sustain its foothold, drawing on long-established diplomatic ties, technical military cooperation with Iran and residual military and political assets in Syria. Although it lacks the capacity to steer major regional events or launch bold new initiatives, Russia can still serve as a secondary diplomatic broker and keep up modest weapons sales. How far can the pact realistically go? The catch is who, exactly, would invade any of the three. Israel functions as a shared threat more than a direct foe, yet an Israeli military strike against any member is hard to imagine. Israel has no cause to attack Pakistan or Turkey – both are American allies as well. And before the Gaza war erupted, Saudi-Israeli normalisation was almost within reach. The pact is unquestionably bad news for Tehran: it unites the three most powerful Sunni states, a dynamic that naturally bodes ill for Shiite-led Iran. Backing proxies like the Houthis and Hezbollah will also become more costly. Yet if even Washington cannot make Iran bend, no regional power will dare launch a direct military assault against Tehran. Conversely, Tehran is highly unlikely to start an open war against any Mecca pact member – its doctrine rests on asymmetric leverage and proxy power, rather than territorial invasion. India, which regards Pakistan as its primary regional threat, will frown on the deal too. With Pakistan now backed by two of the most powerful Muslim nations, New Delhi will have to factor in potential pushback from Saudi Arabia and Turkey when planning military operations in Kashmir. The pact is particularly awkward for India given its traditionally close economic and energy ties with Saudi Arabia, one of India’s largest oil suppliers. Turkey, meanwhile, has long been an outspoken supporter of Pakistan on the Kashmir issue. The pact so far is a straw in the wind – but could it be the first move in a tectonic shift? Throughout its modern history, the region has served as a geopolitical chessboard for external powers. Today, great powers command far less ability to dictate regional outcomes than they did a generation ago. A regional order shaped by regional states is no longer unthinkable.

title: Woman fined HK$4,000 over unleashed dog attack at Hong Kong pet garden
description: Woman pleads guilty after her unleashed dog attacked another and bit its owner, as magistrate urges people to pay more attention to their pets.
content: A woman has been fined HK$4,000 (US$510) after pleading guilty to failing to keep her dog on a leash after it attacked a smaller canine and bit its owner. Eastern Court on Tuesday heard guilty pleas from Chong Oi-lam, 44, who had not leashed her golden retriever while walking it at the pet garden at Wan Chai Temporary Promenade on January 20. The court heard that after the golden retriever pounced on a Pomeranian, its owner picked up the smaller dog to shield it from the attack. The retriever then jumped up in an attempt to reach the other dog and bit the owner’s left arm. After intervening to control her dog after the attack, Chong was warned by the injured person that police had been called and were on their way, but she left the scene. Chong was charged with three summary offences in connection with the incident. In mitigation, she expressed regret and described the court proceedings as a “hard lesson”. She said she had not intended to evade responsibility but had wanted to remove her dog from the scene immediately. She added that she had not realised the pet garden was a public space and that she was required to keep her dog under control. “We have already done dog socialisation training for him and we do want to change his behaviour,” she said. Deputy Magistrate Erica Chong Ching-wai said dog owners should be more vigilant about their pets’ behaviour. “Recently, incidents involved a dog mauling another dog to death and a woman was killed by a dog. Dog owners should pay special attention to your own dogs,” she said. She ordered Chong to pay a total of HK$4,000 for the three charges. Last Thursday, a 33-year-old woman who operated a pet training facility in northern Hong Kong was found dead after being mauled by a mixed-breed dog with suspected pit bull ancestry. A few days before the fatal incident, an unleashed 60kg (132lb) dog mauled two smaller dogs to death in Yuen Long. Its owner faced charges of failing to keep the large dog securely restrained on a leash no longer than two metres.

title: Singapore’s island merger plan fuels nuclear power speculation
description: Analysts say nuclear could be one of Singapore’s options when planning the new island and its supporting infrastructure.
content: Singapore’s plan to merge several islands off its southwest coast into a new hub for industry, defence and “new power generation infrastructure” has stirred speculation over whether the site could one day host a nuclear power plant. The city state is studying advanced nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors (SMRs), as part of its long-term planning for a net-zero power system, but the government has not decided whether to deploy nuclear energy, let alone where any future plant could be sited. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said during Sunday’s National Day Rally that Singapore would, over the coming decades, merge Bukom, Sudong and Semakau, along with other smaller islands, to create a larger island, similar to how it developed Jurong Island. The new western island would not just be used for petrochemicals, it would also support a new generation of industries, including advanced manufacturing facilities and military purposes. “It can accommodate new power generation infrastructure to meet Singapore’s future needs,” said Wong, without specifying what kind of power would be generated there. Social media users were quick to speculate that the island could be used for a nuclear reactor, with one saying: “So that’s where the nuclear plant will be.” Singapore aims to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 by expanding solar power, importing regional clean energy and improving energy efficiency. In May, Wong said Singapore would perform an Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review in 2027, a voluntary assessment by the International Atomic Energy Agency for countries considering nuclear power, to ensure responsible development. A spokesman from the Energy Market Authority (EMA) told This Week in Asia the authority was studying a range of options for Singapore’s energy security and decarbonisation goals including “various energy technologies and infrastructure options for the longer term”. “As Singapore has not made a decision on whether to deploy nuclear energy, it would be premature to discuss the location of any potential nuclear power plant,” the spokesman said. Experts told This Week in Asia that nuclear power was just one of several options that could help Singapore meet its future green energy needs and achieve energy resilience. Sharon Seah, principal fellow and coordinator of the Climate Change in Southeast Asia Programme at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, points out that deploying new technologies, including carbon capture utilisation and storage, green hydrogen, methanol, ammonia and nuclear, would require space, as Singapore is one of the world’s most severely space-constrained countries. “I see this as the Singapore government forward planning and future-proofing their plans,” Seah said. Victor Nian, founding co-chairman of the Centre for Strategic Energy and Resources, stressed that the government had not decided whether to deploy nuclear energy, and the new island would take many years to develop. “But given Singapore’s energy trajectory, advanced nuclear should clearly be one of the options considered when planning the island and its supporting infrastructure,” Nian said. For Alvin Chew, senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, the announcement opens up the possibility of site options for SMRs – an advanced type of nuclear power plant that is smaller in size and power capacity than traditional reactors – or even a conventional nuclear power plant. “Singapore has already made plans to produce hydrogen on the existing Jurong Island. Siting a nuclear power plant on the future western island will complement the hydrogen production as well as the oil refining industry on the connected Jurong Island,” Chew said. The new island’s combined area would be adequate to house a series of SMRs and auxiliary facilities, Chew added. Nian similarly notes that some SMR designs use a plant footprint of about six to 15 hectares for several hundred megawatts, although the total site requirement could be larger once supporting infrastructure and security are included. “Land itself is therefore unlikely to be the decisive constraint if the island is planned with nuclear [power] as a future option,” Nian said. He cautioned, however, that offshore siting did not automatically make nuclear power safe. “The reactor must still meet stringent safety requirements, including for marine hazards, cooling, grid connection, emergency response and security. Ultimately, public confidence will depend more on demonstrated safety, strong regulation and transparency than simply putting a reactor further away,” Nian said. Singapore officials have stressed that safety will be the “overriding priority” in any assessment of nuclear energy, adding that the country is building capabilities in nuclear safety and regulation while working with international partners. Seah notes that perceptions of nuclear energy in Singapore are changing. In the Southeast Asia Climate Outlook Survey 2024, respondents from the city state pointed to solar as the clean energy source with the most potential in their country, followed by green hydrogen and nuclear. Support for nuclear energy in Singapore increased from 14.7 per cent in 2023 to 20.3 per cent in 2024, which marked the highest approval rating in Southeast Asia. Nian said the conversation around nuclear energy was changing and increasingly focused on the conditions under which it could be made safe and viable for Singapore. “That does not mean public acceptance has been achieved, but the conversation is becoming more informed and pragmatic,” Nian said.

title: Trump eyes renaming Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ as Canada trade war deepens
description: Such a change would be reminiscent of Trump’s unilateral action last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
content: President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” as the trade war between the United States and Canada intensifies. Such a change would be reminiscent of the Republican president’s unilateral action last year by executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. The US and Canada are locked in a trade dispute, with Canada expected on Tuesday to announce retaliatory measures after the Trump administration enacted 50 per cent tariffs on US$20 billion of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down. “The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump said on Tuesday on social media. Ontario is Canada’s most populous province and is home to the country’s automobile industry. Canada and the US share one of the world’s largest trading relationships, with deeply integrated supply chains across autos, energy, agriculture and manufacturing, making a prolonged trade fight potentially costly for businesses and workers on both sides of the border. Prime Minister Mark Carney cast doubt on the US’ dependability, saying Canada was finding reliable partners “everywhere in the world, except in the United States. Except in the United States. And Russia”. On Monday, Trump came back with further tariffs, warning that he would impose them on Canada’s auto industry beginning next year. “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump said on social media, criticising what he called the country’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers. Carney said Washington’s auto-sector proposals would gradually have the effect of dismantling Canadian production. “This is the most successful automotive partnership in history,” Carney said, referring to the deeply integrated Canada-US industry. Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unleashed his own tirade. In an interview, he said Trump had underestimated Canadians’ willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to US pressure. “We’re all in,” Ford said. “Up here, we’re at a fever pitch; everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.” Trump responded in a social media post by attacking Ford personally, calling him “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford”, and once again referring to Canada’s prime minister as “Governor Carney”. Ford dismissed the insults: “If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I’m ready.” Ford said “everything is on the table” if the dispute worsens, including cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario. Critical minerals are increasingly important to US national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has sought more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China, which dominates the mining or processing of several strategically important minerals.

title: ‘Normal stability’: US-China Track 1.5 talks offer formula for ties
description: Senior party official Liu Haixing uses unofficial discussions to make the case for disagreements to remain ‘controllable’.
content: China and the US should strive for “normal stability with controllable disagreements” in their relations, a senior Chinese official has urged in the latest semi-official dialogue with Washington. During the talks on Tuesday, Liu Haixing, head of the Communist Party’s International Department, said the two countries should expand the “pie” of shared interests to achieve positive stability anchored in cooperation. “[Both sides] should reject zero-sum games to achieve healthy stability with well-managed competition, and seek common ground while bridging differences to achieve normal stability with controllable disagreements,” Liu said. He made the remarks at the third US-China Track 1.5 Dialogue, a mechanism established in 2023 to bridge official diplomacy and non-governmental exchanges between the two countries. The dialogue brought together roughly 40 Chinese and foreign representatives from local government, think tanks and universities, as well as members of the US strategic and business communities. The US delegation attending the two-day dialogue was led by John Thornton, co-chairman of the Asia Society think tank. The US group also included Kevin Rudd, Asia Society chief and former Australian prime minister; Sean Stein, president of the Washington-based US-China Business Council; and Craig Allen, a former US ambassador. The US delegation described bilateral ties as being “at a unique juncture” and highlighted the rapport between presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump as the “most vital and valuable component” of the relationship, according to the Chinese foreign ministry. “Both sides should deepen dialogue, foster political mutual trust and advance cooperation across trade, cultural exchanges, healthcare, artificial intelligence and food security, while properly managing differences and together addressing global challenges,” the US delegation was quoted as saying. Other members of the delegation included American businessman Craig Mundie, cancer prevention specialist Otis Brawley, Amy Celico, executive director of Tsinghua University’s Schwarzman Scholars programme, and American venture capitalist Gary Rieschel. The dialogue comes just weeks ahead of a trip to the US by Chinese President Xi Jinping, his first state visit to the country since 2015. Both sides are preparing for the summit in September, but Beijing has appeared to be frustrated with the Trump administration’s lack of planning and coordination, with little progress made on deliverables for the meeting. In talks with some of the US group on Monday, Wang Huning, China’s fourth-ranked official, said China stood ready to “enhance correct mutual perceptions and respect each other’s core interests”, according to the Chinese foreign ministry. Wang, chairman of the country’s top political advisory body, said the US and China would also strengthen cooperation across various sectors, “properly manage differences and build a constructive, strategically stable China-US relationship”. Chinese vice foreign minister Ma Zhaoxu also met some of the dialogue participants on Monday. Track 1.5 dialogues are a middle ground between official government-to-government talks and informal or academic exchanges. The first US-China Track 1.5 dialogue took place via video conference in 2023, followed by a second session in Beijing in 2024. At the 2024 meeting, some 30 Chinese and Americans from various governments, universities and think tanks agreed that the two sides should adhere to “peaceful coexistence and avoid conflict and confrontation”. That theme was echoed this year, when Trump travelled to Beijing for a summit in May. During those talks, Xi said the two leaders had “agreed on a new vision of building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability”, framing a new direction for bilateral relations. But frictions since then have tested that stability. On Monday, six months into its war with Iran, the US announced fresh sanctions on entities, individuals and vessels – including some tied to mainland China and Hong Kong – to try to raise the pressure on Tehran’s economy. Beijing criticised the move, calling for de-escalation and a return to dialogue, and vowing to “take all necessary measures” to safeguard its rights and interests. In July, Washington expanded its Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act entity list by targeting dozens of Chinese firms, while simultaneously banning imports and sales of new foreign robotics and power inverters – two industries dominated by China. Beijing retaliated by sanctioning seven US entities and tightening export controls on drones and related technology. Additional reporting by Orange Wang

title: China moves to close regulatory loopholes in overseas investment by wealthy individuals
description: Newly drafted rules would expand oversight of direct offshore investments, with more reporting requirements but limited changes for market-linked schemes.
content: As China is set to flesh out rules that would put individual investors on the same regulatory footing as companies when it comes to outbound investment, covering everything from purchases of overseas property to acquisitions of foreign companies, legal experts said the move will close grey areas long used by wealthy individuals to channel assets abroad. The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) on Friday released a draft revision of its measures governing outbound investment and invited the public to comment through September 20. The draft clarifies that the definition of investors extends beyond corporate entities to include domestic individuals and other organisations. Under the draft rules, “the main channels for individual portfolio investments remain secure, but grey-market workarounds will face a shrinking space to operate”, said Li Fan, a Hefei-based lawyer and partner at the Lantai Partners law firm. While companies making overseas investments have long been subject to requirements such as regulatory approval and filing, the lack of similar, specific rules for individual investors has left more room for them to move money offshore and invest through grey-area structures such as offshore shell companies. Li added that direct outbound investments by individuals, such as establishing companies or acquiring enterprises overseas, would no longer be conducted in a regulatory vacuum. The revision comes as overseas property purchases, direct investments in overseas businesses, and offshore holding platforms have remained popular asset-allocation choices for high-net-worth individuals in China. Over the past year, China has also stepped up its crackdown on illegal cross-border financial activity and tax evasion through the channelling of assets abroad. To circumvent regulatory oversight, many individuals have used so-called offshore nominee arrangements and multilayered structures, while existing rules mainly cover corporate investors and lack a clear basis for “looking through” such structures to the individual investor, said Cheng Xiaxia, head of the Chaoyang district branch of Beijing Guan Ling Law Firm. Under the new rules, individuals would remain subject to domestic compliance obligations even when investments are routed through offshore shell companies or nominee arrangements, Cheng said. The proposed rules would, however, leave established channels for individual overseas financial investment largely unchanged. Investments made through channels such as the Qualified Domestic Institutional Investor scheme and the mainland Chinese-Hong Kong Stock Connect mechanism would remain exempt from the draft’s approval, filing and reporting requirements, unless investors acquire control of a company or obtain equity or voting rights in increments of 10 per cent. Direct investments, including establishing companies overseas, acquiring stakes in foreign entities or investing in overseas real estate, would instead be subject to the relevant approval, filing or reporting requirements, Cheng said. He noted that details such as filing procedures for individual investors were still awaiting further implementation rules. For projects exceeding US$100 million, or those involving diplomatic relations, investors would need to file preliminary work reports 10 business days before starting major groundwork, according to the draft. Furthermore, offshore reinvestment via controlled subsidiaries would face mandatory reporting 20 business days before execution, with previous financial thresholds removed, it added. At the same time, the draft seeks to better protect Chinese investors overseas. If an investor faces discriminatory measures or unreasonable deprivation or restrictions by a foreign organisation or individual, the NDRC may, at the investor’s request, take measures under State Council regulations, including restricting or prohibiting the relevant foreign parties from investing or conducting certain transactions in China. The provision did not target any particular case, Li said, but its wording reflected growing concerns over forced divestment, restrictions on technology transfers and national-security reviews involving Chinese companies overseas, as seen in the case of Dutch chipmaker Nexperia and its parent company, Wingtech Technology. It could be particularly relevant to companies in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, biotechnology and other sensitive technologies, as well as data-heavy platforms and investors in energy, telecommunications and infrastructure, he said. On Tuesday, a draft anti-cross-border corruption law was submitted to the National People’s Congress, the country’s top legislature, for its first reading, as China steps up efforts to curb cross-border corruption and strengthen corporate compliance.

title: Disney Worldbuilders documentary captures ‘magic’ of turning films into theme park lands
description: New Disney+ film interviews masterminds behind Frozen and more to show how on-screen tales are adapted at Disneylands from Hong Kong to Paris.
content: A new documentary that delves into filmmakers and their associated theme park projects is streaming now on Disney+. Disney Worldbuilders uses interviews and file footage to go behind the scenes and into the childhoods of a set of storytellers. The 60-minute film, directed by Leslie Iwerks, starts with former Walt Disney CEO Bob Iger strolling up Main Street at the original Disneyland in California, and wraps up with Iger on the beach in Abu Dhabi, the site of the company’s next major park. There is a global emphasis in “Worldbuilders”, so it is a little light on Walt Disney World, though certain attractions such as Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge and Pirates of the Caribbean translate well across properties. Like many of the filmmakers, Pete Docter made childhood sojourns to Disneyland, and they were big influences. “To this day, I think Pirates [of the Caribbean] is the best ride,” he says. “I just remember feeling as though I had gone into a dream. It’s just such great storytelling. You go in, you fall asleep, you’ve experienced this whole thing and you come up and you wake up out of it and you’re just ‘What just happened?’ It’s magic.” Docter is now chief creative officer of Pixar Animation Studios and one of the forces behind Toy Story (1995), Monsters, Inc (2001) and Inside Out (2015). Monsters, Inc is getting the park treatment at Disney’s Hollywood Studios in Florida. In the documentary, Docter recalls conceptualising the door factory concept for the film. “It literally was like 30 seconds until we were like ‘That would make a great theme park attraction,’” he says. “And for one reason or another – whether the technology wasn’t there or the budget wasn’t quite right – it kept getting postponed. So it’s very exciting now that they’re finally building it.” Nostalgia and sentimentality are peppered through Worldbuilders, but it gets especially emotional as cameras follow Jennifer Lee, co-director of Frozen and Frozen 2, into the World of Frozen at Disneyland Paris for the first time. It opened in March, almost three years after the first edition landed in Hong Kong Disneyland in late 2023. Jared Bush, chief creative officer of Walt Disney Animation Studios, recalls his first reaction to the Zootopia land at Shanghai Disneyland. “I literally bawled my eyes out,” Bush tells Iger in the documentary. Bush was a writer on Moana (2016), which now has a presence in Epcot in Florida, and directed Encanto (2021), which is getting an attraction in the under-construction Tropical Americas section of Disney’s Animal Kingdom in Florida. “For me, seeing all those come to life is incredible and staggering and surreal,” Bush says. I love what the Imagineers do and what they build and how they build it Dave Filoni Lucasfilm president Dave Filoni says Disney’s acquisition of it immediately led to speculation about Star Wars in theme parks. “I think the difficult thing was narrowing it down to what you could actually do,” he says. Filoni and movie director Jon Favreau were asked to help update the Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run attraction. “I love what the Imagineers do and what they build and how they build it,” Filoni says. “It’s just this awesome process of creating this adventure. It’s such an impressive machine, the way that ride functions.” Filoni says when he is in the park, it is usually with Favreau. “We ride stuff together. We always come out of it excited, especially if we’re shooting,” Filoni says. “Because we see the love the people have. We’re like, ‘Alright, we need to get back to work now. We need to give them something great.’” A segment features Kevin Feige, president of Marvel Studios. Viewers will see run-throughs of an attraction for Avengers Campus. “This attraction will take people on a tour throughout the universe,” Feige says. “We are going to move from environment to environment, from screen to screen. “The Imagineers who mock this up in Glendale [California] sit you in a rolling chair and will push you around a version of the track, and you’ve got your 3D glasses, and you look at the screen, and what’s astounding is the point of view of the screen moves with you depending on where you’re looking. Even on my rolling chair in Glendale, it looked amazing,” he says. “I do believe we have only scratched the surface of what can be done with our characters and with our worlds in the parks,” Feige adds as the film images show Epcot’s Guardians of the Galaxy: Cosmic Rewind, Iron Man Experience at Hong Kong Disneyland and Marvel attractions at Disneyland Paris. (A new feature in Toy Story Land and a Marvel-themed expansion at Hong Kong Disneyland were announced at D23, a large Disney fan convention that took place in Anaheim, California, from August 14 to 16, 2026.) “There are so many details within a land,” Feige says. “My favourite detail in a land is a construction wall because a construction wall means more is coming … the adventure continues.”

title: Hong Kong’s Chinese Medicine Hospital to start 24-hour inpatient services in December
description: City’s first dedicated traditional Chinese medicine hospital will also launch 10 additional special disease programmes within this year.
content: The Chinese Medicine Hospital of Hong Kong will launch 24-hour inpatient services in December – a first for the city – and charge patients HK$980 (US$125) per day for subsidised care, more than three times the fee at public hospitals. The city’s first dedicated traditional Chinese medicine hospital will also launch 10 additional special disease programmes within this year to help treat conditions such as eczema and Parkinson’s disease. The hospital, which opened last December in Tseung Kwan O, aims to provide services for more complex cases under a model that features Chinese medicine as the primary approach, integrated with Western medicine. The expansion of services, announced on Tuesday, includes the provision of 24-hour inpatient care from December 11. The hospital will provide 93 inpatient beds – consisting of 60 government-subsidised and 33 non-subsidised ones – as well as 20 beds under its clinical trial and research centre and two high-dependency beds in the first phase. The number of beds is expected to reach 400 by the end of 2030. The subsidised inpatient option will cost HK$980 a day – a fixed, overall package price that covers all treatment-related services, such as room fee, visits by registered practitioners, Chinese medicine interventions, tests and medication. Public hospital inpatient charges in Hong Kong are HK$300 per day for acute general beds, and HK$200 per day for convalescent, rehabilitation, infirmary and psychiatric beds for eligible people. Dr Cheung Wai-lun, project director of the Health Bureau’s Chinese Medicine Hospital Project Office, defended the higher charges compared with public hospitals, describing the fees as affordable. “A sizeable Chinese medicine clinic typically charges HK$980 or more per outpatient consultation, which reflects the current market rate,” he said. “However, when comparing our inpatient model with their outpatient model, the service we provide is far more comprehensive in terms of frequency, scope and Chinese-Western medicine collaboration.” For the hospital’s non-subsidised inpatient services, daily room fees will range from HK$810 to HK$3,100, depending on the type of room. Visits by registered practitioners will cost HK$560 or more per visit. A non-subsidised inpatient package for special diseases will cost between HK$5,520 and HK$14,890 a day. Professor Bian Zhaoxiang, the hospital’s chief executive, said inpatient services would target patients with complex conditions requiring systematic diagnosis and treatment, in addition to unstable cases in need of 24-hour clinical monitoring. They would also cater to those who had temporarily lost self-care ability, and patients with severe symptoms and in need of intensive care, he said. Inpatients can be referred by the hospital’s outpatient services or by other medical institutions. The hospital will offer a medical fee waiver mechanism to support patients with financial difficulties. The hospital will also introduce 10 additional special disease programmes later this year. Five programmes, covering functional gastrointestinal diseases, sub-health conditioning, facial palsy care, menopausal syndrome and skin eczema, will be rolled out in September. Another five, for integrated cancer care, seasonal influenza, prostatic syndrome, Parkinson’s disease and paediatric developmental delay, will be launched in November. The hospital’s annual outpatient attendance is expected to increase from 140,000 in its first year to more than 260,000 in its second year of operation, while the number of day-patient beds will rise from 25 to 35. Tim Pang Hung-cheong, a patients’ rights advocate with the Society for Community Organisation, said the daily fee of HK$980 for subsidised inpatient care at the hospital was appealing, given that it was the first service of its kind in Hong Kong. He noted that patients facing financial difficulties could apply for fee waivers. But he urged the hospital to be more transparent about whether there would be a quota for fee waivers to address public concerns. He also suggested that prices should be adjusted later if the occupancy rate proved unsatisfactory. Lawmaker Chan Wing-kwong, a Chinese medicine practitioner, said the hospital’s inpatient care prices were reasonable, taking into account market rates, residents’ affordability and service costs. He added that the daily fee of HK$980 for subsidised care was comparable to outpatient charges at private clinics. He said it was inappropriate to compare charges at the Chinese Medicine Hospital with those at public hospitals. “The positioning, mission and operating model of the Chinese Medicine Hospital of Hong Kong differ from those of public hospitals – public hospitals receive substantial government subsidies, providing a healthcare safety net for residents, while the Chinese Medicine Hospital of Hong Kong operates under a public-private partnership model,” he said. He called on the hospital to ensure it had sufficient manpower as it expanded its services.

title: Hong Kong jewellery shop slapped with 30-day tour group ban over coerced sales
description: Kaiser Jewellery International barred from receiving any inbound tour group visitors from Wednesday until September 24.
content: Hong Kong’s tourism watchdog has suspended a jewellery shop from receiving tour groups for 30 days after finding it failed to stop a guide from coercing mainland Chinese visitors into making purchases. The Travel Industry Authority (TIA) said on Tuesday that Kaiser Jewellery International would be barred from receiving any inbound tour group visitors from Wednesday until September 24. “The authority adopts a zero-tolerance approach towards coerced shopping and any conduct that damages the reputation of Hong Kong’s tourism industry,” it said in a statement. A check by the South China Morning Post found two locations operated by the company under the TIA’s list of registered shops, including one on the first floor of Hankow Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui trading as “KJI Super Mall”, and another location at Harbourside HQ in Kowloon Bay. The Kowloon Bay branch has been marked as “registration suspended”, though the company has filed an appeal for review and a hearing has been scheduled, according to the authority. The disciplinary action stemmed from a case involving a tour group from the mainland in February. Following an investigation, the authority found the shop had failed to make sufficient efforts to stop the guide from pressuring visitors to shop. It had also failed to take reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorised individuals from promoting or marketing products to tourists on its premises, breaching undertakings made under an administrative scheme governing shops that receive inbound tour groups, it said. In addition to the suspension, the company’s directors, managers and all frontline staff were ordered to complete training courses designated by the authority within a month. The case comes amid continuing concerns over ultra-low-priced Hong Kong tour packages that rely on shopping commissions and paid add-on activities to generate revenue. An investigation by the SCMP earlier this year found one-day Hong Kong tours marketed on mainland online platforms for as little as 1 yuan (14 US cents). A reporter who joined one such tour found that guides repeatedly promoted optional activities and told participants the initial fee was insufficient to cover operating costs. Tourists were also taken to a Tsim Sha Tsui outlet selling health supplements, jewellery and souvenirs, where guides delivered lengthy product pitches and encouraged purchases. Some participants who bought nothing were reprimanded. Industry sources have said such packages cannot cover their costs without commissions from designated shopping stops and revenue from optional activities. The suspension also follows a string of enforcement actions by the authority against coercive shopping and illegal tour guides this year. In June, it revoked a guide’s licence after finding that he had made inappropriate remarks that subjected visitors to coercive shopping while receiving tour groups between February and April. Separately, the authority and the Immigration Department conducted a two-day joint operation in Tsim Sha Tsui and the West Kowloon Cultural District last month, during which two mainland women were arrested on suspicion of breaching their conditions of stay by working as unauthorised guides. In another joint operation at High Island Reservoir’s East Dam in May, a mainland man suspected of illegally leading a hiking group was arrested and subsequently jailed for six weeks. The authority reminded mainland visitors to verify that tour operators were legally qualified and that their Hong Kong itineraries would be handled by licensed local travel agencies. Travellers who encountered unfair treatment or coercive shopping should contact the authority or seek help from police, it added.

title: Exclusive | Jack Ma buys HK$600 million of Alibaba shares, signalling AI confidence: sources
description: Founder’s HK$600 million personal investment comes as Alibaba chairman and CEO also purchased shares after company’s first issuance since 2019.
content: Alibaba Group Holding founder Jack Ma has bought more than HK$600 million worth of the company’s Hong Kong-listed shares on consecutive days, according to people familiar with the matter, a show of confidence in the firm’s long-term prospects for artificial intelligence. The purchases showed Ma’s “strong confidence for Alibaba to realise its AI ambitions and capture the long-term growth opportunities ahead”, one source said. Meanwhile, Alibaba chairman Joe Tsai and CEO Eddie Wu Yongming spent a cumulative HK$202 million acquiring shares over the past two days, according to Hong Kong stock market filings. Tsai bought about HK$82 million in shares on Tuesday, following an HK$80 million purchase on Monday – the same day Wu chipped in roughly HK$40 million. The personal investments came after a new share issuance announced by the company on Sunday, one of the biggest fundraising efforts by a Chinese firm dedicated to AI development. Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. Alibaba shares gained 1.5 per cent to close at HK$114.20 in Hong Kong on Tuesday. The share purchases came as Alibaba continues to advance its AI initiatives. The Sunday share placement, the firm’s first since its 2019 listing in Hong Kong, would improve its “full-stack AI capabilities” and extend its “global AI leadership”, according to a company statement. The deal has drawn strong investor demand. Alibaba met its benchmark of HK$80 billion within hours, with total demand nearly three times oversubscribed, according to people familiar with the deal. The issuance attracted US$28 billion in demand, including US$6 billion from sovereign wealth funds and long-only investors, the people said, adding that anchor demand came from leading sovereign wealth funds across the Middle East, Europe and Asia. More than 40 per cent of the final allocation would go to sovereign wealth and long-only funds, they said. Ma co-founded Alibaba in 1999 with 17 partners. He relinquished his post as group CEO in 2013 and as Alibaba’s executive chairman in 2019. One of the reasons for his departure was to hand the reins to younger generations, he said in a letter to staff members in 2018. In 2023, Ma bought around US$50 million of company stock, the SCMP previously reported. In recent years, Alibaba has been working to pivot from an e-commerce powerhouse into a full-stack AI player with businesses spanning chips, computing infrastructure, large language models and AI applications. Last week, the company reported a 45 per cent year-on-year revenue jump in the June quarter in its cloud and AI operations. During an earnings call, Wu said the company expected its AI investments to break even within three years. It announced a three-year commitment of 380 billion yuan (US$56.54 billion) in AI infrastructure investment in early 2025. Alibaba said this month that its Qwen AI model family had surpassed 3 billion global downloads, while the company’s semiconductor unit, T-Head, also began commercial-scale deployment of its Zhenwu M890 AI processor. On Tuesday, Alibaba Cloud deepened the integration of its cloud infrastructure and consumer AI ecosystem, announcing that users would be allowed to link their “Token Plan” API keys directly to the Qwen app and PC interface. The update enables users to draw from a single token quota – supporting advanced models such as Qwen3.8-Max – to power workplace tools such as email, calendars and cloud storage, according to the company. Additional reporting by Ann Cao

title: US troops a liability for some Kuwaitis amid Iran fury: ‘we’re paying the price’
description: ‘Targeting locations where the Americans are stationed has created fear and anxiety among residents,’ a Kuwaiti national says.
content: Like many Kuwaitis, Ghanim Alsulaimani still vividly remembers Iraqi tanks rolling through his hometown when his small Gulf state faced extinction had US troops not liberated it from invasion. Now, decades later and six months into the US-Iran war, some are seeing those same American troops as more of a liability than an asset, as their presence has put Kuwait in Tehran’s line of fire. Since the Middle East conflict first erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, the Islamic Republic and its allies have hammered Kuwait with recurrent barrages. They have targeted civilian infrastructure, including water desalination plants and energy installations, along with bases hosting American troops. Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz has put Kuwait, which is locked into the waterway and relies on oil exports for revenue, in a difficult economic position. Yet Alsulaimani continues to stand by the United States, even as talks to end the war have stalled, weighing on Gulf economies. “The aim [of Iran] is to use Gulf states as a theatre to pressure the US side into halting its attacks,” Alsulaimani, a political analyst, said. “However, the reality is that the US president is unconcerned. He does not consider stopping or backing down simply because Kuwait is targeted,” he added. On his walls, portraits of Kuwait’s emir and crown prince hang alongside a plaque reading: “There is no place like the homeland, and no homeland like Kuwait.” In private, many Kuwaitis are more scathing in their criticism. Freedom of expression is limited in Kuwait, including open criticism of diplomatic partners. According to Human Rights Watch, “several penal code provisions, as well as the cybercrime law, criminalise speech deemed insulting to religion, the emir or foreign leaders”. In a country where pro-American sentiment has long been a given, some are voicing once unthinkable positions: questioning the presence of foreign troops and US President Donald Trump’s decision to continue the war. “Of course we are paying the price for the presence of US forces,” said a Kuwaiti woman who declined to give her name. But she was reluctant to consider an alternative. “Just imagine if the American forces weren’t in Kuwait,” she said, while buying strawberry pastries for her children at Dunkin’, the US doughnut franchise that remains popular across the Gulf. Although Gulf states are strengthening regional alliances, with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signing a military pact, analysts agree that Kuwait, like many in the region, cannot afford to drop the US as Iran grows emboldened. Positive sentiment towards the US had already taken a hit across the region due to Washington’s support for Israel’s deadly bombing campaign of Gaza after Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attacks. Boycott campaigns of companies seen as supporting illegal Israeli settlements or the Israeli government, including many American firms like Starbucks and McDonald’s, had become popular in Kuwait and elsewhere in the Middle East. After the US-led coalition liberated Kuwait in 1991, American troops dug in. Kuwait hosts one of the region’s largest concentrations of American troops, with US forces active in airfields, bases and training grounds. Their large presence has proven to be an enticing target for Iran. Iranian attacks on Kuwait have killed at least 15 people, including six US troops, four Kuwaiti soldiers and five foreign residents. The situation puts Kuwait in a delicate balancing act. “Kuwait recognises America’s key role in liberating it from Saddam Hussein, but it also recognises that it is now coming under Iranian attack because it hosts American forces,” a senior foreign diplomat based in Kuwait said. “The dilemma is that it faces challenges because of its geographical position and regional power dynamics, making it difficult to find alternatives to the United States.” In restaurants, cafes and public spaces, conversations about the war dominate. Televisions broadcast non-stop coverage of Middle East developments, while breaking news alerts about Iran command attention amid concern the conflict could spiral out of control. A US government spokesman said that security cooperation with Kuwait remains robust. But for Nasser Al-Shammari, a 50-year-old Kuwaiti national, that relationship is now a source of unease. “What Kuwait has recently witnessed was difficult, given the presence of US forces,” he said. “Targeting locations where the Americans are stationed has created fear and anxiety among residents.”

title: Can Anwar’s call for ‘freer’ filmmaking help ease Malaysia’s censorship rules?
description: The prime minister’s remarks come after Malaysia’s top court upheld a ban on the independent film ‘Mentega Terbang’ last month.
content: Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has urged the country’s filmmakers to think more freely, even as recent censorship battles show how tightly the state still controls what can reach the screen. Anwar said an industry forced to repeatedly seek official approval for individual scenes could not become more creative or competitive, calling for fewer restrictions on filmmakers at a time when Malaysian productions were outperforming Hollywood titles at home. But his remarks came less than six weeks after Malaysia’s Court of Appeal upheld the government’s ban on the independent film Mentega Terbang, and nearly three years after Cannes-winning Tiger Stripes reached local cinemas only after cuts its director disowned. The government is also preparing a national film policy through 2035, raising the question of whether Anwar’s call for creative freedom can translate into looser rules or remain bounded by Malaysia’s long-standing sensitivities around religion, culture and morality. “Where is creativity if there are too many constraints and restrictions?” Anwar said on Monday at the opening of the National Film Development Corporation Malaysia (Finas), outside Kuala Lumpur. He said filmmakers should not feel “too pressured and constrained” to the point of having to ask “five times” whether a scene would be approved. Anwar nonetheless kept limits around that freedom, arguing that Malaysia did not need to follow a Western model and that its cinema should remain grounded in “culture, values and morality”. “I don’t want to portray myself as too liberal because I’ll be attacked by the ultra-conservatives,” he said. “But if we want this country to progress, we must accept that young people and audiences want a freer and more open environment.” Under the Film Censorship Act 2002, films intended for public exhibition are submitted to the Film Censorship Board, which can approve them, demand alterations or refuse approval. The home minister can also prohibit a film considered contrary to the public interest. That power was upheld by the Court of Appeal in July in a challenge by the makers of Mentega Terbang, about a Muslim teenager exploring other religions. The Home Ministry banned the film in 2023. Director Khairi Anwar Jailani and producer Tan Meng Kheng were later charged with deliberately wounding religious feelings and pleaded not guilty. Meanwhile, Amanda Nell Eu’s Tiger Stripes won the Critics’ Week Grand Prize at Cannes in 2023 but reached Malaysian cinemas only after cuts. Eu disowned the local version, saying the edits removed “the very essence” of the film. Benjamin YH Loh, a lecturer at Monash University Malaysia, said Anwar’s remarks did not amount to a shift in the government’s approach to regulating creative content. “Right now Anwar is pandering more towards conservative and traditional values, so there has not been any clear shift in policy that would suggest his government would be more open on creative media content regulation,” he told This Week in Asia. “The call to be more open but still remain sensitive to conservative Eastern values shows that his administration has not changed its stance at all.” Cut and thrust Filmmaker Andy Darrel Gomes, who is also a lecturer at Malaysia’s Sunway University, said censorship affected how directors translated their ideas to the screen. “All films are political, reflecting a world view that advocates or protests [against] causes based on the filmmaker’s own moral compass,” Gomes told This Week in Asia. “However, how the filmmaker chooses to put this across in their craft is what’s affected by censorship.” He said filmmakers targeting cinemas or television faced censorship more directly than those aiming for festivals or online releases. Many directors, he added, understood that “it’s not their job to censor themselves, so they leave that to the censorship board”. The Film Censorship Act excludes material transmitted over the internet or intranets from censorship under the legislation. Finas said local films recorded 7.55 million admissions from January to July, compared with 6.94 million for Hollywood releases. Five Malaysian titles grossed more than 10 million ringgit (US$2.47 million) each, led by Tarung: Unforgiven at 23.59 million ringgit. “Finas sees this positive development driven by a significant improvement in the quality of scripts, acting, and the overall process of local film production compared to before,” the agency said. Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil said on Monday that films under Malaysia’s Compulsory Screening Scheme grossed 253.31 million ringgit in 2025, more than double the 125.28 million ringgit recorded in 2024. Finas chief executive Azmir Saifuddin Mutalib said the National Film Policy 2026-2035, in its final stages after two years of consultation, would focus on alternative financing, market access and new technology. “Insya-Allah, we will launch this National Film Policy within the year,” he told reporters on Monday. Across the border, Singapore’s media regulator says it has “moved away from censorship to classification”, using six ratings from G to R21. Freedom Film Network welcomed Anwar’s renewed commitment to artistic freedom but said similar promises had failed to produce meaningful changes for filmmakers. “Promises without political will or actual policy reform do not reflect the reality experienced by local creators,” the group told This Week in Asia, adding that filmmakers had seen “no meaningful improvement on the ground” since Anwar made a similar commitment in 2024. The group has called for the Film Censorship Board to be moved out of the Home Ministry and for mandatory prior censorship to be replaced by an age-classification system.

title: DeepSeek leads surge in low-cost Chinese open-weight models on US platform
description: Open models reached a record share of 62 per cent on a US web development platform on Saturday, a reversal of figures in June.
content: The usage of open-weight AI models from China hit a record high on a popular US web development platform, driven largely by DeepSeek’s latest lightweight model, as business demand for Anthropic’s cutting-edge Fable 5 stalls due to high costs. Open-weight models accounted for 54 per cent of token volume on Vercel’s AI Gateway on Tuesday, surpassing the 46 per cent consumed by proprietary models, according to data on its website. Open models reached a record share of 62 per cent on the platform on Saturday, dwarfing closed systems’ 38 per cent, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said on social media. This was in stark contrast to the breakdown on June 24, when open-weight models accounted for only 28 per cent of Vercel AI Gateway’s token volume, compared with 72 per cent for closed ones, according to Rauch. As of Tuesday, DeepSeek-V4-Flash was the most-used model in terms of token volume, while Chinese models dominated the top five, including Step 3.7 Flash from StepFun, GLM-5.2 from Zhipu, or Z.ai, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s updated 0731 version, which ranked second, fourth and fifth, respectively. The third spot was taken by OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Luna, Vercel data showed. The figures indicate that developers are increasingly choosing cheaper and open models for production workloads, particularly for autonomous agents that can consume large numbers of tokens for reasoning, writing code and calling software tools. “Nowadays, open-source models are more widely used than closed models,” Tomasz Godziek, head of equities at Swiss bank J. Safra Sarasin, said in a media briefing in Hong Kong on Monday. “This is an important driver of the democratisation of AI.” Godziek cited recent remarks by CloudFlare chief executive Matthew Prince that automated agents and bots now generated more than half of web requests for the first time. The proliferation of open-source AI models was a “very good enabler” of this trend, Godziek said. However, their customizability has also raised security concerns. Taiwanese cybersecurity firm TeamT5 said hacking groups linked to Beijing were using models including DeepSeek to automate routine tasks and help develop malware, Bloomberg reported on Monday. Vercel’s data reflects activity on its own platform rather than the broader AI market. However, separate corporate spending data points to growing resistance to the prices charged for the most advanced proprietary models. Anthropic’s Fable 5 represented only 6 per cent of tokens that businesses purchased from the firm in the month after its release, according to an August report from US expense management company Ramp. Despite being Anthropic’s most expensive model, it generated only 11.4 per cent of spending on the company’s models. By comparison, OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol accounted for 25 per cent of OpenAI tokens and 23 per cent of spending. Fable 5 generated about three-quarters as much model-attributed spending as GPT-5.6 Sol. Ramp said the results suggested businesses had found an upper limit to what they would pay for additional AI performance, particularly as open-weight alternatives narrowed the capability gap. The shift has coincided with increased US investment in domestic open-weight models capable of competing with Chinese offerings. Nvidia planned to use a US$6 billion licensing agreement with coding AI start-up Poolside to build a powerful open-weight model that could challenge DeepSeek and Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, the Wall Street Journal reported over the weekend, citing people familiar with the matter. The chip giant would separately invest US$1 billion in Poolside and hire more than 100 of its employees to work on Nvidia’s Nemotron open-model project, according to the report. The deal is not a conventional acquisition, as Poolside’s founders will remain with the company. Nvidia’s push highlights an emerging divide in the AI market: proprietary frontier models continue to capture substantial spending, but lower-cost open-weight systems are taking a growing share of the workloads that developers actually run.

title: Why was Enes Kanter Freedom ejected from a WNBA game? The controversy over trans athletes, explained
description: The former New York Knicks player joined a rally in support of the Indiana Fever’s Sophie Cunningham, before clashing courtside with Natasha Cloud of the Chicago Sky.
content: Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from the WNBA game between the Chicago Sky and Indiana Fever held at the Wintrust Arena in Chicago on Sunday. He was sitting courtside wearing a black T-shirt that read “Woman: noun, adult human female” across the chest. Late in the third quarter, Sky guard Natasha Cloud scored and confronted Freedom during a timeout. He stood up with his arms outstretched and stepped onto the court before security and players intervened. Freedom was then escorted from the arena, displaying his shirt as he walked towards the lobby. “I just got kicked out of a WNBA game for supporting women! Let that sink in, America!” he said in a statement shared on X and Instagram. Cloud responded on Threads, saying: “To every trans kid/person, you are a part of my community and tribe. You belong. You’re loved. You’re seen. You’re perfect as you are and you will always be protected by me.” Cloud evidently interpreted Freedom’s shirt as a statement against transgender women joining the WNBA. The debate surrounding the subject was first sparked when Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham – who also played on Sunday – spoke against the possibility of transgender women joining the WNBA, saying in an ESPN profile in July that she wanted to protect “young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men”. Freedom also took part in a small rally in support of Cunningham held before Sunday’s game. So, how is Enes Kanter Freedom connected to the recent WNBA controversy? Here is what we know. He declared himself ‘eligible’ for WNBA draft Sunday’s incident came after Freedom and fellow former NBA player Royce White declared themselves eligible for the 2027 WNBA draft in recent weeks, claiming they identified as women. The Associated Press reported on Tuesday that the two men are not deemed eligible for the draft, citing a source familiar with the decision. A source also told USA Today that the declarations were “publicity stunts” and that the league would not “give oxygen to efforts designed to mock the league or use this topic to demean or marginalise others”. The WNBA’s collective bargaining agreement states that “only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA”. There has never been a transgender woman player in the league. What is Enes Kanter Freedom’s background? Born Enes Kanter on May 20, 1992, in Zurich, Switzerland, the 34-year-old is of Turkish descent and grew up in Turkey before moving to the US at 17. Selected as the third overall pick in the 2011 NBA Draft by the Utah Jazz, he went on to play 11 seasons in the league for teams including the Oklahoma City Thunder, New York Knicks, Portland Trail Blazers and Boston Celtics. He played his final NBA game on February 8, 2022. As a teenager growing up in Turkey, Freedom was surrounded by anti-American sentiment. He recounts in his 2025 memoir, In the Name of Freedom, how friends once urged him to burn an American flag. “I threw down the flag and the lighter and ran away, with the taunts of my friends ringing in my ears,” he writes. In a 2023 op-ed for The Atlantic, Freedom claimed the Turkish government put a US$500,000 bounty on his head, imprisoned his father and got his brother fired from his basketball team. “I talk about the human rights violations and political prisoners, and that led them to put a bounty on my head and put my innocent father in jail, you know?” he told NewsNation in 2024. In 2021, the athlete legally changed his surname to Freedom upon receiving US citizenship. Who is Enes Kanter Freedom dating? Freedom was dating Australian influencer Emily Sears in 2021, with the couple going Instagram-official on her account, but the current status of their relationship is unclear. Before that, Freedom was reportedly involved with WWE wrestler Dana Brooke in 2019.

title: Why China’s sporting machine fails to turn individual Olympic gold into team success
description: Why has a country that shines in the Olympics struggled so badly on the football pitch and basketball court? Two experts think they know.
content: When it comes to individual success, China can appear to be an unstoppable sporting machine at times, from dominating table tennis, to training divers to enter the water without a splash and weightlifters to shatter world records. But translate that same state-led sports model onto a football pitch, basketball court, and latterly volleyball court, and the system stumbles. In a year when China’s men again watched on as others played in an expanded Fifa World Cup, an economist and a sports executive argue its failures in team sport stem from a structural mismatch: a system built to capitalise on measurable physical traits cannot work with the high cost of identifying talent for teams, low rate of community involvement and rigid training routines. This is evident when you look at football and table tennis. China’s last appearance at a men’s World Cup was in 2002, where they lost all three matches in the group stage and failed to score, and their best result at the AFC Asian Cup was runner-up. Table tennis star Sun Yingsha, on the other hand, has been the women’s world No 1 since 2022 and won multiple Olympic gold medals. Zhu Tian, professor of economics and vice-president at the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS), told the South China Morning Post that in his view, the primary reason for the divide lies in the cost of identifying athletic talent, rather than a simple distinction between individual and team events. According to Zhu, in individual sports such as weightlifting, swimming, or diving, performance depends on measurable physical traits, such as strength, speed and flexibility, that can be identified early. “This allows the state system to select top prospects from relatively small talent pools and concentrate resources effectively,” he said. Conversely, it is more difficult to identify talent through competitive team sports. “Whether a 10-year-old can eventually become a professional footballer cannot be determined through speed tests, strength measurements or technical drills,” Zhu said, noting that crucial attributes such as decision-making under pressure, positioning and tactical awareness “can only be identified, filtered and developed through repeated competitive matches”. This means that population size alone does not give China a competitive advantage; instead, for example, in football, player density is critical. While China had roughly 710,000 registered football players in 2006, a figure that grew to over one million by 2025, registered players represented just 0.054 per cent of the population, compared to 7.7 per cent in Germany and 0.82 per cent in Japan. According to Zhu, low density creates a situation where too few committed players exist locally to support multiple competitive teams, high-quality matches, or scouting networks. “Training intensity cannot substitute for participation density,” he said, adding that skills in team sports emerge from competing against other talented players. While basketball offers more obvious individual metrics, such as points, rebounds and assists, which lowers its measurement costs compared to football, Zhu noted that basketball faces a similar problem where talent pools shrink rapidly as youth drop out after age 12. This economic reality is compounded by practical training habits on the ground. Greg Stolt, senior vice-president at the Asian University Basketball League (AUBL), believes Chinese sports programmes have historically attempted to develop team athletes using rigid, individual-sport frameworks. While individual events such as swimming and diving focus on perfecting form in controlled environments without interference, team sports are constantly evolving and dynamic. “I have seen basketball training in the past that was similar to what they would do in diving or gymnastics,” Stolt added, stressing that preparing for diverse international opponents requires flexible preparation rather than a “one-size-fits-all” repetitive approach. “You do need to work on specific skills that require repetition. But how do you prepare for Slovenia, then Germany, then the US and Canada?” he said. “But again, I think that all depends on the training and experience of the coaches and players,” Stolt added. While China’s women’s teams, particularly in football, basketball and volleyball, have long been viewed publicly as successful exceptions to the country’s struggles, Zhu said their historic triumphs did not contradict this structural logic. Rather, past success occurred when global participation, commercialisation and resource allocation in women’s sports were relatively low, allowing China’s centralised system to yield a significant relative advantage. “As Europe and other Asian countries have significantly increased investment over the past decade, China has slipped from Asia’s dominant force to fourth in the region,” Zhu said, adding that at the grass-roots level, the primary barrier to increasing player density remains the steep opportunity cost faced by Chinese families. Entering a professional sports academy usually requires leaving mainstream education, while also leaving parents to worry about their child’s future if a professional career fails to materialise. The professor noted that unlike Japan and South Korea, which integrated school competitions, community clubs and university pathways to allow youth to play without abandoning education, China maintains a rigid separation between sport and academics. “What China needs to solve is this institutional exit risk,” Zhu said, pointing out that school football in China currently offers too few high-quality matches to develop elite talent. Consequently, he thinks administrative top-down measures, such as naturalising foreign-born players, hiring elite national coaches, or designating specialist sports schools, only address the top of the pyramid without fixing the supply of talent at the bottom. “The national team is the apex of the ecosystem, not its foundation,” Zhu said, adding that sustainable progress means making it cheaper for children to play sport, establishing stable multi-tier regional youth leagues and building seamless connections between education and sports. “There is no short cut to the World Cup,” he said. While his analysis centres heavily on football as the most acute case, Zhu noted that the underlying framework explains the structural challenges facing team sports more broadly. “Only by creating an ecosystem in which more children play meaningful football matches, compete regularly, develop over time and retain viable educational opportunities if professional careers do not materialise, can China gradually build the foundations of a genuine football nation,” Zhu said.

title: China’s J-16s face off against Egypt’s Rafales in combat drills as Iran war rumbles on
description: PLA pilots test strategic reach in 6,000km mission as Middle East conflict pushes Cairo and Beijing closer.
content: Chinese fighter jets have conducted combat training with their Egyptian counterparts in a joint exercise following a major Chinese air force deployment to the Middle East. The drill, which was launched on Saturday and is expected to continue until early next month, is part of the second China-Egypt “Eagles of Civilisation” joint air force training exercises, taking place against the backdrop of the war between the United States and Iran. The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force deployed J-16 fighter jets, YU-20 aerial tankers, KJ-500 airborne early warning and control aircraft and Z-20 helicopters. The aircraft flew more than 6,000km (3,730 miles) over nine hours to reach Egypt, crossing four countries, according to a report by state broadcaster CCTV. However, it did not specify which four countries the PLA Air Force aircraft flew over, or whether their route approached Iran or any Persian Gulf nations. “Through cross-border deployment and rapid loading and unloading operations, the exercise tested the air force’s capabilities in long-range force projection, rapid deployment and integrated operations,” CCTV reported. During the flight, the J-16s conducted aerial refuelling from YU-20 tankers before landing at an airbase in Egypt on August 21, the report said. The PLA Air Force then unloaded supplies, sorted equipment and coordinated briefings ready for training missions within a single day, according to the report. “The joint exercises have provided a valuable platform for us pilots to improve our combat capabilities,” Ning Yiming, a pilot taking part in the drill, was quoted as saying. The exercise comes as tensions in the Middle East remain high amid the US-Iran war. Egypt has maintained a cautious position of neutrality in the conflict. Last week, its top diplomat held talks with the Iranian foreign minister about reviving negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Meanwhile, China has also called for peace talks, with President Xi Jinping on Monday urging a sustained ceasefire during a meeting with visiting King Abdullah II of Jordan. On the first day of training, the Chinese J-16 fighters conducted one-on-one and two-on-two close- and medium-range air combat drills against French-made Rafale fighters operated by the Egyptian Air Force, according to CCTV. It was the J-16’s first deployment outside Asia and its first reported engagement against a mainstream Western-made fighter such as the Rafale. The heavyweight twin-engine J-16 is China’s top-tier fighter, domestically developed and based on the Russian Su-27 jet. Although it lacks stealth features, defence experts regard it as one of the most capable fourth-generation fighters in the world. Both sides have upgraded their participating fighters since last year’s exercise. In the first Eagles of Civilisation, held in 2025, the fighter component consisted of Chinese J-10Cs and Egyptian MiG-29s. With growing defence engagement and arms sales over the past two years, China has noticeably expanded military ties with Egypt, which is also an important US ally in the Middle East. The inaugural Eagles of Civilisation exercise last year marked the PLA Air Force’s first deployment to Africa with a full combat and support package. The Chinese contingent included J-10C fighter jets, Y-20 strategic transport aircraft, KJ-500s and YU-20s. After completing 18 training subjects with their Egyptian hosts, the PLA Air Force conducted a ceremonial fly-past over the pyramids in a formation comprising J-10s and a Y-20. Also in 2025, reports indicated that Egypt had acquired and deployed Chinese-made HQ-9BE air-defence systems and ordered 10 of the WJ-700 drones. Speculation regarding Egyptian interest in the J-10CE fighter has surfaced repeatedly, although Beijing has previously dismissed rumours of a completed deal.

title: Chinese food vendor goes viral after donating US$15 to customer undergoing chemotherapy
description: Father praises stranger’s compassion for bringing warmth to their darkest days.
content: A street food vendor in central China received widespread acclaim after discreetly slipping 100 yuan (US$15) into a takeaway order for a family whose child was undergoing chemotherapy. On August 17, Wang Xianhuang, an egg pancake vendor in Hefei, Anhui province, noticed a heartfelt note attached to a food delivery order that read, “For a child undergoing chemotherapy. Please do not include shredded kelp or lettuce. Make half of it non-spicy.” The message resonated with Wang, prompting him to reflect on the challenges the child and family were facing. After preparing the pancake, Wang added two complimentary cups of soy milk and tucked 100 yuan in cash inside the package. The child’s father, surnamed Zhu, was profoundly moved and subsequently shared the story online. His four-year-old son, Haolin, had been diagnosed with leukaemia in February and was currently undergoing treatment. Zhu wrote in his post: “A stranger showed compassion for a sick child. There is always warmth in this world that can brighten even the darkest days.” For Wang, the donation was significant. The 100 yuan represented about four days’ worth of profit from his modest business. The 33-year-old vendor carries over 200,000 yuan (US$30,000) in entrepreneurial debt and has faced numerous setbacks over the years. At his lowest point, he slept in internet cafes and relied on sink taps for drinking water. After the story went viral, customers from all over China began to flock to his stall, transforming the once-quiet stand into a local hotspot with long queues forming. Both delivery orders and in-person sales reportedly doubled, while some customers who could not visit in person ordered food online to be donated to sanitation workers and delivery riders. On August 22, Wang visited Haolin in hospital, where the child endearingly referred to him as “Uncle Egg Pancake.” Wang donated all of his recent stall earnings, along with a media award, totalling 8,100 yuan (US$1,200), to the family. Recalling the first time he saw photos of Haolin in hospital, with medical tubes attached, Wang expressed profound sadness. “I hope every child in the world can grow up healthy and free from illness,” he remarked. Haolin’s condition is now stable, according to his father, although he will require continued treatment for another 18 months. Shu Zhizhong, founder of the egg pancake brand under which Wang operates, also donated 2,000 yuan to the boy’s family. Shu stated that the brand would grant Wang a cash reward and initiate a free meal programme for outdoor workers. “This is the kind of story that brings me joy online,” one commenter shared. “A small act of kindness can be magnified through the internet, spreading warmth far beyond the initial gesture.”

title: Asia’s super-rich are ‘going all in’ on sustainability as impact investing grows: survey
description: Asian family offices putting more funds into sustainability projects – and adopting ‘systems-level’ approach to make greater impact, survey finds.
content: Family offices in the Asia-Pacific region are putting more funding into sustainability projects and adopting a “systems-level” approach to make a greater impact, a trend that is set to boost Hong Kong’s role as a hub for impact investing, according to a survey released on Tuesday. The proportion of family offices allocating more than half of their portfolios to impact and environmental, social and governance (ESG) strategies climbed to 27 per cent this year, a significant jump from 17 per cent in 2025, the Sustainable Finance Initiative (SFi) found. Allocations of more than 10 per cent to sustainable investments have also grown, rising from 56 per cent last year to 58 per cent in 2026. “Family offices aren’t just committing to impact – they’re polarising around it,” said Katy Yung, CEO of SFi, at a briefing in Hong Kong. “Those who are in, are going all in, whilst a new wave of impact investors are still testing the waters. What’s disappearing is the middle ground.” The annual survey, which polled 121 family office representatives and asset owners, highlights a sharp rise in conviction among impact investors.
