More than half of respondents now view impact through a holistic lens rather than as a stand-alone carve-out. Consequently, reliance on simple portfolio carve-outs dropped to 13 per cent from 18 per cent in 2025. Hong Kong, as an international financial centre, is home to hundreds of family offices. “It’s a very timely moment for Hong Kong as the government has just collected a lot of the submissions for its first five-year plan, which to us provides a clear policy backdrop and opportunity for us to also provide some suggestions on how we can position Hong Kong as a leading impact investing hub,” Yung said. According to the survey, heightened geopolitical risks are affecting the investment priorities of Asia’s family offices. Food and agriculture climbed to the top spot, while WASH (water, sanitation and hygiene) and oceans jumped to second place from fifth last year. In contrast, healthcare slipped to fourth place from third, while nature-based solutions plummeted to seventh place from top position in 2025. Investors also expressed growing interest in evergreen structures offering shorter lock-up periods and greater liquidity during market volatility, alongside philanthropic tools such as grant-making, blended finance and outcome-based funding in new economy sectors, according to the survey. Identifying quality deals with viable exit options remains the top-cited business challenge at 26 per cent, up from 21 per cent in 2025. Additionally, the difficulty in finding like-minded co-investment peers has jumped sharply to 18 per cent, compared with 11 per cent in 2025. The preference for specific private equity or venture capital vehicles has cooled, dropping to 19 per cent from 25 per cent in 2025. The survey also identified two new obstacles this year, as 19 per cent of respondents said they were struggling to find suitable sustainable investment products, while 11 per cent pointed to a lack of standardised reporting from fund managers and ventures. Family offices were cautious about “chasing trends” and taking their time in evaluating the return on these sustainable problem-related solutions, Yung added.

title: Customers facing steeper electricity bills as Hong Kong firms raise fuel charges
description: CLP Power and HK Electric announce higher fuel-related charges, while offering rebates and subsidies to ease the burden on households.
content: Customers will face higher electricity bills next month as Hong Kong’s two power suppliers will raise fuel-related charges, with the firms blaming geopolitical tensions and volatility in international energy markets. As electricity costs rise, CLP Power and HK Electric have introduced rebate and relief schemes as grass-roots households face higher air-conditioning costs after a summer with an unusually high number of very hot days. HK Electric, which supplies electricity mainly to Hong Kong Island and Lamma Island, said on Tuesday that its fuel clause charge would rise to 60.7 HK cents (7.74 US cents) per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in September. The charge will increase by 3.4 cents, or 5.9 per cent, from August, marking the fourth consecutive monthly increase since May. The fuel clause charge has jumped 1.3 times from 26 cents per kWh in May. Together with the basic tariff, the average net tariff will rise to 188.6 cents per unit in September, an increase of 1.8 per cent from August. “International energy prices remain volatile, with spot prices for liquefied natural gas having more than doubled compared with levels before the geopolitical developments earlier this year and still rising,” HK Electric said. “As fuel costs are progressively reflected through the [fuel clause charge] mechanism, the [fuel clause charge] is expected to remain at a relatively high level in the coming months.” CLP Power, which supplies customers in Kowloon, the New Territories, Lantau and other outlying islands, said its fuel cost adjustment would rise to 45.1 cents per unit in September, up 0.1 cent from August. The company said the increase – the sixth consecutive monthly rise since March – reflected changes in actual fuel costs over the previous three months. Its fuel cost adjustment has risen by 15.1 per cent from 39.2 cents per unit of electricity in March. The increases come as Hong Kong experiences a summer with an unusually high number of very hot days, placing an additional financial burden on low-income residents who may find it increasingly difficult to afford air conditioning. Data from the Hong Kong Observatory showed that the city recorded 19 very hot days, defined as days on which the maximum temperature reached at least 33 degrees Celsius (91.4 Fahrenheit), between May and July this year. To ease the impact of higher electricity costs on households, HK Electric said it would provide a special subsidy of eight cents per unit to residential customers whose monthly consumption does not exceed 450 units from August to October. For a household consuming 450 units a month, the monthly electricity bill would rise by HK$15.30 from August after taking the basic tariff and special subsidy into account, the company said. HK Electric also said it had launched a programme providing heat-relief activities, electricity-safety talks and circulating fans to eligible low-income households and elderly residents to help reduce their energy bills. For a household consuming 450 units a month under CLP, the electricity bill will rise by 45 cents per month from August to September, according to calculations by the South China Morning Post. CLP Power has also introduced a three-month special fuel rebate. From August to October 2026, residential customers consuming no more than 900 units per bill will receive a rebate of eight cents per unit. About half of the company’s residential customers are expected to qualify. After the rebate, eligible residential customers would pay a fuel cost adjustment of 37.1 cents per unit in September, lower than the January 2026 level, CLP Power said. Based on an average monthly consumption of 450 units, eligible households would receive more than HK$100 in total rebates over the three-month period, providing timely relief for families, the company added.

title: Singaporean who filmed couple on rooftop and demanded sex, cash gets jail
description: Mohammad Sharulnaim Miswan also targeted another couple having sex in a car and took a photo of them before confronting the pair.
content: A man who hid behind some plants to film a couple having extramarital sex at a rooftop garden in Singapore later used the video to threaten the woman while asking for sex and cash. When the police began investigating, the offender asked the woman to drop the case, even approaching her sister at a supermarket. Despite this ongoing investigation, the man targeted another couple having sex in a parked car and took a photograph of them before confronting them. On Tuesday, Mohammad Sharulnaim Miswan, a 33-year-old Singaporean, was sentenced to two years and 10 months’ jail, along with three strokes of the cane. He pleaded guilty to three charges which include putting a person in fear of harm to commit extortion, obstructing justice and wrongful confinement. Another two charges were taken into consideration. In sentencing, the judge told Sharulnaim that his actions had been most hurtful to his wife, who wept in court with a newborn baby in her arms. Addresses and names of the victims were redacted from court documents due to gag orders protecting their identities. At about 1am on January 15, 2024, Sharulnaim walked past a 35-year-old woman and a 39-year-old man at the rooftop garden of a multi-storey car park. Suspecting they might engage in sexual acts as the man was touching the woman, Sharulnaim hid behind some plants to catch them in the act. He took five videos of the pair having sex, capturing their faces in some of the clips and moving to another spot at one point for a better view. Months later on May 6, 2024, the woman took her son to a clinic and was waiting to see the doctor when she was approached by Sharulnaim. He introduced himself and asked if she was married and whether the boy with her was her son. The woman’s turn at the clinic was next and she took her son to see the doctor. While the woman was waiting to collect medication, Sharulnaim approached her again. He said he had a video of her having sex on the rooftop and showed her a screenshot, getting her to agree to meet him in his car to discuss it. In his vehicle, Sharulnaim told the woman that he wanted to post the video online. She pleaded with him not to do it, saying her son had special needs. Sharulnaim dropped the woman and her son off, exchanged numbers and continued to communicate with her on how to settle the issue. He said he intended to report the video to the police or make it go viral. The woman offered him S$300 (US$236) but he said it was “too low”. Sharulnaim told her that if she was charged with an offence relating to the video, she faced months in jail and a fine of up to S$5,000. He then sought S$2,000 and later S$1,500, but the woman could not afford either sum. Sharulnaim then asked for S$1,000 and for the woman to have sex with him. He said he could pick her up and they could have sex at a car park, after which he would delete the video. The woman refused the sex request and agreed to pay him S$1,300 by the following day. However, on the advice of the man in the sex video, she lodged a police report. Unaware of this development, Sharulnaim sent the woman a photograph of a police station, saying he was going to lodge a report. When the woman did not reply, Sharulnaim called the man in the sex video and repeated the threat. The man felt threatened and said he would pay S$1,000 as the woman had only S$300. He pleaded with Sharulnaim to leave her alone because she had a young son and mother to take care of. No payment was ultimately made and the police arrested Sharulnaim. While his statement was being recorded, he learnt that he was being investigated for putting a person in fear of harm to commit extortion. Months after this, in September 2024, Sharulnaim approached the woman’s sister in a supermarket and said he had an explicit video of her sister. The woman was also present but did not speak to him until Sharulnaim approached her. He asked her to tell the investigation officer that she no longer wished to pursue the case. To placate him, the woman said she would consider it. She refused to take down Sharulnaim’s new number and instead told the investigation officer about what happened. Sharulnaim saw the woman with her sister and son at the supermarket again the following month and begged the woman to drop the case. He asked for forgiveness, saying he was the sole breadwinner and that his parents and wife had learned about what happened. He claimed that he wanted to kill himself. He also asked the woman to tell the police they were family, even though they were not. His friend had told him that this might help get the case dropped. He also offered gifts and financial help to the woman if she let the matter go. The woman’s sister lodged a police report that same day. While the case was ongoing, on February 25, 2025, Sharulnaim came across another couple having sex in a parked car at a multi-storey car park. He took a photograph of them before knocking on the window and gesturing to them to step out. Lying that he was a former police officer, Sharulnaim asked the pair in their 20s for their ages and schools. He said he had taken a video of them having sex and said he would lodge a police report, scaring the man. Sharulnaim said he wanted to lodge a police report against them and that they would be fined for engaging in such acts in public. The couple tried to leave and walked away, but Sharulnaim drove his vehicle and cornered the pair. He rolled down his window and insisted that the man leave while he took the woman home. The woman said her home was nearby and she would walk, but Sharulnaim insisted. He locked the doors and drove off, complimenting the woman on her looks and asking why she was in a relationship with her boyfriend. When Sharulnaim came to the woman’s home, he saw her boyfriend waiting there for her and said he would not let her alight until her boyfriend left. He told the woman she should not be with her boyfriend because she was too pretty for him. Eventually, he unlocked the doors and let her go. She later lodged a police report and Sharulnaim was arrested again. Deputy public prosecutor Niranjan Ranjakunalan sought two years and 11 to 13 months’ jail for Sharulnaim, along with three strokes of the cane. Sharulnaim has prior convictions for theft and desertion from civil defence, among other charges. Defence lawyer S Balarumugan said his client had a daughter and a month-old baby. He said he was also financially supporting his aged parents, who had medical conditions. He said his client apologised to the victims for the ordeal he caused and assured the court he would be “more responsible” in future. District Judge Samuel Wee allowed Sharulnaim’s wife to stay in the courtroom to hear sentencing remarks instead of leaving to tend to her crying baby. He told Sharulnaim that his actions were premeditated and planned. “You know the hurt it has caused your family,” said Judge Wee. “I would say … [it] has been most hurtful to your wife. Despite that, she’s still here today.” Sharulnaim’s wife began to break down in the courtroom, surrounded by family. The judge asked Sharulnaim to look at him as he was talking and told him about the consequences of his actions. “Because of what you did … your children are going to grow up for a short period of time without their father,” Judge Wee said. “And your wife, who has already had to bear the brunt of your very hurtful conduct, is going to be the one continuing to care for them while you are away.” He asked if Sharulnaim had anything to say to his family, to which the man said he had already spoken to his wife and was grateful that she had stayed by his side. The judge then reminded him to think about what he did while in jail and be clear on what he wanted for his future and his family on his release. He allowed Sharulnaim time to speak to his various family members before being taken to jail. He said goodbye to his baby through a hole in the glass. For putting a person in fear of harm to commit extortion, he could have been jailed for between two and five years and caned. For obstruction of justice, he could have been jailed for up to seven years and fined. For wrongful confinement, he could have been jailed for up to three years and fined. This story was first published by CNA

title: Who has Outer Banks star Madelyn Cline dated? Chase Stokes, Pete Davidson, Jackson Guthy and more
description: As the Netflix series wraps up, the actress’ love life remains under scrutiny while she steps into her next film role alongside Johnny Depp and Penélope Cruz.
content: As the cast of Outer Banks bids farewell to the show, all eyes are on Madelyn Cline, who shot to fame after the series began in 2020. She recently appeared in the music video for Sabrina Carpenter’s “House Tour”, and is set to star in the film Day Drinker alongside Johnny Depp and Penélope Cruz. With fame, of course, comes intense scrutiny of Cline’s love life. The actress has been the subject of some relationship speculation over the past few years, being linked to the likes of Outer Banks co-star Chase Stokes and comedian Pete Davidson. So, who has the 28-year-old star been romantically involved with? Here’s what we know about Cline’s dating history. Chase Stokes Cline and Chase Stokes sparked dating rumours after fans noticed his flirtatious comments under the actress’ Instagram while they were quarantining in the same house with the Outer Banks cast. In June 2020, the couple confirmed their relationship in a since-deleted Instagram post. The pair celebrated their one-year anniversary in April 2021, but by November that year, People confirmed that they had broken up. Their characters were love interests in the Netflix series, meaning they had to navigate their real-life break-up in the seasons that followed. “There were moments when it was difficult, absolutely,” Cline told The Hollywood Reporter last week. “But once the dust kind of settled, we were able to just revert to the friendship that we always had. At some point, you look at each other and you’re like, ‘Are you ready to stop being miserable? Because I’m ready.’” “[W]e made a promise to each other before we even started dating that the work was always going to come first,” Stokes also said in an interview with Entertainment Weekly in 2023. Following his split from Cline, Stokes has been in an on-again, off-again relationship with singer Kelsea Ballerini, whom he broke up with in February this year. Jackson Guthy In June 2022, Cline was seen spending time with singer Jackson Guthy. She kept the relationship low profile, only confirming she was dating someone in a December 2022 interview with The Cut, in which she noted that she was living with her boyfriend and their dogs. Speaking with Cosmopolitan in February 2023, Cline briefly spoke about her relationship. “I am happily taken. All I know is he makes me incredibly happy. And I’ve truly never been happier, and I feel very, very empowered.” The relationship was kept largely private, with the pair only occasionally posting on social media. By July 2023, Cline and Guthy appeared to have split when the actress unfollowed him on Instagram, though the couple never explicitly confirmed their break-up. Pete Davidson Pete Davidson has dated his fair share of high-profile ladies, from Ariana Grande to Kim Kardashian, and in September 2023, he was linked to Cline, per Us Weekly. Cline told Nylon magazine in a 2024 interview that she and Davidson had called it quits earlier that year, but gave no further elaboration. When asked what it was like to be with someone whose dating life is so obsessed over on the internet, she simply said, “The jokes write themselves.” Henry Smith Reports of influencer Henry Smith dating Cline emerged this April, after the pair were spotted together watching a show in San Diego. Later that month, Cline made several appearances on Smith’s TikTok page, with one video of the pair dancing to Zara Larsson’s “Lush Life” and another of them giggling as they prepared a yogurt “sweet treat”. Cline also spent Easter with Smith’s family. TMZ reported that after a brief relationship, Cline and Smith had split by late June and unfollowed each other on Instagram. Michael Reyes View this post on Instagram Cline was spotted on a dinner date with luxury property agent Michael Reyes this month. The pair appeared affectionate, holding hands and kissing across the table. While neither Cline nor Reyes has explicitly confirmed their relationship status, they seem to be enjoying the summer in each other’s company and are keeping things private. Other rumoured boyfriends Over the years, Cline has been rumoured to be involved with several other men, including actor Ross Butler, record producer Zack Bia, and Prince Constantine Alexios of Greece and Denmark. Butler was seen dancing with Cline at a restaurant in Milan in 2021, but the actor quickly shut down the rumours, telling TMZ that she was “just a friend”. Bia was spotted having dinner with Cline in late 2021, sparking romance rumours, but the producer told the BFFs podcast that they simply enjoyed spending time together and were not officially dating owing to their busy schedules. In September 2025, Cline was seen spending time with Constantine Alexios in New York, where they appeared to display public affection. However, the pair have not been seen together since.

title: Hong Kong exports jump 50.7% in July, driven by growth in AI-related electronics
description: Government expects robust demand to continue supporting trade development despite geopolitical risks.
content: Hong Kong exports surged by 50.7 per cent year on year in July, driven by “impressive growth” in AI-related electronic products, with the government expecting the robust demand to continue supporting trade development despite geopolitical risks. Provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Tuesday showed that the value of exports jumped to a record HK$672.5 billion (US$86.2 billion) last month after a 53.4 per cent rise in June. A government spokesman attributed July’s strong performance to growth in electronics related to artificial intelligence (AI) and a visible increase in exports to most major markets. “The value of merchandise exports grew by 50.7 per cent over a year earlier, with exports of AI-related electronic products again registering particularly impressive growth,” he said. July’s growth rate was the city’s fourth-highest level in recent decades, only surpassed by 53.4 per cent in June this year, as well as 61.6 per cent and 65.1 per cent in March and January 1984, respectively. The spokesman said global demand for AI-related electronic products was expected to continue to bolster the city’s exports, but warned of geopolitical risks in the Middle East and rising trade protectionism in some advanced economies. Imports rose by 41 per cent year on year to HK$677.4 billion last month. The city still recorded a trade deficit of HK$4.9 billion, equivalent to 0.7 per cent of import value. In July, total exports to Asia grew by 54.6 per cent, with notable increases to most major destinations, in particular, a 95.7 per cent rise to Taiwan, 77.7 per cent to Vietnam and 63.1 per cent to Thailand. Exports to the United States rose by 92.9 per cent. Two goods categories also recorded the largest increases in values for both total exports and imports – electrical machinery or parts, and office machines and automatic data processing machines. Electrical hardware exports increased by 54 per cent year on year to HK$121.6 billion, while office and data processing machine exports surged by 106.5 per cent to HK$54.3 billion. Meanwhile, imports of electrical hardware were valued at HK$104 billion, a 47.1 per cent year-on-year increase, and office and data processing machine imports climbed by 78.9 per cent to HK$33.9 billion. Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, senior economist for Asia-Pacific at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, said July’s export and import figures fell within expectations as the city was expected to benefit from a sustained global demand for AI-related products. These products include chips, semiconductors, servers, routers and other components for firms to build digital infrastructure such as cloud storage or data centres. The economist said the city’s exports to other Asian destinations and the United States had risen due to the high demand and investment for AI-related products. “However, we are still unsure of how the war in the Middle East will develop, and there are also tariffs and export controls to look out for,” he said. Ho Ting-him, Asia economist at Bank of America, said the city’s surge in exports was in line with regional exports, which had also been driven by AI-related goods and components. “The accompanying rise in import growth reflects Hong Kong’s role as an entrepot. It also suggests Hong Kong is deeply involved in the regional supply chain despite without a strong production base,” he said. Ho added that his analysis had found exports of memory chips or semiconductors had contributed to more than a quarter of headline export growth in the city, due to the effect of higher prices. In the first half of 2026, exports increased by 39.1 per cent from a year earlier, while imports grew by 40.6 per cent, resulting in a trade deficit of HK$294.6 billion. Hong Kong’s economy expanded by 5.1 per cent year on year in the first half, marking its strongest half-yearly performance in nearly five years.

title: Why was China’s response to North Korea’s latest missile launches so muted?
description: Missile tests hours after China’s foreign minister left Seoul won’t alter Beijing’s focus on regime stability, analysts say.
content: China’s muted response to North Korea’s latest missile launch, which came soon after top diplomat Wang Yi’s visit to Seoul, underscores how Beijing is prioritising Pyongyang’s stability over near‑term denuclearisation, according to analysts. North Korea started launching more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles just hours after Wang concluded his two-day visit on Thursday, the foreign minister’s first official trip to South Korea in nearly five years. South Korea and Japan condemned the launch as a provocation. Beijing declined to criticise the barrage fired into the sea east of the peninsula, with China’s foreign ministry saying the following day that it had “noted the reports” and did not have any “new comment”. The launch highlighted the gap between Beijing’s diplomatic engagement with both Koreas and its ability, or willingness, to restrain North Korea, said Lee Seong‑hyon, a senior fellow at George H.W. Bush Foundation for US-China Relations. During his meetings in Seoul, Wang urged South Korea to pursue “genuine strategic autonomy”, avoid taking sides between China and the United States and move towards “peaceful coexistence” with its northern neighbour. He also called on Washington to abandon what Beijing calls its “hostile policy” towards Pyongyang, but did not endorse Seoul’s call for multilateral talks involving the North. “Wang Yi’s visit … represents a necessary effort at diplomatic stabilisation and risk management,” Lee said. “For Seoul, maintaining open, predictable channels with Beijing is essential for regional stability and economic continuity. However, the strategic limits of this diplomatic engagement were underscored almost immediately.” Seoul’s dialogue with Beijing remained indispensable for crisis communication, Lee argued, but it “cannot serve as a substitute for robust, sovereign deterrence”. The episode also drew attention to Beijing’s systematic omission of “denuclearisation” from its official readouts. The same pattern was apparent during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Pyongyang in June, his first in seven years. Xi and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un emphasised closer strategic coordination and economic cooperation without referring to Pyongyang’s nuclear programme. Lee described China’s approach as a shift towards managing North Korea’s nuclear reality and prioritising both regime stability and Beijing’s broader strategic interests, rather than pushing for near‑term disarmament, a posture he termed “structural acquiescence”. IIn an analysis for Taiwan’s Prospect Foundation last month, Lee argued that China was not formally recognising North Korea as a nuclear-weapon state but it was putting Pyongyang’s regime stability, bilateral coordination and the US-China rivalry ahead of any near-term push for denuclearisation. That closer relationship provided Pyongyang with what Lee called a more secure “strategic rear”, allowing it to engage selectively with Seoul, Washington and Tokyo while reducing China’s incentive to pressure North Korea over its nuclear arsenal. Other analysts have reached similar conclusions. Zhao Tong, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told the American broadcaster NPR in June that China thought that North Korea’s nuclear issue was mainly a problem for the US and South Korea more than for itself. Still, this shift does not mean it welcomes Kim’s reckless escalation, as Beijing remains wary of regime collapse or a refugee crisis on its border, as well as the risk that conflict could drive closer military cooperation among Washington, Seoul and Tokyo. At the same time, China has sought to prevent South Korea’s alliance commitments with the United States from automatically extending to broader containment measures such as advanced semiconductor restrictions, supply-chain restructuring or Taiwan contingencies, Lee told the South China Morning Post. The challenge for Seoul, therefore, was to maintain engagement with Beijing without making a zero‑sum choice or assuming that Beijing would resolve the security problems posed by Pyongyang, Lee said.

title: Philippine poverty falls to record low, but many still feel insecure
description: Despite cutting poverty to a record-low 9.7 per cent, high costs and climate risks leave millions of Filipino families on edge.
content: The Philippines has cut its official poverty rate to below 10 per cent for the first time, a milestone officials hailed as proof that millions of Filipinos are climbing the economic ladder. Yet for families like Vhan Castro’s, there is a big difference between being officially counted as middle class and actually feeling financially secure. The 34-year-old earns an average of 40,000 pesos (US$650) a month for his family of four through a patchwork of side hustles – from renting out a van for long-haul journeys to running a vehicle repair garage. His wife, a nurse in Saudi Arabia, is taking a year’s unpaid leave to care for their family, having given birth to their second child two weeks ago. Until she returns to work overseas at the end of her maternity leave, the family depends solely on Castro’s income. By the official benchmarks, that income places his family in the middle class. But the lived reality – strained by the Philippines’ rising cost of living and fuel prices – is more complicated. The couple have managed to put aside some savings, but healthcare costs and other concerns weigh heavily on them. “If you’re not hard-working, it really is hard [to live in the Philippines] … when you’re earning well, you need to maximise it because it’s not going to last forever,” he said, adding that he and his wife had not ruled out emigrating. Castro is part of a fast-growing cohort of Filipinos who have cleared the poverty threshold, even as domestic and international headwinds raise doubts about how durable those gains will prove. The scale of the progress became clearer on Friday, when the Philippine Statistics Authority said poverty incidence fell to 9.7 per cent in 2025 – or about 11 million people – down from 15.5 per cent, or 17.5 million, in 2023. It marked the first time the national individual poverty rate had fallen into single digits. Meanwhile, the percentage of families living in poverty also dropped from 10.9 per cent to 6.4 per cent over the same period. The milestone comes a month after the World Bank reclassified the Philippines as an upper-middle-income country, after its gross national income reached US$4,850 per capita – above the bank’s US$4,636 threshold. Defined as the minimum monthly income a family of five needs to cover basic food, shelter, healthcare, education, clothing, utilities and transport costs, the Philippines’ national poverty threshold currently stands at 14,634 pesos (US$237). Households earning more than that are officially classified as “non-poor”, though analysts note that escaping poverty is not the same as being economically secure. “For the first time, fewer than one in 10 Filipinos is living below the poverty line,” Arsenio Balisacan, the country’s chief economist, said in a statement on Friday. “Reaching this milestone ahead of schedule demonstrates that expanding economic opportunities, complemented by effective social protection, can make a meaningful difference in people’s lives.” Balisacan said nominal incomes grew by about 22 per cent across income brackets between 2023 and 2025, pointing to broad-based gains in purchasing power. Yet he warned that poverty reduction was likely to slow “amid the more challenging economic environment in 2026”. “As we enter the final years of the administration, our priority is to ensure that families who have moved out of poverty do not fall back into it,” he said. “Current developments may slow the pace of poverty reduction, but early indications do not point to a reversal of the gains we have achieved.” In July, economic forecasts highlighted the fragility of the Philippine economy, as political uncertainty compounded economic pressures even as inflation eased in June. Analysts have predicted a sharp slowdown in growth, driven by anxiety over US tariffs and the fallout from recent corruption scandals related to flood-control projects. Perception vs reality Official benchmarks contrast sharply with how ordinary citizens feel. A Social Weather Stations survey conducted in late June found that 49 per cent of Filipino families still consider themselves poor, down only slightly from 52 per cent in March. A separate World Bank report on the Philippine middle class, published in June, also found that nearly 28 per cent of the population remained at risk of slipping back into poverty, despite what it called “historic progress” in the overall reduction. “The typical Filipino family earns just enough to stay above the poverty line – but not enough to feel economically secure,” the World Bank report said. “In fact, many families are so close to the edge that a single typhoon, a hospital bill or a lost job can push them back into poverty.” It added that 61 per cent of the population were at high risk from climate-related disasters, with most households lacking savings or insurance to fall back on. Government welfare programmes – such as public works schemes for the very poor and targeted cash subsidies during recent price shocks – have helped nudge vulnerable families over the poverty line, according to Michael Ricafort, chief economist at Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation in the Philippines. Healthcare initiatives such as zero-balance billing in public hospitals have also prevented large medical bills from bankrupting households. But Ricafort said that these programmes had widened the government’s budget deficit and ballooned national debt. To build a genuinely resilient middle class by 2040, the World Bank report said Manila must pivot away from short-term relief towards structural reforms. Ricafort shares this view, believing the Philippines needs longer-term solutions to ensure more people move above the poverty line and stay there. “More sustainable and structural solutions to lift more people from poverty would be enabling education as the biggest equaliser,” he said, pointing towards nutrition programmes as critical to keeping children in school and preparing them for gainful employment. Attracting investment to expand formal job creation was also important, he added, alongside modernising agricultural and manufacturing technology, which would lower production costs, boost global competitiveness, help curb inflation and strengthen food security.

title: How China’s smog-busting pollution plan will clear Shenzhen’s skies for Apec summit
description: Tech hub to curb industrial output, conduct drills and use AI to pinpoint pollution sources, creating ‘crisp air’ as world leaders roll in.
content: The southern megacity of Shenzhen and the broader Guangdong region will curb pollution, reduce some industrial production and conduct a drill to eliminate smog, part of a plan to ensure blue skies over the city in November, when foreign dignitaries descend on the tech hub for the Apec summit. Shenzhen has been designated a “core control area” for smog and air pollution prevention and monitoring, with Guangzhou and eight other neighbouring cities in Guangdong also implementing strict measures, officials with Guangdong’s provincial department of ecology and environment said at a recent press conference. They added arrangements had been put in place for the two special administrative regions of Hong Kong and Macau, which border Guangdong, to “forecast, monitor, warn and tackle pollution” during the two-day Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which starts on November 18. Additionally, officials in the nearby provinces of Fujian, Jiangxi and Hunan, as well as the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, will strengthen supervision of straw burning and steel and cement plants – especially in localities along air pollution corridors – to minimise cross-regional pollution transmission, according to an official work plan. Artificial intelligence will be deployed to pinpoint pollution sources and for more precise atmospheric analysis and forecast, provincial officials said. “We will focus on precision and inter-regional collaboration for clean and crisp air for Apec and these efforts will also benefit residents,” said Zhang Ruifeng, director of the atmospheric environment division at Guangdong’s department of ecology and environment. President Xi Jinping is set to receive leaders from Apec member economies in Shenzhen. United States President Donald Trump is also tipped to visit the southern city for the event, following his trip to Beijing in May. These measures, now being progressively rolled out in Shenzhen and elsewhere, are being compared to China’s all-out war on smog in northern regions in the run-up to the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing as well as the Apec meeting in the capital city in 2014. A separate Shenzhen government document on air and environmental protection has outlined a drill to fight smog, with a goal to achieve the “best air quality” the city has ever seen in November. “Prior to the meeting, we will have citywide drills for Apec meeting air quality assurance to optimise coordination and command for monitoring and the implementation of safeguard measures,” the document said. “We will enhance comprehensive coverage and monitoring throughout the summit and stand ready for quick response … The goal is for air quality in Shenzhen to reach the best level ever recorded in November.” A citywide survey of pollution sources and their emission profiles is already under way, with a focus on industrial manufacturers, construction sites, gas stations, oil storage depots and catering establishments. Based on their proximity to key meeting venues and summit hotels, differentiated and dynamic management and control will be enforced, the document stated, without elaborating. Shenzhen usually experiences some smog in November as a result of cold fronts, coupled with local emissions. But the city – home to Huawei Technologies, Tencent Holdings and DJI, as well as BYD, the world’s biggest electric vehicle (EV) maker – has been harnessing tech to fight pollution. Among other achievements, Shenzhen boasts one of the largest fleets of electric taxies, buses and other public service vehicles among all Chinese cities, with one of the world’s highest EV penetration rates among private cars, according to local government data.

title: Hong Kong government statistician cleared of loitering charge near girls’ school
description: Defendant, 59, admits photographing 16-year-old girl, but judge rules loitering charge unsuitable as his conduct did not amount to a threat to the pupil.
content: A Hong Kong court has acquitted a government statistician accused of loitering near a girls’ school and outside a classroom to photograph a pupil, ruling that his conduct did not pose an actual threat despite leaving the girl feeling unsafe. Eastern Court Magistrate Kestrel Lam Tsz-hong on Tuesday found 59-year-old Patrick Lam Win-hon not guilty of one count of loitering causing concern, despite acknowledging that the defendant had loitered at one of Causeway Bay’s leading girls’ schools on July 5 last year. The court heard that the statistician entered the school on its open day and spent 14 minutes on the fourth floor, where the classroom of the pupil he allegedly targeted was located. Other students alerted teachers to the defendant’s suspicious behaviour, including his taking photographs through the classroom window. The court heard that the target was a 16-year-old girl, who said the defendant had followed her during her daily commute to school for two to three years. The girl said she first noticed the defendant showing interest in her by smiling and nodding at her on the MTR in late 2022. She said she later spotted the same man in the same carriage while travelling from Olympic to Hong Kong station on her daily commute. The girl said she changed her routine, leaving home earlier or later than usual to avoid the defendant. But she found that he would nonetheless wait for her on the platform when she changed trains at Central for Causeway Bay station. After being alerted that the defendant had appeared at the school’s open day and loitered outside her classroom, she told a teacher about the alleged stalking over the years. The school subsequently reported the matter to police. Lam admitted to officers that he had followed the girl. “I want to know her because she resembles an old friend of mine,” he said. Police found 46 photographs taken at the school, 17 of which captured the girl’s face. Lam denied the charge and did not testify in court. In his verdict, Magistrate Lam said the legal test for the offence was whether the loitering behaviour could reasonably cause others to fear for their own safety. He ruled that the defendant had loitered around the school and caused the girl to worry about his intentions, which represented the complainant’s “subjective” view. However, viewed “objectively”, the magistrate said the defendant had not done anything that day to justify a finding that he posed a threat or gave rise to a safety alert. The girl was unaware of his presence until she was told about it. “In my view, although [the girl] raised concern about her own safety, the court is not satisfied that such concern was caused by the defendant’s loitering behaviour,” he said, acquitting the defendant. The magistrate added that the loitering charge was not appropriate for dealing with the incident, as it applied only to threatening behaviour. He also said anti-stalking legislation would be more appropriate for addressing this type of conduct but noted that the proposed law remained under discussion.

title: AI smart glasses force South Korea to rewrite its exam rules
description: Five exam cheats caught in eight weeks are forcing South Korea into a regulatory overhaul.
content: South Korea is preparing to overhaul the rules governing technical qualification exams after five candidates were caught using AI-powered smart glasses to cheat in just over two months. The five cases, reported between May and June, were disclosed in data submitted to the Human Resources Development Service of Korea by opposition politician Kim So-hee, according to a report by The Korea Herald on Monday. In two of the cases – in Gwangju and Daegu – the candidates were caught because examiners spotted a light or electronic sound emitting from their glasses. In another incident in Mokpo, a candidate was seen pressing a button on a pair of glasses, causing a blue display to appear on the lens. In Seoul, a camera lens was found embedded in the frame of glasses worn by a candidate taking an information processing engineer exam, while in Ulsan, a check showed a lens and display on the glasses worn by another candidate. All five were penalised for cheating, and three of them were referred to prosecutors. In June, the incident involving the candidate in Gwangju became the country’s first criminal case, according to the Korea JoongAng Daily. The man in his forties was charged with violating the National Technical Qualification Act. An examiner noticed light reflecting from the lenses of his glasses during the fire protection facilities engineer certification exam. In May, the Human Resources Department expanded its list of prohibited electronic and communications devices, allowing proctors to remove candidates caught using them and invalidate their scores. Smart glasses are not explicitly named in the current list of items forbidden in exam halls – which includes electronic or communications devices such as mobile phones, digital cameras and camera-equipped pens. However, given the pace of technology evolution, the Labour Ministry is planning to use broader language so that new devices can be restricted without the authorities having to constantly change the rules every time to keep up with the trend. “It is difficult to revise the enforcement rules every time a new device emerges, so we are considering making the regulations somewhat more flexible so that we can respond more quickly to technological changes,” a Labour Ministry official said. The public notice process will start in September, and the ministry hopes to complete the revision within the year. Smart glasses are also causing problems in other major exams, including two during the English for international communication tests in May and three during the Test of Proficiency in Korean (TOPIK) exams last year. TOPIK administrator, the National Institute for International Education, installed radio-frequency and metal detectors at all domestic test centres in April to catch cheaters. The Education Ministry is also considering measures to prevent technology-assisted cheating. In June, provincial departments such as the Gyeonggi-do Office of Education and Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education sent their schools circulars showing the most popular devices used in cheating and tips on how to spot AI glasses, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported. A viral clip posted by an internet technology YouTuber in June showed an edge a smart glass user could have over others. In the video, the YouTuber uses a pair of AI glasses to solve all 30 questions in a practice maths test for the college entrance exams, or suneung, in just 18 minutes – scoring 96 out of 100.

title: Opinion | For states, being part of everything doesn’t mean being part of nothing
description: The opposite of commitment is breach, not multiplicity. A nation’s reliability isn’t measured by how many treaties it signs.
content: A coalition may call itself a commitment. It still has to say what that commitment is. The Trump administration is reportedly preparing to send a letter to dozens of countries, pressing them to choose sides in the US-China artificial intelligence race. Those that join Beijing’s proposed AI cooperation framework would be excluded from the US-led AI coalition. “To be part of everything is to be part of nothing,” the draft says. An American official summarised the message more bluntly: countries cannot have it both ways. The letter’s underlying logic reaches far beyond AI. As international institutions become more fragmented and competitive, governments increasingly face the same demand: prove the depth of your commitment by closing the door on everyone else. That is a seductive argument. It is also a dangerous way to organise international cooperation. There are circumstances in which multiple memberships become meaningless. A government may sign declarations for diplomatic display, collect benefits without contributing, make contradictory promises or pass confidential information from one platform to another. But the number of institutions a country joins tells us remarkably little about its reliability. One country may belong to a single alliance and still free-ride. Another may participate in several organisations while paying its dues, implementing their rules and protecting sensitive information. The opposite of commitment is breach, not multiplicity. The crucial distinction is between obligation-based exclusivity and identity-based exclusivity. The first arises when two specific duties cannot be reconciled. A common customs union cannot function if every member sets its tariff. Two military commitments may become incompatible if they require opposing action in the same crisis. Access to classified systems may have to be withdrawn when another relationship creates a demonstrable risk of exposure. Identity-based exclusivity works differently. A country becomes suspect simply because it also enters a forum associated with another power. No conflicting clause needs to be identified. No breach needs to have occurred. Membership elsewhere becomes evidence of disloyalty. The first form of exclusivity can protect cooperation. The second often protects the dominance of whoever designed the club. Consider trade. Australia, Brunei, Japan, Malaysia, New Zealand, Singapore and Vietnam belong to both the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership. The two agreements have different memberships, standards and rules of origin. This overlapping architecture is complicated, but it is hardly empty. If simultaneous participation cancelled every commitment, much of the global trading system would have ceased to function long ago. Even security institutions can accommodate overlapping memberships. Twenty-three of the European Union’s 27 members also belong to Nato. The two organisations have different legal foundations and capabilities, yet they cooperate on military mobility, cybersecurity, resilience and crisis management. Overlap creates friction, but friction can be managed through a division of responsibilities, interoperability rules and information safeguards. Belonging to both organisations has not rendered either meaningless. India provides an even more politically revealing example. It participates in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, remains a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and holds the 2026 Brics chairmanship. India’s participation does not mean it agrees with every member on every issue. It defines the areas in which cooperation remains possible. Indeed, countries sitting in several institutional rooms can become valuable points of interoperability. They understand different regulatory languages, identify conflicts early and carry workable practices between systems that increasingly struggle to speak to one another. Such bridge members require safeguards. Destroying every bridge, however, does not necessarily make either side safer. It can leave rival blocs with fewer channels for communication, crisis management and compromise. Cooperation on public safety, basic standards, disaster response and other shared problems should remain relatively open. Joint investments, proprietary research and sensitive infrastructure may require disclosure rules, independent audits and tiered access. Highly classified systems can be reserved for partners that satisfy much stricter requirements. When cross-membership creates a conflict, members can recuse themselves from decisions, ring-fence data or lose access to a project. Blanket exclusion should be the last remedy. This matters especially to small and middle-sized states. Major powers can use the size of their markets, financial systems and security networks to demand comprehensive alignment. Smaller countries usually obtain trade, energy, investment and security from different partners. For a major power, exclusive alignment produces a tidier map. For a smaller state, it can concentrate national risk in the hands of a sponsor. Forced choices may generate public declarations of loyalty, while governments continue diversifying quietly. The membership list becomes cleaner as the international system grows more brittle. “Being part of everything” can become a substitute for genuine commitment. But that conclusion must follow from conduct, conflicting duties and identifiable risks – not from the mere existence of another membership card. If a coalition cannot name the incompatible obligation, it is not defending commitment. It is demanding allegiance.

title: Philippines to expand military drone fleet as South China Sea tensions rise
description: Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro has pitched a 6.3 per cent budget increase to fund the advanced drones and warships.
content: The Philippines plans to expand its unmanned ⁠capabilities, including through development ⁠and acquisition of drones as part ⁠of efforts to modernise its military, its defence chief said on Tuesday. US defence ally the Philippines also planned to acquire additional guided-missile corvettes and other major defence assets to strengthen its external defence capabilities, Defence Secretary Gilberto ‌Teodoro told a budget hearing in the lower house of Congress. The Philippines has shifted its security focus from internal threats to external security as tensions rise with Beijing in the South China Sea, where confrontations between them over disputed features inside Manila’s exclusive economic zone have grown in frequency in recent years. The armed forces currently operate ⁠a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles that provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, Teodoro said. “As we mature ‌on the cycle, then we can acquire more,” Teodoro said in pitching to lawmakers a 6.3 per cent increase in the defence ministry’s budget for ‌2027, from the 305.5 billion pesos (US$4.95 billion) spending plan approved for this ⁠year. Drone expansion is ⁠part of a proposed 50 billion pesos allocation for the Philippines’ modernisation programme next year, 25 per cent higher ‌than that of the current budget. The priority was also developing the systems, connectivity and operational know-how needed to use ‌drones effectively, Teodoro ‌added. “More than the personnel, it is the integration into the operation, what do you ‌do with them and how do you use them,” he said. Developing secure communications and ⁠network capabilities was crucial, he added. Teodoro declined to identify specific systems under consideration, saying the details ⁠were classified and highly sensitive. “They are very, very sensitive to compromise, particularly with AI,” he said, adding that the Philippines was in close contact with several countries ‌with expertise in drone technology. Yuliia ‌Fediv, Ukraine’s ambassador to the Philippines, said in June that Kyiv had been in discussions with Manila over drone technology cooperation. In June, the United States said it had given the Philippine military four solar-powered sea drones to boost its maritime surveillance.

title: Israel’s strikes push Syria towards Mecca defence pact membership
description: Air strikes intended to curb Turkish expansion risk triggering the very encirclement Israel fears, analysts say.
content: Israel’s escalating campaign to stop Syria rebuilding its military with Turkish help looks set to backfire, after Damascus signalled it was considering joining the new mutual-defence pact formed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Securing a Washington-mediated security deal with Israel was still Damascus’ top priority, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani reportedly told Roman Gofman, the head of Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency, at a meeting in Amman on Sunday. Such a deal would see Israeli forces withdraw from areas of southwest Syria they have occupied since the Assad regime collapsed in December 2024. But according to the official Syrian Arab News Agency, Shaibani made clear that any agreement would not come at the price of capitulating to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s demands for “freedom of action” throughout Syria. Syria was a sovereign state with “the full right to rebuild and develop its national army and determine its alliances and partnerships in accordance with its national interests”, Shaibani reportedly said, adding that Damascus would not accept any arrangement that restricted those rights. The Amman talks were hastily arranged by the United States after Netanyahu ordered air strikes last Tuesday on a Syrian airbase near the Turkish border. He claimed the strikes pre-empted a planned Turkish deployment at the Abu Al-Duhur military airfield in northwest Idlib province – an allegation rejected as false by Ankara, Damascus and US special regional envoy Tom Barrack. Netanyahu described the strikes as a warning to Turkey against expanding its military footprint in northwest Syria southward towards Israel. Barrack countered that they could easily have provoked a clash between the regional powers – a view echoed by other observers, who warned that Israel’s aggressive actions in Syria risked becoming a “self-fulfilling prophecy”. Indeed, the day after the bombing, Shaibani signalled Syria’s defiance by travelling to Pakistan for talks that encompassed the possibility of joining the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. Speaking to reporters in Islamabad on Thursday, he said Damascus had yet to reach a final decision on membership of the alliance, which Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia formed on August 7. Coming just before his meeting with Israel’s intelligence chief, the message was clear: Damascus would do whatever it judged necessary to prevent the escalating turf war between Israel and Turkey from disrupting Syria’s fragile recovery after almost 14 years of civil war. Syrian state media said Sunday’s talks addressed “efforts to bridge differences between Turkey and Israel and ensure that tensions between the two countries do not spill over onto Syrian territory”. Israel’s anxiety Israeli-American geopolitical analyst Shaiel Ben-Ephraim said the Mecca pact was “definitely playing a part in Israel’s anxiety over Syria”. Israel recognised that American power in the region was “waning”, that Saudi Arabia was “turning away” from normalising relations with it and that Turkey and Pakistan were “both hostile states”, he said. “Together, this alliance is stronger than Israel,” said Ben-Ephraim, who is a senior analyst at strategic advisory firm Atlas Global Strategies. “There is a danger that Israel is bringing on strategic encirclement in the region.” He added that the pact could eventually supplant the US-brokered Abraham Accords as the region’s prevailing security framework – a shift that “would make Turkish bases in Syria all the more dangerous”. Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of the Washington-based risk consultancy Gulf State Analytics, said Syria’s possible accession must be seen in the context of a pact that “constitutes an effort on the part of its signatories to establish a new regional order for the post-Iran war period in which Tel Aviv is checked”. Israel has not officially reacted to the alliance’s formation, but Cafiero said it should prompt Israeli leaders to conclude that the cost of attacking any of the three states – particularly Turkey – was now higher than before. Yoni Ben Menachem, a senior Middle East analyst at the Jerusalem Centre for Security and Foreign Affairs, said Israeli officials viewed the Mecca pact as a strategic development capable of gradually altering the regional balance of power. In a research paper published the same day as the Abu Al-Duhur strikes, Menachem – a former head of the Israeli Broadcasting Authority – wrote that Israel’s primary concern was that the trilateral alliance could become “the nucleus of a broader regional framework”, eventually joined by Egypt and other Arab and Muslim states, including Syria. In such a scenario, Israel could find itself facing an independent regional bloc with formidable military, economic and strategic capabilities – one that “does not necessarily rely on the United States and does not necessarily regard Israel’s military superiority as a regional asset”. Menachem said this prospect had pushed Israel’s political establishment to consider building “a network of countervailing alliances” to balance the “emerging Sunni axis”. Retired Israeli Defence Forces colonel Hanan Shai warned against pursuing such counter-alliances, calling the approach a “mistake”. Writing a paper published last Tuesday by the Misgav Institute for National Security and Zionist Strategy, Shai noted that India had long resisted joining any mutual-defence pact, Greece could not align against fellow Nato member Turkey, and Arab states such as the United Arab Emirates would be reluctant to join a bloc “defined from the outset by its opposition to Turkey”. Instead, Shai – now a lecturer in political science and international relations at Bar-Ilan University – said Israel should build “an organisation for security and prosperity” around functioning economic infrastructure, centred on reviving the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor: a US-backed proposal for a network of ports, railways, energy pipelines and data cables connecting the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean via the UAE, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Israel. Rival routes Here too, there was room for both cooperation and confrontation, analysts told This Week in Asia. Ben-Ephraim drew a direct link between Israel’s escalation in Syria and recent moves by the US, Turkey and Gulf Arab states to turn Syria into an alternative energy and logistics corridor to the Gulf, in response to Iran’s chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz. Although officially aimed at Turkey, he said last Tuesday’s strikes also demonstrated “Israel’s ability to disrupt any Syria-routed corridor it doesn’t control”. Israel framed both Turkey’s military role in Syria and recent agreements to rebuild an Ottoman-era railway connecting Turkey to Saudi Arabia via Jordan and Syria “as security-driven rather than economic sabotage”, Ben-Ephraim said. “But the two interests complement each other, and since it [Israel] sees Turkey and Syria as geopolitical rivals, their economic success is also viewed as a negative development,” he said. Nir T. Boms, a counterterrorism expert and research fellow at Tel Aviv University’s Moshe Dayan Centre, had a more optimistic outlook, seeing potential for “a win-win formula with a combined route that will use both the Israeli and the Syrian hubs” – potentially even extending to Gaza. This could “actually serve as the potential for de-escalation and not just for conflict build-up”, Boms said.

title: 3 helpers sacked, issued warnings over use of employer data to secure loans
description: Hong Kong’s privacy watchdog highlights three cases and says helpers’ actions led to their employers being harassed by debt collectors.
content: Three domestic helpers in Hong Kong have been sacked and issued warning letters after providing their employers’ personal data without consent to secure loans, resulting in the households being harassed by debt collectors. Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data Ada Chung Lai-ling said on Tuesday that, in each of the three cases, the names, phone numbers and addresses of employers were originally obtained solely for work purposes. “However, the domestic helpers in question subsequently provided the employers’ personal data to financial institutions for applying for loans,” she said. “And I would say that this went beyond the original purpose for which the data was collected.” In one of the cases, which happened in 2025, the helper provided her employers’ phone number and address to a moneylender in the Philippines as proof of work, but later defaulted on payments due to the high interest rate. The moneylender then texted the employer, requesting that the helper be reminded to make the payments, and threatened to send debt collectors to the address if the transaction was not completed by a deadline. The other two cases took place in January and May this year and involved the helpers disclosing their employers’ personal information to several financial institutions without consent to apply for loans, resulting in their employers being harassed. All three helpers were eventually fired and received warning letters from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data. According to the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance, the commissioner may issue enforcement orders to those who violate the legislation. Failure to comply can lead to criminal liability, resulting in a maximum punishment of two years in jail and a HK$100,000 (US$12,800) fine for repeat offences. Chung also revealed that the privacy watchdog had received 21 inquiries and complaints about helpers’ unauthorised use or disclosure of employers’ personal data to financial institutions in the first half of this year, surpassing the 18 recorded in 2025. But she anticipated the number of cases would stabilise in the second half of this year as the government stepped up regulatory efforts against moneylenders. Under new rules that took effect earlier this month, financial institutions are banned from requesting borrowers to provide loan referees. Anyone earning no more than HK$6,000 per month is also only allowed to borrow up to 35 per cent of their monthly income. The cap is set at 40 per cent for those making between HK$6,001 and HK$12,000 a month. Chung urged domestic workers to obtain their employers’ explicit consent before using their personal data and to avoid recklessly disclosing information to financial institutions to obtain loans. She also encouraged employers to remind helpers not to use their private information for purposes not already agreed on and to carefully handle documents provided by domestic workers that required their signatures. Separately, the watchdog also published a guideline for organisations on protecting personal data when using agentic AI tools. Chung said such artificial intelligence (AI) tools posed a higher risk of a data breach as they could act autonomously on behalf of users to execute various tasks, such as handling emails, making restaurant bookings and even settling payments. The office’s nine recommendations began with three core practices: avoiding excessive or arbitrary collection of personal data for such tools, telling users that the software was in use, and ensuring accuracy of private information with context-based fine-tuning and human review. Another three focused on regularly deleting data deemed no longer relevant, ensuring all personal information was used with consent and verifying the systems’ codes to avoid any malicious programmes. The final three recommendations covered choosing systems with good privacy protection settings, conducting continuous risk assessments and providing training for employees. “If the decisions made by the agentic AI may have a significant impact on individuals … organisations should then adopt a ‘human-in-the-loop’ approach to retain final control over the decision-making process to prevent and mitigate AI-induced errors and automation bias,” said Fiona Lai Ho-yan, assistant privacy commissioner for legal affairs.

title: South Korea’s Hyundai, union agree on tentative wage deal after rare full-day strike
description: Around 40,000 out of roughly 73,000 employees walked off the job on Friday in the first such strike action for a decade.
content: South Korean carmaker Hyundai Motor and the union representing its workers have reached a tentative deal on wages and bonuses, both sides said on Tuesday after a rare full-day strike. Around 40,000 employees of a roughly 73,000-strong domestic workforce at the country’s largest carmaker walked off the job on Friday, according to union figures, in the first such action for a decade. The union said on Monday that it had returned to talks with the company and had postponed shorter strikes planned for this week. Hyundai said on Tuesday that the two sides had struck a “tentative agreement”, while the union indicated that the firm had agreed to partly meet its demands. “We agreed to increase the basic monthly salary by 100,000 won (US$72) and pay a bonus equivalent to four months’ salary,” the union said in a statement. The company will also meet another demand to raise the retirement age once the government passes legislation on a nationwide hike from 60 years to 65. Hyundai will not apply the wage peak system, which gradually reduces the salaries of older workers in their final years, after the retirement age is extended, according to the union. Union members will vote on the proposals on August 31. “We acknowledge the commitment of our employees and appreciate the efforts of our negotiating teams in reaching this tentative agreement,” a Hyundai spokesman said. He also said both parties recognised that advanced technologies such as “physical AI and robotics are essential part” of the future of mobility. The company’s workers have staged a total of 60 hours of strikes this year, causing estimated losses of around US$1.6 billion, according to calculations by local news agency Newsis. Hyundai posted record second-quarter revenue of 49.2 trillion won, although operating profit fell 20.8 per cent year-on-year amid weaker sales. SK Hynix union rejects proposal Another South Korean company facing employee dissent is chipmaker SK Hynix, whose union members narrowly rejected a tentative wage agreement on Tuesday. A total of 50.08 per cent of the 15,045 workers who cast ballots voted against the agreement, according to a source familiar with the matter. The difference was just 25 votes. The agreement, reached last week, included a 6.3 per cent wage increase and a revision to SK Hynix’s profit-sharing bonus scheme, under which 40 per cent of bonuses would be paid in cash and 60 per cent in company shares. The ⁠world’s second-largest memory chipmaker has been reaping strong profits from booming demand for high-bandwidth memory chips ‌used in artificial intelligence applications. Last year, the two sides agreed to set aside 10 per cent of annual operating profit to fund profit-sharing bonus payments ‌under a system to remain in place for 10 years. Under the agreement, ⁠80 per cent of the bonus ⁠is paid in cash in the year it is awarded, while the remaining 20 per cent is deferred over two years. However, ‌this year, management’s proposal to pay more than half of bonuses in shares met with opposition from some workers concerned about ‌the ‌volatility of SK Hynix’s shares. The stock hit a record high in June on enthusiasm ‌over the AI boom before slumping on fears that too much money is being spent ⁠with insufficient reward. In May, Samsung Electronics and its unionised workers agreed on a deal on performance pay, averting a major strike at the chipmaker that had threatened to disrupt supplies. Samsung agreed to allocate 10.5 per cent of its annual semiconductor operating profit to special bonuses ‌for chip workers. The bonuses would ‌be paid in company stock, with the immediate sale of a majority of the shares to be restricted. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Why is Xiaomi doubling down on in-house chips amid a profit slump?
description: Chinese tech giant’s Xring O3 3nm AI processor scheduled to debut aboard folding smartphone in September.
content: Xiaomi’s long-term push into proprietary silicon is laying the groundwork for complex artificial intelligence workloads on smartphones and cars, analysts say, as the Chinese tech giant doubles down on self-developed chips despite an earnings slump and soaring component costs. On Monday it unveiled its flagship Xring O3 3-nanometre AI processor for smartphones, which is scheduled to debut in September aboard its Xiaomi 18 Fold smartphone. The company has also introduced the Xring O100 – a 6nm AI accelerator designed to boost Xiaomi’s MiMo large language model when paired with the O3 – alongside a 3nm Xring D100 chip for autonomous driving. Xiaomi said both the O100 and D100 will be deployed commercially next year. Ivan Lam, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research, said Xiaomi’s semiconductor progress placed it in “the top tier of China’s self-developed mobile systems-on-a-chip (SoC)”. “In the current age of AI, on-chip AI performance has become even more critical as AI workloads are becoming more complex,” Lam said, adding that while semiconductor investments yielded no immediate financial returns, Xiaomi’s long-term commitment remained positive. Xiaomi’s chip expansion comes as the global smartphone industry grapples with surging memory and component costs, squeezing profit margins across handsets and electric vehicles. Last week, Xiaomi reported a 6.1 per cent year-on-year drop in second-quarter revenue to 108.9 billion yuan (US$16.2 billion). Net profit fell 20.3 per cent to 9.46 billion yuan – its third consecutive quarter of decline. Despite financial pressure, the company has ramped up research and development. First-half R&D spending rose 25.6 per cent year on year to 18.2 billion yuan, with AI-related investments accounting for nearly 30 per cent of the total. The Xring O3 builds on the Xring O1, which was released in May last year. The new chip packs 24 billion transistors onto a die with sides of 133mm – representing a 26 per cent increase in transistor count and a 5 per cent gain in density. The company said the chip yields higher performance with lower power consumption. The launch underscores a broader push among Chinese smartphone makers to develop proprietary silicon. Last year, Xiaomi became the world’s fourth tech firm to design a 3nm mobile SoC for mass production, following Apple, Qualcomm and MediaTek. Meanwhile, rival Huawei Technologies is preparing to debut its Kirin 2026 processor, the first to feature its new LogicFolding architecture, in its Mate series handsets.

title: Controversial Malaysian professor sacked; Marcos’ US$3b estate tax: 7 Asia highlights
description: From child-free Singaporeans to a Malaysian politician’s rant against the US, here are a few highlights from SCMP’s recent Asia reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from the SCMP’s coverage of Asia over the past week that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Islamic university sacks professor who claimed Malays could fly A Malaysian Islamic university has formally distanced itself from an academic whose viral claims about ancient Malay civilisation – including that Malays could fly and taught the Chinese “flying kung fu” – have drawn ridicule from historians. 2. ‘No bandwidth left’: why many Singaporeans want to be child-free Nearly one in four Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 surveyed by YouGov in July said they had no children and did not intend to have them in the future. 3. Marcos slammed over US$3b family estate tax, says ‘very busy’ with government Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr has put his anti-corruption drive at the centre of his presidency, but questions over his late father’s estate taxes and the family’s past ill-gotten wealth have prompted critics to question his commitment. 4. Singapore PM unveils major pro-family measures amid record low fertility Singapore will increase its spending on pro-family measures focusing on easing childcare costs, with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong calling them “one of the best investments” as the city state aims to reverse its declining fertility rate. 5. ‘I hate Americans’: Malaysian politician’s anti-US rant draws backlash Malaysian politician Mukhriz Mahathir has triggered a social media storm after declaring in a video that he “hates Americans, all of them”, over Washington’s support for Israel – echoing the fierce anti-US rhetoric long associated with his father, former prime minister Mahathir Mohamad. 6. Why Japan is walking on eggshells over US sanctions on ICC judge Japan has spent years casting the International Criminal Court as a pillar of the rules-based order. This week, its closest ally sanctioned the Japanese judge who leads it. The move has left Tokyo in an uncomfortable bind: defend Tomoko Akane, the Japanese president of The Hague-based court, and risk antagonising US leader Donald Trump, or temper its criticism and appear weak in the face of an attack on an institution central to Japan’s rule-of-law diplomacy. 7. Indonesia takes on Malaysia in battle over palm oil pricing Indonesia produces and exports more palm oil than any other country, but when it comes to setting the price, it still plays second fiddle to Malaysia. President Prabowo Subianto wants to change that. On August 14, he announced a new exchange for commodities including palm oil, nickel and coal, targeted to begin operations on January 1.

title: Serena Williams, Carlos Alcaraz face tricky US Open mixed doubles first-round match
description: Aryna Sabalenka and Novak Djokovic also in the 16-team tournament that was overhauled last year to get top singles players to compete.
content: Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz will open the US Open mixed doubles tournament against a duo that features the reigning women’s doubles champion. Williams and Alcaraz will face Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool on Tuesday in the first round of the championship, which will be Williams’ first match at the US Open since 2022. Aryna Sabalenka and Novak Djokovic might have an even tougher draw. The top seeds, based on having the lowest combined singles ranking in the 16-team field, face Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten — who are the doubles world No 1s. Williams and Alcaraz were drawn to face one of the teams that emerged from the qualifying tournament that was held Monday. That ended up being Routliffe and Glasspool, who won two matches, both requiring match tiebreakers, to secure their place in the main draw. Routliffe teamed with Gabriela Dabrowski to beat Siniakova and Taylor Townsend for last year’s US Open women’s doubles title. They also won the championship in 2023. Sabalenka and Djokovic had been slated to play Leylah Fernandez and Frances Tiafoe. But Tiafoe withdrew from mixed doubles after losing to Arthur Fils in the Cincinnati Open final on Sunday, opening the door for a team that lost in qualifying to earn a spot. Kristina Mladenovic and Marcelo Arevalo, who lost to Routliffe and Glasspool in their second match, got the remaining spot and will play Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik. The eight-team qualifying tournament was added this year to give the traditional doubles specialists an opportunity to compete for the US Open title. When the tournament was overhauled last year — with a US$1 million prize for the winners — in an effort to get top singles players to compete, direct entry was based on singles rankings, essentially shutting out the players who largely focus on doubles. Williams is not planning to play singles in New York. Alcaraz, who has been sidelined since April with a right wrist injury, will return to defend his singles title. The mixed doubles first round and quarter-finals are Tuesday. The semi-finals and final are Wednesday.

title: ‘Children were in pieces’: memories still raw 6 months after Iran school strike
description: Families grieve at least 155 killed in US-linked Tomahawk missile attack on Minab school during opening hours of war.
content: For months, Masoumeh Zakeri has endlessly replayed the last night she spent with her nine-year-old daughter before she was killed in a strike on her school during the opening hours of the US-Israel war with Iran. Motahreh excitedly talked about coming holidays, planned weddings and the clothes she wanted to buy. She had a Ramadan pre-fast meal shortly before dawn and then Zakeri tucked her into bed. “I never saw her again. (That was) the last time,” the 44-year-old mother told Agence France-Presse. Motahreh woke before her parents and took the bus to Shajareh Tayebeh school in Iran’s southern city of Minab. Hours later, the attacks on Iran began and Zakeri received a call telling her to pick up her daughter. She did not make it in time. By the time she arrived, the school had been struck, and Motahreh was among at least 155 people killed, most of them children – the deadliest strike yet reported by Iran. Motahreh was recovered later that day, her mother said, only identified “by her earrings and bracelet”. Six months on, a team of Agence France-Presse journalists obtained rare access to the school which has remained largely in ruins, its collapsed walls and twisted steel now surrounded by portraits of the children killed as Iranian flags flutter above the rubble. Iran says the attack on the school involved two separate US Tomahawk missiles but neither the United States nor Israel has officially claimed responsibility for the strike.
