Rights groups including Amnesty International blamed the US while The New York Times has reported that the school was hit by a US Tomahawk cruise missile. Since an April ceasefire, the intense bombardments have largely come to a halt but diplomatic efforts to end the war have stalled. Zakeri said she did not see her daughter’s body after it was recovered, fearing its condition would replace her last good memory of her. “She was very loving, cheerful and really energetic,” she said, adding that time has done little to dull her grief. “Now our house is completely quiet.” Yaghoub Yazdanpanah, 34, a Persian literature teacher, still remembers the frantic phone calls from his wife and relatives that sent him rushing towards the school to collect his six-year-old daughter Fatemeh. He had to go immediately, he was told, as heavy strikes were already pummelling Tehran and the compound of Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was hit. Then came another call: his daughter’s school had been hit. “I just couldn’t believe it,” said Yazdanpanah, who recalled speeding from work only to be slowed by traffic building around the area as fire and thick smoke billowed over the site. The reality only sank in when he saw men gathering pieces of human flesh scattered by the blast and covering them with fabric. Nearby lay the body of a girl pinned beneath a slab of concrete. “I couldn’t breathe. I went and sat in a corner. I had collapsed and couldn’t really stand on my feet,” he said. His daughter’s body was found later that day. Another father, painter Javad Shahrjou, was struggling to recover from the impact of the second missile strike which blew him and his motorcycle away as soon as he arrived to search for his youngest son, Alireza. “When I entered the yard, children were in pieces … a head here, a foot there. A girl was falling from the second floor,” he said. His seven-year-old son was recovered three days later and identified only by his underwear, socks and shoes. “He was all charred,” he said. Authorities say the school will be preserved as a memorial as people continue to visit the site. Search operations have continued for the bodies of three missing children. The parents say they cannot bring themselves to return. “It’s very difficult for me after what I had seen up close,” said Yazdanpanah. Instead, families visit the cemetery where the children are buried. Arash Tondro, 45, who lives near the school and lost an eight-year-old relative in the strike, said he was still struggling to comprehend why it was targeted. “The place where the school was had been a military base about 10 or 12 years ago,” he told Agence France-Presse while paying respects to his relative at the cemetery. Now, he said, “there is absolutely no military site or anything”. Javad, who said he had lost his job after his son’s death, regularly visits Alireza’s grave and recalls the times when his son used to join him “wherever he went”. Zakeri also visits her daughter’s grave regularly but said grief has left her unable to think beyond the present. “Imagining the future is very difficult for me,” she said. “We have no plans at all. We just can’t bring ourselves to go anywhere or do anything.”

title: America proposes new US$103,265 H-1B visa fee, expanding charge beyond new arrivals
description: The extra upfront cost of hiring skilled foreign workers could make it far less attractive to sponsor Chinese and Indian professionals.
content: The US has proposed a new US$103,265 fee for H-1B visa petitions – a move that could ramp up the cost of hiring skilled foreign workers, with Chinese and Indian professionals particularly hard hit. It comes at a sensitive time for US-China relations, with visas already a long-running source of friction and Beijing stepping up efforts to attract global tech talent as competition intensifies between the world’s two largest economies. The US Department of Homeland Security proposed the additional fee on Monday for every H-1B petition subject to the annual numerical cap of 85,000 visas. That figure includes the 20,000 visas reserved for people holding US master’s degrees or higher. Employers would pay the new charge when filing a petition, on top of existing fees. Universities and certain non-profit or government research organisations would be exempt. The new measure would also go further than an earlier one. A US$100,000 fee imposed by presidential proclamation in September 2025 mainly targeted new H-1B arrivals from overseas. The US$103,265 charge would apply more broadly, including to cap-subject petitions filed for people already in the US seeking a change of status. That means the new policy could have an impact on many international students working in the US under Optional Practical Training. Different legal route The administration’s proposal follows a major legal setback over the previous H-1B fee. In June, a US court in Massachusetts struck down the earlier US$100,000 fee. In a case brought by California and 19 other states, the court ruled that the payment amounted to an unlawful tax that only Congress could authorise. The administration appealed and sought a stay, but the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit declined to pause the ruling. DHS is now pursuing a different legal approach through formal rule-making. Rather than presenting the charge as an entry restriction, the department is framing the new fee as a cost-recovery measure. Officials say the fee could generate about US$8.8 billion a year – money that would help fund immigration adjudication, security vetting, fraud detection and related operations that are currently paid for by taxpayers. The administration also argues that the high cost would encourage companies to hire and train American workers instead of depending on foreign labour. US Vice-President J.D. Vance endorsed the proposal, writing on social media that “if an American corporation needs workers, it should hire and train Americans”. China and India Chinese nationals are the second-largest group of H-1B beneficiaries after Indians, accounting for roughly 12 per cent of approvals in recent years. That translates into some 46,000 to 49,000 petitions annually, with Chinese H-1B professionals heavily represented in technology, engineering, artificial intelligence and semiconductors. Indians account for roughly 70–71 per cent of approvals in recent years with about 283,000 to 284,000 petitions annually. For employers, a six-figure upfront payment – particularly one required without any guarantee that a petition will ultimately be approved – could make sponsoring Chinese and Indian professionals far less attractive. The effect could be especially significant for Chinese professionals already in the US, many of whom entered the country as students before moving into technology and engineering careers. Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian declined to comment on the proposed new visa policy during Tuesday’s press conference. Visa problems Visa access has long been a contentious issue between Washington and Beijing. Chinese students and researchers have faced heightened screening, shorter durations of stay and accusations involving national-security risks. Beijing, meanwhile, has repeatedly complained about what it describes as harassment and the politicisation of academic and professional exchanges. The latest H-1B proposal adds another layer to that dispute. It also arrives as Washington and Beijing compete for the same pool of highly educated workers in fields increasingly viewed as strategically important, including artificial intelligence, advanced engineering and semiconductors. China has responded by making a concerted effort to bring talent home. Domestic AI and semiconductor companies are offering aggressive equity packages and high cash compensation to attract and retain top professionals. Local governments in Beijing, Shanghai and other technology hubs are also offering settling-in subsidies, housing support and tax incentives. Data already show rising numbers of Chinese students and professionals returning home, with US visa uncertainty among the factors driving the trend. Tech rivalry The talent battle is part of a much larger technology rivalry. In mid-July, Chinese President Xi Jinping travelled to Shanghai for the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, delivering a high-profile speech presenting China as a champion of open-source AI and global cooperation. Xi described AI development as a “symphony of global collaboration” rather than a solo performance by any single country. He also hit out at the “overstretching” of national-security concepts to restrict technology sharing. For years, the US has benefited from its ability to attract international students, engineers, researchers and technology specialists. China is now seeking to strengthen its own pull, offering financial incentives and improved support to persuade skilled workers to return. Not yet final The US$103,265 H-1B fee is not yet in force. A 30-day public comment period will follow formal publication in the Federal Register. After that period, the administration could move to finalise the rule. Legal challenges are widely expected, meaning the proposal could face another lengthy battle in the courts. But for Chinese professionals and the US companies that depend on their skills the announcement already sends a powerful signal.

title: German artist Anne Imhof on love, LGBTQ visibility and control ahead of her Hong Kong show
description: Award-winning artist talks about her ballet-infused work at Tai Kwun, challenges of working in Hong Kong and how falling in love inspired her.
content: On the hottest day on record in Hong Kong – when the temperature nudged 37 degrees Celsius (99 degrees Fahrenheit) – contemporary art’s best-known orchestrator of angst found herself forcing her way through the crowd at a former prison compound. This was not the frosty, theatrically sullen Anne Imhof often seen in magazine shoots and society pages. Dressed in her customary black, she appeared not like the enigmatic art-world diva whom Marina Abramović picked as one of the most influential women of 2022. She was just another person trying not to melt in the August heat. She arrived at the Tai Kwun arts and heritage centre in Hong Kong’s Central neighbourhood without an entourage, accompanied only by her partner, Devon Teuscher, a principal dancer at the American Ballet Theatre. Declining Imhof’s suggestion that she join the interview, Teuscher affectionately patted her arm – “Today, it’s all about you” – and slipped away to get a coffee nearby. Shortly afterwards, seated in an air-conditioned meeting room, the German-born Imhof recalled how the couple met during the making of her three-hour production, Doom: House of Hope (2025). The work in New York – Teuscher and Imhof’s home along with Berlin – was a highly stylised adaptation of Romeo and Juliet. True to Imhof’s famously curated gloom, the dystopian set featured brooding young people in school uniform, sports jerseys and joggers, a giant countdown clock, SUVs and a pervasive sense that civilisation had misplaced its keys. Teuscher performed alongside 40 actors and dancers, including Eliza Douglas, Imhof’s former partner and long-time collaborator. LGBTQ visibility in ‘House of Swans’ Imhof’s live performance work, House of Swans, will kick off her first solo exhibition in Asia, starting at Tai Kwun on September 25. The piece, starring Teuscher, expands a ballet sequence from the end of Doom into an origin story for the House of Swans, a faction coexisting alongside the Capulets and Montagues, and it will most definitely be “queered up”, says Imhof, who strongly believes in normalising LGBTQ visibility. In May 2025, shortly after Doom, Imhof and Teuscher posed on the red carpet at the Spring Gala of the American Ballet Theatre and, more recently, they were filmed for Valentino’s 2026 campaign, gazing at each other in a hotel room. Imhof does not care about “bourgeois acceptance of being queer”, but when a major fashion brand wants to say that it is perfectly normal to show two LGBTQ women being intimate together, it is a statement she wholeheartedly supports. The central character in House of Swans is a young woman who travels the world, finds like-minded allies and falls in love with the Queen of the Swans. Teuscher will be joined for the performance by more than a dozen dancers from Hong Kong Ballet (HKB). Imhof promises that any references to classical tales of tragic, passive heroines such as Swan Lake and Giselle will be delivered with attitude. “I’m interested in [classical forms] such as ballet because I want to tell different stories,” she says. “Because autocrats use ballet as a soft power tool par excellence, it doesn’t mean it’s theirs. This is almost like an attempt to claim it back.” I think there’s a depression, a melancholia in my work that people respond to Anne Imhof The 48-year-old artist and former Frankfurt nightclub bouncer defies easy categorisation. She draws, sculpts, composes and, most of all, choreographs and directs large ensemble performances. These works blend dance, drama and potent tableaux to create psychological portraits of urban alienation. Imhof soared to international prominence after winning the Golden Lion at the 2017 Venice Biennale for Faust. That durational performance transformed the German Pavilion into a bleak institution featuring a raised glass floor to establish an internal class system. Outside, Dobermans patrolled behind fences; inside, model-like performers navigated the two levels with a calm intensity punctuated by occasional screams from a topless Douglas. Subsequent works have solidified her reputation for very stylish angst. “I think there’s a depression, a melancholia in my work that people respond to,” Imhof says. “But this melancholia is in almost all of us. In a way, things that I see around me and feel are to be addressed in my work.” She can be funny, though. Aside from performances, Imhof’s Hong Kong show will include an exhibition of video works, drawings and bronze reliefs. Discussing bronze – another “classical” medium she aims to subvert – she adopts a deep, mock-macho voice to parody male artists who created monumental works. Slipping into character, she barks, “Put this in bronze. It’s 30 metres tall!” before clapping her hands to mimic a sycophantic reception. A new bronze relief sculpture in Hong Kong will boast decidedly unclassical subject matter: female pleasure, agency and women existing for purposes other than simply to be looked at. Returning to her normal voice, she adds: “Bronze is annoyingly classical. I tell you, I’m not happy with having to be done with something so early before it is shown. This is contradictory to my nature, which is to want everything in flux until the last minute.” That clashes with Hong Kong’s need for control, Imhof quickly discovered. “At certain moments in the production of the show I have to basically open up about what I’m going to show, and also very precisely say what’s in which position, what’s hanging where … and hand in video texts. It was really hard for me,” she admits. Imhof gives credit to Tai Kwun curators for respecting her creative space while explaining that the requirements were to do with the Temporary Place of Public Entertainment Licence (TPPEL) that all exhibitions in non-governmental venues in Hong Kong, apart from commercial galleries, require. The details requested for approval were tightened with the 2020 national security law. “Generally, in my practice, I don’t give institutions the relief of like, ‘I’m done. Here’s what you get,’” she says. “Why I’m a performance artist is because I believe in this moment of energy when the audience and the artists are in one room, and they create something together and that’s what I live for.” A video work titled Citizen will be shown as part of House of Swans. Based on Doom, it will feature suggestions of violence and scenes involving trans bodies. Consequently, she was told that she either cut out certain scenes or screen the full version in a room with a strict age warning. “Putting the film in a room with an age warning was my choice,” she says. “The process to get the TPPEL was interesting in how it made me feel. I became really aware of how much I wanted to show it in its entirety.” Collaborating with the HKB also required Imhof to learn a new kind of dance. She typically works with the same trusted performers for years – such as dancers from The Forsythe Company – who are accustomed to the free-flowing improvisation she demands. In a strictly hierarchical system such as classical ballet’s, first-timers need more coaxing. “Everybody’s uncomfortable when it comes to doing something where they could make a fool of themselves, including me,” Imhof says. “When I came, I already knew that I needed more of a structure with them. I could get a lot more out of working with the dancers here because Devon is very smart and she is the translator.” Not your traditional muse During this second visit before the premiere, Imhof was still finalising the ensemble. The main cast, however, was set: starring alongside Teuscher will be the brilliantly expressive HKB principal dancer Wang Qingxin. Is House of Swans, which contains significantly more ballet than Imhof’s previous productions, influenced by Teuscher? “The draw towards ballet was always there. It’s not because of her,” Imhof says. “But of course, she is an amazing artist, and it’s amazing to be able to work with one of the best ballet dancers in the world.” House of Swans will be “a fantastical piece about love and peace during a time of war” Anne Imhof Teuscher can be called her “muse” – as was Douglas – though this dynamic is far removed from the outdated trope of a passive woman inspiring a male genius from the sidelines, Imhof stresses. Her collaborative process often blurs the boundaries between her private and public lives. Her relationship with her muses is more Andy Warhol, who was gay, than Pablo Picasso – she has named Warhol’s Factory as a major influence. Even Imhof’s scrappy, early art school productions in Frankfurt’s red-light district relied on close friends to thrash out ideas, perform and heavily shape the creative process with their own distinctive styles. “Maybe this word, muse, is the only one established to describe an admiration and an inspiration,” she says, “and also a presence that becomes enigmatic as an image in the work. “For me, art can only be as good as it can be when there is a lot of agency involved in the collaborators. That means also that I have to relinquish control, which is sometimes not that easy.” Douglas remains a close collaborator and appears in Citizen. Always wary of “white cube” venues that erase local context, Imhof wants to acknowledge Tai Kwun as a loaded historical site. To metaphorically let in the compound’s history of discipline, control and confinement, she has requested that a gallery window remain open. The performance space will see the return of the large countdown screen from Doom, though it will now appear crashed and half-sunken through the floor. In Hong Kong, a countdown clock carries political overtones, but Imhof notes that the prop originated simply as the easiest way for performers and audiences to keep time during durational works. Furthermore, she says, a clock running backwards suggests “some kind of unknown”. Apart from the subversion of traditional gender representation, Imhof tends to resist the notion that her art should deliver overt messages, which has led some critics to dismiss Doom as apolitical, naive and entirely atmospheric. Imhof says she is well aware that the outside world is getting darker. Yet, she has become more determined to create beauty within it – not as an escape from reality, but as a refusal to surrender. Just as in Doom, where the reverse-telling of Romeo and Juliet started with death and ended with love at first sight, Imhof promises that House of Swans will be “a fantastical piece about love and peace during a time of war”. There is no doubt where that uplifting influence is coming from. “It has been such a life-changing experience to meet the love of your life,” Imhof says. “When you fall in love, you just want to be a better person. Period.” “Anne Imhof: House of Swans”, JC Contemporary, Tai Kwun, 10 Hollywood Road, Central, Tue-Sun, 11am-7pm. September 25, 2026 to January 3, 2027. There will only be two full-length public performances featuring Devon Teuscher, on September 25 and 26. For tickets, visit art-mate.net

title: How full equity buyouts could help China’s cooling bubble tea sector turn a new leaf
description: Bain Capital’s acquisition of Gong Cha may signal a shift in bubble tea investment strategy, as sector slows after years of rapid expansion.
content: Fuelled by the recent bubble tea boom and an intensely competitive market, financial investors have shown growing interest in the sector’s major brands, shifting their playbook from early-stage bets and initial public offering subscriptions to full equity buyouts. Growth of mid to high single digits was now expected for the industry in China, down from the double-digit growth projected in previous years, analysts said. The slowdown followed years of capital being raised and deployed to chase the same growth story, said Sandy Lim, director of S&P Global Ratings. In the latest development, global private investment firm Bain Capital said on August 6 that it had reached a deal to buy Taiwan-founded bubble tea brand Gong Cha Global from US private equity firm TA Associates and other shareholders. Bain Capital would work closely with Gong Cha’s management team and focus on its store expansion in Japan, South Korea and the United States, it said in a statement. Gong Cha operates almost 2,200 stores in 33 markets worldwide. Well-established across the Asia-Pacific region – particularly Japan, South Korea and Australia – the brand is also expanding in the Americas and Europe. It currently had no stores in mainland China but operated outlets in Hong Kong and Macau, according to the firm. “Gong Cha primarily operates a capital-light franchise model, generating revenue from franchise and royalty arrangements rather than relying mainly on company-owned outlets. At the parent level, the company directs its spending mainly towards product improvement and brand building,” S&P’s Lim said. “For fresh-tea brands operating in mainland China, most financing transactions remain growth-stage minority investments. We have not seen large-scale private equity buyout cases yet.” With a larger store network and a market crowded with numerous players, the key challenge in China will be improving store economics Sandy Lim, S&P Global Ratings Previously, most Chinese investors backed major domestic bubble tea chains through early-stage financing and IPO subscriptions. Among these are Hong Kong-listed brands Nayuki Holdings and Mixue Group, alongside privately held Heytea. In 2021, Shenzhen-based Heytea closed its Series D financing – its final publicly disclosed round of fundraising – generating US$500 million. Investors in the round included Chinese private equity firms HSG and Hillhouse Investment, and foreign investors Temasek and L Catterton. In the same year, Nayuki went public as China’s first listed bubble tea company. Founding wife-and-husband duo Peng Xin and Zhao Lin remain its largest shareholders. Nayuki debuted in Hong Kong at an IPO price of HK$19.80 per share. It closed at HK$0.73 on Tuesday, a decline of more than 96 per cent over five years. At the time of its listing, China’s private equity firm Tiantu Capital was Nayuki’s top institutional shareholder with an 11.18 per cent stake. Following multiple disclosed stake disposals, its holding fell to 4.98 per cent as of November 2024. Share movements no longer require public disclosure once stakes drop below 5 per cent. From 2023 to 2025, China’s bubble tea chains shifted from net store growth to net closures. The sector saw a net reduction of nearly 30,000 stores last year, as the previous strategy of rapid expansion no longer proved effective, according to domestic consultancy CIC. “With a larger store network and a market crowded with numerous players, the key challenge in China will be improving store economics, including sustaining same-store sales growth and maintaining margin profiles,” said Lim of S&P Global.

title: China’s new traffic safety law set to clarify liability for fully automated cars
description: Lawmakers are set to establish clear liability standards for self-driving cars, a move that could open the floodgates for next-gen vehicles.
content: Beijing could soon hold carmakers legally responsible for traffic violations when autonomous driving systems are in use, marking an important step towards clearing regulatory hurdles to wider commercialisation. The National People’s Congress Standing Committee, China’s top legislative body, is set to review an amended Road Traffic Safety Law on Tuesday. For the first time, the document was set to include a dedicated chapter on governing autonomous vehicles and advanced driving systems, according to state-run news agency Xinhua. “The definitions of autonomous vehicles and driver-assistance functions would be clarified in the amendments,” Xinhua reported, without revealing when the revised law would enter into force. Self-driving systems switched off during a journey would remain subject to existing rules and laws, according to Xinhua, while analysts noted that carmakers could be held accountable for accidents and traffic rule violations when such systems were activated in a vehicle legally recognised as autonomous. “As they are required to shoulder the responsibilities for the cars’ operations on the roads, automotive companies will also be allowed to build and sell cars of this kind to attract consumers,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst based in Shanghai. “When the amended law is promulgated, dozens of new autonomous models will hit the streets.” Next-generation technologies, such as early-stage automated software, sophisticated in-car entertainment systems and phone-linked features, are quickly becoming game changers in China – the world’s largest automotive and electric vehicle (EV) market – amid rising consumer demand for such features, analysts said. Even electric vehicles priced as low as 60,000 yuan (US$8,926) now come equipped with basic automated features, classified as level 2 or level 2+ autonomous driving technologies. These systems still require drivers, who remain responsible for all traffic accidents and violations, to keep their hands on the wheel at all times even when the functions are activated. However, some manufacturers have begun to promise financial liability guarantees. BYD, the world’s largest EV maker, announced in May it would cover any costs from traffic accidents when its “God’s Eye” advanced driver-assistance system was in operation. Founder and chairman Wang Chuanfu told a press conference in Shenzhen on May 28 that BYD aimed to achieve zero traffic accidents through its self-developed autonomous driving technology while designing affordable, next-generation cars for mass-market consumers. He did not disclose a timetable for implementing the policy. Regulatory approvals are also gathering pace. In December, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology gave state-owned Changan Automobile and BAIC the go-ahead to build level 3 vehicles on a trial basis. These systems promise to navigate streets independently, though drivers would still be required to remain fully alert and ready to intervene when necessary, according to criteria set by SAE International, a global standards organisation.

title: As toxic haze spreads, can Indonesia make land burners pay?
description: With thousands of fire hotspots traced to corporate land, the president has vowed action – but past efforts to collect fines have failed.
content: As massive forest and land fires burn across parts of Indonesia, sending haze towards neighbouring Malaysia, President Prabowo Subianto has vowed firm action against big corporations found responsible – reviving a long-running test of whether Jakarta can punish those behind the blazes and finally break the cycle. “We will go after them if they are proven guilty. We will penalise them according to the law,” Prabowo told reporters in Palangka Raya, Central Kalimantan, on Saturday. He flew first to West Kalimantan, then Central Kalimantan, over the weekend to assess the damage in person and meet local officials coordinating the emergency response. The latest fires are part of a wider trend. Forestry ministry data shows more than 202,000 hectares (499,153 acres) of land were burned between January and July, including nearly 95,000 hectares in July alone. Six provinces have been designated priorities: Riau, Jambi and South Sumatra on Sumatra island, alongside West, Central and South Kalimantan on Borneo. Fires have also broken out elsewhere, including Java, Papua and Nusa Tenggara. The blazes have produced choking smoke, forced school closures and blanketed parts of the region in haze that has drifted into Malaysia, with Sarawak among the worst-affected areas. Indonesia has deployed thousands of ground personnel and aircraft including water-bombing helicopters, as well as cloud-seeding technology to contain the fires and slow the haze’s spread. But environmental activists and analysts say containment is no longer enough, pointing to what they describe as chronic weaknesses in prosecution, deterrence and enforcement of Indonesia’s forest-fire laws. Janang Firman Palanungkai, Central Kalimantan executive director of environmental watchdog Walhi, said fire prevention must take precedence. “While we appreciate the efforts to contain the fires, prevention should be the priority here,” he said. Police have named 72 arson suspects nationwide as part of a government crackdown, 14 of them from Kalimantan. Prabowo’s chief of staff, Minister of State Secretariat Prasetyo Hadi, said four companies operating in West Kalimantan were under investigation for land burning. “We won’t hesitate to act sternly, possibly even revoking their licences,” he warned. Under laws passed in 1999 and 2009, deliberately setting fire to forest areas carries a sentence of up to 10 years in prison and heavy fines. Uli Arta Siagian, national campaign coordinator at Walhi, said uncompromising government action was crucial to ushering in a new era of fire mitigation. “We sincerely hope the president will make good on his promise, without fear or favour.” During a televised coordination meeting in Pekanbaru on Monday, Prabowo asked Riau police chief Herry Heryawan if suspect interrogations had uncovered evidence of corporate involvement. Herry said that they had not. But Uli said her organisation had little doubt that most fires in Kalimantan were driven by commercial interests rather than natural causes. “Our data shows that 74 per cent of the hotspots in Kalimantan, numbering 25,524, are within the concession areas of different companies,” she said. In Indonesia, concessions are large tracts of state land licensed to companies for commercial logging, mining or industrial agriculture. Hotspots within concession areas do not in themselves prove corporate responsibility, but activists argue the overlap should trigger deeper investigations and stronger enforcement. Walhi’s own analysis found thousands of hotspots inside company concessions in Kalimantan spanning plantation, mining and forestry activity. “The recurring nature of our forest fire saga is a sure sign that our government has failed to deter corporations from causing harm to the environment,” Uli said. Cheap land clearing Two commercial practices associated with land development heighten fire risk: draining peatlands, which leaves carbon-rich soil dry and highly combustible, and clearing land with fire rather than using machinery or labour. Uli said both practices persisted because they were cheap, despite severe public-health and environmental costs. “Companies torch the land because it’s cheaper than hiring people and machinery, but at a great cost to the environment, not to mention the health hazards incurred,” she said, criticising initial official statements that attributed the crisis primarily to natural factors such as El Nino and a prolonged dry season. “These may be contributing factors, but they don’t negate the fact that there are those who intentionally set fire to the land for commercial gain.” Companies torch the land because it’s cheaper than hiring people and machinery Uli Arta Siagian, environmental activist Rony Teguh, a forest-fire detection technology researcher at the University of Palangka Raya, agreed. He said this year’s fires shared patterns with the disastrous 2015 season, when about 2.6 million hectares burned, costing Indonesia an estimated US$16.1 billion in damages and shrouding the region in haze. “People tend to focus on what’s going on while the fire is raging. But I’d say we must look at what happens after the dust has settled,” Rony said, noting that his past research frequently found palm oil seedlings growing across burned sites once the fires died down. “This happened every time, so it was difficult not to conclude the land had been torched to make way for new plantations.” Uli said Walhi’s field observations over the years corroborated Rony’s findings. An official at the Ministry of Forestry declined to comment when approached by This Week in Asia, citing a lack of adequate information from senior officials. Uli said the problem was not a lack of environmental regulations but weak enforcement of the rules already in place. “The government has actually succeeded in prosecuting a dozen cases against errant companies, but how many were really made to pay through the nose?” she asked. Since 2015, Indonesia’s courts have convicted at least 12 corporations for starting or negligently allowing forest and land fires. Yet authorities have repeatedly struggled to enforce the penalties handed down. According to a report by local news outlet Tempo, by 2024 the government had collected only 400 billion rupiah (US$25 million) of the 20 trillion rupiah (US$1.2 billion) in accumulated fines imposed on companies found negligent over the 2015 fires. Janang said Walhi had begun urging local authorities to act as hotspots began to flare three months ago. “We pushed hard for an environmental audit of the companies and a re-evaluation of their permits, but our pleas fell on deaf ears,” he said. “The question is whether our law enforcement agencies dare to dig further and hold the masterminds behind forest fires to account.”

title: China’s anti-corruption legal framework is about to extend beyond its borders
description: A draft law aimed at combating cross-border corruption has been submitted for its first reading by the country’s top legislature.
content: China’s top legislature has reviewed a draft law aimed at combating cross-border corruption as part of Beijing’s latest efforts to expand its anti-graft legal framework beyond its borders. On Tuesday, the draft Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law was submitted for its first reading during the 24th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People’s Congress (NPC), which runs until Friday. The text of the bill is not yet available to the public. Enacting the law is a vital initiative to complete China’s foreign-related legal framework, protect national interests, promote compliant overseas business growth and “enrich the legal ‘toolbox’ for fugitive repatriation, asset recovery and handling foreign-related corruption cases”, according to state news agency Xinhua. The law codifies a decade of anti-corruption practices to close jurisdictional loopholes and target offshore financial crimes, aiming to resolve long-standing systemic hurdles, specifically the “difficulty in detecting, collecting evidence, repatriating illicit assets” and prosecuting offshore offences, it said. Comprising six chapters and 47 articles, the draft law establishes key principles, scope and national positioning regarding cross-border corruption. It obliged domestic firms operating abroad to adopt rigorous compliance standards, fostering a market-oriented, law-based and internationalised business environment, the report added. China’s institutional architecture for tackling foreign corruption has evolved significantly over the past decade amid President Xi Jinping’s wide-ranging anti-corruption campaign. In a September 2024 article, Song Wei, then dean of the school of Marxism and director of the Clean Governance Research Centre at the University of Science and Technology Beijing, said recent cases increasingly showed a complex entanglement between domestic and overseas corruption. Leaving cross-border corruption “unchecked” not only undermined overall anti-graft efforts and inflicted heavy economic losses, it also directly affected China’s global standing and political image, wrote Song, who joined Tsinghua University as a professor in May. Earlier this year, NPC Standing Committee Chairman Zhao Leji explicitly emphasised in his annual work report that enacting an anti-cross-border-corruption law would be a priority for 2026 to support the implementation of the 15th five-year plan (2026–2030) and improve foreign-related legislation. In a lecture in April, lawyer Li Qichao from the Beijing-based Huicheng Law Firm highlighted that the proposed legislation centred on prevention and punishment by establishing five key frameworks, including extraterritorial jurisdiction and mandatory corporate compliance targeting fugitives, overseas state-owned enterprises, and foreign companies in China. Drawing parallels with international benchmarks such as the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the UK Bribery Act, and the UN Convention Against Corruption, Li noted that the law aligned with recent Supreme People’s Procuratorate guidance cases on covert bribery to provide precise legal standards for tackling complex, foreign-related graft. The latest legislative push comes amid increasingly sophisticated offshore tactics uncovered by state auditors and the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), the party’s corruption-buster. A prime case in point was highlighted in a documentary broadcast during January’s CCDI plenary session, which detailed how the agency worked with law enforcement bodies in “multiple countries and regions” to trace bribes taken by Li Yong, a former general manager of state-owned energy titan China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC). Li, who oversaw CNOOC’s vast international portfolio before his investigation in March 2024, exploited complex commercial structures to conceal millions of dollars in bribes taken overseas, according to the documentary. More than 83 per cent of the illicit funds tied to Li originated offshore, funnelled through foreign business owners who managed, transferred and stored the money across offshore accounts, it said. In one instance, Li used a trusted associate as a “white glove” proxy to insert a shell company into a 2012 deepwater drilling platform charter project. This allowed them to extract millions in illicit commission fees, which were then layered through complex transactions across multiple foreign jurisdictions and deposited in offshore banks. Special task forces breached Li’s web by combining cross-border law enforcement cooperation with big-data intelligence and open-source data analysis, establishing an unbroken chain of evidence across 10 countries and regions. According to Ja Ian Chong, associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, the principle behind a cross-border anti-corruption bill would presumably require surveillance and enforcement mechanisms. That could make the outflow of capital from China to places like Singapore more challenging by adding monitoring requirements, he said. “At a minimum, the flow of capital to and from Singapore could face more scrutiny. That may discourage some people from moving funds to Singapore and using Singapore as a wealth management hub.” Chong added that there were not yet many details available about the legislation. A lot would come down to the final language and implementation, he said. Targets may include foreigners Lau Siu-kai, Professor Emeritus of Sociology with the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said that as economic, trade and financial exchanges between China and other countries and regions increased, cross-border crimes also rose. In recent years, China’s foreign-related legal framework had become increasingly comprehensive, he noted. According to Lau, the targets of the new law may not only be Chinese citizens but could also include foreigners. For Hong Kong, the impact should be limited, as mainland anti-corruption agencies maintain close cooperation with relevant local bodies, particularly the Independent Commission Against Corruption. Nevertheless, once the law was in place, it should provide a stronger legal basis and greater effectiveness in combating cross-border corruption, Lau said.

title: Japan’s famous bonfire monkey zoo to close for major revamp
description: During the closure, the zoo plans to use social media to post updates on its 700 monkeys and hold members-only events.
content: The Japan Monkey Centre, a primate zoo in central Japan known for its winter tradition of monkeys warming themselves by bonfires, will close from mid-October to renovate ageing facilities before reopening in several years. Home to about 700 monkeys of around 50 species, the facility in Inuyama, Aichi prefecture, will open only on weekends and holidays from September, and close its gates from October 19. During the closure, it plans to use social media to post updates on the monkeys and hold events open only to registered members. The zoo’s iconic bonfires date back to 1959, three years after it opened with funding from Nagoya Railroad, when staff burned trees that had fallen in a massive typhoon and resident monkeys were seen gathering around the fire. It later became the first facility in Japan to keep mountain gorillas. Working with partners, including Kyoto University’s Institute for the Evolutionary Origins of Human Behaviour, it is regarded as one of the world’s leading primate care and research facilities. Since 2014, the zoo has been run by a Kyoto University-linked non-profit foundation. Operating costs have been covered by admission fees and donations solicited under the name “Goshien” – a Japanese play on words combining “support” and “monkey”. But fencing, paintwork and other infrastructure have deteriorated, and some buildings lack enough space for the animals or could be damaged in earthquakes and other natural disasters. The renovation will also include improvements to air conditioning and walkways inside the zoo. “We will carry out a complete overhaul to make this a comfortable place for both the monkeys and our visitors,” an official said. The adjacent Japan Monkey Park amusement park, operated by a subsidiary of Nagoya Railroad, will continue normal operations.

title: 58 evacuated, woman taken to hospital after fire at Hong Kong flat
description: Transport Department said Percival Street section closed due to incident, adding traffic in area was heavy.
content: About 60 people were evacuated and a 98-year-old woman was taken to hospital after a fire broke out in a flat in Hong Kong on Tuesday. Police said they received multiple reports of the blaze at 488 Hennessy Road in Causeway Bay at 10.59am. Among the 58 people evacuated were 25 women and 17 men in the building. Another 11 men and five women in a bank on the ground floor were also evacuated. The elderly woman reported feeling unwell and was taken to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai, police said. At 11.39am, the Transport Department said all lanes on the section of Percival Street between Hennessy Road and Russell Street remained closed due to the incident, adding that traffic in the area was heavy. Tram services on the Happy Valley loop were suspended, bus routes 108 and 117 were diverted, and motorists were advised to use alternative routes. The Fire Services Department deployed 12 fire engines and three ambulances during the operation, mobilising a jet and a breathing-apparatus team. The blaze was extinguished at 12.04pm. More than 10 firefighters wearing uniforms labelled “Guangdong Provincial Fire and Rescue Corps” were spotted at the scene. In a social media post, the department said a delegation from the Fire and Rescue Corps of Guangdong Province and the Macau Fire Services Bureau had arrived in the city to take part in a five-day cross-boundary exchange-training programme from August 24 to 28. The delegation observed the firefighting operations on site and gained insight into fire safety facilities in Hong Kong’s buildings, it said. The Transport Department said at 1.15pm that traffic lanes on Percival Street had reopened and affected bus routes were gradually resuming their original routes.

title: Construction safety design needed to reduce fatal accidents in Hong Kong: experts
description: City’s poor industrial safety record, including 15 fatalities so far this year, marked by bad habits and broader systemic and planning issues.
content: Hong Kong should make safety design a part of all building development plans and address the culture of rushing work at construction sites, industry leaders have said after the city recorded 15 fatal industrial accidents earlier this year. Their calls followed the warning by Construction Industry Council chairman Thomas Ho On-sing on Monday that the number of such accidents was on the rise despite stiffer penalties, reflecting that a safety culture had failed to take root. Ho pointed out that up to 70 to 80 per cent of accidents at worksites were caused by bad habits and poor mindsets, while all 15 fatal accidents were triggered by the pressure to finish projects quickly, which he described as among the deadliest factors on construction sites. Chau Sze-kit, chairman of the Hong Kong Construction Industry Employees General Union, said on Tuesday that safety awareness had improved but had yet to become second nature in a sector where “rushing culture” was still prevalent. “For instance, the media recently exposed workers on exterior scaffolding without wearing safety belts or hooking on to independent lifeline ropes. This is a clear case of safety measures not being properly implemented. Ultimately, we need to embed a safety-first culture,” he said. Chau said the issue stemmed from both worker habits and a lack of management supervision, while the provision of safety tools and improved design at the outset of construction would also minimise risks. He said some countries had already incorporated “design for safety” in their construction plans, which effectively reduced the number of deaths on their worksites. Designing for safety involves identifying potential hazards in the early stages of conceptual planning and managing safety during subsequent construction. Studies showed that about 60 per cent of construction accidents could be traced back to lapses in early design and planning, according to a report by the Legislative Council last year. The city’s fatality rate in the construction sector was 17.8 per 100,000 workers in 2023, among the highest across advanced economies. Australia and Singapore have enacted laws to mandate design for safety principles in construction projects, with fatality rates of 2.8 and 3.4 per 100,000 workers, respectively, the Legco report noted. Chau said that a culture of safety had failed to take root in Hong Kong as workers were careless and wanted to take short cuts, while management and safety officers also failed to provide adequate oversight. He added that the “rushing culture” seen on construction sites was caused by tight deadlines and penalties for failing to meet those deadlines. “Under tight deadlines, main contractors face severe financial penalties and serious reputational damage if a project is delayed. At the subcontractor level, they lack bargaining power,” he said. He said frontline workers, who were simply trying to make a living, also had no power to negotiate better safety provisions or longer deadlines. “One could argue they could just refuse the work, but if a worker says no once or twice, no one will hire them again. They are caught in a helpless position where they have to literally choose between their livelihood and their lives,” Chau said. Lawrence Ng San-wa, permanent honorary president of the Hong Kong Construction Sub-contractors Association, said there was still room for the industry to improve its safety record. Echoing Chau, Ng said the industrial accident rate in Hong Kong was tied to individual failings – including workers’ behaviour and inadequate supervision by management – as well as broader, more systemic factors that were sometimes linked to environmental hazards. Ng stressed that it was “unfair to place the blame solely on frontline workers” and that changing mindsets required “the commitment of all construction industry stakeholders” to deal with broader issues of planning. He cited the example of recent extreme weather events, saying they had resulted in tighter construction schedules, which in turn led workers to neglect safety protocols in their rush to meet deadlines. “We all have to understand that work is important, but lives matter most,” Ng said.

title: Loro Piana’s Frédéric Arnault underscores commitment to sustainable Mongolian cashmere at Cop17
description: In Ulaanbaatar, the LVMH-owned maison presents progress on its Resilient Threads initiative as it marks 40 years of sourcing luxury fibre from the region.
content: Italian label Loro Piana marked its 40-year-long relationship with Mongolia at Cop17 – the 17th session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) – currently under way in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia’s capital. The UN-based biennial conference convenes representatives of governments, international organisations, financial institutions and scientists from around the world to find solutions to issues originating from desertification, land degradation and drought. A landlocked country with immense natural resources and a vast, diverse landscape where arid desert sits alongside fertile grasslands, Mongolia is home to the only Loro Piana mill outside Italy. Known for its luxurious garments made of precious yarns such as cashmere, Loro Piana, which was founded in the Piedmont region of northern Italy in 1924, sources its raw materials from countries including Peru, New Zealand and Australia. The brand has been sourcing cashmere from Mongolia for over four decades. In 1997, it officially set up its Mongolian operations before opening a manufacturing plant in Ulaanbaatar in 1999. To support Mongolia’s herding communities and cashmere cooperatives, last year the house launched Resilient Threads, a multi-year programme to protect the biodiversity of Mongolia’s Eastern Steppe and safeguard the well-being of its inhabitants. Created to deal with the challenges posed by climate change, the project is founded upon the One Health principle, a scientific approach that takes into account the interconnected well-being of people, animals and the environment they inhabit. In its first year, the initiative has led to the establishment of a biodiversity centre, a rehabilitation programme for the Bayandelger red goat, and the Dzud Impact Report – Dzud is a winter disaster unique to Mongolia, hampering animal grazing, feed and water, resulting in livestock loss. A One Health masterclass at the Mongolian University of Life Sciences, in partnership with the Royal Veterinary College and University of Liège, is also in the works. The programmes commit to the training of students and professionals on One Health practices, and the preservation of endangered species of goats that not only provide prized fibres like cashmere, but also staples such as goat milk and meat for the local population. Driven by local experts, Resilient Threads also involves initiatives such as the One Health Mobile Hub, a travelling clinic offering herders and their animals healthcare services they wouldn’t be able to access without crossing long distances from their remote locations. “It’s challenging, but it’s rewarding to see these concepts in action after just talking about these things for so long,” said Dr Batkhishig Baival, project lead at Resilient Threads, during a chat at the Loro Piana booth at Cop17. “It’s a learning process, and always evolving also because it requires all of the stakeholders’ engagement and they don’t always agree. The interests of wildlife protection entities, for instance, are often different from [those of the] goat herders, but we always find a [common ground].” Resilient Threads is set to last until 2030, but the Mongolian government is paying close attention to the data being gathered to assess whether to implement the programme long term. Baival added that many provinces have expressed interest in being part of the initiative, which for now only focuses on Sukhbaatar province. Loro Piana has been working to create a protocol to certify responsibly sourced cashmere since 2019 – when it began its partnership with the International Cooperation Committee of Animal Welfare and the Sustainable Fibre Alliance – but Resilient Threads furthers its commitment to empowering local herder communities. Part of LVMH, the largest luxury group in the world, Loro Piana has always prided itself on the excellence of its Made in Italy creations and its vertically integrated supply chain, which begins at the very source – the raw materials – before the fibres travel to Italy and are transformed into yarns that are also used by other luxury brands like LVMH’s Louis Vuitton, and the independent Hermès. Its pristine state-of-the-art factory in Ulaanbaatar, which is on par with its counterparts in Italy, is just an example of the brand’s long history in Mongolia, which began in the 80s, when the Loro Piana family started travelling to the country “in search of the world’s finest cashmere”, as Loro Piana CEO Frédéric Arnault explained at Cop17. “True luxury begins with nature, with exceptional fibres, and with the people and places that make them possible,” Arnault said. “We believe that what we do at Loro Piana, and also more globally, at the LVMH level, at all the 70 houses, cannot exist without an integrated approach to building a healthy and resilient ecosystem,” the CEO added in a speech at the French embassy the day before his appearance at Cop17. This was Arnault’s first trip to the country, a sign of the importance of the relationship between Mongolia and the maison – and also of the ever-growing interest in traceability from luxury consumers, who are becoming more demanding when it comes to matters such as provenance and sustainability.

title: As drug giants grow cautious, can Chinese biotech firms still cash in on licensing deals?
description: Out-licensing deals have overtaken IPOs as the primary lifeline for cash-starved Chinese drug makers, analysts say.
content: Record-breaking cross-border deals helped make some formerly loss-making Chinese biotech companies profitable in the first half of the year, but multinational drugmakers are now signalling plans to tighten deal budgets. Analysts said deals with global partners had overtaken initial public offerings and pre-IPO fundraising as the main funding option for cash-starved Chinese biotech firms wanting to advance the discovery, clinical development and regulatory approval of new drugs. Yet questions remained over whether reliance on overseas licensing income was sustainable in the long run. “Chinese biotech assets remain highly cost-effective relative to global peers,” said Cui Cui, head of healthcare research for Asia at Jefferies, adding that if major pharmaceutical companies became more selective about their expenditures to acquire new drugs, “Chinese biotech assets may look even more attractive”. China’s cross-border deals for innovative drugs hit a record US$110 billion in the first half of the year, according to state news agency Xinhua. Eighty-one agreements were reached – about 80 per cent of the total reported for all of last year. “This is quite sizeable when compared to the IPO proceeds,” said Tony Ren, head of Asia healthcare research at Macquarie Capital. Healthcare and drug companies raised HK$14.1 billion (US$1.8 billion) via 11 first-half listings in Hong Kong, according to Deloitte, while six biotech and healthcare firms went public on mainland China’s A-share market, raising a combined 2.12 billion yuan, according to EY. According to the PharmCube data platform, primary market financing rounds in China’s innovative-drug sector were worth US$5.22 billion last year. Chinese firms can generate data quickly and their assets are not expensive in general Tony Ren, Macquarie Capital A handful of Chinese novel drug developers saw their earnings turn around in the first six months of the year, driven by out-licensing fees. Hong Kong- and Shanghai-listed biotech RemeGen said in a filing on Monday that it swung to a net profit attributable to shareholders of about 4.66 billion yuan (US$693.2 million) in the first half. In the corresponding period last year it made a loss of 449.57 million yuan. The company said the improvement was largely due to a January out-licensing deal with AbbVie for an experimental cancer drug. The agreement brought RemeGen an upfront payment plus potential milestone payments that could total up to US$5.6 billion. Shenzhen-listed CSPC Innovation Pharmaceutical posted a net profit of 1.26 billion yuan in the first half, according to its interim results, after recording a 2.75 million yuan loss a year earlier. It out-licensed eight drug candidates for obesity and weight-related conditions to AstraZeneca in January in a deal worth up to US$18.5 billion. Shanghai-listed Suzhou Zelgen Biopharmaceuticals recorded its first half-year profit – 640 million yuan – since its founding in 2009 after booking a US$100 million upfront payment from a licensing deal signed with AbbVie late last year for an experimental lung cancer treatment. However, multinational companies have been flagging caution over business development spending during their half-year earnings calls. AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot said in an earnings call last month that the company did not need “more business development to deliver” growth after 2030, assuming that “the aggregate probability of success across our pipeline of new products will be at least as we plan it”. Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla said this month that it had “placed the business development bets already … and we are executing on that”. He said the company’s remaining business development capacity stood at about US$6 billion. Ren, from Macquarie, said that while large-scale acquisitions were “out of favour”, smaller acquisitions and licensing “will most likely continue”. “Chinese firms can generate data quickly and their assets are not expensive in general,” he said. “I don’t sense multinationals scaling back their China licensing activities.” Cui, from Jefferies, said: “We expect full-year out-licensing activity [between Chinese biotech firms and their global partners] to continue to grow rapidly.” The Hang Seng SCHK Innovative Drug Select Index has risen about 4.25 per cent over the past month, outperforming Hong Kong’s benchmark Hang Seng Index. However, headwinds still loom for novel drug developers, with Yang Huang, head of China healthcare research at JPMorgan Chase, saying one of “the key overhangs” for first-half and second-quarter earnings was the intensification of the anti-corruption campaign targeting China’s medical sector since May. “Innovative products with clear clinical differentiation have remained relatively resilient, as prescription decisions are increasingly driven by clinical evidence,” he said.

title: Bitcoin tops US$80,000 for first time since May as US moves boost crypto
description: Washington’s buy-back efforts for US debt, cryptocurrency policy support credited for 25 per cent rally.
content: Bitcoin has broken above US$80,000 for the first time in three months, riding a broader rally in alternative assets triggered by Washington’s efforts to tame US bond yields. The world’s largest cryptocurrency traded above US$80,900 on Tuesday, jumping roughly 25 per cent over the past week and signalling an early recovery from a prolonged market slump. While bitcoin remains nearly 36 per cent below its record high of US$126,000 set in October, the sharp rebound has prompted observers to predict an end to this year’s crypto downturn that has seen the original crypto token shed nearly half of its value. Bitcoin’s price hike this week shows characteristics of an early bull market, according to Allen Ding, director of Hong Kong-based Bitfire Research, a unit of Bitfire Group, a Hong Kong-listed crypto asset management firm previously linked to the Chinese crypto exchange Huobi, now known as HTX. The sharp crypto rebound came after the US Treasury announced plans last week to ramp up the buy-backs of long-term US debts in an attempt to lower surging bond yields and boost the economy, pushing up broader investor appetite for hard or alternative riskier assets to hedge against the US dollar. Gold also traded at a three-month high of US$4,698 an ounce on Tuesday, extending a 5.1 per cent gain last week. The bitcoin rally also came amid supportive policy signals from the White House. US President Donald Trump last week urged Congress to pass the Clarity Act, a major crypto bill that aimed to offer clearer definitions on the structure of the digital asset market. The act stalled following debates on whether to allow stablecoin issuers to pay their users interest on their holdings. The cryptocurrency sector had been in nearly a year-long slumber before this week’s bitcoin rebound. Total crypto market capitalisation had fallen to US$2.1 trillion by the end of June, the lowest point since September 2024, and around 52 per cent below the industry’s October 2025 peak, according to a CoinGecko report published in July. June saw the steepest decline of the quarter, CoinGecko said, driven by factors including a hawkish stance by the US Federal Reserve, “flip-flopping” US-Iran tensions, a bitcoin sale by Strategy – the world’s largest so-called bitcoin treasury. Bitcoin’s latest rally, however, should not yet be treated as a confirmed trend, said Ding of Bitfire Research. A significant part of the bitcoin surge was driven by liquidations of overcrowded short positions rather than sustained spot buying, Ding said, citing spot demand as a key indicator for bitcoin momentum.

title: Review | Wakesurf Lovers movie review: Jeffrey Ngai, Renci Yeung defy haters in uneven sports drama
description: Full of beautiful bodies but paper-thin characters, Fung Chih-chiang’s film about wakesurfing and cybershaming drifts nowhere in particular.
content: 2.5/5 stars A sun-kissed sports film that rather awkwardly tackles wakesurfing and cyber-shaming in the same breath, Wakesurf Lovers offers a fluffy excuse to gaze at beautiful, muscled torsos – if you can squint past the paper-thin characters, their nebulous motivations and a romance that barely registers. A well-regarded screenwriter who has worked with Hong Kong film titans such as Stephen Chow Sing-chi, Fung Chih-chiang is notably less reliable as a writer-director of his own films, sometimes fumbling his offbeat, borderline refreshing premises and creating a prevailing sense of tonal whiplash instead. This pattern continues in Wakesurf Lovers. While it has the potential to be a romantic and inspirational comedy-drama about two loners drawn together by a water sport, the film also demoralises the viewer whenever it mires itself in the toxic realm of internet witch-hunts, depicted here with the most puerile imagery possible. Jeffrey Ngai Tsun-sang (Road to Vendetta) plays Rio Wu, a film school graduate and self-professed “slacker” who fails to draw eyeballs to his landscape photography portfolio online – despite his own blinding, albeit unacknowledged, good looks. Then he takes up trolling at the urging of his schoolmate Rizz (Henick Chou Han-ning). Latching onto a baseless accusation hurled by a social media influencer at surfing coach Charmaine (Renci Yeung Sz-wing), Wu swiftly finds viral success after making a slickly produced short-form video mocking her, inadvertently becoming the de facto leader of a digital smear campaign. When a guilty conscience compels Wu, a surfing novice, to join Charmaine’s one-to-one classes to face his victim, he discovers not only an earnest professional being hounded out of business, but also an obvious romantic target with seemingly no one to turn to except her loyal motorboat driver (musician KB, real name Kevin Li Kin-wang). Wakesurf Lovers is most likeable when it simply charts Wu’s enlightenment on the surfboard. It is far less successful when attempting to manufacture conflict via a contrived rivalry between Charmaine and Joe (a perfectly cast Kevin Chu Kam-yin), a star surfer who elicits spontaneous blushing and hooting from his female students. Fung clearly harbours a dim view of today’s mob mentality, but the scenes he devises – Wu surrounded by pedestrians all staring at the same scandalous posts on their phones, or clips from a soapbox channel run by a hate preacher known as The Judge (Chu Pak-him) – provoke more cringes than thoughts. While Wu and Charmaine’s scheme to reshape the online discourse with their wakesurfing displays makes sense to them, it remains implausible for the audience. With even their blossoming romance more implied than portrayed, the film washes up as a half-hearted moral lesson, drifting nowhere in particular. Want more articles like this? title: Hong Kong to revamp senior secondary science and maths curriculum
description: Authorities aim to encourage more students to take science subjects at the senior secondary level.
content:
Education authorities in Hong Kong will revamp the senior secondary school science and extended maths curriculum. It will provide additional syllabus options from the 2029-30 academic year in a bid to attract more students and nurture talent in the field.
The Education Bureau also said it had asked schools to actively encourage students interested in science and mathematics to take two or more science subjects.
The bureau said in a circular to schools on Monday that the revamp was aligned with the strategy in the nation’s 15th five-year plan to “invigorate the country through science and education” and supported Hong Kong’s development as an international innovation and technology centre.
Edith Tse Yuen-ching, principal assistant secretary for innovation technology education at the bureau, said in a blog post that the city was “strengthening the cultivation of innovation and technology talents to respond to the development needs of the country and Hong Kong”.
The circular said a draft of the updated curriculum and assessment for the science subjects – physics, chemistry and biology – had been released for consultation. It said the bureau would brief educators early next month before finalising the draft in the next academic year.
Schools have been invited to give their views on the revamp by the end of next month.
The bureau said the plan was intended to encourage more students to take science subjects at the senior secondary level, making it easier for them to move into science-related programmes at tertiary institutions.
“Schools are required to formulate relevant school-based plans in line with the enhancement measures, with a view to enabling more students to take multiple science and mathematics subjects concurrently at the senior secondary level,” it said.
The government set up an ad hoc committee to review the senior secondary science and maths subjects earlier this year, and the bureau accepted its recommendations.
One initiative is to divide the syllabuses of the three science subjects and extended maths into core and extended parts to cater to students of different abilities.
“[The new syllabuses will] enable more students to choose suitable subjects according to their abilities, as well as their interests and aspirations in innovation and technology,” the bureau said.
It added that schools should actively encourage students with potential to study two or more science and maths subjects starting in 2029-30.
In the past, senior secondary students were mainly divided into arts and science streams.
Since 2009, however, they have only been required to take at least two elective subjects on top of the core subjects of Chinese language, English language and mathematics, as well as citizenship and social development. The electives can be either arts or science subjects.
“This will establish a firm foundation for higher education research and innovation development,” the bureau said, adding that schools should provide information on study pathways, taster lessons and guidance in Form Three when students consider which subjects to study in the following three years.
It also encouraged schools to consider grouping students taking multiple science subjects into the same class to foster a stronger learning environment.
Over the years, some science professors at the city’s universities have complained that undergraduates have insufficient knowledge of science subjects.
The bureau said it would not set hard targets for the proportion of students studying multiple maths and science subjects, nor would it require all senior secondary pupils to study science subjects.
Lee Yi-ying, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Subsidised Secondary Schools Council and principal of Kowloon True Light School, said scientific knowledge was interconnected, and studying more than one science subject would not only help students in their future studies but also help nurture talent for the city.
She said schools might need to provide students with more counselling services to guide them in choosing subjects that would give them the best advantage when applying to university.

title: ‘An intrusion’: data centre fights test Southeast Asia’s AI ambitions
description: From Malaysia to the Philippines, residents have begun resisting power-hungry AI projects planned next to their homes.
content: Residents of Section 9 in Kota Damansara thought they knew what was coming to the vacant land opposite their homes. The site, beside a community forest in the Malaysian township, was expected to become a high street retail development. Instead, they learned that Petaling Jaya City Council (MBPJ) had received an application for two three-storey data centre blocks – part of the vast physical infrastructure now being built across Southeast Asia to support cloud computing and artificial intelligence. To governments, data centres promise foreign investment, digital jobs and a place in the fast-growing AI economy. To nearby residents, however, they can look very different: utility-hungry buildings raising questions over noise, water use, traffic and land suitability. By July 21, the council had received about 290 objections, and nine days later it announced that the developer’s consultant had withdrawn the application to reassess the site’s feasibility and development components. A similar scene played out this month in Oton, a municipality in the central Philippine province of Iloilo, where residents and farmers questioned a proposed 50-megawatt AI data centre during a public hearing. The proponent walked out, and local media reported two days later that the proposal had been withdrawn. Both disputes point to an emerging fault line in Southeast Asia’s race to build the infrastructure of the AI era: national governments want the investment but municipal authorities and residents are often left to decide where its power-hungry, water-dependent footprint should land. Wrong place, not wrong project In Kota Damansara, the 1.1-hectare (2.7-acre) site was zoned for “business and services”, while part of it was marked for transport as a road reserve under MBPJ’s plan. The council said the first notice did not follow its prescribed format and ordered corrections. A fresh objection period was later opened from July 21-27 for homeowners within 20 metres (65 feet). The file on the proposed data centre in Kota Damansara was now fully closed, the council said, although the landowner could still submit a new application for the same site or nearby land, subject to its proposed use, permitted zoning, impact studies and other planning factors. Aiman Zahry, a project director with Kuala Lumpur-based NRY Project Management – a project management consultancy and affiliate of NRY Architects – said the dispute arose less from the building itself than from the absence of an agreed strategy for locating such infrastructure. “Framing it as ‘residents vs data centres’ describes the symptom, not the problem,” Aiman said. The same facility beside an office tower would be infrastructure, he said: “Beside a landed house backing onto a community forest, it is an intrusion. Nothing about the building changes … Only the adjacency,.” Malaysia’s national planning guideline on data centres, approved and published in October 2024, allows data centres larger than one megavolt-ampere, or roughly equal to 1MW, in commercial and industrial zones. For new developments, the guideline calls for 50 metres between a data centre building and a residential lot boundary, with the buffer potentially comprising roads, landscaping or parking. The buffer can be waived if noise is no more than 5 decibels above the original level, but Aiman said the guideline did not specify who should measure it, where or over what period, or whether it must be checked again after operations began. He said the federal guideline contained “no schedule of technical submissions” requiring details such as connected load, water demand, acoustic assessment or cooling design. MBPJ told This Week in Asia the federal guideline was a key reference when assessing the proposal, alongside the city’s own local plan and inputs such as impact reports, comments from technical departments and other relevant agencies, and residents’ feedback. The council said data centre applications should first obtain approval from the Data Centre Task Force, a special national-level committee, before seeking further approval from local authorities. Kota Damansara resident Narindera Pall Singh said he and his fellow residents were not against development but “we are against inappropriate development in the wrong location”. The neighbourhood already had industrial zones, he said, and shop lots would have better served the community. Questions before answers In Oton, residents were brought into the process, but details remained unresolved. Local media reported that Daniel Stefan Robertsen, who presented himself as managing director of Norway Green Energy, proposed a 10-hectare, 50MW data centre in the municipality. A consultation hearing, held on August 14 and broadcast on the Oton council board’s Facebook page, broke down after a local resident questioned the project’s water use and treatment, with Robertsen walking out. That same day, Oton Vice-Mayor Jose Neil P. Olivares refuted claims the council board had endorsed the proposal, saying on social media the project remained at the consultation stage. Local media later reported that Robertsen had emailed the council to say the project would not proceed further in Oton. Metro Pacific Iloilo Water later clarified on social media that it had never entered into any agreement or discussion with Norway Green Energy regarding the proposed Oton data centre, and that the only letter of intent it had received was for a separate, preliminary facility proposed in Pavia, not Oton. Pavia Vice-Mayor Edsel Gerochi was reported by local outlet Panay News as saying the municipal council had received no proposal or communication from the company. The regional test On August 5, Thailand’s cabinet approved a draft regulation establishing a national data centre policy committee to coordinate policies and standards covering energy, water, land use, public safety and community impacts. Thailand’s Board of Investment subsequently said it would tighten its project-screening criteria to align with the committee’s direction, while authorities are also preparing national power and water maps to guide zoning and site selection. Aiman said none of the three countries had developed a system capable of preventing conflict before it emerged; instead, they intervened at different points of the planning and siting process. “Malaysia has the most substantive technical standards, including an alternative to prescribed buffer distances, but lacks mechanisms to verify compliance with their protective provisions,” Aiman said. By contrast, he said, the Philippines provided early consultation at the local level but imposed no equivalent technical baseline. Thailand, meanwhile, was beginning to address power, water, siting and public safety concerns through its new national policy committee, although this remained at the policy stage without an accompanying licensing regime. However, power was the main limiting factor for all three countries. “All three sit in developing economies where grid headroom is finite and the direction of demand is pushing costs up,” Aiman said. Governments needed to develop power generation, grid capacity and data centre policy as a single sequence before demand overwhelmed available infrastructure, he said. Narindera welcomed the data centre’s withdrawal from Kota Damansara but said this was not the end and residents would continue monitoring any new application. “As residents, we simply want development to be carried out in a proper and responsible manner, taking into consideration the surrounding community and existing approved planning,” Narindera said.

title: Debate star and physicist Guo Yanliang leaves a top European quantum lab for China
description: Renmin University recruit aims to probe complex quantum matter using ultracold atomic sandbox with lasers.
content: Guo Yanliang, a champion debater who honed his argumentation skills in international contests and on online variety shows, has left one of Europe’s top quantum laboratories to set up his own research group in Beijing. Guo, 33, says he sees scientific research as a debate between different opinions, which made him more compatible with China than Europe. This year, he returned to China to take a position as associate professor at Renmin University of China where he is building an ultracold atom experiment platform. While he has had papers published in Science and Nature and secured a spot on MIT Technology Review’s “Innovators Under 35 China” list, the physicist says he returned because China offered better support for his long‑term research goals. “The research environment here is more in line with my research characteristics,” he told DeepTech, the Chinese branch of MIT Technology Review, last month. In his future physics research, he aims to use lasers to cool atoms to near absolute zero and probe quantum matter that classical computers cannot simulate. The South China Morning Post has contacted Guo for comment.
