His academic career began in France after he was admitted to the physics department of Wuhan University in central China in 2011 and, through an internal selection, entered the Wuhan University + Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1 (2+2) bachelor’s programme. He received his master’s degree from the University of Paris-Saclay in 2017 and PhD from Sorbonne Paris Nord University in 2021. During this time, he not only confirmed his research direction – quantum physics – but also showcased his talent for debate. “In 2018, I took part in a Chinese-language debate competition held in France and won the championship; in 2019, I also took part in the recording of the sixth season of Qipashuo,” he told DeepTech. Qipashuo is a Chinese online debate variety show in which the country’s most skilled debaters compete on one stage, covering a wide range of social hot topics and entertainment issues. “Writing a paper is like debating,” he said in an interview with Micius Salon, a Chinese quantum science forum. “You gather evidence, anticipate objections and explain things from the audience’s perspective. “When an experiment goes wrong, the machine won’t speak, so you have to design experiments to highlight the contradictions. “I liken debate to a multiplier that amplifies my abilities, provided that my professional competence is strong enough; otherwise, it is meaningless.” In 2021, Guo moved to the University of Innsbruck in Austria as a postdoctoral researcher, where he has been since. His research there focused on ultracold atomic low-dimensional quantum gases, using laser-cooled atoms to create simplified, highly controllable quantum mini-worlds for his research. Within this sandbox, quantum physicists can reproduce complex quantum worlds that classical environments cannot compute, unveiling the physical secrets behind them. Quantum gas refers to placing a gas in a special state, such as ultracold, and then studying its properties. Last year, Guo discovered in simulations a quantum gas that refuses to heat. The study was published in Science, with the results opening a window for examining the physics of driven quantum matter and challenging long-standing assumptions. That year, his laboratory intentionally introduced a contaminant in the form of foreign particles into a quantum gas and analysed its momentum distribution. The research highlighted the value of ultracold quantum gases as a platform for studying complex quantum phenomena. This study was published in another top-tier journal, Nature, with Guo serving as a co-corresponding author. These two publications brought him academic acclaim, and he was promoted to senior postdoctoral researcher at the University of Innsbruck. Guo led the Quantum Science Austria discovery project, ranking first among the 10 recipients and was one of four people to receive Liechtenstein’s Scientific Research Award. This year, he was awarded funding under the Excellent Young Scientists (Overseas) programme. He has returned to the school of physics at Renmin University of China as an associate professor.

title: Philippine retailers tweak recipe to feed consumer demand for cheaper goods
description: Companies are switching ingredients, rethinking expansion and staggering price increases as inflation and a weak peso stress budgets.
content: From switching ingredients to staggering price increases, Philippine companies are rethinking strategies to cover rising costs without losing customers squeezed by inflation and a weak peso. The Philippines is now grappling with the second-weakest growth and fastest inflation among Southeast Asia’s economies after a corruption scandal weighed on confidence and the Iran war stoked consumer prices. The peso, Asia’s third-worst-performing currency this year, is also making imports more expensive. Shifts in consumer spending and higher credit costs are weighing on select names Juan Paolo Colet, managing director at China Bank Capital “Shifts in consumer spending and higher credit costs are weighing on select names across real estate, telecommunication, banking, and consumer discretionary,” said Juan Paolo Colet, managing director at China Bank Capital. Revenue pressures could intensify later this year if growth remained weak and inflation stayed high, Colet said, making it important for companies to strengthen operational efficiencies to better weather the headwinds. For now, restaurants are rethinking expansion, food makers are limiting price increases and telecoms companies are leaning on prepaid plans to support consumption. Food cuts Shakey’s Pizza Asia Ventures, which saw first-half profit fall by a third, said inflation and surging fuel prices weakened non-essential spending. Aside from promotions, the restaurant operator is slowing expansion and being more selective on investments, while restructuring its Peri-Peri chicken chain. Jollibee Foods fared better as customer visits improved from April to June despite higher prices. Still, the Asian fast food giant cut same-store sales forecast, profit growth and outlet openings. Price increases have also been selective, while keeping its cheaper Mix & Match meals for “those who are extremely price sensitive”. The company is on track with its 2.8 billion-peso (US$45 million) “cost containment” programme. Monde Nissin, the nation’s largest instant noodle maker, said it was switching to lower-cost ingredients without sacrificing consumers’ preference. At the same time, it is staggering price increases of 1 to 5 per cent by product. “We want to cushion the blow to our loyal consumers,” its chief financial officer, Jesse Teo, said. Century Pacific Food, which held prices steady for two years, has now raised them by 4 to 5 per cent and plans to do much smaller increases in the third quarter. “We see consumers being more intentional in making every purchase count,” said Dappy San Juan-Tecson, the tuna canner’s investor relations head. San Miguel Food and Beverage is controlling costs. “We are managing our costs carefully, adding capacity where demand is growing, and keeping our brands within reach,” chairman Ramon Ang said. Demand held up for its cheaper food lines in the first half. PLDT’s mobile unit Smart Communications raised selected prepaid packages to 109 pesos from 99 pesos while “adding more data and benefits so customers still see good value”, chief operating officer Butch Jimenez said, after the telco’s income drop. PLDT Home added more speed choices for customers seeking affordable broadband. Globe Telecom is using free service periods, speed upgrades and targeted discounts as consumers become more cautious. Offers include 30 days free, triple speeds on the same plan and 100 pesos off for selected customers. Philippine Seven may benefit from the squeeze. The 7-Eleven operator said as inflation pushes consumers to cheaper products and stores nearer home, was opening more branches in the provinces and leaning on ready-to-eat food and its own drinks, which it said were a “competitive differentiator and margin driver”.

title: Chinese woman, 31, faces lifelong walking issues after water-only diet cuts 20kg in weeks
description: Woman follows ‘bigu,’ a Taoist fasting technique based on the belief that it can lead to transcendence and immortality.
content: A woman from central China undertook a fasting regimen for half a month and lost 20kg, but ultimately suffered from a serious brain disorder from which she may never fully recover. The 31-year-old woman from Henan province, who wishes to remain anonymous, was recently reported by local media to have developed walking difficulties and memory deterioration after consuming nothing but water for 15 consecutive days. Standing at 160 cm tall, the woman, previously weighing 70kg, managed to shed 20kg in mere weeks due to her extreme diet. According to neurologist Sun Guifang from The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, the woman was diagnosed with Wernicke’s encephalopathy, a severe brain disorder resulting from a deficiency of essential vitamins and folic acid. This medical condition can lead to symptoms such as confusion, balance issues while walking, eye movement disorders, and memory impairment. Sun noted that the woman’s gait resembled that of a penguin, and he warned that this symptom might never be resolved. He attributed her condition to the extreme diet, emphasising that the body relies on regular meals for essential nutrients. Both dieting and fasting can pose serious risks to health. The woman informed Sun that she was practising “bigu,” a Taoist fasting technique rooted in the belief that one can achieve transcendence and immortality by subsisting solely on qi – the vital energy circulating throughout the universe. Bigu, which translates literally to “grain avoidance,” is believed to have originated before the Qin dynasty (221 BC–206 BC). While modern approaches to weight loss advocate for a diet rich in minimally processed foods, low in sugar and fat, and high in protein, many individuals still support bigu as an effective method for weight loss and detoxification. On one popular social media platform, the hashtag #bigu boasts 360 million views and has sparked 2.4 million discussions. Some individuals shared experiences of losing over 10kg after consuming only water and vitamin supplements for a month. Other posts encourage bigu practitioners to remember to intake qi by engaging in meditation in well-ventilated spaces. However, there are frequent reports indicating that bigu has led to serious health issues and even fatalities. In 2020, a 26-year-old man from Heilongjiang province in northeastern China died after drinking only water for 52 days, developing dementia-like symptoms just two days before his death. Last year, a woman in Zhejiang province lost 5kg after a week of consuming only water and an “energy pill,” but her fasting led to severe damage to her intestinal mucosa, resulting in a bacterial infection in her bloodstream. She also experienced life-threatening hypokalemia. There is a growing call to ban such content. One commenter stated: “Bigu is not traditional culture but an extremely unhealthy lifestyle.” Another remarked: “I find these individuals ruthless. I can’t even skip one meal in a day.”

title: Letters | Hong Kong needs clearer framework for handling high heat on work sites
description: Readers discuss work supervisors’ dilemma on extremely hot days, and Hongkong Post’s financial woes.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Public debate over Hong Kong’s recent heatwave has rightly focused on protecting frontline workers. However, one group remains largely absent from the discussion: site managers and project supervisors who carry responsibility for worker safety, project delivery and contractual compliance. Increasingly, they are being asked to balance those obligations without a clear framework. Recent criticism of Hong Kong’s Heat Stress at Work Warning system has focused on whether the Hong Kong Heat Index adequately reflects conditions faced by outdoor workers exposed to direct sunlight. Three former directors of the Hong Kong Observatory have argued that the internationally recognised Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) might be more suitable for assessing heat risks at open-air worksites. Regardless of which methodology ultimately prevails, the debate has exposed a gap between contractual requirements and operational reality. What should site managers do when local conditions appear unsafe but the official warning framework does not respond accordingly? The latest generation of construction contracts increasingly recognises extreme heat as a potential ground for extension of time claims. However, such relief is linked to the Labour Department’s Heat Stress at Work Warning system. That helps explain why the heat on August 9 raised concern. Despite temperatures reaching 39.8 degrees Celsius (103.6 Fahrenheit) in Sheung Shui, the Heat Stress at Work Warning remained at amber, the lowest level. Site managers who believed stronger precautions were warranted could have found themselves without the higher-level official trigger on which contractual protections depend. The core issue the Labour Department needs to address is what happens when a site manager believes conditions on the ground warrant stronger precautions, but the official trigger on which contractual protections depend is absent. In such circumstances, a supervisor who allows work to continue could later face questions about worker safety. A supervisor who suspends work could face questions about delays, costs and contractual entitlement. We cannot expect site supervisors to exercise discretion without a clear framework for situations where safety and contractual obligations collide. As the government reviews the Heat Stress at Work Warning system, attention should extend beyond warning thresholds alone. Site-level WBGT monitoring linked to the Smart Site Safety System could provide supervisors with transparent and objective data for safety decisions. While construction workers are at the centre of today’s debate, reforms should also protect workers whose jobs require prolonged exposure to Hong Kong’s extreme summer heat. Roy Ying, senior lecturer, School of Business, Hang Seng University of Hong Kong Hongkong Post needs a sustainable revamp When I was studying in North America, I was happiest when I received a letter from my girlfriend. The person I longed to see was Mr Postman whom I would ask, as the song goes, “Is there a letter in your bag for me?” Now the tide has turned. Globally, the practice of sending traditional mail has dwindled. This is also true of our city, where the postal service is a self-financed operation. Sadly, it has recorded a loss for eight consecutive years, and the government is bailing it out with HK$4.6 billion (US$587 million). Meanwhile, Hongkong Post has announced it will offer new employees, including about 200 people under probation, two-year agreements from September instead of permanent civil service contracts. The move is obviously a blow to those affected, and has alarmed the postal workers union. There is concern that this practice could spread to other civil service departments. Given that the volume of mail being handled has dropped drastically, it’s natural that the number of people hired would have to decline. Hongkong Post is now competing with private services. It seems ridiculous to me that a government department like the postal service can incur a loss of over HK$800 million in a single financial year. In the private sector, this would be cause for massive reform, perhaps even a management shuffle. Hongkong Post needs reform. The government shouldn’t have to inject funds into an organisation with a dismal financial outlook. It may be a long shot, but could Hongkong Post be merged with a profitable private entity? Randy Lee, Ma On Shan

title: Gang attack in Haiti leaves at least 47 dead as anger mounts over police failures
description: Raid on hillside town prompts community fury after police fail to prevent latest assault minutes from local station.
content: At least 47 people were killed and 22 more injured in an overnight gang raid on a neighbourhood overlooking Haiti’s capital of Port-au-Prince, the UN said on Monday, prompting anger over the lack of protection from repeated deadly attacks. The United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti ‌said estimates could still change. The hillside community of Kenscoff, in a strategic position overlooking routes into the capital, has suffered a dozen attacks by armed gangs since last year, forcing thousands to flee their homes. Powerful gangs under a broad alliance have for years cemented their influence over Haiti’s capital and expanded to nearby regions, despite attempts by foreign nations to reinforce the country’s outgunned police. Haitian rights group RNDDH estimated 30 to 40 people were killed and 15 to 20 wounded in the raid, which began around 10.30pm local time, but said it ⁠was difficult to assess a complete tally. Even as Haiti’s government decried a “heinous attack” and promised to reinforce security, residents demanded the local police chief step down, ‌saying officers failed to protect people killed just minutes from the police station. “Kenscoff will not be abandoned,” the prime minister’s office said on social media. “The government’s authority will be restored, without weakness and without delay.” Attacks in ‌Kenscoff over two months in early 2025 saw more than 260 people killed and 200 homes destroyed or set on ⁠fire, forcing 3,000 people to flee, according ⁠to UN estimates. Nearly a dozen more attacks have taken place since, including rapes, kidnapping, arson and livestock theft. “My family are victims,” said Coriolan Kendy, standing by his cousin’s body, lying ‌on the road in a bloodstained sheet. “People in Kenscoff are suffering and the government is to blame.” Another resident, Orisme, who did not share his last name, pleaded for the prime minister’s support. “We ‌live in humiliation ‌and they do nothing for us,” he said. Some residents said several dozen police had tried to rebuff the armed men during the night, ‌and some were injured. They added that they did not identify gang members among the dead. Local media said several houses were set on fire, ⁠including the home of Jean William Pape, a leading public health expert. “The police never gave up,” national police chief Vladimir Paraison told reporters during a ⁠visit to Kenscoff later in the day. Kenscoff overlooks routes into Petion-Ville – home to several embassies, upscale hotels and the temporary seat of government – as well as a major road from the capital into southern Haiti. The violence may deepen concerns over Haiti’s ability to hold an ‌election in December, its first in ‌a decade. Successive governments have repeatedly postponed elections as armed gangs have expanded their influence. The UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, which is mandated to help police fight gangs, aims to reach a capacity of more than 5,500 troops this autumn. A spokesperson did not immediately respond to questions on whether the troops were reinforcing Kenscoff security.

title: On This Day | Landslide kills 18 people in Hong Kong’s Sau Mau Ping – SCMP archive
description: The heavy rainfall-induced landslide occurred just four years after another fatal landslide in the area.
content: This article was first published on August 26, 1976. Tragedy hits Sau Mau Ping At least seven people, including four children, were killed by the landslide that hit Sau Mau Ping Estate yesterday (August 25, 1976). Yesterday’s disaster was only a few blocks away from a slope which slipped on June 18, 1972, killing 67 people. Fire Services teams, assisted by the Army, spent the night under search lights trying to locate people still not accounted for and thought to be buried under tons of mud which engulfed half the ground floor of Block 9 — housing about 1,200 people. The Governor, Sir Murray MacLehose, has ordered an urgent survey of slopes in the area. Sir Murray arrived at the estate a few hours after the disaster occurred to inspect the extent of the damage and to talk to rescue workers. He also talked to some of the affected families in the Estate Office, where about 200 people were temporarily accommodated. Sixteen people were injured in the slip. Six were in fair condition in the United Christian Hospital in Kun Tong last night. The others were treated and discharged. The slip occurred soon after 10 am and totally buried 10 flats at the rear of the ground floor. Tons of mud and debris also buried people in 10 shops at the front of the block. A housewife on the third floor said the noise of the slip was like thunder. “My bed was rocking for a while and I thought there was an earthquake,” Mrs Chow Kwan Kit-kam said. She added: “Babies in neighbouring flats were crying and I didn’t know what to do. “About 15 minutes after the slip, I heard whistling from the street and saw police using loudhailers to advise tenants to evacuate the block,” she said. “Fortunately, there was no panic among the residents and most of them were led to safety very quickly.” Mrs Chow said she also saw a man, with blood all over his face, running from a cafe crying for help. “He was quickly given treatment by rescue workers,” she said. The Divisional Fire Officer for East Kowloon, Mr Lee Kwok-choi, said 60 firemen and all East Kowloon’s rescue vehicles had been rushed to the scene. “We also brought in two rescue vehicles from Tsimshatsui and Hongkong,” he added. Mr Lee said because of traffic congestion, the vehicle from Tsimshatsui was forced to go to Hongkong through the Cross-Harbour Tunnel and then take the vehicular ferry to Kun Tong. He also said the rescue operation was hindered by continuous rain which he feared might cause another slip. The Chief Maintenance Surveyor of the Housing Department, Mr R.A. Bates, later inspected Block 9 and Block 15 and said they were structurally sound and safe. Tenants on the fourth floor and above in Block 9 and those on the second floor and above in Block 15 were advised not to return to their flats last night. Those whose flats were buried, and tenants of the two blocks who preferred to stay away were given temporary accommodation in a Kowloon Bay factory estate. The Social Welfare Department’s Emergency Relief Team distributed hot meals and other necessities to the affected families. Operators of about 30 food and hawking stalls in a single-storey market building on top of the slope were ordered to remove their possessions last night and a Housing Department spokesman said the market will be demolished very soon for safety reasons. Other precautionary measures included the emptying of a 1,000-gallon fuel tank close to the edge of the slope and the trimming back of the damaged slope. A spokesman for the Home Affairs Department last night praised the Mutual Aid Committees and kaifong members for their good work in rendering assistance to tenants affected by the landslide. As soon as news of the disaster reached them, members of MACs in Blocks 3, 10, 15 and 17 rushed to the scene and helped the injured and other tenants to move debris and mud. Some members escorted injured people to the United Christian Hospital in private cars before ambulances arrived. Others remained at the scene to help in evacuation work. “Many committee members and kaifongs continued to give a helping hand to their neighbours in the rain the whole day. They have vividly demonstrated good citizenship,” the spokesman said.

title: Singapore reports rise in home thefts, shoplifting and molestation
description: Total physical crime fell in the first half, but a 25 per cent spike in home thefts pushed key offences higher.
content: The number of theft cases in homes jumped by about 25 per cent in the first half of 2026, even as Singapore’s overall physical crime situation remained stable. There were 459 thefts in dwelling cases at residential premises in the first six months of the year, up 25.1 per cent from 367 cases over the same period in 2025, according to the Singapore police’s midyear crime brief for 2026. Theft in dwelling cases across all types of premises rose just slightly, by 0.6 per cent, from 726 cases in the first half of 2025 to 730 in the same period this year. Such cases accounted for about 7.1 per cent of all physical crime cases. “Theft in dwelling cases typically occurred in premises where belongings were left unsecured or unattended, creating opportunities for theft,” the police said. The increase was largely driven by incidents at residential premises involving people who had access to, or were familiar with, the premises. In light of this, they advised residents, co-tenants and property occupiers to store their personal belongings securely and to refrain from leaving valuables unattended in common spaces and shared facilities. From January to June, the number of physical crime cases in Singapore fell 0.4 per cent to 10,287, from 10,325 over the same period last year. Police described the physical crime situation as “stable”, with robbery and snatch theft recording 12 and nine cases respectively. The top three crimes of concern identified were outrage of modesty – also known as molestation – shop theft and theft in dwellings. Outrage of modesty cases rose by 3.1 per cent to 762 in the first half of 2026, up from 739 a year earlier, making up around 7.4 per cent of the total number of physical crime cases. More than half of the cases involved offenders known to their victims. Residential premises recorded 227 such cases, up from 172 a year earlier, while cases on the public transport network fell to 60 from 84. Cases at public entertainment outlets increased to 58 from 49. Outrage of modesty cases on public transport involving offenders unknown to their victims dropped by 25.7 per cent, from 74 to 55. “Notwithstanding the decrease, the police will continue to sustain enforcement, public education and community vigilance within the public transport network,” the police said, adding that these measures included enhanced police presence through joint patrols with public transport operators. To curb outrage of modesty cases committed at public entertainment outlets, the police said that they would continue to work closely with nightlife operators and stakeholders to strengthen crime prevention efforts and promote a safe environment for patrons. Food tops shoplifting list Shop theft cases rose 2.2 per cent from 2,050 to 2,095, accounting for about 20.4 per cent of the total number of physical crime cases. Commonly stolen items included food and beverages, personal care products, alcoholic drinks and apparel or accessories. Police said that shop theft remained one of the top offences committed by youths, with most of these cases occurring at supermarkets, convenience stores, mini-marts and personal care, health and wellness shops. They said that they were working with retailers and retail associations to strengthen outlet-level crime prevention measures, especially at premises with higher reported shop theft cases. “Retailers are encouraged to review store layouts, strengthen staff vigilance, adopt appropriate detection technologies and participate in the police’s Shop Theft Awareness for Retailers programme,” they said. The police added that they would continue to work with the Ministry of Education to educate students on crimes, including shop theft, through school talks, joint school advisories and other initiatives. “Singapore’s overall physical crime situation remained stable in the first half of 2026, and Singapore continues to be one of the safest places in the world,” said senior assistant commissioner of police Leon Chan, the director of the police’s Operations Department. “While there were some areas of concern, such as outrage of modesty, shop theft and theft in dwelling, we are encouraged by the reduction in outrage of modesty cases involving offenders unknown to victims within the public transport network,” Chan said. “Businesses, community partners and members of the public all have a role to play in preventing, deterring and detecting crime. Police will continue to work closely with our stakeholders and the community to keep Singapore safe and secure.” This article was first published by CNA

title: Gold strategy: how a Chinese vault network could bolster yuan’s role
description: By anchoring yuan trades to gold through Hong Kong and new global vaults, Beijing will add convertibility to its currency, report says.
content: China is building a global network of gold vaults and accelerating central bank reserve buying as part of efforts to promote the yuan’s role in international trade, according to an S&P Global Ratings report on Tuesday. Firms such as Zijin Mining – China’s largest gold processor – and Shandong Gold Mining were also expected to expand “faster than most of their global peers” after Beijing reclassified gold from a financial asset to a “strategic mineral” in 2025, the report said. “If you are trading in renminbi, there’s always a question as to how you are going to use the renminbi,” said Charles Chang, greater China lead for corporate ratings at S&P Global. “But if that renminbi is convertible to gold, then that’s a potentially different picture. Gold is tradeable. It is usable in a lot of places.” The country’s first offshore gold delivery vault was launched in Hong Kong last year under an agreement with the Shanghai Gold Exchange (SGE), with Bank of China (Hong Kong) as the designated operator. Alongside the launch, the SGE listed two new yuan-denominated gold contracts, which can be settled through either physical delivery or cash transfer. Other cities under consideration for China’s vault network included gold trading hubs such as Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Dubai, Riyadh and Moscow, the report said. “The network offers connectivity to the world’s largest physical gold market,” Chang said. “It could also attract countries looking to diversify, onshore or nearshore their gold storage to enhance control.” China’s gold holdings had grown slowly and remained smaller as a share of official reserves, S&P Global data showed. China’s gold reserves ranked sixth globally, behind those of the US, France, Italy, Germany and Russia, a position that Chang said pointed to “sentiment for further build-up through purchases or production” as international tensions and conflicts continued to escalate. As of the end of July, China’s gold reserves stood at 76.08 million ounces, marking the 21st consecutive month of accumulation. Last year, nine of the country’s government departments, including China’s top economic planning agency, the National Development and Reform Commission, published an industrial outline to improve the gold industry’s security, capacity, operations, innovation, scale and mine resources, according to the report. Backed by government support and strong domestic demand for gold bars and coins, Chinese gold miners have accelerated overseas mergers and acquisitions. Zijin Gold International, a unit of Zijin Mining, acquired another two mines in the past year. The two facilities in Ghana and Kazakhstan have already become profitable, helping drive the company’s first-half net profit up 179 per cent year on year to US$1.45 billion in 2026. It terminated a planned takeover of Canada’s Allied Gold in late July, instead taking a 9.2 per cent minority stake for about US$295 million, amid Beijing’s tightening scrutiny of outbound overseas investments.

title: Hottest ocean temperature recorded as ‘super’ El Nino forms
description: Average surface waters reached 21.1 degrees Celsius, months ahead of when peak global ocean temperatures typically occur.
content: Scientists have recorded the highest temperature ever measured in the world’s oceans, as climate change combines with a powerful El Nino in the tropical Pacific. The global average sea-surface temperature hit a record 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 Fahrenheit) on August 22, according to Europe’s Earth observation agency Copernicus, which has been tracking the metric daily since 1979. The previous single-day record of 21.09 degrees was measured in March 2024. “El Nino is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming,” said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus’ European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. “As ocean temperatures continue to rise, the risks to marine ecosystems and coastal communities also increase,” she said. Higher ocean temperatures contribute to sea level rise and increase the chance of extreme weather events, as warmer water transfers more heat and moisture to the atmosphere, intensifying storms and heat on land. Warmer oceans also have a reduced capacity to absorb carbon dioxide. Record temperatures have already been measured in isolated areas of the world’s oceans including the western Mediterranean Sea as well as at the Earth’s poles, driven mainly by man-made climate change. Copernicus expects the trend to continue, with ocean temperatures now being supercharged by El Nino. The August record is particularly worrying because global ocean temperatures are typically highest in March and April, after the Austral summer, Copernicus said. Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at Britain’s national weather agency, told the BBC on Friday: “We are expecting the biggest El Nino for over a century, peaking at something over 3 degrees - that is unheard of in modern climate records”. This means Pacific water would heat up more than 3 degrees above the norm in the coming months. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Hong Kong to revamp senior secondary science and maths curriculum from 2029-30
description: Authorities aim to encourage more students to take science subjects at the senior secondary level.
content: Hong Kong’s education authorities will revamp the senior secondary school science and extended maths curriculum by providing additional syllabus options from the 2029-30 academic year, in a bid to attract more students and nurture talent in the field. The Education Bureau also said it had asked schools to actively encourage students interested in science and mathematics to take two or more science subjects to create a synergistic effect. The bureau said in a circular to schools on Monday that the revamp was aligned with the strategy in the nation’s 15th five-year plan to “invigorate the country through science and education” and supported Hong Kong’s development as an international innovation and technology centre. Edith Tse Yuen-ching, principal assistant secretary for innovation technology education at the bureau, said in a blog post that the city was “strengthening the cultivation of innovation and technology talents to respond to the development needs of the country and Hong Kong”. The circular said a draft of the updated curriculum and assessment for the science subjects – physics, chemistry and biology – had been released for consultation. It said the bureau would brief educators early next month before finalising the draft in the next academic year. Schools have been invited to give their views on the revamp by the end of next month. The bureau said the plan was intended to encourage more students to take science subjects at the senior secondary level, making it easier for them to move into science-related programmes at tertiary institutions. “Schools are required to formulate relevant school-based plans in line with the enhancement measures, with a view to enabling more students to take multiple science and mathematics subjects concurrently at the senior secondary level,” it said. The government set up an ad hoc committee to review the senior secondary science and maths subjects earlier this year, and the bureau accepted its recommendations. One initiative is to divide the syllabuses of the three science subjects and extended maths into core and extended parts to cater to students of different abilities. “[The new syllabuses will] enable more students to choose suitable subjects according to their abilities, as well as their interests and aspirations in innovation and technology,” the bureau said. It added that schools should actively encourage students with potential to study two or more science and maths subjects starting in 2029-30. In the past, senior secondary students were mainly divided into arts and science streams. Since 2009, however, they have only been required to take at least two elective subjects on top of the core subjects of Chinese language, English language and mathematics, as well as citizenship and social development. The electives can be either arts or science subjects. “This will establish a firm foundation for higher education research and innovation development,” the bureau said, adding that schools should provide information on study pathways, taster lessons and guidance in Form Three when students consider which subjects to study in the following three years. It also encouraged schools to consider grouping students taking multiple science subjects into the same class to foster a stronger learning environment. Over the years, some science professors at the city’s universities have complained that undergraduates have insufficient knowledge of science subjects. The bureau said it would not set hard targets for the proportion of students studying multiple maths and science subjects, nor would it require all senior secondary pupils to study science subjects. Lee Yi-ying, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Subsidised Secondary Schools Council and principal of Kowloon True Light School, said scientific knowledge was interconnected, and studying more than one science subject would not only help students in their future studies but also help nurture talent for the city. She said schools might need to provide students with more counselling services to guide them in choosing subjects that would give them the best advantage when applying to university.

title: Meet Luana Lopes Lara, the world’s youngest self-made woman billionaire and Kalshi’s co-founder
description: Having traded professional ballet for MIT, the Brazilian entrepreneur took over the Forbes wealth title from Lucy Guo and Taylor Swift.
content: Prediction platform Kalshi, which allows users to bet on real-life events such as sports games, entertainment awards and even political elections, was sued by the state of New York in late July. Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, alleged that the platform, valued at US$22 billion in May, facilitated gambling addiction, and the site’s offerings are “quintessentially gambling”. Washington state has also ordered Kalshi to shut down. While prediction markets have been on the rise, their future is now uncertain due to the recent legal woes. Luana Lopes Lara, who co-founded Kalshi with Tarek Mansour in 2018, was named by Forbes in December 2025 as the youngest self-made woman billionaire, surpassing Scale AI co-founder Lucy Guo and global pop superstar Taylor Swift. Lopes Lara’s net worth, as of August 21, stands at US$2.6 billion, according to Forbes. So, who is the entrepreneur behind the prediction market platform that is making headlines? Here’s what we know. What is Luana Lopes Lara’s background? Luana Lopes Lara was born in May 1996 in Brazil to an electrical engineer father and a mathematics teacher mother. She has an older sister named Cristiana, who received her PhD from Carnegie Mellon University and is currently a principal research scientist at Amazon. She graduated from MIT Lopes Lara has always had a profound interest in mathematics. During her secondary school years, she took part in academic competitions, winning gold at the Brazilian Astronomy Olympiad and bronze at the Santa Catarina Mathematics Olympiad. In 2018, she graduated with a bachelor’s degree in computer science and engineering from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where she met Mansour. Lopes Lara told The Free Press in January this year that she never thought about the difficulty of becoming a female founder while she was studying at MIT. “I’ve always had such big goals,” she said. Lopes Lara and Mansour were classmates and both ended up interning at trading firm Five Rings Capital, where they came up with the idea for Kalshi on their walks home. The pair made the Forbes 30 Under 30 list in 2022, and have continued to grow their platform since launching it in 2018. She was a professional ballerina Before embarking on the path at MIT that ultimately led her to become a billionaire, Lopes Lara grew up training as a ballerina. She spent three years at the School of the Bolshoi Theater in Joinville, Santa Catarina – around 372km from Rio de Janeiro, where her family was based. The dancer endured extreme conditions, telling Forbes that teachers would hold lit cigarettes under her thigh while keeping her leg extended to test her endurance, and rival dancers would hide glass shards in each other’s shoes to gain an edge. After graduating from secondary school in 2013, she became a professional ballerina, performing Swan Lake for nine months in Salzburg, Austria. She initially thought that she would be able to juggle MIT and ballet, but decided to quit dancing when she realised that she was losing her form after starting her university education. “I decided to go all in on school and completely stop ballet, because otherwise it would consume my mind,” she told The Free Press. “And it was better for me to stop with memories of being good than to see myself slowly decay and fade away.” Who is Luana Lopes Lara married to? 6 years with the love of my life today. I truly believe the most important thing in life is finding your soulmate. Once you do, everything else falls into place. I’m obsessed with you, meu amor. Here’s to the next 6! (factorial, not exclamation) ♥️ — Luana Lopes Lara (@luanalopeslara) July 24, 2026 Lopes Lara has been in a relationship for six years, which she celebrated on her X account in July. “6 years with the love of my life today,” she wrote. “I truly believe the most important thing in life is finding your soulmate. Once you do, everything else falls into place.” Lopes Lara keeps her personal life highly private, only occasionally sharing updates on social media. Although she has never disclosed the identity of her partner, she did share that she got married in May this year.

title: 5 literary classics to dive into this summer, from The Great Gatsby to Dandelion Wine
description: These timeless novels are perfect for a beach read near sand and sea or anywhere under the sun.
content:
There’s nothing quite like sinking into an outdoor chair and getting lost in a great book. While “beach reads” are usually associated with light romances or fast-paced thrillers, summer is also an ideal time to dive into a few literary classics.
Whether you are craving a sun-drenched coastal drama, a high-stakes binge or a comforting, nostalgic read, these five timeless tales deserve a spot in your beach bag this season.
This is the ultimate summer binge-read – a page-turner packed with vengeance, escape, a search for treasure and daring adventure.
The historical fiction follows Edmond Dantès, who is on the cusp of a promising life: newly promoted to captain and engaged to the love of his life.
But his future vanishes overnight when jealous rivals falsely accuse him of treason, sending him to a brutal island prison without a trial.
This beloved 1908 classic is pure comfort, guaranteed to warm your heart on a rainy summer day. The story follows the charmingly chaotic adventures of Anne Shirley, an 11-year-old redheaded orphan girl mistakenly sent to live with Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert. The middle-aged siblings intended to adopt a boy to help them on their farm in the fictional town of Avonlea on the scenic, real-life Prince Edward Island in Canada.
Despite the mix-up, Anne – a fiercely imaginative, free-spirited child – quickly steals their hearts. Brimming with sunshine and nostalgia, Anne of Green Gables is a delightful story about finding belonging in the unlikeliest of places.
If you are looking for delicious writing and sweltering drama, check out this timeless book that explores obsession, class, wealth and desperation. And at under 200 pages, it is an ideal quick weekend read.
Set during the Jazz Age on Long Island, near New York City, the story follows narrator Nick Carraway as he is drawn into the world of his enigmatic neighbour, Jay Gatsby.
The mysterious millionaire is famous for throwing lavish weekend parties for complete strangers, but the grand spectacles exist solely for Daisy Buchanan, the woman he loved and lost. Beneath the glamour and glitz, the novel exposes the raw, destructive weight of social pretence.
Over the course of one magical summer in the US state of Illinois in 1928, 12-year-old Douglas Spaulding comes to two staggering realisations: he is alive, and, one day, he will die.
Through new tennis shoes, lawnmowers and bottles of dandelion wine, Bradbury turns small-town nostalgia into an intoxicating meditation on youth, memory and the bittersweet passage of time. It is, quite simply, the ultimate love letter to summer.
Steinbeck’s lush depictions of the sun-baked Salinas Valley in the US state of California create an unforgettable sense of place. Heavy, philosophical and deeply moving, Steinbeck – who also penned Of Mice and Men and The Grapes of Wrath – considered this sweeping masterpiece his magnum opus.
The multi-generational saga reimagines the biblical story of Cain and Abel through two intertwined families, the Trasks and the Hamiltons. At its core lies a bitter rivalry between brothers, a chilling matriarch driven by dark impulses and the powerful concept of “timshel”. At its centre is free will, a reminder that every human possesses the ultimate power to choose good over evil, regardless of their past or inheritance.

title: Netanyahu says Iran tried to kill one of his sons
description: Israeli leader gives no details on which son was targeted, though elder son Yair has lived under state protection in Miami.
content: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Monday that Iran had attempted to assassinate one of his two sons, without offering further details. “Something incredible happened: Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to kill one of my sons,” Netanyahu said during a phone interview with Israel’s Channel 14. The claim came during a discussion about reports that the Shin Bet domestic security agency had declined to provide a security detail for Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is running neck and neck with Netanyahu ahead of elections on October 27. Netanyahu voiced support for around-the-clock protection for Eisenkot, saying it was “not a luxury”. “Without that, (the Iranians) will succeed,” he said. Netanyahu has two sons and a daughter. It remains unclear which of his sons was allegedly targeted. His elder son, Yair, 35, has spent extended periods in Miami since early 2024, reportedly under Shin Bet protection. His stay in the United States has attracted controversy in Israel over the cost to taxpayers of providing security, while some residents in south Florida have expressed concern that his presence could make the area a target for attacks by Israel’s enemies. Shortly after Netanyahu’s remarks became public on Monday, prominent Israeli journalist Amit Segal wrote on his Telegram channel that the alleged assassination attempt had been known for “months” but was subject to a gag order. Israel killed Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in the opening salvo of US-Israeli strikes on February 28, along with some of his family members. His son Mojtaba, one of Khamenei’s six children, was named the new supreme leader a week later. In a message read out on his behalf on state TV, Mojtaba Khamenei said that in addition to his father, he had lost his wife, his sister, her child and his brother-in-law. Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since his appointment, and was reportedly wounded in the same strikes that killed his father. In another message attributed to him and published on the occasion of funeral ceremonies for his father, the new leader pledged to “avenge the blood” of Ali Khamenei.

title: South Korea pledges to help Trump revive talks with North Korea’s Kim
description: Trump’s recent olive branch to Kim and criticism ‌of Seoul have raised concerns of a strain on long-standing Asian alliances.
content: South Korea and the US agreed to maintain close coordination on efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea, days after Pyongyang rebuffed President Donald Trump’s overtures and launched a barrage of short-range ballistic missiles. South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a phone call late on Monday that Seoul would work to ensure that Trump’s recent messages lead to renewed US-North Korea discussions and peace on the Korean peninsula, Seoul’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Tuesday. The US State Department issued only ‌a brief statement on the phone call, which comes at a period of tension between the allies. Trump recently announced a scaling back of joint military exercises and praised nuclear-armed North Korea, while saying that Seoul had not helped his efforts to try to denuclearise Iran. The State Department said Rubio and Cho discussed “a range of issues in the US-ROK Alliance”, referring to South Korea by the initials of its official name, the Republic of Korea. “The secretary noted the need for the two countries to remain ⁠in close coordination on matters that are integral to the alliance,” it added. In its statement, South Korea’s Foreign ‌Ministry did not mention whether the diplomats reaffirmed their usual commitment to North Korea’s denuclearisation, despite their emphasis on the importance of cooperation on the North Korean nuclear issue. “The minister and secretary agreed to continue close communication and ‌cooperation between South Korea and the US for peace on the Korean peninsula and the resolution of North Korea’s nuclear ⁠issue while maintaining a solid ⁠combined defence posture,” Yonhap quoted the ministry release as saying. Trump’s olive branch to North Korea’s Kim Jong-un last week, coupled with ‌his criticism ‌of Seoul, has raised concern among analysts that his unpredictability could strain alliances that have long maintained peace in Asia. Cho said last week ‌that Trump’s order to curb the military drills appeared aimed in part at pressuring Seoul to support US efforts in the Iran war, ⁠alongside other unresolved issues such as investment. He said one potential source of friction could be South Korea’s pledge to invest US$350 billion in the United ⁠States under a trade deal signed last year. Seoul has yet to announce details of the investment plan, although Cho said Washington had sent Seoul a proposal outlining projects that could be considered. According to the statement, the two sides ‌agreed to work towards “mutually beneficial” outcomes ‌on various pending issues – including tariffs, investment and security cooperation. Cho underscored the Seoul government’s commitment to making substantive contributions to help restore free passage through the Strait of Hormuz, while noting the active leadership of Trump and the US in addressing the Middle East issue. He and Rubio also agreed to meet in person in the near future, the ministry said. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Just Saying | Reflections of a reformed grammar Nazi
description: The evolution of English is an unstoppable force and resisting its ‘dumbing down’ may be futile.
content: “Nothing bad can happen. It can only good happen.” Donald J. Trump It would be easy to write off the regular word salads of America’s 47th president as the increasingly incoherent ramblings of an elderly man in obvious mental and physical decline. However, one can also argue that Trump’s seemingly dyslexic struggles with the English language reflect a deliberate disregard for grammar rules that resonates with his support base. It’s the level of language that up to half of Americans happily use and identify with, if you think about it. Laugh if you will at his limited vocabulary, disrespect for formal syntax and contempt for punctuation, but they have never been detrimental to getting his message across as an effective public speaker and communicator. His very lack of linguistic sophistication – simple words, short sentences, constant repetition, blunt delivery – makes maximum impact with minimum polish, grammar rules and hoity-toity talk be damned. Trump’s dumbing down of the language is but a microcosm of a global shift towards hyper-simplified English usage, stripped bare of formalities and tuned to resonate on digital platforms. All without the encumbrance of archaic or arbitrary rules and the rigid structure that we are expected to adhere to without even remembering why we have to in the first place. “Dumbing down” is one way of looking at it, but in the 1,500-year history of the international lingua franca, it can also be seen as a natural and necessary evolution underpinned by tech-driven advances transforming how we convey and exchange or disseminate information, feelings and ideas. If this evolution is enabling faster and more effective communication, further democratising the vast usage of the language across all countries and cultures, does form really matter as much as function? All this may sound like blasphemous talk for an editor tasked with advising on and overseeing the correct and appropriate use of English – formal British English – at the South China Morning Post. As the crusty old curmudgeon entrusted by our top editors with enforcing a house style, let me assure everyone that these gentle musings in no way reflect any weakening of resolve in that regard. On the contrary, we will continue to insist on consistency to prevent chaos. But here’s the difference: instead of the old “don’t do that, it’s wrong”, the new message to reinforce house style is more like “it may not be wrong per se but that’s not how we do it here”. What it entails overall is a dialling down of the grammar Nazi in people like me. We can get triggered all we want by the increasing irrelevance of rules governing sentence structure, and harrumph all we like at dictionaries embracing and trumpeting seemingly silly new words, but the language is moving on relentlessly with or without us. Take the phrase “it will likely happen” for example: there was a time when it was clearly considered an unacceptable distortion of “it is likely to happen”. Like it or not, “likely” has somehow become a stand-alone adverb and a substitute for “probably” in what is now a widely accepted and even preferred short cut. Speaking of short cuts, I only found out recently that the word “mob” is an abbreviation of the Latin mobile vulgus, meaning “fickle crowd”. There was apparently an intellectual and literary elite backlash against fashionable youth and trendy playwrights who started using the truncated term in the late 1600s. The old guard lost and the “mob” endured. In HBO’s gritty Western series, Deadwood, English usage is an exhilarating combination of mining camp slang, biblical articulation and modern-day profanity stitched together with a poetic rhythm that channels Shakespearean dialogue. In one memorable scene (Season 1, Episode 6) that would be relevant to this article, newspaper editor A.W. Merrick discusses plans to publish an announcement on the free distribution of a smallpox vaccine amid a camp outbreak. One of the key protagonists, villainous saloon keeper Al Swearengen, objects to the use of lofty English to communicate effectively with the “hoopleheads” who form their target audience. Merrick: “The vaccine will be distributed gratis.” Swearengen: “Free gratis.” Merrick: “Free gratis is a redundancy.” Swearengen: “Then leave gratis out.” I inherited my pedantry in correct English usage from one Miss Patricia Russell, a beloved teacher and strict grammarian who encouraged me in school to pursue a career with the language, as she could already see back then that science and mathematics were not my forte. She is sadly no longer with us, but I sometimes wonder how she would feel about my grudging acceptance, and even growing adoption, of contemporary slang and trending jargon in my published work. I like to think she would understand that when it comes to extremely handy phrases such as “I know, right” and “yeah, right”, I daresay there is no classical or academic combination of words that can better express the sentiment or convey the meaning behind them, no matter how clever and learned the writer or speaker. There are, of course, limits to what I can and will tolerate, because being dynamic and adaptable with language is one thing, but outright illiteracy is something else. I am horrified that so many people online these days are unable to distinguish between elementary words such as “loose” and “lose”, or “their” and “there”, or, even worse, “its” and “it’s”. The last example presents an eternal struggle for humanity – the inability to grasp the simple concept that “it’s” can only be a contraction for “it is” and hence should be impossible to confuse with the possessive “its”. And yet here we are, go figure. Other than that, given the way English continues to evolve, who knows, perhaps indeed it can only good happen for the future of human communication.

title: Australia’s top music charts ban AI songs to protect human artists
description: Under the new rules, music must be ‘substantially human made’ but recordings that use AI in a supporting role are still eligible.
content: Music made by artificial intelligence will be banned from Australia’s top charts under new guidelines aimed at protecting “the human nature of artistry”, an industry body said on Tuesday. Under new rules in force from Friday, music must be “substantially human made” to be eligible for the charts, the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) said. “Wholly AI-generated tracks will not be eligible for the ARIA Charts,” the group said. It said its charts would exclude songs that use AI “to generate the entirety or the primary portion of the creative elements”. But “recordings that use generative AI in a supporting role remain eligible”, it added. The move follows growing concern in the music industry over a surge in AI-generated music hitting the airwaves. In July, a cover of Madonna’s “Like a Prayer”, which soared to the top of the charts in Australia, drew scrutiny after it was revealed to have used AI-generated vocals and drums. It peaked at No 2 on the Australian Record Industry Association’s top 20 Australian singles chart in May, and remained in fourth place on Tuesday. Streaming giant Spotify has said it will launch a new “AI Persona” badge clearly identifying content producers that are AI generated and not real people. More than one-third of new uploads to Apple Music are entirely created with AI, a platform executive told Billboard this year. That month several major music industry organisations unveiled a labelling system for content created with generative AI that they would like to see widely adopted. “These changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is – to say the least – a rapidly developing space,” ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd said. “The ARIA Charts will always remain a transparent measurement of the music Australia consumes, but a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent,” she said. The Australian rules are in step with new principles released in July by the London-based International Federation of the Phonographic Industry. The federation represents the recording industry worldwide. The international guidelines state that to qualify for official music charts, a track must be “substantially human made”. Sydney Conservatorium of Music composer and lecturer Alexis Weaver told Australian Broadcasting Corporation the debate around AI in music was “exceptionally fraught and very emotional for a lot of musicians and so everyone will have a different opinion”. Weaver applauded ARIA’s move as a “wonderful step forward” that sent a message ARIA wanted to “prioritise and value human creativity”. “It can be quite hard to avoid AI tools in the current landscape,” Weaver said. “There is a way to use it while you’re still steering the ship and making the main creative choices.” Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: US Treasury bond buy-back reinforces gold debasement trade as Jackson Hole meeting looms
description: Treasury buy-backs bolster gold’s rally as investors await US Federal Reserve’s annual meeting at Jackson Hole.
content: The US Treasury’s decision to boost its buy-backs of long-maturity bonds is strengthening the debasement trade on gold, as investment banks turn more upbeat on the precious metal before the Federal Reserve’s annual meeting in Jackson Hole. Gold traded at a three-month high of US$4,698 an ounce on Tuesday, extending a 5.1 per cent gain last week after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the repurchase programme, which he said was likely to surpass US$4 billion. The announcement renewed immediate concerns about the fiscal stress on Washington and the erosion of the purchasing power of the US dollar, which benefits gold as an alternative to fiat currencies. Morgan Stanley predicted that gold prices would rise to US$5,000 by 2027, while Citigroup raised the three-month price target for the metal to US$4,800 from US$4,500. Dutch bank ING said that gold might face a risk of further upside throughout the year. A dovish tone by Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh at the coming Jackson Hole symposium later this week would add more impetus to bullion, which moves inversely with interest rates. “Gold’s resilience suggests that the rally is not simply a response to lower yields,” said Ewa Manthey, a commodity strategist at ING. “The prospect of larger Treasury buy-backs has refocused attention on government borrowing and fiscal credibility. It has also revived concerns about currency debasement, reinforcing gold’s appeal as a store of value,” she added. While the Treasury’s buy-back programme is much smaller in size than the Fed’s quantitative easing, it signalled that the Trump administration was not serious about capping new bond issuance or reining in the federal debt that had already topped US$40 trillion for the first time in history, according to analysts. The debasement trade has kept demand for gold buoyant over the past few years, with investors boosting exposure to the metal in their portfolios to diversify away from Treasuries and the US dollar. Gold has been on a roller-coaster ride this year. The oil shock induced by the US-Iran war reversed an uptrend by stoking inflation concerns, leading to a more than 30 per cent decline after the unwinding of speculative positions. It recovered part of the loss, with about a 20 per cent rebound from a July low after the de-escalation of Middle East tensions and softer US economic data reduced fears of an immediate interest-rate increase. Gold has risen about 8 per cent this year. Warsh’s changing approach to market communication would also support gold, as the shift was set to cloud the monetary outlook and increase volatility across assets, according to private bank J. Safra Sarasin Group. “Furthermore, Kevin Warsh’s frequent phone calls with President Trump are increasingly under scrutiny,” said Claudio Wewel, a strategist at the bank. “With markets weighing the risks of political influence on monetary policymaking, concerns about Fed independence are on the rise and make a revival of the dollar debasement trade more likely again.” Gold would probably consolidate between a range of US$4,575 and US$4,585 an ounce in the near term before a new bout of gains resumes, according to Stephen Innes, a managing partner at SPI Asset Management. “Gold rarely travels this far without stopping to shake a few passengers from the carriage, and early profit-taking will now collide with traders waiting to buy the dip,” he said. “The bullish argument remains rooted in fiscal anxiety and financial repression, but even strong trends need to breathe.”

title: Want to keep a big dog in Hong Kong? Experts share what you should know
description: Concerns about responsible handling of big dogs raised after attacks last week.
content: Heat, humidity and crowded living spaces could pose challenges for Hongkongers hoping to keep large or aggressive dogs as pets, experts have said, urging potential owners to consider the needs of such animals before deciding to house them. They issued the warning after a woman and two small canines were mauled in two separate attacks last week. The woman was found collapsed in Ping Yeung Tsuen, hours after she was attacked at a dog training centre by a canine suspected of being a mixed-breed fighting dog. She was certified dead at the scene. The smaller dogs were mauled to death in Yuen Long by an unleashed 60kg (132lbs) mastiff-type canine earlier that week. Discussing the importance of correctly caring for big dogs, Lau Yun-yu, chairman of the Hong Kong Society for Pet Nutrition, said large canines, particularly those with thick coats, could face greater challenges in Hong Kong’s hot and humid climate. “Dogs rely primarily on evaporative cooling through panting rather than sweating,” he said, adding that sustained high humidity could significantly reduce their ability to cool themselves. Lau said heat-related risks could increase when temperatures reached about 24 to 26 degrees Celsius (75.2 to 78.8 Fahrenheit), particularly when combined with high relative humidity. “Giant, double-coated dogs face significant thermal strain,” he noted, referring to the condition when high environmental heat exceeds the animals’ ability to cool down. The society chairman said owners needed to be particularly vigilant during Hong Kong’s hot and humid summers. He advised owners of large dogs to pay close attention to cooling measures, ensure access to well-ventilated and cooler spaces, provide sufficient water and schedule outdoor activities during cooler times of the day. The experts warned that Hong Kong’s highly urbanised environment could be unsuitable for large breeds with backgrounds as working dogs, such as guarding livestock or property. Bowie Leung, spokeswoman for the Caucasian Ovcharka & Tibetan Mastiff Club Hong Kong, said such dogs were bred for a very different purpose from modern companion canines. “Their job was to protect the flock from wolves and bears,” she said. “These dogs need a lot of energy, and they need a lot of work to release that energy.” Leung said that given dogs were not commonly needed for such roles in Hong Kong, prospective owners needed to consider whether they could ensure the animals had sufficient activity and space. Lau said owners had to also ensure that their dogs received enough exercise, mental stimulation and consistent care in Hong Kong’s generally crowded living environment. Large dogs could still adapt to living in Hong Kong despite limited living space, but this placed greater demands on owners, particularly in the city’s heat and humidity, he said. Leung warned that some potential owners’ lack of understanding about their dogs could cause the animals’ needs to be underestimated before a decision was made to bring them home. She said some people were attracted to large dogs because they were seen as powerful and loyal protectors. “More than 10 or 20 years ago, breeds such as Tibetan mastiffs, Caucasian ovcharkas and Spanish mastiffs were very popular,” she said. “Many people bought them because they were described as very big, powerful, protective and loyal.” Such dogs were often kept as guard dogs for warehouses, farms or parking areas in rural parts of Hong Kong. But Leung said some owners focused on the image of these dogs without fully understanding what their upkeep involved, such as failing to realise how much the animals would grow. “Some people see them when they are puppies, and they are very cute,” she said. “But they do not think about how big they will become when they grow up, or whether they can actually control them.” She added that when owners could no longer manage large dogs, some animals ended up being confined for long periods or losing the chance to live in a suitable environment. Ivy Tse Yuen-yee, director of animal shelter House of Joy and Mercy, said large dogs could also face difficulties once they entered the rescue system. She said large dogs needed more space, exercise and suitable homes, making them harder to rehome than smaller dogs. Tse noted that some canines retained their hunting instincts. Fast movements or high-pitched sounds from smaller animals could cause dogs to give chase, although such instincts varied between individual animals and were not unique to large breeds. Under local regulations, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) defines a large dog as one weighing 20kg or more. Under the Dangerous Dogs Regulation, large dogs must be securely held on a leash of no more than two metres (6.6 feet) when in public places. Anyone who breaches the requirement can face a maximum fine of HK$25,000 (US$3,200) and three months in prison. Owners who wish to allow their large dogs to exercise off-leash in public areas must pass the government-run Large Dog Exemption Examination, which assesses both the animal’s temperament and the owner’s ability to control it. The AFCD noted that it had sought prosecutions last year in 206 cases involving dog attacks on people or animals under the relevant legislation, compared with 215 in 2024 and 258 in 2023. According to its records, Hong Kong currently has one registered Spanish mastiff and 33 registered Tibetan mastiffs. The department recorded no cases of mastiffs biting people or attacking animals between 2023 and 2025.

title: Viral false claims about quakes, Hiroshima expose Japan’s online conspiracy problem
description: Claims that a deadly quake was artificial and Hiroshima was not hit by an atomic bomb have alarmed experts tracking Japan’s online spaces.
content: Two outlandish claims that gained large audiences online in Japan recently have “shocked” misinformation experts, who say conspiracy-style narratives are feeding on disaster anxiety, fading wartime memory and an online information ecosystem that rewards outrage and suspicion. In the aftermath of the July 28 earthquake in Kumamoto prefecture in southern Japan, a social media user claimed that seismic data from the National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience showed the tremor was “not an earthquake but an artificial explosion waveform”. The post, published about 30 minutes after the magnitude 7.1 quake, was later listed by Yahoo Japan’s real-time search as a popular post, with more than 2,100 reposts and 6,300 likes. Other posts pushed a related claim that the quake had been triggered by HAARP, a research facility in Alaska that has long been a target of disaster-related conspiracy theories. Days later, as Japan marked the August anniversaries of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings and the end of World War II, NHK reported that false claims denying the atomic attacks were gaining traction online, with some posts on X and TikTok drawing more than 1 million views and one YouTube video claiming the bombing was a lie attracting more than 300,000 views. “Both the theory that the earthquake was artificially triggered and the denial of the atomic bombings lack scientific basis, but the contexts in which these conspiracy theories take root differ,” said Yuzuru Kido, a former J-CAST News deputy editor and internet media researcher who tracks Japanese social media discourse. “I believe the denial of the atomic bombings is linked to the fact that more than 80 years have passed since the end of the war, and opportunities to engage directly with memories and testimonies have diminished,” he told This Week in Asia. “On the other hand, with regard to earthquakes, the ‘uncertainty’ inherent in natural disasters – the inability to accurately predict when they will occur or their scale – creates a space for conspiracy theories to take root.” Conspiracy theories long predate the internet and are not exclusive to Japan, Kido pointed out, but years of observing the country’s online space had left him concerned that such claims were becoming easier to revive and circulate. Japan has seen conspiracy claims attach themselves to national traumas before, including suggestions that Japan Airlines Flight 123, which crashed in Gunma prefecture in 1985 with the loss of 520 passengers and crew, was shot down by a missile from a Japanese warship carrying out drills offshore. Historical revisionist claims have also persisted online, including denial of the Nanking massacre that took place in the city now known as Nanjing and occurred over six weeks starting on December 13, 1937, the day Japanese forces captured the city. More recent romance and investment scams have also shown how easily trust can be exploited in digital spaces. “My personal impression is that the number of people accepting conspiracy-theory-style explanations is on the rise,” Kido said. “I believe this stems from a global rise in nationalism, as well as anxiety about the future caused by Japan’s economic stagnation and the weak yen, leading to a demand for narratives that offer simple explanations of causes and solutions.” He added: “Algorithm-driven filter bubbles and echo chambers have made it easier for like-minded people to reinforce and radicalise their convictions.” A Japan-wide survey published by the SmartNews Media Research Institute in September 2025 found that people who used video-based social media sites as their main news sources showed a stronger tendency towards conspiracy-style thinking than those who relied on newspapers. The survey, which examined political and social divisions in Japan as well as media habits, found that 87 per cent of respondents agreed or somewhat agreed that “very important things are happening in the world that ordinary people are never told about”, while 22 per cent believed or somewhat believed that government authorities were closely monitoring all citizens. That people are uncritically accepting claims that are scientifically impossible or simply preposterous is deeply worrying, according to Makoto Watanabe, a professor of communications and media at Hokkaido Bunkyo University in Eniwa, Hokkaido. “A lot of these claims are initially being shared primarily by people who want to earn more views or likes on their social media feeds and really do not care if they are true or not, but they are being accepted as the truth by others,” he said. “There is another group, of course, the people who do make impossible claims based on their beliefs, because they want to influence other people’s way of thinking and also because it makes them feel superior because they feel they have inside information that no one else has.” Schools have introduced classes on media literacy in an effort to encourage young people to think more critically about the information they are presented with, but Watanabe says there will always be a section of the public “that never paid attention in school, are effectively hooked on their mobile phones, believe everything they see on them and are, therefore, really ignorant”. Kido also believes that as long as there are people willing to “seek attention and profit by stoking anxiety,” more such theories will gain traction. “What shocked me the most was the theory denying the atomic bombings,” he said. “I find it deeply troubling that this claim denies not only historical facts, for which numerous records exist, but also the experiences and testimonies of the atomic bomb survivors, thereby undermining their dignity.”

title: ‘His feet are his pillars’: Nepal swimmer gives everything for glory at Asian Para Games
description: ‘If I hit a world record then of course my life will be better. Only then can I speak of inspiring anyone else,’ Harka Man Gharti says.
content: Every morning Harka Man Gharti slices into the blue water of a swimming pool in Nepal’s capital Kathmandu, chasing a dream that stretches far beyond its 25 metres. Unlike the swimmers around him who rely on long strokes of their arms, Gharti powers through his legs and torso because he does not have arms. The 21-year-old is training with three other disabled swimmers who will represent Nepal in the Asian Para Games in Japan in October, chasing medals despite limited resources in the Himalayan country. “It is not my hope, it is my target,” Gharti said after finishing a gruelling session. “Just for a medal, I am giving everything ... every possible thing.” A decade ago an electrocution accident near a hydroelectric project in his native Baglung district in western Nepal changed his life forever, costing him both arms. The tragedy that could have ended his ambitions instead helped forge his extraordinary determination. What began as an experiment with competitive swimming in 2020 soon became a passion and a career pathway. “I love everything about swimming, whether competitive or just for enjoying,” he said. At the hostel where he lives in Kathmandu a row of medals hangs above his bed, proof of a remarkable journey. During training he concentrates on his technique and body position in the water. On race days a different instinct takes over. “I don’t really think about the techniques or my body alignment,” he said. “I just go hard. I just push fast and I just want to push power. That’s it. I just think about speed and for speed I just kick harder and harder.” At last year’s Para Swimming World Series in Japan, Gharti’s times met the minimum qualifying standards for the Asian Para Games, earning him a chance to compete on one of the biggest sporting stages. He will participate in the S5 classification, including the 50m freestyle. China’s Guo Jincheng holds the men’s 50m freestyle record at 29.33 seconds in the category. Sports facilities in Nepal are modest by international standards. Para athletes in the country often face limited funding, scarce specialised infrastructure and a lack of competitive opportunities. His coach, Subha Shrestha, believes Gharti’s greatest strength lies not in what he has lost, but in what he has built. “When we don’t have even a single finger we feel the impact,” Shrestha said. “But he is working so hard with no hands. “His feet are his pillars, his legs are very powerful.” The wider significance of Gharti’s quest is not lost on Nepal’s para swimming community. The nation has had only one Asian Para Games medallist, taekwondo athlete Palesha Goverdhan, who won bronze last time out before also claiming a medal in the Paralympics. For many years Nepali athletes have arrived at major competitions with modest expectations. “In Nepal they often say that we go only for the sake of participation,” Saroj Shrestha, president of the National Para Swimming Association of Nepal, said. “But Harka and we both dream to do something in swimming that even able-bodied athletes have not been able to achieve.” Back on the pool deck, Gharti’s ambitions extend beyond sport. Having recently completed high school, he plans to study computer science. He navigates a computer with his toes, displaying the same determination that has become central to his swimming. “Swimming is a platform for me where it is on me whether I can make my life better or not. “Because if I hit a world record then of course my life will be better,” he said. “Only then can I speak of inspiring anyone else.”

title: Beyond Amsterdam: Amersfoort’s 15th century charm lies in its canals, cafes and tourist-free calm
description: Just 30 minutes from the crowded capital, this historic town offers medieval wall houses, art heritage and vibrant everyday life without the tourist masses.
content: It would be odd to visit the Netherlands without spending time in Amsterdam, the canal-laced city of slender, leaning houses in patterned brick with their toothy stepped gables, famous for its Rembrandts and Van Goghs, and for action-movie speedboat chases along its waterways and under narrow humpbacked bridges.
