Some visitors are attracted less by this culture than by the city’s cheerful open-mindedness; sex workers on display in windows among everyday shopping in a central red-light district and marijuana that was available in cafes for decades before deregulation became fashionable anywhere else. It’s also pleasant just to take a canal-side bench with a lunch of pickled herring, stroopwafels, or chips with peanut-butter sauce, and watch the boats and bicycles go by. However, faced with up to 20 million tourists a year, the city’s 950,000 residents would increasingly like you to consider alternatives, or at least to spread out a bit. It’s not as if the Netherlands’ culture and history stop dead at Amsterdam’s periphery. Within a short train ride (the only kind here; anything more will take you to Belgium or Germany), there are what seem like little bits of Amsterdam that have broken off and floated away. These also have centuries-old tottering houses, ancient churches, canals and the same generally welcoming atmosphere, but each with its own individual style. Amersfoort, for example, was once made prosperous by beer and textiles, as well as its location on the navigable Amer river, later renamed the Eem, but now is a backwater half an hour away from Amsterdam by frequent train. It’s a concentrated and walkable pocket of Dutch culture ancient and modern, best viewed not as a checklist of sights but as a souvenir-shop-free town where ordinary life goes on in a historic setting. Wandering is a pleasure in itself. From Amersfoort Centraal station, it’s a 15-minute walk to the largely pedestrianised Old Town and a landmark that can be seen from some distance away, the 98-metre (321 feet) Gothic Onze Lieve Vrouwetoren, or “Tower of Our Lady”. This solitary finger of reddish brick, built in the 15th century, its accompanying chapel long vanished, rises in steps that change to carved grey stone topped with a shining golden cockerel. From the top, if you can manage the 346-step climb, there are views over the town centre’s labyrinth of narrow streets. But there’s as much pleasure in relaxing with something restorative at a cafe, bar or restaurant in the small square at its base, taken while listening to the sound of the bells reverberating around the ancient facades as the tower’s clock strikes the quarter-hour, the half-hour or the hour. In one corner of the square, the 16th century Kapelhuis (“Chapel House”) is a reminder of when Amersfoort was a major destination for pilgrims, attracted by a supposedly miracle-working stone statue of the Virgin Mary that once perched here. But the continuing survival of the seemingly flimsy stepped frontage, its brickwork in herringbone and circular decorative patterns, seems miracle enough. A little further down the narrow Lieve Vrouwestraat is antiquity of a more domestic nature, in a pair of equally diminutive half-timbered houses that also date from the 16th century, framed in stridently red-painted wood, with dark green shutters. Carry on and the road swings to the left to follow the route of the original city wall along a parade of further ancient housing of particular bricky dignity, walls bulging in some places and studded with the plates of the tie beams holding the buildings together, large ground-floor windows opening onto the thin streets. Dormers with hoists suggest the impossibility of getting furniture up or down steep interior stairs. Many are muurhuizen, or “wall houses”, built in the 15th and 16th centuries on the route of the 13th century city wall using some of its remains. The expanding town had replaced the earlier defences with a larger ring, some of whose impressively fortified water gates still stand. These narrower streets intersect those of regular shopping – shoes, a pharmacy, a bustling bookshop with plenty in English – and cross short and sturdy bridges over tree-lined canals that reflect the ancient frontages alongside. Wandering visitors may happen upon the small, covered 17th century fish market, an 18th century synagogue or fragments of the original city wall. And if they are in need of a souvenir, there’s the Mondriaanhuis. Amersfoort may be short on Rembrandts or Van Goghs, but the town was the birthplace of Pieter Cornelis Mondriaan, more famously known as Piet Mondrian (1872-1944), the master of a grid-like abstraction whose style was picked up and absorbed into the fashion of Saint Laurent and Moschino. The house in which the painter was born shows nine earlier figurative pieces that only hint at the abstraction that was to come, although there are many works by contemporaries clearly influenced by the artist’s later work. A shop sells attractively “Mondrian-ised” merchandise. The finest wall house is the Groot Tinnenburg, which was built before 1414. It was part of the original city wall and connected to a substantial water gate now replaced by a simpler bridge. Still privately owned, and currently up for sale (yours for a rumoured €2.65 million/US$3.08 million), its great mass, towering stepped gables, smart red shutters and location right on a canal make it perhaps Amersfoort’s most photogenic spot, although various water gates compete for that title, too. The gate once attached to the Groot Tinnenburg was rendered redundant by the construction of the Monnikendam, on the second wall, here close to the route of the first. Both protected the water supply and defended the city from waterborne assault where several streams combine to form the Eem. A blank-faced bridge, its flatness relieved only by arrow slits, the Monnikendam connects two squat brick towers capped with witches’ hats of grey slate, the canal passing under an arch low enough to make standing boatmen duck. Walk anticlockwise from the Groot Tinnenburg along the outer bank of a city-circling canal, this section known as the Zuidsingel (“South Canal”), and you’ll discover that several wall houses have long gardens reached rather romantically by private bridges. A clockwise stroll takes you past a small cobbled bridge leading to the Thieves’ Tower, part of a wall house that functioned as a prison from 1434 to 1889, and on to the Kamperbinnenpoort, the only gate from the first city wall to have been preserved, at least partially. Its tall towers, standing over the high road entrance, seem like a version of the Monnikendam that’s been over-fertilised and has bolted skywards. The carving of a windmill and assorted greenery over the ornately framed entrance to a stolid 19th century building here, De Snuif Molen (“Tobacco Mill”; now an Asian grocery store), is a reminder of a later source of revenue for the town. And continuing round to the north, the white-painted Prattenburg house, with a tall, dark-red octagonal tower poking from a steep-sided roof, was once the home and warehouse of a Jewish tobacco dealer. Turning south towards the town centre quickly brings you to the Kanunnikenhuisje, another pocket-sized Gothic brick frontage, from 1520, once home to the priests of the Sint-Joriskerk (“St George’s Church”) opposite. It’s now home to the Tante Cor cafe, with seats outside from which to watch people pass by on their way to market while sipping the Dutch version of coffee with extra milk – the koffie verkeerd, or “wrong coffee”. The medieval Sint-Joriskerk is on a different scale from anything seen since the Tower of Our Lady, with triple steep roofs running its length over nave and aisles, having expanded over time to absorb its formerly external spire-topped tower, which now shoots up unexpectedly from within one roof. There’s carved stone around the entrances but the whole is otherwise domesticated by being constructed of the same materials as the rest of the town, and even more so by having had businesses glue themselves to the church’s outer wall on all sides. These include the rectangular Butter Market hall, which opens onto De Hof square and is supplemented at weekends by a cluster of stalls, all family bustle and with nothing made for tourists. It offers the aromas of fresh baking, waffles and other hot snacks wrapped in gingham paper, and vast wheels of orange cheese. Examining the facades around the square reveals signs of historical trade; the painted head of a helmeted figure with gaping mouth that protrudes from one of them suggests this was long the site of a pharmacy. Proceeding northwest down Havik, following the canal of the same name along the city’s north side, you’ll pass substantial former merchants’ houses to arrive at the Museum Amersfoort. Reached across the canal by its own little bridge, the museum occupies three former wall houses in striking striped brick, linked to form a labyrinth of small spaces containing displays that tell Amersfoort’s history. Within are early landscapes of the city when its first wall was intact, a table model of its historic layout and local treasures such as the keys to the city that French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was too busy to accept when he passed through in 1811. The museum explains the city’s relationship with water, the Eem having been used not only for shipping but also to provide fresh water, vital for both drinking and the development of the brewing and cotton-cloth industries that financed the town’s growth. But the only river that rises within the Netherlands, to drain into the ocean not far to the west, presents something of a threat to Amersfoort’s future, providing a channel for flooding as sea levels rise, and if dykes fail. The best exit from the Old Town is through the nearby Koppelpoort, the most substantial of the city’s remaining gates, uniquely dominating both land and water approaches to the town. Built around 1425, it’s a string of octagonal towers and connecting buildings frowning forbiddingly over roadway and waterway alike. From here, the railway station is a 15-minute walk away, but by now, it’s clear that Amersfoort isn’t just a side trip from Amsterdam; it’s an ideal base from which to explore the larger city and the rest of the region. Its central location, also on a major railway junction, makes access to the rest of the Netherlands easy. For now, it’s quiet and relaxed. The accommodation is relatively cheap and likely to become more competitive still as Amsterdam places further limits on short-term holiday rentals. Perhaps the day-tripping should be done the other way.

title: UK’s Burnham plans US trip to lobby Trump on Ukraine Patriot missiles
description: Following his first international visit to Kyiv, the new UK leader seeks a multi-nation deal to secure vital interceptors for Ukraine.
content: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he and other European leaders plan to travel to the US next month to lobby President Donald Trump to let Ukraine access some of its Patriot air defence missile stocks ahead of the winter. “I’m looking forward to going to New York in September,” Burnham said in an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv on Monday evening, referring to the coming UN General Assembly meeting in New York. It would be his first trip to the US since becoming prime minister. “I’ve not fully confirmed the details yet but it’s likely I will go, particularly after today’s discussion,” he said. “Leaving today, I’m quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks.” Burnham’s comments came on his first international visit since becoming premier, after chairing a meeting of Ukraine’s allies for the first time and holding a bilateral meeting with Ukraine’s President, Volodymyr Zelensky. Zelensky has made repeated pleas to European nations and the US to help Ukraine obtain Patriot missile interceptors and to replenish its stocks in time for winter, when Russia is expected to ramp up attacks on energy infrastructure again. The interceptors are the most potent weapons to shoot down Russian cruise and ballistic missiles. Burnham said he left feeling “really optimistic” that Ukraine’s current struggles defending against Russian ballistic missile strikes due to its low stockpile of interceptors are “fixable”. He said European leaders were considering holding another Coalition of the Willing meeting around the UN General Assembly meeting with a view towards securing American interceptors and stocks from other countries. “That would seem to be the most likely pace of direction,” Burnham said. “Not confirmed yet but that seemed like where most people’s minds were going.” He stressed that while the UK did not use the Patriot missiles required by Ukraine, other European nations needed to step up. “There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with,” Burnham said. “It’s probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation.” Trump has backtracked on an earlier promise to provide or let Kyiv build interceptors for US-made Patriot missile defence systems. The war in Iran has also seriously depleted global stocks of Patriot missiles, leading to delays in supplies and making allies reluctant to provide them to Kyiv. Trump in July told reporters he had not yet agreed to Ukraine’s request to build Patriot missiles. “We’re talking about it but it’s a hard thing to give away that kind of technology,” he said at the time. Burnham, in contrast, has moved aggressively to allow Ukraine access to closely guarded British defence technology. The UK prime minister will allow Ukraine access to classified information on British components for the long-range missile, called SCALP, allowing Kyiv to assemble the cruise missile in Ukraine. “We value the fact that the UK’s course remains unchanged – full support for Ukraine and our defence,” Zelensky said in a post on social media late on Monday outlining his discussions with Burnham. Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that he is seeking 300 Patriot missiles for the winter. He has said previously that if Kyiv could buy 5 per cent of the United States’ Patriot missile stockpile it would survive the winter, and if it could purchase 10 per cent it could destroy all of Russia’s ballistic missiles. Ukraine has already been struggling with an onslaught of Russian ballistic attacks that have led to a rising death toll among its population. At least 437 Ukrainian civilians were killed in July 2026, a 30 per cent increase on a year earlier, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. August has seen several Russian attacks with high civilian death tolls, with 15 killed in ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv on Thursday and 16 killed in a drone attack on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih on Friday.

title: US judge postpones Lockerbie bombing trial over new evidence
description: Defence granted time to review newly disclosed material days before jury selection for former Libyan agent accused in 1988 attack.
content: A federal judge on Monday postponed a trial in the US for a former Libyan intelligence official charged in the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103, citing the discovery of new evidence that defence lawyers want to examine in the nearly 40-year-old case. Jury selection was scheduled to begin Wednesday for the federal trial of Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi in Washington DC. His trial will be the first in the US for the December 21, 1988, bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people, most of them Americans. US District Judge Dabney Friedrich’s order did not specify the nature of the newly discovered evidence. Al-Marimi’s lawyers say prosecutors disclosed the new evidence to them on Saturday and added that their “constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development”. Defence lawyer Laura Koenig, an assistant federal public defender, declined to elaborate in response to an Associated Press inquiry. The judge scheduled a September 1 hearing in Washington to discuss the status of the case. Friedrich’s brief order cited the complex nature of the case, the newly discovered evidence and “the need for the defence to determine how best to defend this case” as reasons to postpone the trial. Al-Marimi is charged in the US with making the bomb that downed the plane. Flight 103 was 31,000 feet (9.45km) over Lockerbie when a bomb in the plane’s forward cargo area exploded 38 minutes after take-off from London Heathrow Airport. The flight was bound for John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York. The blast killed all 259 passengers and crew members and 11 people on the ground in Lockerbie, where the wreckage destroyed an entire city block. Citizens of 21 countries were killed, including 190 Americans and 43 from the United Kingdom. The passengers included 35 Syracuse University students returning home from a semester abroad. Kara Weipz, board president of the non-profit Victims of Pan Am Flight 103, said her organisation had received no details about the new evidence that prompted the trial delay. Weipz’s brother Richard Monetti was among the Syracuse students killed. She called the delay a shock and noted that some victims’ relatives were already packing to head to the trial. “At the same time, for almost 38 years we’ve been seeking the truth of what happened,” Weipz said. “If that’s what this is, then that’s a good thing, and this delay is worth it. … It’s important to hear all the facts.” Prosecutors allege Al-Marimi and others carried out the bombing at the direction of Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was ousted and killed during a 2011 civil war. Two other Libyan intelligence agents were tried by a panel of Scottish judges on a former US military base in the Netherlands in 2000. The tribunal convicted one official and acquitted the other, but the bombmaker’s possible identity remained a mystery for years. Al-Marimi, now in his mid-70s, is charged with two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted. Al-Marimi worked for the Libyan intelligence service from approximately 1973 to 2011, rising to the rank of colonel, according to prosecutors. Prosecutors believe he brought a suitcase containing a bomb to an airport in Malta and gave it to co-conspirators for a flight to Frankfurt, Germany. The suitcase travelled from Frankfurt to London, where it was loaded onto Flight 103, according to investigators.

title: Editorial | Hongkong Post’s survival won’t come from belt-tightening alone
description: The postal service must look to successful examples overseas and not shy away from ambitious reforms.
content: When the pop song “Please Mr Postman” topped the US Billboard charts decades ago, few would have expected the daily sight of a uniformed postman delivering letters to every doorstep to become a rarity. For more than a century, the post office in Hong Kong has not only been an essential public service but also a symbol of connectivity and reliability. Yet like many of its overseas counterparts, the government agency is struggling to survive amid an increasingly challenging environment. Having secured a HK$4.6 billion (US$587 million) bailout from the legislature following eight consecutive years of deficits, Hongkong Post can heave a sigh of relief for now. But it will not be long before it has to face the harsh reality. Unless it can “think out of the postbox” to transform itself and compete with commercial rivals or convince taxpayers to foot its increasingly underutilised and money-losing operation as part of indispensable public services, it may well be consigned to history eventually. The department’s financial woes call for resolute reforms. Worryingly, it has accumulated nearly HK$2.9 billion in losses since 2017-18, with the 2024-25 deficit of HK$821 million the largest in three decades. Meanwhile, mail volume has fallen by an average of 7 per cent a year from 2019-20 to 2024-25, a cumulative drop of 44 per cent that officials expect to continue or worsen. E-commerce, once a bright spot, now accounts for only around a quarter of revenue, down from nearly half in 2020-21, hit by geopolitical tensions and competition from private couriers. In this regard, the HK$4.6 billion injection approved by the Legislative Council earlier – including HK$4.09 billion for operations over the next three years and HK$510 million to refurbish the Air Mail Centre – is less a rescue plan than a time-buying stopgap measure. The government must honour its pledge to complete a comprehensive review of the current self-financing trading fund model within three years. The options include privatisation, corporatisation or reverting to a fully funded department. But it should not rule out other bold choices. Whatever the eventual decision, the department cannot sit back and do nothing in the meantime. It must start cutting costs, exploring new operations and diversifying revenue streams. In a controversial move starting from September, new employees will be offered a two-year contract after probation, instead of the usual permanent civil service appointment. Other cost-saving measures include reviewing the methods and frequency of mail deliveries as well as optimising the post office network and working hours. But survival does not come from belt-tightening alone. The department should take a leaf out of the books of postal services overseas. While it cannot just copy and paste others’ experience because of civil service rules and operational limits under the trading fund, the constraints must not become excuses to stay put and wait for another lifeline from the public coffers. Singapore Post, for instance, is regarded as a successful case of transformation into a global e-commerce logistical enterprise through modernisation and international market expansion. While also facing pressure from declining mail and e-commerce volumes, the publicly listed company boasted net profits of S$60.9 million (US$48 million) in 2025-26. It is also committed to integrating artificial intelligence and automation to reduce costs and serve more. Hongkong Post ought to accomplish more than it already has. As a trusted public agency with an extensive fleet and a presence in almost all districts, it has great potential to deliver more. By borrowing from the playbooks of successful global peers to double down on operational rationalisation and aggressive revenue diversification, there is no reason it cannot become a more financially viable entity. It would be a shame if it shies away from more ambitious reforms and scales back to a basic universal postal service that is kept barely alive by public funds. The digital age does not necessarily spell the end of postal services. Even though the physical delivery of letters may be dying, Hongkong Post need not become a relic of the past. But it must navigate difficult terrain to reinvent itself. That requires making hard choices and obtaining the stamp of approval from the wider society.

title: 6 of the best places to visit during shoulder season, from Japan to Austria and France
description: Travelling in the autumn brings all kinds of benefits. Here are six places worth a visit in 2026, from magical Japan to welcoming Malta.
content: Fewer people, cheaper prices, milder weather – the last quarter of the year can offer a lot for travellers. Much of Europe, for example, is arguably better in September and October than the height of summer. Meanwhile, a lot of the northern hemisphere enjoys vibrant autumn colours, and mountainous regions can offer a real escape from crowds in the off-season. Here, travel experts share their recommendations. 1. Japan Travellers have long flocked to Japan in spring to witness the magic of cherry blossom season, but in autumn the foliage is just as impressive, with leaves transforming into vibrant shades of orange and red. “The autumn colours in Japan are absolutely stunning, and you get to see them without the crowds of the cherry blossom season, which people forget is just as popular with domestic tourists as overseas,” says Emma Otter, from Travel Counsellors. The horticultural splendour does not end there: on September 9, Japan celebrates Chrysanthemum Day. “Across Japan there are flower shows and exhibitions until mid-November dedicated to the chrysanthemum, a bit like the Royal Chelsea Flower Show,” Otter says. 2. Malta Though the summer season is winding down in Malta, parties, festivals and good times certainly do not stop in the autumn, Otter says. In mid-September, the Mediterranean archipelago, one of Europe’s most gay-friendly destinations, ramps up its LGBTQ+ celebrations with its epic annual Pride event. “It’s so much fun; when I went, we even had the Red Arrows fly over,” Otter says, referring to the UK’s Royal Air Force aerobatics display team. “What I love about Malta is that everybody’s welcomed with open arms.” In the autumn, there are also significantly fewer crowds than during the peak summer months, and the temperature is pleasant, ranging from 14 degrees Celsius (57 degrees Fahrenheit) to 28 degrees depending on the month. According to Otter, this makes Malta an underrated family beach destination. “Malta’s not usually known for its beaches, but we stayed at Mellieha Bay, which has this beautiful sandy beach, so it’s ideal for people who don’t have to go away in the school holidays, but still want to take children somewhere warm where the crowds are calming down.” 3. Chamonix, France While Chamonix is best known as a skiing destination, with the season typically running from mid-December to mid-April, travellers should not overlook the Alpine town in autumn, urges Alexander Blunt, co-founder at tour operator Heidi. The pleasant weather makes it the perfect time for a hike, and numerous trails offer stunning views of Mont Blanc, including the famous Tour du Mont Blanc trekking circuit. “There’s also so much to do for non-hardcore hikers as the ski lifts are still running to take you up into the mountains,” Blunt says. “So you can still access these beautiful trails whether you just want a casual 5km [3.1-mile] walk before having a nice lunch or want to hike 40km in a day.” 4. Austria For a twist on the traditional festival circuit, experience Austria’s ceremonial cattle drive, Almabtrieb, which typically takes place from early September to mid-October. “Farming communities take all the cows down from the summer pastures, clean and dress them up,” Blunt says. “There’s also food and music, and it’s this most incredible experience.” If you are looking for a base in Austria, he recommends Zell am See, located on Lake Zell, as the autumn leaves cast a golden glow over the Alpine town. “It’s a beautiful town on a beautiful lake with forest wrapped around it,” Blunt says. “Even in September you can still swim in the lake, and they’ve got all these lidos along it.” He also notes that e-bikes are readily available in mountain towns like Zell am See, opening up alpine access and picturesque trails for older or less active visitors. 5. Nepal Autumn is the perfect time to visit Nepal. As the monsoon rains finish, the days are dry and warm with clear air, ideal for trekking and viewing the high peaks. Autumn is also a culturally important season in Nepal. In October, Nepal’s biggest Hindu festival, Dashain, is a celebration of the victory of the goddess Durga over the demon Mahishasura. The festivities last for 15 days. Tihar, the festival of light and flowers, is a five-day event where towns and villages burst with colour, welcoming prosperity and honouring animals. 6. Albania Albania has experienced a boom in tourism over the past few years, with the summer particularly drawing in large numbers. However, Oliver Browne, chief executive at True Summit Adventures and a resident of the country’s capital, Tirana, says the peak season can be “chaos”, particularly as the main airport is unequipped for high volume. For Browne, autumn is the best time to avoid the crowds, and it is much kinder on the purse strings. “In October, for example, the pricing will be significantly cheaper for hotels than in the summer. Also, in the busy months, there will often be a several-night minimum stay, which is less likely, or not at all, in October,” he says. Meanwhile, September welcomes the country’s first international film festival, the Tirana International Film Festival. This is a must-visit for cinephiles and culture travellers, as it has been approved as an official Academy Awards and European Film Awards qualifying festival.

title: Hong Kong housing rally faces test as property flippers retreat
description: Secondary home prices are the highest in three years, but July short-term trading of those held for less than a year was half the level seen in March.
content: Hong Kong’s housing rally faces a new test as investors who rode the first-half rebound become less active in quick-turn trades, leaving owner-occupiers and longer-term buyers to sustain the recovery. Secondary home prices have continued to rise, with Centaline’s leading index climbing 0.64 per cent to 162.16 on Friday, its highest level in three years. But the short-term trading that accelerated alongside the rebound has pulled back sharply: transactions involving homes held for less than a year fell to 99 in July, down 24 per cent from June. In March, 202 of these transactions were recorded. Despite the decline, Centaline said the average profit per sale rose almost 10 per cent in July to HK$842,000 (US$107,400), the highest monthly average this year. The divergence points to a market in which the gains from the first leg of the recovery have become harder to repeat through quick trades. “Buyers are resisting chasing higher prices as rate expectations shift,” said Louis Chan Wing-kit, Asia-Pacific vice-chairman and chief executive of Centaline’s residential division. Developers were also launching new projects at prices close to those in the secondary market, giving buyers another option and drawing some investors and short-term traders towards first-hand homes, Chan said. Alvin Leung, senior director of project consultancy at Colliers Hong Kong, said he viewed the slowdown in speculative activity as more selective rather than a broad retreat from housing. Residential prices continue to rise even as the volume of quick-flip transactions moderates Alvin Leung, Colliers Hong Kong “Speculative activity has become more selective,” Leung said, adding that investors who entered the market earlier in the year had already captured some capital gains from recovering residential prices, “naturally reducing the urgency to transact again in the near term”. Improving economic sentiment, a stronger stock market and a robust residential rental market were supporting owner-occupier and longer-term investment demand, he said. “Consequently, residential prices continue to rise even as the volume of quick-flip transactions moderates,” Leung said. The remaining flipping activity has been concentrated in cheaper homes. Of 922 short-term transactions recorded in the first seven months of the year, 474 involved properties bought for less than HK$4 million. The average profit on those deals was about HK$520,000. The biggest absolute gain in July came from a 1,288-square-foot flat at Residence Bel-Air in Pok Fu Lam. The owner sold the property for HK$37.18 million after buying it for HK$29.8 million in October, making HK$7.38 million in about 260 days. The biggest percentage gain came from a 293-square-foot flat at Kam On Building in Sham Shui Po. Bought for HK$2.05 million in September, the unit sold for HK$3.29 million in July, generating a 60 per cent gain of HK$1.24 million in about 306 days. At the other end of the market, just 43 of the 922 short-term transactions involved homes bought for more than HK$10 million.

title: In Focus | How China’s anti-corruption fight became Xi Jinping’s most important policy
description: Far from a temporary crackdown, the campaign has proved to be a key tool for enforcing party discipline and driving economic strategy.
content: The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the first part of a series accompanying the data project, Phoebe Zhang looks at how the campaign became one of the Communist Party’s most important policies. In the early years of President Xi Jinping’s first term, when graft fighters were taking down senior officials in ways that raised eyebrows, Chinese authorities constantly had to remind the public that the anti-corruption campaign was not “just a gust of wind”. At that point, Beijing had already locked up dozens of senior officials, including Zhou Yongkang, a former member of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, the highest echelon in China’s political hierarchy. Before his downfall in 2013, Zhou had been one of China’s most influential politicians. Concerns were so widespread that the anti-corruption push would be a flash in the pan, especially at the local level, that Wang Qishan, then the party’s top anti-corruption chief, warned that local governments might fall back on temporary “movement-style” crackdowns. A decade later, few need convincing as the anti-corruption fight expands, netting record numbers of senior officials and unearthing new types of graft involving cryptocurrency schemes and clandestine proxies. A new analysis by the South China Morning Post found that the campaign has widened since its inception. Last year, anti-corruption agencies handed down punishments to 983,000 people, with the fallout ranging from mild warnings to investigations and criminal prosecution. The number of senior officials taken down last year was three times that of 2013. The SCMP’s data bank project also found that from 2013 to 2025, 60 per cent of senior officials felled by China’s anti-corruption drive were serving in regional governments. The campaign has hit provincial administrations particularly hard, with resource-rich areas – notably Jiangxi, Liaoning, Shanxi and Hebei provinces, as well as Inner Mongolia, autonomous region – recording the highest number of dismissals. What began as a crackdown on economic graft has evolved into a systemic overhaul of bureaucratic conduct. While bribery remains the main legal charge, the definition of corruption has expanded to include party discipline and adherence to policy directives. By now, most experts agree that the anti-corruption campaign is among Xi’s most important policies, and one that is key to his vision of China’s future and the party’s ability to rule for generations to come. And the party has shown no interest in pulling any punches. During a January meeting of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, the party’s top anti-graft body, Xi declared that “the situation in the fight against corruption remains grave and complex”, urging officials to come up with new methods to discover, identify and tackle all types of wrongdoing. Just last month, China’s top leadership announced that party governance would be the focus of the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee, expected to be held in October. This meeting is likely to be the party’s most important gathering ahead of its 21st national congress in autumn of next year. The five-yearly party congress is likely to feature a leadership reshuffle and the endorsement of a fourth term for Xi. In a Xinhua report on the coming plenary session, the Politburo said party self-governance “faces new circumstances and challenges” and called for “consistently exercising full and rigorous governance over the party” – a phrase that typically means fighting corruption and tightening party discipline. No end point While generations of Communist Party leaders have pledged to uproot corruption, Xi has tried to convince the country from the outset that his fight is different. In 2013, at the second plenary session of the party’s 18th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), Xi pledged to fight “tigers and flies at the same time” – targeting not only high-ranking officials but also misconduct at the grass-roots level – to underscore a policy of “no forbidden zones, full coverage and zero tolerance”. Soon, Beijing introduced a set of “eight-point austerity rules” to restrict party cadre behaviour. These include banning the use of luxury cars and gifts, banning red carpets, floral arrangements and grand receptions during inspections, simplifying meetings, reducing unnecessary documents and limiting overseas visits. The rules are still in effect today. The anti-corruption campaign has deepened and broadened to cover all policy areas and sectors, including security, finance, education and the graft fighters themselves. In its first three years, it took down top leaders in all 31 provincial-level jurisdictions. The campaign has also hit the military’s top brass, especially in the past two years. The push has become more institutionalised as well. In 2018, the National Supervisory Commission (NSC) was created and merged with the CCDI, giving the party’s anti-corruption campaign a legal basis. Beijing has sought to supplement laws with party regulations. More than 70 per cent of the Communist Party’s regulations have been enacted since 2012. China has also overhauled its corruption-fighting agencies to reflect a “vertical management” style, giving more oversight to higher authorities. It has reinvented the inspection regime, inherited from Imperial China but largely inactive in the years before Xi, so inspectors dispatched from Beijing look for signs of corruption at the local level. Over the past 14 years, Xi has repeatedly emphasised that his anti-corruption campaign has no end point, warning that no official should harbour any illusions of impunity. At the 20th party congress in 2022, Xi said the anti-corruption fight should “never rest, not even for a minute”. Staying disciplined Corruption is the “greatest threat” facing the party, Xi said in a speech at the 19th party congress in 2017. At times, he has argued that purging corruption is crucial for the Communist Party to escape China’s “historical cycles” of dynastic rise and collapse, and ensure its longevity. Xi has said that corruption hinders governance and economic development. “If corruption is allowed to spread, it will eventually lead to the destruction of a party and the fall of a government,” he has warned. Li Jian, a former researcher with the Publicity Department of the Central Committee, wrote in January that the reason that the party could not afford to lose the fight against corruption was because graft harmed the party’s vitality and ability to fight. “[Corruption] seriously undermines fair and just market rules, distorts the efficiency of resource allocation, erodes the fruits of reform and development, and damages the business environment as well as social fairness and justice,” Li wrote. He concluded that there was a need to create a “sound political environment and a level playing field for high-quality development”. “Combating corruption is like sailing against the current – if you do not advance, you will fall back,” said Zhiqun Zhu, a professor of political science and international relations at Bucknell University. “Long-term goals such as rejuvenation of the Chinese nation or unification with Taiwan cannot be achieved any time soon, but the anti-corruption campaign has yielded concrete results, with a cleaner government, a more professional and efficient bureaucracy, and a more loyal and dedicated leadership team,” said Zhu, who is also director of Bucknell’s China Institute. Alfred Wu, associate professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy at the National University of Singapore, said Xi’s views on corruption were shared by his predecessors, though they never pushed the fight to the same level. “Jiang Zemin had repeatedly said that ‘anti-corruption is a serious political struggle that matters to the life and death of the party and the nation’, while Hu Jintao said at the 18th party congress that failure to tackle the issue could prove fatal to the party,” he said, referring to China’s previous two presidents. Beijing has also made the enforcement of its strategies part of the anti-corruption campaign. The latest revision of party disciplinary regulations explicitly prohibits failing to implement the “new concept for development and high-quality development” – Beijing’s term for its new growth model, coined after Xi came to power. This violation has been mentioned in the investigation findings of a handful of disgraced senior officials, including Lan Tianli, the former party secretary of Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, who was investigated last year. Devendra Kumar, an associate fellow at the Centre of Excellence for Himalayan Studies at Shiv Nadar University, said the corruption-fighting efforts under Xi were ultimately about discipline. “In this context, anti-corruption in China cannot be understood in the narrow sense of deviations from institutional rules and laws,” he said. “Rather, it is fundamentally about ‘discipline’, which encompasses not only compliance with regulations but also officials’ political disposition and, increasingly, aspects of their family life, including whom they associate with, where family members work, and where they travel.” Kumar added that the campaign was aimed at enforcing the party’s agenda and preferred modes of thinking through measures such as the campaign on the correct view of political performance, which began in March. With local governments across China preparing for a leadership shuffle, Xi said a “correct view” of performance was particularly vital to ensure new appointments prioritised long-term public benefit over short-term vanity projects. According to Xinhua, local party leaders were tasked with the “top priority” of implementing top leadership’s decisions with “unwavering focus”. Party discipline also figures heavily in “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building”, a new branch of the Chinese leader’s political thought unveiled in June. Its key tenets include insistence on “a centralised, unified leadership of the party Central Committee” as well as “full and rigorous party self-governance” and ensuring that “officials do not have the audacity, opportunity or desire to commit corruption”. Kumar added that there were similarities between Xi and his predecessors’ signature policies in that they all aimed to extend party rule and impose discipline. For example, he said, Mao launched the “continuous revolution” – an ideological extension of the civil war the party won in 1949 – to prevent the party from becoming a stagnant bureaucracy. Xi, by contrast, sees bureaucratisation as a key remedy, with anti-corruption as a tool to fix the problems arising from the party’s organisational structure, according to Kumar. Communist Party institutions lack mechanisms such as public oversight and transparency to foster bottom-up accountability. As a result, he said, top-down methods of enforcing discipline and accountability were necessary for maintaining order and preventing deviations from established regulations and norms, even during periods of weak leadership. Xi laid bare some of those concerns in the report he delivered at the 20th party congress in 2022. He said that China had made great achievements as a result of reform, opening up and socialist modernisation, but “a number of prominent issues and problems – some of which had been building for years and others which were just emerging – demanded urgent action”. Among them, there were a “lack of clear understanding and effective action as well as a slide towards weak, hollow and watered-down party leadership in practice”, according to the Chinese leader. He added that despite repeated warnings, ills including pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance persisted. Another problem Xi saw as serious was “privilege-seeking mindsets and practices”, with some “deeply shocking cases of corruption”. “The intensity with which Xi has pursued disciplinary campaigns must be understood in context,” Kumar said. “When Xi came to power, party institutions were not sufficiently effective in ‘caging’ cadres in their day-to-day functioning, and cadres’ ideological commitment was also considered weak.” He noted there were structural reasons for the campaign to continue, as it had become part of Xi’s broader agenda of revitalising the party, both ideologically and institutionally, and the anti-corruption campaign and institutional changes of the past decade had embedded a “disciplinary regime” into the party’s day-to-day governance. “Consequently, we should expect an intensification of anti-corruption efforts in the run-up to the 21st party congress,” Kumar said.

title: US targets up to 200,000 foreigners in largest-ever mass visa revocation
description: State Department prepares mass revocation of tourist and business visas for foreigners seeking asylum.
content: The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States. If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges. Unless challenged or revised, the State Department was expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by Associated Press and two US officials. The action would be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security. “We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott. He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying “as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis”. The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said. Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travellers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet. Since US President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries. In a social media post on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the United States and then apply for asylum. “People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims,” Landau wrote on X. “Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law.” Landau cited the case of a Colombian citizen who came to the US in 2015 on a tourist visa and then applied for asylum. B1 visas are generally issued for business trips and B2 visas are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care. It was not immediately clear from the documents or the officials how many of these visa holders were seeking or have sought asylum in the United States and would be affected by the revocations. Current applicants for B1 and B2 visas are asked to affirm that they would not apply for asylum in the United States and prove that they intend to return to their home countries. In the past 18 months, the State Department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunken driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against US policies, particularly in the Middle East. The administration has also moved to crack down on so-called birth tourism, a practice the administration claims is used by foreign pregnant women to come to the United States to give birth so that their child will benefit from birthright citizenship. Trump has tried several times to end birthright citizenship, but those challenges have been rejected by courts, including the Supreme Court. The State Department documents obtained by AP suggest screening of current B1 and B2 visa holders began after the State Department received information about asylum requests from the US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

title: US Supreme Court gives Trump temporary win on mail-in ballots as midterms loom
description: Decision permits Trump administration to enforce restrictions for now, leaving final judgment pending as Democrats vow new lawsuits.
content: The US Supreme Court gave President Donald Trump a temporary victory on Monday, lifting a lower court block on his executive order curbing the use of mail-in ballots. The Republican president signed an order in March seeking to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the November midterm elections but it was immediately met with multiple legal challenges. Democratic-led states sued the administration on grounds that under the US Constitution, states – and not the federal government – retain broad control over the administration of elections. A district court in Massachusetts blocked implementation of the executive order but the Supreme Court on Monday lifted the judge’s stay, allowing parts of Trump’s directive to go ahead for now. “The District Court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Government from trying to implement” the executive order, the Supreme Court majority said in an unsigned opinion. But the justices withheld final judgment on the merits of the case pending further litigation. “The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful,” they said. “On that score, time will tell.” The three liberal justices on the nine-member Supreme Court dissented. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat, called the decision a “disgrace”, adding that Trump “wants to make it harder for Americans to vote so they don’t hold him accountable for the skyrocketing costs, illegal war, and rampant corruption that are a hallmark of his administration”. California Governor Gavin Newsom, who is widely tipped to be a Democratic presidential candidate in the next election, said his state would file another lawsuit over the matter. Trump’s March executive order would require the compilation of lists of eligible voters and for the US Postal Service to deliver ballots only to voters who are on the lists. Trump has been a long-time critic of mail-in ballots but has frequently used them himself, including this month when he voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary. Trump has for years claimed without evidence that mail-in voting is highly vulnerable to fraud, repeatedly linking it to his false assertion that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him by Democrat Joe Biden. “Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt,” he said during a July speech on election security. Polls show that Trump’s Republican Party faces a serious threat of losing its narrow control of Congress in the midterm elections in November, particularly in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber. If Democrats win, they have signalled they will block Trump’s agenda and could move to impeach him for the third time.

title: Opinion | Forcing women to drink at business dinners has no place in modern China
description: The alleged assault of a female employee in Hangzhou exposes how such unsavoury practices persist amid Beijing’s anti-extravagance campaign.
content: Reports of a female employee allegedly being assaulted at a drinking party in Hangzhou brought back a version of myself from more than a decade ago. Back then, I was one of those young women routinely invited to business dinners. Seating followed an unwritten rule, with the most powerful person taking the seat of honour, flanked by two young women. Everyone knew what we were there to do: keep the conversation lively, entertain the guests and, above all, keep raising our glasses. I’ve always been a terrible drinker. Yet under the familiar pressure – “Everyone else is drinking. Why aren’t you?” – I would force down a glass or two. I developed little tricks. Baijiu is clear, so I could sometimes discreetly spit it into a napkin without anyone noticing. However, that didn’t always work. Once, I was told to drink what they called a “red apple”, or a full glass of red wine. There was nowhere to hide it. I drank it, blacked out later, vomited three or four times and spent the next day with a splitting headache. What I remember most vividly is not the physical misery. It’s a strange sense of shame. Why could everyone else drink but I couldn’t? The ability to drink was seen as an important professional skill. The women who could drink without flinching seemed admirable. They knew when to stand, whom to toast and, above all, how to manage the mood of the table. I felt that my own body and personality were holding me back. Why was a young female employee expected to be at that dinner in the first place? What role was she expected to play at that table? It never occurred to me that the problem was not my drinking capacity. Why did I need to prove I could drink? More importantly, why did I feel I had no right to refuse? That feeling returned when I read about the Hangzhou incident. On July 26, after a business dinner related to a real estate project, a young female employee was reportedly forced to drink large amounts of alcohol before being assaulted and injured at a karaoke lounge. On August 18, Hangzhou authorities announced Zhao Haifeng, general manager of China Merchants Shekou Industrial Zone Holdings’ Zhejiang branch, and Yu Tingdong, deputy head of Hangzhou’s Binjiang district, had been detained and removed from their positions over allegations they sexually assaulted the woman. The case raises uncomfortable questions. Why was a young female employee expected to be at that dinner in the first place? What role was she expected to play at that table? Perhaps she felt what I once felt. If your boss asks you to come, you come. If everyone drinks, you drink. If you are a young woman, you are expected to know how to keep the table happy. You worry about being seen as difficult. You worry about damaging a business relationship. Even when your body tells you no, you raise the glass anyway. That is one of the most insidious things about drinking culture. It doesn’t always need an explicit command. Power itself can function as an order. That is why I don’t think the Hangzhou case can simply be dismissed as a drunken indiscretion. Business drinking has deep roots in China. A dinner table is rarely just a place to eat. It can be a place to build relationships, exchange information, protect interests and allocate resources. China’s anti-corruption campaigns and the “eight-point rules” introduced after 2012 have curbed lavish official banquets and publicly funded extravagance. Formal regulations can curb excess, but they are much less effective at changing how power operates around a dinner table. Perhaps the most stubborn thing is not the feast itself but the hierarchy behind it. That is what makes the Hangzhou case particularly jarring. Hangzhou is one of China’s most modern and dynamic cities, famous for a new generation of technology start-ups known as the “Six Little Dragons”. However, modern administrative procedures do not automatically produce modern power relations. A city can make entrepreneurs jump through fewer bureaucratic hoops without making it any easier for a young employee to look across a dinner table and simply say, “No, I don’t drink.” When I was attending those dinners, China’s economy was booming. Business dinners became part of the machinery of deal-making, and drinking was the price of admission. The world has changed since then, but the Hangzhou incident is a reminder that some things change much more slowly than economic cycles. Perhaps that is why the story resonates so strongly. It is not simply because we recognise that table. It is because so many of us have sat at one.

title: US targets China’s telecoms grip in Venezuela with new sanctions carve-out
description: Move could test Huawei and ZTE’s long-standing foothold as Washington extends its China reach from oil to another strategic sector.
content: The United States is opening Venezuela’s telecommunications sector to new investment and technology while explicitly excluding Chinese companies, a move that could reshape a market where Huawei and ZTE have become deeply embedded and give Western suppliers an opening as the country expands its 5G networks. The US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on Friday issued two general licences easing some sanctions restrictions on Venezuela’s telecommunications sector, including transactions involving state-owned provider CANTV and mobile operator Movilnet. But both licences specifically exclude transactions involving people or companies in China, Russia, Iran, North Korea and Cuba, as well as entities owned or controlled by, or in joint ventures with, them. The move extends to telecommunications a restriction Washington has already applied as it selectively eases sanctions on Venezuela. Earlier authorisations covering the country’s oil sector similarly opened the door to certain transactions while excluding China-linked entities, allowing the Trump administration to loosen economic restrictions on Caracas without extending the benefits to one of its principal geopolitical rivals. China’s embassy in Washington criticised the restrictions and vowed to defend Chinese companies affected by them. “We stand firmly against illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council,” an embassy spokesperson said. “We will firmly protect Chinese businesses’ legitimate and lawful rights and interests.” The US Treasury Department did not immediately respond to questions about the rationale for excluding Chinese companies or whether the measure was intended to reduce China’s role in Venezuela’s telecommunications infrastructure. The Chinese embassy in Washington also did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In telecommunications, however, the China carve-out could prove particularly consequential. Huawei and ZTE became important suppliers to Venezuela as US sanctions and compliance concerns curtailed other international companies’ ability or willingness to work with government-linked entities. “The importance of Chinese companies and Chinese technology in Venezuela’s telecommunications companies is enormous,” said Alcides Leon, a veteran Venezuelan technology journalist who has covered the sector for decades. In the case of state-owned CANTV and Movilnet, Leon said, most of their technology now comes from Huawei, making a shift away from Chinese suppliers potentially difficult and costly. Restrictions may affect networks’ maintenance, repair and components The restrictions could affect not only future investment but also the maintenance, repair and replacement of components in networks that already rely heavily on Chinese equipment, he said. As one example, Leon estimated that about half of the technology used by Digitel, one of Venezuela’s largest private mobile operators, comes from Huawei, with the other half supplied by Sweden’s Ericsson. The new US authorisations come as Venezuela modernises its telecommunications infrastructure and begins a transition to 5G, potentially creating opportunities for new equipment suppliers and investors. General License 61 allows US persons and companies to provide the goods, technology, software, and services needed to install, maintain, repair, upgrade, or operate telecommunications infrastructure in Venezuela. The authorisation covers equipment and spare parts, fibre-optic capacity, satellite bandwidth, cloud services, data storage, servers, software and network-support services. It also explicitly permits transactions involving CANTV, Movilnet and telecommunications regulator Conatel. However, it does not authorise transactions involving a person located in or organised under the laws of China, or an entity owned or controlled by, or in a joint venture with, such a person. A second authorisation, General License 62, could have more far-reaching implications for the industry’s future. It allows companies to negotiate conditional contracts for new investment in Venezuela’s telecommunications sector, including establishing new telecommunications providers, expanding existing operations and forming joint ventures. The licence also permits companies to submit bids or proposals in response to public tenders, although they cannot perform the resulting contracts or commit capital without separate OFAC authorisation. Chinese companies are again expressly excluded. Leon described the two licences as potentially marking a turning point for Venezuela’s telecommunications industry. The first provides a route for operators to obtain technology, software and support that had become difficult to access under sanctions, while the second could help reopen the sector to future international investment, he said. But excluding China means opening could also redirect Venezuela away from the suppliers that expanded their presence during the sanctions era. Huawei, ZTE ‘came to the rescue of telecommunications in Venezuela’ Huawei and ZTE “came to the rescue of telecommunications in Venezuela” while restrictions were in place, Leon said, allowing significant network deployment using Chinese technology as some other international suppliers pulled back. Their role was not limited to government companies, he added, but extended to private operators. Huawei and ZTE did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Chinese suppliers had been involved in Venezuela’s telecommunications sector well before the latest US sanctions. A CANTV prospectus details a US$144 million contract signed in 2019 by CANTV, Movilnet and Huawei to deploy 4G and 5G technology. The project included the supply, installation and configuration of 900 LTE radio base stations and was financed through Venezuela’s National Development Fund. Huawei and ZTE also took part in earlier generations of Venezuelan mobile and fixed telecommunications infrastructure as economic and technological cooperation between Beijing and Caracas expanded under former president Hugo Chavez and his successor Nicolas Maduro. That history leaves Venezuela facing a potentially complicated technological transition. Leon said opinions among Venezuelan telecommunications specialists differed over the legacy of China’s involvement. Chinese technology allowed networks to continue expanding during a period when access to other suppliers was constrained, he said, but some specialists argue that dependence on Chinese systems also contributed to technological isolation and compatibility problems. The new US rules are therefore likely to “change the landscape of telecom providers in Venezuela”, Leon said, while making it more difficult to maintain some existing networks built with Huawei and ZTE components. Potential beneficiaries could include European suppliers Ericsson and Nokia. “Ericsson and Nokia are going to have an enormous opportunity to gain ground,” Leon said, particularly in the deployment of fibre and 5G infrastructure. The United States does not have a major domestic supplier offering the full range of 5G radio-network equipment produced by Huawei, Ericsson and Nokia, meaning European technology could play an important role in projects enabled by the new US authorisations. Venezuela has already begun allocating spectrum for next-generation networks. Two spectrum auctions last year allocated frequencies to expand 4G and 5G services. In September, Movilnet was awarded 100MHz of spectrum in the 3.5GHz band for 5G deployment, while CANTV obtained additional spectrum in the 2.6GHz band. The changes are taking place amid a potentially broader shake-up of Venezuela’s telecommunications market. Spain’s Telefonica has been pursuing a wider retreat from most of Latin America, raising questions about the future ownership of its Venezuelan subsidiary Movistar, one of the country’s major mobile operators. Leon said the expected departure could change both the ownership structure of Venezuela’s telecommunications industry and relationships between operators and technology suppliers. The sector is closely watching who might acquire the business and whether a change in ownership could bring fresh investment, he said. Applying Washington’s China carve-out to telecommunications puts its Venezuela sanctions policy into a sector at the centre of a much wider US-China technological rivalry. Leon said the licences could be interpreted in two ways: as a further easing of sanctions that could help revive Venezuela’s telecommunications sector, or through a geopolitical lens as an attempt by Washington to push back against China’s ambitions in global 5G networks. Whether the new authorisations ultimately reduce China’s position in Venezuela may depend on how willing Western companies are to enter a market still carrying significant political and economic risks – and how easily Venezuelan operators can diversify away from Chinese technology already embedded in their networks.

title: Trump bought shares in Musk’s SpaceX in June, disclosure reveals
description: White House says third-party manager executed trade without presidential input following rocket maker’s US$1.77 trillion IPO.
content: US President Donald Trump invested as much as US$50,000 ⁠in Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June, according to a public financial disclosure, giving him a financial stake in a major government contractor run by his former adviser. Trump bought between US$15,001 and US$50,000 in shares on June 23, according to a financial disclosure signed ‌by him on August 12 and made public on August 22. The purchase was part of more than 1,000 stock trades the president made in June. SpaceX priced the biggest-ever US IPO on June 12, valuing the space, satellite and AI provider at US$1.77 trillion. In a statement to Reuters, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said third-party financial institutions independently manage the president’s ⁠portfolio and replicate “recognised indexes, such as the Schwab 1000”. “Neither President Trump nor any member of his family ‌has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” Ingle said in the ‌statement. Trump’s investment in SpaceX adds a new financial link between the president and Musk’s ⁠rocket company at a ⁠time when the administration is making decisions that could affect the firm’s fortunes. SpaceX is a US military contractor and often ‌seeks approvals from federal agencies. Trump on Thursday directed his team to help drastically increase the number of US commercial space launches. SpaceX ‌is a ‌dominant player in that sector. US Small Business Administration (SBA) leader and Trump cabinet member Kelly Loeffler ‌earned millions from SpaceX’s IPO, Reuters previously reported. Loeffler first invested in xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence and social media ⁠firm that has since merged with SpaceX. She invested again after Trump nominated her to lead ⁠the SBA. Her first investment in xAI would have been worth between US$7 million and US$2.6 billion on the day of the IPO, depending on the exact amount she invested and the ‌date she made it, ‌said Franco Granda, analyst at data provider PitchBook. The second investment would have been worth between US$2.2 million and US$25.4 million that day, he said. Reuters could not immediately determine the precise amount of Trump’s investment because federal officials use ranges to declare the value of their assets on their financial disclosure forms.

title: Tennis bracelets trend again: from Coco Gauff at Wimbledon to Meghan Markle
description: After soaring in popularity in 2024 thanks to Zendaya’s tennis-themed looks on the Challengers press tour, the style is having another major moment.
content: The tennis bracelet is very much back in the spotlight, courtesy of some major style moments at this year’s Wimbledon. Among the players sporting the classic jewel was two-time major winner Coco Gauff, who chose a gold vermeil and sapphire blue crystal tennis bracelet from London-based jeweller Missoma as part of her on-court look designed by New Balance and Miu Miu. Outside Wimbledon’s hallowed courts, the style has also been seen on the wrists of Hailey Bieber, who stacks her Tiffany & Co. versions up the wrist, Meghan Markle, Brooklyn Beckham and Timothée Chalamet. Interest in the tennis bracelet soared in 2024 with the release of Luca Guadagnino’s Challengers, the sensual tennis romantic drama starring Josh O’Connor, Mike Faist and Zendaya. The actress’ tennis-themed looks on the film’s press tour prompted a 133 per cent spike in online searches for tennis-style jewellery, according to British jewellery retailer The Diamond Store. Originally known as a line bracelet or eternity bracelet, the design’s origins stretch back to the Victorian era, when the discovery of major diamond deposits in South Africa in the 1860s flooded the market with stones and made matched diamond jewellery newly accessible. Tennis bracelets came into their own in the 1920s, when advances in metalworking made platinum, a silvery precious metal far stronger than gold, the material of choice for high-end jewellery. It enabled designers to craft settings so fine they were almost invisible, with diamonds sitting flush against one another in an uninterrupted line. This clean silhouette made it a natural fit for the art deco period, when symmetry and proportion were the hallmarks of design, and the tennis bracelet quickly became a staple of society dressing between the wars. Much like the eternity ring, a continuous band of stones, the tennis bracelet wasn’t short of romantic associations, symbolising enduring love and thus a natural gift for anniversaries and significant milestones. The tennis bracelet’s sporting nickname came in 1987, when former American tennis player Chris Evert paused a US Open match to retrieve her diamond line bracelet after it flew off her wrist mid-match. The moment was broadcast live and permanently attached the sport’s name to the design. The diamond line remains a jewellery box staple, but modern tennis bracelets are just as likely to feature juicy coloured gemstones, unconventional settings and even alternative metals like titanium. For those looking to commission their own tennis bracelet, comfort and wearability should be the starting point, according to the New York-based independent jeweller Jade Trau, whose designs are both relaxed and exceptionally crafted. “What I think is unique about a tennis bracelet is that it’s all about comfort and wearability,” she tells Style. “Our bracelets are linked in a couple of ways to create a really soft, pliable and easily worn bracelet. It’s the kind of diamond bracelet you just wear and becomes a part of you. It’s not an occasion piece,” she adds. Tennis bracelets designed by Trau include modern interpretations like the Envoy, with three pear-shaped diamonds and 22 round, brilliant-cut diamonds in the brand’s antique-influenced Alchemy setting, or the Poppy, with rows of pear, marquise and round-shaped diamonds. Each gold link of Trau’s tennis bracelets is polished and linked together by hand with extruded wire, with each diamond set individually. Whatever route you take, Trau offers advice on what to brief your jeweller. “It should be easy enough to get on and off yourself, but secure enough that you don’t feel it could fall off on its own,” she says. “The right tennis bracelet goes with everything. It’s a piece of jewellery that you just wear and enjoy all the time.” Among the independent jewellers breathing new life into the tennis bracelet is London-based Ananya. The brand offers two white gold versions in the Chakra collection – one set with rainbow sapphires, another with white diamonds – rooted in founder Ananya Malhotra’s love of colours. Los Angeles jeweller Anita Ko goes romantic with her diamond line bracelets, bejewelled with heart-cut coloured stones, while Cece Fein-Hughes, founder of London’s Cece Jewellery, strings her tennis bracelets with champlevé enamelled oval medallions, hand-painted with motifs like crashing waves and English roses, set among round brilliant-cut bezel-set diamonds. Elsewhere, Brazilian jeweller Ara Vartanian launched a capsule of tennis bracelets at the end of last year, timed to coincide with the inaugural SP Open, an international women’s tennis tournament in São Paulo, with three designs set with white, black or brown diamonds. Heavenly London, founded in 1993 by Belinda Scott, offers a more accessible take, with line bracelets set with cubic zirconia rather than diamonds in the classic silhouette. If your loyalties lie with the old guard, the options are plentiful. Graff takes the tennis bracelet into high jewellery territory, building bracelets around the “big four” – emeralds, rubies, sapphires and diamonds – with the occasional yellow and pink diamonds, too. Harry Winston has a range of classic styles, from full white diamonds to alternating white diamonds with blue sapphires or pink diamonds, while Parisian house Messika brings her signature articulation to the format with ultrafine chain-linked styles and gold heart motifs trimmed with diamonds. Tiffany & Co.’s Sixteen Stone bracelet, conceived by legendary designer Jean Schlumberger in 1959, embodies intricate craftsmanship with round brilliant diamonds and yellow gold cross-stitch motifs on the platinum band. Whatever you choose, the jewellery market is flush with both classic and more daring interpretations of the tennis bracelet now more than ever, with something to suit every wrist.

title: US removes Syria from state sponsor of terrorism list in major diplomatic shift
description: Washington lifts decades-old designation, removing final barriers to foreign investment following Assad’s fall.
content: The United States on Monday removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, rescinding a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions and marking another step in warming ties between the countries. The US Department of State also revoked its designation of al-Nusra Front – latterly known as Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) – as a global terrorist organisation. The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief. Rebels led by HTS overthrew long-time Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, with the group’s leader Ahmed al-Sharaa taking over as president as the country rebuilds after more than 13 years of civil war. “Today’s action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Treasury said the moves were “in line with President (Donald) Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria”. But the agency stressed that its removal of restrictions on Syria “does not change Treasury’s posture with regards to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable”. HTS was earlier known as al-Nusra Front and was formerly the branch of al-Qaeda in Syria. It broke ties with the jihadist group in 2016. The United States had initially announced in July its intent to delist Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism, a move seen as a vote of confidence in Sharaa. Trump met on the sidelines of a Nato summit in Turkey with the Syrian president, a former jihadist who has sought to recast himself as a unifying figure after the toppling of the Assad family, which ruled with an iron fist for a half-century. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday’s delistings gave Syrians “a path to prosperity”. The action “eliminates the final major barriers for private sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy,” he said in a statement. Top officials in Damascus hailed the delisting as a major opportunity for the country, still economically devastated after more than a decade of war that rights groups say killed more than half a million people. Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani described Washington’s delisting as a “historic milestone” and said it reflected “the new Syrian state’s commitment to international peace and security”. Finance Minister Mohammed Barnieh described the move as a “success for Syrian diplomacy,” according to the official news agency SANA. It “opens a major and long-awaited door to strengthening Syria’s integration into the global economic and financial system, attracting investment and modern technologies, and supporting development opportunities”. Central bank chief Safwat Raslan lauded the development, adding that his institution was “working to build a modern and reliable financial system capable of evolving with developments and taking advantage of all opportunities”.

title: Mexico ‘optimistic’ on US trade deal after Canada talks collapse
description: President Sheinbaum keeps envoy in Washington to lower US tariffs and avert broader USMCA rift.
content: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum expressed optimism she can reach a trade deal with US President Donald Trump as her chief negotiator leads talks in Washington, just after negotiations between the US and Canada collapsed. “As President Trump said, we hope to reach an agreement with the US,” she told reporters on Monday after being asked about the escalating US-Canada impasse. “I’m optimistic an agreement can be reached.” Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, Sheinbaum’s top trade negotiator, will remain in Washington for several days as he seeks to lower 50 per cent US tariffs on Mexican steel and aluminium, and 25 per cent duties on cars. The six-year-old USMCA trade pact includes the US, Mexico and Canada. Last month, it formally entered a phase of annual reviews. Washington’s negotiations with Ottawa fell apart in recent days, prompting Trump to say he will double tariffs on Canadian cars and parts starting next year. The breakdown also triggered a 50 per cent US levy on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods, while Prime Minister Mark Carney announced retaliatory tariffs to take effect on September 8. As with Mexico, the current import duty on Canadian cars is 25 per cent and applied only to the vehicles’ non-US content. Imported steel also faces 50 per cent levies.

title: China vows to safeguard interests after ‘Economic D-Day’ sanctions over Iran ties
description: Washington warns Iran-linked entities face removal from US dollar system as Trump presses world leaders to cut financial ties.
content: China has condemned fresh US “Economic D-Day” sanctions imposed on Chinese entities over their ties to Iran, pledging “all necessary measures” to protect its interests. Launching the measures on Monday against Iran and its trading partners, the United States unveiled new sanctions against 60 entities, individuals and vessels around the world, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong, and demanded “immediate action” from nations maintaining economic and commercial ties with Iran.
