The measures are part of the Trump administration’s latest efforts to choke off Tehran economically after military strikes and diplomatic negotiations failed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the six-month conflict. In Beijing on Tuesday, the Chinese foreign ministry said Beijing’s cooperation with Tehran was conducted “within the framework of international law and should not be disrupted”. Economic wars and maximum pressure were “not the solutions”, ministry spokesman Lin Jian said. The new actions aim to expand Washington’s secondary sanctions, putting entities in multiple jurisdictions on notice. “Let me be clear: any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. Bessent added that US President Donald Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests” to halt their engagement with the Iranian regime, but did not identify the countries he had contacted. The campaign’s effectiveness may ultimately depend on how far Washington is willing to press China, Iran’s most important remaining economic partner. Although the sanctions announced on Monday target an extensive collection of mainland Chinese and Hong Kong procurement, financial and shipping intermediaries, they stop short of blacklisting major Chinese banks and refiners whose exposure to the US financial system could give Washington substantially greater leverage. “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions,” Bessent said when asked about the possibility of the US imposing secondary sanctions on Chinese banks over their commercial links with Iranian entities. However, he also advocated “quiet diplomacy” and said Washington was “level-setting with every country” to share its expectations. “We know who they are; they know who they are. So when the hammer of US Treasury actions falls upon them, they will have no one to blame but themselves.” The Treasury Department said it had “mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions and fund terror”. “Every country will be given a defined timeline to shut down the Iran-related activity we have identified. If they fail to act, Treasury will act,” it warned. China-based targets The entities targeted on Monday included Hong Kong-based Sweet Ocean Industrial Ltd, accused of serving “as an intermediary for the procurement of sensitive goods, including laser optics equipment” for Iran’s UN-sanctioned Malek Ashtar University of Technology. Among the newly designated Chinese nationals are Li Na, Qiu Xingyu, Tian Jianbai and Zhang Limei. The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control links Li, Tian and Zhang to Sweet Ocean Industrial Ltd, while Qiu is linked to Hong Kong-based BRE International Logistics Corp. The entries carry proliferation-related designations and secondary-sanctions exposure. The new mainland Chinese entities include Bositong Supply Chain Shenzhen Co Ltd, Shenzhen Bositong Logistics Co Ltd, Shenzhen Huamei Lianyun International Logistics Co Ltd and Shenzhen Sweet Ocean Technology Ltd. Newly listed Hong Kong companies include BRE International Logistics Corporation HK Ltd, DEC Photonics Ltd, HK Jiatai Technology Ltd, MT Trading and Logistics HK Ltd, and RPT Technology Ltd. There are also a number of Iranian oil and shipping-related companies, including Feili Co Ltd, Feisu Ltd, Guska Co Ltd, Minvur Ltd, Riqueza Group Ltd, Shipoil Ltd and Sky Oil and Gas Asia Ltd. The Chinese embassy in Washington said Beijing stood firmly against “illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law”. “We will firmly protect Chinese businesses’ legitimate and lawful rights and interests,” embassy spokesman Liu Chang said. More summit headaches The measures could further complicate the fragile US-China truce and come weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to visit Washington for a summit with Trump. Last week, Bessent urged China to join Washington’s latest efforts to economically pressure and isolate Iran, arguing that Beijing’s dependence on Gulf energy supplies gave it a strong incentive to help bring an end to the conflict. The US Treasury has already targeted several Chinese companies, including some based in Hong Kong, over their alleged role in processing billions of dollars in Iranian oil revenue and facilitating arms purchases. It has also warned two large Chinese banks against handling Iranian funds. “Keep in mind, the Chinese get 50 per cent of their energy from the Gulf. So, it would do them a big service to get with the programme,” Bessent told CNBC when asked whether the new economic sanctions would include China. Gulf countries – led by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – accounted for 27.6 per cent of China’s total crude imports in July, according to official customs data released last week. China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, purchasing more than 80 per cent of the country’s total oil exports in 2025, according to data from analytics firm Kpler. “China enables Iran to mitigate global sanctions through trade and financial networks, technology transfers, and dual-use trade,” the US-China Economic and Security Commission alleged in a report released in March. China has denied the allegations. Iran threatens military strikes Iran, meanwhile, has warned that it will retaliate against US sanctions, including possible strikes against its neighbours if they decide to join the US-led economic efforts. “Our hands are not tied,” Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on Monday, adding that “any escalation of this situation will undoubtedly bring about consequences”. “Any country that becomes a partner in creating economic restrictions against us will be regarded by us as an enemy,” Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Iranian state television on Saturday. Iran has faced decades of economic sanctions and isolation, including Washington’s “maximum pressure” campaign during Trump’s first term, as the US has repeatedly sought to constrain Tehran’s access to international markets and the financial system. Even as Washington intensifies economic pressure, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir is visiting Tehran to renew Pakistan’s mediating efforts to end the conflict. Pakistan played an instrumental role in brokering the ceasefire and the signing of a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran in June, but the agreement unravelled less than a month later. The development on Monday marked the latest turn in a conflict that has seen escalating hostilities, repeated collapse of ceasefire agreements and US threats to intensify military operations. Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit route for roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, has pushed up energy prices and added to global inflationary pressures. Additional reporting by Fan Chen

title: Maradona’s ‘Hand of God’ football sells for US$3.35 million
description: Match ball from 1986 World Cup quarter-final against England falls well short of US$10 million estimate.
content: The football with which Diego Maradona scored his “Hand of God” goal against England at the 1986 World Cup has sold at auction for US$3.35 million. The sale price achieved by Heritage Auctions in the United States was around US$6.7 million below the US$10 million estimate. The Dallas-based auction house had placed a US$2.5 million starting price on the Adidas Azteca ball. Maradona scored twice in Argentina’s quarter-final victory over England on June 22, 1986 at Estadio Azteca in Mexico City. He controversially punched the opener beyond England goalkeeper Peter Shilton before scoring a superb individual effort, later voted “Goal of the Century”. The Argentina playmaker, who died aged 60 in November 2020, claimed his contentious first goal was scored “a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God”. Tunisian referee Ali Bin Nasser, who took charge of the match, collected the ball at full-time and kept it for more than three decades. He sold the ball in 2022 for US$2.37 million. Its new owner again put it up for auction in 2023 but it failed to meet the reserve price. After defeating England, Argentina went on to become world champions for the second time following a 3-2 victory over West Germany in the final.

title: Shein’s acquisition of Everlane faces US national security review
description: The review is focused on potential issues linked to the China-founded retailer’s purchase of a firm that handles Americans’ personal data.
content: US authorities are conducting a national security review of Shein Global Holdings’ purchase of American clothing retailer Everlane after Shein sought approval for the deal, people familiar with the matter said, adding to a growing list of regulatory hurdles for the China-founded fast-fashion giant in one of its most important markets. The review by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the US (Cfius), an inter-agency panel led by the Treasury Department, began after the US$80 million transaction was completed in May, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private deliberations. Shein voluntarily initiated the review at that time, which is unusual as companies typically seek Cfius approval before a transaction closes, the people said. Clearance by Cfius usually prevents future challenges, but the body also has the power to block, unwind or impose conditions on transactions it determines threaten US national security. A Shein spokesperson said the company is “committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations in the markets where we operate”. The Treasury did not respond to a request for comment. Cfius reviews are confidential. Shein maintains substantial operations in China even after it moved its headquarters from there to Singapore several years ago. The company remains subject to Chinese regulators, whose blessing it needed to pursue its long-sought initial public offering – launched on Monday – in Hong Kong. At the same time, the US remains among Shein’s top markets for sales. The Cfius review is focused on potential national security issues linked to Shein’s acquisition of a company that handles Americans’ personal data, and it’s unclear what the conclusion will be, according to one of the people familiar with the situation. Such data has become an increasingly sensitive national security issue worldwide, especially in the context of the US-China rivalry with both countries looking to limit the other’s access to citizens’ information. After announcing the Everlane deal closed, Shein engaged a new lawyer from King & Spalding to handle the filing to Cfius, according to the people. That lawyer, Phil Ludvigson, is a former senior Treasury official who built the office that pursues deals that Cfius may want to review but which the parties have not proactively flagged to the committee. A spokesperson for King & Spalding referred questions about the Cfius review to Shein. The company filed for the Cfius review after the deal had closed because Everlane’s financial circumstances required the parties to move quickly on the transaction, according to a person close to the deal, noting that the request was not in response to any government intervention or inquiry. Ludvigson was engaged because of his extensive Cfius expertise and Shein’s long-standing relationship with his firm, the person said. “In the case of Chinese acquirers, Cfius often closely scrutinises the acquisition of any large data sets, particularly those that include geolocational and financial information,” said Rick Sofield, co-chair of Debevoise & Plimpton’s national security practice. National security concerns involving consumer company deals typically revolve around activities such as the collection of customer names and addresses, the use of tracking cookies to build customer profiles, and the implementation of military discount programmes that could identify service members, according to lawyers who represent companies in Cfius reviews. The details of the specific issues raised in the Shein investigation were not immediately clear. Shein’s IPO prospectus includes a section on US regulatory risks as a potential risk factor but does not mention Cfius specifically. Though the Everlane deal is tiny compared with the valuation of up to US$27 billion that Shein is seeking in its IPO, the acquisition has already drawn public criticism in the US. Media commentators, influencers and Everlane’s founder Michael Preysman, who left the company several years ago, have lamented the acquisition as a betrayal of company values rooted in sustainability and supply chain transparency. Shein has faced a range of legal and regulatory hurdles in the US. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued the company in February, alleging it unlawfully sold toxic products to consumers and exposed Americans’ personal data to China’s government. Shein said at the time it “strongly” disagreed with the allegations and is contesting the case. The Federal Trade Commission is also investigating Shein’s US business operations for potential violations of consumer protection laws, Bloomberg has reported. Shein has said it is cooperating with the investigation. Shein abandoned earlier plans to list in New York after facing criticism from lawmakers over its ties to China. Opponents included then-senator Marco Rubio, who is now US President Donald Trump’s secretary of state and acting national security adviser. In 2023, a bipartisan group of lawmakers questioned Shein in a letter about its alleged reliance on forced labour after laboratory testing conducted for Bloomberg found that garments shipped to the US by the company were made with cotton from China’s Xinjiang region. Shein at the time said it has “zero tolerance against forced labour”. The US and other Western countries have accused Chinese officials of engaging in serious human rights abuses in Xinjiang, which Beijing denies.

title: US military kills 2 in eastern Pacific boat strike in first attack in months
description: Lethal attack on low profile vessel ends two-month pause, bringing total campaign death toll to 223 across 67 strikes.
content: After a pause of more than two months, the US military announced Monday that it once again carried out a strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs. It brings the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly year-long US campaign of bombing alleged drug boats off Latin America’s Caribbean coast and in the eastern Pacific Ocean. US Southern Command says the campaign has resulted in the destruction of 64 speedboats, three “low profile” ships and a semi-submersible craft. The command said on social media early Monday that forces “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low profile vessel operating along established narcotrafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”. The military said the strike occurred Sunday, and it marked the first since powerful back-to-back June 24 earthquakes in Venezuela killed thousands of people. As with most of the military’s statements, Southern Command did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists – disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership, and eliminating cartel terror across the region,” said General Francis Donovan, who leads US Southern Command. "This operation is a clear and decisive reminder that SOUTHCOM is taking the fight directly to the cartels." On August 23, under #SOUTHCOM Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan’s direction, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel… pic.twitter.com/aIw1qn36gd — U.S. Southern Command (@Southcom) August 24, 2026 The latest strike comes as the Trump administration pursues deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the US to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal. Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March. The Trump administration’s boat bombing campaign began in early September and has left numerous survivors, but most of them have never been recovered. US Southern Command said in a separate statement Monday that there have been more than 20 search and rescue efforts overall, almost all of which were unsuccessful. According to data compiled from the command’s social media posts, the strikes have generated 28 survivors with only three people ever being rescued – one person during a strike in March who was transferred to the Costa Rican Coast Guard, and two wounded people who were later repatriated to their home countries of Ecuador and Colombia. The very first strike in September 2025 left two survivors who were killed in a second, follow-up strike. When that became public, it drew concern from some lawmakers and those who study military law. The White House insisted it was done “in self-defence” to ensure the boat was destroyed and in accordance with armed conflict laws. But some legal scholars said a second strike killing survivors would have been illegal under any circumstance, armed conflict or not. President Donald Trump has said the US is in “armed conflict” with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing “narcoterrorists”. Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the US over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India. The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the US military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the strikes. However, the evaluation is focused specifically on what’s known as the six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle and not on the legality of the strikes, the inspector general’s office said.

title: Hong Kong woman arrested for allegedly wearing seditious T-shirt outside court
description: Woman was detained on suspicion of disorder in a public place, obstructing police and acting with seditious intention.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a woman for allegedly wearing a T‑shirt with a seditious message outside West Kowloon Court. The force said on Monday night that the woman was detained last week on suspicion of disorder in a public place, obstructing police and acting with seditious intention. “The purpose of the security operation was to ensure public safety and order, though details of the operation cannot be disclosed,” a police spokesman said. The arrest came hours before judges delivered a verdict against two former leaders of the now‑disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil. Shortly after 5am on Friday, more than 50 people had queued outside the courthouse to cover or hear the judgment against former chairman Lee Cheuk‑yan and former vice‑chairwoman Chow Hang‑tung of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China. The pair and the alliance were accused of inciting subversion under the national security law by calling for an end to “one‑party dictatorship” in mainland China. During the wait, a plain‑clothes officer reportedly singled out a woman whose shirt was suspected of carrying seditious intent and escorted her into a police vehicle. The incident was captured on camera by media, with officers reportedly directing reporters to leave as she was taken away. A witness told media she was wearing a black T‑shirt printed with Japanese characters. Hours later, Lee, Chow and the now-disbanded alliance were found guilty of inciting subversion. In a 216‑page ruling, three High Court judges held that any attempt to overthrow or undermine the Communist Party of China’s leadership could amount to subversion, as the country’s constitution did not permit Western‑style democracy. Lee, a former lawmaker, and Chow, a barrister, have been in custody for nearly five years. A fourth defendant, former vice‑chairman Albert Ho Chun‑yan, has been detained for more than four years and awaits sentencing after pleading guilty in January.

title: UK police arrest 12 after deadly wrong-way crash that killed 7
description: Police have denied the collision on Saturday was linked to filming for the TikTok online platform.
content: British police have arrested 12 people after a car pursued by police crashed while driving the wrong way on a major road, killing five youths and two officers. The deaths on Saturday came as officials warned of a trend for young people to carry out dangerous driving stunts to post on social media. However, police on Monday denied the collision was linked to filming for the TikTok online platform. Police in the Cleveland area of northeast England said there was “no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok”. The force revealed that officers were chasing two cars with cloned plates when the deadly accident occurred. It added that 12 had since been arrested on suspicion of taking part in an organised crime group and weapon possession. The crash came days after five teenagers were killed in Ireland while their car drove the wrong way on a motorway. Irish police chief Justin Kelly said that “what makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media”. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday – while visiting Kyiv – that “anybody who glorifies dangerous driving is doing something that’s truly reprehensible and unacceptable”. The government had “raised the issue of this appalling content with social media companies”, including TikTok, Downing Street said. Britain’s communications regulator Ofcom last month launched an investigation into whether TikTok, owned by Chinese company ByteDance, is doing enough under UK law to protect children from harmful content, focusing on its age checks. According to TikTok, it strictly prohibits content that could cause significant physical harm including dangerous driving and proactively removes such content. Ofcom said in a statement sent to Agence France-Presse on Monday that under the Online Safety Act, “platforms must minimise children’s exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges”. The watchdog said it had shown it would “take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short”. National Highways for England said there were 947 reports of wrong-way driving in the year ending May 2026, slightly down on the previous year. Irish police said there had been 62 such incidents so far this year with no marked recent increase.

title: France to press ahead with high school phone ban from next month
description: The ban is expected to take effect from the start of the new school year, which begins in September.
content: The French government said on Monday it would press ahead with a ban on mobile phones in high schools from next month, but trade unions warned that the measure might be hard to implement quickly. In July, France’s parliament approved legislation banning both social media access for children under 15 and mobile phone use in high schools. It is part of a push by President Emmanuel Macron for children to spend less time in front of screens, which the government fears is arresting their development. But earlier this month, the country’s top court struck down the social media provision, dealing a blow to Macron. However the Constitutional Council did not rule on the separate provision banning mobile phone use in high schools. On Monday, government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon said Macron “has decided to promulgate the law” containing the ban on phones, despite the Constitutional Council striking down its flagship provision. “As a result, the ban on mobile phones in high schools can take effect from the start of the new school year, with a stable, consolidated and statutory legal framework,” she said after a cabinet meeting. France’s school year starts in September. The country has already banned children from using mobile phones in colleges – the schools attended between the ages of 11 and 15 – and in primary schools. In early July, high schools had been instructed to prepare for the measure’s implementation in September, ahead of its adoption by parliament later that month. In order to enforce the ban, schools must amend their internal regulations. But many schools may struggle to implement the measure because they have had little time to prepare. Francois Resnais, national secretary of SNPDEN-Unsa, France’s top union of school principals, criticised the timing as “bad”. “Schools are not ready,” Resnais said. “Schools are starting the year with a rule that is not written into their internal regulations, except perhaps for those that tried to anticipate something, but that remains very limited.” Christelle Kauffmann, the union’s deputy secretary general, is among the minority of school leaders who anticipated the measure. At her high school, phones will be banned in corridors and school buildings from the start of term, but allowed outdoors. She said it could take nearly a year before the ban could be fully implemented across all high schools. “It is very difficult for a school community to impose a new rule on young people. Even if the law is supposed to apply automatically, it is not that simple,” she said. “You cannot put a supervisor behind every student.” Kamel Chibli, vice-president of the Occitanie regional council in southern France, said digital pouches and lockers used to store smartphones cost the regional authorities around €40,000 (US$46,675) for a high school with 1,500 students. High school students regularly use their smartphones to check timetable changes, room assignments and other school information. Some teachers also rely on phones in class for research, exercises and document sharing. In its guidance, the education ministry allows exemptions from the ban for “educational uses” or for purposes “necessary for the proper functioning of the school”. Macron’s office has said the president has no plans to give up on his push to bar children from apps such as TikTok and the government would work on a new draft law. “The president’s objective is to have a stable legal framework in place by next spring to protect our children and young people,” Bregeon said. Macron is due to step down next spring after serving the maximum two consecutive terms allowed in office.

title: Mainland China’s ship activity near Taiwan hits record for third month in a row
description: Beijing has ramped up its law-enforcement and survey operations around island since Tokyo and Manila announced boundary talks.
content: Mainland Chinese government vessel sightings around Taiwan have reached record levels for a third straight month, as Beijing expands its law enforcement footprint east of the island following the announcement in late May of Tokyo-Manila maritime boundary talks over the area. Taiwan’s defence ministry said that in the first 24 days of August it detected mainland coastguard, survey and other official vessels a total of 118 times, surpassing the 117 reported in July and 111 in June. Those numbers were far higher than in any previous month on record since Taiwan began releasing detection data in July 2024. Before June, the highest number of sightings of such ships in a single month was 50 in April 2025, according to a tally by the SCMP. That record-breaking intensity of activity aligns with findings from an August 19 report by the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative (AMTI), which noted a “more sustained and assertive presence” by mainland Chinese law-enforcement and survey vessels in waters east of Taiwan. Using commercial automatic identification system data, AMTI – a programme of the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies – showed that the ships’ activity around Taiwan between June and August was concentrated in waters where Chinese, Japanese and Philippine maritime claims overlap. Almost no such activity had been observed in that area between January and late May. Two China Coast Guard vessels accounted for much of the observable activity during that period, while a third had been patrolling the area since August 4, according to AMTI. Within days of the Japan-Philippines announcement, mainland Chinese law-enforcement vessels hailed 198 commercial ships in the area, demanding information about their ports of call and crews, the report noted. Crucially, Beijing’s operations extended well beyond the contested boundary zone. The AMTI report found that survey vessels often operated within 50 nautical miles (93km) of Taiwan – in waters the think tank described as “largely irrelevant to the Japan-Philippines delimitation”. “The scale and character of China’s response suggest that these operations are not just about sending a signal to Tokyo and Manila,” the think tank noted, adding that Beijing might see an opportunity to establish a “semi-permanent presence” and exercise some form of jurisdiction east of Taiwan. Beijing frames the operations differently. Its foreign ministry has condemned the Tokyo-Manila talks as “illegal, null and void” and asserted Beijing’s jurisdiction over the waters. The China Coast Guard has separately described its patrols there as a “necessary response” to what it calls unilateral actions by Japan and the Philippines. The push has also extended to civilian research missions. In June, Beijing’s Ministry of Natural Resources said it carried out a three-day marine environmental survey in waters east of Taiwan, part of what state media said would now be an annual mission rather than the one-off surveys previously run in the area. Beijing sees Taiwan as a breakaway province to be reunited by force if needed. Most countries, including the United States, do not see Taiwan as an independent state, but are opposed to any change to the status quo by force. Taiwanese officials warned in early July that the sustained presence of mainland Chinese government vessels across parts of the first island chain aimed to establish a “new status quo”. The first island chain, which stretches along the East Asian coastline from the Kuril Islands down to Borneo, divides mainland China’s near seas from the open Pacific Ocean. Beyond asserting jurisdiction, sustained law-enforcement patrols east of Taiwan could act as a rehearsal for a maritime quarantine of commercial shipping by mainland China, AMTI said. The survey operations in the area, meanwhile, could also have military uses. The report said that such missions could collect data on subsea environments that could inform undersea warfare capabilities, adding that the surveyed area would be a “critical battleground” in any Taiwan conflict. Ultimately, the report’s authors argued, the pattern mirrored Beijing’s behaviour in other disputed maritime areas, where an expanded operational presence at sea had often outlasted the event Beijing said it was initially responding to. That could make the present expansion particularly consequential. The report pointed out that maritime delimitation was rarely a quick process, with the Japan-Philippines negotiations likely to be measured in years rather than months – potentially giving Beijing an equally extended justification for its operations. “Whatever the original intent,” the report concluded, Beijing’s maritime forces were establishing a “more sustained and assertive presence” east of Taiwan.

title: Trump threatens 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks amid trade row
description: The two countries failed to reach ‌a trade deal late on Friday, with each side blaming the other.
content: US tariffs on all cars and trucks, automotive parts and steel would be increased to 50 per cent starting January 1 next year, President Donald Trump said in a social post on ‌Monday after trade talks with Canada collapsed over the weekend. “Build in the US and there are ZERO TARIFFS. Canada will be treated like a State no longer!” Trump wrote. “On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in ⁠the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE ‌DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment seeking ‌more details on the threatened tariffs. Representatives for the Canadian ⁠government also ⁠did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The two countries failed to reach ‌a trade deal late on Friday, with each side blaming the other as Canada readied tariffs ‌on ‌some US goods in retaliation for 50 per cent levies ordered by Trump ‌on other Canadian products. Major carmakers did not immediately comment on ⁠Trump’s announcement. But auto executives, speaking to Reuters on the condition of anonymity, raised ⁠scepticism about Trump’s threat, noting the president had previously announced large tariffs that never materialised and that any tariff of ‌that size was ‌likely to spark a massive Canadian retaliation. They also noted January was months away following November’s midterm elections and that Trump’s threat could be aimed at restarting talks. The new measures Trump announced on Monday target the Canadian province of Ontario in particular. The province is led by Premier Doug Ford, whose pugnacious approach to talks has riled the Trump administration. Steel and auto production is heavily concentrated in Ontario, which is Canada’s most populous and vote-rich province. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Meet the Indian food safety officer shaking up Mumbai with viral raids
description: Tukaram Mundhe’s crackdown on poor hygiene and unsafe food is forcing businesses in Mumbai to make pre-emptive changes.
content: Tukaram Mundhe is an Indian bureaucrat on a mission. As a state food safety commissioner, the 51-year-old has raided food businesses in the country’s commercial capital Mumbai in an unprecedented crackdown on poor hygiene and unsafe food that has captivated the public nationwide. Mundhe has led the suspension of food permits of four Domino’s and one Pizza Hut outlet in recent weeks, and has also targeted cricket clubs, hotels and well-known restaurants in over 3,000 raids since he took over as Maharashtra’s ‌food safety chief in May. When a Mumbai judge accused Mundhe of selective aggression towards private outlets and asked if court canteens were checked, his teams conducted inspections there within hours, shutting some of them which operated without licences. “Those who try to not comply, they will face what is expected from the regulator,” Mundhe said in an interview with Reuters, talking about his no-nonsense approach. “You are dealing with the lives of people.” Mundhe has won widespread public admiration across India because he has tapped into deep public frustration. Even though foreign chains such as Domino’s and McDonald’s are fast expanding, it is local eateries, roadside kiosks and small restaurants – long dogged by concerns over hygiene – that remain hugely popular. Each year since 2020, Indian food inspectors have checked more than ⁠100,000 food samples and found roughly 20 per cent to be unsafe, substandard or lacking proper labels, government data shows. Nearly 8,000 food business licences have been cancelled in the last three years. “Everyone has tried to ‌normalise this for years by saying it happens in India. It’s basically bottled-up anger,” said Ankur Bisen, a partner at consumer consulting firm The Knowledge Company. “I have never seen anyone like Mundhe. It’s giving people hope.” Mundhe, who is bespectacled and sports a chevron moustache, has an unconventional operating style. He ‌has featured in TV interviews declaring nobody dare bribe him, and that he is not afraid of administrative action despite being transferred numerous times in his 21-year career ⁠as an officer of the highly regarded Indian ⁠Administrative Service. “I get transferred every year,” he said in a 2018 interview. Now, his food safety team’s actions go viral daily – raids lead to detailed public statements and graphic images that show interiors of eateries and grocery warehouses with stained walls, crawling cockroaches ‌and rats, and even expired food – photos that have shocked many Indians. “It was surprising. I did not expect these many violations,” Mundhe said. In Mumbai, Reuters visits last week to 25 street vendors and restaurants showed heightened fear about Mundhe’s raids. One vendor has swapped artificial ‌red dye ‌for natural chilli in Chinese offerings, while another has started changing his frying oil three times a day and requires staff to wear gloves and head caps. Mumbai’s omnipresent street food vada pav – a spicy ‌potato patty in a bun – has not escaped Mundhe’s attention. In June, he prohibited use of newspapers as packaging material – often used to wrap the delicacy. Customers are noticing the change and consuming street food more ⁠confidently. Supriya Wagle, 14, is happy her favourite vada pav is now being packed in cleaner butter paper, saying that is “surely a relief”. After finding lapses at some Domino’s and ⁠Pizza Hut stores, Mundhe’s team on Friday suspended the permit of a McDonald’s outlet after finding “live pest activity (cockroaches)” and “rotting food”. In a statement, McDonald’s India said it had “a zero-tolerance approach” to food safety issues and was reviewing the observations. Domino’s and Pizza Hut did not respond to Reuters queries. Mundhe’s crackdown has included action against a Mumbai British-era cricket club, a 70-year-old ice ‌cream parlour and a 110-year-old Parsi Dairy. He is facing ‌criticism from businesses that say they should be given time to adapt, with some approaching the High Court and accusing his department of high-handedness. In one case, the judges fined his department 500,000 rupees (US$5,225) for continued suspension of an eatery even though it improved its compliance. “If there are observations by the court, we take it seriously … if there is scope for improvement, we improve,” Mundhe said. At an event in New Delhi on Friday, fans clicked quick selfies with Mundhe and jostled to shake his hand. One fan told him Prime Minister Narendra Modi should give him a national role. “I don’t think I’m a celebrity. I’m just a food safety commissioner,” he told Reuters.

title: Chinese tech, pharma firms eye Hong Kong as springboard for global expansion
description: Industry leaders highlight city’s international reach and expertise as state-owned drug maker considers Northern Metropolis project investment.
content: Mainland Chinese technology and pharmaceutical companies are using Hong Kong as a launching pad for global expansion, industry leaders have said, as a major state-owned drugmaker weighs whether to invest in the city’s Northern Metropolis megaproject. The comments highlighting the city’s international background and professional expertise were made during a six-day trip to the rest of the Greater Bay Area, which was arranged by the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office and started on Sunday. “Hong Kong is stepping up efforts to develop its innovation and technology sector. Its unique blend of Chinese and Western cultures, along with its high degree of internationalisation, gives the city a clear advantage in developing the traditional Chinese medicine industry,” Chen Jiehui, vice-chairman of Guangzhou Pharmaceutical Holdings, said on Monday. “Through Hong Kong’s international platform, global languages and standards can be leveraged to help traditional Chinese medicine go global … such as Southeast Asian countries which could serve as a prime example of markets expanding internationally via Hong Kong.” Chen added that his company, a major state-owned pharmaceutical enterprise, was considering investing in the Northern Metropolis and had previously held alignment discussions with relevant parties. He did not reveal details of the possible investment. The Northern Metropolis megaproject aims to turn 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land near the border with the mainland into a technological and economic hub. Wang Yuemiao, executive dean of the central research institute of PCI Technology Group, which focuses on artificial intelligence-based products and services, said on the same day that Hong Kong could help mainland enterprises, such as his company, expand globally. “Hong Kong possesses a mature international business network that can help mainland enterprises engage overseas government agencies, project owners, and industry partners more efficiently, serving as a bridge for businesses to expand abroad,” he said. He added that the city had a mature system of professional services across law, finance, accounting and intellectual property, which could help enterprises lower institutional costs and risks when entering overseas markets. Hong Kong could help enterprises adapt and fine-tune technologies and solutions that had already been proven mature on the mainland to align with international standards, he said. Xue Peng, vice-president of EHang, a company focused on advanced air mobility, also said that the city had strong potential to develop aerial drone transport, starting with cargo delivery. Hong Kong had numerous islands and could also explore cross-border logistics applications, he added. Xue suggested that drones could first be tested and applied in designated locations before their usage was progressively expanded to other parts of Hong Kong. Hong Kong has identified the low-altitude economy, including drone logistics, as a strategic area under a smart city development push. The government earlier established a Task Force on Supporting Mainland Enterprises in Going Global – or GoGlobal Task Force – to encourage firms across the border to use Hong Kong as a platform for expanding overseas. The task force is part of Hong Kong’s efforts to better integrate into national development by capitalising on the bay area strategy and the nation’s Belt and Road Initiative, which aims to improve trade and economic integration across Asia, Europe and Africa.

title: Hong Kong Football Club’s faith in ‘world-class’ ex-Premier League coach to inspire upturn
description: Darren Arnott aiming to turn perennial strugglers into competitive unit, tapping into English connections for emerging potential stars.
content: Darren Arnott likens the ongoing challenge for Football Club to that of someone “hanging on to a cliff and trying to pull themselves up”. When they lost their grip on the precipice last season, local football chiefs handily provided a safety net, sparing the Hong Kong Premier Division’s bottom team from relegation to the First Division. Having finished dead last in the previous campaign, too, they are unlikely to get lucky a third time. Boasting a slim budget and, as a members’ club, confronted with unique challenges, Football Club have got creative in their quest to keep their future in their own hands. A touch more ambitious, too, given they have wrenched Darren Arnott, a head coach with “world-class pedigree and credentials”, according to the club’s director of soccer, Shane Jeffrey, out of the clutches of the same Football Association of Hong Kong, China (HKFA) that waved through their reprieve. Jeffrey, whose official title is congruous with his American nationality, said that former Leeds United coach Arnott, 40, represented “the next phase of [Football Club’s] professional development: tactical sophistication, ruthless structural discipline and a proven commitment to elite high-performance standards”. The Englishman’s appointment to replace Chancy Cooke, who will focus solely on his academy technical director role after two years as first-team boss, coupled with an imaginative summer’s recruitment that exploited Arnott’s “intimate knowledge” of the English and local football scenes, has validated the HKFA’s decision to allow Football Club a top-flight stay of execution. Their well-appointed facilities, respectable attendances and good track record of producing talented local players all added up to a strong argument for their preservation, but that was going to wash for only so long. Still, why would Arnott want to trade his post leading Hong Kong’s under-23 team, on the eve of their Asian Games campaign to boot, for the task of trying to squeeze a quart into a pint pot at Football Club? They do not publicly disclose their annual budget, but it is materially lower than any of their 10 divisional rivals, none of whom spend less than HK$6 million (around US$766,000). Arnott owns an AFC Pro Licence, and he has recently completed the English Premier League’s Elite Coach Accreditation Scheme (ECAS). Along with two spells with Leeds, where he worked with the idiosyncratic Marcelo Bielsa, he has held various posts at Chicago Fire, Astorga and Stromsgodset in the United States, Spain and Norway, respectively. It was slightly vexing for Cooke that people with no insight into the Hong Kong football ecosystem would probably study his bare figures from afar and be wholly unimpressed. Wanting to swap the staccato nature of international management for “being on the grass, getting the passion back into my coaching and developing the staff and players”, Arnott said he tried to shelve concerns over his personal record. “It might be to my detriment, but I just want to produce good work and leave staff in a better place than I found them,” he said. “As a young manager, the chance to install a framework in a club, experiment and help these guys develop the environment is another attraction of the offer. “If in future I have the opportunity to work in another club, I’ll have had the experience that can progress this club and challenge myself in those areas.” Nonetheless, Jeffrey said the target for the forthcoming season was to “set a new standard for what this club can achieve”. “Under Darren’s stewardship, our goals for this season are clear, demanding and uncompromising,” he added. “We want to establish a professional culture, implement high-tempo football, accelerate our elite youth pathway and climb the table.” In limited cases, Football Club have begun employing players full-time to aid visa applications. That was how they secured the 22-year-old former Blackburn Rovers academy and England under-16 midfielder, Charlie Weston, and Cian Coleman, a 21-year-old midfielder who was in the Leeds set-up during Arnott’s time at Elland Road. Weston captained the team in their opening match of the season: a 3-2 defeat by Southern on Saturday. “I’ve been in teams that have struggled and others that have excelled,” he said. “I’ve learned from senior players and want to put that knowledge into this group.” Players must be members of the club, whose football arm has shrunk the application process from six to two weeks to speed signings. Finances have been carefully managed in non-essential areas to release cash for team matters. There is no spare kit for players on matchdays, for example. An offer to manage Football Club’s second team, Lucky Mile, enticed seasoned centre-forward Manuel Bleda to the club, while Alex Dujardin, 27, the commanding former Nanjing City and Tai Po centre-back, was lured back for a third spell. Still “unpacking” the “huge amount” he learned from Argentine Bielsa, Arnott recently finished the two-year ECAS scheme, which seeks to advance the skills of “high-potential coaches”. After the course supplied a sharp focus on leadership, the opportunity of returning to coach across a broader age range will provide Arnott with “real-world development”. “I’m close to the players, they confide in me,” he said. “As you move into a senior leadership role, there is a perception that you have to be more distant. I became more that way, but it wasn’t true to my personality. “I worked with a sports psychologist to develop and understand myself better. My personality doesn’t suit that distance. “I want a family feel and for these guys to believe.” Football Club were moments from a draw with Southern, after levelling from 2-0 down, while the opening weekend of the campaign delivered a series of nail-biters. Giancarlo Italiano, the new Lee Man head coach, was an outlier in enjoying a one-sided 3-0 victory over Kowloon City. “I thought the competition might lean towards the teams that are stacked with a bit of depth, but every side has surprised,” he said. “The league’s really competitive this season.” Arnott’s first job is to make sure his team stay among the city’s elite cohort. “Our expectation is to not get relegated,” he said. “We’re hanging on to the cliff, and trying to pull ourselves up. If we get things right, we can climb onto the top and take our first step forward.”

title: China and Jordan call for Strait of Hormuz to get back to normal after US-Iran conflict
description: The two sides also criticised Israel’s ‘dangerous escalatory actions’ following King Abdullah’s meeting with Xi Jinping in Beijing.
content: China and Jordan have called for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to shipping and for the ceasefire between the United States and Iran to be maintained, in a joint statement issued during King Abdullah’s visit to Beijing. They also said they wanted to see “a comprehensive solution addressing the root causes of tension … through dialogue and negotiation, ensuring full respect for the sovereignty, security and territorial integrity of regional countries”. Peace talks between the US and Iran have stalled and the strait, which was described in the statement as a “vital channel for international commerce and the energy trade”, remains closed to most shipping. The statement, issued after the king’s meeting with President Xi Jinping and other top officials on Monday, called for the “restoration of normal transit through the strait”. The two sides also criticised Israel’s “dangerous escalatory actions” in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, according to state news agency Xinhua. They expressed “deep concern” over Israeli activities that included “land confiscation, the construction and expansion of settlements, and attempts to alter the historic and legal status quo of Islamic and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem”. “Both sides emphasised that all illegal measures aimed at annexing parts or all of the occupied West Bank territory are null and void, holding that such acts violate international law and UN resolutions,” the statement said. Recently, Israel opened tenders for roughly 1,200 settlement homes east of Jerusalem, drawing sharp international condemnation for what was widely seen as an effort to further divide the West Bank and block a future Palestinian state. Jordan has also warned of an “imminent” threat that Israel will take over Jerusalem’s Al-Aqsa mosque, the city’s holiest Muslim site, after around 2,000 rightwingers, many of them settlers, stormed the site last month. During the meeting, Xi vowed to deepen collaboration with Jordan across core sectors, including trade, infrastructure and mining. He added that this could expand into areas such as the digital economy, artificial intelligence and green energy. Meanwhile, the Jordanian ruler pledged to expand cooperation in science and technology, welcomed further investment from Chinese enterprises and commended Beijing’s “just stance” on Middle Eastern affairs, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV. The two countries also signed multiple cooperation agreements spanning diplomacy, judicial affairs, trade, and industrial and supply chains. They also pledged to deepen their strategic partnership following the meeting. The monarch’s trip to China takes place as Jordan is in the crossfire of the US war on Iran. Despite Amman’s official neutrality, military bases in the kingdom hosting US forces have been frequently targeted by Iranian forces. Monday’s meeting came hours before Washington was set to announce what US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has described as the “toughest” sanctions against Iran in history. There has been an international push to de-escalate the conflict, which continues to unsettle the Middle East and the global energy market. However, six months after the war began, hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough have faded. Last week, Beijing hosted Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, who briefed the Chinese side about the latest developments in the Gulf during a meeting with his Chinese counterpart Miao Deyu. According to the Chinese foreign ministry, which announced the meeting on Sunday, Miao reaffirmed China’s commitment to “proactively promoting peace and encouraging talks”. On Sunday, Jordan hosted a high-level meeting between Syria and Israel to achieve “de-escalation” following Israeli strikes on Syrian territory, the state-owned Syrian Arab News Agency reported, citing a diplomatic source. Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah was also in Beijing on Monday as part of a two-day visit at the invitation of Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. The small Gulf state is separated from mainland Iran by a narrow strip of Iraqi coastline and has been hit hard by Iranian missiles and drones since the war began. It hosts several major US military bases, including Camp Arifjan, the logistics, supply and command hub for operations in the Middle East. Meanwhile, Jordan – geographically wedged between Israel, the West Bank, Syria and Iraq – has had to strike a delicate balance between volatile regional dynamics and competing international powers. Long dependent on US military backing and financial aid, Jordan faces rising pressure from Iranian strikes and overseas aid cuts under the administration of US President Donald Trump. While remaining within the US security orbit, Jordan has sought to diversify its partnerships with other nations and strengthen the economy by deepening ties with China. The week-long trip, which started on Tuesday and ended on Monday, was Abdullah’s ninth visit to China since he succeeded his father 27 years ago. During the trip, Abdullah visited Shanghai and Shenzhen – two major hubs for artificial intelligence and robotics – before travelling to the Chinese capital. Speaking to Xinhua before his trip, he highlighted China’s “important role in safeguarding international peace and security”. In the interview, the king spoke of Jordan’s push for a two-state solution that would establish an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel. He said Amman sought to coordinate with China as a key global player to “use its considerable influence and voice on the international stage to help push for the realisation of the two-state solution”. Roughly half of the kingdom’s population is of Palestinian origin. Abdullah also said that deepening China-Arab ties reflected mutual interest in shared development and cooperation and that China had been a key partner in the kingdom’s public sector through training programmes, as well as advancing the country’s energy diversification and self-sufficiency via investments. Traditionally reliant on imported natural gas, Jordan has aggressively pivoted to renewables. King Abdullah told Xinhua that green power had surged from under 1 per cent of the kingdom’s electricity grid a decade ago to 27 per cent today, with a target of 40 per cent by 2035. As a global leader in green tech, China has driven much of this transformation. Over the past decade, nearly 89 per cent of Beijing’s US$3.56 billion investment in the kingdom went to the energy sector, according to the official Jordan News Agency. Trade between the two nations has expanded in tandem, making China Jordan’s biggest trading partner in 2025. Chinese exports to the kingdom – mainly machinery, textiles and vehicles – reached US$6.29 billion. In contrast, Jordanian sales to China totalled US$430 million, concentrated in raw materials such as potash, phosphate, fertilisers and copper.

title: 4 arrested as Kenya investigates 18 elephant deaths in Amboseli
description: Preliminary laboratory ‌results point to the probable involvement of a toxic substance, the tourism and wildlife ministry says.
content: Police have arrested four suspects in an investigation ⁠into the deaths ⁠of 18 elephants in Kenya’s Amboseli ⁠ecosystem, where authorities also seized assorted substances including chemicals, the tourism and wildlife ministry has said. A Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) spokesperson told Reuters on Monday that the four had since been released on bail. Preliminary laboratory ‌results pointed to the probable involvement of a toxic substance, the ministry said in a statement released on Saturday, with earlier indications suggesting cyanide poisoning due to the ingestion of pesticide-contaminated tomatoes from farms bordering Amboseli National Park. Some wildlife experts have expressed doubt that farm pesticide was responsible for the deaths, ⁠citing the absence of reported deaths among other animals in the area. The ministry said ‌investigators were also pursuing a fifth individual believed to have information relevant to the case. A search in Tikondo in Loitoktok ‌sub-county, about 220km (137 miles) southeast of Nairobi, led to the discovery ⁠of assorted substances, including ⁠chemicals believed to have come from a neighbouring country, the statement said. The arrests ‌and recovered substances did not in themselves establish criminal culpability, the ministry said, adding that investigations were ongoing. The first 15 ‌elephant deaths ‌were recorded between June 24 and July 24, the ministry said. In ‌July, KWS said the deaths occurred in Amboseli National Park, Kimana Sanctuary and ⁠the Kuku Ranch area, and that the animals showed symptoms including partial paralysis before dying ⁠within one or two days. The broader Amboseli ecosystem spans the national park and surrounding community land in southern Kenya near the Tanzanian border, providing ‌habitat and movement ‌routes for elephants and other wildlife beneath Mount Kilimanjaro. The area has a history of human-wildlife conflict, with elephants roaming beyond protected areas into community and agricultural land, trampling crops and angering farmers.

title: Meet Dai Zheng, the space veteran betting on China’s reusable rocket revolution
description: LandSpace’s rocket booster recovery has supercharged the country’s commercial space ambitions – and validated a former state engineer’s start-up gamble.
content: Ten years ago, Dai Zheng made a career-defining gamble: he left his secure, prestigious engineering post in China’s state space programme to join an unproven private start-up. On August 19, that risk paid off when a rocket booster returned from orbit and landed upright for the first time in Chinese commercial space history. For Dai, now chief commander of the Zhuque-3 missions at LandSpace, the successful touchdown marked both a major personal milestone and a critical leap forward in China’s drive to develop reusable launch vehicles. The landing followed an intense eight-month recovery effort after a crash during a failed attempt in December. More broadly, it vindicated Dai’s decade-long belief that reusability – recycling parts of a rocket so it can fly again – is essential to cutting launch costs and supporting Beijing’s ambitions for massive satellite constellations. Dai, 42, joined LandSpace in 2016 at the invitation of founder Zhang Changwu. He stepped down from his senior post in rocket research and development at the state-owned China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology (CALT) to serve as deputy general manager at the then one-year-old start-up. The move meant turning his back on a secure path at CALT, where he had worked since 2009 after earning a master’s degree in engineering mechanics from Tsinghua University. As one of the lead architects of the Long March 5, China’s first heavy-lift rocket, Dai had been on a fast-rising trajectory. Leaving the state system was painful. Dai recalled crying the night before resigning as he laid his awards across his bed. “I entered the state aerospace sector straight after graduation and never thought I would leave,” Dai told state broadcaster CCTV in an interview late last year. We cannot let the next generation look up and see only American satellites Dai Zheng, LandSpace There was lots of uncertainty, he said, but “rationally I knew I needed to take that step”. Dai was betting his career on reusable rockets becoming the future of space flight. While fuel accounts for only a small fraction of launch costs, the first-stage booster represents the bulk of the hardware investment. Recovering and reusing boosters allows operators to spread those costs across multiple missions, slashing prices and increasing launch frequency. For China, which needs thousands of launches to deploy proposed low-Earth-orbit satellite constellations, reusability has evolved from an engineering experiment into a strategic necessity. The transition into the commercial space sector quickly tested Dai’s resolve. LandSpace’s debut rocket, Zhuque-1, failed to reach orbit during its maiden launch in October 2018. The setback prompted a decisive pivot: instead of relying on third-party solid fuel, Dai’s team would build its own liquid-propulsion system. That strategy produced the Zhuque-2, powered by the self-developed Tianque liquid oxygen-methane engines. In July 2023, Zhuque-2 made history as the world’s first methane-powered rocket to reach orbit, laying the groundwork for Chinese commercial liquid-propellant rockets. Building on that foundation, Dai spearheaded the development of the larger Zhuque-3, incorporating bold design choices such as replacing traditional aluminium alloys with stainless steel for the rocket’s main body. The approach mirrored SpaceX’s use of stainless steel for its Starship vehicle. Though heavier than aluminium, the material can better withstand re-entry heat, reducing the need for heavy thermal shielding and simplifying refurbishment between flights. For China, closing the commercial space gap with the United States is an urgent priority. US operators, led by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, have already deployed thousands of internet satellites into orbit. “We cannot let the next generation look up and see only American satellites,” Dai said in a CCTV interview aired on Monday. “If we fail to make this happen, future generations will look back and feel that our generation of space workers failed to shoulder our historical responsibility.” Born to teacher parents in Yongan, Fujian province in 1984, Dai said his passion for rocketry began at a fourth-grade summer camp, where he built a cardboard model rocket that soared dozens of metres before releasing a parachute, according to a report by state-run Xinhua News. However, while the Zhuque-3 booster recovery represents a landmark achievement, LandSpace now faces the challenge of turning a one-off breakthrough into routine, reliable reuse. For Dai, the remaining hurdles are necessary steps in a longer process. “Experiencing failure is how you gain experience,” he said. “If you never take that step, you can’t get closer to success. We choose to do things not because they are easy, but because they are correct.”

title: EV maker Xpeng set to challenge Tesla in embodied AI after robotics unit raises US$900m
description: Backers including Alibaba, Tencent and IDG put up a combined US$600 million while Xpeng itself pledges US$200 million.
content: Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker Xpeng has secured US$900 million in funding from high-profile investors including Alibaba Group Holding and IDG Capital to spur its robotics unit, despite a widening second-quarter loss. Dogotix, a subsidiary of Xpeng, raised US$900 million in the latest round of financing, which valued it at US$6.3 billion, Xpeng said in a statement on Monday, adding that the fundraising marked the biggest single private-equity deal involving a Chinese robotics maker. The fresh capital would give Xpeng a shot in the arm as it joins the fray against Tesla to build and sell humanoid robots to tap global investor enthusiasm in embodied artificial intelligence. “I believe Xpeng will not only build one of China’s most valuable humanoid robotics companies, but also become a global leader in physical AI, spearheading the large-scale adoption and commercialisation of advanced general-purpose humanoid robots and autonomous driving technologies in China and overseas,” He Xiaopeng, co-founder and CEO of the company, said in the statement. On Monday, Xpeng said its net loss in the second quarter ending June widened 179 per cent from a year ago to 1.34 billion yuan (US$199.4 million) amid a 32.1 per cent jump in research and development costs. Revenue rose 8 per cent to 19.7 billion yuan year on year. Backers including Alibaba, owner of the South China Morning Post, Tencent Holdings, IDG and Gaorong Ventures agreed to invest a combined US$600 million into Dogotix, while Xpeng itself pledged US$200 million, according to Xpeng. Top executives including He would shell out US$100 million of their own money to participate in this round of financing. “The capital will enable Xpeng to improve its development and production capabilities in constructing advanced robots,” said Ding Haifeng, a consultant at Shanghai-based financial advisory firm Integrity. “Xpeng has the potential to be a real Tesla challenger in EVs and robotics, rather than an imitator.” The proceeds would be used to further develop Xpeng’s robotics technology, build mass production facilities, and reinforce overseas expansion, according to the Monday statement. In July, Xpeng announced it would produce over 1,000 humanoid robots a month by the end of 2026. The first batch of its Iron robots rolling off the production line late this year would initially be deployed as sales assistants at Xpeng’s domestic showrooms. The next-generation of humanoid robots would start commercial deliveries in 2027, it added. In January, Tesla said it was undergoing a structural shift with plans to transform itself from a hardware-centric business into a ­physical AI firm. Tesla has yet to sell any of its Optimus humanoid robots. In December, CEO Elon Musk endorsed Iron on social media while predicting Chinese companies would ­dominate the global robotics market alongside Tesla.

title: America’s US$40tr debt gamble is getting harder to ignore, economists say after ‘grow’ goal
description: Analysts warn that high spending, rising interest costs and tax cuts could impede Washington’s efforts to ‘grow our way out of’ record-high national debt.
content: With Washington claiming that the United States can “grow” out of its mounting fiscal burdens, some economists are sceptical that growth alone could absorb the country’s mountain of national debt, which just surpassed US$40 trillion. The milestone, reached last week, has amplified concerns about the long-term sustainability of maintaining such a massive debt pile – one that has doubled in size from a decade ago. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the trajectory last week, telling CNBC that much of the spending had gone towards investments in factories and equipment, and that the country would “grow our way out of” that debt level. However, some analysts remain doubtful, pointing to elevated government spending, growing debt-servicing costs, and tax cuts as structural barriers that economic growth alone cannot overcome. “The US has no chance of growing out of its debt problem through growth only,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at French investment bank Natixis. Despite high nominal growth rates – boosted by inflation – in recent years, the US has continued accumulating debt, adding US$10 trillion since 2022, as public expenditure remained high, she noted. Under the spending trajectory, the real economic growth rate would have to average around 4.31 per cent annually to eliminate the deficit in the next decade, according to findings published last year by Fiscal Lab on Capitol Hill, an independent research centre. That pace was more than twice the Congressional Budget Office’s projection of average baseline growth of 1.8 per cent per year through 2036, noted Liang Yan, a professor of economics at Willamette University in the United States. “What needs to be done are structural changes in expenditures and revenues,” Liang said, adding that reforming the healthcare system to lower related costs, for instance, could help reduce expenditure. Maybe AI will deliver gains in productivity, but as of yet, they have not materialised at the macro level David Jacks, economics professor Spending on social security and health programmes, including Medicare, alongside net interest payments on debt, forms the largest share of US government expenditure, accounting for 65 per cent of total spending, according to Treasury data. US Treasury bond yields – the cost of government borrowing – have risen to multi-year highs in recent weeks. The yield on the 30-year Treasury touched 5.34 per cent on Tuesday, its highest since 2007, before dropping 0.1 percentage points after the Treasury announced it would at least double its bond buy-back programme. Yields then began to rebound, with the 30-year Treasury yield closing at 5.27 per cent on Friday, while the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 4.73 per cent, higher than in recent weeks leading up to the Treasury’s intervention. When asked by reporters on Friday whether Washington might stage further interventions, US President Donald Trump said that they had “many types” of intervention in their toolbox. “The ultimate intervention is our military,” Trump said. “And if we have to use that, we will.” Liang added that rate cuts would help ease the fiscal pressure. “The current monetary policy – keeping interest rates higher for longer – significantly contributes to the rising interest costs on public debt,” she said. The US Federal Reserve has held rates at between 3.5 and 3.75 per cent in recent quarters and is expected to keep the rates unchanged for the rest of the year, amid mounting inflation and instability from the war in Iran. David Jacks, an economics professor at the National University of Singapore, added that specific policy choices, including 2017’s “Tax Cuts and Jobs Act” and last year’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”, had reduced government revenues and added to the deficit, which stood at 5.8 per cent of gross domestic product last year. “Maybe AI will deliver gains in productivity, but as of yet, they have not materialised at the macro level,” he said. If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can’t be managed without great trauma Ray Dalio, Bridgewater Associates founder Liang noted that, even with a productivity boost from artificial intelligence, projected economic growth remains insufficient to lower the debt-to-GDP ratio. “Much of the tax reforms under Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill must be rewound,” she said, adding that reforms such as raising the top marginal income tax rate and corporate income tax rate were needed. Anxieties over the expanding national debt are already showing in the market. “We’re now in this debasement trade, which means selling the dollar and US Treasuries … and the money is going elsewhere, [such as] to crypto and to gold,” said Garcia-Herrero, though she noted that the process would take time, given the huge size of the market. The three largest foreign holders of US Treasuries – Japan, the United Kingdom and China – all trimmed their holdings in June, according to the latest available data. Billionaire investor Ray Dalio, who founded Bridgewater Associates, on Friday called on investors to underweight debt assets such as bonds and increase allocations in gold and bitcoin, predicting that the US was moving towards a debt crisis. “If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can’t be managed without great trauma,” he said in a social media post, adding that the government had to lower the budget deficit to around 3 per cent of GDP to ease the pressure.

title: US, China diplomats clash over tech spying and trade hub claims in Latin America
description: Weeks before the expected Xi-Trump summit in Washington, officials are trading barbs on social media over the latest competitive arena.
content: Diplomats for China and the US in Latin America have traded brickbats on social media over alleged espionage risks posed by Chinese tech firms in the region, in the latest sign of the two powers’ unfolding strategic tensions in the western hemisphere. US assistant secretary of state for western hemisphere affairs Juan Pablo Segura named telecoms giants Huawei Technologies, ZTE and Hytera, surveillance equipment makers Hikvision and Dahua, and drone heavyweight DJI in a post on social media on Saturday. “Chinese law forces these suppliers to cooperate with Beijing’s intelligence services, creating risks of spying, hacking and network shutdowns,” Segura warned, describing their products as “high-risk technologies”. “We urge US partners in the Americas to quickly switch to trusted suppliers to protect their people and their sovereignty,” Segura concluded in his post, which was shared by the US embassy in Panama minutes later. Beijing’s diplomatic mission in Panama hit back on Sunday with a statement published on its website that rejected Washington’s accusation as lacking “the slightest factual basis”. The statement also suggested that it was the United States that had been engaging in intelligence activities across the region, while acting like a thief shouting “stop thief” and beating the victims. “The true one obsessed with global espionage, without even sparing its own allies, is the US,” the Chinese embassy argued. “For those who only think in terms of geopolitical calculations, even the siu mai might be bugged.” The embassy also denounced the US for “blatant techno-bullying” by stretching the concept of national security to “coerce” regional countries into replacing Chinese products. Latin America has emerged as an arena for the strategic competition between Washington and Beijing – laid bare in the continuing contest over the Panama Canal, a vital artery for global trade. President Donald Trump’s administration has made the western hemisphere a foreign policy priority, designating it a “Homeland Security Zone” and pledging to deny rival powers control over strategically important assets near US shores. Officials have described the approach as the “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, explicitly linking the competition with China to a policy from more than 200 years ago that aimed to drive European powers’ influence away from the Americas. Washington’s change of focus has raised concerns in Beijing that China’s strategic space in the Americas could come under increasing pressure. The latest verbal sparring over Chinese tech companies also comes merely weeks before an expected summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington next month. It follows a White House report, published on August 13, that describes Latin American countries – including Panama, the Dominican Republic and Argentina – as part of what it calls “shadow transshipment network”. The report portrayed this network as “a distributed system of finishing hubs, logistics platforms, processing corridors, free-zone operators, and re-export centres that allow Chinese goods to enter the US market under new national identities”. Segura’s remarks were also shared over the weekend by the US embassy in the Dominican Republic and Peter Lamelas, Washington’s top envoy in Buenos Aires. Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian dismissed Segura’s allegations as full of “fact-distorting fabrications”, saying on Monday that China “firmly rejects them”. “We advise the US to stop its political manipulation [and] stop interfering with sovereign nations’ right to independently choose cooperation partners,” he said. The Chinese embassy in Argentina earlier lashed out at Lamelas, issuing a statement more than a week ago after he accused Beijing of requiring companies to give it access to any data passing through their technology and artificial intelligence networks. “The Chinese government never requests, nor will it ever request, companies to provide, collect, or store data for the Chinese government in violation of local laws,” the statement said.

title: Beijing slams West for criticising Hong Kong court verdict in Tiananmen vigil case
description: Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian hits out at ‘certain countries and organisations’ for using judicial cases to smear Hong Kong.
content: Beijing has slammed Western nations for interfering in China’s internal affairs over their criticism of the conviction of the now-disbanded alliance that organised Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigils and its former leaders for inciting subversion. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian used a regular press briefing on Monday to hit out at “certain countries and organisations” for using the case to smear Hong Kong and denigrate its rule of law. He made the comments in response to questions about expressions of concern from the US and other countries over a Hong Kong court ruling last week, which found the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, ex-chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung guilty of attempting to undermine the fundamental system of the People’s Republic of China under the national security law. Albert Ho Chun-yan, another former alliance chairman, previously pleaded guilty. The ruling triggered criticism from the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Australia, which characterised it as an example of eroding freedoms in Hong Kong. US Assistant Secretary of State Riley Barnes called for the defendants’ immediate release, while UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said residents should be allowed to speak without fear of arrest or prosecution. Lin described such criticisms as interference in China’s internal affairs. He said the alliance’s manifesto aimed to subvert state power, adding that their guilt was clear and that they had caused serious harm. “The Hong Kong government’s actions to combat acts endangering national security in accordance with the law are reasonable and legitimate,” he said. “Hong Kong is a society governed by the rule of law, and the central government firmly supports Hong Kong in safeguarding national security and cracking down on acts that endanger national security. “Hong Kong affairs are purely China’s internal affairs. We urge the parties concerned to respect China’s sovereignty and Hong Kong’s rule of law, stop political manipulation and cease interfering in Hong Kong affairs or China’s internal affairs in any form.” The Hong Kong government also issued a statement on Saturday rejecting what it called “baseless slander and smearing” by Western countries over the convictions. It stressed that the defendants received a fair trial and were not prosecuted for their political beliefs.
