Beijing’s national security office in Hong Kong said on Friday that the defendants should be harshly punished for seriously undermining the city’s fundamental interests and endangering the state’s constitutional order. In a 216-page judgment, three judges found that the alliance, Lee and Chow had incited public hatred towards the Communist Party by likening the 1989 crackdown on protesters to local authorities’ response to the 2019 anti-government protests. The court noted that while it was not unlawful for the alliance to organise the commemorations, the defendants had used the event to attract new supporters and instigate them to take action to oust the party. Set up after the 1989 crackdown, the alliance organised annual candlelight vigils in Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to mark the event and call for accountability and democratic reforms across the border. The event was the only large-scale public gathering on Chinese soil to mark the 1989 crackdown. Separately, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in a Facebook post on Monday that balancing development and security was a long-term endeavour and a challenge not only for Hong Kong but also for countries and regions around the world. He added that security was a prerequisite for development, while development guaranteed security, saying the two coexisted rather than stood in opposition. Lee said the government would fulfil its constitutional responsibility to safeguard national security, while the public should also remain vigilant at all times. He said external hostile forces had never ceased their attempts at infiltration and subversion, while security risks of all kinds were difficult to predict.

title: Opinion | China’s view of Trump’s America has changed from alarm to a shrug
description: Erratic and transactional, the US leader’s approach exposes domestic governance flaws and the limits of Washington’s containment strategy.
content: There is no shortage of Western commentary on US President Donald Trump’s second term. What’s missing is an honest account of how 1.4 billion of us in China see it – or at least how China’s officials and scholars do, since that’s who I can speak for here. I’ve spent a decade watching that view change, from real alarm in 2017 to something closer to a shrug today. Four things now count as consensus among Chinese scholars. One, Trump is undermining America’s alliance system. His first term rattled Washington’s furniture. His second is dismantling the house. He has purged the civil service, stretched executive power, taxed friend and foe alike, and gutted America’s contribution to global public goods. He appears to be governing for the next election, not the next generation – and this is speeding up the arrival of a multipolar world. Two, hostility to China is bipartisan in Washington, but Trump’s version comes with a price tag, which we find oddly reassuring. When tariffs on Chinese goods hit 145 per cent last year, American retailers, farmers and manufacturers howled, inflation bit and the White House backed into a truce. The lesson we draw: his toughness is a negotiating tactic, not a crusade. That leaves room to manage the relationship. Three, pressure has been a poor substitute for actual containment. The 2018 trade war spooked Chinese firms. By 2026, the mood has flipped. Turns out sanctions are quite good at building the thing they’re meant to prevent. Chinese chipmakers have scaled up mature 28-nanometre production. Home-grown chip-design software now holds a quarter of the domestic market. Solar panels and electric vehicles have found new buyers across Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Latin America. America’s share of China’s trade shrank. Four, the real contest is in governance, and time is on China’s side. American policy lurches with every election. China’s five-year plans, for better or worse, tend to survive them. America still leads in technology and firepower, but we’re betting that policy continuity and industrial scale will keep narrowing the gap. Add those four up and what you get is less an argument than a mood – of relaxed, quiet confidence. Eight years ago, China absorbed Trump’s tariffs and improvised. Now it hits back with tools – export controls on rare earths, a blacklist of “unreliable” foreign firms, tariffs of our own on energy – while building alternatives to Washington-led institutions through Brics, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and Belt and Road Initiative. It has gone from rule-taker to rule-shaper. China is not trying to beat the United States. It is trying to improve the lives of its people, hit what we call “common prosperity” and complete national rejuvenation, by which we mean restoring China to what we see as its rightful place in the world. That is both the official and our genuine position. Winning was never the goal. But if you improve your country enough, for long enough, overtaking the country that used to be ahead is simply what ends up happening. China is, by its own account, the only country to have built a fully industrialised green energy system that’s industrialised. Beijing has stuck to the same decade-long strategy while American policy changes with every administration: the Paris Agreement abandoned, rejoined and abandoned again, wind and solar installations stalling as a result. In wind, solar, batteries and electric vehicles, Chinese firms now account for more than half of global capacity, output and exports. The country has built the world’s largest ultra-high-voltage grid and energy storage system, which is how it moves power from where the sun and wind are to where the people are. A state-run satellite network monitors carbon emissions, giving global, high-precision coverage. China has become the country that sets the standard for what a green transition looks like. In AI, America still leads on chips and the underlying algorithms, but China claims the lead on deployment: government services, smart manufacturing and smart cities. In space, the comparison we Chinese scholars like to draw is with Starlink – commercial, narrow, built for coverage – against China’s broader, state-run programme: crewed missions, lunar exploration, the BeiDou satellite network and the Tiangong space station. On governance, China has built the world’s largest digital state and Chinese officials argue it delivers public services and disaster response with a consistency American gridlock can’t match. There are caveats. America still has the deepest capital markets, the best universities, and decades of accumulated research. China still lags in precision manufacturing and some industrial software; external pressure is squeezing its exports in the short term; and the wider geopolitical picture remains genuinely unstable. I’ll admit these caveats read a little like the fine print below an advert for something you didn’t need. Ten years ago, many of us held an admiring, almost idealised view of America. That’s gone. We credit America’s historical contribution to the modern world. We also see, clearly now, 20 years of financial excess, winner-takes-all politics and social fracture. The Trump years have been a blessing in disguise: the pressure stings now, but it is forcing China to fix its weaknesses faster. We don’t reject competing with America. We’d rather China compete without conflict, and coexist. China is not trying to defeat the US. Beijing is trying to out-govern, out-produce and outlast it. Competition without confrontation, if Washington will allow it. Whether that sounds like reassurance or a very patient ultimatum probably depends on where you’re sitting.

title: South Korea says US cut joint marine drill over Iran war constraints
description: The cancellation follows US President Donald Trump’s order last week to scale down the separate annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises.
content: South Korea said on Monday that the United States had cancelled a large joint amphibious landing exercise scheduled for next month due to constraints on force availability caused by the war with Iran. The biennial Ssangyong drills involve marine forces from South Korea and the US and are designed to strengthen combined operations, typically involving warships, aircraft and ground forces rehearsing amphibious landings. The cancellation follows US President Donald Trump’s order last week to scale down the separate annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, cutting the joint drills from 11 days to five. Trump at the time cited their high cost and said they sent an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea, while highlighting his relationship with its leader, Kim Jong-un. “The US Marine Corps formally notified our forces in June that its ability to deploy forces during this year’s Ssangyong exercise would be constrained due to the situation in the Middle East,” Han Seung-jeon, a spokesman for the South Korean Marine Corps, told reporters at a news briefing. Seoul and Washington were continuing consultations on resuming the amphibious exercise, he said, without giving details. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Seoul’s announcement. Trump’s order last week to scale back the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise came as he seeks to revive the relationship he developed with Kim during his first term. The US president said on Wednesday that it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons. Seoul estimates that North Korea has about 80 to 120 such weapons. Trump and Kim met three times during the US leader’s first term, but Pyongyang accelerated its nuclear programmes after their second 2019 summit in Hanoi collapsed without an agreement on North Korea’s denuclearisation.

title: Kerry Properties targets Hong Kong sites, eyes luxury market as mainland growth slumps
description: Developer steps up Hong Kong land bids while shifting Mid-Levels rental project to a potential sale to fund new investments.
content: Kerry Properties is targeting Hong Kong residential land sales and will consider recycling capital from existing assets, betting on a tighter local housing supply even as China’s property downturn weighs on its mainland business. The developer said it acquired three residential sites in Hong Kong in the first half, equal to about 235,000 sq ft of gross floor area, and that it would remain active in government land tenders. “If you look at the government land auctions and MTR land tenders in the past few months, we have basically bid for all of them...and we will continue to invest very actively in the future,” said Calvin Tong, director and general manager for Hong Kong at Kerry Properties, during an earnings briefing on Monday for interim first half results. Its gearing ratio fell to 31.3 per cent at the end of June from 33.3 per cent six months earlier, putting the company on track to reduce leverage to about 30 per cent by year-end. Kerry is also capitalising on Hong Kong’s strong luxury market with a plan to convert a 62-unit Mid-Levels project from a rental asset into a potential sale, freeing up capital for new land acquisitions. The company had planned to hold the flats because of their rare location and views, but “we received quite a lot of inquiries about whether there was an opportunity to sell,” Tong said. “After looking at it again, we think it is a good time,” he added. “We will sell only if it gets the right price; otherwise, we will retain the project.” Hong Kong accounted for HK$5.57 billion (US$710.4 million), or 81 per cent, of Kerry’s contracted sales in the first half, with La Marina, Mont Verra and La Montagne contributing more than 90 per cent. The strong performance, combined with sales carried over from previous years, brought Kerry’s cumulative unrecognised Hong Kong sales backlog to HK$5.9 billion at the end of June, securing a solid revenue pipeline into the second half and 2027. That timing helped drive a 59 per cent decline in recognised Hong Kong property sales revenue to HK$2.54 billion in the first half, while the group’s total revenue fell 33 per cent to HK$6.67 billion. Underlying profit declined 9 per cent to HK$782 million, even as profit attributable to shareholders rose 20 per cent to HK$735 million. The contrast with mainland China was stark. Mainland contracted sales in the first half plunged 88 per cent to HK$1.3 billion, with company management attributing it to projects in second- and third-tier cities “taking longer than expected” to sell. However, “we would not rush to cut prices”, said Suzanne Cheng, the group’s chief financial officer, citing the quality of its developments and stronger balance sheet. Cheng said the group would remain selective on mainland opportunities. Last month, it paid about 2.7 billion yuan (US$402 million) for a commercial site in Shanghai’s Pudong district, citing its strong location, dense surrounding residential population and potential retail catchment. But Kerry would only pursue “particularly attractive sites” on the Chinese mainland, with Hong Kong residential land “remaining the priority,” Cheng added.

title: Former English Premier League player joins Kitchee as Hong Kong league adds star quality
description: Victor Camarasa joins ex-Real Madrid midfielder Asier Illarramendi on books of reigning champions for twin-glory quest.
content: Kitchee have sprinkled more stardust on the local Premier League after confirming the signing of free-agent former Spain under-21 midfielder Victor Camarasa. A spectator from the stands as Kitchee began their Hong Kong title defence with a 3-2 victory at BC Rangers on Saturday, Camarasa played 31 games in the English Premier League during a season-long loan with Cardiff City in 2018-19. The 32-year-old, who joins Asier Illarramendi, the ex-Spain and Real Madrid midfielder, on the books of the 13-time local league champions, has also made 140 La Liga appearances across spells with Levante, Alaves and Real Betis. He was limited to only seven outings off the bench during his single season with Hungarian top-flight club Debrecen last term. “I’ve been lucky to play with and against some very good players, so I understand the game very well,” Camarasa said. “I will bring quality with the ball. I want to achieve something in Asia and give my best every day, and whenever I play.” The arrival of Camarasa, who had a short spell with Crystal Palace after leaving Cardiff, comes at an opportune moment for both Kitchee and Hong Kong football. Poised to continue their domestic season with a tricky trip to North District on Saturday, Kitchee have genuine hopes of making progress in the AFC Champions League Two. Returning to continental football after a two-year absence, they have been drawn in a relatively gentle group with Gangwon FC, Kuching City and Phnom Penh Crown. From a broader perspective, the opening fixture of this Hong Kong Premier League campaign, between newcomers Supreme Sha Tin and Eastern on Friday, drew a crowd of 3,329, marking the league’s highest attendance since 6,489 watched a title decider between Kitchee and Lee Man in May 2023. The Supreme owner, Jim Wong Chi-chuen, is promising to field a marquee Spanish attacking midfielder in a forthcoming match, although he failed in a move for Juan Mata, the former Manchester United and Chelsea attacker. In Bozhidar Kraev, Lee Man have added a 29-year-old Bulgarian forward with 27 international caps and a Danish league winner’s medal from his time with Midtjylland. Now comes Camarasa, whose Alaves team lost the 2017 Spanish Cup final 3-1 to the Barcelona of Lionel Messi, Neymar and Andres Iniesta. He played his last La Liga match for Betis against Espanyol in January 2022, before spells in the Spanish second tier with Real Oviedo and Odense, and that lone campaign in Hungary. Inigo Calderon, the Kitchee head coach, said the capture of Camarasa would wrap up his club’s summer business, after moves for Koldo Obieta, a Spanish centre-forward from Borneo FC, the former Lee Man duo of Everton Camargo and Dudu, and defender Marcao from Tai Po. Camargo hit a double and Obieta added the other in the weekend win over Rangers. Poised for his first experience of Asia, Camarasa said: “This is all new for me, it’s a different culture and different style of football. “But I’m here to play and looking forward to starting. Kitchee is a very important club in Hong Kong. I spoke to the coach and to some of my teammates, and they are very happy at Kitchee and in the city. “There are good players here, and they’re like a family.”

title: Northern Metropolis gets vote of confidence as heavyweights win tender for HK$1.03b
description: Six-company consortium awarded tender for 10.5-hectare project in Hung Shui Kiu, with total investment of HK$16.8 billion expected.
content: A consortium comprising mainland Chinese state-owned and private heavyweights together with a major Hong Kong developer has won the first “large-scale land disposal” project in the Northern Metropolis for HK$1.03 billion (US$132 million), with total investment projected at HK$16.8 billion. The Development Bureau announced the results on Monday, awarding the tender for the 10.5-hectare development project in Hung Shui Kiu to the six-company joint venture, HSK New Development. It comprises subsidiaries of China Merchants Land, China Resources Land (Overseas), China Overseas Land & Investment, Sino Land, CTG Investment and mainland e-commerce titan JD.com. “The consortium of the successful tenderer encompasses not only major enterprises that have long participated in local real estate development, but also market leaders that are well established in other industries,” Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said. “This demonstrates that a large-scale land disposal project can facilitate cooperation across different business sectors,” Linn added, noting their “undeniable experience and capability”. “The six enterprises pool their strengths and join forces to cast a vote of confidence in the Northern Metropolis through concrete actions, setting a new course for the diversified development models in the Northern Metropolis.” According to the bureau, the consortium received 100 marks under a so-called two-envelope tendering system, where bidders submitted proposals for land premium and non-premium elements in two separate packages. A 30 per cent weighting was given to the land premium offered and 70 per cent to non-price factors, including proposals for technology park development and plans to attract strategic industries, investment and jobs. The consortium beat its only competitor – Henderson Land Development, one of the city’s largest developers – which submitted a stand-alone bid. A consortium spokesman said the project would involve technologies and services being introduced in Hong Kong for the first time, including JD.com’s proprietary LangzuTech logistics robots that handle storage, picking, handling, sorting and terminal retail across the entire supply chain. He added that the project would encourage more cold-chain clients to set up operations and introduce “mature, standardised service models from the mainland to Hong Kong, providing residents with more convenient logistics services”. In a statement, Sino Land said the joint venture would leverage the strengths of cross-boundary collaboration across diverse industries to invest in, develop and operate a large-scale smart logistics project. Chairman Daryl Ng Win Kong said: “We are committed to bringing high-value industries and a quality living community to the Northern Metropolis, providing more housing and employment opportunities while enhancing connectivity between Hong Kong and cities across the Greater Bay Area.” The project is located in a future high-end professional services and logistics centre within the Northern Metropolis, a 30,000-hectare area near the mainland border set to be transformed into an economic powerhouse and housing hub. The “large-scale land disposal” scheme requires the winning bidder to collectively develop sizeable land parcels with commercial value and sites earmarked for public facilities. Citing the consortium’s estimate, the bureau said the project would involve an investment of HK$16.8 billion and create more than 6,000 jobs. The bureau said the consortium opted to settle the full tender price, HK$1.03 billion, within 28 days, rather than pay the land premium in instalments. It said the consortium would carry out site formation works on three plots of residential land and build more than 3,000 flats. It would also form a site earmarked for company and technology park developments and build a smart logistics centre, with JD.com participating as a strategic enterprise. JD.com will occupy at least 15,300 square metres, around 30 per cent of the facility’s gross floor area, in 55 months, well ahead of the 96-month minimum requirement. The four sites, totalling 3.6 hectares, will be leased to the consortium for 50 years. The consortium is also responsible for conducting formation works for other sites under the project. Among them, two parcels designated for enterprise and technology park development and a lot reserved for public facilities have to be returned to the government before the end of 2028. The bureau said the two enterprise and technology-related sites, totalling 4.5 hectares, would be granted to the Hung Shui Kiu Industry Park Company, a financially self-sustaining entity set up by the government to facilitate the district’s development. Its land bank was expected to grow from 23 hectares to 27.5 hectares at a nominal land premium for 50 years, it added. Vincent Cheung, managing director of Vincorn Consulting and Appraisal, said the consortium’s ability to bring JD.com into the project was believed to be one of the key factors behind its successful bid. “Its establishment in Hong Kong will help strengthen the local logistics and e-commerce ecosystem and attract upstream and downstream enterprises, professional talent and related investment, marking another step forward in the development of Hong Kong’s logistics, supply-chain and high value-added technology industries,” he said. Cheung said the project would involve substantial construction, financing, site formation and industry-introduction costs, exposing it to risks arising from changes in the property market and economic cycles, fluctuations in construction costs, rising financing costs and industrial operations. He stressed that the project’s overall value should not be judged solely by the land premium but also by the long-term economic benefits arising from the introduction of industries and by its contribution to Hong Kong’s regional competitiveness. Cheung said the tender also set an important foundation for the Northern Metropolis to adopt an industry-oriented land tendering model in the future, rather than relying only on the “highest bidder wins” approach.

title: China’s advanced chip supply to surge by 2035 despite equipment bottlenecks, Goldman says
description: The increase will be driven by aggressive capacity expansion at SMIC, China’s largest contract chipmaker, as well as improving yields.
content: China is on track to dramatically slash its deficit in advanced chips over the next decade as domestic foundries rapidly scale up production, though the weak link of lithography threatens to keep full semiconductor independence out of reach, according to US investment bank Goldman Sachs. The supply of wafers made using 7-nanometre and below advanced processes is projected to grow at a compound annual rate of 46 per cent between 2025 and 2035, far outpacing the 17 per cent growth expected in domestic demand, Goldman analysts said in a report on Monday. That would narrow the gap between domestic supply and demand to 34 per cent by 2035, from 92 per cent in 2025, according to the investment bank. China’s advanced-node wafer supply is expected to reach 410,000 wafers per month by then, compared with demand of 619,000 wafers. The expected increase would be driven by aggressive capacity expansion at Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC), China’s largest contract chipmaker, as well as improving production yields. Goldman’s model assumes SMIC adds monthly capacity of between 30,000 and 50,000 advanced-node wafers each year from 2026 to 2031, before adding another 20,000 wafers per month annually through 2035. It also assumes yields rise from 23 per cent in 2026 to 50 per cent in 2030 and 75 per cent by 2035. The world’s No 1 foundry, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which started mass-producing 7nm chips in 2018, achieves yields that can exceed 90 per cent, depending on chip design and die size. The push for domestic chipmaking accelerated after Washington tightened restrictions on Chinese telecoms giant Huawei Technologies in 2020, cutting off its access to TSMC. Despite subsequent US-led export controls on advanced chipmaking equipment, SMIC was able to produce a 7nm chip for Huawei in 2023. Beijing has continued backing the expansion of both advanced and mature-node capacity, helping to increase the share of chips produced domestically. China’s chip self-sufficiency rate reached about 70 per cent in June in terms of production volume, compared with 38 per cent in January 2010, according to Goldman, although the gap was much wider when measured by value. The rapid buildout is expected to fuel another wave of semiconductor investment in China. Goldman forecast that the country’s chip capital expenditure would grow in double digits annually through the end of the decade, reaching US$82 billion in 2030. Its latest 2030 estimate is 79 per cent higher than the forecast made a year ago. “We remain positive on growing semis capex ahead,” Goldman analysts wrote, citing rising artificial intelligence demand, continued development of the domestic semiconductor ecosystem and a shift towards more advanced chips, packaging and memory products. The spending boom is also providing a larger market for home-grown equipment suppliers. Goldman expects China’s wafer fabrication equipment market to reach US$53 billion in 2027, with local firms accounting for 38 per cent by value in 2028, up from 26 per cent last year. Chinese equipment makers have expanded beyond established strengths such as etching and deposition into more challenging categories including ion implantation, inspection and metrology, according to Goldman’s analysis of the domestic supply chain. Lithography, however, remains the most conspicuous missing link in the domestic equipment ecosystem. China still relies on Dutch supplier ASML for nearly all of its advanced DUV lithography machines, with even some of those models restricted for export by the US, while access to ASML’s cutting-edge EUV machines is blocked entirely. State-owned enterprise Shanghai Micro Electronics Equipment Group, the country’s best hope to develop its own advanced lithography systems, still lags far behind its global peers.

title: China and Switzerland have a new tariff-scrapping trade deal. How will the EU react?
description: The move, seen by analysts as a signal to the EU, will eventually double duty-free coverage included in 12-year-old free-trade agreement.
content: China and Switzerland have concluded negotiations on the scrapping of tariffs on 99.8 per cent of Swiss exports, with analysts saying the deal carries more symbolic than economic weight amid growing trade tensions between China and the European Union. The agreement was announced by the Swiss side on Thursday after a meeting in Bern between Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and Swiss President Guy Parmelin. It will upgrade a 2014 free-trade agreement (FTA) under which only about half of Swiss exports to China were duty-free. Wang said in a statement that the new FTA would create new opportunities for bilateral economic cooperation. “In the current international environment filled with uncertainty, this also demonstrates the clear stance of both sides in choosing certainty and supporting free trade,” Wang said. For Beijing, the upgrade was a way to show that “close economic integration with China remains possible and attractive” for European countries, said Simona Grano, senior lecturer in Chinese Studies at the University of Zurich. The timing was also “convenient from Beijing’s perspective”, said Noah Barkin, senior adviser at Rhodium Group. “It sends a signal to the EU at a time of heightened trade tensions that reduced barriers are possible.” The deal comes as Brussels presses Beijing to deliver “tangible results” by October to address trade imbalances, having already imposed a levy on low-value parcels and opened several anti-subsidy investigations. The bloc’s goods deficit with China reached €360 billion (US$420.5 billion) last year, or roughly €1 billion a day. Countries have sought to shore up trade with China at a time when trade tensions with the US are on the rise Noah Barkin, Rhodium Group As a non-EU country, Switzerland had “traditionally pursued an independent approach towards China”, Grano said. China is Switzerland’s third-largest trading partner after the EU and the United States. Almost all Chinese exports to Switzerland are duty-free under the existing 2014 FTA. Swiss exports to China were worth 15.2 billion Swiss francs (US$19 billion) last year, compared with 18.3 billion francs of imports, according to the Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs. The figures exclude gold, which accounts for the bulk of Swiss shipments. There were “clear economic benefits” for Switzerland, Grano said, pointing to sectors such as watches, machinery and pharmaceuticals. All three sectors will move to full duty-free coverage, from 1 per cent for watches, about 75 per cent for machinery and less than 30 per cent for pharmaceuticals, according to a fact sheet released by the Swiss government. But only 77.5 per cent of Swiss exports will be duty-free when the deal takes effect, with the rest phased in over five to 10 years. The additional tariff savings were estimated at about 244 million francs, the fact sheet said, equivalent to less than 2 per cent of Swiss goods exports to China. Given China’s regulatory and other non-tariff barriers, Grano added that tariff-free access also “does not necessarily mean unrestricted market access”. The existing FTA mainly benefited multinational companies and large industrial firms, while smaller businesses often struggled with red tape and administrative costs, said Peter Bachmann, who was executive director of the Swiss-Chinese Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai from 2014 to 2023. Many Swiss companies already produced in China, he said, limiting the impact of tariff cuts on their sales in the country. For Beijing, analysts said, the value of the agreement lay less in its economic impact than in the signal it sent. Bachmann described the upgrade as more of a “public relations” move for Beijing, allowing it to present the deal as evidence of stronger trade ties with other countries. Bern signalled interest in an upgrade as early as 2018, he noted, while Beijing only showed greater enthusiasm in the past two years. According to the Swiss fact sheet, the pact contains the first reference to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in a Chinese FTA, labour provisions that it said were new to China’s trade deals, and an environmental chapter it called the most ambitious Beijing had accepted. The agreement also comes amid uncertainty over US trade policy. Washington imposed a 39 per cent tariff on Swiss goods in August last year, the highest rate on any Western economy, before cutting it to 15 per cent in November after months of negotiation. While analysts said the US tariffs were not the direct trigger, Barkin said the deal “fits into a pattern in which countries have sought to shore up trade with China at a time when trade tensions with the US are on the rise”. Greater access to China might diversify Swiss companies’ export opportunities, Grano said, “but it does not necessarily diversify Switzerland’s strategic dependencies. In fact, it can deepen them.” She questioned whether that was wise when European countries were trying to reduce their exposure to Beijing. The texts are undergoing legal review, with both sides aiming to sign by the end of the year. The deal would then require Swiss parliamentary approval and could be put to a popular vote in that country.

title: Taiwan unveils Strong Bow anti-ballistic missile specs in push for US$1.13 billion funding
description: Developers disclose details of Chiang Kung hypersonic interceptor with active radar to convince lawmakers to approve funding.
content: Taiwan’s top weapons developer has unveiled details of its Chiang Kung, or Strong Bow, anti-ballistic missile system as it seeks legislative funding for mass production to strengthen the island’s air defences amid growing pressure from Beijing. The government-funded National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology disclosed key specifications of the locally developed system earlier this month, including its hypersonic speed, two-stage solid-fuel propulsion, guidance system and active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar. The disclosure comes as the government prepares another attempt to secure funding after the system was excluded from a pared-back special defence spending package approved by the opposition-controlled legislature in May. The defence ministry plans to resubmit Strong Bow and other programmes through a supplementary budget, which the cabinet could consider as early as Thursday before sending it to lawmakers. The ministry has proposed spending NT$36.1 billion (US$1.13 billion) to produce two Strong Bow systems and 128 interceptor missiles. Strong Bow, also referred to as Tien Kung (Sky Bow) IV, is a land-based mid-tier anti-tactical ballistic missile system designed to intercept incoming missiles at altitudes of at least 70km (43 miles) – higher than Taiwan’s existing Patriot and Tien Kung III systems. According to the institute, the vertically launched missile can reach hypersonic speeds and uses a two-stage solid-fuel rocket motor. It relies on inertial guidance and radar uplink corrections during midcourse flight before switching to an active seeker in the terminal phase. It also uses thrust-vector control to manoeuvre in the thin atmosphere at high altitudes and carries a high-explosive fragmentation warhead. The system includes mobile launchers carrying four missile canisters each, tactical command vehicles and an AESA radar capable of identifying and tracking targets, resisting electronic countermeasures and simultaneously engaging multiple tactical ballistic missiles. The defence ministry said the radar could detect threats at greater ranges and altitudes than those used by the Patriot PAC-3 and Tien Kung III systems. It has described Strong Bow as the outermost layer of Taiwan’s planned multilayered missile defence network, or “T-Dome”, giving defenders an earlier opportunity to intercept ballistic missiles before lower-tier systems engage those that penetrate the first layer. Lu Chien-sheng, deputy director of the institute’s Tien Kung programme, has said Strong Bow was developed specifically to counter tactical ballistic missiles and could operate alongside Patriot and Tien Kung III to create a multilayered interception network. He said its mobile configuration would improve battlefield survivability, while allowing it to command and control other air defence missile units in joint operations. The defence ministry said Strong Bow had completed operational testing and evaluation and was ready for mass production. Funding, however, remains the biggest obstacle. Strong Bow was originally included in the government’s proposed NT$1.25 trillion special defence package, with production scheduled to begin this year and the first integrated locally developed regional air defence system targeted for completion in 2027. The network would initially link Strong Bow with the Tien Kung III and land-based Tien Chien II missiles. A later phase envisages connecting them with United States-made Patriot and National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems through the US Integrated Battle Command System as part of the planned T-Dome. But Strong Bow was among the local programmes excluded after lawmakers approved only about two-thirds of the government’s requested special defence spending earlier this year. Efforts to shift it into the regular 2027 defence budget have also faced difficulties because of commitments to other locally developed weapons and a peak in payments for US arms purchases. The government has now turned to supplementary appropriations. Defence ministry comptroller Hsieh Chi-hsien confirmed last week that additional funding was being planned for missile and drone programmes that failed to secure legislative approval. Analysts have warned that further delays could hamper Taiwan’s efforts to build layered defences against the People’s Liberation Army’s growing ballistic missile arsenal. Su Tzu-yun, a senior analyst at the government-funded Institute for National Defence and Security Research, said Strong Bow was essentially a new missile despite being designated Tien Kung IV. “The tactical advantage is that the higher it can fly, the larger the area it can protect,” he said, estimating that a battery could provide 100km to 150km coverage. Su said Strong Bow had been described as “Taiwan’s version of THAAD”, referring to the US Terminal High Altitude Area Defence system, and estimated its radar detection range was almost 1,000km. Chi Tung-yun, president of the Taiwan Security and Development Association, said deploying Strong Bow alongside Patriot PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors could give defenders one or two additional opportunities to engage each incoming ballistic missile. He urged lawmakers “to fund production as soon as possible”, warning that postponing it until 2028 would be “bad news for Taiwan’s missile defence capability” as the PLA continued expanding its ballistic missile forces. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Ukraine wants peace but won’t ‘simply surrender’, Zelensky says on Independence Day
description: The country marks 35 years of independence from the Soviet Union as Zelensky vows to find a solution to Putin’s ‘ballistic terror’.
content: ⁠Ukraine wants peace but will not just give in to Russia at any price, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said in a defiant speech as foreign leaders gather in Kyiv to mark its Independence Day celebrations. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa were among the foreign dignitaries present on Monday for celebrations of the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s break from the Soviet Union. Burnham, making his first visit to the Ukrainian capital as prime minister, was ‌due to announce British support to help Kyiv boost its domestic production of long-range missiles. He was also scheduled to co-chair a virtual meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing” – a group of countries backing Ukraine – with French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The leaders were expected to discuss Ukraine’s request for more air defence systems to stop Russian ballistic missiles pounding Ukrainian cities. Wearing a traditional Ukrainian embroidered shirt, Zelensky thanked several foreign leaders for travelling to Kyiv to show their support. He vowed to find a solution to what he called Russian President Vladimir Putin’s “ballistic terror”. “Ukraine absolutely wants peace, but it is not ready to simply surrender,” Zelensky said in his video ⁠address posted on Telegram, which showed him standing in front of the golden-domed St Michael’s monastery. Zelensky said Russia’s demand – repeatedly rejected by Ukraine – that Kyiv cede the remaining part of ‌the eastern Donbas area that is not in Russian hands after 4½ years of war would not be enough to stop Russian aggression. “Ukraine is different, and it does not give away what is its own,” he said. Hundreds of thousands of people have been ‌killed, and swathes of Ukrainian territory have been laid waste, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022. US-led peace talks to bring a lasting ⁠end to the war stalled as Ukraine ⁠refused Russian demands to cede more territory, and fighting continues along a 1,200km (750-mile) front line. Zelensky highlighted the achievements of Ukraine’s defence industry during the war, including strikes with naval drones and mid- and long-range strikes deep inside Russia, but ‌said there was more work to do. He urged Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point to accelerate production of its Flamingo cruise missile to take the fight to Russia this winter. Burnham signalled on Monday he would allow the use of classified British technology for ‌Kyiv ‌to start production of European SCALP long-range cruise missiles by Ukraine. The Kremlin said the use of classified British technology would “add fuel to the fire”, and has warned London of “consequences” for ‌supplying drones to Kyiv. Russia’s advances on the battlefield have slowed this year and Ukraine has recaptured some land in the southeast. But Moscow’s forces are threatening the strategic ⁠eastern city of Kostiantynivka in the eastern region of Donetsk which forms part of Donbas, together with the Luhansk region. Exploiting Ukraine’s critical shortage of anti-ballistic missiles, Russia has also stepped up ⁠its campaign of air strikes at cities far from the front line this summer. Ukraine has also increased its long-range attacks on Russian refineries and logistics infrastructure, aimed at undermining Moscow’s war effort. It hit four logistics hubs owned by Russia’s second-largest online retailer Ozon in southern Russia in drone strikes on Monday, the company said. On Saturday, Zelensky ‌said Ukraine’s war effort ‌was complicated by a US$27-billion defence funding gap this year. He also warned that Russia could look to mobilise some 300,000 additional troops after parliamentary elections in September. Paying tribute to the people and soldiers defending Ukraine in the war, Zelensky called on allies to give it “everything” needed to stop the war. “We are not asking you to fight for us,” he said. Urging allies to bring Russia to the negotiating table and hit it with more sanctions, Zelensky said he hoped the United States would lose “all the contradictions and phobias” regarding Russia. “China must no longer remain silent,” he added.

title: Can Singapore’s latest pro-family push change minds on parenthood?
description: Some parents and experts have welcomed the new measures, but say career, housing and time concerns remain unaddressed.
content: Singapore’s latest pro-family push has been welcomed by some parents for tackling the costs of raising children, but others say lower fees and more leave are unlikely on their own to overcome deeper worries over time, careers, housing and lifestyle. During the annual National Day Rally on Sunday night, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a raft of measures to make having children more appealing in the city state. These include increasing childcare leave based on the number of children a family has, topping up funds in children’s post-secondary education accounts and reducing full-day childcare fees in government-supported schools. Singapore’s total fertility rate (TFR) dropped to a historic low of 0.87 in 2025, underscoring the scale of the challenge facing policymakers. The government has set up an inter-agency Marriage and Parenthood Reset workgroup, chaired by Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office Indranee Rajah, to address the trend. In a statement on the National Day Rally measures, the government’s Strategy Group said the announcements were the first set of recommendations from Indranee’s workgroup that Wong’s administration accepted. The recommendations followed consultations with Singaporeans who raised concerns about needing more caregiving time, lower child-raising costs, more affordable preschool and housing support as families grow. The Strategy Group said the workgroup would release a fuller set of recommendations in early 2027, after continuing to study issues including work-life support, fertility and maternity health, relationship formation and education. Experts said the new measures should be judged against more modest benchmarks than a full reversal of Singapore’s fertility decline. Kalpana Vignehsa, senior research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies, said no advanced economy had sustainably restored replacement-level fertility through policy and success should instead be measured by whether such initiatives helped fertility rates stop falling or decline more slowly. “On that score, this package is more promising than its predecessors. It shifts from one-off incentives towards sustained, universal support,” Vignehsa said. Among the policy shifts, childcare leave will now be linked to the number of children a parent has. Currently, every working parent has six days of leave if their youngest child is six years old or younger and two days if their youngest child is aged seven to 12. This will be increased to eight days of leave for one child, aged up to 12, 10 days for two children and 12 days for three or more children. While the government and employers currently share the cost of child-related leave, the former will cover the expenditure for all statutory child-related leave, up to a reimbursement limit. Wong said the government also aimed to reduce full-day childcare fares to S$150 (US$118) a month and infant care fees to S$300 at government-supported schools. Currently, families can pay nearly S$600 a month for full-day childcare and more than S$1,000 monthly for infant care. First-time applicants for the build-to-order scheme, which enables Singaporean families to buy public housing flats directly from the government, will also get an additional ballot chance for every child they have or are expecting, according to Wong. Every Singaporean child would receive almost S$70,000 in direct financial support over the years by the time they turned 17, Wong added. Vignehsa noted that fertility decisions rested on confidence that care would be affordable, careers would survive parenthood, there would be enough time in the week to parent, and that support would not disappear after infancy. “This package builds that confidence more credibly than a larger baby bonus would have,” she said. “The effects will likely be gradual and most visible among couples deciding on a second or third child, rather than [resulting] in a dramatic TFR rebound.” Still, Vignehsa said “two scarcities” remained unaddressed: “the income and career losses that accompany caregiving, and the sheer shortage of time and energy in Singaporean working life”. She suggested making flexible work and reasonable hours a durable, protected feature of working life, offering caregiving compensation and looking upstream at rising singlehood as other methods to slow the fertility rate decline. Danyya Ateera, 34, a health and safety officer, who has two children aged two and five, told This Week in Asia that no additional financial benefit or childcare leave could make her want more children. “No incentive can make me change my mind, although an understanding workplace can lighten the load a bit,” she said, noting that she often felt guilty for taking time off work during busy periods even though her children needed her. For Valerie Ong, 33, who has a two-year-old and is expecting a second child, the need for a bigger home is a key reason she intends to stop at two. On the reduced childcare fees, Ong, who works in advertising, said, “It’s a very tangible cost that families feel. If you give me a S$10,000 lump sum, I just think it’s just cash assistance, but if you lower my school fees, mentally, it changes my opinion of the cost of having a kid.” While having S$70,000 spread across 17 years would help offset costs such as childcare, enrichment and insurance, Ong said the money would not be viewed as funds to upgrade to a bigger property in land-scarce Singapore. “The sum is too small to even come close.” Wong on Sunday touched on larger families wanting bigger homes that cost more and said he had asked National Development Minister Chee Hong Tat to consider additional housing support for larger families. Ong, however, said for couples who decided not to have children at all, no amount of cash incentives or cost-covering from the government would help since they would always have more money as DINKs (dual income no kids). Tan, 31, is one such couple who is married with no children. She told This Week in Asia that while the new measures showed having children could be affordable, there were other trade-offs to consider. “It does sound like a lot of money [to support parents having children] but there’s also other factors to consider like the time costs and giving up our lifestyle now to have a kid,” said Tan, who declined to give her full name. “There are also the expectations we have for ourselves of what we want to give our kid if we have one.”

title: Hong Kong to offer free dental check-ups to preschoolers from September
description: More than 70 per cent of kindergartens join scheme bringing screenings and fluoride treatment to campuses.
content: Hong Kong preschoolers will be offered free dental check-ups starting next month, with more than 70 per cent of the city’s kindergartens having already signed up for the new government initiative. The Department of Health announced on Monday the launch of the Outreach Oral Health Programme for Preschool Children on September 1, aimed at fostering oral hygiene habits and preventing tooth decay at an early stage. Under the scheme, dental teams from 23 participating service providers will visit kindergartens across all 18 districts once each academic year, offering pupils aged 32 months or older free oral screenings and risk assessments. “Children usually have a full set of milk teeth by the age of three. The period between the ages of three and six is the most crucial time to protect these teeth,” said Dr Kitty Hse Mei-yin, consultant in charge of the dental service at the department. “At this stage, children love to eat, which makes reinforcing dental care and oral hygiene extremely important.” Hse said that conducting examinations in a familiar school environment helped ease young children’s anxieties. “With the encouragement of teachers and the support of peers, they view it as a routine school activity, making it much easier for them to accept,” she said. As part of the preventive treatment, medical teams will also apply sodium fluoride varnish to healthy teeth to strengthen them and prevent cavities. For children who already have tooth decay, teams will apply silver diamine fluoride to control the condition. The teams will also issue screening reports to parents, offer individualised dental care advice for children with decayed teeth and provide referrals for eligible students in need. Service providers began contacting kindergartens in June to schedule visits for the 2026-27 academic year. As of Sunday, providers had reached out to 890 of Hong Kong’s 949 schools, with 680 agreeing to participate – representing 71.7 per cent. Hse said that most of the remaining institutions already had existing dental care arrangements in place, while others were facing closure or relocation. She added that providers would continue to follow up with non-participating kindergartens, noting that schools could join at any point during the term. Free oral health workshops for kindergarten teaching staff will also be held by the dental teams to help them deliver oral care messages to their students. “The proportion of children with tooth decay experience has remained high over the past decade, meaning a large proportion of five-year-olds still face the threat of dental decay,” said Dr Alex Chau Man-him, senior dental officer in oral health promotion at the department. According to the department’s 2021 Oral Health Survey, 41.6 per cent of five-year-olds in Hong Kong experienced tooth decay, with an average of 1.8 affected teeth per child. The survey revealed that most of these cavities went untreated, with half of affected children having four or more decayed teeth. Only about a quarter of parents had ever taken their five-year-olds to see a dentist, with nearly half of those visits prompted after dental problems had already developed. With funding support from the Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust, the dental school of the University of Hong Kong has previously organised an oral health project and offered free check-up services to the city’s kindergartens since the 2019-20 school year.

title: Former Hong Kong teacher gets 18 months in prison for molesting student twice
description: Judge Gary Lam describes defendant Cheng Hon-sze’s case as serious and says there is no room for a reduced sentence.
content: A Hong Kong court sentenced a former teacher on Monday to 18 months in prison for molesting a student, aged 15 at the time, on two occasions in 2020. District Judge Gary Lam Kar-yan described defendant Cheng Hon-sze’s case as serious and said there was no room for a reduced sentence, even if it was a first offence. Cheng, now 32, was sentenced at Tsuen Wan Court after being found guilty of two counts of indecent assault for groping the student and making her perform an obscene act in May and October 2020. He was cleared of seven other counts of indecent assault as the court ruled the girl on those occasions had not expressly refused the defendant’s advances or that the acts involved were not considered inherently indecent. The defendant earlier admitted to having repeatedly engaged in intimate acts with the victim in the school’s music storage room and other locations. Lam sentenced Cheng to one year in jail for each count of indecent assault, while ordering that the prison terms be served as a partially consecutive sentence, bringing the overall period down to 18 months. He said the sentencing took into consideration the 11-year age difference between the defendant and the victim, the level of indecency and the damage to the pupil. Cheng taught the girl in Forms One, Two and Four to Six. He was also in charge of the school’s marching band, of which she performed as a trumpeter. Alongside the offences he was convicted of, the defendant was previously accused of repeatedly molesting the girl from November 2019 to June 2024. She was between 14 and 19 at that time. According to a trauma report on the victim, she was still processing her feelings towards the defendant, whom she considered to have both helped and hurt her. The report said she had experienced a contradictory and extreme mental state that had lasted for several years, leading her to neglect personal boundaries and suppress her disgust. The judge, quoting the report, said the girl had developed “twisted values” of accepting the harm caused by someone if they showed care for her. The report attributed this mindset to her inability to fully understand the concerning nature of the incidents. Such an experience at a crucial developmental period had prompted her to view the world as unsafe and untrustworthy, with the victim fearing that, however a person appeared, they could still hurt and betray her, the document read. Lam said the victim’s road to emotional recovery would be a long one. “I can only wish her well and hope she emerges from this dark period as soon as possible,” he added, urging her to seek help if necessary. He cited a clinical psychologist’s report, which noted that the defendant had difficulties in building age-appropriate romantic relationships, and had also failed to fully understand the power imbalance involved or that such behaviour was not socially acceptable. As a result, Cheng would be required to take part in follow-up work with social workers, the judge said. The judge cited the clinical psychologist’s advice that the Correctional Services Department provide the defendant with the appropriate professional help as part of his rehabilitation programme. The report concluded that Cheng had a low to moderate chance of reoffending, but noted he was willing to receive professional help. The defence earlier argued that Cheng’s lack of relationship experience led him to develop feelings for the victim that overrode his judgement and said the defendant deeply regretted the strain his actions had placed on his family. His legal counsel conceded that the teacher-student boundary should never have been crossed and urged the court to consider Cheng’s youth at the time of the offences, among other factors, and impose a lighter sentence. The court also received mitigation letters from the defendant’s sister and a friend, who claimed the incident was out of character and highlighted that he had applied to pursue a master’s degree at Polytechnic University after being barred from teaching.

title: CUHK academic who allegedly hid marital status cleared of indecent assault
description: Peng Peng, 38, acquitted at Sha Tin Court, where he had previously pleaded not guilty to two counts of indecent assault.
content: An associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) has been acquitted of indecently assaulting a woman who reported him upon discovering he was married, after a court found the pair had been mutually attracted and that the man may have wrongly believed she had consented to being touched. Magistrate Raymond Wong Kwok-fai acquitted Peng Peng, 38, at Sha Tin Court on Monday, following hearings that began in July. Peng had pleaded not guilty to two counts stemming from alleged incidents on May 21, 2025, when he and the complainant – a fellow scholar from mainland China – visited CUHK’s art museum before dining in Ma On Shan. The court earlier heard that the two met in April after a conference and went hiking on CUHK’s campus, but the complainant said Peng never mentioned he was a married man or a father. Peng later emailed her, calling the hike an “unforgettable adventure on the campus”. She replied she was “very happy” and looked forward to meeting again in summer. Peng responded: “The views at CUHK are beautiful, but nothing compares to the sight of you beside me.” They later moved their conversations to WeChat. On May 20, the woman invited Peng to the campus but he said he was busy and would see her the next day. She replied: “Nothing, talk to you when we meet.” When Peng asked, “why so mysterious?”, she sent a “doll” emoji and wrote, “keep smiling”. During their museum visit, the court heard, their conversation included sexual innuendo – remarks about her outfit and the colour of her toenails – and Peng patted her on the back. After their dinner on May 21, the complainant spoke with a friend that night and learned of Peng’s marital status. The following day, she went to CUHK to lodge a complaint before reporting the matter to police. Delivering his verdict, Wong said that while the victim complained to police that Peng had touched her waist and hip when they were crossing the road, she only showed that her waist was touched during a demonstration in the court. He also noted that she did not raise this incident to police when she complained about the second one in the restaurant, adding that both parties’ bodies were moving while crossing the road. He ruled that the prosecution could not prove beyond reasonable doubt that Peng had indecently assaulted the complainant. On the second charge, Wong said security camera footage of the restaurant did show that Peng put his hand on the complainant’s waist for 10 seconds. But he concluded that they were “mutually attracted”, judging from their previous email and WeChat exchanges, and the fact that the woman stayed behind for more than two hours and continued to chat cheerfully with Peng after the alleged assault occurred. He also said the woman had no special response after being touched. The magistrate said he could not rule out the possibility that the defendant had a wrongful belief that the complainant consented to him touching her. However, the magistrate said Peng brought suspicion on himself as he actually touched the complainant, thus refusing his application for costs on the second charge. However, his application for costs for the first charge was granted.

title: Why Kyle Chandler, star of Lanterns, loved playing a grouchy Green Lantern
description: Kyle Chandler plays Hal Jordan, the veteran Green Lantern who is assigned to train a rookie, Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart.
content: In the final moments of the first episode of Lanterns, Hal Jordan is shown in an unexpected light. After a 10-year time jump from the main events in the new series’ premiere, the veteran version of Green Lantern played by Kyle Chandler is seen sitting alone in the snowy stands of an otherwise deserted rural school football field – dead. And the ring that gives him his superpowers is nowhere in sight. “That might have been another reason why I said, ‘I want to do this,’” Chandler says. “That sets the tone of the show.” The Hal that the audience gets to know is a bit surly and self-centred. A former military test pilot turned space policeman, Hal knows he is good at his job and has grown used to doing things his way. He has no problem expressing his displeasure at being inconvenienced by his unwanted trainee or earthbound law enforcement officers. “I love the old grouchy characters,” Chandler says. “They always try to do bad but it always falls on top of them. Then, when they do good, it’s heartwarming. You get to play all these different colours inside these guys.” Created by Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof and Tom King, Lanterns follows Hal and new recruit John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), whom Hal has been assigned to train. Considering new Green Lanterns are usually only called up when a current one dies, Hal is not really keen on having to teach his “backup”. The HBO Max series is based on DC comic characters and set within the same universe as films such as Superman and Supergirl and the television series Peacemaker. But don’t worry, familiarity with the comics or other franchise instalments is not required. Mundy and his cohort envisioned their Hal as a Chuck Yeager (legendary flying ace and test pilot) type – someone who is cool and confident with the skills to back it up – and that Chandler’s was a name that had come up immediately. “Kyle has a really, really good sense of himself, in the best way,” says Mundy, who had previously worked with the actor on the Netflix series Bloodline. “Kyle, just as a person, is so likeable and it’s real. [So] it allows you to push the character to be even more of a jerk to John because you know it’s going to fall back on, ‘Oh yeah, it’s Kyle doing it.’ So it can land a little bit softer, and people can tolerate a little bit more.’” I loved the fact that there was humour, and self-deprecating humour and a grouchy character Kyle Chandler Chandler says one of the things that stood out to him the first time he read the script for Lanterns was the writing. “I loved the fact that there was humour, and self-deprecating humour and a grouchy character,” Chandler says. “I could see myself in this role … Did I know anything about Green Lantern? I did not.” Green Lanterns are intergalactic heroes who use a special ring to harness their imagination and willpower to manifest objects, manipulate energy and fly, as we see Hal do, to John’s chagrin. Chandler might not have known much about Lanterns, but he does understand the power of imagination. While growing up in rural Georgia, the characters and stories he encountered while turning the UHF dial on the television were both a refuge and fuel for his own imagination as he played out in the woods by his home. It eventually inspired him to pursue a career in acting and opportunities in Hollywood. Coincidentally, the day Chandler came out to Los Angeles to start work on Lanterns was the anniversary of the day he first left home to chase his acting dreams – January 15, 1989. The actor describes Hal as a “talker” who’s “got far more on his mind than what he’s talking about”. “He’s an older fellow who’s afraid of losing his power and his mortality is coming about and his career is coming to a possible [end],” Chandler says. So when the “young upstart” John comes around, “my character’s thought is, ‘I’m far wiser, I’m far smarter, I’m the only one who’s ever done this before. Don’t forget that kid.’” Hal and John may not have many kind words to say about each other – especially in the 2016 era of the show – but Chandler and Pierre more than make up for it. “I’d never worked with Aaron before … but once we’re acting, it gets very intimate,” Chandler says. “Once we started playing with each other, and you’re still trying to figure out who your character is, working through the other character. It’s such an intimate piece with two people.” Pierre says this process was a “joyful”, “nourishing” and “collaborative experience”. “It’s not a given, nor is it an obligation or mandatory to develop a friendship with individuals that you collaborate with,” Pierre says. “And I was blessed with the gift of … developing a genuine, sincere friendship with Kyle that exists outside the context of work.” As much as Chandler is game to talk about his work on Lanterns, his eyes shine a bit brighter when he mentions his family. This includes the work he and his wife Kathryn do through Patriots’ Hall of Dripping Springs, a sprawling resource centre for veterans and their families in their Texas community that they became involved with during the Covid-19 pandemic. “It’s a place to help veterans job source, to help veterans come together for Taco Tuesdays, and breakfasts and dinners,” Chandler says. “We’ve had so many supporters and people who have donated … and it’s been an incredible experience. Very, very fulfilling.” Pierre likens Hal to a massive puzzle John is trying to piece together without any instructions. Part of John’s journey over the course of the show is coming to understand that Hal is an infinite puzzle and it is OK if he doesn’t understand every nuance and detail. “What he can do is understand who this individual is fundamentally at their core,” Pierre says. “He knows that at his core, there is a mutual love and respect. He could trust Hal with his life, and Hal could trust John with his. At a certain point, John just kind of sets it free.” The John who is taken to see Hal in the final moments of the first episode is closer to the end of that journey. “We had already captured so much of the tension between John and Hal that I was curious what I was going to feel as John seeing Hal in the stands frozen to death,” says Pierre of that 2026 scene that was filmed during a cold night-shoot. “I felt really emotional on the day and I totally just allowed that to present itself on camera. John will deal with that how he deals with it, but I felt this well of [emotion] come all the way up into my throat … and I had to navigate that as John.” And while audiences will have to wait for the mysteries around Hal’s death and the happenings in Rushville, Nebraska, to be resolved in the show’s seven remaining episodes, one thing is certain: no matter how much Hal might come to appreciate John in that time, he is probably not going to admit it out loud. “I think that one of the goals of the arc for these two guys is that they really don’t like each other at the beginning,” Chandler says. “At the end … you realise [it is] a really wonderful friendship that occurred … He’s a friend. I’m not going to tell him that, but he’s a friend, and I’d do anything for him.”

title: Meet Anna Faris’ son with Chris Pratt, Jack – who asked her to ‘accept Jesus Christ’
description: The Scary Movie star and Avengers actor split in 2017, but live nearby to co-parent their son, Jack, who was born prematurely in 2012.
content: Anna Faris recently revealed that her 14-year-old son, Jack, asked her to “accept Jesus Christ”. During an appearance on the Dear Chelsea podcast on August 20, Faris opened up about discussing religion with her son, whom she co-parents with ex-husband Chris Pratt. “He is religious,” Faris told the host Chelsea Handler. The Scary Movie actress explained that she didn’t grow up religious but told her son she would do “anything for him, including this, but it’s going to take a whole lot of long conversations”. The 49-year-old went on to praise her son for his ability to handle complex conversations regarding faith. Her ex-husband, Pratt, is a devout Christian and has frequently spoken about his faith publicly. “[Jack]’s impressive, actually. Because I try to challenge him,” Faris said in the podcast. She would ask her son to consider whether being able to be pro-life was in fact a luxury. “Or I’ll say, ‘What do you think of this mega pastor that’s kind of a grifter?’ And he’s like, ‘Oh, mega pastors are the worst.’ So it’s like, ‘Okay, he’s getting there.’” “I’m appreciative that he’s examining religion the way he is in terms of … starting to recognise hypocrisy, and I’m appreciative that we can have these long conversations,” she continued. So, what else do we know about Anna Faris and Chris Pratt’s son, Jack Pratt? Read on to find out. Anna Faris and Chris Pratt co-parent him Anna Faris and Chris Pratt married in 2009 and separated in 2017. They welcomed their only child together, Jack, in 2012. Both actors have since remarried. Pratt wed Arnold Schwarzenegger’s daughter Katherine in 2019 and shares three children with her, while Faris married cinematographer Michael Barrett in July 2021. The exes co-parent Jack amicably and reportedly agreed to live within 8km of each other for their son’s benefit, according to People. Jack Pratt was born prematurely Jack Pratt, named after Faris’ father, was born several weeks prematurely and weighed just around 1.6kg at birth. While Jack is now healthy, the weeks following his birth were exceptionally challenging for the parents. “The paediatric neurosurgeon sat Chris and me down to tell us that Jack had some severe brain bleeding and there was a chance that he could be developmentally disabled,” Faris wrote in her 2017 memoir Unqualified. “I was in complete shock … So Chris and I did what we could, which was hold hands and hope and face it together.” Jack spent a month in the neonatal intensive care unit and underwent several surgeries alongside physiotherapy. Aside from minor vision and leg muscle issues, he has grown into a thriving teenager. Faris and Pratt are proud parents Jack has occasionally joined his parents on the red carpet. In 2017, he and Faris accompanied Pratt when he received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. “I love you,” Pratt said in his speech. “You’ve given me so much. You gave me the greatest star in the galaxy in my little boy; I love him and I love you.” In August 2024, Pratt shared a heartfelt birthday tribute to his firstborn on Instagram: “Happy Birthday to my wonderful son Jack. I thank God every day for you sweet boy. You are so smart, hilarious, kind, thoughtful, trustworthy and tough. I love you so much kiddo.” Faris also praised her son in an interview with People, saying: “He’s always had such a solid anchor. I don’t know where, being a kid in Hollywood, he got that. I don’t know how he got so down-to-earth, but I’m really grateful.”

title: Hang Seng Bank doubles down on wealth hubs despite Beijing’s tighter investment scrutiny
description: Hong Kong lender says it is expanding its workforce to capture rising demand from high-net-worth clients.
content: Hang Seng Bank says it continues to invest in its wealth centre network to capture growing demand from high-net-worth clients, even as Hong Kong’s wealth management industry faces uncertainty amid Beijing’s tighter scrutiny of mainland Chinese investors’ cross-border investments. The Hong Kong lender recently opened a new wealth management centre at Hysan Place in Causeway Bay, its second such facility after launching its first at Harbour City in Tsim Sha Tsui earlier this year. The 6,300 sq ft facility, which includes a sky bar for clients, marks Hang Seng’s first presence in a grade A commercial building on Hong Kong Island, where more than 30 per cent of its “Prestige Banking” customers are based. Hang Seng said it was expanding its workforce alongside its physical network, and planned to increase its relationship managers in general by about 20 per cent this year. We continue to see very strong demand for account opening and wealth management, whether from domestic or non-domestic customers Rannie Lee, Hang Seng Bank It also planned to open a retail banking centre at Central MTR station and several more wealth centres across the city over the next 12 to 18 months. The opening of the new wealth centre came amid growing concerns over tighter scrutiny by mainland Chinese tax authorities of residents’ overseas investment income, aided by information exchanged under the Common Reporting Standard (CRS). “We continue to see very strong demand for account opening and wealth management, whether from domestic or non-domestic customers,” said Rannie Lee, head of retail banking and wealth at Hang Seng Bank, at a briefing on Monday. Lee added that the CRS and mainland China’s tax framework were not new requirements and had long been in place, with banks continuing to comply with relevant regulations. Hang Seng said its wealth management business maintained “strong double-digit growth” in the first half of the year, despite the challenges. The lender added 60,000 new customers in the second quarter, twice as many as in the previous three months, with its wealth management business also posting growth in the first half of the year. Hang Seng is not alone in expanding its wealth-management presence. AXA Hong Kong and Macau agreed to lease two and a half floors spanning about 97,500 sq ft at Sun Hung Kai Properties’ International Gateway Centre for a new distribution office and one-stop wealth hub, according to a statement co-released by the insurer and the developer on Monday. The insurer had signed a 10-year lease and was expected to occupy the space in early 2028. Located above the West Kowloon high-speed rail terminus, the new hub would serve clients in Hong Kong, Macau and the broader region, including high-net-worth customers, according to the statement. Additional reporting by Cheryl Arcibal

title: Angry Chinese Super League fans attack visiting team bus and make racist, offensive gestures
description: Sudden death of a spectator at another match sparks debate about the readiness of medical equipment at Chinese stadiums.
content: In a chaotic day in the Chinese Super League (CSL) on Saturday, disgruntled Wuhan Three Towns fans directed their anger over their club’s possible relegation at the visiting team’s supporters’ bus, while the sudden death of a spectator sparked widespread debate about medical equipment at stadiums. Off-field chaos erupted following a crucial relegation match between Wuhan and Tianjin Jinmen Tiger that ended in a 0-0 draw despite Wuhan having 28 shots. Frustrated as their club remained deep in the relegation zone, a crowd of Wuhan supporters gathered outside the venue after the final whistle. According to online videos, fans surrounded the Tianjin visiting supporters’ bus, chasing the moving vehicle, shouting abuse, spitting, throwing debris and blocking its exit. In one instance, an individual made a corner-eye pulling gesture, a trope associated with anti-Asian discrimination, causing offence despite both sides being domestic fans. Further incidents occurred inside and outside the venue. Video footage showed what is alleged to be a home venue staff member making an offensive middle-finger gesture towards the away stand. Amid the hostility, an elderly supporter wearing a Wuhan jersey stepped forward to separate the crowd, helping the visitors’ bus depart safely. Supporters tagged Wuhan municipal authorities, the CSL, and the Chinese Football Association (CFA) on social media, calling for an official response and stricter governance. “Hooligan fans have been getting arrogant recently,” one fan commented, while another said: “Is no one going to step in and handle this?” A sports blogger with 68,000 Weibo followers, operating under the account “Paidaxing Jinqiu La”, posted a video to raise awareness of the incident. As one of the original creators who filmed the chaotic scenes outside the venue, she revealed her initial video had been reported and taken down for allegedly infringing on image rights. “Even if you, as a Chinese person discriminating against another Chinese person, indeed possess image rights, I refuse to accept being accused of spreading rumours,” she emphasised in her video. She stated that her footage clearly documented the man making anti-Asian racist gestures three times, including pinching, pulling, and tugging the corners of his eyes. “Under international football standards, such actions severely insult our national image, trample on national dignity, and should be an egregious violation subject to zero tolerance by the league,” she said. Calling on supporters from both cities to remain rational, she urged fans to settle rivalries through match performances and scores instead. “Do not use the trauma of another city as a weapon to hurt your own compatriots, because these are painful memories that can never be forgotten,” she added. “Poking at each other’s wounds is completely meaningless.” On Sunday, another CSL club, Chengdu Rongcheng, released a statement confirming that a spectator collapsed while entering the Chengdu Wuliangye Cultural and Sports Centre before kick-off against Shanghai Shenhua. The club said on-site medical personnel and staff “immediately performed emergency rescue” before transferring the fan to a hospital, where the spectator died despite all resuscitation efforts. “The club expresses deep grief and regret, and will fully assist the family with post-incident arrangements,” the statement read, while urging the public to respect the family and “not believe or spread rumours”. Despite the appeal, the lack of detailed official information regarding the cause of collapse and rescue timeline fuelled online speculation. “I don’t know if the venue was equipped with an AED [automated external defibrillators]; I couldn’t see one in the video,” one netizen wrote. Certified first aid responders among supporters noted that venue medical staff cannot reach every stand in time and called for stadium first aid volunteer teams. Netizens also urged large venues to equip sufficient AEDs and medical centres, pointing to outdated venue standards as a vulnerability in CSL public safety. Reports suggest medical posts at Chinese stadiums are concentrated pitchside mostly, leaving crowded entry gates with fewer patrols. Other users dismissed malicious rumours claiming the fan collapsed over match results. Others attributed the incident to the weather, with temperatures reaching 32 degrees Celsius (89.6 degrees Fahrenheit) before kick-off. “It was extremely hot. People must prioritise their health before attending a match,” another online user commented.

title: China’s Esports World Cup win a showcase for market’s growth potential
