description: With the EWC being held outside Saudi Arabia for the first time, the US$4.3 billion industry looks to grow its market, including in China.
content: China’s AG.AL has been crowned this year’s Esports World Cup (EWC) club champion in Paris on Sunday – a first for a Chinese team – earning US$7 million in prize money after winning or placing in multiple competitions across the 25-tournament series. French President Emmanuel Macron presented the trophy to the team at Grand Palais at the heart of the French capital. Saudi Arabia’s Team Falcons came in second, while French team Vitality rounded out the top three after more than one month of intense competition. Due to the conflict in the Middle East, the EWC was staged in Paris this summer – the first time it has been held outside Saudi Arabia. The event was a reminder of the growing reach of the US$4.3 billion industry, with China among its biggest markets. Some insiders said the bulk of its growth was still to come as EWC looks to match the revenue and cultural pull of sports such as football. “In football in Western markets, you have about US$50 to US$60 which the average fan spends per year. In esports, it’s about 10 per cent of that … so we have a 90 per cent pathway that we still have to unlock,” said Hans Jagnow, director of clubs, national teams and player relations at the EWC Foundation. This year’s EWC saw more than 2,000 athletes compete in 25 tournaments across 24 games, with a total prize pool of more than US$75 million. The Saudi-based esports foundation invested €250 million (US$289 million) to organise the event in Paris, with the French government expecting indirect economic benefits of €600 million. It was that figure that could help explain the enthusiastic response from Macron, who said in May that the chance to host the EWC in Paris was a “historic first and an honour for us”. Scenes of excited fans and news of sold-out finals – the reason the EWC moved its Counter-Strike final from its initial venue to the larger Accor Arena – are crucial for a sector trying to emerge from what has become known as the “esports winter” over the past few years, especially in North America, where organisations have struggled and viewership has dropped sharply. We had this over the last 20 years … it was a constant up and down, but it was more up than down Hans Jagnow, EWC Foundation The League of Legends Champions Series peaked at 183,152 live viewers this year, marking an all-time low for North America’s top League of Legends competition, according to Esports Charts. Activision Blizzard warned back in 2023 that the Overwatch League – based on its popular shooting game Overwatch – was in danger of collapse. However, Jagnow described these difficulties as “growing pains” and emphasised that while some organisations had struggled, other markets were growing. “We had this over the last 20 years in several instances … it was a constant up and down, but it was more up than down,” he said. One of the key markets that continued to grow was China, which reached 29.3 billion yuan (US$4.35 billion) in revenue and an audience of 495 million in 2025, according to an industry report published by Chinese authorities. For China, further growth now depends on broader participation, with organisers outside the game industry getting involved in organising esports events with game publishers, according to Jackie Huang, head of the Honor of Kings global esports division at Tencent Games, the title’s publisher. “I think the challenge is whether more of the broader ecosystem gets involved in this, whether more and more resources across the ecosystem get drawn in,” he said. Local authorities and organisers in China are increasingly reaching out to Honor of Kings asking to host esports events because they recognise the economic benefits they can receive from them, which Huang said was the right path for them to take. “It’s bright, and it’s big,” Huang said, referring to the future of esports. “And the big part is what I keep coming back to: opening it up to the broader ecosystem – because only then can this industry really develop, and the higher its ceiling goes.”

title: China boosts coal’s economic value 700% after turning it to liquids: report
description: The technology has taken years to develop domestically and is transforming the country’s long-defined energy structure.
content: The world’s largest coal-to-liquids plant is turning coal into oil products that can power rockets and serve as machine lubricants while boosting its value sevenfold, according to a Chinese newspaper. The production line, built by China Energy Group Ningxia Coal Industry Co Ltd, began full operations in northwest China’s Ningxia Hui autonomous region last month and processed 24 million tonnes of coal in 2025 – a quarter of the region’s total annual output, according to a report published by Science and Technology Daily on Wednesday. The technology has been a boon this year for China, which sourced more than 40 per cent of its crude oil from the Middle East before the Strait of Hormuz was blocked by the US-Israel war on Iran. At one point, international oil prices rose above US$100 per barrel, making turning coal into oil a very profitable business. According to the report, the project has not only generated substantial economic returns, it has also helped to reduce reliance on imported oil. China’s energy structure has long been defined by its abundant coal, limited oil and scarce natural gas reserves. In Ningxia, coal accounts for more than 90 per cent of the region’s energy use. The facility’s core technology – known as indirect coal liquefaction – involves heating coal with oxygen and steam to turn it into a synthetic gas of carbon monoxide and hydrogen. After purification, the gas is converted into environmentally friendly oil products that are low in sulphur and aromatics. “This technology is the most profound ‘magic’ in the field of coal chemical engineering,” He Peng, a manager with Ningxia Coal Industry, told the newspaper. The process has been long and required enormous investment, with the report noting that as early as 2004 the Chinese government sent Ningxia Coal Industry’s predecessor to negotiate with foreign firms to licence the coal-to-liquids technology. The global pioneer in the field was South African company Sasol, which capitalised on its proprietary know-how by repeatedly raising its price, demanding as much as US$2.5 billion for one synthesis alone. The negotiations dragged on for years without resolution. In 2009, China’s domestic research efforts achieved a breakthrough when Synfuels China Technology completed a 160,000-tonne-per-year indirect coal liquefaction pilot line and produced products that met industry standards. At that point, Ningxia Coal Industry decided to move forward independently, using Synfuels’ fully licensed home-grown technology. The path to self-reliance was beset with challenges, from clogged furnaces to easily broken nozzles and catalysts that were unstable. The most critical component was the gasifier, the first step in turning coal into liquid fuel. The gasifiers built using foreign technical routes could only handle high-quality premium coal and were also prohibitively expensive to modify, forcing the team to start from scratch. In 2012, the domestically developed Shenning furnace was born, opening a new avenue for the clean use of lower-grade coal, thanks to its ability to handle a wide variety in quality. The following year, the National Development and Reform Commission gave formal approval for the megaproject, designed to produce 4 million tonnes of oil products annually. The world-class facility, covering an area larger than 650 football fields, finally produced its first drop of qualified oil in 2016. Coal enters this system and emerges transformed – into diesel, naphtha, liquefied gas, sulphur, high-purity waxes, and a host of other products, each with greater value. The report gave two examples of the uses of these products, across industries. Using its own core technology and working with several partners, China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation developed a coal-based rocket fuel that helped to launch the Long March-12, reducing the industry’s dependence on a single fuel source. The report also named Ningxia Coal Industry’s self-developed C Energy+ series of high-end lubricants, with 11 products for both cars and industrial use. Its 68# anti-wear hydraulic oil performs on a par with leading international products, it said. The upgraded production line means higher-end products and improved safety, with the project standing as a model for China’s coal-to-liquids industry, according to the report. An industry insider told the Science and Technology Daily that “China’s coal-to-liquids sector has very few high-end products” at present. “Most top companies make mid- or low-end items, and high-end ones account for only a small share. Many advanced research findings are still in the lab and haven’t been scaled up for production,” the insider said. Following the latest upgrades, the project’s core processing units were also now operating with 99.8 per cent automated control, enabling long-term unattended operation, the report said. The whole industry should produce more valuable oil products and speciality chemicals, integrate more green hydrogen and green electricity in coal plants to cut emissions, and deploy robots and smart sensors in dangerous areas to keep workers safe, it said. title: China PhD student famous for Christopher Nolan interview accused of widespread plagiarism
description: While silent on allegations, Zhongshu reiterates a sentiment from Nolan interview, ‘We live in an age that demands apology from greatness’.
content: The Chinese podcaster Zhongshu, who garnered widespread international acclaim for her recent interview with filmmaker Christopher Nolan, is now facing allegations of paraphrasing and plagiarism in her podcasts and published works. The interview between Zhongshu and Nolan concerning The Odyssey, released on July 31, quickly went viral and was celebrated as “smart,” “the most interesting and profound,” and “peak journalism” by commentators in media and culture. In the 17-minute video, the PhD candidate in political philosophy at Boston College deviated from the typical promotional questions to delve into the philosophical complexities behind The Odyssey and Nolan’s adaptation. The video interview’s rapid success placed the 29-year-old woman in the spotlight, but she later expressed her willingness to “quit the Internet anytime” in an interview with the Chinese media outlet New Weekly if “my fame begins to consume my time.” Soon after, she found herself embroiled in controversy on Chinese social media. The scrutiny began on Douban, a social networking platform favoured by culture professionals, where some users discovered that her podcast channel Du Shu Bu Cheng Lin (A single tree does not make a forest), which has nearly one million followers, paraphrased the ideas of others without proper attribution. Netizens began to examine her content closely, accusing her of translating and paraphrasing academic publications, open courses, and podcasts from the English-speaking world. Her podcast content was found to exhibit similarities in structure, viewpoints, and even humour with the original materials. In one episode, a guest speaker used the phrase health and literacy “corps” – which was correct – but the AI-generated transcript mistook it for “court.” Zhongshu’s Chinese translation repeated this error by translating it as “court.” As more people joined the campaign, they revealed that her published texts, including the Chinese article, How Universities Combat AI Cheating, released in Caixin Weekly, plagiarised Rose Horowitch’s How AI Killed a 133-Year-Old Princeton Tradition, published in The Atlantic, and contained factual inaccuracies. Caixin Weekly has since removed the article from its website and labelled the page as “pending review.” The translator’s preface she wrote for her translations of works such as ancient Greek scholar Plutarch’s Moralia and Hannah Arendt’s The Human Condition has also been revealed to have plagiarised ideas from other scholars. Simultaneously, netizens investigated Zhongshu’s personal background, questioning whether she had exaggerated her credentials. While Zhongshu often introduced herself as a university lecturer, people sought her real name – Zhuge Yiyang – and discovered that she taught at the Brandeis Osher Lifelong Learning Institute, a learning community for adults aged 50 and over. Given that anyone can apply for a lectureship at the institute, some felt Zhongshu’s profile was less impressive, arguing that the title “university lecturer” implies formal employment with a university. Her page at Boston College indicates no published papers, leading to questions about her academic record as she was six years into her PhD studies. She referred to herself as a “small-town swot,” a Chinese term used by students from rural areas to humorously depict their lack of social and cultural capital, rendering their hard work seemingly futile. Ironically, she attended Groton School, one of the wealthiest boarding schools in the U.S., and continued her studies in the U.S. for her bachelor’s degree. Zhongshu also claimed to have mastered English, German, French, ancient Greek, and Latin. Introducing her recently published Chinese translation of The Human Condition, she referred to herself as “the scholar best suited to translate Hannah Arendt in China,” while disparaging the prior Chinese translator of Arendt’s text as “foolish and shallow,” possessing “a brain as tiny as a walnut.” After the interview with Nolan became a sensation, Zhongshu produced a podcast longer than the original discussion to analyse why it captivated the Western Internet. She mentioned she only viewed the film a day before the interview and prepared her questions on the way home. For many commenters, her unapologetically self-indulgent demeanour, combined with new-found scrutiny of her academic integrity, became increasingly unacceptable. Some even drew parallels between her temperament and that of Donald Trump, noting their shared outspokenness and larger-than-life personas. Zhongshu did not directly confront the allegations but reiterated to the Southern Metropolis Daily what she told Nolan: “We live in an age that demands apology from greatness,” positioning herself as that “greatness.” In a recent podcast, she seemed unfazed by the surrounding criticisms, revealing plans to appear on “a series of Western intellectuals’ podcasts in the U.S.” once her autumn semester commences. The SCMP reached out to Zhongshu and Boston College regarding the plagiarism allegations, but neither responded by the time of this article’s publication. “Plagiarism, paraphrasing, translation without referencing – these are unacceptable behaviours for a scholar,” asserted one online observer. “I prefer talking to AI rather than listening to paraphrased podcasts,” stated another. “Her popularity highlights the superficiality of our time. She skilfully presents herself as a prodigy and intellectual, feeding our yearning for a cultural icon that offers the illusion of shared intellectualism,” a third commented. “I wish I had just one per cent of her confidence. It could help me navigate the world effortlessly,” remarked another.

title: Malaysia says Indonesia to open airspace for cloud seeding to tackle haze
description: Both countries will ‌escalate firefighting and ‌fire prevention programmes ahead of national holidays, Malaysia’s environment minister says.
content: Indonesia has given Malaysian agencies ⁠official permission ⁠to enter its ⁠airspace to conduct cloud seeding operations, Malaysia’s environment minister has said, part of both countries’ efforts to combat the haze blanketing the region. Indonesia has been stepping ‌up efforts to slow the spread of haze caused by forest and land fires across several provinces, which this month led to dozens of school closures, including in neighbouring Malaysia. Malaysia’s national disaster management agency and its meteorological department ⁠were currently preparing schedules for cloud-seeding operations in shared border ‌locations, to be coordinated with the Indonesian military, Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Arthur Joseph Kurup ‌said in a statement. Malaysia was also prepared to ⁠offer help ⁠to Indonesia in extinguishing fires, with any specific requests to be brought to cabinet ‌for further action, Kurup said. He added that both countries would be ‌escalating their firefighting and ‌fire prevention programmes ahead of national holidays in the ‌coming weeks, including the Malaysia Day celebrations in Sarawak state on ⁠September 16. Sarawak, which borders Indonesia’s Kalimantan province on Borneo island, ⁠has been worst hit by the haze. Six districts in Sarawak recorded unhealthy air pollution index (API) readings on ‌Monday, according ‌to data released by the environment department. Unhealthy API levels were also recorded in eight other districts across four states on the Malaysian peninsula, the data showed.

title: Netherlands withdraws from ‘no longer’ neutral Eurovision
description: Its Dutch broadcaster says the contest, which has been hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel’s participation, has ‘become a platform for division’.
content: The Netherlands will not take part in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest, its broadcaster has said, adding that the event can “no longer be considered neutral” given divisions over the Gaza war. “It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character. The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division,” said Taco Zimmerman, director general of AVROTROS in a statement from the broadcaster on Monday. The contest has recently been hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel’s participation. Earlier this month, organisers announced they were excluding any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition. “However, the recently announced changes … do not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored,” said the AVROTROS statement. Israel came close to winning the competition in both 2025 and 2026, ultimately finishing second on each occasion. Next year’s event, the world’s biggest live televised music event, will take place on May 15 in Bulgaria’s Black Sea city of Burgas. It will be the first time that the Balkan nation hosts the contest, coming after Bulgarian singer Darina Yotova, known as Dara, won this year’s contest in the Austrian capital Vienna with the catchy floor-filler “Bangaranga”. Since its launch in 1955, Eurovision has become the ultimate pop platform, catapulting Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame, as well as boosting the likes of Celine Dion, Cliff Richard and Olivia Newton-John. The 2026 competition was watched by 131 million viewers, down 35 million on the year before after five countries boycotted it over Israel’s participation. The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the contest – with the latter three refusing to broadcast the show at all. The Dutch took part in the very first Eurovision Song Contest back in 1956, and have won on five occasions. The most recent winner was Duncan Laurence whose song “Arcade” won the contest in 2019, going on to top charts globally. It became the first Eurovision entry to reach 1 billion streams on Spotify, according to the Eurovision website. The withdrawal was “painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the contest again next year”, Zimmerman said. “As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values. They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts.” Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said the organisation regretted the decision, but understood and respected the choice. Green said organisers would investigate whether another Dutch broadcaster might be willing to take part in the contest. “We very much hope that audiences and artists in the Netherlands can continue to be represented in the Eurovision Song Contest,” Green said. AVROTROS selects and manages the Dutch entry to the contest.

title: Banking veteran Li Yun fills senior Shenzhen posts in countdown to Apec
description: Li takes over from Qin Weizhong as China prepares to showcase the city to the world in November summit.
content: A banking veteran has been appointed the new deputy Communist Party secretary and acting mayor of the southern Chinese metropolis of Shenzhen, just months before the city is scheduled to host a series of Apec meetings. The positions have been filled by Li Yun, who spent more than two decades working in financial institutions and has been the vice-governor of Guangdong province since March last year. As Shenzhen’s new deputy party secretary and acting mayor, Li takes over from Qin Weizhong, the Shenzhen Special Zone Daily reported on Monday. Meeting members of the standing committee of the municipal people’s congress, Li vowed to always “implement the decisions of the Central Committee, provincial and municipal party committees”, as well as push for progress and achievements in Shenzhen’s high-quality development and modernisation drive, the report said. Li, 52, has a doctorate in world economy from Wuhan University and worked for 21 years at Agricultural Bank of China. In 2021, he became vice-president of China Construction Bank and in 2025 he became the vice-governor of Guangdong. Shenzhen is due to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November, an event that the Chinese leadership sees as a great opportunity to showcase China’s technological innovation, build high-level diplomatic engagement and drive regional integration. Qin, Li’s predecessor, was appointed deputy party secretary and mayor of Shenzhen in May 2021. Qin resigned because of a “change in work post”, the report said, without elaborating. He is an alternate member of the party’s 20th Central Committee, which is expected to sit until 2027, when the 21st party congress will be held. Before taking up the positions in Shenzhen, Qin, who has a PhD in chemical engineering from Tsinghua University in Beijing, was responsible for housing, the environment and big data management in Guangdong, the provincial capital. Li’s appointment comes five months after 56-year-old economist Jin Lei was appointed party chief of Shenzhen. Jin, formerly an official in the southwestern province of Sichuan, took over from Meng Fanli nearly six months after Meng was promoted to provincial governor. Shortly after his appointment, Jin inspected preparation work for the Apec meetings and vowed to “resolutely fulfil this major political mission and fully serve the overall national diplomatic strategy”. Since then, the city has launched a series of measures to tackle some long-running issues, including e-bikes and public smoking. It has also ramped up security. Futian district, home to the Apec venues, previously announced it would go “all in” on internationalisation, upgrading services and attracting global companies. Shenzhen has also seized this opportunity to seal deals. Last month, the Port of Shenzhen signed agreements with 16 other ports around the world on routes, port construction and professional development.

title: Hong Kong launches real-name booking system for popular Sai Kung coastal trail
description: Visitors can make bookings for Po Pin Chau section of High Island Geo Trail on Klook’s website, app and WeChat mini-programme.
content: Hong Kong has launched its first countryside real-name reservation system, capping daily visitors to a popular trail in Sai Kung at 2,000 on select dates, with a lawmaker and a district councillor saying the move could gather data to help shape formal arrangements. The trial reservation system for visits to the Po Pin Chau trail in Sai Kung East Country Park went live at 11am on Monday, offering the first batch of slots for September 5 and 6 via Klook’s website, app and WeChat mini-programme. A check by a South China Morning Post reporter on Monday afternoon found that slots for all four time slots – 9am, 11am, 1pm and 3pm – for both dates were still available, with each permitting a maximum of 500 people. To complete the booking, users need to submit all participants’ names, telephone numbers and identity documents, including passports, exit-entry permits for Macau and Hong Kong, or identity cards for mainland Chinese and local residents. Contact information will also be required, and an e-voucher will be sent via email or can be viewed in Klook’s app or mini-programme after registration. According to the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department’s website, the reservation system covers weekends between September 5 and 20, the three-day Mid-Autumn Festival weekend starting on September 25, and the mainland’s National Day “golden week” from October 1 to 7. Lawmaker Chris Ip Ngo-tung, who represents the southeast New Territories, welcomed the move and praised it for managing overcrowding at the site while safeguarding visitors. “An overcrowded tourist spot will not only bring inconvenience and unpleasantness to visitors, but also danger,” he told a radio show, noting that several fatal accidents had previously happened in the area. More than 3,000 people per day visited Po Pin Chau during the Easter holiday, with the influx concentrated over a short period, Ip said, adding that the new arrangement was the result of careful analysis. Ip said he expected the government would use the trial period to collect data and develop a formal arrangement, factoring in actual footfall and the area’s ecological capacity. “If there are a lot of no-shows resulting in the waste of quotas, we can consider introducing a charging or deposit system,” he said. Sai Kung district councillor Chris Cheung Mei-hung said on the same show that the quota system capping daily footfall at 2,000 was a good starting point for managing the site. Cheung noted that most visitors to the spot were mainland tourists, and called on authorities to “fine-tune” the system after the trial period by reserving some quotas for local residents. He also urged setting aside some on-site walk-in quotas. “Some people may not be familiar with mobile apps or online registrations, for example, the elderly, so there should be some walk-in quotas,” he said. Cheung added that authorities should also step up publicity of the system on mainland social media platforms to make tourists aware of the new regulation. Tourists also support the change on social media, with many posting photos taken at the site in comments. “With fewer people, the experience is better too,” a RedNote user said. Another user shared an experience from her visit to the site in November, when she saw someone dropping rubbish on the road, saying that she supported the shake-up.

title: Mainland school operator leases Kowloon tower as talent influx drives city’s education boom
description: The tenant operates top-tier non-tertiary schools in mainland China and is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange.
content: A Hong Kong-listed educational group has completed the largest commercial property leasing deal so far this quarter, as the sector benefits from an influx of immigrant and expatriate families to the city, according to CBRE. The tenant agreed to occupy and transform the entire Tower B at the China Life Centre in Hung Hom, Kowloon into a purpose-built education complex spanning about 36,400 square feet, said Frederick Lai, senior director for capital markets at the property consultancy. “This project showcases the successful repurposing of a commercial asset to support Hong Kong’s expanding education sector,” Lai said. Lai declined to name the tenant, citing a non-disclosure agreement, but said it operated top-tier non-tertiary schools in mainland China and was listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange. “They had been planning to set up a school in Hong Kong for a number of years now and finally they found a perfect opportunity,” Lai added. CBRE predicted the education sector would play a sizeable role in real estate investment and leasing in Hong Kong given the shortage of available school spots for children of expatriates and immigrant families. In the last five years, non-tertiary education groups as well as international private schools had invested HK$1 billion (US$128 million) in real estate, Lai said. On top of that, the sector had leased 280,000 sq ft of space in the past 12 months. As of the third week of August, education investments, including student housing conversions and educational institutions acquiring commercial properties, amounted to HK$10.7 billion, accounting for 37 per cent of the total so far this year, CBRE’s data showed. The investments and leasing covered both school campuses and administrative facilities for the educational groups, Lai said. “Education groups are expanding rapidly in Hong Kong and from a real estate perspective, it’s an emerging sector,” he said. CBRE said more education groups were likely to seek properties for their requirements given that the 280,000 new residents who settled in Hong Kong via various talent schemes since 2022 had brought 250,000 dependents with them, including children of school age. Lai said schools were “very selective” when it came to leasing properties and that they did not just take space because it was available. “It takes a lot of careful planning and discussions before they choose a spot because they would rather have a permanent solution than a temporary one. But when they do find the premises, they invest heavily into that property,” Lai said. Separately, Savills has sold Smart A, an eight-storey, one-stop education-themed commercial building in Kowloon for HK$320 million. Smart A occupies 348-352 Prince Edward Road West, but the 42,000 sq ft total also includes 70 per cent of 354 Prince Edward Road West, which has the potential to be redeveloped, according to Savills. Savills did not identify the buyer, but agents said Hong Kong-listed apparel manufacturer and property developer Crystal International Group purchased the property. Crystal International did not immediately reply to a request for comment on Monday. The property’s basement and ground floor were occupied by ParknShop, while the first to seventh floors were designated for commercial use, Savills said. “Smart A is a well-established tutoring hub in the district, with tenants comprising reputable tutorial centres and related education institutions,” said Jason Wo, senior director for investment at Savills. “The property currently generates a monthly rental income exceeding HK$1.3 million, delivering a yield of over 5 per cent,” Wo said. “Upon full leasing of remaining units, the yield is expected to further improve, approaching 6 per cent, highlighting its strong upside potential.”

title: Brazil presidential debate zeroes in on Chinese investment and US tariffs
description: ‘What matters to Lulism is that we keep buying the finished product from China while we sell ore or sell our grain’: candidate Renan Santos.
content: Brazil’s presidential candidates opened the televised campaign season on Sunday with a debate that turned repeatedly to the country’s position between Washington and Beijing. The exchange comes in an election cycle already shaped by American tariffs, a visa dispute over election monitoring and the Lula government’s warming ties with China. Ronaldo Caiado, Augusto Cury and Renan Santos took to the debate stage in Sao Paulo but the lecterns reserved for President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and former Minas Gerais governor Romeu Zema remained empty. Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro, who are leading in every published poll, refused to take part, with the Brazilian president telling a podcast in July he would skip debates if the exercise meant listening to nonsense. Flavio Bolsonaro has tied his attendance to Lula’s, and Zema withdrew hours beforehand, saying the event had “lost its purpose”. A senator for Rio de Janeiro and the eldest son of Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio became a candidate in December after being named by his father as his heir. Jair was sentenced to 27 years in jail for plotting a coup and masterminding a plan to assassinate Lula after losing his re-election bid in 2022. The Band network has opened the televised campaign in every presidential race since 1989, the first direct vote after two decades of military rule. Broadcasters treat the event as the moment that sets the tone for the season. US-China issue Foreign policy rarely takes up much room in Brazilian presidential debates, which tend to be dominated by security, jobs and inflation. The absence of the two front-runners left the others time for subjects that usually stay at the margins. Washington imposed a 25 per cent tariff on most Brazilian goods on July 22, capping a Section 301 case that ran for a year. It covered digital payment rules, ethanol market access and illegal deforestation. A separate forced labour investigation proposes a further 12.5 per cent duty. The trade dispute has run alongside an argument over the vote itself, which Brasilia treats as a matter of interference. Last month, Brazil denied visas to two US State Department officials who planned to question electoral authorities. And this month, Lula said he would withhold agreement for US President Donald Trump’s nominee as ambassador until the vote was over. Meanwhile, Beijing has moved in the other direction, offering Brasilia support as Washington escalated. President Xi Jinping telephoned Lula on July 26, four days after the tariffs took effect, and said China opposed external interference. The two governments agreed to widen cooperation on artificial intelligence, satellites, critical mineral processing and fertiliser trade. In the debate studio, a radio journalist asked Augusto Cury how he would manage Washington during the second Trump term. The psychiatrist and author, who is running for Avante, argued that the tariffs answered American fiscal pressure rather than any dispute with Brazil. “We cannot be subservient, put 25 per cent, plus 12.5, 37.5 per cent, and damage our export list,” he said. Cury said he would foster equally good relations with China while pushing Brazil out of its raw material role. Caiado, the former Goias governor running for the PSD, or Social Democratic Party, attributed friction with the Trump administration to Lula’s electoral calculations. “Lula is desperate to create this impasse because he saw the presidents of Canada and Australia winning, so he provokes Trump all the time,” he said. Caiado said the foreign ministry had become a mouthpiece for the governing Workers’ Party. He promised to restore its ability to negotiate for a country he said retained leverage in energy, grain and fresh water. However, it was Renan Santos who drew more attention than his two rivals on stage, despite never having held elected office. The 42-year-old co-founded the Free Brazil Movement that organised the protests that preceded former president Dilma Rousseff’s impeachment in 2016. Polling has kept him third for most of the year – at between 5 and 9 per cent – but an AtlasIntel survey in July put him first among Brazilians aged 16 to 24, with 38 per cent. Supporters and opponents call him “the Brazilian Bukele”, a label he encourages by citing controversial Salvadorean president Nayib Bukele – the self-proclaimed “coolest dictator in the world” – when talking about his war on crime. Like Bukele, Santos’ platform pairs mass incarceration and militarised policing with wide deregulation of the economy. On arriving at the studios, Santos was asked how he would handle warming between Lula and Trump as well as their divergence over Chinese investment. “It seems that the sovereignty debate of Lula and Flavio involves choosing who your guardian will be,” he said. “One wants to choose China, the other wants to choose the United States. And that is not what makes a nation sovereign.” Inside the studio he pressed the same charge against the governing party in language aimed at its trade record rather than its diplomacy. “Right now we look at the Workers’ Party [Lula’s party] project wanting to put Brazil on its knees before China, without training a qualified workforce,” he said. “What matters to Lulism is that we keep buying the finished product from China while we sell ore or sell our grain.” Kim Kataguiri, a federal deputy and one of Santos’s main campaign coordinators, said the position amounted to pragmatism rather than an alignment of any kind. “He means that Lula, in exchange for nothing or for very little, automatically aligns with China,” Kataguiri told the South China Morning Post at the studios. Kataguiri drew a sharper line on the other side, separating the American state from the administration that currently runs it. “With Flavio, it is not even in relation to the United States, it is specifically in relation to the Trump government,” he said. “It is not an alignment with the nation, with the American state, but with a figure, and a figure who, by all indications, will have difficulty electing a successor.” He said Brazil should set terms for both the US and China instead of picking one, starting with what Beijing brings to the table. “China wants space inside Brazil, so let it offer investment, let it offer technology, let it offer defence partnership,” he said, naming AI and rare earth processing, sectors he said Beijing led Washington, and added that Brazil could import that technology through strategic partnerships. The same demand applied to the Americans, which he said had a shrinking commercial presence in Brazil. “They do not want us to make more trade partnerships with China, so let them offer more partnership,” Kataguiri said. “American investment in Brazil only falls. The United States took Brazil as a given for the past 20 years and neglected our relations.” Lula tells Trump real target is China While the three candidates argued in the Sao Paulo debate, Record TV aired an exclusive interview with Lula recorded that morning at his official residence in Brasilia. Presenter Mariana Godoy asked what had been settled with Trump on two subjects: the tariffs on Brazilian goods and cooperation against organised crime. Lula described a call with the US president on Friday that ran about 80 minutes in which he reportedly told Trump the grounds for the new sanctions were false, citing record low deforestation and Lula’s own history of fighting forced labour, then placed the pressure elsewhere. “Underneath it all, what he was really getting at was China,” he said. Lula said he offered Trump a joint task force on critical minerals and rare earths, with one condition. “Only this time we are not going to be an exporter of raw material. We want to transform it here, to make mobile phones, to make electric batteries, to make chips,” the president contended.

title: The View | Malaysia’s data centre rules aim to green the sector, not slam the door
description: Unlike the US backlash, Malaysia is drawing up efficiency requirements to guide a sustainable tech boom.
content: In global commercial real estate investment markets, data centres are all the rage. While stock markets continue to suffer bouts of volatility as sentiment oscillates between concerns artificial intelligence (AI) will fall short of expectations and fears it will prove more disruptive than many think, the fundamentals of data centres are exceptionally strong. According to JLL, global data centre occupancy was 97 per cent at the end of last year while 77 per cent of all capacity under construction is committed to tenants. Hyperscalers – leading technology companies and cloud service providers such as Amazon and Meta – occupy more than half of all data centre space, providing security to landlords. This is why data centres account for a fast-growing share of global commercial property fundraising. However, the market has reached an inflection point. The rapid growth of AI workloads has amplified constraints such as power availability, land access, sustainability requirements and community acceptance. In the United States, a fierce backlash against data centres has become “a structural constraint on AI infrastructure” that “has expanded to broader anti-AI sentiment”, Jefferies said in a report. In the first quarter of this year, at least 75 data centre projects worth around US$130 billion were delayed or blocked by local opposition, close to the total value of schemes stymied by local resistance during the whole of 2025. Last month, New York moved to become the first US state to impose a temporary ban on the construction of large new data centres because of fears that the scale and speed of development put too much strain on energy and water resources. Lawmakers in more than a dozen other states are mulling temporary bans on the facilities. Research group Data Centre Watch said “moratoria [have] expanded from local exceptions to a multi-front political battle”. In the past year, there have been signs the growing unease about the pace of development is spreading to Southeast Asia, which accounts for the largest share of data centre capacity under construction in the Asia-Pacific. In Malaysia, whose southern state of Johor was the region’s fastest-growing data centre market last year, the sector is “in a reset mode”, according to S&P Global Ratings, as it shifts from breakneck and indiscriminate expansion to sustainable growth. Last year, the government set up a data centre task force to formulate and coordinate policy, particularly planning, investment approvals and infrastructure requirements. More stringent regulations were introduced, including stricter rules for approving new projects, higher utility tariffs and a stipulation that operators declare their annual electricity demand. Johor, which accounts for 80 per cent of Malaysia’s data centre capacity, halted approvals for projects that are significantly less water- and power-efficient. It also enforced sustainability requirements. “It’s tempting to view what’s happening in Johor through a US lens, but there are huge differences,” said Paul Mah, an adviser and commentator on Asia-Pacific digital infrastructure. First, Johor had to take measures to tame the boom. A huge beneficiary of neighbouring Singapore’s decision in 2019 to impose a temporary ban on data centres, Johor’s operational capacity surged to 1 gigawatt in the space of four years, exceeding Singapore’s installed capacity which took a decade to build, according to data from DC Byte. The tougher regulatory regime is designed to buy Malaysia more time as it ramps up its infrastructure investments to avert major bottlenecks. Far from clamping down on data centres, the government is putting in place measures to ensure the boom does not turn to bust. Second, the government is trying to weed out speculative development by prioritising quality over quantity. S&P noted that actual demand for electricity last year was only 55 per cent of approved capacity. Penalties imposed on data centres that do not meet 85 per cent of their stated annual electricity utilisation should help discourage speculative bids. “Higher barriers to entry in the sector will favour more experienced and better capitalised developers and operators,” said Jamie Tan, managing director at JLL Malaysia. Third, while Thailand is experiencing a surge in data centre investment, fuelling debate over whether Malaysia’s stricter regulations are encouraging operators to invest in markets where costs are cheaper and policies are more permissive, the Malaysian government plans to tighten rules to ease pressure on natural resources and accelerate the shift to renewable energy. Data centres are expected to consume more than 30 per cent of the country’s power by 2035, up from 7 per cent at present. The acute resource-related challenges posed by Malaysia’s data centre boom and the limited spillover benefits in the labour market – given that operational data centres require few staff on-site – put a premium on judicious policies. “It’s not about more permissive or less permissive regulation, but about finding the right way to grow the sector in a sustainable manner,” said Neil Bear-Hetherington, director for Asia-Pacific data centre capital markets at CBRE. Unlike in the US, where some politicians are eager to tout their anti-data centre credentials, Malaysia’s government seeks to bolster and sustain the country’s position as a leading data centre hub.

title: Art, saints, Galileo: Italy’s Padua, 30 minutes from Venice, offers a quiet alternative
description: Escape Venice’s crowds for Padua, less than a 30-minute train ride away and one of the country’s most dynamic cities.
content: My disdain for Venice has been the subject of lively conversations with friends and family. Yes, its picturesque bridges over canals that criss-cross the town are romantic. Yes, it is the birthplace of the modern printing press and a historic melting pot of cultures influenced by significant trade routes. But stopping in Venice also means fighting crowds from cruise ships, paying daily entry fees to breathe its decadence and facing hugely inflated prices for subpar meals. Instead, Padua is less than a 30-minute train ride away. As the setting for William Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew and the birthplace of influential Renaissance architect Andrea Palladio, Padua – Padova in Italian – is close enough to Venice, Vicenza and Verona for easy day trips to explore the Veneto region. On a Trenitalia train heading to the city, we struck up a conversation with a British couple. They raved about their recent stay in Padua, adding that its consistent swell of university students gave it an eternal youthfulness and made it one of the country’s most dynamic cities. “Of course you will see the Giotto frescoes,” said the lady, referring to Italian painter Giotto’s early 14th century collection of 38 paintings found at Scrovegni Chapel that depict scenes in the life of Jesus, his parents and grandparents, as well as his interpretation of The Last Judgment. Since we were staying at Scrovegni Room & Breakfast – a small heritage inn beside the chapel – we could easily visit at some point during our stay. Or so we thought. Due to the delicacy of the frescoes, which were painted between 1303 and 1305 and represent the turning point when Renaissance light emerged from medieval darkness, only 25 people can view them for 15-minute sessions throughout the day; booking far in advance is highly recommended. We found this out the hard way when we tried our luck and discovered that the only available slots were after we had flown home. But it was a beautiful day, and we continued southeast towards the Basilica of St Anthony – another major site on our bucket list. A morning of the sacred The squat Romanesque-Gothic church is the resting place of Lisbon-born Anthony, a celebrated orator who worked the occasional miracle before settling in Padua in his final years. A year after his untimely death due to illness in 1231, aged 36, he was canonised by Pope Gregory IX. Construction on the basilica that bears his name began immediately afterwards. As we entered the church, we looked up to see a statue of St Anthony holding a book – a symbol of his life as a monk studying scripture before embarking on his preaching career. Inside, the relative restraint of the exterior was more than made up for by over-the-top interiors – par for the course, considering that it is an important pilgrimage church for devout Catholics. On the high altar at the end of the nave stood a bronze crucifix alongside seven other statues by Italian sculptor Donatello, who made Padua his home for a decade in the mid-15th century. On the left-hand side of the basilica, St Anthony’s tomb was set within a side chapel surrounded by nine marble reliefs dating to the 1500s that illustrated scenes and miracles from the saint’s life. At the very rear of the basilica was the Chapel of the Reliquaries, where relics such as the tongue and jawbone of St Anthony could be marvelled at, eight centuries after his death – fitting for someone with the gift of the gab. An afternoon of the secular After a morning of the sacred, we were ready to tackle Padua’s secular side. Heading north and west, we stumbled upon the majestic Palazzo della Ragione between two market squares, Piazza delle Erbe and Piazza della Frutta. Though we were captivated by the abundant fruit and vegetable stalls in Piazza delle Erbe, we loved the takeaway options on the ground floor of the 13th century palazzo. Armed with a picnic lunch of octopus salad, we found a shady place to feast while admiring the ornate three storeys of colonnades enveloping the palazzo. Having been the centre of life in Padua for more than eight centuries, it used to house the city’s courts on the upper floor, while popular bars, grocers and craft shops dominate the ground floor today. Piazza delle Erbe was the perfect place for us to observe daily life in Padua while lingering over a gelato. Elderly men nursed espressos as they checked out pretty women strolling by, while young mothers with strollers shopped for the evening’s meal. We strolled east towards increasingly louder musical jubilance, which we discovered was the city’s Pride parade. We were swept up in the energy of the rainbow-hued floats until we found ourselves in the middle of the University of Padua, one of the world’s oldest universities. Established in 1222, it was the alma mater of Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus and where Italian natural philosopher and astronomer Galileo taught for 18 years. After ogling the myriad of stone cherubs and coats of arms of former administrators in a courtyard, we sneaked into a lofty classroom. Perched on polished wooden chairs, we pretended Galileo was at the lectern sharing his observations of the Milky Way as viewed through his new and improved telescope. An evening with delicious food All the day’s activity made our stomachs grumble. We checked our list of restaurant recommendations provided by our inn’s host, a Padua native, and found that several were in the city’s Jewish quarter, a neighbourhood full of alfresco eateries and artisanal shops selling things like handmade leather belts and scrumptious pastries. Among them, along Via Soncin, was Antica Osteria dal Capo, an elegant yet homey restaurant where a queue had already formed outside even though it was not yet open for dinner. Luckily, we were early enough to snag a table in the cosy dining area. We loved the handwritten menu and local dishes such as rich tripe stew and savoury bigoli pasta with anchovy sauce. We finished with a chocolate-drizzled semifreddo allo zabaione, an ideal marriage of mousse and ice cream. Sighing contentedly as we strolled through the quiet streets back to the inn, we congratulated ourselves on a perfect day in Padua.

title: Australia’s bowlers restore order but batting headaches remain ahead of South Africa tour
description: Ex-skipper Ricky Ponting says it is time replacements for Marnus Labuschagne should be considered; others say no urgency for ⁠more changes.
content: Normal service ⁠resumed for Australia as their formidable bowling unit hit their marks in the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay but questions remain over a batting order that continues to misfire at the top. Australia’s innings and 51-run victory was a strong comeback from the Darwin defeat as pace leaders Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins blasted away the tourists’ batters in a timely ‌reminder of their quality ahead of a tough, three-test tour of South Africa in October. Australia’s batting has left selectors with a headache, though, and struggling number three Marnus Labuschagne may be nervous about his place in the squad for South Africa. South Africa-born Labuschagne was already under major scrutiny after two poor dismissals in Darwin before he was bowled for four in Mackay by Shoriful Islam, the ball catching his thigh pad before hitting the stumps. Upon his dismissal, Labuschagne gave the look of a man forsaken by the cricketing gods and later ⁠took scissors to his thigh pad in an unusual gear modification. But behind the theatrics was a batter who had strayed far across his crease and ‌given Shoriful a look at leg stump, further evidence for pundits of a need for change. “There’s some technical deficiency there, but he’s making the margin for error for the bowlers too great,” former Australia captain Ricky Ponting said. “It’s ‌well and truly time to have a look at somebody else.” Labuschagne’s exit would be the second top-order batter dropped in ⁠two matches after opener Jake Weatherald ⁠was dumped in the wake of the fiasco in Darwin, where Australia fell to a shock nine-wicket defeat. Weatherald’s replacement Matt Renshaw hardly inspired in his first Test in more than three years, ‌falling for eight with a nick to the slips, but he will be afforded time to bed into the role. Whether Travis Head should accompany him at the top of the order remains ‌a troublesome ‌question for selectors. Moved up from the middle order for the Ashes as Usman Khawaja struggled with injury, Head has remained there despite not ‌really being seen as a proper opener. Some former players, including Mark Waugh, want Head back down in the middle order but that would mean gambling ⁠with two unproven openers against South Africa, who beat Australia for the World Test Championship title last year. With runs in Darwin and Mackay, Cameron Green ⁠has belatedly shored up his spot at number five, so bringing Head back down would mean upsetting the formula of having wicketkeeper Alex Carey at six and the second all-rounder Beau Webster at seven. Selectors picked a thin 13-man squad for the Bangladesh series ‌but are expected to take at least ‌16 to South Africa and include additional batting cover. Quite who gets the nod among the batters on the fringes is far from certain, with no real stand-out candidates having emerged. Carey said there was no urgency to shake up Australia’s batting line-up further. “I think we felt a little bit like we left some runs out there [against Bangladesh], so we are always looking to improve as a batting unit,” he told reporters in Mackay. “We are hungry. We are working really hard.”

title: Nexperia’s China unit pivots to domestic 12-inch wafers in pursuit of ‘100%’ independence
description: The Chinese division is betting on a high-stakes, home-grown supply chain pivot to bypass suspended European wafer shipments.
content: The China unit of Dutch chipmaker Nexperia has announced plans to shift its entire product line to a domestic 12-inch silicon wafer foundry, pursuing what it calls “independent operations” amid a nearly one-year-long dispute with its European headquarters. Speaking at a press conference themed “based in China, serve the world” on Sunday, Nexperia’s China team – which used to source wafers from the firm’s European fabrication plants – said it was moving towards “100 per cent domestic production”, according to reports by local media outlets. The unit’s supply-chain bottlenecks stem from a dispute between Nexperia’s Dutch headquarters and its Chinese parent company, Wingtech Technology, which owns the semiconductor firm. Caught between the conflicting parties, Nexperia’s Chinese operations have been cut off from crucial European wafer supplies. A central update from the Sunday briefing was a shift to a new 12-inch wafer supply provided by an unnamed “Chinese strategic partner”. Nexperia China is now transferring all its products from its previous 8-inch and 6-inch production lines. In semiconductor manufacturing, chips are cut from thin discs of silicon called wafers. Larger wafers typically produce more individual chips, lowering costs. Nexperia China said its new supply could achieve “unparalleled cost efficiency”, noting that a 12-inch wafer provided about four times the surface area of a 6-inch wafer and 2.25 times that of an 8-inch one. Following a March milestone in which the unit announced it had achieved “small-volume production” of bipolar discrete devices, the firm said on Sunday that its broader product portfolio – including diodes, metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors and logic integrated circuits – would be made entirely from 12-inch wafers. Previously, Nexperia operated under an integrated global supply chain, with raw wafers produced in German and British fabrication plants shipped for assembly to China – which is responsible for about 70 per cent of the firm’s global output – as well as Malaysia and the Philippines. The company’s European facilities lacked 12-inch wafer manufacturing capabilities. Nexperia’s website showed that an 8-inch wafer line in Manchester, United Kingdom, went into operation in 2021, while Wingtech, the Chinese parent, previously committed 12 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion) to build a 12-inch one in Shanghai. The relationship between Nexperia and Wingtech soured in September 2025 after the Dutch government intervened to restrict the Chinese parent company’s operational control over the chipmaker. The following month, Nexperia suspended wafer shipments to its assembly plant in Dongguan, a city in China’s southern Guangdong province. Nexperia China has since operated with limited supplies. On Sunday, it said it had shipped more than 40 billion chips to more than 1,000 customers worldwide over the past 11 months. Addressing the restructuring, John Chang, Nexperia China’s chief operating officer, was quoted by China Daily on Monday as saying the unit’s latest moves were “not about confronting anyone – they are about protecting those we serve”. When contacted for comment on Monday, a representative from Nexperia’s Dutch team reiterated a statement from November, maintaining that the company had “continued to offer alternative supply chain solutions to mitigate disruption”, including “selling and shipping wafers to Nexperia customers directly”. Representatives from Nexperia’s Chinese unit and Wingtech did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The split within the company has led to severe bottlenecks for automotive supply chains, given Nexperia’s role as a major supplier of chips to the industry. The corporate fallout has also expanded into legal channels: Wingtech announced in May that it had filed a lawsuit against Nexperia and three of its executives under China’s anti-foreign sanctions law. At the same time, diplomatic channels have sought to de-escalate the commercial friction. Following an April meeting with Shen Bo, China’s ambassador to the Netherlands, the Dutch government’s economic minister Heleen Herbert said both sides had agreed the dispute should be “solved between the two companies without government interference”. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten is set to visit China next spring, the first by a Dutch leader since the Nexperia saga plunged bilateral ties into crisis, the South China Morning Post reported in July.

title: Letters | Why do the humanities not have awards like the Fields Medal or Nobel Prize?
description: Readers discuss the lack of recognition for outstanding scholarship in the humanities, the lure of toys to children, and elderly mental health.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The recent Fields Medals awarded to Chinese mathematicians Wang Hong and Deng Yu have attracted considerable global attention. Their receiving one of the highest honours in mathematics has generated headlines and wider discussion about scholarly excellence and investment in mathematics. They deserve every bit of that recognition. Their success also prompts a question that those of us in the humanities should ask: if mathematics has the Fields Medal, what do the humanities have? In fact, mathematics has far more than the Fields Medal. The Abel Prize, established by the Norwegian government, is frequently described as mathematics’ equivalent of the Nobel Prize. Other major international honours include the Shaw Prize and the Breakthrough Prize. Beyond mathematics, other scientific disciplines possess an equally extensive system of recognition, including the Nobel Prizes, Kavli Prizes and Lasker Awards. These prizes matter not simply because they reward excellence, but because they make scholarly excellence visible. The media explains the significance of the winners’ research, while the public learns about work that might otherwise remain known only to specialists. The humanities have nothing quite comparable. There is the Nobel Prize in Literature, but it recognises writers rather than scholars of literature. Humanities disciplines certainly have distinguished prizes, but most remain field-specific and receive limited public recognition beyond academic circles. Governments and universities have compelling reasons to invest heavily in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, particularly amid advances in artificial intelligence, biotechnology, medicine and climate science. The question is not whether science deserves such support but why the humanities so often receive comparatively less funding, recognition and public attention. Humanities disciplines, including history, literature and philosophy, produce forms of knowledge whose impact is often difficult to quantify. Yet by helping us understand how people have made sense of their worlds across different times and cultures, the humanities shape how we interpret the past, understand the present and imagine the future. Why not establish major global prizes for outstanding humanities scholarship, modelled on the ambition and prestige of the world’s great scientific prizes? Such awards could recognise transformative scholarship while bringing greater public visibility and support to the humanities. The world has become remarkably good at celebrating those who expand the boundaries of what humanity can calculate and build. We should be equally ambitious about celebrating those who expand the boundaries of what humanity can understand. Jack Meng-Tat Chia, Singapore Beyblade shows toys can still grab children I refer to the letter, “Physical toys aren’t fighting a losing battle. How’s that for hope?” (August 2). The comeback of Beyblade reminds me of when toys shaped how my peers and I spent our free time. Today’s children risk missing out on the tactile play that once defined childhood. Once parents let them use electronic devices, many children trade toys for stretches of screen time. They become passive consumers of online content instead of creating things, competing and forging friendships with playmates. The smartphone might be part of modern life, but it shouldn’t dominate children’s free time. In the early 2010s, before online entertainment took over, toys could easily win their attention. Beyblade’s comeback shows physical toys can still hold their own if they have strong franchises that draw in children. Whether through competitive series such as Beyblade or superhero franchises, children often use toys as springboards for their own stories and games, allowing their imagination to run wild. A franchise might provide the characters and canon, but children make the experience their own. We can’t turn back the clock, but we can demand better alternatives to endless scrolling. Screen-based entertainment has its place, but toys deserve a fighting chance to reclaim some of children’s free time. Sam Ho, Yuen Long Pay attention to elderly mental health Recently there has been much talk about mental health issues concerning the young. How the old battle their own crises is less discussed. By 2046, about 36 per cent of the local population will have reached the age of 65. This is an alarming figure. It is crucial for these seniors not to be isolated or housebound as far as possible. Families must pitch in to take them out. Keeping pets or taking up hobbies would help keep their spirits up. The government must also step up support, especially for elderly living alone. We must also ensure that healthcare services are kept affordable so that the elderly are not deterred from seeking help. Jacqueline Kwan, Sai Ying Pun

title: Louis Vuitton shuts down another store amid fallout from trademark dispute in China
description: The latest China store exit in Guiyang highlights the luxury brand’s struggle to balance prestige with cultural empathy amid legal disputes.
content: Louis Vuitton will close its only store in Guiyang on August 31, according to an on-site notice, further trimming the French luxury brand’s southwestern China footprint, which has fallen to three stores from a peak of six. The closure in the capital of Guizhou province is part of the brand’s plan to optimise its retail network as it recalibrates strategy in the world’s second-largest consumer market amid soft domestic spending and shifting luxury consumption trends. It coincides with a string of trademark lawsuits Louis Vuitton has filed in China. In one case, local tea chain Molly Tea was ordered to pay the brand 10.3 million yuan (US$1.5 million) in July over the use of a similar logo. The verdict sparked heated online debate, but also drew public support for the Chinese company. “We see limited short-term sales impact from the Molly Tea incident. However, the real risk lies in the long-term effect on younger Chinese consumers, who will form the future consumer base for Louis Vuitton,” said Sandy Lim, director at S&P Global Ratings. “They prioritise cultural respect and brand empathy over pure prestige-driven exclusivity. The controversy could create a higher perceived barrier for this cohort, which Louis Vuitton would need to address at some point down the road.” Over the past year, the brand has been scaling back outlets in China. It closed stores in Kunming, Yunnan province, in February and Chengdu Tianfu International Airport in Sichuan province in June, both in the country’s southwest. It also closed its non-duty-free store at the domestic departure section of Terminal 3 at the Beijing Capital International Airport earlier this year, according to an April 30 statement from the city’s customs district, which approved the brand’s application to cancel its health permit for frontier ports. “Louis Vuitton is focusing on quality over quantity in its store network to elevate consumer experience,” Lim said. “This caters to China’s shifting luxury consumption trend, where premium pricing is increasingly justified by immersive brand experiences and high-touch VIP services.” The brand is scaling up its flagship stores in top-tier cities like Beijing and Shanghai. Its new stand-alone store in Beijing’s Taikoo Li Sanlitun North opened in December, after it launched “The Louis”, a boat-themed conceptual landmark, at Shanghai’s HKRI Taikoo Hui in June 2025. China’s personal luxury goods market was expected to see modest growth in 2026, despite ongoing volatility and uncertainty, according to a report earlier this year by consultancy Bain & Company.

title: ‘I hate Americans, all of them’: Malaysian politician’s anti-US rant draws backlash
description: Former PM Mahathir Mohamad’s son Mukhriz defended his anti-US rant, claiming ordinary citizens share blame for Washington’s foreign policy.
content: Malaysian politician Mukhriz Mahathir has triggered a social media storm after declaring in a video that he “hates Americans, all of them”, over Washington’s support for Israel – echoing the fierce anti-US rhetoric long associated with his father, former prime minister Mahathir Mohamad. “I hate Americans. I despise Israelis, but I hate Americans, all of them,” Mukhriz said in the video, posted on Saturday. “It matters not if they’re Republican or Democrat, pro-Israel or pro-Palestine. None of it matters to me,” he said, arguing that ordinary Americans should also share responsibility for the actions of leaders elected in their name. Malaysia, a Muslim-majority nation, has long been one of Southeast Asia’s staunchest backers of the Palestinian cause and does not recognise Israel as a state. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government has repeatedly condemned Israel’s conduct in Gaza, a stance that has increasingly put Kuala Lumpur at odds with Washington over Malaysia’s refusal to admit Israeli citizens. Last month, the US State Department summoned Malaysia’s ambassador to explain the policy. Mukhriz drew a distinction between his own rhetoric and what he characterised as US-backed violence. My hatred is backed by nothing but words Mukhriz Mahathir, Malaysian politician “American hatred is backed by bombs, drones and vetoes. My hatred is backed by nothing but words,” he said. “Theirs kills. Mine does not.” He accused Washington of arming what he called a genocide in Gaza and shielding Israel from accountability, defending his remarks as an exercise of free speech. “My loathing breaks no law. It is my right, my speech,” he said. “But American loathing of Palestinians? That breaks bones, burns tents, ends bloodlines.” The video had been watched more than 350,000 times as of Monday afternoon, drawing some 9,000 reactions and dividing commenters. “I respect your stance, sir. And I share almost the same,” one user wrote. Others objected to Mukhriz assigning collective culpability to an entire nationality. “Criticising a government or its policies is one thing, but saying you hate all Americans is spreading hatred towards an entire people based on nationality,” another user wrote, urging Mukhriz to use his position to promote understanding rather than hatred. “Hate is a very heavy word and it is misplaced here,” a third user said. “Condemning an entire nation of millions of diverse people because of the actions of their government is wrong.” Mukhriz, 61, is a former two-term chief minister of the northern state of Kedah and president of the Malay nationalist Pejuang party. He is also the son of Mahathir, Malaysia’s longest-serving prime minister, whose decades in national politics were marked by fierce criticism of US and Western foreign policy, particularly over Israel, Palestine and the invasion of Iraq. Mahathir once called former US president George W. Bush’s administration a “rogue regime” and accused Washington of terrorising Iraqi civilians. In his 2003 address to an Islamic summit, he said Jews “rule the world by proxy”, attracting international condemnation. Mukhriz himself studied in the United States, graduating from Boston University with a degree in marketing before entering business and later politics. His remarks come as the US-backed ceasefire in Gaza, in place since October 2025, faces renewed strain. Israeli air strikes on Sunday killed at least two Palestinians, including a four-year-old boy, Palestinian health officials told Reuters. More than 1,280 Palestinians and four Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire took effect, Reuters reported. Israel rejects accusations that its campaign amounts to genocide and says its military operations are aimed at Hamas – the Palestinian militant group, designated a terrorist organisation by the US, which led the October 7, 2023 attacks on Israel. The US embassy in Malaysia has been asked for comment on Mukriz’s remarks.

title: Hong Kong mall traffic boosted by Beyblade battles
description: Shopping centres leverage gaming trend to attract crowds and increase sales.
content:
The clanking sound of rotating metal tops, accompanied by cheers, groans of disappointment and calls of “three, two, one … Go shoot!” resonates throughout a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.
Inside stores at Tuen Mun Town Plaza, youngsters and teenagers lean over compact plastic battlefields, launching their tops into the “Beystadiums” for intense matchups in which the one that spins the longest wins.
The toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and elsewhere in Asia early this year, and gatherings are attracting crowds of local players eager to put their models to the test.
Spotting the economic potential behind the hobby, shopping centre operators across Hong Kong are converting open spaces into free battle zones to drive up foot traffic and sales.
Tuen Mun Town Plaza went a step further by scaling up the concept into a mall-wide strategy ahead of a major Beyblade tournament in August, encouraging shop operators to take part in the game and offer discounts to shoppers who present their tops.
“The strategy is about how a tenant can engage with customers through a shared interest, instead of directly selling to them,” said Bella Chhoa Peck-lim, chief commercial officer of Sino Group, which owns the plaza.
What appeared to be a desperate measure by Hong Kong’s retail and catering sectors – still struggling with the trend of residents heading to mainland China for cheaper shopping and dining options – turned into an initial success.
Chhoa said the shopping centre had witnessed a “noticeable” 20 per cent surge in holiday foot traffic following the promotion, and a 10 to 15 per cent rise in weekday attendance.
At Hanamaruken, a ramen shop inside the plaza, co-founder Jelly Tong said her team upgraded the basic Beyblade provided by the landlord to a high-performance model to better compete with visiting players after recognising the game’s potential to boost business.
“Word then spread in their Beyblade chat groups that our store had an exceptionally strong set-up, and some kids ended up bringing six or seven friends over to challenge us,” Tong said. “Afterwards, they stayed here to eat and discuss our custom gear.”
Among dozens of enthusiasts gathered at the shopping complex were 24-year-old warehouse worker Liu Chun-yin and his friend.
“Sometimes I show my spinning top at the nearby ice cream shop here to get special offers or battle against the staff at the tea shop to win a discount,” Liu said.
His friend, a recent Beyblade convert, recalled a visit during which he stayed at the venue from 2pm until 9pm, spending seven hours straight battling fellow players and purchasing food and drinks between matches.
At the D-Park residential and shopping complex in Tsuen Wan, dedicated free-play zones equipped with rows of desks have also drawn parents with young children alongside seasoned adult hobbyists.
Andy Yip, a 34-year-old civil servant from Kowloon East, made a trip to Tsuen Wan with his 11-year-old son and other family members, knowing there would be players at the venue.
“Before my son picked up the hobby, we spent most of our weekends in mainland China, but now we stay in Hong Kong more to accompany him, as he wants to play Beyblade with others,” he said.
Yip added that these outings were typically paired with dining and retail shopping, noting that he typically spent HK$1,000 (US$128) on dinner after his son played at D-Park, while their family members browsed at nearby shops during matches.
At the Pioneer Centre shopping centre in Prince Edward, management has introduced a few Beyblade stadiums to attract a steady stream of parents and children, accompanied by a spend-to-draw promotion offering exclusive models of the tops as prizes.
Eric Cheng, senior leasing manager at the mall, said the set-up and promotion in August had driven a 5 to 10 per cent increase in foot traffic compared with the same period last year, while sales at electronic goods and food and beverage businesses had jumped by 15 and 20 per cent, respectively.
But according to one economist, the Beyblade trend is a temporary solution and not a cure-all for the city’s broader retail sector challenges.
Professor Terence Chong Tai-leung, executive director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance, said shopping centres were ideal venues for Beyblade matches, which required space, and operators could set up play zones at a low cost.
But he stressed that such initiatives were not enough to counter broader macroeconomic headwinds or the flow of residents across the border, noting that price remained the most significant factor driving consumer behaviour.

title: CATL debuts e-commerce platform for direct sales to small buyers, as competition sharpens
description: The platform allows for direct online sales to smaller energy storage buyers.
content: China’s battery king Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) is enabling direct sales to smaller energy storage system makers via its own e-commerce platform, as competition with its domestic peers intensifies. The platform, officially launched on Friday, would offer orders as small as three boxes of its energy storage products, according to a social media post by the firm. CATL is currently the world’s largest producer of lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. The platform, which allows small buyers to skip distributors, was being used by over 1,800 energy storage companies acquired during beta testing, the firm said in the post. The battery giant also said that the small orders would qualify for a five-year quality warranty, the same as it provides for its larger purchasers, and that the delivery period would be within three to five days. While energy storage continues to expand amid the global energy shock and an investment frenzy of artificial intelligence data centres, CATL was facing fiercer competition of late, said Lucas Zhang Liutong, director of Hong Kong-based consultancy WaterRock Energy Economics. “[The e-commerce platform] is probably also to address the potential demand in distributed solar, to bundle with battery energy storage systems, from the residential and small commercial users,” said Zhang, as the spread of price hours driven by China’s power market reform was expected to increase the needs from smaller users. Though the orders via the platform might be small, CATL could command a slightly better price due to its brand reputation, Zhang added. Fujian province-based CATL, which is known for its higher-than-average pricing and bargaining power due to its product quality, has been focusing on large-volume energy storage orders across the globe. However, CATL’s global market share in energy storage-use lithium-ion batteries slid to 27.1 per cent for the first half of the year, down from 30 per cent in 2025 and 38 per cent in 2024, data from Seoul-based SNE Research showed. Its domestic peers like Hithium and EVE Energy were catching up, while a megadeal in the Middle East was ultimately won by BYD and Sungrow Power Supply. Meanwhile, demand for household battery energy storage is rising, a bright spot for CATL after claiming the global crown in grid and commercial segments. The household market saw battery shipments surge 128 per cent year on year during the first half, the fastest among the three segments of grid, commercial and household, according to SNE. In the same period, CATL’s net profit rose 42 per cent year on year to 43.28 billion yuan (US$6.43 billion), but the gross profit margins of EV battery and energy storage – the two largest revenue contributors – both narrowed to 20.63 per cent and 23.96 per cent respectively, levels that were not seen for CATL since 2023.
