title: 78% of low-income elderly Hongkongers report heat-related distress, survey finds
description: Most respondents reported heat-related discomfort, while many lacked awareness of heatstroke risks and available government support.
content: Nearly 80 per cent of low-income elderly people surveyed in Hong Kong reported physical or mental distress during periods of extreme heat, prompting calls for stronger government support and heat-prevention measures. Data from the Department of Health cited by Greenpeace identified elderly people as the city’s demographic most at risk from extreme temperatures. The number of hospital discharges and deaths related to heatstroke among people aged 65 or above rose 16-fold between 2015 and 2024, from four to 68 – the sharpest increase among all age groups. The city has been hit by sweltering weather this summer, with temperatures forecast to reach 33 degrees Celsius (91 Fahrenheit) on Friday. Earlier this month, Hong Kong recorded a maximum temperature of 36.9 degrees, the highest since records began in 1884. For its study released Monday, Greenpeace interviewed 127 residents aged 65 or above in June and July across seven districts with rapidly ageing populations, including Kwai Tsing, Wong Tai Sin and Kowloon City. More than half lived in public housing, while 35 per cent lived in inadequate housing. About 78 per cent of respondents said they had experienced at least one form of physical discomfort because of high temperatures, including dizziness, headaches, vomiting, difficulty breathing and a racing heartbeat. Some also reported mood disturbances and poorer sleep quality. A total of 5.5 per cent said they had been hospitalised for a heat-related illness in the previous year. The survey also found that many elderly people lacked awareness of heat-prevention measures. About 71 per cent believed that staying indoors eliminated the risk of heatstroke, while 35 per cent said they never or rarely turned on their air conditioning during extreme heat, mainly because they wanted to avoid high electricity costs. Greenpeace campaigner Prudence Yeung said older people were often less sensitive to heat because of age-related declines in physiological function. Chronic illnesses also made them particularly vulnerable during periods of extreme weather, she added. “The government’s failure to take action to identify the health risks facing elderly people – and the additional medical costs they may incur – is a policy blind spot,” Yeung said. Although protocols for supporting residents during cold weather – including the distribution of supplies, check-in calls and home visits – were already in place, about 80 per cent of respondents said they had not received heat-related community services, such as heat-safety education or cooling supplies, in the previous two years. The survey also highlighted shortcomings in temporary heat shelters set up under the very hot weather warning. As many as 95 per cent of respondents said they never or rarely used the shelters, with many saying they lived too far away or were unaware that the facilities existed. Nearly 30 per cent said they were unclear about the help available from the government. Yeung urged the Social Welfare Department to coordinate with social welfare agencies and conduct home visits to elderly people during periods of extreme heat, particularly those living alone. She also called for resources to be allocated for the distribution of cooling supplies and electricity subsidies. She urged the government to establish a comprehensive, “people-centred” heat-action plan that would trigger swift, cross-departmental measures and take the lead in providing community support during periods of extreme heat.

title: Professor who said Malays could fly sacked by Malaysian university
description: Solehah Yaacob went viral with her pseudo-history claims. She is fighting against her dismissal.
content: A Malaysian Islamic university has formally distanced itself from an academic whose viral claims about ancient Malay civilisation – including that Malays could fly and taught the Chinese “flying kung fu” – have drawn ridicule from historians. In a statement on Sunday, the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) said Solehah Yaacob, a former linguistics professor, had been terminated from academic service on April 27 and was no longer entitled to claim any affiliation with the institution. The university’s Office for Communication, Advocacy and Promotion said Solehah was now barred from using any official title, position or association with IIUM. “She is no longer a professor nor entitled to claim any association with the university,” it said. “IIUM hopes that this clarification will help avoid any misunderstanding and uphold the integrity and academic standing of the university.” Solehah is challenging her termination before Malaysia’s Industrial Court and has accused the university of unprofessionalism. She told local news outlet Free Malaysia Today that the Higher Education Ministry had awarded her a Malaysia Research Assessment commendation the day before her dismissal. “I was dismissed within 24 hours and was not allowed to appeal,” she was quoted as saying. “IIUM wanted to pay me the equivalent of six months, but I refused.” Solehah stirred controversy last year when she claimed ancient Malays could fly and had taught the Chinese the art of “flying kung fu”. A month later, she claimed ancient Romans had learned shipbuilding techniques from Malay seafarers, and earlier this month suggested that Kedah’s iron ore wealth might have originated from meteor showers, with Gunung Jerai in Kedah among sites she said had been hit by meteorites. Her other disputed claims include that Khadijah, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad, had links to the Malay world. She has also criticised early Malay societies for their Hindu-Buddhist influences and received backlash for a 2018 academic article that cited a satirical piece from The Onion as a source. Historians and academics have repeatedly called her assertions illogical and damaging to historical understanding. James Chin, a scholar of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania, said Solehah’s statements had won a large following among the Malay community, noting that she had gone on to lead paid boat-cruise tours built around her theories. On June 24, Solehah promoted herself as a speaker for the “Islamic Civilisation Voyage 3.0”, a four-day, three-night cruise from Port Klang to Phuket running from November 30 to December 3. Her “The Mystery of the Roman Ship Deception” speech is set to take place aboard the Adora Mediterranea as part of a cruise advertised as halal and casino-free. “These cruises are specifically designed to demonstrate and validate her research findings by taking passengers to the very locations that support her claims. I’m not joking,” Chin said in a statement on August 12. Chin supported IIUM’s decision to terminate Solehah’s services given the reputational damage caused by the controversy and her stated intention to take legal action against the university. For a long time, there was a lot of nonsense going on in Malaysian universities James Chin, Malaysian academic He said Solehah had made a number of similar claims in recent years without apparent consequence until the issue blew up on social media. “It is remarkable that IIUM took action from the backlash on social media,” Chin told This Week in Asia, comparing some of her statements to the style of pseudo-history espoused by controversial US television show Ancient Aliens. Chin also noted that Solehah had built a parallel career outside the university, charging around US$200 for seminars in addition to appearing on halal cruises. This marked the second time in a little over a week that IIUM made headlines, after it cancelled a lecture involving Abdul Razak Baginda, a former adviser to Najib Razak who was found liable by a court over the death of Altantuya Shaariibuu, a Mongolian woman murdered in Malaysia in 2006. “Universities are accountable for what they do because, for a long time, there was a lot of nonsense going on in Malaysian universities, with academics talking about a lot of crazy stuff,” Chin said.

title: Meet Michael Kelly, who plays Byron in Taylor Sheridan’s Lioness
description: Best known for his four-time Emmy-nominated role in House of Cards, the actor now plays a CIA executive alongside Zoe Saldaña and Nicole Kidman.
content: The third season of Lioness is available on Paramount+, with episodes releasing every Sunday until September 20. At present, the season boasts an 85 per cent rating on Rotten Tomatoes. Created by Oscar-nominated screenwriter Taylor Sheridan, the highly anticipated series features a star-studded cast including Zoe Saldaña, Nicole Kidman and Morgan Freeman. Among these established actors is four-time Emmy nominee Michael Kelly, 57, who plays CIA deputy director for operations Byron Westfield in the spy thriller. Kelly has said his character is quite different from who he is in real life. “I always play these guys who never smile. And I never stop smiling myself. So it’s kind of funny,” he told V13 Media. “For me, it’s a change.” In a recent interview with ScreenRant, Kelly praised Sheridan, calling him a “stand-alone talent”. Kelly added that he is eager to act in any of Sheridan’s projects: “There’s nobody who’s doing or has ever done what he’s doing. It’s incredible what he does. And he’s just one of the smartest dudes you’ll ever meet.” So, who is Michael Kelly, who has played various intelligence and law enforcement agents in his acting career? Here’s what we know. What are Michael Kelly’s credits? Michael Kelly was born on May 22, 1969. According to lifestyle publication Bedford and New Canaan Magazine, he was raised in Lawrenceville, Georgia, where he attended public school and self-identified as the “class clown”. He is the oldest of four siblings. Kelly began working at age 14 for a family friend who was a builder – an experience he credits with shaping his work ethic. He later attended Coastal Carolina University, where he initially considered becoming a lawyer, and his adviser suggested that an acting class might help him on that path. He ended up loving performing, and his professor told him that he had “something special”. In 1992, Kelly became the first student to graduate from Coastal Carolina with a performing arts degree. “To be a good actor you have to be willing to make a total a** of yourself, and be willing to fail,” Kelly told Bedford and New Canaan Magazine. “I was good at both of those things.” How did Michael Kelly break into acting? After graduating, Kelly spent a year working at a children’s theatre tour group. His mother subsequently connected him with a Hollywood producer, who advised him to move to Los Angeles or New York. Kelly relocated to New York City, living with friends and relatives while auditioning. His screen debut came in 1994, playing a gym manager in an episode of Lifestories: Families in Crisis. While booking early minor roles, Kelly took on various side hustles, including playing guitar in a band, working as a waiter and bike messenger, and picking up shifts at a consignment shop, in catering, and in construction. “I did absolutely everything I could, and I believe my work ethic is the biggest factor in why I’ve succeeded,” he told the lifestyle magazine. In his twenties, Kelly refined his craft at the Actors Studio, where Tony Award-winning director Arthur Penn mentored him. His persistence paid off. Kelly has since built an extensive résumé across film and television, starring in the Amazon Prime Video series Jack Ryan and feature films Dawn of the Dead and Now You See Me, frequently playing detectives and agents. He earned four Emmy Award nominations for his role as Doug Stamper in Netflix’s political drama House of Cards. Who is Michael Kelly married to? Kelly married Karyn Mendel in December 2005 and they share two children, daughter Franke and son Clinton. The family lives in the town of Bedford in New York. “As proud as I am to have accomplished many of the goals I’ve set for myself in my career, the roles that define me and that I’m most proud of are being husband to my wonderful wife Karyn and father to the two most amazing kids ever,” Kelly said in his profile with Bedford and New Canaan Magazine. While Kelly keeps his family life largely out of the spotlight, his children have previously joined him on set; Franke and Clinton appeared as Doug Stamper’s niece and nephew in an episode of House of Cards.

title: Why Indian intelligence-gathering against China could lead to miscalculation
description: New Delhi is more likely to take ‘unilateral countermeasures’ as routine activities are increasingly framed as threats, researcher says.
content: Routine Chinese activities are increasingly being framed as threats by Indian intelligence agencies, raising the risk of New Delhi miscalculating and taking “unilateral countermeasures” against Beijing, a Chinese academic has warned. India has stepped up intelligence-gathering as ties with neighbouring China turned sour in recent years, according to Zhao Ruoxi, a researcher with the Macau University of Science and Technology. Zhao made the remarks in a paper analysing India’s intelligence operations focused on China from 2020 to 2026. It was published on July 31 in the Chinese-language Journal of Intelligence, run by the Shaanxi Institute of Science and Technology Information. According to Zhao, China’s political and economic footprint in South Asia, its focus on emerging technologies, and naval activities in the Indian Ocean have all come under more scrutiny from India since a border clash in 2020. That confrontation in the Galwan Valley killed 20 Indian and four Chinese troops, plunging relations between the two nations to a historic low. Zhao said India had broadened its intelligence-gathering toolkit in recent years, using space-based reconnaissance, drone surveillance and cyber intelligence to build a multi-agency network against China. India also teamed up with the United States and Middle Eastern countries so that it could track Chinese far-seas naval operations and apply informational pressure on Beijing’s maritime energy supply routes, Zhao wrote in the paper. But she said India’s heavy reliance on foreign data was a “structural weakness” that meant its assessments of China were vulnerable to third-party strategic agendas. Zhao noted that bilateral ties between Beijing and New Delhi began to improve in late 2024, but India’s enhanced intelligence operations targeting China had continued. After agreeing to resume border patrols in 2024, the two countries have worked to mend ties. Direct flights resumed after a five-year halt, Beijing allowed Indian pilgrims to return to the Tibet autonomous region, and India restarted issuing visas for Chinese tourists. Last year, in another sign of thawing ties, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited China for the first time in seven years. During talks with Modi in Tianjin, Chinese President Xi Jinping said border issues should not define the two countries’ relationship. Following the June reopening of the Lipulekh Pass – a move widely viewed as a goodwill gesture by Beijing – the two countries resumed trade through two additional Himalayan passes, Nathu La and Shipki La, in August. In the paper, Zhao said India was expected to increase technical surveillance of the border, which would force China to strengthen its information security. She also warned that Beijing’s diplomatic activities with its South Asian neighbours – particularly efforts to build trust in the region and push forward projects under the Belt and Road Initiative – would face “systemic disruption” from New Delhi. According to Zhao, with more Indian intelligence activities directed at China there was a heightened risk of miscalculation, with routine Chinese activities increasingly framed as threats. “Consequently, the likelihood of triggering unilateral countermeasures rises,” she concluded. Zhao said China should try to counter this pressure by improving its strategic messaging and its communication with South Asian and Indian Ocean littoral countries.

title: Typhoon signal in Hong Kong unlikely in next 2 days but expect unsettled weather
description: Observatory revises earlier prediction that typhoon signal could be issued on Tuesday or Wednesday, but residents can still expect thunderstorms.
content: The likelihood that Hong Kong’s weather forecaster will issue a typhoon signal in the next two days is “relatively low”, although multiple tropical cyclones are set to bring unsettled weather to the city later this week. The Observatory said at noon on Monday that Tropical Storm Narra was expected to skirt the coast of the Leizhou Peninsula in western Guangdong province in the coming days while “maintaining some distance from Hong Kong”. “Unless Narra further edges closer to the vicinity of the Pearl River Delta, the chance of issuing a tropical cyclone warning signal is relatively low,” it said, revising its earlier prediction on Sunday that it could issue a typhoon signal on Tuesday or Wednesday as Narra approached the Guangdong coast. Narra, a name provided by the Philippines, means Burmese rosewood. On Monday, the Observatory said Hong Kong could expect showers and squally thunderstorms in the middle of the week under the influence of a southerly airstream, with occasionally strong winds offshore and on high ground. Another cyclone located near Taiwan on Monday, Tropical Depression Gaenari – named after a type of native Korean flowering bush – had a relatively weak intensity and small circulation. “Its direct threat to Hong Kong is not high. Gaenari is expected to dissipate gradually in the vicinity of the Taiwan Strait [on Monday],” the forecaster said. It added that the weather in Hong Kong in the latter part of this week would be hot, as a third cyclone, Super Typhoon Saudel, edged closer to eastern China. “Under the influence of [Saudel’s] outer subsiding air, the weather will become very hot over southern China in the latter part of this week, but showers will also be triggered by high temperatures,” the Observatory said. “With Saudel moving further inland, showers will increase over the coast of Guangdong early next week.” Saudel is a name provided by the Federated States of Micronesia and refers to the guards of the legendary ruler of the country’s Pohnpei Island.

title: East African troops prepare for Gaza peacekeeping role in US-backed plan
description: Delegations from Burundi and Uganda visited Israel to discuss joining Donald Trump’s International Stabilisation Force.
content: Military officials from Uganda and Burundi visited Israel last week to discuss deploying troops to Gaza as part of an international security force envisioned by US President Donald Trump’s “Board of Peace” for the fragile ceasefire, according to officials. An official with the board said that Ugandan officials had joined a Burundian military delegation and that Uganda was finalising details of its participation after its parliament approved the troop contribution this month. Nothing has been finalised with Burundi, but the official said they looked forward to starting the process. “We shared significant knowledge with one another, and the Burundi representatives expressed interest in our mission,” the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss talks with potential troop-contributing countries ahead of any agreement. A Burundian military official said that three other senior military officers led the delegation to Israel and that Burundi appeared intent on joining. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media. It was not clear what Uganda or Burundi might be offering or what they might receive in return. Neither military responded to requests for comment. If Burundi moves ahead, the African nations would be the latest to join the international force for Gaza after Morocco, Kosovo, Kazakhstan and Albania made commitments. Uganda has committed around 1,200 personnel and Morocco has committed up to 500. Kosovo, Kazakhstan and Albania in total have committed around 80. Indonesia earlier said it was preparing to send 8,000 troops – by far the largest commitment – but put that on hold after the US and Israel attacked Iran. The 20,000-strong force would be led by US Major General Jasper Jeffers. Troops committed remain far short of that goal. Last month, Trump announced a deal for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its forces from Gaza. According to the deal, the International Stabilisation Force would be deployed to areas of the Palestinian territory administered by an incoming technocratic committee and Israeli forces would withdraw. The force would help monitor the ceasefire, train Palestinian police and secure the delivery of aid, among other tasks. The ceasefire that took effect in Gaza last October has stalled due to disagreements regarding Israel’s withdrawal from the strip and Hamas’ disarmament. A US delegation met for hours earlier this month with the Hamas leader and then with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to press them forward. Hamas has agreed to the new US deal. Netanyahu has rejected it, saying Israel would not withdraw from any of the roughly 60 per cent of the territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas had been completely disarmed. Even after Netanyahu’s meeting with the US team, which included negotiator Jared Kushner, officials offered no concrete commitment by Israel. Paul D. Williams, director of the security policy studies programme at George Washington University, said Uganda and Burundi had gained considerable peacekeeping experience through long-term deployments in Somalia as part of an African Union force resisting the al-Qaeda-linked al-Shabab extremist group. Their countries’ leaderships had “shown they are willing to tolerate high numbers of casualties without withdrawing”, he said. Williams added that, with the mission in Somalia winding down, both countries would be searching for ways to accrue financial and material support for their militaries: “Deploying to Gaza with US support is one way to do that.” A Ugandan military officer with knowledge of the coming deployment said troops were being selected to go to Gaza. The officer spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.

title: Beijing warns of ‘policy addiction’, signalling preference for targeted stimulus
description: With an eye on long-term stability, People’s Daily says officials have tools to respond amid weak demand, property risks and local-government debt.
content: In its third consecutive commentary defending China’s economic resilience, Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily emphasised that Beijing was prioritising targeted measures over aggressive stimulus to avoid a potential over-reliance on policy support, while also reiterating confidence in reaching the nation’s economic targets for the year. “China has not taken the path of overrelying on strong policy stimulus,” the piece said. Instead, the commentary added, targeted interventions would function like “acupressure” to address specific vulnerabilities and avoid creating a “policy addiction”. The commentary was published on Monday under the pen name “Zhong Caiwen”, a byline widely believed to be associated with the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission, a key economic decision-making body headed by President Xi Jinping. At the same time, the article noted that China’s macroeconomic policy toolkit remained ample, with substantial room for countercyclical adjustment, allowing Beijing to roll out additional measures as conditions evolve and meet its annual targets. The piece came as China faces prolonged headwinds such as weak domestic demand, a property downturn and persistent geopolitical tensions, which weighed on second-quarter growth. Despite the party’s Politburo pledging stronger fiscal support during its July meeting, data for the month showed key indicators such as retail sales and fixed-asset investment weakening, prompting analyst calls for additional policy stimulus to stave off downside risks. In highlighting the resilience of China’s economy, the commentary pointed to the ability to absorb external shocks and adjust to domestic risks. It said early investment in a new-energy system and oil reserves, along with diversified sourcing, had helped maintain energy supplies despite the US-Israel war on Iran, which has sent oil prices higher. Chinese exports, meanwhile, remained resilient as competitive products and technological advances in areas from electric vehicles and batteries to artificial intelligence and robotics won buyers in more markets amid rising trade tensions and other restrictions. Domestically, the article said efforts to address long-standing risks in local government debt, property and smaller financial institutions had imposed some short-term costs on growth, but argued that these were necessary to secure longer-term economic and social stability. The commentary acknowledged that the imbalance between strong supply and weak demand remained pronounced, particularly as China faces significant pressure to stabilise declining investment. However, it stressed that Beijing’s investment policy was focused on quality and overall benefits rather than speed. It was the third commentary published under the same byline in People’s Daily in as many days, with previous pieces saying domestic risks, such as those linked to property and local government debt, were being contained, while China continued to provide greater stability to the global economy. “The risks and hidden dangers in the economic field are being resolved and contained in an orderly manner,” Saturday’s commentary said. Sunday’s piece then took aim at the “China shock 2.0” narrative, instead describing China as “a stabilising anchor for global industrial and supply chains” that supported the smooth functioning of the global economy. Late last year, an eight-part op-ed series in People’s Daily under the same byline was published before the fourth plenary session of the party’s Central Committee, describing the Chinese economy as an “unsinkable economic aircraft carrier”.

title: Hong Kong urged to adopt trait-based dog tiers, DNA checks after attacks
description: Proposal calls for risk tiers, certified handlers, muzzles or possible confiscation of highest-risk animals as authorities review fighting-dog rules.
content: Hong Kong should introduce a tiered risk framework and carry out DNA testing and physical checks to identify dogs with aggressive traits, a veterinarian and a lawmaker have said after a woman and two pets were mauled within a week. Monday’s calls for policy change came after the woman, 33, was found dead in Ping Yeung Tsuen last week. Hours before her body was discovered, she had been attacked at a dog training centre by a canine suspected of being a mixed-breed fighting dog. Preliminary inspections by authorities revealed the dog shared genetic traits with the pit bull terrier, a banned fighting breed in the city. Yet, the dog’s microchip indicated it was a mongrel. The incident sparked widespread concern about the effectiveness of the city’s dog registration system relying on self-declaration by owners, with residents questioning whether animals with aggressive traits could be identified. Veterinarian Lai Cheong-sang said Hong Kong should replace its breed-specific categorisation system with a trait-based, tiered system to classify dogs’ danger levels and assign corresponding control measures. “If a dog is suspected of having the potential to cause danger after a risk assessment, it can be required to undergo mandatory training, be leashed or otherwise constrained, and receive regular assessments,” he said on a radio show. He also called for a certification system for people who keep or train high-risk breeds. More dangerous dogs should be muzzled and leashed by certified handlers, with the government empowered to confiscate animals posing the highest risk, he said, adding that such breeds should not be imported, bred or sold. In a separate incident in Yuen Long last week, an unleashed 60kg (132lbs) mastiff-type dog mauled two smaller dogs to death in the town centre. The incidents have prompted authorities to review the definition of fighting dogs and other regulations to safeguard public safety. Under Hong Kong law, four types of dogs – pit bull terrier, dogo Argentino, Japanese Tosa and fila Brasileiro – and their crossbreeds are classified as fighting dogs, whose importation and breeding are banned in the city. Existing fighting dogs must be neutered, leashed and muzzled. They are also required to wear a special collar in public places. Under the Dangerous Dogs Regulation, residents can legally possess existing fighting dogs as long as they can produce a valid veterinary certificate certifying that the animal has been neutered, with violators facing a HK$50,000 fine and six months’ imprisonment. Lai said that while Hong Kong required owners to microchip and get a licence for their dogs when they were three to five months old, it was difficult for vets to determine whether a puppy possessed ancestry traits of a specific breed at that stage. Licensing can be completed at the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) and Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals premises, as well as authorised private veterinary clinics. Lai added that the department could require vets to conduct DNA tests for all mongrels, or set standards for physical features to determine their danger levels, before deciding on management measures for a particular dog. Lau Yun-yu, chairman of the Hong Kong Society for Pet Nutrition, said that breed alone did not determine whether a dog would become aggressive. “Body size itself is not the primary determinant of aggression,” he said. “However, when aggression does occur, the difference in size and bite force means that injuries caused by large dogs are typically far more severe.” Bowie Leung, spokeswoman for the Caucasian Ovcharka and Tibetan Mastiff Club Hong Kong, said a dog’s behaviour depended on factors including genetics, bloodline, breeding and whether it had been mixed with other breeds. “You cannot generalise and say all dogs of one breed are aggressive, or all are gentle,” she added. “You have to look at the genes, the bloodline, the breeding, and what the dog has been mixed with.” Appearing on the same radio show, Rebecca Chan Hoi-yan, chairwoman of the Legislative Council’s food safety and environmental hygiene panel, noted that the current classification system under the dog licensing regime relied on owners’ declarations and basic observations. She added that while many residents had called for mandatory DNA tests for all mongrels during licensing, doing so might discourage people from adopting stray dogs. Chan instead suggested dynamic risk assessments for dogs as they matured. “Fighting dogs’ features will emerge as they grow up … if in doubt, the owners can then take them for DNA tests,” she said. Asked whether the list of fighting dogs should be expanded, Chan said she welcomed any discussions between the government and the legislature, but cautioned against making it too broad. “I believe the current regulations on the four types of dogs and their crossbreeds have been effective. The problem is that there is still smuggling and illegal breeding,” she said. Dogs with a history of repeatedly attacking, injuring or killing people and other domestic animals can be classified as “known dangerous dogs” by the court and are subject to similar regulations. According to the AFCD, currently 29 fighting dogs with valid licences and 18 “known dangerous dogs” are registered in Hong Kong. Some jurisdictions have developed established physical and behavioural standards for determining whether a dog belongs to a restricted breed. The United Kingdom, other than the four types of fighting dogs prohibited in Hong Kong, also banned the ownership, breeding, sale and exchange, and advertising for sale of the XL bully in stages in 2024. Ownership is only permitted with an exemption certificate issued by the government, and violators face unlimited fines and jail terms of up to six months. The UK regulations clearly state that the determination of a dog’s type does not lie in its breed, but its physical and behavioural characteristics. Detailed guides for confirming each type of dog, ranging from its height and weight to the shape of its skull, teeth and muscles, and so on, were produced to help police and owners identify whether they fell under a specific type. Applications for exemption certificates were only open for months after a breed was declared banned. Owners who found themselves possessing dangerous dogs without exemption certificates were told to contact police. Police would bring the matter before a magistrate, and the court could hand down a destruction order which would not be executed if the owner complied with conditions set out in the order and the animal did not constitute a threat to public safety. Similarly, in the Australian state of Victoria, the government has gazetted physical and behavioural standards for restricted breeds. Owners of such dogs have to declare whether the animals are from a restricted breed when registering them with the local government, and the authorities have the discretion to reject applications. Failing to provide accurate information about whether a dog is a restricted breed may lead to a fine of A$2,091 (US$1,500). Such dogs cannot be bred, sold or given away, and have to be securely kept in the owners’ premises, which should be labelled with warning signs. They should be muzzled and leashed when outside the owners’ places. Violations of such provisions may result in fines and imprisonment. Additional reporting by Veronica Qi

title: New Zealand plans social media ban for under-16s backed by big fines
description: Wellington is proposing fines of up to 10 per cent of global turnover for tech firms, but a coalition partner has vowed to block the measure.
content: New ⁠Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said on Monday his party would introduce a bill in parliament that seeks to ban children under 16 from using social media, proposing fines of up to 10 per cent of a ‌platform’s global revenue for non-compliance. The bill would require social media platforms to take reasonable steps to verify users’ ages, including by using existing account information, facial technology and digital identity documents. “We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children,” Luxon said in a statement. “Social media is ⁠exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to ‌deal with and it’s affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education.” It was not immediately clear if the bill would garner sufficient ‌support to pass through parliament, with one of Luxon’s coalition partners, the ⁠New Zealand First ⁠party, saying it would not support it. “We have been concerned with the proposed legislation and the direction ‌and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country,” New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, who ‌is also ‌the country’s foreign minister, said in a post on social media. In December, Australia became ‌the world’s first country to ban social media for children under 16, blocking ⁠them from platforms including TikTok, Alphabet’s YouTube and Meta’s Instagram and Facebook. That legislation had been a “colossal ⁠failure”, Peters said, adding that keeping children off social media should be the responsibility of parents. “I won’t pretend that it will be simple or ‌that it will be perfect,” ‌Luxon said at an event. “We won’t get every single child off social media. Some will always find ways around it, but frankly, it’s just way too important not to at least try.”

title: John Lee urges start-ups to seize opportunities through ‘golden gateway’ of Hong Kong
description: City leader makes familiar pitch to attendees at summit, citing Hong Kong’s ability to help global firms enter mainland China and vice versa.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has called on scientists, leading enterprises and investment institutions from around the world to seize opportunities in the city, describing it as a “golden gateway” for overseas companies to enter the mainland Chinese market and mainland unicorn firms to expand globally. Speaking at the first Global Unicorn Summit on Monday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu pointed to the city’s unique advantages as a “superconnector” and a “super value-adder” between the mainland and the world. “On the journey of innovation and entrepreneurship, Hong Kong not only serves as a testing ground for technological breakthroughs, but it will also become an accelerator for the transformation of research outcomes and a new world for global expansion,” he said at the opening of the summit at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. Lee highlighted Hong Kong’s strengths, including its world-leading capital market, common-law system, low-tax business environment, global trade network and pool of top-tier international professional talent. He said these advantages made Hong Kong the premier springboard for mainland start-ups and unicorns – companies valued at more than US$1 billion – to enter international markets and build global supply chains. They also made the city the primary hub for top-tier overseas innovation and technology (I&T) companies to tap into the mainland market, he added. Lee said a record high of more than 11,000 mainland and overseas companies and over 5,200 start-ups were operating in Hong Kong as of last year. The city has also incubated 20 unicorns over the past decade. Lee said the development of the Greater Bay Area would draw on Hong Kong’s high-calibre talent and research strengths, together with the robust advanced manufacturing base in mainland cities, providing a solid foundation for I&T growth. The city leader also reiterated the government’s efforts to develop the sector by creating competitive I&T zones such as the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone and the San Tin Technopole in the Northern Metropolis. Under China’s 15th five-year plan, which guides national development from 2026 to 2030, Hong Kong is tasked with becoming a global innovation and talent hub, with the I&T sector expected to drive the city’s economic growth. Artificial intelligence and research transformation are among the priorities of Hong Kong’s own inaugural five-year blueprint, which the government plans to release next month. At the same event, Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong pledged to support the growth of start-ups by expanding “patient capital”. “Funding is a vital support that helps start-ups grow and cross the ‘valley of death’,” he said, referring to the critical phase between receiving initial seed capital and generating self-sustaining revenue. “The government is reforming its approach to investment in the I&T sector by integrating a capable government with an efficient market.” Sun added that the government would launch the Innovation and Technology Industry-Oriented Fund this year, allocating HK$10 billion (US$1.3 billion) in investment across five key areas, including life and health technology, artificial intelligence and robotics, and semiconductors and smart devices. The innovation chief also reasserted the government’s plan to accelerate the development of the Northern Metropolis, a megaproject that aims to transform 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land along the mainland border into a technological hub, and provide stronger support for research transformation and start-up incubation.

title: Thai teen rocker Nene Royal talks America’s Got Talent and dreaming big
description: The self-taught guitar prodigy has come a long way from Phuket market performances as she prepares for her biggest stage yet.
content: A twist of fate put a guitar in Nene Royal’s hands. Aged seven, she wanted to join the computer science club at her school in Phuket, Thailand, but it was already full. “The only place left was in the music club, and the teacher handed me a guitar,” she told This Week in Asia. “The moment I started playing, something clicked.” Now just 16, the self-taught rocker has a shot at global stardom on the world’s most watched talent show, America’s Got Talent. “I learned by watching YouTube videos, studying musicians and performers I admired and practising for hours every day,” said Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy, in an email. I hope my journey can show other young people in Thailand that it’s OK to dream big Nene Royal Thailand has a long affinity with rock and guitar music, although the scene is dominated by men. Nene said that was never part of her story. “I don’t really think about what I should or shouldn’t be able to do because of my age, where I come from, or because I’m a girl,” she said. “I just focus on the music I love, working hard and becoming the best musician and performer I can be.” Nene first broke through on the small stages of Phuket’s local markets, where the young guitar maestro honed her skills. It was there that she discovered “how much I love performing in front of people, seeing them smile, making them happy through music and feeling that connection with an audience”, she said. From there, she went on to star in Thai talent contests and joined Phuket bands that have built a strong local following. “The more I performed, the more I realised that being on stage and sharing music with people is what I love most,” she said. But the biggest stage her life looms on Tuesday, US time, when Nene will perform in the live rounds of America’s Got Talent – the reality talent show created by British impresario Simon Cowell. She reached the live rounds after storming through two audition stages with towering vocal-and-guitar performances of The Cranberries’ “Zombie” and Muse’s “Hysteria” that have racked up millions of views on YouTube. Her first audition, screened in early July, had judges Sofia Vergara, Howie Mandel, Mel B and even the notoriously hard-to-please Cowell purring with praise over her powerful vocals and mastery of the electric guitar. Her “Zombie” rendition has been watched more than 15 million times on YouTube, as audiences in a country increasingly known for its pop-culture exports, from television series to horror movies and T-pop, closely follow her journey. With “Nene fever” gripping Thailand – including meet-and-greets with royalty and the prime minister – one of the kingdom’s largest conglomerates, CP Group, bought advertising space in New York’s Times Square, imploring people to vote for the teen star-in-the-making. Thai fans have flooded her social media pages ahead of the America’s Got Talent knockout live rounds, vowing to vote in their droves. “Going into the live rounds of AGT feels incredible. I hope my journey can show other young people in Thailand that it’s OK to dream big, even if you’re starting small,” she said. “Seeing so much support from people in Thailand has made the experience even more special. I feel very proud to represent Thailand, but I also feel a responsibility to give everything I have when I step onto that stage.”

title: The Chinese Mulholland Drive? Why Niu Lai is special even in ‘so bad it’s good’ film lore
description: Initially mocked, the low-budget film by a first-time animator and his mum is now being hailed as a bastion of hard work and free expression.
content: Initially derided by audiences for its poor quality, Niu Lai – a home-made, micro-budget animated feature film – has become a cultural sensation in China, one that is being belatedly championed for its wholesome messaging and lo-fi aesthetics. Since premiering in cinemas on August 5, the unlikely commercial hit has taken more than 45 million yuan (US$6.7 million) at the box office and inspired a stream of memes online – as well as a wide range of unlicensed merchandise – in a grass-roots phenomenon that nobody could have predicted. Written and directed by first-time animator Xin Yumeng and his 60-year-old mother, Sun Lifang, Niu Lai tells the story of the eponymous young ox calf, who cannot walk. After befriending a skylark, the timid calf slips into a dream, where he stands up on his hind legs and embarks on a formative journey. In the dream, Niu Lai encounters a snake, a brave leopard protector and a pack of ferocious wolves. As he and his mother travel with their herd across a hostile wilderness, the calf learns to fend for himself, discovering the importance of family and friendship before waking from his dream and taking his first courageous steps into a larger, enlightened world. Xin, who is based in Dalian in China’s Liaoning province, created Niu Lai over five years using second-hand computer equipment bought online to animate a story penned by his mother. The pair provided the voices for all the characters and even composed and performed the film’s theme song. The film was produced by Dalian Jingyuan Culture Film and Television Media – the family’s own interior design company that they rebranded to release the project. Niu Lai was distributed by a family friend who went against the advice of his contemporaries. It opened on 245 screens before it was reduced to just four. It sold only 236 tickets during its first nine days of screening, earning a paltry 7,169 yuan at the box office. From mockery to must-see But then something happened. Word of mouth began to spread online about a film featuring animation so terrible that it had to be seen to be believed. Cynical film-goers started seeking out screenings. Almost overnight, Niu Lai became the must-see film at cinemas, and the number of screenings – followed by its box-office tally – quickly skyrocketed. Perhaps more interesting, however, is that the mockery of the film’s subpar technical quality is subsiding in favour of a more positive response that champions the work. To quote one popular comment on YouTube, where pirated versions of the entire film have been shared numerous times: “You’ll regret watching it for 86 minutes; if you don’t watch it, you’ll probably suffer from regret for the rest of your life”. A history of ‘so bad it’s good’ Of course, this is not the first example of a film achieving success by being “so bad it’s good”. Cult status is frequently bestowed upon films of questionable quality, dating back to the midnight movie boom of the late 1960s and early 1970s. Pink Flamingos (1972), John Waters’ scatological celebration of poor taste starring drag queen Divine, railed against Middle American conservatism. Despite its minuscule budget and abysmal acting, it became a marquee event for marginalised audiences. Reefer Madness (1936) found popularity through derisive mockery decades after its release. Originally financed by a church group to educate parents about marijuana, it was re-released in 1938 by exploitation filmmaker Dwain Esper with newly inserted shocking material. The film’s implausible adolescent antics, escalating to insanity and murder, were ironically rediscovered in the 1970s by stoners celebrating their ludicrous on-screen portrayal. More recently, Tommy Wiseau’s psychodrama The Room (2003) achieved global notoriety as one of the worst movies ever made due to its incomprehensible dialogue and unnatural performances. It sparked a fandom comparable to The Rocky Horror Picture Show, with fans flocking to sold-out screenings to quote lines and act out scenes. The Room’s unlikely success even spawned the Academy Award-nominated film The Disaster Artist (2017). Similarly in China, the questionable quality of supposedly high-end productions such as Sun Jianjun’s Switch (2013), starring Andy Lau Tak-wah, or Zhang Yimou’s misguided epic The Great Wall (2016) – also starring Lau, this time opposite Matt Damon and Pedro Pascal – has attracted cynical audiences interested only in deriving pleasure from the films’ failings. The response to Niu Lai, however, has been something altogether different and without obvious precedent. There is no denying that its quality is objectively poor. When held up alongside contemporary animated blockbusters such as Ne Zha 2 or All Wishes Come True!, Xin’s work cannot compare. One suspects that even the crudest previsualisation renderings on those productions were infinitely more detailed, complex and visually accomplished than Niu Lai’s final product. But for some, that is precisely what appeals. Authenticity in the age of AI Audiences are embracing Niu Lai’s crude simplicity as a bastion of hard work, perseverance and free expression. The film flies in the face of AI-generated slop that has saturated the internet with slick, passion-devoid content created by aggregating the hard work of independent artists such as Xin and Sun. Some have interpreted Niu Lai as a bold statement against this kind of mainstream conformity in favour of a more personal, individual vision. The filmmakers’ inexperience with the medium often gives the film a disjointed, surreal tone. While Niu Lai is clumsy and unfocused for some, the most-liked review on Letterboxd hails it as the “Chinese Mulholland Drive” – in reference to David Lynch’s famously disorientating 2001 thriller, which is also structured largely around a nightmarish dream narrative. Remarkably, Niu Lai’s impact stretches beyond hardcore film aficionados. The title, which translates as “The Bull Comes”, has been seen in financial circles as a premonition of a profitable bull market. Some investors regard tickets for the film as talismans of good luck and have even bought numerous seats in arrangements that spell out fortuitous Chinese characters. The ultimate underdog story What began as cruel mockery has blossomed into a genuine wave of recognition and support for a project that, despite all else, represents the industrious, wholesome endeavours of a family working together towards a well-intentioned, yet seemingly unattainable goal. In a way, the film’s popularity is reminiscent of how the world rallied behind the Cabo Verde national team at the 2026 World Cup this summer, cheering on a squad of part-timers and dreamers as they held future world champions Spain to a goalless draw before taking a ferocious Argentina side all the way to extra time. Everybody loves an underdog story. Is Niu Lai a well-made film? Absolutely not. But is it a good film? Does it tell a compelling and uplifting story with the power to unite and inspire audiences? Against all the odds, and without relying on any of the expensive bells and whistles employed by the industry’s most gifted proponents, the answer is yes – this bull does stand proudly on his own two feet. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Can China’s flash memory giant YMTC smash Shanghai Star Market IPO records?
description: IPO funds to fuel YMTC parent CCSH’s expansion, with nearly US$5 billion set aside to boost chipmaking capacity and accelerate R&D.
content: China is gearing up for what could become its next record-breaking semiconductor stock listing as the parent company of chip giant Yangtze Memory Technologies Corporation (YMTC) prepares to go public on Shanghai’s Star Market. CCSH Corporation, parent of China’s top NAND flash maker, planned to sell between 1.98 billion and 2.43 billion shares, equivalent to 10 to 12 per cent of its enlarged share capital, according to a prospectus made public on Friday. An overallotment option of up to 15 per cent could also be exercised. While the final offer price and total proceeds have yet to be set, the planned size signals a massive fundraising push. CCSH has earmarked 33 billion yuan (US$4.9 billion) specifically for investment projects – 20.8 billion yuan to upgrade mass-production lines and 12.2 billion yuan for research and development. That target already surpasses the 29.5 billion yuan that ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), China’s leading DRAM maker, originally set aside ahead of its float in July. CXMT ultimately raised 66.6 billion yuan, nearly double its baseline plan, in what became the largest Star Market initial public offering on record. YMTC’s final tally could similarly eclipse its baseline 33 billion yuan target depending on final market demand. If successful, the back-to-back floats will give mainland investors direct equity exposure to China’s two leading memory champions, at a time when tight global supply and artificial intelligence demand have sent memory prices and profitability soaring. Investor frenzy surrounding CXMT offers a gauge of the market’s appetite. Its shares surged 466 per cent on their July 27 debut to close at 49 yuan. By August 17, the stock touched 61.80 yuan, driving its market capitalisation to 4.13 trillion yuan and briefly making it China’s most valuable listed company, surpassing Tencent Holdings just 16 trading days after listing. YMTC approaches the market backed by equally strong earnings momentum. CCSH reported first-quarter revenue of 47 billion yuan, close to the 63.2 billion yuan it generated in all of last year. Net profit attributable to shareholders reached nearly 33.4 billion yuan, more than doubling its total 2025 earnings of 14.2 billion yuan. The surge has been underpinned by a persistent global NAND shortage. YMTC’s NAND revenue jumped 393 per cent year on year in the first quarter, pushing gross margin to 78.7 per cent from 36.7 per cent in 2025 as selling prices rose and unit production costs fell. Founded in December 2016, YMTC is China’s leader in 3D NAND flash memory – the non-volatile storage used in solid-state drives, smartphones, PCs and data centres. Unlike companies that only design chips, YMTC operates as an integrated device manufacturer, meaning it handles chip design, wafer fabrication as well as chip packaging and testing under one roof. Washington added the company to its Entity List in December 2022, imposing stringent licensing requirements that sharply restricted its access to US technology, software and equipment. YMTC said in its prospectus that its operations had once fallen into an “extremely difficult” situation during the most severe period of international trade restrictions. Cut off from advanced foreign equipment, YMTC accelerated its shift towards domestic suppliers. Strong demand from China’s home market and continued upgrades across the local semiconductor supply chain allowed it to keep expanding, the company said. YMTC overtook Japan’s Kioxia to rank third in global NAND bit shipments in the second quarter, capturing 14 per cent of the market, data from Counterpoint Research showed. It remained fifth overall by total revenue, reflecting a heavy focus on consumer memory products over high-value data-centre drives.

title: Meet Claudia Spanier, Suzy Menkes’ granddaughter, who DJ’d for Adidas and Asics
description: Known by her moniker ‘Cloud9’, the Brit blends Afrobeats, amapiano and R&B at brand events and Soho House gigs.
content: Suzy Menkes is one of fashion media’s most prolific journalists. The British fashion critic began her career at The Times and served as the editor of Vogue International for several years before stepping down in 2020. At 82, Menkes remains active in fashion journalism, making regular appearances at runway shows during fashion weeks worldwide. Outside her illustrious career, Menkes is a mother to three sons and a grandmother to six grandchildren – three granddaughters and three grandsons. Of all her grandchildren, Menkes regularly highlights Claudia Spanier, who works as a DJ, on her Instagram. Here’s everything you need to know about Suzy Menkes’ DJ granddaughter, Claudia Spanier. What is Claudia Spanier’s background? Claudia Spanier is the daughter of Gideon Spanier, the son of Suzy Menkes and her late husband David Spanier. Like his mother, Gideon works in media as an editor. According to his LinkedIn profile, he has worked at publications such as The Times and currently serves as the UK editor-in-chief at Campaign, a business magazine. Claudia graduated from Hampstead Fine Arts College in London in 2023, where she completed her A-levels in media studies and graphic design. Instead of following in the footsteps of her father and grandmother, Claudia chose to pursue music and now works as a DJ under the moniker “Cloud9”. Where has Claudia Spanier performed? In a 2025 interview with Shift London, Claudia revealed that she discovered her love for DJing after her best friend’s mother, who is a DJ, introduced her to the equipment and let her practise on her decks. “I really like being a DJ. It’s fun to control a room and kind of dictate a night and be in charge of the vibe. That’s one of my favourite things,” she told Shift London. While Claudia originally picked up DJing as a hobby, she quickly fell in love with it and hasn’t looked back since buying her own decks. According to her LinkedIn profile, Claudia works as a freelance DJ, primarily playing Afrobeats, amapiano, funky house and R&B. She has performed at events for major brands including Asics and Adidas, as well as private gigs at Soho House. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkes) On July 31, Menkes showed off her granddaughter’s DJing skills in an Instagram post, writing: “Proud Granny moment watching my Granddaughter Claudia DJ for the Charlotte Tilbury Covent Garden ultimate summer glow pop-up!”

title: Philippines stakes claim as Latin America’s Asean gateway
description: Shared history offers an edge, but analysts say the Philippines must deliver more than nostalgia to rival Singapore or Vietnam.
content: The Philippines is positioning itself as Latin America’s bridge to Southeast Asia, testing whether shared history and culture can translate into hard trade figures as Asean and the Mercosur bloc look beyond their traditional partners. Manila’s Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro made the pitch during visits to Brazil and Chile from August 10 to 13. “Upon this human foundation, commercial bridges thrive: the Philippines stands as the premier strategic gateway for Latin American firms expanding into Asean’s US$4-trillion market,” she told an audience in Chile, referring to the two regions’ shared Spanish colonial history, Catholic faith and people-to-people ties. Lazaro also floated the idea of expanding logistics links – citing the regional presence of Philippine port operator International Container Terminal Services – as a way to cut costs and shield supply chains from global shocks via direct trans-Pacific shipping routes. The pitch lands in a crowded field, however: Singapore remains Southeast Asia’s dominant commercial, financial and logistics hub, while Vietnam and Indonesia have attracted growing interest from companies looking to diversify supply chains. It also comes as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and Mercosur – a South American trade bloc whose members include Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and Uruguay – look for new partners amid US tariffs, energy insecurity and wider geopolitical uncertainty. The two blocs do not have an existing free-trade agreement with each other and most trade is still conducted bilaterally. Combined two-way trade totalled a modest US$33.3 billion in 2023, the latest year for which figures are available. Moves are being made to strengthen ties, however. Brazil has approved negotiating mandates to negotiate preferential trade deals with Indonesia and Vietnam. The South American nation also completed domestic approval of the Mercosur-Singapore Free Trade Agreement earlier this month. “US tariffs have already motivated Mercosur to accelerate the trade agreement with the European Union,” said Alberto Maresca, a doctoral fellow at UNU-CRIS and Ghent University, and a visiting researcher at the Getulio Vargas Foundation’s School of International Relations in Brazil. Maresca said Brazil was leading the push for closer ties with Southeast Asia, adding: “The need for economic and political diversification, motivated by Trump’s foreign policy, would be an important catalyst for a Mercosur-Asean agreement.” Darynaufal Mulyaman, a political economist and assistant professor of international relations at the Christian University of Indonesia who studies both blocs, said the two regions were being pushed to spread risk more widely. “States are no longer operating under the assumption that supply chains and partnerships will remain open and stable indefinitely,” he said. “That assumption breaking down forces both Asean and Mercosur to hedge rather than concentrate their dependencies on a narrow set of traditional partners.” States are no longer operating under the assumption that supply chains and partnerships will remain open and stable indefinitely Darynaufal Mulyaman, political economist The Strait of Hormuz crisis continued to threaten Asia’s energy supplies, while Taiwan Strait tensions “threaten to disrupt the semiconductor and manufacturing chains that both Southeast Asia and, indirectly, Latin America depend on”, Mulyaman said. “These are not abstract risks any more,” he added. Both regions had good reason to diversify trade partners “at a time of heightened geopolitical competition, growing protectionism and uncertainty around traditional markets”, said Ariane Costa, deputy director of the Brazilian Centre for International Relations’ geopolitics programme. Common histories Cultural familiarity could give the Philippines an edge in attracting Latin American companies, analysts say, even if Manila cannot match Singapore’s infrastructure or financial depth. “The Philippines certainly shares cultural similarities with Latin America and Mercosur due to the common histories that both countries and regions share with Spain,” Rodolfo Caffaro Kramer, president of the Mercosur-Asean Chamber of Commerce, told This Week in Asia. “Naturally, these cultural similarities help foster trade, and in this regard, the Philippines is the Asean member with the closest cultural ties to Latin America.” Free-trade agreements that reduce tariffs, cut red tape and harmonise regulations were “always welcome”, Kramer said. Costa said the Philippines could still carve out a role by leaning on its geography, US ties, English-speaking business environment and growing links with other Asian markets. “For Latin American companies seeking to enter Asean, the Philippines could therefore become an important entry point into specific sectors and value chains rather than a direct substitute for Singapore,” she said. Other observers were more cautious, saying the Philippines could not rely on cultural similarities alone to strengthen economic ties. “Filipino society does carry cultural affinities that make the idea of a gateway sound natural on paper,” Mulyaman said. “The real test becomes whether the country is competitive enough to open up genuinely attractive conditions for Latin American investors and traders.” Compared with “capital rich Singapore” and “Vietnam’s aggressive catching up posture”, Manila still needed to do more before the gateway framing became “more than aspiration”, he added. Pragmatic priorities Closer ties would give both blocs “more agency in shaping the rules and institutions of the international economic system”, Costa said, strengthening the negotiation position of the Global South. But she stressed that this “should not be construed as Mercosur choosing Asean and the Global South instead of Europe or North America”, adding: “The objective should be to avoid excessive dependence on any single market or geopolitical axis.” Observers say the most promising areas for cooperation include food, agricultural technology, electronics, biofuels, critical minerals, infrastructure, logistics, energy and manufacturing. “Mercosur has a great opportunity to become a large-scale food producer to supply Asean and help it achieve food security,” Kramer said. Maresca added that Asean technology exports could help Mercosur reduce its reliance on Chinese and US imports, while Costa said Southeast Asia could offer new export markets for higher-value Mercosur goods and services. However, any deeper relationship is likely to emerge gradually rather than through one sweeping bloc-to-bloc agreement. “What is still missing is a broader strategic architecture connecting these initiatives,” Costa said, noting that internal differences, regulatory barriers and sensitivities over competition could slow progress – especially among South American sectors wary of Asian competition. “Trade relationships require logistics, information, financing and networks, not only preferential tariffs,” she said. “For these reasons, I would expect the relationship to develop incrementally: first through bilateral agreements with key Asean economies, followed by greater trade facilitation, investment and regulatory cooperation.”

title: Uefa chief Ceferin rules out Fifa presidency bid but claims Infantino could face challenger
description: Head of European football’s governing body brands World Cup investment project a greater threat to the sport than European Super League plan.
content: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin ruled himself out of running for the Fifa presidency but said Gianni ⁠Infantino would likely face a ⁠challenger if he seeks re-election next year following ⁠a global backlash over a plan to sell part of the World Cup to private investors. Speaking to The Rest Is Politics: Leading podcast, which will air on Monday, Ceferin said he was not interested in succeeding Infantino despite growing uncertainty around the Fifa president’s future after his abandoned investment proposal. “One reason is that I love Uefa ‌and I love working here, and I think that at a certain point you have also, I mean, it’s time also to enjoy life a bit,” Ceferin said. “Let’s see till when. And the second point is, my credibility is much, much, much higher if I’m not interested in the position.” The Uefa chief, who said he has had no contact with Infantino since controversy erupted over the abandoned sell-off plan, suggested the Swiss administrator would likely face opposition if he stands ⁠again in March. “There are two options,” Ceferin said. “One option is that he realises that he doesn’t have the support, and that’s not ‌only a political support of the ones who vote, but the political support of [the] football community, the political support of fans, the political support of the players, former players, coaches. “And the second option that ‌he goes to the elections in March, but in that case, I think he will have a candidate against ⁠him. I don’t know ⁠yet who.” Ceferin also criticised the proposed World Cup investment project, describing it as a greater threat to the sport than the European Super League plan that Uefa successfully ‌fought in 2021. “When you compared in the beginning this plan with the Super League plan, I think this plan is even worse than the Super League plan,” he ‌said. “Football would ‌be literally sold.” Fifa was contacted for comment on Ceferin’s criticism of Infantino and the sport’s global governing body. Ceferin said Uefa’s ‌55 member federations reacted with anger after details of the proposal emerged publicly and rejected suggestions that opposition came only from Europe’s ⁠wealthiest associations. “On one side was England, Germany, who you understand don’t want that, because this money is not so big for them. ⁠But on the other side was San Marino, Cyprus, Liechtenstein ... They said: we’re not for sale,” he said. Ceferin rejected claims that Europe was obstructing efforts to help poorer football nations and took aim at what he described as ‌attempts to portray Uefa as an ‌entitled elite. “What I hear is that they play on, you know, arrogant Europe is against us,” he said. “But I think someone should remind him [Infantino] that he is a European, and that he was supported by Uefa, which he forgot.” Ceferin said neither he nor Uefa had been informed about either the investment proposal or a separate Fifa Peace Prize, awarded in 2025 to US President Donald Trump, before they became public.

title: China team brings X-ray vision to life with a compact high-speed ghost video cam
description: Tabletop imaging camera can capture ‘see-through’ medical videos of beating hearts using a lower radiation dose than traditional methods.
content: Chinese scientists have developed a new tabletop X-ray ghost imaging method that allows them to capture real-time “see-through” video of fast-moving objects. The team’s system could be used to capture dynamic objects such as rotating aircraft engines or biological movements like a beating heart. Importantly, this could all be accomplished with a lower radiation dose and simpler set-up than traditional X-ray methods. “In contrast to other available X-ray imaging techniques for moving objects, our method can be implemented with a conventional tabletop X-ray source,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Communications Physics on August 15. “The set-up is simple, relatively inexpensive and easy to operate.” The researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shanghai Jiao Tong University said their method had “great potential” for medical imaging as well as non-destructive imaging of moving mechanical components. Despite its vital uses in medicine, crystallography and material inspection, conventional tabletop X-ray imaging has operational trade-offs that limit its application to static objects. Conventional X-ray works by shooting radiation through an object, which different structures and materials absorb to varying degrees. The X-rays are then captured by a detector or film on the other side, producing a direct image of the object. X-ray ghost imaging is an indirect technique where an object is lit with X-rays that pass through a patterned filter. These are then measured by a single-pixel detector that picks up on the total intensity of light that reaches it. A computer compares the intensity received by the detector against the known patterns to piece together a final image, according to a news report by the journal Science. This method has emerged as a field of interest because it can achieve imaging at lower radiation doses than conventional X-ray, which could make it safer as well as ideal for long-term or dynamic imaging. Existing X-ray ghost imaging methods face significant challenges due to the very long total acquisition times required to capture an image, making them impractical for real-world applications, the Chinese team said. This is because ghost imaging typically relies on changing the patterned filter after each exposure to reconstruct the final image. To overcome this challenge, the Chinese team’s method uses a spinning filter or mask with tiny patterns that rapidly change as it rotates, enabling faster image acquisition. “Our method has greatly improved the [X-ray ghost imaging] speed and paves the way for X-ray imaging applications of [moving] objects, such as the inspection of rotating aero-engines and in vivo medical imaging,” the team said. Their new method for two-dimensional high-resolution X-ray ghost imaging of moving objects allowed for a rate of up to 200 frames per second. The team tested their system on a spinning copper disk with letters stencilled onto it. Their ghost imaging system was able to accurately image the letters, though the quality degraded as the disk spun faster. When compared with a traditional X-ray camera, their system produced images of lower quality overall but was able to continuously record the full motion of the moving letters. The traditional cameras captured sharper images when the letters were stationary, but suffered from motion blur and frame gaps during movement, leading to distorted or incomplete letters. The imaging speed of the ghost approach is mainly limited by the rotation speed of the spinning mask and the sampling frequency of the detection system. The team said improving both could lead to better and faster imaging. “Notably, our proposed method is not limited to any wavelength but would be particularly suitable for situations where array cameras are cumbersome, extremely expensive and difficult to maintain,” the team said. The peer-reviewed paper was shared online by the journal ahead of final editing to give faster access to the findings.

title: Murder-suicide suspected as woman, 66, found dead after husband jumps from building
description: Hong Kong police investigating after woman found dead in flat shortly after alleged suicide of 80-year-old husband in Kwai Chung Estate.
content: Hong Kong police are investigating a suspected murder-suicide after an 80-year-old man jumped to his death from a residential building, shortly before officers found his 66-year-old wife dead inside their flat with severe head and body injuries. Preliminary investigations found that the couple, married for more than four decades, had planned to divorce due to relationship problems, although authorities had no record of previous domestic disputes between them. The police force said on Monday that a security guard at Kwai Chung Estate, a public housing estate in Kwai Tsing, reported that the retired man had fallen from Chun Kwai House at about 11.30pm the previous night. His wife, who worked as a cleaner, was later found dead in the living room of their flat in the same block. She had sustained serious injuries to her head and body. Wan Chun-hong, the force’s acting assistant district commander (crime) for Kwai Tsing district, said the couple were pronounced dead at the scene. “According to a preliminary forensic examination, the force believes the man died after falling from a height, while the woman died after being struck on the head with hard objects. She is believed to have died between 7pm and 11pm that night,” Wan said. Police found three mobile phones belonging to the couple in the flat, along with bloodstained clothing and hard objects inside a rubbish bin in the communal area on the same floor. The objects included a 60cm-long metal rack, two metal strips and a laundry rack. Wan said police had not found a suicide note or identified any witnesses. But the window and its grilles in the flat were open and faced the direction where the man was found after his fatal fall. Police had not previously received reports of family disputes involving the couple, and neither had a record of mental illness. But Wan said the pair, who had been married for more than 40 years, were on bad terms and that their two daughters had moved out years ago. “The couple had earlier told their family that they planned to divorce because of relationship problems, while the man had also expressed suicidal intentions,” Wan said. He added that the investigation had found no evidence that the couple were under financial pressure. Police will continue investigating the suspected murder-suicide. Officers will examine the couple’s phones, arrange postmortem examinations and look for witnesses. Wan said he believed the incident was an isolated domestic case and urged members of the public to seek professional help for relationship, financial or other problems. He also called on family members to offer support if they noticed anyone struggling with emotional distress. A spokesman of Harmony House, a non-governmental organisation supporting victims of domestic violence, said severe marital distress should never be treated as a private matter. “When a relationship reaches a stage where separation or divorce is being considered, or when one partner feels overwhelmed, hopeless, or emotionally distressed, [they] should regard the situation as a significant warning sign rather than simply a private marital dispute,” he said. Unresolved long-term tensions, emotional distress, persistent arguments, depressive symptoms, or expressions of suicidal or violent thoughts often precede family incidents, he said. To prevent similar tragedies, he said the government and social welfare sector must enhance emotional support and suicide prevention services for older adults and men, who are often reluctant to seek help due to cultural stigma. “In reality, asking for help is often one of the most courageous and responsible steps a person can take,” the spokesman said. Social welfare lawmaker Grace Chan Man-yee said the tragedy shed light on the limitations of existing social support networks in reaching “hidden families”. “The current mechanism of identifying families at risk relies heavily on referrals or voluntary participation, instead of reaching out to them proactively,” she said. “We need to better identify and support the mental health needs of elderly people, while giving caregivers more space and emotional backing.” If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Surge in non-DSE admissions to Hong Kong’s public universities sparks calls for quotas
description: Number of non-DSE students in the city’s public universities jumps to 63 per cent, while local exam-takers fall to 72 per cent of intake.
content:
Public universities in Hong Kong have admitted a record number of students applying outside the local exam system. The intake surged by 63 per cent over seven years to account for nearly 30 per cent of the 15,000 government-funded places, the South China Morning Post has found.
Meanwhile, the intake of home-grown students taking the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) exam has dropped by 7 per cent, causing its proportion to fall from 82 per cent to 72 per cent, sparking calls for a cap on admissions through alternative qualifications to safeguard local interests.
“The decrease in places for DSE students results in driving up admission scores,” said Ng Po-shing, a student guidance consultant at Hok Yau Club and vice-principal of a secondary school. “More students are complaining that they failed to get into certain programmes though they met the median score in the previous cohort.”
The Diploma of Secondary Education is the city’s main university entrance examination.
The SCMP isolated the trends after analysing data sets from the University Grants Committee (UGC) on first-year-first-degree students admitted with DSE and non-DSE qualifications across all eight government-funded universities from 2019-20 to 2025-26.
According to the data, non-DSE admissions to government-funded Year One university places have shown an upwards trend in both overall numbers and proportions over six years.
Admissions for students via non-DSE routes jumped from 2,706 in 2019-20 to 4,401 in 2025-26, marking a 63 per cent increase.
Their share took up only 18 per cent of the total funded university places in 2019-20, but jumped to 22 per cent in 2022-23 and reached 28 per cent in 2025-26.
