The non-DSE route refers to students sitting the International Baccalaureate (IB), GCE A-levels or International A-levels from Hong Kong’s international, private independent and Direct Subsidy Scheme schools, as well as students who studied overseas but returned to Hong Kong’s universities, and talented local students under the School Nominations Direct Admission Scheme (SNDAS).
Conversely, admissions for DSE students to Year One places have shown a declining trend in both overall numbers and proportions.
The number of admitted candidates dropped from 12,355 in 2019-20 to 11,503 in 2025-26, marking a 7 per cent fall.
Their share across the eight universities dropped significantly over the same period, from 82 per cent to a trough of 72 per cent this year.
While 73 per cent of DSE students who attained general admission requirements secured a spot in public universities in 2019, that rate dropped to 70 per cent in 2025.
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and the University of Hong Kong (HKU) recorded the lowest DSE student intake by percentage.
HKUST’s intake comprised only 61 per cent in 2025-26 while HKU took in 62 per cent, down from 83 per cent and 78 per cent, respectively, seven years ago.
Over the same period, the number of non-DSE students admitted by HKUST surged by 156 per cent, while HKU recorded an 87 per cent increase.
The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) was the sole outlier, with its DSE intake edging up to 86 per cent from 84 per cent seven years ago.
The remaining five public universities all recorded declines in local exam admissions over the same period.
An HKUST spokesman said the university did not give preferential treatment based on qualification type or application route, adding that all candidates were assessed independently to ensure fairness and consistency.
An HKU spokesman said its shift was due to diversified educational pathways in Hong Kong, noting that the university also accepted the highest number of students via SNDAS among all institutions.
Education consultant Ng said students from non-DSE curricula often came from families who could afford higher tuition fees and were well equipped to secure good grades, leading to universities preferring to admit them over DSE students, thereby reinforcing their socio-economic status.
“Students with good backgrounds enjoy more resources and then obtain good grades, resulting in good prospects and continued high socio-economic backgrounds or vice versa,” he said.
Due to the shrinking share of DSE students taking up government-funded places, Ng predicted that future candidates might need to secure higher marks to enter public universities.
Lee Yi-ying, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Subsidised Secondary Schools Council, called the DSE a “Hong Kong brand” and said local universities should have greater confidence in admitting DSE students.
Both Ng and Lee observed that candidates securing median admission scores last year – previously considered competitive – still failed to gain entry into certain programmes, which they believed was partly a result of the growing number of non-DSE student admissions.
Both called for a benchmark quota to prevent universities from endlessly expanding alternative admissions, with Lee suggesting that at least 80 per cent of places be reserved for DSE candidates to protect local interests.
A spokesman for the Education Bureau dismissed any direct correlation with the appeal of the DSE.
“Under the university principle of merit-based admission, this phenomenon reflects changes in students’ personal considerations regarding their study destination, and has no direct relationship with the overall attractiveness of the DSE curriculum,” he said.
“Every year, a significant number of top DSE candidates choose to apply directly to prestigious overseas universities or top mainland [Chinese] institutions using their results, with their higher education goals far from being limited to local UGC-funded places.
“In contrast, some students enrolled in non-local curricula such as IB or GCE A-levels in recent years may have shifted to staying in Hong Kong for higher education due to changes in the global situation or personal planning.”
He noted that the proportion of DSE students entering publicly funded university places had largely remained at a high level of more than 70 per cent.

title: Australia sees spike in near-misses amid air traffic controller shortage
description: Staffing gaps are fuelling safety concerns as Sydney Airport records four aircraft close calls in the past month.
content: Australia’s shortage of air traffic controllers is showing signs of nearing a breaking point after the country’s busiest airport recorded at least four near misses in the past month. Since late July, incidents at Sydney Airport included a passenger jet aborting its take-off because there was a plane in its path. In a separate close call, an aircraft that was taxiing had to slam on the brakes to avoid colliding with another jet. Short-staffed control towers have long been a problem globally, but nowhere is the urgency of the matter more on display recently than in Australia. The growing number of incidents is pressing the need for authorities worldwide to crank up hiring and adopt new tools like artificial intelligence. “Air traffic control staffing levels are not at the level required,” said Andrew Marshall, president of the Australian and International Pilots Association, which represents the flight crew at the nation’s flag carrier, Qantas Airways. “Whilst pilots are the last line of defence in aviation safety, it isn’t an appropriate long-term solution.” The problem is there is no quick way to fill the shortfall of air traffic controllers in Australia, largely because it takes years for a new recruit to be fully trained. Meanwhile, flight demand continues to grow. That is becoming the case worldwide as the lack of controllers has turned into one of the aviation industry’s biggest frustrations. More than 70,000 new controllers will be needed globally by 2034, according to forecasts by aviation training provider CAE. At Sydney Airport, staffing pressures have spilled over to the point that a whistle-blower told authorities that short-handed workers held “grave concerns” about safety. That alarm was sounded in June from an experienced air traffic controller, who drew comparisons with the way controllers near Washington pleaded for changes in the months before a mid-air collision that killed 67 people in January 2025. The latest incident emerged on Friday, when authorities said they were investigating an event three days earlier in which two Qantas planes were taxiing towards each other. Both crews reported they had received clearance to proceed. About a week earlier, a Virgin Australia jet aborted its take-off when a Qantas plane started to cross the runway. The same morning, a taxiing Jetstar plane almost collided with a Qatar Airways aircraft that was under tow, injuring one member of the cabin crew. A similar incident occurred between two Qantas planes in late July. These were close calls. An announcement on the Jetstar plane – aired on local media – indicated that the crew spotted the nearby Qatar jet by chance at the last moment. The Virgin Australia aircraft was already applying thrust when it noticed the Qantas plane ahead, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau said. The bureau is investigating all the incidents. The frequency of the events in Sydney has laid bare the fragility of the workforce. Workers inside Sydney Airport’s control tower often struggle to fill all shifts on the roster, and the ranks are so thin that controllers sometimes work 10 days straight without a break, according to their union. “There just aren’t enough people,” said Scott Nugent, president of Civil Air, the controllers’ union. Some days, 20 per cent of rostered shifts were vacant – and that is before anyone called in sick, Nugent said in an interview. The system relied on people doing large amounts of overtime and if they could not fill the gaps, flights started getting delayed, he said. Not enough staff had a sufficient range of skills to carry out different tasks, which made it harder to plug specific holes in the roster when they popped up at short notice, he added. “Recruitment is only one piece of this puzzle,” Nugent said. One tool that could help alleviate the crunch is artificial intelligence. AI could be particularly useful for managing routine jobs like aircraft parking, helping avoid runway and taxiing conflicts, as well as coordinating the growing number of drones and unmanned aircraft, said Ugur Turhan, a trained controller who is now an aviation lecturer at the University of New South Wales Canberra in Australia. At Hong Kong airport, for example, an AI-powered system that is fed with data from high-resolution cameras is designed to prevent tragedies such as the one in March at New York City’s LaGuardia Airport, where an Air Canada Express jet with 76 people on board smashed into a fire truck shortly after landing, killing both pilots. Still, AI systems would require years of testing before being effectively deployed, Turhan said, and human controllers would be needed for the foreseeable future. Meanwhile, the shortage of controllers in Australia has led to an increase in flight delays, disgruntling passengers and airlines. Rob Sharp, CEO at Airservices Australia, a government-owned entity that manages the country’s airspace, has issued a public apology. He said the organisation was building a larger pool of standby controllers to bolster the Sydney roster and that it was in “full recruitment mode”. “We need to fix this problem,” Stephen Beckett, CEO of Airlines for Australia & New Zealand, which represents Qantas, Jetstar and Virgin Australia, said in an interview. It is a common complaint among airlines around the world. Carriers argue that flight delays caused by shortages in control towers create extra costs from staffing, fuel and passenger compensation. According to the International Air Transport Association, air traffic controller delays in the US cost carriers almost US$11 billion between 2015 and 2025, and the situation is only getting worse. In Europe, delays caused by air traffic management in the same period cost airlines and passengers €17.5 billion (US$20 billion), the IATA estimates. For Airservices, like much of the global industry, the shortage of controllers traces its roots to the Covid-19 pandemic, which caused air travel to grind to a near halt and led thousands of aviation workers to leave the industry or lose their jobs. In 2021 and 2022, about 450 employees took voluntary redundancy, Airservices filings show. Airservices had just over 1,000 full-time controllers at the end of June 2025, and added 109 more in the following 12 months, filings show. “They perhaps let too many of the experienced ones go,” said Ian Douglas, a senior lecturer at the School of Aviation at UNSW in Sydney. “You can’t create controllers out of thin air.”

title: Investment market volatility ‘here to stay’ unless global recession strikes: analyst
description: Rich investors put on notice as AI advancement and geopolitical risks continue to change market structure, causing instability, says Nomura.
content: Wealthy investors should be ready for higher volatility “for years” as uncertainties around artificial intelligence development and geopolitical risks are set to persist, according to a major private bank. In the past few years, asset prices underwent several roller coaster rides, from US Liberation Day last year to the sell-off of semiconductor shares and US Treasury in recent months. But volatility came after changes to the market’s structure “over the decades” and was expected to be “here to stay”, said Julia Wang, North Asia chief investment officer of Nomura International Wealth Management, in an interview with the South China Morning Post. “(Periodic high volatility) is already a result of structure changes to the market, so it’s unlikely to change, unless we have a global recession,” said Wang, who joined the international wealth management arm of Japan’s largest investment banking and brokerage firm in November, to advise the offshore investments of clients with at least US$20 million in potential investable surplus. While Wang reaffirmed Nomura’s positive outlook on AI and the global economy, AI was one of the key pushes behind the ups and downs. She explained that expectations for outperforming gains from future productivity drivers resulted in crowded trading and leverage, which usually would be followed by market sell-offs. For instance, after hitting a record high in late June, the memory chip-heavy Korea Composite Stock Price Index plunged 22 per cent last month, sending a Hong Kong-listed SK Hynix-leveraged exchange-traded fund to dive 71 per cent over the month. Despite a quick recovery in early August, Asian fund managers were increasingly cautious about the tremendous AI capital expenditure and rotating into defensive stocks like utilities and healthcare, according to a recent survey. Meanwhile, Wang observed that the expectations of affluent investors on returns have been broadly elevated on the previous phenomenal gains from AI and higher cash rates due to delayed US interest rate cuts, without offering specific numbers given the difference in risk appetite varying from client to client. Moreover, rich investors were asking for a more “flexible” approach to fixed income, taking opportunities in the credit market or in the rates market, she added. Besides AI, Wang warned Asian investors that geopolitical fragmentation and policy uncertainty could bite into the gains from offshore investments, as they could lead to stickier, higher global inflation. While China continued to face deflationary pressures amid sluggish domestic demand, the global headline inflation rate was expected to rise to 4.7 per cent this year before retreating to 3.9 per cent in 2027, according to the International Monetary Fund’s forecast in July. Based on her conversations with clients, Wang said the biggest demand from high net worth individuals in Asia is to protect their existing gains from potential downside risks. Therefore, Nomura suggested clients diversify their assets to hedge the structural risks and manage AI-linked volatility, which global asset managers and private banks have been advocating for in recent years. In addition, Wang advised affluent investors to focus on corporate fundamentals to avoid panic-selling and stay invested to catch the quick rebounds in the market. “The other part is how do you limit the downside. That helps you to stay in the game for longer and then compound,” she added.

title: ‘Hang in there’: Chinese boys offer US$1.50 to struggling store owner, sparking wave of support
description: To express his gratitude, Chen treats the three ‘angel investors’ to a meal, a fishing trip, offering each a red envelope.
content: Three boys from southeastern China offered 10.5 yuan (US$1.50) to a convenience store owner on the brink of closing, igniting a wave of public support. Five years after borrowing money to establish his convenience store in Guangzhou, Chen decided to shut down the shop as business continued to decline. On August 12, three primary school boys visited the store, as they often did, to buy drinks. During a casual conversation, they learned that Chen was preparing to close the establishment. One boy suggested that Chen take his business online, while another proposed they combine their pocket money to support him. The trio then counted their savings and placed 10.5 yuan on Chen’s counter, despite his persistent refusals, before running off with a message of encouragement: “Hang in there!” The sight of the crumpled banknotes brought Chen to tears. After enduring five years of hardships without breaking down, he stated that the children’s genuine act of kindness was what finally caused him to lose his composure. The moment was captured by the store’s surveillance camera and subsequently uploaded by Chen, quickly going viral online. Netizens praised the boys for their kindness, while local residents shared videos of themselves visiting the store and supporting Chen. Chen’s landlord also stepped in, reducing his monthly rent from 5,500 yuan (US$820) to 4,500 yuan. A regular customer set up a stall outside the store selling lemon tea and grilled sausages, donating all proceeds to Chen. Junjie, one of the three boys, also returned to assist in attracting customers by selling goods. Junjie’s father, Wei Sheng, told the SCMP that he was pleasantly surprised by his son’s gesture, viewing it as a simple act of goodwill. “I taught him that giving roses leaves a sweet fragrance on your hands. Helping others is also helping yourself,” he said. Wei, a cement worker at a property management company, and his wife, who works two jobs, have instilled in Junjie the values of independence. During the summer holiday, the 11-year-old often prepares his own meals. Junjie noted that he had never forgotten the complimentary drink Chen once gave him and donated the 3.5 yuan he had on that day, despite having only 15 yuan for his daily meals. On August 17, Chen took the three boys to KFC and went fishing with them to express his gratitude, giving each boy a red envelope. Although Chen has not yet revealed the store’s future, he has already begun live-streaming and selling products online. “The three little ‘angel investors’ are changing my fate,” he told local media. One online observer commented: “Running a bricks-and-mortar store is challenging these days. For Chen, the three children are a ray of light in the darkness.” Another suggested that Chen rename the shop “10.5 Convenience Store” and involve the boys in small-scale charity activities to keep the spirit of kindness alive.

title: Homes crack as London heatwaves trigger record subsidence claims
description: Five successive heatwaves have led to a surge in structural damage claims in the UK capital this summer.
content: Londoners are facing historic levels of subsidence risk after five successive heatwaves dried out the clay soil on which much of the British capital is built. Insurance claims tied to subsidence – a phenomenon associated with bouts of hot, dry weather that shrink the soil and destabilise the foundations on which buildings stand – hit a record last quarter, according to data provided by the Association of British Insurers (ABI). On average, households claimed £20,000 (US$27,200) for the risk, more than in any previous quarter and a 15 per cent jump from the same period in 2025, the ABI said. Laura Hughes, head of general insurance at the ABI, said the upwards trend is likely to continue. “We expect to see more subsidence cases because of the hot weather,” she said in an interview. Londoners have taken to social media to express their dismay. On Reddit, people offered personal accounts telling of “horrendous cracking” in their homes, and “doors sticking” due to subsidence. One said it was “genuinely scary” to discover that their kitchen had moved as the foundations of the home shifted. Another Reddit user described the response of a structural engineer they contacted for help. “Before I could finish explaining he laughed and said, ‘You and 20,000 other people in southeast London’,” the person wrote. “It’s crazy, what’s happening now,” said Otso Lahtinen, chief executive of Geobear, an engineering firm that is regularly called in to repair damage caused by subsidence. “It’s the new norm, and it seems it will happen more often in the next 20 to 30 years.” Data provided by Aviva shows that the areas of London that are most at risk are some of the UK capital’s most sought after, namely the boroughs of Westminster, as well as Kensington and Chelsea. While subsidence has been affecting homes in the British capital for decades, climate change is making it worse. London clay is especially sensitive to fluctuations in moisture, expanding when wet and contracting when dry. The threat of subsidence in the UK is concentrated in and around London as well as in parts of the southeast. In the four years through 2025, insurance payouts for subsidence damage soared roughly 90 per cent to reach a record £297 million, according to data provided by the ABI. The most vulnerable properties are Victorian or Edwardian homes that were built directly onto the upper layers of London clay. By contrast, modern office buildings in the City of London and Canary Wharf have much deeper foundations and are therefore less exposed to such risks. Subsidence is part of a long list of heat-related challenges to which the UK is now struggling to adapt. Over the past months, extreme heat has forced schools to close, led bus drivers to go on strike, and seen banks relax in-office work requirements to protect staff from unbearably hot commutes. Most of England has been gripped by drought and the country’s hospitals have shown signs of buckling under the strain. London Mayor Sadiq Khan has warned that the city would need to turn to private investors to help fund the cost of dealing with the impact of rising temperatures. His office estimates that London now faces an annual bill as high as £36 billion into the 2050s to prepare the city for what climate change has in store. “The impact that climate change is having is undeniable,” said Hughes of the ABI. Subsidence can devalue a property by an average of 20 to 25 per cent, according to the Federation of Master Builders. In some cases, homeowners prefer to cover the cost themselves rather than wade through complicated claims processes. The traditional engineering fix for subsidence damage, known as underpinning, can cost anywhere from £20,000 to more than £100,000. The phenomenon poses “a significant challenge for UK home insurers”, said Cherry Chan, a partner at Deloitte, with subsidence claims making up an ever larger chunk of the payouts they need to make to customers. The consultancy has warned that UK home insurers risk losses in 2026 due in part to the trend. Along with flash floods and wildfires, subsidence is becoming “an increasingly material climate-related risk”, Chan said. It requires that insurers display “careful consideration in long-term exposure and risk management strategies”. Extreme weather patterns in 2026 “will not only impact more new claims in this year, but could cause claims deteriorations for unsettled subsidence claims reported in the past”, she added. That includes 2025, which was a so-called surge year for subsidence impacts. Fresh estimates from the British Geological Survey indicate that under what is known as the RCP 4.5 emissions scenario – reflecting a trajectory that closely aligns with current climate policies – 1.8 million properties, or about 5 per cent of the UK total, were “highly likely or extremely likely” to be susceptible to shrink-swell subsidence by 2070. Under a higher emissions scenario, the figure rises to 4.2 million, or 11 per cent, of British properties. Areas most at risk are densely populated parts of London, Kent and southeast of England. The development has the potential to lead to “increased insurance premiums, depressed house prices and, in some cases, engineering works to stabilise land or property, replacement of utility pipeworks and unstable transport infrastructure”, according to the British Geological Survey. Geobear, which tackles subsidence by injecting resin under buildings, said it had received more homeowner inquiries this summer than ever before. It said insurance clients have confirmed a similar trend, with one telling Geobear it had received 180 claims on a single day, which is significantly more than normal. “It’s a pretty severe situation,” said Lahtinen, the CEO. “If you’re looking to trade, sell or buy property, this is a trend you can’t ignore.”

title: Half of Hong Kong’s public bodies omit emissions data, green group finds
description: The Green Earth’s study of 82 public entities finds that while 41 publish emissions data, about eight use outdated emission factor.
content: Half of Hong Kong’s government departments and public bodies have not disclosed their greenhouse gas emissions data and some calculations have been based on outdated information, a green group has found. The findings from The Green Earth have prompted calls for stronger carbon reporting and the setting of reduction targets across the public sector to align with the city’s goal of achieving carbon neutrality before 2050. The non-profit group’s study of 82 public entities found that while 41 published emissions data, about eight entities relied on an outdated emission factor. An emission factor is a standard multiplier used to calculate the amount of greenhouse gas generated from an activity. The city’s two utility providers, CLP Power and HK Electric, each publish their own emission factors, which are adjusted with changes in the energy mix. Using outdated factors could lead to overestimated emission reductions, said Steven Chan Wing-kit, the green group’s assistant environmental affairs manager. “Mandatory disclosure of carbon emissions in a standardised format would enable progress tracking and channel resources to government bodies with the most pressing reduction needs,” Chan said. Clear emission metrics would also benefit public bodies seeking green finance, serving as indicators for how funded projects contribute to overall environmental performance, he added. The group did not name the departments that failed to publish their emissions data, saying it wanted to focus on the overall carbon reporting situation rather than individual practices. While the government has set an overall energy reduction goal and a plan to be carbon neutral by 2050, it does not mandate carbon reduction targets for all departments. Being carbon neutral means balancing the carbon gas you put into the air with the amount you take out – a net-zero balance of carbon gases. An Environment and Ecology Bureau spokesman said all major government buildings had undergone regular carbon audits since 2017 and must disclose their results in annual environmental performance reports. But he did not define what constitutes a major government building. The Green Earth’s study reviewed annual and environmental reports of 82 public entities on whether they provided data on energy use and greenhouse gas emissions. Just 41 disclosed greenhouse gas emissions data, while 53 provided energy consumption figures. But Chan noted a standardised format for data presentation and measurement units was still lacking. Providing raw data such as actual electricity usage, gas consumption, fuel usage and carbon emissions would help avoid calculation errors and accurately represent the results of their energy-saving efforts, the group said. Additionally, eight government bodies used a citywide default emission factor of 0.7kg (1.54lbs) per kilowatt-hour, an outdated figure based on an official guideline for reporting greenhouse gas emissions dating back to 2008, he pointed out. This has led to overestimated emission reduction figures, Chan said. CLP Power and HK Electric have introduced lower-carbon energy sources in recent years, along with the gradual replacement of coal with natural gas, driving down their respective emission factors to 0.34kg/kWh and 0.59kg/kWh last year. Hong Kong revised its guidelines in March, updating the emission factor. It has also formulated a carbon audit template to help users calculate emissions with simple data such as meter readings and fuel receipts, the bureau said. Singapore and South Korea publish annual carbon emissions and energy usage for their government departments, allowing the public to track the decarbonisation progress. Mainland China has also set reduction targets for its public institutions, aiming for an 8.5 per cent cut in carbon emissions and a 5 per cent reduction in energy consumption per unit of floor area during the 15th five-year-plan period. But the bureau spokesman said it was difficult to formulate a “one-size-fits-all” carbon reduction solution and target, owing to the “differences in the nature and operating conditions of various government bureaus and departments”.

title: In Focus | A rural city, once known for livestock, now provides China’s AI computing fuel
description: Fueled by cheap wind power and a cool climate, Inner Mongolia’s Ulanqab is turning energy produced in its pastureland into power for the AI boom.
content: For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight. Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range. Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands. As the global artificial intelligence boom fuels a scramble for more computing power and electricity, the same climate that has sustained Ulanqab’s pastoral economy is turning this Inner Mongolian city into one of China’s most coveted industrial assets. Earlier this month, Chinese renewable energy company Envision Group brought its Galaxy Campus online in Ulanqab. The AI computing facility has, at its heart, a 120,000-square-metre AI data centre, roughly the area of 20 standard football pitches, according to a company statement. Designed to accommodate up to one million AI accelerators, the campus has a planned power capacity of over two gigawatts, a scale that would make it one of the world’s largest AI computing facilities. For comparison, Colossus 2, the massive US-based AI data centre run by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, has a projected 1.5-gigawatt IT power capacity, according to a ranking by consultancy Epoch AI. Envision selected the Ulanqab location because it could pair computing infrastructure directly with renewable power, with the Galaxy Campus partly powered by Envision wind farms, according to the firm. Ulanqab accounts for about one-tenth of China’s total wind resources and one-third of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region’s, according to China’s Xinhua news agency. “Much of that wind once simply blew past, wasted,” said Yang Wenlong, a project director at Envision Group. “Now it can be turned into electricity for computing, and then into tokens.” About 67 per cent of Ulanqab’s energy was powered by green electricity, including solar power, Yang noted. A decade-long pivot Ulanqab’s shift from raising cattle and potato harvesting to the AI frontier has followed a decade-long path. In 2013, Huawei Technologies began working with the Ulanqab municipal government to expand its data centre presence there. Five years later, US tech giant Apple announced plans to host its iCloud service on data centres in the city, the same year Chinese cloud platform UCloud began building its own facility in Ulanqab. Short video giant Kuaishou initiated construction of a data centre in 2020, and completed the first phase of a centre designed for 300,000 servers several years later. Traditional data centre operators VNET, Centrin Data and Chindata have since added green, AI-focused computing projects in Ulanqab, and Hangzhou-based AI model start-up DeepSeek was reportedly set to add one gigawatt of computing capacity in the city earlier this year. As of June, Ulanqab had signed 89 data centre deals, 86 of which were AI computing projects, according to local government figures. The city has a combined 12.5 gigawatts of capacity under development or planned, three times the 4.2 gigawatts projected for Johor, the southern state of Malaysia that has emerged as one of the largest data centre sites in the Asia-Pacific region, according to recent research by investment bank Goldman Sachs. “We are no longer selling computing power; we are selling tokens,” said Liu Huansuo, deputy director of Ulanqab’s big data management bureau, referring to the industry’s preferred measure for the units of text processed by AI models. China’s appetite for those tokens has exploded in recent years. Daily consumption rose from about 100 billion at the beginning of 2024 to 100 trillion by the end of 2025, before exceeding 140 trillion in March 2026, according to government data. This surge in token demand is driving a greater need for the electricity and computing infrastructure required to produce them. For Ulanqab, the wind blowing across the grasslands is no longer merely an energy resource – it helps to power an AI query. And every AI token comes with a cost. The power economy “Every one million tokens generated requires two to three kilowatt-hours of electricity,” said Luo Xiyong of data centre operator Zhonglian Data. In Ulanqab, data centre operators have access to some of China’s cheapest power. Rates vary by supply arrangement, but some operators have secured electricity for about 0.35 yuan (US$0.05) per kilowatt-hour, less than half the roughly 0.70 yuan charged in eastern provinces. Electricity can account for 60 to 70 per cent of a data centre’s operating costs, making even modest savings significant. At full utilisation, a one-gigawatt AI computing centre might consume as much as 8.76 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity a year. Cutting the electricity cost by just 0.1 yuan per kilowatt-hour might reduce a centre’s annual power bill by about 876 million yuan. For China’s burgeoning AI industry, which is still searching for viable ways to monetise its models, cheap power is no marginal advantage – it is a central part of the business model. But it is only half the equation. The electricity consumed by computing equipment ultimately becomes heat that has to be removed. That is how Ulanqab’s cold, dry climate provides another advantage. With an annual average temperature of about 5 degrees Celsius, the city can use outside air as a natural cooling resource for much of the year, reducing reliance on energy-intensive mechanical systems and leaving more electricity available for computing. Power usage effectiveness (PUE) measures the ratio between a data centre’s total electricity consumption and the electricity delivered to its servers. A PUE of 1.0 means every watt goes directly to computing, while a higher figure indicates more power is consumed by supporting systems such as cooling and power conversion. Leading data-centre clusters in the region have a PUE below 1.15, against a national average of close to 1.5, meaning that more of each watt reaches its chips. A difference of only a few cents can translate into hundreds of millions of yuan in savings at gigawatt scale. Those efficiencies matter because the amount of electricity consumed by computing has been rapidly rising. China’s data centres consumed about 170 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 1.6 per cent of national power use, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA). By 2030, annual consumption by the sector was expected to reach about 800 billion kilowatt-hours, nearly five times 2025 levels, and account for roughly 6 per cent of national electricity use, according to Wang Hongzhi, director of the NEA. A coordinated system The race to secure electricity for AI infrastructure is not unique to China. In the US, the rapid expansion of AI data centres has raised concerns about whether existing power grids can keep pace with demand, with some projects facing delays because of a bottleneck in securing enough electricity. This is in contrast to Ulanqab, where AI giants and tech behemoths are betting that its wind and solar power, combined with a cooler climate, can provide a cheaper and more sustainable foundation for the next generation of AI infrastructure. For China, the challenge is not only generating enough electricity, but also ensuring that electricity supply and computing capacity grow in tandem. In 2026, China’s Government Work Report called for the coordinated development of computing capacity and electricity supply for the first time, reflecting Beijing’s push to better align its rapidly expanding AI infrastructure with the country’s power system. The concept, known as “computing-power and electricity coordination”, aimed to bring together electricity generation, grid capacity, energy storage and computing resources so that renewable power could be used more efficiently to support growing AI demand. Jiang Yi, spokesman for the National Development and Reform Commission, described the new power grid as providing stable, clean electricity, the computing network as the “brain” directing intelligent power-grid scheduling and renewable energy consumption, and the communications network as the “highway” supporting cross-regional computing. That vision goes beyond simply building more data centres. It requires linking electricity, computing and communications infrastructure into a more coordinated, national system. For Ulanqab, that could make its advantages more valuable. Its wind farms provide renewable electricity, data centres then convert that power into computing capacity, and a national network could help deliver that capacity to users far beyond Inner Mongolia. But China’s computing boom has created another challenge: not all that capacity is being used. While demand for AI computing is surging in some of the country’s biggest technology centres, large amounts of capacity elsewhere remain underused, leaving servers, power infrastructure and expensive data centre facilities running below their potential. Data from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT) puts the gap in stark terms. In 2025, China’s intelligent-computing centres had about 3.8 billion card-hours of intelligent-computing capacity available, but only about 1.4 billion card-hours were actually used, putting utilisation at just 36.8 per cent. CAICT has called for closer coordination between computing supply and demand, including better scheduling of computing resources and more precise matching between users and available capacity. The mismatch reflects the geography of China’s computing buildout. Regions such as Ulanqab have attracted data centres because of cheap electricity, abundant land and favourable climates, while much of the demand for AI computing remains concentrated in China’s eastern cities and affluent regions, where technology companies and users are based. Moving up the value chain For Ulanqab, the next challenge is therefore not simply building more servers, but making sure those servers are connected to real demand. The city is now seeking to move up the AI value chain. Under a three-year action plan for 2026-28, Ulanqab plans to expand computing capacity to more than 200,000 petaflops – a measurement of computing capacity – by 2026 and develop a platform for trading and settling AI tokens. The plan calls for Ulanqab to evolve from a data centre hub into a broader computing and AI services centre, focusing on green computing for large AI model training and inference, while encouraging investment in liquid cooling, computing hardware, AI software and talent. The aim is to capture more value from its renewable power: not simply selling electricity or computing capacity, but turning that power into AI computing and ultimately into the tokens generated by AI models. For a user sitting thousands of kilometres away, an AI query may take only seconds to answer. Behind that response, however, is a chain of infrastructure stretching back to places such as Ulanqab: servers drawing electricity, cooling systems removing heat and wind turbines turning the movement of air across the grasslands into power. The next time someone asks a chatbot a question, part of the answer may begin with the wind passing through the grasslands of Inner Mongolia – transformed first into electricity, then computing power and finally into the words that appear on a screen.

title: Style Edit: Chanel’s fall/winter 2026 pre-collection gives womenswear a youthful spin
description: Artistic director Matthieu Blazy loosens formal codes, shortens hemlines and adds colour, echoing founder Gabrielle Chanel’s own playful spirit.
content: It has only been a year since Matthieu Blazy showed his first collection for Chanel, but the Blazy effect, as fashion insiders like to call it, is showing no signs of waning. Since his arrival, the designer has reimagined Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel’s enduring legacy with a playful, youthful spirit that appeals to modern women. Signatures like the tweed suit are transformed into cool, contemporary staples that are versatile and easy to wear, while each collection exudes luxury through the maison’s exquisite craftsmanship and artisanal touches. While Coco’s designs liberated the female body, Blazy’s are helping women reclaim their identity and power in today’s world. This vision continues in the Chanel fall/winter 2026 pre-collection, which is designed for women in motion. Blazy returns to familiar Chanel codes and wardrobe essentials, but re-envisages them through the eyes of everyday heroines and cinema icons walking the streets of Paris. Elegant and self-assured, the collection features soft, fluid pieces such as dresses and silk scarves adorned with prints of the city. Office dressing takes on a more nonchalant attitude with relaxed tailoring, including a signature suit with a skirt cut slightly lower on the hip, styled with shirttails left free and hands in pockets. Chanel’s must-have tweeds are available in simple, whisper-light textures or embellished. A classic jacket-and-skirt ensemble is elevated in quilted denim, while other essentials include supple suede skirts, two-tone corduroy revisited in tweed, multicolour fantasy knits and shearling. The youthful spirit that has become a Blazy hallmark is also evident in shorter hemlines, cropped, fitted jackets and ruffled collars. Modern floral prints, including poppies, bloom across full-skirted dresses, shirts and silk satin pyjamas. A muted, timeless palette of black, navy, beige, denim and grey anchors the collection. Rounding off the look is a covetable collection of accessories that combine Blazy’s playful spirit with the maison’s exceptional craftsmanship. Bag silhouettes are both new and familiar – featuring archival favourites, soft hobos, versatile bucket shapes and the new flap bag, now in a mini format. Pearl and double-C earrings catch the light while chunky link chains trace the neckline. Shoes blend masculine and feminine sensibilities. Chanel’s graphic two-tone is reborn as strappy, square-toed heels, while loafers are reimagined as slingbacks. The double C logo goes beyond simple ornamentation and becomes functional, blending with the wider collection as belt and strap loops. Every piece, from the ready-to-wear down to the shoes, is dynamic and designed for movement, making it the perfect choice for women on the go.

title: Alibaba’s top executives buy US$15m in shares in vote of confidence after AI fundraising
description: The personal investments from Joe Tsai and Eddie Wu follow firm’s 710 million share sale, one of China’s largest AI fundraising efforts.
content: The top two executives at Alibaba Group Holding bought a combined HK$120 million (US$15.3 million) worth of the company’s ordinary shares on Monday in a vote of confidence after the tech giant unveiled one of China’s biggest fundraising rounds dedicated to AI. The share placement, the first since Alibaba’s listing in Hong Kong in 2019, was oversubscribed three times amid strong investor sentiment, according to people familiar with the situation, reflecting what analysts said was “stronger growth visibility” at the company. Group chairman Joe Tsai paid roughly HK$80 million for 720,000 shares, while CEO Eddie Wu Yongming bought 350,000 units for around HK$40 million, according to Hong Kong stock market filings on Monday afternoon. The personal investments, done via the purchase of ordinary shares from the stock market, were separate from Alibaba’s share issuance plan. The 710 million newly issued shares represented around 3.7 per cent of the company’s 19.17 billion total outstanding shares, according to its stock exchange filing Monday morning. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. The order book exceeded the US$10 billion target shortly after launch, attracting US$28 billion in demand, according to the sources. Anchor demand came from leading sovereign wealth funds across the Middle East, Europe and Asia, they said. Long-term investors and sovereign wealth funds accounted for nearly US$6 billion of the bids and secured US$4 billion of the final allocation, one source added. CICC, HSBC, Morgan Stanley and UBS were facilitating the placement, which was expected to close on Wednesday, according to the filing. Alibaba announced the share sale on Sunday, pledging to allocate all proceeds towards investing in its “full-stack AI capabilities” and extending its “global AI leadership”. The company is working to pivot from an e-commerce powerhouse into a full-stack AI player with businesses spanning chips, computing infrastructure, large language models and AI applications. Its Qwen AI model family recently surpassed 3 billion global downloads, Alibaba said this month, while its semiconductor unit, T-Head, also began commercial-scale deployment of its Zhenwu M890 AI processor. The Zhenwu chips have reached more than 650 external customers in over 20 industries, including autonomous driving and financial services. The stock sale “may initially weigh on sentiment” partly due to “immediate dilution and rising depreciation associated with AI infrastructure deployment”, Bank of America Merrill Lynch (BofA) analysts including Joyce Ju wrote in a Monday note. Uncertainties over the duration of capital spending and the possibility of further external funding also added to the concerns, they said. Alibaba’s Hong Kong shares closed down 8.5 per cent to HK$112.50 on Monday. Its New York-listed stock fell 2.2 per cent in the pre-market. Despite the headwinds, BofA maintained a “constructive” view on Alibaba, citing “stronger growth visibility”. Robust customer demand, accelerating revenue and improved AI inference efficiency may allow incremental cloud earnings to grow faster than the associated depreciation burden over time, the analysts noted. Nomura analysts Shi Jialong and Rachel Guo said in a Monday report that they “continue to view Alibaba as one of the best-positioned companies in China’s AI ecosystem because of its full-stack capabilities spanning foundation models, model as a service, cloud infrastructure and proprietary AI chips”. The capital boost comes as Alibaba ramps up spending. Last week, the company reported a 45 per cent year on year jump in April to June quarterly revenue in its cloud and AI operations. Capital expenditure expanded 75 per cent from a year earlier to 67.7 billion yuan (US$10 billion). Alibaba’s overall adjusted earnings before interest, taxes and amortisation (EBITA) – a key measure of operating profit – dropped by 30 per cent year on year to 27.3 billion yuan, beating the analyst consensus forecast of 26.6 billion yuan. However, its latest quarterly profit plunged 75 per cent year on year. Last week during the earnings call, CEO Wu said the company had already spent 190 billion yuan in capital expenditure by the end of June, halfway through a three-year commitment of 380 billion yuan in AI infrastructure investment announced in February 2025. The company expected its AI investments to break even within three years, with the payback period potentially shortened to about two years as gross margins continued to rise, Wu said.

title: Publisher’s Pen | Remembering Zhu Rongji and understanding his legacy
description: The late Chinese premier showed genuine love and support for Hong Kong and kept ‘one country, two systems’ dear to his heart.
content: “History doesn’t repeat itself but it often rhymes.” This famous quote, widely attributed to Mark Twain, keeps playing in my mind as China mourns the death of former premier Zhu Rongji and reflects on his legacy. It was early afternoon on August 12 when I received a message from a friend on the mainland that made my heart sink: “Our much-respected Premier Zhu left us this morning!” As we anxiously waited for the official confirmation that would launch us into a frantically busy news day, my mind went back to those years when I, as a journalist, had multiple opportunities to encounter Zhu up close. I was as impressed by his statesmanship, wisdom and wit on the international stage as I was touched by the genuine love he showed Hong Kong. Zhu became the fifth premier of China in March 1998 as the country was undergoing a tremendous transformation from decades of a planned economy to a “market economy with Chinese characteristics” under then-president Jiang Zemin. It was only about nine months after Hong Kong’s return to Chinese sovereignty following more than a century of British colonial rule. It was an uncertain but exciting time, when the “one country, two systems” governing principle for Hong Kong was being rolled out. The implementation of the special formula designed by paramount leader Deng Xiaoping and officially recognised in China’s constitution – which empowered the establishment of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region and the legislation of the Basic Law – was well received but still a work in progress. Back then there were plenty of concerns, doubts and political narratives about it being “over” for Hong Kong, and some of that remains to this day, although the facts speak louder about the progress the city has made and its transformation for the better after its return to the motherland. Zhu and Jiang kept one country, two systems dear to their hearts, and China’s current leadership has neither changed that approach nor intends to. In his inaugural press conference as premier in 1998, Zhu made his stance clear: he loved Hong Kong and always hoped to visit the city again. Whether he would be welcomed or met with protests, or whatever post-handover activities Hongkongers might organise, “[all] must follow Hong Kong’s Basic Law and relevant laws”, Zhu declared. He was also firm about abiding by the Communist Party leadership’s decisions, reiterating they would firmly stick to their stance on the 1989 political turmoil. While Zhu was a strong reformer, he was also a man of unyielding principle, drawing a red line for Hong Kong in following the law. He dismissed wishful thinking in the West that the break-up of the Soviet Union would lead to a similar change of China’s socialist system. Zhu visited Hong Kong four times before and after 1997, each time to a warm welcome. Zhu was the mastermind behind Beijing’s backing for Hong Kong’s unprecedented fight against big “financial crocodiles” in 1998, when international speculators, in particular American billionaire George Soros, launched attacks on the Hong Kong dollar. Over two turbulent weeks, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority bought back up to HK$118 billion (US$15 billion) in stocks and futures, eventually defeating Soros. Zhu’s full support meant a lot to Hong Kong and its first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, but perhaps more importantly, the premier and the Beijing leadership realised right away that post-1997 Hong Kong was no longer part of the so-called “Western camp”. This reality check prompted Beijing to vigilantly safeguard Hong Kong’s financial security. The matter of Hong Kong’s financial stability becoming a part of national security can thus be traced back to 1998 – it is not something that came about all of a sudden after the city’s implementation of the national security law in 2020. Zhu was never one to mince words, and his candid criticism of Hong Kong’s slow policymaking made headlines when filibustering in the Legislative Council by opposition pan-democrats was a common practice. Democracy did not mean “talks without decisions, decisions without actions”, he warned. Those were the days when Hong Kong reporters, myself included, chased after him wherever he went around the world. We were relentless, and some of us would not let him go when we doorstepped him until we realised he was just taking a break from a long meeting to go to the washroom. I still vividly remember the time, towards the end of Zhu’s five-year term, when I had the nerve to call out loud to him at an event: “Will you serve a second term?” China’s leaders at the time were not quite used to the aggressive style of Hong Kong reporters, and he may well have thought we were “crazy”, but he smiled and waved at us before heading into his next meeting. There was no second term; Zhu retired in 2003. He is gone now, but his remarks resonate to this day in Beijing’s unchanged expectations and core policies for Hong Kong. During Zhu’s time, China successfully fought to prevail and progress amid the Western narrative about an “end of history” after the collapse of the Soviet Union. Under President Xi Jinping’s leadership today, China, including Hong Kong, is facing tremendous geopolitical and economic challenges, but Beijing’s support for the city has not wavered. History does not necessarily repeat itself in exactly the same way because times change; rather, it rhymes with similarities and the lessons can be identical. For Hong Kong, history rhymes by embracing one country while enhancing two systems.

title: Malaysian villages shaken as blasts rock southern Thailand
description: Malaysians near the Thai border heard blasts and saw flashes as insurgent attacks hit 21 districts, injuring at least three people.
content: Residents of Malaysian villages near the Thailand border were left shaken this weekend after hearing loud booms and seeing flashes of light across the frontier, as Thai authorities confirmed more than 50 coordinated attacks on Saturday night. The blasts, heard in Kampung Lubok Gong and Kampung Tersang in Malaysia’s Kelantan state, coincided with a wave of near-simultaneous attacks across 21 districts in Thailand’s Narathiwat, Pattani and Yala provinces beginning around 8pm local time on Saturday, according to Thailand’s Internal Security Operations Command. Preliminary reports indicated three civilians were injured and they were reported to be recovering on Sunday, though authorities said they were still compiling a full casualty count given the scale of the incidents. On the Malaysian side of the border, Ismail Abdul Rahman, 50, of Kampung Lubok Gong, and Malik Zulkarnain, 35, of Kampung Tersang, told national news agency Bernama that the booms were unmistakable. “They were very loud, like booms in the sky during a lightning storm. The house felt as though it was shaking, and we immediately stayed alert,” Ismail said, adding that he kept his family indoors until the noise abated. Malik said the sound was “clearly audible from across the border”, prompting him and his neighbours to stay inside. The violence primarily involved small bombs, arson and other forms of property damage. The highest-profile target was a 7-Eleven convenience store in Pattani. A video circulating on social media appeared to show armed men outside the store while customers and workers fled before it was set on fire. A bomb that damaged rail tracks in Narathiwat forced the suspension of local and long-distance services. It was not clear when they would be restored. As has often been the case with such incidents, no group was immediately publicly blamed or claimed responsibility for the actions. However, such attacks are generally believed to be carried out by the Barisan Revolusi Nasional Melayu Patani, or BRN. It is the major insurgent group in the south with the organisational means and support to stage such an action. It is also the group with which the Thai government has been holding on-again, off-again peace talks. Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul held an urgent meeting on Sunday with high-level security officials in response to the coordinated violence. Security forces had been deployed to inspect affected sites, collect evidence and track down suspects, officials said. Despite the alarm on the Malaysian side, checks by reporters at the Rantau Panjang Immigration, Customs, Quarantine and Security Complex on Sunday morning found operations proceeding as usual, with no disruption to cross-border traffic. Kelantan police chief Mohd Yusoff Mamat confirmed there were no reports of Malaysians affected by the attacks, but urged caution. “Malaysians are urged to exercise caution and postpone travel to the affected areas, especially if there is no urgent need,” he said, adding that those who must travel to Thailand should monitor the security situation and remain vigilant. He said the advice aligned with that of the foreign ministry, which did not bar travel to Thailand but urged precaution. The three southernmost provinces are the only ones with Muslim majorities in predominantly Buddhist Thailand and the BRN has said that it is seeking self-rule for them. Muslim residents have long complained of being treated like second-class citizens in Thailand, and separatist movements have been periodically active for decades. Insurgent violence escalated sharply in 2004 and was met with heavy-handed crackdowns, further fuelling discontent. According to Deep South Watch, a think tank based at the Prince of Songkla University’s campus in Pattani, 7,837 people have died in the violence in the past 22 years. The last major flare-up came in July, when about 10 attackers opened fire and threw pipe bombs at soldiers at a security checkpoint in Narathiwat. Five paramilitary soldiers were killed and six civilians were wounded, including a 10-year-old boy. Don Pathan, an independent security analyst, said the BRN carried out attacks largely for leverage as it negotiated with the Thai government. “From the ground, BRN combatants are turned off by the boasting of military officials and wanted to use the spike in violence to demonstrate their capabilities,” Pathan said. “Many of the targets in these latest incidents were civilians, but BRN combatants were not after body counts. They want to send a stern message to the Thais of what they are capable of doing.” Reporting by The Star and Associated Press

title: Shein seeks to raise up to US$1.76 billion in Hong Kong initial public offering
description: Based on maximum offer price, IPO would value online fast-fashion retailer at over US$27 billion.
content: Fast-fashion retailer Shein Global Holdings is seeking to raise as much as HK$13.85 billion (US$1.76 billion) in a Hong Kong initial public offering that was initially planned four years ago. Shein will sell 279 million shares at HK$47.60 to HK$49.50 each, according to a filing to the city’s stock exchange on Monday. The company began taking investor orders on Monday, with trading expected to start on September 1. Cornerstone investors – who will get guaranteed allocations in exchange for holding the stock for at least six months – have agreed to buy about US$383 million worth of Shein shares. They include Boyu Capital, Tiger Global, General Atlantic, Tencent Holdings, Greenwoods, Taikang Life and UBS. The cornerstone tranche accounted for up to 22.5 per cent of the total funds to be raised, the online fashion platform said. Shein attracted HK$3.58 billion in first-day margin orders for its retail tranche by 5pm, making its HK$1.39 billion public offer 1.6 times oversubscribed, according to data from several brokerages. The IPO would value the company at over US$27 billion, based on the maximum offer price. That would be a significant markdown from its peak valuation of nearly US$100 billion in 2022, as well as its Series D+ funding valuation of around US$64 billion in 2023. The Singapore-headquartered retailer – which was founded in Nanjing, capital of east China’s Jiangsu province – faces multiple headwinds including intense competition, tariffs and regulatory scrutiny. Those challenges have weighed heavily on its revenue growth and profitability, further putting pressure on its valuation. Meanwhile, valuations of industry peers such as Zara’s parent company Inditex and H&M have bounced back significantly since last year. Shein rival PDD Holdings, owner of shopping platform Temu, is valued at a price-to-earnings ratio of nine. Shein will be required to issue additional shares to some pre-IPO investors if its final valuation falls below pre-agreed thresholds, its prospectus said, although specific terms were not disclosed. The company’s financial performance has shown signs of strain. In the first quarter of this year, Shein’s revenue growth nearly stalled, rising only 1.1 per cent year on year to US$9.05 billion. The company also swung to a net loss of US$99 million with an operating profit of US$258 million – down about 25.9 per cent year on year – and its operating margin shrank to 2.9 per cent, according to the prospectus. Shein has said the United States’ decision last year to end the “de minimis” tariff exemption for small packages valued at under US$800 had adversely affected its US sales growth and net revenue. The company added that its US market revenue in the first quarter fell 14.3 per cent year on year. Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs are joint sponsors of Shein’s IPO, while Haitong International Securities, UBS, HSBC, Merrill Lynch (Asia-Pacific), Banco Santander and East West Bank are the joint bookrunners, according to its prospectus.

title: From ‘Jurassic Park’ fan to Hong Kong fossil expert: Natalia Jagielska’s unique journey
description: The palaeontologist blends science and art, researching ancient dinosaurs while illustrating them.
content:
At first sight, Natalia Jagielska’s workspace seems like a mix between a science lab and an art studio. On one side, she studies models of dinosaurs that lived 200 million years ago; on the other, she makes “cute” digital drawings of these ancient creatures.
Jagielska is 28 years old and works as a postdoctoral researcher in palaeontology at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK).
She believes that her two jobs go hand in hand. Besides her research, she also does freelance illustration and gives science advice for TV shows, books and video games.
She was born in Poland and got her master’s degree in Earth science from the University of Manchester. Then, she earned her PhD in fossils at the University of Edinburgh. She became interested in Chinese fossils, and that brought her to Asia.
“There are a lot of sites across China and Hong Kong which have amazing fossils that have not been described yet,” Jagielska said.
Hong Kong has rocks dating to the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. In parts of the New Territories, such as Port Island and Tolo Bay, fossils of ammonites and even a dinosaur have been found. Researchers are still figuring out what type of dinosaur it is.
Jagielska said the soil here is not as rich in discoveries as other areas, such as Shenzhen and Liaoning province.
Since 1996, when the first “fluffy” (feathered) dinosaur was discovered in China’s northeastern Liaoning province, the country has become a destination for palaeontologists.
This discovery showed that dinosaurs were not just scaly reptiles. Many were actually like birds, with pigmented feathers.
It is not easy being a woman in the predominantly male field of science, Jagielska said.
She admires Mary Anning, a 19th century English fossil collector and palaeontologist who worked in southwest England. She discovered the first complete ichthyosaur skeleton and the first pterosaur specimen in Britain.
Having grown up with the Jurassic Park films, Jagielska found it a poetic full-circle moment to work as a scientific consultant for the Jurassic World Evolution 3 video game.
She said the biggest mistake the media makes about dinosaurs is not mentioning their feathers.
The size of these dinosaurs is often wrong, too. “Scary creatures like velociraptors … were actually just slightly bigger than a corgi,” she said.
It is a tough field of science to make it in, Jagielska said. But it is one with many potential career pathways into research, museums, consultancy or even petroleum companies, which Jagielska had previously tried but hated.
“Prepare for failure,” she said to those who are curious about going into palaeontology.
“But when you get lucky, it’s very rewarding. You get to travel, meet interesting people and make tiny kids very happy.”

title: Kazakhstan election: pro-Tokayev party wins landslide as president hints at staying on
description: The Adilet party secured a sweeping victory with over 71 per cent of votes as Tokayev says he has the legal right to seek re-election.
content: A party led by allies of Kazakhstan President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev won a landslide in parliamentary elections on Sunday, hours after he hinted that he may stay in power beyond his current term. The Adilet party won 71.2 per cent of votes in the election to a new single-chamber parliament, Kazakhstan’s central election commission said on Monday. The Auyl party representing agrarian interests was second with 6.3 per cent. “I have the right to be re‑elected in accordance with the law,” Tokayev told reporters earlier, after casting his vote, in response to a question on whether he would seek another term. “Perhaps next year I’ll be able to give you a more specific answer.” Adilet, which means Justice, is led by one of Tokayev’s former top aides with backing from business leaders who have gained influence during his presidency. It was founded only in May, and the former ruling Amanat party, which won the 2023 parliamentary elections, announced in June that it was merging with Adilet. Five of the seven parties that contested the election cleared the 5 per cent threshold for entry to the parliament, with 145 seats allocated by party list for a five-year term. Voter turnout was 74.1 per cent, according to the election commission. The new chamber is the latest element of a constitutional overhaul initiated by Tokayev following deadly 2022 riots that he called an attempted coup in the giant former Soviet republic of about 20 million people. It replaces the previous bicameral parliament, following a referendum in March that also established the post of vice-president, who would succeed the head of state in the event of an early departure from office. Tokayev previously revised the constitution in 2022 to limit the presidency to a single seven-year term in Central Asia’s largest energy producer, which borders Russia and China. He secured re-election in an early ballot under the new system and is due to stand down in 2029. Kazakhstan’s Constitutional Court ruled last month, though, that he is eligible to seek another term because the latest reforms meant the presidential vote would “be considered as the first election or appointment”. Tokayev, 73, said he would announce his nominee for vice-president within the next 10 days. The government would formally resign after the election of the new parliament and there could be changes in some positions, he said in comments to reporters posted by his press office on social media. Under Tokayev, Kazakhstan’s government has supported changes in ownership of large metals producers, a wealth transition that has fostered the rise of a new elite. Following the 2022 violence, which was put down with help from Russian troops, Tokayev moved to consolidate power by dismantling the political legacy of his long-serving predecessor Nursultan Nazarbayev, who handed over power to him in 2019.

title: Hong Kong’s Nocturnal Stationery sparks a quiet connection revolution
description: The shop offers unique, art-inspired stationery, heartfelt community connection and handcrafted design.
content:
In a quiet corner of Hong Kong’s Tsuen Wan district is a stationery shop that offers far more than paper and ink.
At Nocturnal Stationery, people find many fun things. Some crayons look like volcanic rocks and handmade wooden stools shaped like the Chinese character for “moon” (月).
When the stools are next to each other, they spell the word for “friends” (朋).
Beyond the quirky wares he sells, shop owner To Chun-pong has crafted this space to be a hub for connection.
“I try to remember what each customer likes, or at the very least, I make sure to remember who they are. I want every visit to feel like they are coming to see a friend,” the 42-year-old shopkeeper explained.
According to To, this hidden shop’s main appeal for customers is the intimacy and conversation it provides, even outside its normal business hours.
“Back then, even if it was 11pm or the middle of the night, if I wasn’t asleep yet, I would chat with them or help them place orders,” he said.
“Over time, this built a real bond ... between the customers and me.”
Nocturnal’s rows of pens and notebooks are sourced from around the globe.
For To, stationery items are an art form that can compose what he calls “a scenery on the desk”.
“It’s not just something to be used; it can also be a piece of decor,” To said.
“When people say they can get by without stationery, that’s not necessarily true – it might just be that you haven’t realised the impact stationery has on you yet.”
When the Covid-19 pandemic affected To’s job as a graphic designer, he used his free time to learn about e-commerce.
This paved the way for starting an online stationery business, which later became a real store in 2024.
“I wanted to make it more convenient for students to buy stationery. That was the starting point, though of course, I had my own ideas about sourcing more unique items,” To said.
He has a good sense of design, shown in the shop’s bestselling items.
These include memo pads that look and smell like wood. They also include crayons that have the colours of real mountains, lakes and oceans.
He has partnered with Musgrave, a century-old American pencil giant, to launch a set of navy blue pencils.
Embossed in gold is his life motto: “Let the good things connect us.”
This concept has since expanded to include postcards, bookmarks and tote bags.
Nocturnal’s charm has turned many browsers into regulars; some have even become collaborators. Its signature wooden stools, for instance, were a gift from a neighbourhood craftsman who visited the shop for a chat.
“It turns out he has a studio nearby. I asked if he’d be interested in collaborating on a chair themed around our weekend activities,” To recalled.
“I shared my ideas, and he translated them into physical form – proportioned perfectly to resemble a Chinese character.”
While similar nooks exist in other housing estates, To wants this shop to become a fixture of the Tsuen King Circuit neighbourhood.

title: Record non-DSE admissions to Hong Kong’s universities spark calls for quotas
description: Number of non-DSE students in Hong Kong public universities surges 63 per cent, while local exam-takers fall to 72 per cent of intake.
content: Hong Kong public universities have admitted a record number of students applying outside the local exam system, with the intake surging by 63 per cent over seven years to account for nearly 30 per cent of the 15,000 government-funded places, the South China Morning Post has found. Meanwhile, the intake of home-grown students taking the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) exam has dropped by 7 per cent, causing its proportion to fall from 82 per cent to 72 per cent, sparking calls for a cap on admissions through alternative qualifications to safeguard local interests. “The decrease in places for DSE students results in driving up admission scores,” said Ng Po-shing, a student guidance consultant at Hok Yau Club and vice-principal of a secondary school. “More students are complaining that they failed to get into certain programmes though they met the median score in the previous cohort.” The Diploma of Secondary Education is the city’s main university entrance examination. The SCMP isolated the trends after analysing data sets from the University Grants Committee (UGC) on first-year-first-degree students admitted with DSE and non-DSE qualifications across all eight government-funded universities from 2019-20 to 2025-26. According to the data, non-DSE admissions to government-funded Year One university places have shown an upward trend in both overall numbers and proportions over six years. Admissions for students via non-DSE routes jumped from 2,706 in 2019-20 to 4,401 in 2025-26, marking a 63 per cent increase. Their share took up only 18 per cent of the total funded university places in 2019-20, but jumped to 22 per cent in 2022-23 and reached 28 per cent in 2025-26. The non-DSE route refers to students sitting the International Baccalaureate (IB), GCE A-levels or International A-levels from Hong Kong’s international, private independent and Direct Subsidy Scheme schools, as well as students who studied overseas but returned to Hong Kong’s universities, and talented local students under the School Nominations Direct Admission Scheme (SNDAS). Conversely, admissions for DSE students to Year One places have shown a declining trend in both overall numbers and proportions. The number of admitted candidates dropped from 12,355 in 2019-20 to 11,503 in 2025-26, marking a 7 per cent fall. Their share across the eight universities dropped significantly over the same period, from 82 per cent to a trough of 72 per cent this year. While 73 per cent of DSE students who attained general admission requirements secured a spot in public universities in 2019, that rate dropped to 70 per cent in 2025. The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and the University of Hong Kong (HKU) recorded the lowest DSE student intake by percentage. HKUST’s intake comprised only 61 per cent in 2025-26 while HKU took in 62 per cent, down from 83 per cent and 78 per cent, respectively, seven years ago. Over the same period, the number of non-DSE students admitted by HKUST surged by 156 per cent, while HKU recorded an 87 per cent increase. The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) was the sole outlier, with its DSE intake edging up to 86 per cent from 84 per cent seven years ago. The remaining five public universities all recorded declines in local exam admissions over the same period. An HKUST spokesman said the university did not give preferential treatment based on qualification type or application route, adding that all candidates were assessed independently to ensure fairness and consistency. An HKU spokesman said its shift was due to diversified educational pathways in Hong Kong, noting that the university also accepted the highest number of students via SNDAS among all institutions. Education consultant Ng said students from non-DSE curricula often came from families who could afford higher tuition fees and were well equipped to secure good grades, leading to universities preferring to admit them over DSE students, thereby reinforcing their socio-economic status. “Students with good backgrounds enjoy more resources and then obtain good grades, resulting in good prospects and continued high socio-economic backgrounds or vice versa,” he said. Due to the shrinking share of DSE students taking up government-funded places, Ng predicted that future candidates might need to secure higher marks to enter public universities. Lee Yi-ying, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Subsidised Secondary Schools Council, called the DSE a “Hong Kong brand” and said local universities should have greater confidence in admitting DSE students. Both Ng and Lee observed that candidates securing median admission scores last year – previously considered competitive – still failed to gain entry into certain programmes, which they believed was partly a result of the growing number of non-DSE student admissions. Both called for a benchmark quota to prevent universities from endlessly expanding alternative admissions, with Lee suggesting that at least 80 per cent of places be reserved for DSE candidates to protect local interests. A spokesman for the Education Bureau dismissed any direct correlation with the appeal of the DSE. “Under the university principle of merit-based admission, this phenomenon reflects changes in students’ personal considerations regarding their study destination, and has no direct relationship with the overall attractiveness of the DSE curriculum,” he said. “Every year, a significant number of top DSE candidates choose to apply directly to prestigious overseas universities or top mainland [Chinese] institutions using their results, with their higher education goals far from being limited to local UGC-funded places. “In contrast, some students enrolled in non-local curricula such as IB or GCE A-levels in recent years may have shifted to staying in Hong Kong for higher education due to changes in the global situation or personal planning.” He noted that the proportion of DSE students entering publicly funded university places had largely remained at a high level of more than 70 per cent.

title: Letters from readers about teachers, the summer holiday and their favourite things
description: Students argue for choosing their own teachers, explain how they’re spending their summer months and share their best school subjects.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your letters using this form .
Ayra Soni and Shrija Singh (aged 9), Kowloon Junior School
Students should be able to choose their teachers because they could choose a teacher who likes the same things they like. Wouldn’t you like it if you had a teacher who has similar hobbies?
If students could choose their own teachers, they would enjoy going to school more. We believe it would help students have happy, fun, and educational days.
Students would probably work harder because they would have fun. I think most of us would enjoy being able to choose our teachers.
Karen Zhang Chin-wing (aged 9), Po Leung Kuk Camoes Tan Siu Lin Primary School
I was so excited for the summer holidays. This year, my parents didn’t sign me up for classes. Instead, I could do whatever I wanted.
I am preparing for a maths competition. I have already done five years’ worth of past papers.
I have also been reading the Harry Potter books; I read the first three books in about one week. I like them because they’re mysterious and interesting. I persuaded my mum to give me the fourth book, too. She said she would give me the other books for Christmas.
Aubrey Fung San-yuet (aged 9), CPC Yao Dao Primary School
My favourite school subject is science because it is very interesting.
