title: Advice: My parents are glued to their phones and ignore me and my problems
description: On this page, you’ll find advice from our team of psychologists to help you through all the ups and downs of life.
content:
Your desire to share your school life and connect with your parents is natural. Your disappointment and frustration are completely understandable. There is nothing wrong with how you feel.
Go for a quick walk to process how you feel. Try writing down your thoughts. Then, practise saying how you feel out loud in the mirror to build confidence. These steps will make it easier to express yourself clearly and increase the likelihood that your message will be received well.
Some parents are busy with work. They might not realise how much you need attention. But that does not mean they don’t care. They might just need a gentle reminder. Be patient with them.
Choose a peaceful moment when your parents are clearly not busy, like after a meal or during a weekend walk. You can say something simple, like “Hey, can we chat for 10 minutes? I miss talking with you. It’s important to me.” These small steps help everyone feel more relaxed.
Try other ways to communicate: maybe a quick message, voice note, video or short letter. This gives your parents time to think and reply when they are ready.
If things do not improve, you can speak to a trusted teacher, school counsellor or another adult you feel comfortable with.
This question was answered by clinical psychologists from Shall We Talk, a mental health initiative under the Department of Health launched with the Advisory Committee on Mental Health

title: Yuan, Hong Kong dollar bonds surge as issuers seek cheaper funding amid rising US costs
description: Issuance of dim sum, panda and wonton bonds accelerates as Beijing promotes the yuan’s global use and deeper cross-border access broadens demand.
content: Hong Kong and mainland China are set to see continued growth in bond issuance denominated in Hong Kong dollars or the yuan through the rest of the year, as issuers reduce their reliance on US dollar-denominated bonds and seek cheaper funding costs, according to a senior executive at Standard Chartered Bank. “As US dollar funding costs have increased, many bond issuers” have been turning to bonds denominated in other currencies to secure lower borrowing costs, said David Yim Sau-king, head of debt capital markets for Greater China and north Asia at Standard Chartered Bank. “This trend would benefit yuan bonds and Hong Kong dollar bonds.” The yield on the US 30-year Treasury bond reached 5.29 per cent last week, its highest level since 2007. By contrast, the yield on Chinese sovereign bonds was 2.18 per cent on Friday, near the lowest level in more than a year amid slower economic growth. Previously, most international firms focused on issuing US-dollar-denominated bonds because bond markets denominated in other currencies were not sufficiently deep, Yim said. The tide has turned in recent years, he said, as Beijing’s efforts to promote the internationalisation of the yuan have led more overseas companies to consider issuing yuan-denominated bonds this year. Dim sum bonds, referring to offshore yuan-denominated bonds issued in Hong Kong or other overseas markets, reached 683.04 billion yuan (US$101.59 billion) in issuance this year as of August 14 – up 46 per cent, year on year, Yim said. The rapid growth of the dim sum and panda bonds is straightforward, as companies can raise funds much more cheaply in yuan than in the US dollar David Yim Sau-king, Standard Chartered Bank Panda bonds, which are onshore yuan-denominated bonds issued by international firms in mainland China, rose even higher, with an 80 per cent year-on-year increase to 199.68 billion yuan during the same period. “The rapid growth of the dim sum and panda bonds is straightforward, as companies can raise funds much more cheaply in yuan than in the US dollar,” Yim said, adding that it was also because of how the proceeds could be used. “These international companies are now more willing to issue bonds in yuan, as they can use the currency to settle trade or investment.” Wonton bonds, which refer to Hong Kong dollar bonds issued by international firms, are also on the rise because the Hong Kong government has supported the development of the Hong Kong dollar bond market, Yim said. The term “wonton bond” is a play on “dim sum bond” and refers to a Hong Kong dollar-denominated bond issued by an overseas borrower. The amount of wonton bonds issued this year through August 14 stood at HK$671.42 billion (US$85.64 billion), up 76 per cent from the same period a year earlier. “The Bond Connect [programme] also helps to encourage bond issuance in both Hong Kong and on the mainland, as the scheme allows two-way capital flows and adds depth to the bond markets of Hong Kong and mainland China,” Yim added.

title: Ageless Hong Kong women outrigger canoe paddlers more than happy to keep on going
description: A six-paddler female team are among the city’s 43-strong squad taking part in all categories at the World Sprint Championships in Singapore.
content: For a few hardy Hong Kong outrigger canoe paddlers, non-professional athletes in their fifties and sixties taking part in the International Va’a Federation (IVF) World Sprint Championships in Singapore this month, age is “definitely” just a number. “For me, it’s not about proving that I can compete despite my age,” said Adrienne Ng, 54, one of four paddlers who spoke to the South China Morning Post before departing for the tournament at Marina Bay. “It is about proving to myself that there is still so much I can achieve because of the experience, strength and confidence that come with it.” Fellow paddler Polly Snaith started with “a bit of dragon boating and some outrigging” on and off 30 years ago. A bad back injury led to a decade-long absence from the sport for her, and she revisited paddling only in 2017. What was meant to be a “take it easy and very wary of injury” approach quickly became something a lot more serious after the 60-year-old artist also started surf-skiing in 2019. View this post on Instagram A post shared by HK Va’a World Championships 2026 (@hk_vaa_internationals) “I am really excited to experience new waters and races around the world with my paddling mates; we are quite a gang of over 50s,” said Snaith, who is a part of the OC6, or six paddlers, crew. “Queen Lily Race in Hawaii is on the cards for 2027!” Outrigger canoes were originally developed thousands of years ago in Southeast Asia. These seaworthy watercraft were used for transport, enabling ancestral voyagers to migrate across vast stretches of the Pacific and Indian oceans, reaching as far as Hawaii, Tahiti, and Madagascar. Today, it is a growing club sport in which enthusiasts in Hong Kong can participate through local groups including the Victoria Recreation Club (VRC) and the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club. In Singapore, a 43-strong Hong Kong team is competing across the full spectrum of the sport, from solo racing through to six- and 12-person crews, and from elite through to Masters 60+, signalling the growth of outrigger canoeing from a niche pursuit into a sport with some serious and genuine depth in Hong Kong. Among the city’s largest-ever squad fielded at any IVF World Championships are the women’s Masters contingent – women in their fifties and sixties who trained around their full-time jobs, often before sunrise, and funded their own international racing. “I believe you should continue to challenge yourself at every stage of life, but I also believe that the people around you are a huge part of what keeps you motivated,” said Ng, the founder and owner of Treasure Island Group, an outdoor education, events and F&B group based in Pui O on Lantau Island. “Outrigger has reinforced for me that individual strength only gets you so far. It is the team that makes the boat move. “Growing up, my sporting idols were Serena Williams and Michael Jordan. I admired their competitiveness, discipline and determination to keep pushing themselves to be the best. “Today, though, some of my biggest inspirations are the women I train with. Seeing them continue to work hard, compete internationally and support one another is incredibly inspiring. We show that getting older does not mean becoming less ambitious. There are still new goals to set, new challenges to take on and new teams to be part of.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Chad Olsen (@asian.scandinavian) Martha Levin, who is a leadership and talent management trainer and coach in her daily life, was among the city’s outrigging pioneers; she became interested in the sport when she returned to her birthplace from Washington DC in 1995. “I did a lot of road cycling when I was in Washington, but after having ridden the road from Repulse Bay to Stanley, I decided to try something different; the double-decker buses were just too close for comfort,” said the daughter of a United States foreign service officer, who grew up internationally in nine countries and cities. The 63-year-old not only started paddling, but she also enjoyed “dreaming up new things to do”. “We organised an outrigger paddle expedition from Hong Kong to Macau with 48 people, about 70 kilometres from Deep Water Bay to Hac Sa Beach,” said Levin, who is also the chair of the VRC, the oldest sporting club in Hong Kong, having been established in 1849. “In those days, we had to do immigration to get into Macau, so the immigration officer rolled up his pants and brought a little table, and so he stood in the high water line and stamped our passports. “I enjoy bringing other people into the sport, and it’s great to see the spark of excitement: ‘I’ve never seen Lamma from this angle’,” she said. “What started as a way for me to simply meet people and get some exercise when I first came back has become a way of life that I love.” First held in California in 1984, the World Sprint Championships were a biennial event until 2018, when the global pandemic scuppered the next one before its return in Windsor, England, four years later. The distance version debuted in Tahiti in 2017, the same year that Hong Kong started sending teams to compete. It was subsequently held in Australia two years later, followed by Samoa and Brazil in 2023 and 2025. Snaith and Ng competed in the latter two, while Levin has “too many to count”, having competed in all the major races globally for several years. The trio formed part of the 35 athletes donning the Bauhinia flag at the various championships over the past decade before the current edition in Singapore. Joining them this time is newcomer Wang Xiaoxin, who relocated to Hong Kong from Shanghai in 2014, and who has been paddling for only two years, after her husband introduced her to the sport. Previously a brand manager for 15 years and now a jewellery designer with over a decade of experience, the 50-year-old had her first race at the iconic Around The Island Race (ATIR) in Hong Kong last year, and Singapore is her first overseas event. “I have always loved water, and was a competitive youth swimmer for seven years during my teenage years,” said the Anhui native, whose biggest challenge in training was time, having a 10-year-old daughter to take care of. “The greatest [paddling] joy for me is the deep connections between human and nature, and it has taught me to respect nature even more, while enjoying Hong Kong’s breathtaking coastal scenery. “I also treasure the strong sense of unity – everyone moving forward as one heart, one team. A canoe does not move unless you paddle. Life is the same. “The Singapore event will be a beautiful and unforgettable experience, especially for racing alongside so many fellow paddlers from Hong Kong.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by HK Va’a World Championships 2026 (@hk_vaa_internationals) To Ng, who was surfing in her 40s but missed “being part of a team competing at a high level, and being on the water”, prompting her to start paddling. It was the growth and the bond of the community that meant the most to her. “I was amazed by how much experience we had in the training room, both on and off the water when I first joined,” she said. “There is a real maturity that comes with age, and having a community of strong women around you, who motivate each other to stay fit, challenge ourselves and keep improving, is a blessing at this stage of life. “Most of us are juggling families, work and finances, so competing at this level requires commitment and determination. But that is also what makes it so rewarding. “We are not professional athletes. We are women with full lives who have decided that we still want to challenge ourselves and see what we are capable of.”

title: Indonesia takes on Malaysia in battle over palm oil pricing
description: Palm oil is just the start. Indonesia’s new trade exchange also aims to oversee nickel and coal export volumes, prices and taxes.
content: Indonesia produces and exports more palm oil than any other country, but when it comes to setting the price, it still plays second fiddle to Malaysia. President Prabowo Subianto wants to change that. On August 14, he announced a new exchange for commodities including palm oil, nickel and coal, targeted to begin operations on January 1. But analysts say dominance in physical supply does not automatically translate into pricing power. Jakarta’s move to set new benchmarks may not be enough to persuade international traders to ditch Bursa Malaysia’s crude palm oil futures contract (FCPO), the industry’s principal reference for pricing and hedging. The new bourse is part of a broader push by Prabowo for greater state oversight of export prices, volumes and revenue. “We do not merely want to be a producer of global commodities. We must become a setter for prices of global commodities,” Prabowo told lawmakers during his annual budget speech before Indonesia’s House of Representatives. The Strategic Mineral and Commodity Exchange (BMKS) will be supervised by the Financial Services Authority, which said on August 19 that it had appointed Henry Rialdi as deputy commissioner responsible for the exchange’s regulation and oversight. Prabowo said the bourse would establish Indonesian reference prices for major exports – including palm oil, nickel, tin, coal and coffee – and make commodity trading more transparent. For analysts, palm oil looms as the biggest test of that ambition. Indonesia produced 51.66 million tonnes of crude palm oil last year and accounted for more than half of global exports. Malaysia, the second-largest producer, reported a national output of 20.28 million tonnes over the same period. Yet despite Indonesia’s exporting clout, Malaysia’s FCPO remains the global industry’s principal benchmark – not just in futures trading, but in negotiations for physical palm oil contracts worldwide. Siwage Dharma Negara, principal fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and co-coordinator of its Indonesia studies programme, said Prabowo’s plan appeared to serve two related goals. The first was leveraging Indonesia’s export dominance in palm oil, nickel and coal to influence international pricing and strengthen its bargaining position. “The second objective is to give the state better oversight on export prices and volumes, tax payments and possible transfer pricing,” Siwage said. But he said dominance in supply did not automatically confer benchmark status, as Malaysia’s FCPO had been in use for a long time and was widely accepted in global palm oil trading. This would not be Indonesia’s first attempt to challenge the status quo. In 2023, it launched an exchange-based physical CPO market run by the Indonesia Commodity and Derivatives Exchange. Trading activity on the exchange has been limited, however, and it has failed to match FCPO on international hedging and price discovery. David Ng, a proprietary trader at boutique financial derivatives and commodities trading house IcebergX, said FCPO’s appeal came down to deep liquidity. “If the volume is high, you can go in with size, and you can also come out with size,” he said, noting that the contract attracted plantation companies, physical merchants, international participants and speculators, creating a continuous flow of competing orders. Last year, 80,399 FCPO contracts were traded daily, according to Securities Commission Malaysia data sourced from Bursa Malaysia. Ng said that futures and physical prices were closely linked, with physical cargoes typically priced around the FCPO reference, creating built-in incentives for traders to exploit arbitrage. The challenge now for Indonesia, according to both Ng and Siwage, is not simply publishing a domestic reference price, but creating a market participants trust enough to actually use. Siwage said competitive transaction costs, transparent governance and reliable data would all be important if Jakarta hoped to challenge the FCPO’s dominance. “The government may establish the rules, but cannot influence individual prices,” he said, warning that any political intervention in price setting would undermine the exchange’s credibility. Even if Indonesia could not displace FCPO in international contracts for now, Siwage said mandatory transaction reporting could help it establish a useful physical-market reference. Ng flagged a further complication: Indonesia’s oil palm plantations are spread across a far larger and more fragmented geography than Malaysia’s, making consistent, reliable data collection a challenge. Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Jakarta-based Centre of Economic and Law Studies, cautioned against viewing BMKS purely as a bid for international price-setting power. “Prabowo wants to ensure that the price is more transparent and that the government can check transaction data and protect income-tax revenue,” Bhima said. He drew a comparison with Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia (DSI), which was established under sovereign wealth fund Danantara to oversee exports of CPO, coal and ferroalloys. Since June 1, exporters have been required to report transactions through DSI, with further changes planned from January. Bhima was sceptical that establishing a domestic Indonesian benchmark would persuade overseas buyers to abandon established references such as the FCPO. “To ensure that contracts will use Indonesia’s domestic price reference is very hard,” he said, noting that major export contracts with buyers in China and India already had established pricing arrangements. But Siwage said that even without dethroning the FCPO, BMKS could still help Indonesia gain better leverage in commercial negotiations, simply by virtue of its position as the world’s dominant palm oil supplier.

title: In pictures: from film to smartphone – how Hong Kong has been photographed through the decades
description: A look back at how locals and visitors alike documented their days in Hong Kong from the age of film to the day of the smartphone.
content: Before digital screens offered instant previews, taking photographs was an exercise in patient precision. Miscalculating exposure or framing – or later in the process, mishandling rolls of film – could ruin a cherished memory. Through the 1960s and 70s, residents and visiting tourists alike rationed every shutter click, gradually shifting from classic black-and-white to vivid colour stock as film remained a costly luxury. In the 90s, compact cameras – both still and video – became the norm, while shops across Tsim Sha Tsui did a roaring trade, with travellers seeking equipment that was often cheaper than at home. Today, high-resolution smartphones deliver high-definition shots for effortless global sharing, yet many still cherish the warmth and surprise of film photography. Here’s a look at how South China Morning Post photographers used their own cameras to capture the evolving ways in which we have documented our lives and trips.

title: Everland fireflies light up summer darkness in South Korea
description: More than 30,000 people visited the Midsummer Night Firefly Festival in its first two weeks.
content:
Thousands of fireflies illuminated the darkened forest experience zone during Everland’s Midsummer Night Firefly Festival in Yongin, South Korea, earlier this month.
In the cool subterranean dark, a hush fell over the crowd. Against a soft choir of chirping night insects, waves of fireflies took to the air, weaving delicate ribbons of green-gold light through the darkness.
The Midsummer Night Firefly Festival has quietly become a sanctuary for travellers looking to escape the relentless daytime sun and rediscover a childhood sense of awe.
This year, the Firefly Festival and the renowned Summer Night Safari were included free with standard park admission.
Since opening on July 24, the firefly experience alone enchanted roughly 30,000 guests in its first two weeks.

title: Dangers of heavy backpacks for children and how to lighten the load
description: Choose a bag that fits the child and don’t wait for them to show discomfort, experts say.
content:
Backpacks can be fashionable and functional. However, they can also be too heavy – weighed down by digital devices, musical instruments, sports equipment and more.
As families begin back-to-school shopping, here’s how to tell if a backpack is too heavy.
According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, signs a backpack may be too heavy include a child leaning forward to support its weight or having difficulty walking. Straps should not dig into shoulders.
Don’t wait for a child to express discomfort or pain to lighten the load, experts say.
Experts recommend choosing a backpack that fits the child and has two broad, padded shoulder straps, a padded back, compartments to distribute weight and a waist or chest strap to redistribute the load.
Backpacks with wheels can be helpful, especially for children with injuries, but experts say they may be problematic in schools with stairs or crowded walkways.

title: Tibetan cooperative keeps centuries-old weaving tradition alive
description: Founded in 2008 by artisan Pasang, the cooperative employs more than 100 people, including some with disabilities.
content:
More than a dozen men and women sit at wooden looms, sliding shuttles through rows of wool yarn before pulling each thread tight. They repeat it again and again as they weave Pulu, the traditional woollen fabric that has clothed people on the Tibetan plateau for centuries.
They work at the Ethnic Huaji Handwoven Cooperative in Shannan, where artisans are trying to preserve one of Tibet’s oldest weaving traditions while creating jobs for local residents.
Founded in 2008 by Tibetan artisan Pasang, the cooperative employs more than 100 people, including some with disabilities. It teaches younger Tibetans a craft that Pasang feared was disappearing.
The cooperative specialises in Zeter, a finer variety of Pulu made from especially soft wool from the necks and backs of sheep.
Pasang said he learned the craft from his parents. At the time, fewer than 10 people still knew how to weave Zeter.
He added that the craft has been recognised as part of China’s national intangible cultural heritage. Pasang said that he hopes younger generations will continue practising it.

title: UK PM Andy Burnham to visit Kyiv on Monday as Ukraine marks independence anniversary
description: On his first international visit as UK leader, Burnham will co-chair his first Coalition of the Willing meeting of countries supporting Kyiv.
content: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will visit Kyiv on Monday on his first international visit since taking office last month, his office said, as Ukraine marks its 35th independence anniversary. Burnham has vowed to give strong support to Ukraine as it battles Russia’s invasion. The Labour Party leader’s visit comes as he announced that Britain had “agreed that defence firm MBDA can release classified information on UK components for the long-range missile, SCALP, to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine”, a statement said. The missile is the French-produced version of the UK’s Storm Shadow, with both using shared French and British technology. The UK was first to give Ukraine long-range strike weapons for defensive purposes in 2023, according to the premier’s Downing Street office. It said that the decision to release the classified information would “allow the French and Ukrainians to move forward with the Ukrainian assembly of the missile”. “It also complements the major UK effort to rapidly develop low-cost advanced long-range strike weapons for Ukraine through Project Brakestop,” it added. In Kyiv, Burnham will co-chair his first meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, which brings together countries supporting Kyiv. The French presidency confirmed on Friday that the meeting would be held in a “hybrid” format – meaning some participants would attend in person while others joined via video conference. The office of Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin indicated that he would take part remotely. “On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes,” Burnham said in a statement. Burnham’s visit comes weeks after Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky visited London. During that trip, London also announced it would share with Kyiv information on a new battle-tested electronic jamming capability dubbed “Stone Cloak”. When attached to drones, the tablet-sized, military-grade jammers can hinder Russian air defence systems from tracking and targeting such weapons in-flight, Downing Street said. Britain has been one of Ukraine’s strongest backers since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, committing around £25 billion (US$34 billion) in support, including £16 billion in military aid.

title: Editorial | China Evergrande founder’s fall a warning to private sector
description: Case serves as a stark lesson on the limits of corporate survival and the need for business integrity.
content: The sentencing of China Evergrande Group founder Hui Ka-yan to life imprisonment, accompanied by the punishment of more than 50 other individuals, brings a sombre conclusion to the saga of what was once the world’s most indebted property developer. While this case marks a significant moment in the ongoing volatility of the mainland property market, it serves primarily as a stark lesson on the limits of corporate survival and the absolute necessity of business integrity. It is important to distinguish between business failure and criminal conduct. In any market economy, companies rise and fall. While painful, bankruptcy is sometimes an unavoidable consequence of economic cycles. When enterprises face severe financial difficulties, there exists an established, legal path for resolution – through debt restructuring, asset liquidation and transparent negotiations with creditors. Several other major developers in China have faced similar systemic pressures and have chosen this arduous but responsible path. By selling assets and facing the reality of their diminished fortunes, these leaders have navigated crises without resorting to illegal short cuts. Evergrande’s trajectory was fundamentally different. The court’s findings reveal that the company did not simply collapse under the weight of market forces; it crumbled because of systemic deceit. The fabrication of financial reports and the conspiracy to manipulate accounting data represent a profound betrayal of public interest and the law. This was not a business model; it was deception, facilitated by auditors who failed in their duties and a leadership structure that prioritised unchecked expansion over fiscal reality. Hui, who at one time was China’s richest man, was sentenced to life imprisonment for “multiple combined crimes”, with all of his personal property confiscated. Fifty-six people, including the 67-year-old’s two sons, were sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of 22 months to 18 years, with fines or property confiscated as stipulated by the ruling. In 2024, the Chinese auditing arm of PwC, one of the Big Four accountancy firms, was suspended from operating in China for six months and fined about 441 million yuan (US$65.6 million) after Chinese authorities found it had helped to cover up fraud at Evergrande. The consequences of these actions extend far beyond the boardroom. Evergrande was delisted from the Hong Kong stock exchange last year. China’s prolonged real estate slump – triggered by developer defaults such as Evergrande – has severely eroded household wealth, trapped millions in negative equity and choked consumer spending, fundamentally crushing people’s sense of financial security. Millions of families who bought multiple properties as retirement investments or for their children at the market peak are seeing those assets lose significant value or sit empty in oversupplied areas. Pre-sale flats left countless buyers paying steep mortgages on half-built or abandoned blocks of flats. A rising number of distressed owners, including younger workers who are already facing a tough economy, have defaulted. This has led to a surge in heavily discounted court-ordered property auctions as families were forced to liquidate. Thankfully, the worst of the property crash appears to be over. China’s growth model increasingly relies on hi-tech sectors as the economy moves up to the most advanced value and supply chains. For ordinary people, however, a stable property market is a cornerstone of economic health and social stability for any nation. When developers treat housing as a vehicle for reckless speculation rather than homes to be delivered responsibly, the entire ecosystem suffers. The tough but fair punishments for Evergrande’s leadership under the Chinese legal system ought to mark the end of real estate-driven growth that fed so many imbalances into the economy which is still being worked through. Ultimately, this case is a warning to the private sector. Business success can never justify the compromise of legal and ethical standards. Genuine leadership in times of crisis is defined not by the ability to hide liabilities but by the courage to face them legally and transparently. The priority for the property sector must now be sustainable development, ensuring the health of the economy is protected from the hubris of those who believe they are above the rules.

title: How to navigate sex and intimacy when dementia changes a relationship
description: Dementia often alters relationships beyond the sufferer’s urges. Experts share tips on dealing with this part of the condition few discuss.
content: This is the 96th instalment in a series on dementia, including the research into its causes and treatment, advice for carers, and stories of hope. A quiet heartbreak is unfolding behind the closed doors of dementia care, one that few carers dare to speak about openly: the ebb of physical intimacy. A tentative question posted to an online dementia carer support group sparked a flurry of moving responses. That question: “I really don’t know how to approach this subject, but I’m wondering who is still sexually active with a partner who has a dementia diagnosis. I’m struggling with this.” It is a distressing issue for the hundreds of people who weigh in. In emotional comments, both men and women describe their experiences, challenges and concerns, such as these below: “For the past two years, we’ve slept in separate bedrooms. I just can’t go there: there is nothing sexy about a man who never showers or shaves and does nothing all day but sleep.” “I have so many beautiful memories, but today is a very different reality, and I can’t ‘fake’ it. I tell him my hormones don’t work any more and I can’t do it – I tell him it is all my problem – a medical one. I hug him and tell him I am sorry. So far it has worked – but it breaks my heart.” “My wife and I once enjoyed a very active sex life before she presented with [dementia] symptoms. The last time we had sex was a few years ago; she actually initiated it, but during the act, something shifted, her body stiffened visibly, and her expression changed. That was that. For me, consent in my mind was withdrawn and that was the very last time.” Some respondents speak to struggling with partners who exhibit sexual desire that they cannot reciprocate because they feel more like parents than partners: “I feel like he’s my child now.” Some describe a partner’s anger when they do not respond in kind. Some explain that a period of uninhibited sexual interest is a phase of the illness and will wane or can be managed with medication. Others speak of a different sort of intimacy: “We do have moments of tenderness, hand-holding and a kiss when he has episodes of clarity. These are becoming rarer as my nursing role takes precedence.” Amanda Pang, co-founder of Hong Kong home-care company Evercare Health, says a dementia diagnosis “reshapes intimacy in ways people rarely talk about”. Her comment on how the dynamics within a romantic relationship change echoes many of those on the forum. “When a partner becomes a full-time carer, the relationship often shifts from romantic to clinical. They find themselves bathing their spouse, dressing them, monitoring for nighttime wandering – intimate tasks that blur the boundaries that once defined their partnership,” Pang says. Just as experts are quick to remind us that dementia presents differently in every person it affects, the experiences of sexuality and relationships are also unique to individuals. Dr Nathalie Huitema, a US-based specialist in sexuality, ageing and dementia care, agrees that people – even healthcare professionals – are ashamed to talk about sexuality, and especially about sexuality later in life. “Most clinicians aren’t well trained in sexuality across the lifespan, and very few have any education on sexual changes in dementia,” she says. As a result, these concerns are left unspoken – except privately on forums – and add to carers’ already substantial burden. There are many types of dementia and even more types of people, Huitema says. The combination of both, and the effect on relationships and intimacy, is wide-ranging and unpredictable. Huitema firmly rejects the phrase “inappropriate sexual behaviour” when applied to those with dementia. That term, she says, “suggests some sort of moral failure. In dementia, these behaviours are usually the result of disinhibition, confusion or misidentifying a partner. It’s about the brain losing the ability to filter impulses or understand context. I prefer the term ‘misdirected sexual expression’.” Sexual interaction between partners might feel instinctual, but there are a lot of cognitive steps involved in making a move and making out. “First you have or know or feel that you want to have sex, then you have to initiate it, then you have to check in with your partner whether they feel the same way in that moment,” Huitema says. “Then you have to take certain steps, because sexual interaction involves a beginning, a middle and an end.” People with dementia take less initiative in all kinds of activities – not just sex. They can become more self-involved, which means in relationships they focus on themselves and their own sexual desires and not on their partner. Brain changes mean they often become disinhibited. That is one of the causes of misdirected sexual expression, Huitema explains. What’s happening in the brain Understanding how dementia attacks specific regions of the brain helps carers take the sudden shifts in intimacy less personally. When the frontal lobes, which act like a social filter, are damaged, people can lose impulse control or misread social cues and become disinhibited, Huitema says. If the temporal lobes – the brain’s “filing cabinet” that governs memory and emotion – are involved, a person may have trouble recognising their partner or feeling connected to them. The parietal lobes – the sensory processor – can affect how touch is perceived. A gentle, loving touch or a reassuring hug might feel confusing, painful or even threatening. As the brain’s cortex declines, a person’s awareness of the relationship with their significant other fades, but their more primal, deep-seated human needs for warmth, physical comfort and emotional security remain intact, and seeking intimacy becomes instinctive rather than relational. These changes are not intentional, Huitema says, but neurological. “I’m really happy when spouses and partners understand that … so they take it less personally.” Sexuality is not just about attraction but about context and how people feel. After a dementia diagnosis, there could be huge disparities between feelings, and the person with dementia might feel confused, stressed or upset, and their partner exhausted and underappreciated. Huitema says one thing everybody needs is human touch, and that this is true “no matter how the dementia evolves, or even among people with severe cognitive impairment”. “We call it skin hunger,” she adds. “Even when sexuality changes in dementia, the need for physical closeness doesn’t go away … People still need to be held, touched, hugged or have someone sit close to them. “Touch is calming, grounding, and helps people feel safe and connected. So, when sexual behaviour becomes confusing for partners, they can still offer nonsexual touch, such as holding hands, sitting together, gentle massage, cuddling.” Getting the right help can support caring partners who feel exhausted, says Evercare’s Pang. “We’ve worked with spouses who couldn’t sleep for months because they were concerned about their partner wandering in an unfamiliar environment,” she says. “Our carers take on these tasks so the healthy spouse can step back from being a nurse and simply be a partner again. “That creates space for whatever connection remains: holding hands, a quiet moment together, or just the relief of knowing they’re safe.” 5 expert tips on intimacy after a dementia diagnosis 1. Acknowledge your own needs Recognise that your intimacy needs are valid, even if your partner can no longer participate – from the National Institute on Aging (US) 2. Seek a specialised community Connect with carer support groups and join platforms for carers to reduce isolation. Use relationship counselling services; you will feel less alone if you do – Alzheimer’s Society (UK) 3. Use comfort alternatives Offer body pillows, a wrapped hot-water bottle, or a large stuffed animal to satisfy a person’s physical need for a warm body in bed. Keep their hands busy with an activity, such as folding, sorting or squeezing stress balls – Alzheimer Society of Canada 4. Redirect and distract Gentle shifts in environment, like taking a walk or holding hands, can de-escalate misdirected sexual energy – Dementia UK 5. Consult a doctor Sudden spikes in hypersexuality can be managed medically; consult a specialist if behaviours become overwhelming – Mayo Clinic Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Youth membership in Hong Kong uniformed groups drops 8%
description: Some lawmakers have called for the introduction of key performance indicators to ensure wise public spending.
content:
Youth membership in Hong Kong’s uniformed groups has declined by 8 per cent over the past five years despite steady government funding.
The trend has been attributed to low birth rates and a wider array of extracurricular activities for students.
Several lawmakers have called for the introduction of key performance indicators for uniformed groups to ensure careful public spending.
However, some organisations are concerned that linking funding to membership numbers could restrict their development.
The Home and Youth Affairs Bureau grants subsidies to 11 uniformed youth groups to promote positive values, all-round development, and national and ethnic identity.
Such groups received HK$86 million in subsidies during the 2024-25 academic year.
According to the bureau’s figures, the total youth membership across the 11 groups fell from 117,671 in 2020-21 to 108,551 in 2024-25. Over the past decade, membership dropped by nearly 18 per cent.
A bureau spokesman said that social distancing during the Covid-19 pandemic had slowed recruitment and retention efforts, but membership numbers had recently stabilised.

title: Syria holds talks with Israel addressing de-escalation and Israel-Turkey tensions
description: A Syrian government source said Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani met the head of Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency, Roman Gofman.
content: Syria said it held talks with Israel in Jordan on Sunday on de-escalation after recent Israeli strikes, and on keeping the country out of tensions between Israel and Turkey, an ally of Damascus. The high-level negotiations came after the sides in January agreed to establish an intelligence-sharing mechanism as they edge towards a security agreement. They also came after Israel bombed the disused Abu Al-Duhur airbase in the country’s northwest earlier in the week, claiming it wanted to avert Turkish troops deploying to the facility. Ankara denied any visit to the site. Syrian state news agency SANA quoted a diplomatic source at the foreign ministry saying “a high-level Syrian delegation headed by the foreign minister and including the general and military intelligence chiefs” met a high-level Israeli delegation “under American mediation and hosted by Jordan”. The meeting was “part of efforts aiming at de-escalation after recent Israeli bombardment of Syrian territory, escalating tensions in southern Syria, and in support of stability in Syria and the region”, the source said. Discussions also addressed “efforts aimed at bringing closer the viewpoints between Turkey and Israel and ensuring the current tension between the two countries are not reflected on Syria territory”, the report added. A diplomatic source and a Syrian government source said that Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani met the head of Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency Roman Gofman. They discussed issues such as establishing “a special operations room” in Jordan under US supervision to prevent any confrontation in Syria, including involving Turkey, the sources added. US envoy for Syria Tom Barrack had slammed Israel’s attack on the airbase on Tuesday as an “unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability”. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have traded barbs since the incident, with tensions high between the two leaders. The Syrian government source said that Sunday’s talks were the first between Israel and Syria in some time, while the diplomatic source said they were the first in several months. SANA said the discussions addressed “establishing practical mechanisms to stop Israeli attacks … and reviving the negotiations process with the aim of reaching a security agreement that could form the basis of a more comprehensive future agreement”. Israel and Syria’s new authorities have held several rounds of direct talks, and after negotiations in Paris in January they agreed to establish a dedicated communication cell under US supervision to lower bilateral tensions. An Arab diplomat in Damascus said at the time that a joint operations room based in Jordan would follow issues including security co-ordination and border control. Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since the December 2024 toppling of long-time ruler Bashar al-Assad by Islamist forces it considers jihadists. It sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that had long separated Israeli and Syrian forces on the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights. Israel has also carried out repeated incursions deeper into Syrian territory and has vowed to keep troops in a so-called security zone in southern Syria, where it seeks a broader demilitarised area. The talks also came a day after Israel struck what it said was a militant in southern Syria. Damascus said one person was wounded in the strike, which it called a “flagrant violation” of its sovereignty. Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli war and later annexed the areas under its control, a move only recognised by the United States and, this month, Colombia. US President Donald Trump has been pushing for a security deal between Syria and Israel but Israel remains distrustful of Syria’s authorities.

title: Hong Kong homebuyers snap up units at The Sterling as value-focused demand deepens
description: The Sterling residential development drew 46,000-plus subscriptions, highlighting appeal of urban locations with strong transport links as housing recovery matures.
content: Hong Kong homebuyers are still willing to spend, and the sell-out of a major new development on Saturday showed how demand is increasingly concentrated in projects that offer clear value as the housing recovery enters a more mature phase. China Resources Land’s The Sterling in southwestern Kowloon, in Cheung Sha Wan, sold all 180 units offered in its first price-list batch, generating nearly HK$1.6 billion (US$204 million). The project received more than 46,000 subscriptions, or more than 254 times the number of units available, setting a record for first-round subscriptions at a Hong Kong first-hand residential project. The response was driven by the project’s urban location and competitive pricing, rather than a broad return to aggressive buying, according to industry insiders. The project is close to Nam Cheong station, making it a relatively rare large-scale new development in the city area. “The response is part of a broader pattern,” said Roy Ng, head of research at consultancy Newmark. The strong response reflected demand for new, premium stock with good transport connectivity and competitive pricing, he added. The first batch was offered at an average discounted price of about HK$17,880 (US$2,280) per square foot, roughly 27 per cent to 33 per cent below the opening prices of nearby projects launched in 2021. That discounted pricing became particularly compelling because some new developments in the northern New Territories have been marketed at similar levels. The project’s low-price launch strategy successfully attracted buyers and demonstrated that purchasing power remained available Louis Chan, Centaline Property Agency For buyers choosing between a roughly HK$18,000-per-square-foot home in an established urban district and one in an emerging area, immediate transport links, amenities, rental demand and resale liquidity can tip the balance towards the former. The result comes as the market emerges from a sharp slowdown earlier this summer. First-hand private home registrations fell 62 per cent in July to 731 units, according to Land Registry data compiled by Ricacorp Properties, ending a 16-month run above 1,000 units. But that figure largely reflected a lack of major launches and the timing of registrations. The market has since picked up as developers returned with new projects in late July and August, setting up what agents are calling a new-home sales battle. As of August 19, Hong Kong had recorded 642 first-hand private home sales worth HK$7.76 billion, according to market data. The full-month tally is forecast at about 900 units worth HK$10 billion, which would put sales volume 17.2 per cent above July but transaction value 40 per cent lower, with a lack of high-value deals, according to Centaline data. That makes The Sterling’s performance more significant. “The project’s low-price launch strategy successfully attracted buyers and demonstrated that purchasing power remained available,” said Louis Chan, vice-chairman and president of the residential division at Centaline Property Agency. For developers, the launch also highlights the balance between pricing and sales pace. The Sterling is a large, multiphase project that will eventually provide more than 2,200 homes. The first eight months have already recorded 13,869 first-hand transactions, or 67.6 per cent of last year’s full-year total. Full-year sales are forecast at about 18,000 units, which would make 2026 the strongest year since 2019, Centaline said.

title: Activities to learn about fossil hunter Mary Anning
description: Born in England in 1799, she became famous for finding the remains of many ancient reptiles.
content:
Mary Anning was born in England in 1799. She grew up in a beach town called Lyme Regis. Anning’s family didn’t have much money. So Anning and her brother, Joseph, explored the beach. They wanted to find things to sell.
Anning loved to search the coast for unusual objects. She called them curiosities. When she was 12, she and her brother found the skull of an animal sticking out of a cliff.
At first, they thought it was a crocodile. But they had actually found an ancient reptile called an ichthyosaur.
As she grew older, Anning found even more incredible animals. She found a plesiosaur, which is a prehistoric sea reptile with a very long neck. She also found an ancient flying reptile called a Dimorphodon .
She became famous for finding so many fossils. Scientists would visit Anning to seek her advice on fossils.
Today, people remember her as one of the greatest fossil hunters in history.
Write a diary entry from Mary Anning’s point of view. Imagine how she felt when she found the ichthyosaur skeleton.
Location: The cliffs of Lyme Regis, England
Today started out like any other stormy morning on the coast. Joseph and I hurried out to
______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
Suddenly, Joseph shouted and pointed ______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
I immediately _________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
In that moment, I felt _________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
“She sells seashells by the seashore” is a famous tongue twister. It is believed to be inspired by Anning’s life. This sentence is hard to say quickly because of the repeated sounds: “s”, “sh” and “ells”. Write your own tongue twister based on one of her famous fossil discoveries.
1. Pick one of Anning’s famous discoveries. Then, choose a letter that best represents this discovery.
2. Create a list of words that start with your chosen letter. The closer the words sound to one another, the better the tongue twister will be. If you can relate them to the fossil, the beach or digging, that’s even better.
3. Connect your words to form a sentence or two. Try to include as many words as possible starting with your chosen letter.
4. Read your tongue twister aloud to make sure it flows well. Challenge your friends and family to say it quickly.

title: Climate change means more heatwaves. Can humans adapt?
description: Experts say bodies can deal with higher temperatures, but only to a certain extent.
content:
Heatwaves are going to be more frequent, be more intense and last longer, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.
“The summers ahead will be harder,” Hans Kluge said. He is the director of the WHO’s European region.
Human-made climate change is making heatwaves around the world worse. Will the human body be able to adapt to higher temperatures?
Yes, to some extent. However, that adaptation has clear limits, said medical meteorologist Kathrin Graw. She works with Germany’s national weather service, the Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD).
“Within a heatwave, the longer it lasts, the more of a burden it becomes for people day by day,” Graw said. “Especially … when nights remain warm, and sleep quality deteriorates as a result. The heat can be harder to cope with the following day.”
“The longer the heat persists, the more people die,” Graw said.
She pointed to a recent DWD study. It showed that the risk of fatal consequences from heat rises the longer a heatwave lasts.
For people with heart disease, extreme heat can be very dangerous.
In the first few days of a heatwave, deaths increase by 8.5 per cent. By the 11th and 12th days of continuous heat, deaths increase by 18 per cent.
The human body is somewhat able to adapt to heat over the course of a summer, the medical meteorologist said. Weather services like DWD are changing how they issue heat warnings. They send out warnings at lower temperatures at the beginning of summer, or after a cooler period. By the end of summer, they only send warnings when it gets much hotter.
To decide the best time to send a heat warning, meteorologists also rely on the heat index. The heat index looks at both the temperature and the moisture in the air. This tells us how hot it actually feels outside (see graphic).
Graw warned that people cannot adapt to rising temperatures forever. Because of climate change, temperatures have been rising faster in recent years.

title: Macron hosts Saudi’s crown prince for visit ranging from esports to Middle East
description: A French official said agreements, on health, transport and energy, will be signed on Monday alongside talks likely to focus on Iran.
content: French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday welcomed Saudi crown prince and de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman for a two-day visit, hosting him at the Esports World Cup before a second day focused on bilateral deals and the situation in the Middle East. A French presidential official said several agreements, on health, transport and energy, will be signed on Monday alongside talks likely to focus on Iran. But the visit kicked off on Sunday evening on a lighter note with the crown prince being hosted by Macron at the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup hosted by Paris. Fifa President Gianni Infantino was also there and Macron spoke to leading gamers, handing out trophies. The event, which brings together the leading performers in esports ranging from computer games to chess and has been eagerly backed by Riyadh, is being held outside Saudi Arabia for the first time. Paris is keen to emphasise that the crown prince rarely leaves his home country other than for international summits and his trip to France was the first such for almost a year. “The fact that he chose France for this visit is an important signal and testifies to the depth and dynamism of the Franco-Saudi relationship,” said the French presidential official. But three journalists’ unions on Sunday protested against France hosting the Saudi strongman, who is known by his initials “MBS”. In a joint statement, the SNJ-CGT, CFDT-Journalistes and SGJ-FO unions noted that there was a live French investigation for torture and forced disappearance after a complaint lodged in 2021 over the killing of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi. Khashoggi, a Saudi with US residency who was a critic of the Saudi ruling family, was murdered in Saudi Arabia’s consulate in Istanbul in 2018. His body was never recovered. US intelligence concluded that MBS was directly involved in Khashoggi’s killing, and a UN investigation described the journalist’s death as an “extrajudicial killing for which Saudi Arabia is responsible”. The unions said the visit, following a previous one hosted by Macron in July 2022, “looks like a provocation for defenders of media freedom and freedom of expression”. The French presidential official declined to comment on whether the mooted agreements could touch on a vast theme park known as Dragons Ball, based on a Japanese manga and backed by a Saudi fund, which is mooted for the Val-d’Oise region outside Paris. Saudi Arabia is also set to host a string of key global events, notably the Expo 2030 and above all the football World Cup in 2034. Saudi Arabia, a close US ally which has a history of tensions with Iran, is also closely watching developments in the Islamic republic in the wake of the US-Israeli war. On Monday afternoon, Mohammed bin Salman and Macron are to chair the first meeting of the Saudi-French strategic partnership council. Macron and the crown prince “will discuss key regional issues, in a context calling for close coordination between France and its Gulf partners to foster stability and peace” in the Middle East, according to Macron’s office. In December 2021, Macron became one of the first Western leaders to meet the prince in Saudi Arabia in the wake of the Khashoggi killing. The Saudi crown prince has made multiple visits to France since then.

title: Open Questions | US economist Barry Eichengreen on reality of de-dollarisation and next currency reshuffle
description: The former IMF adviser examines how de-dollarisation is gaining pace and what lies ahead for China’s yuan.
content: Barry Eichengreen is a leading American economist and one of the world’s foremost experts on international monetary systems. He is a professor of economics and political science at the University of California, Berkeley, where he has taught since 1987. He served as a senior policy adviser at the International Monetary Fund in 1997-98. Here, he discusses why today’s “de-dollarisation” talk is different from past episodes, how close the world is to a reshuffling of the international monetary system, and what it will really take for the yuan to close the gap. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. Since last year, discussions about “de-dollarisation” have resurfaced with renewed intensity. In your view, how much of this reflects a genuine structural shift? And what, if anything, makes the current moment different from previous episodes of dollar scepticism? My view is that a genuine structural shift is finally getting under way against the backdrop of some long-standing concerns about the US dollar – for example, concerns about the high level of public debt in the United States and whether the growth of the debt is sustainable or not. If there are chronic debt problems, will they have negative implications for the stability of the dollar and the value of foreign central banks’ holdings of US Treasury securities? Those concerns are long-standing, and people have been pointing to them when asking whether the era of dollar dominance may be coming to a close – they have been pointing to them for a long time. What is new and different, however, are two sets of questions that we did not use to ask about the United States and the dollar, but everyone is asking now. First, the strength of US political institutions. The dollar’s stability and confidence in the greenback rest fundamentally on the rule of law, separation of powers, the independence of the central bank and the control of corruption. People are beginning to ask whether those institutional arrangements are more fragile than previously assumed. This has begun to undermine the feeling of security among foreign central banks, governments and other investors holding financial portfolios heavy in dollars. Second, new questions are being asked about US geopolitical alliances. We know from history that central banks, governments and others prefer to hold and use the currencies of their alliance partners, because those partners are viewed as reliable stewards of their reserve holdings. If one is in an alliance with the United States, moreover, holding and using US dollars is a show of good faith in the country. However, US President Donald Trump has raised questions about the continued commitment of the United States to Nato and to its other security arrangements. That has led the Europeans and others to ask: Do we really want to be so reliant on the US and the dollar in this geopolitically uncertain world, or should we look to alternatives, including relying more on our own currency – the euro, in the European case? So, I think questions about both US alliances and the strength of US institutions are new and different, and they imply that the prospects for the dollar may be different going forward as well. It will take years, maybe even decades, for China to close that gap with the United States and the dollar – unless the US shoots itself in the foot Some argue that the US dollar-centred monetary order that emerged after Bretton Woods may be nearing its end, giving way to a more multipolar system. Do you share that view? And what role do you expect the yuan to play in whatever comes next? I have long shared that view. In 2011 – prematurely, perhaps – I published a book called Exorbitant Privilege about the rise and fall of the dollar. My forecast then was that we would be moving gradually towards a more multipolar monetary and financial system, less centred on the dollar – a more multipolar monetary system that better matched our more multipolar global economy. We have moved in that direction as predicted, but more slowly than I expected. The persistence of dollar dominance is very strong because so many banks, firms and governments use dollars, which creates network effects that lock in the use of the dollar. So, I’ve been surprised in the last 15 years that we haven’t moved towards that multipolar system more rapidly. But that movement may now accelerate. I think China’s currency will, over time, come to play a more consequential global role. But the important point to emphasise is that the yuan is starting out very, very far behind the dollar. Hence it will take years, maybe even decades, for China to close that gap with the United States and the dollar – unless the US shoots itself in the foot and confidence in the dollar is abruptly lost. We have seen progress in the yuan’s international use, from broader participation in China’s payment systems to growing panda bond issuance. Do you believe China is now in a particularly important window for advancing yuan internationalisation? How would you characterise the recent progress? The US-Iran war is affording China additional opportunities to increase the use of its currency in global oil and gas trade, and to do more settlements with the energy exporters from the Middle East in its own currency. And now, those energy exporters are likely happy to take yuan in payment. They can use those yuan to buy the services of Chinese construction companies and Chinese exports of solar panels, batteries, electronics and other advanced technologies. The war in the [Persian] Gulf has, I think, accelerated the tendency for other central banks and governments to look for alternatives to the dollar, and in this way created a window for China. Starting from ground zero 15 years ago, China has made impressive progress. But you have to put that in context, where the dollar still accounts for nearly 60 per cent of the foreign exchange reserves of central banks around the world, and the yuan accounts for 2 per cent. And one sees the same thing along other dimensions, such as turnover in global foreign exchange markets, where the dollar is 10 times as important as the yuan. I think China has been making rapid progress, for example, in transactions through China’s Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS). Those transactions had been growing at a 30 or 40 per cent annual rate – really fast, starting from basically nothing 10 years ago. But that growth slowed sharply in 2025. This slowdown suggests that there still are important obstacles to the yuan’s internationalisation. So I would say: impressive progress, but still, the dollar remains in a different league than China’s currency. China has developed the requisite financial and technological infrastructure. China is, in a way, ahead of the United States in terms of the digital financial revolution. But it has to create confidence among bankers that the markets and platforms on which the yuan can be traded constitute a safe, secure and reliable way to make payments. Creating confidence in a new, novel payments platform takes time. More time will be required. The US correspondent banking system clears many more transactions per day than CIPS does. And it will take, as I said before, probably decades before that gap is closed. Looking ahead, what do you see as the next steps for yuan internationalisation? Do you believe Beijing ultimately envisions the yuan on par with the US dollar, or as one of several major currencies in a more multipolar world? China needs to continue to enhance the liquidity of its financial markets. If people are going to make payments using the yuan, they are going to have to hold balances in the currency, so they have the money ready to make those payments. The kinds of securities that foreigners can hold in China are limited by regulation and capital controls. The availability of financial derivatives to hedge the risk of exchange rate changes – those markets are limited in China. So China needs to move slowly but surely to liberalise access to those financial markets, increase the liquidity of its markets, and – where markets barely exist, as in the case of derivatives – to build them out. I want to be clear here: China should move slowly but surely in this direction. It should not move quickly and abruptly, since doing the latter could create financial risks. Back in 2015, China began to move rapidly to relax its capital controls. Money flowed out of the country, the stock market crashed and the authorities reversed course. This episode was a reminder that slow but steady wins the race, and that moving abruptly is not a good idea. Regarding how Beijing envisions the path, the answer is not entirely under Beijing’s control. Whether the dollar remains the leading international currency – and for how long – depends first and foremost on Washington. What Beijing can do is think about what the best Chinese policy is under different scenarios: under the scenario where the dollar remains sound and stable, and banks, governments, and others around the world feel comfortable in holding and using it; or, if there is a crisis of confidence in the dollar caused by the United States itself, how quickly China can ramp up its alternative, namely, own-currency settlement. Beijing should be doing scenario planning, rather than having a blueprint for what they think will happen next. In the event of a crisis of confidence in the US dollar, are widely discussed alternatives such as the euro and the yuan truly ready to step in as viable substitutes? None of the alternatives, including the euro and the yuan, are ready to substitute for the dollar. What they can do is supplement the dollar on the margin. But they lack the scale as international currencies, and they have shortcomings. In the case of China, it is the lack of access to domestic financial markets and the limited liquidity of those markets. In the case of Europe, it is the absence of a stock of safe and liquid assets for international investors to hold and use. Consequently, neither the euro nor the yuan can replace or substitute for the dollar any time soon. While on some dimensions, like the use of currencies as reserves by central banks, the dollar has lost some of its global market share, the euro has gained none of that market share. The yuan has gained only about one-quarter of what the dollar has lost. The other three-quarters have been gained by non-traditional reserve currencies: the South Korean won, the Australian dollar, the Canadian dollar, the Danish krone, the Norwegian krone. So far, you and I have been talking about the currencies of big economies. Traditionally, there has been an association between the widespread international use of a currency and the size of the issuing economy. Big economies engage in more foreign trade and foreign investment, so it makes sense that their currencies would be the dominant units in international transactions. But we now live in a digital world where it is easier to buy, sell, hold and trade the Australian dollar, the Swedish krona, and so forth. These non-traditional reserve currencies are the currencies of small, open, well-managed, inflation-targeting countries. They are becoming more attractive in international use. They too lack the scale to replace the dollar, but they can help to supplement it on the margin. What role do you see Hong Kong playing in the next phase of yuan internationalisation? As Beijing builds up Shanghai’s offshore financial capabilities, do you see the two cities as increasingly competitive? Hong Kong in the next phase will play the same role that it has played in the previous phase – as a kind of sandbox, or pilot scheme, for yuan use, where Chinese authorities experiment with and observe the effects of different financial innovations. This will continue to be the case. If you believe having markets and financial derivatives is important for the use of China’s currency, those markets will be developed, in part, in Hong Kong. And if they work smoothly there, they will be brought onshore. Hong Kong now has a stablecoin ordinance and has issued two stablecoin licences to a couple of big banks. We don’t know whether stablecoins will become important going forward. I, for one, doubt that they will. But Hong Kong can be a place where banks and others can experiment with the payments technology provided by stablecoins. And if that turns out to be important, it’ll be easier for China to catch up, because Hong Kong will already have provided evidence about how that new payments technology works, how it should be regulated, and so forth. As for the competition between Hong Kong and Shanghai, economists generally think that competition is good. Competition forces banks, regulators and others to step up their game to avoid losing market share. So that is what Hong Kong will have to do. Hong Kong has anchored its currency to the US dollar for more than four decades. If the world becomes more multipolar over time, do you believe the arrangement will still make sense? How do you see Hong Kong’s role evolving in a less US dollar-centric world? The dollar peg has served Hong Kong well. It has had more advantages than disadvantages because the global economy has been dollar-dominated. Hong Kong links directly into that because markets for financial instruments denominated in US dollars are so big. This enables Hong Kong banks to act as global banks, because they have a big global market out there that they can service. If people grow more sceptical about the US dollar and move away from it, the global system will become less dollar-centric. At that point, the advantages to Hong Kong of being linked to the US dollar obviously become less. Hong Kong authorities ought to quietly engage in the same kind of scenario planning for different outcomes, depending on what kind of policies – stable or unstable – are followed in the US, so they can respond appropriately. But I would emphasise that they should do their scenario planning quietly. As stablecoins and central bank digital currencies gain traction around the world, do you see them as game-changers that could disrupt the current monetary hierarchy, or will they simply reinforce the existing status quo? If you look at the long sweep of history, you see that financial and payments technology is always changing. We moved from doing transactions using lumps of gold and silver, to tokens and coins, to bank money and bills of exchange, and so forth. We are in another one of those periods where financial and payments technology is changing rapidly. An important new technology is blockchain, or distributed ledger technology. I am convinced that distributed ledger technology will be used to make cross-border payments going forward. The question is: what kind of units run on those new payment rails? Will they be stablecoins on the one hand, or central bank digital currencies and tokenised commercial bank deposits on the other hand? And depending on the answer to that question, in what currency will they be denominated? In US dollars, or something else? The US has taken a bet on stablecoins. If privately issued stablecoins become the dominant unit that runs on those payment rails, it is likely to cement the international role of the dollar, because 99 per cent of stablecoins are linked to the US dollar. And again, the US has a big head start in going down that road. On the other hand, both the euro area and China are looking at central bank digital currencies and tokenised commercial bank deposits. If that turns out to be what runs on these new payment rails, it won’t be the dollar but the euro and the yuan that dominate in the future. So you have to ask, will we be relying more on private digital money, which is what the US is aiming for, or publicly issued and regulated digital money, which is what China and Europe are developing? The arrow of history points towards public provision of the public good of stable money. In the past, we tended to have lots of private issuers of banknotes and coins. Gradually, governments have taken over that function as a public utility. In effect, they have monopolised it. So if I have to bet on one outcome or another, I would bet on central bank digital currencies and tokenised bank deposits. Just as a diverse ecosystem is good for planet Earth, a multipolar monetary system would be good for the global economy Gold has outlasted every major currency in history. As central banks buy gold at the fastest pace in decades, are we witnessing a return of the world’s oldest monetary asset? What role do you see it playing in the future international monetary system? I do not think gold will play a big role in the future. Central banks that inherited very dollar-heavy reserve portfolios in the past want to diversify. One direction they can diversify towards is by using some of their dollars to buy gold. We’ve seen a little bit of that on the margin. If you are a country like Russia that is subject to sanctions, then buying gold is a way of protecting your reserves from being frozen by foreign authorities. You can buy gold, bring it home and vault it in St Petersburg or Moscow. We’ve seen examples of that kind of behaviour in the last decade and a half. But it is important to note, number one: all the gold purchases that we’ve seen in the last 15 years have been by emerging markets that did not inherit a lot of gold from the past. Advanced countries that inherited gold from the Bretton Woods period and the earlier gold standard period have not added to their reserves. And number two, it is important to note that most of the increase in the share of gold in central bank reserves has been due to the run-up in the price, and not active purchases. We may see a little bit more of that behaviour, because every global investor wants a commodity play in their portfolio. Holding a little bit of gold is a way for central banks to acquire that exposure and a bit of additional diversification. Many speak of a “multipolar” monetary system. In practice, how would such a system function? Would it inevitably require greater coordination among major economies, and is meaningful monetary cooperation still possible at a time of growing geopolitical fragmentation? In practice, a multipolar system would be one in which several currencies play consequential international roles – in which several currencies are used in cross-border payments and are regarded as stable stores of value by international investors. Multiple central banks would act as international lenders and liquidity providers of last resort. Just as a diverse ecosystem is good for planet Earth, a multipolar monetary system would be good for the global economy. If there were a shortage of liquidity, and one central bank fell down on the job – for instance, if the Federal Reserve were dominated by isolationist governors – then central banks in China and Europe could step up. When foreign central banks needed liquidity, they would turn to Beijing and Frankfurt, as well as New York and Washington. However, we are in a world now where coordination is difficult to achieve, partly because the current US administration makes it difficult to coordinate – or to use another word, cooperate – smoothly with other governments. The best we can do is hope that the central banks and governments responsible for these different currencies follow sound and stable policies, so that the exchange rates between their currencies remain relatively stable. If they each understand that they have some responsibility for the stability and liquidity of the global system, they can act individually to help to stabilise the system. If the issuers of the currencies that are internationally used all follow sound and stable policies, that would be better than our current dollar-dominated system. Note, however, that my previous statement had a lot of sentences that began with the word “if”. Consider, for example, the Federal Reserve and the dollar currency swap lines that it provides to other countries. By and large, it only provides them to friendly governments – countries that are geopolitically aligned with the United States – rather than providing them more widely. On the other hand, the People’s Bank of China swap lines are very diverse. It provides them to politically aligned countries in Asia, but it also provides them to the Bank of England, the European Central Bank and others. I worry about whether the US model of only providing liquidity to the country’s friends is compatible with global stability. Looking back through history, are there any precedents for a multipolar monetary system, or are we entering an entirely unprecedented paradigm? One that is relevant to us today is the gold standard period before 1913, when currencies were linked to gold, but gold was not really used for international transactions. Gold is very heavy and risky to ship internationally, so currencies were used for payments. The British pound sterling, the French franc, and the German mark – all three of them were widely used for cross-border transactions in that system before 1913. The system worked smoothly because the policies of the issuing central banks and governments were sound and stable. A very different precedent would be the 1920s and 30s, when both the US dollar and the British pound sterling were used internationally. In the 1920s, the two currencies were equal in importance. But neither the issuing central bank nor government followed sound and stable policies. Both the US and the UK had crises of one sort or another in the early 1930s. There was flight from the two international reserve currencies. As a result, that system worked very poorly. We have seen multipolar systems before. Whether they work well or poorly depends on the stability of the underlying policies.

title: Opinion | Hongkong Post should focus on public service, not profit
description: The traditional self-funding operating model is no longer viable in an increasingly competitive e-commerce market.
content: Two years after the Audit Commission called out Hongkong Post for its lack of profitability and other failings, the postmaster finally moved to fix a structural expense: staff costs. But the audit report probably wasn’t the main catalyst for change. Rather, it was the fact the government had to ask the Legislative Council for a HK$4.6 billion (US$510 million) bailout to keep Hongkong Post operating for the next three years that forced the postmaster to act.
