The crisis facing the city’s postal service has been a long time coming – snail mail has been slowing for postal services worldwide for decades, forcing changes to ensure survival. That has included axing jobs and rethinking the purpose they serve in the 21st century. One of the most drastic moves came from Denmark where PostNord ended its letter delivery service at the end of 2025 to focus entirely on parcel delivery. The country is one of the world’s most digitalised nations, with 95 per cent of Danes fully integrated into its digital platforms. Ending its 400-year letter service was the correct move. Obviously, that’s not the case with Hong Kong. We are nowhere near Denmark in terms of development and adoption of digital platforms. But if the government’s ambitious digitalisation plans bear fruit, Hongkong Post’s existential crisis will only deepen. The government is pushing for more residents to use the iAM Smart one-stop digital services platform to access government services and others. Increasingly, there will be fewer letters to deliver. By the end of 2025, iAM Smart had already accumulated over 4 million users. Hongkong Post must brace itself to adapt to this irreversible trend, unless it wants the government’s digitalisation push to fail. Adapt or die – that was the alarm sounded by the Audit Commission in 2024. Given the sluggish pace of change, the government has rightly stepped in and pledged to unveil a reform road map by 2028. At this point, measures such as closing post offices that aren’t reaching productivity key performance indicators and securing lower rents would not be enough. Losing HK$245 million a year like the Hongkong Post did for 2024-25 is not financially sustainable. The Post Office Trading Fund was set up in 1995 to allow the service to finance itself by using revenue from its commercial operations to offset the cost of meeting its postal obligations. The time has come for that to end – it is clear Hongkong Post can no longer self-fund its operations. While it may be unfair to judge a public service purely through the lens of profits and losses, we must acknowledge that the postal service is facing serious competition today. We are not living in 1995. Hongkong Post has recorded a deficit for eight consecutive years. It has, to its credit, been trying to diversify its services and markets, with a focus on cross-border e-commerce with partner countries of the Belt and Road Initiative. But revenues from such e-commerce services, for example, have fallen short of expectations. There is little indication that it can turn this around any time soon. There is just too much competition. Civil service packages for postal staff that were affordable in 1995 are no longer cost-effective. The postmaster had no choice but to move to hire new staff on two-year contracts, instead of the full civil servant package, including pensions. Predictably, that was met with a backlash, including calls for a judicial review. Expectations were not met, for sure, but reality bites. The postmaster general has said that all options would be considered before deciding on the right operating model, including turning Hongkong Post into a government-funded service, creating a joint venture with the private sector or privatising it. But it’s not about what suits Hongkong Post best, but what suits Hong Kong and its people best. The fundamental question for the government is: can the postal service be both a public service and a business? The postal service has a public duty to provide essential services at convenient locations. Its primary duty is not to generate profit. A trading fund is no longer fit for purpose. Experiences from other parts of the world can shed light on how to separate the public service from its commercial operations. The only way forward may be to allow the postmaster to focus on fulfilling its public duties while letting others with the business acumen develop profitable products and services for the commercial operations.

title: Tens of thousands ordered to evacuate in Nevada as fire threatens Reno
description: The Hawk Fire was caused by humans and is under investigation, officials said. 42,000 have been displaced or are under active evacuations.
content: Tens of ⁠thousands of people have been ⁠evacuated this weekend from the ⁠area of Reno, Nevada, and many others were under orders to leave on Sunday as a wildfire reached the outskirts of the state’s third-most-populous city. About 42,000 residents have been displaced or are under active evacuations with an additional 45,000 ‌in “be prepared to evacuate” status as the Hawk Fire threatened northern Reno, local officials said late on Sunday morning. Local television footage showed flames approaching roads. In eyewitness video verified by Reuters, smoke from the hills billowed over nearby residential neighbourhoods. Fire-tracking websites showed evacuation zones extending from the Sierra Nevada hills to the University of Nevada in northwest Reno. The fire ⁠has burned 5,261 hectares (13,000 acres) so far, officials said at a press conference on Sunday. ‌The fire was human-caused and remains under investigation, they said. Three civilians and three first responders have been injured, said Shane Akerson, a commander leading ‌fire and rescue operations. Officials first received reports of a fire off Hawk Meadow Trail ⁠late on Saturday morning, said Richard Edwards, chief of Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District. Firefighters on Saturday worked amid “extreme ‌red flag conditions”, he said. Red flag conditions are a combination of warm temperatures, very low humidity and strong winds that ‌raise the ‌risk of wildfires. “We expect those same strong conditions to come back this afternoon,” Edwards said ‌on Sunday. Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency late on Saturday in Washoe County, ⁠which includes Reno and parts of Lake Tahoe. “This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, ⁠and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials,” Lombardo said in a statement. Lombardo authorised the deployment of two ‌National Guard helicopters to help ‌fight fires and 60 National Guard staff to support operations with the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office, officials said. The Reno-Tahoe International Airport remained outside the evacuation area and commercial flights were operating normally on Sunday.

title: Former cricket captains appeal to Pakistan over jailed ex-PM Imran Khan’s healthcare
description: The group of 21 sportsmen asked that Khan, also a former cricket captain, be allowed family visits and that medical checks be completed.
content: A group of 21 former international cricket captains, including India’s Sunil Gavaskar and Kapil Dev, signed a letter to Pakistan’s government on Sunday regarding the healthcare of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan. Khan has been in prison since 2023 and was sentenced late last year along with his wife to 17 years on corruption charges they both deny. The 73-year-old, who was also a former Pakistan cricket captain, was transferred back to jail on Friday hours after he was taken to hospital for court-ordered medical checks. The Supreme Court had ordered earlier in the week that Khan be taken to the private Shifa International Hospital in the capital Islamabad for treatment after his lawyers filed a petition over health concerns. The cricket captains’ statement, which followed an earlier letter in February about Khan’s medical treatment, laid out three requests. Firstly, they asked that the medical board directed by the Supreme Court “be permitted to complete a full and independent assessment” of Khan’s health, “particularly the reported loss of vision in his right eye”. Secondly, they requested that the weekly visits by Khan’s family be reinstated by the court “be honoured without interruption or administrative delay”. Their final request was that the treatment mandated after the medical assessment “be provided without delay”. Signatories also included Dilip Vengsarkar (India), Michael Atherton, Michael Brearley, Nasser Hussain, Andrew Strauss and David Gower (England), Allan Border, Ian Chappell, Belinda Clark, Adam Gilchrist, Steve Waugh and Kim Hughes (Australia), Clive Lloyd (West Indies) and John Wright (New Zealand). Khan was prime minister from 2018 to 2022 before being removed in a no-confidence vote during a political crisis over tensions between his government and Pakistan’s powerful military establishment. He has since faced multiple legal cases on corruption and other charges. Khan and his party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, maintain that the cases against him are politically motivated. His arrest triggered nationwide protests in May 2023, some of which turned violent and led to hundreds of arrests.

title: US envoy walks back his comments on Golan Heights that contradicted Trump’s position
description: Tom Barrack had said Israel ‘still’ occupies the territory but on Sunday said that was a description of the Golan Heights’ historical status.
content: The US special envoy to Syria and ambassador to Turkey on Sunday walked back his comments from two days ago that Israel “still” occupies the Golan Heights in violation of UN resolutions, remarks that went against US President Donald Trump’s position on the disputed territory. Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it in 1981. The United Nations and most of the international community consider the territory occupied Syrian land and does not recognise Israel’s annexation of it. In 2019, Trump recognised Israeli sovereignty over the territory, reversing decades of US policy. Ambassador Tom Barrack on Friday said Israel “still” occupies the territory in an interview with Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur Mario Nawfal. Barrack now says that was a description of the territory’s historical status, “not an endorsement of the United Nations’ position” on the Golan. “United States policy on the Golan was set by President Trump in 2019 and is unchanged,” he said in a statement to Associated Press on Sunday. He said he intended to explain why he does not anticipate annexation in Lebanon, where Israeli forces were occupying parts of the south after the latest Israel-Hezbollah war, and to argue that negotiated agreements, rather than territorial maps, are more durable and that he had cited the Golan as an example that “territory taken by force remains contested for generations”. In the Friday interview, Barrack had also criticised Israel’s strikes on an airbase in northern Syria earlier last week. Israeli officials said the strikes intended to prevent Turkey from establishing a presence at the base. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz defended the strikes, saying on social media on Sunday that critics who initially called it “unnecessary and politically motivated” changed their position after the government said they were based on “clear intelligence” and at the recommendation of the Israeli army. He added that Israel would not allow Turkey “to establish itself in Syria and threaten Israeli security”. The strikes last Tuesday have highlighted growing tensions between Israel and Turkey over Ankara’s increased influence in Syria following the fall of Bashar al-Assad. Turkey and Syria have denied that Turkish forces were due to be deployed at the Abu Duhur base. Barrack’s comments on the Golan also sparked a backlash in Washington. Florida Republican Senator Rick Scott wrote on social media that the ambassador appears to have “forgotten” Trump’s recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the territory. Barrack went further on the defensive on Sunday, responding to criticism of his assessment of continuing negotiations between Israel and Lebanon over Israeli withdrawal and the disarmament of the militant group. He had said “there are two people missing from that [negotiating] table – Hezbollah and Iran”. That remark prompted speculation Barrack meant Tehran and Hezbollah should join the US-backed negotiations. On Sunday, Barrack stressed that the US does not negotiate with Hezbollah but said he was pointing out that “the weapons in question are supplied and financed by Iran”, which complicates negotiations over their fate. “I was describing the difficulty of the problem, not proposing a new table,” Barrack told Associated Press. “Hezbollah is a designated foreign terrorist organisation. We do not negotiate with it and nothing I said suggests otherwise.” He also defended his remarks questioning who would replace Tehran’s financial support for Shiite communities in southern Lebanon, saying that raising those questions was “not conferring standing on anyone”.

title: Trump takes starring role at Washington’s IndyCar debut
description: The US president waved the green flag to start the Freedom 250 Grand Prix on Sunday, capping celebrations of America’s 250th birthday.
content: US President Donald Trump rode a ceremonial lap in his armoured limousine and waved the green flag to start Sunday’s IndyCar race through the streets of Washington, capping celebrations of America’s 250th birthday. Trump, who created the Freedom 250 Grand Prix by executive order as part of the United States anniversary commemoration, had a prime view of the spectacle as open-wheel cars roared past iconic landmarks at speeds up to 298 km/h (185mph). “It has turned out to be bigger than we ever thought possible,” Trump told race telecaster Fox. “The track is wonderful. I want everyone to be safe and the people to have a good time.” Trump greeted IndyCar series owner Roger Penske, 89, and the seven Indianapolis 500 winners in the field of 25 before the 147-lap event began, telling the racers, “Good luck, do well, have fun.” “Roger told me they had been trying to do it for 20 years and when Trump came along they got it done,” the 80-year-old president said. The race was expected to draw roughly 200,000 spectators, officials said, ‌and tickets were free. Passes to private trackside clubs sold for US$5,000. Trump was inside his armoured limousine known as “The Beast” as the vehicle and his motorcade slowly took a lap around the 2.7km (1.7-mile) layout, which weaves around such landmarks as the Washington Monument, the National Archives and Smithsonian museums, including the National Gallery of Art. “The president wanted to do this. He’s a big fan. We wanted to be part of the 250th anniversary,” Penske said. “This is really a by-product of our team trying to take it to the next level. This is an iconic race.” Flyovers were next, including ones by a stealth bomber and Air Force One, and air traffic was paused at nearby Reagan National Airport due to the race. Trump then waved the green flag at the start-finish line in front of the US Capitol building to begin the 250-mile race. “The 100,000 people who will be coming here today, they care about the country,” Penske said. “They are excited to see us racing here.” Trump has taken major roles in other events to celebrate the anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776, marking the split of 13 original American colonies from Britain. Among the activities was an Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) bout in a huge cage on the White House lawn in June. Spanish pole-sitter Alex Palou, a six-time winner this year, can clinch his fourth consecutive IndyCar season title and fifth in six years. “It’s incredible,” Palou said of the event. “For sure surpassed all my expectations.” IndyCar and Penske Racing are paying much of the US$35 million cost to stage the grand prix, supported by sponsors to boost attention for a series best known for the Indianapolis 500 oval classic. “This is an Indy 500 on the street track,” said New Zealand driver Scott McLaughlin. Kyle Kirkwood was overjoyed at racing around the capital city. “Thrilled to be driving around these amazing streets,” Kirkwood said. “It’s a big moment as an American to be able to drive around DC. It’s an event that America is putting on and something that’s very special.” The race is expected to be a once-in-a-lifetime extravaganza. “I don’t know if we’ll ever drive IndyCars around the nation’s capital again, so the fact we’re doing it is a spectacle,” US racer Josef Newgarden said. “This feels like the Indy 500.” Penske said IndyCar would consider a US capital return. “Never say no. We’ll talk about it,” Penske said. “We’ll have to meet next week and figure out where we’re going next.” Like much of what happens in Washington, it is not entirely smooth running on the streets. Pavement bumps around the course are expected to challenge drivers. “The bumps are so big. There’s not much you can do,” Palou said before the race. “You need to have a car that’s all right over bumps, that’s not trying to kill you every time.”

title: Zelensky details rift with Ukraine’s dismissed defence minister Fedorov
description: The president said inaccurate defence ministry information contributed to an awkward encounter with Trump over the use of Starlink in Russia.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believes actions taken by dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, including his involvement in mass protests and calls for an election, were misguided, as he publicly detailed their dispute for the first time. Zelensky also alluded to problematic decisions over defence spending and said inaccurate information provided by the Defence Ministry contributed to an awkward encounter with US President Donald Trump over the use of Starlink in Russia. Zelensky disclosed figures showing Ukraine’s growing shortage of Patriot air-defence missiles needed to counter Russian ballistic attacks, with deliveries from Western allies declining in the past three years even as Russian missile strikes intensified. He highlighted battlefield gains, however, saying Ukrainian forces have almost completely recaptured the Dnipropetrovsk region, with only about 10 sq km (around 4 square miles) remaining under Russian control. The Ukrainian president made the remarks during a two-hour off-the-record meeting with reporters on Saturday, with a transcript released publicly on Sunday. Zelensky’s first public comments on Fedorov dismissal His comments ranged widely, covering the latest battlefield developments, efforts to counter Russian ballistic attacks, the state of peace negotiations, Ukraine’s budgetary challenges and the political turmoil surrounding Fedorov’s dismissal. “I really had and still have a very positive attitude towards Mykhailo. We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things,” he said. Fedorov, a popular minister credited with modernising Ukraine’s armed forces and accelerating the military’s embrace of technology and drone warfare, was dismissed last month after reportedly falling out with the country’s top military commander. His removal triggered mass protests that lasted for weeks but ultimately failed to force a reversal of the decision. Fedorov later called for an election. Zelensky said he had offered Fedorov four different options to continue working in the government. Fedorov, he said, rejected all of them. The Ukrainian leader told journalists that he believes holding an election during the war would be a huge risk with the potential to “split Ukraine apart”. “I believe elections during a war like this would generally pose enormous risks. Holding elections right now would be a tsunami for the state that would split Ukraine apart,” he said. Zelensky said he had previously faced pressure to hold an election during the war but no partners had come up with a plan for how a poll could be held safely, legitimately and democratically. Inaccurate information led to uncomfortable White House encounter Zelensky appeared to link Fedorov to an awkward episode involving Starlink and Elon Musk. Zelensky said that earlier this year, the defence ministry had told him that SpaceX had agreed to allow Ukraine to use Starlink over Russian territory to carry out deep strike operations, subject to political approval. Acting on that, Zelensky said, he raised the issue directly with US President Donald Trump. He told Trump that Musk had confirmed the proposed use. Zelensky said the two sides subsequently sought Musk’s confirmation and discussed financing for the project. But at a later meeting, Zelensky said Trump told him that Musk had rejected the proposal and accused him of having misled the US president. Musk considered the move a dangerous escalation, according to Zelensky. “He said that I had supposedly deceived him, because Musk had denied Ukraine the use of Starlink on Russian territory. I went back to our ministry of defence and they said that maybe it was so,” he said. Zelensky did not explicitly accuse Fedorov of lying. He said the situation was among the reasons behind “some of the steps”. Zelensky also pushed back against protesters’ vilification of former army chief, General Oleksandr Syrsky, who he dismissed, and current Defence Minister Major Geneneral Yevhen Khmara, saying they had gone too far. “Maybe someone doesn’t like Syrsky for one reason or another. But the slogans ‘Syrsky is the devil, Khmara is the devil’,” he said. “Listen, this is too much. Do you understand? In principle, you can’t treat the military like this and tolerate it, especially when it was the military that made it possible for any peaceful protests to take place in the Ukrainian capital at all.” Pressure on defence budget but military successes Zelensky also described severe financial pressure on Ukraine’s defence effort. He said the Defence Ministry faced a US$27 billion budget shortfall after spending decisions earlier in the year brought forward funds originally intended for the second half of this year. Touching on a corruption inquiry that led Zelensky to fire one of his most senior officials this week, he said anti-corruption investigators do not believe the president was involved. The investigators had named a deputy head of the presidential office among the suspects in a money-laundering case. “The heads of anti-corruption agencies have zero questions for me. They understand perfectly well that I am not involved in anything like that. And this is important to me,” he said. On the battlefield, Zelensky was optimistic. In addition to Ukraine almost completely regaining control of the Dnipropetrovsk region, he said another operation was under way elsewhere and that its results were expected by the end of August. The president said Russia’s principal objective remained the Konstantynivka-Sloviansk-Kramatorsk axis, and that Moscow was still demanding that Ukraine withdraw from the Donbas region as a condition for a settlement. Still struggling for access to Patriot missiles Zelensky said Ukraine was receiving substantially fewer Patriot interceptor missiles even as Russian ballistic attacks are increasing. He said Ukraine received 675 Patriot missiles in 2023, compared with 364 in 2025 and an expected 264 this year. Zelensky said he wanted to secure 300 additional Patriot missiles for the coming winter, while Ukraine’s air force had requested 360. The shortfall is particularly serious, because the United States and European partners are struggling to expand production. Zelensky said Ukraine was also preparing alternatives to Starlink, including a European communications project, as Russia and China work on their own competing system.

title: Landfill collapse kills at least 30 in Guinea as rescuers search for survivors
description: Heavy rains washed over waste at a landfill in Guinea’s capital Conakry on Sunday, triggering a landslide that buried nearby shacks.
content: A landslide at a ⁠landfill in Guinea’s capital killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted the collapse of a massive mound of waste that engulfed nearby tents and shacks. The incident happened less than a week ‌after the government announced plans to close the site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the continuing rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa. The landslide took place at around 2am local time in the Gbessia commune of ⁠Conakry, according to a government statement. The death toll was 30, with six people seriously ‌injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said. Rescuers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which ‌witnesses said was large enough to bury a block of flats along with more ⁠precarious dwellings. One woman, Cire ⁠Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I have lost all my children. All ‌I can do is put my trust in God,” she said. Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite reserves and richest untapped iron ‌ore ‌deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the ‌country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million ⁠people living on less than US$4.20 per day, according to a World Bank report published in ⁠April. Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djenab Toure, announced on Thursday that the government was closing the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to ‌be relocated outside Conakry. Prime Minister ‌Amadou Oury Bah visited the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.

title: Zelensky says Ukraine had no role in Nord Stream pipeline blast after suspect arrested
description: Croatian police have detained a second Ukrainian national in connection with the 2022 sabotage of the pipelines linking Russia to Europe.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country played no role in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines linking Russia to Europe, following the arrest in Croatia of a second Ukrainian suspect sought by Germany. “Ukraine has never even been involved in even the idea of this operation,” Zelensky told reporters during the Ukraine Nordic-Baltic summit in Kyiv on Sunday. “I hope there will be results of the investigation. We are ready to help.” Croatian police arrested a Ukrainian national identified only as Vladimir Z at Germany’s request, the Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office said on Wednesday. He is a trained scuba diver who was allegedly part of a group that used explosives to blow up the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm in September 2022, according to German authorities. Last year, Ukrainian national Serhii K was arrested in Italy and extradited to Germany where he was later charged over the sabotage. The Nord Stream 1 undersea link via the Baltic Sea to Germany was the main route for Russian pipeline gas flows before the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while the second pipeline was completed but never operated. In 2021, the year before the war started, Nord Stream 1 delivered more than a third of Russia’s total gas exports to Europe. There has been intense speculation over who was responsible for the attacks. Russia blamed it on the US, Ukraine and Poland and called them “beneficiaries” of the blasts. Zelensky said the Ukrainian Prosecutor’s Office and the Foreign Ministry were engaged on the issue. “It is important for us now not to lose partnerships with the countries involved,” he told reporters. “We are open to joint steps to clarify all circumstances.”

title: US warns Canada not to think it can win ‘devastating’ trade war
description: Bilateral trade talks have broken down as Ottawa says it would retaliate and match US tariffs affecting US$20 billion of Canadian goods.
content: The Trump administration on Sunday warned that Canada would be “foolish” to think it could win a trade war with the United States, predicting a “devastating” impact on its northern neighbour. Negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down late Friday, putting into force new 50 per cent US tariffs impacting about US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, or 5.5 per cent of Canadian exports to the US. Canada in retaliation said it would match US tariffs, with new levies notably targeting the US steel and dairy industries to take effect on September 8. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Canada would come out worse from tussling with President Donald Trump in a trade war. The United States currently accounts for roughly 70 per cent of Canadian exports. “We’re great trading partners, right? But Canada gets the benefit of trading with the US way more than the US gets the benefit of trading with Canada,” he told the “Fox News Sunday” talk show. “To think that they’re going to go to war with Donald Trump and actually win that war with the US, I think it’s foolish on their part.” He predicted that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney would return to negotiations “very very quickly, because it’s going to be devastating for his country”. Carney was defiant on Saturday, announcing retaliatory tariffs on the US after walking away from a “bad deal” on trade as the rift between the long-time allies deepened. “You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said. Carney cited last-minute US demands that would restrict Canadian trade deals with other countries and unacceptable “threats” to the French language and Quebec culture. Trump hit back early Sunday, saying, “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!” “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” Trump added in a post on Truth Social. The acrimony underscored the deepening rift between the close allies since Trump began his second term in January 2025, including his repeated threats to make Canada the 51st US state. Carney has said bilateral relations have been forever changed, and that Canada must reduce its reliance on the US. Despite the economic fallout, he has won political support at home for his willingness to stand up to Washington since taking office two months after Trump returned to the presidency. “We have a bully in Washington,” Canadian retired teacher Stuart Edwards said on Saturday in Fort Erie, Ontario, in the shadow of the Peace Bridge, a conduit for billions of dollars in annual trade with the United States. “We’re not going to put up with it, Canada isn’t. We’ll fight back,” he said. In the recent talks in Washington, Canada was seeking relief from Trump’s tariffs on autos, steel and aluminium, which have battered the country’s economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an ironclad trade relationship. The White House had alleged “discriminatory treatment” by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told The New York Times on Saturday that the US had offered to reduce its tariffs on steel, aluminium and autos, as well as eliminate a recently imposed tariff on Canadian timber. Greer said those measures would have given Canada “the most preferential treatment of any trading partner”, according to the Times. He also said no new talks were planned with Canadian negotiators.

title: Chinese archaeologists heading to Peru for first joint project to explore ancient sites
description: The partnership – part of a wider effort to expand cultural ties – will explore sites associated with the 5,000-year-old Caral civilisation.
content: Chinese archaeologists will carry out their first joint field project in South America by exploring sites dating back thousands of years in Peru as Beijing steps up its efforts to deepen cultural ties with the region. The Institute of Archaeology of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences said it had signed a cooperation agreement with the Caral Archaeological Zone of the Peruvian Ministry of Culture and the Professional School of Archaeology at the National University of San Marcos to explore sites related to the Caral civilisation. The collaboration will include training, field surveys, joint excavations and projects to preserve cultural heritage. The partnership will later expand to examine sites dating back to the much later Inca period in the Andean highlands to support studies comparing ancient Chinese and South American civilisations. The joint project will start with field surveys of key sites associated with the civilisation, including major population centres such as Caral and Aspero, to develop excavation plans. “This cooperation fills a blank in field archaeology for Chinese archaeological institutions in South America,” the Chinese institute said. The Caral people, often described as the oldest known civilisation in the Americas, flourished around 3000BC to 1800BC along the coast of modern-day Peru. Through the partnership, Chinese researchers will obtain first-hand archaeological data on early American civilisations, contributing what the institute described as “a Chinese academic perspective” to the study of early Pacific Rim societies. The institute also said Peruvian institutions would be able to benefit from Chinese know-how in fields such as archaeological technology and heritage conservation. In recent years, China has been pushing to strengthen relations with Latin American countries through stronger trade ties and major infrastructure projects such as the Chancay megaport in Peru. The impact of US tariffs and Washington’s efforts to assert its influence in the region have also prompted some countries to diversify their partnerships, including closer ties with Beijing. This year, senior officials and business delegations from countries including Uruguay and Brazil have visited China. These trends have also spurred efforts to boost cultural ties, including projects with cultural institutions in Peru and Mexico to stage joint exhibitions showcasing ancient American civilisations. During a state visit to China by then-Peruvian president Pedro Pablo Kuczynski in 2016, the two countries pledged to step up cultural exchanges as part of efforts to strengthen their comprehensive strategic partnership. The cultural alignment was further solidified during President Xi’s state visit to Peru in November 2024, when the two sides agreed to foster closer ties between cultural institutions, performing arts groups and educational bodies, and to step up joint efforts to protect cultural heritage.

title: Indonesia arrests 72 suspected of starting forest fires as haze persists
description: Investigators are tracing financial records to determine whether companies have financed or ordered the land clearing linked to fire cases.
content: Indonesian authorities arrested 72 people suspected of starting some of the forest and peatland fires as huge blazes in central and west Indonesia triggered choking haze. Indonesia has been battling fires driven by an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season, generating dense smoke that crossed into Malaysia, according to Indonesia’s National Disaster Management Agency, or BNPB. Fires are a regular problem in Indonesia that strain relations with neighbouring countries. Plantation owners and traditional farmers often start fires to clear land for farming, according to Mohammad Irhamni, director of special crimes at the National Police’s Criminal Investigation Agency. The arson suspects were being investigated in connection with 89 forest and land fire cases across five provinces on the island of Borneo and four on Sumatra, Irhamni said. Most of the suspects were accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas for plantations at lower cost, he said. Investigators were still tracing financial records to determine whether companies financed or ordered the land clearing, signalling the probe could expand beyond those arrested. “We will not stop at the perpetrators on the ground,” Irhami said in a news conference in the capital, Jakarta, on Sunday. “We will determine who benefited from these activities and who was ultimately behind them.” The suspects faced charges that carried penalties ranging from hefty fines to prison terms of up to 15 years, he said. Blazes on Sunday blanketed parts of Borneo, the world’s third-largest island shared by Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. Indonesia administers about three-quarters of the island, where the country’s Environment Ministry recorded more than 3,700 hotspots on Sunday. BNPB chief Suharyanto said fire activity had increased in West, Central and South Kalimantan provinces on Borneo, where many blazes worsened due to peatlands, prolonging haze in several areas. “Land that appears extinguished on the surface may still contain embers underneath, so sufficient rainfall is crucial to rewet the peat and fully suppress the fires,” said Suharyanto, who, like many Indonesians, uses a single name. The western island of South Sumatra also battled blazes, with more than 1,700 hotspots detected on Sunday, causing choked haze and reducing visibility to only 10 metres (33 feet) in some areas, the ministry said. Cloud-seeding operations resumed over Kalimantan on Sunday, deploying 30 helicopters for water-bombing and aerial patrol missions over Kalimantan and another 22 helicopters covering Sumatra. Meanwhile, Malaysia has suffered severe smoke from the blazes, with its eastern state of Sarawak among the hardest hit. One district recorded “very unhealthy” air quality on Friday, while eight others posted unhealthy readings, prompting the closure of nearly 600 schools and affecting about 200,000 students, the Sarawak government said.

title: Putin wants to draft 300,000 new troops for war, Ukraine’s Zelensky says
description: Russia could draft more troops in 2027 to reach its goal of 500,000 and aims to produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles per year, he adds.
content: Ukraine thinks Russia is planning to draft an additional 300,000 troops for its war effort after Russian parliamentary elections in mid-September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Moscow’s forces are pressing ahead with an effort to capture the rest of eastern Ukraine’s industrialised Donbas region, where its troops have ground ‌forward at what Kyiv says is a great cost. In comments to reporters released on Sunday, Zelensky said Russia could draft more troops in 2027 to reach an overall goal of 500,000, part of what he described as a “peripheral mobilisation” targeting Russia’s far-flung regions. “We believe it will not take place in the central cities,” he said. “But I don’t think they will be able to hide it very well.” Parliamentary elections in Russia are set for September 18 to 20. As fighting rages around the strategic ⁠city of Kostiantynivka, Zelensky said Russia was losing a “maximum” amount of troops in its bid to advance into Ukraine’s so-called fortress belt of eastern ‌cities. He also hailed recent gains by Kyiv’s troops in southeastern Ukraine, adding that the amount of territory occupied by Russia and liberated by Ukrainian forces in 2026 would be equal. Russia is bolstering its battlefield offensive with an escalating air war on Ukrainian cities made worse ⁠by a critical shortage of US-designed ⁠Patriot interceptors. Zelensky said the 264 interceptors Ukraine was expecting to have received in 2026 represented a significant drop from 2025, when Ukraine received 364, and 2023, when ‌it received 675. He added that Russia was aiming to develop a capacity to produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles per year. Over the summer, Ukraine has escalated a campaign ‌of ‌drone strikes targeting Russian economic infrastructure, including oil refineries and online retailers’ warehouses, seeking to destroy infrastructure it says is central to Russia’s ‌war effort. Russian President Vladimir Putin said in comments on Saturday that Kyiv had opened “Pandora’s box” by striking economic targets, saying Russia would hit ⁠back at Ukraine’s “most sensitive economic sectors”. Zelensky said Ukraine was facing another difficult winter of ⁠Russian strikes on its energy grid, a prospect that had prompted Kyiv’s air force to ask for 360 missile interceptors for the season. He also said he had reached an agreement with France on at least one SAMP/T air-defence ‌system this year, and with Germany on ‌the supply of about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors through 2028. Ukraine’s war effort was further complicated by a US$27 billion defence funding gap this year, Zelensky said, a result of higher-than-expected spending in the first half of the year. At least US$8 billion was needed for “a normal start” to 2027, plus about US$20 billion more for military salaries, payments to families of the dead, as well as other financing, he added.

title: Alex Lanier, mixed-doubles pair clinch badminton world titles in France’s golden double
description: An Se-young helps South Korea to double triumph as well, while Chinese top seeds in mixed doubles, women’s doubles lose their finals.
content: Alex Lanier on Saturday became the first singles badminton player from France to clinch the world championship title, moments after the French took gold in the mixed doubles. In the women’s final, South Korea’s world No 1 An Se-young beat Japan’s Akane Yamaguchi 21-17, 21-14 for her second world crown. But it was history for French badminton, after the 21-year-old Lanier beat Japan’s Kodai Naraoka 21-11, 21-11 in a lopsided men’s final that took 50 minutes at New Delhi’s Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium. World No 10 Lanier, who knocked out Hong Kong’s Angus Ng Ka-long in the last 16, smashed the winner as he jumped in delight and hugged his coach before standing on the podium for his gold medal. “I think definitely today was a day for French badminton and it was a day for the whole staff also,” Lanier said after the triumph. “Today it was the day for France, and when the mixed won, everyone was happy, and I just thought that I needed to give them a double smile, double moments, and I needed to make history again.” The finalists went toe-to-toe until the mid-game interval of the opening game with former European champion Lanier leading 11-9. The brawny Lanier, whose parents are professional sailors, then hit the gas to open the gap and take the opener in 23 minutes with a lethal combination of attack and defence. Lanier kept up the momentum in the second game to take five straight points and an 8-3 lead. World No 11 Naraoka, a former finalist, fought back with his power game but soon lost steam to a fitter and inspired Lanier, who also beat world No 2 Kunlavut Vitidsarn and No 7 Canadian Victor Lai en route to the final. Lanier’s win tops off a year of French ‌dominance, after Christo Popov’s World Tour Finals victory last year, and ⁠the French team’s triumph over Denmark to win the continental championships this year. The women’s title clash was much closer, with last year’s winner Yamaguchi giving it her all in a fast-paced battle between No 1 and No 2. Yamaguchi’s returns and jump smashes entertained a large Sunday crowd, but An had answers to everything with her attacking and baseline play. Reigning Olympic champion An, who won her previous world title in 2023, secured the win in 49 minutes and let out a scream and raised her hands to celebrate. Yamaguchi, with a silver, became the first women’s singles player to achieve six medals at the showpiece event. Earlier ⁠in the day, ⁠Thom Gicquel and Delphine Delrue became the first French pair to win a badminton ‌world title after defeating top seeds Feng Yanzhe and Huang Dongping of China 22-20, 19-21, ‌21-15 in ‌the mixed doubles final. In the women’s doubles final, South Korea’s Baek Ha-na and Lee So-hee also beat the Chinese top-ranked pair, Liu Shengshu and Tan Ning, 21-15, 21-15, becoming ‌the country’s first world champions in the event in 31 years.

title: Your backyard could hold a rare earth fortune – and this orange lichen is the clue
description: Chinese scientists discover link between lichen growth and potentially untapped rare-earth-bearing carbonates and mineral deposits.
content: Next time you spot a vivid orange-yellow crust spreading across a rock in your garden, on a country wall or along a hiking trail, take a closer look – you might be standing on a fortune. A Chinese research team has found that a humble lichen could serve as a visible field indicator of unknown rare earth deposits around the world. The researchers said the lichen’s distinctive colour made it easy to spot on exposed rock, and the discovery could be combined with unmanned aerial vehicles and hyperspectral remote sensing to screen large areas for potential rare earth-bearing carbonates. Chinese scientists have spent decades trying to identify biological indicators that could help locate mineral deposits. “This is the second time Chinese scientists have discovered a similar indicator – the first was copper grass in the 1950s – and both are original scientific discoveries in mineral exploration,” said Professor Li Yang of Peking University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences on August 17. The study, titled “Lichen as a Potential Exploration Tool for Rare Earth Element – Enriched Carbonatites”, was published in the peer-reviewed journal Economic Geology on July 27. The lichen, Xanthoria elegans, grows preferentially on rare earth element-enriched carbonates. Researchers found it on 57 of 67 carbonatite rocks mapped at the Bayan Obo mining area in northern China, the world’s largest rare earth deposit. Although the lichen is widely distributed around the world, researchers found it was rarely present on granite, sandstone, quartzite and other non-carbonatite rocks. The chance was typically below 1 per cent when it did occur on these rocks, according to the study. “Once we find it, we can prioritise sampling, which significantly increases the probability of finding [rare earth deposits] compared with searching randomly,” Li said. He said its brownish colour came from the organism itself rather than rare earth elements or iron. “That is why it is such a good indicator, because you can see it from far away.” Chemical analysis provided further evidence of the link, with the lichen containing total rare earth elements of 3,500 to 17,000 parts per million. Its rare earth content also increased with that of the underlying rock. Lichens growing on more highly mineralised carbonates contained more rare earth elements than those growing on barren carbonates or altered surrounding rocks. The researchers found tiny phases enriched in rare earth elements and barium inside the lichen’s organic material. This suggests that particles from the underlying rock may be incorporated during weathering and lichen-rock interactions. “We believe that this lichen likes rare earth elements, but the specific biological mechanism is not yet clear,” Li said. The finding does not mean the lichen actively seeks out rare earth elements. The biological and geochemical processes behind its elemental uptake remain uncertain. The association is particularly strong at Bayan Obo, in China’s Inner Mongolia province, where the lichen preferentially colonises carbonates and areas affected by carbonatite-related alkaline alteration. Early observations suggest the phenomenon may extend beyond Bayan Obo. Li said colleagues working at elevations above 5,000 metres (16,404 feet) in the West Kunlun Mountains, southwest of Xinjiang, had reported a similar association after the paper was published. Broader field studies are still needed to determine whether the lichen can reliably indicate rare earth mineralisation in other geological settings.

title: Singapore’s Lawrence Wong unveils major pro-family measures amid record low fertility
description: The government will fully bear the bill for increasing childcare leave for Singaporean parents, instead of co-sharing it with employers.
content: Singapore will increase its spending on pro-family measures focusing on easing childcare costs, with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong calling them “one of the best investments” on Sunday, as the city state aims to reverse its declining fertility rate. The policy shifts announced by Wong at the annual National Day Rally, Singapore’s biggest political speech of the year, are some of the most significant in years, revolving around boosting support for families to have children. He also spoke about exploring a new offshore power generation infrastructure. The pro-family measures include increasing childcare leave depending on how many children a family has, with the government fully footing the bill, as opposed to sharing it with employers, topping up funds into children’s post-secondary education accounts and reducing full-day childcare fees in government-supported schools. “With these changes, the government will absorb a much larger share of childcare and preschool costs. But I believe this is one of the best investments we can make,” said Wong, without mentioning an estimated figure of increased government spending. Singapore’s total fertility rate dropped to a historic low of 0.87 in 2025. The government has set up an inter-agency workgroup, chaired by Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office Indranee Rajah, to address the trend. Among the policy shifts, childcare leave will now be linked to the number of children a parent has. Currently, every working parent has six days of leave if their youngest child is six years old or below and two days if their youngest child is aged seven to 12. This will be increased to eight leave days for one child, aged up to 12 years old, 10 days for two children and 12 days for three or more children. While the cost of child-related leave is currently shared between the government and employers, the government will cover the expenditure of all statutory child-related leave, up to a reimbursement limit. Wong said the government would also aim to reduce full-day childcare fares to S$150 (US$118) a month and infant care fees to S$300 at government-supported schools. Currently, families can pay nearly S$600 per month for full-day childcare, and more than S$1,000 a month for infant care. Affordable housing will also be available to more buyers under the build-to-order (BTO) scheme, which enables Singaporean families to buy public housing flats directly from the government. The income ceiling for those eligible for this scheme was raised from S$14,000 to S$16,000 for most flats. First-time applicants for a new BTO flat would get an additional ballot chance for every child of theirs or those expecting a child, Wong said. “Ultimately, the decision to have children is a deeply personal one. Policies alone cannot make this happen. But what we can do is make it easier for Singaporeans who want children to start and raise a family,” he added. Norman Li, a psychology professor at Singapore Management University, said that for most people who were reluctant to have children, the perceived burden of raising children in Singapore was a lot more than what any monetary policy could cover and monetary incentives were not very effective. He argued that in modern environments that were more densely populated and where people faced high levels of economic insecurity, there was increased stress and anxiety, prompting them to focus more on themselves than on childcare. “It’s not easy to do, but to get people to reproduce more, it will likely require getting them to feel more secure economically and with their own social status, and to be better connected to and feel supported by their family and friends,” said Li. While measures to entice families to have children would be stepped up, Wong also stressed that it was important for Singapore to continue supplementing its population with new immigrants to support its growing number of seniors. Singapore is one of the fastest-ageing countries in the world. By 2030, one in four citizens will be aged 65 and above. Wong noted that Singapore was built by immigrants and “being Singaporean has never been about ancestry or where your family first came from”. “It has always been about commitment. A commitment to put Singapore first. A commitment to our values and way of life and a belief that, whatever our backgrounds, our future is ours to build together,” Wong added. While the government will always ensure that Singaporeans remain the majority, in the coming years, the overall population and labour force are expected to grow more slowly. On protecting children from harm on social media, Wong said that platforms would be required to have more robust and reliable checks on the age of users. If these safeguards were inadequate, the government would consider additional restrictions, including raising the minimum age for access to beyond 13, he added. Wong also announced major infrastructure plans in the coming decades including on the northeast of the city state, where the government was studying the possibility of building undersea tunnels to the military base at Pulau Tekong. In the southwest, Wong said the plan was to merge some of the islands including Sudong, where there is an airstrip that the armed forces now use in emergencies; Semakau, currently a landfill; and Bukom, where Singapore’s first refinery still operates. He said the new island, formed in a similar way to Singapore’s Jurong Island, would not just be for petrochemicals but could support a new generation of industries, including advanced manufacturing facilities and military operations. It could also accommodate new “power generation infrastructure” to meet Singapore’s future needs, Wong added. Last month, Singapore announced it would rename the Ministry of Trade and Industry to the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry effective October 1, indicating that energy was a key focus of the country. “Jurong Island shaped our economy for the last 50 years. This new Western island can help shape Singapore for the next 50 years and beyond,” Wong said.

title: Opinion | Deutsche Bank’s yuan mandate boosts Chinese currency’s global reach
description: The clearing mandate from China elevates Frankfurt as a primary hub for offshore renminbi settlement, challenging London’s dominance.
content: The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) authorising Deutsche Bank to serve as a renminbi clearing bank in Frankfurt marks a pivotal milestone in the protracted narrative of the currency’s internationalisation. It also carries profound geoeconomic implications that extend far beyond the immediate efficiencies of cross-border payments. By granting this designation to a German institution – the first European lender to receive such a mandate – Beijing has recalibrated the axis of its financial diplomacy, leveraging Germany’s industrial heft and Frankfurt’s position as the European Central Bank’s home to deepen financial integration with the continent’s economic powerhouse. This move is not merely a technical upgrade to clearing infrastructure. It is a calculated geopolitical signal that prioritises bilateral economic resilience with the European Union’s largest economy, even as broader political friction over trade deficits, technology transfer and human rights persists. For Deutsche Bank, the appointment consolidates its long-standing commitment to the renminbi ecosystem. It transforms the bank from a passive participant in China’s financial opening to an active linchpin of European renminbi liquidity, yet the strategic calculus for both signatories appears to be anchored in a shared imperative to de-risk from US dollar dependency while navigating an increasingly fragmented global monetary order. At its core, the clearing mandate functionally elevates Frankfurt as a primary hub for offshore renminbi settlement, directly challenging the traditional dominance of London and, to a lesser extent, Luxembourg in European renminbi trading. Moreover, by designating a German bank, the PBOC implicitly acknowledges the shifting gravity of euro zone financial power. Germany’s export-oriented manufacturing sector can generate renminbi demand through trade in machinery, automobiles and chemical products. Still, the geoeconomic benefit is asymmetric. Deutsche Bank’s appointment as Europe’s first non-Chinese renminbi clearing house accords Beijing with a trusted European institutional vehicle to drive its currency’s internationalisation and draw European corporations deeper into China’s domestic capital ecosystem with lower perceived geopolitical resistance. The geopolitical resonance of this authorisation is equally striking as it unfolds against a backdrop of transatlantic divergence over how to engage with Beijing. The United States has pressured European allies to decouple from Chinese trade, citing national security risks. Another important side effect is that Berlin and Brussels are implicitly asserting a degree of strategic autonomy, prioritising commercial pragmatism over the security-centric discourse emanating from the US. This is not a wholesale embrace of China’s financial model; rather, it is a calibrated bet that deeper renminbi integration can yield tangible economic dividends without ceding political sovereignty, especially as Germany faces competitive pressures from both US tariffs and China’s own industrial policy. From a monetary sovereignty perspective, the clearing bank authorisation signals China’s confidence in the yuan’s international resilience even as the currency’s share of global payments remains modest compared with the US dollar and euro. By outsourcing some clearing functions to a foreign institution, the PBOC is effectively testing the waters for a more decentralised offshore renminbi market, where price discovery and liquidity provision are partly driven by private sector actors rather than state-owned Chinese banks. This devolution could enhance the renminbi’s attractiveness as a reserve currency for European central banks as it reduces the politicisation of access to the currency. The Deutsche Bank appointment also serves as a tacit rebuttal to proponents of de-dollarisation who view renminbi internationalisation as a zero-sum challenge to the US dollar; instead, it positions China’s currency as a complement for specific trade corridors, particularly in green energy and infrastructure, where German and Chinese interests intersect. Ultimately, this geoeconomic gambit is a double-edged sword for all stakeholders. For China, it diversifies offshore clearing beyond Hong Kong and Singapore, creating a European time zone buffer that extends trading hours and reduces reliance on US-based settlement systems – a critical redundancy in an era of financial sanctions. For Europe, it offers a tangible mechanism to bring about the EU’s strategic goal of “de-risking” without full decoupling, allowing firms to access Chinese markets while maintaining ties to Western payment infrastructures. The success of this arrangement hinges on sustained mutual trust and regulatory harmonisation, both of which are strained by divergent data privacy laws, anti-money-laundering standards and geopolitical flashpoints such as Taiwan or Ukraine. The Frankfurt clearing bank is less a harbinger of a bipolar financial world than a stress test for whether economic interdependence can withstand political headwinds, a test whose outcome will shape renminbi internationalisation and the very architecture of 21st century global finance. As Deutsche Bank assumes this mantle, it must balance its commercial obligations with its new-found role as a geopolitical bridge. This position offers immense opportunity but also profound vulnerability in an increasingly contested international order.

title: China delays Chang’e-7 mission to drill for ice near lunar south pole
description: Historic mission expected as early as Monday has been postponed after safety and reliability assessment, China Manned Space Agency says.
content: China’s historic Chang’e-7 mission to drill for ice near the moon’s south pole has been delayed, the country’s human space flight programme authority said on Sunday. The Chang’e-7 – carrying an orbiter, a lander, a rover and a hopper – was expected to lift off aboard a Long March 5 rocket from the Wenchang spaceport in southern China’s Hainan province as early as Monday. The China Manned Space Agency said on Sunday evening that the mission would be postponed following a comprehensive assessment to adhere to principles of safety and reliability. “The Chang’e-7 mission does not meet the launch conditions and cannot be carried out within the scheduled launch window this year,” state news agency Xinhua reported, citing the agency. Earlier on Sunday, the National Astronomical Research Institute of Thailand (Narit) – which developed a scientific instrument on board the spacecraft – announced that the mission would be postponed due to the development of Tropical Storm Narra in the South China Sea. “Due to the target landing site on the lunar south pole, this makes for a very particular launch window in which the sun lined up just right for the lunar crater,” Narit said. “A delay by a few days would mean postponing to the next launch window in a month at the earliest.” Tropical Storm Narra has lingered over Beibu Wan – also known as the Gulf of Tonkin – between Vietnam, China’s southern Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region and the island province of Hainan over the past few days. Over the weekend, the Hainan meteorological bureau issued a blue alert for the storm, the lowest on China’s four-level typhoon warning scale. Once launched, the Chang’e-7 is expected to reach lunar orbit in about five days, where it will spend weeks mapping the landing site before sending a lander down to the surface. The lander – with the rover and hopper on board – aims to touch down at the sunlit rim of a 21km (13-mile)-wide depression called the Shackleton crater, which is located almost exactly at the lunar south pole. While sections of the rim receive sunlight, the crater’s permanently shadowed floor is thought to harbour frozen water. Together, these features could supply a future lunar base with solar power, water, oxygen and rocket fuel. A successful mission could give China a head start over the United States in building a permanent lunar base.

title: 3 elderly people injured after escalator fall at Hong Kong shopping centre
description: Online photos show fire crews and paramedics at scene as escalator remains temporarily closed.
content: A 76-year-old man has been sent to hospital after falling on an escalator at a Hong Kong shopping centre, while two other elderly people sustained minor injuries, according to police. The force received a report at 4.19pm on Sunday that three people had fallen on an escalator in phase one of Shek Lei Shopping Centre, leaving the man trapped. He sustained injuries to his arms and legs and was taken to Princess Margaret Hospital. Photos circulating online show fire services personnel and paramedics at the scene assisting the injured, with the escalator temporarily closed. The same escalator was involved in a similar incident on August 1, when a 75-year-old woman carrying a one-year-old girl lost her balance and fell, landing on a 66-year-old woman and a 72-year-old man standing behind her. All four sustained head injuries and abrasions to their limbs and were taken to the same hospital for treatment.

title: Chinese tennis star Zheng Qinwen to start US Open from qualifiers for first time
description: Paris Olympic champion likely to sit in middle of 32 qualifying hopefuls; Hong Kong’s Coleman Wong to be among top seeds in men’s qualifiers.
content: Chinese tennis star Zheng Qinwen will start from the US Open qualifying rounds for the first time in her career as qualifiers for the final grand slam of the year begin on Monday, New York time. Ranked No 127 in the world, Zheng remained some way off the main draw list, which cut off at No 118 Julia Grabher of Austria, per the women’s singles entry list as of last Wednesday. With an 11-13 record this year including six first-round defeats including at the French Open and Wimbledon, Zheng is expected to sit around the middle pack of the 32 qualifying seeds. The qualifying draw will be announced at noon on Sunday in New York. A player will need to win three matches in a row to reach the main draw, and only then will they receive the guaranteed prize money of US$140,000 for the first round, and the corresponding WTA ranking points. Chinese social media users, however, were split on Zheng’s hopes. “Just finish this season healthily and come back again next year,” said one commentator. Another comment read: “I guess she won’t make it to the main draw; it’s more like she’ll be preparing for the China Open, which she will only play thanks to a wild card.” Still, some fans stood by the Paris Olympic champion. “What you need now is nothing but a win. The confidence gained from consecutive victories is irreplaceable. Come on!” said one Weibo user. Upon arriving in New York, Zheng was seen practising with host player Varvara Lepchenko, as well as world No 7 and Wimbledon runner-up Karolína Muchová. Ranked as high as No 4 in the world in June 2025, Zheng underwent a right elbow injury operation last July and was sidelined for 10 months. Having missed last year’s US Open and this year’s Australia Open, and coupled with her rolling ranking points clearing out, Zheng’s rankings slipped to as low as No 160 in June. Compatriot Yuan Yue, who is ranked one place above Hubei native Zheng, will also play in the qualifiers, which run until Thursday local time. World No 36 Wang Xinyu, world No 54 Zhang Shuai and world No 108 Wang Xiyu will start in the main draw. Separately, Hong Kong star Coleman Wong Chak-lam also missed out on the men’s singles main draw, albeit only narrowly. Ranked No 93 in the world, and only a minor one-place drop from his career-high ranking in the first week of August, Wong was just several places below the cut-off line on the entry list, which was published last Friday. Hongkonger Wong is expected to be among the top few seeds in the qualifying draw, with Chinese player Bu Yunchaokete also among the pack. Wong, who turned 22 in June, famously reached the third round of the US Open last year, before losing to Andrey Rublev in five sets in the third round. Wong also reached the first round of the French Open earlier this year.

title: The African firms adopting Chinese AI as US-China rivalry intensifies
description: Lower costs, downloadable models and greater language flexibility are helping Chinese AI models gain ground across the continent.
content: The United States may want the world to choose sides in the AI race with China, but in Africa, many businesses are pursuing a more pragmatic strategy: using Chinese models where they offer better value or flexibility, while keeping their options open. For example, when African insurtech platform Curacel expanded the range of artificial intelligence (AI) models powering its internal infrastructure, it did not look only to Silicon Valley. Instead, the Nigeria-based firm – which provides AI-powered claims and fraud-detection infrastructure to African insurers and fintech companies – added GLM-5.3, a Chinese model developed by Beijing-based Zhipu AI, alongside models from Western providers. Henry Mascot, chief executive and co-founder of Curacel, said Chinese models delivered comparable results at lower cost on high-volume tasks such as coding, data extraction, classification and customer support, although Western systems remained stronger on the most demanding reasoning and reliability-sensitive work. “In our experience, the leading Chinese models have closed much of the performance gap,” Mascot said. He said Curacel’s multi-model set-up allowed it to use GLM-5.3 selectively. “We can route suitable workloads to it based on quality and cost without moving the entire stack or locking ourselves into one vendor,” Mascot said. “We have also used lower-cost [Chinese] models within client deployments.” Curacel’s approach reflects a broader shift, with models such as DeepSeek, Qwen from Alibaba, the owner of the South China Morning Post, and Moonshot AI’s Kimi challenging established systems from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic. Many Chinese models make their weights – the files that allow companies to adapt them and, with sufficient infrastructure, run them locally – available for download. Their growing use in Africa coincides with Beijing’s efforts to expand its role in the continent’s digital infrastructure, technical training and AI governance. Huawei Technologies is one example of how Chinese companies are combining AI models with the infrastructure needed to run them. In May, its South African cloud business introduced a “model as a service” or MaaS platform, providing pay-per-token access to DeepSeek, Qwen and GLM, together with development and deployment tools. China last month launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), with Beijing presenting its open-weight technology as an alternative to the largely proprietary systems offered by leading American companies. The contest extends beyond models to semiconductors, critical minerals, cloud infrastructure and the rules governing AI. African businesses may choose technology according to price and performance, but governments could face growing pressure to align with Washington or Beijing. That pressure is becoming more explicit. A draft State Department communication reviewed by Reuters on August 14 warned that countries joining Waico could be excluded from the US-led Pax Silica coalition. Michael Michie, co-founder of Nairobi-based EverseTech – an AI consultancy that also builds AI systems for banks, government agencies and other African organisations – said Chinese models had begun to advance more quickly. “A year or so ago, you might have expected to wait quite a long time for a Chinese model release that represented a major step forward. Now we are seeing meaningful improvements within six months or less,” Michie said. EverseTech has moved some of its clients to Chinese models. A legal-sector client switched because of the lower cost per million tokens. Another, which relied heavily on retrieval-augmented generation – a process in which an AI system searches company documents before producing an answer – moved after EverseTech found that a Chinese model could convert the documents into searchable numerical representations faster and more cheaply, Michie said. “For most customers, the question is no longer simply, ‘Which model is the most powerful?’ It is, ‘Which model gives me the capability I need at a price that makes commercial sense?’” he said. Price is far from the only consideration. In Uganda, the developers of Sunflower – an AI model providing farmers with weather updates and agricultural advice in over 30 local languages – built the system on Qwen3 after finding it handled Ugandan languages better than models from Meta Platforms or Google. Djamo, an Ivory Coast fintech company serving francophone Africa, assigns models according to the job at hand. Co-founder and CEO Hassan Bourgi said a lightweight Chinese model could handle a simple customer service task such as closing spam requests, while a more advanced model might be needed for complex work such as writing or reviewing code. “It’s getting commoditised at some point for the simple stuff,” Bourgi said. “But when it’s very complex, I think the Americans are still a bit ahead today.” Bernard Momanyi Nyagaka, co-founder of Sanifu AI, said open weights could allow banks and fintech companies to run models within their own infrastructure instead of sending sensitive information to an outside service. Sanifu helps internal teams build AI agents and data applications that automate manual work. “Open weights mean you can self-host, fine-tune and keep sensitive data – bank records, KYC [know-your-customer] documents – inside your own infrastructure, rather than sending it to a third-party API [application programming interface],” Nyagaka said. However, self-hosting requires computing capacity and technical expertise. Open-weight models may reduce reliance on a model developer, but dependence can shift to the cloud platforms, chips and technical support needed to run them. Nyagaka advised that sensitive data should be kept local, regardless of geopolitics. “For banking, data sovereignty should be a design principle, not a vendor feature. Whatever model you use, the architecture should ensure regulated data doesn’t leave your controlled environment,” he said. And while lower prices can make a model attractive, companies must also consider the cost of leaving the provider later. Michie said: “The strategic mistake would be designing the institution so that five years from now, it has no realistic ability to move away from that model or provider.” He said organisations should examine data-portability rules, termination rights and ownership of organisational data before committing to a provider. Curacel limits that risk through a model gateway – a single interface that can route tasks to Chinese, American, European or self-hosted models. It also tests models against its own workloads rather than relying only on published benchmarks. “That makes switching a routing decision instead of a product rewrite,” Mascot said. Nyagaka argued that open-weight Chinese models could, in some cases, create less dependence than proprietary Western services because companies could retain and host the model weights themselves. “The lock-in risk is highest with closed, hosted APIs of any origin,” he said. But some tech executives have rejected the idea that African businesses must choose between Chinese and American AI. “I would push back on the idea that Africa is merely a testing ground for US-China competition,” Mascot said. “African companies are active buyers. They will choose the technology that solves the problem at the right price, regardless of where it was built.” That pragmatism, according to Michie, should ultimately give African firms more room to manoeuvre. “Africa’s strongest position in the US-China technology competition is not choosing one side,” he said. “It is building enough capability and leverage to work with both and eventually contribute more of our own technology to that ecosystem.”

title: Singapore relaxes screening of dialect films after Dear You film spurs debate
description: Speaking at the National Day Rally, PM Lawrence Wong says the easing comes with the prerequisite that a Mandarin-dubbed version is available.
content: Singapore will no longer restrict the number of cinema screenings for dialect films, relaxing a decades-long policy in a significant move that analysts say was driven by recent discourse over the Chinese blockbuster Dear You. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Sunday the relaxation came with the prerequisite that a Mandarin-dubbed version would be available. Restrictions for pay television content in dialect will also be eased, with details to be announced at a later date. “Even as we promote the use of Mandarin, we can also make more room for dialects,” said Wong, delivering his Mandarin speech at the annual National Day Rally. “Many see dialects as a cultural heritage worth preserving. I agree.” Previously, guidelines dictated that Chinese films meant for theatrical release should generally be in Mandarin, and dialect films were allowed on a case-by-case basis. The policy was in line with Singapore’s Speak Mandarin Campaign, a movement launched in 1979 which originally aimed to replace dialects with Mandarin as the common language of Singapore’s Chinese community. Wong recalled recent discourse sparked by Dear You, a Chinese indie production filmed primarily in Teochew which premiered locally in June. “I believe it is because it reminded us of our pioneers, the sacrifices they made and the hardships they endured, as well as the values they lived by,” said Wong, adding that he had watched the Teochew version of the film. A Mandarin-dubbed version of the blockbuster was screened commercially with highly limited screenings in the dialect, a decision which led to concerns over the loss of dialect, authenticity and heritage. Many also questioned Singapore’s bilingual policies amid waning dialect usage. Following intense public discourse, over 250 additional screenings of the original Teochew version were approved across multiple occasions. The Ministry of Digital Development and Information said recently that a “more flexible approach” would be taken in considering applications for dialect films to be screened in their original form. Lee Cher Leng, an associate professor of Chinese Studies at the National University of Singapore, said the relaxed measures would receive a huge welcome and applause. “I think PM Wong is very much tapping into the pulse of the Singapore Chinese people having the interest of finding out more about their ancestry,” she said. Lee said the government probably did not anticipate the enormous impact of Dear You, which spurred many Chinese Singaporeans to trace their roots and visit their ancestral homes. The policy adjustment was a significant one, reflecting an appreciation of dialects as carriers of identity, memory and culture, said Darlene Machell Espena, associate professor of Southeast Asian studies at Singapore Management University. Greater access to dialect films and television would give younger Singaporeans opportunities to engage with the languages of their grandparents, helping to strengthen intergenerational connections and preserve cultural traditions, she added. “This will help immensely,” said Espena. In his speech, Wong said free-to-air broadcasts would remain mainly in Mandarin. Defending the Speak Mandarin Campaign, he said the movement’s “hard-won gains” had to be protected. The campaign aims to promote Mandarin as a common language to maintain cohesion within Singapore’s linguistically diverse Chinese community. It has restricted the use of Chinese dialects like Hokkien and Cantonese in film, television and radio for decades. “Mandarin also connects us with Chinese communities worldwide. Therefore, our bilingual policy and efforts to promote Mandarin are moving in the right direction and must continue,” said Wong, who noted that dialects were no longer the biggest threat to Mandarin. “Most Chinese Singaporeans know Mandarin but use English more often. The challenge now is to encourage those comfortable in English to speak more Mandarin,” he said. Analysts stress the importance of the campaign. Espena said: “The Speak Mandarin Campaign remains important given Singapore’s social, economic, and geopolitical realities.” Lee noted that the promotion of Mandarin had always been a cornerstone of Singapore’s language policies. “Mandarin really needs to be beefed up a lot more, because English is so pervasive now,” she said. “But dialect will never be a problem any more.”

title: Why Scotland’s modern jewellery is becoming some of the most interesting you can find
description: Scotland is becoming a growing centre for contemporary luxury jewellery as designers draw on the country’s cultural and natural influences.
content: Scotland is quietly becoming one of the most interesting places to find modern jewellery. Its roots in jewellery design run deep, laid by the likes of pre-eminent silversmith Malcolm Appleby, as well as Dorothy Hogg and Jack Cunningham, who respectively led the jewellery departments at the Edinburgh College of Art and The Glasgow School of Art.
