Now, that legacy is expanding its international reach. “Scotland has always produced exceptional makers,” says Keira Wraae-Stewart, founder of Aetla, a fine jewellery gallery that opened in Edinburgh in 2020. “But I think what has changed is the confidence and visibility of the contemporary jewellery scene.” Scottish jewellers, she says, are carving out their own niches and building followings abroad, aided by a network of galleries, schools and events in Scotland that has grown far more robust in recent years. Among these she credits Elements Festival, an annual Edinburgh selling fair and exhibition last held in 2023, with raising the sector’s profile, and highlights Craft Scotland’s Harvest, a contemporary craft fair in the same city held for the first time in October 2025. She adds that the Scottish Gallery and a growing number of independent galleries and retailers are helping connect makers with collectors. Aetla has been a part of that shift. “Since opening Aetla in 2020, we have seen first-hand just how much appetite there is for discovering contemporary jewellery,” says Stewart, who boosts her visibility with a year-round programme of exhibitions, residencies and a permanent collection. Romany Starrs, a jeweller based in Glasgow, says Scotland’s growing status as a jewellery hub comes down to its international reputation. “Our rich history, cultural heritage and tradition of craftsmanship are recognised around the world.” Alison Macleod is a jeweller specialising in bespoke engagement rings and wedding bands who works from a rural atelier in Dumfries and Galloway. She attributes Scotland’s sustained reputation to “an exceptional network of jewellery schools” alongside affordable studio spaces and what she calls “a real spirit of generosity and collaboration” among makers. Drawing on architecture, landscape and more For many of these designers, Scotland’s influence on their work is front and centre. Starrs, for example, nods to Glasgow’s club and creative culture of the 1990s. “It was a community that celebrated self-expression, originality and style, qualities that continue to influence the way I approach jewellery design today,” she says. Her earlier work drew on Glasgow’s architecture, exploring geometry and repetition through primary shapes. More recently, time spent around Loch Lomond, about 30km (19 miles) to the city’s northwest, has pulled her towards something softer, drawn from “the organic forms, movement of the loch and quiet beauty of the landscape”. That has led her to techniques like chasing and repoussé that let her shape metal in a more tactile way, work she describes as shaped by contrast between the urban and the natural. Sarah Brown, a jeweller who works from the island of Islay off Scotland’s west coast, is inspired almost entirely by the landscape around her. “Scotland has completely shaped my identity as a jeweller,” she says. “Growing up on an island on the west coast surrounded by nature, I developed my love for art, being drawn to artists that capture its essence.” She went on to study at the Glasgow School of Art, where she fell in love with the art nouveau style of the “Glasgow Girls” – women artists in Glasgow at the turn of the 20th century – who became major influences on her early work. Scotland’s ancient jewellery-making heritage, with its intricate patterns drawn from nature, has shaped her work from the start, she says, but it is the Scottish island of Islay that now dominates her practice. “The rugged coastline surrounding Islay, with its vast and powerful waters, has always fascinated me and shaped my jewellery,” she says, describing how rock pools, foaming waves and the changing light over the water all feed into her pieces. “Each piece becomes a collage of observations that aim to portray the boundless facets of my island home.” ‘Jewellery that could only have been imagined here’ The landscape surrounding Macleod, who lives inland, has a similar impact on her work. She draws on the hedgerows, woodlands and changing seasons around her, often starting a piece from “seed heads, leaf skeletons and tiny natural forms that might easily be overlooked”. Living rurally, she says, “brings a slower pace of life, giving me the time to make thoughtfully and by hand, rather than rushing the creative process”. She adds that Scotland has given her both her visual language and way of working. “The changing seasons, wild landscapes and slower rhythm of rural life encourage me to notice small details that find their way into my jewellery, while our strong tradition of making has instilled a respect for skill, honesty and creating pieces that are made to last for generations.” Scotland is just as central to the work of Edinburgh-based luxury jeweller Hamilton & Inches, which is now marking its 160th anniversary. “Rather than simply taking inspiration from Scotland, we strive to create jewellery that could only have been imagined and crafted here,” says Victoria Houghton, the brand’s chief executive. The house became one of two jewellers in the world licensed to work with and sell Scottish gold in 2019. In 2023, it acquired what it describes as the largest known private collection of Scottish freshwater river pearls, material it now works with under licence from NatureScot, Scotland’s nature agency. “That level of stewardship reflects a broader shift within luxury, where authenticity, scarcity and provenance have become as important as craftsmanship itself,” Houghton says. “Rather than looking to emulate other luxury capitals, Scotland is carving out its own identity, one rooted in authenticity, heritage and a strong sense of place.” It’s all about community None of this, Stewart says, would matter as much if Scotland’s jewellery scene amounted to a scattering of individually talented makers working in isolation. “I think it is a genuine community,” she says. “Although many jewellers work independently in their own studios, I have always found people in the Scottish jewellery scene to be incredibly generous with their time, knowledge and encouragement.” That community, she adds, extends well beyond the makers themselves, taking in galleries, exhibitions, retailers and institutions such as the Edinburgh Assay Office. Its small scale, she believes, is actually part of its might. “Scotland is a relatively small jewellery community, and I think that is one of its strengths,” she says. “From my experience, there is a real willingness to champion one another’s work and celebrate each other’s successes. There is always more that can be done, but it feels like there is a genuine desire to see the wider sector continue to grow.” As evidence of how far the scene’s range has grown, Stewart names a current generation of makers building on the foundations laid by Appleby, Hogg and Cunningham, among them jewellers Ellis Mhairi Cameron and Ruth Leslie. She points to “the breadth of approaches and the confidence with which designers are developing their own distinct voices”. Stewart is also careful to frame this less as a sudden arrival than a shift in recognition. “Scotland has always had the talent,” she says. “I think we are simply becoming much better at celebrating it.” Brown, meanwhile, points to the steady flow of “new and innovative designers coming out of the art schools and establishing themselves within the UK and globally” as evidence that Scotland’s status as a growing centre for contemporary jewellery is no longer really in question.

title: Divorcing devices: how digital detox helps Hongkongers ‘carve out moments’
description: From phone-free habits to weekend breaks, residents are embracing digital detoxes to ease stress, improve sleep and reclaim focus in an always-on culture.
content: In the second instalment of a five-part Health Matters wellness series on Hong Kong’s growing wellness trends, Fiona Sun looks into how residents are embracing digital detox, as experts warn that excessive screen use is linked to anxiety, depression and sleep disorders. For Robert Broad, stepping away from electronic devices has become part of a self-care routine he developed after the Covid-19 pandemic. The 56-year-old recalled how spending long hours in front of screens while working remotely affected his physical and mental health and reduced the time he spent with family and friends. “I became a lot more anxious, I wasn’t sleeping as much, I gained weight – all of those things started to snowball and take a toll on me and my relationships,” he said. Determined to restore a sense of balance, Broad began with small, manageable steps that could develop into lasting habits. When he returns home from work, he puts his mobile phone in a drawer. He has disabled news alerts and keeps notifications on only for his parents and anyone who may need to reach him in an emergency. He has also switched his phone to greyscale to make it less appealing and checks his emails in batches rather than as they arrive. He stops checking them at 8.30pm each day. Electronic devices are banned from the dinner table and the bedroom. At weekends, he makes a point of leaving his phone at home for short periods, including during 20-minute walks with his dog. “What I try to do with my detox is carve out moments when I can be mindful and present in the activities I’m doing, particularly when there are kids around,” he said. Broad, who has an 11-year-old son, is the founder of Look Up Hong Kong, a group that promotes children’s well-being in the digital age. “In a city like Hong Kong, a realistic detox is sort of small, repeatable, screen-free pockets of the day,” he said. “Start with just one thing. Don’t try to do too many things at once because that tends to fail like any restriction. If you go on a very strict diet, for example, and only eat cabbage for five days, it’s not going to work.” In a city built on speed, constant connectivity and packed schedules, more people in Hong Kong are trying to step away from screens. From phone-free habits and weekend breaks to meditation and spa retreats, digital detox is gaining momentum as residents seek to manage stress, sleep better and reclaim their attention in an always-on culture. No longer merely a wellness buzzword, digital detox has become a coping strategy for navigating a world in which work, social life and even family communication often take place through electronic devices. Hong Kong has a high rate of digital-device ownership. Official statistics showed that 96.8 per cent of people aged 10 and above had a smartphone last year. Data also showed that 96.4 per cent of those aged 10 and above had used the internet last year. Chan Kai-tai, a clinical professional consultant and associate professor in the department of psychiatry at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said that although internet addiction was not a recognised medical condition, excessive use of digital devices was associated with inattention, emotional problems such as anxiety and depression, and sleep disorders. “Is it really toxic? Is it like diabetes, where you have to restrict your diet? Yes, it is,” he said. Chan said young people were among those most vulnerable to unhealthy uses of digital devices, having grown up with smartphones and tablet computers as part of their socialisation, learning and leisure. Older residents had also become more susceptible as they grew increasingly reliant on digital devices to communicate with their children and combat social isolation, he said. People experiencing emotional problems or stress might be more likely to seek comfort online, while those in certain professions, such as influencers and online media employees, were also vulnerable, Chan added. “When you find it difficult to stop or even feel genuine cravings, or when your mood clearly worsens whenever you are not using electronic devices, you need to take it seriously,” he warned. Chan said a digital detox could take many forms, but the key was to cultivate healthy and rational screen-time habits. “Digital detox is essentially about the regulation of usage, namely controlling the duration of digital activities to minimise the negative impact on oneself, such as mood, sleep and addiction problems,” he said. Experts said even simple measures could make a difference, including turning off non-essential notifications, setting daily screen-time limits, keeping phones away from the dinner table and bedroom, or taking a day offline. They also recommended replacing screen time with offline activities such as playing sports, meeting friends, attending concerts or museum exhibitions and taking weekend breaks in parks or the countryside to reconnect with nature and greenery. Tim Li Man-ho, an assistant professor in the department of psychiatry at Chinese University, said blue light from screens could suppress melatonin production and disrupt sleep. He advised avoiding electronic devices for at least two hours before bedtime. Instead, he suggested winding down with calming activities such as listening to music, reading, or practising meditation or yoga to help the body and mind relax before sleep. But experts said people who found themselves unable to control their screen use should seek professional help. A programme run by the Hong Kong Christian Service to help young people with internet addiction receives about 100 new cases each year, most of them pupils in Forms One to Three, according to Joe Tang Chun-yu, who is in charge of the charity’s online addiction counselling centre. Tang said internet addiction was increasingly affecting younger age groups, with primary school pupils accounting for about 30 per cent of service users. The most commonly used devices among them were iPads and mobile phones, he said. In the most serious cases, youngsters dropped out of school or came into conflict with their families because of excessive screen use, he added. Many of them faced difficulties in the real world, including social isolation, bullying at school and difficulty expressing themselves, prompting them to turn to the internet as an escape, Tang said. “The key is to identify the dissatisfaction with reality that led to their addiction and address it so they can regain balance in their lives,” he said. Tang suggested that parents engage more with their children, learn about their thoughts and arrange activities to replace screen use. Youngsters should also be encouraged to develop new interests away from electronic devices, he said. As awareness grows, more parents are becoming mindful of how their use of electronic devices may affect their children. Jeannie Leung is cutting back on her own screen time to shield her eight-year-old daughter from the harms of excessive device use and set a better example at home. “She said, ‘Mummy, I feel that when you’re on the phone, you’re not really with me, you’re not really paying attention to me’,” Leung recalled of a conversation with her daughter about three years ago. “That caught me off guard and I realised this was an issue that I needed to address.” Leung, who is in her forties and works in education and charity, has drawn a clear line at home: no phones at the dinner table and no electronic devices in the bedroom. She has gone further, deleting social media apps from her phone and switching off mobile data for other apps to curb the urge to scroll. During her MTR commute, she now swaps her phone for a book or simply sits back and relaxes. Leung said she had reduced her daily screen time to about three hours, including work-related use such as messaging on WhatsApp. Since setting these boundaries, she said she had more time to engage with her daughter, as well as better sleep and less anxiety. “It’s been a process to do it on a diligent basis and to do it so that in a way it becomes second nature,” she said.

title: US efforts to secure AI supply chains are doomed to fail: Chinese academic
description: Washington’s initiatives such as Pax Silica will not succeed by targeting third parties, a conference hears over the weekend.
content: The latest US artificial intelligence (AI) and supply chain initiatives are doomed to fail, according to a prominent political scientist who also argued that efforts to restrict US companies’ access to low-cost Chinese models would backfire. Instead, he argued, the United States and China should collaborate on driving global economic development to generate the external demand needed to sustain long-term growth. “US frameworks such as Pax Silica, the chip alliance and the rare earth alliance explicitly target a third party, which is bound to fail,” Zheng Yongnian, dean of the school of public policy at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, told a conference on Sunday. The escalating technological rivalry between the world’s two largest economies has prompted Washington to set up the international groupings Zheng referred to, as part of efforts to curb Beijing’s momentum and secure supply chains in areas such as AI, semiconductors and critical minerals. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that a draft State Department document had warned that members of Pax Silica could be excluded if they signed up to the alternative Chinese-led World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. Last month, US media outlet Axios also reported that the White House was considering adding several Chinese AI labs to a blacklist that could restrict their ability to use US technology. The AI leadership contest between Washington and Beijing has reached a critical juncture with American firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic pushing high-cost models while cheaper Chinese models are rapidly expanding around the world. Some US officials have called for a ban on using foreign open-source models – a move that one researcher has estimated could cost businesses up to US$12 billion per year. Zheng said any efforts to curb the use of Chinese technology would be ignoring commercial reality. “If the US bans American enterprises from using Chinese AI, it is self-harm and, from a corporate perspective, runs entirely counter to their development interests,” Zheng said in a recorded video address. He also told the event, which was hosted by the Institute of Public Policy at South China University of Technology, that the two countries were catering to different markets. American tech firms favoured an expensive, closed-source approach suited to affluent economies such as Japan and South Korea, whereas China’s cost-efficient open-source models offered near-peer performance accessible to developing nations, he said. Zheng also said America’s AI-driven growth model contained systemic risks, adding that over 40 per cent of current US economic expansion was tied to the technology. “A bursting of Washington’s AI bubble would trigger a cascading disaster for itself, spill over to all its economic partners and destabilise the entire global economy,” Zheng said. He added that the US must instead ensure there were sufficient practical uses for its AI technology. Despite political efforts in Washington to force a rift, complete economic decoupling was unfeasible because the world’s two largest economies were highly complementary, he argued. Zheng said the US was ahead in areas such as basic scientific research, capital markets, software development, and agriculture and energy production, while China excelled at translating fundamental scientific research into applied technology, software, agricultural goods and energy. To achieve genuine global economic rebalancing, he urged both powers to look beyond their frictions and focus on helping to boost economic growth in developing regions of Africa, Asia and Latin America as a way of increasing consumer demand. Rather than engaging in zero-sum competition, Zheng said China and the US could cooperate on raising world consumption levels as a way of helping their economies to continue to grow.

title: China’s overlooked internet army is quietly embedding AI into everyday businesses
description: From RedNote to Meituan, digital platforms are bypassing third-party providers to build in-house AI models.
content: While China’s new “AI tigers” have captured global attention for challenging Silicon Valley front-runners, a quieter wave of domestic technology companies is building in-house artificial intelligence systems serving everyday users. Beyond pure-play AI labs like DeepSeek, Z.ai (also known as Zhipu AI), Moonshot AI and MiniMax, consumer-facing platforms that span e-commerce, video gaming, social media and travel are developing foundation models tailored to their own business ecosystems, in efforts that have drawn far less attention. RedNote, the lifestyle platform often described as China’s answer to Instagram, underscored the trend earlier this month with its latest release. Its AI research arm, Dots Studio, introduced Dots3-Note Preview, a 280-billion-parameter open-weight model. Citing benchmark tests, the company said the system matched or outperformed models from US labs OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as domestic leaders DeepSeek and Z.ai, in specific tasks. The release highlights a growing technical focus for a platform best known for fashion, travel and shopping recommendations. Dots Studio said in a blog post that it aimed to “build AI that benefits everyone and helps people solve the many problems they encounter in life”. Industry analysts said the effort reflected a broader operational shift across China’s technology sector, where digital platforms are building custom AI rather than relying solely on third-party providers. “When non-AI companies invest in AI models, it is primarily because AI has become critical to their business operations,” said Su Lian Jye, a chief analyst focusing on applied intelligence market research across the Asia-Oceania region at Omdia. Su noted that these consumer platforms were “digital native and extremely data-rich”. By marrying proprietary business data with custom AI models, companies could streamline workflows, predict demand, personalise services and unlock new revenue streams, he added. Similar strategies are taking shape across the industry. Meituan, the food delivery and local services giant, has invested substantially in its LongCat model family as it seeks to integrate AI across areas including merchant services, logistics, customer support and recommendations. Trip.com, China’s largest online travel agency, developed its own travel-focused AI system, Wendao, to support applications including itinerary planning, customer service and travel recommendations. Chinese video streaming platform Bilibili and gaming developer miHoYo, meanwhile, have focused on using AI to enhance content creation and develop more interactive digital experiences. Bilibili developed the Index family of language models, including IndexTTS, a multilingual speech synthesis system, which has been used in areas including AI subtitles, translation, video creation and voice generation. miHoYo developed Glossa, an in-house generative AI model aimed at making game characters more interactive, and reportedly uses it in AI features for Honkai: Star Rail, its globally popular role-playing game. The company is also exploring AI applications in game development, including content generation, voice synthesis and production workflows. However, building and scaling in-house AI infrastructure presents steep operational hurdles. According to Omdia’s AI Market Maturity Survey, the biggest barriers included a lack of business data or poor-quality data, regulatory and compliance concerns, shortages of qualified in-house talent and challenges of integrating AI into existing systems. Investing in AI could also “introduce budget pressure due to high infrastructure and personnel costs”, though “the long-term impact can be strongly positive”, Omdia’s Su said.

title: Chinese robots tackle tennis, smash track records at World Humanoid Robot Games
description: Event highlights robots’ remaining weaknesses, including balance issues, limited autonomy and battery constraints, while underscoring need for faster networks.
content: A tennis ball flew across the net. On the other side, a humanoid robot crouched, shuffled sideways in a series of quick steps, adjusted its position and swung its racquet to send the ball back. The robot traded forehands and backhands with human players during singles and mixed-doubles demonstrations. At one point, while chasing a ball, it lost its balance and toppled backwards, drawing gasps from the crowd. It then rolled over, pushed itself back to its feet and resumed playing. The robot was developed by Beijing-based Galbot and took part in what the company described as the world’s first human-robot tennis match. The demonstration took place as the second World Humanoid Robot Games opened on Saturday night at Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, the speed-skating venue used for the 2022 Winter Olympics. The five-day event brings humanoid robots together to compete in sports ranging from running and football to table tennis and combat events. This year’s games feature 51 events and 1,301 matches involving more than 600 teams and 2,056 humanoid robots, according to the organiser. New competitions include table tennis and kickboxing, while scenario-based events have been expanded to cover tasks in industrial production, hotels, homes and logistics. Tennis presents a demanding challenge for humanoid robots. The tennis robot had to track an incoming ball, predict where it would land, move to the right position, and coordinate its torso and arms to return the shot, all within a matter of seconds. The tennis court was not the only place where the robots were pushing sporting limits. A Tien Kung robot won the 400-metre large-robot race final on Sunday in 38.15 seconds, beating the human men’s world record of 43.03 seconds. The second- and third-place robots also finished below 40 seconds, with times of 39.45 and 39.66 seconds, respectively. The improvement from last year was particularly striking. The winning time in the same event a year ago was 88.03 seconds. On Saturday, a Tien Kung Ultra robot developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre clocked 9.39 seconds in the 100 metres, faster than Usain Bolt’s men’s world record of 9.58 seconds. Still, the competition also produced plenty of reminders that these were robots learning to operate at their limits. During one football match, a robot that was attempting to play the ball knocked over one of its own teammates. On the running track, robots that fell and could not continue were carried away by staff on stretchers or wheeled off in wheelchairs. If AI computing is also put on the robot, battery consumption will increase further David Li, Huawei Technologies A year ago, robots placed relatively limited demands on communications networks because many were still operated by remote control, with competitions focused more on their mechanical agility, according to Yang Lifan, deputy general manager of China Unicom’s Beijing branch, which is providing network services for the games. That began to change as competitions increasingly required robots to operate autonomously, Yang said, pointing to Beijing’s humanoid robot half-marathon in April as an early test. Unlike an indoor competition, where Wi-fi could sometimes be used, a road race over a wide area required continuous mobile-network coverage. “Now the network has become an indispensable part of it, and its importance will only continue to grow,” Yang said. At this year’s games, more robots are equipped with 5G-advanced modules that can send data collected by on-board sensors to an embodied-intelligence system for processing before receiving instructions back. David Li, an executive at Huawei Technologies, said battery life remained a major constraint for humanoid robots, with much of their power already consumed by motors controlling movement. “If AI computing is also put on the robot, battery consumption will increase further,” he said. Some advanced robot makers are therefore moving more AI processing to the cloud, allowing on-board batteries to focus on motion – a shift that makes network coverage increasingly important.

title: Why Chinese media says US historians are giving ‘ammunition’ to separatists
description: As ethnic issues grow ever more sensitive, Beijing is alleging the New Qing History movement seeks to fracture the nation.
content: China has stepped up its offensive against a US-born school of thought on China’s last imperial dynasty, accusing it of providing “theoretical ammunition” for attempts to divide the country. The denunciation comes as online debates over the Qing dynasty (1644-1911) continue to give rise to inflammatory rhetoric, and as Beijing’s ethnic policies and historical narratives are increasingly becoming an arena for international political competition. An article published by the state-run China Ethnic News last Monday warned that New Qing History was “seriously eroding the historical foundations of the community for the Chinese nation in the real world” and should be “forcefully refuted”. That marked the latest broadside in a two-year campaign by the outlet to attack the loosely defined scholarly movement, which began to take shape in the late 1980s. Rather than being an organised movement with a unified doctrine, New Qing History refers to a broad revisionist approach to understanding how the Manchu-led Qing managed both China’s Han majority and the many other ethnic groups under their rule. Scholars taking this approach have drawn on Manchu-language sources to question the long-held assumption that “Sinicisation” – the idea that conquerors of China and even neighbouring peoples were transformed by Chinese culture, often portrayed as a spontaneous and largely one-way process – was the only explanation. They also draw on anthropological and sociological perspectives to explain the Manchu rulers’ relations with Tibetan religious leaders, Mongolian chieftains and Turkic elites in Xinjiang. The China Ethnic News article reiterated several criticisms that Chinese historians have long levelled at New Qing History, including accusations that the approach undermined the Qing’s historical status as a truly Chinese dynasty. It said historians were “fracturing the integrity of the Chinese nation” by treating frontier regions under Qing rule such as Mongolia and Xinjiang as separate units from China’s interior. The piece argued that this “erroneous view of history” could lead to “multiple real-world harms” amid the complex international political environment. “By deconstructing the Qing’s territory into ‘pluralistic modules’ and denying the historical affiliation of frontier regions and China, New Qing History is effectively providing ‘theoretical ammunition’ for various separatist forces,” warned the authors Li Defeng and Zhang Yide from Inner Mongolia University. For at least a decade, Chinese scholars have explicitly or implicitly accused New Qing History of being part of an “academic intrigue” aimed at dividing China. In the article, Li and Zhang said that New Qing History could be traced back to theories advanced by scholars in imperial Japan who argued that Manchuria and Mongolia were not part of China. In a since-deleted interview with Chinese digital outlet The Paper, Georgetown University professor James Millward argued that the allegations that New Qing History was part of an anti-China conspiracy were a “misunderstanding”. He added that the movement’s purpose was to refine the scholarship of earlier historians – such as John K. Fairbank – on topics such as the tribute system, Sinicisation and the idea of China as the civilisational centre. In a 2017 interview with The Paper, Ding Yizhuang, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), praised the school’s focus on Manchu-language sources and acknowledged its value in inspiring research in China. “As for whether the ‘New Qing History’ has some political agenda or even a conspiracy behind it, I think we should first … at least understand what they are talking about before criticising it. Only then can such criticism be convincing,” she said. However, at an academic symposium in 2019, Ding said that “New Qing History is an American thing, not our thing” and rejected any affiliation with the movement. Liu Xiaomeng, another CASS scholar, wrote in a piece published in 2012 that New Qing History had helped to move research from an excessively Han-centric approach and set a higher bar for Chinese scholars working in the field. However, Liu also warned that denying the Qing dynasty was part of Chinese history would inevitably push the school towards an extreme position. Over the past few years, the debate has become more politically charged as Beijing has sought to reshape the relationship between ethnic minorities and the state – such as through the recently enacted Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which some observers have described as providing a statutory mandate for assimilation. In an academic research guideline issued in 2024, the National Ethnic Affairs Commission – a central government agency overseen by the Communist Party’s United Front Work Department – called for resistance to a range of “erroneous historical views”, including New Qing History. The criticism of New Qing History also comes as Beijing steps up efforts to build a “Chinese intellectual system in philosophy and social sciences” capable of explaining China’s practices to the outside world without what officials describe as the monopoly or distortion of Western concepts and narratives. Monday’s article said New Qing History applied modern Western theories of the nation-state to China’s long-standing model of a “unity in diversity” Chinese nation, while using concepts such as “empire” and “colonialism” rooted in European historical experiences to describe centuries of two-way interaction among different regions of China. The Chinese government began compiling an official history of the Qing in 2002, with the project originally expected to take little more than a decade. But it remains unfinished, a potential sign of the political sensitivity surrounding the period. “New Qing History has produced a lot of books and many arguments. We need to catch up. A complete rebuttal cannot be built on just one or two articles,” read one comment below Monday’s article. Rebuttals of New Qing History perspectives have not exclusively been aimed at foreign scholars – the movement has found support among some fringe Chinese nationalists. Some influencers – often labelled “Han chauvinists” – have blamed China’s backwardness compared to Western powers and its descent into a “century of humiliation” in modern times on the Manchu rulers’ takeover of the Han-dominated Ming dynasty. They portrayed the Manchus as foreign “barbarians” who colonised China and stalled its civilisation. That echoes New Qing History’s approach of treating the Qing as more than simply another Chinese dynasty and comparing it with the Mughal and Ottoman empires. The view reached a peak in popularity in the second half of last year before being rebuked by state media, but its supporters remain active online today.

title: Exam scores reveal increased student interest in China’s newer, smaller universities
description: Research-focused universities with close ties to entrepreneurs and scientists seen as offering competitive advantage in job market.
content: A growing number of China’s top high school students are looking beyond traditional elite universities to smaller, newer, research-intensive institutions that offer curricula focused on technological innovation and its commercialisation. In Guangdong province, two-year-old Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology and one-year-old Great Bay University, in Dongguan, had minimum admission scores from the national entrance exam above 625 this year, higher than many departments at more established universities, according to data released by the city government of Guangzhou, the provincial capital. Amid China’s broader push to foster research-focused universities as a way of bolstering strategic industries, the newer universities have focused on more specialised fields of research and closer links with industry than is common at traditional universities. They include Westlake University in Hangzhou, ShanghaiTech University, Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology, Fuyao University of Science and Technology in Fuzhou and Eastern Institute of Technology in Ningbo. For some families navigating an increasingly competitive graduate job market, the roles that prominent entrepreneurs, scientists and industry leaders play at such universities suggest graduates might have an advantage in career competition. Steve Zheng, from Shenzhen, scored in the top 1.6 per cent of the 433,000 physics-stream high school students who took the National Higher Education Entrance Examination last year and sought to study mathematics at his home city’s Southern University of Science and Technology, which was founded 16 years ago, for that reason. But the fierce competition for places ultimately led him to enrol at a longer-established comprehensive university in the province. The value of new research-focused universities was not to create another group of prestigious names Xiong Bingqi, 21st Century Education Research Institute “Universities backed by leading academics and industry figures are more likely to attract strong job opportunities,” he said in explaining his initial choice. But Xiong Bingqi, director of the Beijing-based 21st Century Education Research Institute and an authority on Chinese education policy and reform, said most of the newer, smaller universities – often supported by wealthy entrepreneurs or local governments – were created to train researchers and build scientific capabilities over the long term rather than generate immediate employment opportunities for graduates. “The value of new research-focused universities was not to create another group of prestigious names, but to explore different models for cultivating research talent and strengthening China’s innovation capacity,” he said. Xiong said, however, that long-term funding remained a challenge. Fuyao University of Science and Technology, founded with a 10 billion yuan (US$1.48 billion) donation from entrepreneur Cao Dewang, has attracted public attention after he said that academic departments should become financially self-sufficient through the commercialisation of research. Xiong said cultivating new world-class research universities would require long-term and diversified funding sources, including government support, philanthropic donations and professional input to commercialise the fruits of academic research.

title: Wall Street helped build modern China. But is it now being cast aside?
description: Beijing once courted Wall Street’s titans, hailing them as ‘old friends of China’. But the relationship today is far frostier.
content: For decades, Wall Street titans – from former Goldman Sachs chief Henry Paulson to Blackstone co-founder Stephen Schwarzman and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio – were hailed as “old friends of China”, feted by senior officials and granted rare access to the country’s top leadership. Today, while American financiers continue to visit China and maintain commercial links, those private meetings with the top leadership have largely diminished, even as Beijing gradually opens its capital markets. The shift has raised a crucial question for global investors: can Wall Street maintain its bridge to Beijing amid a changing US-China relationship? “The decline of such roles suggests they have stopped being useful,” said Christopher Marquis, Sinyi professor of Chinese management at Cambridge Judge Business School. “China’s economy no longer needs foreign bankers’ capital and expertise the way it did 20-plus years ago.” The “honeymoon period” for Wall Street and Beijing dates to China’s reform era in the late 1990s and 2000s, when Beijing relied heavily on foreign financial expertise to modernise its economy. That era was epitomised by the 1995 establishment of China International Capital Corporation, the country’s first joint-venture investment bank, launched with Morgan Stanley to restructure state enterprises and build capital markets. Goldman Sachs was another major beneficiary, paying US$2.58 billion for a stake in the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China in 2006 – then its largest-ever principal investment – and helping underwrite some of the country’s largest overseas listings. Others, including Morgan Stanley, built similarly close ties with Chinese banks and companies. The partnership yielded massive returns. Alibaba Group Holding’s US$25 billion debut on the New York Stock Exchange in 2014 became the largest initial public offering in history at the time, paving the way for a wave of tech listings. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. At the same time, Chinese capital was flowing into global markets. The China Investment Corporation, Beijing’s sovereign wealth fund, ploughed a combined US$8 billion into Blackstone and Morgan Stanley in 2007 alone, opening another channel of engagement between Wall Street and Beijing. “The relationship was two-way, mutually beneficial and trusting during those years,” said Kevin Chen Kaifeng, chief economist at Horizon Financial in New York. “Almost all of those driving factors are now gone,” he added, citing the slowdown in Chinese listings in US markets, Wall Street’s exit from major stakes in Chinese state-owned banks, and declining Chinese investment in the US. Regulators on both sides have added friction. Nasdaq’s tighter rules have piled pressure on Chinese issuers already facing strict US audit scrutiny, while Beijing requires mainland firms to clear rigorous national security and data privacy reviews before listing abroad. Only two mainland Chinese companies completed US debuts in the first half of the year, raising a combined US$59.5 million – the weakest half-year showing in five years in terms of both deal count and proceeds, according to a June report by accounting firm EY. Chinese authorities have also tightened controls on cross-border capital flows by cracking down on unauthorised offshore brokerages, expanding outbound investment rules to individual residents, and applying a 20 per cent tax on offshore family trusts and insurance structures. “The two-way streets of deals dried up on both ends,” Chen said. Wall Street’s leverage has waned in another way. Marquis said its traditional role as an advocate for market access had also lost much of its currency. Banks once lobbied heavily for policies that kept the pipeline of China deals open, but with Washington’s bipartisan hawkish turn on China, that advocacy carried far less weight than it once did, he said. I don’t foresee future ‘old friend of China’ roles for Wall Street bankers Christopher Marquis, Cambridge Judge Business School During the 2018 US-China trade war, top Wall Street executives – traditionally Beijing’s strongest allies in Washington – attempted to leverage their political access to broker a truce, only to find their lobbying efforts powerless in the face of US President Donald Trump’s tariff and export ban agenda. “No amount of Goldman or Blackstone advocacy can soften export controls or investment restrictions,” Marquis said. “Wall Street can no longer deliver its half of the bargain.” The retreat also reflected a shift in Beijing’s own financial priorities, analysts said. Today, Beijing is pursuing national self-sufficiency to insulate its economy from geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions and the risk of decoupling from the United States and its allies, with technology innovation as a central priority. China’s top leadership has repeatedly stressed that finance should “serve the real economy”, part of a stated ambition – formalised in this year’s five-year plan – to build China into a “financial powerhouse” on its own terms. The policy is explicitly distanced from the profit-driven model long associated with Wall Street. Finance had been defined “as an arm of state power rather than a sector to be developed with foreign help”, Marquis said. Yet the market has not shut. At least seven foreign firms, including Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase, now wholly own mainland securities brokerages after Beijing removed foreign-ownership caps in 2020. A high-profile business delegation – including Schwarzman, BlackRock’s Larry Fink, Goldman’s David Solomon, and Citi’s Jane Fraser – accompanied Trump on a state visit to Beijing in mid-May, where President Xi Jinping assured executives that China would expand access for foreign capital. While some financiers continued to maintain strong links with China, analysts said those individual relationships were unlikely to restore Wall Street’s former role. “I don’t foresee future ‘old friend of China’ roles for Wall Street bankers,” Marquis said. “There may still be a legitimate, narrower commercial role … but they should treat access for what it is: conditional and transactional.” Chen struck a more hopeful note, arguing the bridge could be rebuilt if China reopens its financial markets further to foreign institutions and Chinese investment in the US recovers. “The future depends on whether China can open up institutions, and revamp Chinese investments in the US,” he said. “If this happens, the future of the Wall Street bridge is bright.”

title: Indonesian teen with ‘Superman’ cape fights haze fires, minister hails ‘forest hero’
description: The teen has been using his free time after school to help his father douse fires since 2023, as videos of his feats have gone viral.
content: Dressed as his favourite superhero, Indonesian teenager Rudiyansah walks along a charred landscape, helping douse wildfires that have razed large parts of Borneo island. The Southeast Asian country has been battling infernos that have left a thick, blanketing smog over parts of the island that Indonesia shares with Malaysia and Brunei. Rudiyansah’s red and blue Superman costume stood out against the stark, scorched landscape surrounding the town of Palangkaraya, where he has joined a local volunteer firefighting group set up by his father to put out smouldering peatland. The 17-year-old said he had been using his free time after school to help his father douse fires since 2023. But this year, he decided to don the brightly coloured tights when fighting fires, creating a striking image that has drawn attention to the struggle to contain the blazes. While Rudiyansah said dressing as the Man of Steel was “just for fun”, video of him using a hosepipe to wet foliage has gone viral, garnering millions of views and earning him the title of “forest hero” from the country’s forestry minister. “Honestly, I’m really happy because I can help locals, even though it feels really tiring,” Rudiyansah, who like many Indonesians only uses one name, said on Sunday while still wearing his cape. He said that he wet his costume slightly before heading into the fields to prevent it from burning, and washed it every night to keep it clean. His father, Mulyadi, said the haze from this year’s fire season was the worst his volunteer firefighter group had seen since it was established in 2020. “In the house, he’s like a normal kid,” he said when asked about his cape-clad son. “But when he saw me going out, he asked, ‘Are you going to put out fires? I’ll go with you,’” he said. The lack of water was the main challenge for firefighters, Mulyadi said, with wells and other water sources drying up during drought. Fires between January and July burned more than 200,000 hectares of land – an area three times the size of the capital Jakarta, the government said this week. That is already larger than during previous El Nino seasons – a weather pattern that triggers worldwide changes in winds, atmospheric pressure and rainfall – in 2019 and 2023. The government has ordered more troop and aircraft deployments to help contain the spread of the blazes and smog, which has reached Malaysia. El Nino is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that typically brings drought, which increases the risks of wildfires, in Indonesia. Human-caused climate change can amplify its impact because a warmer ocean and atmosphere make more energy and moisture available to feed extreme weather events. Rudiyansah, who dreams of becoming a forest ranger someday, called on firefighters to carry on despite the challenges in putting out the fires. “To volunteers and firefighters across Indonesia, keep up the spirit in the fight against the flames,” he said.

title: Ultra quick: Chinese robots beat Usain Bolt’s 100m world record at Beijing games
description: The results mark a sharp improvement from last year’s inaugural event, when Tiangong Ultra won over the same distance in 21.50 seconds.
content: Two Chinese humanoid robots have eclipsed the achievement of the man widely regarded as the fastest human in history. Racing in the 100 metres at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, Tiangong Ultra clocked 9.39 seconds in a preliminary heat, beating the men’s world record of 9.58 seconds held by Jamaican sprinting great Usain Bolt since 2009. Another robot in the heat, Lightning, also finished faster than Bolt in a time of 9.47 seconds. Unitree Robotics’ robot was not as quick, finishing last with a time of 12.41 seconds. Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre, won its heat at the opening of the games’ second edition on Saturday. The robot overtook smartphone maker Honor’s Lightning near the finish after falling behind early in the race. 在北京世界人形机器人运动会上，一个人形机器人以 9.39 秒的成绩跑完 100 米，打破了博尔特 9.58 秒的世界纪录！ pic.twitter.com/eE4LnQ0qvu — Eason Mao☢ (@KELMAND1) August 23, 2026 “Our initial acceleration is slightly slower compared to Honor, but our top speed is higher,” Guo Xuanjie, head of the innovative humanoid department at the centre, said. “Once our top speed kicked in during the second half, we were able to make the pass.” Earlier on Saturday, state media reported that Lightning had clocked 9.32 seconds during a preparatory test, reaching a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second. However, despite their historic times, neither had quite the same finesse of human athletes after crossing the line. Lacking a gradual braking system, they slammed into a thick protective mat. Tiangong Ultra then stumbled wildly into the crowd, forcing onlookers to scramble out of the way, while Lightning collapsed and was carried off on a stretcher. The chaotic finish capped a dramatic leap in performance from last year’s inaugural event, where Tiangong Ultra won the 100m in 21.50 seconds before winning the world’s first humanoid half-marathon in Beijing in two hours and 40 minutes over 21.1km. This year’s half-marathon was won by Lightning in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the human world record pace. Guo attributed the dramatic speed gains over the past year primarily to core hardware upgrades. “A key area of progress is joint performance, with joint torque and rotational speeds seeing substantial increases,” he said, adding that high-power racing demands strict component reliability and high battery discharge capacity to support “high-dynamic competition”. Guo revealed that Tiangong Ultra will also compete in the 400m, 1,500m and 4x100m relay, while its smaller counterpart, Tiangong Omni, enters the youth division sprints and obstacle races. The record-breaking sprint sparked widespread discussion on Chinese social media. “This really shows how times are changing and technology is advancing,” one netizen wrote, echoing a sentiment shared by many marvelling at the rapid year-over-year progress. Others poked fun at the violent stopping methods, jokingly dubbing the machines “disposable 100m athletes” after watching them slam into the mats. “Can’t they have a dignified way to stop?” one commenter asked. Some questioned the practical value of the competition. “What’s the point of running fast? Where can this actually be applied?” one user asked, while another cheekily suggested: “Wouldn’t it be even faster if they put wheels on the bottom of their feet?” The Beijing games, running through Wednesday, have attracted 2,056 robots from 666 teams across 16 countries competing in 51 events, ranging from football and dancing to industrial challenges.

title: People’s Daily defends China’s economic resilience, says annual targets will be met
description: Risks are ‘being resolved and contained’, back-to-back weekend commentaries assert after second-quarter GDP misses mark.
content: The flagship newspaper of China’s ruling Communist Party has run back-to-back commentaries defending the resilience of the world’s second-largest economy, saying domestic risks were being contained while China continued to provide greater stability to the global economy. The People’s Daily commentaries, published on Saturday and Sunday, came as weak domestic demand and persistent imbalances weighed on second-quarter growth, with July data showing little improvement. “In the second half of the year, as major projects … get under way and macroeconomic policies take effect in a timely and effective manner, China’s economic performance will remain within a reasonable range, and the country will successfully achieve its annual targets,” Saturday’s commentary said. The two pieces were published under the pen name of “Zhong Caiwen”, which is widely believed to be associated with the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission, a key economic decision-making body headed by President Xi Jinping. Saturday’s article argued that China’s economic resilience should be assessed not only through headline figures, but also through the quality of growth. It pointed to continued expansion in hi-tech and equipment manufacturing, while noting that risks linked to property, local government debt and smaller financial institutions were being systematically addressed. “The risks and hidden dangers in the economic field are being resolved and contained in an orderly manner,” the commentary said, adding that China had maintained the bottom line of preventing systemic risks. China reported 4.3 per cent gross domestic product growth in the second quarter, the slowest quarterly growth rate since the end of 2022. Retail sales, a major gauge of consumer spending, grew by only 0.6 per cent year on year last month. Saturday’s article came a day after China’s Ministry of Finance unveiled new measures aimed at boosting spending on big-ticket items such as vehicles and home renovations, with more action pledged for later in the year. Sunday’s piece, meanwhile, took aim at the “China shock 2.0” narrative, instead describing China as “a stabilising anchor for global industrial and supply chains” that supported the smooth functioning of the global economy. China’s strength in new energy had helped it reduce oil imports and ease pressure on global oil prices at a time when the US-Israel war on Iran was tightening global crude supplies and driving up raw material costs, the article noted. The commentary also cited strong European demand for Chinese-made air conditioners during recent heatwaves as evidence of Chinese manufacturers’ ability to respond quickly to overseas demand, backed by integrated supply chains, energy-efficient technologies and fast delivery. Late last year, an eight-part op-ed series in the People’s Daily under the same byline was published before the fourth plenary session of the party’s Central Committee, describing the Chinese economy as an “unsinkable economic aircraft carrier”. The plenum approved recommendations for China’s 15th five-year plan, covering the 2026-2030 period.

title: Opinion | Asia is reaching for the open road that Chinese AI offers
description: Countries seeking sovereign AI want to control their own AI capabilities rather than rent them from a foreign platform.
content: At a recent Apec digital technology and AI forum in Chengdu, ministers across the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum issued a statement in support of open-source artificial intelligence models – a rare point of agreement in a debate often framed as a zero-sum US-China contest. It pointed towards an AI order that cuts against the assumption of a contest with a single winner, an assumption that still shapes Washington’s alarm over every Chinese AI breakthrough. Across Asia, governments are building their own systems, and most are building on open Chinese models. Because the leading Chinese systems are open weight, free to download and reshape, they are producing an AI order in which no single company or country owns the field. That openness matches what many states pursuing sovereign AI want: a multipolar landscape where they control their own capabilities rather than rent them from a foreign platform. Across the region, countries are entering that order along three distinct roads: the flagship national model built directly on a Chinese base, the government pilot that puts Chinese systems into public services, and the private start-up that ships on whatever is most open. China’s rising influence flows from aligning with those goals rather than from any strategy that has outpaced Washington’s. The economics leave little room for hesitation. Building a frontier model costs billions of dollars and demands rare talent, leaving just China and the United States still training at the frontier. For everyone else, an open Chinese model removes the barrier: the weights are free, they run on local servers without sending data abroad, and they cost 60 to 90 per cent less to operate than the leading American systems while trailing by only months. The flagship national model The most visible of the three roads is the flagship national model. Last year, AI Singapore moved from using Meta’s Llama in its Southeast Asian Languages in One Network (SEA-LION) project to running SEA-Lion large-language models on Qwen by Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post. And Kazakhstan’s AlemLLM was developed by Chinese start-up 01.AI on a DeepSeek base, the only option for a country with only a few hundred ageing chips. A model assembled this way stays tied to its base, yet in an open ecosystem that reliance is shared rather than captive: the weights are owned outright, the code can be adapted freely, and a government that could never train a frontier model alone gets a working system it controls. The government pilot A second road runs through the government pilot. In Malaysia, the Prime Minister’s Office and communications ministry were among the first users of a domestic platform running DeepSeek. Vietnam passed a law last December asserting sovereignty over its AI infrastructure, a legal frame the cheapest open foundation will end up filling. Each pilot leaves behind domestic expertise and options no single supplier can revoke. The private start-up The third road runs through private developers, and it reaches well beyond the developing world. In Japan, companies such as Abeja and Lightblue build their models on Qwen, which outperform American systems on Japanese-language tasks. In South Korea, where DeepSeek is restricted on security grounds, commercial developers still reach for Qwen because of its permissive licensing. In Kenya and Nigeria, start-ups build on Chinese models because inference costs can be as much as 90 per cent lower. What this adds up to is not Chinese domination. As Asia builds on its open models, a shared set of tools and standards spreads, and China gains influence as its most useful contributor. The US, meanwhile, keeps confirming the fear that drives the shift: being shut out of the technology altogether. In June, the Trump administration ordered Anthropic to cut off foreign access to its most capable models, briefly extending the block to treaty allies alongside adversaries. Each time Washington treats frontier models as capabilities to be licensed and withheld, it validates the anxiety. Malaysia showed how little unilateral pressure can achieve against an open system. Last year, it walked back its involvement in a platform running DeepSeek on Huawei chips, dropping the hardware claim within a day under US export-control pressure while the model stayed in place. The pattern holds inside Washington’s coalition; the Pax Silica initiative counts Singapore and Kazakhstan among its members. When Chinese President Xi Jinping urged countries at the World AI Conference in Shanghai last month to embrace open-source development and warned against hoarding technology behind national security, the message landed because it described a world that states were already building. China is gaining ground in Asia less through industrial strategy than through alignment with that vision; the American approach asks countries to stake their future on a supplier that has shown it will cut them off. For much of the region, the sovereign choice has been made, and it runs along an open road that happens to go through China.

title: What new analysis of Joshua Reynolds’ masterpiece The Portrait of Mai tells us
description: The Getty Museum is conducting a thorough study of the 18th century painting ahead of its Los Angeles debut on September 14.
content: A nearly eight foot (2.4-metre) canvas by the great 18th century English portrait painter Joshua Reynolds recently made the journey from London’s National Portrait Gallery (NPG) to the Getty Museum in Brentwood, Los Angeles, where it will make its grand West Coast debut next month. The Portrait of Mai, which depicts a regal-looking young Tahitian man who arrived in London with Captain James Cook in 1774, was bought by the Getty two years ago in a celebrated and rare joint acquisition with NPG after the privately held painting was put up for sale by its Dublin-based owner for more than US$61 million. The painting has received royal treatment since being unpacked at the Getty late last month. The museum’s conservation team performed a technical study that included capturing new imaging and uncovering pigments and materials used by Reynolds. The team is also confirming any alterations that may have been made to the painting over the past 250 years. On a recent sunny Tuesday morning at the Getty – in a back room filled with other paintings, tucked into a corner of the hilltop museum – NPG’s visiting conservator Sally Higgs joins the Getty’s associate conservator of paintings, Kari Rayner, in an examination of the painting, which was first exhibited in 1776 at the Royal Academy in London. The women peer closely at the canvas wearing headband magnifiers as they pass a small bright light across its surface to study the brushstrokes, paint and process Reynolds used to create the painting, which was made in the Grand Manner that defined the artist’s work. “When we do these types of studies, we end up with different questions,” Rayner says. “That’s one of the things about such a condensed study period that’s been a little bit challenging.” The project is an example of the interdisciplinary, cross-institutional work that happens all the time at the Getty, says Catherine Patterson, a scientist for the Getty Conservation Institute. “It’s important to note that a huge amount of the work of gathering that data is what we’re doing in this very intense period,” Patterson says. “Understanding what it means and what additional questions we have, it takes months.” The art of conservation is not about changing the subject matter or making a classical painting look new. It is about preserving the historical artefact to decipher the artist’s intentions and better understand what went into the piece, without disturbing its originality. The Portrait of Mai stands out for telling the story of the first Polynesian to visit Britain, and is a rare example of a Grand Manner painting done of a person of colour. The artwork introduced tension between indigenous traditions and Western conventions through the inclusion of Mai’s robe, turban and hand tattoos. Upon his arrival in London, Mai became something of a celebrity among the aristocracy, and was welcomed by King George III. “We work for the art. It’s not about us. We’re here to serve the object,” Patterson says. “We do our job the best if nobody notices we’ve done anything,” Higgs says. “You’ll often read articles about conservation or about art that has been conserved and the name of the conservator is never mentioned.” The most telling details of the painting are revealed through technical analysis, using a number of scans and a conservator’s favourite tool: the headband magnifiers known as optivisors. The journey of discovery began with a chemical image analysis to better understand the materials present. X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy scans identified the chemical elements that make up the painting, including lead. Reflectance imaging spectroscopy was then used to measure how the materials interact with light. The scans revealed layers of paint and reworked areas, including Mai’s hand placement and head. The research also revealed that the pigments Reynolds used contained lead as well as vermilion, carbon black, and one or more iron-earth pigments. “[Reynolds] is notoriously someone that never is satisfied with what he’s done,” Higgs says. “And you can really see that in this painting that he just can’t stop – it’s never finished.” Happily for the conservators, their work also showed that the painting does not require any kind of additional treatment. “It’s in very good condition, especially for a Reynolds,” Rayner says. “That’s why we’re now carrying out this technical study with the idea that, if and when treatment is needed in the future, it will help inform the treatment.” The work is ongoing. The next phase includes analysing the binding media and examining the paint layer structure. The research is ultimately about preserving what the painting represents: a monumental encounter of cultures, says Davide Gasparotto, senior curator of paintings at the Getty. “It’s not just a painting, it’s also an anthropological artefact,” Gasparotto says. “It talks about this incredibly important moment of encounter of cultures, sometimes difficult, problematic.” The painting will make its Los Angeles debut on September 14 with a private Polynesian blessing ceremony where guests will experience the living cultural traditions of Tahiti through music, dance and food. After its welcoming party, The Portrait of Mai will be displayed among other portraits owned by the Getty, including those by Thomas Gainsborough, Pompeo Batoni and Francisco Goya, as well as sculptures by Jean-Antoine Houdon, Franz Xaver Messerschmidt and Francis Hardwood. “But [Mai] will have the place of honour,” Gasparotto says. The painting will remain at the Getty until March 14, 2027, after which the museum will close for renovations. The painting will then be transferred to the Getty Villa for about six months. It will again return to the Getty when it reopens, just in time for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

title: ‘Huge influx’: expat retirees projected to drive Hong Kong’s premium home demand
description: Wealthy expats increasingly choose Hong Kong as retirement base, lured by its low-tax regime and international connectivity, analysts say.
content: Hong Kong is tipped to see more luxury home sales with expatriates increasingly choosing the city as their retirement base, drawn to its low-tax environment as well as business opportunities, according to analysts. “A huge influx of expats who used to live in Hong Kong are moving back with a long-term view to retirement,” said Victoria Allan, founder and CEO of Habitat Property. “Many expats who previously would have left to retire are staying and purchasing [property] for the first time.” Notable high-end property deals recently involved non-local top executives and business founders, among others. A growing number of ultra-wealthy expatriates are choosing to remain in Hong Kong beyond their working years … rather than relocate elsewhere William Lau, Knight Frank About 30 per cent of Habitat’s recent sales were contributed by expat clients, Allan said. “Previously, people were buying property as an investment. While they are still doing that, clients are also buying with a lifestyle plan in place – for retirement along with the long-term benefits of being based in Hong Kong, primarily for tax status,” she added. “And, yes, we are seeing expat clients back in the market – the first time since 2019.” Among those who recently bought upscale homes were Swire Pacific chairman Guy Bradley, who bought a HK$50 million (US$6.37 million) 2,832 sq ft property on Stanley Beach Road in September. Sachin Tulshyan, managing director for equity products at Nomura Holdings, bought a detached luxury house at Villa Rosa in Tai Tam for HK$75 million in December. Allan said one of Habitat’s recent sales was a penthouse at the Verano on Repulse Bay Road, also in Southern district, snapped up by an expat client “looking to have Hong Kong as a retirement base”. Knight Frank has observed the same trend, according to William Lau, senior director and residential agency head at the consultancy. “A growing number of ultra-wealthy expatriates are choosing to remain in Hong Kong beyond their working years … rather than relocate elsewhere,” Lau said. “Many have established deep personal, family and business connections in the city over decades and continue to appreciate Hong Kong’s role as an international financial centre, its low-tax environment, world-class healthcare system, excellent connectivity and high standard of living.” Hong Kong’s salaries tax is capped at 15 per cent for the first HK$5 million, lower than the UK’s progressive rates starting at 20 per cent, and far below the more than 50 per cent levies in parts of Europe. “Many wealthy individuals who have traditionally maintained multiple residences around the world are increasingly viewing Hong Kong as their long-term Asian base due to its convenience, lifestyle offering and proximity to key business and family interests across the region,” Lau said. Both Allan and Lau anticipate a gradual stream of wealthy retirees settling permanently in Hong Kong. “From a residential perspective, many of these individuals are likely to adopt a ‘rent first, buy later’ strategy,” Lau said. “It would not be unusual for them to lease ultra-prime residences with monthly rents exceeding HK$500,000, while familiarising themselves with different neighbourhoods and evaluating their long-term requirements before making a purchase decision.” Lau added that a segment of this cohort comprised “ultra-wealthy retirees looking to acquire trophy assets immediately, particularly large single-family houses in traditional luxury districts such as The Peak, Deep Water Bay, Repulse Bay, Shouson Hill and other prestigious low-density residential areas where privacy, exclusivity and space remain highly sought after”. While Hong Kong continues to attract high-net-worth individuals for business, investment and wealth management opportunities, retirement is a different proposition Cathie Chung, JLL in Hong Kong Analysts predict higher premiums for prime properties, given the city’s limited stock. “The influx will drive structural polarisation within the residential sector,” said Derek Chan Hoi-chiu, head of research at Ricacorp Properties. “A flight-to-quality trend will decouple ultra-luxury valuations – particularly in coveted enclaves like The Peak and Southern district – from the broader mass market. The market will also experience heightened demand for premier serviced luxury rentals as temporary bases prior to acquisition.” Chan said while “general housing inventory remains ample, true ultra-luxury stock – such as detached mansions on The Peak, Southside estates, or expansive penthouses – is exceptionally scarce”. He added this “chronic undersupply will underwrite price resilience and compel some buyers to acquire established, legacy properties for multimillion-dollar modern retrofits”. Not all agencies foresee a surge. “While Hong Kong continues to attract high-net-worth individuals for business, investment and wealth management opportunities, retirement is a different proposition,” said Cathie Chung, senior director of research at JLL in Hong Kong. “The city’s high cost of living, particularly housing and day-to-day expenses, remains a key consideration.” A study last month by British financial advice and wealth management company St James’s Place found that two-thirds of ultra-rich expatriates living in Hong Kong planned to retire in the city.

title: Chinese, Southeast Asian ride-hailing firms eye Hong Kong amid licensing roll-out
description: Transport chief says more than 7,500 people have applied for new combined taxi and ride-hailing vehicle written test.
content: More ride-hailing platform operators from mainland China and Southeast Asia have approached the Hong Kong government about entering the city’s market ahead of the launch of licensed operations, the transport minister has revealed. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also said on Sunday that more than 7,500 people had applied for the new combined taxi and ride-hailing vehicle written test, calling the number a “very good and positive” sign. “We hope there will be more competition and greater diversity, which will provide more choices for residents and future ride-hailing drivers,” she said on a television programme. Hong Kong legalised ride-hailing services earlier this year, requiring platforms, vehicles and drivers to obtain separate licences or permits. Although the new regulatory regime took effect on August 3, the first licensed services are not expected to launch until later this year. Chan said the operators included established companies that Hongkongers might have encountered while visiting the mainland or Southeast Asia, but she did not identify them or disclose how many had made contact. Uber already operates in Hong Kong, while Chinese platforms Didi and Amap also offer local booking services. Amap is owned by Alibaba Group Holding, which also owns the South China Morning Post. Geely-backed CaoCao Mobility, China’s second-largest ride-hailing operator, signed a strategic partnership agreement with Octopus in June aimed at operating licensed services in the city. Singapore-headquartered Grab is Southeast Asia’s largest ride-hailing platform, providing services in more than 900 cities across eight countries. Other major mainland operators include T3 Chuxing and Meituan’s mobility platform, but neither has an established ride-hailing presence in the city. The government hoped to invite interested companies to apply for platform licences within the next few months, Chan said. An exam for prospective ride-hailing drivers was introduced as part of the new regulatory regime, combined with the existing test for taxi drivers to create a single assessment for both services. Those who pass can take the required pre-service course before applying for relevant permits. The first batch of candidates for the combined written test would sit the examination from mid-September, Chan said. Applications opened on August 3. Existing taxi drivers can apply directly for a ride-hailing permit without taking the exam. Chan said the Transport Department would begin a baseline survey before the end of the third quarter to examine residents’ travel patterns and assess passenger demand. Licensed platforms will later be required to send operational data to a government monitoring system, allowing authorities to dynamically assess supply and demand. She said that platforms would be asked to explain how they planned to provide sufficient capacity, including by attracting taxis to offer bookings through their apps. Licence renewal requirements could also be designed to encourage drivers to work more regularly, Chan said.

title: Hong Kong to launch AI training for workers in November with big tech firms
description: Finance chief warns frontier tech will challenge the job market, urging faster action to equip young people with AI skills and workplace opportunities.
content: Hong Kong will partner with major technology firms to launch an AI training programme for the labour force in November as part of a government drive to equip workers with new skills, the city’s finance chief has said. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po also said on Sunday the separate HK$50 million (US$6.4 million) “AI for All” push announced in February would feature more than 200 activities and was expected to benefit 50,000 people within two years. Writing in his weekly blog, Chan noted the training programme would be carried out by the Employees Retraining Board “The Employees Retraining Board will work with major tech enterprises to roll out AI courses in November to the employed population,” he said. The board, which coordinates and funds market-oriented training courses, will be renamed Upskill Hong Kong as part of a revamp to promote continuous learning and skill improvement across the workforce. “The development and application of frontier technology will pose challenges to the job market. We must speed up our response, helping young people master the skills and giving them opportunities to apply them in the workplace,” he said. Chan cited a survey finding that almost 70 per cent of Hong Kong residents were proficient in using artificial intelligence (AI), while about 20 per cent were highly proficient and leveraged the technology to automate daily tasks. “The budget has set aside HK$50 million for an ‘AI for All’ programme, which will provide diverse AI training to employees, students and the general public under the leadership of Cyberport, the Hong Kong Science Park and the Productivity Council … The target is to hold over 200 activities this year and next, which are expected to benefit around 50,000 people,” he said. Chan said the government had also launched 30 AI projects across 13 departments to boost efficiency in areas such as licensing approvals, facility bookings, environmental hygiene and complaint handling. By the end of the year, the Transport Department will use AI in vehicle licence renewals, cutting processing time from 10 working days to one. It will also pilot real-time, AI-driven traffic signal adjustments in the first quarter of next year to shorten pedestrian waiting times. But Armstrong Lee Hon-cheung, managing director of Worldwide Consulting Group, said spending HK$50 million to benefit 50,000 people over two years was “a drop in the bucket”. “Our working population is over 3.5 million. An initiative reaching 50,000 people is far from enough to upskill the workforce,” he said. He said the per-capita amount should be comparable to the digital education initiative for primary and secondary school students, which totals HK$2 billion, or an average of HK$3,000 per pupil. He suggested the government provide tax incentives to businesses that invest in AI upskilling, for example by hiring dedicated trainers for their employees. Lee pointed out that the lack of a qualification framework or structure for AI education often left employers confused when they saw candidates claim to be highly proficient in the technology. “When we see 70 per cent of people described as proficient in AI, most of them may simply be using DeepSeek or Doubao,” he said. “We need to know the level someone has reached after completing a given AI training programme – beginner, intermediate or advanced – and what they are capable of doing, so we can assess their competitiveness in recruitment and promotion exercises.”
