title: Why Trump’s economic pain could spark more Iranian attacks on Gulf nations
description: The plan is likely to prompt Tehran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf in a bid to push up oil prices and force Trump to retreat.
content: President Donald Trump is betting new sanctions, a naval blockade and ramped-up economic pressure against Iran’s trading partners can accomplish what thousands of bombs and missiles could not: force Tehran to accept a deal to end the war on US terms. But like other US efforts to force Iran into capitulation, there is one main problem: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has claimed control of the vital Strait of Hormuz and sent volleys of attack drones across the Gulf, may be impervious to such pressure – and has plenty of ways to retaliate. A major part of the US effort will come on Monday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has promised to unveil details of a plan designed to shift the conflict from tit-for-tat strikes across the Middle East to full-blown economic isolation – a campaign that could touch nations ranging from China and India to Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. Yet significant new economic pressure is likely to prompt Iran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf, including against energy infrastructure, in an attempt to push up oil prices and raise the cost of the US effort, forcing Trump to shift his approach once again. “If this is actually effective, at some point, Iran will lash out again – they just will have no alternative,” said Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who worked on Iran issues at the State Department and White House National Security Council until last year. “Trump may see this as a different phase of the war, but I don’t think Iran does.” Since the US and Israel first attacked Iran on February 28, Iran has repeatedly shown the ability to endure air strikes on thousands of targets, layers of sanctions and a US navy blockade – yet still retain the ability to hit back. Tehran has used Shahed attack drones and ballistic missiles to hit both US bases and civilian sites across the Gulf, including water and power infrastructure. That has kept Hormuz largely shut, raised global energy prices and forced wealthy Gulf nations to lobby the US into finding a diplomatic off-ramp to the unpopular conflict. Iran’s grip on Hormuz also gives it immense leverage in any potential talks with the US. Bessent suggested this week that the shift to an economic campaign “means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart”. But analysts are not so sure that Iran will refrain from a return to open hostilities, even if the US does. “If this new economic pressure campaign works – and that’s a big if – it’s more likely that we would see military action coming out of Iran than that we would see capitulation, at least as a first step,” said Chris Kennedy, the economic statecraft lead at Bloomberg Economics. “Just because the US has decided to pause its full-blown military operation doesn’t mean Iran will follow suit.” It is not clear exactly how the US could ramp up economic pressure on Iran, other than going after China – the main buyer of Iranian oil – and risking blowback. Going after smaller entities in countries such as Iraq, Turkey or the UAE would be unlikely to break Tehran’s will. Still, the US economic pressure campaign is having an impact. It now risks triggering one of Iran’s worst ever economic crises, despite the country weathering years of broad isolation. Even before the war, a slump in the Iranian rial triggered nationwide protests, with the government killing thousands. Since the war began, the nation’s citizens have seen their purchasing power evaporate under inflation that is now above 80 per cent and with a currency that has lost almost 30 per cent of its value this year alone. This week, Iran’s central bank governor said the nation’s oil exports had “virtually stopped” under the US blockade, ending the government’s main source of revenue. The International Monetary Fund said in April it expected Iran’s economy to shrink 6.1 per cent this year, the worst contraction in decades. On Friday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian urged an end to the war with the US. But his responsibilities are mostly limited to domestic economic policy, while hardline Iranian officials, including some in the nation’s powerful military leadership, have argued that Iran is winning and should continue the fight. It is possible the new measures Bessent will announce on Monday and the ongoing naval blockade will eventually spur Iran to return to the interim diplomatic deal it reached with the US in June, said David Schenker, a US diplomat for the Middle East during Trump’s first term. But it could take six months for any measures to have a significant impact, testing the patience of the Trump administration, he said, noting the Iranian government has shown it can endure major economic pain while largely ignoring the suffering of the nation’s people. “It could drag on for some time,” said Schenker, now a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. “The Iranian regime still sees itself as having leverage and being in a good position.”

title: European wine producers seek new markets as China sales dream sours
description: Imports of bottled wine from the EU fell 16.6 per cent by volume in the first half of this year, according to Chinese customs data.
content: Chinese-French wine merchant Arsen Zhao says business remains strong in Paris, but he is welcoming far fewer customers from Asia than before. “We’ve seen a much sharper drop in customers from China,” Zhao said. “Consumers are trading down, while large volumes of European wine imported previously have yet to be sold, leaving inventories high and weighing on new orders.” As demand has weakened and unsold inventory has piled up, prices have come under pressure. “Some high-end French wines are now selling for less in China than in France,” he said. Zhao is among a growing number of wine merchants shipping fewer bottles to China – formerly one of the industry’s most promising markets. Demand has withered as consumers tighten their purse strings amid weaker income growth, drinking habits shift and Beijing tightens its scrutiny over lavish banquets and official entertaining. By volume, China’s bottled wine imports from the European Union fell 16.6 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026, according to Chinese customs data, with their value dropping 7.9 per cent to US$251 million. Shipments from Spain fell 24.9 per cent, by volume, those from Italy were down 17.7 per cent and France witnessed a fall of 14.3 per cent. The retreat has been years in the making. China’s per-capita wine consumption peaked in the mid-2010s, while wine sales plunged 47 per cent between 2019 and 2022, compared with declines of 17 per cent for spirits and 9 per cent for beer, according to a study published last year by University of Adelaide economist Kym Anderson. Wineries in regions including Shangri-La in Yunnan, the eastern foothills of the Helan Mountains in Ningxia and Shandong have developed rapidly Arsen Zhao, Paris wine merchant While slower income growth and disruptions from the Covid-19 pandemic accelerated the decline, alcohol consumption had already begun falling three years before the pandemic, the study noted, pointing to a broader structural shift in drinking habits. Zhao said that as China’s vast wine market weakened, many merchants had begun shifting their focus towards markets with stronger consumer spending power, such as Singapore and South Korea. European producers were also facing growing competition from China’s domestic wine industry, Zhao said. “Wineries in regions including Shangri-La in Yunnan, the eastern foothills of the Helan Mountains in Ningxia and Shandong have developed rapidly, with improving quality encouraging some consumers to turn to home-grown bottles,” he said. A wine merchant in Madrid said China was never the biggest part of his business, but it was a steady one. Some years he shipped more than 3,000 bottles a year to China, mainly to Western restaurants in major cities such as Shanghai and Shenzhen, but this year he expected that figure would fall to below 900 bottles. “Business has been difficult this year, and wine merchants everywhere are struggling,” he said. “Even here in Spain, we always complain that young people either don’t drink wine any more or simply can’t afford it.” He said he began noticing a change when Australian wine returned to the Chinese market in early 2024, after China removed punitive duties imposed in 2021 amid a broader deterioration in relations sparked by Australian calls for an international investigation into the origins of the Covid-19 pandemic. “To be honest, I haven’t really asked why, but since China started importing Australian wine again, our business has become more difficult,” he said. “Australian wines are more competitive on price.” However, according to Chinese customs data, imports of bottled Australian wine fell 11.6 per cent year on year by volume in the first half of 2026, even as their value rose 20 per cent to US$297 million, making Australia China’s largest source of imported wine by value. Others have responded to China’s slowdown by looking elsewhere. Victorien Renier, a wine merchant from Dijon, France, said American buyers had increasingly filled the gap left by Chinese customers. “I personally felt that the American market took over from the Chinese market, with a wider variety of clients and bigger numbers,” he said. The volume of wine consumed in China fell by 13 per cent last year, according to the Paris-based International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV), the global intergovernmental body for the wine sector. Wine demand in China was particularly sensitive to changes in income and prices because of its discretionary nature, OIV said in a report released in May, while consumption was moving away from its traditional reliance on official entertaining and gift-giving towards more fragmented, consumer-led drinking. It said global wine consumption had fallen 14 per cent since 2018, with China recording the largest contraction among major markets. Some smaller European producers are wondering whether selling to China is worth the cost. An employee at Ysios, a winery in Alava in northern Spain, said high shipping and other export costs meant it would need to sell substantially more wine to make the Chinese market commercially viable. “We are still divided over our China strategy,” she said. “To make the costs work, we would have to ship much larger volumes, like the bigger producers do. But that risks compromising both our quality and the exclusivity our brand is built on, especially as demand from China is declining.”

title: South Koreans ‘intoxicated by stocks’ swarmed market frenzy – and lost everything
description: ‘I don’t think I will ever invest in the Kospi again,’ says an emotionally drained retiree who, like others, is reeling from the rout.
content: It was a ⁠vision to give South Korea a stock market that reflected its true economic ⁠dynamism, by shedding regulatory taboos and encouraging bolder bets – instead, it created an investor trauma that could take years to shake. The ⁠30 per cent decline in the Kospi benchmark since its June 19 peak has hurt President Lee Jae Myung’s government politically and turned the spotlight on an economic system that drove retail investors into poorly understood leveraged products. It has also raised questions about how South Korea, a tech powerhouse, can progress to developed market status when it hosts such extreme behaviour by retail investors, known locally as “ants” for their tendency to swarm into trades. “Ultimately many who entered the market may have suffered severe losses and a majority of them could become so traumatised that they lose interest in investing altogether,” said Jeon Suk-jae, a YouTuber whose investment channel has 3.7 million subscribers. In the two months since the market’s peak, Jeon has seen the comments on his channel, which hosts videos like the ‌one titled “the entire nation is intoxicated by stocks”, flip from euphoria to gloom, broadly tracking the national mood. Beyond the losses – some realised, some still on paper – there is a psychological reckoning that the nation’s leaders are dealing with. Demand for psychiatric help is rising and other signs of stress are rattling the public. Police in Busan said they had arrested a man in his 20s who is suspected of attempted murder over the stabbing of a YouTuber he allegedly blamed for his stock losses. President Lee took office last year with a promise to eliminate the market’s “Korea discount”, the tendency for local stocks to lag global peers due to the dominance of family-owned conglomerates and weak governance. To close the gap, regulators began discussing more sophisticated products in January, including single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds that use derivatives to multiply a stock’s daily return. Such products, popular with Korean investors trading abroad, had backing from the presidential office. “Why is something permitted on the Nasdaq not allowed in Korea?” Kim Yong-beom, the presidential chief of staff for policy, told the Hankyoreh newspaper then. Such discussions became the catalyst for regulators’ decision to allow the ETFs to launch on May 27. Concerns were internally raised ⁠over whether domestic investors understood the risk of heavy losses, but the products were still approved. The only barriers to entry were an hour-long mandatory training course and a 10 million won (US$7,208) minimum deposit. The presidential office and economic ministries said they reviewed the introduction of single-stock leveraged ETFs after thoroughly assessing risk factors. “The ‌government remains committed to maintaining market stability,” the Blue House said. The Financial Services Commission, South Korea’s top financial regulator, said while there was no standardised procedure for reviewing risks, the agency “comprehensively examined various risk factors at each stage”. I don’t think I will ever invest in the Kospi again. South Korean stock investor Dalbo Park On paper, the timing looked perfect. The push to give markets a little more pep coincided with a global AI boom that made Korean memory chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both US$1 trillion companies, firing ‌up a leveraged domestic stock mania. As markets surged, financial influencers and commentators turned investment into a national obsession. Analysts called it a “once-in-a-generation” earnings surge. Sales of books on domestic stocks more than tripled between January and June, according to online bookstore Yes24. Many retail investors ⁠who felt shut out of the AI windfall were now taking the biggest ⁠risks chasing quick profits. To supercharge returns, investors took on debt, with margin loans for Kospi investment jumping about 75 per cent from the start of the year to 30 trillion won by late June. Investors said they were driven by the belief that leverage was the quickest way to overcome odds stacked against them, amid the country’s widest-ever wealth inequality. “Even though reckless, leveraged or margin ‌trading is the only way to climb the broken ladder, at least by just a little,” said Kwon Soon-kuk, a 34-year-old investor, adding that he earned as much as 66 per cent on his investment at the market’s height. Margin loan balances hit a record 29.8 trillion won on June 24, according to the Korea Financial Investment Association. Park Jung-jae, an economics professor at Yonsei University, attributed the herd behaviour to past ‌economic shocks ‌that amplified fear of missing out, or FOMO. Global investors, by contrast, pulled back through the surge as they rebalanced portfolios, even as the Kospi rose 5 per cent to 8 per cent in a day on multiple occasions. The leveraged ETFs launched just as the Kospi, already more than doubled from October levels, crossed 8,000 points. ‌Such funds must trade shares and derivatives to match the leverage, amplifying price swings in both directions. The effect was magnified because SK Hynix and Samsung together account for over 53 per cent of the Kospi’s total value. Sentiment shifted in early July, when the VKospi volatility gauge – the “Korean fear index” – spiked to 97.99, its highest level since ⁠data collection began in 2009. A Citi client note on July 28 estimated retail investors had lost US$38.7 billion on leveraged ETFs. Chun Wang, a director of multi-asset strategies at Leuthold Group in an August 7 note, likened South Korea’s long history of bad speculative bets to Squid Game, the wildly popular Netflix drama. “Episode after episode, ⁠ordinary people under intense financial pressure get lured into increasingly high-risk games by the promise of a life-changing payout, only to end up losing everything,” he said. The fallout has been emotional and political. Park Jongsuk, a Seoul psychiatrist treating stock-related distress, said his caseload had dipped to seven or eight patients a day last year. “But since June of this year, the numbers have exploded again. Currently I am treating an average of 11 patients a day,” he said. Some investors have instead turned back to Wall Street, with appetite for US leveraged ETFs ‌still strong, according to the Korea Securities Depository. While politicians have apologised and authorities ‌have imposed new restrictions on individual investment in such ETFs, investor confidence remains shaken. Elevating the Kospi to global index provider MSCI’s developed market list has been a flagship goal for the Lee administration. Some analysts said this is likely to damage foreign views of the market even though measures to address the Korea discount are still seen positively. “However, because volatility increased too much before the achievements of corporate governance measures are fully established in the market, it will be difficult to make long-term investments for foreign investors,” said Huh Jae-hwan, an analyst at Eugene Investment Securities in Seoul. Some investors have lost faith in the Korean market, even though the Kospi still trades more than double its October level. “I’ve been a stock investor for 30 years but never experienced something like this before,” said Dalbo Park, a retiree in his 80s who lost 35 per cent of his investment in the rout. “I don’t think I will ever invest in the Kospi again.”

title: Washington pushes ‘America first’ agenda in Apec talks ahead of Chinese leader’s visit
description: Washington says it wants to ‘break down barriers’ for its companies in talks being held in the run-up to Xi Jinping’s visit next month.
content: The United States has pledged to take an “America first” approach to the latest round of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation talks, which are taking place in China weeks before President Xi Jinping’s visit to America. The US State Department said: “US leadership in Apec is a key dimension to pursuing America first policies that foster prosperity and advance economic growth in the United States and across the region by breaking down barriers for US business, boosting fair and reciprocal trade and supporting American job growth.” It added that the delegates, led by Casey Mace, the senior official for Apec affairs, would seek to create more opportunities for American businesses in fields such as agriculture and fisheries, energy, transport, health and food security. The US also pledged to boost services exports and supply-chain innovation, as well as lead discussions on trade and labour-related matters. Trade is expected to be one of the main items on the agenda when Xi visits the US next month in the latest effort between the two countries to stabilise relations in the wake of last year’s tariff war. Xi hosted his US counterpart Donald Trump in Beijing in May, a trip that resulted in plans for US-China boards of trade and investment, although the latter has yet to get off the ground. The meeting of Apec senior officials is the third of its kind this year and the largest yet, according to China’s foreign ministry. The event, in the port city of Dalian, started last week and will run until Friday, bringing together more than 2,300 representatives from member states. It will include nearly 130 events covering trade, transport, food security, customs, technology, energy and health, laying the groundwork for the Apec summitin November in Shenzhen, southern China. According to the State Department, Ruth Perry, a senior US official overseeing ocean, fisheries and polar affairs, will lead a workshop designed to highlight American innovations such as satellite monitoring as part of Apec’s efforts to combat illegal fishing and marine debris. At a separate meeting in Dalian on Saturday, Zhang Baofeng, deputy head of China’s General Administration of Customs, called on Apec economies to do more to remove trade barriers and ease cross-border bottlenecks amid increasingly fragmented global supply chains, according to state news agency Xinhua. He said the need to align rules and standards and strengthen supply-chain resilience “had never been more urgent”. Zhang called for greater regulatory coordination, lower transaction costs and more efficient customs procedures to create a safer, more transparent and predictable business environment.

title: After gaining EV dominance, Chinese carmakers shift goal to take on full-hybrid behemoths
description: Chinese EV leaders are pushing into full-hybrid tech to challenge industry titans on mainland and abroad.
content: Chinese carmakers, already at the vanguard of electric vehicle (EV) technology and production, are looking to make a dent in international marques’ full-hybrid vehicle stronghold as they continue to disrupt the global car industry’s pecking order. Major car builders including Geely Auto and Changan Automobile have reported impressive sales of hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), luring domestic consumers away from the likes of Toyota’s Prius. “Chinese-developed HEVs, banking on the carmakers’ strength in developing intelligent features and computing power, have an edge over their international rivals in smart driving and in-car entertainment,” said Chen Jinzhu, CEO of the Shanghai Mingliang Auto Service consultancy. “Now they are developing new models that may prove to be superior in terms of pricing and fuel efficiency,” he added. An HEV is equipped with an internal combustion engine to drive an electrical generator, which either charges batteries or directly powers electric motors. Unlike pure electric or plug-in hybrid cars, a battery in an HEV cannot be recharged by charging facilities. In China, nearly all carmakers have been prioritising development of pure electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles since Beijing granted cash subsidies for buyers in 2009. HEV cars are not categorised as new-energy vehicles in mainland China, meaning they are not eligible for government incentives, such as subsidies or tax exemptions. Chinese carmakers, from Geely and Changan, to Great Wall Motor and Chery Automobile, have been doubling down on their full-hybrid technology after HEV models were well received by consumers in regions with limited power supply. The HEV segment had been dominated by international brands like Toyota and Honda over the past two decades, with the segment seeing annual sales of about 1.2 million units, accounting for around 5 per cent of the total car deliveries nationwide, according to estimates by analysts. “With the full empowerment of Geely’s new energy and AI technologies, our [next-generation] i-HEV’s technical specifications proved to have far surpassed those of Japanese products,” Jerry Gan Jiayue, the newly appointed CEO of Geely Auto, told reporters in a media briefing on August 17. “We feel it [is] safe to term our technology as the global benchmark [for HEV],” he added. Gan, who was formerly head of Geely Auto’s car development and sales, made the statement following the announcement of his promotion at the event. The i-HEV intelligent hybrid system, rolled out early this year, was supported by an artificial intelligence energy management platform capable of monitoring temperature, humidity and altitude to enhance fuel efficiency, according to a statement by Geely. A highway test showed it consumed an average of 2.22 litres of fuel per 100 kilometres, the lowest among all the world’s HEV models, the company added. Geely, the mainland’s second-largest carmaker only behind BYD, the world’s largest EV assembler, said it aimed to achieve monthly HEV deliveries of 30,000 units on the domestic market by the end of 2026. Its new HEV models would be exported to markets outside the mainland from 2027, it added. The European Union now levies tariffs of 17.8 per cent to 45.3 per cent on Chinese-made pure electric cars, while HEV exports from the mainland are subject to a duty of just 10 per cent.

title: Why Cambodia is reviving US military drills despite close China ties
description: Restarting Angkor Sentinel drills lets Phnom Penh signal strategic autonomy without abandoning Beijing, analysts say.
content: Cambodia is preparing to restart joint military exercises with the United States next year, in a move analysts described as a pragmatic reset of defence ties strained since 2017 – though not a pivot away from China. Senior officials from both countries discussed restarting the Angkor Sentinel drills last weekend, alongside expanded training and military reforms, Cambodian media reported. Washington has also signalled interest in further visits to Ream, a strategically located Cambodian naval base built with extensive Chinese assistance. The announcements followed a visit by Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s under secretary of defence for policy, to Phnom Penh for meetings with Prime Minister Hun Manet and Defence Minister Tea Seiha on August 14 and 15 – the last stop on a four-nation tour aimed at rebuilding military relationships. Bora Chhay, a policy analyst and managing director of strategic advisory firm BowerGroupAsia’s Cambodia practice, called it a “significant but pragmatic reset”. The previous US approach, including a since-lifted arms embargo Washington imposed in 2021 over Cambodia’s deepening ties with Beijing and its human rights record, “has not prevented China’s influence from expanding”, he said. Since 2022, China has bankrolled an extensive upgrade of the Ream base, with the Pentagon noting in a report to the US Congress last year that two Chinese naval combatants had been continuously stationed at the base even before the opening of a joint logistics and training centre last April. Washington worries that Ream, on Cambodia’s Gulf of Thailand coast, could become China’s first regional military outpost, handing it an operational advantage near the South China Sea that might unsettle the balance of power. Last year, China and Cambodia staged their largest-ever joint exercises, some of which were held at Ream, involving nearly 900 Chinese and more than 1,300 Cambodian troops, backed by warships, artillery, helicopters and reconnaissance drones. China currently maintains only one officially acknowledged and fully dedicated permanent overseas military base, in Djibouti. ‘Steadily atrophied’ ties Phnom Penh has long been one of Beijing’s staunchest Southeast Asian allies, having received billions of dollars in Chinese investment. China is also Cambodia’s dominant defence partner, according to Cambodian-American political scientist Sophal Ear, an associate professor at the Arizona State University’s Thunderbird School of Global Management. Against this backdrop, restarting Angkor Sentinel – the joint drills with the US that ran for seven years before Cambodia cancelled them in early 2017, months after holding its first Golden Dragon drills with China – carried symbolic weight, Ear said. Washington’s objective “is probably not to ‘win Cambodia back’”, he said. “It is to prevent Cambodia from becoming strategically exclusive to China. That is a much more achievable objective.” Ear points to a pattern of American self-sabotage: years spent voicing concerns over Ream, Beijing’s influence and Phnom Penh’s democratic backsliding, all while US-Cambodia military ties “steadily atrophied”. “The result was somewhat self-defeating: the more Washington disengaged, the fewer alternatives Cambodia had to Chinese military cooperation,” Ear said. “Washington appears to have concluded that if it wants to limit Chinese strategic dominance in Cambodia, engagement is more effective than isolation.” That dynamic has played out before, according to defence analyst Abdul Rahman Yaacob, a research fellow at the Rabdan Security and Defence Institute in the United Arab Emirates. He cited Thailand’s 2014 coup, after which the US scaled down its Cobra Gold exercises and froze some military aid. China responded to Washington’s move by ramping up arms sales and launching new joint drills, including Falcon Strike. A similar scenario unfolded after Cambodia forcibly deported 20 Uygur asylum seekers to China in 2009, triggering US aid cuts. Rahman said this illustrated how Beijing had moved in whenever Washington pulled back from Cambodia or Thailand over democracy and rights concerns in the past. For Phnom Penh, expanding ties with Washington demonstrated its “strategic autonomy”, he said. “This is something that Phnom Penh is keen to show to the rest of the world – that it is not China’s puppet,” Rahman said, pointing to a proposal Cambodia reportedly submitted to the US embassy months ago seeking to restart joint drills and rebuild the bilateral relationship. “The Americans could have accepted a number of recommendations in the proposal,” he added. The Thai factor Cambodia’s recent deadly border clashes with Thailand had exposed the limits of its close ties with China, Rahman said, since Bangkok was not deterred from striking Cambodian territory. Meanwhile, joint training with the US military would enable Cambodia to learn more modern warfare techniques, he said. Noting that Cambodia was militarily weaker than Thailand, Ear said that deeper engagement with the US offered “diplomatic and strategic reassurance even if it does not alter the military balance overnight”. “A Cambodia that conducts exercises with both the Chinese and American militaries, receives Japanese security assistance and maintains relationships with other regional partners is harder to portray as diplomatically isolated or simply a Chinese client,” he said. Chhay said stronger US defence ties could also bolster Cambodia’s deterrence capabilities and diplomatic visibility, while increasing its “strategic space in supporting peaceful border management, confidence building” and engagement with the rest of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. For Washington, “Cambodia offers an opportunity to rebuild US influence and preserve strategic choice in Southeast Asia”, he added.

title: All hands on deck at charity hoping to inspire Hong Kong youth with sailing
description: Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club Charity Foundation has hosted an event bringing young people out for a day at sea.
content:
About 60 young people and their family members took to Hong Kong’s waters last month – for many of them, it was their first time on sailing boats.
“Charity Sailing Day for Tai Po Youth and Family” was organised by the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club Charity Foundation to introduce local youth to water sports.
The event offered participants a two-hour sailing session with seven sailors who volunteered their time and lent their personal boats for the day.
“I hope they learn that sport can change lives. Whether there is wind or not, you can steer your own course in life and keep the helm in your own hands,” said Adrian Pang, spokesman for the charity.
“Good athletes train through heavy winds and rough waves so that when they face life’s impacts, they become stronger and grow.”
Pang also emphasised the practical and social values that students learned from the experience, such as the importance of staying safe on board and looking after one another while out at sea.
The charity was established in 2012 to grant underprivileged youth and individuals with special needs access to water sports by leveraging the resources and volunteer network of the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club. Operating from its primary base at Kellett Island – a former naval magazine site – the club in Causeway Bay is one of Hong Kong’s oldest institutional sports organisations.
Pang added that the foundation aimed to give Tai Po youth a fun experience during the summer holiday while promoting sailing to groups who rarely have the chance to participate in the elite sport.
Following the time at sea, the event continued ashore with a buffet lunch, interactive discussion sessions, quizzes and games.
Although the day began with sunny skies, heavy rain poured down towards the end of the voyage.
“It was a perfect mix of weather – to have a very sunny start and end with rain, it provided a complete experience of sailing for the students,” Pang said.
Three young participants, Marcus Yung, Daniel Wong and Mira Man, spent their session on board Next Generation, a yacht skippered by Eddy Lee, a director at Lee Kum Kee.
Daniel Wong, a nine-year-old pupil at Wai Chow Public School (Sheung Shui), said he was excited about learning how to steer a boat.
“It was super fun, and I was surprised to see a bedroom on the sailing boat,” he said, noting that while he had always been interested in water sports, this was his first sailing experience.
Another nine-year-old participant, Mira, a student at Hong Kong and Kowloon Kaifong Women’s Association Sun Fong Chung Primary School, said she felt comfortable on the water despite her initial worries about the weather.
“I wasn’t scared on the boat. The most memorable part was sticking my legs out to feel the sea breeze – it was very comfortable,” she said.
“I was worried it would be very hot, so I brought sunscreen and a hat. But it turned out to be quite cool. I want to keep going out to sea on boats even though I don’t think I know how to control one yet.”
Marcus, a 10-year-old pupil at Pentecostal Yu Leung Fat Primary School, described the outing as an unforgettable experience.
“We sang along to my favourite songs together while we sailed. It was fun! I hope I can have another chance to sail again,” he said.

title: Untapped market: Hong Kong’s craft breweries push for permits to serve guests
description: Brewers in industrial buildings say licensing rules prevent them from hosting tours and walk-in customers, missing out on tourist revenue.
content: When a 100-member tour group from South Korea approached a Hong Kong craft beer manufacturer about a visit and tasting session, the operator declined their request. The refusal was not due to a lack of confidence in the product or a staff shortage. The brewery simply lacked a licence to serve beer on the premises. “It is not easy doing manufacturing in Hong Kong,” said Luke Yardley, founder of local craft beer brewery Yardley Brothers. “It is just a missed opportunity when in every other country – if you are in London, New York, Dublin – customers can go for a day out and visit the brewery. They get to have a nice experience where they can consume alcohol on site. And the key thing is they can buy alcohol on site.” Yardley is not alone. Many of Hong Kong’s craft beer manufacturers operate in industrial buildings under food factory licences to house their giant equipment and save costs, which makes applying for liquor licences difficult. The situation has prompted calls for a review of the licensing regime governed by the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department to allow breweries to offer samples for walk-in customers, which industry leaders and a lawmaker have said could help support tourism. Hong Kong has about 15 home-grown craft breweries producing more than 30 distinct brands, with some being exported for international consumption. In Hong Kong, catering operators that want to serve alcohol must obtain a licence from the Liquor Licensing Board, and they are usually given to restaurants or clubhouses. For other premises, an application must undergo extra scrutiny from other government arms, including the Planning Department, Fire Services Department and buildings authorities, leading to lengthier approval times. Yardley has been running his brewery for 10 years, and the factory in Kwai Chung now produces about 15,000 litres (3,963 gallons) of beer per month. He said Hong Kong was home to a few top beer makers in Asia, but the regulatory hurdles made it difficult for producers to promote themselves “confidently”. Yardley called for a review of the current licensing regime and urged authorities to explore the feasibility of introducing a dedicated liquor licence for breweries, allowing them to offer samples to visitors, which he said could also attract more tourists to Hong Kong. “A concern [could be] having it out of control where you have nightclubs in industrial buildings and that is not what we are proposing,” he said. Also expressing similar frustration was Christopher Wong See-wai, head brewer and a co-founder of Heroes Beer in Yau Tong, who said it was a pity that all household beer brands in Hong Kong came from overseas. “The reason why microbreweries in other countries can win support from their neighbourhood community, expanding their influence to a broader area, is through residents’ visits to learn what they are doing,” said Wong, who is also the co-founder of a few other local breweries. “The biggest problem in Hong Kong is that people do not even know we exist.” For a niche brand such as Heroes, which specialises in “experimental beer” and produces about 40,000 litres of beer per year, building a reputation to rival established names such as Blue Girl, San Miguel and Carlsberg is difficult without local community engagement, according to Wong. “There are many luxury homes in Yau Tong. If I have a licence, people can come to my brewery, sit down, have a glass of beer after work and join a tour to learn more about us,” he said. Also a restaurant operator, Wong said many breweries were able to meet the conditions for obtaining liquor licences. He questioned the government’s reluctance to expand the licensing regime to them, when there were already many retail and even gym operators in industrial buildings. Lawmaker Adrian Pedro Ho King-hong said breweries in Hong Kong were facing “massive challenges” in running tasting tours because of the licensing regime, as well as land-use restrictions. He agreed that authorities should explore introducing a dedicated “taproom licence” with certain restrictive conditions such as size and capacity to avoid turning factories into entertainment venues. “Introducing a taproom licence regime can on the one hand enhance the international publicity of Hong Kong brands, and on the other hand, it is good for the tourism industry as many visitors would like to tour our local breweries,” he said. During a recent public consultation session for Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu acknowledged that the city needed globally recognised local brands and pledged to provide policy support. Ho said he would meet authorities to discuss the matter after collecting information and opinions from the industry, but cautioned that progress required cross-departmental collaboration. Even if the department approved serving alcohol at breweries, there could be further restrictions on land use stipulated by authorities and the deeds of mutual covenant governing use of the buildings, he added. “It takes time and I think we need a starting point in promoting industrial building revitalisation,” he said. In response to a South China Morning Post inquiry, the department stressed that the operation of commercial or retail activities in industrial buildings must also comply with other statutory requirements, such as zoning plans, government lease conditions and building and fire safety legislation. “The [department] will continue to work closely with relevant policy bureaus and departments to examine feasible options that support local food trade while upholding regulatory standards and community interests,” it said. The Development Bureau said catering services were permissible in wholesale converted industrial buildings under its revitalisation scheme. It added that it was reviewing the scheme and would explore the possibility of widening non-industrial uses in non-wholesale converted industrial buildings, taking into account emerging market needs and interdepartmental feedback.

title: Patient arrested after bedding, restraint belts set ablaze at Hong Kong hospital
description: No injuries reported after fire broke out at Kwong Wah Hospital at 12.36am.
content: A patient has been arrested on suspicion of setting fire to bedding and restraint belts at a Hong Kong hospital, with no injuries reported. Police arrested the 25-year-old man surnamed Wong at Kwong Wah Hospital in Yau Ma Tei for alleged arson. He remains in custody. The fire was reported at 12.36am on Sunday after a security guard alerted police. The suspect allegedly set fire to bedding and restraint belts at the hospital. Following a preliminary investigation, the Fire Services Department classified the blaze as suspicious, and police have taken over the case. Arson carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment under Hong Kong law.

title: Alibaba to issue US$10 billion in new shares for huge AI push amid strong investor demand
description: The Chinese tech giant is going ‘full stack’, expanding beyond retail into chips, cloud and large language models as surging spending weighs on quarterly profits.
content: Alibaba Group Holding will issue HK$80 billion (US$10.2 billion) worth of new shares and use all of the proceeds to invest in AI, the Chinese tech giant said on Sunday. The move aims to “extend the company’s global AI leadership”, it said, adding that Alibaba would use the funds raised to “invest in its full-stack AI capabilities”, including expanding and enhancing its AI infrastructure. The decision underscores Alibaba’s efforts over the past few years to transform from an e-commerce giant into a full-stack AI player with businesses spanning chips, computing infrastructure, large language models and AI applications. Banks have received pre-launch indications of interest in excess of the deal size “on the back of strong interest received from sovereign wealth funds and global long-only investors”, according to a person familiar with the matter. Alibaba increased the size of the offering to HK$80 billion because of strong investor demand, the source added. Last week, Alibaba announced a 45 per cent year-over-year jump in its April-to-June quarterly revenue in cloud and AI businesses, with capital expenditure expanding 75 per cent from a year earlier to 67.7 billion yuan (US$10 billion). Alibaba was expecting its investments in AI computing to break even within three years, with the payback period potentially shortened to about two years as gross margins continued to rise, Alibaba Group CEO Eddie Wu Yongming said during an earnings call on Thursday. This news reflects Alibaba’s plan to continue ramping up its AI investments Kenny Ng, Everbright Securities International The e-commerce and AI giant will also use the share-sale proceeds to boost AI innovation, according to another person familiar with the deal. The offering would be one of China’s largest AI-dedicated financing cases, as well as Alibaba’s first new share placement following its Hong Kong listing in 2019. No further details about the offering were disclosed. Alibaba’s latest AI-financing plans are set to further intensify the US-China AI competition as top US labs and hyperscalers also move to raise substantial new capital. “This news reflects Alibaba’s plan to continue ramping up its AI investments, as its past earnings have already shown rapid growth in AI-related spending,” said Kenny Ng, a strategist at Everbright Securities International. He noted that the company’s capital expenditures would likely remain high to support this push. The immediate market reaction, however, looks to depend on the final pricing of the new shares. “If the placement price comes with a steep discount, it could put more pressure on the stock,” Ng added. “If the discount is narrower, the pressure on the share price will be relatively mild.” During Thursday’s earnings call, Wu added that the company had already spent 190 billion yuan in capital expenditure by the end of June. In February 2025, Alibaba announced a three-year commitment of 380 billion yuan in AI infrastructure investment. Alibaba operates the Qwen family of large language models, which the company recently said had recorded more than 3 billion downloads globally. More than 2 billion Qwen downloads were recorded in 2026, far ahead of all other AI model providers, according to a report earlier this month by the open-source developer platform Hugging Face. The platform attributed Qwen’s popularity to factors including a consistent pace of flagship model releases and offerings covering a wide range of sizes and use cases. Alibaba has also reported growing momentum from its T-Head semiconductor unit. The company’s Zhenwu chips had served more than 650 customers on Alibaba Cloud, while its Zhenwu M890 AI processor began commercial-scale deployment this month. Alibaba’s AI Cloud and Compute Services, a new reporting segment that covers its cloud business and T-Head unit, recorded 48.4 billion yuan in revenue for the three months ended June 30, marking its fastest growth in 22 quarters. Alibaba Group owns the South China Morning Post. “We expect supply to continue ramping up in the second half of the year to meet strong customer demand,” Wu said last week. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude large language models, confidentially filed its prospectus in June, paving the way for what many expect to be the largest-ever initial public offering. The company was valued at US$965 billion after a US$65 billion Series H funding round in May. As of July 9, investment-grade bond issuance from Google, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Nvidia, Oracle and SpaceX reached around US$240 billion, more than double the total for 2025, according to Morningstar. Alibaba is among global AI players locked in a fierce race to secure market leadership despite mounting pressure to justify their ever-expanding AI investments. While Alibaba’s AI revenue climbed, its latest quarterly profit plunged 75 per cent, year over year. The company’s New York-listed shares fell 8.57 per cent on Friday, while its Hong Kong-listed shares slid 2.54 per cent. Domestic rival Tencent Holdings also said earlier this month that its AI capital expenditure jumped 176 per cent, year on year, to 52.8 billion yuan for the quarter ended in June. Net profit increased merely 0.8 per cent to 68.4 billion yuan from 63.1 billion yuan in the same period last year. US Big Tech’s AI spending, however, dwarfs that of Chinese tech giants. Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta are collectively expected to spend around US$700 billion this year, translating to an average of US$44 billion per company per quarter.

title: Hong Kong may issue typhoon signal on Tuesday or Wednesday as Narra approaches
description: Observatory says storm expected to head towards southwestern tip of Guangdong province early next week.
content: The Hong Kong Observatory may issue a typhoon signal on Tuesday or Wednesday as a tropical storm edges closer to the region. “Tropical Cyclone Narra is expected to linger over the vicinity of Beibu Wan today and tomorrow, and then turn northeastwards gradually later on Monday to Tuesday, edging closer to the vicinity of Leizhou Peninsula,” the forecaster said on Sunday. Leizhou Peninsula sits at the far southwestern tip of Guangdong province, some 400km (248.5 miles) west-southwest of Hong Kong. “The Observatory will closely monitor its movement and the change in local wind conditions, and assess the need for issuing tropical cyclone warning signals on Tuesday or Wednesday,” it added, urging the public to pay attention to the latest weather information. Narra is named after a tree species in the Philippines. According to the forecast, there will be showers and squally thunderstorms early next week. The city’s temperatures will rise from 27 degrees Celsius (80.6 Fahrenheit) to 33 degrees on Friday.

title: Michelin and Black Pearl young chef awardee Justin Yang opens restaurant in Hong Kong
description: The Divine Dish star Justin Yang blends his Fujianese heritage with modern flair at Quan, a contemporary Chinese restaurant in Central.
content: By the time chef Justin Yang Yanbin took part in the reality cooking show The Divine Dish (also known as Chef of China) in 2025, he was already a culinary star, having received the Michelin Guide Chengdu’s young chef award the previous year – despite having nearly two decades of training under his belt. Then, six months after achieving first runner-up on the cooking show, he received another young chef award – this time from the Black Pearl Restaurant Guide 2026. Trained under legendary Min cuisine master Luo Bingfu, the now 32-year-old Yang has held executive chef positions at several acclaimed restaurants, including Chic 1699 in Xiamen, Hokklo at Waldorf Astoria Xiamen and Hokkien Cuisine in Chengdu, where he led the team to its first Michelin star as its youngest-ever executive Chinese chef. For him, joining The Divine Dish was never about winning. “Taking part in the show was more about showing my own personality and expressing the image and creative process of a modern head chef,” he explains. “I wanted the audience to know that fine food is not easy to create – that there is much more to it. “Only knowing how to cook is not enough. That can only be called a ‘talent’ – someone with skill. But if you also know how to think, how to express yourself on top of that – that is called ‘genius’. “Being on shows doesn’t guarantee good results, but it helps me learn. I always have to keep learning to think, and thinking to learn, because this industry requires you to grow step by step, to broaden your horizons. You have to dare to express yourself, dare to do it.” Drawing from traditional Chinese cosmology Now, Yang has brought his expertise in Cantonese and Min cuisine to Hong Kong with Quan, a new contemporary Chinese restaurant in Central. “The character quan actually refers to my hometown, Quanzhou,” he says. “But it’s not just about making Fujian cuisine or Quanzhou cuisine. That is my starting point, where my roots are, but we want to evolve with the times, and our flavours are being elevated. So it’s not just Quanzhou cuisine or Fujian cuisine – it’s me, it’s what I want to present as Justin Yang.” At the restaurant, Yang introduces his “five elements” philosophy – earth, water, metal, fire and wood – with representative dishes such as chilled mantis shrimp with sea urchin, braised beef short ribs in a clay pot, and Fujian old wine drunken crab. The concept draws from traditional Chinese cosmology but is interpreted through a culinary lens, reflecting both Yang’s Fujian heritage and his modern, global approach to cooking. Earth grounds every culinary creation in the deep, fertile heritage of Fujian flavours. It represents the traditional techniques and ingredients that Yang learned from his mentor as well as the flavours of his childhood in Quanzhou. Water celebrates Quanzhou’s geographic identity, cradled between the Daiyun Mountains and the Taiwan Strait, where the culinary tradition is defined by fresh local seafood. Metal represents shaping refined flavours with the painstaking precision of a master goldsmith. It speaks to Yang’s rigorous attention to detail – he describes himself as being a “detail freak and perfectionist”. “I have very high standards and always look at the smallest things,” he says. “I push myself constantly to improve.” Fire sits as the vital energy of the wok, breathing life and warmth into every plate, while wood represents the growth of culinary artistry. “Your vision is very important,” he says about his creative process. “It’s like a fountain – every day you want to improve, so naturally ideas start to combine and flow from your mind.” Always starting over Now in his 19th year of cooking, Yang marks his arrival in Hong Kong with a playful sense of timing. “I turned 18 in the industry, which means my culinary career has officially come of age,” he says. “And since I’ve come of age, I chose to leave home and come to Hong Kong as my first stop.” Yang’s approach to his career is defined by a single, recurring practice: starting over. “Throughout the years, every time I achieve something, I reset to zero. I don’t let achievements make me proud. Every year, after I achieve something, the next year I reset to zero, and I start from zero, again and again.” This is also what he looks forward to almost every time he has to relocate for his career, having transitioned from Fujian to Xiamen to Chengdu to Shanghai and now to Hong Kong. “I especially love the process of opening a new restaurant – building a new team, creating new dishes, discovering new inspiration in the process and creating something new,” he says. “I don’t treat this as just a job. I treat it as my life’s career and my own cultivation. So I care deeply about whether I’m making progress on this journey.” When asked if there is any dish or cuisine that still challenges him, he speaks with the certainty of a man who knows his path. “Culinary art has no borders, and it never stops. You can only keep creating along this path – you can never stop. Art only has width, not length.” Quan, 5/F, CCB Tower, 3 Connaught Road Central, Central, Hong Kong

title: Fan Zhendong enjoys ‘fitting, warm welcome’ in home debut for Borussia Dusseldorf
description: German club says they have to seize the moment and capitalise on Chinese star’s winning ways, pulling power in the Table Tennis Bundesliga.
content: Borussia Dusseldorf manager Andreas Preuss said Chinese table tennis star Fan Zhendong’s first home match was “only a beginning” and that the German club had to ride the wave and seize the moment to make it sustainable. In his second season in Germany, but the first with new team Dusseldorf, Fan on Saturday secured two points in his team’s 3-1 win over TSV Bad Konigshofen in the Table Tennis Bundesliga. Preuss, who spoke exclusively to the South China Morning Post on Sunday, said it was a “fitting, warm welcome” for China’s Paris Olympics champion. Despite Kanak Jha losing his match against Filip Zeljko, Fan secured two points with a pair of identical 3-1 wins over Andre Bertelsmeier and Zeljko, enough to help the home team claim their second league win in as many matches. “I am thrilled. They were very exciting matches played at a high level,” Preuss said. “It was a fitting, warm welcome for Fan Zhendong, and he thanked everyone in his own way by scoring two points for the team today. “I am extremely pleased; it was a celebration of table tennis.” Fan, 29, helped attract 3,800 spectators at the Mitsubishi Electric Hall for the team’s first home fixture of the season. The club are playing some of their games at the bigger arena in Dusseldorf as their usual home court ARAG Centre Court can host only 1,100 spectators. “There were a lot of learnings for us in the past few months. We kind of knew what was to come, and so we proceeded on many things in parallel,” Preuss said. “We started with merchandising, with social media, we even have a community. “We have more than 40 people working in the club, and we are doing many things every weekend. We had the chance to learn from Saarbrucken [Fan’s previous club] and start on a higher level.” Preuss estimated that around 40 per cent of the spectators at the Mitsubishi Hall were Chinese, including a group of about 100 tourists who arrived from China on the day. The team are starting to negotiate with sponsors, as well as starting a shop in China. Preuss said the team now had around 60 sponsors, up from about 35 at the end of last season. Merchandise including jerseys, scarves and other souvenirs were sold out at the arena after the match. “We now have a mascot, Bo, so there is this lion running around in the arena,” said the 64-year-old Preuss. “We’re developing step by step, we don’t want to do everything from the start. “There will be souvenirs specially designed for the Chinese market, which is different [from what we used to deal with]. This is also a different culture, so we have to adapt.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by D.SPORTS (@dsports.sportstadtduesseldorf) Fan’s new teammate Qiu Dang, who also won a point, heaped praise on the “incredibly fantastic event” and the full-house arena. “Even coming out onto the floor was amazing,” the German international said. “We had to give everything today; even Fan Zhendong dropped two games as well, but I think he played really well after such a long break from competition. “I think there’s no pressure, but it surely felt different being on the same team as Fan. I am thrilled to be playing alongside him; we all feel relieved to have him. We can learn a lot from his game, and hopefully we can win a lot of matches this season.” Borussia Dusseldorf are Germany’s most successful table tennis team, having won the league 34 times, along with 28 German Cup titles and seven European Champions League trophies. The decorated team, however, did not win anything in the 2024-25 season, which was the swansong for the legendary Timo Boll, as well as the season that followed, when former world No 1 Fan swept the league, the cup and Europe in his first overseas season with 1. FC Saarbrucken. Manager Preuss said there was an overwhelming response to Fan joining the club in March, with attention and engagement on the team’s social media increasing to 500 times higher than normal. Sport1, a German television channel, said Fan has gained “at least 100 million loyal fans in Dusseldorf in a very short period of time”, referring to the news that a story about the 29-year-old joining the team was viewed that many times. Fan is expected to be rested in the next match against SV Werder Bremen on Thursday, but will return for the German Cup first-round tie versus Ochsenhausen. Fan is also expected to feature against Bergneustadt – in the fourth league match – at ARAG Centre Court on September 5.

title: Gaokao reforms could leave Chinese public vulnerable to pseudo-history, top academic warns
description: University dean’s cautionary words come as Beijing is increasingly on guard about historical views at odds with the official line.
content: China’s secondary school students are dropping history as an exam subject, a trend that could leave the public more vulnerable to distorted narratives in the future, an academic at a top university has warned. The note of caution comes as Beijing steps up efforts to counter “historical nihilism” – the official term for narratives that contradict or undermine the state’s official historical line – as well as pseudo-history, such as claims that Ancient Greece did not exist. “History education in secondary schools is an important means of preserving historical, cultural, ethnic and national identity,” said Liu Linhai, dean of the school of history at Beijing Normal University, in a commentary in the state-backed China Teacher Paper. “Its current weakening and even marginalisation should be a matter of urgent concern for policymakers, who should take coordinated and effective measures to address the structural problems affecting the subject,” Liu wrote. Authorities in China have become increasingly alert to challenges to the orthodox view of the country’s history. On Thursday, a newspaper published by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences ran two front-page pieces framing pseudo-history as a “new variant” of historical nihilism. In a strongly worded editorial, Chinese Social Sciences Today warned that such narratives could sow confusion in society, threaten ideological security and undermine cultural confidence and national identity. The second article, by two staff reporters, examined how claims that the Tang dynasty (618-907) never existed went viral – to highlight how influencers and traffic-driven social media algorithms could turn fringe theories into viral narratives. They also mentioned the so-called “1644 historical perspective”, which has been seen as a particularly sensitive issue. Central to this narrative is the view that China was prosperous and powerful under the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), whose rulers came from China’s majority Han ethnic group, and its decline began with the country’s conquest by the ethnic Manchus who established Qing rule in 1644. By emphasising a historical break and blaming a specific ethnic group for China’s relative decline in that period, these narratives challenge the idea of China’s 5,000-year historical continuity, which Beijing uses today to cast itself as the inheritor of a long-unified, multi-ethnic nation. Liu noted that the importance of history education had become more pronounced as the internet, social media and artificial intelligence transformed how historical knowledge was produced and consumed, warning that the rise of amateur historical research had fuelled the spread of inaccurate historical narratives online. “A sound history education in secondary schools is extremely important,” Liu said. “It is the foundation for ensuring that students acquire sound knowledge and correct values, and any measures that weaken or marginalise the subject could have serious consequences.” Yet, while the need for a sound history education had grown, the subject had also come under greater pressure, he said. China’s reforms to its highly competitive college entrance examination or gaokao had caused a “structural disruption” across secondary education, with history bearing the brunt, he noted. Since 2014, reforms have sought to give students greater flexibility to choose subjects based on their interests and strengths by moving the exam away from its traditional science-humanities divide. Under the new system, only Chinese, mathematics and English remain compulsory, while students can choose several additional science and humanities subjects that also contribute to their final score. Although high school students were “theoretically free” to choose subjects based on their interests, Liu said their choices were constrained by the requirements of the zhongkao or high school entrance exam and the admission requirements of universities, limiting the flexibility envisioned by the reforms. “The college entrance exam is a competitive selection examination, and students’ eventual choices tend to be rational and pragmatic,” he wrote. He noted that the proportion of students choosing history had dropped sharply in most provinces and continued to fall each year, prompting a reduction in classroom hours for history teachers. Chinese media reports have described similar consequences. Facing declining student numbers and reduced workloads, some middle-school history teachers have either had to start teaching other subjects or leave the profession. Policy reforms had reduced the weight given to history in the high school entrance exam, with some provinces even excluding it altogether, making students less likely to prioritise the subject, Liu said. “Without a solid foundation in history during junior high school, the subject may struggle to attract students in high school,” he noted. In some provinces, students had to choose between history and physics, further squeezing history as relatively few university programmes required the subject, while physics was required for a much wider range of courses, he said. According to the Southern Weekly newspaper, among those provinces, nearly half saw a roughly 7:3 split in favour of physics, with the ratio reaching 8:2 in some provinces. Even students interested in history would opt for physics if they felt it would give them a better shot at a higher exam score, Liu added. He stressed that a sound foundation in history had become all the more necessary today as “erroneous” views of history were proliferating. Liu argued that policymakers should address the structural pressures facing history education if the subject was to play its role in “strengthening national and ethnic identity and safeguarding national security”. He highlighted the unique role of secondary school history, noting that most students received no formal history education after graduation and that their understanding of the past was largely shaped during their school years. Chinese Social Sciences Today also said that strengthening historical education and improving historical literacy among the public was a long-term solution to countering pseudo-history.

title: Meet comedian Ziwe, the talk show host putting Law Roach and Kevin Hart in the hot seat
description: Her satirical interviews have gone viral and her blunt questions – like whether Zendaya will ever wear Saint Laurent – keep fans thoroughly entertained.
content: Comedian Ziwe Fumudoh – best known simply as Ziwe – has repeatedly gone viral over the past year with her hit talk show Ziwe: You’d Be an Iconic Guest. Known for her disarmingly blunt and satirical interview style, she puts celebrity guests in the hot seat with unfiltered and sometimes uncomfortable questions. Most recently, she featured image architect Law Roach on her show, where she asked the famous celebrity stylist about his journey with “pettiness” and his “unofficial red carpet boycott [of] Saint Laurent, Dior, Valentino, Chanel and Gucci” when styling Zendaya after those fashion houses refused to dress the actress early in her career. “I think that there is an importance of being petty, but I’ve outgrown my pettiness. I think that holding grudges makes you ugly, so in my quest to become more beautiful, I’ve released some of the grudges that I held,” Roach replied. “And I’m actually wearing Saint Laurent right now.” However, his journey of releasing grudges has only gone so far. When asked if Zendaya would also be wearing those brands during public appearances, Roach simply told Ziwe “no”. In the past, Ziwe’s interviews with Kevin Hart and Vince Staples have garnered millions of views on YouTube. She frequently asks her guests for their views on societal issues such as matters of race. In several exchanges, she has pointedly asked her guests, “How many Black friends do you have?” Ziwe’s inimitable interview style has earned her a dedicated fan base and a following of over 1.2 million on Instagram. Here’s everything you need to know about Ziwe Fumudoh. What is Ziwe’s background? Ziwerekoru Fumudoh was born in February 1991 in Massachusetts to Nigerian immigrant parents and is the second of three children. She attended Phillips Academy, a prep school in Andover, before studying at Northwestern University in Illinois. Originally a mathematics major, Ziwe told Variety in 2020 that she found herself falling in love with writing after a professor told her it’s “how you’ll have power as a Black woman”. She went on to study African-American studies, film, and poetry, but quickly realised she couldn’t earn a living writing poetry. Ziwe had mulled going back to school to become a civil rights lawyer, but she found her footing in comedy after working for satirical outlet The Onion and news programme The Colbert Report. She also started doing stand-up comedy and fell in love with the medium. How did Ziwe break into showbiz? Ziwe moved to New York after graduating from university and began working for comedy studio Above Average Productions, founded by Lorne Michaels. She launched her YouTube series Baited in 2017, where she featured her white friends and questioned them about race, often “baiting” them into committing a racial faux pas. She was also the host of Pop Show, a live performance where she sang original satirical tracks with her comedian friends. Between 2019 and 2020, she worked as a writer for the late-night talk show Desus & Mero, hosted by Desus Nice and The Kid Mero. Ziwe later shifted her Baited series from YouTube to Instagram Live, where she interviewed guests such as Caroline Calloway, Alyssa Milano, and Rose McGowan. The show’s popularity landed the comedian her eponymous late-night show with Showtime, where she discussed race and politics with guests who were subjected to the game “Enslave, Appropriate, Silence” – an awkward (for her guests) twist on “F***, Marry, Kill”. The Showtime series was cancelled after two seasons in 2023. Currently, the comedian and writer hosts her wildly popular interview series, Ziwe: You’d Be an Iconic Guest, on YouTube.

title: Quake-prone Indonesia’s first nuclear power plant plan stokes safety fears
description: While some people see the proposed project on an uninhabited island with ‘pride’, others warn of safety issues.
content: Coal-dependent Indonesia is reviving decades-old plans to build nuclear power plants that were put on hold following the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster in Japan, as it seeks to meet its decarbonisation targets. Some members of the public and experts, however, have voiced concerns about the risks of a nuclear disaster in the quake-prone country, despite one of the leading candidate sites being an uninhabited island considered not to be in an active seismic zone. The government began discussing the revival of the plan last year as it seeks to reshape its energy policy. Deputy Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Yuliot told an international nuclear forum in Jakarta in December that a new energy strategy would “explicitly” require the use of nuclear energy “to balance the energy mix and achieve decarbonisation targets”. Plans to build nuclear power plants were first made in the mid-1990s under then president Suharto. Although Indonesia in 2014 designated nuclear power as a “last option” as an energy source following the meltdown at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant caused by the March 2011 earthquake and tsunami, the country shifted to treating it as a “strategic choice” last year. The Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources says that it aims to have Indonesia’s first nuclear power plant operational by 2032 at the earliest, with a target for nuclear energy to account for up to 12.1 per cent of the primary energy mix by 2060, with an installed capacity of 35-42 gigawatts. Zainal Arifin, acting head of the Nuclear Energy Regulatory Agency, said in Jakarta earlier this year, “It is a good moment for Indonesia to make a decision [on nuclear power plants].” The energy ministry is still awaiting presidential approval to establish an organisation to implement the nuclear energy programme and formally select a site. Leading candidates reportedly include Semesak Island in West Kalimantan province on Borneo and the island province of Bangka Belitung. The government has indicated a preference for Semesak Island and has repeatedly held briefings for residents living nearby. Some local officials and businesspeople appear to welcome the prospect of a nuclear power plant. Sebastianus Darwis, the regent of Bengkayang regency, where the island is located, said that he wants the plant to serve as a catalyst for attracting industries to the area, whose economy is based on agriculture and fisheries. “Nuclear power is clean energy. It is proof of a developed nation. It brings pride,” he said. “We aim to become the first in Southeast Asia to operate a nuclear power plant.” Semesak Island is located 900 metres (2,952 feet) off Sungai Raya village in Bengkayang regency. Referring to Indonesia’s new capital Nusantara, under construction in East Kalimantan province, Sebastianus added that the planned nuclear plant “would serve as a power source [for the new capital] and we would also like to sell electricity abroad”. Although Semesak has no inhabitants, fishermen from Sungai Raya frequent the waters surrounding it, which are rich shrimp fishing grounds, and take breaks on its shore. Ramli Umar, 61, a resident of Sungai Raya, expressed mixed feelings about the project, citing the prospect of economic growth but also concerns about radiation. “If this area is selected as a national project, we have no choice but to comply,” he said. Haripan, 62, a fisherman who has been living in the village for decades, said he would prefer to be relocated to another area if a nuclear power plant is built on the island. “Of course, I have concerns. I am afraid of the impact of a nuclear power plant. I am also worried that an accident like those at Chernobyl and Fukushima could happen,” he said, referring to the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear power plant disaster and that at the Fukushima plant. The national government plans to expropriate a total of 300 hectares (741 acres) across the island and a buffer zone on the opposite shore in the regency, according to Sebastianus. Indonesia’s plans for nuclear power have also attracted interest overseas. Japan’s Economy, Trade and Industry Ministry signed a memorandum of understanding with the Indonesian energy ministry in March to assist with the introduction of nuclear energy. The move came as Japan itself shifts its stance on nuclear power, with its industry ministry in June last year proposing the replacement of two to five ageing nuclear reactors by the 2040s and a total of 11 to 14 by the 2050s, setting such a numerical target for the first time since the Fukushima disaster. Russia appears particularly eager to offer technical cooperation. Alexey Likhachev, director general of the state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom, met Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in May in Jakarta, promising to support the construction plan. The Indonesian government has said it would prioritise constructing small modular reactors, a technology pioneered by Russia that allows reactor components to be factory-assembled and transported to a location for installation. Although there have been no large-scale protests against nuclear power in Indonesia in recent years, some opposition remains among members of the public and experts in a country that is frequently hit by earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Fabby Tumiwa, executive director of the Institute for Essential Services Reform, a think tank and NGO promoting clean energy, said: “I am very critical of this. And the reason for that is not because of ideology or something. I only found that it’s not economically feasible and there are safety issues.” Warning that new active faults have been discovered in the country in recent years, he cautioned that there is “nothing safe” about siting nuclear power plants in Indonesia. Fabby noted that Japan’s restart of nuclear reactors years after the Fukushima disaster has likely encouraged Indonesia’s policy shift as well. “We don’t really need nuclear power plants,” he said, arguing that Indonesia has plenty of renewable energy to replace coal thermal power and achieve its decarbonisation targets.

title: Letters | Solution to Asia’s ageing workforce could be sitting at home retired
description: Readers discuss second-career pathways for older professionals, and why Indonesia and China should innovate together.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Your report, “China’s state agencies are hiring retirees as the workforce rapidly ages” (July 19), highlights an intriguing response to one of Asia’s defining demographic challenges. China’s universities, hospitals and government agencies are discovering something societies often forget: retirement from a job does not necessarily mean retirement of one’s usefulness. As a physician who has spent decades in medicine, I see ageing differently from the conventional calendar. Chronological age tells us how many birthdays someone has celebrated; functional age tells us what that person can still contribute. A healthy 65- or 70-year-old physician, professor, engineer, scientist or administrator might possess something no university can quickly manufacture and no artificial intelligence can fully replicate: decades of accumulated judgment. China’s experiment therefore deserves attention across Asia. Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Hong Kong and, eventually, much of Southeast Asia face similar demographic pressures. Instead of viewing population ageing primarily as an expanding pension and healthcare burden, governments should also ask how healthy longevity can become productive longevity. This does not mean indiscriminately raising retirement ages. A construction worker whose body has endured four decades of physical labour faces a very different reality from a professor able to teach or mentor part-time at 70. The better approach is flexible, voluntary and health-sensitive: phased retirement, part-time consultancy, mentoring, research, telemedicine and intergenerational skills transfer. Governments and employers should create second-career pathways that allow older professionals to contribute without blocking opportunities for younger workers. The best arrangement might unite the two generations: senior workers provide judgment and institutional memory; younger colleagues contribute technological fluency and fresh perspectives. There are health benefits too. Purpose, social engagement and continued intellectual activity are important components of healthy ageing, provided work remains voluntary and appropriate to individual capacity. Asia might discover that one answer to its ageing workforce has been sitting at home all along. The demographic challenge, therefore, is not simply how to support millions of older citizens. It is how to stop prematurely retiring their wisdom. Rafael R. Castillo, Manila, Philippines Indonesia and China should innovate together For more than a decade, Indonesia-China relations have been defined by impressive investment figures. From the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed railway to nickel processing plants and industrial estates, cooperation has helped reshape Indonesia’s economic landscape. These projects have created jobs, strengthened infrastructure and accelerated industrialisation. The next phase of the partnership should not be measured simply by the value of new investments. It should be judged by how much knowledge, technology and innovation the two countries create together. The global economy is entering a period when competitiveness depends less on cheap labour and more on research, digital capabilities and advanced manufacturing. China has become one of the world’s leading innovation economies, investing heavily in research and development. Indonesia has a young population, abundant natural resources and ambitious plans to move beyond commodity dependence. These strengths are complementary. Rather than focus on financing new industrial projects, both governments should expand cooperation in university partnerships, joint research centres, technology transfer, vocational education and talent development. Indonesian researchers and students would gain greater access to China’s rapidly evolving innovation ecosystem, while Chinese institutions would deepen their engagement with Southeast Asia’s largest economy.
