Such cooperation would also make bilateral relations more resilient. Investment flows fluctuate with global economic conditions, commodity prices and geopolitical tensions. However, knowledge partnerships create long-term trust and shared capacity that endure beyond economic cycles. For Indonesia, this would support its ambition to escape the middle-income trap by developing higher-value industries and improving productivity. For China, it would reinforce its role as a partner in sustainable regional development rather than merely a source of capital. As Asia navigates technological competition and an increasingly uncertain global economy, the success of international partnerships will depend on how much money is invested as well as how much innovation is shared. Indonesia and China have already shown they can build railways, factories and industrial zones together. The greater challenge is to build laboratories, research networks and future innovators. That would be a partnership measured in billions of dollars and ideas capable of shaping Asia’s next chapter. Budi Kristanto, Banjarmasin, Indonesia

title: Hong Kong rules out Wang Fuk Court buy-back extension as 100 owners hesitate
description: Deputy finance chief Michael Wong warns of ‘substantially lower’ compensation at later stage if government uses legal means to acquire flats.
content: About 100 homeowners at fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court in Hong Kong have yet to accept the government’s buy-back offer that expires next week, Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun has said, stressing that the sign-up period will not be extended. “The deadline is a very serious timeline … it will not be extended, nor will better terms and a higher acquisition price suddenly be offered,” Wong told a radio programme on Sunday. “I hope [the homeowners] will understand and take the appropriate action within the remaining eight days.” He emphasised that given the government could later turn to legal means to acquire any remaining flats, the compensation offered under statutory requirements would be substantially lower. “Under the statutory mechanism, compensation is based on the market value at the time of acquisition. That would mean the value after the fire … which is substantially lower than the government’s offer of HK$8,000 or HK$10,500 [US$1,020 or US$1,340] per square foot,” he said. The hold-outs, accounting for 5 per cent of all homeowners at the estate, have until August 31 to submit acceptance letters. After selling their homes and receiving compensation, they can either buy a property on the open market or join a special sales programme to acquire a new subsidised flat, using cash or a flat-for-flat arrangement. As of August 21, 1,878 households had submitted acceptance letters, accounting for 94.7 per cent of flats, while 74.1 per cent of owners had already signed sale and purchase agreements with the government, according to Wong. He noted that 91.5 per cent of owners in Wang Chi House – the only block undamaged by the fire – had accepted the offer, and 67.7 per cent had signed sale and purchase agreements. The city’s deadliest blaze in decades swept through seven of the Tai Po estate’s eight blocks last November, killing 168 people and displacing about 5,000 residents. The government announced in February it would spend about HK$6.8 billion to acquire the affected flats, using HK$4 billion in public money and HK$2.8 billion from a donation-backed support fund. The government later extended the offer to owners at Wang Chi House, adding another HK$1 billion to the cost of the scheme. Wong stressed that the government would not extend the sign-up period as subsequent work, including flat selection for the special sales scheme, could not be delayed given rehousing must be swiftly arranged. He acknowledged that some owners were discontented with the acquisition price, but urged them to accept the offer. Since the use of public money required legislative approval, the government would not raise the acquisition price at the last minute as private developers might, he added. “This arrangement has fully balanced various factors,” Wong said. “It is a highly compassionate approach.” The government would consider using legal means to acquire any remaining flats but would not pursue this avenue until next year at the earliest, he said. Earlier, authorities released the sales brochure and price list for the 10 subsidised housing projects under the special sales programme. Prices for the 4,400 flats ranged from HK$1.51 million to HK$5.37 million. The most expensive flats are at Hemma Sapphire, the Housing Authority’s Anderson Road Quarry site project in Kwun Tong, while the lowest-priced homes are at Yu Fung Court in Tung Chung. Two new projects in Tai Po, scheduled for completion in 2029 and 2031, will offer more than 1,500 flats priced between HK$2.71 million and HK$3.69 million. Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho Wing-yin said a balloting exercise would be conducted next month to determine the order of flat selection, allowing the first batch of owners to choose homes by the end of the month. She expected about 50 to 60 owners could select flats each day, adding that government outreach teams could accompany them during the process. Ho said about 2,800 flats under the programme, or 60 per cent, were more than 400 sq ft and would be sufficient to meet the needs of the affected families. Around 330 homeowners had already opted for a cash offer, with some purchasing a flat on the second-hand Home Ownership Scheme (HOS) market, Ho said. Wong emphasised that if homeowners were unable to select a preferred flat in the special sales programme, authorities would allow them to take a cash payment instead, which they could then use to buy a second-hand HOS flat within two years or a property on the private market. Betty Ho, a resident of Wang Shing House, is among the homeowners who have refused to sell to the government. “I started paying my mortgage in my twenties. There is no reason why, after I have finished paying for my home, the government can now just take it away,” she said. Dissatisfied with the government’s consultation on rehousing options, Ho remained adamant that in situ resettlement should have been included. She said she would reject the buy-back offer. Ho, who is currently living in government-arranged transitional housing, said authorities had not told her what would happen if she continued to decline the offer. “I cannot plan my next step, and I do not know where I will be living,” she added. “If they force me to move out of the transitional housing, I will have nowhere to stay.”

title: Are humanoid robots the future? Chinese makers instead highlight practical design
description: The industry is seeing a shift from flashy demonstrations, like kickboxing and dancing, to real-world deployment.
content: Humanoid robots were still among the biggest crowd-pleasers at this year’s World Robot Conference (WRC) in Beijing, though other types of robots, such as wheeled machines, were gaining momentum as the industry moves from demonstration to deployment. At Unitree Robotics’ packed booth at the conference, bipedal models played table tennis or squared off in fighting matches, showing off levels of speed, balance and coordination that the industry has only seen in the last few years. But elsewhere across the exhibition halls, robots were sorting parcels, loading production lines, or moving materials. Many moved on wheels instead of legs, while others had conventional-looking robotic arms. “If wheels can get the job done, do we really need two legs?” asked Yang Li, senior engineer of start-up X Square Robot. Bipedal robots may be more impressive to spectators if they can punch, run and jump, but industrial users ultimately cared about factors such as payload, reliability and return on investment, he said. During an hour-long, controlled test this month, a two-armed WALL-B embodied model designed by X Square Robot was able to sort 1,816 packages, according to the company. It said that it was more efficient than the bipedal Figure 03 robot, from US start-up Figure AI, which handled an average of 1,248 parcels an hour. At the WRC, AI2 Robotics, another Chinese start-up, had a wheeled robot making coffee and ice cream for visitors. The machine used different end effectors for different jobs, with a gripper on one arm and a dexterous hand on the other. Mo Lei, AI2 Robotics vice-president and head of strategy, said its robots had progressed from a single demonstration to performing multiple jobs for one customer and replicating similar tasks across different customers. In factories, he added, a more basic test was whether the same robot could reliably work for eight to 16 hours a day. The shift to non-humanoids, however, does not indicate a decline in market enthusiasm for bipeds. Morgan Stanley data showed that half-size bipeds remained the largest category in China in the first half, accounting for 50 per cent of shipments, followed by wheel-based humanoids at 29 per cent and full-size bipeds at 21 per cent. But wheeled platforms were expanding rapidly in industrial and commercial settings because their greater stability made them a practical choice for manipulation and embodied-AI applications, the investment bank said. Besides the form factor, the competition is also shifting from the body towards the robotic “brain”. Unitree founder Wang Xingxing told the WRC that AI models had become the company’s biggest area of investment in terms of both capital and personnel. Its prospectus also earmarked 2.02 billion yuan (US$300.52 million) for intelligent robot model research and development, accounting for nearly half of the 4.2 billion yuan it had originally planned to raise in its Shanghai initial public offering. He said the biggest challenge was generalisation, for example, where a robot can complete tasks in an unpredictable environment, rather than simply performing scripted movements. That could happen in two or three years if progress was fast, he said. At the same time, instead of a new robot, Unitree unveiled a seven-axis biomimetic robotic arm, R1, priced from 9,900 yuan (US$1,472). Another challenge was data, as growing demand drives growth of relevant firms. Lumos Robotics, a robot maker, also provides data-collection equipment and data-processing services. Company founder and CEO Yu Chao said that the data-collection business contributes roughly half of its revenue. Lumos is currently working with Mitsubishi Electric, one of its investors, on a robotic project involving assembly, packaging, material handling and inspection at Mitsubishi’s factories in China. What was more important than the number of robots Mitsubishi bought was the access it offered to data generated in a real factory environment, Yu said.

title: Exodus from New Territories brownfield relieves pressure on industrial property market
description: The Northern Metropolis project is forcing a wave of brownfield tenants to relocate, lifting demand for floor space in industrial buildings.
content: For years, brownfield sites in Hong Kong’s New Territories have hosted a range of businesses looking for cheap space – from storage depots to recycling centres to scrapyards. Now, the massive Northern Metropolis project is forcing many of these brownfield tenants to relocate, lifting demand for floor space in industrial estates across the city. The wave of relocations had driven nearly 20 per cent of the new leases for industrial properties recorded so far this year, a major uplift that has helped slow the decline in rental prices in the sector, according to analysts. Samuel Lai, head of CBRE Hong Kong’s industrial and logistics division, said that 994 hectares of brownfield land were set to be acquired for the Northern Metropolis in four phases. The first phase – from 2024 to the end of 2026 – involved about 320 hectares of land, more than 100 hectares of which had already been acquired, he added. Nearly half of the businesses operating on the brownfield sites were in logistics and warehousing sectors, according to Lai. Other facilities on the sites included car parks, sawmills, storage depots, recycling centres and scrapyards. “While most brownfield operations displaced by land resumption relocate to other brownfield sites to continue business, some move into urban industrial buildings and compliant logistics warehouses,” Lai said. “Industrial properties in Fanling have benefited the most, as they are relatively close to the Northern Metropolis brownfield sites and offer rental rates within a range acceptable to these operators,” he added. According to CBRE data, a total of 2.3 million sq ft of space in industrial buildings and warehouses has been leased in Hong Kong so far this year. More than 400,000 sq ft of that leased space involved storage businesses that had relocated from brownfield sites to urban logistics centres due to the Northern Metropolis. The figures indicate that nearly 20 per cent of newly recorded leasing activity originated from the Northern Metropolis, according to Lai. “Rising vacancy levels in industrial buildings and warehouses over the past two years have prompted some landlords to lower rents to accommodate relocation demand from brownfield operations,” Lai said. Hong Kong’s warehouse vacancy rate hit a peak of 13.2 per cent at the end of last year, but has since fallen slightly to 11.6 per cent, according to Lai. Joseph Lam, head of JLL’s logistics and industrial department, said that some brownfield tenants had relocated to compliant industrial buildings or modern warehouses, as rents for compliant warehouses had fallen by about 30 per cent from historical highs over the past two years. According to JLL, Japanese multinational toy manufacturer Bandai relocated from a brownfield site to the Hutchison Logistics Centre two years ago. The three-year lease commenced in May 2024, covering an area of 50,808 sq ft at a monthly rent of HK$787,524 (US$100,400). Building materials supplier Mapei Hong Kong recently signed a new lease to relocate from a brownfield site to the entire Jing Hin Godown, a compliant warehouse facility in Yuen Long. The two-year lease, commencing this March, covers an area of 70,291 sq ft at a monthly rent of HK$423,360 for the first year and HK$500,000 thereafter. SJ Logistics, a company with mainland Chinese backing, has also shifted from brownfields, buying the entire G2000 warehouse building in Fanling from G2000 Group chairman Michael Tien for HK$380 million in November 2025. The building has a total floor area of about 112,590 sq ft and cost around HK$3,375 per square foot. Although the relocation of brownfield operations in the Northern Metropolis has driven increased demand for urban industrial buildings, rents for urban industrial properties have not rebounded accordingly. According to CBRE, overall rents for industrial buildings and warehouses had fallen by about 3 per cent in the year to date. Liz Ling, executive director at House Property, believed that the relocation of operations from brownfield sites would have a limited impact on the urban industrial property market. “Most operators currently renting simple sheet-metal warehouses in brownfields would find it very difficult to move into urban industrial buildings or logistics warehouses, as the rents are significantly higher,” she said. The current rent for simple sheet-metal warehouses in brownfields was typically less than HK$10 per square foot, whereas the rent for logistics warehouses in urban areas is at least around HK$14 per square foot, according to Ling. “There are currently many vacant industrial units in Kwun Tong, with a particularly high number of large units sitting empty,” she said. Rents for industrial properties in the area had dropped by about 10 per cent, while transaction prices per square foot had fallen by 50 per cent compared with their 2019 peak, she added. JLL’s Lam, however, believes that the relocation of brownfield operations has triggered a structural shift in demand in the medium to long term, even though it has not yet directly driven up the sale prices or rents of industrial buildings in the short term. “Once supply and demand returned to equilibrium, rents for compliant warehouses were expected to recover steadily, with an average annual growth rate of 5 to 10 per cent,” he said. Lai from CBRE said the industrial property market would not only benefit from the relocation of brownfield tenants, but also from the artificial intelligence boom, which was leading to a surge in demand for new data centres. The vacancy rate for industrial properties would likely fall further, narrowing to between 10 and 11 per cent by the end of the year, Lai added, while the overall decline in rents for industrial buildings and warehouses for the year would narrow to about 5 per cent.

title: Bites to bytes: Thai street food app feeds into hunger for authenticity
description: The Thai Street Gold Star app lists approved vendors, shows menus and gives users directions to each stall.
content: Bangkok’s best street food has always existed on a kind of mental map for Thai food writer Choltanutkun Tun-atiruj. It is built from habit, cravings and neighbourhood rhythms: the office crowds, the schools, the university nearby and the vendors selling everything from moo ping (grilled pork skewers) and sticky rice to pad thai and kuay teow reua – a bowl of rice noodles in dark broth flavoured with cow or pig’s blood, then topped with meat and spices. “I can’t tell you my favourite because I rotate between vendors, depending on what I’m craving that day, but ever since I moved to this area a few years ago, I’ve never had to order anything on [food delivery and ride-hailing super-app] Grab ever again,” said Choltanutkun, who lives in Sukhumvit in the heart of the Thai capital. Officials are now trying to turn mental maps like hers into a more formal one. The Thai Street Gold Star app, developed by the Office of Small and Medium Enterprises Promotion and Suan Dusit University, was launched in late July. It is being rolled out across Bangkok, Pattaya in Chonburi province and Chiang Mai. The app aims to boost the visibility and reach of food vendors while supporting efforts to lift the sector to international standards. Users can search for approved vendors, browse menus and find directions to each stall. To receive certification, vendors must meet requirements covering food hygiene and sanitation, the identity and memorability of their dishes and customer service standards. The use of digital technology alongside higher standards would improve operators’ competitiveness, generate income for small and medium-sized enterprises, stimulate tourism and help establish Thailand as a global gastronomy and wellness-tourism destination, said deputy government spokeswoman Lalida Persvivatana. Aphisavadh Sirivadhanawaravachara, a researcher on hospitality management and tourism in Thailand, said the app had potential to elevate the sector by increasing vendors’ visibility and creating new marketing opportunities. “It should not be viewed simply as a way to regulate or relocate vendors, but as an opportunity to create an ecosystem that helps vendors develop their businesses, build their brands, access new markets, and connect more effectively with tourism,” Aphisavadh said. Thailand had an enormous advantage in the diversity of its local cuisine, he said, suggesting that the app could eventually showcase the distinctive food, ingredients, culinary traditions and experiences of each region. Food and lifestyle writer Sansern Srisawat said the app could help locals and tourists navigate the myriad food stalls around the country. “Nowadays, I see people using Google Maps as a guide, but it isn’t designed specifically for food,” he said. “It will help customers make decisions and trust those vendors more.” It could also serve as an alternative marketing avenue for vendors facing lower profits after signing up for food delivery platforms to reach more customers, Sansern said. Big money For many tourists, Thailand’s street food is a major reason to visit the country. Government figures put the value of the country’s street food market at more than 261 billion baht (US$7.9 billion). But researchers say its importance goes far beyond tourism. “Street food is not a tourist attraction added on top of Thai cities; it is how urban Thailand feeds itself every day,” said Weerapak Samsiripong, a researcher for the Institute for Population and Social Research at Mahidol University. Weerapak, whose research spans street food and urban security in Thailand, said many locals relied on street food, but it was especially important for lower-income populations, accounting for two-thirds of their household food budget. That made the app design important, he said, particularly because Thailand already had several street food certifications. “Gold Star will be most useful if it is aligned with the existing standards … It can become the unifying mark this landscape needs.” But he said gaps remained in the level of support, communication and practical guidance that some vendors received, especially when policies were carried out at the local level. Street food policy needed to involve vendors, Aphisavadh said, pointing to the apprehension of those operating in unauthorised areas. “Of course, regulations and public order are important. But we can also look at these situations as opportunities rather than simply problems,” he said. Weerapak said policymakers needed a clearer picture of the sector itself, adding that government figures on street food income accounted only for the “visible” parts of the sector, while the contributions of vendors operating without fixed addresses remained unknown. “Without knowing how many vendors there are, where they operate and what they need, it is difficult to design support that actually fits them,” he said. Lost in translation The local government’s recent attempt to manage kerbside stalls by moving vendors into designated market areas has also raised concerns that the city could lose some of the charm that has made it popular among visitors. “Unless you go somewhere like Chinatown or Khao San Road … there are fewer vendors than from a few years ago. Many street vendors have been moved or organised away,” Choltanutkun said. While she appreciated Bangkok’s cleaner footpaths, especially in areas such as Sukhumvit, Choltanutkun said street food vendors brought “so much charm and character to the city”. Sansern said he still wanted to see long-standing vendors “thrive while staying true to their originality”, rather than transforming themselves into stalls in large department stores or tourist-heavy areas. But it did not have to be an either-or solution, Weerapak said, because Thailand did not need to choose between preserving the charm of its street food stalls and making them more organised. “Good street food management is not about banning or permitting; it is about the balance between control and support,” he said. “Street food policy works best when economic promotion, tourism, city orderliness and health are pursued as one synergistic package rather than separately.” Aphisavadh added that the initiative had the potential to preserve and elevate Thai street food culture, provided it helped vendors become more professional while protecting their authenticity. “If we can achieve that, the Thai Street Gold Star app could become much more than an app for finding street food,” he said. “It could become a strategic tool for Thai street food development, culinary tourism and local economic development.”

title: Tech paradox: fear of being left behind drives China non-programmers to build own AI tools
description: While some AI anxiety builds useful vigilance, an expert suggests focusing on adaptability rather than chasing every new tech advancement.
content: A growing number of non-programmers across China are developing their own AI tools, primarily motivated by concerns about falling behind as technology reshapes work and daily life. The anxiety surrounding this shift is almost palpable. AI courses and side-hustle tutorials have flooded mainland social media as employers increasingly expect their workers to develop AI literacy. Simultaneously, enrolment and interest in humanities programmes at universities are declining. Together, these trends underscore a central paradox of the AI age: the more that AI can accomplish, the more humans must explore and navigate to discover the tasks that only they can perform. Mainland media outlet Jizhou Studio profiled three non-programmers currently building their own AI tools, as generative AI and agents have made coding capabilities accessible to ordinary users. Congcong, 46, a former product manager, closely follows new AI models and applications, fearing that others may master them before she does. Using ChatGPT, she created a spoken English training agent for herself and her daughter, followed by a bot to monitor her child’s homework and breaks. When her daughter experienced verbal bullying at school, the girl sought advice from the AI. The chatbot analysed the situation, reassured her that she was not to blame, and suggested ways to respond, providing instant support that busy parents may not always be able to offer. Congcong recognised that AI’s constant positive feedback, while comforting, could potentially foster a form of reliance that extends beyond its intended role as a tool. Heisen, a 36-year-old new-media editor, employed AI coding tools to develop a meal-planning mini-programme for his mother, capable of generating menus and shopping lists. Without having to write the code himself, he described the desired functions and interface through prompts, enabling AI to turn his ideas into a working product. However, the mini-programme did not replace the family routine it aimed to enhance. His mother still asked him daily: “What should we eat tomorrow?” and struggled to use it effectively, relying mostly on her handwritten notebook. Lucy, 40, who works in internet operations, built an AI-powered wardrobe tool after frequently grappling with clothing choices. The tool organises her clothes and recommends outfits based on various occasions. Yet, despite improving daily efficiency, the rise of AI agents has intensified her worries about the future of work. At her company, increasing productivity through AI has become a clear priority, leading internet firms to compete in adopting technology. She noted that managers now sometimes directly inquire whether a task could be handled by AI. Peng Kaiping, a professor of psychology and cognitive sciences at Tsinghua University, argues that some anxiety about AI can be beneficial, sharpening vigilance amid uncertainty. In a discussion with the Chinese Qiushi Journal, he stated that the goal should not be to chase every technological advancement but to cultivate adaptability. He cautioned that AI’s pressures extend beyond job concerns; overreliance can create an illusion of knowledge while undermining attention, memory, and deep thinking, and highly personalised systems may weaken genuine social skills. Peng urged people to learn how to use AI while nurturing traits that are harder to automate, such as empathy, aesthetic judgment, intrinsic motivation, and critical thinking. He also called for more genuine parental involvement in education and a less rigid focus on key performance indicators (KPIs) and time efficiency in the workplace. For Lucy, an antidote to AI anxiety has come from an unexpected source: tai chi. In a world increasingly driven by speed and efficiency, the slow, graceful movements of tai chi have offered her a way to pause and reconnect with herself. Her late father, who cherished the practice, inspired her to take it up, serving as a reminder of what AI cannot replicate. As she expressed, while AI may mimic a person’s voice, mannerisms, or personality, it cannot restore a lost relationship.

title: China builds world’s first custom plant immunity system for epidemic response
description: Tailored biological tools could enable crops to quickly develop immunity against emerging viruses, bacteria and fungi, researchers say.
content: Chinese scientists have created an AI-guided platform to engineer custom plant immune receptors to rapidly combat emerging diseases that threaten plants, including commercial crops vulnerable to devastating outbreaks. Their programmable synthetic immune receptors can be introduced into plants to help them detect proteins made by specific bacteria, viruses and fungi, triggering an immune response to neutralise the threat, according to the team. By leveraging protein design guided by artificial intelligence (AI), custom receptors could be engineered within weeks rather than years, fast-tracking the breeding of disease-resistant crops and enabling a quicker response to emerging plant diseases, the researchers said. “This work establishes a versatile platform for efficient plant immunity engineering,” the team from the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology and biotechnology company Qi Biodesign said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Science last month. Around the world, essential crops are threatened by plant pathogens that can devastate agricultural yields and compromise global food security. Plant breeding programmes often introduce resistance genes that encode receptors capable of recognising proteins secreted by pathogens. When these receptors bind to their protein target, it can trigger an immune response. “However, this resistance is often rapidly overcome by fast-evolving pathogens, particularly in modern agricultural systems characterised by large-scale monoculture of genetically uniform crops,” the team said. This biological vulnerability is what heightens the threat of agro-terrorism and plant bioweapons, or pathogens purposefully introduced or modified to target specific crops. To counter new pathogens, receptors must be identified to engineer more resistant plant varieties. However, this process can take years, as the limited diversity of natural plant immune receptors makes the process difficult and time-consuming. Synthetic immune receptors offer a way to accelerate the development of disease-resistant crops. Instead of years, the rapid design of synthetic receptors could enable the “rapid recognition of new and emerging pathogen proteins within weeks”. “To address the vast diversity of pathogens, we aimed to develop a universal strategy for engineering synthetic immune receptors that can recognise specific pathogen proteins.” To create their synthetic receptor, the team spliced AI-designed proteins – which act as binders to pathogen proteins – into a natural rice immune receptor. “These synthetic receptors successfully conferred recognition and immune activation against proteins from diverse plant pathogens, including 14 viruses, two bacteria, a fungus and an oomycete,” they said. Oomycetes are fungus-like micro-organisms that can cause destructive plant diseases. The team said it tested 391 synthetic receptors and found that about 18 per cent triggered robust and specific immune responses, about 58 per cent displayed varying levels of autoimmunity and nearly 24 per cent showed no immune activity against targets. Some of the pathogens that the receptors worked against target vital crops such as potatoes and tomatoes. According to the paper, a lack of immune activity could result from improper protein expression in the plants, failure of the designed binders to engage with their target pathogen proteins, or an inability to trigger the conformational changes – or physical shape – needed to induce immune activation. “Nevertheless, the overall design success rate was encouraging and demonstrated the broad applicability of our synthetic receptor strategy for enabling recognition of diverse pathogen-derived proteins,” the team wrote. As crops are often threatened with infections by multiple pathogens, the team also developed a strategy to stack synthetic receptors which it said “offers a scalable and multiplexed framework for engineering broad-spectrum and durable disease resistance in crops”. “The establishment of synthetic plant immune receptors will open new avenues for synthetic plant immunity and provide a versatile foundation for engineering disease resistance against diverse pathogens in crops.” The team said designing synthetic receptors for certain kinds of pathogens could still be challenging, and that the overall success rate was still low, but that identifying new natural receptor scaffolds to graft binders onto and expanding AI-guided binder design could improve the system.

title: Yuki Kurihara, 11-year-old Japan whizz-kid, chases Asian Games history
description: Yuki will become Japan’s youngest athlete in history of the Asian Games next month.
content:
Yuki Kurihara will become Japan’s youngest athlete in Asian Games history next month, and the 11-year-old eSports champ wants to be the continental multi-sport competition’s youngest-ever medallist, too.
The bespectacled primary school student joined his Japan teammates this week for an inauguration ceremony ahead of their home Games, which take place in Nagoya city and the wider Aichi prefecture area from September 19 to October 4.
Yuki will compete in the eSports event Puyo Puyo Champions, a puzzle game where players try to clear their screen of coloured blobs by lining them up and popping them.
He is aiming to outshine a previous child medallist in Indonesia’s Bunga Nyimas, who won bronze in women’s skateboarding aged 12 in Jakarta in 2018.
“I want to win so that I can bring a gold medal back for Team Japan,” Yuki said.
The Asian Games, which were first held in 1951, have seen numerous school-age athletes in recent editions.
Cui Chenxi, 13, became China’s youngest Asian Games gold medallist when she won the women’s street skateboarding event three years ago in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province. Cui was not even the youngest skateboarder appearing at the Games.
Nine-year-old Mazel Paris Alegado competed for the Philippines in the women’s park final, and the women’s street final had a pair of Thai competitors aged 11 and 12.
Kurihara started playing Puyo Puyo in his first year of primary school and soon started competing in and winning tournaments. He obtained his pro licence in April this year and regularly competes against adults.
“It’s hard having to balance it with school and cram school, but it’s really fun,” he said. “It’s the summer holidays now, so I have a lot of time to practise. I want to practise a lot and develop some new strengths.”
Kurihara says his favourite food is eel, and his “win rate is better” if he eats it before a contest.
Puyo Puyo is a game of skill and dexterity, with players looking to set off chains to clear their screens of coloured blobs. Kurihara says he has pulled off a maximum chain of 19 and is looking to further polish his skills.
“It feels great when you set off a massive chain,” he said. “I’d love for newcomers to see a massive chain too.”

title: Canada’s Carney refuses to take Trump’s ‘bait’, confronting US in trade war
description: The prime minister’s tough stance on Washington draws strong support from the Canadian public and politicians despite the economic risks.
content: Siding with Canadians weary of provocations from Washington, Prime Minister Mark Carney stood up to US President Donald Trump, rejecting what he called an “unfair” trade deal – a gamble that could prove economically risky. “We will not allow any nation to determine our future. We will set our own course to keep building Canada strong for all,” Carney said on Friday, as negotiations for a bilateral trade deal were crumbling. After weeks of talks with US officials in an effort to avoid punitive duties, Carney walked away just ahead of the deadline set by Trump. That triggered 50 per cent US tariffs affecting some US$20 billion worth of goods, from hockey sticks to cement, effective Saturday. Carney then announced retaliatory duties on US goods, notably steel and dairy products, to take effect on September 8. “Our government understood before many that America would transform all of its commercial relationships, that it would put a series of tariffs on its closest allies, and use economic integration as a weapon,” Carney said on Saturday. “We recognise that sometimes its signature was written in pencil.” He pledged that his country would match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses”. Trump hit back at the neighbouring nation on Sunday, saying “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one”. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” he said on social media. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called the breakdown “a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States”, saying no ‌new talks were planned with Ottawa. “We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation,” Greer told Fox News. “They’ve always had the best deal and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that.” Carney, the former head of the central banks of Canada and Britain, earned full support across Canada’s political spectrum, with opposition leader Pierre Poilievre calling on citizens to “stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses”. The Globe and Mail in an editorial said: “In the end, Prime Minister Mark Carney took the hint from the Canadian public rather than the bait from the American president.” A poll published earlier in the week revealed that 56 per cent of Canadians surveyed wanted their government to take a “hard line” and make no more concessions to Washington on trade. Since Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025, Canada has been in his crosshairs on the subject. The Republican billionaire was irked by Carney’s widely-touted January speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in which the prime minister declared a “rupture” in the US-led world order. Trump has also repeatedly said he wants to make the Group of Seven nation the 51st US state. Canadians have taken it badly. Many provinces, which have authority over the sales of alcohol, removed US wine and spirits from their shelves. In recent months, Carney has faced increasing calls to play the energy card to put pressure on Trump. So far, he has not gone that far. “Canada fuels American growth, supplying 99 per cent of their natural gas imports, 85 per cent of their electricity imports, 60 per cent of their crude oil imports,” Carney said on Saturday. “I don’t think they want us to stop sending any of that energy.” The US remains by far Canada’s biggest trading partner, with Canadian exports to its neighbour representing 70 per cent of its overall total. Tariffs are already having a deep impact on major sectors in Canada such as the steel and auto industries. Standing up to Trump thus is hardly risk-free for Carney, who hopes that his plans to diversify Canada’s economy by developing new trade partners will allow Ottawa to reduce its dependence on Washington. While the new US duties only affect 5.5 per cent of those exports, “the economic cost of the increase is real nonetheless”, according to analysts at the Royal Bank of Canada. Quebec and Ontario provinces in eastern Canada, the country’s economic powerhouses, are especially expected to feel the pinch, they said. Beyond the immediate consequences, the Trump administration’s “unpredictability” with respect to Canada “is a weight on business confidence across all trade-exposed industries, not just those directly targeted with tariffs”, the RBC analysts said. Trevor Tombe, a professor of economics at the University of Calgary, said in a social media post that if the tariffs remain in place over the long run, it could result in the loss of 90,000 Canadian jobs. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Opinion | Hong Kong can open a lucrative new frontier as Chinese tech IP hub
description: As the city works more closely with mainland tech firms seeking to expand internationally, it can carve out a distinctive role.
content: Since 2021, Hong Kong’s development as a regional intellectual property (IP) trading centre has featured in China’s five-year plans and the policy addresses of chief executives Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor and John Lee Ka-chiu. There are good strategic reasons to see considerable potential in developing the city as an IP servicing centre for the Greater Bay Area, and potentially the whole of China and wider Asia-Pacific region. Hong Kong has several natural advantages. Major international IP agreements apply to the city, either through China or Hong Kong’s World Trade Organization membership. Its robust IP regime is backed by effective enforcement. The reputation of Hong Kong’s Customs and Excise Department is reflected in the prominent role it has played in the World Customs Organisation, particularly in the Asia-Pacific since 2000. Hong Kong protects seven major forms of IP: patents, trademarks, designs, copyright, trade secrets, plant varieties and integrated-circuit layout designs. Most Hong Kong people are probably most familiar with trademark and copyright protection, given the occasional high-profile corporate disputes over logos, designs and entertainment-related properties. The importance of trademark protection was illustrated by the long-running legal battle between French fashion house Lacoste and Hong Kong-based Crocodile Garments over their crocodile logos. Such disputes show IP is not merely a legal entitlement: for companies, it can be a valuable commercial asset whose protection can have a direct bearing on brand value and market access. IP is demonstrably much more than a legal matter. It is an economic asset that can be traded, licensed, financed and commercialised. Globally, digital platforms and specialised marketplaces have emerged to facilitate the buying, selling and licensing of patents and other IP. In Hong Kong, however, some of the most visible IP trading activity in recent years has involved something rather less conventional: collectible cards. At Hong Kong’s inaugural Comic Con exhibition in May, card trading attracted considerable interest. Entrepreneur Derek Cheung Pui-sang has also established a trading-card and gaming hub in Tsim Sha Tsui, supported by services for authenticating, grading and valuing rare and vintage cards. A new ecosystem based on the commercialisation of creative content appears to be emerging. The challenge is to develop a similar ecosystem around technology and innovation. For many years, Hong Kong’s relatively low private-sector research and development investment limited patent activity. Government assistance to small and medium-sized enterprises, including the Original Grant Patent (OGP) system launched in 2019, has yet to transform the situation. That could change as Hong Kong accelerates its drive up the technology ladder and works more closely with mainland technology companies seeking to expand internationally. Schools are putting greater emphasis on STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) education, while universities are paying more attention to commercialising their research. The impressive performance of Hong Kong inventors at international competitions, including winning major awards at the recent Silicon Valley International Invention Festival, suggests the city has a growing reservoir of research and innovation that could generate more commercially valuable patents. The development of technology hubs in the Northern Metropolis should strengthen this trend. As more mainland enterprises in areas such as biotechnology, artificial intelligence, microelectronics and quantum computing establish a presence in Hong Kong, demand for sophisticated patent and other IP-related services should rise. This is where Hong Kong can carve out a distinctive role. Its common law system offers familiarity and confidence to international investors, while its close economic and technological integration with mainland China gives it access to one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing technology markets. Hong Kong is well placed to become a neutral and trusted venue for technology licensing agreements, patent portfolio acquisitions, joint research and development contracts, franchising arrangements and IP due diligence in mergers and acquisitions. Its legal and financial professionals can help start-ups and technology companies navigate patent registration, license technologies to overseas partners, package IP into investment opportunities, obtain professional valuations and raise capital through IP-backed lending as well as, where appropriate, securitisation. But turning this potential into a viable industry will require investment in talent. The government needs to expand training and strengthen the capacity of the Intellectual Property Department, which handles patent registration under Hong Kong’s original grant system as well as the re-registration of standard patents granted in mainland China and Europe. If Hong Kong is to become an IP management centre for mainland technology companies, the city must ensure its patent professionals meet international standards. Advanced economies have developed rigorous professional pathways combining scientific or technical expertise with specialised legal and patent training. Hong Kong needs to expand similar interdisciplinary training. Some local universities have introduced postgraduate certificate courses and cross-disciplinary degree programmes designed to produce legal professionals with stronger technological expertise. More such programmes are needed, particularly those that equip practitioners to understand both the science behind an invention and the commercial opportunities surrounding it. Hong Kong is on the cusp of becoming a significant technology centre. But technology hubs cannot thrive on laboratories, researchers and capital alone. They also need an ecosystem of professionals who can turn inventions into valuable assets, protect those assets, connect them with investors and markets, and take them across borders. IP services can become an important part of that ecosystem. Hong Kong has a strong foundation in law, finance, international connectivity and IP protection. The opportunity is to build on those strengths to serve mainland enterprises, help Chinese technology go global and create a potentially lucrative business frontier for Hong Kong.

title: How Hong Kong beauty retail tactics echo global Dead Sea sales scams
description: WikiLeaks files reveal pushy sales operations for Dead Sea beauty products have been problematic in several countries for decades.
content: Allegedly aggressive sales tactics and business operations in Hong Kong’s beauty product sector closely mirror the global “Dead Sea sales scams” uncovered years ago, documents on WikiLeaks have shown. The controversy has prompted calls from experts for the city’s government to strengthen regulation by expanding proposed cooling-off period legislation to cover retail beauty goods. A check of the whistle-blower website WikiLeaks by the South China Morning Post found that shops and kiosks selling Dead Sea products using allegedly pushy sales tactics had been reported in several countries over the past two decades, affecting customers in the United States, New Zealand, Australia and Europe. Diplomatic cables released by the website in earlier years shed light on the operation behind the billion-dollar industry, which involves alleged immigration fraud, illegal labour, money laundering and worker exploitation in the United States. One cable, prepared by former US ambassador to Israel James Cunningham in 2009, revealed that many young Israelis, generally newly released military draftees, worked in the industry on tourist visas or expired work visas, prompting US investigators to crack down. “The financial incentive is great; post-IDF [Israel Defence Forces] salaries are low and jobs scarce – hence their ‘need’ to find a way to quickly finance their university education and/or onward travels,” the cable read. Last week, Hong Kong customs officers arrested two staff members from Sayles Retail, the local distributor of the Opatra London skincare brand, following claims of aggressive sales tactics. The move was made after a woman complained that she was cheated into paying more than HK$60,000 (US$7,700) for products. Opatra’s London headquarters said it would cooperate fully with any inquiries. Sayles Retail operates beauty brands in Hong Kong, such as Opatra London and Lux Boutique, which market luxury skincare with some containing Dead Sea salts and minerals. Company search records showed Israeli directors were behind both the local operator and the UK headquarters. In the cable, Cunningham, who also served as US consul general in Hong Kong between 2005 and 2008, wrote to the secretary of state that many Israelis were well coached for interviews when applying for US visas, lying to officers that they intended to visit family and friends. Many were in fact hired to sell Dead Sea cosmetics through recruitment websites or word of mouth. The cable revealed that Dead Sea product companies were usually structured under “parent” companies that bought kiosks at shopping centres across the US and sublet the contract to kiosk managers, who were controlled by regional managers responsible for hiring workers. Parent companies created a series of “legitimate managerial layers” between themselves and illegal workers. “Thus, it has been extremely difficult for investigators working to combat Dead Sea fraud,” the cable read, which also identified a key player in the industry holding more than 50 companies. “Shoppers are besieged by a determined crop of salespeople: young Israelis who man mobile carts and have a no-holds-barred selling style,” Cunningham added. Another cable, prepared by Wendy Vincent, a fraud prevention manager at the US consulate in Tel Aviv, in 2010, indicated that the embassy suspected there were hundreds of Dead Sea companies and thousands of kiosks across the US, drawing thousands of Israelis into jobs paying US$1,000 to US$3,200 per month. According to Vincent, Tel Aviv had been investigating visa fraud in the industry since 2007 and realised the same business model had been deployed to sell pillows, toys and even roasted nuts. In some cases, Israeli workers’ passports were held by employers. They worked 11 hours a day, six days per week, earned only commission and had US$500 deducted from their salaries for living expenses, according to the cables. Professor Sibylle Heilbrunn, head of the master’s programme in innovation and entrepreneurship management at Kinneret College on the Sea of Galilee in Israel, said that while sellers inflicted harm on customers, they themselves were exploited and exposed to arrest and deportation. She said such sales tactics were “barely visible” in Israel. The legitimate Dead Sea product industry began in the country in the late 1980s and 1990s, while the kiosk model emerged in the 1990s and 2000s, run by Israeli operators abroad. According to Heilbrunn, Dead Sea products carried an “exotic” appeal, with unverifiable claims and no baseline reference price – factors exploited by overseas operators. She added that a large cohort of youth, aged 21 to 23, were discharged from the army every year, supplying a labour force to the industry seeking workers that could tolerate hierarchy and quotas. Employers sought workers who could live with eight strangers in one flat without unravelling, showed resilience despite constant rejection, could endure 12-hour shifts and obey a chain of command. In Israel, according to Heilbrunn, only about 10 per cent of the workforce was employed in the high-wage innovative sector, reserved for a small elite group to enter at the age of 18. The rest earned only half as much. She said Israel was an expensive country where housing, university and post-army trips all came with a steep price tag. “A young person with no capital … is offered a job that promises tens of thousands of shekels in a few months plus a flight and a place to sleep. It is not mysterious that they take it,” she said. Roy Ying Fai, senior lecturer of marketing at the Hang Seng University of Hong Kong, who frequently travelled to North America, said he witnessed such aggressive sales tactics more than 10 years ago in the US. He added he had not seen such practices any more, believing authorities had cracked down on the practice. Ying said he did not know if the same syndicate was behind the Dead Sea products sold in Hong Kong and the US. But from his observation, the mode of operation was slightly different in Hong Kong. Instead of Israelis, locals were hired and trained to deploy similar sales tactics. Some operators still hired expatriates to distribute free samples at the door. It was understood that local law enforcement agencies intended to look into the Opatra case to see if it involved any illegal workers or overstayers. But Catherine Yeung Wing-man, an associate professor of marketing at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said such aggressive sales tactics targeting impressionable customers could occur across any industry or country. She noted salespeople created an anxious state in customers by pointing out their pores and wrinkles using magnifying mirrors, then offering immediate relief through their products. They then overwhelmed shoppers with pseudoscientific jargon and lured them into making purchases through artificial urgency, such as time-limited discounts, she added. Roy Ying said such tactics highlighted a loophole in proposed cooling-off measures for the wellness sector. He was referring to government proposals for a statutory seven-day cooling-off period and a 14-day refund window for prepaid beauty and fitness contracts. The two-month consultation will end on August 31. Ying said the government should consider extending the proposed cooling-off period to cover more areas such as retail beauty products. Yeung agreed that the cooling-off period should be “applied to any product and any environment”, because the psychological underpinnings behind aggressive sales tactics of services and products were the same. A spokesman for the Commerce and Economic Development Bureau said prepaid consumer contracts for beauty and fitness services accounted for the highest number of complaints. Beauty products rarely involved prepayments and were usually immediately supplied to customers shortly after payment, which might not fall within the proposed scope of the legislation, he said. Customs would take decisive enforcement action against aggressive commercial practices, regulated by the Trade Descriptions Ordinance, he added. The controversy surrounding Opatra started with a video going viral online, which showed a woman crying outside an outlet in New Town Plaza shopping centre, claiming she had been cheated. Yeung said shopping centres had a responsibility to do more, for example, carrying out due diligence checks before leasing out premises and reviewing tenants’ business operations from time to time. She said property developers presented their shopping centres as a family-friendly, community-oriented retail ecosystem, a commercial strategy designed to capture habitual foot traffic and maximise long-term profits. “Having monetised this brand identity as a trusted ‘community partner’, developers face a fundamental commercial contradiction if they were to turn around and claim they were merely passive landlords leasing floor space,” she said, adding that she did not think developers were currently doing so. Ying agreed and proposed designating an official channel for landlords to report suspected business malpractices to authorities. In 2014, a kiosk selling Dead Sea cosmetics was evicted from a shopping centre in New Zealand by the mall owner after an elderly woman complained that she was coerced into buying NZ$3,000 worth of wrinkle creams.

title: China is building a vast ‘national ring road’ circling the country’s borderlands
description: The vast ‘border-coast loop’ is designed to boost development and national unity, but will have to navigate geopolitical and ecological barriers.
content: China has outlined plans to build a massive road link snaking along the country’s land borders and coastlines – an ambitious project that could boost incomes in a string of remote regions, but also provoke geopolitical and ecological risks. The project is framed as an effort to boost economic development, social stability and national unity, with the more than 25,000km (15,500-mile) route set to run through several regions with large ethnic-minority populations – including Tibet and the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. But Beijing will need to navigate some tricky geopolitical terrain to complete the road, which will run close to areas subject to territorial disputes, while also managing ecological hazards in rugged landscapes with fragile ecosystems. The road project – dubbed the “golden border-coast loop” by Chinese state media – is due to be completed by 2030 and will be made up of three sections, according to a five-year blueprint issued by China’s Ministry of Transport in July. The first section – the G219 highway – runs through China’s southwest and far west, from Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region through Yunnan province and Tibet autonomous region to the northernmost tip of Xinjiang. Stretching 10,000km, the route will closely follow China’s borders with Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, India, Bhutan, Nepal, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Russia. Part of the road linking southern and northern Xinjiang will run beneath the seismically active Tianshan mountains, with a 15.7km tunnel slated to become operational next year. The G219 will connect to another highway, the mostly completed G331, which winds from Xinjiang across China’s northern borderlands, taking in Inner Mongolia autonomous region, as well as Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning provinces. The 9,200km route will run near China’s borders with Russia, Mongolia and North Korea. The third section is the 7,000km G228, a highway along the nation’s coastline that is already mostly open to traffic. It runs from Liaoning down through Hebei, Tianjin, Shandong, Jiangsu, Shanghai, Zhejiang, Fujian and Guangdong, before arriving back in Guangxi. “This entire transport loop will not only offer the public a fresh road trip experience, but will also unlock tremendous benefits in industrial synergy, border consolidation and border-area stability and development,” the Ministry of Transport said. Beautiful yet remote areas in Tibet, Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia that had long been inaccessible for most tourists would now become easily reachable, it added. The entire loop, when fully open, will resemble similar roads in the United States, such as the California Pacific Coast Highway, US Route 1 and Interstate 95 along the Atlantic coast, as well as Interstate 90 and Interstates 8 and 10 that run along the US’ borders with Canada and Mexico, respectively. The project also appears to dovetail with Beijing’s new ethnic unity law, which came into effect in July and signals a shift in policy towards assimilation. But Beijing is likely to run into challenges as it pushes forward with construction. For one thing, the thaw in relations between China and India remains shaky after years of border disputes that at times spilled over into deadly confrontations. India views the G219 highway with concern. In 2024, New Delhi protested the road upgrades and extensions taking place in disputed border areas – part of the preparatory work for the G219 project – which it framed as an attempt by China to alter the facts on the ground in the region. Environmental protection is another concern. In June, a report by China’s Ministry of Ecology and Environment on its key projects for the next five years noted that several areas near the road would require continuous monitoring, including the alpine border regions of Tibet, desert areas in southern Xinjiang, and Tianshan mountains’ glacial regions. The ministry plans to undertake careful environmental impact assessments in these areas to ensure local ecosystems and species are protected, including the Tibetan antelope, which has benefited from intensive conservation efforts in recent years. Despite these challenges, China’s connectivity push goes far beyond the loop project. The country has already built the world’s largest highway and rail networks, which increasingly extend into Tibet and Xinjiang. In August, Beijing established the Xinjiang-Tibet Railway Company to oversee the construction of a 1,980km line running from the Tibetan capital of Lhasa to Hotan in Xinjiang. In 2022, China unveiled plans for a new highway between Lhunze in Tibet and Mazha in Xinjiang, which will also run near areas subject to overlapping claims from Beijing and New Delhi. The road, which will intersect with the G219, is currently under construction.

title: Hong Kong’s young balance bike stars face early retirement due to lack of space
description: Sport serves a crucial developmental purpose for entry points into youth athletics and helps former riders in BMX, table tennis and swimming.
content: At just nine years old, Hong Kong’s Wong Tsz-ching is already approaching the end of his competitive balance bike career. A keen rider, Tsz-ching started at four years old and entered his first race six months later. His five-year-old sister, Wong Tsz-yau, followed suit, competing at two and a half. However, even though Tsz-ching has faced the best riders across Asia and represented Hong Kong at a world cup-level balance bike event in Japan, back home he has nearly run out of tracks. While children in Tokyo, Taipei, or mainland China can race balance bikes until they are 12 or 13, lack of space, safety limits and academic pressures force Hong Kong’s young riders into early retirement just as they reach primary school. Their father, Wong Siu-cheong, has invested roughly HK$30,000 (about US$3,800) in modified equipment for the siblings, alongside monthly coaching fees of HK$1,000 per child. The investment yielded results. At the end of 2025, Tsz-ching finished in the top 10 of the eight-year-old category at the King of Runbike World Cup, mainland China’s largest children’s balance bike competition, competing against top riders from across Asia. But Wong said that his son has only one local event left before he must officially retire from Hong Kong competitions. “If we could, we would love for him to keep competing a couple of years longer ... but Hong Kong has its limitations.” The sport’s early exit age is tied directly to Hong Kong’s lack of space. Balance bikes were introduced to mainland China and Hong Kong around 2015 through early childhood education and parent-child communities. While mainland China experienced an explosive boom that peaked around 2020 with dedicated indoor arenas and corporate sponsorship, Hong Kong developed on a different trajectory. Andrew Li, who founded the Balance Bike Group Hong Kong a decade ago, pointed out that the lack of space in the city has created an unavoidable safety paradox. “Our racing venues are small. If older, larger children ride fast in a confined space, the risk of collisions and injury increases significantly,” Li said. “In other regions, tracks are wider, so 10- or 11-year-olds can compete safely. But in Hong Kong, we have to be cautious.” He said Hong Kong lacks large indoor sports halls dedicated to balance bikes, adding that most events rely on outdoor venues like football pitches or private sites such as Central’s event space, leaving organisers vulnerable to weather disruptions. Even public facilities present contradictions for parents. “The Leisure and Cultural Services Department has balance bike parks, but when we take our kids there, officials tell them they cannot ride too fast,” Wong said. “It feels contradictory. How do you define fast or slow on a balance bike? It’s a race – are they supposed to just stroll?” Along with the lack of space, the children also have to deal with educational demands. In Hong Kong, children aged eight enter Primary 3, a milestone marked by a sharp rise in the academic workload and exam pressure. “Around eight years old, study pressures become quite intense in Hong Kong. Parents inevitably put academics first,” Li said, adding that low local birth rates have further shrunk the pool of young participants. Having endured a total shutdown of over a year during the Covid-19 pandemic, Li said that Hong Kong’s balance bike scene is currently in a phase of “starting over”. He said unlike the mainland market, which saw a rapid surge followed by a visible decline after 2020, Hong Kong’s scene avoided an abrupt crash, steadily rebuilding its grass-roots foundation. Despite early retirement ages, balance bikes serve a crucial developmental purpose in Hong Kong as an entry point for youth athletics. Li emphasised that balance bikes offer a low-barrier, high-aerobic activity that builds motor skills, core balance and reaction speed in children as young as 18 months, without the complex rules of basketball or football. “Balance bikes require substantial physical endurance,” Wong said, noting that his son’s athletic performance in track and field ranks in the upper tier among his peers. “When he started track and field at five or six, the coach had him run for long periods, and he didn’t tire easily. It gave him a great physical foundation.” This foundation has helped older riders transition into mainstream sports after hanging up their balance bike helmets. Li mentioned former riders from his club have moved on to Hong Kong’s BMX squad, top-10 youth rankings in table tennis and elite primary school swimming teams, including Diocesan Boys’ School. The culture surrounding balance bikes in Hong Kong is also evolving. Li noted that while hyper-competitive trophy hunting surged years ago as commercial coaching expanded, recent years have brought a healthier shift. “Around 60 to 70 per cent of parents now view it as a recreational activity rather than a high-pressure competition,” Li said. Looking ahead, Li hopes to steer the local scene towards a balanced “carnival” model, similar to European events, combining festive, low-stress play areas with structured races on shared grounds. “Sports should be fun for young kids. If you force two- or three-year-olds into intense competition, it’s not suitable,” Li said. “Our goal is to build an environment where children can enjoy riding without excessive pressure, giving them a solid start for whatever sport they choose next.”

title: In Malaysia, voter anger fuels a third force against Anwar
description: Barely three months old, Rafizi Ramli’s breakaway party is already siphoning crucial votes away from Anwar Ibrahim’s coalition.
content: Malaysian politics runs on grudges and few illustrate that better than the one nursed by Rafizi Ramli. A year after losing the deputy presidency of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s People’s Justice Party (PKR), he has built a vehicle for the disaffected, aimed squarely at the coalition of which he was once part. Parti Bersama Malaysia – or Bersama, meaning “together” – is barely three months old under its new leadership, yet it has already rattled Malaysia’s governing alliance. Taken over in May by Rafizi and fellow ex-minister Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad, Bersama recently gained another PKR defector in the form of Wong Chen, a three-term MP who spent almost 20 years in Anwar’s party before resigning his Subang seat on August 10. The timing could hardly be worse for the ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, which has suffered back-to-back drubbings in state elections at the hands of Barisan Nasional, its erstwhile enemy turned federal partner. Bersama now threatens to open a second front, drawing away reform-minded voters that PH cannot afford to lose – even as it insists it is a progressive alternative and more than a just spoiler. During his time as PKR’s former deputy president, Rafizi built a reputation as a campaigner fluent in data-driven attacks, viral messaging and bread-and-butter grievances before his falling out with the party leadership. His Bersama co-leader Nik Nazmi is philosophical about the split from PH and what it means for the future. “We feel that Pakatan Harapan has lost its way. It was no longer true to its ideals,” he told This Week in Asia. “What Bersama is, is a progressive, multiracial party, but it is also very much looking at providing solutions for today’s era, rather than looking at the past with the baggage of the past.” Had power been the only objective, defecting to BN would have been easier, Nik Nazmi said. The new Bersama’s first electoral outing, in Johor, was modest yet consequential. In Perling, a seat that PH member the Democratic Action Party (DAP) once considered safe, Bersama’s Boo Wei Han won 2,996 votes. BN’s candidate then beat the DAP’s by just 1,611 – narrow enough that Bersama’s presence made the difference. Nik Nazmi rejects the “spoiler” label, however, saying that PH losing votes does not mean those votes were ever its to lose. “Why would anyone assume that all of them would have voted for PH if we did not run?” he asked. “They may have stayed at home.” Losing but hurting PH Not everyone agrees. Azmi Hassan, a political analyst and senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, said the Johor result proved Bersama did not need to win seats to leave a mark. “Bersama is considered just a spoiler, but a very effective spoiler if you look at what happened in Johor,” he said. “The party that will lose most with the presence of Bersama, there is no doubt it is specifically PKR.” But Azmi argues that siphoning off votes from rivals without building a coalition of its own is not much of a strategy. “How long does Bersama want to be a spoiler? It won’t benefit them much,” he said. Indeed, much of Bersama’s early support may not even be the party’s own. Public policy expert Ahmad Mohsein Azman, a senior analyst at strategic advisory firm BowerGroupAsia, thinks frustration with Anwar’s government is doing much of the heavy lifting for now. “Bersama will need to show the voters that its appeal is more than just being a rehash of PKR, and that they have a sustainable political vision and ideals that they can commit to,” he said. Weak turnout in PH strongholds across the Johor and Negeri Sembilan state elections hinted that reform-minded Malaysians were “spoilt for choice given how many fledgling parties are positioning as pro-reform alternatives, or are discouraged out of frustration given the state of Malaysian politics today”. Bersama, as it stood, was inseparable from Rafizi and would need to evolve beyond being simply PKR minus the parts he disliked, Ahmad Mohsein said. Nik Nazmi appeared unmoved by the criticism. “For Bersama, we want to build and we want to scale up on our terms, and we are no longer looking at PH,” he said. “Good luck to PH. I think the BN wave is just so big right now, but it’s also a way for PH to look at themselves and reflect.” For now, most observers – including Rafizi, by his own admission – saw Bersama less as a government-in-waiting than a shot across the bows of a coalition that had grown too comfortable with its founding myth, Ahmad Mohsein said. “However, if the party plays its cards right, it may be on track to assert itself within the political scene in the next five to 10 years.”

title: Meet Kathryn Chandler, wife of Lanterns star Kyle Chandler
description: The model-turned-screenwriter met her future husband at a dog park; their daughter Sydney plays the lead in Disney+’s Alien: Earth.
content: Kyle Chandler stars as Hal Jordan, a veteran crime-fighting Green Lantern, in HBO’s latest superhero series Lanterns. Based on the DC comic Green Lantern, the series builds on director James Gunn’s growing DC Universe and follows Chandler’s character who is paired with Green Lantern newbie John Stewart (played by Aaron Pierre), to solve a series of crimes. The eight-part series premiered on August 16 and has already built buzz about a possible second season despite only two episodes being released so far. Chandler, an Emmy Award-winning actor whose Hollywood career spans nearly four decades, arrived at the show’s Los Angeles premiere on August 13 with his wife, Kathryn Chandler. The pair have been married since 1995, and Chandler has previously credited Kathryn for keeping him grounded despite his fame. “She knows who I really am and still appreciates me,” Kyle told Men’s Health magazine during a 2010 interview. “My wife knows I’m a complete idiot, and she reminds me every day that success is meaningless if I’m pretending to be someone I’m not.” Here’s everything you need to know about Kyle Chandler’s wife, Kathryn Chandler. Their meet-cute was straight out of a romcom Kyle and Kathryn first met at a dog park where the two would pass by each other and exchange friendly smiles while walking their pets. After multiple run-ins, Kathryn told the Chicago Sun-Times in a 1999 interview that she decided to take matters into her own hands and instructed her dog, Otis, to “Go over and jump on that guy.” Thanks to Otis, the pair finally introduced themselves but did not start dating until several months later when Kathryn, who turned out to live on the same street as Chandler, noticed the actor had a moving van outside his house. “I saw a moving van in front of his house, and I thought, ‘Ohmigod! It’s never going to happen!’” she told the Chicago Sun-Times. “So I took my dog and slowly strolled by his house. I said, ‘Hey, are you moving?’ And he said his neighbours were.” The conversation led to a movie date and the beginning of their relationship. The couple wed in 1995 and have two daughters, Sydney and Sawyer. Sydney, now 30, is following in her father’s footsteps and has starred in films such as Don’t Worry Darling (2022). She is currently playing the lead character in the Disney+ series Alien: Earth (2025-present). Kathryn worked as a model Kathryn was a former model when she first met Chandler, as per the Chicago Sun-Times. The mother of two briefly put her career on hold after having her children and today works as a screenwriter. Despite Chandler’s fame, he and his family live a quiet life on a 33-acre ranch outside Austin, Texas, according to People. She founded a non-profit organisation In 2019, Kathryn co-founded Patriot’s Hall in Dripping Springs, Texas. Patriot’s Hall is a non-profit dedicated to providing “connection, resources, and a centralised support hub” to veterans, per the organisation’s website. Kyle also serves on the board of directors. During an appearance on The Kelly Clarkson show in July 2023, Kathryn explained how there are “so many veterans and families in Texas” and how the community rallied round to help build the centre. Sitting on 10 acres, the Patriot’s Hall campus aims to “empower veterans of all ages and their families by cultivating new friendships, reigniting purpose and discovering new ways for continued service”, according to the website.

title: How to be a good tourist; a guide for the modern traveller
description: With the world’s most popular destinations bursting at the seams – and neither residents nor visitors happy with the fact – it would be in everyone’s interests for travellers to rethink their approach.
content: From Tenerife to Thessaloniki, demonstrators’ chants and roadside graffiti alike say, “Tourists go home”, although sometimes in rather stronger language. Around the world, the residents of “must-see” destinations can no longer see each other for the crowds, and increasingly view tourists less as benefactors and more as a bane. Local authorities are responding ever more robustly to their complaints. To drink alcohol in certain Amsterdam streets now attracts a fine of €95 (US$110), while in the village of Varenna, on Italy’s Lake Como, it’s twice as much for wearing swimwear away from the beach. Not far away, in seaside Portofino, the introduction of no-loitering zones has effectively put an end to selfies, unless you’re a professional narcissist and the income to be expected from sponsors or followers is greater than the potential €275 (US$317) penalty for blocking traffic. However, much of the globally growing ill will is not about bad behaviour but merely about numbers. Destinations that have seen many long-term rental properties turned into more profitable short-term accommodation for tourists are introducing strict regulations (British Columbia) or banning Airbnb and its ilk altogether (Barcelona). Local satisfaction is crucial to success, but if the visited are unhappy, so are the visitors. Tourists discover soaring head taxes, 90-minute queues and compulsory advance-purchase tickets with a timed entry, and that the quiet stroll between two pretty mountain villages they have come back to enjoy for a second time now has an entrance fee and one-way-only traffic, and yet is still a conga line. Individual residents, municipal authorities and national tourism bureaus alike declare that they don’t dislike tourists, and don’t want to discourage them, but they do want to choose the visitors they get. An official online Tokyo travel guide, How to stay safe and be respectful in Tokyo at night, has little to say about safety in what anyway ranks as one of the world’s least dangerous cities. Instead, it explains how not to offend locals by littering, or by drinking or smoking in public. But if the Japanese are too polite to say straight out, “Don’t come unless you obey the rules”, José Antonio Donaire, Barcelona’s commissioner for sustainable tourism, feels no such restraint. He wants to restrict visitors to no more than the 15.7 million the city hosted in 2025, and he wants half of those to be cultural tourists – presumably people who swoon at the sight of Joan Miro’s surrealist art or Antoni Gaudi’s soaring Sagrada Família rather than their 15th Estrella Damm lager of the day. In terms of accommodation capacity, all tourists may be equal, but some are more equal than others. These regulations, fines and fees suggest a definition of good tourists: it’s those who stay longer, spend more with local businesses, respect the needs of residents, do not congregate all in one spot and neither dive into historic fountains (€500/US$576 fine in Rome) nor indulge in drunken caterwauling at 3am (€140/US$161 in Amsterdam). However, concentrating on attracting good tourists will still not solve the problem of volume, and some destinations are looking to spread the load. Japan has offered some international visitors free domestic flights to destinations beyond the well-worn Tokyo-Kyoto-Osaka trail that two-thirds of them take. Spain’s new policy is to encourage visitors to avoid the summer peak, and to look beyond the supply of sun, sea, sand and potential sexual partners along its crowded Mediterranean beaches towards the equally sun-baked sleepy villages of the interior. These are all sugar-cube houses, crumbling castles and excellent walking among hills hatched with olives and vines, where good tourists eat local dishes, rather than fish and chips or pizza. All these schemes ignore the jumbo jet in the room, though.
