If we don’t want a future in which the world’s major cities are to be toured by boat rather than by hop-on, hop-off bus, there must be a reduction in the emissions that make such catastrophes ever more likely. One per cent of fliers produce 50 per cent of airline emissions, so the rest typically urge the elite to cut back first. But the good tourist understands that simply to board a plane is to be a member of an elite. Eighty per cent of the world’s population never takes to the air, so perhaps halving your own flying is not an unreasonable idea. This would reduce emissions, although the only true ecotourism is just staying at home. In China and Europe, extensive rail systems offer less damaging ground-level travel as an easy substitute. Or there’s the option to halve the number of trips but stay for twice as long. The good tourist leaves the rentals to the locals who need the space and opts for a hotel instead. Good tourists also avoid getting bogged down in the slough of meme-driven, artificial-intelligence-derived ignorance that is most online travel commentary. That leads to the taking of well-trodden paths between sights ranging from those of genuine cultural and historical significance to those merely of social-media-driven popularity, where the idea of being there, and being seen to be there, is more important than the actual experience. Today, social media merely ensures that a location may go from overlooked to overwhelmed in the blink of a smartphone’s camera shutter, the image repeated in increasingly dishonest “I was here, too” postings. The hydroelectric project next to the cliffside temple is cropped out, the sky is edited into an improbable blue and the camera angle narrowed to exclude the hordes of others taking the near-identical shot. The resulting image is of perfect beauty in tranquil solitude while the reality is anything but. And the blame cannot be laid solely at the perfectly pedicured feet of influencers. Every step you take, every post you make, people are watching you. The good tourist travels flexibly, and keeps quiet about new discoveries. But if you follow the crowd, then it’s unsurprising that crowds are what you find. As the late Irish travel writer Dervla Murphy told The Guardian newspaper in 2009, “Choose your country, use guidebooks to identify the areas most frequented by foreigners – and then go in the opposite direction.” Of course, if significant numbers go in the opposite direction, there will no longer be an opposite direction, although when there are no longer “hidden gems” to be found “off the beaten track”, this will at least result in a merciful release from cliché. There was a time when travel writing was not all how-to guides, or thinly disguised advertising, but written by a tiny number of people who ventured abroad to be a substitute for those who couldn’t. It’s time to lead the way by sometimes going nowhere, perhaps instead sitting down with a well-informed account from the past of somewhere you might go in the future. Or might not. Travel less, but travel better.

title: Editorial | As Hong Kong boosts governance efficiency with AI, balance is key
description: The use of artificial intelligence to speed up environmental impact assessments is welcome, but care must be taken to ensure accuracy and reliability.
content: Hong Kong has never had the luxury of abundant land for development. A small territory supporting a large and highly urbanised population must constantly make difficult choices about housing, transport and infrastructure. This is especially true when every decision carries an environmental cost that is often irreversible. Yet the way forward is not to stand still, but to ensure that development is necessary, properly designed and compatible with the protection of the city’s natural heritage. The government’s use of artificial intelligence to accelerate environmental impact assessments – a statutory requirement to evaluate and mitigate possible damage before major development projects can proceed – is therefore a welcome step. According to the Environmental Protection Department, the application of AI shortened the time frame for collecting environmental data and completing the process from 36 to 48 months to 15 to 24 months. The new technology has also enabled real-time surveillance for environmental and bird monitoring, and reduced the time for tree baseline surveys by 70 per cent. The gain is substantial. However, speed alone should not be the ultimate goal. Equally essential is accuracy and reliability. There have been legal challenges against the findings of some key environmental impact assessments in the past, resulting in prolonged litigation and delays in implementing key infrastructure projects. The real test is whether AI enables Hong Kong to reach decisions that are both efficient and environmentally sound. Unlike some policies and measures that can be tweaked or withdrawn, the damage caused by poorly designed and implemented infrastructure projects often cannot be undone. AI must therefore be used to strengthen scientific and objective assessments rather than to justify short cuts and administrative efficiency. Hong Kong’s rich biodiversity has made the job more challenging. Despite its reputation as a forest of glitzy skyscrapers and concrete towers, the city contains a remarkable variety of habitats, including a thousand kilometres of rugged coastline, mountain ranges, country parks and wetlands. There are 25 country parks and 22 special conservation areas, covering about 40 per cent of the territory’s total land mass. Some 3,300 plant species, 55 terrestrial mammal species, 116 species of amphibians and reptiles, 203 freshwater fish species, 135 dragonfly species and 249 butterfly species make their homes here. The city also boasts one third of the total bird species in China, with over 580 species recorded. Conservationists recently pointed to species such as the brown wood owl, Chinese barbet and black-chinned yuhina as evidence that Hong Kong’s biodiversity may be richer than previously understood. Several new species, which had been unknown worldwide, have also been discovered in Hong Kong. They include two new soft coral species off Sung Kong Island early this year, the Mai Po box jellyfish in 2023, a jumping spider in 2019 and the Hong Kong tree gecko in 2018. That richness cannot be taken for granted, though. A 2025 study on the conservation status of 886 species across eight animal groups fuelled concern, after 21 species, including the black-headed ibis, were found to have disappeared from the local habitat. Some experts were worried that many of the vulnerable species and habitat types lacked sufficient protection and called for a special “red list” to conserve vulnerable local species. Hong Kong’s growing appetite for development places continuous pressure on wildlife and their habitats. Even though a single project may not result in catastrophic impact immediately, environmental damage is often cumulative. The Northern Metropolis mega-project aims to transform about 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) near the border with Shenzhen into an integrated living, economic and hi-tech hub, housing an estimated 2.5 million residents and providing 650,000 jobs upon full implementation. The potential impact on the environment cannot be ignored. The use of AI in environmental impact assessment and other public services is part of a broader and necessary drive to make governance more efficient and effective. With careful planning, mitigation and protection, Hong Kong can strike a fine balance between conservation and development.

title: Milk vs plant-based alternatives: 7 claims put to the test
description: Experts look at cow’s milk and alternatives like soy, almond and oat, comparing the benefits, allergy safety, climate impact and more.
content: Oat, soy, almond – look in anyone’s fridge or head to a cafe and you might find a slew of plant-based drinks. We hear multiple claims about health and the environment, but are these drinks actually – as is so often claimed – better than cow’s milk, better for the climate or better for those of us with allergies? Some of these claims are true, some are not. Our fact-checkers assess seven popular statements. 1. Plant-based drinks are healthier than cow’s milk False. Milk and dairy products naturally contain easily digestible protein, which is essential for building and maintaining muscle. The German Nutrition Society says they also provide calcium for bone health, as well as vitamins and iodine. You only find meaningful amounts of such micronutrients in fortified plant-based alternatives. If you are cutting out dairy products, check the ingredients in plant-based drinks or find another way to add in the nutrients you are missing. 2. Organic plant-based drinks replace the nutrients in cow’s milk False. Organic goods are not necessarily healthy. Organically produced plant-based drinks lack important nutrients such as calcium, vitamins and iodine. Under the EU Organic Regulation 2018/848, vitamins and minerals may be added to organic foods only if required by law. There is no such regulation for plant-based milk alternatives, meaning no nutrients may be added to them. Some producers circumvent the ban by offering combination drinks, such as an oat-and-seaweed drink that uses calcium-rich organic seaweed. However, legal controversy surrounds this practice. 3. Plant-based drinks are better for people with allergies Mostly false. People who are allergic to milk protein or who are lactose intolerant often turn to plant-based drinks. However, they are not always the solution, as they can come with risks for people with allergies depending on the raw materials, production methods and labelling involved. Many milk alternatives contain allergens that must be declared and labelled accordingly, for example if they are based on soy, nuts or gluten/oats. The German Allergy and Asthma Association also highlights uncertainties when packaging refers to “traces of” potential allergens. This is because even if the drink does not deliberately include an allergen, unintended contamination can occur via production facilities or supply chains. 4. Children need cow’s milk for healthy growth Partially correct. Scientists say young children need an adequate supply of nutrients such as calcium, iodine, vitamin B2, vitamin B12 and protein. Unlike cow’s milk, however, plant-based drinks – regardless of the raw material they are made from – naturally contain none or only negligible amounts of these nutrients typically found in milk. “Plant-based drinks are therefore not an equivalent substitute for cow’s milk,” says a specialist network set up by Germany’s Federal Ministry of Food and Agriculture. Specialists recommend qualified nutritional advice to ensure an adequate supply of all essential nutrients for any parents seeking to avoid dairy products. It is difficult to quantify the actual risk factors because of limited data. The effects on later health and growth have not been sufficiently investigated, according to scientists at Germany’s Max Rubner Institute for nutrition and food. However, comparative cross-sectional or cohort studies have shown that high consumption of plant-based milk alternatives in early life may increase the risk of health problems. 5. Plant-based drinks are good for the climate Largely correct. Milk is a staple food in many countries, but it makes up a significant part of the carbon footprint of our diet. A 2018 review study found that, comparatively per litre, cow’s milk performs significantly worse in environmental metrics than all plant-based options. For example, around three times as many greenhouse gases, around 10 times the land area, significantly higher water consumption and greater over-fertilisation were recorded, says science writer Hannah Ritchie in findings for the non-profit organisation Our World in Data. However, there are significant differences between the plant-based alternatives. Almond milk requires less land and causes fewer emissions than soy cultivation, but can consume more water and contribute more to over-fertilisation. So there is no clear winner across all environmental criteria. 6. Soy milk robs men of their masculinity False. “Soy boy” is a derogatory term often seen on social media, based on the myth that soy can “feminise” men, as consuming it causes testosterone to fall or oestrogen levels to rise. The fact is that soy contains isoflavones, which are similar to oestrogen. Nevertheless, science does not support the rumour that soy is a “masculinity killer”. A meta-analysis of dozens of clinical studies published in the journal Reproductive Toxicology in 2020 found no measurable effects of soy foods or isoflavone supplements on testosterone or oestrogen levels in men. 7. Milk and cheese come only from animals True, with exceptions. Under European food law, terms such as “milk”, “cream” or “cheese” may only be used for products derived from the udders of mammals such as cows, buffalo, sheep or goats. That means terms such as oat milk, almond milk or soy cream are not permitted. However, an exemption is made for the use of traditionally established terms such as coconut milk, cocoa butter or peanut butter.

title: Panama Canal to reduce shipping over El Nino-fuelled drought
description: Further restrictions on the Atlantic-Pacific waterway are likely due to low water levels in artificial lakes that feed the canal.
content: The Panama Canal will cut the number of ships passing through it starting next month because of drought caused by the El Nino phenomenon, the operator of the strategic waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific said on Thursday. From September 3, the number of vessels allowed through each day will fall from 36 to 34 due to low water levels in two artificial lakes that feed the canal, the Panama Canal Authority said. It will drop to 32 from September 15 on, the agency said. Central America is in the throes of a severe drought driven by El Nino, a weather pattern that warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, triggering worldwide changes in winds, atmospheric pressure and rainfall. In the area of the canal rainfall from May to August is down by 34 per cent from its historical average, the authority said, adding that El Nino could cut it even more. The Panama Canal handles five per cent of global maritime trade and around 40 per cent of US container traffic. The canal operator said that “lower than forecast rainfall in the canal’s watershed” called for measures to bolster the “long-term sustainability” of the waterway. It has already implemented other water conservation measures, such as lowering the maximum draft – the vessel’s depth in the water – for the largest ships. In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low the waterway’s operators cut the daily ship transit number from 38 to 22. It said on Thursday that with the coming reduction, waiting times for ships trying to get through without making a reservation beforehand will increase. Nine of 10 ships using the canal do so with a reservation and the remaining slots are auctioned off. Before the Iran war the average winning bid in these auctions was US$135,000. But in April one shipping company eager to use the canal paid a whopping US$4 million. The operator said it does not rule out further restrictions on shipping depending on how much it rains in the coming weeks. The US-built canal’s main users are the United States, China, Japan, Chile and South Korea. Water is a touchy issue in Panama because the lakes that feed the canal also provide water for half the population of 4.2 million people. El Nino occurs on average every two to seven years. This year’s El Nino is shaping up as one of the strongest on record. On Wednesday, the government of Honduras placed 80 per cent of that Central American country on drought alert.

title: India rescues 2 Chinese nationals from sunken cargo ship, searches for others
description: The Panama-flagged vessel had ‌24 crew on board, including 20 Chinese nationals, according to India’s coastguard.
content: ⁠India’s coastguard ⁠and navy continued search-and-rescue operations off the eastern coast on Sunday after a Panama-flagged cargo vessel carrying 24 crew sank, with two Chinese nationals rescued, a ‌senior official said. The two rescued Chinese seafarers said the vessel developed a list on Friday and sank within eight minutes, forcing crew to abandon ship, Shyam Jagannathan, director general of India’s Maritime Administration, said. Jagannathan said the chances ⁠of finding survivors generally fall sharply after 12 hours, but ‌rescuers were continuing the search. Twenty-two crew members remain missing from the Ocean Winner, including 18 Chinese nationals, ‌three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi, according to the ⁠Indian coastguard. The Indian navy is closely coordinating with the coastguard to locate ‌the remaining crew, the navy said in a post on social media. The coastguard has ‌sent two vessels from Sri Vijaya Puram, formerly known ‌as Port Blair, for the search-and-rescue operation, a coastguard spokesperson ⁠said. The Ocean Winner was carrying iron ore bound for ⁠China after departing from India’s eastern Paradip port on Friday, according to an initial report prepared from India’s Maritime Administration. The ‌cargo ship ‌sank about 240 nautical miles (448km) from the port, according to government sources. The cause of the sinking was not immediately known.

title: In Focus | How Pacific nations walk a tightrope between Western security and Chinese trade
description: As Australia expands defence pacts in the region, Beijing courts local communities with ‘small and beautiful’ aid.
content: On paper, Western countries are rushing to sign defence pacts in the South Pacific, ensuring their influence in a region long neglected as a geopolitical backwater. But on the water, the island nations are playing a very different game. Instead of taking sides, local leaders are leveraging the geopolitical tug of war between China and the West, winning security guarantees from the latter while Beijing builds infrastructure and deepens its economic footprint. In June, Vanuatu – an archipelago nation around 1,750 km (1,090 miles) east of Australia – signed a security pact with Canberra. A week later in early July, Fiji signed its first mutual defence treaty with Australia. The treaty is open for other Pacific nations to join. Beijing issued similar responses to both developments, saying the countries’ cooperation should not target any third party or be used to “engage in geopolitical games”. These manoeuvres represent Australia’s latest efforts in what Foreign Minister Penny Wong has described as a “permanent contest” for influence in the region against an increasingly assertive China. They also shed light on Australia’s ambition of becoming the Pacific’s preferred security partner and shutting out China’s influence, said Connor Graham, a research fellow at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute. The art of hedging For Pacific island nations, these pacts are a calculated hedge. Balancing major powers was a core survival strategy for the countries, said Graeme Smith, deputy director of the Coral Bell School of Asia-Pacific Affairs at Australian National University. “Nearly all Pacific countries’ major trading partner is China, but also the Pacific Ocean is filled with US military facilities and you do not have the capacity to shut them out,” Smith said. “You have no choice but to balance and make the best of it.” The US’ permanent military presence in the South Pacific dates back to the end of the 19th century, when Washington annexed American Samoa and soon after built its first naval base south of the equator. During World War II, the Allies operated airbases and naval airfields across the South Pacific – including in Papua New Guinea, Fiji and the Solomon Islands. After the war, Washington shifted its security focus northwards to Guam and Hawaii, largely leaving it to Australia and New Zealand to further Western interests in the South Pacific. Graham of the Lowy Institute said that not becoming “a theatre for great-power competition” had been a priority for local leaders. For Pacific nations, Australia might be the preferred security partner, but they still looked to China for trade and development, he said. Such balancing acts are evident across the region. Last month, Papua New Guinea ordered the closure of Taiwan’s representative office in its capital just days after the Pacific country’s first defence alliance treaty with Australia came into effect. That was a signal to Beijing that it was still welcome “to come in and have a presence”, Graham noted. In May, Vanuatu balanced its new security alliance with Australia by simultaneously entering into talks with Beijing on a strategic cooperation pact. Canberra and Port Vila agreed to water down key clauses that were apparently aimed at limiting Chinese investment in Vanuatu’s ports, airports and telecommunications, replacing what was functionally a veto with a weaker provision for consultation. Last year, months after granting Australia veto power over several kinds of pacts the country could seal with third parties in exchange for A$140 million (US$98 million) in aid, Nauru hedged its bets by signing a A$1 billion investment proposal with a Chinese state-linked company without consulting Canberra. The delicacy of the region’s balancing act was most clearly evident last month, when a People’s Liberation Army submarine test-launched a long-range ballistic missile with a dummy warhead, which was believed to have landed near the exclusive economic zones of Tuvalu and Kiribati, over 1,000 km northeast of the Solomon Islands. Canberra immediately accused Beijing of “destabilising” the region and the United States criticised China for providing only a few hours’ notice of its launch. Speaking alongside Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese a day after China’s missile test, Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale confirmed that his government had lodged an official diplomatic protest. “China is a good friend of Solomon Islands, but this is not something a friend does. This is not good in our region,” Wale said. Xu Shaomin, deputy director of the Centre for Oceanian Studies at the Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou, southern China, said Honiara’s rhetoric was “nuanced” and “measured”, a reflection of the tightrope the nation must walk. The Solomon Islands is widely viewed as China’s closest partner in the region. It signed a security pact with Beijing in 2022, less than three years after cutting diplomatic ties with Taiwan. Months after signing the pact, it also turned a US Coast Guard vessel away from its ports. However, Wale’s administration has re-engaged with the US since taking office in May, signing a pact on July 28 that allows the US Coast Guard to patrol its waters with local police aboard. Beijing, which sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification, objects to any official exchanges with the self-ruled island. Most countries, including the US – Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise it as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Xu said Pacific nations were well aware of China’s red lines, particularly regarding Taiwan, and were not looking to cross them. “If China were to withdraw, they would lose a vital piece of leverage in their geopolitical game with Australia, New Zealand and the US,” Xu said. Smith said that Beijing was likely to capitalise on the Pacific Island nations’ desire to balance competing major powers. “I think China is probably quite sanguine about all these agreements being signed and looking to use them as an opportunity to push for closer bilateral ties with countries signing the agreements,” he said. Domestic reality Besides their geopolitical position, the countries have to manage domestic frustrations, with the public seeing such international manoeuvring as a distraction from pressing needs like health, education and the rising cost of living, according to Smith. Despite strong post-pandemic economic rebounds as tourism resumed, South Pacific nations remain vulnerable to external shocks, especially energy prices. In May, the World Bank projected that economic growth across 11 Pacific nations would slow to 2.8 per cent in 2026. Youth unemployment rates are high and rising. Many skilled workers such as teachers and medical professionals are emigrating in search of better wages. Moreover, the countries’ physical future is in doubt as rising sea levels threaten to submerge swathes of their territory. In December, the first climate migrants arrived in Australia from Tuvalu, where more than one-third of its 11,000 people have applied for a climate visa to migrate to Australia under a deal struck between the two countries two years ago. Nasa scientists have projected that half of Tuvalu’s main atoll of Funafuti may be submerged by 2050. “Small and beautiful” China funded and constructed major infrastructure in the Solomon Islands after Honiara’s 2019 diplomatic switch. That included US$119 million for a national sports stadium complex and aquatic centre in Honiara to host the 2023 Pacific Games. Australia, meanwhile, provided a Pacific Games Partnership of about US$11.4 million to support the event. In November, Beijing signed a framework agreement with five Pacific island nations – Micronesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Vanuatu and Fiji – to upgrade their economic partnership and “boost trade, attract investment, and accelerate industrialisation through flexible trade negotiations”, China’s Ministry of Commerce said at that time. While China is known for using its trade clout and megaproject expertise to woo developing nations, it is also trying out a more niche strategy to win over locals in the South Pacific. After Pacific leaders shelved a sweeping regional trade and security deal proposed by China in 2022, Beijing began to deliver “small and beautiful” projects in the Pacific, following President Xi Jinping’s pledges at a Belt and Road Initiative forum in 2023. A popular buzzword in China’s foreign diplomacy, “small and beautiful” refers to low-budget, small-scale projects that focus on public welfare and communities’ needs. For instance, China donated and installed hundreds of solar street lights across Nauru and Kiribati, and sent medical teams to remote villages and outlying islands. In Nauru, a tiny coral reef nation suffering from the devastating environmental impact of decades of mining, Chinese agriculture specialists have introduced soilless cultivation factories, allowing residents who once relied on expensive imports to access locally grown vegetables. In May, Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown joined Chinese officials in Wuzhou to launch the MV Tuitui Moana, a 43-metre (141-foot) multipurpose vessel built in southern China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region to improve transport links and cargo delivery among multiple islands. Xu of Sun Yat-sen University said delivering tangible local improvements could help secure the public support necessary for sustained engagement. “These projects are insulated from unpredictable political shifts, such as a government changing hands or a former opposition party coming to power,” he said. This could also be more cost-effective, Xu said, adding that maintenance costs for large-scale projects – such as highways, ports and shipyards – had been quite high for local governments. At the same time, such small projects were less likely to trigger caution and pushback from regional powers like Australia and New Zealand, avoiding Western anxieties that Beijing’s infrastructure investments were a form of strategic pre-positioning, he added. “In this sense, looking at the situation in reverse, China’s future relations and aid programmes with Pacific island nations are likely to have to pivot entirely towards ‘small and beautiful’ initiatives,” Xu said. Yet, China’s strategic shifts have not gone unanswered. Australia has reinforced its Pacific ties and ramped up funding following China’s reported attempt to establish a permanent military base in Vanuatu in 2018 and its successful 2022 security agreement with the Solomon Islands. For the first time since 2021, Canberra overtook Beijing as the dominant lender and infrastructure investor across the Pacific in 2024, providing about 37 per cent of all development spending across the region, according to estimates published by the Lowy Institute on July 28. China accounted for 6 per cent of the regional development flows, the report said.

title: Skincare in your 30s: a new routine for acne, fine lines and sensitivity
description: Introduce retinol gradually, try vitamin C serums like SkinCeuticals’ C E Ferulic, and wear SPF daily – while prioritising barrier care.
content: At some point in your 30s, your skin stops playing by the rules you’d come to rely on. The routine that worked fine at 26 starts feeling like it’s missing something. A breakout appears on your chin the week before your period; you catch a fine line under harsh bathroom light that definitely wasn’t there last summer; your cleanser, the same one you’ve used for years, suddenly leaves your face feeling stripped. It’s not a dramatic change, but more of a quiet, slightly confusing recalibration that nobody really warned you about. “As we move through our 30s, oestrogen and progesterone naturally begin to fluctuate while our androgen levels often remain relatively stable,” says Marlee Bruno, a physician associate at Mind Body & Soul Medical. “That creates what we call relative androgen dominance – in simple terms, the hormones responsible for oil production suddenly have more influence.” At the same time, cell turnover slows: Bruno notes that research suggests it drops by roughly 20 per cent across this decade, which means oil, debris and dead skin cells don’t clear the pores as efficiently as they once did, leading to dullness that takes longer to shift, a loss of firmness that reads as tiredness even when you’re not tired, and breakouts that tend to cluster along the jawline and chin. One of the most persistent myths dermatologists deal with is the idea that acne is something you simply outgrow. “Even if hormone levels fall within a normal range on lab work, that shift in balance can be enough to increase oil production and trigger breakouts,” says Dr Melanie Palm, a dermatologist and cosmetic surgeon at Art of Skin MD. Dr Omodamola Aje, endocrinologist at Berkshire Medical Center, adds that this is also why adult acne tends to land where it does: the jawline, chin and lower face are most sensitive to sebum-driving hormones, which is why those are the spots that flare when the balance tips. And when something like polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) or insulin resistance is involved, she points out, no skincare routine is going to fully compensate, as the underlying cause matters just as much as what’s on the shelf. Stress adds another layer to an already complicated picture. Cortisol, the body’s primary stress hormone, disrupts the same hormonal feedback loop that’s already shifting in your 30s, spiking oil production, slowing skin repair and making the barrier more reactive. It’s why a difficult week at work or a run of bad sleep has a way of showing up on your face within days, usually in exactly the spots that are already prone to flaring. But the particular headache of 30s skin is that all of this happens at the same time. You’re managing breakouts with one hand and preventing wrinkles with the other, and the ingredients that address one can easily aggravate the other. “People see a breakout and a fine line at the same time and immediately want to throw every active ingredient they own at their face,” Bruno says. “The reality is that you can’t treat acne or ageing if you’ve destroyed your skin barrier.” Palm sees the same pattern: many of her patients arrive in their 30s still using the harsh cleansers and multiple exfoliants they relied on a decade earlier, not realising that skin gets more sensitive with age and what once felt clarifying now tips the barrier into irritation. The reality is that you can’t treat acne or ageing if you’ve destroyed your skin barrier Marlee Bruno, Mind Body & Soul Medical This is also when the retinol conversation usually starts. Retinol, a vitamin A derivative, speeds up cell turnover and supports collagen synthesis, which means it works both sides of the 30s problem at once. It helps clear congestion and smooth texture while quietly building skin density over months and years. The catch is that people tend to introduce it wrong: too high a concentration, too often, no buffer, and then they get irritated and give up. “In dermatology, consistency tends to outperform intensity,” Palm says. “A product used comfortably and regularly will almost always deliver better long-term results than an aggressive routine that someone abandons after a few weeks.” Starting low, two or three nights a week, over a thin layer of moisturiser is the standard entry point for a reason. But the bigger routine update this decade asks for isn’t really about adding more. It’s about being smarter with what’s already there. Bruno is a firm believer in recovery nights: not every evening needs to be an active treatment night, and sometimes the skin needs ceramides, hydration and barrier support more than it needs another acid. SPF, which should already have been a fixture since your 20s, becomes genuinely non-negotiable here: UV exposure is the single biggest driver of early collagen breakdown, and cumulative damage tends to become visible exactly in this decade. Vitamin C earns its place for the collagen support and antioxidant protection it provides alongside brightening. That’s why formulas that do double duty on brightening and collagen synthesis, like SkinCeuticals’ C E Ferulic or Medik8’s C-Tetra Luxe, are where most dermatologists point you first. On the moisture side, ceramides and peptides tend to serve 30s skin better than heavier occlusives, which can congest pores that are already working overtime. None of this needs to feel like a countdown, though. The 30s are early enough that most of what’s happening is still in the preventive window, which means the decisions made now are the ones that actually compound. A slightly more considered routine, a couple of well-chosen actives, and the willingness to admit that what worked at 25 might simply not be the right tool any more – that’s more or less the whole brief.

title: Nvidia customers notified of AI-related price rises above 15%
description: The rises will impact systems including those with the Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips, according to people familiar with the process.
content: Some of Nvidia’s biggest customers have been told that the prices of servers containing its artificial intelligence chips are going up more than 15 per cent in many cases with memory chip costs soaring. The price rises will go into effect on systems shipped early next year and will impact systems including those with the flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips, according to people familiar with the process, who asked not to be identified commenting on communications that have not yet been made public. The increases will depend on the generation of Nvidia chips and the memory configurations, they said. Companies who build the servers under contract for large data centre operators such as Microsoft, Alphabet’s Google and Oracle have recently notified their customers of the forthcoming increases, the people said. Nvidia representatives did not respond to requests for comment. The inability of the industry’s most dominant company to hold the line on prices or absorb growing costs shows how much leverage makers of memory chips – Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology – have amid a surge in demand for AI infrastructure. Major technology companies including Apple and Qualcomm have recently said they have been forced to charge more for their products because of chip shortages. Nvidia’s accelerator processors are the heart of computers that create and run AI software. Their effectiveness depends on how much dynamic random access memory, or DRAM, they are paired with. The two Korean companies and Micron Technology account for most of the world’s production of that type of chip. While they have been increasing output, they still have not caught up with surging demand. That has driven the price of the commodity-like components up massively and given their manufacturers unprecedented influence in technology. Nvidia is one of the most profitable companies in semiconductors. It is able to charge tens of thousands of dollars per chip because supply – from contract manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing – still cannot meet runaway demand. The company has a gross margin, or percentage of sales remaining after deducting the cost of production, of 75 per cent. Originally derived from PC gaming chips that sold for hundreds of dollars, AI accelerators have seen prices driven up by incessant demand and, as yet, a dearth of viable alternatives for Nvidia’s offerings. Nvidia has also raised prices for its gaming-oriented PC graphics cards, industry news site Tom’s Hardware reported earlier this month. How Nvidia’s customers react to this latest move and whether it will create an opening for its competitors is likely to depend on whether they are able to secure enough memory themselves. Major customers such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta are all pursuing their own in-house chip programmes but are still dependent on purchases from Nvidia for their data centre build-outs. Their ability to push forward with greater independence will also depend on their access to supply from Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron Technology. The price increases are also likely to add complexity to the industry’s massive AI data centre buildout ambitions. Project delays, labour shortages, tightening capital markets and community resistance to developments have already complicated many plans. Nvidia is reporting second-quarter earnings next week. The updates by the world’s most valuable publicly traded company have become a key update for the technology industry and investors who have poured money into AI infrastructure on the promise that it will transform the economy.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong must abandon superiority complex over mainland China
description: The city’s future lies in discarding the prejudice that has clouded its judgment to embrace mainland success and align with the national trajectory.
content: After many years in Hong Kong, with some sadness, I left the city for greener pastures, though my link with it remains an emotional one. When I moved my two dogs across the border to Shenzhen, I was told by agents, officials, even artificial intelligence, that the mainland bureaucracy would be rigid and unhelpful. My experience was the opposite. The young customs officers at Shenzhen Bay answered my phone calls, gave candid advice and treated my situation – a single parent relocating with a daughter and two elderly pets – with warmth. At the crossing, the tone of the officials was almost playful: “Are they kitties or doggies?” Once it was clear the dogs had been mine for years and that their vaccinations were valid, there was no problem at all. By contrast, Hong Kong’s Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, which must endorse the papers prepared by private vets, while helpful, also seemed rigid. While waiting there, I overheard another applicant say she had no confidence in Chinese bureaucracy, insisting Hong Kong’s was better. That assumption, in my experience, was simply not true. Too many in Hong Kong still cling to an outdated picture of mainland China, assuming superiority while ignoring its rapid improvements. China’s central and local governments have invested heavily in improving the country, and the results have been acknowledged, even by sceptics. I often think of Diwu Lun, a minister in the Eastern Han dynasty who had a reputation for impartiality. He said he once rejected a man who offered an excellent horse as a bribe in return for a recommendation but couldn’t stop thinking about it. He also said that when his nephew was ill, he visited the boy 10 times in a night but could sleep soundly afterwards, yet when his own son took ill, he slept not a wink. How, he asked, can one be truly impartial? The lesson was simple: partiality is human and pragmatism demands that we make room for imperfection. Nepotism exists, yes, but it is not a trait specific to any political system; rather it is a human condition, and one that societies must manage rather than deny. In Hong Kong, however, an extreme pursuit of impartiality – even, an overthinking of it – has sometimes led to paralysis. Its systems have been elevated through rigidity, and suspicion has been mistaken for wisdom. For years, the idea persisted that in “one country, two systems”, it must be Hong Kong’s system that is better. Yet is it right to talk down mainland China when its achievements in the last decade have eclipsed even those of the United States? Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s system has led to inflated property prices and forced ordinary people to live in cramped, degrading conditions. Across the border in Shenzhen, and even the smaller towns and villages on the mainland, people live more freely, help each other more and enjoy a richer daily life. Crime levels are low, but not because, as the nonsense I often hear repeated goes, China is a police state. The reality is that social trust, community solidarity and effective governance have created a society where ordinary people have dignity and security. Just as the US is learning that China-bashing does not work and that it must live with the fact of China’s equal status, Hong Kong, too, must confront its own illusions. The city must reposition itself as a Chinese city, find its niche and produce leadership capable of both safeguarding national security and ensuring prosperity. The mentality that “Hong Kong is better” can no longer be sustained. Its future lies not in clinging to an outdated superiority complex but in embracing the reality of the Chinese mainland’s success. Only by re‑examining this mindset, discarding the prejudice that has long clouded its judgment and aligning itself with the broader national trajectory can Hong Kong hope to prosper in the new era. And perhaps the clearest image of that future is not found in policy papers but in a simple crossing: a father, a daughter and two old dogs, met not with suspicion but with warmth, duly checked for rabies shots but waved through with kindness. That moment at Shenzhen Bay shows what Hong Kong must learn – that dignity, trust and humanity are not weaknesses but strengths. If the city can carry that lesson into its politics as well as its daily life, it will not merely observe China’s rise; it will share in it.

title: Iran condemns US plans to announce new sanctions
description: Warning that nations joining the US ‘economic war’ would be deemed enemies, Iran said the move could affect trading partners including China.
content: Iran on Saturday denounced US plans to announce ⁠new sanctions that could put further strain on the Islamic Republic’s economy and have an impact on its most important trading partners including China. Iran on Saturday warned countries against taking part in the United States’ “economic war” against the Islamic Republic, saying they would be considered enemies. “We declare to all countries … do not join the economic war waged by the United States. Any country participating in the imposition of economic restrictions against us is considered an enemy,” said Mohsen Rezai, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, on state television. After nearly six months of war since the US and Israel launched air strikes against Iran on February 28, the sides are not firing at each other but also showing no sign of pursuing peace talks. Oil shipments are at a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran threatening to strike any unauthorised oil tankers that try to transit the vital waterway, and Iran’s economy is already ‌under immense pressure from sanctions. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to hold a press conference on Monday after threatening “the toughest sanctions in history” on Iran. Bessent has also urged cooperation with Washington from China, which buys more than 80 per cent of Iran’s shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. Beijing has urged diplomacy. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, said on Saturday the imminent US announcement of new economic sanctions was an “assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent member state of the United Nations”. “Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law,” he said in a post on social media. The secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, told state television that Tehran would target the interests of countries helping the United States. US President Donald Trump, who has warned of economic consequences against any country that provides “any type of lifeline to Iran”, ‌said on Friday that Washington was observing “what happens” in the conflict. “They would love to make a deal but they’re not ready to make the right deal, in my opinion,” Trump said of Iran. While the US had effectively blockaded Iranian vessels in their ports, the Strait of Hormuz remained bottled up with thousands ‌of seafarers stranded on hundreds of vessels. Only four commodity ships sailed along the strait on Thursday, none of them large crude carriers or liquefied natural gas tankers, ship-tracking data ⁠showed. However, Iran has granted permission for a number ⁠of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait following repeated requests from Baghdad, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported on Saturday. IRNA said obtaining special permission for Iraqi tankers was one of Baghdad’s main requests during a visit to Iraq by Parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf. US ‌Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US military helped move a seven-day average of 8 million barrels a day of oil through the strait. That is down from more than 20 million per day before the war, or about one of every five barrels consumed worldwide. US attacks have ‌severely diminished ‌Iran’s economy and devastated its navy and air force, but Tehran maintains enough missile and drone capability to impede oil tanker traffic and attack regional rivals. Abdollahi, the armed forces chief of staff, sought to underline Iran’s ‌missile capabilities during a visit to an underground plant manufacturing ballistic missiles that was reported by state television on Saturday. “This plant has been able, much better than in the past, to produce equipment superior both in ⁠capacity and quality and in quantity,” he said. Qalibaf, Iran’s parliamentary speaker, said Tehran had received “numerous messages” from neighbouring countries about establishing new regional security arrangements and economic cooperation. Qalibaf, who did not say which countries he was referring ⁠to, accused the US of endangering the security of its allies in the region for the sake of Israel, adding that an independent, “home-grown” regional order would deliver peace and security. Trump, meanwhile, has yet to achieve objectives he set at the start of the war such as dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme – the state of which remains uncertain given that United Nations inspectors have been shut ‌out since 2025 – and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow ‌their clerical rulers. Thousands have been killed, mainly in Iran, where 168 Iranian schoolchildren were killed on the first day of the war. The US has reported more than 750 military staff wounded and 18 killed. While Iran remains defiant, President Masoud Pezeshkian has also called for a diplomatic solution. “It would be better to end the war today, when we are powerful and have dignity, and the whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasises that America, contrary to all regulations, attacked our schools, hospitals, and infrastructure and is hated in the world,” the ISNA news agency quoted him as saying on Friday.

title: Israel targets ‘terrorist’ in southern Syria; Damascus condemns attack
description: Tensions between Israel and Syria flared this week after Israel bombed an airbase, a move ‌US special envoy Tom Barrack called ‘unnecessary’.
content: Israel said it targeted a “terrorist” ⁠in southern Syria ⁠on Saturday in ⁠what Syria’s foreign ministry said was a drone strike on a civilian vehicle on the outskirts of Damascus in a “blatant” violation of its ‌territory. The Syrian foreign ministry said the drone had hit a vehicle on a road near Beit Jinn village in the countryside west of the capital, which caused injuries among civilians. Syrian state television ⁠reported one person was injured. The Israeli military said in ‌a statement that it fired in southern Syria towards what it described as a ‌terrorist, whose activity posed an immediate threat to its ⁠soldiers. ⁠It did not say how it fired. Tensions between Israel and Syria flared this week after Israel bombed an airbase in the northwest on ‌Tuesday, an escalation ‌US special envoy to Syria, Tom Barrack, ‌called “unnecessary”. Syria’s foreign ministry said the strike was part of ⁠a pattern of repeated Israeli attacks on Syrian territory and ⁠was a “blatant violation” of its sovereignty. It held Israel accountable for the consequences of such actions. Barrack, who also serves as ambassador to Turkey, said the attack on Tuesday on the Abu Duhur base could have been Israel “baiting the Turks … that was the serious and worrying part”. However, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz contradicted the US envoy’s remarks about there being no warning, saying in a statement that Israel decided to alert senior members of the Syrian government. “Simultaneously, we transferred the intelligence reports to the relevant authorities in the US,” Katz said. Barrack said it was likely that Israel had intelligence suggesting Turkey may be bolstering its presence in the area and “a commander somewhere in the field made a decision ‘We’re not going to let that happen’… What they didn’t do is tell us or Turkey”. He added that another possible reason for the attack on Abu Duhur, around 80km (50 miles) east of the Turkish border, was a miscommunication between the Israeli military and the country’s intelligence agency. “When they [the Turkish military] see these jets coming towards the border and they don’t know what the purpose, direction or intention is, they start to say ‘We’re going to have to scramble our own’,” Barrack said as he outlined how close Israel and Turkey came to direct confrontation. Israeli ‌troops continue to ‌operate in southern Syria and Israel occupies territory in southwest Syria it seized after the toppling of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: 7 dead in UK after vehicle travelling in wrong direction hits police car
description: Following recent head-on crashes in Ireland, police have warned that some young people are driving the wrong way ‘for social media ‌likes’.
content: Seven people, including two police officers, died in a car crash in northeast England on Saturday after a car heading the wrong ‌way down a major road hit a marked police armed response car, the local police force said. Cleveland Police said the incident took place in the early hours of Saturday near the South Bank area east of Middlesbrough and that all occupants of the two cars ⁠died at the scene. “This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland,” ‌Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said. The police force said it had formally identified the passengers in the other car, ‌a Volkswagen Passat, and was contacting their families. Fuller named the ⁠two dead ⁠officers as police constables Matthew Blades, 37, and Tom Clough, 38, describing them as “brave officers … ‌who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift”. Prime Minister Andy Burnham ‌also ‌released a brief statement expressing his sadness at the incident, which ‌as usual in such cases will be reviewed by Britain’s Independent Office ⁠for Police Conduct. Following two recent head-on crashes near Dublin, one of which killed five ⁠people, Ireland’s police chief this week warned that some young people were driving the wrong way on the motorway “for social media ‌likes”. An Irish parliament ‌committee has asked short-form video platform TikTok to explain how it removes content “that appears to glorify dangerous and illegal behaviour on our roads”. On Tuesday, Ireland’s media regulator made a similar request.

title: Ukrainian drones kill at least 10, hit warehouse of Russian online retailer Ozon
description: Ukraine has opened a ‘Pandora’s box’ of Russian retaliation, Putin said. Kyiv said it is seeking to choke financing for Russia’s war effort.
content: Ukrainian drones killed at least 10 people in attacks against targets across Russia and Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine, including a warehouse owned by online retailer Ozon and an industrial facility, Russian officials said on Saturday. Russia and Ukraine are both ramping up drone campaigns ‌aiming to cripple each other’s economic infrastructure, often striking targets far beyond the war’s front lines, as fighting on the battlefield grinds towards the four-and-a-half-year mark. On Friday, at least 16 people were killed and more than 130 wounded when several Russian drones struck a shopping centre in central Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine’s strikes, which Kyiv says seek to choke off financing for Moscow’s war effort, had opened a “Pandora’s box” of Russian retaliation. French President Emmanuel Macron, meanwhile, promised to accelerate ⁠the delivery of new French equipment to Ukraine after discussing Kyiv’s shortage of air defences in a call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. In a post on Telegram on Saturday, Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, governor of Russia’s Samara region, said an elderly woman had been killed in a strike on the city ‌of Novokuibyshevsk, which he said caused damage to industrial facilities. Ukraine’s military said it had struck the city’s oil ⁠refinery, causing a fire. Ozon, Russia’s second-largest ⁠online retailer, said in a statement on Telegram that work at its Samara region logistics centre in the town of Chapayevsk had been halted after the strike, which ‌it said caused injuries. The attack is the first on Ozon following weeks of drone strikes on its larger rival Wildberries, which Ukraine has cast as part of a wider ‌campaign ‌against economic infrastructure underpinning the Russian war in Ukraine. Elsewhere, in the southern Russian region of Krasnodar, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said three ‌people, two of them children, had been killed and another adult was wounded in a strike on the Sea of Azov port ⁠town of Yeysk. He said a fire had broken out at an unnamed facility at the town’s port. The governor of Russia’s Belgorod ⁠region, which borders Ukraine, said two people had been killed and 13 wounded in Ukrainian attacks. In Bryansk, another frontier region, four people were wounded, the local governor said. On the Crimean peninsula, seized from Ukraine by Russia in ‌2014, the Moscow-backed governor of Sevastopol, Mikhail ‌Razvozhayev, said at least two people had been killed and 10 injured when a Ukrainian drone struck a city bus. In Luhansk region, an eastern Ukrainian province almost all of which is controlled by Russia, Moscow-installed governor Leonid Pasechnik said two civilians, including a 16-year-old boy, had been killed and nine more were wounded. Russia’s Defence Ministry said it downed a total of 457 Ukrainian drones overnight.

title: Canada’s PM hits back with new US tariffs after trade talks fail
description: ‘We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked,’ Mark Carney said, accusing Trump of starting a trade war.
content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Saturday he would slap retaliatory tariffs on the United States after walking away from a “bad deal” on trade, deepening the rift between the long-time allies. Negotiations between the neighbouring countries broke down on Friday in Washington, allowing new 50 per cent US tariffs impacting some US$20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 per cent of Canadian exports to the United States, to come into force. Impacted products range from hockey sticks to cement. US President Donald Trump had said Washington “should be able to have a deal with Canada”, citing his “good relationship” with Carney. But on Saturday, the Canadian prime minister said Trump had set conditions that were ultimately unacceptable. “We believed earlier this week that we were moving towards a mutually beneficial agreement,” Carney said in the Canadian capital, Ottawa. “In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada, and called into question the reliability of any deal. In short, they asked too much and they offered too little,” he said. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered, and we will not give what they’ve asked,” Carney said, accusing Trump of launching a trade “war”. “You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said. New Canadian tariffs will notably target the US steel and dairy industries, and take effect on September 8. Carney said further details would come next week. On Friday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington had offered “significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminium, autos and lumber” in exchange for concessions from Canada. A senior US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, characterised the talks as candid and not acrimonious but said there were no further scheduled meetings. Canada has been seeking relief from Trump’s tariffs on cars, steel and aluminium, which have battered the country’s economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an ironclad trade relationship. Canadian negotiators had been camped out in Washington this week to firm up a deal that aimed to address various flashpoints. The White House had alleged “discriminatory treatment” by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties. They were originally set to take effect on Wednesday, before Trump issued a last-minute delay of three days, citing major progress in talks. Ryan Majerus, a former US commerce official who now is a trade lawyer with King & Spalding, told Agence France-Presse that “both sides will face significant pressure in the coming days to find an off-ramp”. Beyond the latest tariffs, the United States and Canada still have to agree on revisions to the North American free trade agreement, USMCA, which Trump declined to renew in its current form. Bilateral ties also have been hurt by Trump’s repeated threats to make Canada the 51st US state. Trump was irked by Carney’s widely touted January speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in which the prime minister declared that the global order was experiencing a “rupture”. The Canadian leader has repeatedly said relations with the United States have been forever changed and that the country must reduce its reliance on the United States, which currently accounts for roughly 70 per cent of Canadian exports. “We’ve been under no illusions. We recognised from the start that America has changed,” Carney told reporters on Saturday.

title: Sword attack that killed 1 at Sweden high school prompts social media probe
description: Police are investigating whether the teenager who carried out the attack was involved in online communities promoting school violence.
content: Swedish police are investigating whether an 18-year-old man who attacked students at a high school with a sword on Friday, killing one, was involved in online communities promoting school violence, a police source said. The attacker struck at a school in the central ‌Swedish town of Fagersta, also severely injuring two teenage boys before being arrested by police. The parents of a 17-year-old girl told local newspaper Fagersta-Posten that their daughter was killed in the attack. Police are investigating whether a TikTok account that posted a picture of a sword 20 minutes before the assault belonged to the suspect, the source told reporters. According to the Dagens Nyheter newspaper, the image appeared to have been taken in a ⁠restroom at the school. Before it was taken down on Friday, the month-old account contained videos that referred to two ‌episodes of mass violence in Sweden and to Norwegian far-right mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik. One of the videos referenced a 2015 attack in which a masked swordsman killed a ‌teaching assistant and two boys at a school in Trollhättan, western Sweden, before being shot dead by ⁠police. “The investigators are looking ⁠into various online communities which might have egged on the suspect to carry out the attack,” the police source said. Political party leaders pause campaigning Several ‌party leaders cancelled planned speeches on Saturday, pausing campaigning ahead of the September 13 election. Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson travelled to Fagersta ‌to ‌offer condolences to the bereaved family and visit the injured. “What should never happen has happened again,” Kristersson told reporters ‌in Fagersta. “Our thoughts go first and foremost to the families who have been incredibly hard hit by this,” he said. Sweden’s ⁠worst mass shooting took place in February 2025 at a school in the south-central city of Orebro, when a gunman ⁠killed 10 people before turning the gun on himself. On Saturday, police clarified that the suspect in the Fagersta attack had not been shot, contrary to what they had said on Friday. “Service weapons were ‌used but the perpetrator has ‌not been injured in connection with the arrest, and has not been in need of medical attention,” a police spokesperson said. Prosecutors ordered the man’s detention on suspicion of murder and several counts of attempted murder. “The investigation is at an intense stage. We are conducting interrogations and gathering information, but I cannot go into specifics,” Prosecutor Ann-Sofie Trossing told reporters.

title: Elderly woman allegedly pressured into spending HK$100,000 on beauty products
description: Customs launches investigation after woman claims 88-year-old mum left exhausted and confused with huge bill from company already under scrutiny.
content: Hong Kong customs is investigating whether an 88-year-old was pressured into spending HK$100,000 (US$12,750) on beauty products at an outlet linked to a company already accused of aggressive sales tactics. In a social media post on Saturday, a woman surnamed Ng wrote that her mother was targeted during a three-hour ordeal in April at the Avinichi booth in the Wing On department store in Sheung Wan. The allegations are the latest in a string of complaints over Hong Kong’s beauty product sector following a crackdown on the local operations of Opatra London. In the post, Ng said that her mother visited the store in April. After the first transaction, the salesperson allegedly did not return the mother’s credit card and instead kept it in a folder while trying to sell her more products. Ng claims the credit card was swiped four times over a three-hour period, with charges amounting to HK$100,000 for skincare products, a beauty treatment device and 24 detoxifying sessions. The daughter claimed her mother’s helper tried to intervene and suggest leaving, but the “selling continued”. “My mother was left exhausted and confused afterwards, and said she felt as if she had been hypnotised,” Ng wrote. She said the family had asked for a refund, but Avinichi refused and only offered an exchange. She said she had reported the case to the Customs and Excise Department, as well as the Consumer Council. In a response to the South China Morning Post, the department said it was “actively investigating the case” and would take “appropriate enforcement” action should any contravention of the Trade Descriptions Ordinance be found. “Customs has always attached great importance to consumer rights protection and has zero tolerance for unfair trade practices, pledging to continue its stringent enforcement action against unscrupulous traders,” it said. When an SCMP reporter visited the store on Saturday, the two staff present said they were not aware of the allegations. After speaking to a manager over the phone, one of the employees asked for the reporter’s contact information and said a company spokesperson would get in touch. The staff member declined to allow the reporter to speak to the manager directly. As of 9pm on Saturday, the SCMP had yet to receive a response. Avinichi is one of a series of beauty brands managed by Apex Retail, a company with locations across Hong Kong and Singapore. It operates about a dozen shops in Hong Kong, under the brands Earth, Napara, Privilege Boutique, Dualsonic and others. A store for another of its brands, Lionesse, recently faced similar accusations of aggressive sales tactics. Addressing the previous case, Apex Retail declined to comment on individual allegations or circumstances that did not involve identifiable customer matters. According to its website, the company launched two Avinichi “experience boutiques” in 2025. It also lists the Wing On department store in Sheung Wan as one of its “mall partners”. The Avinichi trademark is owned by Exclusive Label, based in the United States. A statement at the bottom of Avinichi’s website notes that all retail locations are independently owned and managed. Hong Kong’s beauty sector has come under heightened scrutiny following the arrest of two managers at the Hong Kong operator of beauty chain Opatra London over alleged coercive sales practices. The company has suspended local operations, while customs officers are investigating six customer complaints involving disputed sums between HK$1,800 and HK$100,000. The Mineral Boutique, a brand under Beauty Express Group, has also come under scrutiny for allegedly aggressive sales practices. Legal experts previously told the SCMP that such practices – including credit card abuse, unwanted physical contact and pressure to buy costly products – could breach the Trade Descriptions Ordinance. The ordinance prohibits harassment, coercion and misleading conduct used to pressure consumers into making purchases they otherwise would not have made.

title: Hong Kong and Shenzhen test crossings at revamped Huanggang Port ahead of opening
description: Latest drill checked for any hiccups in how private cars will cross into Shenzhen and use of ‘joint clearance’ e-channels.
content: Hong Kong has conducted its first test involving Shenzhen authorities of clearance procedures and private car access at the revamped Huanggang border crossing, ahead of a massive exercise next week involving 20,000 people to fully assess the facility’s capacity. No 2 official Eric Chan Kwok-ki said Saturday’s drill went smoothly and passenger flows were orderly, with speedy pickup by public transport, although a motorist association reported traffic jams along the San Tin Interchange roundabout leading to the crossing. “We will conduct a further stress test with a continuous peak-level passenger and traffic flow to ensure smooth operations,” Chan said, describing next Saturday’s exercise as a “large-scale cross-border drill”. Hong Kong authorities have conducted several drills at the Huanggang Port crossing at the mainland Chinese border this month as a part of final preparations before the checkpoint opens, which sources have said could come as early as next month. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said next Saturday’s drill would increase pressure on capacity and feature a full test of 90 clearance channels within the building, as well as assess how private vehicles would use a new clearance machine. “Through today’s exercise, we have identified further improvement measures, such as how to line up buses and different transport,” Tang added. The latest 10,000-strong drill focused on vehicle clearance operations. Private cars were arranged to simulate the vehicle clearance process for entry to Shenzhen. Cars first passed through a customs kiosk before immigration clearance to avoid having to back up midway through the clearance channel for a spot check. Vehicles then stopped in front of the immigration checkpoint, where an “integrated information collective device” will complete the clearance, occupant temperature check and biometric data collection in one go, although the cars did not use the machine. Authorities also tested how cars would turn back should problems with occupant identity documents arise or if they were refused entry by Shenzhen authorities. Following the vehicle flow trial, dozens of civil servants used the “joint clearance” e-channels, equipped with three gates instead of the two in traditional clearance machines, to cross into Shenzhen. The revamped checkpoint will be the first to deploy the “joint clearance” model, where people only need to show one type of identity document required by their destination for e-channel clearance. Traditionally, crossing the border requires visiting a departure and arrival counter. Authorities have staged three peak traffic stress tests, each involving about 2,000 civil servants crossing into Hong Kong and descending into the arrival hall. Authorities also simulated situations where a passenger found to have a fever was sent for a further check and another in which a traveller was caught smuggling illicit cigarettes and an endangered tortoise into the city. Ringo Lee Yiu-pui, honorary life president of the Hong Kong, China Automobile Association, told the South China Morning Post that 400 drivers had volunteered to take part in Saturday’s drill, with each car making at least two trips to the crossing. Lee said the drivers had started out in Fanling and Sheung Shui, with the latter route along the Yuen Long Highway proving more congested. Some drivers had taken a wrong turn at the San Tin Interchange roundabout, while others were slowed by works on roads leading to the port building and slip roads condensing into single-lane traffic. A minor traffic accident also occurred at around 1pm at the interchange, he said, adding authorities could introduce clearer signage. “In our experience, the time stuck in traffic could be as long as an hour, as besides the roundabout being jammed, roads leading to Huanggang would also be congested,” Lee said. Tang said traffic flow leading to the crossing was “heavy but smooth”.

title: The last lap: fans, drivers bid fond farewell to ‘old school’ Dutch Grand Prix
description: ‘It’s definitely going to be missed, for sure. It’s always been really fun to drive,’ four-time world champion Max Verstappen says.
content: For three days a year, the quiet residential street of Van Speijkstraat in the sleepy Dutch beach resort of Zandvoort transforms itself into a sea of orange streamers and chequered flags, welcoming Formula One fans from around the world. Party tunes blast out from house parties, children sell home-made lemonade and friendship bracelets from little “pit stop” stalls and colossal posters of local hero – four-time world champion Max Verstappen – flutter in the sea breeze. But to the regret of fans and drivers alike, Sunday marks the last edition of the Dutch Grand Prix, which returned to the circuit in 2021 but simply isn’t generating enough profits for the promoters. “We try to make the greatest party ever,” said housewife Sabine Volkers, 38, as her children danced on the street and tried to entice passers-by to buy lemonade. “Like no other,” proclaim promotional banners flying all over Zandvoort and most people in Formula One agree that the fans and circuit combine to create a unique experience. Often referred to as “old school” (it hosted its first race in 1952), the track snakes through sand dunes only a short walk from the North Sea beach. Drivers relish the steep banks at the corners while the proximity to the coast makes for unusual conditions – sand gets blown onto the tarmac and torrential rain often appears out of nowhere, dramatically changing the driving challenge. “Honestly, I think it’s a great track. From a driving perspective, especially in qualifying, it’s super fun,” teen sensation Kimi Antonelli, who is leading this year’s championship, said. “It’s definitely a shame to lose a track like this,” added Antonelli, as many drivers praised the “character” of Zandvoort compared to purpose-built tracks in places like the Middle East. The fans are closer to the track than at other venues, creating a raucous atmosphere as the Dutch “orange army” roar on their beloved champion Verstappen. “It’s proper old-school driving. It’s definitely one of the best tracks on the calendar compared to some tracks that we go to now that ... lack a bit of character,” Verstappen said. “So, yeah, it’s definitely going to be missed, for sure. It’s always been really fun to drive. Even if I would not be Dutch, you know, to drive here would have been always amazing,” he added. But in some ways Zandvoort’s charm has also been its downfall – a tiny beach resort struggles to accommodate the global circus that comes with a grand prix. Transport is a challenge, with huge traffic jams and long queues at the station, despite the operator running special trains – rebaptised the “Max Express”. A lack of space means there is no room to expand the stands and, despite attracting near capacity crowds, the sums don’t add up. “We and the British Grand Prix at Silverstone are the only races that have to operate without any government support,” Motorsport Magazine quoted race director Robert van Overdijk as saying. The Dutch GP needs a full house on all three days simply to break even, he said. Uncertainty over Verstappen’s success and even continued participation in Formula One was another risk hanging over promoters. “If you go on for another three or five years and Max stops at some point, you don’t know what’s happening,” van Overdijk told the De Boordradio podcast. Ironically, just as the last edition was getting going, Verstappen committed to Red Bull until 2030, but for now there seems to be no going back on the decision. “We’re going out with a bang. Of course it also makes us a bit sad, but more than anything else, we’re proud,” van Overdijk said. Not everyone is sad the race is ending: environmental groups had complained for years about the pollution and noise generated by the event. “For me, it’s incredible to see so many happy faces in my town,” Zandvoort mayor David Moolenburgh said. “We’re really going to miss it,” he said, adding that it boosted his town’s global reputation, as well as providing welcome cash to Zandvoort businesses. Zandvoort resident Erik Romijn, 54, said he was very proud that “a small city of 15,000 people can make a party for 100,000 people every year”. “The whole world saw that we can create a big party,” the engineer said.

title: Why China may have little to lose as ‘weakened’ Trump seeks North Korea talks
description: The US president’s push to revive negotiations with Kim Jong-un could see Washington scaling back its military presence in the South.
content: China may have “little to lose” from talks between the United States and North Korea which, analysts say, may lead to Washington watering down its security commitments. US President Donald Trump has already ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the scale of the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise with South Korea, criticising the exercise for both its cost and for sending “totally inappropriate and hostile” signals to Pyongyang. Citing his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, Trump said Pyongyang had been “unthreatening and respectful”, adding that Seoul had said “No thanks!” when asked to join the US in the “denuclearisation” of Iran. Following Trump’s order, the South Korean defence ministry announced that the joint exercise would end on Friday, six days earlier than initially planned, while also cancelling counter-attack exercises and scaling back field training. The US leader also said he wanted to meet Kim, whom he met twice during his first term in office, later this year. He also added that North Korea possessed 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons. The North Korean leader’s sister, Kim Yo-jong, said on Wednesday that she knew nothing about communication between the two countries, describing the scaling back of the military exercise as “not even worth evaluating” and “completely uninteresting”. Troy Stangarone, a visiting senior fellow at the Korea Economic Institute of America, said Trump would find himself in a “weakened negotiating position”. He said North Korea’s relationship with Russia had weakened the impact of sanctions, given it an “economic lifeline” and transferred new military technology to the regime. Pyongyang has sent troops and weapons to Ukraine in exchange for conventional and nuclear weapons technology from Moscow. “With China joining Russia in backing off calls for denuclearisation, North Korea has political and economic cover it did not have during Trump’s first term,” Stangarone said. “In reducing the US-Korea military exercises, Trump has gone off his own playbook of seeking leverage and instead given it away. He’s made a concession and with everyone knowing that he needs a win after the challenges with Iran, Trump will have even less leverage. “It’s likely China would have little to lose from US-North Korea talks because of the weakened US position.” Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, said: “From China’s perspective, there is no reason to openly oppose dialogue between North Korea and the US. “[However] they want to ensure a mechanism is in place where they are consulted and not sidelined. “Ultimately, China wants to project an image to the outside world that it is coordinating with North Korea on foreign policy and approaches towards the US.” Lim Eul-chul, professor of North Korean studies at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies, Kyungnam University, said Pyongyang “keenly understands” that Trump needed a diplomatic breakthrough in the face of the ongoing war with Iran and growing domestic pressure. “Kim Jong-un is well aware that even if a summit is arranged, the process could be derailed at any moment due to domestic US opposition or his own political calculations,” Lim said. “From North Korea’s perspective, the global disorder and uncertainty created by Trump are viewed … as a strategic opportunity to maximise Kim’s own leverage.” He added that the North was likely to conclude that it was “far more advantageous to adopt a ‘wait-and-see’ approach”. Andrew Yeo, a senior fellow and the SK-Korea Foundation chair at the Brookings Institution’s Centre for East Asia Policy Studies, said Trump wanted a “foreign policy win”.
