He said that unlike the meetings in his first term, Trump would focus less on denuclearisation and more on efforts to limit the growth of North Korea’s weapons programme. “The US now is at a point where we don’t really publicly mention denuclearisation … that itself would be a win [by accepting what] North Korea currently has in terms of its nuclear programme,” Yeo said. Henry Haggard, a former US diplomat stationed in South Korea, said Kim felt he had “little reason” to engage with Trump, who was only offering a “photo opportunity” in contrast to closer ties with Russia and China. “[Kim] likely will seek recognition of his nuclear programme from Trump, which Trump might be willing to consider if it leads to a breakthrough.” Chinese President Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June – his first visit to the country in seven years – and promised to “enhance exchanges in diplomacy, law enforcement and military affairs”. However, denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula was notably excluded from the joint statement issued after his meeting with Kim. This was a stark contrast to Xi’s previous visit in 2019, when he praised the North’s commitment to denuclearisation as part of wider efforts to safeguard peace and stability. Lami Kim, Korea chair in advanced technologies, national security and defence at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, said Trump had often referred to North Korea as a “nuclear power” and was increasingly likely to formally recognise it as such. She said this could see trade-offs such as suspending joint military exercises with South Korea or reducing the number of troops in South Korea in exchange for a moratorium on North Korean intercontinental-range ballistic missile tests. “From Trump’s perspective, such an arrangement could appear to be a win-win: the United States would reduce both its military costs and the threat posed directly to the US mainland by North Korea,” she said. “China, meanwhile, could have reasons to welcome a rapprochement between Washington and Pyongyang, especially if it resulted in a reduced US security commitment to the Korean peninsula and the broader region.”

title: 1,500 Indonesian soldiers deployed to fight Borneo wildfires
description: Fires between January and July burned over 200,000 hectares of land, driven by a powerful El Nino weather pattern causing dry conditions across the country.
content: Indonesia is deploying an additional 1,500 soldiers to Borneo, an official said on Saturday, to help tackle wildfires that have burned through swathes of the island and created thick smog choking some areas. Fires between January and July burned over 200,000 hectares of land – an area three times the size of the capital Jakarta, the government said this week, as dry conditions driven by a powerful El Nino weather pattern take hold. President Prabowo Subianto, on a visit to Borneo on Saturday to lead wildfire response meetings, ordered increased troop deployment, said Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya. “An additional three Indonesia National Armed Forces battalions, or around 1,500 personnel, will be brought in from outside Kalimantan starting today,” Teddy said in a statement. Kalimantan is Indonesia’s part of Borneo, which the country shares with Brunei and Malaysia. Six helicopters were also set to arrive on Saturday to boost waterbombing operations, Teddy said. The government is monitoring the situation closely, mobilising resources to help contain the spread of the blaze, Prabowo told reporters in the Central Kalimantan provincial capital of Palangkaraya. “We’re taking mitigation measures. The important thing is to immediately stop the spread of fire spots,” said the president. Smog from the fires has prompted local governments in Borneo, home to pristine rainforest and vast plantations, to advise residents to wear masks and reduce outdoor activities. The fires have sent smoke into Malaysian Borneo, with six areas of Sarawak state recording “unhealthy” air quality. The area burned is already larger than during previous El Nino seasons in 2019 and 2023, but not as large as in 2015, during a particularly strong El Nino. El Nino is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns. It typically brings drought in Indonesia. Human-caused climate change can amplify its impacts because a warmer ocean and atmosphere make more energy and moisture available to feed extreme weather events.

title: 20 sailors kidnapped by Somali pirates near Yemen on US-sanctioned ship
description: The hijacking comes amid a resurgence of piracy that has seen six commercial vessels seized since April across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.
content: Somali pirates hijacked an oil products tanker off Yemen, a Somali maritime security official said, the latest in a resurgence of piracy that has seen six commercial vessels seized since April across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. Six armed pirates hijacked the Eritrean-flagged M.T. Sibu 1 on Thursday about 136 nautical miles (252 kilometres) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen, and took it towards Somalia’s Puntland coast, the official, who has knowledge of the incident, told journalists on Friday. He spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not allowed to discuss the matter publicly. The Sibu 1, managed by the UAE-based Qatrat Alnada Almasi Ship Management, was sanctioned by the US Treasury Department last year for allegedly belonging to an Iranian “shadow fleet” used to transport petroleum products seeking to evade US sanctions. The tanker had 20 crew members aboard – 16 Indians, one Syrian, one Sudanese, and one Iraqi. The nationality of one crew member was not immediately known. The vessel’s previous port of departure and intended destination remained unclear. The hijacking came three days after pirates seized the Lutuf, a Cameroon-flagged general cargo vessel, off Somalia’s coast. The vessel had 10 crew aboard, including six Indians, a Turkish national, a Georgian national and two Serbian security guards, according to maritime tracking reports. The Sibu 1 is the sixth commercial vessel hijacked by Somali pirates since April 21, when the Palau-flagged tanker Honor 25 was seized off Somalia. Pirates later seized the Sward on April 26, the Eureka on May 2, the Asana on July 17 and the Lutuf on August 17. The attacks have occurred increasingly far from Somalia’s coastline, including the hijacking of the Eureka while anchored off Yemen and the Asana about 65 nautical miles (120 kilometres) southwest of al-Mukalla. The International Maritime Bureau recorded 38 piracy and armed robbery incidents worldwide during the first half of 2026, including five hijackings. Somali pirates accounted for 94 per cent of crew members taken hostage during that period, the bureau said. Puntland’s Security Ministry said on Friday that its investigations indicated that forces beyond Puntland’s control were behind the renewed piracy, but did not identify any group or country. The claim could not be independently verified. Puntland said it had deployed security forces along its coast and condemned air strikes that it said struck fishing vessels and property near coastal communities where hijacked ships were being held. It called on the countries involved to explain strikes near Garacad on August 18 and 20. The ministry did not identify who carried out the strikes, and the allegations could not be independently confirmed.

title: Chinese J-16 fighters arrive in Egypt ahead of Eagles of Civilisation 2026 joint drill
description: Multi-role PLA fighters travel 6,000km to take part in their first African deployment, refuelling in mid-air along the way.
content: A fleet of Chinese J-16 fighters has arrived in Egypt ahead of a joint exercise that will be the aircraft’s first-ever deployment to Africa. The planes and aviators taking part in the Eagles of Civilisation 2026 exercise arrived at an Egyptian airbase on Friday morning after a 6,000km (3,700-mile) journey that took nine hours and required the planes to refuel in mid-air, according to the People’s Liberation Army. It added that the service personnel involved in the exercise had started preparations for the joint exercise. The PLA has previously said the drills would finish early next month. The J-16, a twin-seat multi-role fighter nicknamed the Hidden Dragon, regularly patrols along China’s east coast and potential flashpoints such as the South China Sea and Taiwan Strait. The jet has previously featured in other overseas drills, including with Russia and Pakistan, but this is the first time it is taking part in an exercise with the Egyptian air force. During its inaugural joint exercise with the North African country last year, China deployed J-10C fighters, which are lighter, single-engine multi-role jets. The Chinese defence ministry said this year’s exercise would focus on air combat tactics and air superiority operations among other elements. It added that the drills would deepen trust and cooperation between the two militaries and contribute to regional peace and stability. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military commentator and former PLA instructor, said the deployment of the J-16s reflected Beijing’s push to train its air force in unfamiliar places and conditions. “The different aircraft types across China’s air force units all need to go abroad, to go out and take a look, in order to strengthen their combat training and readiness capabilities,” he said. “There need to be as many exercises like this as possible in order to increase our capability to operate in unfamiliar airspace, in different types of airspace. Going up against different opponents can also greatly improve our own capabilities.” Song said the journey to Egypt – the J-16’s longest-range deployment to date – would have been a “major test” for the pilots’ tactical and technical skills as well as the aircraft’s technical performance. He suggested such exercises were likely to become more frequent as the air force tried to improve its coordinated combat abilities – something that was becoming increasingly important as China’s overseas interests increased. “China is a major global power in terms of development, and we also need to rely on cooperation with other countries to support our own development,” he said. “So building up the navy and air force’s global power-projection capability is therefore critically important. We can’t rely only on diplomatic capability. We also need hard power, including military capability, to safeguard our overseas interests.”

title: Hong Kong-built greenhouse gas tracker device ‘functioning well’ on space station
description: Tech minister Sun Dong says Multi‑Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory has ‘successfully captured images with good clarity’.
content: A greenhouse gas monitoring instrument developed by a university in Hong Kong is operating successfully aboard the Tiangong space station and is expected to contribute to sustainable development, the city’s technology minister has said. Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong also revealed more details in a blog post on Saturday about the life of the city’s first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, who he said had a busy schedule at the space station. The Multi‑Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory (Musico), developed by a team led by scientists at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and funded by the city government, has been deployed to China’s space station. “Musico is equipped with four sensors for detecting carbon dioxide, methane, oxygen, and aerosols. They have all successfully captured images with clear imaging quality and demonstrated good overall performance,” he said. “Over the next two years or more, the instrument will provide autonomous, controllable, and highly accurate greenhouse gas (carbon dioxide and methane) emission monitoring data, contributing to efforts to address climate change and promote global sustainable development.” Musico is considered the world’s first lightweight, high-resolution, high-precision synergistic observatory for carbon dioxide and methane. Although the instrument is smaller than a household washing machine, it can accurately detect specific sources of greenhouse gas emissions on Earth, according to the university. Five other projects, led by scholars from Polytechnic University, the University of Hong Kong, City University and the Chinese University of Hong Kong, had received funding from the special call for aerospace technology under the government’s Innovation and Technology Support Programme, Sun said. The minister also revealed that Lai, who has been working at the space station for about three months, had “completed a series of experiments and scientific studies with her teammates, while also performing daily station maintenance, health monitoring and emergency pressure drills” amid a busy schedule. He added that the government had brought nearly 400 local students to visit mainland China’s aerospace research bases during the summer holiday, with the aim of cultivating their interest in the area. “I hope more and more Hong Kong youth will follow the example of Dr Lai, aim high, work hard and pursue their dreams in innovation and technology,” he said.

title: Why Stand by Me remains a dark coming-of-age masterpiece 40 years after its release
description: This landmark of 1980s cinema is a bittersweet experience when watched today, with two of its biggest talents lost to tragic deaths.
content: One of the greatest films of the 1980s, Rob Reiner’s Stand by Me turns 40 this month. And, just as its hero discovers while looking back on the events of a summer long past, time and tragedy have only made it burn brighter. Based on a novella by Stephen King and sensitively adapted by Raynold Gideon and Bruce A. Evans, Stand by Me is a film about, rather than for, kids. As with much of King’s work, the main theme is the harm that adults do to children, and the scars it leaves. In the years since the film’s release, its cast and crew have come to all kinds of harm themselves. Lead River Phoenix died aged 23 of a drug overdose in 1993. Co-star Corey Feldman, a sexual abuse survivor, has struggled with addiction throughout his career. And in 2025, Reiner was stabbed to death alongside his wife, Michele Singer Reiner, in their Los Angeles home. Their son, Nick Reiner, remains the chief suspect. The wraparound story begins in 1986. After hearing that his childhood friend, Chris Chambers (Phoenix), has been killed trying to stop a knife fight, writer Gordie (Richard Dreyfuss) reminisces about the summer of 1959, when they were bored 12-year-olds scratching around their hometown of Castle Rock, Oregon. Along with pals Teddy Duchamp (Feldman) and Vern Tessio (Jerry O’Connell), Chris and Gordie (played as a child by Wil Wheaton) leave Castle Rock on a mission to find the body of a local boy, Ray Brower, who has been hit and killed by a train. But town bully Ace Merrill (Kiefer Sutherland) and his goons have other ideas. Real life, not acting Casting directors Janet Hirshenson and Jane Jenkins helped choose leads who, according to Wheaton, were uncannily close to their roles. “I was awkward and nerdy and shy and uncomfortable in my skin and sensitive,” Wheaton says. “River was cool and smart and passionate, and even at that age, kind of like a father figure to some of us. Jerry was one of the funniest people I had ever seen in my life, either before or since, and Corey was unbelievably angry and in an incredible amount of pain and had a terrible relationship with his parents.” Before filming started, Reiner made sure the four stars had rehearsed enough to be able to disappear into their roles completely. As Wheaton puts it, “When you saw the four of us being comrades, that was real life, not acting.” They are helped by a beautiful script, which was nominated for an Academy Award for best adapted screenplay, and should have won. Funny, warm and wise, it combines witty dialogue with a complete lack of condescension towards its protagonists, although older Gordie’s voice-over plays a touch mawkish these days. Whether swearing, smoking or swapping pop-cultural epithets (“Mickey’s a mouse, Donald’s a duck, Pluto’s a dog. What’s Goofy?”), Gordie and co always feel like real kids. And their adventures, whether dodging trains or running from mad dogs, never seem like Amblin-style escapist fantasies. Innocence, corruption and untrustworthy adults Despite its sunny aspect and glorious 1950s soundtrack, the film never lets you forget the darkness lurking beneath. In King’s world, innocence and corruption are always intertwined. Brower is killed while out picking blueberries of all things; in the fireside story Gordie tells, a pie-eating contest ends up in vomit-fuelled revenge; and Chris is disgraced for stealing the school milk money – no matter that he tried to return it. But it is the adults who are not to be trusted. The boys’ parents are neglectful and, in Teddy’s case, outright abusive – his father having burnt his face by holding him too close to a stove. The junkyard owner delights in setting his dog on them. And Chris’ teacher kept the milk money because she knew he would get the blame. Gordie is ignored by his dad (Marshall Bell), who openly favours his late brother Denny (John Cusack). Reiner, meanwhile, was overshadowed by his own father, the comedian Carl Reiner. “He was a big force,” he says. “I felt that he didn’t see me.” Reiner was a much better role model to his young cast. O’Connell called him “the single most important thing that’s ever happened to me”. Wheaton says: “Rob was one of the first men in my life who treated me like a person. He believed in me. I wanted to make him proud.” In fact, the director was so happy with the results he named his production company Castle Rock. And King told him, “That’s the best film ever made out of anything I’ve written, which isn’t saying much. But you’ve really captured my story. It is autobiographical.” Watching the film today, with two of its biggest talents lost to tragic deaths, is a bittersweet experience. While some, like Gordie – and King – managed to fight their way out of the darkness, others were not so lucky. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Man arrested for driving under influence of drugs after 3-vehicle crash
description: Two hospitalised after accident along Pok Fu Lam Road involving large truck and two light goods vehicles, police say.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a 38-year-old man on suspicion of driving under the influence of drugs following a three-vehicle crash that left two people injured. Police said they received a report at 1.48pm on Saturday of a traffic accident along Pok Fu Lam Road involving a large truck and two light goods vehicles. The force said the 38-year-old driver of one of the light goods vehicles failed a drug test that was administered at the scene. He was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence of drugs and dangerous driving causing grievous bodily harm. The 61-year-old male driver of the other light goods vehicle and a 59-year-old female passenger were injured and sent to Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam for treatment. The force added that the 56-year-old male driver of the large truck also complained of chest pain following the incident, but refused medical treatment. The arrested driver has been detained pending further investigation.

title: Myanmar air strike kills 14 praying at monastery, rebel witnesses say
description: Public buildings, most often monasteries and schools, are frequently the sites of reported air strikes according to a UN report from last week.
content: A Myanmar military air strike on a monastery where civilians were gathered for a meditation retreat marking Buddhist Lent killed 14 people, two rebel fighters who witnessed the aftermath said. Myanmar has been consumed by civil war since the military staged a 2021 coup ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and detaining the Nobel Peace Prize laureate. Over the past five years, more than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed across all sides as the military battles an array of pro-democracy and ethnic minority rebels. The Friday air strike hit a monastery hall around 9.00am in Myaung township of central Sagaing region, killing 11 men and three women, according to Nway Oo Myaung, a pro-democracy rebel who helped clear bodies. “Older people had entered the meditation centre for three months” to mark the period of Buddhist Lent, which roughly coincides with Myanmar’s rainy season, he said on Friday. “Those who were killed, their ages were between 50 and 70,” Nway Oo Myaung added. “It wasn’t a mistaken target, they intentionally attacked a monastery.” It was not immediately possible to contact the Myanmar military for comment. But second local opposition fighter, speaking on condition of anonymity, said on Saturday, “Five dead people were from our village and the other nine were from other villages.” “While we were trying to rescue people, the aircraft came to bomb a second time,” he said. Myanmar’s military often relies on its Chinese- and Russian-supplied jets to keep rebels at bay, analysts say. UN investigators from the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) last week published a report accusing the military of “indiscriminate and intentional aerial attacks against civilians”. Public buildings, most often monasteries and schools, are frequently the sites of reported air strikes. Myanmar’s government called the IIMM publication “one-sided allegations against Myanmar’s security forces based on unverifiable and inaccurate information”. After five years of martial law, Myanmar’s military staged elections around the start of 2026 – touting the exercise as a return to normality. The IIMM report said it “observed a notable escalation in aerial attacks in the months preceding the elections”. Democracy watchdogs derided the vote as a charade to rebrand military rule while excluding the popular Suu Kyi, sidelining her party and punishing dissenters with prison time. It resulted in coup-leader Min Aung Hlaing taking over as civilian president in April. He is currently spearheading a diplomatic blitz to shake off Myanmar’s post-coup pariah status and gain diplomatic recognition abroad. India, China, Laos and Thailand have all openly embraced him with visits to their capitals – drawing criticism from campaigners who complain they have granted him undue legitimacy. This week, Min Aung Hlaing visited Russia and Belarus, which have remained steadfast allies with Myanmar since the coup.

title: Man hospitalised after bamboo scaffolding collapses in Sham Shui Po
description: Victim suffers head injuries after being trapped under scaffolding on Nam Cheong Street, police say.
content: A Hong Kong man has been hospitalised after being trapped by fallen bamboo scaffolding at a building in Sham Shui Po, prompting authorities to launch an investigation. Emergency services were called to 105-107 Nam Cheong Street at around 3.49pm on Saturday following reports scaffolding measuring about 15 metres by 33 metres (49 feet by 108 feet) had partially collapsed and trapped the victim. According to police, the victim, who is believed to be in his fifties or sixties, suffered head injuries but was conscious when taken to Princess Margaret Hospital in Kwai Chung for treatment. Police have classified the case as an industrial accident, and an investigation into the cause of the collapse is ongoing. The Hong Kong and Kowloon Bamboo Scaffolding Workers Union said that according to workers interviewed at the scene, the scaffolding collapsed after heavy construction materials were stored on an upper platform, causing the supporting base poles to snap. A worker at the site told the union that his colleague on the upper platform was using ropes to lower bags of construction waste to other labourers below just before the incident. The union said the platform was suspected to have been used as a temporary storage area for construction waste, with severe overloading causing the collapse. The union pointed out that under the Code of Practice for Bamboo Scaffolding Safety, working platforms were categorised into light-duty and heavy-duty tiers. Under safety guidelines, load limits apply to evenly distributed weight across a platform rather than at concentrated points. The Buildings Department told the South China Morning Post that officers sent to inspect the building after the accident found a section of scaffolding running from the ground floor to the first floor had collapsed. But it stressed that the main building scaffolding and the upper platform section posed no immediate danger. The department said the contractor involved had promptly removed the fallen bamboo, adding it would continue to liaise with the building owners’ corporation and contractor over taking apart the remaining structure. It vowed to investigate the cause of the collapse and consider prosecuting the contractor or taking disciplinary action if any breaches of the Buildings Ordinance were found.
